nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, the real Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$: $n$-tuples of reals with the standard inner product and norm.
nodes.title: Ambient Euclidean space of the Platonic classification

nodes.summary: A convex polytope in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is given by its vertex set: a finite nonempty set $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ that equals the set of extreme points of its convex hull $\operatorname{conv}(V)$. The polytope itself is the convex set $\operatorname{conv}(V)$.
nodes.title: Convex polytope

nodes.summary: The underlying set of a convex polytope $P$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the convex hull of its vertex set.
nodes.title: Underlying set of a convex polytope

nodes.summary: The dimension of a convex polytope $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is its affine dimension: the dimension of the real vector space spanned by the differences $x - y$ of points $x, y \in P$.
nodes.title: Dimension of a convex polytope

nodes.summary: A convex polytope $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is full-dimensional if its dimension equals $n$.
nodes.title: Full-dimensional convex polytope

nodes.summary: A face of a convex polytope $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a nonempty set of the form $\{x \in P : \ell(y) \le \ell(x) \text{ for all } y \in P\}$ for some linear functional $\ell$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, that is, the set of points where $\ell$ attains its maximum over $P$. Taking $\ell = 0$ shows that $P$ itself is a face.
nodes.title: Face of a convex polytope

nodes.summary: For a subset $F \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, its affine dimension is the dimension of the real vector space spanned by the differences $x - y$ with $x, y \in F$. The empty set and every single point get dimension $0$.
nodes.title: Affine dimension of a set

nodes.summary: A flag of a convex polytope $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a sequence $F_0, F_1, \dots, F_{n-1}$ of faces of $P$ such that each $F_k$ has affine dimension $k$ and $F_i \subsetneq F_j$ whenever $i < j$.
nodes.title: Flag of a convex polytope

nodes.summary: The rigid motions of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are the affine isometric bijections $\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$.
nodes.title: Rigid motions

nodes.summary: An affine isometry $\varphi$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a symmetry of a convex polytope $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ if $\varphi(P) = P$.
nodes.title: Symmetry of a convex polytope

nodes.summary: A convex polytope $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is regular (Platonic) if it is full-dimensional and for any two flags $(F_0, \dots, F_{n-1})$ and $(G_0, \dots, G_{n-1})$ of $P$ there is an affine isometry $\varphi$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $\varphi(P) = P$ and $\varphi(F_k) = G_k$ for every $k < n$.
nodes.title: Regular convex polytope

nodes.summary: Two convex polytopes $P$ and $Q$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ are similar when there are a real number $a > 0$ and an affine isometry $\varphi$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ such that the underlying set of $Q$ is $\{a\,\varphi(x) : x \in P\}$.
nodes.title: Similar polytopes

nodes.summary: For $d \in \mathbb{N}$, this is the set of regular (Platonic) convex polytopes in $\mathbb{R}^d$: the convex polytopes in $\mathbb{R}^d$ that are full-dimensional and whose symmetry group acts transitively on their flags.
nodes.title: Regular polytopes

nodes.summary: For regular convex polytopes $P$ and $Q$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, $P$ is related to $Q$ when they are similar as convex polytopes, that is, when there are a real number $a > 0$ and an affine isometry $\varphi$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ such that the underlying set of $Q$ is $\{a\,\varphi(x) : x \in P\}$.
nodes.title: Similarity of regular polytopes

nodes.summary: For $d \in \mathbb{N}$, $p_d \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ is the number of similarity classes of regular convex polytopes in $\mathbb{R}^d$, with $p_d = \infty$ when there are infinitely many classes.
nodes.title: Number of Platonic polytopes

nodes.summary: For $d \in \mathbb{N}$ let $p_d \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ be the number of regular convex polytopes in $\mathbb{R}^d$ up to similarity. Then $p_2 = \infty$, $p_3 = 5$, $p_4 = 6$, and $p_d = 3$ for every $d \ge 5$.
nodes.title: Classification of the Platonic polytopes
Points and spanned hyperplanes

reading_title.source: Affine hyperplanes in $\mathbb{R}^d$

nodes.summary: An affine subspace $A$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ is an affine hyperplane when there are a nonzero linear functional $\ell \colon \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ and a real number $c$ such that $A = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^d : \ell(x) = c\}$.
nodes.title: Affine hyperplanes in $\mathbb{R}^d$

nodes.summary: For a set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, the hyperplanes spanned by $P$ are the affine hyperplanes of $\mathbb{R}^d$ that equal the affine span of some subset of $P$.
nodes.title: Hyperplanes spanned by a point set

nodes.summary: The statement that for every $d \ge 1$ and every set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ whose affine span is all of $\mathbb{R}^d$, writing $\mathcal{H}$ for the set of affine hyperplanes of $\mathbb{R}^d$ that equal the affine span of some subset of $P$, there is an injective map $f \colon P \to \mathcal{H}$ with $p \in f(p)$ for every $p \in P$.
nodes.title: Injective point-to-hyperplane matching question

nodes.summary: For every $d \ge 1$ and every set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ whose affine span is all of $\mathbb{R}^d$, let $\mathcal{H}$ be the set of affine hyperplanes of $\mathbb{R}^d$ that equal the affine span of some subset of $P$. Then there is an injective map $f \colon P \to \mathcal{H}$ with $p \in f(p)$ for every $p \in P$.
nodes.title: Spanning point sets have injective point-to-hyperplane matchings
Point–line incidences

nodes.summary: For a finite set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, this is the multiset of the numbers $|\ell \cap P|$, where $\ell$ ranges over the lines determined by $P$, that is, the distinct lines through two distinct points of $P$, each counted once.
nodes.title: Line sizes of a planar point set

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, $f(n)$ is the number of distinct multisets that arise as the line sizes of some $n$-point set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, that is, as the multiset of the numbers $|\ell \cap P|$ over the distinct lines $\ell$ through two distinct points of $P$, each line counted once. These multisets are the line-compatible sequences for $n$; there are finitely many, since each has at most $n^2$ entries,…
nodes.title: Number of line-compatible sequences

nodes.summary: The proposition that there is a real constant $C$ such that for every natural number $n$, the number $f(n)$ of line-compatible sequences for $n$ is at most $e^{C \sqrt{n}}$; that is, there are at most $\exp(O(\sqrt{n}))$ line-compatible sequences. This is Erdős Problem 733.
nodes.title: Subexponential count of line-compatible sequences (statement)

nodes.summary: There is a real constant $C$ such that for every natural number $n$, the number of line-compatible sequences for $n$, that is, of distinct multisets of the numbers $|\ell \cap P|$ over the distinct lines $\ell$ through two distinct points of an $n$-point set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, each line counted once, is at most $e^{C \sqrt{n}}$. This answers Erdős Problem 733.
nodes.title: Szemerédi–Trotter bound on line-compatible sequences

nodes.summary: For a finite set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, $A(P)$ is the set of the numbers $|\ell \cap P|$ over the lines $\ell$ determined by $P$, that is, the lines through at least two distinct points of $P$.
nodes.title: Line-incidence set of a finite planar point set

nodes.summary: For a finite set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, let $A(P)$ be the set of the numbers $|\ell \cap P|$ over the lines $\ell$ through at least two distinct points of $P$. For a natural number $n$, $F(n)$ is the number of distinct sets $A(P)$ over all $n$-point sets $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$. Every such $A(P)$ is a subset of $\{0, \dots, n\}$.
nodes.title: Number of line-incidence sets

nodes.summary: For a finite set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, let $A(P)$ be the set of the numbers $|\ell \cap P|$ over the lines $\ell$ through at least two distinct points of $P$, and let $F(n)$ be the number of distinct sets $A(P)$ over all $n$-point sets $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$. This is the statement that there is a real constant $C$ such that $F(n) \le e^{C\sqrt{n}}$ for every natural number $n$, that is,…
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 607: subexponentially many line-incidence sets

nodes.summary: For a finite set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, let $A(P)$ be the set of the numbers $|\ell \cap P|$ over the lines $\ell$ through at least two distinct points of $P$, and let $F(n)$ be the number of distinct sets $A(P)$ over all $n$-point sets $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$. There is a real constant $C$ such that $F(n) \le e^{C\sqrt{n}}$ for every natural number $n$.
nodes.title: Szemerédi–Trotter bound for line-incidence sets (Erdős Problem 607)
Steiner ratio

nodes.summary: The space $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the Euclidean distance, in which the point sets of the Steiner ratio problem lie.
nodes.title: The Euclidean plane of the Steiner ratio problem

nodes.summary: For points $x$ and $y$ of the Euclidean plane, the length of the unordered pair $\{x, y\}$ is the Euclidean distance between $x$ and $y$.
nodes.title: Length of an edge

nodes.summary: For a finite set $V$ of points in the Euclidean plane and a simple graph $G$ with vertex set $V$, the total length of $G$ is the sum, over all edges $\{x, y\}$ of $G$, of the Euclidean distance between $x$ and $y$.
nodes.title: Total length of a graph on points of the plane

nodes.summary: For a finite set $V$ of points in the Euclidean plane, this is the set of real numbers $\ell$ such that some tree with vertex set $V$ has total length $\ell$, the total length being the sum of the Euclidean lengths of its edges.
nodes.title: Lengths of spanning trees

nodes.summary: For a finite set $V$ of points in the Euclidean plane, this is the set of real numbers $\ell$ such that, for some finite set $W$ of points of the plane containing $V$, some tree with vertex set $W$ has total length $\ell$. The points of $W$ outside $V$ are the Steiner points.
nodes.title: Lengths of Steiner trees

nodes.summary: For a finite set $V$ of points in the Euclidean plane, the minimum spanning tree length of $V$ is the infimum of the total lengths of the trees with vertex set $V$. For nonempty $V$ this set of lengths is finite and nonempty, so the infimum is a minimum; for empty $V$ the value is $0$ by convention.
nodes.title: Minimum spanning tree length

nodes.summary: For a finite set $V$ of points in the Euclidean plane, the Steiner length of $V$ is the infimum of the total lengths of the trees whose vertex set is a finite set of points of the plane containing $V$. This set of lengths is nonempty and bounded below by $0$, so the infimum exists.
nodes.title: Steiner minimal tree length

nodes.summary: For every nonempty finite set $V$ of points in the Euclidean plane, the Steiner minimal tree length of $V$ is at most the minimum spanning tree length of $V$: allowing Steiner points never increases the optimal length.
nodes.title: The Steiner length is at most the minimum spanning tree length

nodes.summary: The Steiner ratio constant is the infimum, over all finite sets $V$ of at least two points in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, of the ratio of the Steiner minimal tree length of $V$ to the minimum spanning tree length of $V$.
nodes.title: The Steiner ratio of the Euclidean plane

nodes.summary: The Steiner ratio of the Euclidean plane, that is, the infimum of the ratio of the Steiner minimal tree length to the minimum spanning tree length over all finite sets of at least two points in the plane, equals $\sqrt{3}/2$.
nodes.title: Gilbert–Pollak conjecture

nodes.summary: The Steiner ratio constant, the infimum over finite sets $V$ of at least two points in the Euclidean plane of the length of a Steiner minimal tree for $V$ divided by the length of a minimum spanning tree of $V$, is at most $\sqrt{3}/2$.
nodes.title: Gilbert–Pollak upper bound for the Steiner ratio

nodes.summary: The Steiner ratio constant, the infimum over finite sets $V$ of at least two points in the Euclidean plane of the length of a Steiner minimal tree for $V$ divided by the length of a minimum spanning tree of $V$, is at least $0.824$.
nodes.title: Chung–Graham lower bound for the Steiner ratio
Part 2 of 2

nodes.summary: There are an integer $n > 1$ and real numbers $x_i$, $y_i$ and $s_i > 0$ for $i = 1, \dots, n$, with the $s_i$ pairwise distinct, such that the union of the closed squares $[x_i, x_i + s_i] \times [y_i, y_i + s_i]$ is the unit square $[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$ and any two of these squares with different indices have disjoint interiors.
nodes.title: Squaring the square with distinct squares

nodes.summary: Every finite non-collinear subset of the real Euclidean plane determines an ordinary line: two points of the set such that no third point of the set is collinear with them.
nodes.title: Sylvester–Gallai theorem

nodes.summary: Optimal arrangements of congruent bodies in space and the smallest sets or fewest translates needed to cover given families of shapes.
nodes.title: Packings and coverings

nodes.summary: There is a real constant $c > 0$ such that for every integer $n \ge 1$ there is a linear map $\varphi : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ for which the ellipsoid $E = \varphi(B)$, the image of the open Euclidean unit ball $B$ about the origin, has volume exactly $c n^2$ and the origin is the only point of $E$ whose coordinates are all integers.
nodes.title: Klartag's lattice packing theorem
Goodman–Goodman circle covering theorem

nodes.summary: Write $B(c, r)$ for the closed ball with centre $c$ and radius $r$ in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$. Call balls $B(c_1, r_1), \dots, B(c_n, r_n)$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ *nonseparable* if for every nonzero vector $v$ and every real $t$ such that no point $p$ of any of the balls satisfies $\langle v, p \rangle = t$, either $\langle v, c_i \rangle < t$ for all $i$ or $\langle v, c_i \rangle > t$ for all $i$. The statement…
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 1121 (circle covering)

nodes.summary: Both parts of Erdős Problem 1121 hold. For every natural number $d$, and in particular in the plane ($d = 2$): if $B(c_1, r_1), \dots, B(c_n, r_n)$ are closed balls in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$ with centres $c_i$ and radii $r_i > 0$ such that every hyperplane meeting none of the balls has all the centres $c_i$ strictly on the same side, then some closed ball of radius $r_1 + \dots + r_n$ contains all of the…
nodes.title: Circle covering theorem (Erdős Problem 1121)
Hadwiger covering and illumination problem

nodes.summary: A set $K$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a convex body when it is compact and convex and its interior in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is nonempty.
nodes.title: Convex bodies in Euclidean space

nodes.summary: For sets $K$ and $L$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ and a natural number $q$, $K$ is covered by $q$ translates of $L$ when there are vectors $v_1, \dots, v_q \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $K \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^{q} (v_i + L)$, where $v + L = \{v + y : y \in L\}$.
nodes.title: Covering by translates

nodes.summary: A set $K$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is covered by $q$ interior translates, for a natural number $q$, when there are vectors $v_1, \dots, v_q \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that $K \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^{q} (v_i + \operatorname{int} K)$, where $\operatorname{int} K$ is the interior of $K$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $v + S = \{v + y : y \in S\}$.
nodes.title: Covering by interior translates

nodes.summary: For $n, q \in \mathbb{N}$, the uniform interior translate bound holds when every convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (a compact convex set with nonempty interior) is covered by $q$ translates of its interior $\operatorname{int} K$, that is, $K \subseteq (v_1 + \operatorname{int} K) \cup \dots \cup (v_q + \operatorname{int} K)$ for some $v_1, \dots, v_q \in \mathbb{R}^n$.
nodes.title: Uniform bound for covering convex bodies by interior translates

nodes.summary: A set $K$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is centrally symmetric when there is a point $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $x \in K$ if and only if $2c - x \in K$.
nodes.title: Central symmetry about some center

nodes.summary: For $n, q \in \mathbb{N}$, the uniform symmetric interior translate bound holds when every convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (a compact convex set with nonempty interior) that is centrally symmetric, meaning that there is $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that for all $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $x \in K$ if and only if $2c - x \in K$, is covered by $q$ translates of its interior, that is,…
nodes.title: Uniform bound for covering centrally symmetric convex bodies by interior translates

nodes.summary: A set $K$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is covered by $q$ smaller positive homothets, for a natural number $q$, when there are real numbers $r_1, \dots, r_q$ with $0 < r_i < 1$ for every $i$ and vectors $v_1, \dots, v_q \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that every point of $K$ lies in $v_i + r_i K = \{v_i + r_i y : y \in K\}$ for some $i$.
nodes.title: Covering by smaller positive homothets

nodes.summary: For sets $K, L \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, the translate covering number of $K$ by $L$ is the least natural number $q$ for which there are vectors $v_1, \dots, v_q \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $K \subseteq (v_1 + L) \cup \dots \cup (v_q + L)$, and it is $\infty$ if no such $q$ exists.
nodes.title: Translate covering number

nodes.summary: The Hadwiger covering number of dimension $n$, an element of $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, is the least natural number $q$ such that every convex body $K$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is covered by $q$ translates of its interior $\operatorname{int} K$, and it is $\infty$ if no such $q$ exists.
nodes.title: Hadwiger covering number

nodes.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the symmetric Hadwiger covering number in dimension $n$ is the least natural number $q$ such that every centrally symmetric convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (a compact convex set with nonempty interior that is symmetric about some point) is covered by $q$ translates of its interior, and it is $\infty$ if no such $q$ exists.
nodes.title: Symmetric Hadwiger covering number

nodes.summary: For sets $K$ and $L$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ and a natural number $q$, $K$ is covered by $q$ translates of $L$ if and only if there are vectors $v_1, \dots, v_q \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that every $x \in K$ lies in $v_i + L = \{v_i + y : y \in L\}$ for some $i$.
nodes.title: Pointwise form of covering by translates

nodes.summary: For every set $K$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ and every natural number $q$, $K$ has a cover by $q$ interior translates if and only if $K$ is covered by $q$ translates of the set $L = \operatorname{int} K$, the interior of $K$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
nodes.title: Interior-translate covers unfold to translate covers

nodes.summary: Let $K, L \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and let $q \in \mathbb{N}$. If $q$ is the least natural number $r$ such that $K$ is covered by $r$ translates of $L$, then the translate covering number of $K$ by $L$ equals $q$.
nodes.title: The translate covering number is the least covering count

nodes.summary: If $q$ is the least natural number such that every convex body $K$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is covered by $q$ translates of its interior, then the Hadwiger covering number of dimension $n$ equals $q$.
nodes.title: A least uniform bound is the Hadwiger covering number

nodes.summary: If $q$ is the least natural number such that every centrally symmetric convex body $K$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is covered by $q$ translates of its interior, then the symmetric Hadwiger covering number of dimension $n$ equals $q$.
nodes.title: A least uniform bound is the symmetric Hadwiger covering number

nodes.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the coordinate cube is the set $[-1, 1]^n$ of points $x$ of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $-1 \le x_i \le 1$ for every coordinate $i$.
nodes.title: Coordinate cube

nodes.summary: For every $n$, the coordinate cube in $\mathbb{R}^n$ equals the set of points $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $|x_i| \le 1$ for every coordinate $i$.
nodes.title: The coordinate cube as an absolute-value box

nodes.summary: A set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is an affine cube if $K = e([-1, 1]^n)$ for some affine bijection $e : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$, where $[-1, 1]^n$ is the coordinate cube $\{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : -1 \le x_i \le 1 \text{ for all } i\}$.
nodes.title: Affine cube

nodes.summary: A point $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ lies in the interior of the coordinate cube $[-1, 1]^n$ if and only if $-1 < x_i < 1$ for every coordinate $i$.
nodes.title: Interior of the coordinate cube

nodes.summary: For every $n$, the coordinate cube $[-1, 1]^n$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a convex body: it is compact and convex, and its interior in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is nonempty.
nodes.title: The coordinate cube is a convex body

nodes.summary: For every $n$, the coordinate cube $[-1, 1]^n$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is centrally symmetric: there is a point $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $x$ lies in the cube if and only if $2c - x$ does.
nodes.title: The coordinate cube is centrally symmetric

parts: Covering the cube by translates of its interior needs
reading_title.source: Covering the cube by translates of its interior needs $2^n$ translates

nodes.summary: Let $C_n = [-1, 1]^n$ be the coordinate cube in $\mathbb{R}^n$. If $C_n$ is contained in the union of $q$ translates $v_1 + \operatorname{int} C_n, \dots, v_q + \operatorname{int} C_n$ of its interior, then $2^n \le q$.
nodes.title: Covering the cube by translates of its interior needs $2^n$ translates

reading_title.source: Lower bound $2^n$ for uniform interior-translate covering

nodes.summary: Let $n$ and $q$ be natural numbers. If every convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (a compact convex set with nonempty interior) can be covered by $q$ not necessarily distinct translates of its interior, then $2^n \le q$.
nodes.title: Lower bound $2^n$ for uniform interior-translate covering

nodes.summary: If $q$ is a natural number such that every convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ is contained in the union of $q$ translates of its interior $\operatorname{int} K$, then $8 \le q$.
nodes.title: Uniform interior-translate bounds in dimension three are at least eight

reading_title.source: Lower bound $2^n$ for centrally symmetric interior-translate covering

nodes.summary: Let $n$ and $q$ be natural numbers. If every centrally symmetric convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (a compact convex set with nonempty interior that is symmetric about some point) can be covered by $q$ not necessarily distinct translates of its interior, then $2^n \le q$.
nodes.title: Lower bound $2^n$ for centrally symmetric interior-translate covering

nodes.summary: Let $C_3 = [-1, 1]^3$ be the coordinate cube in $\mathbb{R}^3$. There are vectors $v_1, \dots, v_8 \in \mathbb{R}^3$ such that $C_3$ is contained in the union of the translates $v_1 + \operatorname{int} C_3, \dots, v_8 + \operatorname{int} C_3$ of its interior.
nodes.title: Eight translates of the interior cover the three-dimensional cube

nodes.summary: Let $C_3 = [-1, 1]^3$ be the coordinate cube in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Then $8$ is the least natural number $q$ such that $C_3$ is contained in the union of $q$ translates of its interior $\operatorname{int} C_3$.
nodes.title: Eight is the least number of interior translates covering the three-dimensional cube

nodes.summary: Let $C_3 = [-1, 1]^3$ be the coordinate cube in $\mathbb{R}^3$. The translate covering number of $C_3$ by its interior $\operatorname{int} C_3$, the least number of translates of $\operatorname{int} C_3$ whose union contains $C_3$, equals $8$.
nodes.title: Translate covering number of the three-dimensional cube by its interior

nodes.summary: Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a set and let $v, x \in \mathbb{R}^n$. The direction $v$ illuminates $x$ with respect to $K$ when $x$ lies on the boundary of $K$, $\|v\| = 1$, and $x + tv$ lies in the interior of $K$ for some real $t > 0$.
nodes.title: Illumination by a direction

reading_title.source: Illumination by $q$ directions

nodes.summary: A set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is illuminated by $q$ directions, for a natural number $q$, if there are unit vectors $v_1, \dots, v_q \in \mathbb{R}^n$ (not necessarily distinct) such that for every boundary point $x$ of $K$ there are an index $i$ and a real $t > 0$ with $x + tv_i$ in the interior of $K$.
nodes.title: Illumination by $q$ directions

nodes.summary: Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a set and let $p, x \in \mathbb{R}^n$. The point $p$ illuminates $x$ with respect to $K$ when $p \notin K$, $x$ lies on the boundary of $K$, and $p + t(x - p)$ lies in the interior of $K$ for some real $t > 1$; that is, the ray from $p$ through $x$ meets the interior of $K$ at a point beyond $x$.
nodes.title: Illumination by an external point

reading_title.source: Illumination by $q$ external points

nodes.summary: A set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is illuminated by $q$ external points, for a natural number $q$, if there are points $p_1, \dots, p_q \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus K$ (not necessarily distinct) such that for every boundary point $x$ of $K$ there are an index $i$ and a real $t > 1$ with $p_i + t(x - p_i)$ in the interior of $K$.
nodes.title: Illumination by $q$ external points

nodes.summary: The directional illumination number of a set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is the least natural number $q$ such that $K$ is illuminated by $q$ directions, and $\infty$ if there is no such $q$.
nodes.title: Directional illumination number

nodes.summary: The external-point illumination number of a set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is the least natural number $q$ such that $K$ is illuminated by $q$ external points, and $\infty$ if there is no such $q$.
nodes.title: External-point illumination number

nodes.summary: The following statements are equivalent: for every $n \ge 1$, every convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is covered by at most $2^n$ homothets $v_i + r_i K$ with $v_i \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $0 < r_i < 1$; and for every $n \ge 1$, every convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is covered by $2^n$ translates of its interior $\operatorname{int} K$, repetitions allowed.
nodes.title: Two equivalent formulations of Hadwiger's covering conjecture

nodes.summary: Every convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ is covered by $16$ translates of its interior $\operatorname{int} K$, repetitions allowed.
nodes.title: Papadoperakis's bound for Hadwiger's covering problem in dimension 3

nodes.summary: Every convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ is covered by $14$ translates of its interior $\operatorname{int} K$, repetitions allowed.
nodes.title: Prymak's bound for Hadwiger's covering problem in dimension 3

nodes.summary: The number $8$ is the least natural number $q$ such that every centrally symmetric convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ is covered by $q$ translates of its interior $\operatorname{int} K$, repetitions allowed. Here $K$ is centrally symmetric when there is a point $c$ with $x \in K$ if and only if $2c - x \in K$.
nodes.title: Lassak's theorem for centrally symmetric bodies in dimension 3

nodes.summary: Let $n \ge 1$, let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a convex body and let $q$ be a natural number. Then some $q$ unit vectors $v_1, \dots, v_q$ illuminate $K$ if and only if some $q$ points $p_1, \dots, p_q$ outside $K$ illuminate $K$. nodes.summary: Planar arcs are parametrized by the closed unit interval $[0, 1]$ of real numbers.
nodes.title: Parameter interval of unit arcs

nodes.summary: A unit arc is a continuous map $\gamma$ from the closed interval $[0, 1]$ to the complex plane whose length, the total variation of $\gamma$ on $[0, 1]$, equals $1$.
nodes.title: Unit arc

nodes.summary: For a real angle $\theta$ and a complex number $\tau$, the motion with angle $\theta$ and translation $\tau$ sends $z \in \mathbb{C}$ to $e^{i\theta} z + \tau$: a rotation about the origin by $\theta$ followed by translation by $\tau$, with neither reflection nor rescaling.
nodes.title: Direct rigid motion of the plane

nodes.summary: For every real angle $\theta$ and every complex number $\tau$, the map $z \mapsto e^{i\theta} z + \tau$ of the complex plane is an isometry: it preserves the distance $|z - w|$ between any two points $z, w \in \mathbb{C}$.
nodes.title: Direct rigid motions of the plane are isometries

nodes.summary: The straight path is the continuous map from the interval $[0, 1]$ to the complex plane that sends each $t \in [0, 1]$ to $t$ viewed as a complex number; it traces the segment from $0$ to $1$.
nodes.title: Straight path

nodes.summary: The total variation of the inclusion $[0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}$, $t \mapsto t$, over the whole interval $[0, 1]$ equals $1$.
nodes.title: The identity on the unit interval has total variation one

nodes.summary: The path $[0, 1] \to \mathbb{C}$, $t \mapsto t$, which traces the segment from $0$ to $1$ on the real axis, has total variation (length) exactly $1$ over $[0, 1]$.
nodes.title: The straight segment has length one

nodes.summary: The straight unit arc is the unit arc whose curve is the straight path $t \mapsto t$ from $[0, 1]$ to the complex plane, which traces the segment from $0$ to $1$ and has length $1$.
nodes.title: Straight unit arc

nodes.summary: A set $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ covers every unit arc when for every unit arc $\gamma : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{C}$, that is, every continuous map whose total variation (length) is exactly $1$, there are an angle $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ and a translation $\tau \in \mathbb{C}$ such that $e^{i\theta} \gamma(t) + \tau \in \Omega$ for every $t \in [0, 1]$.
nodes.title: Sets that cover every unit arc

nodes.summary: If a set $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ covers every unit arc, that is, contains a rotated and translated copy of every continuous curve $[0, 1] \to \mathbb{C}$ of length exactly one, then $\Omega$ is nonempty.
nodes.title: Sets covering every unit arc are nonempty

nodes.summary: The empty set $\emptyset \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ does not cover every unit arc: not every continuous curve $\gamma : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{C}$ of length exactly $1$ can be mapped into $\emptyset$ by a rotation followed by a translation.
nodes.title: The empty set does not cover every unit arc

nodes.summary: A set $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is a convex universal cover when it is nonempty, convex (as a subset of the real plane $\mathbb{C} \cong \mathbb{R}^2$), and covers every unit arc: for every continuous curve $\gamma : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{C}$ of length exactly $1$ there are $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\tau \in \mathbb{C}$ with $e^{i\theta} \gamma(t) + \tau \in \Omega$ for all $t \in [0, 1]$.
nodes.title: Convex universal covers

nodes.summary: A set $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is a universal cover when it is nonempty and covers every unit arc: for every continuous curve $\gamma : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{C}$ of length exactly $1$ there are $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\tau \in \mathbb{C}$ with $e^{i\theta} \gamma(t) + \tau \in \Omega$ for all $t \in [0, 1]$. Neither convexity nor measurability of $\Omega$ is required.
nodes.title: Universal covers

nodes.summary: If $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is a convex universal cover of unit arcs, then $\Omega$ is a null-measurable set for Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{C}$.
nodes.title: Convex universal covers are null-measurable

nodes.summary: Every convex universal cover $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is a universal cover.
nodes.title: Convex universal covers are universal covers

nodes.summary: The set of convex cover areas is the set of all values $\operatorname{vol}(\Omega) \in [0, \infty]$, where $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ ranges over the convex universal covers and $\operatorname{vol}$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{C} \cong \mathbb{R}^2$.
nodes.title: Areas of convex universal covers

nodes.summary: The set of values $\lambda(\Omega) \in [0, \infty]$, where $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ ranges over the universal covers and $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{C} \cong \mathbb{R}^2$, applied as an outer measure since $\Omega$ need not be measurable.
nodes.title: Areas of universal covers

nodes.summary: The convex cover area infimum is the infimum in $[0, \infty]$ of the set of convex cover areas, that is, the infimum of the Lebesgue areas of all convex universal covers $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$.
nodes.title: Infimal area of convex universal covers

nodes.summary: The infimum in $[0, \infty]$ of the areas $\lambda(\Omega)$ of the universal covers $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$, where $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{C} \cong \mathbb{R}^2$, applied as an outer measure since $\Omega$ need not be measurable.
nodes.title: Infimal area of a universal cover

nodes.summary: For every continuous curve $\gamma : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{C}$ of length exactly $1$ there are an angle $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ and a translation $c \in \mathbb{C}$ such that $|e^{i\theta}\gamma(t) + c| \le 1$ for every $t \in [0, 1]$; that is, the closed disk of radius $1$ centred at $0$ covers every unit arc.

nodes.summary: The closed disk $\{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| \le 1\}$ is a convex universal cover: it is nonempty, convex, and covers every unit arc.
nodes.title: The closed unit disk is a convex universal cover

nodes.summary: The cover area infimum, the infimum in $[0, \infty]$ of the Lebesgue areas of all universal covers in $\mathbb{C}$ (nonempty sets that cover every unit arc, not necessarily convex), is not $\infty$.

nodes.summary: The sphere-packing density $\Delta_4 \in [0, \infty]$ is the supremum, over all packings $P$ of congruent balls in $\mathbb{R}^4$, of the upper density of $P$. Here the upper density of $P$ is the limit superior, as the real radius $R > 0$ tends to infinity, of the supremum over all points $p \in \mathbb{R}^4$ of the ratio of the volume of the part of the open ball $B(p, R)$ covered by $P$ to the volume of $B(p, R)$.

Then some point $x$ in the convex hull of $\{p_1, \dots, p_n\}$ has at least $n/(d+1)$ of the points in every closed halfspace containing it: for all $v \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}$ with $\langle v, x \rangle \le t$, the number of indices $i$ with $\langle v, p_i \rangle \le t$ is at least $n/(d+1)$.

Suppose that for every nonzero continuous linear functional $F : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$ and every real $c$ such that the plane $\{x : F(x) = c\}$ meets the interior of $K$, the intersection of this plane with the boundary (frontier) of $K$ is homeomorphic to the unit circle. Then $K$ is convex.

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a set in an extended pseudometric space and let $k$ be a natural number. The set $s$ has a $k$-piece Borsuk cover if there are $k$ sets whose union contains $s$, each of extended diameter strictly smaller than that of $s$.
nodes.title: Borsuk covers

nodes.summary: The Borsuk number of a set $s$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the least natural number $k$ such that $s$ has a $k$-piece Borsuk cover, that is, $s$ is covered by $k$ sets each of strictly smaller extended diameter than $s$; it is $\infty$ if no such $k$ exists.

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, the Borsuk number of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the supremum, in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, of the Borsuk numbers of the bounded subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with at least two points.

nodes.summary: The first Borsuk failure dimension is the least positive integer $n$ such that the Borsuk number of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is greater than $n + 1$, and $\infty$ if there is no such $n$.

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, a set $s$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ has a $k$-piece Borsuk cover if and only if there are subsets $c_1, \dots, c_k$ of $s$ with $s = c_1 \cup \dots \cup c_k$, each of extended diameter strictly smaller than that of $s$.

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, a set $s$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ has a $k$-piece Borsuk cover if and only if there are $k$ closed subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ whose union contains $s$, each of extended diameter strictly smaller than that of $s$.
nodes.title: Borsuk covers by closed sets

nodes.summary: Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers. If a nonempty set $s$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ has a $k$-piece Borsuk cover, then $0 < k$.
nodes.title: Borsuk covers of nonempty sets have at least one piece

nodes.summary: Let $n$, $k$ and $l$ be natural numbers with $k \le l$. If a nonempty set $s$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ has a $k$-piece Borsuk cover, then $s$ has an $l$-piece Borsuk cover.
nodes.title: Enlarging a Borsuk cover

nodes.summary: For a nonempty set $s$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ and a natural number $k$, the Borsuk number of $s$ is at most $k$ if and only if $s$ has a $k$-piece Borsuk cover.
nodes.title: Bounds on the Borsuk number of a set

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the Borsuk number of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is at most $k$ if and only if every bounded subset $s$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with at least two points has a $k$-piece Borsuk cover, that is, $s$ is covered by $k$ sets, each of extended diameter strictly smaller than that of $s$.
nodes.title: Upper bounds on the Borsuk number of a Euclidean space

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, Borsuk's conjecture in dimension $n$ is the statement that the Borsuk number of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is at most $n + 1$.
nodes.title: Borsuk's conjecture in a given dimension

nodes.summary: The first Borsuk failure dimension is $\infty$ if and only if, for every positive integer $n$, the Borsuk number of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is at most $n + 1$.
nodes.title: When the first Borsuk failure dimension is infinite

nodes.summary: A set $s$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a two-distance set if there are reals $0 < a < b$ such that the distance between any two distinct points of $s$ is $a$ or $b$, and both $a$ and $b$ occur as the distance between some two points of $s$.
nodes.title: Two-distance sets

reading_title.source: Two-distance Borsuk number in dimension $n$

nodes.summary: The two-distance Borsuk number in dimension $n$ is the supremum, taken in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, of the Borsuk numbers of all bounded two-distance sets with at least two points in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$.
nodes.title: Two-distance Borsuk number in dimension $n$

nodes.title: Brunn–Minkowski inequality

nodes.summary: Let $d \ge 0$ and let $S_0, \dots, S_d$ be subsets of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$ such that the origin lies in the convex hull of each $S_i$. Then there are points $c_0 \in S_0, \dots, c_d \in S_d$ such that the origin lies in the convex hull of $\{c_0, \dots, c_d\}$.

nodes.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the Hanner cube $C_n \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is defined by recursion on $n$: $C_0$ is the centered unit segment $[-1, 1] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^1$, and $C_{n+1} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+2}$ is the $\ell_\infty$ sum of $C_n$ and the centered unit segment.
nodes.title: Hanner cube

nodes.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the Hanner cross-polytope $P_n \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is defined by recursion on $n$: $P_0$ is the centered unit segment $[-1, 1] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^1$, and $P_{n+1} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+2}$ is the $\ell_1$ sum of $P_n$ and the centered unit segment.

nodes.summary: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the Hanner cross-polytope $P_n \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is a Hanner polytope.
nodes.title: The Hanner cross-polytopes are Hanner polytopes

reading_title.source: Membership in the $\ell_\infty$ Hanner sum

nodes.summary: Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ and $L \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. A point $x \in \mathbb{R}^{m+n}$ lies in the $\ell_\infty$ Hanner sum of $K$ and $L$ if and only if $(x_1, \dots, x_m) \in K$ and $(x_{m+1}, \dots, x_{m+n}) \in L$.
nodes.title: Membership in the $\ell_\infty$ Hanner sum

nodes.summary: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the Hanner cube $C_n \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ equals the coordinate cube $\{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1} : -1 \le x_i \le 1 \text{ for every } i\} = [-1, 1]^{n+1}$.
nodes.title: The Hanner cube is the coordinate cube

nodes.summary: If $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a Hanner polytope, then $0 < n$.
nodes.title: Hanner polytopes live in positive dimension

nodes.summary: Every Hanner polytope $K$ is centrally symmetric about the origin: $-K = K$.
nodes.title: Hanner polytopes are centrally symmetric

nodes.summary: For every Hanner polytope $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $-x \in K$ if and only if $x \in K$.
nodes.title: Negation preserves membership in a Hanner polytope

nodes.summary: Every Hanner polytope $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is convex.

nodes.summary: The origin belongs to every Hanner polytope.

nodes.summary: Every Hanner polytope is compact.

nodes.summary: The feasible region of a linear program with $m$ variables, constraint matrix $A$ and right-hand side $b$ is the set of vectors $x \in \mathbb{R}^m$ with $A x \le b$ and $x \ge 0$, both inequalities holding componentwise. It is a convex polyhedron in $\mathbb{R}^m$.

If $P$ is nonempty and bounded, then some $x \in P$ maximises $f$ on $P$ and is an extreme point of $P$, that is, $x$ does not lie in the open segment between two distinct points of $P$.

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a real normed space and $E^*$ its continuous dual. For $h : E^* \to \mathbb{R}$ and $x, v \in E^*$, the difference quotients of $h$ at $x$ in direction $v$ form the set $\{(h(x + t v) - h(x))/t : t > 0\}$.
nodes.title: Difference quotients

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a real normed space with continuous dual $E^*$. For $h : E^* \to \mathbb{R}$ and $x, v \in E^*$, the directional derivative of $h$ at $x$ in direction $v$ is the infimum of the difference quotients, $h'(x; v) = \inf_{t > 0} \frac{h(x + t v) - h(x)}{t}$, which is taken to be $0$ when these quotients are not bounded below.
nodes.title: Directional derivative

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a real normed space with continuous dual $E^*$, and let $h : E^* \to \mathbb{R}$ be convex. For all $x, v \in E^*$, the function $s \mapsto h(x + s v)$ is convex on $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.title: Restriction of a convex function to a line

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a real normed space, $E^*$ its continuous dual, and $h : E^* \to \mathbb{R}$ a convex function. For all $x, v \in E^*$, the set of difference quotients $\{(h(x + t v) - h(x))/t : t > 0\}$ is bounded below.
nodes.title: Difference quotients of a convex function are bounded below

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a real normed space with continuous dual $E^*$, let $h : E^* \to \mathbb{R}$ be convex, and write $h'(x; v)$ for the directional derivative of $h$ at $x$ in direction $v$. For all $x, v, w \in E^*$, $h'(x; v + w) \le h'(x; v) + h'(x; w)$.
nodes.title: Subadditivity of the directional derivative

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a real normed space with continuous dual $E^*$ and let $h : E^* \to \mathbb{R}$ be any function. For every $x \in E^*$, the directional derivative of $h$ at $x$ in direction $0$ is $0$.
nodes.title: Directional derivative in direction zero

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a real normed space with continuous dual $E^*$, let $h : E^* \to \mathbb{R}$ be convex, and write $h'(x; v)$ for the directional derivative of $h$ at $x$ in direction $v$. For all $x, v \in E^*$, $h'(x; v) + h'(x; -v) \ge 0$.

nodes.summary: For a set $K$ in a real normed space $E$, the support function of $K$ sends a continuous linear functional $\ell$ on $E$ to the supremum $\sup_{x \in K} \ell(x)$ of the values of $\ell$ on $K$.
nodes.title: Support function

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a nonempty compact subset of a real normed space $E$, and let $h_K(l) = \sup_{x \in K} l(x)$ be its support function on the continuous dual $E^*$. For every $l \in E^*$ there is $x \in K$ with $l(x) = h_K(l)$.
nodes.title: The support function of a compact set is attained

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a nonempty compact subset of a real normed space $E$. Its support function $h_K(l) = \sup_{x \in K} l(x)$ is a convex function on the whole continuous dual $E^*$.
nodes.title: The support function of a compact set is convex

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a nonempty compact subset of a real normed space $E$, and let $h_K(l) = \sup_{x \in K} l(x)$ be its support function on the continuous dual $E^*$. There is a constant $C \ge 0$ such that $h_K(l_1) - h_K(l_2) \le C \|l_1 - l_2\|$ for all $l_1, l_2 \in E^*$, where $\|\cdot\|$ is the operator norm.
nodes.title: The support function of a compact set is Lipschitz

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a nonempty compact subset of a real normed space $E$. Its support function $h_K(l) = \sup_{x \in K} l(x)$ is continuous on the continuous dual $E^*$ with the operator norm.
nodes.title: The support function of a compact set is continuous

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a real normed space, $E^*$ its continuous dual, and $h : E^* \to \mathbb{R}$. For $x, v \in E^*$ let $h'(x; v)$ be the infimum of the difference quotients $(h(x + t v) - h(x))/t$ over $t > 0$, taken to be $0$ when they are unbounded below. A point $x \in E^*$ is a Gateaux point of $h$ when $h'(x; v) + h'(x; -v) \le 0$ for every $v \in E^*$.
nodes.title: Gateaux points

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a real normed space with continuous dual $E^*$, let $K \subseteq E$ be a nonempty compact set with support function $h_K$, and write $h_K'(x; v)$ for the directional derivative of $h_K$ at $x$ in direction $v$. For every $v \in E^*$ and every real $c$, the set of $x \in E^*$ with $h_K'(x; v) + h_K'(x; -v) < c$ is open.
nodes.title: Strict sublevel sets of the symmetrized directional derivative are open

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a real normed space with continuous dual $E^*$, let $K \subseteq E$ be a nonempty compact set with support function $h_K$, and write $h_K'(x; w)$ for the directional derivative of $h_K$ at $x$ in direction $w$. For every $x \in E^*$, the map $w \mapsto h_K'(x; w)$ is continuous on $E^*$.
nodes.title: Continuity of the directional derivative of a support function in the direction

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a real normed space with continuous dual $E^*$, let $K \subseteq E$ be a nonempty compact set with support function $h_K$, and write $h_K'(x; w)$ for the directional derivative of $h_K$ at $x$ in direction $w$. If $C$ is a real number with $h_K(\ell_1) - h_K(\ell_2) \le C \|\ell_1 - \ell_2\|$ for all $\ell_1, \ell_2 \in E^*$, then $h_K'(x; w) \le C \|w\|$ for all $x, w \in E^*$.
nodes.title: Lipschitz bound on directional derivatives of a support function

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space with continuous dual $E^*$, let $K \subseteq E$ be a nonempty compact set with support function $h_K$, and write $h_K'(\ell; v)$ for the directional derivative of $h_K$ at $\ell$ in direction $v$. Then the Gateaux points of $h_K$, that is, the functionals $\ell \in E^*$ with $h_K'(\ell; v) + h_K'(\ell; -v) \le 0$ for every $v \in E^*$, form a dense subset of $E^*$.
nodes.title: Mazur's theorem for support functions

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a nonempty compact subset of a real normed space $E$, let $h_K(l) = \sup_{y \in K} l(y)$ be its support function on the continuous dual $E^*$, and write $h_K'(u; v)$ for the directional derivative of $h_K$ at $u$ in direction $v$. If $u \in E^*$ and $z \in K$ satisfy $u(z) = h_K(u)$, then $v(z) \le h_K'(u; v)$ for every $v \in E^*$.
nodes.title: A maximizer bounds the directional derivative of the support function from below

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a nonempty compact subset of a real normed space $E$, and let $h_K(l) = \sup_{y \in K} l(y)$ be its support function on the continuous dual $E^*$. If $l \in E^*$ is a Gateaux point of $h_K$ and $z_1, z_2 \in K$ satisfy $l(z_1) = h_K(l)$ and $l(z_2) = h_K(l)$, then $z_1 = z_2$.
nodes.title: Maximizers at a Gateaux point of the support function are unique

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a nonempty compact set in a real normed space $E$, let $\ell$ be a continuous linear functional on $E$, and let $h_K$ be the support function of $K$. If $z \in K$ satisfies $\ell(z) = h_K(\ell)$ and every $y \in K$ with $\ell(y) = h_K(\ell)$ equals $z$, then $z$ is an exposed point of $K$.

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space and let $A \subseteq E$ be a compact convex set. Then every extreme point of $A$ lies in the closure of the set of exposed points of $A$.

Let $u : B \to \mathbb{R}$ and $b \in B$. If $g'_b(v, w) = u(b)\, g_b(v, w)$ for all $v, w \in E_b$ and $E_b$ contains a nonzero vector, then $u(b) > 0$.

nodes.title: Conformal class of a Riemannian metric

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a $C^\infty$ manifold modeled on a real normed space, and let $g$ and $g'$ be $C^\infty$ Riemannian metrics on $M$, with inner products $g_x$ and $g'_x$ on the tangent space $T_x M$. Then $g'$ lies in the conformal class of $g$ if and only if there is a $C^\infty$ function $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ with $g'_x(v, w) = e^{f(x)}\, g_x(v, w)$ for all $x \in M$ and all $v, w \in T_x M$.

Then the conformal scaling $u g$ of $g$ by $u$ lies in the conformal class of $g$.
nodes.title: Conformal scalings lie in the conformal class

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a $C^\infty$ manifold modeled on a real normed space, and let $g$ and $g'$ be $C^\infty$ Riemannian metrics on $M$. If $g'$ lies in the conformal class of $g$, then $g$ lies in the conformal class of $g'$.

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a $C^\infty$ manifold modeled on a real normed space, and let $g$, $g'$ and $g''$ be $C^\infty$ Riemannian metrics on $M$. If $g'$ lies in the conformal class of $g$ and $g''$ lies in the conformal class of $g'$, then $g''$ lies in the conformal class of $g$.

nodes.summary: Let $(M, g)$ be a $C^\infty$ Riemannian manifold modeled on a finite-dimensional real space (boundary and corners allowed), and let $x \in M$, $u \in T_x M$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$. nodes.title: Sectional curvature bounded above

nodes.summary: A $C^\infty$ Riemannian manifold $M$ has scalar curvature at least $k \in \mathbb{R}$ when its scalar curvature at every point $x \in M$ is at least $k$.

nodes.summary: A $C^\infty$ Riemannian manifold $(M, g)$ is Einstein when there is a real constant $\lambda$ such that $\operatorname{Ric}_x(v, w) = \lambda \, g_x(v, w)$ for every point $x \in M$ and all tangent vectors $v, w \in T_x M$, where $\operatorname{Ric}$ is the Ricci curvature ([Lang], Einstein manifolds). Ricci-flat is the case $\lambda = 0$.

Then the Lie bracket $[X, Y]$ vanishes at every point $y \in F$.

nodes.title: Line lying in a graph

nodes.summary: The graph of a real-valued function $f$ of two real variables is doubly ruled when for every point $(x_0, y_0) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ there are $(u_1, v_1, w_1)$ and $(u_2, v_2, w_2)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ such that the lines through $(x_0, y_0, f(x_0, y_0))$ with directions $(u_1, v_1, w_1)$ and $(u_2, v_2, w_2)$ both lie in the graph of $f$, and $(u_2, v_2)$ is not a real multiple of $(u_1, v_1)$.

nodes.summary: Let $f$ be a real-valued function of two real variables whose graph is doubly ruled; no continuity of $f$ is assumed. Then there are real numbers $a, b, c, d, e, g$ such that $f(x, y) = ax^2 + bxy + cy^2 + dx + ey + g$ for all real $x$ and $y$, and either $a = b = c = 0$ (the graph is a plane) or $b^2 - 4ac > 0$ (the graph is a hyperbolic paraboloid).

If the total curvature of $r$ is at most $4\pi$, then $r$ is unknotted: there is a real-analytic isotopy from $r$ to the standard circle through smooth knots.

nodes.summary: The unit strip is the set of points $(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ with $0 \le x \le 1$, that is, $[0, 1] \times \mathbb{R}$.

Then $f$ is a Moebius embedding of aspect ratio $a$ if $f(1 - x, y + a) = f(x, y)$ for every $(x, y) \in S$, $f$ is $C^\infty$ on $S$, at every point of $S$ the derivative of $f$ within $S$ is a linear isometry $\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3$, and $f$ is injective on $[0, 1] \times [0, a)$.

nodes.summary: Let $a > 0$. If $f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ is a Moebius embedding of aspect ratio $a$, then $a > \sqrt{3}$. That is, a smooth embedded paper Moebius band has aspect ratio greater than $\sqrt{3}$.

Knots, links and ambient isotopy

nodes.summary: An oriented parametrized smooth knot in Euclidean 3-space is a $C^\infty$ curve $\gamma \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^3$ that is $2\pi$-periodic ($\gamma(t + 2\pi) = \gamma(t)$ for all $t$), injective on $[0, 2\pi)$, and an immersion ($\gamma'(t) \neq 0$ for all $t$).
nodes.title: Parametrized knot

nodes.summary: An oriented labeled parametrized smooth link with $n$ components in Euclidean 3-space is a family $(\gamma_i)_{i < n}$ of parametrized knots whose traces $\gamma_i(\mathbb{R})$ are pairwise disjoint.
nodes.title: Parametrized link

nodes.summary: A smooth ambient isotopy of $\mathbb{R}^3$ consists of two families of maps $H_t, G_t \colon \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$, indexed by times $t \in \mathbb{R}$, such that $(t, x) \mapsto H_t(x)$ and $(t, x) \mapsto G_t(x)$ are $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^3$, $G_t(H_t(x)) = x$ and $H_t(G_t(x)) = x$ for all $t$ and $x$, and $H_0$ is the identity.
nodes.title: Smooth ambient isotopy of Euclidean 3-space

nodes.summary: The identity ambient isotopy of $\mathbb{R}^3$ has forward and inverse families $H_t$ and $G_t$ equal to the identity map of $\mathbb{R}^3$ for every time $t$.
nodes.title: Identity ambient isotopy

nodes.summary: The inverse of an ambient isotopy with forward family $(H_t)$ and inverse family $(H_t^{-1})$ is the ambient isotopy whose forward family is $(H_t^{-1})$ and whose inverse family is $(H_t)$; at each time $t$ it is the inverse diffeomorphism of $H_t$.
nodes.title: Inverse ambient isotopy

nodes.summary: If $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ are smooth ambient isotopies of $\mathbb{R}^3$ with forward families $H_t, H'_t$ and inverse families $G_t, G'_t$, their composition (first $\Phi$, then $\Psi$, at the same time parameter) is the ambient isotopy with forward family $H'_t \circ H_t$ and inverse family $G_t \circ G'_t$.
nodes.title: Composition of ambient isotopies

nodes.summary: An orientation-preserving smooth reparametrization of the circle is given by maps $f, g \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, both $C^\infty$ and inverse to each other ($g(f(t)) = t$ and $f(g(t)) = t$ for all $t$), such that $f(t + 2\pi) = f(t) + 2\pi$ and $g(t + 2\pi) = g(t) + 2\pi$ for all $t$, and $f$ is strictly increasing. Here $f$ is a lift of the reparametrization and $g$ is a lift of its inverse.
nodes.title: Orientation-preserving reparametrization of the circle

nodes.summary: The identity circle reparametrization has lift and inverse lift both equal to the identity map of $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.title: Identity reparametrization of the circle

nodes.summary: The inverse of a circle reparametrization with lift $f$ and inverse lift $f^{-1}$ is the circle reparametrization whose lift is $f^{-1}$ and whose inverse lift is $f$.
nodes.title: Inverse circle reparametrization

nodes.summary: If $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are circle reparametrizations with lifts $f_\sigma, f_\tau$ and inverse lifts $g_\sigma, g_\tau$, their composition (first $\sigma$, then $\tau$) is the circle reparametrization with lift $f_\tau \circ f_\sigma$ and inverse lift $g_\sigma \circ g_\tau$.
nodes.title: Composition of circle reparametrizations

nodes.summary: Two parametrized knots $\gamma_1, \gamma_2$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are isotopic (oriented ambient isotopy) if there are a smooth ambient isotopy of $\mathbb{R}^3$ with forward family $H_t$ and an orientation-preserving reparametrization of the circle with lift $f$ such that $H_1(\gamma_1(t)) = \gamma_2(f(t))$ for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$.
nodes.title: Isotopy of parametrized knots

nodes.summary: Two parametrized links in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with $n$ components $\gamma^1_i$ and $\gamma^2_i$ ($i < n$) are isotopic (oriented, labeled ambient isotopy) if there are a single smooth ambient isotopy of $\mathbb{R}^3$ with forward family $H_t$ and, for each $i < n$, an orientation-preserving reparametrization of the circle with lift $f_i$, such that $H_1(\gamma^1_i(t)) = \gamma^2_i(f_i(t))$ for every $i < n$ and every…
nodes.title: Isotopy of parametrized links

nodes.summary: The trace of a parametrized link $L$ in Euclidean 3-space is the union of the images of its component curves: the set of all points $\gamma(t)$, where $\gamma$ is a component of $L$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}$.
nodes.title: Trace of a parametrized link

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a parametrized link in Euclidean 3-space with components $\gamma_1, \dots, \gamma_n$, each a $2\pi$-periodic curve. The total contour length of $L$ is the sum over all components $\gamma_i$ of the contour length of $\gamma_i$ on one period $[0, 2\pi]$. It is a value in $[0, \infty]$.
nodes.title: Total contour length of a parametrized link

nodes.summary: For a parametrized link $L$, the ropelength ratio of $L$ is its total contour length divided by the thickness of its trace (the union of the images of its components), a value in $[0, \infty]$ computed with the division of $[0, \infty]$.
nodes.title: Ropelength ratio of a parametrized link

nodes.summary: For a parametrized link $L$ with $n$ components, the ropelength of $L$ is the infimum, in $[0, \infty]$, of the ropelength ratios of all parametrized links $L'$ with $n$ components that are isotopic to $L$. It is the ropelength of the oriented, labeled ambient-isotopy type of $L$.
nodes.title: Ropelength of a parametrized link

nodes.summary: Let $L$ and $L'$ be parametrized links with $n$ components. If $L'$ is isotopic to $L$, then the ropelength of $L$ is at most the ropelength ratio of $L'$.
nodes.title: Ropelength is at most the ratio of any isotopic link

nodes.summary: For every parametrized link $L$ with $n$ components, the ropelength of $L$ is at most the ropelength ratio of $L$.
nodes.title: Ropelength is at most the ropelength ratio

nodes.summary: Let $L_1$ and $L_2$ be parametrized links with $n$ components. If $L_1$ is isotopic to $L_2$ (by an oriented, labeled ambient isotopy), then the ropelength of $L_1$ equals the ropelength of $L_2$.
nodes.title: Ropelength is an isotopy invariant

nodes.summary: A parametrized knot $K$ determines the parametrized link with one component, whose single component is $K$; the pairwise disjointness condition holds trivially.
nodes.title: Parametrized knot as a one-component link

nodes.summary: If $K_1$ and $K_2$ are parametrized knots and $K_1$ is isotopic to $K_2$, then the one-component parametrized link of $K_1$ is isotopic to the one-component parametrized link of $K_2$.
nodes.title: Isotopic knots give isotopic one-component links

nodes.summary: The ropelength of a parametrized knot $K$ is the ropelength of the one-component parametrized link determined by $K$: the infimum, in $[0, \infty]$, of the ropelength ratios of all one-component parametrized links that are isotopic to the one-component link of $K$.
nodes.title: Ropelength of a parametrized knot

nodes.summary: Let $v_0, \dots, v_{n-1}$ be a list of $n \ge 1$ points of $\mathbb{R}^3$. The polyline curve is the $n$-periodic map $\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^3$ with $\gamma(k + \alpha) = (1 - \alpha) v_k + \alpha v_{k+1}$ for integers $0 \le k < n$ and reals $0 \le \alpha < 1$, where indices are taken modulo $n$ (so $v_n = v_0$). For the empty list the curve is constantly $0$.
nodes.title: Parametrization of a closed polyline

nodes.summary: A PL knot is a list $v_0, \dots, v_{n-1}$ of points of $\mathbb{R}^3$ with $n \ge 3$, viewed as the vertices, in order, of the closed polyline with edges from $v_i$ to $v_{i+1}$ for $i < n - 1$ and from $v_{n-1}$ back to $v_0$.

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a PL knot with vertices $v_0, \dots, v_{n-1}$. Its image is the subset of $\mathbb{R}^3$ traced by the closed polyline through these vertices: the image of the half-open interval $[0, n)$ under the parametrization that sends $k + \alpha$, for an integer $0 \le k < n$ and a real $0 \le \alpha < 1$, to $(1 - \alpha) v_k + \alpha v_{k+1}$, with indices taken modulo $n$.
nodes.title: Image of a PL knot

nodes.summary: A PL knot $K$ with vertices $v_0, \dots, v_{n-1}$ is simple if its closed polyline parametrization, which sends $k + \alpha$, for an integer $0 \le k < n$ and a real $0 \le \alpha < 1$, to $(1 - \alpha) v_k + \alpha v_{k+1}$ (indices modulo $n$), is injective on the half-open interval $[0, n)$.
