Frames in Hilbert spaces

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be an inner product space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. A finite family $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ in $E$ is a frame with frame bounds $A, B \in \mathbb{R}$ if $A > 0$, $B > 0$ and, for every $x \in E$, $A \|x\|^2 \le \sum_{i \in \iota} |\langle f_i, x \rangle|^2 \le B \|x\|^2$.
nodes.title: Finite frame

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be an inner product space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. If a finite family $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ in $E$ is a frame with frame bounds $A$ and $B$, then $A > 0$.
nodes.title: The lower frame bound is positive

nodes.summary: If a finite family $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ in an inner product space $E$ over $\mathbb{K}$ ($\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$) is a frame with frame bounds $A$ and $B$, then $0 < B$.
nodes.title: The upper frame bound is positive

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be an inner product space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a finite frame in $E$ with frame bounds $A$ and $B$. Then $A \|x\|^2 \le \sum_{i \in \iota} |\langle f_i, x \rangle|^2$ for every $x \in E$.
nodes.title: Lower frame inequality

nodes.summary: If a finite family $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ in an inner product space $E$ over $\mathbb{K}$ ($\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$) is a frame with frame bounds $A$ and $B$, then $\sum_{i} |\langle f_i, x \rangle|^2 \le B \|x\|^2$ for every $x \in E$.
nodes.title: Upper frame inequality

nodes.summary: For a finite family $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ in an inner product space $E$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, the frame operator is the bounded linear operator $S \colon E \to E$ given by $S x = \sum_{i \in \iota} \langle f_i, x \rangle f_i$, the sum of the rank-one operators $x \mapsto \langle f_i, x \rangle f_i$. The inner product is conjugate-linear in its first argument.
nodes.title: Frame operator

nodes.summary: For a finite family $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ in an inner product space $E$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, the frame operator $S$ of the family satisfies $S x = \sum_{i \in \iota} \langle f_i, x \rangle f_i$ for every $x \in E$, where the inner product is conjugate-linear in its first argument.
nodes.title: Frame operator formula

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be an inner product space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, with inner product conjugate-linear in the first argument, and let $S$ be the frame operator of a finite family $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ in $E$. Then $\langle S x, y \rangle = \sum_{i \in \iota} \overline{\langle f_i, x \rangle} \, \langle f_i, y \rangle$ for all $x, y \in E$.
nodes.title: Inner product against the frame operator

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be the frame operator of a finite family $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ in an inner product space $E$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. For every $x \in E$, $\langle S x, x \rangle = \sum_{i \in \iota} |\langle f_i, x \rangle|^2$; the right side is a real number, viewed as an element of $\mathbb{K}$.
nodes.title: Quadratic form of the frame operator

nodes.summary: Let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a finite family in an inner product space $E$ over $\mathbb{K}$ ($\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$), with frame operator $S$. For every $x \in E$, $\operatorname{Re} \langle S x, x \rangle = \sum_{i} |\langle f_i, x \rangle|^2$.
nodes.title: Real part of the frame quadratic form

nodes.summary: Let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a finite family in an inner product space $E$ over $\mathbb{K}$ ($\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$), with frame operator $S$. For all $x, y \in E$,
nodes.title: Cauchy–Schwarz bound for the frame operator

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a Hilbert space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. For every finite family $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ in $E$, not necessarily a frame, the frame operator of $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ is self-adjoint.
nodes.title: The frame operator is self-adjoint

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be an inner product space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a finite frame in $E$ with frame bounds $A$ and $B$ and frame operator $S$. Then $A \|x\| \le \|S x\|$ for every $x \in E$.
nodes.title: The frame operator is bounded below

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a Hilbert space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a finite frame in $E$ with frame bounds $A$ and $B$. Then its frame operator $S$ is a unit in the algebra of bounded linear operators on $E$, that is, $S$ has a bounded linear two-sided inverse.
nodes.title: The frame operator of a frame is invertible

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be an inner product space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a finite frame in $E$ with frame bounds $A$ and $B$ and frame operator $S$. Then the operator norm of $S$ satisfies $\|S\| \le B$.
nodes.title: The frame operator has norm at most the upper frame bound

nodes.summary: Let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$, with $\iota$ finite, be a frame with bounds $A$ and $B$ in a Hilbert space $E$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. Its frame operator $S$ is invertible in the algebra of bounded linear operators on $E$, and the inverse frame operator $S^{-1}$ is its inverse there.
nodes.title: Inverse frame operator

nodes.summary: Let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$, with $\iota$ finite, be a frame with bounds $A$ and $B$ in a Hilbert space $E$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, with frame operator $S$ and inverse frame operator $S^{-1}$. Then $S \circ S^{-1}$ is the identity operator on $E$.
nodes.title: The inverse frame operator is a right inverse

nodes.summary: Let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$, with $\iota$ finite, be a frame with bounds $A$ and $B$ in a Hilbert space $E$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, with frame operator $S$ and inverse frame operator $S^{-1}$. Then $S^{-1} \circ S$ is the identity operator on $E$.
nodes.title: The inverse frame operator is a left inverse

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a Hilbert space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a finite frame in $E$ with frame bounds $A$ and $B$. Then the inverse $S^{-1}$ of its frame operator $S$ is self-adjoint.
nodes.title: The inverse frame operator is self-adjoint

nodes.summary: Let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$, with $\iota$ finite, be a frame with bounds $A$ and $B$ in a Hilbert space $E$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $S^{-1}$ be the inverse of its frame operator. Then every $x \in E$ satisfies $x = \sum_{i \in \iota} \langle f_i, S^{-1} x \rangle f_i$.
nodes.title: Frame reconstruction formula

nodes.summary: Let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$, with $\iota$ finite, be a frame with bounds $A$ and $B$ in a Hilbert space $E$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $S^{-1}$ be the inverse of its frame operator. The canonical dual frame is the family $(S^{-1} f_i)_{i \in \iota}$.
nodes.title: Canonical dual frame

nodes.summary: Let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$, with $\iota$ finite, be a frame with bounds $A$ and $B$ in a Hilbert space $E$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $S^{-1}$ be the inverse of its frame operator. Then the frame operator of the canonical dual frame $(S^{-1} f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ is $S^{-1}$.
nodes.title: Frame operator of the canonical dual frame

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a Hilbert space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a finite frame in $E$ with frame bounds $A$ and $B$ and frame operator $S$. Then the canonical dual frame $(S^{-1} f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ is a frame with lower frame bound $1/B$ and upper frame bound $1/A$.
nodes.title: The canonical dual frame is a frame

nodes.summary: Let $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$, with $\iota$ finite, be a frame in a Hilbert space $E$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ whose lower and upper frame bounds are both equal to $A$. Then its frame operator is $S = A \cdot I$, where $I$ is the identity operator on $E$.
nodes.title: Tight frames have scalar frame operator
Hilbert projection theorem

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a nonempty complete convex subset of a real inner product space $F$. For every $x \in F$ there is exactly one $p \in K$ with $\|x - p\| = \inf_{w \in K} \|x - w\|$, that is, exactly one point of $K$ nearest to $x$.
nodes.title: Existence and uniqueness of the nearest point

nodes.summary: For every subset $K$ of a real inner product space $F$ and every $x \in F$, there is a point $p \in F$ such that, if $K$ is nonempty, complete and convex, then $p \in K$ and $\|x - p\| = \inf_{w \in K} \|x - w\|$.
nodes.title: Totalized existence of the convex projection

nodes.summary: For a subset $K$ of a real inner product space $F$ and a point $x \in F$, the nearest-point projection $P_K(x)$ is a chosen point of $F$ such that, whenever $K$ is nonempty, complete and convex, $P_K(x) \in K$ and $\|x - P_K(x)\| = \inf_{w \in K} \|x - w\|$; it is then the unique point of $K$ nearest to $x$. When $K$ fails one of these hypotheses, the value of $P_K(x)$ is unspecified.
nodes.title: Nearest-point projection onto a convex set

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a nonempty complete convex subset of a real inner product space $F$, and let $P_K$ be the nearest-point projection onto $K$. For every $x \in F$, $P_K(x) \in K$ and $\|x - P_K(x)\| = \inf_{w \in K} \|x - w\|$.
nodes.title: Defining property of the convex projection

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a nonempty complete convex subset of a real inner product space $F$, and let $P_K$ be the nearest-point projection onto $K$. Then $P_K(x) \in K$ for every $x \in F$.
nodes.title: The convex projection lies in the set

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a nonempty complete convex subset of a real inner product space $F$, and let $P_K$ be the nearest-point projection onto $K$. Then $\|x - P_K(x)\| = \inf_{w \in K} \|x - w\|$ for every $x \in F$.
nodes.title: The convex projection minimizes the distance to the set

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a nonempty complete convex subset of a real inner product space $F$, and let $P_K$ be the nearest-point projection onto $K$. For every $x \in F$ and every $w \in K$, $\langle x - P_K(x), w - P_K(x) \rangle \le 0$.
nodes.title: Variational inequality for the convex projection

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a nonempty complete convex subset of a real inner product space $F$, let $P_K$ be the nearest-point projection onto $K$, and let $x \in F$. If $p \in K$ satisfies $\|x - p\| = \inf_{w \in K} \|x - w\|$, then $P_K(x) = p$.
nodes.title: Nearest points coincide with the convex projection

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a nonempty complete convex subset of a real inner product space $F$, and let $P_K$ be the nearest-point projection onto $K$. Then $P_K(x) = x$ for every $x \in K$.
nodes.title: The convex projection fixes the points of the set

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a nonempty complete convex subset of a real inner product space $F$, and let $P_K$ be the nearest-point projection onto $K$. Then $P_K(P_K(x)) = P_K(x)$ for every $x \in F$.
nodes.title: Idempotence of the convex projection

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a convex subset of a real inner product space $F$, let $x, y \in F$, and let $p, q \in K$ satisfy $\|x - p\| = \inf_{w \in K} \|x - w\|$ and $\|y - q\| = \inf_{w \in K} \|y - w\|$, so that $p$ is a point of $K$ nearest to $x$ and $q$ is a point of $K$ nearest to $y$. Then $\|p - q\| \le \|x - y\|$.
nodes.title: Nonexpansiveness of nearest-point selection

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a convex subset of a real inner product space $F$, let $x, y \in F$, and let $p, q \in K$ satisfy $\|x - p\| = \inf_{w \in K} \|x - w\|$ and $\|y - q\| = \inf_{w \in K} \|y - w\|$, so that $p$ is a point of $K$ nearest to $x$ and $q$ is a point of $K$ nearest to $y$. Then $\|p - q\|^2 + \|(x - p) - (y - q)\|^2 \le \|x - y\|^2$.
nodes.title: Firm nonexpansiveness of nearest-point selection

reading_title.source: The convex projection is $1$-Lipschitz

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a nonempty complete convex subset of a real inner product space $F$, and let $P_K$ be the nearest-point projection onto $K$. Then $\|P_K x - P_K y\| \le \|x - y\|$ for all $x, y \in F$, that is, $P_K$ is $1$-Lipschitz.
nodes.title: The convex projection is $1$-Lipschitz

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a nonempty complete convex subset of a real inner product space $F$, and let $P_K$ be the nearest-point projection onto $K$. For all $x, y \in F$, $\|P_K(x) - P_K(y)\|^2 + \|(x - P_K(x)) - (y - P_K(y))\|^2 \le \|x - y\|^2$.
nodes.title: Firm nonexpansiveness of the convex projection
Kirszbraun theorem

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a real inner product space (not necessarily complete), let $F$ be a complete real inner product space, let $s \subseteq E$ and let $K \ge 0$. Every map $f : E \to F$ that is $K$-Lipschitz on $s$ agrees on $s$ with some map $g : E \to F$ that is $K$-Lipschitz on all of $E$.
nodes.title: Kirszbraun extension theorem

nodes.summary: Let $E$ and $F$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $s \subseteq E$ and let $K \ge 0$. Every map $f : E \to F$ that is $K$-Lipschitz on $s$ agrees on $s$ with some map $g : E \to F$ that is $K$-Lipschitz on all of $E$.
nodes.title: Kirszbraun extension theorem for Hilbert spaces

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be an inner product space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, not necessarily complete, let $(u_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $H$ and let $x \in H$. The gradient descent trajectory of $f$ from $x_0$ with steps $s$ is the sequence $(x_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ in $E$ starting at $x_0$ with $x_{k+1} = x_k - s_k \nabla f(x_k)$.
nodes.title: Gradient descent with a step schedule

reading_title.source: Convex functions with $1$-Lipschitz gradient

nodes.summary: A function $f : E \to \mathbb{R}$ on a real Hilbert space $E$ is unit-smooth convex if it is convex, differentiable, and its gradient is $1$-Lipschitz: $\lVert \nabla f(x) - \nabla f(y) \rVert \le \lVert x - y \rVert$ for all $x, y \in E$.
nodes.title: Convex functions with $1$-Lipschitz gradient

nodes.summary: A step schedule $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ achieves a uniform last-iterate rate with exponent $c \in \mathbb{R}$ if there are a real number $C > 0$ and an integer $K \ge 1$ with the following property. For every $d \in \mathbb{N}$, every convex differentiable function $f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ whose gradient is $1$-Lipschitz for the Euclidean norm, every $x^\star \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with…
nodes.title: Uniform last-iterate rate of a step schedule

nodes.summary: The gradient descent exponent is the supremum, in the extended reals $[-\infty, +\infty]$, of the set of real numbers $c$ such that some step schedule $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ achieves a uniform last-iterate rate with exponent $c$. In particular, it is $-\infty$ if there is no such $c$, and $+\infty$ if these exponents are unbounded above.
nodes.title: The gradient descent exponent

nodes.summary: The silver ratio is the real number $\rho = 1 + \sqrt{2}$.

nodes.summary: The silver exponent is $\log_2 \rho = \log \rho / \log 2$, where $\rho = 1 + \sqrt{2}$ is the silver ratio.

nodes.summary: The silver step schedule is the sequence $s_t = 1 + \rho^{\nu_2(t + 1) - 1}$ for $t \in \mathbb{N}$, where $\rho = 1 + \sqrt{2}$ is the silver ratio and $\nu_2(n)$ is the exponent of $2$ in the prime factorization of $n$.
nodes.title: Silver step schedule

nodes.summary: The step schedule with every step size equal to $1$ achieves a uniform last-iterate rate with exponent $1$.
nodes.title: Constant unit steps achieve exponent one

nodes.summary: The gradient descent exponent is at least $1$.

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a real Hilbert space, $f : E \to \mathbb{R}$ and $x_0 \in E$. If every step size is $0$, then for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$ the $k$-th gradient descent iterate of $f$ from $x_0$ equals $x_0$.
nodes.title: Gradient descent with zero step sizes stays put

Moreau decomposition

nodes.summary: Variational characterization of the projection onto a cone with complete carrier: `p` is the projection of `x` iff the residual pairs nonpositively with the cone and is orthogonal to `p`. The ambient space need not be complete.

Mountain pass theorem

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a real Banach space and $f : E \to \mathbb{R}$. A point $x \in E$ is a critical point of $f$ when the Fréchet derivative of $f$ at $x$ vanishes, $f'(x) = 0$. Here $f'(x)$ is taken to be $0$ when $f$ is not differentiable at $x$, so such points are critical as well.
nodes.title: Critical point

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a real Banach space. A function $f : E \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfies the Palais–Smale condition when every sequence $(u_k)$ in $E$ such that $(f(u_k))$ is bounded and the Fréchet derivatives $f'(u_k)$ tend to $0$ in operator norm has a subsequence converging in $E$. Here $f'(x)$ is taken to be $0$ at points where $f$ is not differentiable.
nodes.title: Palais–Smale condition

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a real Banach space, $f : E \to \mathbb{R}$, $a, b \in E$ and $\varepsilon, r \in \mathbb{R}$. The points $a$ and $b$ are separated by a mountain range of $f$ at height $\varepsilon$ and radius $r$ when $f(a) = 0$, $\varepsilon > 0$, $r > 0$, $f(y) \ge \varepsilon$ for every $y \in E$ with $\|y - a\| = r$, $\|b - a\| > r$ and $f(b) \le 0$.
nodes.title: Mountain range

nodes.title: Mountain pass level

nodes.title: Mountain pass theorem
Polar sets

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a real inner product space. The polar of a set $A \subseteq E$ is the set $A^\circ = \{y \in E : \langle x, y \rangle \le 1 \text{ for all } x \in A\}$. This uses the one-sided bound $\langle x, y \rangle \le 1$, not $|\langle x, y \rangle| \le 1$.
nodes.title: Polar of a set

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a real inner product space, $A \subseteq E$ and $y \in E$. Then $y$ lies in the polar $A^\circ$ of $A$ if and only if $\langle x, y \rangle \le 1$ for every $x \in A$.
nodes.title: Membership in the polar

nodes.summary: In a real inner product space $E$, the polar of the empty set is all of $E$, since the defining condition is vacuous.
nodes.title: Polar of the empty set

nodes.summary: In a real inner product space $E$, for every set $A \subseteq E$ the origin $0$ lies in the polar $A^\circ$ of $A$, since $\langle x, 0 \rangle = 0 \le 1$ for every $x \in A$.
nodes.title: The origin lies in every polar

nodes.summary: Let $A$ and $B$ be subsets of a real inner product space. If $A \subseteq B$, then the polar $B^\circ$ of $B$ is contained in the polar $A^\circ$ of $A$.
nodes.title: The polar reverses inclusion

nodes.summary: In a real inner product space $E$, the polar of the closed unit ball $\{x \in E : \|x\| \le 1\}$ is the closed unit ball itself.
nodes.title: The closed unit ball is self-polar

parts: The polar of the cube is the
reading_title.source: The polar of the cube is the $\ell^1$ unit ball

nodes.summary: For every $n$, the polar of the coordinate cube $[-1, 1]^n$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$, that is the set of all $y$ with $\langle x, y \rangle \le 1$ for every $x$ in the cube, is the closed $\ell^1$ unit ball $\{y \in \mathbb{R}^n : \sum_i |y_i| \le 1\}$.
nodes.title: The polar of the cube is the $\ell^1$ unit ball

nodes.summary: Let $E$ and $F$ be finite-dimensional real inner product spaces, let $f : E \to F$ be a linear map with adjoint $f^* : F \to E$, and let $K \subseteq E$. Writing $S^\circ$ for the polar of a set $S$, we have $(f(K))^\circ = (f^*)^{-1}(K^\circ)$, that is, $y \in F$ lies in the polar of $f(K)$ if and only if $f^*(y)$ lies in the polar of $K$.
nodes.title: Polar of a linear image

nodes.summary: On the whole space, a variational-inequality solution satisfies `A u = f`.
nodes.title: Variational inequality on the whole space reduces to an equation

nodes.summary: For a coercive bounded linear operator `A` on a real Hilbert space, a nonempty closed convex set `K`, and `f ∈ E`, there is exactly one `u ∈ K` with `⟪A u - f, v - u⟫_ℝ ≥ 0` for all `v ∈ K`.
nodes.title: Stampacchia's theorem, operator form

nodes.summary: For a coercive bounded bilinear form `B` on a real Hilbert space, a nonempty closed convex set `K`, and a continuous linear functional `φ`, there is exactly one `u ∈ K` with `B u (v - u) ≥ φ (v - u)` for all `v ∈ K`.
nodes.title: Stampacchia's theorem, bilinear-form form

nodes.summary: A coercive bounded linear operator on a real Hilbert space is surjective. This is the whole-space case of Stampacchia's theorem (compare Mathlib's Lax–Milgram theorem, which is the analogous statement for bilinear forms).
nodes.title: Coercive bounded operators on a real Hilbert space are surjective

nodes.summary: Fixed points of nonexpansive, Lipschitz and affine maps: the Browder–Göhde–Kirk theorem and Kirk's normal structure, Markov–Kakutani, Browder's demiclosedness principle, maps with contracting iterates.
nodes.title: Fixed-point theory

nodes.summary: Let $X$ be a nonempty complete metric space, let $f : X \to X$, and write $f^n$ for the $n$-th iterate of $f$. Let $(q_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of nonnegative real numbers with $q_n \to 0$ such that $d(f^n(x), f^n(y)) \le q_n \, d(x, y)$ for every $n \ge 1$ and all $x, y \in X$. Then $f$ has a fixed point: there is $x \in X$ with $f(x) = x$.
nodes.title: Fixed points of maps whose iterates have null Lipschitz constants

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a nonempty compact convex subset of a real normed space $E$, and let $(F_i)_{i \in I}$ be a family of continuous affine maps $E \to E$ such that each $F_i$ maps $K$ into $K$ and $F_i(F_j(x)) = F_j(F_i(x))$ for all $i, j \in I$ and all $x \in E$. Then there is $x \in K$ with $F_i(x) = x$ for every $i \in I$.
nodes.title: Markov–Kakutani fixed-point theorem
Browder's demiclosedness principle

nodes.summary: If `T` is nonexpansive, `u n ⇀ x` weakly, and `u n - T (u n) → 0`, then `T x = x`.
nodes.title: Browder's demiclosedness principle

nodes.summary: The fixed-point set of a nonexpansive map is weakly sequentially closed: if every `u n` is a fixed point of `T` and `u n ⇀ x` weakly, then `T x = x`.
nodes.title: Fixed points of a nonexpansive map are weakly sequentially closed
Browder–Göhde–Kirk fixed-point theorem

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a uniformly convex real Banach space and let $K \subseteq E$ be a nonempty, closed, bounded, convex set. If a map $f : E \to E$ sends $K$ into $K$ and is nonexpansive on $K$, that is, $\|f(x) - f(y)\| \le \|x - y\|$ for all $x, y \in K$, then $f$ has a fixed point in $K$: there is $y \in K$ with $f(y) = y$.
nodes.title: Browder–Göhde–Kirk fixed point theorem

nodes.summary: The diameter of a set $s$ in a real normed space is the supremum in $\mathbb{R}$ of the distances $\operatorname{dist}(x, y)$ over all $x, y \in s$; by the convention for real suprema it is $0$ when $s$ is empty or these distances are unbounded.
nodes.title: Diameter of a set

nodes.summary: The radius of a point $x$ in a set $s$ of a real normed space is the supremum in $\mathbb{R}$ of the distances $\operatorname{dist}(x, y)$ over all $y \in s$; by the convention for real suprema it is $0$ when $s$ is empty or these distances are unbounded.
nodes.title: Radius of a point in a set

nodes.summary: A point $x$ of a real normed space is diametral in a set $s$ if $x \in s$ and the radius of $x$ in $s$ equals the diameter of $s$.
nodes.title: Diametral point

nodes.summary: A set $K$ in a real normed space has normal structure if every convex subset $H \subseteq K$ with at least two points contains a point that is not diametral in $H$.
nodes.title: Normal structure

nodes.summary: A map $T : K \to K$ from a subset $K$ of a real normed space to itself is nonexpansive if $\|T(x) - T(y)\| \le \|x - y\|$ for all $x, y \in K$, that is, if $T$ is $1$-Lipschitz for the distance inherited from the space.
nodes.title: Nonexpansive self-map

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a reflexive real Banach space, meaning that the canonical embedding of $E$ into its double dual is surjective, and let $K \subseteq E$ be a nonempty, closed, bounded, convex set with normal structure. Then every nonexpansive self-map $T : K \to K$ has a fixed point.
nodes.title: Kirk's fixed-point theorem for sets with normal structure

nodes.summary: Approximation and interpolation of functions: Chebyshev equioscillation, best approximation, Lagrange interpolation, Bernstein polynomials and Voronovskaya, Korovkin, Müntz–Szász, Runge, Kolmogorov superposition, universal approximation.
nodes.title: Approximation theory

nodes.summary: Let $\Lambda : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be strictly increasing with $\Lambda(0) = 0$. The real linear span of the monomials $x \mapsto x^{\Lambda(n)}$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$, restricted to $[0, 1]$, is dense in $C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ with the uniform norm if and only if the series $\sum_{n \ge 0} 1/\Lambda(n+1)$ diverges, that is, the sequence $(1/\Lambda(n+1))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is not summable.
nodes.title: Müntz–Szász theorem for integer exponents

nodes.summary: Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ be compact, let $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ be open with $K \subseteq U$, and let $f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ be analytic at every point of $U$. Then for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there are complex polynomials $p$ and $q$ such that $q(z) \ne 0$ for every $z \in K$ and $|f(z) - p(z)/q(z)| < \varepsilon$ for every $z \in K$.
nodes.title: Runge's theorem

Then for every function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ that is continuous on $K$ and every…

Bernstein polynomials

nodes.summary: For `n ≠ 0`, `∑ k : Fin (n + 1), (x - k / n) * bernstein n k x = 0`: the binomial frequency `S / n` has mean `x`.

nodes.summary: Every point of a normed space has a nearest point in a finite-dimensional subspace (proximinality). No completeness hypothesis on the ambient space is needed: completeness enters only through the finite-dimensional subspace, whose closed balls are compact.
nodes.title: Existence of best approximations in finite-dimensional subspaces

nodes.summary: In a strictly convex real normed space, a convex set contains at most one point nearest to a given point: the midpoint of two distinct nearest points would be strictly closer, by `norm_midpoint_lt_iff`.

Chebyshev equioscillation theorem

nodes.summary: A polynomial `p` of degree at most `n` equioscillates against `f` on `[a, b]` with amplitude `E` and sign `σ = ±1` at the `n + 2` points `x 0 < ⋯ < x (n+1)`, if `f (x i) - p (x i) = σ * (-1) ^ i * E` for every `i ≤ n + 1`, and `|f y - p.eval y| ≤ E` for every `y ∈ [a, b]`.
nodes.title: Equioscillation of a polynomial approximation

nodes.summary: If `p` equioscillates against `f` on `[a, b]`, then `p` is the unique polynomial of degree at most `n` whose uniform error on `[a, b]` is at most `E`. In particular `p` is the unique best uniform approximation to `f` among polynomials of degree at most `n`.
nodes.title: Uniqueness of the equioscillating best approximation

nodes.summary: If `p` equioscillates against `f`, then no polynomial of degree at most `n` has uniform error strictly less than `E` on `[a, b]`: `p` is a best uniform approximation.
nodes.title: Chebyshev equioscillation theorem (sufficiency)

nodes.summary: If the error `f - p` of a polynomial `p` of degree at most `n` alternates with a one-sided lower bound `η` at `n + 2` strictly increasing points of `[a, b]`, `η ≤ σ * (-1) ^ i * (f (x i) - p (x i))`, then every polynomial of degree at most `n` has uniform error at least `η` on `[a, b]`.

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a real-linear operator on $C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ that is positive: $(L f)(x) \ge 0$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$ whenever $f(x) \ge 0$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$. If $g, h \in C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ satisfy $|g(y)| \le h(y)$ for all $y \in [0, 1]$, then $|(L g)(x)| \le (L h)(x)$ for every $x \in [0, 1]$.

nodes.summary: Let $f \in C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ have sup norm $\|f\|$, let $x \in [0, 1]$, and let $\delta > 0$, $\varepsilon \ge 0$ and $C \ge 0$ be real numbers with $2\|f\| \le C \delta^2$. If $|f(y) - f(x)| < \varepsilon$ for every $y \in [0, 1]$ with $|y - x| < \delta$, then $|f(y) - f(x)| \le \varepsilon + C (y - x)^2$ for every $y \in [0, 1]$.

Lagrange interpolation

nodes.summary: For real nodes $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$, an index $k < n$ and a real number $t$, the value at $t$ of the $k$-th Lagrange basis polynomial is $\ell_k(t) = \prod_{j \ne k} (x_k - x_j)^{-1} (t - x_j)$, the product running over the indices $j < n$ with $j \ne k$.
nodes.title: Evaluated Lagrange basis polynomial

nodes.summary: For real nodes $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ and a real number $t$, the Lebesgue function of the nodes at $t$ is $L_n(t) = \sum_{k < n} |\ell_k(t)|$, where $\ell_k$ is the $k$-th evaluated Lagrange basis polynomial for these nodes.
nodes.title: Lebesgue function

nodes.summary: For real nodes $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$, a function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and a real number $t$, the Lagrange interpolant of $f$ at $t$ is $\mathcal{L}^n f(t) = \sum_{k < n} f(x_k)\, \ell_k(t)$, where $\ell_k$ is the $k$-th evaluated Lagrange basis polynomial for these nodes.
nodes.title: Lagrange interpolant

nodes.summary: If the real nodes $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ are pairwise distinct, then $\ell_k(x_k) = 1$ for every $k < n$, where $\ell_k$ is the $k$-th evaluated Lagrange basis polynomial for these nodes.
nodes.title: Lagrange basis polynomials equal one at their own node

nodes.summary: For real nodes $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ and indices $k \ne j$ below $n$, the $k$-th evaluated Lagrange basis polynomial $\ell_k$ for these nodes satisfies $\ell_k(x_j) = 0$.
nodes.title: Lagrange basis polynomials vanish at the other nodes

nodes.summary: If the real nodes $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ are pairwise distinct, then for every function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and every $j < n$, the Lagrange interpolant of $f$ on these nodes satisfies $\mathcal{L}^n f(x_j) = f(x_j)$.
nodes.title: The Lagrange interpolant matches the function at the nodes

nodes.summary: If the real nodes $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ are pairwise distinct, then their Lebesgue function satisfies $L_n(x_j) = 1$ for every $j < n$.
nodes.title: The Lebesgue function equals one at the nodes
Uniform approximation by partial sums of one power series

nodes.title: The claim of Scottish Book Problem 159

nodes.title: Scottish Book Problem 159 has a negative answer

nodes.summary: Measure theory provides the language of size and integration underlying probability and modern analysis.
nodes.title: Measure Theory

nodes.summary: Hausdorff measures and dimension, dimension functions and codimension, fractal sets such as attractors of iterated function systems, and the measure and dimension of distance sets.
nodes.title: Geometric measure theory
Dimension functions for Hausdorff measures

nodes.summary: A Hausdorff dimension function (gauge) is a continuous, non-decreasing function $\psi : [0,\infty) \to [0,\infty)$ with $\psi(0) = 0$ and $\psi(r) > 0$ for every $r > 0$. In particular $\psi(r) \to 0$ as $r \to 0^+$.
nodes.title: Hausdorff dimension function

nodes.summary: Every Hausdorff dimension function $\psi : [0,\infty) \to [0,\infty)$ is continuous.
nodes.title: Continuity of a Hausdorff dimension function

nodes.summary: Every Hausdorff dimension function $\psi : [0,\infty) \to [0,\infty)$ is non-decreasing: if $r \le s$ then $\psi(r) \le \psi(s)$.
nodes.title: Monotonicity of a Hausdorff dimension function

nodes.summary: Every Hausdorff dimension function $\psi$ satisfies $\psi(0) = 0$.
nodes.title: A Hausdorff dimension function vanishes at zero

nodes.summary: If $\psi$ is a Hausdorff dimension function and $r > 0$ is a real number, then $\psi(r) > 0$.
nodes.title: A Hausdorff dimension function is positive at positive radii

nodes.summary: If $\psi$ is a Hausdorff dimension function and $r \ge 0$, then $\psi(r) = 0$ if and only if $r = 0$.
nodes.title: A Hausdorff dimension function vanishes only at zero

nodes.summary: Every Hausdorff dimension function $\psi$ satisfies $\psi(r) \to 0$ as $r \to 0^+$, that is, as $r$ tends to $0$ through positive values.
nodes.title: A Hausdorff dimension function tends to zero at zero
Falconer distance set problem

nodes.summary: For a set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, the distance set of $E$ is $\Delta(E) = \{\lvert x - y \rvert : x, y \in E\}$, the set of Euclidean distances between pairs of points of $E$.
nodes.title: Euclidean distance set

nodes.summary: An element $s \in [0, \infty]$ has the planar threshold property when every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with Hausdorff dimension $\dim_H E > s$ has a distance set $\{|x - y| : x, y \in E\}$ of positive one-dimensional Lebesgue measure.
nodes.title: Planar Falconer threshold property

nodes.summary: An extended nonnegative real $s$ is an admissible planar threshold when $0 \le s \le 2$ and $s$ has the planar threshold property: every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with Hausdorff dimension $\dim_H E > s$ has a distance set of positive one-dimensional Lebesgue measure.
nodes.title: Admissible planar threshold

nodes.summary: The planar distance threshold is the infimum, taken in $[0, \infty]$, of the admissible planar thresholds, that is, of all $s \in [0, 2]$ such that every compact subset $E$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ with Hausdorff dimension greater than $s$ has a distance set of positive Lebesgue measure.
nodes.title: Planar distance threshold

nodes.summary: For every set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, the distance set of $E$ is contained in $[0, \infty)$.
nodes.title: Distances are nonnegative

nodes.summary: For every $d$, the distance set of the empty subset of $\mathbb{R}^d$ is empty.
nodes.title: Distance set of the empty set

nodes.summary: For every point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the distance set of $\{x\}$ is $\{0\}$.
nodes.title: Distance set of a singleton

nodes.summary: If $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is compact, then the distance set of $E$ is a compact subset of $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.title: Distance sets of compact sets are compact

nodes.summary: If $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is compact, then the distance set of $E$ is a Borel measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.title: Distance sets of compact sets are Borel

nodes.summary: Let $s \le t$ be elements of $[0, \infty]$. If $s$ has the planar threshold property, that is, every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with Hausdorff dimension $\dim_H E > s$ has a distance set of positive one-dimensional Lebesgue measure, then $t$ has the planar threshold property.
nodes.title: The planar threshold property is upward closed

nodes.summary: Every subset $E$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ satisfies $\dim_H E \le 2$.
nodes.title: Subsets of the plane have Hausdorff dimension at most two

nodes.summary: The number $2$ is an admissible planar threshold: $2 \in [0, 2]$, and every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with Hausdorff dimension $\dim_H E > 2$ has a distance set of positive Lebesgue measure. This holds vacuously, since no subset of the plane has Hausdorff dimension greater than $2$.
nodes.title: Two is an admissible planar threshold

nodes.summary: There is an admissible planar threshold, that is, the set of admissible planar thresholds is nonempty.
nodes.title: Admissible planar thresholds exist

nodes.summary: For every $s \in [0, \infty]$ that is an admissible planar threshold, the planar distance threshold is at most $s$.
nodes.title: Admissible thresholds bound the planar distance threshold

nodes.summary: The planar distance threshold is at most $2$.
nodes.title: The planar distance threshold is at most two

nodes.summary: The planar distance threshold, an element of $[0, \infty]$, is not $\infty$.
nodes.title: The planar distance threshold is finite

nodes.summary: Let $\tau \in [0, \infty]$ be the planar distance threshold and let $\tau_{\mathbb{R}}$ be its value as a real number (with the convention that $\infty$ goes to $0$). Viewing $\tau_{\mathbb{R}}$ again as an element of $[0, \infty]$ gives back $\tau$.
nodes.title: Real round trip of the planar distance threshold

nodes.summary: The planar distance threshold is at least $0$.
nodes.title: Trivial lower bound for the planar distance threshold

nodes.summary: Thresholds up to two with the planar threshold property bound the planar distance threshold. For every $s \in [0, \infty]$ with $s \le 2$ that has the planar threshold property, the planar distance threshold is at most $s$.
nodes.title: Thresholds up to two with the planar threshold property bound the planar distance threshold

nodes.summary: Let $t \in [0, \infty]$. If $E$ is a compact subset of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose Hausdorff dimension $\dim_H E$ satisfies $t \le \dim_H E$ and whose distance set has Lebesgue measure zero, then $t$ is at most the planar distance threshold.
nodes.title: Zero-measure distance sets give lower bounds for the planar distance threshold

nodes.summary: For every real number $s \ge 0$, $s$ is an admissible planar threshold (as an element of $[0, \infty]$) if and only if $s \in [0, 2]$ and $s$ has the planar threshold property.
nodes.title: Real form of admissible planar thresholds

nodes.summary: Let $s_0 \in [0, \infty]$ be the planar distance threshold, the infimum of the admissible planar thresholds. Every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with Hausdorff dimension $\dim_H E > s_0$ has a distance set of positive one-dimensional Lebesgue measure.
nodes.title: The planar distance threshold is itself a threshold

nodes.summary: The planar distance threshold is an admissible planar threshold: it lies in $[0, 2]$ and has the planar threshold property.
nodes.title: The planar distance threshold is admissible

nodes.summary: The planar distance threshold is the least admissible planar threshold: it is itself an admissible planar threshold, and it is at most every admissible planar threshold.
nodes.title: The planar distance threshold is attained

nodes.summary: The set of real numbers $r \in [0, 2]$ such that $r$, viewed as an element of $[0, \infty]$, has the planar threshold property equals the image of the set of admissible planar thresholds under the map $[0, \infty] \to \mathbb{R}$ that is the identity on finite values and sends $\infty$ to $0$.
nodes.title: Real form of the admissible threshold family

nodes.summary: The value of the planar distance threshold as a real number (with the convention that $\infty$ goes to $0$) equals the infimum in $\mathbb{R}$ of the set of real numbers $r \in [0, 2]$ that, as elements of $[0, \infty]$, have the planar threshold property.
nodes.title: The planar distance threshold as a real infimum

nodes.summary: This is the proposition that for every integer $d \ge 2$ and every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ whose Hausdorff dimension is strictly greater than $(d+1)/2$, the distance set $\{\|x - y\| : x, y \in E\}$ has positive one-dimensional Lebesgue measure.
nodes.title: Statement of Falconer's distance set theorem

nodes.summary: The proposition that every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with Hausdorff dimension greater than $4/3$ has a distance set $\{|x - y| : x, y \in E\}$ of positive Lebesgue measure.
nodes.title: Wolff's planar distance set condition, as a proposition

nodes.summary: This is the proposition that $5/4$ has the planar threshold property: every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ whose Hausdorff dimension is strictly greater than $5/4$ has a distance set $\{\|x - y\| : x, y \in E\}$ of positive one-dimensional Lebesgue measure.
nodes.title: Statement of the Guth–Iosevich–Ou–Wang planar distance set theorem

nodes.summary: This is the proposition that for every integer $d \ge 2$ and every $s$ with $0 \le s \le d/2$, there is a compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ of Hausdorff dimension exactly $s$ whose distance set $\{\|x - y\| : x, y \in E\}$ has one-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero.
nodes.title: Statement of Falconer's measure-zero distance set examples

reading_title.source: Statement of the upper bound $3/2$ for the planar distance threshold

nodes.summary: This is the proposition that the planar distance threshold, the infimum of all $s \in [0, 2]$ such that every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ of Hausdorff dimension strictly greater than $s$ has a distance set $\{\|x - y\| : x, y \in E\}$ of positive one-dimensional Lebesgue measure, is at most $3/2$.
nodes.title: Statement of the upper bound $3/2$ for the planar distance threshold

nodes.summary: Every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with Hausdorff dimension greater than $4/3$ has a distance set $\{|x - y| : x, y \in E\}$ of positive Lebesgue measure.
nodes.title: Wolff's planar distance set theorem

nodes.summary: Every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ whose Hausdorff dimension is strictly greater than $5/4$ has a distance set $\{\|x - y\| : x, y \in E\}$ of positive one-dimensional Lebesgue measure.
nodes.title: Guth–Iosevich–Ou–Wang planar distance set theorem

nodes.summary: The planar distance threshold, the infimum of all $s \in [0, 2]$ such that every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ of Hausdorff dimension strictly greater than $s$ has a distance set $\{\|x - y\| : x, y \in E\}$ of positive one-dimensional Lebesgue measure, is at most $3/2$.
nodes.title: Falconer's upper bound for the planar distance threshold

nodes.summary: The planar Falconer distance threshold, the infimum of the $s \in [0, 2]$ such that every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with Hausdorff dimension greater than $s$ has a distance set $\{|x - y| : x, y \in E\}$ of positive Lebesgue measure, is at most $4/3$.
nodes.title: Wolff's upper bound for the planar Falconer threshold

nodes.summary: The planar Falconer distance threshold, the infimum of the $s \in [0, 2]$ such that every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with Hausdorff dimension greater than $s$ has a distance set $\{|x - y| : x, y \in E\}$ of positive Lebesgue measure, is at most $5/4$.
nodes.title: Guth–Iosevich–Ou–Wang upper bound for the planar Falconer threshold

nodes.summary: The planar distance threshold, the infimum of all $s \in [0, 2]$ such that every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ of Hausdorff dimension strictly greater than $s$ has a distance set $\{\|x - y\| : x, y \in E\}$ of positive one-dimensional Lebesgue measure, is at least $1$.

Hausdorff codimension

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a subset of an extended metric space and let $n, c$ be natural numbers. The set $S$ has Hausdorff codimension at least $c$ in dimension $n$ if $S$ is empty or its Hausdorff dimension satisfies $\dim_H S + c \le n$, the inequality being taken in $[0, \infty]$.
nodes.title: Lower bound on Hausdorff codimension

nodes.summary: In an extended metric space, the empty set has Hausdorff codimension at least $c$ in dimension $n$ for all natural numbers $n$ and $c$.
nodes.title: The empty set has every codimension

nodes.summary: Let $T \subseteq S$ be subsets of an extended metric space and let $n, c$ be natural numbers. If $S$ has Hausdorff codimension at least $c$ in dimension $n$, then so does $T$.
nodes.title: Subsets inherit a codimension bound

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a subset of an extended metric space and let $n < c$ be natural numbers. If $S$ has Hausdorff codimension at least $c$ in dimension $n$, then $S$ is empty.
nodes.title: Sets of codimension larger than the dimension are empty

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a subset of an extended metric space and let $c \le n$ be natural numbers. If the Hausdorff dimension of $S$ satisfies $\dim_H S \le n - c$, then $S$ has Hausdorff codimension at least $c$ in dimension $n$.
nodes.title: A dimension bound gives a codimension bound

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a subset of an extended metric space and let $n, c$ be natural numbers. Then $S$ has Hausdorff codimension at least $c$ in dimension $n$ if and only if either $S$ is empty, or both $c \le n$ and the Hausdorff dimension of $S$ satisfies $\dim_H S \le n - c$.
nodes.title: Characterization of Hausdorff codimension
Hausdorff dimension of self-similar sets

nodes.summary: Let $X$ be a topological space and let $(f_i)_{i < n}$ be a finite family of maps $X \to X$. A set $S \subseteq X$ is an attractor of the family if it is nonempty and compact and is fixed by the Hutchinson operator, that is, $S = \bigcup_{i < n} f_i(S)$.
nodes.title: Attractor of an iterated function system

nodes.summary: Let $(f_i)_{i < n}$ be a finite family of maps $f_i \colon \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d$ on Euclidean space. nodes.summary: A finite family of maps $f_i \colon \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d$, $i < n$, satisfies the open set condition if there is a nonempty open set $G \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ such that $f_i(G) \subseteq G$ for every $i < n$ and the images $f_i(G)$ and $f_j(G)$ are disjoint whenever $i \neq j$.
nodes.title: Open set condition

nodes.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $(f_i)_{i < n}$ be an affine-symmetric iterated function system on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with common contraction factor $\lambda \in (0,1)$ that satisfies the open set condition. Then every attractor $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ of the system has Hausdorff dimension

nodes.title: Measures and measurable sets

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a subset of the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that every subset $T$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ homeomorphic to $S$ (as a subspace) is Lebesgue measurable, that is, Carathéodory measurable with respect to Lebesgue outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^2$. Then $S$ is absolutely measurable: for every measure $\mu$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb{R}^2$, the set $S$ is Carathéodory measurable with respect to the outer…

nodes.title: Vitali's theorem
Atomless measures

nodes.summary: A measure $\mu$ on a measurable space is atomless when every measurable set $s$ with $\mu(s) > 0$ contains a measurable subset $t \subseteq s$ with $0 < \mu(t) < \mu(s)$.
nodes.title: Atomless measure

nodes.summary: The restriction of an atomless measure to a measurable set is atomless.
nodes.title: Restriction of an atomless measure

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a finite atomless measure. For every measurable set $s$ and every $t \in [0, \infty]$ with $t \le \mu(s)$, there is a measurable set $u \subseteq s$ with $\mu(u) = t$.
nodes.title: Sierpiński's theorem on atomless measures
Banach–Tarski paradox

nodes.summary: Let $X$ be a metric space. Subsets $A$ and $B$ of $X$ are finitely equidecomposable by isometries if there are a natural number $n$, sets $A_1, \dots, A_n$ and $B_1, \dots, B_n$ in $X$, and isometric bijections $g_1, \dots, g_n$ of $X$ onto itself such that the sets $A_i$ are pairwise disjoint, the sets $B_i$ are pairwise disjoint, $A = A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_n$, $B = B_1 \cup \dots \cup B_n$, and $g_i(A_i) = B_i$…
nodes.title: Finite equidecomposability by isometries

nodes.summary: Let $A$ and $B$ be subsets of a metric space $X$. Then $A$ is finitely equidecomposable by isometries with $B$ if and only if there are a map $f : X \to X$ and a finite set $S$ of isometric bijections of $X$ onto itself such that $f$ restricts to a bijection from $A$ onto $B$ and for every $x \in A$ there is $g \in S$ with $f(x) = g(x)$.
nodes.title: Equidecomposability via piecewise-isometric bijections

nodes.summary: Every subset $A$ of a metric space $X$ is finitely equidecomposable by isometries with itself.
nodes.title: Finite equidecomposability by isometries is reflexive

nodes.summary: Let $A$ and $B$ be subsets of a metric space $X$. If $A$ is finitely equidecomposable by isometries with $B$, then $B$ is finitely equidecomposable by isometries with $A$.
nodes.title: Finite equidecomposability by isometries is symmetric

nodes.summary: Let $A$, $B$ and $C$ be subsets of a metric space $X$. If $A$ is finitely equidecomposable by isometries with $B$ and $B$ is finitely equidecomposable by isometries with $C$, then $A$ is finitely equidecomposable by isometries with $C$.
nodes.title: Finite equidecomposability by isometries is transitive

nodes.summary: Let $A_1$, $A_2$, $B_1$ and $B_2$ be subsets of a metric space $X$ with $A_1 \cap A_2 = \emptyset$ and $B_1 \cap B_2 = \emptyset$. If $A_1$ is finitely equidecomposable by isometries with $B_1$ and $A_2$ is finitely equidecomposable by isometries with $B_2$, then $A_1 \cup A_2$ is finitely equidecomposable by isometries with $B_1 \cup B_2$.
nodes.title: Finite equidecomposability by isometries respects disjoint unions

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be an isometric bijection of a metric space $X$ onto itself. Then every subset $A$ of $X$ is finitely equidecomposable by isometries with its image $g(A)$.
nodes.title: Equidecomposability of a set with its isometric image

nodes.summary: In three-dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^3$, write $\bar B(c, r)$ for the closed ball of radius $r$ about $c$. There are points $c_1, c_2 \in \mathbb{R}^3$ such that $\bar B(c_1, 1)$ and $\bar B(c_2, 1)$ are disjoint and the closed unit ball $\bar B(0, 1)$ is finitely equidecomposable by isometries with $\bar B(c_1, 1) \cup \bar B(c_2, 1)$.
nodes.title: Banach–Tarski paradox for the closed unit ball

nodes.summary: If $\mathcal{A}$ is an algebra of sets on $\alpha$, then $\mathcal{A}$ is a semiring of sets: $\emptyset \in \mathcal{A}$, $s \cap t \in \mathcal{A}$ for all $s, t \in \mathcal{A}$, and for all $s, t \in \mathcal{A}$ the difference $s \setminus t$ is the union of finitely many pairwise disjoint members of $\mathcal{A}$.

nodes.summary: If $\mathcal{A}$ is an algebra of sets on $\alpha$, then $\mathcal{A}$ is a $\pi$-system: for all $s, t \in \mathcal{A}$ with $s \cap t$ nonempty, we have $s \cap t \in \mathcal{A}$.

Congruence-invariant extensions of Lebesgue measure

nodes.summary: Two sets $E$ and $F$ in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ are congruent when some isometry of the plane onto itself maps $E$ onto $F$.
nodes.title: Congruent plane sets

nodes.summary: A function $\mu$ that assigns to every subset of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ a value in $[0, \infty]$ is congruence invariant when $\mu(E) = \mu(F)$ for all congruent plane sets $E$ and $F$.
nodes.title: Congruence-invariant set functions on the plane

nodes.summary: `μ` is countably additive on pairwise-disjoint families. This is the countably-additive reading of "additive" in Problem 169; the typescript does not say whether finite or countable additivity is meant.
nodes.title: Countably additive set function

Independent bases of atomless measures

nodes.summary: A measure $\mu$ on a measurable space $X$ is convex (in Fréchet's sense, "sans singularités") if $\mu(X) = 1$ and every measurable set $A$ with $\mu(A) > 0$ contains a measurable subset $B$ with $0 < \mu(B) < \mu(A)$.
nodes.title: Convex measure

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $X$. A class $B$ of subsets of $X$ is stochastically independent with respect to $\mu$ if for every finite collection of distinct sets $A_1, \dots, A_n$ in $B$, including the empty one, $\mu(A_1 \cap \dots \cap A_n) = \mu(A_1) \cdots \mu(A_n)$. The empty intersection is $X$ and the empty product is $1$, so this forces $\mu(X) = 1$. The sets in $B$ need not be measurable;…
nodes.title: Stochastically independent class of sets

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $X$. A class $B$ of subsets of $X$ is a base of $\mu$ if every set in $B$ is measurable, $B$ is stochastically independent with respect to $\mu$, and every measurable set $A \subseteq X$ agrees up to a null set with a set $C$ in the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $B$, that is, $\mu(A \triangle C) = 0$.
nodes.title: Base of a measure

nodes.summary: The proposition, Szpilrajn's Problem 191 from the Scottish Book in its original form, that for every measurable space $X$, every convex measure $\mu$ on $X$ has a base, that is, some class $B$ of subsets of $X$ is a base of $\mu$.
nodes.title: The claim of Szpilrajn's Problem 191

nodes.summary: The claim of Szpilrajn's Problem 191 is false: not every convex measure possesses a base. That is, there are a measurable space $X$ and a convex measure $\mu$ on $X$ such that no class of subsets of $X$ is a base of $\mu$.
nodes.title: Szpilrajn's Problem 191 has a negative answer
Lyapunov convexity theorem

nodes.summary: For a measure $\mu$ on a measurable space $\alpha$ and a function $f : \alpha \to E$ into a real normed space $E$, the Lyapunov range of $f$ with respect to $\mu$ is the set $\lbrace \int_s f \, d\mu : s \subseteq \alpha \text{ measurable} \rbrace$ of integrals of $f$ over measurable subsets of $\alpha$.
nodes.title: Lyapunov range

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a finite atomless measure on a measurable space $\alpha$, let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, and let $f : \alpha \to E$ be Bochner integrable with respect to $\mu$. Then the Lyapunov range of $f$ with respect to $\mu$, the set of integrals $\int_s f \, d\mu$ over measurable sets $s \subseteq \alpha$, is compact and convex.
nodes.title: Lyapunov convexity theorem
Measures on complete Boolean algebras

nodes.summary: A real-valued function $\mu$ on a complete Boolean algebra $B$ is a measure in von Neumann's sense when $\mu(\bot) = 0$, $\mu(a) > 0$ for every $a \ne \bot$, and $\mu$ is countably additive: for every sequence $(a_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ of pairwise disjoint elements of $B$ (that is, $a_i \wedge a_j = \bot$ whenever $i \ne j$), the series $\sum_i \mu(a_i)$ converges and $\mu(\bigvee_i a_i) = \sum_i \mu(a_i)$.
nodes.title: Von Neumann measures on a complete Boolean algebra

nodes.summary: A complete Boolean algebra $B$ satisfies the countable chain condition (von Neumann's condition (5)) when every subset $S \subseteq B$ whose distinct elements are pairwise disjoint (that is, $a \wedge b = \bot$ for all distinct $a, b \in S$) is at most countable.
nodes.title: The countable chain condition for complete Boolean algebras

nodes.summary: A complete Boolean algebra $B$ satisfies the generalized distributivity law (von Neumann's condition (6)) when, for every double sequence $(a_{i,j})_{i, j \in \mathbb{N}}$ of elements of $B$ that is increasing in $j$ for each fixed $i$ (that is, $a_{i,0} \le a_{i,1} \le \cdots$ for every $i$),
nodes.title: Von Neumann's generalized distributivity law

nodes.summary: The statement that every complete Boolean algebra satisfying the countable chain condition and the generalized distributivity law carries a measure in von Neumann's sense.
nodes.title: Von Neumann's sufficiency claim

nodes.summary: There is a complete Boolean algebra that satisfies the countable chain condition and the generalized distributivity law but carries no measure in von Neumann's sense; that is, von Neumann's sufficiency claim is false. This answers Problem 163 of the Scottish Book in the negative, in its stated form.
nodes.title: Von Neumann's conditions do not guarantee a measure

nodes.summary: The transition function of a rate matrix is row-stochastic for `t ≥ 0` (Norris 1997, Theorem 2.1.2).
nodes.title: Transition function of a rate matrix is row-stochastic
Finite continuous-time Markov chains as path processes

nodes.summary: The jump matrix `Π` of a matrix `Q` (Norris 1997, §2.6): for a state with exit rate `q i = -Q i i ≠ 0`, `Π i j = Q i j / q i` for `j ≠ i` and `Π i i = 0`; a state with `q i = 0` is absorbing, `Π i j = δ i j`.
nodes.title: Jump matrix of a rate matrix

nodes.summary: The entries of the jump matrix of a rate matrix are nonnegative.
nodes.title: Nonnegativity of the jump matrix

nodes.summary: The rows of the jump matrix of a rate matrix sum to `1`.
nodes.title: Rows of the jump matrix sum to one

nodes.summary: The jump matrix of a rate matrix is row-stochastic.
nodes.title: Jump matrix is row-stochastic

nodes.summary: Row `i` of the jump matrix of a rate matrix, as a probability mass function on `ι`.
nodes.title: Row of the jump matrix as a probability mass function

nodes.summary: The law of one step `(ξ, E)` of the construction: `ξ : ι → ι` has independent coordinates with `ξ i ∼ Π i`, and `E` is an independent exponential clock of rate `1`.
nodes.title: Law of one step of the chain construction

nodes.summary: The law of the i.i.d. step sequence `ω : ℕ → (ι → ι) × ℝ` driving the chain.
nodes.title: Law of the driving step sequence of a Markov chain

nodes.summary: The jump chain started at `i`: `Y 0 = i` and `Y (n + 1) = ξ n (Y n)`.
nodes.title: Jump chain of a continuous-time Markov chain

nodes.summary: The `n`-th holding time `S n = E n / q (Y n)`, where `q k = -Q k k`; it is `∞` when `Y n` is absorbing (`q (Y n) = 0`). Negative clock values, a null event, give `S n = 0`.
nodes.title: Holding times of a continuous-time Markov chain

nodes.summary: The `n`-th jump time `T n = S 0 + ⋯ + S (n - 1)`, with `T 0 = 0`.
nodes.title: Jump times of a continuous-time Markov chain

nodes.summary: The path of the chain started at `i`: `X t = Y n` for the `n` with `T n ≤ t < T (n + 1)`. If `t` is at or after the explosion time `sup T n` (a null event, by `IsRateMatrix.ae_tendsto_ctmcJumpTime`), the value is an arbitrary state that does not depend on `i`, `Q` or `ω`.
nodes.title: Path of a continuous-time Markov chain

nodes.summary: The shift of the step sequence by `n`: `(shift n ω) m = ω (n + m)`.
nodes.title: Shift of the step sequence of a Markov chain

nodes.summary: The jump times are nondecreasing.
nodes.title: Jump times are nondecreasing

nodes.summary: If `T n ≤ t < T (n + 1)`, then `X t = Y n`.
nodes.title: Path value between consecutive jump times

nodes.summary: The jump chain of the shifted steps started at `Y n` is the jump chain after `n`.
nodes.title: Jump chain of the shifted steps

nodes.summary: The holding times of the shifted steps started at `Y n` are the holding times after `n`.
nodes.title: Holding times of the shifted steps

nodes.summary: `T (n + m) = T n + T' m`, where `T'` are the jump times of the shifted steps started at `Y n`.
nodes.title: Additivity of jump times under shifting

nodes.summary: After a finite jump time `T n`, the path is the path started at `Y n` driven by the shifted steps: `X (T n + s) = X' s` with `X'` built from `shift n ω` started at `Y n`.
nodes.title: Path restarts at a jump time

nodes.summary: First-jump decomposition of the path: before the first holding time the chain is at `i`; afterwards it is the chain started at `ξ 0 i` driven by the shifted steps.

nodes.summary: The jump chain `Y n` is a measurable function of the steps.

nodes.summary: The path `(t, ω) ↦ X t` is jointly measurable in the time and the steps.

nodes.summary: The state `X t` is a measurable function of the steps.
nodes.title: Measurability of the chain state at a fixed time

nodes.summary: Non-explosion (Norris 1997, §2.7, for a finite state space): almost surely the jump times of the chain started at `i` tend to `∞`, so `X t` is a genuine state of the jump chain for every `t ≥ 0`.
nodes.title: Non-explosion

nodes.summary: Strong Markov property at jump times (Norris 1997, §2.6–2.7): let `A` be a measurable set of histories of the first `n` steps such that `T n < ∞` whenever the history lies in `A`; these histories determine `Y 0, …, Y n` and `S 0, …, S (n - 1)`. Then for every state `k` and every measurable set `B` of paths, the path after `T n` is independent of the event `{history ∈ A, Y n = k}` and distributed as the chain…
nodes.title: Strong Markov property at jump times

nodes.summary: Kolmogorov (Norris 1997, §2.8, Theorem 2.8.2 for a finite state space): the chain built from the jump chain and the holding times has transition function `exp (t • Q)`: `P_i(X t = j) = exp (t Q) i j` for every `t ≥ 0`.
nodes.title: Kolmogorov

nodes.summary: Restart law at a fixed time (cf. the Markov property, Norris 1997, §2.8), for events of `X s` and of the path after `s` only: for the chain started at `i`, the probability that `X s = k` and that the path after `s` lies in a measurable set `B` is `exp (s Q) i k` times the probability that the chain started at `k` lies in `B`. This is weaker than the Markov property with respect to the natural filtration: arbitrary…
nodes.title: Restart law at a fixed time

nodes.summary: Finite-dimensional distributions (Norris 1997, §2.8, Theorem 2.8.2 (c)): with increments `s 0, …, s (n - 1) ≥ 0`, times `t k = s 0 + ⋯ + s k`, and states `j 0, …, j (n - 1)`, `P_i(X (t k) = j k for all k) = ∏ₖ exp (s k Q) (j (k - 1)) (j k)`, where `j (-1) = i`.
nodes.title: Finite-dimensional distributions
Hitting times of finite continuous-time Markov chains

nodes.summary: The hitting time `inf {t ≥ 0 | X t ∈ A}` of a set of states `A` by the chain `X = ctmcPath Q i ω` started at `i`, valued in `ℝ≥0∞` (it is `∞` if `A` is never visited).
nodes.title: Hitting time of a continuous-time Markov chain

nodes.summary: From a state `i ∉ A`, the hitting time of `A` is the first holding time plus the hitting time of the chain restarted after the first jump.
nodes.title: First-jump decomposition of a hitting time

nodes.summary: From a state `i ∈ A`, the hitting time of `A` is `0` as soon as the first holding time is positive (which fails only on a null event, see `ctmcHoldingTime`).
nodes.title: Hitting time from inside the target set is zero

nodes.summary: Mean hitting time, first-step equation (compare Norris 1997, §3.3): from `i ∉ A` with `q i = -Q i i ≠ 0`, `E_i H_A = 1 / q i + ∑ⱼ Π i j E_j H_A` in `ℝ≥0∞`.
nodes.title: Mean hitting time, first-step equation

nodes.summary: From a state of `A`, the mean hitting time of `A` is `0`.
nodes.title: Mean hitting time from inside the target set is zero

nodes.summary: Minimality of the mean hitting time (compare Norris 1997, §3.3): if every state off `A` has a positive exit rate, every `m : ι → ℝ≥0∞` with `1 / q i + ∑ⱼ Π i j m j ≤ m i` off `A` dominates `E_i H_A`.
nodes.title: Minimality of the mean hitting time

nodes.summary: From `i ∉ A ∪ B` with `q i ≠ 0`, `E_i (H_A H_B) = (E_i H_A + E_i H_B) / q i + ∑ⱼ Π i j E_j (H_A H_B)` in `ℝ≥0∞`.
nodes.title: Product moment of two hitting times, first-step equation

nodes.summary: From a state of `A ∪ B`, the product moment of the hitting times of `A` and `B` is `0`.
nodes.title: Product moment of hitting times from inside their union is zero

nodes.summary: If `mA`, `mB` are supersolutions of the mean equations of `A` and `B` (as in `lintegral_ctmcHittingTime_le`) and `F` satisfies `(mA i + mB i) / q i + ∑ⱼ Π i j F j ≤ F i` off `A ∪ B`, then `F` dominates `E_i (H_A H_B)`.
nodes.title: Minimality of the product moment

nodes.summary: Backward equations for the mean hitting time (compare Norris 1997, §3.3): if `m : ι → ℝ` is nonnegative and `(Q m) i = -1` for `i ∉ A`, then `E_i H_A ≤ m i` (so it is finite), `E_i H_A = 0` on `A`, and the real vector `E_i H_A` solves the same backward equations. With uniqueness of the solution, this identifies `E_i H_A`.
nodes.title: Backward equations for the mean hitting time

nodes.summary: Let `mA`, `mB`, `f` be nonnegative with `(Q mA) i = -1` off `A`, `(Q mB) i = -1` off `B` and `(Q f) i = -(mA i + mB i)` off `A ∪ B`. Then `E_i (H_A H_B) ≤ f i` (so it is finite), it is `0` on `A ∪ B`, and its real part `p` solves `(Q p) i = -(E_i H_A + E_i H_B)` off `A ∪ B`.
nodes.title: Backward equations for the product moment of two hitting times
Stationarity and detailed balance for finite continuous-time Markov chains

nodes.summary: The row vector `π` is in detailed balance with the matrix `Q`: `π i * Q i j = π j * Q j i` for all `i j` (Norris 1997, §3.7). This is only the algebraic equation: it holds for `π = 0` and every `Q`. For a probability vector `π` and a stochastic matrix it is the reversibility of the chain started from `π`.
nodes.title: Detailed balance

nodes.summary: `π Q = 0` if and only if `π P t = π` for every real `t` (Norris 1997, §3.5, finite state space).
nodes.title: Invariance under the semigroup

nodes.summary: Detailed balance with a matrix whose rows sum to `0` implies invariance `π Q = 0` (Norris 1997, §3.7).
nodes.title: Detailed balance implies invariance for the generator

nodes.summary: Detailed balance for `Q` implies `π i P t i j = π j P t j i` for every `t` (Norris 1997, §3.7). For a probability vector `π` and a rate matrix `Q` this is the reversibility of the chain started from `π`.
nodes.title: Detailed balance propagates to the transition function

nodes.summary: Detailed balance with a matrix whose rows sum to `0` (for instance a rate matrix) makes `π` invariant for every `P t`.
nodes.title: Detailed balance implies invariance for the transition semigroup
The sticky (equal-input) kernel on a finite state space

nodes.summary: The equal-input matrix `𝟙 πᵀ`: every row equals `π`.
nodes.title: Equal-input matrix

nodes.summary: The sticky kernel with persistence `c`: `c • 1 + (1 - c) • 𝟙 πᵀ`. Started from `i`, it stays at `i` with probability `c` and otherwise redraws the state from `π`.
nodes.title: Sticky kernel

nodes.summary: The equal-input generator `κ • (𝟙 πᵀ - 1)` with rate `κ` (Felsenstein's F81 model on an arbitrary finite state space): jumps at rate `κ` to a state drawn from `π`.
nodes.title: Equal-input generator (F81 model)

nodes.summary: Entrywise form of the equal-input matrix.
nodes.title: Entries of the equal-input matrix

nodes.title: Equal-input matrix is idempotent

nodes.summary: Entrywise form of the sticky kernel.
nodes.title: Entries of the sticky kernel

nodes.summary: The sticky kernel at persistence `1` is the identity.
nodes.title: Sticky kernel at persistence one is the identity

nodes.summary: The sticky kernel at persistence `0` is `𝟙 πᵀ`.
nodes.title: Sticky kernel at persistence zero is the equal-input matrix

nodes.summary: For `0 ≤ c ≤ 1` and `π ≥ 0` the entries of the sticky kernel are nonnegative.

Long-distance limit

nodes.title: Rows of the sticky kernel sum to one

nodes.title: Sticky kernel is row-stochastic

nodes.title: Stationary vector of the sticky kernel

nodes.summary: With `∑ π = 1`, `K c * K c' = K (c c')` for all real `c`, `c'`.
nodes.title: Composition

nodes.summary: With `∑ π = 1`, `K c ^ n = K (c ^ n)`: `n` steps of the sticky kernel are one step with persistence `c ^ n`.

nodes.title: Equal-input generator is a rate matrix

nodes.summary: With `∑ π = 1`, `exp (t • κ (𝟙 πᵀ - 1)) = K (e^{-κ t})` for all real `κ` and `t`.
nodes.title: The sticky kernel is the equal-input transition function

nodes.summary: Semigroup law of the sticky kernel in time: `K (e^{-κ s}) * K (e^{-κ t}) = K (e^{-κ (s + t)})` (with `∑ π = 1`).
nodes.title: Semigroup law

nodes.summary: If `(X, Y)` has joint law `P(X = i, Y = j) = π i K i j` (stationary start, one step of the kernel), then `Cov(f X, g Y) = c Cov_π(f, g)`. The algebraic identity holds for all real `π`, `f`, `g`, `c`; it is a covariance of a probability law when `π` is a probability vector and `0 ≤ c ≤ 1`.

Then $\sigma(X_0, \dots, X_k) \subseteq \sigma(X_0, \dots, X_{k+1})$ for every $k$.

nodes.summary: Let $X_0, X_1, \dots$ be maps from a measurable space $\Omega$ to a measurable space $S$, and write $\sigma(X_0, \dots, X_k)$ for the σ-algebra on $\Omega$ generated by $\omega \mapsto (X_0(\omega), \dots, X_k(\omega))$, with the product σ-algebra on $S^{k+1}$. If $C$ is measurable with respect to $\sigma(X_0, \dots, X_k)$ and $B \subseteq S$ is measurable, then $C \cap X_{k+1}^{-1}(B)$ is measurable with respect…

Write $\sigma(X_0, \dots, X_k)$ for the σ-algebra on $\Omega$ generated by $\omega \mapsto (X_0(\omega), \dots, X_k(\omega))$, with the product σ-algebra on $S^{k+1}$. Suppose that for every $k$, every measurable…
nodes.title: The Markov property for measurable functions

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a measure on a measurable space $\Omega$, let $X : \Omega \to S$ be a measurable map to a measurable space $S$, let $A \subseteq S$ be measurable, let $C \subseteq \Omega$ be any set and let $f : S \to [0, \infty]$ be any function. Then $\int_{C \cap X^{-1}(A)} f(X(\omega)) \, dP(\omega) = \int_C \mathbf{1}_A(X(\omega)) \, f(X(\omega)) \, dP(\omega)$.

Write $\sigma(X_0, \dots, X_k)$ for the σ-algebra on $\Omega$ generated by $\omega \mapsto (X_0(\omega), \dots, X_k(\omega))$, with the product σ-algebra on $S^{k+1}$, and $\mathrm{FDD}_n(\mu, \kappa; A_0, \dots, A_n)$ for the…
nodes.title: Finite-dimensional distributions given the past

Write $\sigma(X_0, \dots, X_k)$ for the σ-algebra on $\Omega$ generated by $\omega \mapsto (X_0(\omega), \dots, X_k(\omega))$, with the product σ-algebra on $S^{k+1}$. Kolmogorov's criterion for reversibility

nodes.summary: For a natural number $M$, a stochastic matrix of size $M + 1$ is a square matrix $P = (P_{ij})$ indexed by the states $\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$, with real entries $P_{ij} \ge 0$ for all states $i, j$, whose rows sum to $1$: $\sum_j P_{ij} = 1$ for every $i$. It is the transition matrix of a Markov chain on these $M + 1$ states.
nodes.title: Stochastic matrix

nodes.summary: For a stochastic matrix $P$ on the finite state space $\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the $n$-th matrix power $P^n$ is defined by $P^0 = I$, the identity matrix, and $(P^{n+1})_{ij} = \sum_k P(i, k) (P^n)_{kj}$. The entry $(P^n)_{ij}$ is the probability of moving from state $i$ to state $j$ in exactly $n$ steps.
nodes.title: Matrix powers of a stochastic matrix

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a stochastic matrix on the finite state space $\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$ and write $P^n$ for its $n$-th matrix power. Then $P$ is irreducible if for all states $i$ and $j$ there is an $n \ge 1$ with $(P^n)_{ij} > 0$; that is, every state can be reached from every state, itself included, in a positive number of steps.
nodes.title: Irreducible stochastic matrix

nodes.summary: A probability distribution on the finite state space $\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$ is a function $\pi$ from the states to $\mathbb{R}$ with $\pi(i) \ge 0$ for every state $i$ and $\sum_i \pi(i) = 1$.
nodes.title: Probability distribution on a finite state space

nodes.summary: A probability distribution $\pi$ on the finite state space $\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$ is stationary for a stochastic matrix $P$ on the same states if $\pi P = \pi$, that is, $\sum_i \pi(i) P(i, j) = \pi(j)$ for every state $j$.
nodes.title: Stationary distribution

nodes.summary: A probability distribution $\pi$ and a stochastic matrix $P$ on the finite state space $\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$ satisfy the detailed balance (reversibility) equations when $\pi(i) P(i, j) = \pi(j) P(j, i)$ for all states $i$ and $j$.
nodes.title: Detailed balance

nodes.summary: A stochastic matrix $P$ on the finite state space $\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$ is reversible if there is a probability distribution $\pi$ on the states that is stationary for $P$ and satisfies the detailed balance equations $\pi(i) P(i, j) = \pi(j) P(j, i)$ for all states $i, j$.
nodes.title: Reversible stochastic matrix

nodes.summary: A stochastic matrix $P$ on the finite state space $\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$ satisfies Kolmogorov's cycle condition when (1) for all states $x, y$, $P(x, y) > 0$ implies $P(y, x) > 0$; and (2) for every $n \ge 0$ and every loop of states $x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n$ with $x_n = x_0$ and $\prod_{i=0}^{n-1} P(x_{i+1}, x_i) > 0$, we have $\prod_{i=0}^{n-1} P(x_i, x_{i+1}) = \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} P(x_{i+1}, x_i)$.
nodes.title: Kolmogorov's cycle condition

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a stochastic matrix on the finite state space $\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$ and let $\pi$ be a probability distribution on the same states. If $\pi$ and $P$ satisfy the detailed balance equations $\pi(i) P(i, j) = \pi(j) P(j, i)$ for all states $i, j$, then $\pi$ is stationary for $P$: $\sum_i \pi(i) P(i, j) = \pi(j)$ for every state $j$.
nodes.title: Detailed balance implies stationarity

nodes.summary: Every entry of every power of a stochastic matrix is nonnegative.
nodes.title: Powers of a stochastic matrix are nonnegative

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be an irreducible stochastic matrix on the finite state space $\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$. If a probability distribution $\pi$ satisfies the detailed balance equations $\pi(i) P(i, j) = \pi(j) P(j, i)$ for all states $i, j$, then $\pi(i) > 0$ for every state $i$.
nodes.title: Detailed balance distributions of irreducible chains are positive

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be an irreducible stochastic matrix on the finite state space $\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$. If $P$ is reversible, that is, some probability distribution $\pi$ is stationary for $P$ and satisfies the detailed balance equations $\pi(i) P(i, j) = \pi(j) P(j, i)$ for all states $i, j$, then $P$ satisfies Kolmogorov's cycle condition: (1) for all states $x, y$, $P(x, y) > 0$ implies $P(y, x) > 0$; and (2) for every…
nodes.title: Kolmogorov's cycle theorem, necessity half

nodes.summary: For a stochastic matrix $P$ and a path of states $x_0, x_1, \dots, x_k$, the path product is the real number $\prod_{i=0}^{k-1} P(x_i, x_{i+1})$, the product of the forward transition probabilities along the path. For the empty path and for a path consisting of a single state it is $1$.
nodes.title: Forward path product

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a stochastic matrix on the states $\{0, \dots, M\}$. For every path (finite list of states), the product of the forward transition probabilities $P(x, y)$ over consecutive states $x, y$ along the path is nonnegative.
nodes.title: Path products are nonnegative

nodes.summary: For a stochastic matrix $P$ and a path of states $x_0, x_1, \dots, x_k$, the ratio product is the real number $\prod_{i=0}^{k-1} \frac{P(x_i, x_{i+1})}{P(x_{i+1}, x_i)}$, where a quotient with denominator $0$ is taken to be $0$. For the empty path and for a path consisting of a single state it is $1$.
nodes.title: Ratio product along a path

nodes.summary: For a stochastic matrix $P$, the ratio product along every path of states is nonnegative.
nodes.title: The ratio product is nonnegative

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a stochastic matrix such that $P(x, y) > 0$ implies $P(y, x) > 0$ for all states $x$ and $y$. If the forward path product along a path of states is positive, then the ratio product along that path is positive.
nodes.title: Positive paths have positive ratio product

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a stochastic matrix on the states $\{0, \dots, M\}$. If $n > 0$ and the $(i, j)$ entry of the $n$-th matrix power $P^n$ is positive, then there is a path from $i$ to $j$ (a finite list of states starting at $i$ and ending at $j$) along which the product of the transition probabilities $P(x, y)$ over consecutive states $x, y$ is positive.
nodes.title: Paths from positive matrix powers

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be an irreducible stochastic matrix on the states $\{0, \dots, M\}$. For any two states $i, j$ there is a path from $i$ to $j$ (a finite list of states starting at $i$ and ending at $j$) along which the product of the transition probabilities $P(x, y)$ over consecutive states $x, y$ is strictly positive.
nodes.title: Irreducible chains have positive paths

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a stochastic matrix, $n$ a natural number and $c_0, c_1, \dots, c_{n+1}$ states. Then the ratio product along $c_0, c_1, \dots, c_{n+1}$ equals $\frac{P(c_0, c_1)}{P(c_1, c_0)}$ times the ratio product along $c_1, \dots, c_{n+1}$, where a quotient with denominator $0$ is taken to be $0$.
nodes.title: First step of the ratio product

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a stochastic matrix, $n$ a natural number and $c_0, c_1, \dots, c_n$ states. Then the ratio product along $c_0, c_1, \dots, c_n$ equals $\prod_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{P(c_i, c_{i+1})}{P(c_{i+1}, c_i)}$, where a quotient with denominator $0$ is taken to be $0$.
nodes.title: The ratio product as a finite product

nodes.summary: If some power `w` of a stochastic matrix is all-positive, then every later power `m ≥ w` is all-positive: write `m = (m - w) + w`, use `matPow_add`, and note that row `i` of `matPow (m - w)` sums to `1`, so some entry of that row is positive, and that entry times the positive `matPow w` entry gives a positive summand.
