nodes.summary: An ergodic chain has, for every pair of states, some positive power with a positive `(i, j)`-entry. (This is the per-pair form; it is strictly weaker than ergodicity, which asks for one power working for all pairs at once.)
nodes.title: Pairwise positive powers of an ergodic chain

nodes.summary: Once a power of an ergodic chain is all-positive, every later power is all-positive: there is a threshold `w` past which every power is all-positive.
nodes.title: Powers of an ergodic chain are eventually all positive

nodes.summary: The `p`-th power of a stochastic matrix, as a stochastic matrix.
nodes.title: Power of a stochastic matrix

nodes.summary: The underlying matrix of `P.pow p` is the `p`-th matrix power of `P`.
nodes.title: Underlying matrix of a stochastic matrix power

nodes.summary: Powers of a power: `(P.pow p).matPow n = P.matPow (p * n)`.
nodes.title: Recursive powers of a stochastic matrix power

nodes.summary: Every positive power of an ergodic chain is ergodic.
nodes.title: Powers of an ergodic Markov chain are ergodic

nodes.summary: The uniform chain: every transition has probability `1 / (M + 1)`.
nodes.title: Uniform Markov chain on finitely many states

nodes.summary: The uniform chain has constant transition probabilities `1 / (M + 1)`.
nodes.title: Transition probabilities of the uniform chain

nodes.summary: The uniform chain is ergodic, with witness `n = 1`.
nodes.title: The uniform Markov chain is ergodic

nodes.summary: The identity chain: `prob i j` is `1` on the diagonal and `0` elsewhere.
nodes.title: Identity Markov chain

nodes.summary: The identity chain has the displayed transition probabilities.
nodes.title: Transition probabilities of the identity chain

nodes.summary: Every power of the identity chain is the identity matrix.
nodes.title: Powers of the identity chain are the identity matrix

nodes.summary: The identity chain is not ergodic (for `M ≥ 1`): every power has a zero off-diagonal entry.
nodes.title: The identity Markov chain is not ergodic

nodes.summary: Doeblin's argument (Levin, Peres and Wilmer, proof of Theorem 4.9): if the `r`-step transition probabilities dominate `δ π`, then the total variation distance of `Pⁿ(x, ·)` from the stationary distribution `π` is at most `(1 - δ) ^ ⌊n / r⌋`. The bound is informative when `r > 0` and `0 < δ`; for `r = 0` (`n / 0 = 0`) or `δ ≤ 0` it reads `d_TV ≤ 1` or weaker.
nodes.title: Doeblin's argument

nodes.summary: The convergence theorem (Levin, Peres and Wilmer, Theorem 4.9): a primitive (irreducible and aperiodic) stochastic matrix with stationary distribution `π` converges to `π` geometrically fast in total variation, uniformly in the starting state.
nodes.title: The convergence theorem

nodes.summary: For a primitive stochastic matrix with stationary distribution `π`, every row of `Pⁿ` converges to `π`: `Pⁿ(x, y) → π(y)`.
nodes.title: Convergence of matrix powers to the stationary distribution

nodes.summary: A primitive stochastic matrix has at most one stationary distribution. In fact `π'` may be any stationary vector of total mass `1`, not necessarily nonnegative.
nodes.title: Uniqueness of the stationary distribution of a primitive chain

nodes.summary: The stationary distribution of a primitive stochastic matrix has full support.
nodes.title: Stationary distribution of a primitive chain has full support

nodes.summary: Continuous-time processes with continuous paths or independent increments: Kolmogorov's continuity theorem, Blumenthal-type zero–one laws, Markov property for independent-increment processes, quadratic variation, the Itô integral and Itô's formula, stochastic differential equations, the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, and Fokker–Planck equations for diffusions.
nodes.title: Brownian motion and stochastic calculus
Blumenthal zero–one law

nodes.summary: The *germ σ-algebra at `0`* of a filtration `𝓕` indexed by `NNReal`, defined as the intersection `⨅_{t > 0} 𝓕_t`. For Brownian motion this is the `𝓕_0^+` σ-algebra of events observable "immediately after" time `0`. Ported verbatim from `v1/Atlas/TheoryOfProbability/code/Blumenthal01.lean`.
nodes.title: Germ sigma-algebra at time zero

nodes.summary: A continuous process `B : NNReal → Ω → E` with independent increments, started at `x` and adapted to `𝓕`. The measure is a probability measure, `B 0 = x` a.e., each increment after `s` is independent of `𝓕 s`, and a.e. paths are continuous. These are the five meaningful fields of the archived v1 specification; its tautological pushforward-law field is omitted. No Gaussian-law or stationary-increment condition is…
nodes.title: Continuous process with independent increments

nodes.summary: Each coordinate of the adapted continuous process is measurable.
nodes.title: Coordinates of a continuous independent-increment process are measurable

nodes.summary: The natural filtration of a process: `𝓕^nat_t = σ(B_u : u ≤ t)`. Unlike Mathlib's `Filtration.natural`, this is built from measurability rather than strong measurability, which is all that is available from adaptedness.
nodes.title: Natural filtration of a process

nodes.summary: The germ σ-algebra of the natural filtration of `B`.
nodes.title: Germ sigma-algebra of the natural filtration

nodes.summary: Each `B u` is measurable with respect to the natural filtration at any later time `t`.
nodes.title: Process is measurable for its natural filtration at later times

nodes.summary: The natural filtration is contained in any filtration to which `B` is adapted.
nodes.title: Natural filtration is the smallest adapted filtration

nodes.summary: The germ σ-algebra is contained in every positive-time component of the filtration.
nodes.title: Germ sigma-algebra lies in every positive-time level

nodes.summary: Every event in the natural germ of a continuous process with independent increments and a deterministic a.e. initial value has probability `0` or `1`. This general form includes the classical Brownian natural-filtration law.
nodes.title: Blumenthal zero-one law
Fokker–Planck equation

nodes.summary: The free energy `F(t) = ∫ₐᵇ (Ψ p + D p log p) dx` of the density `p(t, ·)` on `[a, b]` (potential `Ψ`, diffusion coefficient `D`).
nodes.title: Free energy of a Fokker–Planck density

nodes.summary: The (negative) probability flux `p Ψ' + D ∂ₓ p` of the gradient-drift Fokker–Planck equation at `(t, x)`; the flux itself is `-(p Ψ' + D ∂ₓ p)`.
nodes.title: Negative probability flux of the Fokker–Planck equation

nodes.summary: `p` solves the gradient-drift Fokker–Planck equation `∂ₜ p = ∂ₓ (p Ψ' + D ∂ₓ p)` on `[a, b]` with zero flux at both ends, for times `t ∈ I`.
nodes.title: No-flux solution of the gradient-drift Fokker–Planck equation

nodes.summary: Let `p` be `C²` in `(t, x)`, positive for times in an open set `I`, and solve the no-flux gradient-drift Fokker–Planck equation on `[a, b]` for `t ∈ I`, with `C²` potential `Ψ` (any real `D`). Then for `t ∈ I`, `F'(t) = -∫ₐᵇ p (Ψ' + D ∂ₓ log p)² dx`. Only the values of `p` on `[a, b]` enter `F`; positivity is asked of the whole `C²` function `p t` so that `log (p t)` is `C²`.
nodes.title: Dissipation identity

nodes.summary: Under the hypotheses of `hasDerivAt_freeEnergy`, on a convex open time set `I` the free energy is nonincreasing.
nodes.title: Free-energy decay

nodes.summary: If `p` is `C²` and solves the no-flux equation on `[a, b]` for times in `I` (positivity is not needed), the total mass `∫ₐᵇ p(t, x) dx` has zero time derivative at every `t ∈ I`.
nodes.title: Mass conservation

nodes.summary: The partial derivative `∂ᵢ f (x) = Df(x) eᵢ` on `Fin n → ℝ`.
nodes.title: Partial derivative on Euclidean coordinate space

nodes.summary: The gradient `∇f(x) = (∂ᵢ f(x))ᵢ`.
nodes.title: Gradient of a function on Euclidean coordinate space

nodes.summary: The divergence `div F (x) = ∑ᵢ ∂ᵢ Fᵢ (x)` of a vector field.
nodes.title: Divergence of a vector field

nodes.summary: The probability flux `J = b p - D ∇p` of the diffusion `dX = b dt + √(2D) dW` with density `p`.
nodes.title: Probability flux of a diffusion

nodes.summary: The Fokker–Planck operator `-div J`: the density evolves by `∂ₜ p = fokkerPlanckOp D b p`, and `p` is stationary iff this vanishes.
nodes.title: Fokker–Planck operator

nodes.summary: The (unnormalized) Gibbs density `e^{-Ψ(x) / D}`.
nodes.title: Gibbs density

nodes.summary: The Gibbs density has zero flux under the gradient drift `-∇Ψ`: for differentiable `Ψ`, `D ≠ 0` and any constant `c`, `J = -∇Ψ · c e^{-Ψ/D} - D ∇(c e^{-Ψ/D}) = 0`.
nodes.title: The Gibbs density has zero flux

nodes.summary: The Gibbs density is stationary for the gradient drift: `-div J = 0`.
nodes.title: The Gibbs density is stationary

nodes.summary: If `p > 0` is differentiable and the gradient drift `-∇Ψ` has zero flux for `p`, then `∂ᵢ Ψ = -D ∂ᵢ log p`.
nodes.title: A zero-flux density determines the drift

nodes.summary: Two differentiable potentials whose gradient drifts both have zero flux for the same positive differentiable density differ by a constant.
nodes.title: Identifiability of the potential

nodes.summary: The flux of the Gibbs density under the drift `-(∇Ψ + A ∇Ψ)` is the rotational part `-(A ∇Ψ) e^{-Ψ / D}` (for differentiable `Ψ`, `D ≠ 0`, any matrix `A`).
nodes.title: Flux of the Gibbs density under a rotational gradient drift

nodes.summary: Rotational drifts share the Gibbs stationary density (non-identifiability): for a `C²` potential `Ψ`, `D ≠ 0` and an antisymmetric matrix `A` (`Aᵀ = -A`), the drift `-(∇Ψ + A ∇Ψ)` satisfies `div J = 0` for `p = e^{-Ψ / D}`.
nodes.title: Rotational drifts share the Gibbs stationary density

nodes.summary: An explicit rotational drift with nonzero flux (our derivation): on `ℝ²` with `Ψ(x) = (x₀² + x₁²) / 2`, `D = 1` and the rotation generator `A = [[0, 1], [-1, 0]]`, the drift `-(∇Ψ + A ∇Ψ)` has the Gibbs (standard Gaussian, up to normalization) density as a stationary density, yet its flux at `(1, 0)` is nonzero, so it is not the gradient drift.
nodes.title: An explicit rotational drift with nonzero flux
Kolmogorov continuity theorem

nodes.summary: The set of dyadic rationals: real numbers of the form `k / 2 ^ n` for some integer `k` and natural number `n`.
nodes.title: Dyadic rationals

nodes.summary: If every adjacent dyadic increment at level `m` is at most `D * 2^{-mγ}`, then `f` is `γ`-Hölder on the dyadic rationals of `[0, 1]`, with an explicit constant.
nodes.title: Deterministic chaining

nodes.summary: A single full-measure set carries a Hölder bound for the original process on the dyadic rationals of `[0, 1]`. The moment-integrability correction in the module docstring is required for this Bochner formulation.
nodes.title: Almost sure Hölder bound on the dyadic rationals

nodes.summary: Kolmogorov continuity theorem, in the original modification formulation. The direct dyadic bound permits choosing `Y = X`. See the module docstring for the necessary moment-integrability correction to the archived v1 statement.
nodes.title: Kolmogorov continuity theorem

nodes.summary: The canonical Kolmogorov-process condition implies a common a.e. Hölder bound for `X` on the dyadics of `[0, 1]`. Its measurable-pair and finite lintegral fields supply the Bochner hypotheses internally, including when `M = 0`. No claim is made about the raw paths at every real time.
nodes.title: Hölder bound on dyadics for a Kolmogorov process

nodes.summary: A real-valued Kolmogorov process on `NNReal` whose time exponent is greater than one has one modification with measurable coordinates and continuous paths on every sample. The same modification agrees exactly at time zero and preserves every closed set containing an original sample path. Fixed-time almost-everywhere equality is asserted separately at each time; no indistinguishability claim is made for the raw…
nodes.title: Kolmogorov continuous-modification theorem for real-valued processes
Markov property of processes with independent increments

nodes.summary: For a finite set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, the predecessor of $t$ in $S$ is the largest element of $S$ strictly below $t$, or $0$ if there is no such element.
nodes.title: Predecessor of a time in a finite set

nodes.summary: Let $(B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a real-valued process on $\Omega$, let $s \ge 0$, and let $S \subset \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ be a finite set. For $t \ge 0$ let $t^-$ be the largest element of $S$ strictly below $t$, or $0$ if there is none. The increment at $t$ is the random variable $\omega \mapsto B_{s+t}(\omega) - B_{s+t^-}(\omega)$.
nodes.title: Increment over the predecessor interval

nodes.summary: For a real-valued process $(B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ on $\Omega$ indexed by $t \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ and a time $s \ge 0$, the shifted path is the map sending $\omega \in \Omega$ to the path $t \mapsto B_{s+t}(\omega)$ in $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}}$.
nodes.title: Shifted path of a process

nodes.summary: Let $(B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a real-valued process on $\Omega$ and let $s \ge 0$. The centered shifted path at time $s$ sends $\omega \in \Omega$ to the function $t \mapsto B_{s+t}(\omega) - B_s(\omega)$ on $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$.
nodes.title: Centered shifted path

nodes.summary: Let $(B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a real-valued process on a measure space $(\Omega, \mu)$ and let $s \ge 0$. This is the pushforward of $\mu$ under the map sending $\omega \in \Omega$ to the path $t \mapsto B_{s+t}(\omega) - B_s(\omega)$, a measure on the space of functions $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{R}$ with its product σ-algebra.
nodes.title: Law of the centered shifted path

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\Omega$, let $(B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a real process on $\Omega$ indexed by $t \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, let $s \ge 0$, and let $\nu_s$ be the law under $\mu$ (the pushforward of $\mu$) of the centered shifted path $\omega \mapsto (t \mapsto B_{s+t}(\omega) - B_s(\omega))$. For a real function $Y$ on paths $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{R}$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}$, the path expectation is the…
nodes.title: Time-dependent path expectation

nodes.summary: A real-valued process $(B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ on $\Omega$, indexed by $t \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, is adapted to a filtration $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \ge 0}$ when $B_t$ is $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable for every $t \ge 0$.
nodes.title: Adapted real process

nodes.summary: A real-valued process $(B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ on $\Omega$ has independent increments with respect to a filtration $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \ge 0}$ and a measure $\mu$ when, for all $0 \le s \le t$, the σ-algebra generated by $B_t - B_s$ is independent of $\mathcal{F}_s$ under $\mu$.
nodes.title: Independent increments with respect to a filtration

nodes.summary: Let $B = (B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a real process on a measurable space $\Omega$, adapted to a filtration $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \ge 0}$ of its σ-algebra, and give the space $\mathbb{R}^{[0, \infty)}$ of real paths indexed by $t \ge 0$ the product σ-algebra. For every $s \ge 0$, the map from $\Omega$ to $\mathbb{R}^{[0, \infty)}$ sending $\omega$ to the path $t \mapsto B_{s+t}(\omega)$ is measurable.
nodes.title: Measurability of the shifted path

nodes.summary: Let $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a filtration on a measurable space $\Omega$ indexed by $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, and let $(B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a real-valued process adapted to it (each $B_t$ is $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable). Then for every $s \ge 0$ the map $\omega \mapsto (t \mapsto B_{s+t}(\omega) - B_s(\omega))$ from $\Omega$ to $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}}$, with the product σ-algebra, is measurable.
nodes.title: Measurability of the centered shifted path

nodes.summary: Let $B = (B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a real process on a measurable space $\Omega$, adapted to a filtration $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \ge 0}$ of its σ-algebra, let $S$ be a finite set of nonnegative reals and let $s, t, u \ge 0$. Write $p_S(t)$ for the largest element of $S$ strictly below $t$, or $0$ if there is none. If $s + t \le s + u$ and $s + p_S(t) \le s + u$, then the increment $B_{s+t} - B_{s+p_S(t)}$ is…
nodes.title: Measurability of an increment before a given time

nodes.summary: For a finite set $T \subseteq \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, call the largest element of $T$ strictly below $t$ (or $0$ if there is none) the predecessor of $t$ in $T$. Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ be finite and let $t, a \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ with $t < a$. Then the predecessor of $t$ in $S \cup \{a\}$ equals the predecessor of $t$ in $S$.
nodes.title: Inserting a larger element does not change the predecessor

nodes.summary: For a finite set $T \subseteq \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, call the largest element of $T$ strictly below $t$ (or $0$ if there is none) the predecessor of $t$ in $T$. Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ be finite and let $a \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ with $x < a$ for every $x \in S$. Then the predecessor of $a$ in $S \cup \{a\}$ is the supremum of $S$ in $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, that is, its…
nodes.title: Predecessor of a new maximum

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a probability measure and let $(B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a real process adapted to a filtration $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \ge 0}$ such that $B_t - B_s$ is independent of $\mathcal{F}_s$ under $\mu$ whenever $s \le t$. Let $s \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ and let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ be finite. For $t \in S$ let $\Delta_t = B_{s+t} - B_{s+t^-}$, where $t^-$ is the largest element of $S$ strictly below $t$, or…
nodes.title: Past events factor against grid increments

nodes.summary: Let $(B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a family of real functions on $\Omega$, let $s \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ and let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ be a nonempty finite set. For $u \in S$ let $\Delta_u = B_{s+u} - B_{s+u^-}$, where $u^-$ is the largest element of $S$ strictly below $u$, or $0$ if there is none. Then for every $\omega \in \Omega$, $\sum_{u \in S} \Delta_u(\omega) = B_{s + \max S}(\omega) - B_s(\omega)$.
nodes.title: Telescoping sum of grid increments

nodes.summary: Let $(B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a real-valued process on $\Omega$, let $s \ge 0$, and let $S \subset \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ be a finite set. For $u \ge 0$ let $u^-$ be the largest element of $S$ strictly below $u$, or $0$ if there is none. Then for every $t \in S$ and every $\omega \in \Omega$, $B_{s+t}(\omega) - B_s(\omega) = \sum_{u \in S : u \le t} (B_{s+u}(\omega) - B_{s+u^-}(\omega))$.
nodes.title: Telescoping the centered shifted path over a finite set

nodes.summary: Let $B = (B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a real process on a measurable space $\Omega$, adapted to a filtration $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \ge 0}$ of its σ-algebra. For every finite set $S$ of nonnegative reals and all $s, t \ge 0$, the increment $B_{s+t} - B_{s+p_S(t)}$ is measurable, where $p_S(t)$ is the largest element of $S$ strictly below $t$, or $0$ if there is none.
nodes.title: Measurability of the increments

nodes.summary: Let $(B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a real-valued process on $\Omega$, let $s \ge 0$, and let $S \subset \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ be a finite set. For $t \ge 0$ let $t^-$ be the largest element of $S$ strictly below $t$, or $0$ if there is none. The increment rectangles are the events $\bigcap_{t \in S} \{\omega \in \Omega : B_{s+t}(\omega) - B_{s+t^-}(\omega) \in C_t\}$, where each $C_t \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a Borel set.
nodes.title: Increment rectangles

nodes.summary: Let $(B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a real-valued process on $\Omega$, let $s \ge 0$, and let $S \subset \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ be a finite set. For $t \ge 0$ let $t^-$ be the largest element of $S$ strictly below $t$, or $0$ if there is none. This is the σ-algebra on $\Omega$ generated by the increment rectangles, the events $\bigcap_{t \in S} \{\omega \in \Omega : B_{s+t}(\omega) - B_{s+t^-}(\omega) \in C_t\}$ with each…

For $u \ge 0$ let $p_S(u)$ be the largest element of $S$ strictly below $u$, or $0$ if there is none, and let $\Delta_u = B_{s+u} - B_{s+p_S(u)}$. Let $\mathcal{G}_S$ be the σ-algebra on $\Omega$ generated by the sets $\bigcap_{u \in S} \{\omega : \Delta_u(\omega) \in E_u\}$…

Then for every $t \in S$, the increment $\omega \mapsto B_{s+t}(\omega) - B_{s+t^-}(\omega)$ is measurable with respect to the σ-algebra generated by the events…
nodes.title: Measurability of an increment in the increment σ-algebra

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\Omega$, let $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a filtration indexed by $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, and let $(B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a real-valued process that is adapted (each $B_t$ is $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable) and has independent increments (for $u \le t$, the increment $B_t - B_u$ is independent of $\mathcal{F}_u$ under $\mu$). For a finite set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ and…
nodes.title: Independence of future increments from the present

nodes.summary: Let $(B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a real-valued process on $\Omega$ and let $s \ge 0$. The centered cylinders at time $s$ are the events $\bigcap_{t \in S} \{\omega \in \Omega : B_{s+t}(\omega) - B_s(\omega) \in C_t\}$, where $S \subset \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ is a finite set and each $C_t \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a Borel set.
nodes.title: Cylinder events of the centered shifted path

nodes.summary: Let $B = (B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a real process on a measurable space $\Omega$, let $s \ge 0$ and let $S$ be a finite set of nonnegative reals. For $u \ge 0$ let $p_S(u)$ be the largest element of $S$ strictly below $u$, or $0$ if there is none, and let $\Delta_u = B_{s+u} - B_{s+p_S(u)}$. Let $\mathcal{G}_S$ be the σ-algebra on $\Omega$ generated by the sets $\bigcap_{u \in S} \{\omega : \Delta_u(\omega) \in E_u\}$…

nodes.summary: For every $t \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ and every Borel set $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, the set of paths $f : \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f(t) \in D$ is measurable for the product σ-algebra on the space of all such paths.
nodes.title: Evaluation events are measurable

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\Omega$, let $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a filtration indexed by $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, and let $(B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a real-valued process that is adapted (each $B_t$ is $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable) and has independent increments (for $u \le t$, the increment $B_t - B_u$ is independent of $\mathcal{F}_u$ under $\mu$). Then for every $s \ge 0$, $\mathcal{F}_s$ is independent…
nodes.title: Independence of the centered future path from the present

nodes.summary: The collection of sets of paths $f : \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{R}$ of the form $\bigcap_{t \in S} \{f : f(t) \in C_t\}$, where $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ is a finite set and each $C_t$ is a measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.title: Cylinder sets of path space

nodes.summary: Consider the subsets of $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}}$ of the form $\bigcap_{t \in S} \{f : f(t) \in C_t\}$, where $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ is finite and every $C_t \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is Borel. They form a π-system: whenever two of them have nonempty intersection, the intersection is again of this form.
nodes.title: Path cylinders form a π-system

nodes.summary: The product σ-algebra on the space of paths $f : \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{R}$ equals the σ-algebra generated by the cylinders, the sets $\{f : f(t) \in C_t \text{ for all } t \in S\}$ with $S$ a finite subset of $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ and $(C_t)_{t \ge 0}$ a family of Borel subsets of $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.title: Cylinders generate the product σ-algebra on path space

nodes.summary: Write $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}}$ for the space of functions $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{R}$. These are the subsets of $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}}$ of the form $U \times \{f : f(t) \in V_t \text{ for all } t \in S\}$, where $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a Borel set, $S \subset \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ is a finite set, and each $V_t \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a Borel set.
nodes.title: Rectangles of a Borel set and a path cylinder

nodes.summary: Consider the subsets of $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}}$ of the form $U \times \bigcap_{t \in S} \{f \in \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}} : f(t) \in V_t\}$, where $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is Borel, $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ is finite and every $V_t \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is Borel. They form a π-system: whenever two of them have nonempty intersection, the intersection is again of this form.
nodes.title: Rectangles of a Borel set and a path cylinder form a π-system

nodes.summary: Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be a Borel set and let $V$ be a set of paths $f : \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{R}$ that is measurable for the product σ-algebra. nodes.summary: For a type $V$ and $0 \le p \le 1$, the Bernoulli($p$) bond law on $V \times \mathbb{Z}$ is the product measure on configurations $\omega$, which assign true (open) or false (closed) to every unordered pair $\{a, b\}$ of points of $V \times \mathbb{Z}$ (with $a = b$ allowed), under which the values $\omega(e)$ are independent and each is true with probability $p$ and false with probability $1 - p$.

nodes.summary: Let $V$ be a type, let $p$ be a real number with $0 \le p \le 1$, and let $P$ be a property of configurations $\omega$, that is, of functions assigning true or false to every unordered pair $\{a, b\}$ of points of $V \times \mathbb{Z}$ (with $a = b$ allowed). We say that $P$ holds almost surely if $P(\omega)$ holds for almost every $\omega$ with respect to the Bernoulli($p$) bond law on $V \times \mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.summary: The FKG inequality (Fortuin, Kasteleyn, Ginibre 1971). Let `π` be a probability weight on `ConfigSpace E` (`π ≥ 0`, `∑ π = 1`) satisfying the FKG lattice condition. Then any two monotone functions `f g : ConfigSpace E → ℝ` are positively correlated: `E_π[f] * E_π[g] ≤ E_π[f * g]`.
nodes.title: FKG inequality

nodes.summary: The FKG inequality for events: under a probability weight `π` satisfying the FKG lattice condition, two increasing events are positively correlated, `π(A) * π(B) ≤ π(A ∩ B)`.

nodes.summary: The Holley inequality for increasing events (Holley 1974). If `μ₁, μ₂ ≥ 0` have equal total mass and satisfy `μ₁ a * μ₂ b ≤ μ₁ (a ⊓ b) * μ₂ (a ⊔ b)`, then `μ₁(A) ≤ μ₂(A)` for every increasing event `A`. This is Mathlib's `holley` applied to the indicator of `A`.
nodes.title: Holley inequality for increasing events

nodes.summary: The finite measure `∑_ω μ(ω) δ_ω` on `ConfigSpace E` with point masses `μ(ω)` (negative masses are truncated to `0`). For a normalized nonnegative `μ` it is the measure of the `PMF` `PMF.ofFintype μ`; see `measOfMass_eq_toMeasure`.

nodes.summary: For a normalized nonnegative mass function, `measOfMass μ` is the measure of the `PMF` `PMF.ofFintype (ENNReal.ofReal ∘ μ)`.
nodes.title: Normalized point masses give the probability mass function's measure

nodes.summary: If `μ₁, μ₂ ≥ 0` on `{0,1}^E` have equal total mass and satisfy the Holley lattice condition `μ₁(a) μ₂(b) ≤ μ₁(a ∧ b) μ₂(a ∨ b)`, then `measOfMass μ₁` is stochastically dominated by `measOfMass μ₂`. Strict positivity, assumed in Holley's paper, is not needed. See R. Holley, *Remarks on the FKG inequalities*, Comm. Math. Phys. 36 (1974); the real-valued form is `StatMech.holley_dominates`, from Mathlib's `holley`.

nodes.summary: If `μ₁, μ₂` are strictly positive probability mass functions on `{0,1}^E` satisfying the Holley lattice condition `μ₁(a) μ₂(b) ≤ μ₁(a ∧ b) μ₂(a ∨ b)`, there is a finite measure on pairs with marginals `measOfMass μ₁` and `measOfMass μ₂`, concentrated on `{(a, b) | a ≤ b}`. See R. Holley, *Remarks on the FKG inequalities*, Comm. Math. Phys. 36 (1974), and G. Grimmett, *The Random-Cluster Model* (2006), Chapter 2.

nodes.summary: A planar point is a point of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$: a pair $(x, y)$ of real numbers, with the Euclidean norm $\lVert (x, y) \rVert = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$.

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$ and an index $i$ with $0 \le i < n$, the cyclic successor of $i$ is $(i + 1) \bmod n$; in particular the successor of $n - 1$ is $0$. For $n = 0$ there are no indices.

nodes.summary: For points $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ in the Euclidean plane and a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the tour length is $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \lVert x_{\sigma(i)} - x_{\sigma(i+1 \bmod n)} \rVert$, the length of the closed tour that visits $x_{\sigma(0)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(n-1)}$ in this order and returns to its start.
nodes.title: Length of a closed tour

nodes.summary: For points $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ in the Euclidean plane, $L_n$ is the minimum, over all permutations $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, of the length of the closed tour that visits $x_{\sigma(0)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(n-1)}$ in this order and returns to its start.
nodes.title: Shortest tour length

nodes.summary: Let $\Omega$ be a set and let $X_0, X_1, X_2, \dots \colon \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be functions. For an outcome $\omega \in \Omega$ and $n \ge 1$, the normalized tour length is $L_n(\omega)/\sqrt{n}$, where $L_n(\omega)$ is the length of a shortest closed tour through $X_0(\omega), \dots, X_{n-1}(\omega)$. For $n = 0$ it is defined to be $0$.
nodes.title: Normalized tour length

nodes.summary: Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $M$ be a matrix over $\mathbb{K}$ whose rows and columns are indexed by finite sets $n$ and $m$. Its smallest singular value is the real number $\sigma_{\min}(M) = \inf_{x \in \mathbb{K}^m,\ \lVert x \rVert_2 = 1} \lVert Mx \rVert_2$, where $\lVert \cdot \rVert_2$ is the Euclidean norm. When $m$ is empty there are no unit vectors, and $\sigma_{\min}(M) = 0$.

nodes.summary: Let $0 < p \le 1/2$. For each $n$, let $B_n$ be a random $n \times n$ real matrix on a probability space $(\Omega_n, P_n)$ whose $n^2$ entries are mutually independent and each equal to $1$ with probability $p$ and to $0$ with probability $1 - p$. Then there is a function $o : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $o(n) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$ such that $P_n(\det B_n = 0) = (1 - p + o(n))^n$ for every $n \ge 1$.

Thin-shell conjecture

nodes.summary: A function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is a log-concave density when it is measurable, $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x$, and $f(x)^{1-t} f(y)^t \le f((1-t)x + ty)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and every real $t$ with $0 < t < 1$.
nodes.title: Log-concave densities

nodes.summary: A measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is isotropic log-concave when it is a probability measure, it has density $f$ with respect to Lebesgue measure for some log-concave density $f$, and for all coordinates $i, j$ the functions $x \mapsto x_i$ and $x \mapsto x_i x_j$ are $\mu$-integrable with $\int x_i \, d\mu(x) = 0$ and $\int x_i x_j \, d\mu(x) = \delta_{ij}$, that is, $1$ if $i = j$ and $0$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Isotropic log-concave probability measures

nodes.summary: For a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the normalized radius variance of $\mu$ is $\frac{1}{n} \int (\|x\|^2 - n)^2 \, d\mu(x)$, computed in $[0, \infty]$, where $\|x\|$ is the Euclidean norm (for $n = 0$ the integral is $0$ and so is the value).
nodes.title: Normalized radius variance

nodes.summary: Write $|x|$ for the Euclidean norm. The thin-shell variance constant is the supremum, taken in $[0, \infty]$, of the normalized radius variance $\frac{1}{n} \int (|x|^2 - n)^2 \, d\mu(x)$ over all dimensions $n \ge 1$ and all isotropic log-concave probability measures $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
nodes.title: Thin-shell variance constant

nodes.summary: Write $|x|$ for the Euclidean norm. For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the thin-shell width in dimension $n$ is the square root of the supremum, taken in $[0, \infty]$, of $\int (|x| - \sqrt{n})^2 \, d\mu(x)$ over all isotropic log-concave probability measures $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, with $\sqrt{\infty} = \infty$.
nodes.title: Thin-shell width

nodes.summary: For all real numbers $r \ge 0$ and $d > 0$, $(r - \sqrt{d})^2 \le (r^2 - d)^2 / d$.
nodes.title: Elementary radius deviation bound

nodes.summary: For every $n > 0$ and every measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the integral $\int (\|x\| - \sqrt{n})^2 \, d\mu(x)$, taken in $[0, \infty]$ with $\|x\|$ the Euclidean norm, is at most the normalized radius variance of $\mu$.
nodes.title: Radius fluctuation is bounded by the normalized radius variance

nodes.summary: The thin-shell variance constant bounds the normalized radius variance of isotropic log-concave measures. For every $n > 0$ and every isotropic log-concave probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the normalized radius variance of $\mu$ is at most the thin-shell variance constant.
nodes.title: The thin-shell variance constant bounds the normalized radius variance of isotropic log-concave measures

nodes.summary: For every $C \in [0, \infty]$, the thin-shell variance constant is at most $C$ if and only if, for every $n > 0$ and every isotropic log-concave probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the normalized radius variance of $\mu$ is at most $C$.
nodes.title: Characterization of bounds on the thin-shell variance constant

nodes.summary: For every $n > 0$ and every isotropic log-concave probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the integral $\int (\|x\| - \sqrt{n})^2 \, d\mu(x)$, taken in $[0, \infty]$ with $\|x\|$ the Euclidean norm, is at most the thin-shell variance constant.
nodes.title: The thin-shell variance constant bounds the radius fluctuation

nodes.summary: The thin-shell variance constant, a value in $[0, \infty]$, is at least $0$.
nodes.title: The thin-shell variance constant is nonnegative

nodes.summary: For every dimension $n \ge 1$, the thin-shell width in dimension $n$ is at most the square root of the thin-shell variance constant, computed in $[0, \infty]$ with $\sqrt{\infty} = \infty$.
nodes.title: Thin-shell width is at most the square root of the variance constant

nodes.summary: If $C$ is a real number such that for every $n > 0$ and every isotropic log-concave probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ the normalized radius variance of $\mu$ is at most $\max(C, 0)$, then the thin-shell variance constant is finite.
nodes.title: A uniform variance bound makes the thin-shell variance constant finite

nodes.summary: There are a real $C > 0$ and a natural number $N \ge 3$ such that for every natural number $n \ge N$ the thin-shell width $\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ of dimension $n$ satisfies $\sigma_n \le C \sqrt{n / \log n}$.
nodes.title: Klartag's first thin-shell bound

nodes.summary: For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there are a constant $C > 0$ and an integer $N \ge 3$ such that for every dimension $n \ge N$ the thin-shell width $\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ satisfies $\sigma_n \le C n^{2/5 + \varepsilon}$. Here $\sigma_n$ is the square root of the supremum of $\mathbb{E}\,(|X| - \sqrt{n})^2$ over isotropic log-concave random vectors $X$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
nodes.title: Klartag's power-law thin-shell bound

nodes.summary: There are a real $C > 0$ and a natural number $N \ge 3$ such that for every natural number $n \ge N$ the thin-shell width $\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ of dimension $n$ satisfies $\sigma_n \le C n^{3/8}$.
nodes.title: Fleury's thin-shell bound

nodes.summary: There are a real $C > 0$ and a natural number $N \ge 3$ such that for every natural number $n \ge N$ the thin-shell width $\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ of dimension $n$ satisfies $\sigma_n \le C n^{1/3}$.
nodes.title: Guédon–Milman thin-shell bound

nodes.summary: There are a constant $C > 0$ and an integer $N \ge 3$ such that for every dimension $n \ge N$ the thin-shell width $\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ satisfies $\sigma_n \le C n^{1/4}$. Here $\sigma_n$ is the square root of the supremum of $\mathbb{E}\,(|X| - \sqrt{n})^2$ over isotropic log-concave random vectors $X$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
nodes.title: Lee–Vempala thin-shell bound

nodes.summary: For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a natural number $N \ge 3$ such that for every natural number $n \ge N$ the thin-shell width $\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ of dimension $n$ satisfies $\sigma_n \le \exp\big((\log n)^{1/2 + \varepsilon}\big)$.
nodes.title: Chen's thin-shell bound

nodes.summary: There are a real $C > 0$ and a natural number $N \ge 3$ such that for every natural number $n \ge N$ the thin-shell width $\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ of dimension $n$ satisfies $\sigma_n \le C (\log n)^4$.
nodes.title: Klartag–Lehec polylogarithmic thin-shell bound

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha = \big(1 + 7\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{53 - 4\sqrt{2}}\big)/8$. There are a real $C > 0$ and a natural number $N \ge 3$ such that for every natural number $n \ge N$ the thin-shell width $\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ of dimension $n$ satisfies $\sigma_n \le C (\log n)^{\alpha}$.
nodes.title: Jambulapati–Lee–Vempala thin-shell bound

nodes.summary: There are a constant $C > 0$ and an integer $N \ge 3$ such that for every dimension $n \ge N$ the thin-shell width $\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ satisfies $\sigma_n \le C \sqrt{\log n}$. Here $\sigma_n$ is the square root of the supremum of $\mathbb{E}\,(|X| - \sqrt{n})^2$ over isotropic log-concave random vectors $X$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, and $\log$ is the natural logarithm.
nodes.title: Klartag's square-root-logarithmic thin-shell bound

nodes.summary: There are a real $C > 0$ and a natural number $N \ge 3$ such that for every natural number $n \ge N$ the thin-shell width $\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ of dimension $n$ satisfies $\sigma_n \le C \log \log n$.
nodes.title: Guan's thin-shell bound

nodes.summary: There is a real $C > 0$ such that for every natural number $n \ge 1$ and every isotropic log-concave measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the normalized radius variance $\frac{1}{n} \int (|x|^2 - n)^2 \, d\mu(x)$ is at most $C$.
nodes.title: Klartag–Lehec thin-shell variance bound

nodes.summary: There is a real $C > 0$ such that for every natural number $n \ge 1$ the thin-shell width $\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ of dimension $n$ satisfies $\sigma_n \le C$.
nodes.title: Klartag–Lehec bounded thin-shell width

nodes.summary: The thin-shell variance constant, the supremum in $[0, \infty]$ of the normalized radius variances $\frac{1}{n} \int (|x|^2 - n)^2 \, d\mu(x)$ over all dimensions $n \ge 1$ and all isotropic log-concave probability measures $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, is finite.

nodes.summary: The thin-shell variance constant, the supremum in $[0, \infty]$ of the normalized radius variances $\frac{1}{n} \int (|x|^2 - n)^2 \, d\mu(x)$ over all dimensions $n \ge 1$ and all isotropic log-concave probability measures $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, is at least $2$.

nodes.summary: For a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the covariance matrix of $\mu$ is the $n \times n$ real matrix whose $(i, j)$ entry is $\int (x_i - m_i)(x_j - m_j) \, d\mu(x)$, where $m_i = \int x_i \, d\mu(x)$ is the mean of the $i$-th coordinate.

nodes.summary: For a function $f \colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, usually the Lebesgue density of a probability law, the differential entropy of $f$ is $-\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x) \log f(x) \, dx$, with the natural logarithm and $0 \log 0 = 0$.

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, a full-dimensional convex body in dimension $n$ is a nonempty compact convex set $K$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ whose interior is nonempty, where $n$ is required to be positive.

nodes.summary: For every log-concave law $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the covariance matrix of $\mu$ is positive semidefinite.

nodes.summary: If $\mu$ is an isotropic log-concave probability measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$, then the covariance matrix of $\mu$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix.
nodes.title: Isotropic log-concave laws have identity covariance

nodes.summary: For a full-dimensional convex body $K$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, the uniform law on $K$ is the probability measure obtained by restricting Lebesgue measure to $K$ and dividing by the volume of $K$; it gives a set $A$ the mass $\operatorname{vol}(A \cap K) / \operatorname{vol}(K)$.

nodes.summary: For a full-dimensional convex body $K$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, let $\operatorname{Cov}(K)$ be the covariance matrix of the uniform probability law on $K$ and let $\operatorname{vol}(K)$ be the Lebesgue volume of $K$. The isotropic constant of $K$ is the real number $L_K = \left(\det \operatorname{Cov}(K) / \operatorname{vol}(K)^2\right)^{1/(2n)}$.

nodes.title: Isotropic constant of a log-concave law

nodes.title: Supremum of isotropic constants of convex bodies

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, a full-dimensional convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is centrally symmetric when $K = -K$, that is, for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $x \in K$ if and only if $-x \in K$.
nodes.title: Centrally symmetric convex body

nodes.summary: This is the value $\sup_{n \ge 1} \sup_K L_K \in [0, \infty]$, where for each dimension $n \ge 1$ the inner supremum runs over the full-dimensional convex bodies $K$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that are centrally symmetric, that is $K = -K$, and $L_K$ is the isotropic constant of $K$.
nodes.title: Supremum of isotropic constants of symmetric convex bodies

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, the squared-radius thin-shell width in dimension $n$ is the supremum, in $[0, \infty]$, of $\left(\int (|x|^2 - n)^2 \, d\mu(x) / n\right)^{1/2}$ (with $0/0 = 0$) over all isotropic log-concave probability measures $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, that is, those with a log-concave Lebesgue density, mean zero and identity covariance.

nodes.summary: This is the supremum, in $[0, \infty]$, of the isotropic constant $L_\mu = e^{-h(f)/n} (\det \mathrm{Cov}(\mu))^{1/(2n)}$ over all positive integers $n$ and all log-concave laws $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with Lebesgue density $f$, where $h(f) = -\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f \log f$ is the differential entropy of $f$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(\mu)$ is the covariance matrix of the coordinates under $\mu$.

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$ and let $K \subseteq \alpha$ be a measurable set with $\mu(K) \neq 0$. Then the conditional measure $\mu(\cdot \mid K)$, that is $\mu(K)^{-1}$ times the restriction of $\mu$ to $K$, equals the measure with density $x \mapsto \mu(K)^{-1} \mathbf{1}_K(x)$ with respect to $\mu$. nodes.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a full-dimensional convex body, so that its Lebesgue measure $\mathrm{Vol}(K)$ is finite and positive. The uniform density of $K$ is the function $f_K \colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ equal to $1/\mathrm{Vol}(K)$ on $K$ and to $0$ outside $K$.

nodes.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a full-dimensional convex body of Lebesgue measure $\mathrm{Vol}(K)$. The uniform law of $K$ is the log-concave law on $\mathbb{R}^n$ whose probability measure is Lebesgue measure restricted to $K$ and divided by $\mathrm{Vol}(K)$, and whose density is the uniform density of $K$.

nodes.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a full-dimensional convex body with Lebesgue measure $\mathrm{Vol}(K)$ and uniform density $f_K$, equal to $1/\mathrm{Vol}(K)$ on $K$ and to $0$ outside $K$. Expectation under a probability mass function

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type carrying a σ-algebra in which singletons are measurable, let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\alpha$ and let $f : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$. The expectation of $f$ under $p$ is the Bochner integral $\int f \, d\mu_p$, where $\mu_p$ is the probability measure on $\alpha$ associated to $p$.

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a probability mass function on a finite measurable space $\alpha$ in which singletons are measurable, and let $f : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$. Then the expectation of $f$ under $p$ equals the finite sum $\sum_{a \in \alpha} p(a) f(a)$.

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\mathbb{R}$ with cumulative distribution function $F_\mu$ (for a probability measure, $F_\mu(x) = \mu((-\infty, x])$). The quantile function of $\mu$, the generalized inverse of $F_\mu$, is the function $Q_\mu : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ given by $Q_\mu(u) = \inf \lbrace x \in \mathbb{R} : u \le F_\mu(x) \rbrace$ for $u \in (0, 1)$ and $Q_\mu(u) = 0$ for $u \notin (0, 1)$.

nodes.summary: The likelihood family `L : ℕ → ℝ → ℝ` (observation, parameter) has a monotone likelihood ratio on the parameter set `S`: `L` is nonnegative on `S`, and for observations `n ≤ m` and parameters `θ ≤ θ'` in `S`, `L m θ * L n θ' ≤ L n θ * L m θ'` (total positivity of order two). For positive likelihoods this is monotonicity of `θ ↦ L m θ / L n θ`. The nonnegativity is part of the predicate: without it the downstream…
nodes.title: Monotone likelihood ratio

nodes.summary: The likelihood family has an antitone likelihood ratio on `S`: `L` is nonnegative on `S`, and for `n ≤ m` and `θ ≤ θ'` in `S`, `L n θ * L m θ' ≤ L m θ * L n θ'`. For positive likelihoods this says `θ ↦ L m θ / L n θ` is nonincreasing (larger counts favor smaller parameters).
nodes.title: Antitone likelihood ratio

nodes.summary: Posterior stochastic ordering, cross-multiplied form (Milgrom 1981, Prop. 1). If the family `L` has a monotone likelihood ratio on a set `S` carrying the prior `μ` (`μ Sᶜ = 0`), and every `L n` is `μ`-integrable, then for `n ≤ m` and every threshold `t`, `(∫_{θ > t} L n dμ) (∫ L m dμ) ≤ (∫_{θ > t} L m dμ) (∫ L n dμ)`.
nodes.title: Posterior stochastic ordering, cross-multiplied form

nodes.summary: Posterior probability of `{θ > t}` after observing `n`, by Bayes' formula for the prior `μ` and likelihood `L`: `(∫_{θ > t} L n θ dμ) / ∫ L n θ dμ`. Meaningful when the marginal likelihood `∫ L n dμ` is positive (otherwise the division returns the junk value `0`), and a genuine posterior probability only when `L` is nonnegative (as in the MLR predicates: a signed `L` can give a value outside `[0, 1]`).

nodes.summary: The posterior is stochastically nondecreasing in the observation for an MLR family and every prior (Milgrom 1981, Prop. 2): if `n ≤ m` and both marginal likelihoods are positive, then `P(θ > t ∣ n) ≤ P(θ > t ∣ m)` for every `t`.

nodes.summary: The posterior is stochastically nonincreasing in the observation for a family with an antitone likelihood ratio and every prior: if `n ≤ m` and both marginal likelihoods are positive, then `P(θ > t ∣ m) ≤ P(θ > t ∣ n)` for every `t`.

nodes.summary: At the BH step-up index `k`, at least `k` p-values are at most `q k / m`.
nodes.title: Benjamini–Hochberg index satisfies the step-up condition

nodes.summary: The BH step-up index is the largest `k ≤ m` with at least `k` p-values at most `q k / m`.
nodes.title: Maximality of the Benjamini–Hochberg index

nodes.summary: The BH procedure at level `q ≥ 0` rejects exactly `bhIndex q p` hypotheses.
nodes.title: Number of Benjamini–Hochberg rejections

nodes.summary: If the p-values are independent and every true-null p-value is uniformly distributed on `[0, 1]`, the BH procedure at level `q ∈ [0, 1]` has false discovery rate at most `q |H0| / m`. Nothing is assumed about the false-null p-values beyond measurability and independence. (For `m = 0` both sides are `0`.)
nodes.title: Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control

nodes.summary: At a level `q ≥ 0`, hypothesis `i` is rejected by the BH procedure exactly when replacing its p-value by `0` leaves the BH step-up index unchanged. No sign condition is imposed on the p-values.
nodes.title: Benjamini–Hochberg rejection as leave-one-out index invariance

nodes.summary: At a level `q ≥ 0`, hypothesis `i` is rejected by the BH procedure exactly when its p-value is at most `q k⁰ / m`, where `k⁰` is the BH step-up index computed after replacing the `i`-th p-value by `0`. No sign condition is imposed on the p-values.
nodes.title: Leave-one-out criterion for Benjamini–Hochberg rejection
Bonferroni correction

nodes.summary: The hypotheses rejected by the Bonferroni procedure at level `α`: those whose p-value is at most `α / m`.
nodes.title: Bonferroni rejection set

nodes.summary: If every true-null p-value is valid and `c ∈ [0, 1]`, the probability that some true null has p-value at most `c` is at most `|H0| c`. No independence is assumed.
nodes.title: Union bound for valid p-values

nodes.summary: If every true-null p-value is valid, the probability that some true null has p-value at most `α / m` is at most `α |H0| / m`, for `α ∈ [0, 1]`. No independence is assumed. (For `m = 0` there is no hypothesis and both sides are `0`.)
nodes.title: Bonferroni inequality

nodes.summary: If every true-null p-value is valid, the probability that the Bonferroni procedure at level `α ∈ [0, 1]` rejects at least one true null is at most `α`.
nodes.title: The Bonferroni procedure controls the FWER
Holm–Bonferroni method

nodes.summary: Holm's step-down count at level `α`: the largest `r ∈ {0, …, m}` such that for every `k ∈ {1, …, r}` the `k`-th smallest p-value is at most `α / (m - k + 1)`, i.e. at least `k` p-values are at most `α / (m - k + 1)`. (`r = 0` always qualifies.)
nodes.title: Holm's step-down count

nodes.summary: The hypotheses rejected by Holm's step-down procedure at level `α`: those whose p-value is at most `α / (m - r + 1)` with `r = holmIndex α p`; these are the hypotheses with the `r` smallest p-values.
nodes.title: Hypotheses rejected by Holm's step-down procedure

nodes.summary: Holm's step-down count is at most `m`.
nodes.title: Holm's step-down count is at most the number of tests

nodes.summary: Every step up to Holm's count succeeds: for `1 ≤ k ≤ holmIndex α p`, at least `k` p-values are at most `α / (m - k + 1)`.
nodes.title: Every step up to Holm's count succeeds

nodes.summary: Holm's count is the largest index up to which every step succeeds.
nodes.title: Holm's count is the largest index where every step succeeds

nodes.summary: The rejection set is closed under smaller p-values.
nodes.title: Holm's rejection set is closed under smaller p-values

nodes.summary: Holm's procedure at level `α ≥ 0` rejects exactly `holmIndex α p` hypotheses.
nodes.title: Number of hypotheses rejected by Holm's procedure

nodes.summary: If Holm rejects a hypothesis in `J`, then some `j ∈ J` has p-value at most `α / |J|`: the first hypothesis of `J` in sorted order sits at a position `k ≤ m - |J| + 1`. This is the shared Holm rejection bound, used both for Holm's FWER control below and for identifying Holm's procedure with the closure of the Bonferroni local tests.
nodes.title: Holm rejection bound for a set of hypotheses

nodes.summary: If every true-null p-value is valid, the probability that Holm's step-down procedure at level `α ∈ [0, 1]` rejects at least one true null is at most `α`. No independence is assumed.
nodes.title: Holm's procedure controls the FWER
Closed testing principle

nodes.summary: The closed testing procedure: given the decisions `φ J` of local tests of the intersection hypotheses `H_J`, reject `Hᵢ` exactly when `φ J` holds for every `J` containing `i`.
nodes.title: Closed testing procedure

nodes.summary: Membership in the closed rejection set.
nodes.title: Membership in the closed rejection set

nodes.summary: If the closed procedure rejects a hypothesis in `H0`, then the local test of the intersection hypothesis `H_{H0}` rejects.
nodes.title: Closed testing rejection implies the intersection test rejects

nodes.summary: If `H0` is the set of true nulls and the local test of `H_{H0}` rejects with probability at most `α`, then the closed procedure rejects some true null with probability at most `α`. Applied to every possible `H0`, local level-`α` tests give strong control of the family-wise error rate. No assumption on the dependence between local tests is made.
nodes.title: The closed testing principle

nodes.summary: The Bonferroni local test of the intersection hypothesis `H_J` at level `α`: reject when some `j ∈ J` has `p j ≤ α / |J|`. (It never rejects `H_∅`.)
nodes.title: Bonferroni local test of an intersection hypothesis

nodes.summary: The Bonferroni local test of `H_{H0}` has level `α ∈ [0, 1]` when the p-values in `H0` are valid.
nodes.title: Level of the Bonferroni local test

nodes.summary: For `α ≥ 0`, the hypotheses rejected by Holm's step-down procedure are exactly those rejected by the closed testing procedure built on the Bonferroni local tests.
nodes.title: Holm's procedure is a closed test
Permutation tests

nodes.summary: The permutation (group-invariance) p-value of the statistic `T` at `ω`: the fraction of group elements `g` with `T (g • ω) ≥ T ω`.
nodes.title: Permutation p-value

nodes.summary: Counting lemma: for any family of reals `t` indexed by `G` and any `k`, at most `k` elements `h` have rank count `#{g | t h ≤ t g}` at most `k`.
nodes.title: Counting lemma for rank counts

nodes.summary: Lehmann and Romano (2005), §15.2; Hemerik and Goeman (2018): if the law `μ` is invariant under the action of a finite group `G`, the permutation p-value of any measurable statistic is valid.
nodes.title: Validity of permutation p-values

nodes.summary: The Monte Carlo permutation p-value `(1 + #{b | T(g_b • ω) ≥ T(ω)}) / (B + 1)` of the statistic `T` at the data `ω` with the `B` drawn group elements `g`.
nodes.title: Monte Carlo permutation p-value

nodes.summary: Phipson and Smyth (2010); Hemerik and Goeman (2018): if the null law `μ` is invariant under a finite group `G` and `g₁, …, g_B` are drawn independently and uniformly from `G`, independently of the data, then `(1 + #{b | T(g_b • ω) ≥ T(ω)}) / (B + 1)` is a valid p-value under the joint law.
nodes.title: Validity of Monte Carlo permutation p-values
Two-groups model and local false discovery rates

nodes.summary: The two-groups model of Efron et al. (2001): prior null probability `π₀ ∈ [0, 1]`, null density `f₀` and non-null density `f₁` of the z-value (probability densities on `ℝ`).
nodes.title: Two-groups model

nodes.summary: The mixture density `f = π₀ f₀ + (1 - π₀) f₁` of the z-values.
nodes.title: Mixture density of the two-groups model

nodes.summary: The law `P₀` of a null z-value.
nodes.title: Law of a null z-value

nodes.summary: The law `P₁` of a non-null z-value.
nodes.title: Law of a non-null z-value

nodes.summary: Joint law of (null indicator, z-value) on `Bool × ℝ`; `true` means the case is null.
nodes.title: Joint law of null indicator and z-value

nodes.summary: Efron's local false discovery rate `fdr(z) = π₀ f₀(z) / f(z)` (zero where `f(z) = 0`).
nodes.title: Local false discovery rate

nodes.summary: The tail-area false discovery rate of a region `Γ`: `Fdr(Γ) = π₀ P₀(Γ) / P(Γ)`, written with the densities. Efron's `Fdr(z)` is `tailFdr (Set.Iic z)`. It is `0` when `P(Γ) = 0`.
nodes.title: Tail-area false discovery rate

nodes.summary: The mixture density is nonnegative.
nodes.title: Mixture density is nonnegative

nodes.summary: The null part of the mixture is dominated by the mixture: `π₀ f₀ ≤ f`.
nodes.title: Null part of the mixture is dominated by the mixture

nodes.summary: The mixture density is measurable.
nodes.title: Mixture density is measurable

nodes.summary: The mixture density is integrable.
nodes.title: Mixture density is integrable

nodes.summary: The local false discovery rate is measurable.
nodes.title: Local false discovery rate is measurable

nodes.summary: The basic identity `fdr(z) f(z) = π₀ f₀(z)`, for every `z` (where `f(z) = 0` both sides vanish because `π₀ f₀ ≤ f`).
nodes.title: Local fdr times mixture density equals the null part

nodes.summary: The local false discovery rate is nonnegative.
nodes.title: Local false discovery rate is nonnegative

nodes.summary: The local false discovery rate is at most one.
nodes.title: Local false discovery rate is at most one

nodes.summary: `P₀(A) = ∫_A f₀`.
nodes.title: Null law as the integral of the null density

nodes.summary: `P₁(A) = ∫_A f₁`.
nodes.title: Non-null law as the integral of the non-null density

nodes.summary: `P(H = 0, Z ∈ A) = π₀ P₀(A)`.
nodes.title: Joint probability of a null case in a set
Joint probability of a non-null case in a set

nodes.summary: The z-value has the mixture law: `P(Z ∈ A) = ∫_A f`.
nodes.title: z-value has the mixture law

nodes.summary: The law of the z-value under the joint law is the mixture `f · Lebesgue`.
nodes.title: Marginal z-value law of the joint law is the mixture

nodes.summary: Efron et al. (2001): `P(H = 0, Z ∈ A) = ∫_A fdr(z) dP_Z(z)` for every measurable `A`, so `fdr(Z)` is a version of the posterior null probability `P(H = 0 | Z)`.
nodes.title: Null probability as an integral of the local fdr

nodes.summary: Efron et al. (2001): `fdr(Z) = P(H = 0 | Z)` almost surely, as a conditional expectation of the null indicator given the z-value.
nodes.title: Local fdr is the posterior null probability

nodes.summary: `P(H = 0 | Z ∈ Γ) = Fdr(Γ)`: the tail-area false discovery rate is the posterior null probability given `Z ∈ Γ` (Storey 2002, Theorem 1; Efron 2010, ch. 2). Both sides are `0` when `P(Z ∈ Γ) = 0`.
nodes.title: Tail-area fdr is the posterior null probability given a region

nodes.summary: `E[fdr(Z) | Z ∈ Γ] = Fdr(Γ)`, written with densities: the tail-area false discovery rate is the `f`-weighted average of the local false discovery rate over `Γ` (Efron 2010, ch. 5).
nodes.title: Tail-area fdr is the average local fdr over the region

nodes.summary: The true-null set of an outcome vector `x : Fin m → Bool × Bool`, where `(x i).1` records that hypothesis `i` is null and `(x i).2` that it is rejected.
nodes.title: True-null set of a test outcome vector

nodes.summary: The rejection set of an outcome vector.
nodes.title: Rejection set of a test outcome vector

nodes.summary: The probability `∏ᵢ q(xᵢ)` of an outcome vector when the `m` (null, rejected) pairs are i.i.d. with law `q`.
nodes.title: Probability of a test outcome vector

nodes.summary: Storey's positive false discovery rate `pFDR = E[V / R | R > 0]` for `m` tests whose (null, rejected) indicator pairs are i.i.d. with law `q`: `V / R` is the false discovery proportion.
nodes.title: Storey's positive false discovery rate

nodes.summary: Storey (2002), Theorem 1: for `m ≥ 1` i.i.d. tests, `pFDR = P(H = 0 | T ∈ Γ)`, where `q (true, true) = P(H = 0, T ∈ Γ)` and `q (false, true) = P(H = 1, T ∈ Γ)`. The identity is homogeneous in `q`, so only `q ≥ 0` is assumed; when `P(T ∈ Γ) = 0` both sides are `0`.
nodes.title: Storey's theorem: pFDR is a posterior null probability

nodes.summary: The law of one test's (null, rejected) pair in the two-groups model when the test rejects iff its z-value lies in `Γ`.
nodes.title: Law of a test's null and rejection pair

nodes.summary: Storey (2002), Theorem 1, in the two-groups model: for `m ≥ 1` i.i.d. tests rejecting on `Γ`, `pFDR(Γ) = π₀ P₀(Γ) / P(Γ) = Fdr(Γ)`.
nodes.title: Storey's theorem in the two-groups model

nodes.summary: Storey's estimator `π̂₀(t) = #{i | pᵢ > t} / (m (1 - t))` of the proportion of true nulls, for a tuning parameter `t ∈ [0, 1)`.
nodes.title: Storey's estimator of the null proportion

nodes.summary: Conservative bias of Storey's (2002) estimator for a fixed set `H0` of true nulls: if their p-values are valid, then `E[π̂₀(t)] ≥ m₀ / m` for every `t ∈ [0, 1)`. No independence is assumed; the non-null p-values are arbitrary measurable functions.
nodes.title: Conservative bias of Storey's null proportion estimator

nodes.summary: Storey's (2003) q-value for a nested family of rejection regions `Γ_s = {T ≤ s}` with `pFDR(Γ_s) = pfdr s`: `q(t) = inf_{s ≥ t} pfdr s`, the smallest pFDR over the regions that contain the observed statistic `t`.
nodes.title: Storey's q-value

nodes.summary: The q-value is at most the pFDR of the smallest region containing the statistic.
nodes.title: q-value is at most the pFDR of the smallest region

nodes.summary: The q-value is monotone in the statistic.
nodes.title: q-value is monotone in the statistic

nodes.summary: When the pFDR is nondecreasing along the nested regions, the q-value is the pFDR.
nodes.title: q-value equals the pFDR when the pFDR is monotone

nodes.summary: Multivariate normal theory and linear models: Gaussian maximum likelihood, Cochran's theorem on quadratic forms, t and F sampling laws, Gauss–Markov and generalized least squares, principal component analysis, and Gaussian graphical models. Ridge and lasso regression are under least squares, ridge and lasso regression, and probabilistic principal component analysis, with the factor-analysis marginal, under…
nodes.title: Linear models and multivariate analysis

nodes.summary: Let $X$ be a real $m \times n$ matrix such that $X^\top X$ is invertible, and let $B = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top$. Then $BX = I_n$, and for every real $n \times m$ matrix $A$ with $AX = I_n$ the matrix $AA^\top - BB^\top$ is positive semidefinite.
nodes.title: Gauss–Markov covariance minimality
Cochran's theorem

nodes.summary: Rank criterion (Cochran 1934): square matrices `A k` over a field that sum to the identity have ranks adding up to the size iff they are idempotent and pairwise annihilating.
nodes.title: Rank criterion

nodes.summary: Under the standard Gaussian law, orthogonal projections onto pairwise orthogonal subspaces are mutually independent.
nodes.title: Independence of orthogonal projections of a standard Gaussian

nodes.summary: Under the standard Gaussian law, the squared lengths `‖P_{K k} Z‖²` of the projections onto pairwise orthogonal subspaces are mutually independent.
nodes.title: Independence of squared lengths of orthogonal Gaussian projections

nodes.summary: The mean of the observations `x i` with `grp i = g` (`0` for an empty group).
nodes.title: Group mean of observations

nodes.summary: For i.i.d. `N(μ, v)` observations `xᵢ` labelled by groups `grp i`, the vector of group means is independent of the vector of within-group residuals `xᵢ - x̄_{grp i}`.
nodes.title: Gaussian one-way layout

nodes.summary: For i.i.d. `N(μ, v)` observations labelled by groups, the between-group sum of squares `∑ᵢ (x̄_{grp i} - x̄)²` is independent of the within-group sum of squares `∑ᵢ (xᵢ - x̄_{grp i})²`.
nodes.title: One-way analysis of variance

nodes.summary: For an i.i.d. sample `X₁, …, Xₙ ~ N(μ, v)` with `n ≥ 1`, the sample mean has the law `N(μ, v / n)`.
nodes.title: Law of the Gaussian sample mean

nodes.summary: Cochran's theorem, independence part: if `Z` has independent standard normal coordinates and symmetric matrices `A k` sum to the identity with ranks adding up to the dimension, the quadratic forms `Zᵀ (A k) Z` are mutually independent.
nodes.title: Cochran's theorem

nodes.summary: For an i.i.d. sample `X₁, …, Xₙ ~ N(μ, v)`, the sample mean is independent of the residual vector `(Xᵢ - X̄)ᵢ`.
nodes.title: Independence of the Gaussian sample mean and residuals

nodes.summary: For an i.i.d. sample `X₁, …, Xₙ ~ N(μ, v)`, the sample mean `X̄` is independent of the sum of squared deviations `∑ (Xᵢ - X̄)² = (n - 1) S²`.
nodes.title: Independence of the Gaussian sample mean and sum of squared deviations

nodes.summary: For independent standard normal coordinates, the sum of the squares of the coordinates in a nonempty finite set `s` has the chi-square law with `|s|` degrees of freedom.
nodes.title: Sum of squares of independent standard normals is chi-square

nodes.summary: Coordinates of the standard Gaussian law in an orthonormal basis `b`: the sum of the squared coordinates `⟪b i, x⟫` over a nonempty set `s` of indices is chi-square with `|s|` degrees of freedom.
nodes.title: Squared orthonormal coordinates of a standard Gaussian are chi-square

nodes.summary: Cochran's theorem, projection form: for the standard Gaussian law on a finite-dimensional real inner product space `E` and a subspace `K` of positive dimension, the squared norm of the orthogonal projection onto `K` is chi-square with `dim K` degrees of freedom.
nodes.title: Cochran's theorem

nodes.summary: Cochran's theorem, matrix form: if `Z` has independent standard normal coordinates and `A` is a symmetric idempotent matrix of positive rank, the quadratic form `Zᵀ A Z` is chi-square with `rank A` degrees of freedom.
nodes.title: Cochran's theorem
Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem

nodes.summary: Frisch–Waugh–Lovell for weighted least squares with a symmetric weight matrix `W`: if `(b, t)` solves the normal equations of the regression of `y` on `[A | z]` and `z⊥ = z - A u` is the weighted residual of `z` on `A` (`Aᵀ W z⊥ = 0`), then `t ⟪z⊥, z⊥⟫_W = ⟪z⊥, y⟫_W`, where `⟪x, y⟫_W = x ⬝ᵥ W y`.
nodes.title: Frisch–Waugh–Lovell

nodes.summary: Under the hypotheses of `frischWaughLovell`, if also `y⊥ = y - A v` is the weighted residual of `y` on `A` (`Aᵀ W y⊥ = 0`), then `t ⟪z⊥, z⊥⟫_W = ⟪z⊥, y⊥⟫_W`: the coefficient of `z` in the full regression is the coefficient of the regression of the residualized response on the residualized regressor.
nodes.title: Frisch–Waugh–Lovell, residualized form

nodes.summary: Under the hypotheses of `frischWaughLovell_residual`, if `⟪z⊥, z⊥⟫_W ≠ 0` then `t = ⟪z⊥, y⊥⟫_W / ⟪z⊥, z⊥⟫_W`.
nodes.title: Frisch–Waugh–Lovell, solved form
Gaussian graphical models

nodes.summary: For positive definite `S` on `ι ⊕ κ`, `S₁₁ - S₁₂ S₂₂⁻¹ S₂₁ = ((S⁻¹)₁₁)⁻¹`.
nodes.title: The conditional covariance is the inverse of a precision block

nodes.summary: The partial correlation of coordinates `0` and `1` given the `κ`-block, computed from the conditional covariance `C = S₁₁ - S₁₂ S₂₂⁻¹ S₂₁`: `C₀₁ / √(C₀₀ C₁₁)`.
nodes.title: Partial correlation from the conditional covariance

nodes.summary: The partial correlation from the precision matrix: `ρ₁₂·rest = -Ω₀₁ / √(Ω₀₀ Ω₁₁)`.
nodes.title: Partial correlation from the precision matrix

nodes.summary: The `κ`-block (the conditioning coordinates) of a vector on `Fin 2 ⊕ κ`.
nodes.title: Conditioning block of a vector

nodes.summary: The `κ`-block is a measurable function of the vector.
nodes.title: Measurability of the conditioning block

nodes.summary: If `V = (X₀, X₁, Y) ~ N(μ, S)` with `S` positive definite, then `X₀` and `X₁` are conditionally independent given `Y` iff `(S⁻¹)₀₁ = 0`. (The standard Borel sample space is the setting of Mathlib's conditional independence.)
nodes.title: Pairwise Markov property of Gaussian vectors

nodes.summary: The sample second-moment matrix `m⁻¹ ∑ₛ xₛ xₛᵀ` of `m` observations in `ℝ^ι`.
nodes.title: Sample second-moment matrix

nodes.summary: The quadratic forms of a sample add up to `m · tr (S K)`.
nodes.title: Sum of sample quadratic forms as a trace

nodes.summary: The Gaussian log-likelihood objective `log det K - tr (S K)` of a precision matrix `K`.
nodes.title: Gaussian log-likelihood of a precision matrix

nodes.summary: A matrix vanishes off the edges of `G`: `K i j = 0` for distinct non-adjacent `i, j`.
nodes.title: Matrix supported on the edges of a graph

nodes.summary: Dempster's covariance-selection MLE (sufficiency): a positive definite `K̂` supported on `G` whose inverse agrees with `S` on the diagonal and the edges maximizes `log det K - tr (S K)` over positive definite `K` supported on `G`.
nodes.title: Dempster's covariance-selection MLE

nodes.summary: Under the hypotheses of `gaussLogLik_le_of_inv_eq_on_graph`, a positive definite `K` supported on `G` with the same objective value is `K̂`.
nodes.title: Uniqueness of Dempster's MLE
Generalized least squares

nodes.summary: The generalized least-squares matrix `(Xᵀ V⁻¹ X)⁻¹ Xᵀ V⁻¹`; `glsMatrix X V *ᵥ y` is the GLS estimate of `b` in `y = X b + e` with `Cov e = V`.
nodes.title: Generalized least-squares matrix

nodes.summary: The GLS estimator is unbiased: `B X = 1` when `Xᵀ V⁻¹ X` is invertible.
nodes.title: Unbiasedness of the generalized least-squares estimator

nodes.summary: The covariance of the GLS estimator: `B V Bᵀ = (Xᵀ V⁻¹ X)⁻¹`.
nodes.title: Covariance of the generalized least-squares estimator

nodes.summary: The GLS estimator has minimal covariance among linear unbiased estimators: for every `A` with `A X = 1`, `A V Aᵀ - B V Bᵀ` is positive semidefinite, where `B = glsMatrix X V`.
nodes.title: Aitken's theorem
Principal component analysis

nodes.summary: The sample mean of column `j` of an `n × p` data matrix (rows are observations). For `n = 0` it is the junk value `0`.
nodes.title: Sample mean of a data matrix column

nodes.summary: The column-centered data matrix `X i j - x̄ⱼ`.
nodes.title: Column-centered data matrix

nodes.summary: The unbiased sample covariance matrix `(n - 1)⁻¹ (X - x̄)ᵀ (X - x̄)` of an `n × p` data matrix. The divisor needs `2 ≤ n`; for `n = 1` the factor is the junk value `(0 : ℝ)⁻¹ = 0` (and for `n = 0` the product is the zero matrix).
nodes.title: Unbiased sample covariance matrix

nodes.summary: The principal-component scores `(X - x̄) w` of the observations along a direction `w`.
nodes.title: Principal component scores

nodes.summary: The centered columns sum to zero (for at least one observation).
nodes.title: Centered columns sum to zero

nodes.summary: Entries of the sample covariance matrix: `Sⱼₖ = (n - 1)⁻¹ ∑ᵢ (Xᵢⱼ - x̄ⱼ)(Xᵢₖ - x̄ₖ)`.
nodes.title: Entries of the sample covariance matrix

nodes.summary: The sample covariance matrix is symmetric.
nodes.title: Sample covariance matrix is symmetric

nodes.summary: The sample covariance matrix is positive semidefinite (for every `n`).
nodes.title: Sample covariance matrix is positive semidefinite

nodes.summary: The trace of the sample covariance matrix is the total sample variance, the sum of the column sample variances.
nodes.title: Trace of the sample covariance is the total sample variance

nodes.summary: The scores along any direction have sample mean zero.
nodes.title: Principal component scores have sample mean zero

nodes.summary: The sample variance of the scores along `w` is the quadratic form `wᵀ S w`.
nodes.title: Sample variance of scores is a quadratic form

nodes.summary: The eigenvalues `λ₀ ≥ λ₁ ≥ ⋯ ≥ λ_{p-1}` of a real symmetric `p × p` matrix, in decreasing order (Mathlib's `LinearMap.IsSymmetric.eigenvalues` of `Matrix.toEuclideanLin S`).
nodes.title: Eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix in decreasing order

nodes.summary: An orthonormal eigenbasis of a real symmetric matrix, ordered to match `orderedEigenvalues`; for a covariance matrix these are the principal axes.
nodes.title: Ordered orthonormal eigenbasis of a symmetric matrix

nodes.summary: The Rayleigh quotient `wᵀ S w / wᵀ w` of a real matrix (junk value `0` at `w = 0`).
nodes.title: Rayleigh quotient of a matrix

nodes.summary: The ordered eigenvalues are decreasing.
nodes.title: Ordered eigenvalues are decreasing

nodes.summary: The `k`-th basis vector is an eigenvector for the `k`-th eigenvalue.
nodes.title: Ordered eigenbasis vectors are eigenvectors

nodes.summary: The quadratic form expanded in the ordered eigenbasis: `xᵀ S x = ∑ λᵢ ⟪vᵢ, x⟫²`.
nodes.title: Quadratic form expanded in the ordered eigenbasis

nodes.summary: The ordered eigenvalues sum to the trace.
nodes.title: Ordered eigenvalues sum to the trace

nodes.summary: The eigenvalues of a positive semidefinite matrix are nonnegative.
nodes.title: Eigenvalues of a positive semidefinite matrix are nonnegative

nodes.summary: The Rayleigh quotient of the `k`-th eigenvector is the `k`-th eigenvalue.
nodes.title: Rayleigh quotient of an eigenvector is its eigenvalue

nodes.summary: On nonzero directions orthogonal to the first `k` eigenvectors, the Rayleigh quotient is at most the `k`-th eigenvalue; the bound is attained at the `k`-th eigenvector (`rayleigh_orderedEigenbasis`).
nodes.title: Hotelling's characterization of the principal axes

nodes.summary: Dual of `rayleigh_le_of_orthogonal`: on nonzero directions orthogonal to the eigenvectors after index `k`, the Rayleigh quotient is at least the `k`-th eigenvalue.
nodes.title: Lower bound on the Rayleigh quotient for orthogonal directions

nodes.summary: Every subspace of dimension `p - k` contains a nonzero vector whose Rayleigh quotient is at least `λₖ`.
nodes.title: Courant–Fischer min–max, matrix form

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a measurable space, $W : S \to \mathbb{R}$ an estimator, $\mu$ a probability measure on $S$ for which $W$ is integrable, and $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ a target. Likelihood and maximum likelihood estimators

nodes.summary: Let $\Omega$ be a measurable space with a measure $\mu$ and let $\Theta$ be a set of parameters. A normalized density family on $\Omega$ indexed by $\Theta$ with dominating measure $\mu$ consists of a function $f_\theta : \Omega \to [0, \infty]$ for each $\theta \in \Theta$ such that $f_\theta$ is $\mu$-almost everywhere measurable and $\int_\Omega f_\theta \, d\mu = 1$.
nodes.title: Normalized density family

nodes.summary: Let $F$ and $G$ be normalized density families on a measurable space $\Omega$ with the same parameter set $\Theta$ and the same dominating measure $\mu$. If for every $\theta \in \Theta$ and every $x \in \Omega$ the density of $F$ at $\theta$ and the density of $G$ at $\theta$ take the same value at $x$, then $F = G$.
nodes.title: Normalized density families are determined by their densities

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a normalized density family on a measurable space $\Omega$ with parameter set $\Theta$, dominating measure $\mu$ and densities $f_\theta$. The population law at $\theta \in \Theta$ is the measure $P_\theta$ on $\Omega$ with density $f_\theta$ with respect to $\mu$, so that $P_\theta(A) = \int_A f_\theta \, d\mu$ for every measurable set $A \subseteq \Omega$.
nodes.title: Population law

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a normalized density family on $\Omega$ with parameter set $\Theta$, dominating measure $\mu$ and densities $f_\theta$. For every $\theta \in \Theta$, the population law $P_\theta$, the measure with density $f_\theta$ with respect to $\mu$, is a probability measure.
nodes.title: Population laws are probability measures

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a normalized density family on $\Omega$ with parameter set $\Theta$ and densities $f_\theta$ for $\theta \in \Theta$. For a sample size $n$, a parameter $\theta \in \Theta$ and a sample $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}) \in \Omega^n$, the iid likelihood of $\theta$ at $x$ is $L_n(\theta; x) = \prod_{i < n} f_\theta(x_i)$, a value in $[0, \infty]$. For $n = 0$ this is the empty product $1$.
nodes.title: Likelihood of an iid sample

nodes.summary: For a normalized density family $F$, every parameter $\theta$ and the empty sample $x$ (sample size $n = 0$), the iid likelihood of $\theta$ at $x$ equals $1$, the empty product.
nodes.title: Likelihood of the empty sample

A map $\hat\theta$ from $\Omega^n$ to $\Theta$ is a maximum likelihood estimator for samples of size $n$ if for every sample $x \in \Omega^n$ the parameter $\hat\theta(x)$ maximizes…

Then $\hat\theta$ is a maximum likelihood estimator for samples of size $n$ if and only if $L_n(\theta; x) \le L_n(\hat\theta(x); x)$ for every sample…

nodes.summary: For `X ~ N(μ, v)` and an everywhere differentiable `g` with integrable derivative, `(X - μ) g(X)` is integrable and `E[(X - μ) g(X)] = v E[g'(X)]`. For `v = 0` both sides vanish.

Unlike the one-dimensional case, this integrability does not follow from that of `dh`: `h(x) = exp(x₁²)` has `∂₀ h = 0` but `x₀ h(x)` is…

nodes.summary: For `X ~ N(θ, I_p)` and an estimator `X + g(X)` whose coordinates `gᵢ` are square integrable and satisfy the hypotheses of Stein's lemma in the `i`-th coordinate with partial derivative `dgᵢ`, the quadratic risk is `p + E[∑ gᵢ(X)² + 2 ∑ dgᵢ(X)]`.

nodes.summary: The James–Stein estimator `δ(x) = (1 - (p - 2) / ‖x‖²) x` of the mean of `N(θ, I_p)`. At `x = 0` the factor is `1` by Lean's `a / 0 = 0` convention, so `δ(0) = 0`.

Sufficient statistics and the factorization theorem

nodes.summary: A sub-σ-algebra `m` is *sufficient* for the family of measures `P` on `(Ω, m₀)` if `m ≤ m₀`, every `P θ` is finite, and for every `m₀`-measurable set `s` one `m`-measurable function is a version of the conditional probability `P_θ[1_s | m]` under every `P θ`. Bundling `m ≤ m₀` and finiteness into the predicate means an `IsSufficient` hypothesis itself represents a sufficient sub-σ-algebra for statistical laws: the…
nodes.title: Sufficient sub-σ-algebra

nodes.summary: If `m` is sufficient for a family of probability measures, every `m₀`-measurable real function `W` that is integrable under all the measures has one `m`-measurable version of the conditional expectation `P_θ[W | m]` for every `θ`. (Measurability of `W` itself, not only under each `P θ`, is what lets one approximating sequence serve every parameter.)
nodes.title: Common conditional expectation under a sufficient σ-algebra

nodes.summary: Factorization implies sufficiency (Halmos–Savage, the sufficiency half). If every `P θ` has a density `g θ` with respect to one measure `ν` that is σ-finite on `m`, and each `g θ` is `m`-measurable, then `m` is sufficient for `P`.
nodes.title: Factorization implies sufficiency

nodes.summary: Factorization criterion, sufficiency direction, for a statistic, under an extra σ-finiteness hypothesis. If `dP_θ/dμ = g_θ(T) · h` with `g_θ` and `h` measurable and `h · μ` σ-finite on the σ-algebra generated by `T`, then `T` is sufficient for `P`.
nodes.title: Factorization criterion, sufficiency direction, for a statistic, under an extra σ-finiteness hypothesis

nodes.summary: A statistic `T : X → τ` is *sufficient* for the discrete family `P : Θ → PMF X` if the conditional probability `P θ x / P_θ(T = T x)` of `x` given `T = T x` is the same under any two parameters `θ, θ'` for which `{T = T x}` has positive probability. Here `P_θ(T = t) = (P θ).map T t`.
nodes.title: Sufficient statistic for a discrete family

nodes.summary: If `T` is sufficient for `P`, then `P θ x = g θ (T x) * h x` with `g θ t = P_θ(T = t)` and a parameter-free `h` with values in `[0, 1]`.
nodes.title: Factorization, necessity

nodes.summary: If `P θ x = g θ (T x) * h x` for nonnegative real `g`, `h` with `h` free of `θ`, then `T` is sufficient for `P`.
nodes.title: Factorization, sufficiency

nodes.summary: The Fisher–Neyman factorization theorem (discrete case). A statistic `T` is sufficient for the family of mass functions `P` if and only if there are nonnegative functions `g` and `h`, with `h` free of the parameter, such that `P θ x = g θ (T x) * h x` for every `θ`, `x`.
nodes.title: The Fisher–Neyman factorization theorem

nodes.summary: If the family of probability measures `P` is dominated by a σ-finite measure `μ` and the statistic `T` is sufficient for `P`, then the densities factor as `dP_θ/dμ = g_θ(T) · h` with measurable `g_θ` and `h`, `h` free of `θ`.
nodes.title: Halmos–Savage factorization, necessity

nodes.summary: For a convex loss `L`, `L ∘ μ[W | m]` is integrable whenever `W` and `L ∘ W` are.
nodes.title: Integrability of a convex loss of a conditional expectation

nodes.summary: For `W` with a finite second moment and any target `c`, `E (W - c)² = E (μ[W | m] - c)² + E (W - μ[W | m])²`. This is the Pythagorean identity `MeasureTheory.integral_sq_sub_eq_integral_sq_sub_condExp_add` with the constant predictor `fun _ => c`, with the two summands commuted; it is not a second Pythagorean proof.
nodes.title: Squared-error decomposition

nodes.summary: Conditioning leaves the squared-error risk at `c` unchanged if and only if `W` already equals `μ[W | m]` almost everywhere.
nodes.title: Equality case under squared error

nodes.summary: Let `m` be sufficient for the family of probability measures `P`, and let `W` be a measurable estimator that is integrable under every `P θ`. There is one parameter-free `m`-measurable estimator `η`, a version of `P_θ[W | m]` for every `θ`, with the same mean as `W` under every `θ` and no larger risk under every loss `ℓ θ` that is convex in the estimate (for which `ℓ θ ∘ W` is integrable).
nodes.title: The Rao–Blackwell theorem

nodes.summary: If the statistic `T` is sufficient for `P` and `W` is a measurable estimator with finite second moment under every `P θ`, there is a measurable `φ` such that `φ ∘ T` is a version of every `E_θ[W | T]`, has the same mean as `W`, and for every target `τ θ` satisfies `E_θ (W - τ θ)² = E_θ (φ(T) - τ θ)² + E_θ (W - φ(T))²`.
nodes.title: The Rao–Blackwell theorem for a sufficient statistic
