nodes.summary: Let $X_0, X_1, X_2, \dots$ be real-valued functions on a set $\Omega$. For a natural number $n$, a point $\omega \in \Omega$ and a real number $x$, the empirical count is the number of indices $i \in \{0, 1, \dots, n\}$ with $X_i(\omega) \le x$. Divided by $n + 1$, it is the value at $x$ of the empirical distribution function of $X_0(\omega), \dots, X_n(\omega)$.

Write $F(x) = P(X_0 \le x)$ for the distribution function of $X_0$, and $C_n(\omega, x)$ for the empirical count, the number of indices $i \in \{0, 1, \dots, n\}$ with $X_i(\omega) \le x$.…

Potential outcomes and causal identification

nodes.summary: The mean of `y` over a set of units `S`, `(1/|S|) ∑_{i ∈ S} yᵢ` (the junk value `0` for `S = ∅`).
nodes.title: Sample mean over a set of units

nodes.summary: The sample variance of `y` over `S` with divisor `|S| - 1`; meaningful for `|S| ≥ 2` (for `|S| ≤ 1` it is the junk value `0`).
nodes.title: Sample variance over a set of units

nodes.summary: The mean of a finite population of `N = Fintype.card ι` units, `(1/N) ∑ᵢ yᵢ`.
nodes.title: Mean of a finite population

nodes.summary: The variance of a finite population with divisor `N - 1`, `S² = ∑ᵢ (yᵢ - ȳ)² / (N - 1)`; meaningful for `N ≥ 2`.
nodes.title: Variance of a finite population

nodes.summary: The finite-population average treatment effect `(1/N) ∑ᵢ (y₁ᵢ - y₀ᵢ)`.
nodes.title: Finite-population average treatment effect

nodes.summary: The difference in means for the treated set `S`: the mean of the treated outcomes `y₁` over `S` minus the mean of the control outcomes `y₀` over the complement.
nodes.title: Difference-in-means estimator

nodes.summary: Neyman's variance estimator `s₁² / n₁ + s₀² / n₀` for the treated set `S`.
nodes.title: Neyman's variance estimator

nodes.summary: The expectation of a statistic `f` of the treated set under complete randomization: the treated set is uniform among the `(N choose n₁)` sets of `n₁` units (`n₁ ≤ N`; for `n₁ > N` there is no such set and the value is `0`).
nodes.title: Expectation of a statistic under complete randomization

nodes.summary: Under complete randomization with `n₁ ≥ 1` treated and `n₀ ≥ 1` control units, the difference in means is unbiased for the finite-population average treatment effect.
nodes.title: Neyman (1923)

nodes.summary: The variance of the difference in means under complete randomization is `S₁²/n₁ + S₀²/n₀ - S_τ²/N`, where `S_τ²` is the population variance of the unit-level effects `τᵢ = y₁ᵢ - y₀ᵢ` and `n₀ = N - n₁`.
nodes.title: Neyman (1923)

nodes.summary: The expectation of Neyman's variance estimator under complete randomization with at least two treated and two control units is `S₁²/n₁ + S₀²/n₀` (the sample variances are unbiased for the population variances under sampling without replacement).
nodes.title: Expectation of Neyman's variance estimator under complete randomization

nodes.summary: Its expectation under complete randomization is at least the variance of the difference in means, with equality exactly when the treatment effect `y₁ᵢ - y₀ᵢ` is the same for all units.
nodes.title: Neyman's variance estimator is conservative

nodes.summary: The observed outcome: `Y₁` on the treated event `T`, `Y₀` off it (consistency).
nodes.title: Observed outcome from potential outcomes

nodes.summary: The propensity of the event `T` given `W = w`, `P(T ∩ {W = w}) / P(W = w)`. Meaningful for `P(W = w) > 0`; it is `0` (a junk value) when `P(W = w) = 0`.
nodes.title: Propensity score

nodes.summary: The event `T` is conditionally independent of `V` given `W`, stated through the values of `W`: `P(T, V ∈ B, W = w) P(W = w) = P(T, W = w) P(V ∈ B, W = w)` for all measurable `B` and all `w`. For a `W` with countably many values this is the conditional independence of the indicator of `T` and `V` given `W`.
nodes.title: Conditional independence given a discrete variable

nodes.summary: Strong ignorability of the treatment `T` given `W` for the potential outcomes `V` (Rosenbaum & Rubin 1983): `T ⊥ V | W` and overlap, `0 < P(T | W = w) < 1` for every value `w` of positive probability.
nodes.title: Strong ignorability

nodes.summary: Strong ignorability is inherited by measurable functions of the potential outcomes.
nodes.title: Strong ignorability passes to functions of the potential outcomes

nodes.summary: The propensity score `e(X) = P(T | X)` is a balancing score: given `e(X)`, the treatment is conditionally independent of the covariate `X`.
nodes.title: Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983), Theorem 1

nodes.summary: The propensity score is calibrated: among units with score `c` (an event of positive probability), the proportion treated is `c`.
nodes.title: Calibration of the propensity score

nodes.summary: A function `b(X)` of the covariate is a balancing score (`T ⊥ X | b(X)`) if and only if it is finer than the propensity score: covariate values of positive probability with the same `b` have the same propensity. (Theorem 1 is the case `b = e`.)
nodes.title: Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983), Theorem 2

nodes.summary: If treatment assignment is strongly ignorable given the covariate `X`, it is strongly ignorable given any balancing score `b(X)`.
nodes.title: Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983), Theorem 3

nodes.summary: Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983), Theorem 3 for the propensity score: if treatment assignment is strongly ignorable given the covariate `X`, it is strongly ignorable given `e(X)`.
nodes.title: Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983), Theorem 3

nodes.summary: Inverse probability weighting (Horvitz & Thompson 1952; Rosenbaum 1987): under strong ignorability of `T` given a finitely-valued covariate `X` for the treated potential outcome `Y₁`, `E[1_T Y / e(X)] = E[Y₁]`, where `Y` is the observed outcome.
nodes.title: Inverse probability weighting

nodes.summary: Inverse probability weighting, control arm: under strong ignorability of `T` given `X` for `Y₀`, `E[1_{Tᶜ} Y / (1 - e(X))] = E[Y₀]`.
nodes.title: Inverse probability weighting

nodes.summary: Under strong ignorability of `T` given a finitely-valued `X` for the pair `(Y₀, Y₁)`, `E[1_T Y / e(X) - 1_{Tᶜ} Y / (1 - e(X))] = E[Y₁ - Y₀]`.
nodes.title: Identification of the average treatment effect by inverse probability weighting

nodes.summary: Let the covariate information be a sub-σ-algebra `m` (for example the one generated by `X`), and `e = P(T | m)` the propensity score. If `Y₁` is integrable, the treatment is mean-ignorable for `Y₁`, `E[1_T Y₁ | m] = e E[Y₁ | m]` (implied by `Y₁ ⊥ T | m`), and overlap holds in the strong form `e ≥ ε > 0`, then `E[1_T Y / e] = E[Y₁]` for the observed outcome `Y`.
nodes.title: Inverse probability weighting with a general covariate

nodes.summary: The U-statistic with kernel `h` of degree `m` on a sample `x` of size `n`: the average of `h (x ∘ f)` over the `n.descFactorial m` injective maps `f : Fin m ↪ Fin n`. For `m > n` there are no such maps and the value is `0` (Lean's `a / 0 = 0`).
nodes.title: U-statistic

nodes.summary: Hoeffding's `c`-th projection of a kernel `h` of degree `m` under `μ`: `h_c(y) = E h(y₁, …, y_c, X_{c+1}, …, X_m)` with `X_{c+1}, …, X_m` i.i.d. `μ`.
nodes.title: Hoeffding projection of a kernel

nodes.summary: For an i.i.d. sample of size `n ≥ m` and an integrable kernel, the U-statistic has mean `E h(X₁, …, X_m)`.
nodes.title: Unbiasedness

nodes.summary: Hoeffding's variance formula (1948, §5): for an i.i.d. sample of size `n ≥ m` and a symmetric square-integrable kernel `h` of degree `m`, `Var U = C(n, m)⁻¹ ∑_{c=1}^{m} C(m, c) C(n - m, m - c) Var h_c`.
nodes.title: Hoeffding's variance formula

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a measurable space. A set $A \subseteq S^{\mathbb{N}}$ is an exchangeable (or permutable) event if it is measurable for the product σ-algebra and $\{x : x \circ \sigma \in A\} = A$ for every permutation $\sigma$ of $\mathbb{N}$ that moves only finitely many indices.
nodes.title: Exchangeable event

nodes.summary: Let $\Omega$ and $S$ be measurable spaces and let $X_0, X_1, \ldots : \Omega \to S$ be a sequence of maps. An event $E \subseteq \Omega$ is exchangeable with respect to $(X_n)$ if there is an exchangeable event $A \subseteq S^{\mathbb{N}}$ such that $E = \{\omega \in \Omega : (X_n(\omega))_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \in A\}$.

nodes.summary: Let $\Omega$ and $S$ be measurable spaces and let $X_0, X_1, \ldots : \Omega \to S$ be measurable maps. If $E \subseteq \Omega$ is exchangeable with respect to $(X_n)$, then $E$ is measurable.

If an event $E \subseteq \Omega$ is exchangeable with respect to $(X_n)$, then $\mu(E) = 0$ or $\mu(E) = 1$.

Then $\mu_f$ is a probability measure, $\mu_f((a, b]) = f(b) - f(a)$ for all real $a \le b$, and every finite measure $\nu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ with $\nu((a, b]) = f(b) - f(a)$ for all…

Then there is exactly one measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ that is a probability measure and satisfies $\mu((a, b]) = f(b) - f(a)$ for all real $a \le b$.

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\alpha$ and let $X : \alpha \to \beta$ and $Y : \alpha \to \Omega$ be maps. A kernel $\kappa$ from $\beta$ to $\Omega$ is a regular conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X$ under $\mu$ if $X$ and $Y$ are measurable, $\kappa$ is a Markov kernel, and for every measurable set $s \subseteq \Omega$ the real-valued function $a \mapsto \kappa(X(a))(s)$ is $\mu$-almost everywhere equal to the…
nodes.title: Regular conditional distribution (kernel form)

nodes.summary: Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty standard Borel space, $\mu$ a finite measure on $\alpha$, and $X : \alpha \to \beta$, $Y : \alpha \to \Omega$ measurable maps. Then the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X$ under $\mu$, the kernel from $\beta$ to $\Omega$ obtained by disintegrating the joint law of $(X, Y)$ under $\mu$, is a regular conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X$ under $\mu$.
nodes.title: The conditional distribution kernel is a regular conditional distribution

nodes.summary: Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty standard Borel space, $\mu$ a finite measure on $\alpha$, and $X : \alpha \to \beta$, $Y : \alpha \to \Omega$ measurable maps. Then there exists a kernel $\kappa$ from $\beta$ to $\Omega$ that is a regular conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X$ under $\mu$; in particular $\kappa$ is a Markov kernel.

nodes.summary: Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty standard Borel space, $\mu$ a finite measure on a measurable space $(\alpha, \mathcal{F})$, $\mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{F}$ a sub-σ-algebra, and $Y : \alpha \to \Omega$ an $\mathcal{F}$-measurable map. Then some family of measures on $\Omega$ indexed by $\alpha$ is a measure-valued regular conditional distribution of $Y$ given $\mathcal{G}$ under $\mu$.

nodes.summary: Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty standard Borel space, $\mu$ a finite measure on $\alpha$, and $X : \alpha \to \beta$, $Y : \alpha \to \Omega$ measurable maps. Then some family of measures on $\Omega$ indexed by $\alpha$ is a measure-valued regular conditional distribution of $Y$ given the σ-algebra $\sigma(X)$ on $\alpha$ generated by $X$, under $\mu$.

nodes.summary: Let $X$ and $Y$ be measurable real random variables on a probability space. If $X$ and $Y$ are independent and $X + Y$ has a Gaussian law, then $X$ and $Y$ each have a Gaussian law. Here a Gaussian law may be degenerate, that is, a point mass.
nodes.title: Cramér's decomposition theorem

nodes.summary: Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$, let $(\mu_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of probability measures on the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$, and let $\varphi : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{C}$. Suppose that for every $t \in \mathbb{R}^d$ the characteristic functions $\hat\mu_n$ of the $\mu_n$ satisfy $\hat\mu_n(t) \to \varphi(t)$ as $n \to \infty$, and that $\varphi$ is continuous at $0$. Then there is a probability measure…
nodes.title: Lévy's continuity theorem
Bochner's theorem

nodes.summary: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$. Then $f$ is continuous, satisfies $f(0) = 1$, and is positive definite, meaning that for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, all points $x_1, \dots, x_n \in \mathbb{R}$ and all coefficients $c_1, \dots, c_n \in \mathbb{C}$ the sum $S = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \overline{c_i}\, c_j\, f(x_i - x_j)$ is a nonnegative real number, if and only if there is a Borel probability measure $\mu$…
nodes.title: Bochner's theorem

nodes.summary: A function $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ is positive definite when for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, all $t_1, \dots, t_n \in \mathbb{R}$ and all $z_1, \dots, z_n \in \mathbb{C}$, the sum $S = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \varphi(t_i - t_j) \, z_i \, \overline{z_j}$ is real and nonnegative, that is, $\operatorname{Im} S = 0$ and $\operatorname{Re} S \ge 0$.
nodes.title: Positive definite functions

nodes.summary: A function $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is positive definite when its composition with the inclusion $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ is positive definite, that is, when for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, all $t_1, \dots, t_n \in \mathbb{R}$ and all $z_1, \dots, z_n \in \mathbb{C}$, the sum $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \varphi(t_i - t_j) \, z_i \, \overline{z_j}$ is a nonnegative real number.
nodes.title: Positive definite real-valued functions

nodes.summary: A function $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ is a characteristic function when there is a probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ whose characteristic function equals $\varphi$, that is, $\int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{itx} \, d\mu(x) = \varphi(t)$ for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$.
nodes.title: Characteristic functions

nodes.summary: A function $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a real-valued characteristic function when its composition with the inclusion $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ is a characteristic function, that is, when there is a probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ with $\int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{itx} \, d\mu(x) = \varphi(t)$ for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$.
nodes.title: Real-valued characteristic functions

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ be the characteristic function of a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$. Then $\varphi$ is continuous, positive definite, and satisfies $\varphi(0) = 1$.
nodes.title: Forward direction of Bochner's theorem

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$ with characteristic function $\varphi_\mu(t) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{itx} \, d\mu(x)$. Then $\varphi_\mu$ is positive definite: for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, all $t_1, \dots, t_n \in \mathbb{R}$ and all $z_1, \dots, z_n \in \mathbb{C}$, the sum $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \varphi_\mu(t_i - t_j) \, z_i \, \overline{z_j}$ is a nonnegative real number.
nodes.title: Characteristic functions are positive definite

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a real-valued characteristic function, that is, a function whose composition with the inclusion $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ is the characteristic function of a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$. Then $\varphi$ is continuous, $\varphi$ is positive definite in the sense that its composition with the inclusion $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ is positive definite, and…
nodes.title: Real-valued characteristic functions are continuous and positive definite
Lattice distributions

nodes.summary: A measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ with characteristic function $\varphi(t) = \int e^{itx} \, d\mu(x)$ is a lattice random variable if $\varphi(l) = 1$ for some real $l \ne 0$ and $\varphi(t) \ne 1$ for some real $t$.
nodes.title: Lattice random variable

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$ with characteristic function $\varphi(t) = \int e^{itx} \, d\mu(x)$, and let $l \ne 0$ be real. Then $\varphi(l) = 1$ if and only if $\mu$ gives mass $1$ to the lattice $\{(2\pi / l) k : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$.
nodes.title: A characteristic function equal to one detects lattice support

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$ that is a lattice random variable. Then there is a real number $h \ne 0$ such that $\mu$ gives mass $1$ to the lattice $\{hk : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$.
nodes.title: Lattice random variables are supported on a lattice
Probability generating functions

nodes.summary: For a measure $\mu$ on $\Omega$ and a function $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{N}$, the probability generating function of $X$ under $\mu$ is the function $G_X : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ given by
nodes.title: Probability generating function

reading_title.source: Integrability of $s^X$ for $|s| \le 1$

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\Omega$, let $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{N}$ be measurable, and let $s$ be a real number with $|s| \le 1$. Then the function $\omega \mapsto s^{X(\omega)}$ is integrable with respect to $\mu$.
nodes.title: Integrability of $s^X$ for $|s| \le 1$

reading_title.source: The generating function at $s = 1$

nodes.summary: For every probability measure $\mu$ on $\Omega$ and every function $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{N}$, the probability generating function $G_X(s) = \int_\Omega s^{X(\omega)} \, d\mu(\omega)$ of $X$ under $\mu$ satisfies $G_X(1) = 1$.
nodes.title: The generating function at $s = 1$

reading_title.source: The generating function at $s = 0$

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\Omega$ and let $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{N}$ be measurable. Then the probability generating function $G_X(s) = \int_\Omega s^{X(\omega)} \, d\mu(\omega)$ of $X$ under $\mu$ satisfies $G_X(0) = \mu(\lbrace \omega : X(\omega) = 0 \rbrace)$, where the measure of the event is read as a real number, an infinite value being read as $0$.
nodes.title: The generating function at $s = 0$

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\Omega$, let $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{N}$ be measurable, and let $s$ be a real number with $|s| \le 1$. Then the probability generating function $G_X(s) = \int_\Omega s^{X(\omega)} \, d\mu(\omega)$ of $X$ under $\mu$ satisfies
nodes.title: Series form of the probability generating function

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\Omega$, and for $Z : \Omega \to \mathbb{N}$ write $G_Z(s) = \int_\Omega s^{Z(\omega)} \, d\mu(\omega)$ for the probability generating function of $Z$ under $\mu$. If $X, Y : \Omega \to \mathbb{N}$ are measurable and independent under $\mu$, then $G_{X+Y}(s) = G_X(s) \, G_Y(s)$ for every real $s$ with $|s| \le 1$.
nodes.title: Generating function of a sum of independent variables
Taylor bounds for characteristic functions

nodes.summary: For every real number $u$, $|e^{iu} - 1 - iu| \le u^2$, with no restriction on the size of $u$.
nodes.title: Global second-order bound for the imaginary exponential

nodes.summary: Let $X$ be a measurable real random variable on a probability space with $X^2$ integrable, and let $\varphi_X$ be the characteristic function of the law of $X$. Then for every real $t$, $|\varphi_X(t) - 1 - it\,\mathbb{E}[X]| \le t^2 \, \mathbb{E}[X^2]$.
nodes.title: Second-order Taylor bound for the characteristic function

nodes.summary: Let $X$ be a measurable real random variable on a probability space with $|X|$ integrable, and let $\varphi_X$ be the characteristic function of the law of $X$. Then for every real $t$, $|\varphi_X(t) - 1| \le |t| \, \mathbb{E}|X|$.
nodes.title: First-order Taylor bound for the characteristic function

nodes.summary: Let $X$ be a measurable real random variable on a probability space with $\mathbb{E}[X] = 0$ and $X^2$ integrable, and let $\varphi_X$ be the characteristic function of the law of $X$. Then for every real $t$, $|\varphi_X(t) - 1| \le t^2 \, \mathbb{E}[X^2]$.
nodes.title: Characteristic-function second-order bound

nodes.summary: Infinitely divisible and stable distributions, convolution powers, the Lévy–Khintchin representation, and regularly varying and slowly varying functions (Karamata's theorem, Potter bounds, generalized inverses) with the truncated moments and tail integrals of heavy-tailed laws.
nodes.title: Infinitely divisible laws and regular variation

nodes.summary: For every measure $\nu$ on an additive commutative monoid $M$ with a σ-algebra, the zeroth convolution power of $\nu$ is the Dirac measure $\delta_0$ at the identity element $0$ of $M$.
nodes.title: The zeroth convolution power

nodes.summary:
Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid with a σ-algebra and let $
u$ be a measure on $M$. For every natural number $n$, the $(n+1)$-st convolution power of $

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid with a measurable structure. If $\nu$ is an s-finite measure on $M$, then for every natural number $n$ its $n$-fold convolution power $\nu^{*n}$ is s-finite.
nodes.title: Convolution powers of an s-finite measure are s-finite

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid with a measurable structure. If $\nu$ is a probability measure on $M$, then for every natural number $n$ its $n$-fold convolution power $\nu^{*n}$ is a probability measure.

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid with a measurable structure in which addition is jointly measurable. A measure $\mu$ on $M$ is infinitely divisible if for every natural number $n \ge 1$ there is a probability measure $\nu$ on $M$ whose $n$-fold convolution power $\nu^{*n}$ equals $\mu$.

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid with a measurable structure in which addition is jointly measurable. Every infinitely divisible measure on $M$ is a probability measure.

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid with a measurable structure in which addition is jointly measurable. If $\mu$ and $\eta$ are infinitely divisible measures on $M$, then their convolution $\mu * \eta$ is infinitely divisible.
nodes.title: Infinite divisibility is closed under convolution

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid with a σ-algebra for which addition $M \times M \to M$ is measurable. For every point $x \in M$ and every natural number $n$, the $n$-th convolution power of the Dirac measure $\delta_x$ is $\delta_{nx}$, where $nx$ is the sum of $n$ copies of $x$ (so $0x = 0$).
nodes.title: Convolution powers of a Dirac measure

nodes.summary: For every real number $a$, the Dirac measure $\delta_a$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is infinitely divisible: for every $n \ge 1$, $\delta_a$ is the $n$-fold convolution power of $\delta_{a/n}$.
nodes.title: Dirac measures on the real line are infinitely divisible

nodes.summary: For every real rate $r \ge 0$ and every natural number $n$, the $(n+1)$-st convolution power of the Poisson measure on $\mathbb{N}$ with rate $r$ is the Poisson measure on $\mathbb{N}$ with rate $(n+1)r$.
nodes.title: Convolution powers of a Poisson measure

nodes.summary: For every real $r \ge 0$, the Poisson distribution with parameter $r$, as a measure on $\mathbb{N}$, is infinitely divisible: for every $n \ge 1$ it is the $n$-fold convolution power of the Poisson distribution with parameter $r/n$.
nodes.title: Poisson distributions are infinitely divisible
Regular variation

nodes.summary: A function $L : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is slowly varying (at infinity) if $L(x) > 0$ for all sufficiently large $x$ and, for every real $c > 0$, $L(cx) / L(x) \to 1$ as $x \to \infty$.
nodes.title: Slowly varying function

nodes.summary: Let $L : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and $a > 0$. If $L(x) > 0$ for all sufficiently large $x$ and $L(x) \to a$ as $x \to \infty$, then $L$ is slowly varying.
nodes.title: Functions with a positive limit are slowly varying

nodes.summary: The constant function $x \mapsto 1$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is slowly varying.
nodes.title: The constant function one is slowly varying

nodes.summary: For every real $c > 0$, the constant function $x \mapsto c$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is slowly varying.
nodes.title: Positive constants are slowly varying

nodes.summary: If $L_1, L_2 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ are slowly varying, then so is their pointwise product $x \mapsto L_1(x) L_2(x)$.
nodes.title: Products of slowly varying functions

nodes.summary: If $L : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is slowly varying and $c > 0$, then $x \mapsto c L(x)$ is slowly varying.
nodes.title: Positive multiples of slowly varying functions

reading_title.source: The function $1 + (1 + x)^{-1}$ is slowly varying

nodes.summary: The function $x \mapsto 1 + (1 + x)^{-1}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is slowly varying; it tends to the positive limit $1$ at infinity.
nodes.title: The function $1 + (1 + x)^{-1}$ is slowly varying

nodes.summary: Let $f, g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$. If $f$ is slowly varying and $f(x) = g(x)$ for all sufficiently large $x$, then $g$ is slowly varying.
nodes.title: Slow variation is preserved by eventual equality

nodes.summary: A function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is regularly varying with index $\rho \in \mathbb{R}$ if there is a slowly varying function $L : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $f(x) = x^{\rho} L(x)$ for all sufficiently large $x$.
nodes.title: Regularly varying function

nodes.summary: For every real number $\rho$, the function $x \mapsto x^\rho$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is regularly varying with index $\rho$.
nodes.title: Powers are regularly varying

nodes.summary: If $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is regularly varying with index $\rho$ and $g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is regularly varying with index $\sigma$, then the pointwise product $fg$ is regularly varying with index $\rho + \sigma$.
nodes.title: Products of regularly varying functions

nodes.summary: If $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is regularly varying with index $\rho$ and $c > 0$, then $x \mapsto c f(x)$ is regularly varying with index $\rho$.
nodes.title: Positive multiples of regularly varying functions

nodes.summary: For real numbers $c > 0$ and $\rho$, the function $x \mapsto c x^\rho$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is regularly varying with index $\rho$.
nodes.title: Positive multiples of powers are regularly varying

nodes.summary: Let $f, g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and $\rho \in \mathbb{R}$. If $f$ is regularly varying with index $\rho$ and $f(x) = g(x)$ for all sufficiently large $x$, then $g$ is regularly varying with index $\rho$.
nodes.title: Regular variation is preserved by eventual equality

nodes.summary: If $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is regularly varying with some index $\rho$, then $f(x) > 0$ for all sufficiently large $x$.
nodes.title: Regularly varying functions are eventually positive

nodes.summary: For a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}$, the right tail of $\mu$ at $x$ is the real number $\mu((x, \infty))$ when $\mu((x, \infty)) < \infty$, and $0$ when $\mu((x, \infty)) = \infty$.
nodes.title: Right tail of a measure

nodes.summary: For a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and a real $x$, the left tail of $\mu$ at $x$ is the real number $\mu((-\infty, -x))$, where an infinite value is sent to $0$.
nodes.title: Left tail of a measure

nodes.summary: For a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and a real number $x$, the combined tail of $\mu$ at $x$ is the real number $\mu((x, \infty)) + \mu((-\infty, -x))$, where each of the two measures is converted from $[0, \infty]$ to a real number, an infinite value becoming $0$.
nodes.title: Combined tail of a measure

nodes.summary: For every probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and every $x \in \mathbb{R}$, the right tail of $\mu$ at $x$ is at most $1$.
nodes.title: The right tail of a probability measure is at most one

nodes.summary: For every probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and every real $x$, the left tail of $\mu$ at $x$ is at most $1$.
nodes.title: The left tail of a probability measure is at most one

nodes.summary: For every probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and every real number $x$, the combined tail of $\mu$ at $x$ satisfies $\mu((x, \infty)) + \mu((-\infty, -x)) \le 2$.
nodes.title: The combined tail of a probability measure is at most two

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\mathbb{R}$. If $x \le y$, then the right tail of $\mu$ at $y$ is at most the right tail of $\mu$ at $x$.
nodes.title: The right tail of a finite measure is antitone

nodes.summary: For every finite measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$, the left tail of $\mu$ is antitone in the threshold: if $a \le b$, then $\mu((-\infty, -b)) \le \mu((-\infty, -a))$.
nodes.title: Monotonicity of the left tail

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\mathbb{R}$ and write $T(x) = \mu((x, \infty)) + \mu((-\infty, -x))$ for its combined tail at a real number $x$. Then $T$ is antitone: $T(b) \le T(a)$ whenever $a \le b$.
nodes.title: The combined tail is antitone

nodes.summary: For every measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and every $x \in \mathbb{R}$, the right tail of $\mu$ at $x$ is at most the combined tail of $\mu$ at $x$.
nodes.title: The right tail is at most the combined tail

nodes.summary: For every measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and every real $x$, the left tail of $\mu$ at $x$ is at most the combined tail of $\mu$ at $x$.
nodes.title: The left tail is at most the combined tail

nodes.summary: For every finite measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$, the right tail $\mu((x, \infty))$, taken as a real number, tends to $0$ as $x \to \infty$.
nodes.title: The right tail of a finite measure vanishes at infinity

nodes.summary: For every finite measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$, the left tail $\mu((-\infty, -x))$, taken as a real number, tends to $0$ as $x \to \infty$.
nodes.title: The left tail of a finite measure vanishes at infinity

nodes.summary: For every finite measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$, the combined tail $\mu((x, \infty)) + \mu((-\infty, -x))$, with both masses taken as real numbers, tends to $0$ as $x \to \infty$.
nodes.title: The combined tail of a finite measure vanishes at infinity

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\mathbb{R}$ and $p$ a real number. Write $R(x) = \mu((x, \infty))$ for the right tail and $T(x) = \mu((x, \infty)) + \mu((-\infty, -x))$ for the combined tail of $\mu$. The measure $\mu$ has tail balance $p$ when $0 \le p \le 1$, $T(x) > 0$ for all sufficiently large $x$, and $R(x) / T(x) \to p$ as $x \to \infty$.
nodes.title: Tail balance

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\mathbb{R}$. If $\mu((x, \infty)) = 0$ for all sufficiently large $x$ and the combined tail $\mu((x, \infty)) + \mu((-\infty, -x))$ is positive for all sufficiently large $x$, then $\mu$ has tail balance $0$.
nodes.title: Tail balance zero from a vanishing right tail

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\mathbb{R}$ and let $p \in \mathbb{R}$. If the combined tail of $\mu$ at $x$ equals $0$ for all sufficiently large $x$, then $\mu$ does not have tail balance $p$.
nodes.title: Eventually vanishing combined tail rules out tail balance

nodes.summary: For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ and every $p \in \mathbb{R}$, the Dirac measure $\delta_a$ at $a$ does not have tail balance $p$.
nodes.title: Dirac masses have no tail balance

nodes.summary: For a regularly varying function `f` of index `-α` with `α > 0` that is eventually non-increasing, there exists a sequence `a : ℕ → ℝ` of positive reals such that `n · f (a n) → 1` as `n → ∞`.
nodes.title: Generalized inverse of a regularly varying function

nodes.summary: A regularly varying function has the expected ratio limit.
nodes.title: Ratio limit of a regularly varying function

nodes.summary: Potter's bound for antitone functions with a ratio limit. If `W` is antitone, bounded, eventually positive and `W (c * x) / W x → c ^ ρ` for every `c > 0`, then for every `δ > 0` there are `C > 0` and `Y` such that `W (x * u) / W x ≤ C * u ^ (ρ - δ)` for all `x ≥ Y` and `u ∈ (0, 1]`. The proof chains the ratio limit at the dyadic scales `1/2` and `2`.
nodes.title: Potter's bound

nodes.summary: Karamata's integral theorem for antitone functions with a ratio limit. If `W` is antitone, nonnegative, bounded, eventually positive and `W (c * x) / W x → c ^ ρ` for every `c > 0`, then for `β ≥ 0` and `β + 1 + ρ > 0`, `(∫ t in (0)..x, t ^ β * W t) / (x ^ (β + 1) * W x) → 1 / (β + 1 + ρ)`. The proof substitutes `t = x * u` and applies dominated convergence with Potter's bound as the dominator.
nodes.title: Karamata's integral theorem
Stable distributions and domains of attraction

nodes.summary: The convolution power of a Gaussian is Gaussian with the mean and the variance multiplied by `n`: the law of the sum of `n` i.i.d. `N(μ, v)` variables is `N(nμ, nv)`.
nodes.title: Convolution powers of a Gaussian are Gaussian

nodes.summary: Indexed stability fixes the positive-n dilation to `n^(1/α)` and allows arbitrary centering. Degenerate Dirac identities may satisfy several indices.
nodes.title: Stable distribution of a given index

nodes.summary: A Dirac law satisfies the fixed-dilation identity at every admissible index. These are degenerate rescaling identities, with centering `na - n^(1/α)a`.
nodes.title: Dirac measures are stable of every index

nodes.summary: Every real Gaussian measure is stable of index `2`: the sum of `n` i.i.d. `N(μ, v)` variables is `N(nμ, nv)`, which is the pushforward of `N(μ, v)` under `x ↦ √n · x + (n - √n) μ`.
nodes.title: Gaussian measures are stable of index 2

nodes.summary: A nondegenerate Gaussian cannot have fixed stability index one. The n=4 convolution variance is `4v`, while every such affine dilation has variance `16v`.
nodes.title: Nondegenerate Gaussian is not stable of index 1

nodes.summary: A measure `μ` on `ℝ` is *nondegenerate* if it is not a point mass `δ_a` for any `a`.
nodes.title: Nondegenerate measure on the real line

nodes.summary: A Gaussian with nonzero variance is nondegenerate: it gives mass `0` to every singleton, while `δ_a` gives mass `1` to `{a}`.
nodes.title: Gaussian with nonzero variance is nondegenerate

nodes.summary: A Dirac measure is degenerate, by definition.
nodes.title: Dirac measure is degenerate

nodes.summary: The probability measure `μ` is *in the domain of attraction* of `G` if there exist sequences of normalizing constants `a n > 0` and centering constants `b n` such that the law of `(S_n - b n) / a n` (where `S_n` has law `μ^{*n}`) converges weakly to `G`, expressed here as integration against arbitrary bounded continuous functions.

nodes.summary: A stable law is a normalized weak limit of its own convolution powers. The positive-n inverse affine identity is exact; order zero uses normalizer one.

Legendre transform

nodes.summary: Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$, give $\mathbb{R}^d$ its standard inner product, and let $\Lambda : \mathbb{R}^d \to [-\infty, \infty]$. The Legendre transform of $\Lambda$ at $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the Fenchel conjugate of $\Lambda$ at the linear functional $y \mapsto \langle x, y \rangle$, that is, the extended real number $\Lambda^*(x) = \sup_{y \in \mathbb{R}^d} \big(\langle x, y \rangle - \Lambda(y)\big)$.
nodes.title: Legendre transform

nodes.summary: Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $\Lambda : \mathbb{R}^d \to [-\infty, \infty]$. For every $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the Legendre transform $\Lambda^*$ of $\Lambda$ satisfies $\Lambda^*(x) = \sup_{l \in \mathbb{R}^d} \big(\langle l, x \rangle - \Lambda(l)\big)$.
nodes.title: Supremum formula for the Legendre transform

nodes.summary: Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $\Lambda : \mathbb{R}^d \to [-\infty, \infty]$, with Legendre transform $\Lambda^*$. For all $x, l \in \mathbb{R}^d$, we have $\langle l, x \rangle - \Lambda(l) \le \Lambda^*(x)$ in $[-\infty, \infty]$.
nodes.title: Fenchel–Young inequality for the Legendre transform

nodes.summary: Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $\Lambda_1, \Lambda_2 : \mathbb{R}^d \to [-\infty, \infty]$, with Legendre transforms $\Lambda_1^*$ and $\Lambda_2^*$. If $\Lambda_1(y) \le \Lambda_2(y)$ for every $y \in \mathbb{R}^d$, then $\Lambda_2^*(x) \le \Lambda_1^*(x)$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$.
nodes.title: The Legendre transform is order-reversing

nodes.summary: Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $\Lambda : \mathbb{R}^d \to [-\infty, \infty]$, with Legendre transform $\Lambda^*$. Then the set $\{(x, t) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R} : \Lambda^*(x) \le t\}$ is convex.
nodes.title: The epigraph of the Legendre transform is convex

nodes.summary: Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $\Lambda : \mathbb{R}^d \to [-\infty, \infty]$, with Legendre transform $\Lambda^*$. If $\Lambda^*(x)$ is a real number for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, then $\Lambda^*$, viewed as a function $\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$, is convex on $\mathbb{R}^d$.
nodes.title: A finite Legendre transform is convex

nodes.summary: Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $\Lambda : \mathbb{R}^d \to [-\infty, \infty]$ be a function that never takes the value $-\infty$, with Legendre transform $\Lambda^*$. Then $X$ (under $\mu_X$) is convexly dominated by $Y$ (under $\mu_Y$) when every convex function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ for which $f \circ X$ is $\mu_X$-integrable and $f \circ Y$ is $\mu_Y$-integrable satisfies…

Return probabilities of random walks on Cayley graphs

nodes.summary: For a group $G$ and a natural number $k$, the data of a $k$-regular Cayley graph on $G$ is a finite set $S \subseteq G$ of generators such that $S$ is closed under inverses ($s \in S$ implies $s^{-1} \in S$), the identity $1$ does not belong to $S$, every element of $G$ is the product of a finite (possibly empty) list of elements of $S$, and $S$ has exactly $k$ elements.
nodes.title: Regular Cayley graph

nodes.summary: Let $\Gamma$ be a $k$-regular Cayley graph on a group $G$ with generating set $S$. For $n \ge 1$, the first-return probability of $\Gamma$ at time $n$ is the real number obtained by dividing by $k^n$ the number of words $(s_1, \dots, s_n) \in S^n$ with $s_1 s_2 \cdots s_n = 1$ and $s_1 \cdots s_m \ne 1$ for every $0 < m < n$; at time $n = 0$ it is $0$.
nodes.title: First-return probability

nodes.summary: The return probability of a $k$-regular Cayley graph $\Gamma$ is the sum $\sum_{n \ge 0} p_n$, where $p_n$ is the first-return probability of $\Gamma$ at time $n$.
nodes.title: Return probability

nodes.summary: The statement that for every natural number $k > 1$ there is a real number $C < 1$ such that for every group $G$ and every $k$-regular Cayley graph $\Gamma$ on $G$, if the return probability of $\Gamma$ is less than $1$ (that is, $\Gamma$ is transient), then it is at most $C$.
nodes.title: Uniform return-probability gap

nodes.summary: For every natural number $k > 1$ there is a real number $C < 1$ such that for every group $G$ and every $k$-regular Cayley graph $\Gamma$ on $G$ whose return probability is less than $1$, the return probability of $\Gamma$ is at most $C$.
nodes.title: Uniform return-probability gap for transient Cayley graphs

nodes.summary: Given maps $X_0, X_1, X_2, \dots$ from a set $\Omega$ to a set $S$ and a map $T : \Omega \to \mathbb{N}$, the post-stopping-time sequence is the sequence $(Y_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ of maps from $\Omega$ to $S$ given by $Y_k(\omega) = X_{T(\omega)+k+1}(\omega)$. When $T$ is a stopping time, this is the sequence of observations immediately after time $T$.

nodes.summary: Galton–Watson processes, extinction probabilities, total progeny and the hitting-time theorem, and linear birth–death processes.
nodes.title: Branching processes
Galton–Watson process

nodes.summary: The law of the generation size `Z_n` of the Galton–Watson process with offspring law `ν` started from one individual: `Z_0 = 1` and, given `Z_n = z`, `Z_{n+1}` has law `ν^{∗z}` (`Measure.convPow ν z`).
nodes.title: Generation-size law of a Galton–Watson process

nodes.summary: The mean offspring number `m = E ξ = ∑ k ν{k} ∈ [0, ∞]`.
nodes.title: Mean offspring number

nodes.summary: The extinction probability `q = sup_n P(Z_n = 0)`, the limit of the probabilities of extinction by generation `n` (`tendsto_law_real_zero`). On a path space carrying the process the events `{Z_n = 0}` increase with `n` (`0` is absorbing), so `q` is the probability of eventual extinction; this file describes the process through its generation laws and does not construct the path space.
nodes.title: Extinction probability of a Galton–Watson process

nodes.summary: The iterates `f^[n](s)` of the offspring generating function stay in `[0, 1]` for `s ∈ [0, 1]`.
nodes.title: Iterates of the offspring generating function stay in (0, 1)

nodes.summary: The iterates `f^[n](0)` of the offspring generating function are non-decreasing.
nodes.title: Iterates of the generating function at zero are nondecreasing

nodes.summary: `sup_n f^[n](0)` is the least fixed point of `f` in `[0, 1]` (Athreya–Ney 1972, ch. I).
nodes.title: Limit of generating-function iterates is the least fixed point

nodes.summary: The least fixed point is `1` iff the mean offspring number is at most `1`, provided the offspring number is not almost surely `1` (Athreya–Ney 1972, ch. I).
nodes.title: Least fixed point equals one iff mean offspring is at most one

nodes.summary: The generating function of `Z_n` is the `n`-th iterate of the offspring generating function on `[0, 1]` (Athreya–Ney 1972, ch. I).
nodes.title: Generating function of the n-th generation size
Probability of extinction by generation n

nodes.summary: The mean generation size is `E Z_n = m ^ n` (Athreya–Ney 1972, ch. I).
nodes.title: Mean generation size of a Galton–Watson process

nodes.summary: `P(Z_n = 0)` is non-decreasing in `n`.
nodes.title: Extinction by generation n is nondecreasing in n

nodes.summary: `P(Z_n = 0)` converges to the extinction probability.
nodes.title: Extinction by generation n converges to the extinction probability

nodes.summary: The extinction probability is the least fixed point of the offspring generating function in `[0, 1]` (Athreya–Ney 1972, ch. I).
nodes.title: Extinction probability is the least fixed point

nodes.summary: Extinction is certain iff the mean offspring number is at most `1`, provided the offspring number is not almost surely `1` (Athreya–Ney 1972, ch. I).
nodes.title: Galton–Watson extinction criterion
Linear birth–death process

nodes.summary: Kendall's extinction probability `α t = P(X t = 0 | X 0 = 1)` of the linear birth–death process with per-capita birth rate `b` and death rate `d`: `d (E - 1) / (b E - d)` with `E = exp ((b - d) t)` if `b ≠ d`, and `b t / (1 + b t)` if `b = d`. Meaningful for `0 ≤ b`, `0 ≤ d`, `0 ≤ t`.
nodes.title: Kendall's extinction probability for the birth–death process

nodes.summary: Kendall's ratio `β t` of the geometric tail of the law of `X t`: `b (E - 1) / (b E - d)` with `E = exp ((b - d) t)` if `b ≠ d`, and `b t / (1 + b t)` if `b = d`.
nodes.title: Kendall's geometric tail ratio

nodes.summary: Kendall's law of the linear birth–death process at time `t` started from one individual: `prob b d t 0 = α t` and `prob b d t (n + 1) = (1 - α t) (1 - β t) (β t) ^ n`.
nodes.title: Kendall's law of the linear birth–death process

nodes.summary: At time `0` the population is one individual: `prob b d 0 = δ₁`.
nodes.title: Linear birth–death law at time zero

nodes.summary: Kendall's probabilities are nonnegative.
nodes.title: Nonnegativity of Kendall's probabilities

nodes.summary: Kendall's probabilities sum to `1`: no mass escapes to infinity.
nodes.title: Kendall's probabilities sum to one

nodes.summary: The mean population size at time `t` started from one individual is `E[X t] = exp ((b - d) t)` (Kendall 1948; Bailey 1964, ch. 8).
nodes.title: Mean population size of the linear birth–death process

nodes.summary: Forward Kolmogorov equation for state `0`: `p_0' = d p_1`.
nodes.title: Forward Kolmogorov equation for the empty state

nodes.summary: Forward Kolmogorov equation for state `n + 1`: `p_(n+1)' = b n p_n - (b + d) (n + 1) p_(n+1) + d (n + 2) p_(n+2)`.
nodes.title: Forward Kolmogorov equation for positive states

nodes.summary: Backward Kolmogorov equation for the extinction probability: `α' = d - (b + d) α + b α²` (Karlin–Taylor 1975, ch. 4).
nodes.title: Backward Kolmogorov equation for the extinction probability

nodes.summary: The extinction probability is the only `[0, 1]`-valued solution `q` on `[0, ∞)` of the backward equation `q' = d - (b + d) q + b q²` with `q 0 = 0`.
nodes.title: Uniqueness of the extinction probability solving the backward equation

nodes.summary: Supercritical case: if `d < b`, the extinction probability tends to `d / b`.
nodes.title: Limiting extinction probability in the supercritical case

nodes.summary: Critical and subcritical cases: if `b ≤ d` and `0 < d`, extinction is certain in the limit.
nodes.title: Certain extinction in the critical and subcritical cases
Total progeny and the hitting-time theorem

nodes.summary: The exploration walk started at `k` with steps `x_i - 1` stays positive at every time `j < n`: `j < k + ∑_{i < j} x_i`. Together with `∑ x_i + k = n` this says that the walk first hits `0` at time `n`.
nodes.title: First passage of the exploration walk

nodes.summary: The cyclic shift `i ↦ x_{(i + r) mod n}` of a tuple.
nodes.title: Cyclic shift of a tuple

nodes.summary: Cycle lemma (Dvoretzky–Motzkin 1947). If `x : Fin n → ℕ` satisfies `∑ x_i + k = n` with `1 ≤ k`, then exactly `k` of the `n` cyclic shifts of `x` (counted by shift `r < n`) are first-passage sequences.
nodes.title: Cycle lemma

nodes.summary: The weight `W_p(k, n) = ∑ ∏_i p(x_i)` over the step sequences `x : Fin n → ℕ` with `∑ x_i + k = n` (the walk from `k` is at `0` at time `n`). For `p(j) = P(ξ = j)` this is `P(ξ_1 + ⋯ + ξ_n = n - k)` when `k ≤ n`, and `0` when `k > n`.
nodes.title: Walk weight of step sequences ending at zero

nodes.summary: The weight `H_p(k, n) = ∑ ∏_i p(x_i)` over the step sequences with `∑ x_i + k = n` along which the walk from `k` first hits `0` at time `n`. For `p(j) = P(ξ = j)` this is the probability `P(T = n)` that the total progeny of `k` ancestors is `n`.
nodes.title: Hitting weight of first-passage step sequences

nodes.summary: Hitting-time theorem, weighted form: `n · H_p(k, n) = k · W_p(k, n)` for every weight `p` with values in a commutative semiring and all `k, n`. For probability weights this is the hitting-time theorem of van der Hofstad–Keane (2008); the proof double counts cyclic shifts with the cycle lemma.
nodes.title: Hitting-time theorem

nodes.summary: Under `ν^{⊗n}`, the event that the walk from `k` first hits `0` at time `n` has measure `H_p(k, n)` with `p(j) = ν{j}`. When `ν` is a probability measure this is the probability `P(T = n)`.
nodes.title: Probability of first passage at time n

nodes.summary: Under `ν^{⊗n}`, the event `ξ_1 + ⋯ + ξ_n + k = n` has measure `W_p(k, n)` with `p(j) = ν{j}`. When `ν` is a probability measure this is the probability `P(ξ_1 + ⋯ + ξ_n = n - k)`.
nodes.title: Probability of the offspring walk event as a walk weight

nodes.summary: For i.i.d. offspring numbers with law `ν` and `k` ancestors, the finite-measure identity `n · P(T = n) = k · P(ξ_1 + ⋯ + ξ_n = n - k)` holds as an identity of event masses (Otter 1949; Dwass 1969); the two sides are probabilities when `ν` is a probability measure.
nodes.title: Otter–Dwass formula

nodes.summary: For Poisson(`r`) step weights, `W_p(k, n) = e^{-rn} (rn)^{n-k} / (n-k)!` when `k ≤ n`: the sum of `n` independent Poisson(`r`) variables is Poisson(`rn`).
nodes.title: Walk weights for Poisson offspring

nodes.summary: For Poisson(`r`) offspring and `k ≤ n` ancestors, `n · P(T = n) = k e^{-rn} (rn)^{n-k} / (n-k)!` (Tanner 1961; Haight–Breuer 1960).
nodes.title: Borel–Tanner law

nodes.summary: For Poisson(`r`) offspring and one ancestor, the total progeny satisfies `P(T = n) = e^{-rn} (rn)^{n-1} / n!` for `n ≥ 1` (Borel 1942).
nodes.title: Borel law

nodes.summary: The mean total progeny `∑_n E Z_n` of the Galton–Watson process started from one individual. By Tonelli this is `E ∑_n Z_n` for any process with the generation laws `law ν n`.
nodes.title: Mean total progeny of a Galton–Watson process

reading_title.source: Mean total progeny equals $1/(1-m)$

nodes.summary: The mean total progeny is `(1 - m)⁻¹` in `[0, ∞]`: it is `1 / (1 - m)` for `m < 1` and `∞` for `m ≥ 1` (`m` the mean offspring number).
nodes.title: Mean total progeny equals $1/(1-m)$

Poisson point processes

nodes.summary: The counting measure `∑_{i < n} δ_{x_i}` of a finite tuple of points.
nodes.title: Counting measure of a finite tuple of points

nodes.summary: The law of the Poisson point process with finite intensity `μ` on `E`: `∑_n e^{-μ(E)} / n! • (μ^{⊗n}).map countingMeasure`, a probability measure on `Measure E` (Last–Penrose Prop. 3.5, mixed binomial construction).

nodes.summary: `(∑ δ_{x_i})(s) = #{i | x_i ∈ s}`, as a sum of indicators.
nodes.title: Counting measure of a set as a sum of indicators

nodes.summary: The counting measure of a tuple depends measurably on the tuple.

Integral against a counting measure

nodes.summary: The Poisson weights sum to one: `∑_n e^{-μ(E)} μ(E)^n / n! = 1`.

Integral of a coordinate function under a product measure

nodes.summary: The image of `∑ δ_{x_i}` under `T` is `∑ δ_{T(x_i)}`.
nodes.title: Image of a counting measure under a map

nodes.summary: The number of points `η(B)` in a measurable set `B` has the Poisson law of mean `μ(B)`.
nodes.title: Point counts of a Poisson point process are Poisson

nodes.summary: The counts `η(A i)` of pairwise disjoint measurable sets are independent, and `η(A i)` has the Poisson law of mean `μ(A i)`: the mixed binomial process is a Poisson process with intensity `μ` in the sense of Last–Penrose Def. 3.1 (Last–Penrose Prop. 3.5).
nodes.title: Mixed binomial process is a Poisson process

nodes.summary: `E ∫ f dη = ∫ f dμ` for measurable `f : E → [0, ∞]` (Last–Penrose Prop. 2.7).
nodes.title: Campbell's formula

nodes.summary: For measurable `f : E → [0, ∞)`, `E exp(-∫ f dη) = exp(-∫ (1 - e^{-f}) dμ)` (Last–Penrose Thm. 3.9). The integral `∫ f dη` is a finite sum `∑ f(x_i)` for every configuration charged by the process.
nodes.title: Laplace functional

nodes.summary: For measurable `h : E × Measure E → [0, ∞]`, `E ∫ h(x, η) η(dx) = ∫ E h(x, η + δ_x) μ(dx)` (Mecke 1967; Last–Penrose Thm. 4.1).
nodes.title: Mecke equation

nodes.summary: The image `η ∘ T⁻¹` of a Poisson point process under a measurable map `T : E → F` is the Poisson point process with intensity `μ ∘ T⁻¹` (Last–Penrose Thm. 5.1).
nodes.title: Mapping theorem

nodes.summary: The restrictions `η|_{A i}` of a Poisson point process with finite intensity `μ` to pairwise disjoint measurable sets `A i` are independent Poisson point processes with intensities `μ|_{A i}` (Last–Penrose Thm. 5.2).
nodes.title: Restriction theorem
Poisson processes

nodes.summary: `N : ℝ≥0 → Ω → ℕ` is a Poisson process of rate `r` under `P` (Kingman 1993, ch. 4; Karlin–Taylor 1975, ch. 4): `N 0 = 0` and the paths are nondecreasing almost surely, the increments over consecutive intervals are independent, and for `s ≤ t` the increment `N t - N s` has the Poisson law of mean `r (t - s)`.
nodes.title: Poisson process

nodes.summary: The `n`-th arrival time `S n = T 0 + ⋯ + T (n - 1)` of the interarrival times `T`.
nodes.title: Arrival times from interarrival times

nodes.summary: The counting process of the interarrival times `T`: `count T t ω` is the number of arrivals `n ≥ 1` with `S n ≤ t`. When that set is infinite (a null event for exponential interarrivals of positive rate) `Set.ncard` returns `0`.
nodes.title: Counting process of interarrival times

nodes.summary: The `(n + 1)`-th arrival time of i.i.d. rate-`r` exponential interarrivals has the Gamma (Erlang) law with shape `n + 1` and rate `r` (Karlin–Taylor 1975, §4.2).
nodes.title: Arrival times of exponential interarrivals are Erlang

nodes.summary: The number of arrivals in `[0, t]` of i.i.d. rate-`r` exponential interarrivals has the Poisson law of mean `r t` (Karlin–Taylor 1975, §4.2, Theorem 2.1).
nodes.title: Arrival counts of exponential interarrivals are Poisson

nodes.summary: The counting process of i.i.d. rate-`r` exponential interarrivals starts at `0` almost surely (all interarrival times are positive almost surely).
nodes.title: Counting process starts at zero almost surely

nodes.summary: The counting process of i.i.d. rate-`r` exponential interarrivals has nondecreasing paths almost surely (the arrival times tend to infinity almost surely, so every arrival set in `[0, t]` is finite).
nodes.title: Counting process has nondecreasing paths almost surely

nodes.summary: Superposition (Kingman 1993, §2.2): the sum of two independent Poisson processes of rates `r₁` and `r₂` is a Poisson process of rate `r₁ + r₂`. Independence is of the two processes as random paths.
nodes.title: Superposition

nodes.summary: The thinning of `N` by the marks `B`: the number of indices `i < N t` with `B i`, i.e. the number of points of `N` in `[0, t]` that are kept when the `i`-th point (in time order, from `0`) is kept iff `B i`.
nodes.title: Thinning of a Poisson process

nodes.summary: Thinning (Kingman 1993, §5.1; Karlin–Taylor 1975, §4.1): keeping each point of a Poisson process of rate `r` independently with probability `p`, independently of the process, gives a Poisson process of rate `p r`. The marks `B i` are i.i.d. with `P(B i) = p` and independent of `N` as a random path.
nodes.title: Thinning

nodes.summary: The increments of the counting process of i.i.d. rate-`r` exponential interarrivals over consecutive intervals `(t i, t (i + 1)]` are independent with the Poisson laws of means `r (t (i + 1) - t i)`: the increment vector has the product law (Kingman 1993, ch. 4; Karlin–Taylor 1975, ch. 4).
nodes.title: Independent Poisson increments of the counting process

nodes.summary: Exponential interarrivals give a Poisson process (Kingman 1993, ch. 4; Karlin–Taylor 1975, ch. 4): the counting process of i.i.d. rate-`r` exponential interarrival times is a Poisson process of rate `r`.
nodes.title: Exponential interarrivals give a Poisson process

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\Omega$, and let $v$ assign to each real $t$ a function $v_t : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$. A map $T : \Omega \to \Omega$ is aperiodic with respect to $\mu$ if the set of periodic points of $T$, the points $x$ with $T^k(x) = x$ for some $k \ge 1$, where $T^k$ is the $k$-fold iterate of $T$, has (outer) $\mu$-measure zero. Equivalently, for $\mu$-almost every $x$, no positive iterate of $T$ fixes $x$.
nodes.title: Aperiodic transformation

nodes.summary: For a map $T : \Omega \to \Omega$, a set $B \subseteq \Omega$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the level-$k$ floor with base $B$ is the image $T^k(B)$ of $B$ under the $k$-fold iterate $T^k$ of $T$; the level-$0$ floor is $B$.
nodes.title: Floor of a Rokhlin tower

nodes.summary: For a map $T : \Omega \to \Omega$, a set $B \subseteq \Omega$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the union of the tower with base $B$ and height $n$ is the set $\bigcup_{k=0}^{n-1} T^k(B)$ of its floors $B, T(B), \dots, T^{n-1}(B)$, where $T^k(B)$ is the image of $B$ under the $k$-fold iterate of $T$. It is empty when $n = 0$, and no disjointness of the floors is required.
nodes.title: Union of a Rokhlin tower

nodes.summary: Let $\Omega$ be a measurable space, $T : \Omega \to \Omega$ a map and $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A set $B \subseteq \Omega$ is the base of a Rokhlin tower of height $n$ for $T$ if $B$ is measurable and the floors $B, T(B), \dots, T^{n-1}(B)$ are pairwise disjoint, that is, $T^i(B) \cap T^j(B) = \emptyset$ for all $i \ne j$ with $i, j < n$; here $T^k(B)$ is the image of $B$ under the $k$-fold iterate of $T$.
nodes.title: Rokhlin tower

nodes.summary: Let $\Omega$ be a standard Borel space with a probability measure $\mu$, and let $T : \Omega \to \Omega$ be a measure-preserving map that is aperiodic with respect to $\mu$. Then for every integer $n \ge 1$ and every $\varepsilon \in (0, \infty]$ there is a measurable set $B \subseteq \Omega$ such that the floors $B, T(B), \dots, T^{n-1}(B)$ are pairwise disjoint, where $T^k(B)$ is the image of $B$ under the…

Birkhoff ergodic theorem

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on a measurable space $\alpha$, let $T : \alpha \to \alpha$ preserve $\mu$, and let $f : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ be measurable and $\mu$-integrable. For a natural number $n$ write $S_n f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(T^k x)$. Then the integral of $f$ with respect to $\mu$ over the set of points $x \in \alpha$ such that $S_n f(x) > 0$ for some natural number $n$ is nonnegative.
nodes.title: Hopf maximal ergodic theorem

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a measurable space, $T : \alpha \to \alpha$ a map, $g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ a function and $c$ a real number. The maximal divergence set of $T$, $g$ and $c$ is the set of points $x \in \alpha$ for which there is a rational number $q > c$ such that $n q < \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} g(T^k x)$ for infinitely many natural numbers $n$.
nodes.title: Maximal divergence set

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$, let $T : \alpha \to \alpha$ preserve $\mu$, and let $g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ be measurable. Then for every real number $c$, the maximal divergence set of $T$, $g$ and $c$ is a measurable set.
nodes.title: Measurability of the maximal divergence set

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a measurable space, $T : \alpha \to \alpha$ a map, $g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ a function, $c$ a real number and $x \in \alpha$. Then $x$ lies in the maximal divergence set of $T$, $g$ and $c$ if and only if there is a rational number $q > c$ such that for every natural number $N$ there is a natural number $n \ge N$ with $n q < \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} g(T^k x)$.
nodes.title: Membership in the maximal divergence set

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a measurable space. For every map $T : \alpha \to \alpha$, every function $g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ and every real number $c$, the preimage under $T$ of the maximal divergence set of $T$, $g$ and $c$ equals that set.
nodes.title: Invariance of the maximal divergence set

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a measurable space, $T : \alpha \to \alpha$ a map, $g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ a function and $c$ a real number. For every natural number $k$ and every $x \in \alpha$, the point $T^k x$ lies in the maximal divergence set of $T$, $g$ and $c$ if and only if $x$ does.

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on a measurable space $\alpha$, let $T : \alpha \to \alpha$ be ergodic with respect to $\mu$ (in particular $T$ preserves $\mu$), and let $g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ be $\mu$-integrable. Then for $\mu$-almost every $x \in \alpha$, the Birkhoff averages $\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} g(T^k x)$ converge to $\int g \, d\mu$ as $n \to \infty$.
nodes.title: Birkhoff pointwise ergodic theorem (ergodic case)

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$, let $T : \alpha \to \alpha$ preserve $\mu$, and let $g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ be $\mu$-integrable. Then for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ the Birkhoff sum $x \mapsto \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} g(T^k x)$ is $\mu$-integrable.
nodes.title: Integrability of Birkhoff sums

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$, let $T : \alpha \to \alpha$ preserve $\mu$, and let $g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ be $\mu$-integrable. Then for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ the Birkhoff average $x \mapsto \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} g(T^k x)$ is $\mu$-integrable (for $n = 0$ it is the zero function).
nodes.title: Integrability of Birkhoff averages

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$, let $T : \alpha \to \alpha$ preserve $\mu$, and let $u : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ be $\mu$-integrable. Then for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, writing $T^k$ for the $k$-th iterate of $T$, we have $\int u(T^k x) \, d\mu(x) = \int u \, d\mu$.
nodes.title: Invariance of the integral under iterates

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\alpha$, let $T : \alpha \to \alpha$ preserve $\mu$, and let $u : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ be $\mu$-integrable. Then for every $n \ge 1$, $\int \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} u(T^k x) \, d\mu(x) = \int u \, d\mu$.
nodes.title: Birkhoff averages preserve the integral

nodes.summary: Let $T : \alpha \to \alpha$ be a map. For $f : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ and $n \ge 1$ write $A_n f(x) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(T^k x)$ for the $n$-th Birkhoff average of $f$, and $A_0 f = 0$. Then for every $u : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$, every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and every $x \in \alpha$, writing $|u|$ for the function $y \mapsto |u(y)|$, we have $|A_n u(x)| \le A_n |u|(x)$.
nodes.title: Triangle inequality for Birkhoff averages

nodes.summary: Let $T : \alpha \to \alpha$ be a map. For $u : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$, $n \ge 1$ and $x \in \alpha$, write $A_n u(x) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} u(T^k x)$ for the $n$-th Birkhoff average of $u$ at $x$, and $A_0 u(x) = 0$. If $u, v : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $u(y) \le v(y)$ for every $y \in \alpha$, then $A_n u(x) \le A_n v(x)$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and every $x \in \alpha$.
nodes.title: Monotonicity of Birkhoff averages

nodes.summary: Let $T : \alpha \to \alpha$ be a map, let $M \ge 0$, and let $g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $|g(x)| \le M$ for every $x \in \alpha$. Then for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and every $x \in \alpha$, the Birkhoff average $\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} g(T^k x)$ (taken to be $0$ for $n = 0$) has absolute value at most $M$.

For a function $f : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ and $n \ge 1$ write $A_n f(x) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(T^k x)$, and $A_0 f = 0$. Then for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\int |A_n g(x) - A_n h(x)| \, d\mu(x) \le \int |g(x) - h(x)| \, d\mu(x)$.

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type. If a sequence $u : \mathbb{N} \to \alpha$ is eventually periodic, then there are natural numbers $p > 0$ and $n_0$ such that $u(n + p) = u(n)$ for every natural number $n \ge n_0$.

nodes.summary: For $N \in \mathbb{N}$, the configuration space of the two-sided full shift on $N$ symbols is the set $\{0, \dots, N-1\}^{\mathbb{Z}}$ of all bi-infinite sequences $x = (x_i)_{i \in \mathbb{Z}}$ of symbols. It carries the product of the discrete topologies.

nodes.summary: For $c \in \mathbb{C}$, let $T_c(z) = z^2 + c$ and let $T_c^n$ be its $n$-fold iterate. The filled Julia set $K_c$ is the set of $z \in \mathbb{C}$ whose orbit under $T_c$ is bounded: there is a real $M$ such that $|T_c^n(z)| \le M$ for every $n \ge 0$.
nodes.title: Filled Julia set

nodes.summary: For $c \in \mathbb{C}$, let $K_c$ be the filled Julia set of $T_c(z) = z^2 + c$ and let $M$ be the Mandelbrot set. If $c \in M$, then $K_c$ is nonempty and connected. If $c \notin M$, then $K_c$ is homeomorphic to the Cantor space $\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ of binary sequences with the product topology.

nodes.summary: For each complex number $c$, the map $T_c : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ is given by $T_c(z) = z^2 + c$.

Max-min indecomposable sequences and lunar primes

nodes.summary: The max-min product of sequences $g, h \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is the sequence $g \otimes h$ with $(g \otimes h)_k = \max_{i + j = k} \min(g_i, h_j)$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the maximum running over pairs of natural numbers $(i, j)$. This is the product of the max-min semiring $(\mathbb{N}, \max, \min)$ on coefficient sequences.
nodes.title: Max-min product

nodes.summary: For all sequences $g, h \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, the max-min product satisfies $(g \otimes h)_0 = \min(g_0, h_0)$.
nodes.title: Constant coefficient of a max-min product

nodes.summary: For all sequences $g, h \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, the max-min product satisfies $(g \otimes h)_1 = \max(\min(g_0, h_1), \min(g_1, h_0))$.
nodes.title: Linear coefficient of a max-min product

nodes.summary: A coefficient sequence $g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ over the max-min semiring is a monomial when exactly one of its entries is nonzero, that is, when it is $c x^i$ for some index $i$ and some coefficient $c \neq 0$.
nodes.title: Monomials over the max-min semiring

nodes.summary: The zero coefficient sequence $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is not a max-min monomial: a monomial has exactly one nonzero entry, and the zero sequence has none.
nodes.title: The zero sequence is not a monomial

nodes.summary: A coefficient sequence $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is indecomposable (in the arXiv version: irreducible) when for all sequences $g, h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $g \otimes h = f$, where $\otimes$ is the max-min product, $g$ or $h$ is a max-min monomial, that is, a sequence with exactly one nonzero term.
nodes.title: Max-min indecomposable sequences

nodes.summary: The zero coefficient sequence $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is not indecomposable over the max-min semiring: it factors as $0 = 0 \otimes 0$, where $\otimes$ is the max-min product, and the zero sequence is not a monomial.
nodes.title: The zero sequence is decomposable

nodes.summary: Let $n$ and $b$ be natural numbers. The coefficient sequence of a digit string $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ with digits in $\{0, \dots, b - 1\}$ is the sequence $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ whose $k$-th term is $a_k$ for $k < n$ and $0$ for $k \ge n$.
nodes.title: Coefficient sequence of a digit string

nodes.summary: Let $n$ and $b$ be natural numbers and let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be a digit string with digits in $\{0, \dots, b - 1\}$. Then for every $k \ge n$, the $k$-th term of the coefficient sequence of $a$ is $0$.
nodes.title: A digit string has no coefficients beyond its length

nodes.summary: For a natural number $b$, the lunar unit of base $b$ is the coefficient sequence $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ whose constant term is $b - 1$ and whose other terms are all $0$, that is, the constant polynomial $b - 1$ over the max-min semiring. The subtraction is truncated, so the lunar unit of base $0$ is the zero sequence.
nodes.title: Lunar unit

nodes.summary: For every natural number $b \ge 2$, the lunar unit of base $b$, the sequence with constant term $b - 1$ and all other terms $0$, is a max-min monomial: it has exactly one nonzero term.
nodes.title: The lunar unit is a monomial

nodes.summary: Let $b$ be a natural number. The lunar unit of base $b$ is the constant polynomial $b - 1$, the sequence with constant term $b - 1$ and all other terms $0$. A coefficient sequence $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is a lunar prime of base $b$ (Applegate, LeBrun and Sloane) when for all sequences $g, h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with all terms less than $b$ and $g \otimes h = f$, where $\otimes$ is the max-min…
nodes.title: Lunar primes

nodes.summary: For every integer $b \ge 2$, the zero sequence is not a lunar prime of base $b$: $0 = 0 \otimes 0$, where $\otimes$ is the max-min product, and $0$ is not the lunar unit, the constant polynomial $b - 1$ with coefficient sequence $(b - 1, 0, 0, \dots)$.
nodes.title: Zero is not a lunar prime

nodes.summary: Let $b$ be a natural number. A coefficient sequence $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is a prime candidate in base $b$ when its constant term $f_0$ is nonzero and some term $f_i$ equals $b - 1$, where the subtraction is truncated, so that $b - 1 = 0$ when $b = 0$. For $f$ with all terms less than $b$, the second condition says that the largest coefficient of $f$ is $b - 1$.
nodes.title: Lunar prime candidates

nodes.summary: For every natural number $b \ge 2$, the lunar unit of base $b$, the sequence with constant term $b - 1$ and all other terms $0$, is a prime candidate in base $b$: its constant term is nonzero and one of its terms equals $b - 1$.
nodes.title: The lunar unit is a prime candidate

nodes.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, consider the Boolean polynomials of degree exactly $n$ with nonzero constant term, that is, the base-$2$ lunar numbers given by digit strings $(a_0, \dots, a_n) \in \{0, 1\}^{n+1}$ with $a_0 \ne 0$ and $a_n \ne 0$. For natural numbers $g$ and $n$, a finite set $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ is a $g$-difference basis for $[n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$ if $r_{A-A}(x) \ge g$ for every $x \in [n]$, and $\eta_g(n)$ is the least size of such a set.

nodes.summary: For an abelian group $G$ and $g \in \mathbb{N}$, a $g$-difference basis of $G$ is a finite set $A \subseteq G$ such that every $x \in G$ equals $a - a'$ for at least $g$ ordered pairs $(a, a') \in A \times A$. The difference basis number $\eta_g(G)$ is the least size of a $g$-difference basis of $G$, and $0$ if $G$ has none.
