nodes.summary: Let $q$ and $g$ be natural numbers with $g \mid q - 1$, let $K$ be a finite field with $q^2$ elements, and let $\theta \in K$ be a primitive $(q^2 - 1)$-th root of unity, that is, a generator of $K^\times$. If $a$ and $b$ are natural numbers less than $q^2 - 1$ with $(\theta^a - \theta)^q = \theta^a - \theta$ and $(\theta^b - \theta)^q = \theta^b - \theta$, and $(q^2 - 1)/g$ divides $a - b$, then $a = b$.
nodes.title: Nonzero differences of the Bose–Chowla set avoid the subgroup of order $g$

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $g$ and $n$, let $\alpha_g(n)$ be the largest size of a set $A \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$ such that every nonzero integer $x$ is the difference $a - a'$ of at most $g$ ordered pairs $(a, a') \in A \times A$. If $g \ge 1$, then for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ we have $\alpha_g(n) \le (1 + \varepsilon)\sqrt{gn}$ for all sufficiently large $n$; that is, $\alpha_g(n) \le (1 + o(1))\sqrt{gn}$.
nodes.title: Upper bound for sets with bounded difference multiplicities

nodes.summary: For every integer $g \ge 1$ there are finite sets $A_n \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$ of integers, one for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, such that for every $n$ each nonzero integer $x$ equals $a - a'$ for at most $g$ ordered pairs $(a, a') \in A_n \times A_n$, and $|A_n| / \sqrt{gn} \to 1$ as $n \to \infty$.
nodes.title: Lower-bound construction for sets with bounded difference multiplicities

nodes.summary: For a finite set $A$ of integers and an integer $x$, write $r_{A-A}(x)$ for the number of ordered pairs $(a, a') \in A \times A$ with $a - a' = x$. For every integer $g \ge 1$, let $\alpha_g(n)$ be the largest size of a set $A$ of integers in the interval $[1, n]$ with $r_{A-A}(x) \le g$ for every nonzero integer $x$. Then $\alpha_g(n) / \sqrt{gn} \to 1$ as $n \to \infty$, that is,…
nodes.title: Asymptotics of the largest sets with bounded difference counts
Difference sets of sparse sets

nodes.summary: The proposition asserts the following for every infinite set $A$ of natural numbers. Write $A(N) = |A \cap \{1, \dots, N\}|$ for its counting function and $D(N)$ for the number of integers $d \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ of the form $d = a - b$ with $a, b \in A$. If $A(N)/N \to 0$ as $N \to \infty$, then $\limsup_{N \to \infty} D(N)/A(N) = +\infty$.
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 899 on difference sets of sparse sets

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be an infinite set of natural numbers whose counting function $A(N) = |A \cap \{1, \dots, N\}|$ satisfies $A(N)/N \to 0$ as $N \to \infty$, and let $D(N)$ be the number of integers $d \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ of the form $d = a - b$ with $a, b \in A$. Then $\limsup_{N \to \infty} D(N)/A(N) = +\infty$, where the ratio is computed in the extended reals and taken to be $0$ when $A(N) = 0$.
nodes.title: Ruzsa's theorem on difference sets of sparse sets
Greedy B_h-sets

reading_title.source: Next term of a greedy $B_h$-set

nodes.summary: Let $h$ and $a$ be natural numbers and $A$ a set of natural numbers. Then $a$ is the next greedy $B_h$ choice after $A$ if $a$ is greater than every element of $A$, the set $A \cup \{a\}$ is a $B_h$-set, and for every natural number $b < a$ that is greater than every element of $A$, the set $A \cup \{b\}$ is not a $B_h$-set.
nodes.title: Next term of a greedy $B_h$-set

parts: Fourth positive term of the greedy
reading_title.source: Fourth positive term of the greedy $B_h$-set

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $h$ and $a$, we say that $a$ is the fourth positive element $a_4(h)$ of the greedy $B_h$-set if $1$ is the next greedy $B_h$ choice after $\{0\}$, $h + 1$ is the next greedy $B_h$ choice after $\{0, 1\}$, $h^2 + h + 1$ is the next greedy $B_h$ choice after $\{0, 1, h + 1\}$, and $a$ is the next greedy $B_h$ choice after $\{0, 1, h + 1, h^2 + h + 1\}$.
nodes.title: Fourth positive term of the greedy $B_h$-set

reading_title.source: Quasipolynomial for the fourth greedy $B_h$ term

nodes.summary: For a natural number $h$, the value $v(h)$ is $(h^3 + 3h^2 + 3h + 1)/2$ if $h$ is odd and $(h^3 + 2h^2 + 3h + 2)/2$ if $h$ is even.
nodes.title: Quasipolynomial for the fourth greedy $B_h$ term

reading_title.source: Formula for the fourth greedy $B_h$ term

nodes.summary: For every integer $h \ge 1$, the fourth positive element $a_4(h)$ of the greedy $B_h$-set is $(h^3 + 3h^2 + 3h + 1)/2$ if $h$ is odd and $(h^3 + 2h^2 + 3h + 2)/2$ if $h$ is even.
nodes.title: Formula for the fourth greedy $B_h$ term

parts: Lower bound for the fourth greedy
reading_title.source: Lower bound for the fourth greedy $B_h$ term

nodes.summary: Let $h$ and $a$ be natural numbers with $h \ge 2$. If $a$ is the fourth positive element $a_4(h)$ of the greedy $B_h$-set, then $a \ge v(h)$, where $v(h) = (h^3 + 3h^2 + 3h + 1)/2$ if $h$ is odd and $v(h) = (h^3 + 2h^2 + 3h + 2)/2$ if $h$ is even.
nodes.title: Lower bound for the fourth greedy $B_h$ term

parts: Upper bound for the fourth greedy
reading_title.source: Upper bound for the fourth greedy $B_h$ term

nodes.summary: Let $h$ and $a$ be natural numbers with $h \ge 1$. If $a$ is the fourth positive element $a_4(h)$ of the greedy $B_h$-set, then $a \le v(h)$, where $v(h) = (h^3 + 3h^2 + 3h + 1)/2$ if $h$ is odd and $v(h) = (h^3 + 2h^2 + 3h + 2)/2$ if $h$ is even.
nodes.title: Upper bound for the fourth greedy $B_h$ term
Sidon sets

nodes.summary: A set in an additive commutative monoid is Sidon when every equality of two pairwise sums is trivial up to swapping the summands. Repeated summands are included.
nodes.title: Sidon set

nodes.summary: A finite set $A$ of natural numbers is a Sidon set when every equality $a + b = c + d$ with $a, b, c, d \in A$ is trivial, that is, $a = c$ and $b = d$, or $a = d$ and $b = c$.
nodes.title: Finite Sidon sets of natural numbers

nodes.summary: For a finite set $A$ of natural numbers, the sumset $A + A$ is the finite set of all sums $x + y$ with $x, y \in A$.
nodes.title: Sumset of a finite set of natural numbers

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a finite set of natural numbers. A natural number $a$ is isolated in $S$ when $a \in S$, $a + 1 \notin S$, and either $a = 0$ or $a - 1 \notin S$.
nodes.title: Isolated elements of a set of natural numbers

nodes.summary: For a finite set $S$ of natural numbers, the isolated count of $S$ is the number of elements $a \in S$ with $a + 1 \notin S$ and either $a = 0$ or $a - 1 \notin S$.
nodes.title: Number of isolated elements

nodes.summary: A finite set $A$ of natural numbers is a Sidon set when $a + b = c + d$ with $a, b, c, d \in A$ implies $\{a, b\} = \{c, d\}$, and its sumset is $A + A = \{x + y : x, y \in A\}$. An element $s$ of a finite set $S$ of natural numbers is isolated in $S$ when $s + 1 \notin S$ and either $s = 0$ or $s - 1 \notin S$. The proposition asserts that for every natural number $M \ge 1$ there is a natural number $K$ such that…
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 152 on isolated sums of Sidon sets

nodes.summary: For every natural number $M \ge 1$ there is a natural number $K$ such that every finite Sidon set $A$ of natural numbers with at least $K$ elements has at least $M$ isolated elements in its sumset $A + A = \{x + y : x, y \in A\}$. Here $A$ is a Sidon set when $a + b = c + d$ with $a, b, c, d \in A$ implies $\{a, b\} = \{c, d\}$, and an element $s$ of $A + A$ is isolated when $s + 1 \notin A + A$ and either $s = 0$…
nodes.title: Large Sidon sets have many isolated sums
Golomb rulers

nodes.summary: For a natural number $m$, the set of Golomb ruler lengths with $m$ marks consists of the natural numbers $L$ for which there is a finite Sidon set $S$ of natural numbers with $S \subseteq \{0, 1, \dots, L\}$, exactly $m$ elements, and $L \in S$. A mark at $0$ is not required.
nodes.title: Golomb ruler lengths

nodes.summary: For $m \ge 1$, the optimal Golomb ruler length $G(m)$ is the infimum in $\mathbb{N}$ of the set of Golomb ruler lengths with $m$ marks, that is, of the natural numbers $L$ such that some $m$-element Sidon set of natural numbers contained in $\{0, 1, \dots, L\}$ contains $L$; for $m = 0$ we set $G(0) = 0$.
nodes.title: Optimal Golomb ruler length

nodes.summary: The optimal Golomb ruler lengths with $m = 3, 4, \dots, 11$ marks are, in order, $3, 6, 11, 17, 25, 34, 44, 55, 72$.
nodes.title: Optimal Golomb rulers with 3 to 11 marks

nodes.summary: The optimal Golomb ruler length with $27$ marks is $553$.
nodes.title: Optimal 27-mark Golomb ruler

nodes.summary: The optimal Golomb ruler length with $28$ marks is $585$.
nodes.title: Optimal 28-mark Golomb ruler
Number of Sidon sets

reading_title.source: Sidon subsets of $\{1, \dots, N\}$

nodes.summary: For a natural number $N$, this is the finite family of all subsets of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ that are Sidon sets of natural numbers, including the empty set and the singletons.
nodes.title: Sidon subsets of $\{1, \dots, N\}$

reading_title.source: Largest Sidon subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ (Erdős Problem 861)

nodes.summary: For a natural number $N$, $f(N)$ is the largest cardinality of a Sidon subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$.
nodes.title: Largest Sidon subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ (Erdős Problem 861)

nodes.summary: Let $A(N)$ be the number of Sidon subsets of $\{1, \dots, N\}$, including the empty set and the singletons, and let $f(N)$ be the largest size of a Sidon subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$. The statement is that $A(N) / 2^{f(N)} \to \infty$ as $N \to \infty$.
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 861, first question

nodes.summary: Let $A(N)$ be the number of Sidon subsets of $\{1, \dots, N\}$, including the empty set and the singletons, and let $f(N)$ be the largest size of a Sidon subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$. The statement is that $\log_2 A(N) / f(N) \to 1$ as $N \to \infty$, that is, $A(N) = 2^{(1 + o(1)) f(N)}$.
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 861, second question

nodes.summary: Let $A(N)$ be the number of Sidon subsets of $\{1, \dots, N\}$, including the empty set and the singletons, and let $f(N)$ be the largest size of a Sidon subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$. Then $A(N) / 2^{f(N)} \to \infty$ as $N \to \infty$.
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 861, first question: positive answer

nodes.summary: Let $A(N)$ be the number of Sidon subsets of $\{1, \dots, N\}$, including the empty set and the singletons, and let $f(N)$ be the largest size of a Sidon subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$. Then the ratio $\log_2 A(N) / f(N)$ does not tend to $1$ as $N \to \infty$; that is, $A(N) = 2^{(1 + o(1)) f(N)}$ fails.
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 861, second question: negative answer
Sidon ideal

nodes.summary: A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a *weak Sidon set* (or *well spread*) if sums of two distinct elements of $A$ are distinct: whenever $a, b, c, d \in A$ satisfy $a < b$, $c < d$ and $a + b = c + d$, then $a = c$.
nodes.title: Weak Sidon set

nodes.summary: Every Sidon set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a weak Sidon set.
nodes.title: Sidon sets are weak Sidon sets

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a property of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$. The ideal generated by $P$ is the family of all sets $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ that are contained in the union of finitely many sets with property $P$. The empty union is allowed, so the empty set always belongs to it.
nodes.title: Ideal generated by a property

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a property of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$. Every set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ with property $P$ lies in the ideal generated by $P$, the family of all subsets of finite unions of sets with property $P$.
nodes.title: Sets with a property lie in the ideal it generates

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a property of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$. If $A$ lies in the ideal generated by $P$ and $B \subseteq A$, then $B$ also lies in the ideal generated by $P$.
nodes.title: Generated ideals are closed under subsets

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a property of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$, and consider the ideal generated by $P$, the family of all subsets of finite unions of sets with property $P$. If $A$ and $B$ lie in this ideal, then so does $A \cup B$.
nodes.title: Generated ideals are closed under unions

nodes.summary: The Sidon ideal $\mathrm{Si}$ is the ideal on $\mathbb{N}$ generated by the Sidon sets: it consists of all sets $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ contained in a finite union of Sidon subsets of $\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: Sidon ideal

nodes.summary: A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is *gap-lacunary* (called *lacunary* in the source) if it is infinite and, writing $A(n)$ for its $n$-th element in increasing order (counting from $n = 0$), the gaps $A(n+1) - A(n)$ tend to infinity as $n \to \infty$.
nodes.title: Gap-lacunary set

nodes.summary: Every gap-lacunary set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is infinite.
nodes.title: Gap-lacunary sets are infinite

nodes.summary: A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is *almost thin* if it is infinite and, writing $A(n)$ for its $n$-th element in increasing order (counting from $n = 0$), there is a real number $\alpha < 1$ such that $A(n)/A(n+1) \le \alpha$ for all sufficiently large $n$.
nodes.title: Almost thin set

nodes.summary: Every almost thin set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is infinite.
nodes.title: Almost thin sets are infinite

nodes.summary: The van der Waerden ideal $W$ consists of the sets $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ for which there is an $n > 0$ such that $A$ contains no arithmetic progression $a, a + r, \dots, a + (n - 1) r$ of $n$ terms with $a \in \mathbb{N}$ and $r > 0$.
nodes.title: Van der Waerden ideal

nodes.summary: The empty subset of $\mathbb{N}$ belongs to the van der Waerden ideal.
nodes.title: The empty set lies in the van der Waerden ideal

nodes.summary: For a set $Z \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, the positive difference set $D(Z)$ is the set of all differences $a - b$ with $a, b \in Z$ and $a > b$.
nodes.title: Positive difference set

nodes.summary: For a set $Z \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, let $D(Z) = \{a - b : a, b \in Z,\ b < a\}$ be its set of positive differences. The ideal $D_{\mathrm{fin}}$ consists of the sets $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ for which there is a natural number $n$ such that $D(Z) \not\subseteq A$ for every $n$-element set $Z \subseteq \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: The ideal of sets avoiding large difference sets

nodes.summary: The empty set belongs to the ideal $D_{\mathrm{fin}}$ of sets $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ for which some natural number $n$ satisfies $D(Z) \not\subseteq A$ for every $n$-element set $Z \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, where $D(Z)$ is the set of positive differences $a - b$ with $a, b \in Z$ and $b < a$.
nodes.title: The empty set lies in the difference-set ideal

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$, $C$, $M$ and $K$, the block $\mathrm{Block}(n, C, M, K)$ is the set of natural numbers $M l + C \cdot 2^k$ with $0 \le k < n$ and $1 \le l \le K$.
nodes.title: Block sets

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $C$ and $M$, the block $\mathrm{Block}(1, C, M, 1) = \{M l + C \cdot 2^k : 0 \le k < 1,\ 1 \le l \le 1\}$ is the singleton $\{M + C\}$.
nodes.title: One-term blocks

nodes.summary: Every weak Sidon set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is the union of two disjoint Sidon sets $B$ and $C$.
nodes.title: Weak Sidon sets split into two Sidon sets

nodes.summary: The ideal on $\mathbb{N}$ generated by the weak Sidon sets equals the Sidon ideal.
nodes.title: Weak Sidon sets generate the Sidon ideal

reading_title.source: The Sidon ideal is $F_\sigma$

nodes.summary: Give the Cantor space $\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ the product topology and identify each set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ with its indicator function. Then the set of indicator functions of the members of the Sidon ideal is a countable union of closed subsets of $\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$.
nodes.title: The Sidon ideal is $F_\sigma$

nodes.summary: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ with $0 \notin A$, and write $A(n)$ for the $n$-th element of $A$ in increasing order, counting from $n = 0$, with $A(n) = 0$ when $A$ has at most $n$ elements. If $2 A(n) \le A(n+1)$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then $A$ is a Sidon set.
nodes.title: Positive sets whose elements at least double are Sidon

nodes.summary: Call a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ lacunary if it is infinite and the gaps $A(n + 1) - A(n)$ between consecutive elements tend to infinity, where $A(n)$ is the $n$-th element of $A$ in increasing order. Every set in the Sidon ideal is contained in a finite union of lacunary sets, that is, it lies in the ideal $\mathrm{Lac}$ generated by the lacunary sets.
nodes.title: The Sidon ideal is contained in the lacunary ideal

nodes.summary: There exist a Sidon set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and a real constant $c > 0$ such that $|A \cap \{1, \dots, n\}| > c\, n^{1/3}$ for every natural number $n \ge 1$.
nodes.title: Mian–Chowla lower bound for an infinite Sidon set

nodes.summary: There exist a Sidon set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and a real constant $c > 0$ such that $|A \cap \{1, \dots, n\}| > c\, (n \log n)^{1/3}$ for every natural number $n \ge 1$, where $\log$ is the natural logarithm.
nodes.title: Ajtai–Komlós–Szemerédi lower bound for an infinite Sidon set

nodes.summary: There is a Sidon set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that for every real $\varepsilon > 0$, the inequality $|A \cap \{1, \dots, n\}| > n^{\sqrt{2} - 1 - \varepsilon}$ holds for all sufficiently large natural numbers $n$; that is, $|A \cap \{1, \dots, n\}| > n^{\sqrt{2} - 1 - o(1)}$.
nodes.title: Ruzsa's lower bound for an infinite Sidon set

nodes.summary: There is a Sidon set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ that is not contained in any finite union of almost thin sets; that is, $A$ does not belong to the ideal generated by the almost thin sets.
nodes.title: A Sidon set outside the almost thin ideal

nodes.summary: Every set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ that is contained in a finite union of almost thin sets is contained in a finite union of Sidon sets; that is, the ideal generated by the almost thin sets is contained in the Sidon ideal.
nodes.title: The almost thin ideal is contained in the Sidon ideal

nodes.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and $C \ge 1$ be natural numbers, and put $M = C \cdot 2^n + 1$ and $K = (n - 1)\binom{n}{2} + 1$. Then the block $\mathrm{Block}(n, C, M, K) = \{M l + C \cdot 2^k : 0 \le k < n,\ 1 \le l \le K\}$ is not contained in the union of any $n - 1$ Sidon subsets of $\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: A block not covered by few Sidon sets

nodes.summary: There is a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ that belongs to the van der Waerden ideal, is contained in a finite union of gap-lacunary sets (infinite sets whose gaps between consecutive elements tend to infinity), and belongs to the ideal $D_{\mathrm{fin}}$ of sets avoiding large difference sets, but is not contained in any finite union of Sidon sets.
nodes.title: A set in the van der Waerden, lacunary and difference-set ideals outside the Sidon ideal
Sidon sets and perfect difference sets

reading_title.source: Perfect difference sets modulo $v$

nodes.summary: A set $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a perfect difference set modulo a natural number $v$ when every nonzero residue $x$ modulo $v$ satisfies $x \equiv a - b \pmod{v}$ for exactly one ordered pair $(a, b)$ of elements of $B$.
nodes.title: Perfect difference sets modulo $v$

nodes.summary: The proposition that for every finite Sidon set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ there are a prime $p$ and a set $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ with $A \subseteq B$ such that $B$ is a perfect difference set modulo $p^2 + p + 1$.
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 707

nodes.summary: The proposition that for every finite Sidon set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ there are a natural number $m \ge 1$ and a set $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ with $A \subseteq B$ such that $B$ is a perfect difference set modulo $m^2 + m + 1$.
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 707, weak form

nodes.summary: It is not the case that every finite Sidon set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is contained in a perfect difference set modulo $p^2 + p + 1$ for some prime $p$: there is a finite Sidon set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that for every prime $p$, no set $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ with $A \subseteq B$ is a perfect difference set modulo $p^2 + p + 1$. Here $A$ is Sidon when $w + x = y + z$ with $w, x, y, z \in A$ forces…
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 707 is false

nodes.summary: It is not the case that every finite Sidon set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is contained in a perfect difference set modulo $m^2 + m + 1$ for some natural number $m \ge 1$: there is a finite Sidon set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that for every $m \ge 1$, no set $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ with $A \subseteq B$ is a perfect difference set modulo $m^2 + m + 1$. Here $A$ is Sidon when $w + x = y + z$ with $w, x, y, z \in A$…
nodes.title: The weak form of Erdős Problem 707 is false
Sidon sets meeting every infinite progression

nodes.summary: The proposition that the complement of every Sidon set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ contains an infinite arithmetic progression: for every Sidon set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ there are natural numbers $a$ and $d \ge 1$ such that $a + kd \notin A$ for every natural number $k$.
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 198

nodes.summary: It is not the case that the complement of every Sidon set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ contains an infinite arithmetic progression: there is a Sidon set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that for all natural numbers $a$ and $d \ge 1$ some term $a + kd$, $k \in \mathbb{N}$, lies in $A$. Here $A$ is Sidon when $w + x = y + z$ with $w, x, y, z \in A$ forces $\{w, x\} = \{y, z\}$.
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 198 is false
Upper bounds for Sidon sets

reading_title.source: Largest Sidon subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ (Green's Problem 31)

nodes.summary: For a natural number $N$, $F(N)$ is the largest cardinality of a Sidon subset of $[N] = \{1, \dots, N\}$.
nodes.title: Largest Sidon subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ (Green's Problem 31)

nodes.summary: Let $F(N)$ be the largest size of a Sidon subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$. The statement is that there are a real constant $c < 1$ and a natural number $N_0$ such that $F(N) \le \sqrt{N} + c N^{1/4}$ for all $N \ge N_0$.
nodes.title: Green's Problem 31: improving Lindström's upper bound

nodes.summary: Let $F(N)$ be the largest size of a Sidon subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$. There are a real constant $c < 1$ and a natural number $N_0$ such that $F(N) \le \sqrt{N} + c N^{1/4}$ for all $N \ge N_0$.
nodes.title: Lindström's upper bound for Sidon sets can be improved

nodes.summary: Sets with no solution to x+y=z or similar: sum-free sets in abelian groups and intervals, counts of sum-free and maximal sum-free sets, large sum-free subsets, square-sum-free, divisor-sum-free and non-averaging sets.
nodes.title: Sum-free sets

nodes.summary: A set $S$ in a type $M$ with a multiplication is product-free if $xy \notin S$ for all $x, y \in S$, where $x$ and $y$ need not be distinct.
nodes.title: Product-free set
Divisor-sum-free sets

nodes.summary: A finite set $S$ of natural numbers is divisor-sum-free if no element $x \in S$ divides the sum of the elements of any nonempty subset of $S \setminus \{x\}$.
nodes.title: Divisor-sum-free sets

nodes.summary: The proposition that for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a natural number $N_0$ such that for every natural number $N \ge 1$ with $N \ge N_0$ there is a set $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ with $|S| > N^{1/2 - \varepsilon}$ that is divisor-sum-free: no element $x \in S$ divides the sum of the elements of any nonempty subset of $S \setminus \{x\}$.
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 131: large divisor-sum-free sets

nodes.summary: It is not true that for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a natural number $N_0$ such that for every natural number $N \ge 1$ with $N \ge N_0$ there is a set $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ with $|S| > N^{1/2 - \varepsilon}$ that is divisor-sum-free, meaning that no element $x \in S$ divides the sum of the elements of any nonempty subset of $S \setminus \{x\}$.
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 131 has a negative answer
Large sum-free subsets

nodes.summary: A finite set $S$ of natural numbers is sum-free if $x + y \notin S$ for all $x, y \in S$, where $x = y$ is allowed.
nodes.title: Sum-free sets of natural numbers

nodes.summary: The statement that there is a function $\omega$ from the natural numbers to the real numbers with $\omega(n) \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$ such that every finite set $A$ of positive integers contains a sum-free subset $B \subseteq A$ with $|B| \ge |A|/3 + \omega(|A|)$.
nodes.title: Green's Problem 1 on large sum-free subsets

nodes.summary: There is a function $\omega$ from the natural numbers to the real numbers with $\omega(n) \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$ such that every finite set $A$ of positive integers contains a subset $B \subseteq A$ with $x + y \notin B$ for all $x, y \in B$ (a sum-free subset) and $|B| \ge |A|/3 + \omega(|A|)$.

Square-sum-free sets

nodes.summary: A finite set $A$ of natural numbers is square-sum-free if for all $a, b \in A$, not necessarily distinct, the sum $a + b$ is not a perfect square.

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a set with an addition. A subset $S \subseteq G$ is sum-free if $x + y \notin S$ for all $x, y \in S$, where $x = y$ is allowed; that is, $S$ contains no Schur triple $x + y = z$ with $x, y, z \in S$.
nodes.title: Sum-free set

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a set with an addition. A subset $S \subseteq G$ is distinct sum-free if there are no pairwise distinct $x, y, z \in S$ with $x + y = z$, that is, if $S$ contains no distinct Schur triple.

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a set with an addition and $S \subseteq G$. Write $\mu(S)$ for the supremum in $\mathbb{N}$ of the sizes of the finite sum-free subsets of $S$ (sets $T$ with $x + y \notin T$ for all $x, y \in T$), taken to be $0$ if these sizes are unbounded. For finite $S$ this is the largest size of a sum-free subset of $S$, and $\mu(G)$ is the value for $S = G$.

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a set with an addition. The number $f^*_{\max}(G)$ is the number of subsets of $G$ that are maximal, with respect to inclusion, among the distinct sum-free subsets of $G$, and it is $0$ if there are infinitely many such subsets. Here $S \subseteq G$ is distinct sum-free if $x + y \notin S$ for all $x, y \in S$ such that $x$, $y$ and $x + y$ are pairwise distinct.
nodes.title: Number of maximal distinct sum-free sets

nodes.summary: For a subset $F$ of a set $G$ with an addition, this is the number of ordered pairs $(x, y)$ with $x, y \in F$ such that $x$, $y$ and $x + y$ are pairwise distinct and $x + y \in F$, that is, the number of ordered distinct Schur triples $(x, y, x + y)$ in $F$. If there are infinitely many such pairs, the value is $0$ by convention.

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid, $A \subseteq M$ and $n$ a natural number. $A$ is an asymptotic additive basis of order $n$ if all but finitely many elements of $M$ are sums of exactly $n$ (not necessarily distinct) elements of $A$, that is, $M \setminus nA$ is finite, where $nA = \{a_1 + \dots + a_n : a_1, \dots, a_n \in A\}$ and $0A = \{0\}$.

Schnirelmann density

nodes.summary: For a set $A$ of natural numbers, let $\sigma(A) = \inf_{n \ge 1} |A \cap \{1, \dots, n\}| / n$ be its Schnirelmann density. If $A$ and $B$ are sets of natural numbers that both contain $0$, then their sumset $A + B = \{a + b : a \in A,\ b \in B\}$ satisfies $\sigma(A) + \sigma(B) - \sigma(A)\sigma(B) \le \sigma(A + B)$.

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be a set of natural numbers with $0 \in A$ whose Schnirelmann density $\sigma(A) = \inf_{n \ge 1} |A \cap \{1, \dots, n\}| / n$ is positive. Then $A$ is an additive basis of finite order: there is a natural number $h$ such that every natural number $n$ can be written as $n = a_1 + \dots + a_h$ with $a_1, \dots, a_h \in A$, repetitions allowed.

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an abelian group, $s = (s_i)_{i \in \iota}$ a family in $G$ indexed by a finite type $\iota$ (a colored multiset), and $g \in G$. nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an abelian group, $m$ a natural number and $s = (s_i)_{i \in \iota}$ a family of elements of $G$ indexed by a finite set $\iota$ (a colored multiset: repeated values count separately). The family $s$ is a perfect $m$-cover of $G$ when every $g \in G$ equals $\sum_{i \in I} s_i$ for exactly $m$ subsets $I \subseteq \iota$ (the empty subset has sum $0$).

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an abelian group, let $s = (x_1, \dots, x_{k+1})$ be a family in $G$ that is a perfect $2^j$-cover of $G$, and let $S_1 = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$. For every $a \in G$, if $S_1$ covers $a$ exactly $c$ times, then $S_1$ covers $a + x_{k+1}$ exactly $2^j - c$ times.
nodes.title: Removing the last element of a perfect $2^j$-cover

parts: Shifting by multiples of the last element of a perfect
reading_title.source: Shifting by multiples of the last element of a perfect $2^j$-cover

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an abelian group, let $s = (x_1, \dots, x_{k+1})$ be a family in $G$ that is a perfect $2^j$-cover of $G$, and let $S_1 = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$. For every $b \in G$, if $S_1$ covers $b$ exactly $c$ times, then for every integer $t$ it covers $b + 2t\,x_{k+1}$ exactly $c$ times and $b + (2t + 1)\,x_{k+1}$ exactly $2^j - c$ times.
nodes.title: Shifting by multiples of the last element of a perfect $2^j$-cover

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of order $2^n$ and let $a, b \in G$ be nonzero. Then $b = (2j+1)a$ for some integer $j$ if and only if, for every perfect cover $S$ of $G$ with $a \in S$, the set $(S \setminus \{a\}) \cup \{b\}$ is again a perfect cover of $G$. If moreover $a \ne b$, then $b = (2j+1)a$ for some integer $j$ if and only if no perfect cover of $G$ contains both $a$ and $b$.
nodes.title: Odd multiples and replacement in perfect covers

reading_title.source: Replacing an entry of a perfect $2^k$-cover by an odd multiple

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an abelian group, let $k$ and $N$ be natural numbers, and let $a, b, s_1, \dots, s_N \in G$. If the family $(a, s_1, \dots, s_N)$ is a perfect $2^k$-cover of $G$ and $b = (2j + 1)a$ for some integer $j$, then the family $(b, s_1, \dots, s_N)$ is also a perfect $2^k$-cover of $G$.

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an abelian group of order $2^n$ and $S$ a perfect cover of $G$. For a finite $A \subseteq G$, let $\mathcal{T}(A)$ be the set of combinations $\sum_{x \in A} c_x x$ in which every integer coefficient $c_x$ is $0$ or odd. Then: (a) for disjoint $A, B \subseteq S$, $\mathcal{T}(A) \cap \mathcal{T}(B) = \{0\}$; (b) if $A \subseteq S$ and $s \in S \setminus A$, then $s \notin \mathcal{T}(A)$.

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a vertex set $V$, and let $w$ assign a natural-number cost $w(uv)$ to each unordered pair of vertices $\{u, v\}$. For configurations $C, C' : V \to \mathbb{N}$, there is a pebbling step from $C$ to $C'$ if there is an edge $uv$ of $G$ with $0 < w(uv) \le C(u)$ such that $C'$ is obtained from $C$ by removing $w(uv)$ pebbles from $u$ and adding one pebble to $v$.

A configuration $C : V \to \mathbb{N}$ of pebbles is *solvable* if for every target vertex $r$ there is a finite, possibly empty, sequence of pebbling steps on $G$ with costs $w$ leading from $C$ to a configuration with at least one pebble on $r$.

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $d$ and $k$, the $d$-dimensional grid $P_k^d = \square_{i\lt d} P_k$ is the simple graph on $\{0, \dots, k-1\}^d$ in which $x$ and $y$ are adjacent when there is a coordinate $i$ with $x_j = y_j$ for all $j \ne i$ and $|x_i - y_i| = 1$. nodes.summary: Let $d$ and $k$ be natural numbers and let $w_0, \dots, w_{d-1}$ be natural numbers. The grid cost with cost $w_i$ in coordinate $i$ assigns to each unordered pair $\{x, y\}$ of points of $\{0, \dots, k-1\}^d$ the sum of the $w_i$ over the coordinates $i$ with $x_i \ne y_i$. On an edge of the grid exactly one coordinate differs, so an edge in coordinate $i$ costs $w_i$.

If $x_i \ne y_i$ and $x_j = y_j$ for every $j \ne i$, then the grid cost of the pair $\{x, y\}$ with cost $w_j$ in coordinate $j$ is $w_i$.

nodes.summary: Density versions: Szemerédi's and Roth's theorems and Roth-number bounds, Sárközy's theorem, cap sets, counts of three-term progressions, progressions in complements and in walks, arithmetic progression API, and polynomial triangle removal in vector spaces.
nodes.title: Arithmetic progressions in dense sets

nodes.summary: For every natural number $k \ge 1$ and every real number $\delta > 0$ there is a natural number $N$ such that for every $n \ge N$, every set $A \subseteq \{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ with $\delta n \le |A|$ contains an arithmetic progression of length $k$: there are natural numbers $a$ and $d > 0$ with $a + i d \in A$ for all $i < k$.
nodes.title: Szemerédi's theorem
Arithmetic progressions and progression-free sets

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid, $l \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ and $a, d \in M$. A set $s \subseteq M$ is an arithmetic progression of length $l$ with first term $a$ and difference $d$ if $s = \{a + n d : n \in \mathbb{N},\ n < l\}$ and $s$ has exactly $l$ elements, counting the size of an infinite set as $\infty$; here $n d$ is the sum of $n$ copies of $d$.
nodes.title: Set arithmetic progressions with given first term and difference

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an additive commutative monoid and $l \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$. A set $s \subseteq \alpha$ is an arithmetic progression of length $l$ if there are $a, d \in \alpha$ such that $s = \{a + nd : n \in \mathbb{N},\ n < l\}$ and $s$ has exactly $l$ elements (infinitely many when $l = \infty$). Here $nd$ denotes the sum of $n$ copies of $d$.
nodes.title: Sets that are arithmetic progressions

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid and $l \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$. If a set $s \subseteq M$ is an arithmetic progression of length $l$, then $s$ has exactly $l$ elements, counting the size of an infinite set as $\infty$.
nodes.title: Cardinality of a set arithmetic progression

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid and $l \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$. If a set $s \subseteq M$ is an arithmetic progression of length $l$, then there are $a, d \in M$ with $s = \{a + n d : n \in \mathbb{N},\ n < l\}$, where $n d$ is the sum of $n$ copies of $d$.
nodes.title: First term and difference of a set arithmetic progression

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid, $l \in \mathbb{N}$ and $a, d \in M$. A list $s$ of elements of $M$ is an arithmetic progression of length $l$ starting from $a$ with difference $d$, in either direction, if $s = (a, a + d, \dots, a + (l - 1)d)$ or $s = (a + (l - 1)d, \dots, a + d, a)$, where $n d$ is the sum of $n$ copies of $d$; when $l = 0$ both lists are empty.
nodes.title: List arithmetic progressions with given start and difference

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid and $l \in \mathbb{N}$. A list $s$ of elements of $M$ is an arithmetic progression of length $l$ if there are $a, d \in M$ such that $s = (a, a + d, \dots, a + (l - 1)d)$ or $s = (a + (l - 1)d, \dots, a + d, a)$, where $n d$ is the sum of $n$ copies of $d$.
nodes.title: Arithmetic progressions of lists

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid, $\beta$ a preordered type, $f : \beta \to M$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Then $f$ contains a monotone arithmetic progression of length $k$ if there are $x_1 < x_2 < \dots < x_k$ in $\beta$ such that the list $(f(x_1), \dots, f(x_k))$ is an arithmetic progression of length $k$: for some $a, d \in M$ it equals $(a, a + d, \dots, a + (k - 1)d)$ or its reverse.
nodes.title: Monotone arithmetic progressions in a function

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid and $l \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$. A set $s \subseteq M$ is free of nontrivial arithmetic progressions of length $l$ if every subset of $s$ that is an arithmetic progression of length $l$ forces $l \le 1$; equivalently, $l \le 1$ or no subset of $s$ is an arithmetic progression of length $l$.
nodes.title: Progression-free sets

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a set in an additive commutative monoid and $l \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ with $l > 1$. If $s$ is an arithmetic progression of length $l$, then $s$ is not free of nontrivial arithmetic progressions of length $l$.
nodes.title: A progression of length greater than one is not progression-free

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid and $l \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$. A finite set $s \subseteq M$ is free of nontrivial arithmetic progressions of length $l$ if it is so as a set: $l \le 1$, or no subset of $s$ is an arithmetic progression of length $l$.
nodes.title: Progression-free finite sets

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a set of natural numbers such that $a = b$ whenever $a, b, c \in s$ satisfy $a + c = 2b$. Then $s$ is free of nontrivial arithmetic progressions of length $3$: no subset of $s$ is an arithmetic progression of length $3$.
nodes.title: Sets of naturals without three-term progressions

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $k$ and $N$, $r_k(N)$ is the largest cardinality of a subset $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ that is free of nontrivial arithmetic progressions of length $k$, meaning that if $k \ge 2$ then no subset of $S$ is an arithmetic progression of length $k$ (for $k \le 1$ every subset qualifies).
nodes.title: Largest size of a progression-free subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $k$ and $N$, the largest size $r_k(N)$ of a subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ free of nontrivial arithmetic progressions of length $k$ satisfies $r_k(N) \le N$.
nodes.title: Trivial upper bound for the largest progression-free subset

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $k$ and $N$, let $r_k(N)$ be the largest size of a subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ free of nontrivial arithmetic progressions of length $k$. Then some subset $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ free of nontrivial arithmetic progressions of length $k$ has exactly $r_k(N)$ elements.
nodes.title: A largest progression-free subset is attained

nodes.summary: Let $k$ and $N$ be natural numbers, and let $S$ be a finite set of natural numbers with $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ that is free of nontrivial arithmetic progressions of length $k$. Then $|S| \le r_k(N)$, where $r_k(N)$ is the largest size of a subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ containing no nontrivial $k$-term arithmetic progression.
nodes.title: Progression-free subsets are bounded by the extremal size

nodes.summary: A $k$-term descending wave is a sequence $x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{k-1}$ of natural numbers with $x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_{k-1}$ and $x_{j-1} + x_{j+1} \le 2 x_j$ for every $j$ with $0 < j < k - 1$.
nodes.title: Descending wave

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, the statement that for every colouring of the natural numbers with two colours there is a monochromatic $k$-term descending wave all of whose terms lie in $\{1, \dots, n\}$. Equivalently, every colouring of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ with two colours has a monochromatic $k$-term descending wave, so the statement says $f(k) \le n$, where $f(k)$ is the least $n$ with this property.
nodes.title: Forcing a monochromatic descending wave

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, say that $n$ forces a $k$-term wave if every colouring of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ with two colours has a monochromatic $k$-term descending wave. The statement that for every natural number $k \ge 1$ the number $k^2 - k + 1$ forces a $k$-term wave and the number $k^2 - k$ does not; that is, $f(k) = k^2 - k + 1$ for every $k \ge 1$, where $f(k)$ is the least $n$ that forces a $k$-term wave.

Progression-free Ramsey sets

nodes.summary: This is the statement that for all natural numbers $k \ge 2$ and $r \ge 2$ there is a set $A$ of natural numbers that contains no arithmetic progression of $k + 1$ distinct terms and such that for every colouring $c$ of the natural numbers with $r$ colours there are a subset $t \subseteq A$ that is an arithmetic progression of $k$ distinct terms and a colour $i$ with $c(x) = i$ for every $x \in t$.

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a colouring of the natural numbers with the two colours true and false, let $b$ be a colour and let $l, N$ be natural numbers. Then $c$ has a monochromatic progression of colour $b$ and length $l$ in $\{1, \dots, N\}$ when there are natural numbers $a \ge 1$ and $d \ge 1$ with $a + (l - 1) d \le N$, where $l - 1$ is read as $0$ when $l = 0$, such that $c(a + j d) = b$ for every $j < l$.

Then the generalized Schur number $S_m(k, l)$, the largest $n$ such that $\{1, \dots, n\}$ admits a partition into $k$ classes that are $l$-sum-free modulo $m$, equals $m - 1$.
nodes.title: Modular Schur numbers attaining $m - 1$

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a prime, let $i$ and $l$ be positive integers with $l \not\equiv 1 \pmod p$, and let $k$ be a natural number with $k \ge p^i - 1$. Then the generalized Schur number modulo $p^i$ satisfies $S_{p^i}(k, l) = p^i - 1$.

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a prime and let $l$ be a positive integer with $l \ge p - 1$ and $l \not\equiv 1 \pmod p$. nodes.summary: Let $a_1, \dots, a_k$ be integers, the coefficients of the linear equation $a_1x_1 + \cdots + a_kx_k = 0$. The equation has a canceling partition when its indices split into pairs of distinct indices $i, j$ with $a_i + a_j = 0$; precisely, when there is a permutation $\sigma$ of the indices $1, \dots, k$ such that for every $i$ we have $\sigma(\sigma(i)) = i$, $\sigma(i) \ne i$ and $a_i + a_{\sigma(i)} = 0$.

nodes.summary: A subset $A$ of a commutative semigroup $(S, +)$ is thick when for every finite set $E \subseteq S$ there is an $x \in S$ with $E + x \subseteq A$, that is, $e + x \in A$ for every $e \in E$.

nodes.summary: A subset $A$ of a commutative semigroup $(S, +)$ is a CR-set (combinatorially rich) when for every natural number $n$, including $n = 0$, there is a natural number $r$ such that for every $r \times n$ matrix $(m_{ij})$ with entries in $S$ there are a nonempty set $\alpha \subseteq \{1, \ldots, r\}$ and an element $s \in S$ such that $s + \sum_{i \in \alpha} m_{ij} \in A$ for every column $j \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$.

A subset $A$ of $S$ is an essential CR-set when there is an ultrafilter $p$ on $S$ with $p + p = p$, all of whose members are CR-sets, such that $A \in p$.

Let $a_n$ be the number of words of length $n$ over $\{0, 1, 2\}$ that contain no abelian cube as a factor. Then $2^{n/24} = O(a_n)$ as $n \to \infty$: there is a constant $C$ such that $2^{n/24} \le C a_n$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

Square-free words

nodes.summary: A word $w$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a square if $w = xx$ for some nonempty word $x$, where $xx$ denotes the concatenation of $x$ with itself.
nodes.title: Square word

nodes.summary: A finite word $w$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ is square-free if no factor of $w$ is a square, where a factor of $w$ is a word $s$ with $w = psq$ for some words $p$ and $q$, and a square is a word $xx$ with $x$ nonempty.
nodes.title: Square-free finite word

nodes.summary: An infinite word $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ is square-free if it contains no two adjacent equal nonempty blocks: for all $i \ge 0$ and all $k \ge 1$ there is some $j < k$ with $u_{i+j} \ne u_{i+k+j}$.

nodes.summary: An infinite word $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ over the ternary alphabet is a square-free infinite ternary word if it is square-free as an infinite word.

nodes.summary: If a finite word $v$ is square-free and $u$ is a factor of $v$, that is, $v = puq$ for some words $p$ and $q$, then $u$ is square-free.

nodes.summary: A finite word $w$ is square-free if and only if, for every prefix $s$ of a suffix of $w$ and every nonempty prefix $x$ of $s$, we have $s \ne xx$, where $xx$ denotes the concatenation of $x$ with itself.

Then $f$ maps every square-free word over $\{a, b, c\}$ to a square-free word if and only if it maps every square-free word over $\{a, b, c\}$ of length at most $5$ to a square-free word.

Factor complexity of infinite words

nodes.summary: A right-infinite word over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a sequence $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ of letters $u_n \in \alpha$. For natural numbers $k$ and $i$, the length-$k$ factor of $u$ at position $i$ is the word $u_i u_{i+1} \cdots u_{i+k-1}$, given as the map $\{0, \ldots, k-1\} \to \alpha$, $s \mapsto u_{i+s}$.
nodes.title: Factor of an infinite word

nodes.summary: For a right-infinite word $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ and a natural number $k$, the set of length-$k$ factors of $u$ is the set of the maps $\{0, \ldots, k-1\} \to \alpha$, $s \mapsto u_{i+s}$, for $i \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: Set of factors of a given length

nodes.summary: For a right-infinite word $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ and a natural number $k$, the length-$k$ initial segment of $u$ is the word $u_0 u_1 \cdots u_{k-1}$, given as the map $\{0, \ldots, k-1\} \to \alpha$, $s \mapsto u_s$; it is the length-$k$ factor of $u$ at position $0$.
nodes.title: Initial segment of an infinite word

nodes.summary: If the alphabet $\alpha$ is finite, then for every right-infinite word $u$ over $\alpha$ and every natural number $k$, the set of length-$k$ factors of $u$ is finite.
nodes.title: Finitely many factors of each length

nodes.summary: For a right-infinite word $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ and natural numbers $k$ and $i$, the length-$k$ factor of $u$ at position $i$, as a list, is $[u_i, u_{i+1}, \ldots, u_{i+k-1}]$ (the empty list when $k = 0$).
nodes.title: Factor as a list

nodes.summary: A finite list $w$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a factor of a right-infinite word $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ over $\alpha$ when, writing $\ell$ for the length of $w$, there is a position $i \in \mathbb{N}$ with $w = [u_i, u_{i+1}, \ldots, u_{i+\ell-1}]$. In particular, the empty list is a factor of every right-infinite word over $\alpha$.
nodes.title: Lists occurring in an infinite word

nodes.summary: Let $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ be a right-infinite word over an alphabet $\alpha$, viewed as a map $\mathbb{N} \to \alpha$. A finite word $w = w_0 w_1 \cdots w_{n-1}$ over $\alpha$ is a nonempty factor of $u$ when $n \ge 1$ and there is a position $i \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $w_j = u_{i+j}$ for every $j < n$.
nodes.title: Nonempty factors of an infinite word

nodes.summary: Let $w$ be a finite list of length $\ell$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ and $u$ a right-infinite word over $\alpha$. Then $w$ is a factor of $u$ if and only if there is a position $i \in \mathbb{N}$ such that the length-$\ell$ factor of $u$ at position $i$, as a list, equals $w$.
nodes.title: Occurrence via list-valued factors

nodes.summary: Let $w$ be a finite list of length $\ell$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ and $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ a right-infinite word over $\alpha$. Then $w$ is a nonempty factor of $u$ if and only if $w$ is nonempty and there is a position $i \in \mathbb{N}$ with $[u_i, u_{i+1}, \ldots, u_{i+\ell-1}] = w$.
nodes.title: Nonempty factors via list-valued factors

nodes.summary: For a finite list $w$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ and a right-infinite word $u$ over $\alpha$, $w$ is a nonempty factor of $u$ if and only if $w$ is nonempty and $w$ is a factor of $u$.
nodes.title: Nonempty factors are the factors that are nonempty

nodes.summary: Let $k$ be a natural number, $v$ a map $\{0, \ldots, k-1\} \to \alpha$, written $j \mapsto v_j$, and $u$ a right-infinite word over $\alpha$. Then the list $[v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_{k-1}]$ is a factor of $u$ if and only if $v$ belongs to the set of length-$k$ factors of $u$. This holds also for $k = 0$.
nodes.title: Factors as lists and as tuples agree

nodes.summary: Let $w = w_0 w_1 w_2 \cdots$ be an infinite word over a finite alphabet $A$. For $n \ge 0$ and a position $i \ge 0$, the factor of $w$ of length $n$ at position $i$ is the word $w_i w_{i+1} \cdots w_{i+n-1}$. The factor complexity $p_w(n)$ is the number of distinct factors of $w$ of length $n$, each word being counted once however often it occurs in $w$.
nodes.title: Factor complexity of an infinite word

nodes.summary: For every infinite word $w$ over a finite alphabet, the factor complexity of $w$ at length $0$ equals $1$, that is, $p_w(0) = 1$: the empty word is the only factor of $w$ of length $0$.
nodes.title: Factor complexity at length zero
Fibonacci word

nodes.summary: The Fibonacci substitution sends each letter of the binary alphabet $\{0, 1\}$ to a finite binary word: it maps $0$ to $01$ and $1$ to $0$.
nodes.title: Fibonacci substitution

nodes.summary: The Fibonacci morphism $\varphi$ extends the Fibonacci substitution $\sigma$, which maps $0$ to $01$ and $1$ to $0$, to finite binary words by concatenation: $\varphi$ maps the empty word to the empty word, and $\varphi(bw) = \sigma(b)\varphi(w)$ for every letter $b$ and every finite binary word $w$.
nodes.title: Fibonacci morphism

nodes.summary: The finite Fibonacci words $f_n$, for natural numbers $n$, are the words in the letters $0$ and $1$ defined by $f_0 = 0$ and $f_{n+1} = \varphi(f_n)$, where $\varphi$ is the Fibonacci morphism, which replaces each letter $0$ by $01$ and each letter $1$ by $0$.
nodes.title: Finite Fibonacci words

nodes.summary: Let $f_0 = 0$ and let $f_{k+1}$ be the image of $f_k$ under the Fibonacci morphism ($0 \mapsto 01$, $1 \mapsto 0$), so that $f_0, f_1, f_2, \ldots$ are the finite Fibonacci words $0, 01, 010, 01001, \ldots$. The one-sided infinite Fibonacci word is the infinite binary word whose letter at index $n$ (indices start at $0$) is the letter of $f_{n+2}$ at index $n$.
nodes.title: Infinite Fibonacci word

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi$ be the Fibonacci morphism on finite binary words, induced by $0 \mapsto 01$ and $1 \mapsto 0$. For all finite binary words $a$ and $b$, $\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b)$, where juxtaposition denotes concatenation.
nodes.title: The Fibonacci morphism respects concatenation

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi$ be the Fibonacci morphism on finite binary words, induced by $0 \mapsto 01$ and $1 \mapsto 0$. For every finite binary word $w$, the length of $\varphi(w)$ is at least the length of $w$, that is, $|w| \le |\varphi(w)|$.
nodes.title: The Fibonacci morphism does not shorten words

reading_title.source: Finite Fibonacci words begin with $0$

nodes.summary: Let $f_0 = 0$ and let $f_{k+1}$ be the image of $f_k$ under the Fibonacci morphism ($0 \mapsto 01$, $1 \mapsto 0$). For every natural number $n$, there is a finite binary word $t$ such that $f_n = 0t$, that is, the first letter of $f_n$ is $0$.
nodes.title: Finite Fibonacci words begin with $0$

nodes.summary: Let $f_0 = 0$ and let $f_{k+1}$ be the image of $f_k$ under the Fibonacci morphism ($0 \mapsto 01$, $1 \mapsto 0$). For every natural number $n$, the word $f_n$ has length at least $n + 1$.
nodes.title: Lower bound on the length of the finite Fibonacci words

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$, the $n$-th finite Fibonacci word $f_n$ is a prefix of $f_{n+1}$: there is a finite word $t$ in the letters $0$ and $1$ with $f_{n+1} = f_n t$.
nodes.title: Consecutive finite Fibonacci words are nested

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $n \le m$, the $n$-th finite Fibonacci word $f_n$ is a prefix of the $m$-th finite Fibonacci word $f_m$: there is a finite word $t$ in the letters $0$ and $1$ with $f_m = f_n t$.
nodes.title: Earlier finite Fibonacci words are prefixes of later ones

nodes.summary: Let $a$ and $t$ be finite words in the letters $0$ and $1$, and let $k$ be a natural number smaller than the length of $a$. Then the letter at position $k$ of the concatenation $a t$ equals the letter at position $k$ of $a$, counting positions from $0$.
nodes.title: Appending a word does not change earlier letters

nodes.summary: Let $f_0 = 0$ and let $f_{k+1}$ be the image of $f_k$ under the Fibonacci morphism ($0 \mapsto 01$, $1 \mapsto 0$). For all natural numbers $n \le m$ and every index $i$ less than the length of $f_n$ (indices start at $0$), the letter of $f_m$ at index $i$ equals the letter of $f_n$ at index $i$.
nodes.title: Letters of the finite Fibonacci words stabilize

nodes.title: The finite Fibonacci word of index $n + 2$ has more than $n$ letters

nodes.summary: Let $f_0 = 0$ and let $f_{k+1}$ be the image of $f_k$ under the Fibonacci morphism ($0 \mapsto 01$, $1 \mapsto 0$). For all natural numbers $m$ and $n$ such that $n$ is less than the length of $f_m$, the letter of $f_m$ at index $n$ equals the letter at index $n$ of the one-sided infinite Fibonacci word (indices start at $0$). nodes.summary: Let $f_0, f_1, f_2, \ldots$ be the finite Fibonacci words. For every natural number $n$, $f_{n+2} = f_{n+1} f_n$, where juxtaposition denotes concatenation.

nodes.summary: For every natural number $N$, prepending the letters $0$ and $1$ to the concatenation $f_0 f_1 \cdots f_{N-1}$ of the first $N$ finite Fibonacci words gives $f_{N+1}$: that is, $0\,1\,f_0 f_1 \cdots f_{N-1} = f_{N+1}$, where the concatenation is empty when $N = 0$.

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$, the finite Fibonacci word $f_n$ is the word formed by the first $|f_n|$ letters of the infinite Fibonacci word.
nodes.title: Finite Fibonacci words are prefixes of the infinite Fibonacci word

nodes.summary: Let $f$ be the infinite Fibonacci word and let $f_0, f_1, f_2, \ldots$ be the finite Fibonacci words. For every natural number $N$, the finite word $w_N = 0\,1\,f_0 f_1 \cdots f_{N-1}$ (so $w_0 = 01$) consists of the first $|w_N|$ letters of $f$, and for every natural number $k$ the first $k$ letters of $f$ form a prefix of $w_N$ for some $N$. In this sense $f = 0 \cdot 1 \cdot f_0 \cdot f_1 \cdot f_2 \cdots$.

nodes.summary: For an infinite word $w = w_0 w_1 w_2 \cdots$ over $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, its first difference is the infinite word $\Delta w$ over $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ with $(\Delta w)_i = w_{i+1} - w_i$ for every natural number $i$.
nodes.title: First difference of an infinite binary word

nodes.summary: For a finite word $w = w_0 w_1 \cdots w_m$ over $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, its first difference is the word $(w_1 - w_0)(w_2 - w_1) \cdots (w_m - w_{m-1})$ of length $m$, computed in $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. The first difference of the empty word is the empty word.
