Morphic words

nodes.summary: Given a map $f$ sending each letter of an alphabet $A$ to a finite word over $A$, its extension to finite words sends a word $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_m$ over $A$ to the concatenation $f(a_1) f(a_2) \cdots f(a_m)$ of the images of its letters in order; the empty word is sent to the empty word.
nodes.title: Extension of a letter map to finite words

nodes.summary: Let $f$ send each letter of an alphabet $A$ to a finite word over $A$, extended to finite words by concatenation. The iterates of $f$ on finite words over $A$ are defined by $f^0(w) = w$ and $f^{n+1}(w) = f(f^n(w))$ for every finite word $w$ over $A$ and every natural number $n$.
nodes.title: Iterates of a letter map

nodes.summary: Let $f$ send each letter of an alphabet $A$ to a finite word over $A$, extended to finite words by concatenation. Then $f(uv) = f(u)f(v)$ for all finite words $u$ and $v$ over $A$.
nodes.title: Extended letter maps preserve concatenation

nodes.summary: Let $k$ be a natural number and let $f$ send each letter of an alphabet $A$ to a word of length exactly $k$ over $A$, extended to finite words by concatenation, with iterates $f^n$ (where $f^0$ is the identity). Then for every natural number $n$ and every finite word $w$ over $A$, the word $f^n(w)$ has length $k^n$ times the length of $w$.
nodes.title: Length of iterates of a uniform letter map

nodes.summary: A map $f$ sending each letter of an alphabet $A$ to a finite word over $A$ is non-erasing when the word $f(a)$ is nonempty for every letter $a \in A$.
nodes.title: Non-erasing letter maps

nodes.summary: Let $f$ send each letter of an alphabet $A$ to a finite word over $A$, extended to finite words by concatenation, with iterates $f^n$ (where $f^0$ is the identity). Then $f$ is prefix-preserving (prolongable) at a letter $a \in A$ when $f(a) = a\alpha$ for some finite word $\alpha$ over $A$ such that the word $f^n(\alpha)$ is nonempty for every natural number $n$, including $n = 0$.
nodes.title: Prolongable letter maps

nodes.summary: Let $f$ send each letter of an alphabet $A$ to a finite word over $A$, extended to finite words by concatenation, with iterates $f^n$ (where $f^0$ is the identity), let $a \in A$, and let $w = w_0 w_1 w_2 \cdots$ be an infinite word over $A$. Then $w$ is the limit of the iterates of $f$ at $a$ when the lengths of the words $f^n(a)$ (iterates applied to the one-letter word $a$) are unbounded as $n$ ranges over the…
nodes.title: Infinite word as the limit of iterates

nodes.summary: An infinite word $w$ over a finite alphabet $A$ is pure morphic when there are a map $f$ sending each letter of $A$ to a finite word over $A$ and a letter $a \in A$ such that $f$ is prolongable at $a$ and $w$ is the limit of the iterates of $f$ at $a$.
nodes.title: Pure morphic words

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be a finite alphabet, $B$ any alphabet, $u$ an infinite word over $A$, $\tau : A \to B$ a map (a coding) and $w$ an infinite word over $B$. Then $w$ is morphic with generator $u$ and coding $\tau$ if $u$ is a pure morphic word and $w(n) = \tau(u(n))$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: Morphic words via a coding

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be a finite alphabet, $u$ a pure morphic infinite word over $A$, $\tau : A \to B$ a map and $w$ an infinite word over $B$. If $w(n) = \tau(u(n))$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then $w$ is morphic with generator $u$ and coding $\tau$.
nodes.title: Building a morphic word from its generator

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be a finite alphabet, $u$ an infinite word over $A$, $\tau : A \to B$ a map and $w$ an infinite word over $B$. If $w$ is morphic with generator $u$ and coding $\tau$, then $u$ is a pure morphic word.
nodes.title: The generator of a morphic word is pure morphic

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be a finite alphabet, $u$ an infinite word over $A$, $\tau : A \to B$ a map and $w$ an infinite word over $B$. If $w$ is morphic with generator $u$ and coding $\tau$, then $w(n) = \tau(u(n))$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: A morphic word is the coding of its generator

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and $u$ a pure morphic infinite word over $A$. Then $u$ is morphic with generator $u$ and the identity coding of $A$.
nodes.title: Pure morphic words are morphic
Palindromic fixed points of morphisms

nodes.summary: The alphabet is the three-letter set $\{0, 1, 2\}$.
nodes.title: The ternary alphabet of Labbé's counterexample

nodes.summary: A morphism of the ternary alphabet $\{0, 1, 2\}$ is given by its letter map: a function $\varphi$ that sends each letter $a$ to a finite word $\varphi(a)$ over $\{0, 1, 2\}$, possibly the empty word.
nodes.title: Morphisms of the ternary alphabet

nodes.summary: A morphism $\varphi$ acts on a word $w = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_k$ by $\varphi(w) = \varphi(w_1) \varphi(w_2) \cdots \varphi(w_k)$, the concatenation of the images of its letters; the empty word is sent to the empty word.
nodes.title: Image of a word under a morphism

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi$ be a morphism of the ternary alphabet $\{0, 1, 2\}$, acting on finite words letter by letter. Its iterates $\varphi^n$ on finite words are defined by $\varphi^0(w) = w$ and $\varphi^{n+1}(w) = \varphi(\varphi^n(w))$ for every natural number $n$ and every finite word $w$ over $\{0, 1, 2\}$.
nodes.title: Iterated images of words under a morphism

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi$ be a morphism of the ternary alphabet $\{0, 1, 2\}$, sending each letter to a finite word, and let $\varphi^n$ be the $n$-th iterate of its letter by letter extension to finite words, with $\varphi^0$ the identity. Then $\varphi$ is primitive when there is a natural number $n$ such that for all letters $a$ and $b$, the letter $b$ occurs in the word $\varphi^n(a)$.
nodes.title: Primitive morphisms

nodes.summary: A finite word $w$ over the alphabet $\{0, 1, 2\}$ is a palindrome when it equals its reversal, that is, reads the same backwards; in particular the empty word is a palindrome.
nodes.title: Palindromes

nodes.summary: A morphism $\varphi$ is in class P (Hof–Knill–Simon) when there is a palindrome $p$ such that for every letter $a$, $\varphi(a) = p q_a$ for some palindrome $q_a$. The palindromes $p$ and $q_a$ may be empty.
nodes.title: Class P

nodes.summary: An infinite word over the alphabet $\{0, 1, 2\}$ is a sequence $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ of letters indexed by the natural numbers, that is, a map $\mathbb{N} \to \{0, 1, 2\}$.
nodes.title: Infinite words

nodes.summary: A finite word $w = w_0 w_1 \cdots w_{n-1}$ over the ternary alphabet $\{0, 1, 2\}$ occurs in an infinite word $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ over the same alphabet at position $k$ when $w_i = u_{k+i}$ for every $i < n$.
nodes.title: Occurrence of a word at a position

nodes.summary: A finite word $w$ is a factor of an infinite word $u$ when it occurs in $u$ at some position: there is $k \in \mathbb{N}$ with $w_i = u_{k+i}$ for every $i < |w|$ (letters of $w$ indexed from $0$). In particular the empty word is a factor of every infinite word.
nodes.title: Factors of an infinite word

nodes.summary: An infinite word $u$ is a fixed point of a morphism $\varphi$ when it is the limit of the iterates of a prolongable letter: there is a letter $a$ such that $\varphi(a)$ begins with $a$, the words $\varphi^m(a)$ ($m \ge 0$) are arbitrarily long, and every $\varphi^m(a)$ is a prefix of $u$.
nodes.title: Fixed point of a morphism

nodes.summary: An infinite word $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ over the ternary alphabet $\{0, 1, 2\}$ is palindromic when it has arbitrarily long palindromic factors: for every natural number $N$ there is a finite word $w = w_0 \cdots w_{n-1}$ with $n \ge N$ that reads the same backwards and occurs in $u$: for some position $k$, $w_i = u_{k+i}$ for all $i < n$.
nodes.title: Palindromic infinite words

nodes.summary: Let $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ be an infinite word over the ternary alphabet $\{0, 1, 2\}$, and say that a finite word $w = w_0 \cdots w_{n-1}$ occurs in $u$ at position $m$ when $w_i = u_{m+i}$ for every $i < n$. Then $u$ is uniformly recurrent when for every finite word $w$ that occurs in $u$ at some position, there is a natural number $B$ such that for every position $k$, the word $w$ occurs in $u$ at position…
nodes.title: Uniformly recurrent infinite words

nodes.summary: Let $\psi$ and $\theta$ be morphisms of the ternary alphabet $\{0, 1, 2\}$, each sending every letter to a finite word, and write $xy$ for the concatenation of words $x$ and $y$. Then $\psi$ and $\theta$ are conjugate when there is a finite word $w$ such that $\psi(a) w = w \theta(a)$ for every letter $a$, or there is a finite word $w$ such that $\theta(a) w = w \psi(a)$ for every letter $a$.
nodes.title: Conjugate morphisms

nodes.summary: A morphism $\psi$ is the identity morphism when $\psi(a)$ is the one-letter word $a$ for every letter $a$.
nodes.title: Identity morphism

nodes.summary: The proposition that there exist a primitive morphism $\varphi$ on the alphabet $\{0, 1, 2\}$ and an infinite word $u$ such that $u$ is a fixed point of $\varphi$, $u$ is palindromic and uniformly recurrent, and no morphism $\psi$ that has $u$ as a fixed point and is not the identity is conjugate to a morphism in class P.
nodes.title: Palindromic uniformly recurrent fixed point outside class P

nodes.summary: The conjecture holds: there exist a primitive morphism $\varphi$ on the alphabet $\{0, 1, 2\}$ (some power $\varphi^n$ maps every letter to a word containing every letter) and an infinite word $u$ such that $u$ is a fixed point of $\varphi$, $u$ is palindromic (it has arbitrarily long palindromic factors) and uniformly recurrent (for every factor $w$ of $u$ there is $B$ such that, for every $k$, $w$ occurs in $u$…
nodes.title: Labbé's palindromic fixed point outside class P
Sturmian words

nodes.summary: For an infinite binary word $x = x_0 x_1 x_2 \cdots$ over $\{0, 1\}$ and natural numbers $i$ and $n$, this is the number of indices $k < n$ with $x_{i+k} = 1$, that is, the number of $1$s in the factor $x_i x_{i+1} \cdots x_{i+n-1}$ of length $n$ starting at position $i$ (it is $0$ when $n = 0$).
nodes.title: Number of ones in a factor

nodes.summary: An infinite binary word $x = x_0 x_1 x_2 \cdots$ over $\{0, 1\}$ is balanced when for all natural numbers $i$, $j$ and $n$, the numbers of $1$s in the factors $x_i x_{i+1} \cdots x_{i+n-1}$ and $x_j x_{j+1} \cdots x_{j+n-1}$ of length $n$ differ by at most $1$.
nodes.title: Balanced infinite words

nodes.summary: An infinite binary word $x = x_0 x_1 x_2 \cdots$ over $\{0, 1\}$ is aperiodic when it is not ultimately periodic: there are no natural numbers $p > 0$ and $N$ such that $x_{n+p} = x_n$ for all $n \ge N$.
nodes.title: Aperiodic infinite words

nodes.summary: An infinite binary word $x = x_0 x_1 x_2 \cdots$ over $\{0, 1\}$ is Sturmian when it is both aperiodic and balanced.
nodes.title: Sturmian words
Thue–Morse sequence and its generalizations

nodes.summary: For $L \in \mathbb{N}$ and letters $a, t$ of the alphabet $\{0, \dots, L-1\}$, the cyclic shift of $a$ by $t$ is the letter $(a + t) \bmod L$. Writing the letters as $a_0, \dots, a_{L-1}$, it sends $a_i$ to $a_{(i + t) \bmod L}$.
nodes.title: Cyclic letter shift

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a natural number and let $t$ be a letter of the alphabet $\{0, 1, \dots, L - 1\}$. The cyclic shift by $t$ of a word $w = a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ over this alphabet is the word $\sigma_t(a_1) \sigma_t(a_2) \cdots \sigma_t(a_n)$ of the same length, where $\sigma_t(a) = (a + t) \bmod L$ is the cyclic shift of a letter.
nodes.title: Cyclic shift of a word

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a natural number and let $t$ and $b$ be letters of the alphabet $\{0, 1, \dots, L - 1\}$. For a letter $a$ write $\sigma_t(a) = (a + t) \bmod L$ for its cyclic shift by $t$, and for a word $w$ over this alphabet write $\sigma_t(w)$ for the word obtained by shifting each letter of $w$. Then $b$ occurs in $\sigma_t(w)$ if and only if $b = \sigma_t(a)$ for some letter $a$ occurring in $w$.
nodes.title: Letters of a cyclically shifted word

nodes.summary: For every $L \in \mathbb{N}$, every letter $t$ of the alphabet $\{0, \dots, L-1\}$ and every finite word $w$ over that alphabet, the word obtained from $w$ by shifting each letter cyclically by $t$ has the same length as $w$.
nodes.title: Cyclic shifting preserves word length

nodes.summary: For every $L \in \mathbb{N}$ and all letters $a, t$ of the alphabet $\{0, \dots, L-1\}$, the cyclic shift of $a$ by $t$ is the letter $(a + t) \bmod L$.
nodes.title: Value of the cyclic letter shift

nodes.summary: Let $L > 1$ and $k > 1$ be natural numbers, take the letters $0, 1, \dots, L-1$ (the elements of $\mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z}$), and let $\kappa$ assign a shift $\kappa(j, n) \in \mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z}$ to each $j \in \{1, \dots, k-1\}$ and each $n \ge 0$. For a word $w$ and $t \in \mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z}$, let $f^t(w)$ be the word obtained from $w$ by adding $t$ modulo $L$ to every letter. The blocks $A_n$ of the…
nodes.title: Blocks of the generalized Thue–Morse sequence

nodes.summary: Let $l$ be a list of lists over a type and let $m \in \mathbb{N}$. If every list in $l$ has length $m$, then the concatenation of the lists in $l$ has length $n \cdot m$, where $n$ is the number of lists in $l$.
nodes.title: Length of a concatenation of equal-length lists

nodes.summary: Let $L > 1$ and $k > 1$ be natural numbers and let $\kappa$ assign a shift $\kappa(j, n) \in \mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z}$ to each $j \in \{1, \dots, k-1\}$ and each $n \ge 0$. For every $n \ge 0$, the block $A_n$ of the $(L, k, \kappa)$-Thue–Morse sequence has exactly $k^n$ letters.
nodes.title: Length of the generalized Thue–Morse blocks

nodes.summary: Let $L > 1$ and $k > 1$ be natural numbers and let $\kappa$ assign a shift $\kappa(j, n) \in \mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z}$ to each $j \in \{1, \dots, k-1\}$ and each $n \ge 0$. For every $n \ge 0$, the block $A_n$ of the $(L, k, \kappa)$-Thue–Morse sequence is a prefix of $A_{n+1}$: there is a word $w$ with $A_{n+1} = A_n w$.
nodes.title: Each generalized Thue–Morse block is a prefix of the next

nodes.summary: Let $L > 1$ and $k > 1$ be natural numbers and let $\kappa$ assign a shift $\kappa(j, n) \in \mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z}$ to each $j \in \{1, \dots, k-1\}$ and each $n \ge 0$. For all natural numbers $m \le n$, the block $A_m$ of the $(L, k, \kappa)$-Thue–Morse sequence is a prefix of $A_n$: there is a word $w$ with $A_n = A_m w$.
nodes.title: The generalized Thue–Morse blocks form a chain of prefixes

nodes.summary: For every natural number $k > 1$ and every $m \in \mathbb{N}$, we have $m < k^{m+1}$.
nodes.title: A crude exponential bound

nodes.summary: Let $l_1$ and $l_2$ be lists over a type, and let $m$ be a natural number less than the length of $l_1$. Then the entry at position $m$ of the concatenation of $l_1$ followed by $l_2$ equals the entry at position $m$ of $l_1$ (positions start at $0$).
nodes.title: Indexing into a concatenation

nodes.summary: Let $L, k \ge 2$, let $\kappa : \{1, \dots, k-1\} \times \mathbb{N} \to \{0, \dots, L-1\}$ be a shift schedule, and let $A_0, A_1, \dots$ be the blocks of the $(L, k, \kappa)$-Thue–Morse sequence. The infinite word $A_\infty$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, L-1\}$ has, for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$, as its letter at position $m$ (positions start at $0$) the letter at position $m$ of the block $A_{m+1}$, which has…
nodes.title: The infinite generalized Thue–Morse word

nodes.summary: Let $L, k \ge 2$, let $\kappa : \{1, \dots, k-1\} \times \mathbb{N} \to \{0, \dots, L-1\}$ be a shift schedule, and let $A_0, A_1, \dots$ be the blocks and $A_\infty$ the infinite word of the $(L, k, \kappa)$-Thue–Morse sequence. For all $m, N \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m + 1 \le N$ and $m$ less than the length of $A_N$, the letter at position $m$ of $A_N$ equals the letter at position $m$ of $A_\infty$ (positions start…
nodes.title: Later blocks agree with the infinite word

nodes.summary: The classical shift schedule is the map $\kappa$ that assigns to the index $j = 1$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ the letter $\kappa(1, n) = 1$ of the alphabet $\{0, 1\}$. It is the schedule of the classical Thue–Morse sequence, the $(L, k, \kappa)$-Thue–Morse sequence with $L = k = 2$.
nodes.title: Classical shift schedule

nodes.summary: The classical Thue–Morse blocks are the blocks $A_n$ of the $(2, 2, \kappa)$-Thue–Morse sequence with $\kappa(1, n) = 1$ for every $n \ge 0$. Thus $A_0$ is the one-letter word $0$, and $A_{n+1}$ is $A_n$ followed by the word obtained from $A_n$ by exchanging the letters $0$ and $1$.
nodes.title: Classical Thue–Morse blocks

nodes.summary: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the classical Thue–Morse block $A_n$ (the block $A_n$ of the $(L, k, \kappa)$-Thue–Morse sequence with $L = k = 2$ and $\kappa(1, i) = 1$ for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$) has exactly $2^n$ letters.
nodes.title: Length of the classical Thue–Morse blocks

nodes.summary: The classical Thue–Morse block $A_0$ is the one-letter word $0$.
nodes.title: Classical Thue–Morse block of order 0

nodes.summary: The classical Thue–Morse block $A_1$ is the word $01$.
nodes.title: Classical Thue–Morse block of order 1

nodes.summary: The classical Thue–Morse block $A_2$ is the word $0110$.
nodes.title: Classical Thue–Morse block of order 2

nodes.summary: The classical Thue–Morse block $A_3$ is the word $01101001$.
nodes.title: Classical Thue–Morse block of order 3

nodes.summary: Let $A_\infty$ be the infinite word of the $(2, 2, \kappa)$-Thue–Morse sequence with $\kappa(1, n) = 1$ for every $n \ge 0$. The letters of $A_\infty$ at positions $0, 1, \dots, 7$ are $0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1$, so $A_\infty$ begins with $01101001$.
nodes.title: The classical Thue–Morse word begins with 01101001

nodes.summary: The Thue–Morse substitution $\sigma$ on the alphabet $\{0, 1\}$ sends each letter to a word of length two: $\sigma(0) = 01$ and $\sigma(1) = 10$.
nodes.title: Thue–Morse substitution

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be the Thue–Morse substitution, $\sigma(0) = 01$ and $\sigma(1) = 10$, applied to finite words over $\{0, 1\}$ letter by letter. For a natural number $n$, the $n$th Thue–Morse block is the finite word $\sigma^n(0)$: the $0$th block is the one-letter word $0$, and the $(n+1)$st block is obtained from the $n$th by replacing each letter $a$ with $\sigma(a)$.
nodes.title: Thue–Morse blocks

nodes.summary: The Thue–Morse sequence $t_0 t_1 t_2 \cdots$ over $\{0, 1\}$ is indexed from $0$, and $t_n = 1$ exactly when the binary expansion of $n$ has an odd number of digits equal to $1$; otherwise $t_n = 0$.
nodes.title: Thue–Morse sequence
Reduced factor complexity

nodes.summary: The reduction $\operatorname{red}(w)$ of a binary word $w$ is the word obtained by collapsing each maximal run of equal consecutive letters of $w$ to a single letter; for example $\operatorname{red}(0011101) = 0101$.
nodes.title: Reduction of a binary word

nodes.summary: The number of alternations of a binary word $w$ is the number of occurrences of the factors $01$ and $10$ in $w$, that is, the number of positions $i$ with $w_i \ne w_{i+1}$.
nodes.title: Alternations of a binary word

nodes.summary: The morphism $\mu$ sends each letter to a word of length two, $\mu(0) = 01$ and $\mu(1) = 10$, and a binary word $w_1 w_2 \cdots w_k$ to the concatenation $\mu(w_1) \mu(w_2) \cdots \mu(w_k)$.
nodes.title: Extension of the Thue–Morse substitution to binary words

nodes.summary: The regular paperfolding sequence $f = f_0 f_1 f_2 \cdots$ over $\{0, 1\}$ is indexed from $0$: for each $i$, write $i + 1 = m \cdot 2^k$ with $m$ odd; then $f_i = 0$ if $m \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $f_i = 1$ if $m \equiv 3 \pmod 4$.
nodes.title: Regular paperfolding sequence

nodes.summary: For a finite binary word $w$, let $\mathrm{red}(w)$ be the word obtained from $w$ by collapsing each run of equal letters to a single letter. For an infinite binary word $x = x_0 x_1 x_2 \cdots$ and a natural number $n$, the reduced factor complexity $\rho^{\mathrm{red}}_x(n)$ is the number of distinct words $\mathrm{red}(w)$ as $w$ ranges over the length-$n$ factors of $x$.
nodes.title: Reduced factor complexity

nodes.summary: For a binary sequence $x = x_0 x_1 x_2 \cdots$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the reduced abelian complexity $\rho^{\mathrm{ab,red}}_x(n)$ is the number of distinct pairs $(|\mathrm{red}(v)|, |\mathrm{red}(v)|_0)$, where $v$ ranges over the length-$n$ factors of $x$, $\mathrm{red}(v)$ is the reduction of $v$ (each run of equal letters collapsed to a single letter) and $|w|_0$ is the number of letters $0$ in $w$.…
nodes.title: Reduced abelian complexity

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, $m_n$ is the least number of alternations (positions where two adjacent letters differ) among the length-$n$ factors of the Thue–Morse sequence.
nodes.title: Minimum number of alternations in Thue–Morse factors

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, $M_n$ is the largest number of alternations (positions where two adjacent letters differ) among the length-$n$ factors of the Thue–Morse sequence.
nodes.title: Maximum number of alternations in Thue–Morse factors

nodes.summary: Let $\mu$ be the morphism on binary words with $\mu(0) = 01$ and $\mu(1) = 10$. If $w$ is a nonempty binary word of length $|w|$ with $\alpha$ alternations (positions where two adjacent letters differ), then $\mu(w)$ has exactly $2|w| - 1 - \alpha$ alternations.
nodes.title: Alternations of the Thue–Morse image of a word

nodes.summary: For a natural number $k$, let $m_k$ and $M_k$ be the least and the largest number of alternations (positions where two adjacent letters differ) among the length-$k$ factors of the Thue–Morse sequence. Then for every $n \ge 2$, $m_{2n} = 2n - 1 - M_{n+1}$, $M_{2n} = 2n - 1 - m_n$, $m_{2n+1} = 2n - M_{n+1}$ and $M_{2n+1} = 2n - m_{n+1}$.
nodes.title: Doubling recurrences for Thue–Morse alternation extrema

nodes.summary: For a natural number $k$, let $m_k$ and $M_k$ be the least and the largest number of alternations (positions where two adjacent letters differ) among the length-$k$ factors of the Thue–Morse sequence. Then for every $n \ge 1$, $m_{4n} = 2n - 1 + m_{n+1}$, $M_{4n} = 2n + M_{n+1}$, $m_{4n+2} = 2n + m_{n+1}$ and $M_{4n+2} = 2n + 1 + M_{n+1}$.
nodes.title: Quadrupling recurrences for Thue–Morse alternation extrema

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be the Thue–Morse sequence and $\rho^{\mathrm{red}}_t$ its reduced factor complexity. For every odd natural number $n$, $\rho^{\mathrm{red}}_t(n) = \rho^{\mathrm{red}}_t((n+1)/2)$.
nodes.title: Reduced complexity of the Thue–Morse word at odd lengths

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be the Thue–Morse sequence and $\rho^{\mathrm{red}}_t$ its reduced factor complexity. For every natural number $m \ge 1$, $\rho^{\mathrm{red}}_t(4m) = \rho^{\mathrm{red}}_t(m+1) + 2$, and for every natural number $m \ge 0$, $\rho^{\mathrm{red}}_t(4m+2) = \rho^{\mathrm{red}}_t(m+1) + 2$.
nodes.title: Reduced complexity of the Thue–Morse word at even lengths

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number and let $w = w_0 w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a binary word of length $2n + 1$ with $w_{2i} \ne w_{2i+2}$ for every $i < n$, so that its even positions read $abab\cdots$ with $a \ne b$ and its odd positions are arbitrary. Then the reduction of $w$, the word obtained by collapsing each maximal run of equal letters of $w$ to a single letter, has length $n + 1$; that is, $w$ has exactly $n + 1$…
nodes.title: Runs in a word whose even-position letters alternate

nodes.summary: Let $f$ be the regular paperfolding sequence and let $\rho^{\mathrm{red}}_f(n)$ be the number of distinct reductions of length-$n$ factors of $f$. For every $n \ge 1$, $\rho^{\mathrm{red}}_f(2n) = 4$.
nodes.title: Reduced complexity of the paperfolding word at even lengths

nodes.summary: Let $f$ be the regular paperfolding sequence and let $\rho^{\mathrm{red}}_f(n)$ be the number of distinct reductions of length-$n$ factors of $f$. For every $n \ge 1$, $\rho^{\mathrm{red}}_f(8n+1) = 4$.
nodes.title: Reduced complexity of the paperfolding word at lengths 8n + 1

nodes.summary: Let $f$ be the regular paperfolding sequence and let $\rho^{\mathrm{red}}_f(n)$ be the number of distinct reductions of length-$n$ factors of $f$. For every natural number $n$, $\rho^{\mathrm{red}}_f(8n+3) = 6$.
nodes.title: Reduced complexity of the paperfolding word at lengths 8n + 3

nodes.summary: Let $f$ be the regular paperfolding sequence and let $\rho^{\mathrm{red}}_f(n)$ be the number of distinct reductions of length-$n$ factors of $f$. For every natural number $n$, $\rho^{\mathrm{red}}_f(8n+5) = 6$.
nodes.title: Reduced complexity of the paperfolding word at lengths 8n + 5

nodes.summary: Let $f$ be the regular paperfolding sequence and let $\rho^{\mathrm{red}}_f(n)$ be the number of distinct reductions of length-$n$ factors of $f$. For every natural number $n$, $\rho^{\mathrm{red}}_f(8n+7) = 6$.
nodes.title: Reduced complexity of the paperfolding word at lengths 8n + 7

nodes.summary: Let $f$ be the regular paperfolding sequence and let $\rho^{\mathrm{red}}_f(n)$ be the number of distinct reductions of length-$n$ factors of $f$. For every $n \ge 2$, $\rho^{\mathrm{red}}_f(n) = 4$ if $n \equiv 0, 1, 2, 4$ or $6 \pmod 8$, and $\rho^{\mathrm{red}}_f(n) = 6$ if $n \equiv 3, 5$ or $7 \pmod 8$.
nodes.title: Reduced complexity of the paperfolding word

nodes.summary: Let $f$ be the regular paperfolding sequence and let $\rho^{\mathrm{ab,red}}_f(n)$ be the number of reductions of length-$n$ factors of $f$, counted up to rearrangement of their letters. For every even $n > 0$, $\rho^{\mathrm{ab,red}}_f(n) = 3$.
nodes.title: Reduced abelian complexity of the paperfolding word at even lengths

nodes.summary: Let $f$ be the regular paperfolding sequence and let $\rho^{\mathrm{ab,red}}_f(n)$ be the number of reductions of length-$n$ factors of $f$, counted up to rearrangement of their letters. For every $n > 1$ with $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, $\rho^{\mathrm{ab,red}}_f(n) = 4$.
nodes.title: Reduced abelian complexity of the paperfolding word at lengths 1 mod 4

nodes.summary: Let $f$ be the regular paperfolding sequence and let $\rho^{\mathrm{ab,red}}_f(n)$ be the number of reductions of length-$n$ factors of $f$, counted up to rearrangement of their letters. For every natural number $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, $\rho^{\mathrm{ab,red}}_f(n) = 5$.

nodes.summary: The Tribonacci word is written over the three-letter alphabet whose letters are $a$, $b$ and $c$.

nodes.summary: The finite Tribonacci words $W(n)$, for $n \ge 0$, are the words over the alphabet $\{a, b, c\}$ defined by $W(0) = a$, $W(1) = ab$, $W(2) = abac$ and $W(n + 3) = W(n + 2)\,W(n + 1)\,W(n)$ for every $n \ge 0$, where juxtaposition denotes concatenation.
nodes.title: Finite Tribonacci words

nodes.summary: For every $n \ge 0$, the finite Tribonacci word $W(n + 3)$ is the concatenation $W(n + 2)\,W(n + 1)\,W(n)$.
nodes.title: Recursion for the finite Tribonacci words

nodes.summary: Writing $|w|$ for the length of a word $w$, for every $n \ge 0$ the finite Tribonacci words satisfy $|W(n + 3)| = |W(n + 2)| + |W(n + 1)| + |W(n)|$.
nodes.title: Length recurrence for finite Tribonacci words

nodes.summary: For every $n \ge 0$, the finite Tribonacci word $W(n)$ has length at least $n + 1$.
nodes.title: Length lower bound for finite Tribonacci words

nodes.summary: For every $n \ge 0$, the finite Tribonacci word $W(n)$ is a prefix of $W(n + 1)$.
nodes.title: Each finite Tribonacci word is a prefix of the next

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $m \le n$, the finite Tribonacci word $W(m)$ is a prefix of $W(n)$.

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $m \le n$, the length of the finite Tribonacci word $W(m)$ is at most the length of $W(n)$.
nodes.title: Lengths of finite Tribonacci words are monotone

nodes.summary: The infinite Tribonacci word is the sequence over the alphabet $\{a, b, c\}$ whose letter at each position $k \ge 0$ (positions counted from $0$) is the letter at position $k$ of the finite Tribonacci word $W(k)$; this position exists because $W(k)$ has length at least $k + 1$.

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a prime, $r \ge 1$ a natural number, and $K$ a finite field of characteristic $p$ with $q = p^r$ elements. A formal power series $f = \sum_n f_n X^n \in K[[X]]$ is algebraic over the polynomial ring $K[X]$ (it is a root of a nonzero polynomial with coefficients in $K[X]$) if and only if its coefficient sequence $n \mapsto f_n$ is $p$-automatic, that is, its $p$-kernel is finite.

nodes.summary: A substitution is a map $\eta$ sending each letter of an alphabet $A$ to a finite word over $A$, extended to finite words by concatenation, such that $\eta$ is non-erasing (the word $\eta(a)$ is nonempty for every letter $a \in A$) and some letter $a \in A$ is growing, that is, $|\eta^k(a)| \to \infty$ as $k \to \infty$, where $\eta^k$ is the $k$-th iterate of $\eta$. The alphabet $A$ need not be finite.

nodes.summary: Let $\eta$ be a letter map, $b$ a letter, $i$ a digit and $w$ a digit word. If $i < |\eta(b)|$, then the value of the substitution automaton started at $b$ on the word $iw$ (the digit $i$ followed by $w$) equals its value started at $\eta(b)_i$ on $w$, where $\eta(b)_i$ is the letter of $\eta(b)$ at position $i$, counting from $0$. If $i \ge |\eta(b)|$, the run on $iw$ is undefined.

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be Kimberling's morphism on the alphabet $\{0, 1\}$, given by $h(1) = 110$ and $h(0) = 11$ and extended to finite words by concatenation. Then the simple map $\varphi_i$ of $a$ negates the letters of $u$ at positions $i, \dots, i + m$ and leaves every other letter unchanged: for every position $j$, $\varphi_i(u)_j = \neg u_j$ if $i \le j \le i + m$, and $\varphi_i(u)_j = u_j$ otherwise.

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be a binary keyword and $u$ a binary word. A list $[j_1, \dots, j_r]$ of indices acts completely on $u$ when applying the simple maps $\varphi_{j_1}, \varphi_{j_2}, \dots, \varphi_{j_r}$ of $a$ in this order changes the word at every step: with $u_0 = u$ and $u_q = \varphi_{j_q}(u_{q-1})$, we have $u_q \ne u_{q-1}$ for $1 \le q \le r$. nodes.summary: A nonempty finite word is primitive if it is not a proper power of another word.
nodes.title: Primitive word

nodes.summary: Let $r$ be a natural number. The content of a word $w$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$ is the function that assigns to each letter $i$ the number of occurrences of $i$ in $w$.
nodes.title: Content of a word

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered alphabet, and order the words over $\alpha$ lexicographically. A word $w$ over $\alpha$ of length $n$ is a Lyndon word if it is nonempty and, for every $k$ with $0 < k < n$, $w$ is strictly smaller than its rotation by $k$, the word obtained by moving the first $k$ letters of $w$ to the end.
nodes.title: Lyndon word

nodes.title: Content is additive under concatenation

nodes.summary: Let $r$ be a natural number. For every letter $i$ of the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$, the content of the one-letter word $i$ takes the value $1$ at $i$ and the value $0$ at every other letter.
nodes.title: Content of a one-letter word

nodes.summary: Let $r$ be a natural number, let $w$ be a word over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$, let $i$ be a letter, and write $c(u)$ for the content of a word $u$ (the number of occurrences of each letter in $u$). If $iw$ denotes $w$ with $i$ prepended, then $c(iw)(i) = c(w)(i) + 1$ and $c(iw)(j) = c(w)(j)$ for every letter $j \ne i$.
nodes.title: Content of a word after prepending a letter

nodes.summary: For a natural number $r$ and a word $w$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$, summing over all letters $i$ the number of occurrences of $i$ in $w$ gives the length of $w$.
nodes.title: The content of a word sums to its length

nodes.summary: Let $r$ be a natural number. Given a function $d$ from the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$ to the natural numbers, the words of content $d$ are the words $w$ over this alphabet whose content equals $d$, that is, in which each letter $i$ occurs exactly $d(i)$ times.
nodes.title: Words with prescribed content

nodes.summary: For a natural number $r$ and natural numbers $n_0, \dots, n_{r-1}$, the set of Lyndon words over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$, ordered as the natural numbers, in which each letter $i$ occurs exactly $n_i$ times.
nodes.title: Lyndon words of given content

nodes.summary: Let $r$ be a natural number, let $n_0, \dots, n_{r-1}$ be natural numbers, and let $n = n_0 + \dots + n_{r-1}$. The number of words over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$ in which each letter $i$ occurs exactly $n_i$ times is the multinomial coefficient $\binom{n}{n_0, \ldots, n_{r-1}} = \frac{n!}{n_0! \cdots n_{r-1}!}$.
nodes.title: Words of given content are counted by the multinomial coefficient

nodes.summary: Let $w$ be a word of length $n$, and for $0 \le k < n$ let $w_k$ be the rotation of $w$ by $k$, obtained by moving the first $k$ letters of $w$ to the end. Then $w$ is primitive if and only if $w$ is nonempty and the $n$ words $w_0, w_1, \dots, w_{n-1}$ are pairwise distinct.
nodes.title: Primitivity via distinct rotations

nodes.summary: If $w$ is a primitive word of length $n$ and $0 < k < n$, then the rotation of $w$ by $k$, obtained by moving the first $k$ letters of $w$ to the end, is different from $w$.
nodes.title: Nontrivial rotations move a primitive word

nodes.summary: For a natural number $r$ and natural numbers $n_0, \dots, n_{r-1}$, the set of primitive words over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$ in which each letter $i$ occurs exactly $n_i$ times.
nodes.title: Primitive words of given content

nodes.summary: Every Lyndon word over a linearly ordered alphabet is primitive.
nodes.title: Lyndon words are primitive

nodes.summary: Let $r$ be a natural number and let $n_0, \dots, n_{r-1}$ be natural numbers with $n = n_0 + \dots + n_{r-1} > 0$. Order the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$ as the natural numbers and order words over it lexicographically. Then the number of Lyndon words over this alphabet in which each letter $i$ occurs exactly $n_i$ times equals, as a rational number, Witt's multigraded value…
nodes.title: Witt's formula for the number of Lyndon words of given content
Rectangles in nondecreasing words

reading_title.source: Number of $r \times s$ rectangles in a bargraph

nodes.summary: Let $w = w_0 w_1 \cdots w_{m-1}$ be a word of natural numbers, drawn as a bargraph whose column $i$ has height $w_i$. The number of occurrences of an $r \times s$ rectangle (height $r$, width $s$) in $w$ is the number of pairs $(i, y)$ of natural numbers with $i < m$, $i + s \le m$ and $y \le w_0 + \cdots + w_{m-1}$ such that $y + r \le w_{i+j}$ for every $j < s$.

Reverse-permute equivalence of strings

reading_title.source: $k$-strings

nodes.summary: For a natural number $k$, a $k$-string is a finite sequence (possibly empty) of elements of $\{0, 1, \ldots, k-1\}$.
nodes.title: $k$-strings

nodes.summary: For a natural number $k$, a $k$-string $s$ is related to a $k$-string $t$ by the reverse-permute (RP) relation when there is a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, 1, \ldots, k-1\}$ such that $t$ is obtained, either from $s$ or from the reversal of $s$, by replacing each entry $x$ with $\sigma(x)$.
nodes.title: The reverse-permute relation
Ulam words

nodes.summary: For a natural number $f$ (the fuel) and a word $w$ in the letters $0$ and $1$, the test returns false when $f = 0$. With fuel $f + 1$ it returns true when $w$ has length $1$; otherwise it returns true exactly when there is exactly one $k$ with $1 \le k < |w|$ such that the prefix $w_1 \cdots w_k$ and the suffix $w_{k+1} \cdots w_{|w|}$ are distinct and both pass the test with fuel $f$.
nodes.title: Fuel-bounded Ulam test

nodes.summary: Ulam words are finite words over the alphabet $\{0, 1\}$, defined by recursion on the length. The empty word is not an Ulam word, and the two words $0$ and $1$ of length $1$ are Ulam words. A word $w$ of length at least $2$ is an Ulam word if and only if there is exactly one way to write $w = uv$ with $u$ and $v$ nonempty, distinct Ulam words.
nodes.title: Ulam words

nodes.summary: The empty word is not an Ulam word, and both words $0$ and $1$ of length one are Ulam words. The Ulam words of length two are exactly $01$ and $10$, and the Ulam words of length three are exactly $001$, $011$, $100$ and $110$.
nodes.title: Ulam words of length at most three

nodes.summary: The words $0001$ and $1011$ are Ulam words, while $0011$ and $0110$ are not.
nodes.title: Ulam words of length four: examples

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, $\#U_n$ denotes the number of Ulam words of length $n$, that is, of words $w_1 \cdots w_n$ of length $n$ in the letters $0$ and $1$ that are Ulam words.
nodes.title: Number of Ulam words of a given length

nodes.summary: There are $2$, $2$, $4$ and $8$ Ulam words of length $1$, $2$, $3$ and $4$ respectively: $\#U_1 = 2$, $\#U_2 = 2$, $\#U_3 = 4$ and $\#U_4 = 8$, where $\#U_n$ is the number of Ulam words of length $n$.
nodes.title: Numbers of short Ulam words

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $N$ and $n$ and a residue class $a \in \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$, this is the number of Ulam words $w$ of length $n$ in the letters $0$ and $1$ whose binary value $\pi(w)$, read with the most significant letter first, lies in the class $a$ modulo $N$. For $N = 0$, $\mathbb{Z}/0\mathbb{Z}$ is $\mathbb{Z}$ and the condition is $\pi(w) = a$.
nodes.title: Ulam words in a residue class

nodes.summary: Read the Ulam words of length $2$ as binary numerals, most significant letter first. None of their values is congruent to $0$ modulo $3$, exactly one is congruent to $1$, and exactly one is congruent to $2$.
nodes.title: Residues of the Ulam words of length 2 modulo 3

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, this is the list $u_1 < u_2 < \dots < u_k$ of the distinct binary values $\pi(w)$, read with the most significant letter first, of the Ulam words $w$ of length $n$, in increasing order.
nodes.title: Sorted binary values of Ulam words

nodes.summary: The increasing list of the distinct binary values $\pi(w)$, read with the most significant letter first, of the Ulam words $w$ of length $3$ has exactly the entries $1, 3, 4, 6$.
nodes.title: Binary values of the Ulam words of length 3

nodes.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, read each Ulam word of length $n$ as a binary numeral, most significant letter first, and list the resulting values in increasing order as $u_1 < u_2 < \dots < u_k$. The mean gap of these values is the rational number
nodes.title: Mean gap of the Ulam values

nodes.summary: The stages $S_n \subseteq \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ of the discrete Sierpiński triangle are defined by $S_0 = \{(2, 1)\}$ and $S_{n+1} = S_n \cup (S_n + (2^n, 0)) \cup (S_n + (2^n, 2^n))$, where $S + (u, v) = \{(x + u, y + v) : (x, y) \in S\}$ denotes a translate.
nodes.title: Stages of the discrete Sierpiński triangle

nodes.summary: The discrete Sierpiński triangle is the set $\mathcal{S} = \bigcup_{n \ge 0} S_n \subseteq \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, the union of all the stages $S_n$ of the discrete Sierpiński triangle.
nodes.title: The discrete Sierpiński triangle

nodes.summary: The stage $S_1$ of the discrete Sierpiński triangle is $\{(2, 1), (3, 1), (3, 2)\}$.
nodes.title: The first stage of the discrete Sierpiński triangle

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $a$ and $b$ with $a + b \ge 1$, the binary word $0^a 1111 0^b$ ($a$ zeros, then four ones, then $b$ zeros) is an Ulam word if and only if $a + b \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.
nodes.title: Ulam words with a block of four ones

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$, $(\#U_n)^2 \le \sum_{i=n}^{2n} \#U_i$, where $\#U_i$ is the number of Ulam words of length $i$.
nodes.title: Square of the Ulam word count is at most a block sum

nodes.summary: For every $n \ge 3$, the word $1^3 0^{n-3}$ (three ones followed by $n - 3$ zeros) is an Ulam word if and only if $n \equiv 0 \pmod 4$ or $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.
nodes.title: Ulam words with three leading ones

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n \ge 6$, the number of Ulam words of length $n$ is at least $2n + 4$.
nodes.title: Linear lower bound on the number of Ulam words

nodes.summary: Let $\#U_n$ be the number of Ulam words of length $n$ and $\alpha_0 = (\#U_{30} / (2 \cdot 31))^{1/30}$. For every real $\alpha$ with $1 < \alpha < \alpha_0$, every real $C$ and every natural number $N$, there is some $n \ge N$ with $C \alpha^n \le \#U_n$; that is, $\limsup_{n \to \infty} \#U_n / \alpha^n = \infty$.
nodes.title: Exponential lower bound for Ulam word counts along a subsequence

nodes.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ let $U_n$ be the set of Ulam words of length $n$, and let $\mu_g(n)$ be the mean gap of the binary values of the words in $U_n$. Then $2^n / |U_n|$ (the reciprocal of the density $|U_n| / 2^n$) and $\mu_g(n)$ have the same order of growth as $n \to \infty$: there are constants $c, C > 0$ such that $c \, \mu_g(n) \le 2^n / |U_n| \le C \, \mu_g(n)$ for all sufficiently large $n$.
nodes.title: The inverse Ulam density has the order of the mean gap

nodes.summary: For every $n \ge 1$, the number of $a \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ for which the word $0^a 1 0^{n-1-a}$ ($a$ zeros, then a one, then $n - 1 - a$ zeros) is an Ulam word equals $2^{s_2(n-1)}$, where $s_2(m)$ is the sum of the binary digits of $m$. This number is the term $G(n - 1)$ of Gould's sequence.
nodes.title: Counting Ulam words with a single one

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $a$ and $b$, the binary word $0^a 11 0^b$ ($a$ zeros, then two ones, then $b$ zeros) is an Ulam word if and only if $a + b$ is odd.
nodes.title: Ulam words with a block of two ones

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $a$ and $b$ with $a + b \ge 2$, the binary word $0^a 101 0^b$ ($a$ zeros, then the letters $1, 0, 1$, then $b$ zeros) is an Ulam word if and only if $a + b$ is odd.
nodes.title: Ulam words with one 101 block

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $a$ and $b$, the binary word $0^a 1 0^b$ ($a$ zeros, then a one, then $b$ zeros) is an Ulam word if and only if the binomial coefficient $\binom{a + b}{a}$ is odd.
nodes.title: Parity criterion for Ulam words with a single one

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $x$ and $y$ with $1 \le y \le x$, the word $1^y 0^{x-y}$ ($y$ ones followed by $x - y$ zeros) is an Ulam word if and only if $(x, y) = (1, 1)$ or $(x, y)$ belongs to the discrete Sierpiński triangle $\mathcal{S}$.
nodes.title: Ulam words made of ones followed by zeros

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $a$ and $b$ with $a + b \ge 1$, the word $0^a 10101 0^b$ ($a$ zeros, then $10101$, then $b$ zeros) is an Ulam word if and only if $a$ and $b$ are both even and at least one of $a$ and $b$ is zero.
nodes.title: Padding the word 10101 with zeros

nodes.summary: For a word $w$ over $\{0, 1\}$, let $\bar w$ be its complement (every letter swapped) and let $\pi(w)$ be the integer whose binary expansion is $w$, most significant letter first. If $w$ is an Ulam word of length $n$, then $\bar w$ is an Ulam word and $\pi(\bar w) + \pi(w) = 2^n - 1$. Moreover, for all natural numbers $N$ and $n$ and every $a \in \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$, the number of Ulam words $w$ of length $n$…
nodes.title: Complement symmetry of Ulam words

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $N$ and $n$ and a residue $a \in \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$, let $c_{a,N}(n)$ be the number of Ulam words of length $n$ whose value as a binary numeral, most significant letter first, is congruent to $a$ modulo $N$. Then for every $n \ge 1$ we have $c_{0,2}(n) = c_{1,2}(n)$, and for every $a \in \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ we have $c_{a,3}(n) = c_{-a,3}(n)$ if $n$ is even and…
nodes.title: Residue symmetries of Ulam words modulo 2 and 3

reading_title.source: Universal cycle for $k$-subsets

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, let $N = \binom{n}{k}$. A sequence $c_0, \dots, c_{N-1}$ of elements of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, read cyclically, is a universal cycle for the $k$-subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ when, for every starting position $i < N$, the $k$ consecutive entries $c_i, c_{i+1}, \dots, c_{i+k-1}$ (indices taken modulo $N$) are pairwise distinct, and every $k$-element subset of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is…
nodes.title: Universal cycle for $k$-subsets

nodes.summary: The statement that for every natural number $k$ there is a natural number $N$ such that every $n \ge N$ for which $k$ divides $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ admits a universal cycle for the $k$-subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Here $n - 1$ and $k - 1$ are truncated at $0$, so for $k = 0$ the divisibility condition reads $0 \mid 1$ and never holds.
nodes.title: Chung–Diaconis–Graham universal cycle conjecture

reading_title.source: Existence of universal cycles for $k$-subsets

nodes.summary: For every natural number $k$ there is a natural number $N$ such that for every $n \ge N$ for which $k$ divides $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$, there is a universal cycle for the $k$-subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Here $n - 1$ and $k - 1$ are truncated at $0$, so for $k = 0$ the divisibility condition reads $0 \mid 1$ and never holds.
nodes.title: Existence of universal cycles for $k$-subsets

For $k \ge 1$ let $A_{k+1} = \mathrm{mex}(U_k)$, $B_{k+1} = \mathrm{mex}(U_k \cup \{A_{k+1}\})$, $C_{k+1} = \mathrm{mex}(U_k \cup \{A_{k+1}, B_{k+1}\})$, $D_{k+1} = A_{k+1} + B_{k+1} + C_{k+1}$ and…

nodes.summary: For $n \ge 1$, $A_n$ is the first entry of the $n$-th quadruple $(A_n, B_n, C_n, D_n)$ of the anti-Tribonacci construction: $A_1 = 1$, and for $n \ge 2$, $A_n$ is the least positive integer that is not among the values $A_k$, $B_k$, $C_k$, $D_k$ with $1 \le k < n$. At $n = 0$ the definition gives $A_0 = A_1 = 1$.
nodes.title: First summands of the anti-Tribonacci construction

nodes.summary: For $n \ge 1$, $B_n$ is the second entry of the $n$-th quadruple $(A_n, B_n, C_n, D_n)$ of the anti-Tribonacci construction: $B_1 = 2$, and for $n \ge 2$, $B_n$ is the second smallest positive integer that is not among the values $A_k$, $B_k$, $C_k$, $D_k$ with $1 \le k < n$. At $n = 0$ the definition gives $B_0 = B_1 = 2$.
nodes.title: Second summands of the anti-Tribonacci construction

nodes.summary: For $n \ge 1$, $C_n$ is the third entry of the $n$-th quadruple $(A_n, B_n, C_n, D_n)$ of the anti-Tribonacci construction: $C_1 = 3$, and for $n \ge 2$, $C_n$ is the third smallest positive integer that is not among the values $A_k$, $B_k$, $C_k$, $D_k$ with $1 \le k < n$. At $n = 0$ the definition gives $C_0 = C_1 = 3$.
nodes.title: Third summands of the anti-Tribonacci construction

nodes.summary: For $n \ge 1$, the anti-Tribonacci number $D_n$ (OEIS A265389) is the fourth entry of the $n$-th quadruple $(A_n, B_n, C_n, D_n)$ of the anti-Tribonacci construction, so $D_n = A_n + B_n + C_n$ and $D_1 = 6$. At $n = 0$ the definition gives $D_0 = D_1 = 6$.

nodes.summary: A positive integer $p$ is an *upper Wythoff number* when the letter at index $p - 1$ (indices start at $0$) of the infinite Fibonacci word $0100101001001\ldots$ is $1$; that is, the upper Wythoff numbers are the positions of the letter $1$ in the Fibonacci word counted from one. A positive integer $x$ is an *unsum* (OEIS A260317) if there are no upper Wythoff numbers $p < q$ with $p + q = x$.
nodes.title: Unsums of upper Wythoff numbers

nodes.summary: The positive integers $p < 30$ such that the letter at index $p - 1$ (indices start at $0$) of the infinite Fibonacci word is $1$, that is, the upper Wythoff numbers below $30$, are exactly $2, 5, 7, 10, 13, 15, 18, 20, 23, 26, 28$.

nodes.summary: The unsums (OEIS A260317) that are at most $21$ are exactly $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 11, 13, 14, 16, 19, 21$.
nodes.title: The unsums up to 21

nodes.summary: Let $a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$ be the unsums (OEIS A260317): the positive integers that are not a sum $p + q$ of upper Wythoff numbers $p < q$. For $i \ge 0$, the $i$-th gap between consecutive unsums (counted from zero) is $a_{i+2} - a_{i+1}$; this is OEIS A260311 shifted by one.

nodes.summary: Call a gap index $i$ a marker if $i \ge 10$ and the $i$-th gap between consecutive unsums (counted from zero) equals $2$. For $j \ge 0$, the $j$-th marker is the $j$-th marker in increasing order, counted from zero, so the $0$-th marker is the smallest one.

nodes.summary: Let $g_0, g_1, g_2, \ldots$ be the gaps between consecutive unsums, and call an index $i \ge 10$ with $g_i = 2$ a marker. Let $m_0 < m_1 < m_2 < \cdots$ be the markers in increasing order. For each $j$, the $j$-th word between markers is $g_{m_j + 1} g_{m_j + 2} \cdots g_{m_{j+1} - 1}$, the word of the gaps strictly between the $j$-th and the $(j+1)$-th marker.

The word $W_1$ of the gaps $g_k$ with $m_0 < k < m_1$, in increasing order of $k$, consists of the single digit $3$.

nodes.summary: For a finite list of natural numbers, a leading letter $2$ is replaced by the two letters $1, 1$, and two leading letters $1, 1$ are replaced by the single letter $2$; the empty list and every list beginning otherwise (with a letter other than $1$ or $2$, or with a $1$ not followed by another $1$) are left unchanged.

nodes.summary: For a finite list $A$ of natural numbers, the mirror image $A^r$ is obtained by reversing $A$ and then complementing the first letter: a leading $2$ of the reversed list becomes $1, 1$, two leading letters $1, 1$ become $2$, and any other list is left unchanged. For example $(1, 1, 2)^r = (1, 1, 1, 1)$ and $(1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1)^r = (2, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1)$.

nodes.summary: For a natural number $r$, the position following row $j$, zero-based column $k$, is row $j$, column $k + 1$ if $k + 1 < 1 + r(j - 1)$ (the length of row $j$, with $j - 1$ read as $0$ when $j = 0$), and row $j + 1$, column $0$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Next position in the Connell triangle

nodes.summary: For a natural number $r$, the position $p_n = (j_n, k_n)$ (row $j_n$, zero-based column $k_n$) of index $n \ge 0$ is defined by $p_0 = (1, 0)$ and $p_{n+1} = (j_n, k_n + 1)$ if $k_n + 1 < 1 + r(j_n - 1)$ (the length of row $j_n$, with $j_n - 1$ read as $0$ when $j_n = 0$), and $p_{n+1} = (j_n + 1, 0)$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Position of a term in the Connell triangle

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $m \ge 2$ and $r \ge 1$, the Connell $(m, r)$ sequence $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ reads the Connell triangle row by row: row $j \ge 1$ has $\ell_j = 1 + r(j - 1)$ entries $s_j, s_j + m, \dots, s_j + m(\ell_j - 1)$, where $s_1 = 1$ and $s_{j+1} = s_j + m(\ell_j - 1) + 1$. Thus $a_n = s_j + mk$, where row $j$, zero-based column $k$ is the position reached from row $1$, column $0$ after $n$ steps, each step…

nodes.title: Regular fractal sequence

nodes.summary: In a regular fractal sequence with position array $p$, for every $i \ge 0$ the map $j \mapsto p_i(j)$, sending $j$ to the position of the $j$-th occurrence of $i + 1$ (counting from $j = 0$), is injective.
nodes.title: Occurrence positions are distinct

nodes.summary: Let $(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a regular fractal sequence. Then for every positive integer $k$ there are infinitely many $n$ with $x_n = k$.

Gijswijt's sequence

nodes.summary: The curling number $\mathcal{C}(S)$ of a finite string $S$ of natural numbers is the largest integer $k$ such that $S = X Y^k$ for some strings $X$ and $Y$ with $Y$ nonempty; for the empty string $\varepsilon$ it is $\mathcal{C}(\varepsilon) = 1$.

reading_title.source: Terms of the $m$th order Gijswijt sequence

nodes.summary: For $k \ge 1$, $A^{(m)}(k)$ is the $k$th term of the $m$th order sequence $A^{(m)}$, that is, the last entry of the list of its first $k$ terms. For $k = 0$ the value is $0$ by convention.
nodes.title: Terms of the $m$th order Gijswijt sequence

nodes.summary: The first nine terms of Gijswijt's sequence $A^{(1)}$ are $1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3$.
nodes.title: First terms of Gijswijt's sequence

nodes.summary: The first eight terms of the second-order sequence $A^{(2)}$ are $2, 2, 2, 3, 2, 2, 2, 3$.
nodes.title: Initial terms of the second-order Gijswijt sequence

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $m$ and $n$, the first occurrence of $n$ in the $m$th order Gijswijt sequence $A^{(m)}$ is the least position $k \ge 1$ with $A^{(m)}(k) = n$, and it is $0$ if $n$ does not occur in $A^{(m)}$.
nodes.title: First occurrence of a value in a Gijswijt sequence

nodes.summary: For a natural number $m$, write $A^{(m)}(k)$ for the $k$th term of the $m$th order sequence. The block lengths $\beta^{(m)}(t)$ are defined by $\beta^{(m)}(0) = 0$, $\beta^{(m)}(1) = 1$ and, for $t \ge 1$, $\beta^{(m)}(t+1)$ is the least $k > (m+1)\,\beta^{(m)}(t)$ with $A^{(m)}(k+1) = m$, or $0$ if there is no such $k$.
nodes.title: Block lengths of the higher-order Gijswijt sequences

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $m$ and $t$, the block $B_t^{(m)}$ is the prefix of length $\beta^{(m)}(t)$ of the $m$th order Gijswijt sequence $A^{(m)}$, where $\beta^{(m)}(t)$ is the $t$th block length.
nodes.title: Gijswijt blocks

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $m$ and $t$, the glue string $S^{(m)}_t$ is the block $B^{(m)}_{t+1}$ of the $m$th order Gijswijt sequence with its first $(m+1)\,\beta^{(m)}(t)$ elements removed, where $\beta^{(m)}(t)$ is the length of the block $B^{(m)}_t$.
nodes.title: Glue strings of a Gijswijt sequence

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $m$ and $t$, the string $T^{(m)}_t$ is the concatenation $S^{(m)}_1 S^{(m)}_2 \cdots S^{(m)}_{t-1}$ of the glue strings of the $m$th order Gijswijt sequence; it is empty when $t \le 1$.
nodes.title: Concatenated glue strings of a Gijswijt sequence

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $m$ and $n$, let $p$ be the position of the first occurrence of $n$ in the $m$th order Gijswijt sequence $A^{(m)}$, with $p = 0$ if $n$ does not occur. Then $t(m, n)$ is the least $t \ge 1$ such that the block length $\beta^{(m)}(t)$ equals $p$, so that when $n$ occurs, this first $n$ is the last element of the block $B_t^{(m)}$; if there is no such $t$, then $t(m, n) = 0$.
nodes.title: Block index of the first occurrence

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $m$ and $u$ and exponents $a_1, a_2, \ldots$, the block word of order $m$ is the concatenation $B_{u-1}^{a_{u-1}} \cdots B_2^{a_2} B_1^{a_1}$, where $B_i = B_i^{(m)}$ is the $i$th block of the $m$th order Gijswijt sequence and $B_i^{a_i}$ is $a_i$ copies of $B_i$ in a row. Only $a_1, \ldots, a_{u-1}$ are used, and the word is empty when $u \le 1$.
nodes.title: Block words

nodes.summary: For every natural number $m$, the first block length $\beta^{(m)}(1)$ of the $m$th order Gijswijt sequence equals $1$.
nodes.title: The first block has length one

nodes.summary: For every $m \ge 1$, the first block $B_1^{(m)}$ of the $m$th order Gijswijt sequence is the one-term string $m$.
nodes.title: The first block

nodes.summary: For every natural number $m$, the concatenated glue string $T^{(m)}_1$ is the empty string.
nodes.title: The first concatenated glue string is empty

nodes.summary: For every natural number $m$ and every sequence of exponents $a_1, a_2, \ldots$, the block word $B_{u-1}^{a_{u-1}} \cdots B_1^{a_1}$ of order $m$ with $u = 1$, where $B_i$ is the $i$th block of the $m$th order Gijswijt sequence, is a product of no blocks and hence the empty string.
nodes.title: The empty block word

nodes.summary: For every $n \ge 4$ there is a real number $\alpha$ with $n - 2 < \alpha < n - 1$ such that the first occurrence of $n$ in Gijswijt's sequence is at position $2^{2^{3^{\cdot^{\cdot^{(n-2)^{\alpha}}}}}}$, a power tower whose bases are $2, 2, 3, \ldots, n-2$ from the bottom up and whose top exponent is $\alpha$; for $n = 4$ it is $2^{2^{\alpha}}$.
nodes.title: Van de Pol's tower formula for first occurrences

nodes.summary: For strings $S$ and $T$ of natural numbers, if $T$ is a suffix of $S$, then $\mathcal{C}(T) \le \mathcal{C}(S)$.
nodes.title: The curling number is monotone under suffixes

nodes.summary: Let $m \ge 1$ and $t \ge 2$. The element $m$ followed by the concatenated glue string $T^{(m)}_t$ is a suffix of the block $B^{(m)}_t$, and whenever $B^{(m)}_t = X\,T^{(m)}_t\,Y$ for strings $X$ and $Y$, the string $Y$ is empty; that is, $T^{(m)}_t$ occurs in $B^{(m)}_t$ only as a suffix.
nodes.title: Concatenated glue strings occur in a block only at its end

nodes.summary: Let $m \ge 1$. A finite string $P$ of natural numbers is a prefix of the $(m+1)$th order Gijswijt sequence $A^{(m+1)}$ with curling number $\mathcal{C}(P) \le m$ if and only if $P = T^{(m)}_t$ for some $t \ge 1$, where $T^{(m)}_t$ is the concatenated glue string.
nodes.title: Concatenated glue strings are the next-order prefixes with small curling number

nodes.summary: Let $m \ge 1$ and $t \ge 2$, and consider the block $B_t^{(m)}$ of the $m$th order Gijswijt sequence. Every maximal run of consecutive terms equal to $m$ in $B_t^{(m)}$ has length exactly $m + 1$, and the term right after the run exists and equals $m + 1$.
nodes.title: Runs of the smallest term in a block

nodes.summary: Let $1 \le m \le n$, and write $\beta^{(m)}(t)$ for the length of the block $B_t^{(m)}$ of the $m$th order Gijswijt sequence $A^{(m)}$. Then there is a $t \ge 1$ such that $A^{(m)}(\beta^{(m)}(t)) = n$ and $\beta^{(m)}(t)$ is the position of the first occurrence of $n$ in $A^{(m)}$; that is, the first $n$ in $A^{(m)}$ is the last term of the block $B_t^{(m)}$.

Self-generating sets

nodes.summary: A finite set $F$ of functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ has strict growth when $x < f(x)$ for every $f \in F$ and every $x \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: Strict growth of a set of generators

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a finite set of functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and let $s \in \mathbb{N}$. A set $\Gamma \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is self-generating for $s$ and $F$ when $s \in \Gamma$ and $f(x) \in \Gamma$ for every $f \in F$ and every $x \in \Gamma$.
nodes.title: Self-generating sets

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a finite set of functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and let $s \in \mathbb{N}$. A set $C \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a fixed-point set for $F$ and $s$ when, for every $y \in \mathbb{N}$, $y \in C$ if and only if $y = s$ or $y = f(x)$ for some $f \in F$ and some $x \in C$; equivalently, $C = \{s\} \cup \bigcup_{f \in F} f(C)$.
nodes.title: Fixed-point sets for a seed and generators

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a finite set of functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and let $s \in \mathbb{N}$. Reachability from $s$ is the least predicate on $\mathbb{N}$ that holds at $s$ and holds at $f(w)$ whenever it holds at $w$ and $f \in F$. Thus $y$ is reachable exactly when $y = f_k(\cdots f_1(s) \cdots)$ for some $k \ge 0$ and $f_1, \ldots, f_k \in F$; the case $k = 0$ is $s$ itself.
nodes.title: Reachability from a seed by generators

nodes.summary: For a finite set $F$ of functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a seed $s \in \mathbb{N}$, the set generated from $s$ by $F$ consists of all numbers $f_k(\cdots f_1(s) \cdots)$ with $k \ge 0$ and $f_1, \dots, f_k \in F$; the case $k = 0$ gives $s$ itself.
nodes.title: Set generated from a seed

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a finite set of functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and $s \in \mathbb{N}$. Every fixed-point set $C$ for $F$ and $s$ is self-generating: $s \in C$, and $f(x) \in C$ for every $f \in F$ and every $x \in C$.
nodes.title: Fixed-point sets are self-generating

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a finite set of functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and $s \in \mathbb{N}$. The set generated from $s$ by $F$ contains $s$ and is closed under every $f \in F$: if $x$ is in it and $f \in F$, then $f(x)$ is in it.
nodes.title: The generated set is self-generating

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a finite set of functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and let $s \in \mathbb{N}$. If a set $G \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ contains $s$ and satisfies $f(x) \in G$ for every $f \in F$ and every $x \in G$, then $G$ contains the set generated from $s$ by $F$, that is, every number obtained from $s$ by applying finitely many (possibly no) functions of $F$ in succession.
nodes.title: The generated set lies in every self-generating set

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a finite set of functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and $s \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $\Gamma$ be the set generated from $s$ by $F$. Then for every $y \in \mathbb{N}$, $y \in \Gamma$ if and only if $y = s$ or $y = f(x)$ for some $f \in F$ and $x \in \Gamma$.
nodes.title: The generated set is a fixed-point set

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a finite set of functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $x < f(x)$ for every $f \in F$ and every $x \in \mathbb{N}$, let $s \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $C \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a fixed-point set for $F$ and $s$: $y \in C$ exactly when $y = s$ or $y = f(x)$ for some $f \in F$ and $x \in C$. Then $C$ equals the set generated from $s$ by $F$, the numbers obtained from $s$ by applying finitely many…
nodes.title: Under strict growth, a fixed-point set is the generated set

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a finite set of functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and $s \in \mathbb{N}$. The set generated from $s$ by $F$ equals the intersection of all sets $G \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ that contain $s$ and are closed under every $f \in F$.
nodes.title: The generated set is the intersection of all self-generating sets

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a finite set of functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $x < f(x)$ for every $f \in F$ and every $x \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $s \in \mathbb{N}$. If $C$ is a fixed-point set for $F$ and $s$, then $C$ is the intersection of all sets $G \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ that contain $s$ and are closed under every $f \in F$.
nodes.title: Under strict growth, a fixed-point set is the intersection of all self-generating sets

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a finite set of functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $x < f(x)$ for every $f \in F$ and every $x \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $s \in \mathbb{N}$. If $C$ is a fixed-point set for $F$ and $s$, then $C$ contains $s$ and is closed under every $f \in F$, and $C \subseteq G$ for every set $G \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ that contains $s$ and is closed under every $f \in F$.
nodes.title: Under strict growth, a fixed-point set is the least self-generating set

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a finite set of functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and let $s \in \mathbb{N}$. Call a set $G \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ self-generating if $s \in G$ and $f(x) \in G$ for every $f \in F$ and every $x \in G$. If $C$ is self-generating and is contained in every self-generating set, then $C$ equals the set generated from $s$ by $F$.
nodes.title: The least self-generating set is the generated set

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a finite set of functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $x < f(x)$ for every $f \in F$ and every $x \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $s \in \mathbb{N}$. If $C_1$ and $C_2$ are both fixed-point sets for $F$ and $s$, then $C_1 = C_2$.
nodes.title: Under strict growth, fixed-point sets are unique
Smarandache permutation sequence

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, the $n$-th block is the list of the odd numbers $1, 3, \ldots, 2n - 1$ in increasing order followed by the even numbers $2n, 2n - 2, \ldots, 2$ in decreasing order; the $0$-th block is empty.
nodes.title: Blocks of the Smarandache permutation sequence

nodes.summary: For a natural number $N$, this is the list of natural numbers obtained by concatenating, in order, the Smarandache blocks numbered $1, 2, \dots, N$, where block $n$ is the list $(1, 3, \dots, 2n - 1, 2n, 2n - 2, \dots, 2)$ of the odd numbers below $2n$ in increasing order followed by the even numbers from $2n$ down to $2$. For $N = 0$ it is the empty list.
nodes.title: Prefix of the Smarandache permutation sequence

nodes.summary: The Smarandache permutation sequence (OEIS A004741) is the sequence $(a_i)_{i \ge 0}$ of natural numbers, indexed from $0$, obtained by concatenating the blocks $(1, 3, \ldots, 2n - 1, 2n, 2n - 2, \ldots, 2)$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$ in order; it begins $1, 2, 1, 3, 4, 2, 1, 3, 5, 6, 4, 2, \ldots$, so $a_0 = 1$.

nodes.summary: Let $s = (s_0, s_1, s_2, \dots)$ be a sequence of elements of a set $A$, each element $a$ carrying a weight $w(a) \in \mathbb{N}$. nodes.summary: Four natural numbers $a, b, c, d$ form a Van der Laan window when the largest of them equals the sum of the two smallest, that is, when $\max(a, b, c, d) = \min(a + b, a + c, a + d, b + c, b + d, c + d)$.
nodes.title: Van der Laan windows

nodes.summary: A sequence $s \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is a Van der Laan sequence when, for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the four consecutive terms $s(n), s(n + 1), s(n + 2), s(n + 3)$ form a Van der Laan window, that is, the largest of them equals the sum of the two smallest.

nodes.summary: A sequence $w$ of natural numbers contains a sequence $p = p_1 \cdots p_k$ as a consecutive pattern if some $k$ adjacent entries $w_{i+1}, \dots, w_{i+k}$ of $w$ have the same relative order as $p$: for all $a, b \in \{1, \dots, k\}$, $w_{i+a} < w_{i+b}$ if and only if $p_a < p_b$.

nodes.summary: The standardization $\mathrm{st}(s)$ of a finite sequence $s = s_1 s_2 \cdots s_k$ of natural numbers is obtained by replacing each entry $s_i$ by the number of indices $j$ with $s_j \le s_i$. When the entries of $s$ are distinct, this number is the rank of $s_i$: the $r$th smallest entry becomes $r$.
nodes.title: Standardization

nodes.summary: Given an optional previous entry $y$ and a sequence $s_1 s_2 \cdots s_\ell$ of natural numbers, this lists, in order, the entries $s_i$ with $s_i \ne s_{i-1} + 1$, where $s_0 = y$; if there is no previous entry, $s_1$ is always listed. With no previous entry, these are the minima $a$ of the maximal blocks $a, a + 1, \dots, a + k$ of adjacent consecutive integers of the sequence.
nodes.title: Heads of runs of consecutive integers

nodes.summary: The reduction $\operatorname{red}(s)$ of a finite sequence $s$ of natural numbers is obtained in two steps. First, every maximal block of adjacent entries of the form $a, a + 1, \ldots, a + k$ is replaced by its first entry $a$. Then the resulting sequence is standardized: each of its entries $x$ is replaced by the number of its entries that are at most $x$, which for distinct entries is the rank of $x$.
nodes.title: Reduction of a sequence

nodes.summary: The standardization of $315$ is $\mathrm{st}(315) = 213$, and the reduction of $16783425$ is $\mathrm{red}(16783425) = 15324$. Here $\mathrm{st}$ replaces each entry by its rank, and $\mathrm{red}$ replaces each maximal block of adjacent consecutive integers $a, a + 1, \dots, a + k$ by its minimum $a$ and then standardizes.

nodes.summary: For finite sequences $a$ and $b$ of natural numbers, $\mathrm{push}(a, b)$ is the sequence obtained by taking the first entry of $b$, then the next two entries of $a$ (only one if just one is left), and repeating; once one of the two sequences is exhausted, the remaining entries of the other follow in order.

Then $\mathrm{si}(\sigma_1, \sigma_2)$ is the reversal of $p$: the stack obtained by pushing the entries of $p$ in order onto an empty stack, read from top to bottom.

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, $\xi_n$ is the sequence listing the elements of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ whose parity differs from that of $n$ in increasing order, followed by the elements with the same parity as $n$ in increasing order. Thus $\xi_n = 1, 3, \dots, n-1, 2, 4, \dots, n$ for even $n$, and $\xi_n = 2, 4, \dots, n-1, 1, 3, \dots, n$ for odd $n$.

Pattern avoidance in inversion sequences

nodes.summary: A sequence $e = e_0 e_1 \cdots e_{n-1}$ of natural numbers contains the length-3 pattern $p = p_0 p_1 p_2$ of natural numbers when there are positions $i_0 < i_1 < i_2$ in $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ such that, for all $a, b \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, $e_{i_a} < e_{i_b}$ if and only if $p_a < p_b$; that is, the subsequence $e_{i_0} e_{i_1} e_{i_2}$ is order-isomorphic to $p$.
nodes.title: Containment of a length-3 pattern

nodes.summary: If $n < 3$, then no sequence $e_0 e_1 \cdots e_{n-1}$ of natural numbers contains a length-3 pattern $p$.
nodes.title: Short sequences contain no length-3 pattern

nodes.summary: An inversion sequence of length $n$ is a sequence $e = e_0 e_1 \cdots e_{n-1}$ of natural numbers with $e_i \le i$ for every $i$. It contains a length-3 pattern $p = p_0 p_1 p_2$ (a triple of natural numbers) when some subsequence $e_a e_b e_c$ with $a < b < c$ is order-isomorphic to $p$. For a set $B$ of length-3 patterns, $|I_n(B)|$ is the number of inversion sequences of length $n$ that contain no pattern of $B$.
nodes.title: Number of inversion sequences avoiding a set of patterns

nodes.summary: For every set $B$ of length-3 patterns, the number $|I_1(B)|$ of inversion sequences of length one that avoid every pattern in $B$ equals $1$: the only inversion sequence of length one is $0$, and it avoids every length-3 pattern.
nodes.title: One inversion sequence of length one

nodes.summary: For a set $B$ of length-3 patterns, $F_B(x) = \sum_{n \ge 1} |I_n(B)| x^n$ is the formal power series in $\mathbb{Q}[[x]]$ with constant coefficient $0$ whose coefficient of $x^n$, for $n \ge 1$, is the number $|I_n(B)|$ of inversion sequences of length $n$ that avoid every pattern in $B$.

nodes.summary: For every set $B$ of length-3 patterns and every $n \ge 0$, the generating function $F_B(x) = \sum_{m \ge 1} |I_m(B)| x^m \in \mathbb{Q}[[x]]$ has constant coefficient $0$, and its coefficient of $x^{n+1}$ is $|I_{n+1}(B)|$, the number of inversion sequences of length $n + 1$ that avoid every pattern in $B$.

Pattern avoidance in weak ascent sequences

nodes.summary: For a word $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_m$ of natural numbers, $\mathrm{wasc}(a_1 \cdots a_m)$ is the number of weak ascents, that is, of positions $j$ with $1 \le j < m$ and $a_j \le a_{j+1}$; in particular the empty word and every word of length one have no weak ascents.
nodes.title: Number of weak ascents of a word

nodes.summary: A word $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ over $\mathbb{N}$ is a weak ascent sequence if either $n = 0$, or $a_1 = 0$ and $a_i \le 1 + \operatorname{wasc}(a_1 \cdots a_{i-1})$ for every $2 \le i \le n$, where $\operatorname{wasc}(u)$ is the number of weak ascents of $u$, that is, of positions $j$ with $u_j \le u_{j+1}$.
nodes.title: Weak ascent sequence

nodes.summary: A word $w$ over $\mathbb{N}$ contains a pattern $p$ (another word over $\mathbb{N}$) if $w$ has a subsequence $s$, not necessarily contiguous, of the same length as $p$ that is order-isomorphic to $p$: for all positions $i$ and $j$, $s_i < s_j$ if and only if $p_i < p_j$.

nodes.summary: A permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ is a king permutation if adjacent entries never differ by exactly $1$: for every position $i$ with $i + 1 < n$, neither $\sigma(i + 1) = \sigma(i) + 1$ nor $\sigma(i) = \sigma(i + 1) + 1$. Equivalently, $|\sigma(i + 1) - \sigma(i)| > 1$ for all adjacent positions $i$ and $i + 1$.

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a permutation of $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$. A position $i$ is a peak of $\sigma$ if $i + 2 < n$ and $\sigma(i) < \sigma(i+1) > \sigma(i+2)$. Thus the peak entry is $\sigma(i+1)$, and the position recorded is $i$, that of the first of the three entries.

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number. nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, the Dedekind number $M(n)$ is the number of antichains with respect to inclusion among the subsets of the $n$-element set $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$, that is, of families of subsets in which no member is contained in a different member; the empty family and the family $\{\emptyset\}$ are counted.

Self-dual monotone Boolean functions

nodes.summary: The complement of a Boolean vector $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ is the vector $\bar x \in \{0,1\}^n$ obtained by negating every coordinate: $\bar x_i = \lnot x_i$ for every $i < n$.
nodes.title: Complement of a Boolean vector

nodes.summary: For a Boolean function $f \colon \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$, its dual is the Boolean function $f^\star \colon \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ given by $f^\star(x) = \lnot f(\bar x)$, where $\bar x$ is the coordinatewise complement of $x$.
nodes.title: Dual of a Boolean function

nodes.summary: A Boolean function $f \colon \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ is self-dual monotone when it is monotone, that is, $f(x) \le f(y)$ for all $x, y \in \{0,1\}^n$ with $x_i \le y_i$ for every $i < n$, and it equals its dual, that is, $f = f^\star$, where $f^\star(x) = \lnot f(\bar x)$ and $\bar x$ is the coordinatewise complement of $x$.
nodes.title: Self-dual monotone Boolean functions

nodes.summary: For every $n$ and every Boolean vector $x \in \{0,1\}^n$, writing $\bar x$ for the coordinatewise complement of $x$, we have $\bar{\bar x} = x$.
nodes.title: Complementation of Boolean vectors is an involution

nodes.summary: For every $n$ and every Boolean function $f \colon \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$, writing $f^\star$ for the dual of $f$, we have $(f^\star)^\star = f$.
nodes.title: Duality of Boolean functions is an involution

nodes.summary: For every $n$ and every index $i < n$, the projection $x \mapsto x_i$ on $\{0,1\}^n$ is a self-dual monotone Boolean function.
nodes.title: Coordinate projections are self-dual monotone

nodes.summary: For a natural number $m$, let $D_m$ be the poset of monotone Boolean functions $\{0,1\}^m \to \{0,1\}$, where $0 < 1$, inputs are ordered coordinatewise and functions are ordered pointwise. Then for all natural numbers $n$ and $k$, $D_{n+k}$ is order-isomorphic to the poset of monotone maps $\{0,1\}^k \to D_n$, ordered pointwise.

Unate and monotone Boolean functions

nodes.summary: The weight $\mathrm{wt}(f)$ of an $n$-variable Boolean function $f \colon \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ is the number of inputs $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ with $f(x) = 1$.

nodes.summary: An $n$-variable Boolean function $f$ is monotone increasing in the variable $x_i$ if for every input $x$ with $x_i = 0$, changing $x_i$ to $1$ does not decrease the value: $f(x) \le f(x')$, where $x'$ agrees with $x$ except that $x'_i = 1$.
nodes.title: Boolean functions increasing in a variable

nodes.summary: An $n$-variable Boolean function $f$ is monotone decreasing in the variable $x_i$ if for every input $x$ with $x_i = 0$, changing $x_i$ to $1$ does not increase the value: $f(x') \le f(x)$, where $x'$ agrees with $x$ except that $x'_i = 1$.
nodes.title: Boolean functions decreasing in a variable

nodes.summary: A Boolean function $f$ on $n$ variables, with Boolean values $0 < 1$, is unate when for each variable $i$ either $f$ is increasing in $x_i$ (changing $x_i$ from $0$ to $1$, with the other variables fixed, never decreases the value of $f$) or $f$ is decreasing in $x_i$ (that change never increases the value of $f$).
nodes.title: Unate Boolean function

nodes.title: Monotone Boolean functions are unate

nodes.summary: An $n$-variable Boolean function $f$ is non-degenerate on the variable $x_i$ when flipping $x_i$ changes the value of $f$ at some input: there is $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ with $f(x) \ne f(x')$, where $x'$ is $x$ with its $i$-th coordinate negated.
nodes.title: Non-degeneracy in a variable

nodes.summary: An $n$-variable Boolean function $f$ is non-degenerate when it is non-degenerate on every variable $x_i$, $1 \le i \le n$: for each $i$ there is an input $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ with $f(x) \ne f(x')$, where $x'$ is $x$ with its $i$-th coordinate negated. For $n = 0$ the condition is vacuous, so both $0$-variable (constant) functions are non-degenerate, matching the paper's convention.

nodes.summary: The concatenation $g \,\|\, h$ of two $n$-variable Boolean functions $g$ and $h$ is the $(n+1)$-variable function whose truth table is that of $g$ followed by that of $h$: its value at $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{n+1})$ is $g(x_2, \dots, x_{n+1})$ if $x_1 = 0$ and $h(x_2, \dots, x_{n+1})$ if $x_1 = 1$. Equivalently, $(g \,\|\, h)(x) = \bar{x}_1 g(x_2, \dots, x_{n+1}) \oplus x_1 h(x_2, \dots, x_{n+1})$.

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a vertex type $V$ and let $k$ be a natural number. A $k$-linear partition of $G$ is a set of exactly $k$ blocks, each block a nonempty finite sequence of pairwise distinct vertices, such that every vertex of $G$ lies in exactly one block and any two consecutive vertices of a block are nonadjacent in $G$. The blocks themselves are unordered; only the vertices within a block are ordered.

In particular $p(j, k, 0) = 1$ for all $j$ and $k$, while $p(0, k, n) = p(j, 0, n) = 0$ for $n \ge 1$.

nodes.summary: For a finite board $B \subseteq \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, whose cell $(i, j)$ lies in row $i$ and column $j$, the max-rook number of $B$ is the largest size of a subset of $B$ that contains at most one cell of each row and at most one cell of each column, that is, the largest number of non-attacking rooks that can be placed on $B$.

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number. nodes.summary: A double-perfect partition of $N$ of order $r$ is a finite multiset $\lambda$ of positive integers with sum $N$ such that, for every integer $m$ with $1 \le m \le N$, the number of distinct sub-multisets of $\lambda$ with sum $m$ is $2$ if $r + 1 \le m \le N - r - 1$ and $1$ otherwise. Their set is denoted $U_r(N)$; order $1$ gives the double-perfect partitions.

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, $\mathrm{po}(n)$ is the number of overpartitions of $n$ all of whose parts are odd.
nodes.title: Overpartitions into odd parts

nodes.summary: The number $\mathrm{po}(0)$ of overpartitions of $0$ into odd parts equals $1$: the empty overpartition is the only one.
nodes.title: Overpartitions of zero into odd parts

nodes.summary: Let $\mathrm{po}(j)$ be the number of overpartitions of $j$ into odd parts. For every natural number $n$, the sum $\sum_k (-1)^k \, \mathrm{po}(n - k(3k+1)/2)$ over the integers $k$ with $k(3k+1)/2 \le n$ equals $(-1)^{\lceil m/2 \rceil}$ if $n = m(3m+1)/2$ for some integer $m$, and $0$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Pentagonal recurrence for overpartitions into odd parts

nodes.summary: Write $\mathrm{po}(m)$ for the number of overpartitions of $m$ into odd parts. For every natural number $n$, the sum $\sum_{k \ge 0,\ k(k+1)/2 \le n} (-1)^{\lceil k/2 \rceil} \, \mathrm{po}(n - k(k+1)/2)$ equals $1$ if $n = m(m+1)/2$ for some natural number $m$, and equals $0$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Triangular recurrence for overpartitions into odd parts

nodes.summary: Write $\mathrm{po}(m)$ for the number of overpartitions of $m$ into odd parts. For every natural number $n$, the sum $\mathrm{po}(n) + 2 \sum_{k \ge 1,\ 2k^2 \le n} (-1)^k \, \mathrm{po}(n - 2k^2)$ equals $1$ if $n = 0$, equals $2$ if $n = m^2$ for some integer $m \ge 1$, and equals $0$ otherwise.

nodes.summary: Let $\mathrm{po}(m)$ be the number of overpartitions of $m$ into odd parts and $p(m)$ the number of partitions of $m$. For every natural number $n$, $\mathrm{po}(n) = \sum_k (-1)^{\lceil k/2 \rceil} p(n - k(3k+1)/2)$, the sum running over the integers $k$ with $k(3k+1)/2 \le n$.

nodes.summary: Let $\operatorname{ped}(m)$ be the number of partitions of $m$ in which no even part is repeated. For every $n \ge 0$, the sum $\sum_j (-1)^j \operatorname{ped}(n - 2j^2)$ over the integers $j$ with $2j^2 \le n$ equals $1$ if $n = k(k+1)/2$ for some integer $k \ge 0$, and $0$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Merca's square recurrence for partitions with distinct even parts

nodes.summary: Let $\mathrm{po}(m)$ be the number of overpartitions of $m$ into odd parts and $\mathrm{pod}(m)$ the number of partitions of $m$ whose odd parts are distinct. For every natural number $n$, $\mathrm{po}(n) = \sum_k \mathrm{pod}(n - k(k+1)/2)$, the sum running over the natural numbers $k$ with $k(k+1)/2 \le n$.

nodes.summary: Let $\operatorname{pod}(m)$ be the number of partitions of $m$ in which no odd part is repeated. For every $n > 0$, the sum $\sum_{k \ge 0} \operatorname{pod}(n - k(k+1)/2)$ over the $k$ with $k(k+1)/2 \le n$ is even.

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, $p(n)$ is the number of partitions of $n$, that is, of ways of writing $n$ as a sum of positive integers, disregarding order.
