nodes.summary: Let $p(n)$ be the number of partitions of $n$. Then $p(0) = 1$: the only partition of $0$ is the empty one.

nodes.title: The partition number of one

nodes.summary: Let $p(n)$ be the number of partitions of $n$. Over the integers, $\sum_{n \ge 0} p(n)\, x^n$ equals the weighted partition generating function $\sum_{n \ge 0} \sum_{\lambda} \prod_{i} f(i, c_i(\lambda))\, x^n$ with all weights $f(i, c) = 1$, where $\lambda$ runs over the partitions of $n$, $i$ over the distinct parts of $\lambda$, and $c_i(\lambda)$ is the number of times $i$ occurs in $\lambda$.
nodes.title: Partition generating function with unit weights

nodes.summary: Let $p(n)$ be the number of partitions of $n$. Over the integers, $\left(\sum_{n \ge 0} p(n)\, x^n\right) \cdot \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^k x^{k(3k-1)/2} = 1$. By the pentagonal number theorem the second factor equals $\prod_{i \ge 1} (1 - x^i)$.

nodes.summary: Let $p(n)$ be the number of partitions of $n$, and for an integer $k$ let $g(k) = k(3k - 1)/2$ be the generalized pentagonal number of $k$. For every natural number $n \ge 1$, $p(n) = \sum_{k} (-1)^{k+1}\, p(n - g(k))$, where the sum runs over the nonzero integers $k$ with $g(k) \le n$.

nodes.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ let $T_n$ be the central trinomial coefficient, the coefficient of $X^n$ in $(1 + X + X^2)^n$. Let $M : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be any function with $M_n = \sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} \binom{n}{2k} C_k$ for every $n$, where $C_k$ is the $k$-th Catalan number (these sums are the Motzkin numbers). Then for every $n \ge 1$, $T_{n+1} = T_n + 2n \, M_{n-1}$.

The word $p$ satisfies the bounded Motzkin prefix condition for $h$ when, for every $m \in \{0, 1, \dots, n\}$, the sum of the displacements of $p_0, \dots, p_{m-1}$ is nonnegative, and the sum of the displacements of all $n$…
nodes.title: Bounded Motzkin prefix condition

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a word of length $n$ in the steps $D$, $F$, $U$ and let $h \in \mathbb{Z}$. Then $p$ satisfies the bounded Motzkin prefix condition for $h$, in which the prefix length $m$ ranges over $\{0, 1, \dots, n\}$, if and only if $p$ is a Motzkin prefix ending at height $h$, in which $m$ ranges over all natural numbers with $m \le n$.
nodes.title: Bounded form of the Motzkin prefix condition

nodes.summary: Write a path of length $n$ as a sequence of steps $p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}$, and let $s(p_r) \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$ be the vertical displacement of the step $p_r$ (down, flat or up). For a natural number $k$ and positions $i, j < n$, the pair $(i, j)$ is a hump of height $k$ if and only if $i < j$, $s(p_i) = 1$, $s(p_j) = -1$, $s(p_r) = 0$ for every $r$ with $i < r < j$, and $\sum_{r \le i} s(p_r) = k$.
nodes.title: Characterization of Motzkin humps

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a word of length $n$ in the steps $D$, $F$, $U$, let $k \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $i, j \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$. The pair $(i, j)$ is a peak of height $k$ in $p$ when it is a hump of height $k$ in $p$ and $j = i + 1$, that is, when the down step $p_j$ immediately follows the up step $p_i$.
nodes.title: Motzkin peak

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a word of length $n$ in the steps $D$, $F$, $U$, let $k \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $i, j \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Then $(i, j)$ is a peak of height $k$ in $p$ if and only if $(i, j)$ is a hump of height $k$ in $p$ and $j = i + 1$.
nodes.title: Peaks are humps with adjacent endpoints

nodes.summary: A word $p = p_0 p_1 \cdots p_{n-1}$ of length $n$ in the steps $U$ (up), $F$ (flat) and $D$ (down) has last non-flat step up when some position $i$ has $p_i = U$ and every later step $p_j$ with $j > i$ is $F$. In particular, such a word contains an up step.
nodes.title: Paths whose last non-flat step is up

nodes.summary: Let $p = p_0 p_1 \cdots p_{n-1}$ be a word of length $n$ in the steps $D$, $F$, $U$. Then the last non-flat step of $p$ is $U$ if and only if there is a position $i$ with $p_i = U$ such that $p_j = F$ for every position $j > i$.
nodes.title: Characterization of words whose last non-flat step is up

nodes.summary: Write a path of length $n$ as a sequence of steps $p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}$, each $D$ (down), $F$ (flat) or $U$ (up), encoded as $0$, $1$, $2$. The path has first non-up step down when there is a position $i$ with $p_i = D$ and $p_j = U$ for every $j < i$. In particular, a path all of whose steps are up steps, including the empty path, does not qualify.

nodes.summary: Write a path of length $n$ as a sequence of steps $p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}$, each $D$ (down), $F$ (flat) or $U$ (up), encoded as $0$, $1$, $2$. The path has first non-up step $D$ if and only if there is a position $i$ with $p_i = D$ and $p_j = U$ for every $j < i$.
nodes.title: Characterization of paths whose first non-up step is down

nodes.summary: Write a path of length $n$ as a sequence of steps $p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}$, each $D$ (down), $F$ (flat) or $U$ (up), encoded as $0$, $1$, $2$. The path ends with an up step when it has a last position, that is, some $i < n$ with $i + 1 = n$, and $p_i = U$.

nodes.summary: A standard Young tableau of order $n$ is encoded by a map $T$ that assigns to each entry $i \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ a cell $T(i) = (r_i, c_i)$ with row and column indices in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. The map $T$ is a standard Young tableau when it is injective and, for every entry $i$ and every cell $(r, c)$ with $r \le r_i$ and $c \le c_i$, there is an entry $j \le i$ with $T(j) = (r, c)$.

nodes.summary: The Motzkin discriminant is the formal power series $1 - 2X - 3X^2 \in \mathbb{Q}[[X]]$, the discriminant in the generating functions for the Motzkin triangle.
nodes.title: Motzkin discriminant

nodes.summary: A formal power series $s \in \mathbb{Q}[[X]]$ is a Motzkin square root when $s^2 = 1 - 2X - 3X^2$ and the constant coefficient of $s$ is $1$.
nodes.title: Square roots of the Motzkin discriminant

nodes.summary: The canonical square root is the power series $s = \sum_{n \ge 0} \binom{1/2}{n} (-2X - 3X^2)^n \in \mathbb{Q}[[X]]$, obtained by substituting $-2X - 3X^2$ for $Y$ in the binomial series $(1 + Y)^{1/2} = \sum_{n \ge 0} \binom{1/2}{n} Y^n$.
nodes.title: Canonical square root of the Motzkin discriminant

nodes.summary: Let $s = \sum_{n \ge 0} \binom{1/2}{n} (-2X - 3X^2)^n \in \mathbb{Q}[[X]]$ be the canonical square root of $1 - 2X - 3X^2$. The power series $h \in \mathbb{Q}[[X]]$ has $n$-th coefficient $\frac{1}{2} [X^{n+1}] (1 - X - s)$ for every $n \ge 0$. Since $1 - X - s$ has constant coefficient $0$, this is the quotient $h = (1 - X - s)/(2X)$.
nodes.title: Second component of the Motzkin Riordan pair

nodes.summary: Let $s = \sum_{n \ge 0} \binom{1/2}{n} (-2X - 3X^2)^n \in \mathbb{Q}[[X]]$ be the canonical square root of $1 - 2X - 3X^2$, which has constant coefficient $1$. The power series $g \in \mathbb{Q}[[X]]$ is the multiplicative inverse $g = s^{-1}$ of $s$, that is, $g = 1/\sqrt{1 - 2X - 3X^2}$.
nodes.title: First component of the Motzkin Riordan pair

nodes.summary: Formal power series $g, h \in \mathbb{Q}[[X]]$ form a Motzkin Riordan pair when there is a power series $s \in \mathbb{Q}[[X]]$ with $s^2 = 1 - 2X - 3X^2$ and constant coefficient $1$ such that $g s = 1$ and $2 X h = 1 - X - s$.
nodes.title: Motzkin Riordan pairs

nodes.summary: A bundled Motzkin Riordan pair consists of formal power series $g, h \in \mathbb{Q}[[X]]$ together with a proof that they form a Motzkin Riordan pair: there is $s \in \mathbb{Q}[[X]]$ with $s^2 = 1 - 2X - 3X^2$ and constant coefficient $1$ such that $g s = 1$ and $2 X h = 1 - X - s$.
nodes.title: Bundled Motzkin Riordan pairs

nodes.summary: For a Motzkin Riordan pair $(g, h)$ and natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the $(n, k)$ entry is the rational number $[X^n]\, g h^k$, the coefficient of $X^n$ in the power series $g h^k \in \mathbb{Q}[[X]]$.
nodes.title: Entries of a Motzkin Riordan array

nodes.summary: Let $s \in \mathbb{Q}[[X]]$ be the canonical square root of $1 - 2X - 3X^2$, given by the binomial series, which has constant coefficient $1$. The canonical Motzkin Riordan pair is $(g, h)$ with $g = s^{-1}$ and $h = (1 - X - s)/(2X)$, the Motzkin Riordan pair conditions being witnessed by $s$.
nodes.title: The canonical Motzkin Riordan pair

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be the square root of $1 - 2X - 3X^2$ in the ring of formal power series over $\mathbb{Q}$ with constant coefficient $1$, and let $g = 1/s$ and $h = (1 - X - s)/(2X)$. For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the $(n, k)$ entry of the Motzkin triangle (OEIS A094531) is the rational number given by the coefficient of $X^n$ in $g h^k$.

Gessel words

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, the Gessel alphabet over $S = [n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$ is the disjoint union of an unbarred copy and a barred copy of $[n]$: it has an unbarred letter $i$ and a barred letter $\bar{i}$ for each $i \in [n]$.
nodes.title: Gessel alphabet

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number, let $w$ be a word (a finite sequence of letters) over the Gessel alphabet over $[n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$ and let $m$ be a natural number. The unbarred count of $m$ in $w$ is the number of positions of $w$ that hold the unbarred letter $m$; it is $0$ when $m \notin [n]$.

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number, let $w$ be a word (a finite sequence of letters) over the Gessel alphabet over $[n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$ and let $m$ be a natural number. nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number, let $w$ be a word over the Gessel alphabet over $[n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$ and let $m$ be a natural number. The signed balance of $m$ in $w$ is the integer obtained by subtracting the number of occurrences of the barred letter $\bar{m}$ in $w$ from the number of occurrences of the unbarred letter $m$ in $w$; it is $0$ when $m \notin [n]$.

nodes.summary: A word $w$ over the Gessel alphabet of $S = [n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$ is a complete Gessel word when it is a Gessel word and, for every $m \in [n]$, the unbarred letter $m$ and the barred letter $\bar m$ occur the same number of times in $w$.
nodes.title: Complete Gessel words

nodes.summary: A word $w$ over the Gessel alphabet of $[n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$ is a complete Gessel word if and only if it is a Gessel word and, for every $m \in [n]$, the signed balance of $m$ in $w$ (the number of occurrences of the unbarred letter $m$ minus the number of occurrences of the barred letter $\bar m$) is zero.

k-box paths and skew Dyck paths

nodes.summary: A skew Dyck path is built from three kinds of step: the up step $U = (1,1)$, the down step $D = (1,-1)$ and the left step $L = (-1,-1)$.
nodes.title: Skew Dyck steps

nodes.summary: A word $w$ in the steps $U$, $D$, $L$ is a skew Dyck word when neither $UL$ nor $LU$ occurs in $w$ as two consecutive letters, the number of $U$s in $w$ equals the number of $D$s and $L$s together, and no prefix of $w$ has more $D$s and $L$s together than $U$s.

nodes.summary: For $m \in \mathbb{N}$, the skew Dyck paths of semilength $m$ are the words of length $2m$ over $\{U, D, L\}$ that avoid the factors $UL$ and $LU$, have as many $U$s as $D$s and $L$s together, and have no prefix with more $D$s and $L$s together than $U$s.

Equivalently, it is the number of positions of $w$ at which an occurrence of $f$ as a contiguous block starts, overlapping occurrences all being counted; in particular the empty word has factor count $|w| + 1$ in $w$.

Marked Dyck paths

nodes.summary: A step of a marked Dyck path is one of three kinds: a horizontal step $E = (1, 0)$, an unmarked vertical step $N = (0, 1)$, or a marked vertical step $N^* = (0, 1)$.
nodes.title: Steps of a marked Dyck path

nodes.summary: For a finite sequence $P$ of marked Dyck steps, $E(P)$ is the number of horizontal steps $E$ in $P$.
nodes.title: Number of horizontal steps in a marked Dyck step sequence

nodes.summary: For a finite sequence $P$ of marked Dyck steps, $N(P)$ is the number of unmarked vertical steps $N$ in $P$.
nodes.title: Number of unmarked vertical steps

nodes.summary: For a finite sequence $P$ of marked Dyck steps, $N^*(P)$ is the number of marked vertical steps $N^*$ in $P$.
nodes.title: Number of marked vertical steps

nodes.summary: Let $E(Q)$, $N(Q)$ and $N^*(Q)$ denote the numbers of horizontal steps $E$, unmarked vertical steps $N$ and marked vertical steps $N^*$ in a finite sequence $Q$ of marked Dyck steps. A marked Dyck path is a finite sequence $P$ of marked Dyck steps such that $E(P) = N(P) + N^*(P)$ and every prefix $Q$ of $P$ satisfies $N(Q) + N^*(Q) \le E(Q)$: a lattice path from $(0, 0)$ that ends on the diagonal and never goes…
nodes.title: Marked Dyck path

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a marked Dyck path with $\ell$ steps. For a position $i$ with $0 \le i < \ell$, the step of $P$ at position $i$ is marked when it is the marked vertical step $N^*$ (rather than an unmarked vertical step $N$ or a horizontal step $E$).
nodes.title: Marked step of a marked Dyck path

nodes.summary: The size of a marked Dyck path $P$ is $N^*(P) + E(P)$, where $N^*(P)$ is the number of marked vertical steps of $P$ and $E(P)$ the number of its horizontal steps.
nodes.title: Size of a marked Dyck path

nodes.summary: For every marked Dyck path $P$, the size of $P$ equals $N(P) + 2N^*(P)$, where $N(P)$ and $N^*(P)$ are the numbers of unmarked and marked vertical steps of $P$.
nodes.title: Size of a marked Dyck path in vertical steps

nodes.summary: A step of a multi-marked Dyck path is one of the horizontal step $E = (1, 0)$, the plain vertical step $N = (0, 1)$, or, for an integer $t \ge 2$, the marked vertical step $N^*_t = (0, 1)$ of index $t$. There are no marked steps of index less than $2$.
nodes.title: Steps of a multi-marked Dyck path

nodes.summary: For a finite sequence $P$ of multi-marked steps (horizontal steps $E$, plain vertical steps $N$ and marked vertical steps $N^*_t$ with index $t \ge 2$), $E(P)$ is the number of horizontal steps $E$ in $P$.
nodes.title: Number of horizontal steps in a multi-marked step sequence

nodes.summary: For a finite sequence $P$ of multi-marked steps (horizontal steps $E$, plain vertical steps $N$ and marked vertical steps $N^*_t$ with index $t \ge 2$), $N(P)$ is the number of plain (unmarked) vertical steps $N$ in $P$.
nodes.title: Number of plain vertical steps

nodes.summary: For a finite sequence $P$ of multi-marked steps (horizontal steps $E$, plain vertical steps $N$ and marked vertical steps $N^*_t$ with index $t \ge 2$), this is the number of vertical steps in $P$, plain steps $N$ and marked steps $N^*_t$ counted together.
nodes.title: Number of vertical steps

nodes.summary: For a finite sequence $P$ of multi-marked steps (horizontal steps $E$, plain vertical steps $N$ and marked vertical steps $N^*_t$ with index $t \ge 2$), this is the total number of steps in $P$, that is, the length of $P$.
nodes.title: Number of steps

nodes.summary: For a finite sequence $s$ of steps of a multi-marked Dyck path, the index sum of $s$ is the sum of the indices $t$ over all occurrences of marked steps $N^*_t$ in $s$, each occurrence counted separately; the steps $E$ and $N$ contribute nothing.
nodes.title: Index sum of a multi-marked step sequence

nodes.summary: For a finite sequence $s$ of steps of a multi-marked Dyck path, the shifted index sum of $s$ is the sum of $t - 1$ over all occurrences of marked steps $N^*_t$ in $s$, each occurrence counted separately; the steps $E$ and $N$ contribute nothing.
nodes.title: Shifted index sum of a multi-marked step sequence

nodes.summary: For a finite sequence $P$ of multi-marked steps (horizontal steps $E$, plain vertical steps $N$ and marked vertical steps $N^*_s$ with index $s \ge 2$) and a natural number $t$, $N^*_t(P)$ is the number of marked steps in $P$ whose index is exactly $t$.
nodes.title: Number of marked steps of a given index

nodes.summary: The size of a finite sequence $s$ of steps of a multi-marked Dyck path is $E(s) + \sum (t - 1)$, where $E(s)$ is the number of horizontal steps $E$ in $s$ and the sum runs over all occurrences of marked steps $N^*_t$ in $s$.
nodes.title: Size of a multi-marked step sequence

nodes.summary: A multi-marked Dyck path is a finite sequence $P$ of steps, each a horizontal step $E = (1,0)$, a plain vertical step $N = (0,1)$ or a marked vertical step $N^*_t = (0,1)$ carrying an index $t \ge 2$, such that every prefix of $P$, including the empty prefix and $P$ itself, has at most as many vertical steps (plain and marked) as horizontal steps, and $P$ has exactly as many vertical steps as horizontal steps.
nodes.title: Multi-marked Dyck path

nodes.summary: For every multi-marked Dyck path $P$, the number $E(P)$ of horizontal steps of $P$ equals the number of vertical steps of $P$, plain steps $N$ and marked steps $N^*_t$ counted together.
nodes.title: Equal horizontal and vertical step counts

nodes.summary: For every finite sequence $s$ of steps of a multi-marked Dyck path, the number of vertical steps of $s$ plus the shifted index sum of $s$ equals the number of plain vertical steps $N$ of $s$ plus the index sum of $s$.
nodes.title: Vertical count plus shifted index sum

nodes.summary: For every multi-marked Dyck path $P$, the size $E(P) + \sum (t - 1)$ of $P$ equals $N(P) + \sum t$, where $E(P)$ is the number of horizontal steps $E$ of $P$, $N(P)$ is the number of plain vertical steps $N$ of $P$, and both sums run over all occurrences of marked steps $N^*_t$ in $P$.
nodes.title: Two expressions for the size of a multi-marked Dyck path

nodes.summary: A step of a multi-marked Dyck path is vertical when it is the plain step $N$ or a marked step $N^*_t$; the horizontal step $E$ is not vertical. This test delimits the final run of vertical steps of a step sequence.
nodes.title: Vertical steps of a multi-marked Dyck path

nodes.summary: The final run of vertical steps of a finite sequence $s$ of steps of a multi-marked Dyck path is the longest suffix of $s$ consisting of vertical steps ($N$ or $N^*_t$): the part of $s$ after its last horizontal step $E$, or all of $s$ if $s$ has no step $E$.
nodes.title: Final run of vertical steps

nodes.summary: A multi-marked Dyck path $P$ has a marked tail when its final run of vertical steps (the steps after its last horizontal step $E$, or all of $P$ if $P$ has no step $E$) contains a marked vertical step $N^*_t$ for some index $t \ge 2$.
nodes.title: Marked tail

nodes.summary: A multi-marked Dyck path $P$ has an unmarked tail when it does not have a marked tail, that is, when its final run of vertical steps (the steps after its last horizontal step $E$, or all of $P$ if $P$ has no step $E$) contains no marked vertical step.
nodes.title: Unmarked tail

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, $\tilde P_n$ is the set of multi-marked Dyck paths $P$ of size $n$. Here the size of $P$ is $E(P) + \sum (t - 1)$, where $E(P)$ is the number of horizontal steps of $P$ and the sum runs over the marked steps $N^*_t$ of $P$, each occurrence counted separately.
nodes.title: Multi-marked Dyck paths of a given size

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, $\tilde R_n$ is the set of multi-marked Dyck paths of size $n$ with an unmarked tail, that is, whose final run of vertical steps contains no marked step.
nodes.title: Multi-marked Dyck paths with an unmarked tail
Peak descents of Dyck paths

nodes.summary: Let $l$ be a finite sequence of up steps $U$ and down steps $D$. A peak of $l$ is a position where a step $U$ is immediately followed by a step $D$. The peak descents of $l$ form the list that has, for each peak from left to right, the length $j$ of the maximal run of consecutive steps $D$ that starts at the $D$ of that peak, so that the peak and its descent form the primitive block $U D^j$.
nodes.title: Peak descents

nodes.summary: The Dyck path $UUUUDDDUDDUUDUUDDD$, which factors as $U\,U\,U\,(UD^3)(UD^2)\,U\,(UD)\,U\,(UD^3)$, has four peaks $UD$, and the lengths of the maximal runs of $D$ steps starting at the $D$ of each peak are, from left to right, $3, 2, 1, 3$.
nodes.title: Peak descents of a sample Dyck path

The empty composition gives $a(0, k) = 1$, and $k = 0$ gives Arndt compositions.

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, $c^{2k}_o(n)$ is the number of compositions of $n$, with any number of parts, in which every part is odd or at most $2k$. For $k = 0$ these are De Morgan's compositions of $n$ into odd parts.

nodes.summary: For a natural number $N$ and a property $P$ of compositions of $N$, the signed count of the compositions of $N$ satisfying $P$ is the number of them with an odd number of parts minus the number with an even number of parts. Equivalently, it is the sum of $(-1)^{\ell(c) + 1}$ over all compositions $c$ of $N$ satisfying $P$, where $\ell(c)$ is the number of parts of $c$.
nodes.title: Signed count of compositions

nodes.summary: The only composition of $0$ is the empty one, which has no parts and so is even. Hence the signed count of all compositions of $0$, the number of odd compositions minus the number of even ones, is $-1$.

nodes.summary: Let $k$ be a natural number. A finite sequence $(a_0, \dots, a_{\ell - 1})$ of natural numbers satisfies the placement condition for $k$ when every entry $a_i < k$ has a preceding entry and a following entry, the preceding entry satisfies $a_{i-1} \ge k$, and the following entry $a_{i+1}$ is either the last entry (that is, $i + 2 = \ell$) or satisfies $a_{i+1} > k$.
nodes.title: Huang's placement condition for small parts

nodes.summary: If every entry of a finite sequence of natural numbers is at least $k$, then the sequence satisfies Huang's placement condition for $k$, vacuously.

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, let $E(n)$ and $O(n)$ be the numbers of partitions of $n$ into distinct parts with an even and an odd number of parts, respectively. If $2n = j(3j + 1)$ or $2n = j(3j - 1)$ for some integer $j \ge 0$, then $E(n) - O(n) = (-1)^j$; otherwise $E(n) - O(n) = 0$.

For a natural number $r$, the $r$-fold binomial transform of $a$ is obtained by applying the binomial transform $r$ times in succession; the $0$-fold transform of $a$ is $a$ itself.

In both cases the equality is one of integer sequences.

Hypersequences

nodes.summary: Let $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a sequence in an additive commutative monoid. Its hypersequence of generation $r$, written $a^{(r)}_n$, is defined by recursion on $r$: $a^{(0)}_n = a_n$ and $a^{(r+1)}_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a^{(r)}_k$ for all natural numbers $r$ and $n$. Thus each generation is the sequence of partial sums of the previous one.

nodes.summary: The INVERT transform of an integer sequence $a = (a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ is the integer sequence $b = (b_n)_{n \ge 0}$ in which $b_n$ is the coefficient of $x^{n+1}$ in the inverse of $1 - \sum_{m \ge 0} a_m x^{m+1}$ in $\mathbb{Z}[[x]]$ (the inverse exists because the constant coefficient is $1$). In the one-based indexing of the source, $a_n$ and $b_n$ are the terms of index $n + 1$.

Then $(1 - A(x))(1 + B(x)) = 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}[[x]]$, that is, $1 + B(x)$ is the inverse of $1 - A(x)$.

nodes.summary: Parking functions and their variants (partial, weakly increasing, k-Naples, metered) and statistics on them: lucky cars, descents, displacement, and lucky statistics of Stirling permutations read as parking preferences.
nodes.title: Parking functions

nodes.summary: Let $s, t \in \mathbb{N}$ and number the $t$ spots $0, \dots, t-1$. A map $f : \{0, \dots, s-1\} \to \{0, \dots, t-1\}$, giving the preferred spot of each of $s$ cars, is a partial parking function if for every spot $k \in \{0, \dots, t-1\}$, at most $t - k$ cars $i$ satisfy $f(i) \ge k$.
nodes.title: Partial parking function

nodes.summary: Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and number the $n$ spots $0, \dots, n-1$. A map $f : \{0, \dots, n-1\} \to \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, giving the preferred spot of each of $n$ cars, is a parking function if it is a partial parking function with $n$ cars and $n$ spots, that is, if for every spot $k$, at most $n - k$ cars $i$ satisfy $f(i) \ge k$.
nodes.title: Parking function

nodes.summary: Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, number the $n$ spots $0, \dots, n-1$, and let $f : \{0, \dots, n-1\} \to \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ give the preferred spot of each of $n$ cars. Then $f$ is a parking function if and only if, for every spot $k \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, at least $k + 1$ cars $i$ satisfy $f(i) \le k$.
nodes.title: Lower-tail characterization of parking functions

nodes.summary: Let $s$ and $t$ be natural numbers with $0 < s \le t$. A partial parking function with $s$ cars and $t$ spots is a map $f : \{0, \dots, s - 1\} \to \{0, \dots, t - 1\}$ such that for every spot $k \in \{0, \dots, t - 1\}$ at most $t - k$ cars $i$ have $f(i) \ge k$. The number of partial parking functions with $s$ cars and $t$ spots is $(t + 1 - s)(t + 1)^{s - 1}$.

nodes.summary: Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers. nodes.summary: When the spots in a finite list $O$ of integers are occupied, a car preferring $a \in \mathbb{Z}$ parks in $a$ if $a$ is free; otherwise in the first free spot among $a - 1, \dots, a - k$, checked in decreasing order with no lower bound; otherwise in the first free spot among $a + 1, \dots, a + |O| + 1$, checked in increasing order (one of them is free, so this is the first free spot after $a$).

nodes.summary: For every integer $n \ge 4$, the set $\{1, n - 1, 2n - 2\}$ is an $n$-admissible lucky set if and only if $n$ is even.
nodes.title: When $\{1, n - 1, 2n - 2\}$ is an admissible lucky set

nodes.summary: Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a Stirling permutation of order $n$ and let $\sigma$ be a permutation of $\{1, \dots, 2n\}$. Read words of length $2n$ as parking functions, and let $d(v)$ denote the total displacement of a word $v$, the sum of the displacements of its cars. Then the rearranged word $w \circ \sigma = w_{\sigma(1)} \cdots w_{\sigma(2n)}$ satisfies $d(w \circ \sigma) = d(w)$.
nodes.title: Total displacement of a Stirling permutation is invariant under rearrangement

nodes.summary: Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a Stirling permutation of order $n$, read as a parking function of length $2n$. Then the total displacement of $w$, the sum $d(1) + \dots + d(2n)$ of the displacements of its cars, is $n^2$.
nodes.title: Total displacement of a Stirling permutation

nodes.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $w$ be a Stirling permutation of order $n$, read as a parking function of length $2n$. The number of cars $i \in \{1, \dots, 2n\}$ with displacement $d(i) = 0$ is at least $1$ and at most $n$.
nodes.title: Number of cars with zero displacement

nodes.summary: Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a Stirling permutation of order $n$ that is extremely lucky, that is, its set $\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$ of lucky cars has exactly $n$ elements, and let $1 \le i \le n$. If car $j$ is unlucky and exactly $i - 1$ of the cars $1, \dots, j - 1$ are unlucky, then car $j$ prefers spot $w_j = n - i + 1$ and has displacement $d(j) = 2i - 1$.
nodes.title: Unlucky cars of an extremely lucky Stirling permutation

nodes.summary: Let $w$ and $w'$ be Stirling permutations of order $n$, and suppose that $w$ is extremely lucky, that is, its set $\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$ of lucky cars has exactly $n$ elements. If every car has the same displacement in $w'$ as in $w$ (that is, $\mathrm{dis}(w') = \mathrm{dis}(w)$), then $w' = w$.
nodes.title: Extremely lucky Stirling permutations are determined by their displacements

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$, the number of Stirling permutations $w$ of order $n$ in which exactly $n$ cars have nonzero displacement (equivalently, whose displacement composition $\mathrm{dis}(w)$ has exactly $n$ nonzero parts) is the Catalan number $C_n$.

nodes.summary: Let $t, n \in \mathbb{N}$, number the $n$ spots $0, \dots, n-1$, and let $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_{m-1}$ be a list of preferences in $\mathbb{N}$. Cars arrive in order, and car $i$ parks in the least spot $s$ with $a_i \le s < n$ that is not taken by one of the previous $t$ cars (cars $\max(0, i - t), \dots, i - 1$) that parked; if there is no such spot, car $i$ fails. nodes.summary: In the $1$-metered parking scheme on two spots $\{0, 1\}$, if three cars arrive all preferring spot $0$, then they park in spots $0$, $1$ and $0$, in that order.

nodes.summary: In the $1$-metered parking scheme on two spots $\{0, 1\}$, if three cars arrive with preferences $0$, $0$, $1$, then the first two cars park in spots $0$ and $1$ and the third car fails to park.

nodes.summary: Let $t$, $m$, $n$ be natural numbers, let $f : \{0, \dots, m - 1\} \to \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ be a preference function and let $i < m$ be a car. Under the $t$-metered parking scheme on $n$ spots, if car $i$ parks in spot $s$ then $s \le f(i) + t$, that is, its displacement is at most $t$; and if car $i$ fails to park then $f(i) + t \ge n$.

nodes.summary: For every natural number $t \ge 1$ and every natural number $n$, the number of $t$-metered $(2, n)$-parking functions is $\mathrm{mpf}_{2,n}(t) = \max(n^2 - 1, 0)$, that is, $n^2 - 1$ for $n \ge 1$ and $0$ for $n = 0$.

nodes.summary: Let $0 < m \le n$ and let $\alpha = (a_1, \dots, a_m)$, with each $a_i \in \{1, \dots, n\}$, be any sequence of preferred spots of $m$ cars on $n$ spots. Under the $1$-metered parking scheme, car $i$ is lucky (it parks in its preferred spot $a_i$) if and only if position $i$ is the first position of one of the laces of the lace decomposition $\mathrm{lace}(\alpha)$.

nodes.summary: Let $0 < m \le n$ and $f : \{0, \dots, m-1\} \to \{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Then $f$ is a $1$-metered parking function if and only if, in the lace decomposition of $(f(0), \dots, f(m-1))$, the last spot $n - 1$ occurs in no lace other than as its first entry.

nodes.summary: Let $m \ge 1$ and $f : \{0, \dots, m-1\} \to \{0, 1\}$. Then $f$ is a $1$-metered parking function with $m$ cars and $2$ spots if and only if every lace of the lace decomposition of $(f(0), \dots, f(m-1))$ that contains the value $1$ has length $1$.

nodes.summary: For a partition $P$ of a finite set $s$, a commutative monoid $R$ and a function $f : \mathbb{N} \to R$, the block-size product of $f$ over $P$ is $\prod_{B \in P} f(|B|)$, the product over the blocks $B$ of $P$ of $f$ applied to the cardinality of $B$.
nodes.title: Product over block sizes

nodes.summary: If $P$ is a partition of a finite set $s$ and $B$ is a block of $P$, then $|B| \le |s|$.
nodes.title: Blocks are no larger than the ground set

nodes.summary: Every block $B$ of a partition of a finite set $s$ satisfies $|B| \ge 1$.
nodes.title: Blocks are nonempty

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a partition of a finite set $s$ that is not the coarsest partition $\top$ of $s$ (the one whose only block is $s$ when $s$ is nonempty). Then every block $B$ of $P$ satisfies $|B| < |s|$.
nodes.title: Blocks of a partition other than the coarsest are smaller than the ground set

nodes.summary: If $P$ is a partition of a nonempty finite set $s$, then $P$ is the coarsest partition $\top$ of $s$, whose only block is $s$, if and only if $P$ has exactly one block.
nodes.title: Recognizing the one-block partition

nodes.summary: A partition $P$ of a finite set $s$ has at least one block, that is, its number of blocks is positive, if and only if $s$ is nonempty.
nodes.title: A partition has a block exactly when its ground set is nonempty

nodes.summary: A partition $P$ of a finite set $s$ is the finest partition $\bot$ of $s$, whose blocks are the singletons $\{a\}$ for $a \in s$, if and only if the number of blocks of $P$ equals $|s|$.
nodes.title: Recognizing the partition into singletons by its number of blocks

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a partition of a finite set $s$, let $R$ and $S$ be commutative monoids, let $f : \mathbb{N} \to R$, and let $g : R \to S$ be a monoid homomorphism. Then $g\bigl(\prod_{B \in P} f(|B|)\bigr) = \prod_{B \in P} g(f(|B|))$, where both products run over the blocks $B$ of $P$.

nodes.summary: A set partition of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is a finite collection of nonempty, pairwise disjoint subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, called blocks, whose union is $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$.
nodes.title: Set partition

nodes.summary: A set partition $P$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ has a crossing if there are $a < b < c < d$ in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ such that $a$ and $c$ lie in the same block of $P$, $b$ and $d$ lie in the same block of $P$, and these two blocks are different.
nodes.title: Crossing in a set partition

nodes.summary: A set partition of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is noncrossing if it has no crossing.

nodes.summary: A noncrossing partition of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is a set partition of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ that is noncrossing.

nodes.summary: For a noncrossing partition $P$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and a point $a \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the block of $P$ at $a$ is the block of the underlying set partition that contains $a$.

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$, the discrete partition of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, whose blocks are the singletons, is noncrossing.

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$, the indiscrete partition of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the coarsest partition of this set, is noncrossing.
nodes.title: The indiscrete partition is noncrossing

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, the discrete noncrossing partition of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is the finest partition of this set, whose blocks are the singletons $\{a\}$ for $a \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$; it is noncrossing.
nodes.title: Discrete noncrossing partition

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, the indiscrete noncrossing partition of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is the coarsest partition of this set: its only block is the whole set when $n > 0$, and it has no blocks when $n = 0$. It is noncrossing.
nodes.title: The indiscrete noncrossing partition

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$ and every $a \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the block containing $a$ in the discrete noncrossing partition of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is the singleton $\{a\}$.
nodes.title: The block of a point in the discrete noncrossing partition

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$ and every $a \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the block containing $a$ in the indiscrete noncrossing partition of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is the whole set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$.
nodes.title: The block of a point in the indiscrete noncrossing partition

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$, the set of blocks of the discrete noncrossing partition of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is exactly the set of singletons $\{a\}$ with $a \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$.
nodes.title: The discrete noncrossing partition consists of the singletons

nodes.summary: For $n = 0$, the set of blocks of the indiscrete noncrossing partition of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the empty set, is empty.
nodes.title: The indiscrete partition of the empty set has no blocks

nodes.summary: For $n = 0$, the discrete noncrossing partition of the empty set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ has no blocks: its set of blocks is empty.
nodes.title: The discrete partition of the empty set has no blocks

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$ with $0 < n$, the set of blocks of the indiscrete noncrossing partition of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is $\{\{0, \dots, n-1\}\}$: its only block is the whole set.
nodes.title: The indiscrete partition of a nonempty set has a single block

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number. A noncrossing partition $P$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ equals the discrete noncrossing partition if and only if $P$, viewed as a set partition, is the finest partition of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$.
nodes.title: Characterization of the discrete noncrossing partition

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number. A noncrossing partition $P$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ equals the indiscrete noncrossing partition if and only if $P$, viewed as a set partition, is the coarsest partition of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$.
nodes.title: Characterization of the indiscrete noncrossing partition

nodes.summary: A cell of the $3 \times n$ rectangle is a pair $(r, c)$ of a row $r \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ and a column $c \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$.
nodes.title: Cells of the $3 \times n$ rectangle

nodes.summary: Two cells $x$ and $y$ of the $3 \times n$ rectangle are adjacent when they share an edge: they lie in the same row and their columns differ by $1$, or they lie in the same column and their rows differ by $1$.
nodes.title: Adjacent cells

nodes.summary: A set $d$ of cells of the $3 \times n$ rectangle is a square-or-domino tile when it consists of exactly one cell, or of exactly two cells that are adjacent.
nodes.title: Square and domino tiles

nodes.summary: A set $d$ of cells of the $3 \times n$ rectangle is a square-or-domino tile if and only if either $d = \{x\}$ for some cell $x$, or $d = \{x, y\}$ for some distinct adjacent cells $x$ and $y$.
nodes.title: Characterization of square and domino tiles

nodes.summary: A square-and-domino tiling of the $3 \times n$ rectangle is a finite family $T$ of sets of cells such that every member of $T$ is a square-or-domino tile (a single cell or two adjacent cells), any two distinct members of $T$ are disjoint, and every cell of the rectangle lies in some member of $T$.
nodes.title: Square-and-domino tilings

nodes.summary: A family $T$ of sets of cells of the $3 \times n$ rectangle, with columns numbered $0, \dots, n-1$, is vertical-fault-free when for every natural number $k$ with $k + 1 < n$ some member of $T$ contains two cells of the same row lying in columns $k$ and $k + 1$. For a square-and-domino tiling this says that every internal vertical boundary is crossed by a horizontal domino.

nodes.summary: For a natural number $d$, a lattice cell in dimension $d$ is a point of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, that is, a function assigning an integer to each of the $d$ coordinate axes.
nodes.title: Lattice cells

nodes.summary: Two lattice cells $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ are face adjacent when there is an axis $k$ such that $x_j = y_j$ for every axis $j \ne k$ and $|x_k - y_k| = 1$.
nodes.title: Face adjacency of lattice cells

nodes.summary: A finite set $S$ of lattice cells in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ is a polycube when it is nonempty and any two cells $x, y \in S$ are joined by a finite sequence of cells of $S$, starting at $x$ and ending at $y$, in which consecutive cells are face adjacent.
nodes.title: Polycube

nodes.summary: A finite set $S$ of lattice cells in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ is in canonical position when, for every axis $k$, every cell $x \in S$ has $x_k \ge 0$ and some cell $x \in S$ has $x_k = 0$; that is, the minimum of each coordinate over $S$ is $0$.
nodes.title: Canonical position of a cell set

nodes.summary: The proper dimension of a finite set $S$ of lattice cells in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ is the number of axes $k$ on which $S$ varies, that is, for which there are cells $x, y \in S$ with $x_k \ne y_k$.
nodes.title: Proper dimension

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $d$ and $n$, the fixed $n$-cell polycubes in dimension $d$ are represented by the finite sets $S$ of lattice cells in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ that are polycubes (nonempty and connected through face adjacency), have exactly $n$ cells, and are in canonical position (the minimum of each coordinate over $S$ is $0$).

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $d$ and $n$, $A_d(n)$ is the number of fixed $n$-cell polycubes in dimension $d$, that is, the number of $n$-cell polycubes in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ that are in canonical position.

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $i$, the fixed $n$-cell polycubes proper in dimension $i$ are the fixed $n$-cell polycubes in dimension $i$ whose proper dimension is $i$, that is, which vary along each of the $i$ axes.
nodes.title: Proper fixed polycubes

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $i$, $\mathrm{DX}(n,i)$ is the number of fixed $n$-cell polycubes proper in dimension $i$, that is, of fixed $n$-cell polycubes in dimension $i$ whose proper dimension is $i$.

Periodic tiling conjecture

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an abelian group and let $F, A \subseteq G$. Then $F$ tiles $G$ with tiling set $A$ if the map $A \times F \to G$, $(a, f) \mapsto a + f$, is a bijection; equivalently, every element of $G$ lies in $a + F$ for exactly one $a \in A$.
nodes.title: Tiling of an abelian group by translates

nodes.summary: A subset $A$ of an abelian group $G$ is periodic if there exist a subgroup $H$ of $G$ of finite index and a finite set $S \subseteq G$ such that $A = S + H$, that is, $A$ is the union of finitely many cosets of $H$.
nodes.title: Periodic tiling set

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an abelian group. A set $F \subseteq G$ forms an aperiodic tiling equation if $F$ tiles $G$ with some tiling set $A \subseteq G$, and no tiling set $A \subseteq G$ with which $F$ tiles $G$ is periodic.
nodes.title: Aperiodic tiling equation

nodes.summary: There exist a finite abelian group $G_0$ and a finite non-empty set $F \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^2 \times G_0$ that forms an aperiodic tiling equation in the group $\mathbb{Z}^2 \times G_0$.
nodes.title: Greenfeld–Tao counterexample to the periodic tiling conjecture

nodes.summary: There is a natural number $d_0$ such that for every natural number $d \ge d_0$ there exists a finite non-empty set $F \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^d$ that forms an aperiodic tiling equation in $\mathbb{Z}^d$.
nodes.title: Aperiodic tiling equations in high-dimensional integer lattices

nodes.summary: For $d \in \mathbb{N}$, a set $\sigma \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ continuously tiles $\mathbb{R}^d$ with tiling set $\Lambda \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ if for almost every $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ (with respect to Lebesgue measure) there is exactly one $v \in \Lambda$ with $x \in v + \sigma$.
nodes.title: Continuous tiling of Euclidean space

nodes.summary: For $d \in \mathbb{N}$, a set $\Lambda \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is periodic if there exist a lattice $L \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, that is, a discrete additive subgroup that spans $\mathbb{R}^d$ over $\mathbb{R}$, and a finite set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ such that $\Lambda = S + L$, so that $\Lambda$ is the union of finitely many cosets of $L$.
nodes.title: Periodic continuous tiling set

nodes.summary: For $d \in \mathbb{N}$, a set $\sigma \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ forms an aperiodic continuous tiling equation if $\sigma$ continuously tiles $\mathbb{R}^d$ with some tiling set $\Lambda \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, and no tiling set $\Lambda$ with which $\sigma$ continuously tiles $\mathbb{R}^d$ is periodic.
nodes.title: Aperiodic continuous tiling equation

nodes.summary: There is a natural number $d_0$ such that for every natural number $d \ge d_0$ there exists a bounded measurable set $\sigma \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ of positive Lebesgue measure that forms an aperiodic continuous tiling equation.
nodes.title: Aperiodic continuous tiling equations in high-dimensional Euclidean space
Self-avoiding walks on the honeycomb lattice

nodes.summary: A vertex of the honeycomb lattice is a triple $(x, y, s)$ with $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $s$ a boolean recording which of the two classes of the bipartition the vertex belongs to.
nodes.title: Vertices of the honeycomb lattice

nodes.summary: For a vertex $v = (x, y, s)$ and a direction label $d \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, the step from $v$ in direction $d$ is a vertex on the other side of the bipartition. If $s$ is true, it is $(x, y, \mathrm{false})$, $(x + 1, y, \mathrm{false})$ or $(x, y + 1, \mathrm{false})$ for $d = 0, 1, 2$ respectively. nodes.title: Steps are involutions

nodes.summary: For every vertex $v$ of the honeycomb lattice, the steps from $v$ in the directions $0$, $1$ and $2$ are three distinct vertices.
nodes.title: Distinct labels give distinct neighbors

nodes.summary: The origin is the vertex $(0, 0, \mathrm{false})$.
nodes.title: Origin of the honeycomb lattice

nodes.summary: For a finite word $d_1 d_2 \cdots d_k$ of direction labels in $\{0, 1, 2\}$, its endpoint is the vertex reached from the origin by taking the step in direction $d_1$, then the step in direction $d_2$, and so on through $d_k$. The endpoint of the empty word is the origin.
nodes.title: Endpoint of a direction word

nodes.summary: For a word $(d_1, \ldots, d_n)$ of direction labels in $\{0, 1, 2\}$ and an integer $0 \le i \le n$, the $i$-th vertex of the word is the endpoint of its prefix $(d_1, \ldots, d_i)$, the vertex reached from the origin after the first $i$ steps.
nodes.title: Vertices along a direction word

nodes.summary: For a word $(d_1, \ldots, d_n)$ of direction labels in $\{0, 1, 2\}$, the set of visited vertices is the finite set of its $i$-th vertices for $0 \le i \le n$; it contains the origin (for $i = 0$) and the endpoint of the word.

nodes.summary: A word $(d_1, \ldots, d_n)$ of direction labels in $\{0, 1, 2\}$ is self-avoiding when its set of visited vertices has exactly $n + 1$ elements, that is, when its $n + 1$ vertices, the $i$-th vertices for $0 \le i \le n$, are pairwise distinct.
nodes.title: Self-avoiding direction words

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, this is the number of self-avoiding walks with $n$ steps on the honeycomb lattice starting at the origin.
nodes.title: Number of self-avoiding walks on the honeycomb lattice

nodes.summary: There are exactly $12$ self-avoiding walks with $3$ steps on the honeycomb lattice starting at a fixed vertex.
nodes.title: Three-step self-avoiding walks on the honeycomb lattice

nodes.summary: There are exactly $90$ self-avoiding walks with $6$ steps on the honeycomb lattice starting at a fixed vertex.
nodes.title: Six-step self-avoiding walks on the honeycomb lattice

nodes.summary: Let $c_n$ be the number of $n$-step self-avoiding walks on the honeycomb lattice starting at the origin. Then $c_n^{1/n} \to \sqrt{2 + \sqrt{2}}$ as $n \to \infty$.
nodes.title: The connective constant of the honeycomb lattice
Tilings of grids, cylinders and tori up to symmetry

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, the reflection $f$ acts on the cells $(x, y) \in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$ of the $n \times m$ grid by $(x, y) \mapsto (-1 - x, y)$, that is, $(x, y) \mapsto (n - 1 - x, y)$ with the first coordinate taken modulo $n$.

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, the half-turn $r^2$ acts on the cells $(x, y) \in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$ of the $n \times m$ grid by $(x, y) \mapsto (-1 - x, -1 - y)$, that is, $(x, y) \mapsto (n - 1 - x, m - 1 - y)$ with the coordinates taken modulo $n$ and $m$.
nodes.title: Cell map of the half-turn r²

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, the reflection $r^2 f$ acts on the cells $(x, y) \in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$ of the $n \times m$ grid by $(x, y) \mapsto (x, -1 - y)$, that is, $(x, y) \mapsto (x, m - 1 - y)$ with the second coordinate taken modulo $m$.
nodes.title: Cell map of the reflection r²f

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, the quarter-turn $r$ acts on the cells $(x, y) \in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ of the $n \times n$ grid by $(x, y) \mapsto (-1 - y, x)$, that is, $(x, y) \mapsto (n - 1 - y, x)$ modulo $n$.
nodes.title: Cell map of the quarter-turn r

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, the three-quarter turn $r^3$ acts on the cells $(x, y) \in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ of the $n \times n$ grid by $(x, y) \mapsto (y, -1 - x)$, that is, $(x, y) \mapsto (y, n - 1 - x)$ modulo $n$.

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, the diagonal reflection $rf$ acts on the cells $(x, y) \in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ of the $n \times n$ grid by $(x, y) \mapsto (y, x)$.

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite set, $\varphi$ a permutation of $\alpha$ and $c \in \alpha$. The orbit of $c$ under $\varphi$ is the finite set $\{\varphi^k(c) : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$ of images of $c$ under the nonnegative powers of $\varphi$. Since $\alpha$ is finite, this is the orbit of $c$ under the cyclic group generated by $\varphi$.

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite set and $\varphi$ a permutation of $\alpha$. For $c \in \alpha$ let $O(c) = \{\varphi^k(c) : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$ be the orbit of $c$ under $\varphi$. The set of orbits of $\varphi$ is the set $\{O(c) : c \in \alpha\}$ of subsets of $\alpha$, in which each orbit occurs once.

nodes.summary: For a natural number $m$ and a finite set $F$ of cells $(i, j)$ (column $i$, row $j$), let $f_j$ be the number of cells of $F$ in row $j$. The $m$-weight of $F$ is $\mathrm{wt}_m(F) = \prod_j 1\downarrow_{f_j, m}$, the product over the rows $j$ that contain a cell of $F$, where $x\downarrow_{k, m} = \prod_{i < k} (x - m i)$ is the $m$-falling factorial.

nodes.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the Robbins number $A_n$ is the natural number obtained by dividing $\prod_{k=0}^{n-1} (3k+1)!$ by $\prod_{k=0}^{n-1} (n+k)!$, where the division is division of natural numbers rounded down.

nodes.summary: Let $n \ge 2$. There are nonzero real numbers $c, d$ and real numbers $r_0 \le \dots \le r_{n-1}$ and $s_0 \le \dots \le s_{n-2}$ such that the type-A minuscule polynomials factor over $\mathbb{R}$ as $N_{n+1}(x) = c \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} (x - r_i)$ and $N_n(x) = d \prod_{j=0}^{n-2} (x - s_j)$, and $r_j \le s_j \le r_{j+1}$ for every $j$ with $0 \le j \le n - 2$.

reading_title.source: $(3+1)$-free posets

nodes.summary: A partially ordered set $P$ is $(3+1)$-free when there are no elements $a, b, c, d \in P$ with $a < b < c$ such that $d$ is incomparable to each of $a$, $b$ and $c$ (neither $d \le x$ nor $x \le d$ for $x = a, b, c$).
nodes.title: $(3+1)$-free posets

nodes.summary: The incomparability graph $\operatorname{inc}(P)$ of a partially ordered set $P$ is the simple graph on $P$ in which two distinct elements $x$ and $y$ are adjacent when they are incomparable, that is, neither $x \le y$ nor $y \le x$.
nodes.title: Incomparability graph of a poset

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$ with $n = |V|$ elements, $X_G$ is the polynomial with integer coefficients in the variables $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ given by $X_G = \sum_{\kappa} \prod_{v \in V} x_{\kappa(v)}$, where $\kappa$ ranges over the proper colourings $\kappa : V \to \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ of $G$, that is, the maps with $\kappa(u) \ne \kappa(v)$ whenever $u$ and $v$ are adjacent.

nodes.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a family $F$ of subsets of $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, the number of comparable pairs of $F$ is the number of ordered pairs $(A, B)$ of members of $F$ with $A \subsetneq B$. Sunflower lemma

nodes.summary: Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers. A family $F$ of subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ contains a $k$-sunflower if some subfamily $T \subseteq F$ with exactly $k$ members satisfies $A \cap B = C \cap D$ for all $A, B, C, D \in T$ with $A \ne B$ and $C \ne D$, that is, all pairwise intersections of distinct members of $T$ are equal.

nodes.summary: Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers. A family $F$ of subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is $k$-sunflower-free if it does not contain a $k$-sunflower.
nodes.title: Sunflower-free families

reading_title.source: Erdős–Szemerédi sunflower conjecture for $k \ge 4$

nodes.summary: The proposition asserts that for every natural number $k \ge 4$ there is a real number $c$ with $0 < c < 2$ such that, for all sufficiently large $n$, every $k$-sunflower-free family of subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ has at most $c^n$ members.
nodes.title: Erdős–Szemerédi sunflower conjecture for $k \ge 4$

reading_title.source: The Erdős–Szemerédi sunflower bound for $k \ge 4$

nodes.summary: For every natural number $k \ge 4$ there is a real number $c$ with $0 < c < 2$ such that, for all sufficiently large $n$, every family of subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ that contains no $k$-sunflower has at most $c^n$ members. Here a $k$-sunflower in a family is a choice of $k$ distinct members whose pairwise intersections are all equal.
nodes.title: The Erdős–Szemerédi sunflower bound for $k \ge 4$

nodes.summary: Let $r \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $S$ be a family of subsets of a type $X$. Then $S$ is an $r$-sunflower if $S$ has exactly $r$ members (its cardinality is taken to be $0$ when $S$ is infinite) and any two distinct members $A \ne B$ of $S$ satisfy $A \cap B = \bigcap S$, the intersection of all members of $S$.

Union-closed families

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$ and a subset $A$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$, the binary code of $A$ is the natural number $b(A) = \sum_{i \in A} 2^i$.
nodes.title: Binary code of a subset

nodes.summary: For subsets $A$ and $B$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, $A$ precedes $B$ in the set order, written $A < B$, if $|A| > |B|$, or $|A| = |B|$ and $b(A) < b(B)$, where $b(A) = \sum_{i \in A} 2^i$ is the binary code of $A$.
nodes.title: Set order

nodes.summary: For a subset $A$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the sort key of $A$ is the natural number $(n - |A|) \cdot 2^n + b(A)$, where $b(A) = \sum_{i \in A} 2^i$ is the binary code of $A$.
nodes.title: Sort key of a subset

nodes.summary: For a family $U$ of subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the string $s(U)$ is the list of the sort keys of the nonempty members of $U$, in increasing order.
nodes.title: String of a family

nodes.summary: For a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and a family $U$ of subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the permuted image $\sigma(U)$ is the family $\{\sigma(A) : A \in U\}$, where $\sigma(A) = \{\sigma(a) : a \in A\}$.
nodes.title: Permuted image of a family

nodes.summary: A family $U$ of subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is union-closed if $A \cup B \in U$ for all $A, B \in U$.
nodes.title: Union-closed family

nodes.summary: A family $U$ of subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is canonical, the canonical representative of its isomorphism class, if for every permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ the string $s(U)$ is lexicographically at most the string $s(\sigma(U))$ of the permuted family $\sigma(U)$.
nodes.title: Canonical family

nodes.summary: For all subsets $A$ and $B$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, $A < B$ in the set order if and only if the sort key of $A$ is less than the sort key of $B$.
nodes.title: The sort key encodes the set order

nodes.summary: Let $A_1, \dots, A_k$ be nonempty subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with $A_i < A_j$ in the set order whenever $i < j$, and suppose the family $U = \{\emptyset, A_1, \dots, A_k\}$ is canonical. Then for every $m \le k$, including $m = 0$, the family $\{\emptyset, A_1, \dots, A_m\}$ is canonical.

nodes.summary: A family $F$ of finite sets is union-free over its subfamilies if no member $A \in F$ is the union of a nonempty subfamily of $F$ that does not contain $A$.
nodes.title: Families in which no member is a union of other members

nodes.summary: A family $F$ of subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is union-free if there are no pairwise distinct $A, B, C \in F$ with $A \cup B = C$.

nodes.summary: The assertion that, for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ and all sufficiently large $n$, the maximum size of a union-free family of subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is at most $(1 + \varepsilon)\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}$; that is, it is at most $(1 + o(1))\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}$.

Then $\mathrm{ex}_3(n) / n^2 \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, that is, $\mathrm{ex}_3(n) = o(n^2)$.

reading_title.source: Generalized triangle $\mathcal{T}_r$

nodes.summary: Let $r, n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $G$ be a family of subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, typically an $r$-uniform hypergraph. Then $G$ contains a generalized triangle $\mathcal{T}_r$ (the book $B_{r,2}$) when there are edges $D_1, D_2, D_3 \in G$, not necessarily distinct, with $|D_1 \cap D_2| + 1 = r$, $D_1 \triangle D_2 \subseteq D_3$ and $D_3 \cap D_1 \cap D_2 = \emptyset$.
nodes.title: Generalized triangle $\mathcal{T}_r$

nodes.summary: For $r, n \in \mathbb{N}$, the Turán number $\mathrm{ex}(n, \mathcal{T}_r)$ is the largest number of edges of an $r$-uniform hypergraph on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ that contains no generalized triangle $\mathcal{T}_r$.
nodes.title: Turán number of the generalized triangle

reading_title.source: Steiner system $S(t, r, m)$

nodes.summary: Let $t, r, m \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $D$ be a family of subsets of $\{0, \dots, m-1\}$. Then $D$ is a Steiner system $S(t, r, m)$ when every block of $D$ has exactly $r$ elements and every $t$-element subset of $\{0, \dots, m-1\}$ is contained in exactly one block of $D$.
nodes.title: Steiner system $S(t, r, m)$

nodes.summary: Let $D$ be a family of subsets of $\{0, \dots, m-1\}$, let $r \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $\varphi : \{0, \dots, n-1\} \to \{0, \dots, m-1\}$. The $r$-uniform blow-up of $D$ along $\varphi$ is the family of $r$-element subsets $e \subseteq \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ such that $\varphi$ is injective on $e$ and the image $\varphi(e)$ is a block of $D$.
nodes.title: Blow-up of a hypergraph along a map

nodes.summary: Let $D$ be a family of subsets of $\{0, \dots, m-1\}$ and let $r, n \in \mathbb{N}$. The largest blow-up size of $D$ is the maximum, over all maps $\varphi : \{0, \dots, n-1\} \to \{0, \dots, m-1\}$, of the number of edges of the $r$-uniform blow-up of $D$ along $\varphi$; it is $0$ when there is no such map.
nodes.title: Largest blow-up of a hypergraph

nodes.summary: Let $n$, $s$, $r$ be natural numbers. A family $H$ of subsets of $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ is a Turán $(n, s, r)$-system when $0 < r < s \le n$, $H$ is $r$-uniform (every member of $H$ has exactly $r$ elements), and every $s$-element subset of $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ contains some member of $H$.

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$, $s$, $r$ with $0 < r < s \le n$, the set of realized sizes for $n$, $s$, $r$ is nonempty: some natural number $k$ is the number of members of a Turán system with parameters $n$, $s$, $r$.

nodes.summary: Let $n$, $s$, $r$ be natural numbers with $0 < r < s \le n$ and let $T(n, s, r)$ denote the Turán number. Then some Turán system with parameters $n$, $s$, $r$ has exactly $T(n, s, r)$ members.

nodes.summary: Let $n$, $s$, $r$ be natural numbers and let $T(n, s, r)$ denote the Turán number. If $H$ is a Turán system with parameters $n$, $s$, $r$, then $T(n, s, r) \le |H|$.
