reading_title.source: $(0,2)$-graphs

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, a simple graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is a $(0,2)$-graph when every two distinct vertices of $G$ have either exactly zero or exactly two common neighbors.
nodes.title: $(0,2)$-graphs

reading_title.source: The three-chromatic $(0,2)$-graph conjecture

nodes.summary: It asserts that there are a natural number $n$ and a simple graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which every two distinct vertices have either zero or two common neighbors, such that the chromatic number of $G$ is $3$.
nodes.title: The three-chromatic $(0,2)$-graph conjecture

reading_title.source: No finite $(0,2)$-graph has chromatic number three

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$ and every simple graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which every two distinct vertices have either zero or two common neighbors, the chromatic number of $G$ is not $3$. In particular, the three-chromatic $(0,2)$-graph conjecture is false.
nodes.title: No finite $(0,2)$-graph has chromatic number three
Chromatic number of wheel-free graphs

nodes.summary: A simple graph $G$ has an induced wheel if there are a natural number $\ell \ge 4$, distinct vertices $r_0, \dots, r_{\ell-1}$ of $G$ (the rim) and a vertex $h$ of $G$ (the hub) with $h \ne r_i$ for every $i$, such that for all $i, j < \ell$ the vertices $r_i$ and $r_j$ are adjacent in $G$ exactly when $i - j \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{\ell}$, and $h$ is adjacent to $r_i$, $r_j$ and $r_k$ for some pairwise distinct…
nodes.title: Induced wheels

nodes.summary: A simple graph $G$ is wheel-free if it has no induced wheel, that is, no induced cycle of length at least four together with a vertex outside the cycle that is adjacent to at least three vertices of the cycle.
nodes.title: Wheel-free graphs

nodes.summary: This is the proposition that for every positive integer $k$ there are a natural number $n$ and a simple graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ such that $G$ contains no triangle, $G$ is wheel-free (it has no induced wheel) and the chromatic number of $G$ is at least $k$.
nodes.title: Triangle-free wheel-free graphs of large chromatic number (proposition)

nodes.summary: For every positive integer $k$ there are a natural number $n$ and a simple graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ such that $G$ contains no triangle, $G$ is wheel-free (it has no induced wheel) and the chromatic number of $G$ is at least $k$.
nodes.title: Davies's theorem on triangle-free wheel-free graphs
Color-critical graphs

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a graph and $S$ a set of unordered pairs of its vertices. Then $S$ is critical for $G$ if deleting the edges of $G$ that lie in $S$ strictly lowers the chromatic number, as an element of $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$.
nodes.title: Critical edge sets

nodes.summary: For a graph $G$ and an unordered pair $e$ of vertices, $e$ is a critical edge of $G$ if removing $e$ from the edge set of $G$ strictly lowers the chromatic number of $G$, taken in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$.
nodes.title: Critical edge

nodes.summary: Let $G'$ be a subgraph of a graph $G$. A set $S$ of vertices is critical for $G'$ if deleting the vertices in $S$ from $G'$ strictly lowers the chromatic number of $G'$, viewed as a graph on its own vertex set, with chromatic numbers taken in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$.
nodes.title: Critical vertex sets of a subgraph

nodes.summary: Let $G'$ be a subgraph of a graph $G$. A vertex $v$ is critical for $G'$ if $\{v\}$ is a critical vertex set of $G'$, that is, deleting $v$ from $G'$ strictly lowers the chromatic number of $G'$, viewed as a graph on its own vertex set, with chromatic numbers taken in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$.
nodes.title: Critical vertices of a subgraph

nodes.summary: Let $k$ be a natural number. A graph $G$ is $k$-critical (or vertex-critical) if its chromatic number equals $k$ and every vertex $v$ of $G$ is critical, that is, deleting $v$ from $G$ strictly lowers the chromatic number.
nodes.title: Vertex-critical graphs

nodes.summary: A graph $G$ is cocolorable with $n$ colors if there is a map from its vertices to the colors $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ such that each color class induces either an independent set or a complete graph in $G$.
nodes.title: Cocolorable graphs

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$, if a graph $G$ has a proper coloring with $n$ colors, then $G$ is cocolorable with $n$ colors.
nodes.title: Colorable graphs are cocolorable

nodes.summary: Every graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$ is cocolorable with $|V|$ colors.
nodes.title: Finite graphs are cocolorable

nodes.summary: The cochromatic number of a graph $G$, an element of $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, is the least natural number $n$ such that $G$ is cocolorable with $n$ colors, that is, the least number of colors in a coloring of the vertices of $G$ in which each color class induces either an independent set or a complete graph. It is $\infty$ exactly when $G$ is not cocolorable with any finite number of colors.
nodes.title: Cochromatic number

nodes.summary: If a graph $G$ is cocolorable with $n$ colors for some natural number $n$, then the cochromatic number of $G$ equals the least natural number $m$ such that $G$ is cocolorable with $m$ colors.
nodes.title: Cochromatic number as a minimum

nodes.summary: For every graph $G$ on a finite vertex set, the cochromatic number of $G$, converted from $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ to $\mathbb{N}$ by sending $\infty$ to $0$, equals the least natural number $m$ such that $G$ is cocolorable with $m$ colors.
nodes.title: Cochromatic number of a finite graph

nodes.summary: The chromatic cardinal is the minimal number of colors need to color it. In contrast to `chromaticNumber`, which assigns `⊤ : ℕ∞` to all non-finitely colorable graphs, this definition returns a `Cardinal` and can therefore distinguish between different infinite chromatic numbers.
nodes.title: Chromatic cardinal of a graph

nodes.summary: For a graph $G$ on a finite vertex set and a natural number $k$, this is the maximum number of vertices in a union of $k$ (possibly empty, possibly overlapping) independent sets of $G$.
nodes.title: Largest union of independent sets

nodes.summary: A graph $G$ on a finite vertex set is CDS-colorable if it has a proper coloring $C$ with colors in $\mathbb{N}$ such that for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the number of vertices whose color under $C$ is less than $k$ equals the maximum size of a union of $k$ independent sets of $G$.
nodes.title: CDS-colorable graphs

nodes.summary: Let $f$ be a graph homomorphism from $H$ to $G$ and let $c$ be a labeling of the edges of $G$ by elements of a type $K$. Then $f$ is rainbow for $c$ if distinct edges of $H$ are mapped to edges of $G$ with distinct labels, that is, the labeling $e \mapsto c(f(e))$ of the edges of $H$ is injective.
nodes.title: Rainbow homomorphisms

nodes.summary: For a graph $H$ on a finite vertex type and a natural number $n$, the anti-Ramsey number $\mathrm{AR}(n, H)$ is the largest $k$ for which there is a coloring of the edges of the complete graph $K_n$ on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with colors $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$, every color used, that contains no rainbow copy of $H$. Here a copy of $H$ is an injective homomorphism from $H$ to $K_n$, and it is rainbow when distinct edges of…
nodes.title: Anti-Ramsey number
Cycle lengths in graphs of large chromatic number

nodes.summary: The statement that both of the following hold: (i) for every natural number $k$ there is a simple graph $G$ with chromatic number $4$ in which any two distinct cycle lengths of $G$ differ by at least $k$; (ii) for all natural numbers $k$ and $g$ there is a simple graph $G$ with chromatic number $4$ and girth at least $g$ in which any two distinct cycle lengths of $G$ differ by at least $k$.
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 751

nodes.summary: It is not the case that both of the following hold: (i) for every natural number $k$ there is a simple graph $G$ with chromatic number $4$ in which any two distinct cycle lengths of $G$ differ by at least $k$; (ii) for all natural numbers $k$ and $g$ there is a simple graph $G$ with chromatic number $4$ and girth at least $g$ in which any two distinct cycle lengths of $G$ differ by at least $k$.
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 751 is false

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a graph on an arbitrary vertex set that has no proper colouring with finitely many colours. Then the family $(1/\ell)$, indexed by the odd cycle lengths $\ell$ of $G$ (the odd numbers $\ell$ such that $G$ contains a cycle of length $\ell$), is not summable; that is, $\sum_\ell 1/\ell = \infty$.
nodes.title: Odd cycle lengths and infinite chromatic number (Erdős Problem 57)

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a graph on an arbitrary vertex set that has no proper colouring with finitely many colours. Then the family $(1/\ell)$, indexed by the odd cycle lengths $\ell$ of $G$ (the odd numbers $\ell$ such that $G$ contains a cycle of length $\ell$), is not summable; that is, $\sum_\ell 1/\ell = \infty$.
nodes.title: Resolution of the Erdős–Hajnal odd cycle problem (Liu–Montgomery)

nodes.summary: The proposition that every simple graph $G$ with infinite chromatic number has cycles of length $2^n$ for infinitely many $n$: for every natural number $N$ there is some $n \ge N$ such that $G$ contains a cycle of length $2^n$.
nodes.title: Statement of Erdős Problem 63

nodes.summary: Every simple graph $G$ with infinite chromatic number has cycles of length $2^n$ for infinitely many $n$: for every natural number $N$ there is some $n \ge N$ such that $G$ contains a cycle of length $2^n$.
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 63 (Liu–Montgomery)
Degeneracy and greedy coloring

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex type $V$, let $U \subseteq V$ and let $k$ be a natural number. Then $G$ is $k$-degenerate on $U$ if every nonempty subset $W \subseteq U$ contains a vertex $v$ with at most $k$ neighbors in $W$.
nodes.title: Degeneracy on a vertex set

nodes.summary: A simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex type $V$ is $k$-degenerate, for a natural number $k$, if it is $k$-degenerate on the full vertex set $V$: every nonempty set $W$ of vertices contains a vertex with at most $k$ neighbors in $W$.
nodes.title: Degenerate graph

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex type $V$, let $U \subseteq V$, and let $k \le l$ be natural numbers. If $G$ is $k$-degenerate on $U$, then $G$ is $l$-degenerate on $U$.
nodes.title: Degeneracy on a vertex set is monotone in the degree bound

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex type $V$, let $T \subseteq U \subseteq V$ and let $k$ be a natural number. If $G$ is $k$-degenerate on $U$, then $G$ is $k$-degenerate on $T$.
nodes.title: Degeneracy on a vertex set passes to subsets

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex type $V$ and let $k$ be a natural number. If $G$ is $k$-degenerate, then $G$ is $k$-degenerate on every subset $U \subseteq V$.
nodes.title: A degenerate graph is degenerate on every vertex set

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$ and let $s \subseteq V$ be nonempty. If $G$ is $k$-degenerate on $s$, then some vertex $v \in s$ has at most $k$ neighbors in $s$.
nodes.title: A degenerate vertex set has a vertex of small degree

nodes.summary: For every natural number $k$, the edgeless graph on a finite vertex set is $k$-degenerate.
nodes.title: The edgeless graph is degenerate

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set. If $G$ is $k$-degenerate and $k \le l$, then $G$ is $l$-degenerate.
nodes.title: Degeneracy is monotone in the bound

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set. If every vertex of $G$ has degree at most $k$, then $G$ is $k$-degenerate.
nodes.title: Bounded maximum degree implies degeneracy

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$ and let $k$ be a natural number. A map $e : V \to \mathbb{N}$ is a degeneracy ordering of $G$ with bound $k$ if $e$ is injective and every vertex $v$ has at most $k$ neighbors $w$ with $e(v) < e(w)$.
nodes.title: Degeneracy ordering

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$ and let $s \subseteq V$. If $G$ is $k$-degenerate on $s$, then there is a map $e : V \to \mathbb{N}$, injective on $s$, such that every $v \in s$ has at most $k$ neighbors $w \in s$ with $e(v) < e(w)$.
nodes.title: Degeneracy orderings of a vertex set

nodes.summary: If $G$ is a $k$-degenerate simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$, then $G$ has a degeneracy ordering with bound $k$: an injective map $e : V \to \mathbb{N}$ such that every vertex $v$ has at most $k$ neighbors $w$ with $e(v) < e(w)$.
nodes.title: Degenerate graphs have degeneracy orderings

reading_title.source: Coloring a $k$-degenerate vertex set with $k + 1$ colors

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$, let $s \subseteq V$ and let $k$ be a natural number. If $G$ is $k$-degenerate on $s$, then there is a map $f : V \to \{0, 1, \dots, k\}$ such that $f(a) \ne f(b)$ for all adjacent vertices $a, b \in s$.
nodes.title: Coloring a $k$-degenerate vertex set with $k + 1$ colors

reading_title.source: $k$-degenerate graphs are $(k + 1)$-colorable

nodes.summary: Let $k$ be a natural number. Every $k$-degenerate simple graph on a finite vertex set is $(k + 1)$-colorable.
nodes.title: $k$-degenerate graphs are $(k + 1)$-colorable

nodes.summary: Let $k$ be a natural number. If $G$ is a $k$-degenerate simple graph on a finite vertex set, then the chromatic number of $G$ is at most $k + 1$.
nodes.title: Chromatic number of a degenerate graph
Edge coloring

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on $V$. An edge labeling $C$ of $G$ with colors in $K$ is a proper edge coloring when any two distinct edges of $G$ that share a vertex receive different colors: whenever a vertex $v$ is adjacent to $w_1$ and to $w_2$ with $w_1 \ne w_2$, the edges $v w_1$ and $v w_2$ have different colors under $C$.
nodes.title: Proper edge coloring

nodes.summary: König's line coloring, regular multigraph case: a `d`-regular bipartite multigraph (given by endpoint projections) is `d`-edge-colorable. The proof extracts a perfect matching by Hall's theorem and inducts. Shared API also used by the multigraph Galvin development.
nodes.title: König's edge coloring theorem for regular bipartite multigraphs

nodes.summary: König's line coloring, bounded-degree multigraph case: a bipartite multigraph of maximum degree at most `d` is `d`-edge-colorable. The proof pads both sides with dummy edges to reach the regular case. Shared API also used by the multigraph Galvin development.
nodes.title: König's edge coloring theorem for bounded-degree bipartite multigraphs

nodes.summary: Every finite bipartite simple graph $G$ has a proper edge coloring with $\Delta(G)$ colors, where $\Delta(G)$ is the maximum degree of $G$.
nodes.title: König's line coloring theorem

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on $V$. A map $c$ that assigns a color in $K$ to every unordered pair of elements of $V$ is a proper coloring of unordered pairs for $G$ when, for all vertices $x, y, z$ such that $x$ is adjacent to both $y$ and $z$ and $y \ne z$, the pairs $\{x, y\}$ and $\{x, z\}$ receive different colors under $c$.
nodes.title: Proper coloring of unordered pairs

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on $V$ and let $c$ assign a color in $K$ to every unordered pair of elements of $V$. If $c$ is a proper coloring of unordered pairs for $G$, then the edge labeling of $G$ that gives each edge $e$ the color $c(e)$ is a proper edge coloring of $G$.
nodes.title: Proper colorings of unordered pairs restrict to proper edge colorings

nodes.summary: Let $G$ and $H$ be simple graphs on $V$ such that every edge of $H$ is an edge of $G$. If a map $c$ from unordered pairs of elements of $V$ to $K$ is a proper coloring of unordered pairs for $G$, then it is also a proper coloring of unordered pairs for $H$.
nodes.title: Proper colorings of unordered pairs pass to subgraphs

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set and let $\Delta$ be its maximum degree. Then $G$ has a proper edge coloring with $\Delta + 1$ colors: there is an assignment of colors from $\{0, 1, \dots, \Delta\}$ to the edges of $G$ such that any two distinct edges sharing a vertex receive different colors.
nodes.title: Vizing's theorem
Four color theorem

reading_title.source: Graphs with a $K_5$ minor

nodes.summary: A simple graph $G$ has $K_5$ as a minor if there are five nonempty, pairwise disjoint sets of vertices $S_1, \dots, S_5$ such that any two vertices in the same set are joined by a walk in $G$ all of whose vertices lie in that set, and for all distinct $i, j$ some vertex of $S_i$ is adjacent in $G$ to some vertex of $S_j$.
nodes.title: Graphs with a $K_5$ minor

reading_title.source: Graphs with a $K_{3,3}$ minor

nodes.summary: A simple graph $G$ has $K_{3,3}$ as a minor if there are six nonempty, pairwise disjoint sets of vertices $L_1, L_2, L_3, R_1, R_2, R_3$ such that any two vertices in the same set are joined by a walk in $G$ all of whose vertices lie in that set, and for all $i, j \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ some vertex of $L_i$ is adjacent in $G$ to some vertex of $R_j$.
nodes.title: Graphs with a $K_{3,3}$ minor

nodes.summary: A simple graph $G$ is called planar here if it has neither $K_5$ nor $K_{3,3}$ as a minor.
nodes.title: Planarity by forbidden minors

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$ that has neither $K_5$ nor $K_{3,3}$ as a minor, and let $\ell$ assign a natural number $\ell(u, v)$ to every ordered pair of vertices $u, v$ such that $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $G$ if and only if $u \ne v$ and $\ell(u, v) > 0$. Then $G$ has a proper vertex coloring with four colors.
nodes.title: Four color theorem
Fractional coloring

nodes.summary: Let $X$ be a graph with finite vertex set $V(X)$. A *fractional clique* of $X$ is a function $f \colon V(X) \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f(v) \ge 0$ for every vertex $v$, such that $\sum_{v \in S} f(v) \le 1$ for every independent set $S$ of $X$. The *weight* of $f$ is $\sum_{v \in V(X)} f(v)$. The *fractional clique number* $\omega^*(X)$ of $X$ is the supremum of the weights of all fractional cliques of $X$.
nodes.title: Fractional clique number

nodes.summary: Let $X$ be a graph with finite vertex set $V(X)$. A *fractional colouring* of $X$ assigns to each set $S$ of vertices of $X$ a real weight $f(S) \ge 0$, with $f(S) = 0$ unless $S$ is independent, such that $\sum_{S \ni x} f(S) \ge 1$ for every vertex $x$ of $X$, the sum running over all sets of vertices containing $x$. The *weight* of $f$ is the sum of $f(S)$ over all sets $S$ of vertices of $X$. The *fractional…
nodes.title: Fractional chromatic number

nodes.summary: Let $X$ be a finite simple graph. A fractional colouring of $X$ assigns to each set $S$ of vertices of $X$ a real weight $f(S) \ge 0$, with $f(S) = 0$ unless $S$ is independent, such that $\sum_{S \ni x} f(S) \ge 1$ for every vertex $x$, the sum running over all sets of vertices containing $x$. The fractional colouring $f$ is *regular* if $\sum_{S \ni x} f(S) = 1$ for every vertex $x$ of $X$. Since $f$ vanishes off…
nodes.title: Regular fractional colouring
Hajnal–Szemerédi theorem

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set with maximum degree $\Delta(G)$, and let $k$ be a natural number with $\Delta(G) < k$. Then $G$ has a proper coloring with the $k$ colors $0, 1, \dots, k-1$ that is equitable: for any two colors $i$ and $j$, the number of vertices of color $i$ is at most one more than the number of vertices of color $j$.
nodes.title: Equitable coloring with more colors than the maximum degree

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set with maximum degree $\Delta(G)$, and let $k$ be a natural number with $\Delta(G) < k$. Then $G$ has a proper coloring with the $k$ colors $0, 1, \dots, k-1$ that is equitable: for any two colors $i$ and $j$, the number of vertices of color $i$ is at most one more than the number of vertices of color $j$.
nodes.title: Hajnal–Szemerédi theorem

nodes.summary: The proposition asserts that for all integers $r \ge 2$ and $m \ge 1$ and every finite simple graph $G$ with exactly $rm$ vertices, (a) if every vertex of $G$ has degree at least $m(r - 1)$, then $G$ contains $m$ pairwise disjoint cliques of $r$ vertices each, and (b) if every vertex of $G$ has degree at most $m - 1$, then $G$ has a proper colouring with $m$ colours in which every colour class has exactly $r$…
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 914 on clique factors and equitable colourings

nodes.summary: For all integers $r \ge 2$ and $m \ge 1$ and every finite simple graph $G$ with exactly $rm$ vertices, (a) if every vertex of $G$ has degree at least $m(r - 1)$, then $G$ contains $m$ pairwise disjoint cliques of $r$ vertices each, and (b) if every vertex of $G$ has degree at most $m - 1$, then $G$ has a proper colouring with $m$ colours in which every colour class has exactly $r$ vertices.
nodes.title: Hajnal–Szemerédi theorem in clique-factor and equitable-colouring form

Kneser graphs

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $v$ and $k$, the Kneser graph $K_{v:k}$ has as vertices the $k$-element subsets of the $v$-element set $\{0, 1, \dots, v-1\}$, with two distinct vertices adjacent when they are disjoint.
nodes.title: Kneser graph

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $k$ and $k$-element subsets $x$ and $y$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$, the vertices $x$ and $y$ of the Kneser graph $K(n, k)$ are adjacent if and only if $x$ and $y$ are disjoint and $x \ne y$.
nodes.title: Adjacency in the Kneser graph

nodes.summary: Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers with $0 < k$ and $2k \le n$. The Kneser graph $K(n, k)$, whose vertices are the $k$-element subsets of $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ and in which two such subsets are adjacent when they are disjoint and distinct, has chromatic number $n - 2k + 2$.
nodes.title: Kneser–Lovász theorem
List coloring

nodes.summary: A simple graph $G$ is $q$-list-colorable if, for every set of colors and every assignment of a finite list $L(v)$ of at least $q$ colors to each vertex $v$, there is a proper coloring $c$ of $G$ with $c(v) \in L(v)$ for every vertex $v$.
nodes.title: List colorability

nodes.summary: A natural number $q$ is the choice number of a simple graph $G$ if $G$ is $q$-list-colorable but is not $r$-list-colorable for any $r < q$.
nodes.title: Choice number

nodes.summary: If a simple graph $G$ is $q$-list-colorable and $q \le r$, then $G$ is $r$-list-colorable.
nodes.title: Monotonicity of list colorability

nodes.summary: If a simple graph $G$ is $q$-list-colorable, then $G$ is $q$-colorable, that is, it has a proper coloring with $q$ colors.
nodes.title: List-colorable graphs are colorable

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph and assign to each vertex $v$ a finite list $L(v)$ of colors. A finite set $S$ of vertices is partially list-colorable from $L$ when the subgraph of $G$ induced by $S$ has a proper coloring $c$ with $c(v) \in L(v)$ for every $v \in S$. No colors are assigned to vertices outside $S$.
nodes.title: Partial list colorability

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph on $n$ vertices whose choice number $q$ is positive, let $t \le q$ be a natural number, and assign to each vertex $v$ a list $L(v)$ of exactly $t$ colors. Then there is a set $S$ of vertices of $G$ that is partially list-colorable from $L$ (the subgraph of $G$ induced by $S$ has a proper coloring giving each vertex a color from its list) and satisfies $tn \le q|S|$, that is,…
nodes.title: Albertson–Grossman–Haas partial list coloring conjecture

nodes.summary: There exist a finite simple graph $G$ on $n$ vertices whose choice number $q$ is positive, a natural number $t \le q$, and an assignment to each vertex $v$ of a list $L(v)$ of exactly $t$ colors, such that every set $S$ of vertices of $G$ whose induced subgraph has a proper coloring giving each vertex a color from its list satisfies $q|S| < tn$.
nodes.title: The partial list coloring conjecture is false

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a graph on a finite vertex set $V$, let $L$ assign to each vertex $v$ a finite list $L(v)$ of colours (natural numbers), and let $S \subseteq V$. A map $f : V \to \mathbb{N}$ is a proper $L$-colouring of $S$ when $f(v) \in L(v)$ for every $v \in S$ and $f(v) \ne f(w)$ for all adjacent $v, w \in S$.
nodes.title: Proper list colouring of a vertex subset

nodes.summary: For a graph $G$ on a finite vertex set and an assignment $L$ of a finite list $L(v)$ of natural-number colours to each vertex $v$, $\lambda_L$ is the largest $k$ such that some set of $k$ vertices of $G$ has a proper $L$-colouring.
nodes.title: Maximum number of list-colourable vertices

reading_title.source: The partial list colouring number $\lambda_t$

nodes.summary: For a graph $G$ on a finite vertex set and a natural number $t$, $\lambda_t$ is the minimum of $\lambda_L$ over all assignments $L$ of a list $L(v)$ of exactly $t$ natural-number colours to each vertex $v$, where $\lambda_L$ is the largest $k$ such that some set of $k$ vertices of $G$ has a proper $L$-colouring.
nodes.title: The partial list colouring number $\lambda_t$

nodes.summary: For every finite graph $G$ with choice number $\chi_\ell$ and all natural numbers $r$, $s$ with $1 \le r \le s \le \chi_\ell$, one has $\lambda_r / r \ge \lambda_s / s$, where $\lambda_t$ is the minimum, over all assignments of lists of exactly $t$ colours to the vertices, of the largest number of vertices of $G$ that can be properly coloured from their lists.
nodes.title: Iradmusa's partial list colouring conjecture

nodes.summary: There exist a finite graph $G$ with choice number $\chi_\ell$ and natural numbers $r$, $s$ with $1 \le r \le s \le \chi_\ell$ such that $\lambda_r / r < \lambda_s / s$, where $\lambda_t$ is the minimum, over all assignments of lists of exactly $t$ colours to the vertices, of the largest number of vertices of $G$ that can be properly coloured from their lists. So Iradmusa's partial list colouring conjecture fails.

nodes.summary: The odd distance graph is the simple graph on the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ in which two points $x$ and $y$ are adjacent when their Euclidean distance is an odd integer.

Perfect graphs

nodes.summary: A finite simple graph $G$ is perfect if, for every set $S$ of its vertices, the induced subgraph $G[S]$ has chromatic number equal to its clique number, the largest size of a clique in $G[S]$.
nodes.title: Perfect graph

nodes.summary: A finite simple graph $G$ satisfies condition (P) if, for every set $S$ of its vertices, the induced subgraph $G[S]$, with independence number $\alpha(G[S])$ and clique number $\omega(G[S])$, satisfies $|S| \le \alpha(G[S]) \cdot \omega(G[S])$.
nodes.title: Gasparian's condition (P)

nodes.summary: Every finite perfect graph $G$ satisfies Gasparian's condition (P): for every set $S$ of its vertices, the induced subgraph $G[S]$, with independence number $\alpha(G[S])$ and clique number $\omega(G[S])$, satisfies $|S| \le \alpha(G[S]) \cdot \omega(G[S])$.

nodes.title: Valid adjacency-matrix instance

nodes.summary: A valid instance with $n$ vertices and adjacency matrix $A$ determines the simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which vertices $x$ and $y$ are adjacent exactly when $A_{xy}$ is true.

Subgraphs of large cochromatic number

nodes.summary: The proposition asserts two statements. First, there is a real number $c > 0$ such that for every simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set with chromatic number $m$ there are a subgraph $H$ of $G$ and a natural number $k$ with $k \ge c\,m / \log m$ such that the cochromatic number of $H$ is at least $k$. Second, there is a real number $c > 0$ with the same property for the bound $k \ge c\sqrt{m / \log m}$.

Moreover, there is a real number $c > 0$ with the same property for the bound $k \ge c\sqrt{m / \log m}$.

Chromatic numbers may be infinite.

nodes.summary: Let $X$ be a finite graph and $s$ a natural number. An *$s$-arc* in $X$ is a sequence $(v_0, \dots, v_s)$ of vertices of $X$ such that $v_{i-1}$ and $v_i$ are adjacent for $1 \le i \le s$, and $v_{i-1} \ne v_{i+1}$ for $0 < i < s$.

nodes.summary: A finite graph $G$ is $s$-arc transitive if its automorphism group acts transitively on its $s$-arcs: for any two $s$-arcs $(u_0, \dots, u_s)$ and $(v_0, \dots, v_s)$ of $G$ there is an automorphism $\varphi$ of $G$ with $\varphi(u_i) = v_i$ for every $i \le s$.

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $p$ and $s$, the coconut tree $\mathrm{CT}(p, s)$ is the graph whose vertices are the path vertices $v_1, \dots, v_p$ and the leaves $v_{\ell_1}, \dots, v_{\ell_s}$, in which $v_i$ and $v_{i+1}$ are adjacent for $1 \le i < p$, every leaf is adjacent to $v_p$, and there are no other edges. Then $y$ is an ancestor of $x$, and $x$ a descendant of $y$, when $y$ is obtained from $x$ by a finite, possibly empty, sequence of smoothings, each performed at a vertex where the current $d$-label equals $1$: either at a path vertex other than the central vertex, or at a leaf.
nodes.title: Ancestors of labelings of coconut trees

nodes.summary: Let $s \ge 1$ and let $(d, r)$ be an arithmetical structure on the coconut tree $CT(p + 1, s)$, whose path vertices are $v_1, \dots, v_{p+1}$ with central vertex $v_{p+1}$. If $d(v_k) = 1$ for some non-central path vertex $v_k$ (that is, $1 \le k \le p$), then smoothing $(d, r)$ at $v_k$ gives an arithmetical structure on $CT(p, s)$.
nodes.title: Path smoothing preserves arithmetical structures on coconut trees

nodes.summary: Let $p$ and $s$ be natural numbers with $p + s \ge 2$, let $(d, r)$ be an arithmetical structure on the coconut tree $CT(p, s + 1)$, and let $\ell$ be a leaf with $d(\ell) = 1$. Then the labelings $(d', r')$ obtained by smoothing $(d, r)$ at $\ell$ form an arithmetical structure on $CT(p, s)$.
nodes.title: Smoothing a leaf preserves arithmetical structures

nodes.summary: If $(d, r)$ is an arithmetical structure on the coconut tree $CT(p, s)$, whose path vertices are $v_1, \dots, v_p$, then for every $1 \le k \le p$, subdividing $(d, r)$ at position $k$ (inserting a new path vertex just before $v_k$) gives an arithmetical structure on $CT(p + 1, s)$.
nodes.title: Subdivision preserves arithmetical structures on coconut trees

nodes.summary: Let $s \ge 1$ and let $(d, r)$ be an arithmetical structure on the coconut tree $CT(p, s)$ with $d(\ell_j) \ge 2$ at every leaf $\ell_j$. Then there is exactly one pair consisting of a number $q$ with $1 \le q \le p$ and a smooth arithmetical structure on $CT(q, s)$ that is a coconut ancestor of $(d, r)$, that is, one obtained from $(d, r)$ by a possibly empty sequence of smoothings, each performed at a vertex…
nodes.title: Unique smooth ancestor

nodes.summary: Let $s \ge 2$ and $1 \le i \le p$, and let $(d, r)$ be a smooth arithmetical structure on the coconut tree $\mathrm{CT}(i, s)$. Then exactly $B(p - 1, p - i)$ arithmetical structures on $\mathrm{CT}(p, s)$ are descendants of $(d, r)$, where $B(n, k)$ is the ballot number.
nodes.title: Number of descendants of a smooth coconut structure

Cycle-continuous maps

nodes.summary: A multigraph $G$ consists of a type $V$ of vertices, a type $E$ of edges, and a map assigning to each edge an ordered pair of vertices, its two endpoints. Distinct edges may have the same endpoints (parallel edges), and the two endpoints of an edge may coincide (a loop). Neither $V$ nor $E$ is required to be finite.
nodes.title: Multigraphs with loops and parallel edges

nodes.summary: A multigraph $G$ is finite and nontrivial when its set of vertices and its set of edges are both finite and it has at least one edge. These are the graphs on which the cycle-continuous order is considered.
nodes.title: Finite multigraphs with at least one edge

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a multigraph. A set $S$ of edges of $G$ is a binary cycle when $S$ is finite and every vertex $v$ is an endpoint of an even number of edges of $S$, where only edges with exactly one endpoint equal to $v$ are counted; loops are not counted, which agrees modulo $2$ with counting each loop twice. The cycle space of $G$ is the set of all binary cycles of $G$.
nodes.title: Binary cycle space

nodes.summary: Let $G$ and $H$ be multigraphs. A map $f$ from the edges of $G$ to the edges of $H$ is cycle-continuous when, for every binary cycle $C$ of $H$, the preimage $f^{-1}(C)$ is a binary cycle of $G$.
nodes.title: Cycle-continuous maps

nodes.summary: There is a sequence $G_0, G_1, G_2, \dots$ of pairwise distinct finite multigraphs, each with at least one edge, such that for all $i \ne j$ there is no cycle-continuous map from the edges of $G_i$ to the edges of $G_j$.
nodes.title: Infinite antichains in the cycle-continuous order

nodes.summary: There is a sequence $G_0, G_1, G_2, \dots$ of pairwise distinct finite multigraphs, each with at least one edge, such that for all $i \ne j$ there is no cycle-continuous map from the edges of $G_i$ to the edges of $G_j$.
nodes.title: Samal's theorem: infinite antichains in the cycle-continuous order exist
Deza graphs

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$, and let $n, k, b, a$ be natural numbers. Then $G$ is a Deza graph with parameters $(n, k, b, a)$ when $a \le b \le k < n$, $V$ has exactly $n$ elements, every vertex of $G$ has degree $k$, and any two distinct vertices of $G$ have exactly $a$ or exactly $b$ common neighbours, whether or not they are adjacent.
nodes.title: Deza graph

nodes.summary: If a finite simple graph $G$ is a Deza graph with parameters $(n, k, b, a)$, then $a \le k$.

Graph homomorphisms, cores and covers

nodes.summary: Let $Y$ be a subgraph of a graph $X$. A *retraction* from $X$ to $Y$ is a homomorphism $f$ from $X$ to $Y$, regarded as a graph in its own right, whose restriction to the vertex set of $Y$ is the identity map. We say that $Y$ is a *retract* of $X$ if there is a retraction from $X$ to $Y$.
nodes.title: Retract

nodes.summary: A finite graph $X$ is a *core* if every homomorphism from $X$ to itself is a bijection. For finite graphs $X$ and $Y$, $Y$ is a *core of* $X$ if $Y$ is a core, there is a homomorphism from $X$ to $Y$, and there is an injective homomorphism from $Y$ to $X$; that is, $Y$ is isomorphic to a subgraph of $X$.
nodes.title: Core of a graph

nodes.summary: A homomorphism $f$ from a finite graph $X$ to a finite graph $Y$ is a *local injection* if any two distinct vertices of $X$ with the same image under $f$ are at distance at least $3$ in $X$.
nodes.title: Local injection

nodes.summary: A homomorphism $f$ from a finite graph $X$ to a finite graph $Y$ is a *local isomorphism* if for every vertex $x$ of $X$, $f$ maps the set of neighbours of $x$ bijectively onto the set of neighbours of $f(x)$.
nodes.title: Local isomorphism

nodes.summary: A finite graph $X$ *covers* a finite graph $Y$ if there is a surjective local isomorphism from $X$ to $Y$.
nodes.title: Graph cover

nodes.summary: A homomorphism from X to Y is a *simple folding* if it has one fibre consisting of two vertices at distance two, and all other fibres are singletons. A homomorphism is a *folding* if it is the composition of a non-negative number of simple foldings.
nodes.title: Folding of a graph homomorphism
Grassmann graphs

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $k$ and $\ell$, the vertices of the Grassmann graph $\mathrm{Gr}(k, \ell)$ are the $\ell$-dimensional linear subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_2^k$.
nodes.title: Vertices of the Grassmann graph

reading_title.source: Grassmann graph over $\mathbb{F}_2$

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $k$ and $\ell$, the Grassmann graph $\mathrm{Gr}(k, \ell)$ has as vertices the $\ell$-dimensional linear subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_2^k$, and two distinct such subspaces $L$ and $L'$ are adjacent when $\dim(L \cap L') = \ell - 1$.
nodes.title: Grassmann graph over $\mathbb{F}_2$

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $k$ and $\ell$ and linear subspaces $A$ and $B$ of $\mathbb{F}_2^k$, $\mathrm{Gr}(k, \ell)[A, B]$ is the finite set of vertices $L$ of the Grassmann graph $\mathrm{Gr}(k, \ell)$, that is of $\ell$-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_2^k$, with $A \subseteq L \subseteq B$. If $A \not\subseteq B$ the set is empty.
nodes.title: Grassmann vertices between two subspaces

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$ and let $S \subseteq V$ be nonempty. Let $d$ be the degree in $G$ of a fixed vertex of $S$, chosen once for each $S$. The expansion of $S$ is the rational number $\Phi_G(S) = |E(S, V \setminus S)| / (d \cdot |S|)$, where $E(S, V \setminus S)$ is the set of edges of $G$ with one endpoint in $S$ and the other in $V \setminus S$; it is $0$ when $d = 0$.

Integral Cayley graphs

nodes.summary: A square integer matrix is integral: every complex root of its characteristic polynomial (every eigenvalue) is an integer.
nodes.title: Integer matrix with integral spectrum

With the points numbered $0, 1, \dots, n - 1$, these are the permutations $(0\,1\,k) = (0\,1)(1\,k)$ with $2 \le k < n$, products composed right to left; the set is empty when $n < 3$.

Then the Cayley graph $\mathrm{Cay}(A_n, R)$, whose vertices are the elements of $A_n$ with distinct $x$ and $y$ adjacent when $x^{-1} y \in R$ or $y^{-1} x \in R$, is integral: every eigenvalue of its integer adjacency matrix (every complex root of the characteristic…

Johnson graphs

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $v$, $k$ and $i$, the generalized Johnson graph $J(v,k,i)$ is the graph whose vertices are the $k$-element subsets of $\{0, 1, \dots, v-1\}$, in which two distinct vertices are adjacent if and only if their intersection has exactly $i$ elements.
nodes.title: Generalized Johnson graph

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the Johnson graph $J(n, k)$ has as vertices the $k$-element subsets of $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$, and two vertices $s$ and $t$ are adjacent when $|s \cap t| + 1 = k$, that is, when $s$ and $t$ share exactly $k - 1$ elements.
nodes.title: Johnson graph

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $k$ and $k$-element subsets $s$ and $t$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$, the vertices $s$ and $t$ of the Johnson graph $J(n, k)$ are adjacent if and only if $|s \cap t| + 1 = k$.
nodes.title: Adjacency in the Johnson graph
Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$, the integer Laplacian of $G$ is the $V \times V$ integer matrix $L$ with $L_{uu} = \deg u$ for every vertex $u$, $L_{uv} = -1$ when $u \ne v$ are adjacent, and $L_{uv} = 0$ when $u \ne v$ are not adjacent.
nodes.title: Integer Laplacian of a graph

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$ and a vertex $r \in V$, the reduced Laplacian of $G$ at $r$ is the integer Laplacian of $G$ with the row and the column of $r$ deleted, a matrix indexed by the vertices of $G$ other than $r$.
nodes.title: Reduced Laplacian

nodes.summary: A subgraph $T$ of a simple graph $G$ is a spanning tree of $G$ if it contains every vertex of $G$ and, regarded as a graph on its own vertex set, it is a tree (connected and acyclic).
nodes.title: Spanning tree

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set, the number of spanning trees of $G$ is the number of subgraphs of $G$ that are spanning trees, that is, subgraphs that contain every vertex of $G$ and are trees.
nodes.title: Number of spanning trees

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set, the integer Laplacian of $G$ equals $D - A$, where $D$ is the diagonal matrix of vertex degrees and $A$ is the adjacency matrix of $G$, both with integer entries.
nodes.title: The integer Laplacian is degree minus adjacency

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$ and let $L = D - A$ be its Laplacian matrix over $\mathbb{Z}$, where $D$ is the diagonal matrix of vertex degrees and $A$ is the adjacency matrix of $G$. For every vertex $r \in V$, the reduced Laplacian of $G$ at $r$ equals the submatrix of $L$ obtained by deleting the row and the column of $r$.
nodes.title: The reduced Laplacian is a principal submatrix

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$ on a vertex set $V$, there is an equivalence between the spanning trees of $G$ (subgraphs of $G$ that contain every vertex and are trees) and the simple graphs $H$ on $V$ that are trees with $H \le G$, that is, every edge of $H$ is an edge of $G$. It sends a spanning tree to the graph on $V$ with the same edges.
nodes.title: Spanning trees as trees contained in the graph

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$, the number of spanning trees of $G$ equals the number of simple graphs $H$ on $V$ such that every edge of $H$ is an edge of $G$ and $H$ is a tree.
nodes.title: Spanning trees as trees on the whole vertex set

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$ and let $r \in V$. Then the determinant of the reduced Laplacian of $G$ at $r$, that is, the integer Laplacian of $G$ with the row and the column of $r$ deleted, equals the number of spanning trees of $G$.
nodes.title: Matrix-tree theorem for a chosen root

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$, let $L = D - A$ be its Laplacian matrix over $\mathbb{Z}$, where $D$ is the diagonal matrix of vertex degrees and $A$ is the adjacency matrix of $G$, and let $r \in V$. Then the determinant of the submatrix of $L$ obtained by deleting the row and the column of $r$ equals the number of spanning trees of $G$.
nodes.title: Matrix-tree theorem for principal minors of the Laplacian

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite nonempty vertex set $V$ and let $r \in V$. Then the determinant of the reduced Laplacian of $G$ at $r$, that is, the integer Laplacian of $G$ with the row and the column of $r$ deleted, equals the number of spanning trees of $G$.

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$, let $\varepsilon$ be a real number and let $S \subseteq V$. Let $L$ be the real Laplacian matrix of $G$ and $L_S$ the real Laplacian matrix of the graph on $V$ whose edges are the edges of $G$ with both endpoints in $S$. The set $S$ is $\varepsilon$-light in $G$ if $\varepsilon L - L_S$ is positive semidefinite.

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$ with edge set $E$, the average degree of $G$ is the rational number $2|E|/|V|$; it equals $0$ when $V$ is empty.
nodes.title: Average degree of a finite graph

nodes.summary: A simple graph $G$ has a matching cut if some matching $M$ of $G$, that is, a set of pairwise disjoint edges of $G$, is such that deleting the edges of $M$ from $G$ leaves two vertices $u$ and $v$ that are not joined by any path. The matching may be empty, in which case this says that $G$ itself has two vertices not joined by any path.

nodes.summary: For every real number $d$ there is a natural number $g$ such that every simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set with at least two vertices, whose average degree is less than $d$ and whose girth is at least $g$, has a matching cut. An acyclic graph has infinite girth, so it meets the girth bound for every $g$.

nodes.summary: Let $V$ be a finite set, $c : V \times V \to \mathbb{R}$ a capacity function and $s, t \in V$. A function $f : V \times V \to \mathbb{R}$ is a feasible $s$-$t$ flow for $c$ if $0 \le f(u, v) \le c(u, v)$ for all $u, v \in V$ and $f$ is conserved at every vertex $v \ne s, t$, that is, $\sum_{u \in V} f(u, v) = \sum_{w \in V} f(v, w)$.
nodes.title: Feasible flow

nodes.summary: For a finite set $V$, a vertex $s \in V$ and a function $f : V \times V \to \mathbb{R}$, the value of $f$ is its net outflow from the source $s$, $\sum_{v \in V} f(s, v) - \sum_{u \in V} f(u, s)$.
nodes.title: Flow value

nodes.summary: For a finite set $V$ and vertices $s, t \in V$, an $s$-$t$ cut is a subset $S \subseteq V$ with $s \in S$ and $t \notin S$.
nodes.title: Source–sink cut

nodes.summary: Let $V$ be a finite set and $c : V \times V \to \mathbb{R}$ a capacity function. The capacity of a subset $S \subseteq V$ is the total capacity of the arcs leaving $S$, $\sum_{u \in S} \sum_{v \in V \setminus S} c(u, v)$.
