nodes.summary: A strict total order on a type $\alpha$ is a binary relation $<$ on $\alpha$ that is irreflexive ($a < a$ holds for no $a$), transitive ($a < b$ and $b < c$ imply $a < c$) and total on distinct elements ($a \ne b$ implies $a < b$ or $b < a$). In the Gale–Shapley development it models strict preference.
nodes.title: Strict preference order

nodes.summary: A binary relation $<$ on a set $\alpha$ that is irreflexive ($a \not< a$ for all $a$), transitive ($a < b$ and $b < c$ imply $a < c$) and total on distinct elements ($a \ne b$ implies $a < b$ or $b < a$) defines a strict total order on $\alpha$ whose relation is $<$.
nodes.title: Building a strict total order from a relation

nodes.summary: The relation of a strict total order $T$ on a set $\alpha$ is its underlying binary relation $\lt _T$ on $\alpha$, which is irreflexive, transitive, and relates any two distinct elements in one direction or the other.
nodes.title: Relation of a strict total order

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a strict total order on a set $\alpha$, with relation $\lt _T$. Then $a \lt _T a$ fails for every $a \in \alpha$.
nodes.title: Irreflexivity of a strict total order

nodes.summary: Let $<$ be the relation of a strict total order on a type $\alpha$. If $a, b, c \in \alpha$ satisfy $a < b$ and $b < c$, then $a < c$.
nodes.title: Transitivity of a strict total order

nodes.summary: Let $<$ be the relation of a strict total order on a type $\alpha$. If $a, b \in \alpha$ and $a \ne b$, then $a < b$ or $b < a$.
nodes.title: Strict total orders are total on distinct elements

nodes.summary: Let $T$ and $T'$ be strict total orders on a set $\alpha$, with relations $\lt _T$ and $\lt _{T'}$. If $x \lt _T y \iff x \lt _{T'} y$ for all $x, y \in \alpha$, then $T = T'$.
nodes.title: Strict total orders are determined by their relation

nodes.summary: For sets $M$ (men) and $W$ (women), a preference profile of the men assigns to each $m \in M$ a strict total order on $W$, the preferences of $m$.
nodes.title: Men's preferences

nodes.summary: For types $M$ and $W$, a preference profile of $W$ over $M$ assigns to each $w \in W$ a strict total order on $M$, read as the strict preference of $w$ among the elements of $M$.
nodes.title: Women's preference profile

nodes.summary: A perfect matching between sets $M$ and $W$ is a bijection $\mu \colon M \to W$, which matches each $m \in M$ with $\mu(m) \in W$.
nodes.title: Perfect matching

nodes.summary: Let $M$ and $W$ be sets. Suppose that each $m \in M$ has a strict total order $\lt _m$ of preference on $W$ and each $w \in W$ has a strict total order $\lt _w$ of preference on $M$, where $x \lt _m y$ means that $m$ prefers $x$ to $y$, and likewise for $\lt _w$. For a perfect matching $\mu$ between $M$ and $W$, a pair $(m, w) \in M \times W$ is a blocking pair when $w \lt _m \mu(m)$ and $m \lt _w \mu^{-1}(w)$,…
nodes.title: Blocking pair

nodes.summary: Let $M$ and $W$ be sets. Suppose that each $m \in M$ has a strict total order of preference on $W$ and each $w \in W$ has a strict total order of preference on $M$. A perfect matching $\mu$ between $M$ and $W$ is stable for these preferences when no pair $(m, w) \in M \times W$ is a blocking pair for $\mu$.
nodes.title: Stable perfect matching

nodes.summary: Let $M$ and $W$ be finite sets with the same number of elements. Suppose that each $m \in M$ has a strict total order of preference on $W$ and each $w \in W$ has a strict total order of preference on $M$. Then some perfect matching between $M$ and $W$ is stable for these preferences.
nodes.title: Existence of stable perfect matchings

nodes.summary: Let $M$ and $W$ be finite sets with the same number of elements. Suppose that each $m \in M$ has a strict total order of preference on $W$ and each $w \in W$ has a strict total order of preference on $M$. Then some perfect matching between $M$ and $W$ is stable for these preferences.
nodes.title: Gale–Shapley theorem

reading_title.source: Preference profile for $n$ men and $n$ women

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, number $n$ men and $n$ women by $0, \dots, n - 1$. A preference profile $P = (M, W)$ for them consists of a permutation $M_i$ of $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ for each man $i$ and a permutation $W_j$ of $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ for each woman $j$: $M_i(r)$ is the woman man $i$ ranks at zero-based position $r$, and $W_j(r)$ is the man woman $j$ ranks at position $r$.
nodes.title: Preference profile for $n$ men and $n$ women

nodes.summary: For a preference profile of $n$ men and $n$ women, the rank of woman $j$ for man $i$ is the zero-based position $r \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ at which $i$ ranks $j$, so his favorite has rank $0$ and his least favorite has rank $n - 1$.
nodes.title: Rank of a woman for a man

nodes.summary: For a preference profile for $n$ men and $n$ women, the rank that woman $j$ gives man $i$ is the zero-based position at which she ranks him, that is, the paper's ranking minus one.
nodes.title: A woman's rank of a man

nodes.summary: For a preference profile of $n$ men and $n$ women, man $i$ and woman $j$ are soulmates when each ranks the other first: $j$ is the first choice of $i$ and $i$ is the first choice of $j$.
nodes.title: Soulmate pair

nodes.summary: The number of soulmate pairs of a preference profile $P$ for $n$ men and $n$ women is the number of pairs $(i, j)$ of a man $i$ and a woman $j$ that are soulmates in $P$, that is, each ranks the other first.
nodes.title: Number of soulmate pairs

nodes.summary: For a preference profile of $n$ men and $n$ women, each man $i$ gets the strict total order on the women in which $i$ prefers woman $a$ to woman $b$ exactly when he ranks $a$ at an earlier position than $b$.
nodes.title: Men's preferences induced by rankings

nodes.summary: For a preference profile $P$ for $n$ men and $n$ women, each woman $j$ gets the strict total order on the men in which man $a$ comes before (is preferred to) man $b$ exactly when woman $j$ ranks $a$ at an earlier position than $b$.
nodes.title: Women's preference orders of a profile

nodes.summary: For a preference profile of $n$ men and $n$ women, a matching $\mu$, in which man $i$ marries woman $\mu(i)$, is stable when no man and woman both strictly prefer each other to their own spouses. Equivalently, $\mu$ is a stable perfect matching for the strict preferences induced by the men's and the women's rankings.
nodes.title: Stable matching

nodes.summary: For a preference profile of $n$ men and $n$ women, a matching $\mu$, in which man $i$ marries woman $\mu(i)$, is stable if and only if there are no man $i$ and woman $j$ such that $i$ ranks $j$ strictly above his wife $\mu(i)$ and $j$ ranks $i$ strictly above her husband $\mu^{-1}(j)$.
nodes.title: Stability in terms of ranks

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a preference profile of $n$ men and $n$ women, and let $\mu$ be a matching in which man $i$ marries woman $\mu(i)$. Man $i$ and his wife $\mu(i)$ form a hell-couple when each ranks the other last: $i$ ranks $\mu(i)$ in his last position and $\mu(i)$ ranks $i$ in her last position.
nodes.title: Hell-couple

nodes.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $L_n$ is the number of Latin squares of order $n$: families $(M_0, \dots, M_{n-1})$ of permutations of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ (the rows) such that for every position $r$ the entries $M_0(r), \dots, M_{n-1}(r)$ (column $r$) are pairwise distinct.
nodes.title: Number of Latin squares

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a preference profile for $n$ men and $n$ women, with positions in each ranking numbered $0, \dots, n - 1$, and consider the state of the men-proposing Gale–Shapley algorithm in which each man $i'$ has proposed to the women at the positions $r' < p(i')$ of his ranking. Man $i$ is provisionally engaged in this state if $1 \le p(i) \le n$ and the woman $w$ at his position $p(i) - 1$ (the last woman he…
nodes.title: Provisional engagement in the Gale–Shapley algorithm

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a preference profile for $n$ men and $n$ women. The number $p_t(i)$ of women man $i$ has proposed to after $t$ rounds of the men-proposing Gale–Shapley algorithm on $P$ is defined by $p_0(i) = 0$ and, for every $t$, $p_{t+1}(i) = p_t(i)$ if man $i$ is provisionally engaged in the state $p_t$ and $p_{t+1}(i) = p_t(i) + 1$ otherwise: in each round every man who is not provisionally engaged proposes to his…
nodes.title: Proposal counts in the Gale–Shapley algorithm

nodes.summary: For a preference profile $P$ for $n$ men and $n$ women, the number of rounds of the men-proposing Gale–Shapley algorithm on $P$ is the least $t$ such that every man is provisionally engaged after $t$ rounds (or $0$ if there is no such $t$).
nodes.title: Number of Gale–Shapley rounds

nodes.summary: For every preference profile, after zero rounds of the men-proposing Gale–Shapley algorithm every man has made zero proposals.
nodes.title: No proposals before the first round

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a preference profile for $n$ men and $n$ women and let $t$ be a natural number. After $t + 1$ rounds of the men-proposing Gale–Shapley algorithm on $P$, a man who is provisionally engaged after $t$ rounds has made as many proposals as after $t$ rounds, and every other man has made one proposal more than after $t$ rounds.
nodes.title: One round of the Gale–Shapley algorithm

nodes.summary: For the preference profile with no men and no women, the men-proposing Gale–Shapley algorithm takes zero rounds.
nodes.title: Gale–Shapley rounds with no participants

reading_title.source: A profile has at most $n$ soulmate pairs

nodes.summary: Every preference profile for $n$ men and $n$ women has at most $n$ soulmate pairs, since a man's soulmate is his first choice.
nodes.title: A profile has at most $n$ soulmate pairs

nodes.summary: There is exactly one Latin square of order $0$, that is, $L_0 = 1$.
nodes.title: Latin squares of order zero

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a preference profile for $n$ men and $n$ women in which all men rank the women in the same order. Then the men-proposing Gale–Shapley algorithm on $P$ ends in exactly $n$ rounds.
nodes.title: Gale–Shapley rounds when all men have the same preferences

nodes.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $P$ be a preference profile for $n$ men and $n$ women. The men-proposing Gale–Shapley algorithm on $P$ ends in exactly one round if and only if every woman is the first choice of exactly one man.
nodes.title: When the Gale–Shapley algorithm ends in one round

nodes.summary: Call a preference profile for $n$ men and $n$ women disjoint if for every pair of positions $(r, s)$ there is exactly one man–woman pair in which the man ranks the woman at position $r$ and the woman ranks the man at position $s$. For every natural number $n$, the number of disjoint profiles is at most $(n^2)!$ and is divisible by $(n!)^2$.
nodes.title: Counting disjoint preference profiles

nodes.summary: Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers, where $n - k$ is read as $0$ when $k > n$. Consider the $n - k$ men $k, \dots, n - 1$ and the $n - k$ women $k, \dots, n - 1$ among $n$ men and $n$ women numbered from $0$, where each of these men ranks all $n$ women and each of these women ranks all $n$ men. The number of ways to choose these rankings so that no man and woman among them each rank the other first is
nodes.title: Outsiders without soulmate pairs

reading_title.source: Number of profiles with exactly $k$ soulmate pairs

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the number $F(k, n)$ of preference profiles for $n$ men and $n$ women with exactly $k$ soulmate pairs is
nodes.title: Number of profiles with exactly $k$ soulmate pairs

reading_title.source: Profiles with $n - 1$ soulmate pairs

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a preference profile for $n$ men and $n$ women with exactly $n - 1$ soulmate pairs (read as $0$ when $n = 0$). Then $P$ has exactly one stable matching. Moreover, for every stable matching $\mu$ of $P$ and every man $i$ who has no soulmate, the men-proposing Gale–Shapley algorithm on $P$ ends after $r + 1$ rounds, where $r$ is the zero-based position at which man $i$ ranks his wife $\mu(i)$.
nodes.title: Profiles with $n - 1$ soulmate pairs

nodes.summary: For all $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$, the number of preference profiles of $n$ men and $n$ women in which, for every position $r$, different men rank different women at position $r$ (the men's rankings form a Latin square), and which have exactly $k$ soulmate pairs, is
nodes.title: Profiles with Latin-square men's preferences, counted by soulmate pairs

reading_title.source: Mutually Latin profiles with $k$ soulmate pairs

nodes.summary: Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers and let $L_n$ be the number of Latin squares of order $n$. Call the men's preferences of a preference profile for $n$ men and $n$ women Latin when, for every position $r$, distinct men rank distinct women at position $r$, and likewise for the women's preferences. The number of preference profiles whose men's and women's preferences are both Latin and that have exactly $k$ soulmate…
nodes.title: Mutually Latin profiles with $k$ soulmate pairs

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a preference profile of $n$ men and $n$ women, and let $\mu$ be a stable matching for $P$, in which man $i$ marries woman $\mu(i)$. Then at most one man $i$ forms a hell-couple with his wife $\mu(i)$.
nodes.title: At most one hell-couple in a stable matching

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a preference profile for $n$ men and $n$ women and let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be stable matchings for $P$. If man $i$ and his wife $\mu(i)$ form a hell-couple in $\mu$ (each ranks the other last), then $\nu(i) = \mu(i)$.
nodes.title: A hell-couple belongs to every stable matching

nodes.summary: In a preference profile for $n$ men and $n$ women, a man $i$ and a woman $j$ form a pair of outcasts when every man other than $i$ ranks $j$ last and every woman other than $j$ ranks $i$ last. The number of preference profiles with at least one pair of outcasts is $14$ if $n = 2$ and $n^4 ((n-1)!)^{2n}$ if $n \ne 2$ (this is $0$ for $n = 0$).
nodes.title: Profiles with a pair of outcasts

nodes.summary: Walks, paths and cycles in graphs, Eulerian and Hamiltonian cycles, and vertex and edge connectivity, including Menger's theorem and Fleischner's theorem on squares of 2-connected graphs.
nodes.title: Paths, cycles and connectivity

nodes.summary: Two paths that meet only at their common endpoint `m` concatenate to a path.
nodes.title: Concatenation of paths meeting at one endpoint is a path
Bridges and bridgeless graphs

nodes.summary: A simple graph is bridgeless when no edge is a bridge.
nodes.title: Bridgeless graph

nodes.summary: A simple graph $G$ is bridgeless if and only if no edge of $G$ is a bridge.
nodes.title: Characterization of bridgeless graphs

nodes.summary: If no edge of a simple graph $G$ is a bridge, then $G$ is bridgeless.
nodes.title: Bridgeless from non-bridge edges

nodes.summary: Every edge of a bridgeless graph is not a bridge.
nodes.title: Edges of a bridgeless graph are not bridges

nodes.summary: The edgeless graph on any vertex set is vacuously bridgeless.
nodes.title: The edgeless graph is bridgeless
Cycle covers

nodes.summary: A cycle in a simple graph $G$ consists of a base vertex $v$ of $G$ together with a closed walk $v = v_0, v_1, \dots, v_n = v$ in $G$ such that $n \ge 1$, the $n$ edges $v_{k-1} v_k$ of the walk are pairwise distinct, and the vertices $v_1, \dots, v_n$ are pairwise distinct. In a simple graph this forces $n \ge 3$.
nodes.title: Cycles in a graph

nodes.summary: The edges of a cycle $c$ in a simple graph form the list of the edges of its closed walk, in the order in which $c$ traverses them starting from its base vertex; each edge is the unordered pair of its two endpoints.
nodes.title: Edges of a cycle

nodes.summary: The length of a cycle in a simple graph is the number of edges of its closed walk.
nodes.title: Length of a cycle

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph. A finite multiset $C$ of cycles in $G$ is a cycle cover of $G$ when every edge of $G$ is an edge of at least one cycle in $C$.
nodes.title: Cycle covers

nodes.summary: The total length of a finite multiset $C$ of cycles in a simple graph is the sum of the lengths of the cycles in $C$, each counted with its multiplicity.
nodes.title: Total length of a multiset of cycles
Cycle lengths and circumference

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$, the set of cycle lengths of $G$ is the set of natural numbers $m$ such that $G$ contains a cycle of length $m$.
nodes.title: Cycle lengths

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$, the set of odd cycle lengths of $G$ is the set of those cycle lengths of $G$ that are odd, that is, the odd natural numbers $m$ such that $G$ contains a cycle of length $m$.
nodes.title: Odd cycle lengths

nodes.summary: A cycle is globally longest if no cycle in the graph has more edges.
nodes.title: Longest cycle in a graph
Eulerian circuits

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph and let $p$ be an Eulerian trail in $G$, that is, a walk between any two vertices that uses every edge of $G$ exactly once. Then for every vertex $x$, the number of edges of $p$ that contain $x$, counted with multiplicity along $p$, equals the degree of $x$ in $G$.
nodes.title: Edges at a vertex of an Eulerian trail

nodes.summary: Every finite connected simple graph in which every vertex has even degree has a closed Eulerian trail, that is, a closed walk that uses every edge of the graph exactly once.
nodes.title: Euler circuits in connected even graphs

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph and let $u$ and $v$ be non-isolated vertices of $G$, that is, vertices with at least one neighbour. If $v$ is reachable from $u$ in $G$, then $v$ is reachable from $u$ in the subgraph of $G$ induced on the set of non-isolated vertices.
nodes.title: Reachability among non-isolated vertices

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph in which every vertex has even degree, and suppose that the subgraph of $G$ induced on its non-isolated vertices is connected (in particular nonempty, so $G$ has at least one edge). Then $G$ has a closed Eulerian trail, that is, a closed walk that uses every edge of $G$ exactly once.
nodes.title: Euler circuits in simple graphs whose non-isolated vertices are connected

nodes.summary: An edge-indexed multigraph with vertex type $V$ and edge type $E$ assigns to each edge $e \in E$ an unordered pair of endpoints in $V$, such that no edge has two equal endpoints. Distinct edges may have the same endpoints, so parallel edges are distinguished by their elements of $E$.
nodes.title: Edge-indexed multigraph

nodes.summary: In an edge-indexed multigraph, an indexed walk is a walk that records which edge it traverses at each step. Indexed walks are defined inductively: for every vertex $v$ there is the empty indexed walk from $v$ to $v$, and if $e$ is an edge with endpoints $u$ and $v$ and $p$ is an indexed walk from $v$ to $w$, then traversing $e$ from $u$ to $v$ and then following $p$ is an indexed walk from $u$ to $w$.
nodes.title: Indexed walk

nodes.summary: The support of an indexed walk $p$ from $u$ to $v$ in an edge-indexed multigraph is the list of the vertices that $p$ visits, in order and with repetitions, including both endpoints: the empty walk at $w$ has support $[w]$, and a walk that starts at $u$ with an edge and continues with an indexed walk $q$ has support $u$ followed by the support of $q$.
nodes.title: Vertex list of an indexed walk

nodes.summary: The edge list of an indexed walk is the list of the edge identities it traverses, in order and with repetitions: the empty walk has the empty edge list, and the walk that traverses an edge $e$ and then follows an indexed walk $p$ has edge list $e$ followed by the edge list of $p$.
nodes.title: Edge list of an indexed walk

nodes.summary: An indexed walk $p$ in an edge-indexed multigraph is a trail when its edge list has no repeated entries, that is, $p$ traverses each edge of the multigraph at most once.
nodes.title: Indexed trail

nodes.summary: An indexed walk is a trail exactly when its edge list has no duplicates.
nodes.title: Characterization of indexed trails

nodes.summary: An indexed walk is Eulerian when it is a trail, that is, it uses no edge identity twice, and every edge identity of the multigraph occurs in its edge list.
nodes.title: Eulerian indexed walk

nodes.summary: An indexed walk is Eulerian exactly when it is a trail whose edge list contains every edge identity of the multigraph.
nodes.title: Characterization of Eulerian indexed walks

nodes.summary: The support of the empty indexed walk at a vertex $v$ is the one-element list $[v]$.
nodes.title: Support of the empty indexed walk

nodes.summary: If $e$ is an edge with endpoints $u$ and $v$ and $p$ is an indexed walk starting at $v$, then the support of the walk that traverses $e$ from $u$ to $v$ and then follows $p$ is $u$ followed by the support of $p$.
nodes.title: Support of a walk extended at the front

nodes.summary: For every vertex $v$ of an edge-indexed multigraph, the edge list of the empty indexed walk at $v$ is the empty list.
nodes.title: The empty indexed walk has no edges

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be an indexed walk from $v$ to $w$ in an edge-indexed multigraph $M$, and let $e$ be an edge of $M$ with endpoints $u$ and $v$. The edge list of the walk from $u$ to $w$ that traverses $e$ and then follows $p$ is $e$ followed by the edge list of $p$.
nodes.title: Edge list of an extended indexed walk

nodes.summary: In an edge-indexed multigraph, a vertex $v$ is incident with an edge $e$ when $v$ belongs to the unordered pair of endpoints of $e$.
nodes.title: Incidence

nodes.summary: In an edge-indexed multigraph, a vertex $v$ is incident with an edge $e$ if and only if $v$ belongs to the unordered pair of endpoints of $e$.
nodes.title: Incidence is membership in the endpoint pair

nodes.summary: The underlying simple graph of an edge-indexed multigraph $M$ with vertex set $V$ is the simple graph on $V$ whose edges are the unordered pairs $\{u, v\}$ that are the endpoint pair of some edge of $M$; such pairs have $u \ne v$ because $M$ is loopless. It forgets edge multiplicities.
nodes.title: Underlying simple graph of an edge-indexed multigraph

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an edge-indexed multigraph. Two vertices $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in the underlying simple graph of $M$ if and only if some edge $e$ of $M$ has endpoint pair $\{u, v\}$.
nodes.title: Adjacency in the underlying graph

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an edge-indexed multigraph. An indexed walk $p$ in $M$ from $u$ to $v$ yields a walk from $u$ to $v$ in the underlying simple graph of $M$ by forgetting edge identities: the empty indexed walk at $w$ goes to the empty walk at $w$, and an indexed walk that first traverses an edge $e$ with endpoints $\{u, x\}$ and then continues with an indexed walk $q$ goes to the walk that first steps from $u$ to $x$, an…
nodes.title: From an indexed walk to a walk in the underlying graph

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an edge-indexed multigraph and $p$ an indexed walk in $M$ from $u$ to $v$. The walk from $u$ to $v$ in the underlying simple graph of $M$ obtained from $p$ by forgetting edge identities visits the same vertices as $p$, in the same order: the two supports are equal as lists.
nodes.title: Forgetting edge identities preserves the vertex sequence

nodes.summary: For every indexed walk $p$ from $u$ to $v$ in an edge-indexed multigraph, the edge list of the walk in the underlying simple graph obtained from $p$ by forgetting edge identities is the list of the endpoint pairs of the edges of $p$, taken in the same order.
nodes.title: Edges of the forgetful walk

nodes.summary: For an indexed walk $p$, the walk in the underlying simple graph obtained by forgetting edge identities has the same length as $p$, namely the number of entries in the edge list of $p$.
nodes.title: Forgetting edge identities preserves length

nodes.summary: The degree of a vertex $v$ in an edge-indexed multigraph $M$ is the number of edges of $M$ incident with $v$, that is, the cardinality of the set of edges whose endpoint pair contains $v$; it is defined to be $0$ when this set is infinite.
nodes.title: Degree in an edge-indexed multigraph

nodes.summary: For every vertex $v$ of an edge-indexed multigraph $M$, the degree of $v$ equals the cardinality of the set of edges of $M$ whose endpoint pair contains $v$, where this cardinality is taken to be $0$ when the set is infinite.
nodes.title: Degree as the number of incident edges

nodes.summary: Given edge-indexed multigraphs $M$ and $N$ on the same vertex type $V$, with edge types $E$ and $F$, their disjoint sum is the edge-indexed multigraph on $V$ whose edge type is the disjoint union $E \sqcup F$, where an edge coming from $E$ has its endpoints in $M$ and an edge coming from $F$ has its endpoints in $N$.
nodes.title: Disjoint sum of edge-indexed multigraphs

nodes.summary: Let $M$ and $N$ be edge-indexed multigraphs on the same vertex type. Every edge $e$ of $M$, viewed as an edge of the disjoint sum of $M$ and $N$, has the same endpoints as in $M$.
nodes.title: Endpoints of edges from the first summand

nodes.summary: Let $M$ and $N$ be edge-indexed multigraphs on the same vertex type. Every edge $f$ of $N$, viewed as an edge of the disjoint sum of $M$ and $N$, has the same endpoints as in $N$.
nodes.title: Endpoints of edges from the second summand

nodes.summary: Let $M$ and $N$ be edge-indexed multigraphs on the same vertex type, each with finitely many edges. Then for every vertex $v$, the degree of $v$ in the disjoint sum of $M$ and $N$ equals the degree of $v$ in $M$ plus the degree of $v$ in $N$.
nodes.title: Degrees add under disjoint sums

nodes.summary: Let $M$ and $N$ be edge-indexed multigraphs on the same vertex type. If the underlying simple graph of $M$ is connected, then the underlying simple graph of the disjoint sum of $M$ and $N$ is connected.
nodes.title: Adding edges preserves connectedness

nodes.summary: In an edge-indexed multigraph with finitely many vertices and finitely many edges, the sum of the degrees of all vertices is even.
nodes.title: Handshake lemma for edge-indexed multigraphs

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an edge-indexed multigraph with finitely many vertices and finitely many edges. If the underlying simple graph of $M$ is connected and every vertex of $M$ has even degree, then there are a vertex $u$ and a closed indexed walk from $u$ to $u$ that is Eulerian, that is, it traverses every edge of $M$ exactly once.
nodes.title: Euler circuits in edge-indexed multigraphs

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an edge-indexed multigraph with finitely many vertices and finitely many edges. Suppose that the subgraph of the underlying simple graph of $M$ induced on its non-isolated vertices is connected, and that every vertex of $M$ has even degree. Then there are a vertex $u$ and a closed indexed walk from $u$ to $u$ that is Eulerian, that is, it traverses every edge of $M$ exactly once.
nodes.title: Euler circuits in edge-indexed multigraphs whose non-isolated vertices are connected

nodes.summary: The line graph of an edge-indexed multigraph is the simple graph whose vertices are the edge identities, two of them being adjacent when they are distinct and share an endpoint. In particular, parallel edges are adjacent.
nodes.title: Line graph of an edge-indexed multigraph

nodes.summary: Two edge identities $e_1$ and $e_2$ are adjacent in the line graph of an edge-indexed multigraph exactly when $e_1 \ne e_2$ and some vertex is incident with both of them.
nodes.title: Adjacency in the line graph of a multigraph

nodes.summary: For an edge-indexed multigraph with finitely many vertices and finitely many edge identities, the maximum degree is the largest degree of a vertex, and $0$ when there are no vertices.
nodes.title: Maximum degree of a multigraph

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an edge-indexed multigraph with finitely many vertices and finitely many edges. Then every vertex of $M$ has degree at most the maximum degree of $M$.
nodes.title: Degrees are bounded by the maximum degree

nodes.summary: In an edge-indexed multigraph with finitely many edges, the degree of every vertex $v$ equals the number of edges incident with $v$.
nodes.title: Degree counts incident edges
Menger's theorem

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set and let $s$ and $t$ be distinct, nonadjacent vertices of $G$. Then there is a natural number $n$ with the following two properties. First, there is a set $C$ of exactly $n$ vertices with $s \notin C$ and $t \notin C$ such that every walk from $s$ to $t$ passes through a vertex of $C$, and every set of vertices with these three properties has at least $n$ elements.…
nodes.title: Menger's theorem, vertex form

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph with vertices $s$ and $t$, and let $P_0, \dots, P_{n-1}$ be a family of paths from $s$ to $t$ in $G$, indexed by $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. The family is internally vertex-disjoint when for all indices $i \ne j$, every vertex lying on both $P_i$ and $P_j$ is $s$ or $t$.
nodes.title: Internally vertex-disjoint paths

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set, let $s$ and $t$ be vertices of $G$, and let $C$ be a set of vertices of $G$. Then $C$ is an $s$-$t$ vertex cut when $s \notin C$, $t \notin C$, and $t$ is not reachable from $s$ in the graph obtained from $G$ by deleting every edge that has an endpoint in $C$.
nodes.title: Vertex cuts separating two vertices

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set, let $s$ and $t$ be vertices of $G$, and let $C$ be a set of vertices of $G$. Then $C$ is an $s$-$t$ vertex cut if and only if $s \notin C$, $t \notin C$, and every walk from $s$ to $t$ in $G$ passes through a vertex of $C$.
nodes.title: Vertex cuts are walk separators

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set and let $s$ and $t$ be distinct, nonadjacent vertices of $G$. Then there is a natural number $k$ such that there exist $k$ internally vertex-disjoint paths from $s$ to $t$ and an $s$-$t$ vertex cut with exactly $k$ vertices, every family of internally vertex-disjoint paths from $s$ to $t$ has at most $k$ members, and every $s$-$t$ vertex cut has at least $k$…
nodes.title: Menger's theorem for vertex cuts and internally disjoint paths

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph with vertices $s$ and $t$. A family $P_0, \dots, P_{n-1}$ of paths from $s$ to $t$ in $G$ is edge-disjoint when, for all indices $i \ne j$, no edge of $P_i$ is an edge of $P_j$.
nodes.title: Edge-disjoint paths

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices of $G$. A finite set $C$ of unordered pairs of vertices is an $s$-$t$ edge cut when every element of $C$ is an edge of $G$ and $t$ is not reachable from $s$ in the graph obtained from $G$ by deleting the edges in $C$.
nodes.title: Edge cuts separating two vertices

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set and let $s$ and $t$ be distinct vertices of $G$. Then there is a natural number $k$ such that there exist $k$ edge-disjoint paths from $s$ to $t$ and an $s$-$t$ edge cut with exactly $k$ edges, every family of edge-disjoint paths from $s$ to $t$ has at most $k$ members, and every $s$-$t$ edge cut has at least $k$ edges. In words, the maximum number of edge-disjoint…
nodes.title: Menger's theorem for edge cuts and edge-disjoint paths
Reachability and connectedness

nodes.summary: In a connected graph every vertex `v ≠ s` has a neighbor `p` one step closer to `s` (a parent of `v` in a breadth-first tree rooted at `s`).
nodes.title: Parent vertex towards a root in a connected graph

nodes.summary: Two walks $p$ and $q$ in a simple graph $G$ are internally disjoint if no vertex is an interior vertex of both, where the interior vertices of a walk are the entries of its vertex sequence other than the first and the last.
nodes.title: Internally disjoint walks

nodes.summary: A simple graph $G$ is infinitely connected if it has at least two vertices and, for any two distinct vertices $u$ and $v$, there is an infinite set of paths from $u$ to $v$ in $G$ that are pairwise internally disjoint.
nodes.title: Infinitely connected graphs

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set and a set $s$ of vertices, this is the set of vertices that lie in $s$ or are adjacent to some vertex of $s$, that is, $s$ together with all neighbours of its vertices.
nodes.title: One round of breadth-first search

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set, a natural number $n$ and a set $s$ of vertices, this applies rounds of breadth-first search to $s$ (each round adds all neighbours of the current vertices), stopping after $n$ rounds or as soon as a round adds no new vertex, whichever comes first, and returns the resulting set.
nodes.title: Breadth-first search with a round limit

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$ and a vertex $u$, this is the set obtained from $\{u\}$ by breadth-first search with at most $|V|$ rounds, stopping early as soon as a round adds no new vertex.
nodes.title: Vertices reachable from a vertex
Vertex connectivity

reading_title.source: $k$-vertex-connected graph

nodes.summary: Let $k$ be a natural number. A simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$ is $k$-vertex-connected if $V$ has more than $k$ elements and, for every set $S$ of fewer than $k$ vertices, the subgraph of $G$ induced on $V \setminus S$ is connected.
nodes.title: $k$-vertex-connected graph

reading_title.source: Characterization of $k$-vertex-connectivity by vertex deletion

nodes.summary: Let $k$ be a natural number and let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$. Then $G$ is $k$-vertex-connected if and only if $V$ has more than $k$ elements and, for every set $S$ of fewer than $k$ vertices, the subgraph of $G$ induced on $V \setminus S$ is connected.
nodes.title: Characterization of $k$-vertex-connectivity by vertex deletion

reading_title.source: Vertex count of a $k$-vertex-connected graph

nodes.summary: Let $k$ be a natural number. If a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$ is $k$-vertex-connected, then $V$ has more than $k$ elements.
nodes.title: Vertex count of a $k$-vertex-connected graph

reading_title.source: Deleting fewer than $k$ vertices from a $k$-vertex-connected graph

nodes.summary: Let $k$ be a natural number and let $G$ be a $k$-vertex-connected simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$. Then for every set $S$ of fewer than $k$ vertices, the subgraph of $G$ induced on $V \setminus S$ is connected.
nodes.title: Deleting fewer than $k$ vertices from a $k$-vertex-connected graph

reading_title.source: A $k$-vertex-connected graph with $k \ge 1$ is connected

nodes.summary: Let $k \ge 1$ be a natural number. Every $k$-vertex-connected simple graph on a finite vertex set is connected.
nodes.title: A $k$-vertex-connected graph with $k \ge 1$ is connected

reading_title.source: Deleting one vertex from a $k$-vertex-connected graph with $k \ge 2$

nodes.summary: Let $k \ge 2$ be a natural number and let $G$ be a $k$-vertex-connected simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$. Then for every vertex $v$, the subgraph of $G$ induced on $V \setminus \{v\}$ is connected.
nodes.title: Deleting one vertex from a $k$-vertex-connected graph with $k \ge 2$

nodes.summary: A simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$ is 2-vertex-connected if and only if $V$ has more than two elements, $G$ is connected, and for every vertex $v$ the subgraph of $G$ induced on $V \setminus \{v\}$ is connected.
nodes.title: Characterization of 2-vertex-connected graphs

nodes.summary: Every vertex of a 2-vertex-connected simple graph on a finite vertex set has degree at least two.
nodes.title: Degrees in a 2-vertex-connected graph are at least two

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a 2-vertex-connected simple graph on a finite vertex set. Then for every vertex $x$ of $G$ there is a cycle in $G$ that starts and ends at $x$.
nodes.title: Cycles through each vertex of a 2-vertex-connected graph
Hamiltonian cycles

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph with $n \ge 3$ vertices in which every vertex has degree at least $n/2$. Then $G$ is Hamiltonian, that is, it has a cycle that visits every vertex exactly once.
nodes.title: Dirac's theorem

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$, and let $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_n$ be a list of vertices with $v_0 = v_n$ in which $v_{i-1}$ and $v_i$ are adjacent in $G$ for each $1 \le i \le n$. If $v_1, \dots, v_n$ are pairwise distinct, every vertex of $V$ is among them, and $n \ge 3$, then $G$ is Hamiltonian: it has a cycle that visits every vertex exactly once.
nodes.title: A cyclic listing of the vertices gives a Hamiltonian cycle

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$ with $|V| \ge 3$. If $\deg u + \deg v \ge |V|$ for every pair of distinct nonadjacent vertices $u$ and $v$, then $G$ is Hamiltonian.
nodes.title: Ore's theorem

nodes.summary: For every finite simple graph $G$ that is $3$-vertex-connected and straight-line planar, the prism $G \mathbin{\square} K_2$, the Cartesian product of $G$ with the complete graph on two vertices, is Hamiltonian.
nodes.title: Prism-Hamiltonicity conjecture for 3-connected planar graphs

nodes.summary: The prism-Hamiltonicity conjecture for 3-connected planar graphs is false: there is a finite simple graph $G$ that is $3$-vertex-connected and straight-line planar whose prism $G \mathbin{\square} K_2$ is not Hamiltonian.
nodes.title: Špacapan's counterexample to prism-Hamiltonicity
Square of a graph

nodes.summary: The square of a simple graph $G$ is the simple graph on the same vertex set in which two distinct vertices $u$ and $v$ are adjacent when they are adjacent in $G$ or have a common neighbor in $G$, that is, a vertex $w$ adjacent in $G$ to both $u$ and $v$.
nodes.title: Square of a graph

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$ and vertices $u$ and $v$, the vertices $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in the square of $G$ if and only if $u \ne v$ and either $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $G$ or there is a vertex $w$ with $u$ adjacent to $w$ and $w$ adjacent to $v$ in $G$.
nodes.title: Adjacency in the graph square

nodes.summary: Let $G$ and $H$ be simple graphs on the same vertex set such that every edge of $G$ is an edge of $H$. Then every edge of the square of $G$ is an edge of the square of $H$.
nodes.title: Monotonicity of the graph square

nodes.summary: If a simple graph $G$ is connected, then the square of $G$ is connected.
nodes.title: The square of a connected graph is connected

nodes.summary: Let $G$ and $H$ be simple graphs on the same finite vertex set such that every edge of $G$ is an edge of $H$. If the square of $G$ is Hamiltonian, then the square of $H$ is Hamiltonian.
nodes.title: Adding edges preserves a Hamiltonian square

nodes.summary: Let $G$ and $H$ be simple graphs on the same vertex set. Then $H$ equals the square of $G$ if and only if, for all vertices $u$ and $v$, the vertices $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $H$ exactly when $u \ne v$ and either $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $G$ or there is a vertex $w$ with $u$ adjacent to $w$ and $w$ adjacent to $v$ in $G$.
nodes.title: Characterization of the graph square

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph and let $u, w, v, x_1, \dots, x_k$ (with $k \ge 0$) be a sequence of vertices in which consecutive vertices are adjacent in $G$. If $u \ne v$, then in the sequence $u, v, x_1, \dots, x_k$ consecutive vertices are adjacent in the square of $G$.
nodes.title: Skipping a vertex of a walk in the graph square

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$, and let $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_n$ be vertices with $n \ge 3$ and $v_0 = v_n$, such that $v_1, \dots, v_n$ are pairwise distinct and every vertex of $V$ is among them. If for each $i < n$ the vertices $v_i$ and $v_{i+1}$ are distinct and either adjacent in $G$ or have a common neighbor in $G$, then the square of $G$ is Hamiltonian.
nodes.title: A cyclic listing by square adjacencies gives a Hamiltonian square

nodes.summary: In a 2-vertex-connected simple graph on a finite vertex set with at least five vertices, every vertex has at least four neighbors in the square of the graph.
nodes.title: Minimum degree in the square of a 2-connected graph
Říha's cycle lemma

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a closed walk in a simple graph $G$. A vertex $y$ is bound to $c$ when $y$ lies on $c$ and every neighbor of $y$ in $G$ lies on $c$.
nodes.title: Bound vertices of a closed walk

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a closed walk in a simple graph $G$. A vertex $y$ is bound to $c$ if and only if $y$ lies on $c$ and every neighbor of $y$ in $G$ lies on $c$.
nodes.title: Characterization of bound vertices

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite $2$-vertex-connected simple graph. Then for every vertex $x$ of $G$ there is a cycle $c$ through $x$ and a vertex $y \ne x$ that is bound to $c$: $y$ lies on $c$ and every neighbor of $y$ in $G$ lies on $c$.
nodes.title: Říha's cycle lemma
Fleischner's theorem

nodes.summary: For a set $D \subseteq V$, the collapse map sends $V$ to $D$ together with one new vertex, the contraction vertex: each $v \in D$ is sent to itself, and each $v \notin D$ is sent to the contraction vertex.
nodes.title: Collapsing the complement of a set

nodes.summary: For a set $D \subseteq V$, the collapse map from $V$ to $D$ together with the contraction vertex sends each $v \in D$ to $v$ itself.
nodes.title: The collapse map fixes the retained set

nodes.summary: For a set $D \subseteq V$, the collapse map from $V$ to $D$ together with the contraction vertex sends each vertex $v \notin D$ to the contraction vertex.
nodes.title: The collapse map sends the complement to the contraction vertex

nodes.summary: For a set $D \subseteq V$, a vertex $v \in V$ and an element $a \in D$, the collapse map from $V$ to $D$ together with the contraction vertex sends $v$ to $a$ if and only if $v = a$.
nodes.title: Preimages of retained vertices under the collapse map

nodes.summary: For a set $D \subseteq V$ and a vertex $v \in V$, the collapse map from $V$ to $D$ together with the contraction vertex sends $v$ to the contraction vertex if and only if $v \notin D$.
nodes.title: Preimage of the contraction vertex under the collapse map

nodes.summary: For a set $D \subseteq V$ whose complement $V \setminus D$ is nonempty, the collapse map from $V$ to $D$ together with the contraction vertex is surjective.
nodes.title: The collapse map is surjective

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a vertex set $V$ and let $D \subseteq V$. Contracting the complement of $D$ to a single vertex gives the simple graph whose vertices are the elements of $D$ together with one new vertex $\ast$, in which two vertices $a, b \in D$ are adjacent exactly when they are adjacent in $G$, and a vertex $a \in D$ is adjacent to $\ast$ exactly when $a$ has a neighbour in $G$ outside $D$. The new…
nodes.title: Contracting the complement of a vertex set

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a graph on $V$, let $D \subseteq V$, and contract $V \setminus D$ to a single vertex. Two vertices $a, b \in D$ are adjacent in the contracted graph if and only if they are adjacent in $G$.
nodes.title: Contraction preserves adjacency among retained vertices

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a graph on $V$, let $D \subseteq V$, and contract $V \setminus D$ to a single vertex. A vertex $a \in D$ is adjacent to the contraction vertex in the contracted graph if and only if $a$ is adjacent in $G$ to some vertex $v \notin D$.
nodes.title: Neighbors of the contraction vertex

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a 2-vertex-connected graph on a finite vertex set $V$, and let $D \subseteq V$ be a set with at least two elements that induces a connected subgraph of $G$ and whose complement $V \setminus D$ is nonempty. Then the graph obtained from $G$ by contracting $V \setminus D$ to a single vertex is 2-vertex-connected.
nodes.title: Contracting the complement preserves 2-connectivity

nodes.summary: Let $V$ be a finite set and $D \subseteq V$. If the complement $V \setminus D$ has at least two elements, then $D$ together with one new vertex has fewer elements than $V$, that is, $|D| + 1 < |V|$.
nodes.title: Cardinality bound for contracting the complement

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a graph on a finite vertex set $V$ and let $x \in V$. Then $G$ has a strong square cycle at $x$ if the square $G^2$ of $G$ has a Hamiltonian cycle that starts and ends at $x$ and whose two edges at $x$, its first and its last edge, are edges of $G$.
nodes.title: Strong square cycle at a vertex

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a graph on a finite vertex set $V$ and let $x \in V$. Then $G$ has a strong square cycle at $x$ if and only if the square $G^2$ of $G$ has a Hamiltonian cycle $p$ that starts and ends at $x$ such that $x$ is adjacent in $G$ to the second vertex of $p$ and the second-to-last vertex of $p$ is adjacent in $G$ to $x$.
nodes.title: Characterization of strong square cycles

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph that is 2-vertex-connected, that is, $G$ has at least three vertices and stays connected after deleting at most one vertex. Let $G^2$ be the square of $G$: the graph on the same vertices in which two distinct vertices are adjacent if and only if they are adjacent in $G$ or have a common neighbour in $G$. Then for every vertex $x$ of $G$, the graph $G^2$ has a Hamiltonian cycle whose…
nodes.title: Strengthened Fleischner theorem

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph that is 2-vertex-connected, that is, $G$ has at least three vertices and stays connected after deleting at most one vertex. Let $H$ be the square of $G$: the graph on the same vertices in which two distinct vertices are adjacent if and only if they are adjacent in $G$ or have a common neighbour in $G$. Then $H$ is Hamiltonian: it has a cycle that passes through every vertex exactly…

nodes.summary: Independent sets, cliques and dominating sets in graphs, with bounds on their sizes and polynomials counting them.
nodes.title: Independence, cliques and domination
Caro–Wei theorem

nodes.summary: Every finite graph has an independent set of size at least the sum over its vertices of the reciprocal of one more than the degree.
nodes.title: Caro–Wei bound

nodes.summary: For every finite simple graph $G$, the independence number of $G$ is at least $\sum_{v} \frac{1}{\deg(v) + 1}$, the sum running over all vertices $v$ of $G$.
nodes.title: Caro–Wei bound for the independence number
Dominating sets

nodes.summary: A set $S$ of vertices of a simple graph $G$ dominates $G$ when every vertex of $G$ lies in $S$ or is adjacent to some vertex of $S$.
nodes.title: Dominating set

nodes.summary: A set $S$ of vertices of a simple graph $G$ is an independent dominating set of $G$ when no two vertices of $S$ are adjacent and $S$ dominates $G$.
nodes.title: Independent dominating set

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set, the domination number of $G$ is the least number of elements of a dominating set of $G$.
nodes.title: Domination number

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set, the independent domination number of $G$ is the least number of elements of an independent dominating set of $G$.
nodes.title: Independent domination number

nodes.summary: Every finite graph has an independent dominating set.
nodes.title: Existence of independent dominating sets

nodes.summary: Every simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set has an independent dominating set whose number of elements equals the independent domination number of $G$.
nodes.title: A minimum independent dominating set exists

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set. If $S$ is an independent dominating set of $G$, then the independent domination number of $G$ is at most the number of elements of $S$.
nodes.title: Independent dominating sets are at least as large as the independent domination number

nodes.summary: Every simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set has a dominating set whose number of elements equals the domination number of $G$.
nodes.title: A minimum dominating set exists

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set. If $S$ is a dominating set of $G$, then the domination number of $G$ is at most the number of elements of $S$.
nodes.title: Dominating sets are at least as large as the domination number
Domination in rook graphs

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, the rook graph on the $n \times m$ board is the simple graph whose vertices are the cells $(i, j)$ with $0 \le i < n$ and $0 \le j < m$, in which two cells are adjacent if and only if they are distinct and lie in the same row (same $i$) or the same column (same $j$).
nodes.title: Rook graph

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, a finite set $S$ of cells of the $n \times m$ board dominates the rook graph on that board if and only if for every cell $(i, j)$, some cell of $S$ lies in row $i$ or some cell of $S$ lies in column $j$.
nodes.title: Dominating sets of the rook graph

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$, $m$ and $k$, $E_{n,m}(k)$ is the number of $k$-element sets of cells of the $n \times m$ board that contain a cell in every row and a cell in every column (Mertens' $E_{n,m}(k)$).
nodes.title: Rook placements covering all rows and columns

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$, $m$ and $k$, $d_{n,m}(k)$ is the number of $k$-element sets of cells of the $n \times m$ board that are dominating sets of the rook graph on that board (Mertens' $d_{R_{n,m}}(k)$).
nodes.title: Dominating rook placements

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, the rook domination polynomial of the $n \times m$ board is the integer polynomial $D_{n,m}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{nm} d_{n,m}(k)\, x^k$, where $d_{n,m}(k)$ is the number of $k$-element sets of cells of the $n \times m$ board that are dominating sets of the rook graph on that board.
nodes.title: Domination polynomial of the rook graph

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n, m \ge 1$ and $k$, let $d_{n,m}(k)$ be the number of $k$-element sets of cells of the $n \times m$ board that are dominating sets of the rook graph on that board, and let $E_{a,b}(k)$ be the number of $k$-element sets of cells of the $a \times b$ board that contain a cell in every row and a cell in every column. Then
nodes.title: Dominating rook placements via covering placements

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n, m \ge 1$ and $k$, let $E_{a,b}(k)$ denote the number of $k$-element sets of cells of the $a \times b$ board that contain a cell in every row and a cell in every column. Then
nodes.title: Recursion for rook placements covering all rows and columns

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n, m \ge 1$ and $k$ with $k > nm - n - m - \min(n, m) + 2$, let $d_{n,m}(k)$ be the number of $k$-element sets of cells of the $n \times m$ board that are dominating sets of the rook graph on that board. Then
nodes.title: Dominating rook placements at high density

nodes.title: Single-sum formula for the rook domination polynomial

Domination polynomials of grids

nodes.summary: A domination state is one of three labels: uncovered, covered or occupied.
nodes.title: Domination states

nodes.summary: For a finite graph $G$, the domination polynomial of $G$ is the polynomial $\sum_S z^{|S|}$ with integer coefficients, the sum running over the dominating sets $S$ of $G$.
nodes.title: Domination polynomial

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph, $S$ a finite set of vertices of $G$ and $v$ a vertex of $G$. The domination state of $v$ relative to $S$ in $G$ is occupied if $v \in S$, covered if $v \notin S$ and $v$ is adjacent in $G$ to some vertex of $S$, and uncovered otherwise.
nodes.title: Domination state of a vertex

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a simple graph on a vertex set $V$ (the row). A map $\sigma$ assigning to each vertex of $V$ a domination state (uncovered, covered or occupied) is a signature for $R$ if no uncovered vertex is adjacent in $R$ to an occupied vertex: for all vertices $i, j$ adjacent in $R$, it is not the case that $\sigma(i)$ is uncovered and $\sigma(j)$ is occupied.
nodes.title: Domination signature

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $R$ on a vertex set $V$ (the row), a signature of $R$ is a map $\sigma$ assigning to each vertex of $V$ a domination state (uncovered, covered or occupied) such that $\sigma$ is a domination signature for $R$, that is, no uncovered vertex is adjacent in $R$ to an occupied vertex. This is the type of all signatures of $R$; when $R$ is a cycle they are the paper's cyclic signatures.
nodes.title: Signatures of a row graph

nodes.summary: For a graph $R$ (the row), the all-covered signature $\sigma_\bullet$ of $R$ is the signature that gives every vertex of $R$ the state covered; it is a signature because it has no uncovered vertex.
nodes.title: All-covered signature

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a graph (the row) and let $\sigma$ and $\tau$ assign a domination state (uncovered, covered or occupied) to each vertex of $R$. The new row $\tau$ is compatible with the previous row $\sigma$ when, for every vertex $i$ of $R$: if $\sigma(i)$ is uncovered then $\tau(i)$ is occupied; if $\sigma(i)$ is occupied then $\tau(i)$ is not uncovered; and if $\tau(i)$ is covered then $\sigma(i)$ is occupied or some…
nodes.title: Compatible row signatures

nodes.summary: Let $V$ be a finite set and let $\sigma$ assign a domination state (uncovered, covered or occupied) to each element of $V$. The occupied count $\operatorname{occ}(\sigma)$ is the number of elements $i \in V$ such that $\sigma(i)$ is occupied.
nodes.title: Number of occupied vertices

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set (the row). The transfer matrix $A$ of $R$ is the matrix with entries in $\mathbb{Z}[z]$, rows indexed by the new signature $\tau$ and columns by the old signature $\sigma$, both ranging over the signatures of $R$, whose entry $A_{\tau\sigma}$ is $z^{\operatorname{occ}(\tau)}$ if $\tau$ is compatible with $\sigma$ and $0$ otherwise; here $\operatorname{occ}(\tau)$ is…
nodes.title: Domination transfer matrix

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a finite graph (the row), $n$ a natural number and $\sigma$ an assignment of a domination state to each vertex of $R$. Let $H$ be the box product of $R$ with the path on the vertices $0, \dots, n$, so that the last row of $H$ consists of the vertices $(i, n)$. Relative to a vertex set $S$ of $H$, a vertex is occupied if it lies in $S$, covered if it lies outside $S$ but is adjacent to a vertex of $S$,…
nodes.title: Almost dominating polynomial

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph, $S$ a finite set of vertices of $G$ and $v$ a vertex of $G$. Then the domination state of $v$ relative to $S$ in $G$ is occupied if and only if $v \in S$.
nodes.title: A vertex is occupied exactly when it lies in the set

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph and $S$ a finite set of vertices of $G$. Then $S$ dominates $G$ if and only if no vertex of $G$ has domination state uncovered relative to $S$ in $G$.
nodes.title: Dominating sets have no uncovered vertex

nodes.summary: For every finite graph $G$, the value at $1$ of the domination polynomial of $G$ equals the number of dominating sets of $G$.

nodes.summary: For a natural number $z$, the zero indicator of $z$ is the Boolean value that is true if $z = 0$ and false otherwise.

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a vertex type $V$ and let $A$ be a finite independent set of $G$. The characteristic vector of $A$ is the Boolean function on $V$ that sends a vertex $v$ to true if $v \in A$ and to false otherwise.
nodes.title: Characteristic vector of an independent set

nodes.summary: Let $V$ and $W$ be finite types, let $R$ be a relation between $V$ and $W$, and let $a$ and $b$ be Boolean functions on $V$ and on $W$. The pairing of $a$ and $b$ along $R$ is the natural number of pairs $(v, w) \in V \times W$ such that $R(v, w)$ holds and both $a(v)$ and $b(w)$ are true.

The transfer matrix of $G$ and $H$ along $R$ is indexed by pairs $(A, B)$ where $A$ is a finite independent set of $G$ and $B$ is a finite independent set of $H$. Independence polynomial of claw-free graphs

nodes.summary: A simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$ is claw-free if it has no induced claw $K_{1,3}$: there are no vertices $c, \ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_3 \in V$ such that $\ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_3$ are pairwise distinct, each is adjacent to $c$ and different from $c$, and no two of them are adjacent.
nodes.title: Claw-free finite graph

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a claw-free simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$, and let $I(G) = \sum_{k=0}^{|V|} i_k X^k \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ be its independence polynomial, where $i_k$ is the number of independent sets of $G$ with $k$ vertices. Then $I(G)$, viewed as a polynomial with real coefficients, splits over $\mathbb{R}$: it is a constant times a product of linear factors $X - r$ with $r \in \mathbb{R}$, so all its roots are…
nodes.title: Chudnovsky–Seymour theorem

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set. Then $G$ is claw-free if and only if the claw $K_{1,3}$, the star graph on four vertices whose center is adjacent to the other three, is not an induced subgraph of $G$, that is, there is no injective map from its vertices to those of $G$ that preserves both adjacency and nonadjacency.
nodes.title: Claw-free finite graphs have no induced claw

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$, and let $I(G) = \sum_{k=0}^{|V|} i_k X^k \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ be its independence polynomial, where $i_k$ is the number of independent sets of $G$ with $k$ vertices. Then for every natural number $k$, the coefficient of $X^k$ in $I(G)$ is the number of independent sets of $G$ with exactly $k$ vertices.
nodes.title: Coefficients of the independence polynomial

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$, and let $I(G) = \sum_{k=0}^{|V|} i_k X^k \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ be its independence polynomial, where $i_k$ is the number of independent sets of $G$ with $k$ vertices. Then for every element $x$ of a commutative ring $R$, the value of $I(G)$ at $x$ is $\sum_S x^{|S|}$, the sum running over all independent sets $S \subseteq V$ of $G$, the empty set included.
nodes.title: Evaluating the independence polynomial

nodes.summary: Let $V$ be a finite set. For a simple graph $G$ on $V$, let $I(G) = \sum_{k=0}^{|V|} i_k X^k \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ be its independence polynomial, where $i_k$ is the number of independent sets of $G$ with $k$ vertices. If $G$ is the graph on $V$ with no edges, then $I(G) = (1 + X)^{|V|}$.
nodes.title: Independence polynomial of the edgeless graph

nodes.summary: Let $V$ be a finite set. For a simple graph $G$ on $V$, let $I(G) = \sum_{k=0}^{|V|} i_k X^k \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ be its independence polynomial, where $i_k$ is the number of independent sets of $G$ with $k$ vertices. If $G$ is the complete graph on $V$, then $I(G) = 1 + |V|\,X$.
nodes.title: Independence polynomial of the complete graph

nodes.summary: A simple graph $G$ on a vertex set $V$, not necessarily finite, is claw-free if it has no induced claw $K_{1,3}$: there are no vertices $c, \ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_3 \in V$ such that $\ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_3$ are pairwise distinct, each is adjacent to $c$ and different from $c$, and no two of them are adjacent.
nodes.title: Claw-free graph

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on an arbitrary vertex set. Then $G$ is claw-free if and only if the claw $K_{1,3}$, the star graph on four vertices whose center is adjacent to the other three, is not an induced subgraph of $G$, that is, there is no injective map from its vertices to those of $G$ that preserves both adjacency and nonadjacency.
nodes.title: Claw-free graphs have no induced claw

nodes.summary: A simple graph on a finite vertex set is a claw-free finite graph if and only if it is a claw-free graph in the sense defined for graphs on arbitrary vertex sets.
nodes.title: The two definitions of claw-free agree
Maximal cliques and triangles

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$, this is the set of natural numbers $k$ such that some finite clique of $G$ with exactly $k$ vertices is maximal under inclusion among the finite cliques of $G$, that is, no finite clique of $G$ strictly contains it.
nodes.title: Sizes of maximal cliques

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set and an edge $uv$ of $G$, this is the finite set of triangles of $G$ that contain the edge $uv$, where a triangle is the vertex set of a $3$-clique of $G$; that is, the $3$-cliques of $G$ containing both $u$ and $v$.
nodes.title: Triangles containing an edge
Odd independent sets

nodes.summary: A set $S$ of vertices of a simple graph $G$ is odd independent if $S$ is an independent set of $G$ and, for every vertex $v \notin S$, the set of neighbours of $v$ that lie in $S$ is finite and is either empty or has an odd number of elements.
nodes.title: Odd independent set

nodes.summary: If $S$ is an odd independent set of a simple graph $G$, then $S$ is an independent set of $G$: no two distinct vertices of $S$ are adjacent.
nodes.title: Odd independent sets are independent

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be an odd independent set of a simple graph $G$ and let $v$ be a vertex with $v \notin S$. Then only finitely many neighbours of $v$ lie in $S$.
nodes.title: Outside vertices have finitely many neighbours in an odd independent set

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be an odd independent set of a simple graph $G$ and let $v$ be a vertex with $v \notin S$. Then the set of neighbours of $v$ that lie in $S$ is either empty or has an odd number of elements.
nodes.title: Outside vertices see an empty or odd part of an odd independent set

nodes.summary: The empty set is odd independent in any simple graph.
nodes.title: The empty set is odd independent

nodes.summary: For every vertex $a$ of a simple graph $G$, the singleton $\{a\}$ is odd independent in $G$.
nodes.title: Singletons are odd independent

Books in graphs

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph. The book number of $G$ is the maximum, over ordered pairs $(u, v)$ of adjacent vertices, of the number of common neighbors of $u$ and $v$ (the number of triangles containing the edge $uv$); it is $0$ if $G$ has no edges.
nodes.title: Book number

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph. If $u$ and $v$ are adjacent vertices of $G$, then the number of common neighbors of $u$ and $v$ is at most the book number of $G$.
nodes.title: Common neighbors of an edge are bounded by the book number

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph and $b$ a natural number. If every pair of adjacent vertices $u$, $v$ of $G$ has at most $b$ common neighbors, then the book number of $G$ is at most $b$.
nodes.title: Bounding the book number

nodes.summary: The proposition asserts that for every natural number $n$ and every simple graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with more than $n^2/4$ edges, some edge of $G$ lies in at least $n/6$ triangles of $G$.
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 905 on edges in many triangles

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$, every simple graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with more than $n^2/4$ edges has an edge that lies in at least $n/6$ triangles of $G$.
nodes.title: Edwards–Khadzhiivanov–Nikiforov theorem on edges in many triangles
Erdős–Faudree triangle conjecture

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a vertex type $V$ and let $T$ and $Y$ be finite sets of vertices. The set $Y$ is joined to two vertices of $T$ in $G$ if every vertex $y \in Y$ is adjacent in $G$ to two distinct vertices $u, v \in T$.
nodes.title: Vertices joined to two vertices of a set

nodes.summary: For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the following holds for all sufficiently large $n$: every simple graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with more than $n^2/4$ edges contains a triangle $T$ and a set $Y$ of vertices, each adjacent in $G$ to two distinct vertices of $T$, with $|Y| > (1/2 - \varepsilon)n$.
nodes.title: Erdős–Faudree triangle conjecture

nodes.summary: The proposition that the Erdős–Faudree triangle conjecture fails, that is, that it is not the case that for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ and all sufficiently large $n$, every simple graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with more than $n^2/4$ edges contains a triangle $T$ and a set $Y$ of vertices, each adjacent in $G$ to two distinct vertices of $T$, with $|Y| > (1/2 - \varepsilon)n$.
nodes.title: Negation of the Erdős–Faudree triangle conjecture

nodes.summary: For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the following holds for all sufficiently large $n$: every simple graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with more than $n^2/4$ edges contains a triangle $T$ and a set $Y$ of vertices, each adjacent in $G$ to two distinct vertices of $T$, with $|Y| \ge (1/6 - \varepsilon)n$.
nodes.title: Book lower bound for Erdős Problem 1034

nodes.summary: For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the following holds for all sufficiently large $n$: there is a simple graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with more than $n^2/4$ edges such that for every triangle $T$ of $G$, every set $Y$ of vertices each adjacent in $G$ to two distinct vertices of $T$ satisfies $|Y| \le (2 - \sqrt{5/2} + \varepsilon)n$.
nodes.title: Ma–Tang upper bound for Erdős Problem 1034

reading_title.source: $K_4$-free upper bound for Erdős Problem 1034

nodes.summary: For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the following holds for all sufficiently large $n$: there is a simple graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ that contains no $K_4$ and has more than $n^2/4$ edges, such that for every triangle $T$ of $G$, every set $Y$ of vertices each adjacent in $G$ to two distinct vertices of $T$ satisfies $|Y| \le (2\sqrt{3} - 3 + \varepsilon)n$.
nodes.title: $K_4$-free upper bound for Erdős Problem 1034

nodes.summary: It is not true that for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ and all sufficiently large $n$, every simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with more than $n^2/4$ edges contains a triangle $T$ and a set of more than $(1/2 - \varepsilon)n$ vertices, each adjacent to two distinct vertices of $T$.
nodes.title: The Erdős–Faudree triangle conjecture is false
Extremal graphs of girth five

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, $\mathrm{ex}(n; \{C_3, C_4\})$ is the largest number of edges of a simple graph on $n$ vertices whose girth is at least $5$, that is, which contains no triangle and no four-cycle (OEIS A006856). An acyclic graph has infinite girth, so the empty graph always qualifies.
nodes.title: Girth-five extremal number

nodes.summary: For $n = 1, 2, \dots, 20$ the girth-five extremal numbers $\mathrm{ex}(n; \{C_3, C_4\})$, the largest numbers of edges of a simple graph on $n$ vertices that contains no triangle and no four-cycle, are, in order, $0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 16, 18, 21, 23, 26, 28, 31, 34, 38, 41$.
nodes.title: Girth-five extremal numbers up to twenty vertices

nodes.summary: The girth-five extremal number $\mathrm{ex}(50; \{C_3, C_4\})$, the largest number of edges of a simple graph on $50$ vertices that contains no triangle and no four-cycle, equals $175$.
nodes.title: Girth-five extremal number on fifty vertices
Four-cycle-free graphs

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, let $\mathrm{ex}(n; C_4)$ be the largest number of edges of a simple graph on $n$ vertices that contains no four-cycle $C_4$ as a (not necessarily induced) subgraph. For $n = 1, 2, \dots, 20$ the values of $\mathrm{ex}(n; C_4)$ are, in order, $0, 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 11, 13, 16, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, 33, 36, 39, 42, 46$.
nodes.title: Extremal numbers of the four-cycle up to twenty vertices

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, let $\mathrm{ex}(n; C_4)$ be the largest number of edges of a simple graph on $n$ vertices that contains no four-cycle $C_4$ as a (not necessarily induced) subgraph. For every prime power $q > 13$, $\mathrm{ex}(q^2 + q + 1; C_4) = q (q + 1)^2 / 2$; the division is exact because $q (q + 1)$ is even.
nodes.title: Füredi's theorem on four-cycle-free graphs
Generalized Turán numbers

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number and let $T$ and $H$ be simple graphs, where $T$ has finitely many vertices. A copy of a graph in a graph $G$ is a subgraph of $G$ isomorphic to it, and $G$ is $H$-free if it contains no copy of $H$. The generalized Turán number $\mathrm{ex}(n, T, H)$ is the largest number of copies of $T$ in an $H$-free simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$, and is $0$ if there is no such…
nodes.title: Generalized Turán number

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number and let $T$ and $H$ be simple graphs, where $T$ has finitely many vertices. Then the generalized Turán number $\mathrm{ex}(n, T, H)$ is the supremum in $\mathbb{N}$, with the supremum of the empty family taken to be $0$, of the number of copies of $T$ in $G$ over all simple graphs $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ that contain no copy of $H$ (a subgraph isomorphic to $H$).
nodes.title: The generalized Turán number as a supremum

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number and let $T$ and $H$ be simple graphs, where $T$ has finitely many vertices. If $G$ is a simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ that contains no copy of $H$ (a subgraph isomorphic to $H$), then the number of copies of $T$ in $G$ is at most the generalized Turán number $\mathrm{ex}(n, T, H)$.
nodes.title: The generalized Turán number is an upper bound

nodes.summary: Let $n$ and $m$ be natural numbers and let $T$ and $H$ be simple graphs, where $T$ has finitely many vertices. Then the generalized Turán number $\mathrm{ex}(n, T, H)$ is at most $m$ if and only if every simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ that contains no copy of $H$ (a subgraph isomorphic to $H$) has at most $m$ copies of $T$.
nodes.title: Upper bounds for the generalized Turán number

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number and let $T$ and $H$ be simple graphs, where $T$ has finitely many vertices. If some simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ contains no copy of $H$ (a subgraph isomorphic to $H$), then some such graph $G$ has exactly $\mathrm{ex}(n, T, H)$ copies of $T$, where $\mathrm{ex}(n, T, H)$ is the generalized Turán number.
nodes.title: The generalized Turán number is attained
Graph saturation

nodes.summary: Let $F$ and $G$ be simple graphs. A pair of vertices $x, y$ of $G$ is an $F$-saturating non-edge of $G$ if $x \ne y$, $x$ and $y$ are not adjacent in $G$, and the graph $G + xy$ obtained from $G$ by adding the edge $xy$ contains a copy of $F$ (a subgraph isomorphic to $F$, not necessarily induced).
nodes.title: Saturating non-edge

reading_title.source: A saturating non-edge of an $F$-free graph creates a copy of $F$

nodes.summary: Let $F$ and $G$ be simple graphs, and let $xy$ be an $F$-saturating non-edge of $G$. If $G$ is $F$-free, that is, $G$ contains no copy of $F$, then the graph $G + xy$ obtained from $G$ by adding the edge $xy$ contains a copy of $F$, and $G$ does not.
nodes.title: A saturating non-edge of an $F$-free graph creates a copy of $F$

nodes.summary: Let $F$ and $G$ be simple graphs. The graph of $F$-saturating non-edges of $G$ is the simple graph on the vertices of $G$ whose edges are exactly the $F$-saturating non-edges of $G$.
nodes.title: Graph of saturating non-edges

nodes.summary: Let $F$ and $G$ be simple graphs such that $G$ has only finitely many $F$-saturating non-edges. Then $f_F(G)$ is the number of $F$-saturating non-edges of $G$, counted as unordered pairs $\{x, y\}$, that is, the number of edges of the graph of $F$-saturating non-edges of $G$.
nodes.title: Number of saturating non-edges

reading_title.source: $H$-saturated graphs

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a simple graph. A simple graph $G$ is $H$-saturated if $G$ is $H$-free (it contains no copy of $H$ as a subgraph) and is maximal with this property: every $H$-free simple graph $G'$ on the same vertex set as $G$ with $G \subseteq G'$ equals $G$.
nodes.title: $H$-saturated graphs

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a simple graph. A simple graph $G$ is $H$-saturated if and only if $G$ is $H$-free and every simple graph $G'$ on the same vertex set with $G \subsetneq G'$ contains a copy of $H$.
nodes.title: Saturation via strict supergraphs

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a simple graph. A simple graph $G$ is $H$-saturated if and only if $G$ is $H$-free and, for all distinct vertices $s$ and $t$ of $G$ that are not adjacent in $G$, the graph $G + st$ obtained from $G$ by adding the edge $st$ contains a copy of $H$.
nodes.title: Saturation via missing edges

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a simple graph. The complete graph on any vertex set is $H$-saturated if and only if it is $H$-free.
nodes.title: Saturation of complete graphs

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a simple graph and $n$ a natural number. The set of saturated edge counts of $H$ on $n$ vertices is the set of natural numbers $m$ such that some $H$-saturated simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ has exactly $m$ edges.
nodes.title: Edge counts of saturated graphs

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a simple graph and $n$ a natural number. The saturation number $\operatorname{sat}(n, H)$ is the minimum number of edges of an $H$-saturated simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$, and is $0$ when no such graph exists.
nodes.title: Saturation number

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a simple graph, $n$ a natural number, and $\operatorname{sat}(n, H)$ the saturation number of $H$ on $n$ vertices. If the set of saturated edge counts of $H$ on $n$ vertices is empty, that is, no $H$-saturated simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ exists, then $\operatorname{sat}(n, H) = 0$.
nodes.title: The saturation number is zero when no saturated graph exists

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a simple graph, $n$ a natural number, and $\operatorname{sat}(n, H)$ the saturation number of $H$ on $n$ vertices. Every $H$-saturated simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ has at least $\operatorname{sat}(n, H)$ edges.
nodes.title: Saturated graphs bound the saturation number

nodes.summary: Attainment: when a saturated graph exists, some saturated graph has exactly `sat(n, H)` edges.
nodes.title: Saturation number is attained by a saturated graph

Turán problems in the hypercube

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, the $n$-dimensional hypercube $Q_n$ is the simple graph whose vertices are the functions from $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ to the Booleans $\{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$, with an edge between two vertices exactly when they differ in exactly one coordinate.
nodes.title: Hypercube graph

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$ and all vertices $x, y$ of the $n$-dimensional hypercube $Q_n$ (functions from $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ to the Booleans), $x$ and $y$ are adjacent in $Q_n$ if and only if there is exactly one coordinate $i$ with $x_i \ne y_i$.
nodes.title: Adjacency in the hypercube

nodes.summary: For all vertices $x, y$ of the $0$-dimensional hypercube $Q_0$, $x$ and $y$ are not adjacent in $Q_0$.

nodes.title: Subgraphs of the hypercube have at most as many edges

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$ and a simple graph $H$, let $Q_n$ be the $n$-dimensional hypercube. If $S$ is a subgraph of $Q_n$ that contains no copy of $H$, then $S$ has at most $\mathrm{ex}(Q_n, H)$ edges.

If $Q_n$ has at least one subgraph (not necessarily spanning) that contains no copy of $H$, then some subgraph $S$ of $Q_n$ contains no copy of $H$ and has exactly $\mathrm{ex}(Q_n, H)$ edges.

nodes.summary: Let $G$ and $H$ be graphs on the same vertex set $V$. Then $G$ is a unique subgraph of $H$ if exactly one subgraph of $H$ is isomorphic to $G$. Here a subgraph of $H$ means a spanning subgraph: a graph on $V$ all of whose edges are edges of $H$ (not necessarily induced).
nodes.title: Unique subgraph

nodes.title: Number of unique subgraphs

nodes.summary: For a graph $H$ on a finite vertex set, let $u(H)$ be the number of spanning subgraphs of $H$ that are isomorphic to no other spanning subgraph of $H$ (its unique subgraphs). The statement is that there is a real constant $c > 0$ such that for infinitely many $n$ some graph $H$ on $n$ vertices has $u(H) \ge c \cdot 2^{\binom{n}{2}} / n!$.

This is the proposition that there is no real constant $c > 0$ such that for infinitely many $n$ some graph $H$ on $n$ vertices has $u(H) \ge c \cdot 2^{\binom{n}{2}} / n!$.

Chromatic symmetric function

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$, let $k$ be a natural number and let $m : \{0, \dots, k-1\} \to \mathbb{N}$. The chromatic profile count of $G$ at $k$ and $m$ is the number of proper colorings $c : V \to \{0, \dots, k-1\}$ of $G$ such that for every color $i$, exactly $m(i)$ vertices $v$ satisfy $c(v) = i$.
nodes.title: Chromatic profile count

nodes.summary: Let $G$ and $H$ be simple graphs on finite vertex sets. We say that $G$ and $H$ have the same chromatic symmetric function when, for every natural number $k$ and every $m : \{0, \dots, k-1\} \to \mathbb{N}$, the chromatic profile count of $G$ at $k$ and $m$ equals that of $H$: both graphs have equally many proper colorings with colors $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$ in which each color $i$ is used on exactly $m(i)$ vertices.
nodes.title: Graphs with the same chromatic symmetric function

nodes.summary: Every simple graph on a finite vertex set has the same chromatic symmetric function as itself.
nodes.title: Reflexivity of having the same chromatic symmetric function

nodes.summary: Let $G$ and $H$ be simple graphs on finite vertex sets. If $G$ has the same chromatic symmetric function as $H$, then $H$ has the same chromatic symmetric function as $G$.
nodes.title: Symmetry of having the same chromatic symmetric function

nodes.summary: Let $G$, $H$ and $K$ be simple graphs on finite vertex sets. If $G$ has the same chromatic symmetric function as $H$, and $H$ has the same chromatic symmetric function as $K$, then $G$ has the same chromatic symmetric function as $K$.
nodes.title: Transitivity of having the same chromatic symmetric function

nodes.summary: If $G$ and $H$ are isomorphic simple graphs on finite vertex sets, then $G$ and $H$ have the same chromatic symmetric function.
