Edge-graceful labelings

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$, let $q$ be a natural number and let $\ell$ be a bijection from the edge set of $G$ to $\{0, 1, \dots, q-1\}$. The incident-edge sum at a vertex $v$ is $\sum_{e \ni v} (\ell(e) + 1)$, the sum over the edges $e$ of $G$ that contain $v$; in other words, the edges carry the labels $1, \dots, q$.
nodes.title: Incident-edge sum

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$, let $q$ be a natural number and let $\ell$ be a bijection from the edge set of $G$ to $\{0, \dots, q-1\}$. The induced residue of a vertex $v$ is the incident-edge sum at $v$ (with edge labels $\ell(e) + 1$) reduced modulo $|V|$, viewed as an element of $\{0, \dots, |V| - 1\}$. When $|V| = 0$ there are no vertices, so there is nothing to define.
nodes.title: Induced vertex residue

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite nonempty vertex set $V$, let $q$ be a natural number and let $\ell$ be a bijection from the edge set of $G$ to $\{0, \dots, q-1\}$. For every vertex $v$, the induced residue of $v$ with respect to $\ell$, read as a natural number, equals the incident-edge sum at $v$ with respect to $\ell$ modulo $|V|$.
nodes.title: Value of the induced residue

nodes.summary: A simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$ is edge-graceful when there are a natural number $q$ and a bijection $\ell$ from the edge set of $G$ to $\{0, \dots, q-1\}$ such that the induced residue map, sending each vertex $v$ to the sum of $\ell(e) + 1$ over the edges $e$ containing $v$ taken modulo $|V|$, is a bijection from $V$ to $\{0, \dots, |V| - 1\}$.
nodes.title: Edge-graceful graph

nodes.summary: A simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$ is edge-graceful if and only if there are a natural number $q$, a bijection $\ell$ from the edge set of $G$ to $\{0, \dots, q-1\}$ and a bijection $\lambda$ from $V$ to $\{0, \dots, |V| - 1\}$ such that for every vertex $v$, $\lambda(v)$ is the induced residue of $v$ with respect to $\ell$ and, if $V$ is nonempty, $\lambda(v)$ equals the incident-edge sum at $v$ with…

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$, the induced forest number $a(G)$ is the maximum number of vertices of an induced forest in $G$, that is, the maximum cardinality of a set $S \subseteq V$ such that the subgraph of $G$ induced on $S$ is acyclic.
nodes.title: Induced forest number

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$. For every set $S \subseteq V$ such that the subgraph of $G$ induced on $S$ is acyclic, $|S|$ is at most the induced forest number of $G$.

Nash-Williams arboricity theorem

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph and $k$ a natural number. A labeling of the edges of $G$ with labels in $\{0, 1, \dots, k - 1\}$ is an arboricity coloring when, for each label $i$, the graph on the vertices of $G$ whose edges are the edges of $G$ labeled $i$ is acyclic, that is, a forest.
nodes.title: Arboricity colorings

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$ and let $k$ be a natural number. Then $G$ has an arboricity coloring with $k$ labels, that is, its edges can be labeled with $k$ labels so that the edges of each label form a forest, if and only if for every nonempty set $U \subseteq V$, the number of edges of $G$ with both endpoints in $U$ is at most $k(|U| - 1)$.

nodes.summary: Let $q$ and $n$ be natural numbers. A finite set $A$ of words of length $n$ over $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ is an independent code for the $q$-cycle when every difference $x = a_1 - a_2$ with $a_1, a_2 \in A$ whose coordinates all lie in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$ is the zero word. For $q \ge 3$ this says exactly that $A$ is an independent set in the $n$-th strong power of the cycle graph $C_q$.
nodes.title: Independent codes for the modular cycle

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $q$ and $n$, a cycle code of length $n$ modulo $q$ is a finite set of words of length $n$ over $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ that is an independent code for the $q$-cycle.
nodes.title: Cycle codes

nodes.summary: For every nonzero natural number $q$ and every natural number $n$, there are only finitely many cycle codes of length $n$ modulo $q$.
nodes.title: Finitely many cycle codes of each length

nodes.summary: For a natural number $q$, a positive integer $n$ and a cycle code $A$ of length $n$ modulo $q$, the rate of $A$ is $|A|^{1/n}$, the $n$-th root of the number of codewords of $A$, taken in the extended nonnegative reals $[0, \infty]$.
nodes.title: Rate of a cycle code

nodes.summary: For a natural number $q$, the Shannon capacity of the $q$-cycle is the supremum, in $[0, \infty]$, of the rates $|A|^{1/n}$ over all positive integers $n$ and all cycle codes $A$ of length $n$ modulo $q$.
nodes.title: Shannon capacity of the modular cycle

nodes.summary: For every natural number $q$, every positive integer $n$ and every cycle code $A$ of length $n$ modulo $q$, the rate of $A$ is at most the Shannon capacity of the $q$-cycle.
nodes.title: Code rates are at most the cycle capacity

nodes.summary: Let $q$, $n$ and $M$ be natural numbers with $n \ge 1$. nodes.summary: A BPZ profile is an arbitrary quadruple of integers, called its code, pairs, auxiliary and neutral coordinates: the four integer coordinates propagated by the valid-tuple product of Buys, Polak and Zuiddam. No validity condition is imposed on the quadruple.

nodes.summary: For $i = 1, 2$ let $p_i = (c_i, \pi_i, a_i, z_i)$ be a BPZ profile, with integer code, pairs, auxiliary and neutral coordinates. The product $p_1 \star p_2$ is the BPZ profile with code coordinate $(c_1 - \pi_1)(c_2 - \pi_2) + a_1 \pi_2 + \pi_1 a_2$, pairs coordinate $z_1 \pi_2 + \pi_1 z_2$, auxiliary coordinate $a_1 a_2$ and neutral coordinate $z_1 z_2 + (a_1 - z_1)(a_2 - z_2)$.

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph with vertex set $V$ and let $k$ be a natural number. The $k$-th strong power $G^{\boxtimes k}$ is the simple graph whose vertices are the words $x = (x_1, \dots, x_k) \in V^k$ of length $k$, in which two words $x$ and $y$ are adjacent (confusable) when $x \neq y$ and for every $i$ either $x_i = y_i$ or $x_i$ and $y_i$ are adjacent in $G$.
nodes.title: Strong power of a graph

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set and let $\theta$ be a real number. For $k \ge 1$ let $G^{\boxtimes k}$ be the $k$-th strong power of $G$ and $\alpha(G^{\boxtimes k})$ its independence number. The graph $G$ has Shannon capacity $\theta$ when $\alpha(G^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k} \to \theta$ as $k \to \infty$.
nodes.title: Shannon capacity of a graph

nodes.summary: The cycle graph $C_5$ on five vertices has Shannon capacity $\sqrt{5}$: writing $\alpha(C_5^{\boxtimes k})$ for the independence number of the $k$-th strong power of $C_5$, we have $\alpha(C_5^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k} \to \sqrt{5}$ as $k \to \infty$.
nodes.title: Lovász's theorem: the Shannon capacity of the pentagon

nodes.title: Directed graphs and tournaments
Connectivity of directed graphs

nodes.summary: A directed path in a digraph $D$ is a finite, possibly empty, sequence of vertices of $D$ with no vertex repeated in which each vertex is joined to the next by an arc of $D$.
nodes.title: Directed paths

nodes.summary: The internal vertices of a path given as a vertex list (all but the first and the last).
nodes.title: Internal vertices of a path

nodes.summary: Let $D$ be a digraph, $r$ a natural number and $y$, $x$ vertices of $D$. We write $\kappa(y, x) \ge r$ when there are $r$ pairwise distinct directed paths in $D$ from $y$ to $x$, no two of which share an internal vertex. Here a directed path from $y$ to $x$ is a sequence of distinct vertices starting at $y$ and ending at $x$ in which each vertex is joined to the next by an arc of $D$, and its internal vertices are…

Dichromatic number

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a vertex set $V$. A binary relation $D$ on $V$ is an orientation of $G$ if $D(u, v)$ holds only when $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $G$, and for every pair of adjacent vertices $u$ and $v$ exactly one of $D(u, v)$ and $D(v, u)$ holds.
nodes.title: Orientations of a graph

nodes.summary: Let $D$ be a binary relation on a set $V$, viewed as a digraph, let $n$ be a natural number, and let $f_0, f_1, \dots, f_{n+1}$ be elements of $V$. The sequence $(f_0, \dots, f_{n+1})$ is a closed directed walk of length $n + 1$ in $D$ if $f_0 = f_{n+1}$ and $D(f_i, f_{i+1})$ holds for every $i$ with $0 \le i \le n$.
nodes.title: Closed directed walks

reading_title.source: Dichromatically $k$-colourable graphs

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a vertex set $V$ and let $k$ be a natural number. Then $G$ is dichromatically $k$-colourable if for every orientation $D$ of $G$ there is a map $c \colon V \to \{0, \dots, k - 1\}$, not required to be a proper colouring, such that no closed directed walk of positive length in $D$ has all of its vertices of the same colour under $c$.
nodes.title: Dichromatically $k$-colourable graphs

nodes.summary: The dichromatic number of a simple graph $G$ is the least natural number $k$ such that $G$ is dichromatically $k$-colourable, taken in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$; it is $\infty$ if $G$ is dichromatically $k$-colourable for no natural number $k$.
nodes.title: Dichromatic number

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph. If $G$ is dichromatically $n$-colourable for some natural number $n$, then the dichromatic number of $G$ equals the least natural number $k$ such that $G$ is dichromatically $k$-colourable.
nodes.title: The dichromatic number as a least natural number

nodes.summary: If a simple graph $G$ has no edges, then the empty relation on its vertex set, the digraph with no arcs, is an orientation of $G$.
nodes.title: The empty orientation of an edgeless graph

reading_title.source: Edgeless graphs are dichromatically $1$-colourable

nodes.summary: If a simple graph $G$ has no edges, then $G$ is dichromatically $1$-colourable.
nodes.title: Edgeless graphs are dichromatically $1$-colourable
Labeled directed graphs

nodes.summary: A labeled directed graph with vertex set $V$, edge set $E$ and label set $L$ consists of a source map $s : E \to V$, a target map $t : E \to V$ and a label map $\ell : E \to L$; the edge $e$ goes from $s(e)$ to $t(e)$ and carries the label $\ell(e)$. Loops and parallel edges are allowed.
nodes.title: Labeled directed graph

nodes.summary: Two labeled directed graphs $G$ and $H$ with the same vertex set, edge set and label set are equal if they have the same source map, the same target map and the same label map.
nodes.title: Extensionality for labeled directed graphs

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a labeled directed graph with vertex set $V$ and label set $L$, and let $p$ be a predicate on $V$. The restriction of $G$ to $p$ is the labeled directed graph with label set $L$ whose vertices are the vertices $v$ of $G$ with $p(v)$, whose edges are the edges of $G$ whose source and target both satisfy $p$, and in which each edge has the same source, target and label as in $G$.
nodes.title: Restriction of a labeled directed graph

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a labeled directed graph, $p$ a predicate on its vertices, and $e$ an edge of $G$ whose source and target satisfy $p$, viewed as an edge of the restriction of $G$ to $p$. The source of $e$ in the restriction, viewed as a vertex of $G$, is the source of $e$ in $G$.
nodes.title: Source of an edge in a restriction

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a labeled directed graph, $p$ a predicate on its vertices, and $e$ an edge of $G$ whose source and target satisfy $p$, viewed as an edge of the restriction of $G$ to $p$. The target of $e$ in the restriction, viewed as a vertex of $G$, is the target of $e$ in $G$.
nodes.title: Target of an edge in a restriction

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a labeled directed graph, $p$ a predicate on its vertices, and $e$ an edge of $G$ whose source and target satisfy $p$, viewed as an edge of the restriction of $G$ to $p$. The label of $e$ in the restriction is its label in $G$.
nodes.title: Label of an edge in a restriction
Modular orientations

nodes.summary: Consider a multigraph with vertex set $V$ and edge set $E$ in which each edge has a first and a second endpoint. For a set $S \subseteq V$, an edge crosses the cut at $S$ when exactly one of its two endpoints lies in $S$.
nodes.title: Edges crossing a cut

nodes.summary: Consider a multigraph with finitely many edges in which each edge has a first and a second endpoint. For a set $S$ of vertices, the size of the cut at $S$ is the number of edges crossing it, that is, having exactly one endpoint in $S$. Distinct parallel edges are counted separately.
nodes.title: Size of a cut

nodes.summary: For a natural number $k$, a finite multigraph is $4k$-edge-connected when it has at least two vertices and, for every set $S$ of vertices such that both $S$ and its complement are nonempty, at least $4k$ edges cross the cut at $S$, that is, have exactly one endpoint in $S$. Parallel edges are counted separately. For $k \ge 1$ the condition implies that the multigraph is connected.
nodes.title: 4k-edge-connected multigraphs

nodes.summary: Each edge $e$ of the multigraph has a reference direction from its first endpoint to its second endpoint, and an orientation chooses for each edge whether to reverse it. The tail of $e$ is its first endpoint if $e$ is not reversed and its second endpoint if $e$ is reversed.
nodes.title: Tail of an oriented edge

nodes.summary: Each edge $e$ of the multigraph has a reference direction from its first endpoint to its second endpoint, and an orientation chooses for each edge whether to reverse it. The head of $e$ is its second endpoint if $e$ is not reversed and its first endpoint if $e$ is reversed.
nodes.title: Head of an oriented edge

nodes.summary: In a multigraph with finitely many edges and a chosen orientation, the indegree of a vertex $v$ is the number of edges whose head is $v$, parallel edges counted separately.
nodes.title: Indegree

nodes.summary: In a multigraph with finitely many edges and a chosen orientation, the outdegree of a vertex $v$ is the number of edges whose tail is $v$, parallel edges counted separately.
nodes.title: Outdegree

nodes.summary: For a natural number $k$, an orientation of a multigraph with finitely many edges is a modulo $(2k+1)$ orientation when at every vertex the indegree minus the outdegree is congruent to $0$ modulo $2k + 1$.
nodes.title: Modular orientations

nodes.summary: This is the statement that for every integer $k \ge 1$, every finite multigraph (loops and parallel edges allowed) that has at least two vertices, and in which every partition of the vertices into two nonempty sets is crossed by at least $4k$ edges, admits an orientation of its edges in which, at every vertex, the indegree minus the outdegree is divisible by $2k + 1$.
nodes.title: Jaeger's modular orientation conjecture

nodes.summary: There exist an integer $k \ge 1$ and a finite multigraph (loops and parallel edges allowed) with at least two vertices, in which every partition of the vertices into two nonempty sets is crossed by at least $4k$ edges, such that no orientation of the edges makes the indegree minus the outdegree of every vertex divisible by $2k + 1$.
nodes.title: Jaeger's modular orientation conjecture is false

Suppose that the graph is strongly connected (for all $u, v \in V$ there is a directed walk, possibly of length $0$, from $u$ to $v$), aperiodic (for every integer $d > 1$ there is a closed directed walk of positive length not divisible by $d$), and of constant positive…

Suppose that the graph is strongly connected (for all $u, v \in V$ there is a directed walk, possibly of length $0$, from $u$ to $v$), aperiodic (for every integer $d > 1$ there is a closed directed walk of positive length not divisible by $d$), and of constant positive…

Robbins' theorem

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite nonempty vertex set $V$. Then $G$ is connected and, after deleting any single edge of $G$, every vertex is still reachable from every vertex (that is, $G$ is 2-edge-connected) if and only if $G$ has a strongly connected orientation: a relation $D$ on $V$ such that $D(u, v)$ holds only when $u$ and $v$ are adjacent, for every edge $uv$ exactly one of $D(u, v)$ and $D(v, u)$…
nodes.title: Robbins' theorem

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite, possibly empty, vertex set $V$. Then every vertex of $G$ is reachable from every vertex and, after deleting any single edge of $G$, every vertex is still reachable from every vertex, if and only if $G$ has a strongly connected orientation: a relation $D$ on $V$ such that $D(u, v)$ holds only when $u$ and $v$ are adjacent, for every edge $uv$ exactly one of $D(u, v)$ and…
nodes.title: Robbins' theorem, allowing the empty graph
Tournaments and score sequences

nodes.summary: A tournament on the players $1, \dots, n$ is a binary relation $T$, where $T(i, j)$ means that $i$ beats $j$, such that no player beats itself and for any two distinct players $i$ and $j$ exactly one of $T(i, j)$ and $T(j, i)$ holds.
nodes.title: Tournament

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a binary relation on the players $1, \dots, n$, where $T(i, j)$ means that $i$ beats $j$. The score of a player $i$ is the number of players $j$ such that $T(i, j)$ holds, that is, the number of players that $i$ beats.
nodes.title: Score of a player

nodes.summary: A tournament is reducible if some nonempty proper set of players loses all games against the complement.
nodes.title: Reducible tournament

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a binary relation on the players $1, \dots, n$, where $T(i, j)$ means that $i$ beats $j$. A set $S$ of players is a circular triad of $T$ if $S$ has exactly three elements and every $i \in S$ beats exactly one $j \in S$.
nodes.title: Circular triad

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $a$ and $b$, let $g(n) = n! \binom{n-a+b}{b}$ for $n \ge a$ and $g(n) = 0$ for $n < a$, and let $A(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} g(n) x^n / n!$ be its exponential generating function, a formal power series over $\mathbb{Q}$. Then $(1 - x)^{b+1} A(x) = x^a$; equivalently, $A(x) = x^a (1 - x)^{-(b+1)}$.
nodes.title: Exponential generating function of a shifted binomial sequence

nodes.summary: Let $s_1 \le s_2 \le \dots \le s_n$ be a nondecreasing sequence of natural numbers. There is a tournament on $n$ players in which player $i$ has score $s_i$ for every $i$ if and only if $\sum_{i=1}^{k} s_i \ge \binom{k}{2}$ for every $k$ with $1 \le k \le n$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n} s_i = \binom{n}{2}$.
nodes.title: Landau's theorem on score sequences

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a tournament on $n$ players in which the score $s_i$ of player $i$ satisfies $s_1 \le s_2 \le \dots \le s_n$. Then $T$ is reducible if and only if $\sum_{i=1}^{k} s_i = \binom{k}{2}$ for some integer $k$ with $1 \le k < n$.
nodes.title: Moon's reducibility criterion

nodes.summary: In a tournament on $n$ players with scores $s_1, \dots, s_n$, the number of circular triads is $\binom{n}{3} - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \binom{s_i}{2}$.
nodes.title: Moon's count of circular triads
Transitive subtournaments

nodes.summary: Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A relation $T$ on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is a tournament when $T(x, x)$ holds for no $x$ and, for all distinct $x$ and $y$, exactly one of $T(x, y)$ and $T(y, x)$ holds.
nodes.title: Tournaments

nodes.summary: Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $T$ be a relation on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $S$ be a set of its elements. Then $T$ is transitive on $S$ when, for all $x, y, z \in S$, $T(x, y)$ and $T(y, z)$ imply $T(x, z)$. For a tournament $T$ this says that the subtournament of $T$ on $S$ is transitive.
nodes.title: Transitivity on a vertex set

nodes.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $f(n)$ is the largest $m$ such that every tournament $T$ on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is transitive on some set of exactly $m$ vertices, that is, contains a transitive subtournament on $m$ vertices.
nodes.title: Transitive subtournament number

nodes.summary: For every $n \ge 1$, $f(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$, where $f(n)$ is the largest $m$ such that every tournament on $n$ vertices contains a transitive subtournament on $m$ vertices.
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 1216 (the Erdős–Moser formula)

nodes.summary: It is not the case that $f(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$ for every $n \ge 1$, where $f(n)$ is the largest $m$ such that every tournament on $n$ vertices contains a transitive subtournament on $m$ vertices.
nodes.title: Erdős Problem 1216 is false

nodes.summary: The backward arcs of $T^*$. The list of ordered pairs $(5, 0)$, $(5, 2)$, $(4, 1)$, $(3, 0)$ of vertices in $\{0, \dots, 5\}$. These are the arcs of the six-vertex tournament $T^*$ that go from a larger to a smaller vertex: $6 \to 1$, $6 \to 3$, $5 \to 2$ and $4 \to 1$ in the source's labelling $1, \dots, 6$, with every vertex lowered by one.
nodes.title: The backward arcs of $T^*$

reading_title.source: The six-vertex tournament $T^*$

nodes.summary: The six-vertex tournament $T^*$. The tournament $T^*$ is the relation on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, 5\}$ with an arc $i \to j$ if and only if either $(i, j)$ is one of the backward arcs $(5, 0)$, $(5, 2)$, $(4, 1)$, $(3, 0)$, or $i < j$ and $(j, i)$ is not a backward arc.
nodes.title: The six-vertex tournament $T^*$

reading_title.source: Containing $T^*$ as a subtournament

nodes.summary: Containing $T^*$ as a subtournament. A relation $T$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ contains $T^*$ when there is an injective map $f$ from the vertex set $\{0, \dots, 5\}$ of $T^*$ to $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ such that for all vertices $i, j$ of $T^*$, $i \to j$ in $T^*$ if and only if $T(f(i), f(j))$ holds.
nodes.title: Containing $T^*$ as a subtournament

parts: The Erdős–Hajnal problem for the tournament
reading_title.source: The Erdős–Hajnal problem for the tournament $T^*$

nodes.summary: The Erdős–Hajnal problem for the tournament $T^*$. There is a real number $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for every natural number $n$ and every tournament $T$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ that does not contain $T^*$ as a subtournament, there is a set $S$ of vertices on which $T$ is transitive with $|S| \ge n^{\varepsilon}$.
nodes.title: The Erdős–Hajnal problem for the tournament $T^*$

reading_title.source: Nguyen–Scott–Seymour: $T^*$ has the Erdős–Hajnal property

nodes.summary: Nguyen–Scott–Seymour: $T^*$ has the Erdős–Hajnal property. Binary encoding of CNF formulas

nodes.summary: On a list of Booleans that begins with $k$ copies of $\mathrm{true}$ followed by $\mathrm{false}$, the reader returns $k$ together with the rest of the list after that $\mathrm{false}$. On a list containing no $\mathrm{false}$, including the empty list, it fails.
nodes.title: Reading a unary length prefix

nodes.summary: The code of $n \in \mathbb{N}$ is the self-delimiting block of the binary representation of $n$ (least significant bit first, with $0$ represented by the empty list): each bit $c$ is written as the two bits $\mathrm{true}, c$, and the block ends with a terminating $\mathrm{false}$.
nodes.title: Prefix-free code of a natural number

nodes.summary: Given a bit string $w$, writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, the decoder reads one self-delimiting block $1\,b_1\,1\,b_2 \cdots 1\,b_k\,0$ from the front of $w$, with payload $b_1 \cdots b_k$ and remaining bits $r$. If the payload is the binary expansion of some natural number $n$, least significant bit first and without trailing zeros (empty for $n = 0$), the result is $(n, r)$. Decoding fails if $w$ does not…
nodes.title: Decoding a prefix-coded natural number

nodes.summary: A literal $(n, b)$, with variable index $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and polarity $b \in \{\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true}\}$, is encoded as the prefix-free code of $n$ followed by the single bit $b$.
nodes.title: Binary code of a literal

nodes.summary: Given a bit string $w$, the decoder reads a prefix-coded natural number $n$ from the front of $w$ and then one more bit $b$. The result is the literal $(n, b)$, with variable index $n$ and polarity $b$, together with the bits left after $b$. Decoding fails if no prefix-coded natural number can be read or no bit follows it.
nodes.title: Decoding a literal

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$ and a bit string $w$, the decoder reads $n$ literals one after another from the front of $w$ with the literal decoder. The result is the clause made of these literals, in order, together with the bits left after them; for $n = 0$ it is the empty clause together with $w$. Decoding fails if one of the $n$ literals cannot be read.
nodes.title: Decoding a fixed number of literals

nodes.summary: Writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, the code of a clause $C = (\ell_1, \dots, \ell_k)$ is $1^k 0$ ($k$ ones followed by a zero) followed by the binary codes of $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_k$ in order, where a literal $(x, b)$ with variable index $x$ and polarity $b$ is coded by the prefix-free code of $x$ followed by the bit $b$.
nodes.title: Length-prefixed binary code of a clause

nodes.summary: Given a bit string $w$, writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, the decoder reads a unary length prefix $1^n 0$ ($n$ ones followed by a zero) from the front of $w$, then reads exactly $n$ literals from the remaining bits with the literal decoder. The result is the clause made of these literals, in order, together with the bits left after them. Decoding fails if $w$ does not begin with such a prefix or one of the…
nodes.title: Decoding a length-prefixed clause

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$ and a bit string $w$, the decoder reads $n$ clauses one after another from the front of $w$ with the length-prefixed clause decoder. The result is the CNF formula made of these clauses, in order, together with the bits left after them; for $n = 0$ it is the empty formula together with $w$. Decoding fails if one of the $n$ clauses cannot be read.
nodes.title: Decoding a fixed number of clauses

nodes.summary: Writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, the code of a CNF formula $\varphi = (C_1, \dots, C_m)$ is $1^m 0$ ($m$ ones followed by a zero) followed by the length-prefixed binary codes of the clauses $C_1, \dots, C_m$ in order.
nodes.title: Length-prefixed binary code of a CNF formula

nodes.summary: Given a bit string $w$, writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, the decoder reads a unary length prefix $1^n 0$ ($n$ ones followed by a zero) from the front of $w$, then reads exactly $n$ clauses from the remaining bits with the length-prefixed clause decoder. nodes.title: Decoding a length-prefixed CNF formula

nodes.summary: Given a bit string $w$, the decoder reads one CNF formula $\varphi$ from the front of $w$ with the length-prefixed CNF decoder, which also returns the bits left after $\varphi$. The result is $\varphi$ if no bits are left; decoding fails if no formula can be read or if bits remain after it.
nodes.title: Decoding a complete length-prefixed CNF formula

nodes.summary: For all lists of Booleans $u$, $p$ and $r$, parsing one self-delimiting block from the front of $u$ succeeds with payload $p$ and remainder $r$ if and only if $u$ is the self-delimiting block of $p$ followed by $r$.
nodes.title: Parsing a self-delimiting block

nodes.summary: For every bit string $w$ and every CNF formula $\varphi$, the complete CNF decoder returns $\varphi$ on input $w$ if and only if $w$ is the length-prefixed binary code of $\varphi$.

nodes.summary: A list $x$ of Booleans encodes a satisfiable CNF formula when $x$ is the binary code of some CNF formula $\varphi$ and $\varphi$ is satisfiable.

nodes.summary: SAT is the set of lists of Booleans that encode a satisfiable CNF formula.

nodes.summary: A clause is a finite list of slots, where slot $j$ records how the variable $x_j$ occurs: the slot is either empty (the variable is absent) or holds a Boolean $b$, meaning the literal $x_j = b$; so $b$ true gives $x_j$ and $b$ false gives $\lnot x_j$.

nodes.summary: A CNF formula is a finite list of dense clauses, read as the conjunction of its clauses.
nodes.title: Dense CNF formula

nodes.summary: A finite bit sequence $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ satisfies a clause $c$ when there are an index $j$ and a Boolean $b$ such that slot $j$ of $c$ holds the literal $x_j = b$, $j < n$, and $a_j = b$. Variables $x_j$ with $j \ge n$ are unassigned and satisfy no literal.
nodes.title: Satisfaction of a dense clause

nodes.summary: A finite bit sequence $a$ satisfies a CNF formula $\varphi$ when $a$ satisfies every clause of $\varphi$.
nodes.title: Satisfaction of a dense CNF formula

nodes.summary: The CNF formula decoded from a bit string $w$ is the result of the accumulator decoding of $w$ started with no slots read for the current clause: $w$ is read two bits at a time, $00$ ends a clause, $01$ is an empty slot, $10$ a positive and $11$ a negative literal, and a trailing unterminated clause and a dangling odd bit are ignored.
nodes.title: Dense decoding of CNF formulas

nodes.summary: Slot $j$ of a dense clause is empty (variable $x_j$ is absent), holds the positive literal $x_j$, or holds the negative literal $\neg x_j$. Its code is $01$ when empty, $10$ for the positive literal and $11$ for the negative literal.
nodes.title: Two-bit code of a slot

nodes.summary: The bit string encoding a clause is the concatenation of the two-bit codes of its slots, in order (empty slot $01$, positive literal $10$, negative literal $11$), followed by the terminator $00$.
nodes.title: Dense encoding of a clause

nodes.summary: The dense encoding of a CNF formula $\varphi$ is the bit string obtained by concatenating, in order, the encodings of the clauses of $\varphi$, where a clause is encoded as the two-bit codes of its slots followed by the terminator $00$.
nodes.title: Dense encoding of a CNF formula

nodes.summary: For every CNF formula $\varphi$, decoding the bit string that encodes $\varphi$ gives back $\varphi$. In particular, every CNF formula is the decoding of some bit string.

nodes.summary: Let $k_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $c$ be a dense clause with slots $s_0, \dots, s_{L-1}$. nodes.summary: Let $\varphi$ be a dense CNF formula all of whose clauses have the same length $V$. Every natural number $j < H$ satisfies $j < p$, or $j = u + p$ for some natural number $u < H - m$, or $j = H - c + p + r$ for some natural number $r < c - p$, where $c - p$ is truncated subtraction (zero when $c \le p$).
nodes.title: Coverage of target depths

nodes.summary: Let $p, c, H$ be natural numbers with $p \le H$ and $c \le H$, and let $m = \max(p, c)$. For every natural number $u < H - m$ we have $p \le u + p$, $u + p < H - c + p$ and $u + p < H$. For every natural number $r < c - p$, where $c - p$ is truncated subtraction, we have $H - m + p = H - c + p$ and $H - c + p + r < H$.

nodes.summary: A 1-in-3-SAT instance is a pair $(n, \varphi)$ of a natural number $n$, the number of variables, and a CNF formula $\varphi$.

3-SAT with bounded occurrences

nodes.summary: A bounded-occurrence 3-SAT instance is a pair $(n, \varphi)$ of a natural number $n$, the number of variables, and a CNF formula $\varphi$.
nodes.title: Bounded-occurrence 3-SAT instances

nodes.summary: A bounded-occurrence 3-SAT instance $(n, \varphi)$ is well formed when every clause of $\varphi$ is a list of exactly three literals, not necessarily distinct, every literal of $\varphi$ has a variable less than $n$, and for every variable $v < n$ at most four of the literals in the clauses of $\varphi$, counted with multiplicity and with either polarity, have variable $v$.
nodes.title: Well-formed bounded-occurrence 3-SAT instances

nodes.summary: A bounded-occurrence 3-SAT instance $(n, \varphi)$ is satisfiable when there is a list $(a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ of booleans such that $\varphi$ is satisfied by the assignment sending each variable $x < n$ to $a_x$ and every variable $x \ge n$ to false.
nodes.title: Satisfiable bounded-occurrence 3-SAT instances

nodes.summary: The decision problem 3-SAT WITH BOUNDED OCCURRENCES accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of bounded-occurrence 3-SAT instances, to an instance that is well formed and satisfiable; it rejects every other bitstring, including every bitstring that does not decode.
nodes.title: 3-SAT with bounded occurrences as a decision problem

nodes.summary: The decision problem 3-SAT WITH BOUNDED OCCURRENCES over bitstrings belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

Betweenness

nodes.summary: An instance of BETWEENNESS is a pair $(n, T)$ of a natural number $n$ (the number of elements) and a list $T$ of triples of natural numbers.
nodes.title: BETWEENNESS instances

nodes.summary: A BETWEENNESS instance $(n, T)$ is well formed when every triple $(a, b, c)$ in $T$ satisfies $a < n$, $b < n$ and $c < n$, and $a$, $b$, $c$ are pairwise distinct.
nodes.title: Well-formed BETWEENNESS instances

nodes.summary: A BETWEENNESS instance $(n, T)$ is feasible when there is an ordering of the numbers $0, \dots, n-1$ such that for every triple $(a, b, c)$ in $T$, either $p(a) < p(b) < p(c)$ or $p(c) < p(b) < p(a)$, where $p(m)$ is the position of $m$ in the ordering, counting from $0$, and $p(m) = n$ when $m$ is not among $0, \dots, n-1$.
nodes.title: BETWEENNESS feasibility

nodes.summary: BETWEENNESS accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of pairs $(n, T)$ of a natural number and a list of triples of natural numbers, to a BETWEENNESS instance that is both well formed and feasible. Bitstrings that do not decode to such a pair are rejected.
nodes.title: The BETWEENNESS decision problem

nodes.summary: The BETWEENNESS decision problem belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.
nodes.title: BETWEENNESS is NP-complete
Binary constraint satisfaction

nodes.summary: A binary CSP instance is a pair consisting of a list $(D_0, \dots, D_{n-1})$ of lists of natural numbers, where $D_j$ is the domain of variable $j$, and a list of constraints, each a triple $(j, k, P)$ of two variable indices $j, k \in \mathbb{N}$ and a list $P$ of allowed value pairs in $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: Binary CSP instances

nodes.summary: A binary CSP instance with domain list $(D_0, \dots, D_{n-1})$ and constraint list $C$ is well formed when every constraint $(j, k, P) \in C$ has $j < n$ and $k < n$.
nodes.title: Well-formed binary CSP instances

nodes.summary: A binary CSP instance with domain list $(D_0, \dots, D_{n-1})$ and constraint list $C$ is feasible when there is a list $(a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ of natural numbers with $a_j \in D_j$ for every $j < n$ and $(a_j, a_k) \in P$ for every constraint $(j, k, P) \in C$, where $a_i$ is read as $0$ for every index $i \ge n$.
nodes.title: Feasible binary CSP instances

nodes.summary: The decision problem BINARY CONSTRAINT SATISFACTION accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of binary CSP instances, to an instance that is well formed and feasible; it rejects every other bitstring, including every bitstring that does not decode.
nodes.title: Binary constraint satisfaction as a decision problem

nodes.summary: The decision problem BINARY CONSTRAINT SATISFACTION over bitstrings belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.
nodes.title: BINARY CONSTRAINT SATISFACTION is NP-complete

Let $b$ be the array $(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}, v_0, \dots, v_{s-1})$, where $v_j$ is the value of gate $j$ of $c$ on input $x$. Then $b$ has length $n + s$ and the Boolean certificate verifier accepts $b$.

The cost counted by the Boolean certificate verifier on $b$ is $2 + s + \sum_{j < s} a_j$ if $m = n + s$, where $a_j$ is the number of arguments of gate $j$, and $1$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Cost of the Boolean certificate verifier

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a natural number and let $c$ be a circuit over the Boolean signature with $n$ inputs, $s$ gates and one output in which every gate has at most $K$ arguments. Then for every array $b$ of truth values, the cost counted by the Boolean certificate verifier on $b$ is at most $2 + (K + 1)s$.

nodes.title: Evaluating a circuit

nodes.summary: A NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT instance $(n, \varphi)$ is well-formed when every clause of $\varphi$ is a list of exactly three literals, repetitions allowed, and every literal $(x, b)$ in it has variable index $x < n$.
nodes.title: Well-formed NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT instances

Balanced biclique

nodes.summary: An instance of BALANCED BICLIQUE is a triple $(n, es, K)$ consisting of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a list $es$ of pairs of natural numbers (the edges) and a natural number $K$ (the bound).
nodes.title: Balanced biclique instances

nodes.summary: The graph of a balanced biclique instance $(n, es, K)$ is the simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which distinct vertices $u$ and $v$ are adjacent when $(u, v)$ or $(v, u)$ belongs to $es$.
nodes.title: Graph of a balanced biclique instance

nodes.summary: A balanced biclique instance $(n, es, K)$ is well formed when the entries of the list $es$ are distinct and every pair $(u, v)$ in $es$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$, $u \neq v$ and $(v, u) \notin es$.
nodes.title: Well-formed balanced biclique instances

nodes.summary: A balanced biclique instance $(n, es, K)$ is feasible when there are disjoint sets $A$ and $B$ of exactly $K$ vertices each in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ such that every vertex of $A$ is adjacent to every vertex of $B$, where distinct vertices $u$ and $v$ are adjacent when $(u, v)$ or $(v, u)$ belongs to $es$. In other words, the graph contains a complete bipartite subgraph $K_{K,K}$, not necessarily induced.

Biclique edge cover

nodes.summary: An instance of BICLIQUE EDGE COVER is a tuple $(L, R, E, K)$ of natural numbers $L$, $R$ and $K$ and a finite list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers. Here $L$ counts the left vertices, $R$ counts the right vertices, each pair $(a, b)$ in $E$ is an edge from left vertex $a$ to right vertex $b$, and $K$ is the bound on the number of bicliques.
nodes.title: Biclique edge cover instances

nodes.summary: An instance $(L, R, E, K)$ of BICLIQUE EDGE COVER is well formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(a, b)$ in $E$ satisfies $a < L$ and $b < R$.
nodes.title: Well-formed biclique edge cover instances

nodes.summary: An instance $(L, R, E, K)$ of BICLIQUE EDGE COVER is feasible when there is a list of at most $K$ pairs $(A, B)$ of finite lists of natural numbers, with every element of $A$ less than $L$ and every element of $B$ less than $R$, such that for every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ some listed pair $(A, B)$ has $u \in A$, $v \in B$ and $(a, b)$ in $E$ for all $a \in A$ and $b \in B$.
nodes.title: Feasible biclique edge cover instances

nodes.summary: BICLIQUE EDGE COVER is the decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of biclique edge cover instances, to an instance that is well formed and feasible; it rejects every bitstring that fails to decode.

nodes.title: Karp's SAT-to-CLIQUE map on bit strings

nodes.summary: Writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, the map sends a bit string $1^k\,0\,1^n\,0\,b$ to $1^k\,0\,1^n\,0\,\bar b$, where $\bar b$ is $b$ with every bit complemented. A bit string with fewer than two zeros goes to the fixed no-instance $1\,0\,0$.

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number, and let the pair list of $n$ be the list of pairs $(i, j)$ with $i < j < n$ in encoding order. For all $i < j < n$, the bit of the pair $(i, j)$ in $b$ is the entry of $b$ at the position of $(i, j)$ in the pair list of $n$.

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f$ be a function from pairs of natural numbers to bits, and let $b$ be the list obtained by applying $f$ to each entry of the pair list of $n$ (the pairs $(i, j)$ with $i < j < n$ in encoding order). Then for all $i < j < n$, the bit of the pair $(i, j)$ in $b$ is $f(i, j)$.

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $k$ and a list of bits $b$, the graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ read off $b$ has a clique of exactly $k$ vertices if and only if there is a set $s$ of exactly $k$ of these vertices meeting the clique-mode pair condition on every pair $i < j$: whenever $i$ and $j$ both lie in $s$, the bit of the pair $\{i, j\}$ in $b$ is set.

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $k$ and a list of bits $b$, the graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ read off $b$ has a vertex cover of exactly $k$ vertices if and only if there is a set $s$ of exactly $k$ of these vertices meeting the cover-mode pair condition on every pair $i < j$: whenever the bit of the pair $\{i, j\}$ in $b$ is set, $i$ or $j$ lies in $s$.

It is the adjacency of two occurrences in different clauses in Karp's graph.

nodes.summary: For a list of literal occurrences (clause index, variable, polarity), the row-by-row pair bits are defined recursively: the empty list has none, and for a list $o, o_1, \dots, o_k$ they are the adjacency bits of $o$ with $o_k, \dots, o_1$, in that order, followed by the row-by-row pair bits of $o_1, \dots, o_k$. Two occurrences are adjacent when they lie in different clauses and are not complementary.

Then for every list of occurrences $o_1, \dots, o_k$, the row-by-row pair bits of $f(o_1), \dots, f(o_k)$ equal those of $o_1, \dots, o_k$.

Connected dominating set

nodes.summary: An instance of CONNECTED DOMINATING SET is a triple $(n, E, K)$ of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers (the edges) and a natural number $K$ (the bound).
nodes.title: Instances of CONNECTED DOMINATING SET

nodes.summary: For an instance $(n, E, K)$ of CONNECTED DOMINATING SET, its graph is the simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $E$.
nodes.title: Graph of a CONNECTED DOMINATING SET instance

nodes.summary: An instance $(n, E, K)$ of CONNECTED DOMINATING SET is well formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ has $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, with the reversed pair $(v, u)$ not in $E$.
nodes.title: Well-formed CONNECTED DOMINATING SET instances

nodes.summary: An instance $(n, E, K)$ of CONNECTED DOMINATING SET is feasible when there is a set $S$ of vertices of its graph $G$ with at most $K$ elements such that every vertex of $G$ lies in $S$ or is adjacent in $G$ to a vertex of $S$, and the subgraph of $G$ induced by $S$ is connected (in particular, $S$ is nonempty).
nodes.title: Feasible CONNECTED DOMINATING SET instances

nodes.summary: CONNECTED DOMINATING SET accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to an instance of CONNECTED DOMINATING SET that is well formed and feasible. Bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are rejected.
nodes.title: The decision problem CONNECTED DOMINATING SET

nodes.summary: The decision problem CONNECTED DOMINATING SET belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.
nodes.title: CONNECTED DOMINATING SET is NP-complete
Densest k-subgraph

nodes.summary: An instance of DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH is a quadruple $(n, E, k, m)$ consisting of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers (the edges), a natural number $k$ (the size of the vertex set sought) and a natural number $m$ (the edge threshold).
nodes.title: Instances of DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH

nodes.summary: An instance $(n, E, k, m)$ of DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH is well formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, with the reversed pair $(v, u)$ not in $E$.
nodes.title: Well-formed DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH instances

nodes.summary: An instance $(n, E, k, m)$ of DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH is feasible when there are a finite set $S$ of exactly $k$ natural numbers, each less than $n$, and a sublist $E'$ of $E$ (obtained by deleting entries and keeping the order) with at least $m$ entries such that both components of every pair in $E'$ lie in $S$.
nodes.title: Feasibility for DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH

nodes.summary: The decision problem DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when bitstring decoding of $x$ as a quadruple $(n, E, k, m)$ succeeds and returns an instance of DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH that is both well formed and feasible; every bitstring that does not decode is rejected.
nodes.title: DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH as a decision problem

nodes.summary: The decision problem DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH belongs to the class NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.
nodes.title: DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH is NP-complete

nodes.summary: An instance with vertex count $n$, edge list $E$ and bound $K$ is feasible when some sublist $D$ of $E$ (its entries taken in order) has at most $K$ entries and dominates every edge of $E$: for every $e \in E$ there is $d \in D$ such that one of the two entries of $d$ equals one of the two entries of $e$.

nodes.summary: EDGE DOMINATING SET is the decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to an EDGE DOMINATING SET instance $(n, E, K)$ that is well formed and feasible, that is, some sublist of $E$ with at most $K$ entries contains, for every edge of $E$, an edge sharing an endpoint with it. nodes.summary: An instance of BANDWIDTH is a triple $(n, E, K)$ of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a list $E$ of ordered pairs of natural numbers (the edges) and a natural number $K$ (the bound).
nodes.title: BANDWIDTH instances

nodes.summary: A BANDWIDTH instance $(n, E, K)$ is well formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, and its reverse $(v, u)$ does not occur in $E$. Thus $E$ lists the edges of a loopless undirected graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, each edge exactly once.
nodes.title: Well-formed BANDWIDTH instances

nodes.summary: A BANDWIDTH instance $(n, E, K)$ is feasible when there is an ordering of the numbers $0, \dots, n-1$ such that $|p(u) - p(v)| \le K$ for every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$, where $p(m)$ is the position of $m$ in the ordering, counting from $0$, and $p(m) = n$ when $m$ is not among $0, \dots, n-1$.
nodes.title: BANDWIDTH feasibility

nodes.summary: BANDWIDTH accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of triples $(n, E, K)$ of a natural number, a list of pairs of natural numbers and a natural number, to a BANDWIDTH instance that is both well formed and feasible. Bitstrings that do not decode to such a triple are rejected.

nodes.title: List-coloring instances

nodes.summary: A list-coloring instance $(n, E, L)$ is well formed when the edge list $E$ has no repeated entries, every edge $(u, v)$ in $E$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$ and its reversal $(v, u)$ does not occur in $E$, and the list $L$ of color lists has length $n$.

nodes.summary: A list-coloring instance $(n, E, L)$ is feasible when there is a list $c = (c_0, \dots, c_{n-1})$ of $n$ natural numbers such that for every $v < n$ the number $c_v$ belongs to the $v$-th entry $L_v$ of $L$ (taken to be the empty list when $L$ has at most $v$ entries), and $c_u \ne c_v$ for every edge $(u, v)$ in $E$, where $c_w$ is read as $0$ when $w \ge n$.

nodes.title: Well-formed MAXIMUM CUT instances

nodes.summary: An instance $(n, es, K)$ of MINIMUM BISECTION is feasible when there is a set $S \subseteq \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ with $\lfloor n / 2 \rfloor$ elements such that no sublist of $es$ (a list obtained from $es$ by deleting entries) with $K + 1$ entries consists only of entries $(u, v)$ with exactly one of $u$ and $v$ in $S$; that is, at most $K$ entries of $es$ have exactly one endpoint in $S$.

Here $\pi(v)$ is the position of $v$ in $\pi$, counted from $0$, and is $n$ when $v \ge n$; the sum runs over the list $E$, so a repeated pair is counted once for each occurrence.

Asymmetric traveling salesperson problem

nodes.summary: An instance of the asymmetric traveling salesperson problem is a triple $(n, w, B)$ consisting of a natural number $n$ (the number of cities), a weight matrix $w$ given as a list of rows, each row a list of natural numbers, and a natural number $B$ (the bound).
nodes.title: Asymmetric TSP instances

nodes.summary: Let $w$ be a weight matrix, given as a list of rows of natural numbers, and let $t = (t_0, \dots, t_{L-1})$ be a list of natural numbers. The length of the tour $t$ under $w$ is $\sum_{j=0}^{L-1} w_{t_j, t_{(j+1) \bmod L}}$, the sum of the weights along the closed walk including the return edge from $t_{L-1}$ to $t_0$, where $w_{a,b}$ denotes the entry in row $a$ and column $b$ of $w$, taken to be $0$ when that…
nodes.title: Length of a tour in the asymmetric TSP

nodes.summary: An asymmetric TSP instance $(n, w, B)$, with $n$ the number of cities, $w$ the weight matrix and $B$ the bound, is well formed when $n > 0$, $w$ has exactly $n$ rows, every row of $w$ has length $n$, and the diagonal entry $w_{a,a}$ in row $a$ and column $a$ is $0$ for every $a < n$.
nodes.title: Well-formed asymmetric TSP instances

nodes.summary: An asymmetric TSP instance $(n, w, B)$ is feasible when there is a list $t$ of natural numbers with no repeated entries, of length $n$ and containing every $v < n$ (so $t$ lists the cities $0, \dots, n - 1$ in some order), whose tour length under $w$ is at most $B$.
nodes.title: Feasible asymmetric TSP instances

nodes.summary: The asymmetric TSP decision problem accepts a bitstring $x$ when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of asymmetric TSP instances, to an instance $(n, w, B)$ that is well formed and feasible, and rejects $x$ otherwise; in particular it rejects every bitstring that does not decode to an instance.

Capacitated vehicle routing

nodes.summary: A capacitated vehicle routing instance is a tuple $(n, d, D, m, C, K)$ consisting of a natural number $n$ (the number of customers), a list $d$ of natural numbers (the demands), a list $D$ of lists of natural numbers (the distance matrix, whose rows and columns include the depot), and natural numbers $m$ (the number of vehicles), $C$ (the capacity) and $K$ (the bound on the total length).
nodes.title: Capacitated vehicle routing instances

nodes.summary: Let $D$ be a list of lists of natural numbers, read as a distance matrix whose entry $D_{u,v}$ is the entry at position $v$ of the row at position $u$ (positions counted from $0$), or $0$ if there is no such entry, and let $o$ be a natural number, the depot. The length of the empty route is $0$, and the length of a route given by a list $(r_1, \dots, r_k)$ of natural numbers with $k \ge 1$ is…
nodes.title: Length of a route

nodes.summary: A capacitated vehicle routing instance $(n, d, D, m, C, K)$ is well formed when the demand list $d$ has length $n$, the distance matrix $D$ has $n + 1$ rows, and every row of $D$ has length $n + 1$.
nodes.title: Well-formed capacitated vehicle routing instances

nodes.summary: Let $(n, d, D, m, C, K)$ be a capacitated vehicle routing instance, with customers $0, \dots, n - 1$ and depot $n$, and let the demand $d_c$ of $c$ be the entry of the list $d$ at position $c$ (counting from $0$), or $0$ if $d$ has no such entry. The instance is feasible when there is a list of at most $m$ routes, each a list of natural numbers, such that every route has no repeated entries and only entries less…

nodes.summary: The decision problem CAPACITATED VEHICLE ROUTING accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a capacitated vehicle routing instance that is well formed and feasible; it rejects every bitstring that does not decode.

Degree-constrained spanning tree

nodes.summary: An instance of DEGREE-CONSTRAINED SPANNING TREE is a triple $(n, E, K)$ consisting of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers (the edges) and a natural number $K$ (the degree bound).
nodes.title: Instances of DEGREE-CONSTRAINED SPANNING TREE

nodes.summary: An instance $(n, E, K)$ of DEGREE-CONSTRAINED SPANNING TREE is well formed when $n > 0$, the list $E$ has no repeated entries, and every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, with the reversed pair $(v, u)$ not in $E$.
nodes.title: Well-formed DEGREE-CONSTRAINED SPANNING TREE instances

nodes.summary: An instance $(n, E, K)$ of DEGREE-CONSTRAINED SPANNING TREE is feasible when there is a list $T$ of pairs of natural numbers such that $T$ is a sublist of $E$ (obtained by deleting entries and keeping the order), $T$ has no repeated entries, $T$ has exactly $n - 1$ entries, the graph of $T$ on $n$ vertices is connected, and for every vertex $v < n$ there is no sublist of $T$ with $K + 1$ entries each of which has…
nodes.title: Feasibility for DEGREE-CONSTRAINED SPANNING TREE

nodes.summary: The decision problem DEGREE-CONSTRAINED SPANNING TREE accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when bitstring decoding of $x$ as a triple $(n, E, K)$ succeeds and returns an instance of DEGREE-CONSTRAINED SPANNING TREE that is both well formed and feasible; every bitstring that does not decode is rejected.
nodes.title: DEGREE-CONSTRAINED SPANNING TREE as a decision problem

nodes.summary: The decision problem DEGREE-CONSTRAINED SPANNING TREE belongs to the class NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

Directed Hamiltonian cycle

nodes.summary: An instance of HAMILTONIAN CYCLE (DIRECTED) is a pair $(n, E)$ of a natural number $n$, the number of vertices, and a finite list $E$ of ordered pairs of natural numbers, the arcs.
nodes.title: Instances of HAMILTONIAN CYCLE (DIRECTED)

nodes.summary: For a finite list $E$ of ordered pairs of natural numbers and natural numbers $u$ and $v$, the directed adjacency of $u$ to $v$ in $E$ is the boolean value that is true exactly when the pair $(u, v)$ occurs in $E$.
nodes.title: Directed adjacency for HAMILTONIAN CYCLE (DIRECTED)

nodes.summary: An instance $(n, E)$ of HAMILTONIAN CYCLE (DIRECTED), with $n$ a natural number and $E$ a finite list of ordered pairs of natural numbers, is well formed when $n > 0$, the list $E$ has no repeated entries, and every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$.
nodes.title: Well-formed instances of HAMILTONIAN CYCLE (DIRECTED)

nodes.summary: An instance $(n, E)$ of HAMILTONIAN CYCLE (DIRECTED), with $n$ a natural number and $E$ a finite list of ordered pairs of natural numbers, has a directed Hamiltonian cycle when there is a list $(v_0, \dots, v_{n-1})$ of $n$ distinct natural numbers containing every natural number below $n$ such that the pair $(v_j, v_{(j+1) \bmod n})$ occurs in $E$ for every $j < n$.

nodes.title: The directed Hamiltonian cycle decision problem

A list $p$ is a Hamiltonian path from $s$ to $t$ when it lists each of the vertices $0, \dots, n - 1$ exactly once, starts at $s$, ends at $t$, and each two consecutive entries of $p$ form an arc.

nodes.title: Distinct variables of a formula

nodes.summary: In the HAMPATH construction with $m$ clauses, the top of diamond $i$ is the vertex $m + i(3m + 2)$; it is also the bottom of diamond $i - 1$.
nodes.title: Tops of the diamonds

nodes.summary: In the HAMPATH construction with $m$ clauses, write $T(i)$ for the top of diamond $i$. Row vertex $l$ of diamond $i$ is the number $T(i) + 1 + l$; the row of diamond $i$ consists of the vertices with $l \le 3m$.
nodes.title: Row vertices of a diamond

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula with $m$ clauses, and write $T(i)$ for the top of diamond $i$ and $R(i, l)$ for its row vertex $l$. The arcs of diamond $i$ for variable $x$ are $T(i) \to R(i, 0)$, $T(i) \to R(i, 3m)$, $R(i, 0) \to T(i + 1)$ and $R(i, 3m) \to T(i + 1)$; for every $l < 3m$, both $R(i, l) \to R(i, l + 1)$ and $R(i, l + 1) \to R(i, l)$; and for every clause $j < m$, the arcs $R(i, 3j + 1) \to j$ and…
nodes.title: Arcs of a variable diamond

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula and let $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ be its distinct variables, in the order of the distinct-variable list of $\varphi$. The arcs of the construction for $\varphi$ are the arcs of diamond $i$ for variable $x_i$, for $i = 0, \dots, k - 1$, concatenated in this order.
nodes.title: Arcs of the HAMPATH construction

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula with $m$ clauses, numbered $0, \dots, m - 1$, and let $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ be its distinct variables, in the order of their last occurrences in $\varphi$ (clauses read in order, and the literals of each clause in order). Put $T_i = m + i(3m + 2)$ and $R_{i,l} = T_i + 1 + l$. The result is the encoded PATH instance with vertices $0, \dots, T_k$, source $T_0$, target $T_k$, and, for…
nodes.title: Sipser's HAMPATH instance of a CNF formula

nodes.summary: The encoded PATH instance on the two vertices $0$ and $1$, with no arcs, whose source and target are both $0$.
nodes.title: A fixed HAMPATH no-instance

nodes.summary: A bit string $x$ that decodes to a CNF formula $\varphi$ is sent to Sipser's HAMPATH instance of $\varphi$, and a bit string that does not decode to a CNF formula is sent to the fixed HAMPATH no-instance (two vertices, no arcs, source and target $0$).
nodes.title: The SAT-to-HAMPATH reduction map

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula with $m$ clauses and $k$ distinct variables, and write $R(i, l)$ for row vertex $l$ of diamond $i$ in the HAMPATH construction for $\varphi$. A list of vertices $p$ has normal detours when for every clause $j < m$ there is a diamond $i < k$ such that $p$ contains $R(i, 3j + 1), j, R(i, 3j + 2)$ or $R(i, 3j + 2), j, R(i, 3j + 1)$ as consecutive entries.
nodes.title: Normal clause detours

nodes.summary: In the HAMPATH construction with $m$ clauses, if $i \le i'$ then the top of diamond $i$ is at most the top of diamond $i'$.
nodes.title: Tops are monotone in the diamond index

nodes.summary: In the HAMPATH construction with $m$ clauses, for every diamond $i$ and every $l \le 3m$, row vertex $l$ of diamond $i$ is a smaller number than the top of diamond $i + 1$.
nodes.title: Row vertices lie below the next top

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $u, v$ and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, the bit encoding of the edge list whose first edge is $(u, v)$ and whose remaining edges are $E$ is: $u$ copies of true, then false, then $v$ copies of true, then false, then the bit encoding of $E$.
nodes.title: Bits of an edge list, first edge first

nodes.summary: The edge-list bit encoding of the empty list of edges is the empty bit string.
nodes.title: Edge bits of the empty edge list

nodes.summary: For all lists $E$ and $E'$ of pairs of natural numbers, the bit encoding of the concatenation of $E$ and $E'$ is the bit encoding of $E$ followed by the bit encoding of $E'$.
nodes.title: Bits of concatenated edge lists

nodes.summary: The witness encoding of a list $p$ of natural numbers (the vertices of a candidate path) is the bit string obtained by writing each entry $v$ of $p$, in order, as $v$ copies of true followed by one false, and concatenating the results.
nodes.title: Witness encoding

nodes.summary: The witness decoder reads a list $w$ of bits as a list of natural numbers. On the empty list it returns the empty list. Otherwise it reads a unary number $v$ from the front of $w$, a run of $v$ copies of true ended by false, and if decoding the remaining bits gives a list $p$, it returns $v$ followed by $p$. It fails if no unary number can be read from a nonempty list, or if decoding the remaining bits fails.
nodes.title: Witness decoder

nodes.summary: The witness encoding of the empty list of vertices is the empty bit string.
nodes.title: Witness encoding of the empty list

nodes.summary: For a natural number $v$ and a list $p$ of natural numbers, the witness encoding of the list with first entry $v$ followed by $p$ is the bit string made of $v$ copies of true, then one false, then the witness encoding of $p$.
nodes.title: Witness encoding of a nonempty list
The witness encoding respects concatenation to Length of an encoded PATH instance

nodes.summary: For lists $p$ and $p'$ of natural numbers, the witness encoding of the concatenation of $p$ and $p'$ is the witness encoding of $p$ followed by the witness encoding of $p'$.
nodes.title: The witness encoding respects concatenation

nodes.summary: The witness decoder succeeds on the empty list of bits and returns the empty list of vertices.
nodes.title: Decoding the empty witness

nodes.summary: If a list $w$ of bits is nonempty and reading a unary number (a run of true ended by false) from the front of $w$ fails, that is, every bit of $w$ is true, then the witness decoder fails on $w$.
nodes.title: Witness decoding fails on a cut-off first number

nodes.summary: If reading a unary number from the front of a list $w$ of bits returns $v$ with remaining bits $r$, that is, $w$ is $v$ copies of true, then false, then $r$, then the witness decoder succeeds on $w$ exactly when it succeeds on $r$, and its result on $w$ is $v$ followed by its result on $r$.
nodes.title: Decoding peels off the first number

nodes.summary: For every list $p$ of natural numbers, the witness decoder applied to the witness encoding of $p$ (each entry $v$ written as $v$ copies of true followed by false) succeeds and returns $p$.
nodes.title: Decoding inverts the witness encoding

nodes.summary: For every bit string $w$ and every list $p$ of natural numbers, if the witness decoder returns $p$ on $w$, then $w$ is the witness encoding of $p$.
nodes.title: The witness decoder succeeds only on encodings

nodes.summary: For every list $w$ of bits and every list $p$ of natural numbers, the witness decoder returns $p$ on $w$ if and only if $w$ is the witness encoding of $p$, which writes each entry $v$ of $p$ as $v$ copies of true followed by false.
nodes.title: The witness codec

nodes.summary: For every list $p = (v_1, \dots, v_k)$ of natural numbers, the witness encoding of $p$ has length $\sum_{i=1}^{k} (v_i + 1)$.
nodes.title: Witness length

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$ and every list $p$ of natural numbers all below $n$, the witness encoding of $p$ has length at most $|p| \cdot n$.
nodes.title: Witness length bound

nodes.summary: For every list $p$ of natural numbers, the witness encoding of $p$ has length at least $|p|$.
nodes.title: A witness is at least as long as its vertex list

nodes.summary: Given $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, the arc check of a list $p$ of natural numbers returns true when every two consecutive entries $u, v$ of $p$ satisfy $(u, v) \in E$, $u < n$ and $v < n$, and false otherwise; in particular every list with fewer than two entries passes.
nodes.title: Arc check of a vertex list

nodes.summary: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, every list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers and every list $p$ of natural numbers, the arc check of $p$ against $n$ and $E$ returns true if and only if every two consecutive entries $u, v$ of $p$ form an arc of the digraph on $0, \dots, n - 1$ listed by $E$, that is, $(u, v) \in E$, $u < n$ and $v < n$.
nodes.title: Checking a vertex list against the arcs

nodes.summary: Given a natural number $n$, an edge list $E$, vertices $s$ and $t$ and a list $p$ of natural numbers, the Boolean test that $p$ has no repeated entries, has length $n$, has all entries below $n$, has first entry $s$ and last entry $t$, and that every two consecutive entries $u, v$ of $p$ satisfy $(u, v) \in E$, $u < n$ and $v < n$.
nodes.title: The Hamiltonian path check

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $n$, $s$, $t$, every edge list $E$ and every list $p$ of natural numbers, the Hamiltonian path check on $(n, E, s, t, p)$ returns true if and only if $p$ is a Hamiltonian path from $s$ to $t$ in the digraph on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with edge list $E$.
nodes.title: The Hamiltonian path check is correct

nodes.summary: Given bit strings $x$ and $w$, the verifier decodes $x$ as a PATH instance, consisting of a start vertex $s$, a target vertex $t$, a vertex count $n$ and an edge list $E$, and decodes $w$ as a witness, a list $p$ of natural numbers each written in unary. If both decodings succeed, it accepts exactly when the Hamiltonian path check passes, that is, when $p$ is a Hamiltonian path from $s$ to $t$ in the digraph on…
nodes.title: The HAMPATH verifier

nodes.summary: For bit strings $x$ and $w$, the HAMPATH verifier accepts $(x, w)$ if and only if there are natural numbers $s$, $t$, $n$, a list $es$ of pairs of natural numbers and a list $p$ of natural numbers such that $x$ is the PATH encoding of $(s, t, n, es)$, $w$ is the witness encoding of $p$, and $p$ is a Hamiltonian path from $s$ to $t$ in the digraph on $0, \dots, n - 1$ with edge list $es$.
nodes.title: What the HAMPATH verifier accepts

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $s$, $t$, $n$, a list $es$ of pairs of natural numbers and a list $p$ of natural numbers, the HAMPATH verifier applied to the PATH encoding of $(s, t, n, es)$ and the witness encoding of $p$ returns the same boolean as the Hamiltonian path check on $n$, $es$, $s$, $t$ and $p$.
nodes.title: The verifier on an encoded instance and witness

nodes.summary: If the PATH instance decoder fails on a bit string $x$, then for every bit string $w$ the HAMPATH verifier rejects $(x, w)$, that is, returns false.
nodes.title: Instances that do not decode are rejected

nodes.summary: If the witness decoder fails on a bit string $w$, then for every bit string $x$ the HAMPATH verifier rejects $(x, w)$, that is, returns false.
nodes.title: Witnesses that do not decode are rejected

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $s$, $t$, $n$ and every edge list $E$, the encoding of the PATH instance $(s, t, n, E)$ has length $s + t + n + 3 + \ell$, where $\ell$ is the length of the bit encoding of the edge list $E$.

Let $i$ and $l \le 3m$ be natural numbers, and let $(v, R_{i,l})$ be an arc of Sipser's construction for $\varphi$. Then $l < 3m$ and $v = R_{i,l+1}$; or $0 < l$ and $v = R_{i,l-1}$; or $l \in \{0, 3m\}$ and $v = T_i$; or $v < m$ and $l \in \{3v + 1, 3v + 2\}$.

Longest cycle

nodes.summary: An instance of LONGEST CYCLE is a triple $(n, E, K)$ of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers (the edges), and a natural number $K$ (the bound).
nodes.title: Instances of LONGEST CYCLE

nodes.summary: For an instance $(n, E, K)$ of LONGEST CYCLE, its graph is the simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $E$. Loops are dropped, and pairs with an endpoint at least $n$ contribute no edge.
nodes.title: Graph of a LONGEST CYCLE instance

nodes.summary: An instance $(n, E, K)$ of LONGEST CYCLE is well formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$, $u \ne v$ and $(v, u) \notin E$.
nodes.title: Well-formed LONGEST CYCLE instances

nodes.summary: An instance $(n, E, K)$ of LONGEST CYCLE is feasible when there are pairwise distinct vertices $v_1, \dots, v_m$ of the graph of the instance, with $m \ge K$ and $m \ge 3$, such that $v_j$ is adjacent to $v_{j+1}$ for every $1 \le j < m$ and $v_m$ is adjacent to $v_1$. That is, the graph has a simple cycle with at least $K$ edges and at least three vertices.
nodes.title: Feasible LONGEST CYCLE instances

nodes.summary: LONGEST CYCLE accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of instances, to an instance of LONGEST CYCLE that is well formed and feasible. Bitstrings that do not decode, and bitstrings that decode to instances that are not well formed, are rejected.

nodes.summary: A longest-path instance $(n, E, K, s, t)$ is feasible when the graph of $E$ on $n$ vertices has a simple path from $s$ to $t$ with at least $K$ edges, that is, a list $v_0, \dots, v_m$ of pairwise distinct vertices with $m \ge K$, $v_0 = s$ and $v_m = t$, in which $v_j$ and $v_{j+1}$ are adjacent for every $j < m$.

Minimum equivalent digraph

nodes.summary: An instance of MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH is a triple $(n, E, K)$ consisting of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a finite list $E$ of ordered pairs of natural numbers (the arcs) and a natural number $K$ (the bound on the number of arcs).
nodes.title: Instances of MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH

nodes.summary: For a finite list $E$ of ordered pairs of natural numbers and natural numbers $u$ and $v$, the directed adjacency test of $E$ at $(u, v)$ returns true when the pair $(u, v)$ occurs in $E$, and false otherwise.
nodes.title: Directed adjacency for MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a finite list of ordered pairs of natural numbers, read as the arcs of a directed graph, and let $n$, $u$ and $v$ be natural numbers. Then $v$ is reachable from $u$ within $n$ steps along $E$ when there are natural numbers $w_0, w_1, \dots, w_k$ with $k \le n$, $w_0 = u$ and $w_k = v$ such that $(w_j, w_{j+1})$ occurs in $E$ for every $j < k$.
nodes.title: Bounded reachability in a digraph

nodes.summary: An instance $(n, E, K)$ of MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH is well formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(a, b)$ in $E$ satisfies $a < n$, $b < n$ and $a \ne b$; that is, $E$ lists distinct arcs without loops between vertices among $0, \dots, n - 1$.
nodes.title: Well-formed MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH instances

nodes.summary: An instance $(n, E, K)$ of MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH is feasible when some sublist $F$ of $E$ (obtained by deleting entries of $E$) has at most $K$ entries and, for all vertices $u < n$ and $v < n$, $v$ is reachable from $u$ within $n$ steps along $E$ if and only if $v$ is reachable from $u$ within $n$ steps along $F$.

nodes.summary: An instance $(n, E, K)$ of DIRECTED PATH COVER is well formed when the edge list $E$ has no repeated entries and every edge $(a, b)$ in $E$ satisfies $a < n$, $b < n$ and $a \ne b$.

nodes.summary: An instance $(n, E, K)$ of DIRECTED PATH COVER is feasible when there is a list of at most $K$ paths, each a list of natural numbers, such that every path has no repeated vertex, every vertex on a path is less than $n$, and whenever $v$ immediately follows $u$ on a path the pair $(u, v)$ occurs in $E$; and such that every vertex $v < n$ lies on some path, and all paths containing $v$ are equal.

nodes.title: Symmetric TSP instances

Rows and columns are numbered from $0$.
nodes.title: Well-formed symmetric TSP instances

nodes.summary: A symmetric TSP instance $(n, w, B)$ is feasible when there is a list of $n$ pairwise distinct natural numbers containing every $v < n$, that is, an ordering of the cities $0, 1, \dots, n-1$ visiting each exactly once, whose tour length with respect to $w$ (the sum of the weights of consecutive edges, including the return edge) is at most $B$.

nodes.summary: Let $(a, B)$ be a 3-partition instance with $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{N-1})$, and let $m = \lfloor N/3 \rfloor$. Unbounded knapsack problem

nodes.summary: An instance of the unbounded knapsack problem is a triple $(I, C, K)$ of a finite list $I = ((s_1, v_1), \dots, (s_m, v_m))$ of items, where item $j$ has weight $s_j \in \mathbb{N}$ and value $v_j \in \mathbb{N}$, a capacity $C \in \mathbb{N}$ and a target value $K \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: Unbounded knapsack instances

nodes.summary: An unbounded knapsack instance with items $(s_1, v_1), \dots, (s_m, v_m)$, capacity $C$ and target value $K$ is feasible when there are multiplicities $c_1, \dots, c_m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $\sum_{j=1}^{m} c_j s_j \le C$ and $\sum_{j=1}^{m} c_j v_j \ge K$.
nodes.title: Feasible unbounded knapsack instances

nodes.summary: The unbounded knapsack problem is the decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of unbounded knapsack instances, to a feasible instance. Bitstrings that fail to decode are rejected.
nodes.title: Unbounded knapsack as a decision problem

nodes.summary: The unbounded knapsack decision problem belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.
nodes.title: UNBOUNDED KNAPSACK is NP-complete

nodes.summary: An instance of EXACT COVER is a pair $(n, C)$ of a natural number $n$, the size of the universe $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, and a finite list $C$ of finite lists of natural numbers, the candidate subsets. nodes.summary: An instance $(n, C)$ of EXACT COVER is feasible when $C$ has a sublist $S$, obtained by deleting some entries of $C$, such that for every natural number $x < n$ there is exactly one list that occurs in $S$ and contains $x$.

Set cover

nodes.summary: A set-cover instance is a triple $(n, C, K)$ consisting of a natural number $n$, the size of the universe, a finite list $C$ of finite lists of natural numbers, the subsets, and a natural number $K$, the bound.
nodes.title: Set-cover instances

nodes.summary: A set-cover instance $(n, C, K)$ is well formed when every list $s$ in $C$ has no repeated entries and every entry of $s$ is less than $n$, that is, each member of $C$ lists the elements of a subset of $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ without repetition.
nodes.title: Well-formed set-cover instances

nodes.summary: A set-cover instance $(n, C, K)$ is feasible when there is a sublist $D$ of $C$ (a list obtained from $C$ by deleting entries while keeping their order) with at most $K$ entries such that every natural number $x < n$ belongs to some list in $D$.

Precedence-constrained multiprocessor scheduling

nodes.summary: An instance is a tuple $(d, P, m, D)$ in which $d = (d_0, \dots, d_{n-1})$ is a list of natural numbers, $d_j$ being the duration of job $j$; $P$ is a list of pairs $(a, b)$ of natural numbers, each read as the precedence constraint that job $a$ precedes job $b$; $m$ is a natural number, the number of machines; and $D$ is a natural number, the deadline.

Resource-constrained project scheduling

nodes.summary: An instance of resource-constrained project scheduling (an RCPSP instance) is a quadruple $(J, P, C, D)$: a list $J$ of jobs, each a pair $(p, r) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ of a duration $p$ and a resource demand $r$; a list $P$ of precedence pairs $(a, b) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ of job indices; a resource capacity $C \in \mathbb{N}$; and a deadline $D \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: Instances of resource-constrained project scheduling

It fails if some block fails to parse. The bound never binds, since every block uses at least one bit. So the parse succeeds exactly when $s$ is a concatenation of self-delimiting blocks.

Relativization and oracle separations

nodes.summary: For an oracle $O$, a function from bitstrings to booleans, write $\mathsf{P}^O$ and $\mathsf{NP}^O$ for the classes of decision problems decidable in polynomial time, respectively in nondeterministic polynomial time, by machines that may query $O$. There is an oracle $O$ such that $\mathsf{P}^O \ne \mathsf{NP}^O$, and there is an oracle $O$ such that $\mathsf{P}^O = \mathsf{NP}^O$.

nodes.summary: There is a decision problem that belongs to PSPACE but not to the class $\mathsf{L}$ of decision problems decidable in deterministic logarithmic space.
