Sequential transducers, Mealy and Moore machines

nodes.summary: A sequential transducer with states in a type $Q$, input letters in a type $\Sigma$ and output letters in a type $\Gamma$ consists of a transition function assigning to each state $q \in Q$ and input letter $a \in \Sigma$ a successor state in $Q$ and an output word over $\Gamma$, a start state in $Q$, a set of accepting states $F \subseteq Q$, an initial output word over $\Gamma$, and, for each state in $Q$, a…
nodes.title: Sequential transducer

nodes.summary: The run of a sequential transducer $S$ from a state $q$ on an input word $a_1 \cdots a_n$ is the pair $(q_n, w_1 w_2 \cdots w_n)$, where $q_0 = q$ and, for each $1 \le i \le n$, $S$ moves from $q_{i-1}$ on $a_i$ to $q_i$ emitting the word $w_i$. The initial output and the final outputs of $S$ are not included.
nodes.title: Run of a sequential transducer

nodes.summary: For a sequential transducer $S$, a state $q$ and an input word $w$, the final state of the run of $S$ from $q$ on $w$ is obtained by starting in $q$, reading the letters of $w$ in order, moving at each letter to the successor state given by the transition function of $S$, and taking the state reached at the end.
nodes.title: Final state of a sequential transducer run

nodes.summary: For a sequential transducer $S$, a state $q$ and an input word $x$, the output word of the run from $q$ on $x$ is the concatenation of the output words that $S$ emits on the successive letters of $x$, starting in $q$ and moving to the successor state after each letter; the initial and final outputs are not included.
nodes.title: Output word of a sequential transducer run

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a sequential transducer, $q$ a state, $a$ an input letter and $w$ an input word, and let $q'$ be the successor state of $q$ on $a$ under the transition function of $S$. Then the final state of the run of $S$ from $q$ on the word $aw$ equals the final state of the run of $S$ from $q'$ on $w$.
nodes.title: Final state of a sequential transducer run on a nonempty word

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a sequential transducer, $q$ a state, $a$ an input letter and $x$ an input word, and let $q'$ and $w$ be the successor state and the output word of $S$ in state $q$ on letter $a$. The output word of the run of $S$ from $q$ on $ax$ is $w$ followed by the output word of the run from $q'$ on $x$.
nodes.title: Output of a sequential transducer on a nonempty word

nodes.summary: For a sequential transducer $S$, a state $q$ and input words $x$ and $y$, the final state of the run of $S$ from $q$ on $xy$ is the final state of the run on $y$ from the final state of the run from $q$ on $x$.
nodes.title: Final state of a sequential transducer on a concatenation

nodes.summary: For a sequential transducer $S$, a state $q$ and input words $x$ and $y$, the output word of the run of $S$ from $q$ on $xy$ is the output word of the run from $q$ on $x$ followed by the output word of the run on $y$ from the final state of the run from $q$ on $x$.
nodes.title: Output of a sequential transducer on a concatenation

nodes.summary: A sequential transducer $S$ translates an input word $x$ to an output word $y$ when the run of $S$ on $x$ from its start state ends in an accepting state $q$ and $y$ is the concatenation of the initial output of $S$, the output words emitted by the transitions along the run, and the final output of $S$ at $q$.
nodes.title: Translation by a sequential transducer

nodes.summary: Let $S_1$ be a sequential transducer from $I$ to $M$ with start state $s_1$, initial output $\iota_1$ and final output map $\phi_1$, and let $S_2$ be one from $M$ to $O$ with start state $s_2$, initial output $\iota_2$ and final output map $\phi_2$. For a transducer $S$, a state $q$ and a word $w$, write $\delta_S(q, w)$ for the state $S$ reaches by reading $w$ from $q$ and $\lambda_S(q, w)$ for the concatenation…
nodes.title: Composition of sequential transducers

nodes.summary: Let $S_1$ be a sequential transducer from $I$ to $M$, $S_2$ one from $M$ to $O$, and $C$ their composition. Let $q_1$ be a state of $S_1$, $q_2$ a state of $S_2$ and $a \in I$ a letter, and suppose that $S_1$, reading $a$ in state $q_1$, moves to $q_1'$ and emits the word $w$. Then $C$, reading $a$ in state $(q_1, q_2)$, moves to $(q_1', q_2')$, where $q_2'$ is the state $S_2$ reaches by reading $w$ from $q_2$.
nodes.title: One step of a composite transducer: the successor state

nodes.summary: Let $S_1$ be a sequential transducer from $I$ to $M$, $S_2$ one from $M$ to $O$, and $C$ their composition. Let $q_1$ be a state of $S_1$, $q_2$ a state of $S_2$ and $a \in I$ a letter, and let $w$ be the word $S_1$ emits when it reads $a$ in state $q_1$. Then the word $C$ emits when it reads $a$ in state $(q_1, q_2)$ is the concatenation of the words $S_2$ emits while reading $w$ from $q_2$.
nodes.title: One step of a composite transducer: the output

nodes.summary: Let $S_1$ be a sequential transducer from $I$ to $M$, $S_2$ one from $M$ to $O$, and $C$ their composition. For a transducer $S$, a state $q$ and a word $w$, write $\delta_S(q, w)$ for the state $S$ reaches by reading $w$ from $q$ and $\lambda_S(q, w)$ for the concatenation of the words it emits along the way (without initial or final output). Then for all states $q_1$ of $S_1$ and $q_2$ of $S_2$ and every word $x$…
nodes.title: States reached by a composite sequential transducer

nodes.summary: Let $S_1$ be a sequential transducer from $I$ to $M$, $S_2$ one from $M$ to $O$, and $C$ their composition. For a transducer $S$, a state $q$ and a word $w$, write $\lambda_S(q, w)$ for the concatenation of the words $S$ emits while reading $w$ from $q$ (without initial or final output). Then for all states $q_1$ of $S_1$ and $q_2$ of $S_2$ and every word $x$ over $I$,…
nodes.title: Output of a composite sequential transducer

nodes.summary: Let $S_1$ be a sequential transducer from $I$ to $M$ and $S_2$ one from $M$ to $O$, with start states $s_1$ and $s_2$. For a transducer $S$, a state $q$ and a word $w$, write $\delta_S(q, w)$ for the state $S$ reaches by reading $w$ from $q$ and $\lambda_S(q, w)$ for the concatenation of the words it emits along the way (without initial or final output); juxtaposition of words is concatenation. For a word $x$ over…
nodes.title: State of the second transducer after the first one's whole output

nodes.summary: Let $S_1$ be a sequential transducer from $I$ to $M$ and $S_2$ one from $M$ to $O$, with start states $s_1$ and $s_2$. For a transducer $S$, a state $q$ and a word $w$, write $\delta_S(q, w)$ for the state $S$ reaches by reading $w$ from $q$ and $\lambda_S(q, w)$ for the concatenation of the words it emits along the way (without initial or final output); juxtaposition of words is concatenation. For a word $x$ over…
nodes.title: Output of the second transducer on the first one's whole output

nodes.summary: Let $S_1$ be a sequential transducer from $I$ to $M$, $S_2$ one from $M$ to $O$, and $C$ their composition. For a sequential transducer $S$ with start state $s$, initial output $\iota$ and final output map $\phi$, and a word $x$, let $\delta_S(s, x)$ be the state $S$ reaches by reading $x$ from $s$ and $\lambda_S(s, x)$ the concatenation of the words it emits along the way, and call the concatenation…
nodes.title: Total output of a composite sequential transducer

nodes.summary: Let $S_1$ be a sequential transducer from an alphabet $A$ to an alphabet $B$, and $S_2$ one from $B$ to an alphabet $C$. For every word $x$ over $A$ and every word $y$ over $C$, the composition of $S_1$ and $S_2$ translates $x$ to $y$ if and only if there is a word $z$ over $B$ such that $S_1$ translates $x$ to $z$ and $S_2$ translates $z$ to $y$.
nodes.title: Translations of a composite sequential transducer

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a sequential transducer with input alphabet $\Sigma$ and output alphabet $\Gamma$, and let $L$ be a language over $\Gamma$. The preimage of $L$ under $S$ is the language over $\Sigma$ consisting of the words $x$ for which there is a word $y \in L$ such that $S$ translates $x$ to $y$.
nodes.title: Preimage of a language under a sequential transducer

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a sequential transducer with state type $Q$, input alphabet $\Sigma$ and output alphabet $\Gamma$, and let $M$ be a DFA over $\Gamma$ with state type $P$. The product DFA of $S$ and $M$ is the DFA over $\Sigma$ with state type $Q \times P$ defined as follows. In state $(q, r)$ on a letter $a$, if $S$ moves from $q$ to $q'$ emitting the word $w$, it moves to $(q', r')$, where $r'$ is the state $M$ reaches…
nodes.title: Product DFA of a sequential transducer and a DFA

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a sequential transducer and $M$ a DFA over the output alphabet of $S$. For every input word $x$, state $q$ of $S$ and state $r$ of $M$, the product DFA of $S$ and $M$, started in $(q, r)$ and run on $x$, ends in the state $(q', r')$, where $q'$ is the final state of the run of $S$ from $q$ on $x$ and $r'$ is the state that $M$ reaches from $r$ on the output word of that run.
nodes.title: Runs of the product DFA

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a sequential transducer with output alphabet $\Gamma$ and let $M$ be a DFA over $\Gamma$. The language accepted by the product DFA of $S$ and $M$ equals the preimage under $S$ of the language accepted by $M$, that is, the set of input words that $S$ translates to some word accepted by $M$.
nodes.title: The product DFA recognizes the preimage

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a sequential transducer with finitely many states, input alphabet $I$ and output alphabet $O$, and let $L$ be a regular language over $O$. Then the preimage of $L$ under $S$, the set of words over $I$ that $S$ translates to some word of $L$, is regular.
nodes.title: Inverse sequential transduction preserves regular languages

nodes.summary: A Mealy machine with state set $Q$, input alphabet $I$ and output alphabet $O$ consists of a start state in $Q$ and a transition function that, given a state $q \in Q$ and an input letter $a \in I$, returns a successor state in $Q$ and a single output letter in $O$; thus the output of a transition depends on the state and the input letter.
nodes.title: Mealy machine

nodes.summary: The run of a Mealy machine $M$ from a state $q$ on an input word $a_1 \cdots a_n$ is the pair $(q_n, o_1 \cdots o_n)$, where $q_0 = q$ and, for each $1 \le i \le n$, $M$ moves from $q_{i-1}$ on $a_i$ to $q_i$ emitting the output letter $o_i$.
nodes.title: Run of a Mealy machine

nodes.summary: For a Mealy machine $M$, a state $q$ and an input word $x$, the final state of the run from $q$ on $x$ is the state reached by starting in $q$ and moving, on each successive letter of $x$, to the successor state given by the transition function of $M$; on the empty word it is $q$.
nodes.title: Final state of a Mealy machine run

nodes.summary: For a Mealy machine $M$, a state $q$ and an input word $x$, the output word of $M$ from $q$ on $x$ is the second component of the run of $M$ from $q$ on $x$: the word of output letters emitted along that run, one per input letter.
nodes.title: Output word of a Mealy machine run

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a Mealy machine, $q$ a state, $a$ an input letter and $x$ an input word, and let $q'$ be the successor state of $M$ in state $q$ on letter $a$. The final state of the run of $M$ from $q$ on $ax$ is the final state of the run from $q'$ on $x$.
nodes.title: Final state of a Mealy machine on a nonempty word

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a Mealy machine, $q$ a state, $a$ an input letter and $x$ an input word, and let $q'$ and $o$ be the successor state and the output letter of $M$ in state $q$ on letter $a$. The output word of the run of $M$ from $q$ on $ax$ is $o$ followed by the output word of the run from $q'$ on $x$.
nodes.title: Output of a Mealy machine on a nonempty word

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a Mealy machine with start state $q_0$. On an input word $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$, for each $i$ let $q_i$ and $b_i$ be the state that $M$ moves to and the letter that it outputs when it reads $a_i$ in state $q_{i-1}$. The transduction of $M$ on this word is the output word $b_1 b_2 \cdots b_n$.
nodes.title: Transduction of a Mealy machine

nodes.summary: The sequential transducer of a Mealy machine $M$ has the states and the start state of $M$; on an input letter $a$ in a state $q$ it moves to the state that $M$ moves to and emits the one-letter word consisting of the letter that $M$ outputs on this transition. Every state accepts, and the initial and final outputs are empty.
nodes.title: Mealy machine as a sequential transducer

nodes.summary: For a Mealy machine $M$, a state $q$ and an input word $w$, the final state of the run from $q$ on $w$ of the sequential transducer associated with $M$ equals the final state of the run of $M$ from $q$ on $w$.
nodes.title: The sequential transducer of a Mealy machine has the same final states

nodes.summary: For a Mealy machine $M$, a state $q$ and an input word $w$, the output word of the run from $q$ on $w$ of the sequential transducer associated with $M$ (excluding its initial and final outputs) equals the output word of the run of $M$ from $q$ on $w$.
nodes.title: The sequential transducer of a Mealy machine has the same run outputs

nodes.summary: For a Mealy machine $M$, the set of accepting states of the sequential transducer associated with $M$ is the set of all states.
nodes.title: Every state of the sequential transducer of a Mealy machine is accepting

nodes.summary: For every Mealy machine $M$, the initial output of the sequential transducer of $M$ is the empty word.
nodes.title: Initial output of the sequential transducer of a Mealy machine

nodes.summary: For every Mealy machine $M$ and every state $q$, the final output of the sequential transducer of $M$ at $q$ is the empty word.
nodes.title: Final outputs of the sequential transducer of a Mealy machine

nodes.summary: For every Mealy machine $M$, input word $x$ and output word $y$, the sequential transducer of $M$ translates $x$ to $y$ if and only if the transduction of $M$ on $x$ is $y$.
nodes.title: The sequential transducer of a Mealy machine computes its transduction

nodes.summary: A Moore machine with state type $Q$, input alphabet $\Sigma$ and output alphabet $\Gamma$ consists of a transition function, assigning to each state $q$ and input letter $a$ a successor state $\delta(q, a) \in Q$, an output function $\lambda : Q \to \Gamma$, and a start state $q_0 \in Q$. The output depends only on the state.
nodes.title: Moore machine

nodes.summary: The run of a Moore machine $M$ with output function $\lambda$ from a state $q$ on an input word $a_1 \cdots a_n$ is the pair $(q_n, \lambda(q_0) \lambda(q_1) \cdots \lambda(q_n))$, where $q_0 = q$ and, for each $1 \le i \le n$, $q_i$ is the successor of $q_{i-1}$ on $a_i$. The output word has $n + 1$ letters and begins with the output of the starting state.
nodes.title: Run of a Moore machine

nodes.summary: For a Moore machine $M$, a state $q$ and an input word $x$, the final state of the run from $q$ on $x$ is the state reached by starting in $q$ and moving, on each successive letter of $x$, to the successor state given by the transition function of $M$; on the empty word it is $q$.
nodes.title: Final state of a Moore machine run

nodes.summary: For a Moore machine $M$, a state $q$ and an input word $x$, the output word of $M$ from $q$ on $x$ is the second component of the run of $M$ from $q$ on $x$: the outputs of the states visited along that run, starting with the output of $q$; it has one more letter than $x$.
nodes.title: Output word of a Moore machine run

nodes.summary: For a Moore machine $M$ with transition function $\delta$, a state $q$, an input letter $a$ and an input word $w$, the final state of the run of $M$ from $q$ on the word $aw$ equals the final state of the run of $M$ from $\delta(q, a)$ on $w$.
nodes.title: Final state of a Moore machine run on a nonempty word

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a Moore machine, $q$ a state, $a$ an input letter and $x$ an input word, and let $q'$ be the successor state of $M$ in state $q$ on letter $a$. The output word of the run of $M$ from $q$ on $ax$ is the output of $q$ followed by the output word of the run from $q'$ on $x$.
nodes.title: Output of a Moore machine on a nonempty word

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a Moore machine with start state $q_0$, and write $o(q)$ for the output of a state $q$. On an input word $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$, let $q_i$ be the state that $M$ moves to from $q_{i-1}$ on $a_i$. The transduction of $M$ on this word is the output word $o(q_0)\, o(q_1) \cdots o(q_n)$, of length $n + 1$.
nodes.title: Transduction of a Moore machine

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a Moore machine with transition function $\delta$, output function $\lambda$ and start state $q_0$. Its sequential transducer has the same states and the start state $q_0$; reading a letter $a$ in state $q$ it moves to $\delta(q, a)$ and emits the one-letter word $\lambda(\delta(q, a))$; every state is accepting; the initial output is the one-letter word $\lambda(q_0)$; and every final output is empty.
nodes.title: The sequential transducer of a Moore machine

nodes.summary: For a Moore machine $M$, a state $q$ and an input word $x$, the output word of the run of $M$ from $q$ on $x$ is the output of $q$ followed by the output word of the run of the sequential rendering of $M$ from $q$ on $x$.
nodes.title: Moore machine output via its sequential rendering

nodes.summary: For a Moore machine $M$, the set of accepting states of the sequential transducer associated with $M$ is the set of all states.
nodes.title: Every state of the sequential transducer of a Moore machine is accepting

nodes.summary: For every Moore machine $M$, the initial output of the sequential transducer of $M$ is the one-letter word consisting of the output of the start state of $M$.
nodes.title: Initial output of the sequential transducer of a Moore machine

nodes.summary: For a Moore machine $M$ and every state $q$, the final output word at $q$ of the sequential transducer associated with $M$ is empty.
nodes.title: Final outputs of the sequential transducer of a Moore machine

nodes.summary: For every Moore machine $M$, input word $x$ and output word $y$, the sequential transducer of $M$ translates $x$ to $y$ if and only if the transduction of $M$ on $x$ is $y$.
nodes.title: The sequential transducer of a Moore machine computes its transduction
Star height

nodes.summary: The star height of an ordinary regular expression is the nesting depth of the Kleene star in it: the expressions for the empty language and the empty word and the single letters have star height $0$; a union $e_1 + e_2$ and a concatenation $e_1 e_2$ have the larger of the star heights of $e_1$ and $e_2$; and $e^*$ has star height one more than $e$.
nodes.title: Star height of a regular expression

nodes.summary: A generalized regular expression over an alphabet $\alpha$ is built from ordinary regular expressions over $\alpha$ by complement, union, concatenation and Kleene star: every ordinary regular expression over $\alpha$ is one, and if $e$, $e_1$, $e_2$ are generalized regular expressions, then so are the complement $\neg e$, the union $e_1 + e_2$, the concatenation $e_1 e_2$ and the star $e^*$.
nodes.title: Generalized regular expressions

nodes.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$, the language over $\alpha$ denoted by a generalized regular expression over $\alpha$ is defined recursively, for generalized regular expressions $e$, $e_1$, $e_2$: an ordinary regular expression denotes the language it matches; the complement $\neg e$ denotes the complement, in the set of all words over $\alpha$, of the language of $e$; the union $e_1 + e_2$ denotes the union and the…
nodes.title: Language of a generalized regular expression

nodes.summary: The generalized star height of a generalized regular expression is the nesting depth of the Kleene star in it, counting the stars inside its ordinary regular subexpressions: for generalized regular expressions $e$, $e_1$, $e_2$, an ordinary regular expression has its usual star height; the complement $\neg e$ has the star height of $e$; the union $e_1 + e_2$ and the concatenation $e_1 e_2$ have the larger of the…
nodes.title: Generalized star height

nodes.summary: A language $L$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ has generalized star height at most $n$, for a natural number $n$, if some generalized regular expression over $\alpha$ whose generalized star height is at most $n$ denotes $L$.
nodes.title: Bounded generalized star height
Thompson's construction

nodes.summary: Over an alphabet $\alpha$, this is the ε-NFA whose set of states is empty; consequently it has no start states, no accepting states and no transitions.
nodes.title: The ε-NFA with no states

nodes.summary: The ε-NFA over the alphabet $\alpha$ with a single state, which is both its start state and its accepting state, and no moves at all (neither letter moves nor ε-moves).
nodes.title: One-state automaton

nodes.summary: For a letter $a$ of the alphabet $\alpha$, this is the ε-NFA over $\alpha$ with two states, a start state and an accepting state, and a single move, which reads $a$ and goes from the start state to the accepting state; it has no other moves and no ε-moves.
nodes.title: Single-letter automaton

nodes.summary: Given ε-NFAs $M$ with state set $\sigma$ and $N$ with state set $\tau$ over the same alphabet, their union is the ε-NFA on the disjoint union $\sigma \sqcup \tau$ whose moves are the moves of $M$ and the moves of $N$, whose start states are the start states of $M$ and of $N$, and whose accepting states are the accepting states of $M$ and of $N$.
nodes.title: Union of ε-NFAs

nodes.summary: Given ε-NFAs $M$ with state set $\sigma$ and $N$ with state set $\tau$ over the same alphabet, their concatenation is the ε-NFA on the disjoint union $\sigma \sqcup \tau$ whose moves are the moves of $M$, the moves of $N$, and an ε-move from every accepting state of $M$ to every start state of $N$. Its start states are the start states of $M$ and its accepting states are the accepting states of $N$.
nodes.title: Concatenation of ε-NFAs

nodes.summary: Given an ε-NFA $M$ with state set $\sigma$, its star automaton has the states of $M$ together with one new state $q_0$, which is its only start state and its only accepting state. Its moves are the moves of $M$, an ε-move from $q_0$ to every start state of $M$, and an ε-move from every accepting state of $M$ to $q_0$.
nodes.title: Kleene star of an ε-NFA

nodes.summary: The state set $S(r)$ of Thompson's automaton of a regular expression $r$ is defined by structural recursion: $S(0)$ is empty, $S(\varepsilon)$ has one element, $S(a)$ has two elements for a letter $a$, both $S(P + Q)$ and $S(PQ)$ are the disjoint union $S(P) \sqcup S(Q)$, and $S(P^*)$ is $S(P)$ together with one new element.
nodes.title: States of Thompson's automaton

nodes.summary: To each regular expression $r$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ it assigns an ε-NFA over $\alpha$ with state set $S(r)$, the states of Thompson's automaton of $r$, by structural recursion: $0$ goes to the automaton with no states, $\varepsilon$ to the one-state automaton, a letter $a$ to the single-letter automaton of $a$, $P + Q$ to the union of the automata of $P$ and $Q$, $PQ$ to their concatenation, and $P^*$ to the…
nodes.title: Thompson's construction

nodes.summary: The automaton accepts exactly the words the regular expression matches.
nodes.title: Correctness of Thompson's construction

nodes.summary: The state count $n(r)$ of a regular expression $r$ is defined by structural recursion: $n(0) = 0$, $n(\varepsilon) = 1$, $n(a) = 2$ for a letter $a$, $n(P + Q) = n(P) + n(Q)$, $n(PQ) = n(P) + n(Q)$ and $n(P^*) = n(P) + 1$.
nodes.title: Thompson state count

nodes.summary: For every regular expression $r$, the number of states of Thompson's automaton of $r$ is $n(r)$, the Thompson state count of $r$: $n(0) = 0$, $n(\varepsilon) = 1$, $n(a) = 2$ for a letter $a$, $n(P + Q) = n(P) + n(Q)$, $n(PQ) = n(P) + n(Q)$ and $n(P^*) = n(P) + 1$.
nodes.title: Number of states of Thompson's automaton
Two-way finite automata

nodes.summary: A deterministic two-way automaton with state set $Q$ over the alphabet $\Sigma$ consists of a partial transition function, which assigns to each state $q \in Q$ and input symbol $a \in \Sigma$ at most one pair of a successor state and a head move (left, stay or right), together with a single start state and a set of accepting states.
nodes.title: Deterministic two-way automaton

nodes.summary: A deterministic two-way automaton $A$ is viewed as the nondeterministic two-way automaton with the same states and accepting states, whose only start state is the start state of $A$, and which can go from state $q$ reading a symbol $a$ to state $q'$ with head move $m$ exactly when the step function of $A$ at $q$ and $a$ returns $q'$ and $m$.
nodes.title: A deterministic two-way automaton as a nondeterministic one

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be a deterministic two-way automaton, viewed as a nondeterministic two-way automaton. On reading the symbol $x$ in state $q$, it has a transition to state $q'$ with head move $m$ if and only if the transition function of $A$ sends $(q, x)$ to the pair $(q', m)$.
nodes.title: Transition relation of a deterministic two-way automaton

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be a deterministic two-way automaton, viewed as a nondeterministic two-way automaton. If, on reading the symbol $x$ in state $q$, it has a transition to state $q'$ with head move $m$ and a transition to state $q''$ with head move $m'$, then $m = m'$ and $q' = q''$.
nodes.title: Deterministic two-way automata have unique transitions

nodes.summary: The language of a deterministic two-way automaton $A$ is the set of words accepted by $A$ viewed as a nondeterministic two-way automaton: a word $w$ belongs to it when, starting in the start state with the head at the first position of $w$ and following the step function of $A$ (which moves the head one position left, keeps it in place, or moves it one position right, and gets stuck when it is undefined or would…
nodes.title: Language of a deterministic two-way automaton

nodes.summary: For every deterministic two-way automaton $A$ and every word $w$, $w$ belongs to the language of $A$ if and only if $w$ is accepted by $A$ viewed as a nondeterministic two-way automaton.
nodes.title: Membership in the language of a two-way deterministic automaton

nodes.summary: The language of every deterministic two-way automaton with finitely many states is regular.
nodes.title: Finite two-way deterministic automata accept regular languages

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ with transition function $\delta$, this is the deterministic two-way automaton with the same states, start state and accepting states as $M$ which, in state $q$ reading a symbol $a$, goes to state $\delta(q, a)$ and moves its head one symbol to the right.
nodes.title: A DFA as a two-way deterministic automaton

nodes.summary: For every DFA $M$, the deterministic two-way automaton that simulates $M$, viewed as a nondeterministic two-way automaton, equals the nondeterministic two-way automaton obtained by viewing $M$ as an NFA and letting that NFA always move its head one symbol to the right.
nodes.title: The two-way simulation of a DFA agrees with that of its NFA

nodes.summary: For every DFA $M$, the deterministic two-way automaton that simulates $M$ by always moving its head one symbol to the right has exactly the language accepted by $M$.
nodes.title: The two-way simulation of a DFA accepts the same language

nodes.summary: For every regular language $L$ over an alphabet, there is a deterministic two-way automaton with finitely many states whose language is exactly $L$.
nodes.title: Regular languages are accepted by two-way deterministic automata

nodes.summary: Every nondeterministic two-way automaton with finitely many states accepts a regular language.
nodes.title: Finite two-way nondeterministic automata accept regular languages

nodes.summary: For every regular language $L$ over an alphabet, there is a nondeterministic two-way automaton with finitely many states that accepts exactly the words of $L$.
nodes.title: Regular languages are accepted by two-way nondeterministic automata

nodes.summary: Nerode equivalence, the minimal automaton and its universal property, and the minimization algorithms of Moore, Hopcroft and Brzozowski with their correctness and cost.
nodes.title: Automaton minimization
Myhill–Nerode theorem

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. Two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$ when they have the same left quotient, that is, $\{z \in \Sigma^* \mid xz \in L\} = \{z \in \Sigma^* \mid yz \in L\}$.
nodes.title: Nerode equivalence

nodes.summary: For a language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the Nerode setoid of $L$ is the set $\Sigma^*$ of words equipped with Nerode equivalence for $L$, which is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
nodes.title: The Nerode setoid

nodes.summary: For a language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the Nerode classes of $L$ are the elements of the quotient of the set of words over $\Sigma$ by Nerode equivalence for $L$, under which two words $x$ and $y$ are equivalent when they have the same left quotient, that is, when for every word $z$ we have $xz \in L$ if and only if $yz \in L$.
nodes.title: Nerode classes

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. Two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$ if and only if, for every word $z \in \Sigma^*$, $xz \in L$ holds exactly when $yz \in L$.
nodes.title: Continuation characterization of Nerode equivalence

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language. If two words $x$ and $y$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$, then $x \in L$ if and only if $y \in L$.
nodes.title: Nerode equivalent words agree on membership

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$, then for every word $z \in \Sigma^*$ the words $xz$ and $yz$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$.
nodes.title: Nerode equivalence is a right congruence

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$, then for every symbol $a \in \Sigma$ the words $xa$ and $ya$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$.
nodes.title: Appending a symbol preserves Nerode equivalence

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. For every word $x \in \Sigma^*$, the word $x\varepsilon$ obtained by appending the empty word $\varepsilon$ is Nerode equivalent to $x$ for $L$.
nodes.title: Appending the empty word preserves the Nerode class

nodes.summary: For a language $L$ and a word $x$, the Nerode class $[x]$ of $x$ is the equivalence class of $x$ under Nerode equivalence for $L$.
nodes.title: Nerode class of a word

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language. The residual map sends the Nerode class $[x]$ of a word $x$ to the left quotient $x^{-1}L = \{ y \mid xy \in L \}$, viewed as an element of the set $\{ w^{-1}L \mid w \text{ a word} \}$ of left quotients of $L$. It is well-defined because Nerode equivalent words have the same left quotient.
nodes.title: Residual map on Nerode classes

nodes.summary: For every language $L$, the map sending the Nerode class $[x]$ of a word $x$ to the left quotient $x^{-1}L = \{ y \mid xy \in L \}$ is a bijection from the set of Nerode classes of $L$ onto the set $\{ w^{-1}L \mid w \text{ a word} \}$ of left quotients of $L$.
nodes.title: Bijection between Nerode classes and left quotients

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$ and $a \in \Sigma$ a symbol. Appending $a$ sends the Nerode class of a word $x$ to the Nerode class of $xa$; this is well defined because Nerode equivalence is preserved by appending a symbol.
nodes.title: Transition on Nerode classes

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language. The accepting Nerode classes of $L$ are those whose words belong to $L$: the Nerode class $[x]$ of a word $x$ is accepting if and only if $x \in L$. This is well-defined because Nerode equivalent words are either both in $L$ or both outside $L$.
nodes.title: Accepting Nerode classes

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. The Nerode automaton of $L$ is the deterministic automaton over $\Sigma$, not necessarily finite, whose states are the Nerode classes of words for $L$, whose start state is the class of the empty word, which on reading a symbol $a \in \Sigma$ moves from the class of a word $x$ to the class of $xa$, and whose accepting states are the classes of the words in $L$.
nodes.title: The Nerode automaton

nodes.summary: For every language $L$, the language accepted by the Nerode automaton of $L$ is exactly $L$.
nodes.title: The Nerode automaton recognizes its language

nodes.summary: For every language $L$ and every Nerode class $q$ of $L$, there is a word $x$ such that the Nerode automaton of $L$, started in its start state and reading $x$, ends in the state $q$.
nodes.title: Every state of the Nerode automaton is reachable

nodes.summary: For every language $L$, writing $x^{-1}L = \{ y \mid xy \in L \}$ for the left quotient of $L$ by a word $x$, there are finitely many Nerode classes of $L$ if and only if the set $\{ x^{-1}L \mid x \text{ a word} \}$ of left quotients of $L$ is finite.
nodes.title: Finitely many Nerode classes iff finitely many left quotients

nodes.summary: A language $L$ is regular, that is, accepted by some deterministic finite automaton, if and only if $L$ has finitely many Nerode classes.
nodes.title: Myhill–Nerode theorem, quotient form

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. Two words $x$ and $y$ over $\Sigma$ are distinguishable by $L$ when there is a word $z$ over $\Sigma$ such that exactly one of $xz$ and $yz$ belongs to $L$.
nodes.title: Distinguishable words

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA and let $L$ be the language it accepts. If $M$ reaches the same state from its start state on reading the words $x$ and $y$, then $x$ and $y$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$.
nodes.title: Words reaching the same DFA state are Nerode equivalent

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language and let $M$ be a DFA that accepts exactly $L$. If two words $x$ and $y$ are distinguishable by $L$, then the states that $M$ reaches from its start state on reading $x$ and on reading $y$ are different.
nodes.title: Distinguishable words reach different DFA states

nodes.summary: Two states $p$ and $q$ of a DFA $M$ are equivalent when they accept the same continuation language: for every word $z$, running $M$ from $p$ on $z$ ends in an accepting state if and only if running $M$ from $q$ on $z$ does.
nodes.title: Equivalent states of a DFA

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA and let $L$ be the language it accepts. Two words $x$ and $y$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$ if and only if the states that $M$ reaches from its start state on reading $x$ and on reading $y$ are observationally equivalent, that is, $M$ accepts the same language from both states.
nodes.title: Nerode equivalence is equivalence of the reached states

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ and a state $q$ of $M$, let $L_q$ be the language of words $z$ such that running $M$ from $q$ on $z$ ends in an accepting state. The reachable residuals of $M$ form the set of the languages $L_q$ over all states $q$ that $M$ reaches from its start state on some input word.
nodes.title: Residual languages of reachable states

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language and let $M$ be a DFA that accepts exactly $L$. This is the bijection from the Nerode classes of $L$ to the reachable residuals of $M$, the languages accepted by $M$ from states it reaches from its start state. It sends the Nerode class of a word $x$ to the left quotient $\{z \mid xz \in L\}$, which is the language $M$ accepts from the state it reaches on reading $x$.
nodes.title: Nerode classes correspond to reachable residuals

nodes.summary: For a language $L$ and a Nerode class $q$ of $L$, the representative of $q$ is a word whose Nerode class is $q$, chosen once and for all.
nodes.title: Representative of a Nerode class

nodes.summary: For a language $L$ and a DFA $M$ over the same alphabet, this map sends each Nerode class $q$ of $L$ to the state that $M$ reaches from its start state on the chosen representative of $q$.
nodes.title: Nerode classes to DFA states

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA that accepts exactly the language $L$. Then the map sending each Nerode class of $L$ to the state that $M$ reaches from its start state on the chosen representative of the class is injective. In particular, $M$ has at least one distinct state for each Nerode class.
nodes.title: Distinct Nerode classes reach distinct states

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language with finitely many Nerode classes, and let $M$ be a DFA with a finite set of states $Q$ that accepts exactly $L$. Then the number of Nerode classes of $L$ is at most $|Q|$.
nodes.title: Nerode classes bound the number of DFA states

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language and let $M$ be a DFA with a finite set of states $Q$ that accepts exactly $L$. For a word $x$, the left quotient of $L$ by $x$ is the language $\{z \mid xz \in L\}$. Then the number of distinct left quotients of $L$ is at most $|Q|$.
nodes.title: Myhill–Nerode lower bound via left quotients

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language with finitely many Nerode classes, and let $M$ be a DFA with a finite set of states $Q$ that accepts exactly $L$. Send each Nerode class of $L$ to the state that $M$ reaches from its start state on the chosen representative word of the class. Then the number of Nerode classes of $L$ equals $|Q|$ if and only if every state in $Q$ is the image of some Nerode class under this map.
nodes.title: Equality case of the Nerode state bound

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language with finitely many Nerode classes, and let $M$ be a DFA with a finite set of states $Q$ that accepts exactly $L$. Send each Nerode class of $L$ to the state that $M$ reaches from its start state on the chosen representative word of the class. If some state in $Q$ is not the image of any Nerode class under this map, then the number of Nerode classes of $L$ is strictly less than $|Q|$.
nodes.title: Strict Nerode state bound

nodes.summary: A state is reachable when some input word reaches it from the start state.
nodes.title: Reachable state of a DFA

nodes.summary: A DFA is accessible when every state is reachable.
nodes.title: Accessible DFA
Minimal deterministic automaton

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA, write $\delta^*(q, x)$ for the state $M$ reaches from the state $q$ by reading the word $x$, and let $L_M(q)$ be the language of words accepted by $M$ when started in $q$. For every state $q$ and every word $x$, the left quotient $\{z : xz \in L_M(q)\}$ of $L_M(q)$ by $x$ equals $L_M(\delta^*(q, x))$.
nodes.title: Left quotients of continuation languages

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ and a word $x$, the minimized state of $x$ is the language accepted by $M$ starting from the state that $M$ reaches on reading $x$ from its start state, viewed as an element of the reachable residuals of $M$.
nodes.title: Residual reached by a word

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA accepting the language $L$. The set of left quotients $\{z : xz \in L\}$ of $L$ by words $x$ equals the set of reachable residuals of $M$ (the languages accepted by $M$ from the states it reaches from its start state). The bijection from the first set to the second sends each language to itself.
nodes.title: Left quotients as reachable residuals

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA accepting the language $L$. The minimized DFA of $M$ has as states the reachable residuals of $M$, that is, the languages accepted by $M$ from the states it reaches from its start state. Its start state is $L$; on a letter $a$ it moves from a state $K$ to the left quotient $\{z : az \in K\}$; and its accepting states are those that contain the empty word.
nodes.title: Minimized DFA

nodes.summary: For every language $L$ and every word $x$, the state that the residual-language DFA of $L$ reaches on reading $x$ is the left quotient $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$. This automaton has the left quotients of $L$ as states, start state $L$, transition from $K$ on a letter $a$ to $a^{-1}K$, and accepts $K$ when $K$ contains the empty word.
nodes.title: States reached in the residual-language DFA

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA accepting the language $L$, and consider the automaton whose states are the left quotients of $L$, with start state $L$, moving from $K$ on a letter $a$ to $\{z : az \in K\}$. For every word $x$, the state that the minimized DFA of $M$ reaches on $x$, carried to the left quotients of $L$ by the bijection that sends each language to itself, is the state that this automaton reaches on $x$.
nodes.title: Evaluation in the minimized DFA agrees with the left-quotient automaton

nodes.summary: For every DFA $M$ and every word $x$, the state that the minimized DFA of $M$ reaches on $x$ is the language accepted by $M$ from the state that $M$ reaches on $x$.
nodes.title: States reached in the minimized DFA

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA. For every reachable residual $K$ of $M$ (a state of the minimized DFA of $M$) and every letter $a$, the minimized DFA of $M$ moves from $K$ on input $a$ to the left quotient $\{z : az \in K\}$ of $K$ by $a$.
nodes.title: Transitions of the minimized DFA

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA, and for a word $x$ let $[x]$ be the language accepted by $M$ from the state that $M$ reaches on $x$. For every word $x$ and every letter $a$, the minimized DFA of $M$ moves from the state $[x]$ on input $a$ to the state $[xa]$.
nodes.title: Transitions of the minimized DFA on reached states

nodes.summary: For every DFA $M$, the minimized DFA of $M$ accepts exactly the language accepted by $M$.
nodes.title: The minimized DFA accepts the same language

nodes.summary: For every language $L$, the residual-language DFA of $L$ is accessible. This automaton has as states the left quotients $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$ for words $x$, start state $L$, transition from $K$ on a letter $a$ to $a^{-1}K$, and accepts $K$ when $K$ contains the empty word.
nodes.title: The residual-language DFA is accessible

nodes.summary: For every DFA $M$, every state of the minimized DFA of $M$ is reached from its start state by reading some word.
nodes.title: The minimized DFA is accessible

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ accepting the language $L$, there is a bijection from the Nerode classes of $L$ to the reachable residuals of $M$; it sends the class of a word $x$ to the left quotient $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$.
nodes.title: Nerode classes and reachable residuals

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA accepting the language $L$. The reachable residuals of the minimized DFA of $M$ and the reachable residuals of $M$ both form the set of left quotients $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$ of $L$ by words $x$, and this is the bijection from the first set to the second that sends each language to itself.
nodes.title: Reachable residuals of the minimized DFA

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA accepting the language $L$. If the set of reachable residuals of $M$ (the states of the minimized DFA of $M$) and the set of Nerode classes of $L$ are both finite, then they have the same number of elements.
nodes.title: When finite, the minimized DFA has as many states as there are Nerode classes

nodes.summary: A CSLib deterministic automaton $M$ on finite words is viewed as a Mathlib DFA with the same states, the same transition function, the same start state and the same set of accepting states as $M$.
nodes.title: CSLib automata as Mathlib DFAs

nodes.summary: A Mathlib DFA $M$ is viewed as a CSLib deterministic automaton on finite words with the same states, the same transition function, the same start state and the same set of accepting states as $M$.
nodes.title: Mathlib DFAs as CSLib automata

nodes.summary: For every deterministic automaton $M$ on finite words, the DFA with the same states, transition function, start state and accepting states as $M$ accepts exactly the language of $M$.
nodes.title: Converting a CSLib automaton to a Mathlib DFA preserves its language

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$ and let $x, y \in \Sigma^*$. Then $x$ and $y$ are related by the Nerode congruence of $L$, that is, $xz \in L \iff yz \in L$ for every word $z$, if and only if they are Nerode equivalent for $L$, that is, their left quotients $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$ and $y^{-1}L$ are equal.
nodes.title: The Nerode congruence relates words with equal left quotients

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$, and write $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$ for the left quotient of $L$ by a word $x$. This is the map from the classes of the Nerode congruence of $L$ to the set $\{w^{-1}L : w \in \Sigma^*\}$ of residual languages of $L$ that sends the class of each word $x$ to $x^{-1}L$; it is well defined because Nerode-congruent words have the same left quotient.
nodes.title: The residual language of a Nerode class

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$, and write $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$ for the left quotient of $L$ by a word $x$. This is the bijection from the classes of the Nerode congruence of $L$ onto the set $\{x^{-1}L : x \in \Sigma^*\}$ of residual languages of $L$ that sends the class of each word $x$ to $x^{-1}L$.
nodes.title: Nerode classes are the residual languages

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$, and write $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$ for the left quotient of $L$ by a word $x$. Consider the canonical automaton of $L$ as a DFA: its states are the classes $[x]$ of the Nerode congruence of $L$, its start state is the class of the empty word, on a letter $a$ it goes from $[x]$ to $[xa]$, and its accepting states are the classes of words of $L$. Renaming each…
nodes.title: The Nerode automaton is the residual-language automaton

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over an alphabet $\Sigma$ accepting the language $L$, and write $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$ for the left quotient of $L$ by a word $x$. Consider the canonical automaton of $L$ as a DFA: its states are the classes $[x]$ of the Nerode congruence of $L$, its start state is the class of the empty word, on a letter $a$ it goes from $[x]$ to $[xa]$, and its accepting states are the classes of words of…
nodes.title: The canonical automaton of a DFA's language is its minimized DFA

nodes.summary: Let $M$ and $N$ be DFAs over the same alphabet with transition functions $\delta_M$ and $\delta_N$. A morphism from $M$ to $N$ is a map $f$ from the states of $M$ to the states of $N$ that sends the start state of $M$ to the start state of $N$, satisfies $f(\delta_M(q, a)) = \delta_N(f(q), a)$ for every state $q$ of $M$ and every symbol $a$, and such that each state $q$ of $M$ is accepting if and only if $f(q)$ is…
nodes.title: Morphisms of DFAs

nodes.summary: If $f$ is a morphism from a DFA $M$ to a DFA $N$, then for every state $q$ of $M$ and every word $x$, running $N$ on $x$ from $f(q)$ ends in the image under $f$ of the state reached by running $M$ on $x$ from $q$.
nodes.title: DFA morphisms commute with evaluation from a state

nodes.summary: If $f$ is a morphism from a DFA $M$ to a DFA $N$, then for every word $x$, the state that $N$ reaches on input $x$ from its start state is the image under $f$ of the state that $M$ reaches on input $x$ from its start state.
nodes.title: DFA morphisms commute with evaluation

nodes.summary: If $f$ is a morphism from a DFA $M$ to a DFA $N$ over the same alphabet, then $M$ and $N$ accept the same language.
nodes.title: DFA morphisms preserve the accepted language

nodes.summary: For every DFA $M$, the identity map on the states of $M$ is a DFA morphism from $M$ to itself.
nodes.title: Identity DFA morphism

nodes.summary: If $f$ is a DFA morphism from $M$ to $N$ and $g$ is a DFA morphism from $N$ to $P$, where $M$, $N$, $P$ are DFAs over the same alphabet, then the composite of $g$ and $f$ is the DFA morphism from $M$ to $P$ whose state map is $g \circ f$.
nodes.title: Composition of DFA morphisms

nodes.summary: A DFA $M$ is state-separated when any two equivalent states of $M$ are equal: if $p \ne q$, then the languages of words accepted by $M$ starting from $p$ and from $q$ are different.
nodes.title: State-separated DFA

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an accessible DFA accepting the language $L$. The residual-language DFA of $L$ has as states the left quotients $x^{-1}L = \{y \mid xy \in L\}$ for words $x$, start state $L$, transitions $K \mapsto a^{-1}K$ on a symbol $a$, and a state $K$ is accepting when it contains the empty word. The canonical residual map is the DFA morphism from $M$ to this DFA that sends each state $q$ of $M$ to its continuation…
nodes.title: The canonical residual map

nodes.summary: For an accessible DFA $M$, every state of the residual-language DFA of the language accepted by $M$ is the image of some state of $M$ under the canonical residual map.
nodes.title: The canonical residual map is surjective

nodes.summary: For an accessible DFA $M$, the canonical residual map from $M$ to the residual-language DFA of its accepted language is injective if and only if $M$ is state-separated, that is, any two states of $M$ with the same continuation language are equal.
nodes.title: Injectivity of the canonical residual map

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA that is accessible and state-separated, and let $L$ be the language it accepts. The map sending each state $q$ of $M$ to the language of words accepted by $M$ starting from $q$ is a bijection from the states of $M$ onto the set of left quotients $\{z : xz \in L\}$ of $L$ by words $x$.
nodes.title: States of an accessible, state-separated DFA correspond to residuals

nodes.summary: For an accessible DFA $M$ accepting the language $L$, every DFA morphism from $M$ to the residual-language DFA of $L$ equals the canonical residual map.
nodes.title: Uniqueness of the canonical residual map
Brzozowski's algorithm

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ with finitely many states, the determinized reversal of $M$ is the subset construction applied to the reversal of $M$: its states are the sets of states of $M$; reading a letter $a$ from a set $S$ leads to the set of states $q$ whose $a$-successor in $M$ lies in $S$; its start state is the set of accepting states of $M$; and it accepts exactly the sets that contain the start state of $M$.
nodes.title: Determinized reversal of a DFA

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with finitely many states and $w$ a word. On input $w$, the determinized reversal of $M$ reaches the set of states $q$ of $M$ from which $M$, reading $w$ backwards starting at $q$, ends in an accepting state.
nodes.title: States reached in the determinized reversal

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with finitely many states and $L$ its language, and write $w^R$ for the word $w$ read backwards. The determinized reversal of $M$ accepts exactly the reversed language $L^R = \{w \mid w^R \in L\}$.
nodes.title: The determinized reversal accepts the reversed language

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with finitely many states in which every state is reached from the start state by some word, and let $L$ be its language. Write $u^R$ for the word $u$ read backwards, $L^R = \{u \mid u^R \in L\}$ for the reversed language, and $w^{-1}K = \{v \mid wv \in K\}$ for the left quotient of a language $K$ by a word $w$. Then two words $w$ and $w'$ lead the determinized reversal of $M$ from its start state…
nodes.title: Brzozowski's lemma

nodes.summary: For a deterministic finite automaton $M$ over a finite alphabet with finite state set $Q$, the subsets of $Q$ reachable from the start state in the subset construction of the reversal of $M$.
nodes.title: States of the intermediate Brzozowski automaton

nodes.summary: For a deterministic finite automaton $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, the subset construction of the reversal of $M$, restricted to the subsets reachable from its start state.
nodes.title: The intermediate Brzozowski automaton

nodes.summary: For a deterministic finite automaton $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, the subsets of states of the intermediate Brzozowski automaton of $M$ that are reachable from the start state in the subset construction of its reversal.
nodes.title: States of Brzozowski's automaton

nodes.summary: For a deterministic finite automaton $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, the subset construction of the reversal of the intermediate Brzozowski automaton of $M$, restricted to the subsets reachable from its start state. Equivalently: reverse, determinize by the subset construction and keep the reachable subsets, twice.
nodes.title: Brzozowski's automaton

nodes.summary: For a deterministic finite automaton $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, every state of the intermediate Brzozowski automaton of $M$ (the subset construction of the reversal of $M$ restricted to its reachable subsets) is reached from its start state by some word.
nodes.title: Every state of the intermediate Brzozowski automaton is reachable

nodes.summary: For a deterministic finite automaton $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, every state of Brzozowski's automaton of $M$ is reached from its start state by some word.
nodes.title: Every state of Brzozowski's automaton is reachable

nodes.summary: For a deterministic finite automaton $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, Brzozowski's automaton of $M$ accepts exactly the language of $M$.
nodes.title: Brzozowski's automaton accepts the language of the original automaton

nodes.summary: For a deterministic finite automaton $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states and words $w$ and $w'$, Brzozowski's automaton of $M$ reaches the same state on $w$ as on $w'$ if and only if $w$ and $w'$ are Nerode equivalent for the language of $M$, that is, have the same left quotient.
nodes.title: Brzozowski's automaton identifies exactly the Nerode equivalent words

nodes.summary: For a deterministic finite automaton $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, the map that sends a state $p$ of Brzozowski's automaton of $M$ to the language accepted by $M$ from the state that $M$ reaches on $w$, where $w$ is a chosen word leading Brzozowski's automaton from its start state to $p$; this language is one of the residual languages of the reachable states of $M$.
nodes.title: Residual language of a state of Brzozowski's automaton

nodes.summary: For a deterministic finite automaton $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, the bijection from the states of Brzozowski's automaton of $M$ to the residual languages of the reachable states of $M$ that sends each state $p$ to the language accepted by $M$ from the state that $M$ reaches on $w$, where $w$ is a chosen word leading Brzozowski's automaton from its start state to $p$.
nodes.title: States of Brzozowski's automaton as residual languages

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, and let $L$ be its language. For a language $K$ and a word $w$, write $w^{-1}K = \{v \mid wv \in K\}$ for the left quotient of $K$ by $w$. Every state of Brzozowski's automaton of $M$ is reached by some word $w$; rename that state to $w^{-1}L$, which does not depend on the choice of $w$. The renamed automaton is exactly the minimized DFA of $M$: its…
nodes.title: Brzozowski's automaton is the minimal automaton
Moore's algorithm

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with state set $S$ and transition function $\delta$. One round of Moore's refinement sends a set $E \subseteq S \times S$ of pairs of states to the set of pairs $(p, q) \in S \times S$ such that $p$ is accepting if and only if $q$ is accepting and, for every letter $a$, the pair $(\delta(p, a), \delta(q, a))$ lies in $E$.
nodes.title: Moore refinement step

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, and write $R$ for one round of Moore's refinement. For a set $E$ of pairs of states of $M$ and a budget $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the stopping Moore iteration is defined by recursion on $n$: with budget $0$ it returns $E$; with budget $n + 1$ it returns $E$ if $R(E) = E$, and otherwise the stopping Moore iteration from $R(E)$ with budget $n$.
nodes.title: Stopping Moore iteration

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, and write $R$ for one round of Moore's refinement. For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and every set $E$ of pairs of states of $M$, there is $k \le n$ such that the stopping Moore iteration from $E$ with budget $n$ returns $R^k(E)$, and if $k < n$ then $R^k(E)$ is a fixed point of $R$, that is, $R(R^k(E)) = R^k(E)$.
nodes.title: Output of the stopping Moore iteration

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet with finite set of states $Q$, Moore's relation is the set of pairs of states obtained from $Q \times Q$ by repeating rounds of Moore's refinement until a round changes nothing, for at most $|Q \times Q|$ rounds.
nodes.title: Moore's relation

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA. If a set $Z$ of pairs of states of $M$ is contained in its image under one round of Moore's refinement, then $Z$ is contained in Moore's relation of $M$.
nodes.title: Moore's relation contains every post-fixed point

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, two states $p$ and $q$ of $M$ are related by Moore's relation if and only if they have the same continuation language: for every word $w$, $M$ started at $p$ accepts $w$ exactly when $M$ started at $q$ accepts $w$.
nodes.title: Correctness of Moore's refinement

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$, two reachable states $p$ and $q$ of $M$ are related when the pair $(p, q)$ lies in Moore's relation of $M$; this relation is an equivalence relation on the reachable states of $M$.
nodes.title: Moore equivalence on reachable states

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$, these are the equivalence classes of the reachable states of $M$ under Moore equivalence, that is, under Moore's relation of $M$ restricted to reachable states. They are the states of Moore's minimal automaton.
nodes.title: States of Moore's automaton

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet with finitely many states. For a reachable state $s$ of $M$, its Moore class is the equivalence class of $s$ among the reachable states of $M$ under Moore's relation; it is a state of Moore's minimal automaton of $M$.
nodes.title: Moore class of a reachable state

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, Moore's minimal automaton of $M$ has as states the classes of reachable states of $M$ under Moore's relation. Its start state is the class of the start state of $M$; reading a letter $a$ sends the class of a reachable state $s$ to the class of the state that $M$ reaches from $s$ on $a$; and the class of $s$ is accepting exactly when $s$ is an accepting…
nodes.title: Moore's minimal automaton

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, Moore's minimal automaton of $M$ accepts exactly the language accepted by $M$.
nodes.title: Moore's automaton accepts the same language

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet with finitely many states. Each state of Moore's minimal automaton of $M$, a class of reachable states of $M$, is sent to the continuation language of any member $s$, the set of words that $M$ accepts when started at $s$; this is a reachable residual language of $M$. It does not depend on the choice of $s$, because Moore-related states have the same continuation language.
nodes.title: Continuation language of a Moore class

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet with finitely many states. The states of Moore's minimal automaton of $M$ are in bijection with the reachable residual languages of $M$: the bijection sends the class of a reachable state $s$ to the continuation language of $s$, the set of words that $M$ accepts when started at $s$.
nodes.title: Moore classes are the reachable residuals

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA. Renaming each state of Moore's minimal automaton of $M$, a class of reachable states, to the continuation language accepted from its members turns Moore's automaton into exactly the minimized DFA of $M$, whose states are the reachable continuation languages of $M$.
nodes.title: Moore's automaton is the minimal automaton

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, Moore's minimal automaton of $M$ has exactly as many states as there are Nerode classes of the language accepted by $M$.
nodes.title: Moore's automaton has one state per Nerode class
Hopcroft's algorithm

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ with transition function $\delta$, a set $C$ of states and a letter $a$, the preimage of $C$ under $a$ is the set of states $q$ with $\delta(q, a) \in C$.
nodes.title: Preimage of a set under a letter

nodes.summary: A set $D$ of states is split by a set $P$ of states when $D$ contains both a state in $P$ and a state not in $P$, that is, when $D \cap P$ and $D \setminus P$ are both nonempty.
nodes.title: A set of states split by another

nodes.summary: For sets $P$ and $D$ of states, splitting $D$ by $P$ gives the two-element list $[D \cap P,\ D \setminus P]$ if both of these sets are nonempty, and the one-element list $[D]$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Splitting a block by a set

nodes.summary: For finite sets $A$ and $B$ of states, the smaller one is $A$ if $|A| \le |B|$ and $B$ otherwise; on a tie in cardinality it is $A$.
nodes.title: Smaller of two finite sets of states

nodes.summary: Given a waiting list $W$ of pairs of a set of states and a letter and sets $S$ and $D$ of states, write $D_1 = D \cap S$ and $D_2 = D \setminus S$. The new waiting entries for $D$ consist, for each letter $b$ in the enumeration order of the alphabet, of both $(D_1, b)$ and $(D_2, b)$ if $(D, b)$ is in $W$, and otherwise of the single entry $(E, b)$, where $E$ is the smaller of $D_1$ and $D_2$ by cardinality ($D_1$…
nodes.title: New splitters for a split block

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ with transition function $\delta$, a list $P$ of blocks of states, a set $C$ of states and a letter $a$, let $S = \{q : \delta(q, a) \in C\}$ be the preimage of $C$ under $a$. The partition after the splitter $(C, a)$ replaces each block $D$ of $P$, in order, by the two blocks $D \cap S$ and $D \setminus S$ when both are nonempty, and keeps $D$ otherwise.
nodes.title: One refinement round of the partition

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ with transition function $\delta$, a list $P$ of blocks of states, a list $W$ of pairs of a set of states and a letter, a set $C$ of states and a letter $a$, let $S = \{q : \delta(q, a) \in C\}$ be the preimage of $C$ under $a$, and say that $S$ splits a set $D$ when $D$ meets both $S$ and its complement. The waiting list after the splitter $(C, a)$, from the rest $W$ of the waiting list, consists of…
nodes.title: One update of the waiting list

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ with finite state set $Q$, this is the set $F \subseteq Q$ of accepting states of $M$, as a finite set.
nodes.title: Block of accepting states

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ with state set $Q$ and set of accepting states $F$, the rejecting block is the set $Q \setminus F$ of states of $M$ that are not accepting.
nodes.title: Rejecting states

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ with finite state set $Q$ and set of accepting states $F$, the initial partition is the list of blocks $F$, $Q \setminus F$, in this order, with any empty block removed.
nodes.title: Hopcroft's initial partition

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with finite state set $Q$, set of accepting states $F$ and finite alphabet $\Sigma$. If $F$ and $Q \setminus F$ are both nonempty, the initial waiting list consists of the splitters $(S, b)$ for every letter $b \in \Sigma$, where $S = F$ if $|F| \le |Q \setminus F|$ and $S = Q \setminus F$ otherwise; if one of $F$ and $Q \setminus F$ is empty, the initial waiting list is empty.
nodes.title: Hopcroft's initial waiting list

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA. Given a round budget $k$, a partition $P$ of the states of $M$ (a list of blocks) and a waiting list $W$ of splitters $(C, a)$, each a block $C$ with a letter $a$, the loop returns the pair $(P, W)$ unchanged if $k = 0$ or $W$ is empty. Otherwise it removes the first splitter $(C, a)$ from $W$, replaces $P$ by the partition after the splitter $(C, a)$ and the remaining waiting list by the waiting…
nodes.title: Hopcroft's refinement loop

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with finite state set $Q$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$. Hopcroft's partition of $M$ is the partition returned by Hopcroft's loop run from the initial partition and the initial waiting list with a budget of $|\Sigma| \cdot (|Q| + 1)$ rounds.
nodes.title: Hopcroft's partition

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ with finitely many states, Hopcroft's relation is the set of pairs $(p, q)$ of states of $M$ such that $p$ and $q$ lie in a common block of Hopcroft's partition.
nodes.title: Hopcroft's relation

nodes.summary: A list $P$ of sets of states is a partition into nonempty blocks when entries of $P$ at different positions are disjoint, every entry of $P$ is nonempty, and every state lies in some entry of $P$.
nodes.title: Partitions of the states

nodes.summary: For a list $P$ of sets of states, two states $p$ and $q$ are related by $P$ when some block $D$ of $P$ contains both $p$ and $q$.
nodes.title: Lying in a common block

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a list of sets of states that is a partition into nonempty blocks, let $C$ be an entry of $P$, and let $p$ and $q$ be states lying in a common entry of $P$. Then $p \in C$ if and only if $q \in C$.
nodes.title: A block contains both or neither of two related states

nodes.summary: If a list $P$ of sets of states is a partition into nonempty blocks, then the length of $P$ is at most the number $|Q|$ of states.
nodes.title: A partition has at most as many blocks as there are states

nodes.summary: Let $S$ and $D$ be sets of states. Every piece of $D$ split by $S$ (the two sets $D \cap S$ and $D \setminus S$ if $D$ meets both $S$ and its complement, and $D$ itself otherwise) is contained in $S$ or disjoint from $S$: any two states $x$ and $y$ of the piece satisfy $x \in S \iff y \in S$.
nodes.title: Pieces of a split block lie on one side

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with transition function $\delta$, $P$ a list of blocks of states, $C$ a set of states and $a$ a letter. Two states $p$ and $q$ lie in a common block after the splitter $(C, a)$ is applied to $P$ if and only if they lie in a common block of $P$ and $\delta(p, a) \in C \iff \delta(q, a) \in C$.
nodes.title: Effect of one splitter on the common-block relation

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with transition function $\delta$, let $P$ be a list of sets of states, $C$ a set of states and $a$ a letter, and let $\mathrm{pre} = \{q : \delta(q, a) \in C\}$. The partition after the splitter $(C, a)$, which replaces each entry $D$ of $P$ meeting both $\mathrm{pre}$ and its complement by $D \cap \mathrm{pre}$ and $D \setminus \mathrm{pre}$, has length equal to the length of $P$ plus the number…
nodes.title: Number of blocks after one round

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with transition function $\delta$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, let $P$ be a list of sets of states with no repeated entries, let $W$ be a list of pairs of a set of states and a letter, let $C$ be a set of states and $a$ a letter, and let $S = \{q : \delta(q, a) \in C\}$ be the preimage of $C$ under $a$. Then the waiting list after the splitter $(C, a)$, computed from the blocks $P$ and the rest…
nodes.title: Growth of the waiting list in one round

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with transition function $\delta$. A list $P$ of sets of states and a waiting list $W$ of pairs $(C, b)$ of a set of states $C$ and a letter $b$ satisfy the invariants when: (i) $P$ is a partition of the states into nonempty blocks; (ii) for every $(C, b)$ in $W$, $C$ is an entry of $P$; (iii) for every letter $b$ and all states $p$, $q$ lying in a common entry of $P$, if for every $C$ with…
nodes.title: Invariants of Hopcroft's loop

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA, $P$ a list of blocks of states, $W$ a list of pairs of a set of states and a letter, $C$ a set of states and $a$ a letter. If $P$ and the waiting list obtained by putting $(C, a)$ in front of $W$ satisfy the invariants of Hopcroft's loop, then so do the partition after the splitter $(C, a)$ and the waiting list after the splitter $(C, a)$ from the rest $W$.
nodes.title: One round preserves the invariants

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA and $P$ a list of blocks of states such that $P$ with the empty waiting list satisfies the invariants of Hopcroft's loop. Then two states $p$ and $q$ lie in a common block of $P$ if and only if they accept the same continuation languages, that is, $M$ accepts a word from $p$ exactly when it accepts it from $q$.
nodes.title: With an empty waiting list, blocks are the classes of equal continuation languages

nodes.summary: For every DFA $M$ with finitely many states over a finite alphabet, Hopcroft's initial partition and initial waiting list satisfy the invariants of Hopcroft's loop.
nodes.title: The invariants hold initially

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with finite state set $Q$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, let $P$ be a partition of the states given as a list of blocks, let $W$ be a waiting list of splitters, and let $k$ be a natural number. If $P$ and $W$ satisfy the invariants of Hopcroft's loop and $|W| + |\Sigma| \cdot (|Q| - |P|) \le k$, where $|P|$ and $|W|$ are the lengths of the lists, then Hopcroft's loop run from $(P, W)$ with a…
nodes.title: Termination of Hopcroft's loop

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with finite state set $Q$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$. Hopcroft's loop, run from the initial partition and the initial waiting list with a budget of $|\Sigma| \cdot (|Q| + 1)$ rounds, ends with an empty waiting list.
nodes.title: Hopcroft's waiting list is exhausted

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$, Hopcroft's final partition of $M$ is a partition of the states of $M$ into nonempty blocks.
nodes.title: Hopcroft's final partition is a partition

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$, two states $p$ and $q$ share a block of Hopcroft's final partition of $M$ exactly when the language accepted by $M$ from $p$ equals the language accepted by $M$ from $q$.
nodes.title: Correctness of Hopcroft's algorithm

nodes.summary: For every DFA $M$ with finitely many states over a finite alphabet, Hopcroft's relation of $M$, the set of pairs of states lying in a common block of Hopcroft's partition, equals Moore's state equivalence of $M$ as a set of pairs of states.
nodes.title: Hopcroft's partition is Moore's relation

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ and reachable states $p$ and $q$ of $M$, the classes of $p$ and $q$ under Moore's equivalence on reachable states (the states of Moore's minimal automaton) are equal if and only if $p$ and $q$ share a block of Hopcroft's final partition of $M$.
nodes.title: Moore classes are Hopcroft blocks

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA, $D$ a block of Hopcroft's final partition of $M$ and $p$ a state in $D$. Then a state $q$ lies in $D$ if and only if the language accepted by $M$ from $q$ equals the language accepted by $M$ from $p$.
nodes.title: Blocks of Hopcroft's partition are language classes

nodes.summary: The smaller of two sets has at most half their combined size: it is one of the two sets, so twice its size is at most the sum of the two sizes.
nodes.title: The smaller of two sets has at most half their total size

nodes.summary: If two disjoint sets union to `D`, the smaller of them has at most half the size of `D`.
nodes.title: The smaller part of a split has at most half the size

parts: Halving chains shrink blocks by a factor of at least
reading_title.source: Halving chains shrink blocks by a factor of at least $2^k$

nodes.summary: After `k` halving steps, the initial block is at least `2 ^ k` times the final block. The halving hypothesis is stated for the cardinalities only; no subset hypothesis is needed.
nodes.title: Halving chains shrink blocks by a factor of at least $2^k$

nodes.summary: In a chain of blocks where each step at least halves the size, a block containing a given state can occur at most `Nat.log 2 n` times past the start, where `n` is the number of states. In Hopcroft's algorithm, the successive smaller halves containing one fixed state form such a chain: each of them is the smaller half of a split of the previous block containing that state.
nodes.title: The smaller-half counting lemma

nodes.summary: Every entry `newSplitters` adds for a block `D` is a half of `D` (one of the two sides of the split by `pre`), or the smaller half.
nodes.title: New splitters are halves of the split block

nodes.summary: A smaller-half entry added by `newSplitters` for a block `D` has at most half the size of `D`: the two halves are disjoint and union to `D`. No split hypothesis is needed: the halves of any block partition it.
nodes.title: Smaller-half splitters have at most half the block size

nodes.summary: The splitters popped by Hopcroft's loop, in order: the same recursion as `DFA.hopcroftLoop`, collecting each popped splitter. The cost of processing one popped splitter `(C, a)` is `(preimage M C a).card + 1`: one predecessor visit per state whose `a`-successor lies in `C`, plus `O(1)` per-splitter overhead. See `hopcroftCost`. `hopcroftLoop_eq_hopcroftLoop_of_length` proves this trace records exactly the splitters…
nodes.title: Trace of splitters popped by Hopcroft's algorithm

nodes.summary: The predecessor cost of a splitter trace: for each popped splitter `(C, a)`, one predecessor visit per state in the preimage `preimage M C a`, plus `1` per-splitter overhead. This is the quantity the total-work bound constrains to `O(|Σ| n log n)`. Charging splitter size `C.card` instead would undercount: if all `n` states transition on `a` to one state `q`, processing the singleton splitter `({q}, a)` costs `n`…
nodes.title: Predecessor cost of a Hopcroft splitter trace

nodes.summary: The loop and the trace recurse on the same state, so they take the same number of steps. The two theorems below make the correspondence usable: the trace length is at most `k`, and running the loop for exactly the trace's length gives the full loop result, so the trace contains every splitter the loop pops and no others.
nodes.title: The splitter trace records exactly the splitters the loop pops

nodes.summary: The trace and the loop take the same number of steps: the trace length is the fuel the loop consumed, i.e. the loop would stop after exactly that many rounds if run with only that much fuel.
nodes.title: Hopcroft splitter trace length equals loop fuel

nodes.summary: Number of splitters with letter `b` containing `q`, with multiplicity. This applies both to the waiting list and to the actual popped trace.
nodes.title: Splitter count of a state and letter

nodes.summary: Replacement contributes one token at a state in the parent block; otherwise only membership in the smaller half contributes a token.
nodes.title: Splitter count of newly added splitters

nodes.summary: The exact token update at a state. Only its unique parent block can contribute a new token, even when other blocks split in the same round.
nodes.title: Splitter count update after one Hopcroft round

nodes.summary: A waiting entry supplies a token; duplicate entries remain counted.
nodes.title: Waiting entries give positive splitter count

nodes.summary: A refined block containing `q` is a subset of the old block containing `q`. Both partitions are the canonical Hopcroft partitions.
nodes.title: Refined Hopcroft blocks lie inside their old blocks

nodes.summary: One refinement cannot increase logarithmic block-size credit plus pending-token credit. Replacing a pending splitter spends no new credit; adding a nonpending smaller half spends one logarithmic unit.
nodes.title: Potential inequality for one Hopcroft refinement round

nodes.summary: Total state/letter charging along the actual execution. The bound includes initial tokens and tokens still pending through replacements. No amortized bound is assumed in the execution invariant.
nodes.title: Splitter count bound along a Hopcroft execution

nodes.summary: Initially there is at most one token for each state and letter.
nodes.title: Initial splitter count is at most one

reading_title.source: Hopcroft visits each of $n$ states at most $\log_2 n + 1$ times per letter

nodes.summary: Each state is processed with a fixed letter at most `log₂ n + 1` times during any prefix of the actual initialized Hopcroft execution.
nodes.title: Hopcroft visits each of $n$ states at most $\log_2 n + 1$ times per letter

nodes.summary: Every popped splitter has a nonempty block, including splitters whose predecessor set is empty.
nodes.title: Popped Hopcroft splitters are nonempty

nodes.summary: Double counting visits by source state and letter, retaining every incoming transition even when many sources have the same successor.
nodes.title: Hopcroft predecessor-work as splitter counts plus pops

nodes.summary: A nonempty popped block pays for its pop, even if its preimage is empty. This bounds the `+1` term independently of predecessor visits.
nodes.title: Number of pops bounded by the total splitter count

nodes.summary: Total predecessor-work bound, including one unit for every pop, for every prefix of the initialized execution. No runtime claim is made for the scanning implementation or for initialization.
nodes.title: Total predecessor-work bound

reading_title.source: $O(|\Sigma| n \log n)$ bound on Hopcroft predecessor-work

nodes.summary: A uniform `O(|Σ| n log n)` bound, with the explicit constant `4`. The condition `n ≥ 2` is essential when absorbing the additive unit into the logarithm. This concerns predecessor-work, not scan runtime.
nodes.title: $O(|\Sigma| n \log n)$ bound on Hopcroft predecessor-work

nodes.summary: The bound for the complete terminating minimization execution. `DFA.hopcroftLoop_waiting_eq_nil` proves this fuel exhausts the queue; `hopcroftLoop_eq_hopcroftLoop_of_length` ties the trace to its result.
nodes.title: Predecessor-work bound for the complete Hopcroft run

nodes.summary: With at most one state, the accepting/rejecting split has an empty side, so the algorithm has no initial splitters.
nodes.title: No initial Hopcroft splitters with at most one state

nodes.summary: Zero predecessor-work for zero/one-state boundary parameters. This does not assert that constructing the initial partition costs zero.
nodes.title: Zero Hopcroft predecessor-work with at most one state

nodes.summary: An empty alphabet causes no predecessor-work, for any state count.
nodes.title: Zero Hopcroft predecessor-work over an empty alphabet
