nodes.summary: The recorded cost is exactly the work of the actual popped trace.
nodes.title: Recorded Hopcroft cost equals the work of the popped trace

nodes.summary: The canonical cost monad records the proved total predecessor-work bound for every initialized execution prefix.
nodes.title: Recorded Hopcroft cost obeys the predecessor-work bound

nodes.summary: At the proved terminating fuel, instrumentation returns the original correct minimization partition and an empty waiting list.
nodes.title: Instrumented complete Hopcroft run returns the minimization partition

nodes.summary: Recognition of languages by monoid morphisms, syntactic congruences and monoids, transition monoids, language contexts and quotients, and inverse images under word morphisms.
nodes.title: Syntactic monoids and algebraic recognition
Syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. Two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$ when, for all words $u, v \in \Sigma^*$, $uxv \in L$ if and only if $uyv \in L$.
nodes.title: Syntactic equivalence

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then for every word $w \in \Sigma^*$ the words $wx$ and $wy$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$.
nodes.title: Syntactic equivalence is stable under left multiplication

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then for every word $w \in \Sigma^*$ the words $xw$ and $yw$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$.
nodes.title: Syntactic equivalence is stable under right multiplication

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$ and let $w, x, y, z \in \Sigma^*$ be words. If $w$ and $x$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, and $y$ and $z$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then $wy$ and $xz$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$.
nodes.title: Syntactic equivalence is compatible with concatenation

nodes.summary: For a language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the syntactic congruence of $L$ is the monoid congruence on the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ that relates words $x$ and $y$ when, for all words $u$ and $v$, $uxv \in L$ if and only if $uyv \in L$.
nodes.title: Syntactic congruence

nodes.summary: For a language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the syntactic monoid of $L$ is the quotient of the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ of words by the syntactic congruence of $L$, which relates words $x$ and $y$ when $uxv \in L \iff uyv \in L$ for all words $u$ and $v$.
nodes.title: Syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: For a language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the syntactic morphism of $L$ is the monoid homomorphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ of words to the syntactic monoid of $L$ that sends each word to its class under the syntactic congruence of $L$.
nodes.title: Syntactic morphism

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then $x \in L$ if and only if $y \in L$.
nodes.title: Syntactically equivalent words agree on membership

nodes.summary: For a language $L$, the accepting set of the syntactic monoid of $L$ is the set of syntactic classes of words of $L$: a class belongs to it when its representatives lie in $L$, which does not depend on the representative chosen.
nodes.title: Accepting set of the syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. For every word $x \in \Sigma^*$, $x \in L$ if and only if the image of $x$ under the syntactic morphism of $L$ lies in the accepting set of the syntactic monoid of $L$, the set of syntactic classes of words of $L$.
nodes.title: The syntactic morphism recognizes the language

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then they are Nerode equivalent for $L$: the sets $\{z : xz \in L\}$ and $\{z : yz \in L\}$ are equal.
nodes.title: Syntactic equivalence refines Nerode equivalence

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language. For all words $x$ and $y$, if the syntactic morphism of $L$ sends $x$ and $y$ to the same element of the syntactic monoid of $L$, then $x$ and $y$ have the same Nerode class with respect to $L$.
nodes.title: Equal syntactic classes give equal Nerode classes

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ and a word $x$, the transition action of $x$ is the map sending each state $q$ of $M$ to the state that $M$ reaches by reading $x$ starting from $q$.
nodes.title: Transition action of a word

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over an alphabet $\Sigma$ and let $L$ be the language accepted by $M$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ have the same transition action on $M$, that is, for every state $q$, running $M$ from $q$ on $x$ ends in the same state as running $M$ from $q$ on $y$, then $x$ and $y$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$.
nodes.title: Words with the same transition action are syntactically equivalent

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA that is accessible (every state is reachable from the start state) and state-separated (two states with the same continuation language are equal). If two words $x$ and $y$ are syntactically equivalent for the language accepted by $M$, then $x$ and $y$ have the same transition action on $M$: for every state $q$, reading $x$ from $q$ and reading $y$ from $q$ lead to the same state.
nodes.title: Syntactically equivalent words act identically

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over an alphabet $\Sigma$ that is accessible (every state is reached from the start state by some word) and state-separated (distinct states have distinct continuation languages), and let $L$ be the language accepted by $M$. Then two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$ if and only if they have the same transition action on $M$: for every state $q$, running $M$ from $q$ on…
nodes.title: Syntactic equivalence via transition actions

nodes.summary: For a type $Q$ of states, the state transformation monoid of $Q$ consists of all functions $Q \to Q$, multiplied by composition in the opposite order: the product $fg$ first applies $f$ and then $g$, so $(fg)(q) = g(f(q))$, and the unit is the identity function.
nodes.title: State transformation monoid

nodes.summary: For a type $Q$ of states, the bijection from the state transformations of $Q$ to the functions $Q \to Q$ that sends each transformation to its underlying function; it forgets the multiplication of state transformations.
nodes.title: State transformations as functions

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ and a word $x$, the transition transformation of $x$ is the transition action of $x$, the map sending each state $q$ to the state that $M$ reaches by reading $x$ from $q$, regarded as an element of the monoid of state transformations of $M$ (multiplied in reading order: $fg$ applies $f$ first, then $g$).
nodes.title: Transition transformation of a word

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$, the transition morphism is the monoid homomorphism from the free monoid of words to the state transformations of $M$ that sends each word $x$ to its transition action, the map taking each state $q$ to the state that $M$ reaches by reading $x$ from $q$. State transformations are multiplied in reading order, so the product $fg$ applies $f$ first and then $g$; with this order, the word $xy$ is sent to…
nodes.title: Transition morphism of a DFA

nodes.summary: The transition monoid of a DFA $M$ is the image of the transition morphism of $M$: the submonoid of state transformations of $M$ consisting of the transition actions of all words, where a word $x$ acts by sending each state $q$ to the state that $M$ reaches by reading $x$ from $q$. State transformations are multiplied in reading order, so the product $fg$ applies $f$ first and then $g$.
nodes.title: Transition monoid of a DFA

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over an alphabet $\Sigma$. Each word $x \in \Sigma^*$ determines the element of the transition monoid of $M$ given by the state transformation that sends each state $q$ to the state $M$ reaches from $q$ after reading $x$.
nodes.title: Transition monoid element of a word

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an accessible, state-separated DFA and let $L$ be the language $M$ accepts. The syntactic congruence of $L$ equals the kernel of the transition morphism of $M$: two words are syntactically equivalent for $L$ if and only if they induce the same transformation of the states of $M$.
nodes.title: Syntactic congruence as a kernel

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an accessible, state-separated DFA with state type $Q$, and let $L$ be the language $M$ accepts. This is the monoid homomorphism from the syntactic monoid of $L$ to the state transformation monoid of $Q$ that sends the syntactic class of each word $x$ to the map taking each state $q$ to the state $M$ reaches from $q$ by reading $x$. It is well defined because syntactically equivalent words act…
nodes.title: Action of the syntactic monoid on states

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be an accessible, state-separated DFA and let $L$ be the language $M$ accepts. The image of the action of the syntactic monoid of $L$ on the states of $M$, the monoid homomorphism sending the syntactic class of each word $x$ to the state transformation induced by reading $x$, is exactly the transition monoid of $M$.
nodes.title: Image of the syntactic action

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$, let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on $\Sigma$ into a monoid $M$, and let $A \subseteq M$. Then $\varphi$ recognizes $L$ through $A$ when, for every word $w \in \Sigma^*$, $w \in L$ if and only if $\varphi(w) \in A$.
nodes.title: Recognition of a language by a monoid morphism

nodes.summary: For every language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the syntactic morphism of $L$, from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ to the syntactic monoid of $L$, recognizes $L$ through the accepting subset of the syntactic monoid, namely the set of syntactic classes of words in $L$.
nodes.title: The syntactic morphism recognizes its language

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$ and let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to C$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ that recognizes $L$ through a subset $A \subseteq C$. If $\varphi = f \circ \psi$ for monoid morphisms $\psi : \Sigma^* \to T$ and $f : T \to C$, then $\psi$ recognizes $L$ through the preimage $f^{-1}(A)$.
nodes.title: Recognition pulls back along a factorization

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on an alphabet $\Sigma$ into a monoid $M$ that recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a set $A \subseteq M$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ satisfy $\varphi(x) = \varphi(y)$, then $x$ and $y$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$: for all words $u, v \in \Sigma^*$, $uxv \in L$ if and only if $uyv \in L$.
nodes.title: Words with equal recognizer images are syntactically equivalent

nodes.summary: If a monoid morphism $\varphi$ from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a subset $A$ of its codomain, then the kernel congruence of $\varphi$ is contained in the syntactic congruence of $L$: any words $x, y$ with $\varphi(x) = \varphi(y)$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$.
nodes.title: Recognizer kernels refine the syntactic congruence

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$, let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on $\Sigma$ into a monoid $M$, and let $A \subseteq M$ be such that $\varphi$ recognizes $L$ through $A$. Since the kernel congruence of $\varphi$ (words $x, y$ with $\varphi(x) = \varphi(y)$) is contained in the syntactic congruence of $L$, there is a monoid morphism from the quotient of…
nodes.title: Canonical map from a recognizer's kernel quotient to the syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: If a monoid morphism $\varphi$ from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a subset $A$ of its codomain, then the canonical monoid morphism from the quotient of $\Sigma^*$ by the kernel congruence of $\varphi$ to the syntactic monoid of $L$, which sends the class of a word $x$ to its syntactic class, is surjective.
nodes.title: The kernel quotient of a recognizer maps onto the syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ that recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a subset $A \subseteq M$. This is the monoid morphism from the image $\varphi(\Sigma^*)$ to the syntactic monoid of $L$ that sends $\varphi(x)$ to the syntactic class of $x$ for every word $x$. It is well defined because words with the same image under $\varphi$ are syntactically…
nodes.title: Map from a recognizer's image to the syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ that recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a subset $A \subseteq M$. Then the canonical monoid morphism from the image $\varphi(\Sigma^*)$ to the syntactic monoid of $L$, which sends $\varphi(x)$ to the syntactic class of $x$, is surjective.
nodes.title: The image of a recognizer maps onto the syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: If a monoid morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ to a finite monoid $M$ recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through some subset of $M$, then the syntactic monoid of $L$ is finite.
nodes.title: Finite recognizers give finite syntactic monoids

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$, let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on $\Sigma$ into a monoid $M$, and let $A \subseteq M$. Then $\varphi$ recognizes $L$ through $A$ if and only if the set of words of $\Sigma^*$ that belong to $L$ equals $\varphi^{-1}(A)$.
nodes.title: Recognition as an inverse image

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ that recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a subset $A_1 \subseteq M$. If $A_2 \subseteq M$ satisfies $\varphi(x) \in A_1 \iff \varphi(x) \in A_2$ for every word $x$, then $\varphi$ also recognizes $L$ through $A_2$.
nodes.title: Changing the accepting set off the image of a recognizer

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. The syntactic DFA of $L$ has the syntactic monoid of $L$ as its set of states, the identity $1$ as start state, and the syntactic classes of the words of $L$ as accepting states; from a state $q$, reading a letter $a \in \Sigma$ leads to $q \cdot [a]$, where $[a]$ is the syntactic class of the one-letter word $a$.
nodes.title: The syntactic DFA

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. For every state $q$ of the syntactic DFA of $L$ (an element of the syntactic monoid of $L$) and every word $x \in \Sigma^*$, the state reached from $q$ by reading $x$ is $q \cdot [x]$, where $[x]$ is the image of $x$ under the syntactic morphism of $L$.
nodes.title: Runs of the syntactic DFA

nodes.summary: For every language $L$, the syntactic DFA of $L$ accepts exactly $L$.
nodes.title: The syntactic DFA accepts its language

nodes.summary: For every language $L$, every state of the syntactic DFA of $L$ is reachable: some word leads to it from the start state.
nodes.title: The syntactic DFA is accessible

nodes.summary: Every language whose syntactic monoid is finite is regular.
nodes.title: Finite syntactic monoid implies regularity

nodes.summary: If the syntactic monoid of a language $L$ is finite, then the syntactic DFA of $L$ has finitely many states and accepts exactly $L$.
nodes.title: The syntactic DFA of a language with finite syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over an alphabet $\Sigma$ with state set $Q$, start state $q_0$ and set of accepting states $F$. The transition morphism of $M$, from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ to the monoid of state transformations of $Q$, recognizes the language accepted by $M$ through the set of transformations $f$ with $f(q_0) \in F$.
nodes.title: The transition morphism of a DFA recognizes its language

nodes.summary: Every language accepted by a DFA with finitely many states has a finite syntactic monoid.
nodes.title: Languages of finite automata have finite syntactic monoids
Transition monoids and regularity

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ with set of states $Q$, start state $q_0$ and accepting states $F$, the accepting transformations of $M$ are the state transformations $f$ of $Q$ with $f(q_0) \in F$.
nodes.title: Accepting transformations of a DFA

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with start state $q_0$ and accepting states $F$. The transition morphism of $M$, from words to state transformations, recognizes the language accepted by $M$ through the accepting transformations of $M$: a word is accepted by $M$ exactly when the transformation it induces sends $q_0$ into $F$.
nodes.title: The transition morphism recognizes through accepting transformations

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with start state $q_0$ and accepting states $F$. The map sending each word to the element of the transition monoid of $M$ that it induces recognizes the language accepted by $M$, with accepting set the elements $f$ of the transition monoid such that $f(q_0) \in F$: a word is accepted by $M$ exactly when the transformation it induces sends $q_0$ into $F$.
nodes.title: The transition monoid recognizes the accepted language

nodes.summary: If $Q$ is a finite set, then the monoid of state transformations of $Q$, consisting of all functions $Q \to Q$ multiplied in diagrammatic order, is finite.
nodes.title: Finitely many state transformations

nodes.summary: For every DFA $M$ with a finite set of states, the transition monoid of $M$ is finite.
nodes.title: Transition monoids of finite automata are finite

nodes.summary: If $L$ is a regular language, then the syntactic monoid of $L$ is finite.
nodes.title: Regular languages have finite syntactic monoids

nodes.summary: A language $L$ is regular if and only if the syntactic monoid of $L$ is finite.
nodes.title: Regular languages are those with finite syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ accepting the language $L$, this is the monoid homomorphism from the transition monoid of $M$ to the syntactic monoid of $L$ that sends the transformation induced by each word $w$ to the syntactic class of $w$.
nodes.title: The transition monoid maps to the syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA accepting the language $L$, and suppose that the transition monoid of $M$ and the syntactic monoid of $L$ are both finite. Then the syntactic monoid of $L$ has at most as many elements as the transition monoid of $M$.
nodes.title: The syntactic monoid is no larger than the transition monoid

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with a finite set of states $Q$, and suppose the syntactic monoid of the language accepted by $M$ is finite. Then that syntactic monoid has at most $|Q|^{|Q|}$ elements.
nodes.title: Endofunction bound for the syntactic monoid
Inverse homomorphic images of regular languages

nodes.summary: Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. The alphabet preimage of $L$ under $f$ is the language over $\Sigma$ consisting of the words $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ such that $f(a_1) f(a_2) \cdots f(a_n) \in L$.
nodes.title: Alphabet preimage

nodes.summary: Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. The alphabet preimage morphism of $f$ and $L$ is the monoid morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ to the syntactic monoid of $L$ that sends a word $w$ to the syntactic class of $f^*(w)$, the word obtained by applying $f$ to each letter of $w$. It is the composite of the letterwise map $f^* \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$…
nodes.title: Alphabet preimage morphism

nodes.summary: Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. Write $f^*(w)$ for the word obtained by applying $f$ to each letter of a word $w$, $[u]_L$ for the class of a word $u$ in the syntactic monoid $M(L)$ of $L$, $A_L \subseteq M(L)$ for the accepting set of classes of words in $L$, and $\varphi \colon \Sigma^* \to M(L)$ for the alphabet preimage morphism…
nodes.title: The alphabet preimage morphism recognizes the alphabet preimage

nodes.summary: Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets, $L$ a language over $\Gamma$, and $K$ the alphabet preimage $\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid f^*(w) \in L\}$, where $f^*(w)$ is the word obtained by applying $f$ to each letter of $w$. If $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are words such that $f^*(x)$ and $f^*(y)$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then $x$ and $y$ are syntactically equivalent for $K$.
nodes.title: Syntactic equivalence pulls back along an alphabet map

nodes.summary: Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets, $L$ a language over $\Gamma$ with syntactic monoid $M(L)$, and $\varphi \colon \Sigma^* \to M(L)$ the alphabet preimage morphism, which sends a word $w$ to the class in $M(L)$ of the word $f^*(w)$ obtained by applying $f$ to each letter of $w$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ satisfy $\varphi(x) = \varphi(y)$, then $x$ and $y$ are syntactically congruent…
nodes.title: The alphabet preimage morphism refines the preimage's syntactic congruence

nodes.summary: Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. Write $f^*(w)$ for the word obtained by applying $f$ to each letter of a word $w$, $[u]_L$ for the class of a word $u$ in the syntactic monoid $M(L)$ of $L$, $K$ for the alphabet preimage $\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid f^*(w) \in L\}$, and $\varphi \colon \Sigma^* \to M(L)$ for the alphabet preimage morphism…
nodes.title: Division map for the syntactic monoid of an alphabet preimage

nodes.summary: Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$ whose syntactic monoid is finite. Then the syntactic monoid of the alphabet preimage $\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid f^*(w) \in L\}$ is finite, where $f^*(w)$ is the word obtained by applying $f$ to each letter of $w$.
nodes.title: Alphabet preimages preserve finiteness of the syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets. If $L$ is a regular language over $\Gamma$, then its alphabet preimage $\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid f^*(w) \in L\}$ is regular, where $f^*(w)$ is the word obtained by applying $f$ to each letter of $w$.
nodes.title: Regular languages are closed under alphabet preimages

nodes.summary: Let $e \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a bijection between alphabets and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. The alphabet preimage $\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid e^*(w) \in L\}$, where $e^*(w)$ is the word obtained by applying $e$ to each letter of $w$, is regular if and only if $L$ is regular.
nodes.title: Renaming letters by a bijection preserves and reflects regularity

nodes.summary: Let $e \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a bijection between alphabets and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. The syntactic monoid of the alphabet preimage $\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid e^*(w) \in L\}$, where $e^*(w)$ is the word obtained by applying $e$ to each letter of $w$, is finite if and only if the syntactic monoid of $L$ is finite.
nodes.title: Finiteness of the syntactic monoid is invariant under renaming letters

nodes.summary: Let $\Sigma$ and $\Gamma$ be alphabets, $h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ a monoid morphism between their free monoids of words, and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. The inverse image of $L$ under $h$ is the language $h^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid h(w) \in L\}$ over $\Sigma$.
nodes.title: Inverse image under a word morphism

nodes.summary: Let $h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid morphism between free monoids. For every word $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n \in \Sigma^*$ (including the empty word, $n = 0$), we have $h(a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n) = h(a_1) h(a_2) \cdots h(a_n)$, the concatenation of the images of its letters.
nodes.title: Word morphisms act letter by letter

nodes.summary: Let $h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid morphism between free monoids and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. The inverse image $h^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid h(w) \in L\}$ consists exactly of the words $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n \in \Sigma^*$ such that the concatenation $h(a_1) h(a_2) \cdots h(a_n)$ of the images of their letters lies in $L$.
nodes.title: Letterwise description of the inverse image under a word morphism

nodes.summary: Let $h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid morphism between free monoids and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$ with syntactic monoid $M(L)$. The recognizing morphism of $h$ and $L$ is the monoid morphism $\Sigma^* \to M(L)$ that sends a word $w$ to the syntactic class $[h(w)]_L$ of $h(w)$; it is the composite of $h$ with the syntactic morphism of $L$.
nodes.title: Recognizing morphism of an inverse image

nodes.summary: Let $h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid morphism between free monoids, $L$ a language over $\Gamma$, and $K = h^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid h(w) \in L\}$ its inverse image. If $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are words such that $h(x)$ and $h(y)$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then $x$ and $y$ are syntactically equivalent for $K$.
nodes.title: Syntactic equivalence pulls back along a word morphism

nodes.summary: Let $h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid morphism between free monoids and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. Write $[u]_L$ for the class of a word $u$ in the syntactic monoid $M(L)$ of $L$, $K$ for the inverse image $h^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid h(w) \in L\}$, and $\varphi \colon \Sigma^* \to M(L)$ for the recognizing morphism $w \mapsto [h(w)]_L$. This is the monoid morphism from the submonoid…
nodes.title: Division map for the syntactic monoid of an inverse image

nodes.summary: Let $h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid morphism between free monoids and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$ whose syntactic monoid is finite. Then the syntactic monoid of the inverse image $h^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid h(w) \in L\}$ is finite.
nodes.title: Inverse images under word morphisms preserve finiteness of the syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: Let $h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid morphism between free monoids. If $L$ is a regular language over $\Gamma$, then its inverse image $h^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid h(w) \in L\}$ is regular.
nodes.title: Regular languages are closed under inverse word morphisms

nodes.summary: Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets, $f^* \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ the monoid morphism that applies $f$ to each letter of a word, and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. Then the alphabet preimage of $L$ under $f$ equals the inverse image $(f^*)^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid f^*(w) \in L\}$ of $L$ under $f^*$.
nodes.title: Alphabet preimages are inverse images under word morphisms
Language quotients and syntactic monoids

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $A$ and let $u, v$ be words over $A$. The context quotient of $L$ by $(u, v)$ is the language $u^{-1} L v^{-1} = \{x \in A^* \mid uxv \in L\}$ of words that land in $L$ when placed between $u$ and $v$.
nodes.title: Context quotient

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $A$, and for words $u, v$ over $A$ write $u^{-1} L v^{-1} = \{x \mid uxv \in L\}$. Then for all words $u_1, v_1, u_2, v_2$ over $A$, $u_2^{-1} (u_1^{-1} L v_1^{-1}) v_2^{-1} = (u_1 u_2)^{-1} L (v_2 v_1)^{-1}$.
nodes.title: Composing context quotients

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi \colon A^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on an alphabet $A$ to a monoid $M$, let $P \subseteq M$, and let $u, v$ be words over $A$. The accepting set for the context $(u, v)$ is $\{m \in M \mid \varphi(u)\, m\, \varphi(v) \in P\}$.
nodes.title: Accepting set for a context quotient

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi \colon A^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on an alphabet $A$ to a monoid $M$ that recognizes a language $L$ over $A$ through $P \subseteq M$, that is, a word $x$ lies in $L$ exactly when $\varphi(x) \in P$. Then for all words $u, v$ over $A$, $\varphi$ recognizes the context quotient $\{x \mid uxv \in L\}$ through the set $\{m \in M \mid \varphi(u)\, m\, \varphi(v) \in P\}$.
nodes.title: Recognizers recognize context quotients

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $A$, let $u, v$ be words over $A$, and write $u^{-1} L v^{-1} = \{x \mid uxv \in L\}$. Let $\eta$ be the syntactic morphism of $L$ and $\eta'$ the syntactic morphism of $u^{-1} L v^{-1}$. This is the monoid morphism from the image of $\eta$ to the syntactic monoid of $u^{-1} L v^{-1}$ that sends $\eta(x)$ to $\eta'(x)$ for every word $x$ over $A$.
nodes.title: The canonical map to the syntactic monoid of a context quotient

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $A$, let $u, v$ be words over $A$, and write $u^{-1} L v^{-1} = \{x \mid uxv \in L\}$ for the context quotient. If the image of the syntactic morphism of $L$ and the syntactic monoid of $u^{-1} L v^{-1}$ are both finite, then the syntactic monoid of $u^{-1} L v^{-1}$ has at most as many elements as the image of the syntactic morphism of $L$.
nodes.title: Size bound for the syntactic monoid of a context quotient

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $A$ whose syntactic monoid is finite. Then for all words $u, v$ over $A$, the syntactic monoid of the context quotient $u^{-1} L v^{-1} = \{x \mid uxv \in L\}$ is finite.
nodes.title: Context quotients preserve finiteness of the syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: If $L$ is a regular language over an alphabet $A$, then for all words $u, v$ over $A$, the context quotient $u^{-1} L v^{-1} = \{x \mid uxv \in L\}$ is regular.
nodes.title: Regular languages are closed under context quotients

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $A$. Two words $x, y$ over $A$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$ if and only if, for all words $u, v$ over $A$, $x$ lies in the context quotient $u^{-1} L v^{-1} = \{w \mid uwv \in L\}$ exactly when $y$ does.
nodes.title: Syntactic equivalence via context quotients

nodes.summary: For a language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$ and a word $w \in \Sigma^*$, the right quotient of $L$ by $w$ is the language $\{x \in \Sigma^* : xw \in L\}$ of all words $x$ whose concatenation $xw$ with $w$ lies in $L$.
nodes.title: Right quotient of a language by a word

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi \colon A^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on an alphabet $A$ to a monoid $M$, let $P \subseteq M$, and let $u$ be a word over $A$. The accepting set for the left quotient by $u$ is $\{m \in M \mid \varphi(u)\, m \in P\}$.
nodes.title: Accepting set for a left quotient

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi \colon A^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on an alphabet $A$ to a monoid $M$, let $P \subseteq M$, and let $u$ be a word over $A$. The accepting set for the right quotient by $u$ is $\{m \in M \mid m\, \varphi(u) \in P\}$.
nodes.title: Accepting set for a right quotient

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi \colon A^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on an alphabet $A$ to a monoid $M$ that recognizes a language $L$ over $A$ through $P \subseteq M$, that is, a word $x$ lies in $L$ exactly when $\varphi(x) \in P$. Then for every word $u$ over $A$, $\varphi$ recognizes the left quotient $\{x \mid ux \in L\}$ through the set $\{m \in M \mid \varphi(u)\, m \in P\}$.
nodes.title: Recognizers recognize left quotients

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi \colon A^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on an alphabet $A$ to a monoid $M$ that recognizes a language $L$ over $A$ through $P \subseteq M$, that is, a word $x$ lies in $L$ exactly when $\varphi(x) \in P$. Then for every word $u$ over $A$, $\varphi$ recognizes the right quotient $\{x \mid xu \in L\}$ through the set $\{m \in M \mid m\, \varphi(u) \in P\}$.
nodes.title: Recognizers recognize right quotients

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $A$, let $u$ be a word over $A$, and write $u^{-1} L = \{x \mid ux \in L\}$. Let $\eta$ be the syntactic morphism of $L$ and $\eta'$ the syntactic morphism of $u^{-1} L$. This is the monoid morphism from the image of $\eta$ to the syntactic monoid of $u^{-1} L$ that sends $\eta(x)$ to $\eta'(x)$ for every word $x$ over $A$.
nodes.title: The canonical map to the syntactic monoid of a left quotient

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $A$, let $u$ be a word over $A$, and write $L u^{-1} = \{x \mid xu \in L\}$. Let $\eta$ be the syntactic morphism of $L$ and $\eta'$ the syntactic morphism of $L u^{-1}$. This is the monoid morphism from the image of $\eta$ to the syntactic monoid of $L u^{-1}$ that sends $\eta(x)$ to $\eta'(x)$ for every word $x$ over $A$.
nodes.title: The canonical map to the syntactic monoid of a right quotient

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $A$ whose syntactic monoid is finite. Then for every word $u$ over $A$, the syntactic monoid of the left quotient $u^{-1} L = \{x \mid ux \in L\}$ is finite.
nodes.title: Left quotients preserve finiteness of the syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $A$ whose syntactic monoid is finite. Then for every word $u$ over $A$, the syntactic monoid of the right quotient $L u^{-1} = \{x \mid xu \in L\}$ is finite.
nodes.title: Right quotients preserve finiteness of the syntactic monoid

nodes.summary: If $L$ is a regular language over an alphabet $A$, then for every word $u$ over $A$, the right quotient $L u^{-1} = \{x \mid xu \in L\}$ is regular.
nodes.title: Regular languages are closed under right quotients by fixed words

nodes.summary: If $L$ is a regular language over an alphabet $A$, then for every word $u$ over $A$, the left quotient $u^{-1} L = \{x \mid ux \in L\}$ is regular.
nodes.title: Regular languages are closed under left quotients by fixed words

nodes.summary: Context-free grammars and derivations, normal forms, parsing algorithms, pushdown automata, deterministic and ambiguous languages, closure and non-closure properties, pumping and Ogden's lemmas, and Parikh images.
nodes.title: Context-free languages

nodes.summary: Grammar basics and derivation forests, Chomsky and Greibach normal forms, ε- and unit-production elimination, CYK and Earley recognizers, leftmost derivations and (inherent) ambiguity, pushdown automata, deterministic context-free languages, and the grammar–PDA equivalence.
nodes.title: Grammars, parsing and pushdown automata

nodes.summary: Over a finite alphabet, every regular language is context-free.
nodes.title: Regular languages over a finite alphabet are context-free
Context-free grammars

nodes.summary: Under an assignment $V$ of languages to nonterminals, a terminal $a$ denotes the language containing only the one-letter word $a$, and a nonterminal $A$ denotes its assigned language $V(A)$.
nodes.title: Interpretation of a grammar symbol

nodes.summary: Under an assignment $V$ of languages to nonterminals, a sentential form denotes the concatenation, in order, of the languages its symbols denote: a terminal $a$ denotes the language containing only the one-letter word $a$, and a nonterminal $A$ denotes $V(A)$. The empty sentential form denotes the language containing only the empty word.
nodes.title: Interpretation of a sentential form

nodes.summary: For every assignment $V$ of languages to nonterminals and all sentential forms $u$ and $v$, the language that $uv$ denotes under $V$ is the concatenation of the languages that $u$ and $v$ denote under $V$.
nodes.title: Interpretation of a concatenation

nodes.summary: Under every assignment of languages to nonterminals, a terminal word $w$, read as a sentential form, denotes the singleton language $\{w\}$.
nodes.title: A terminal word denotes its singleton

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar with terminals $T$, and let $V$ assign a language over $T$ to each nonterminal of $g$. Interpret a sentential form under $V$ by sending each terminal $a$ to the language $\{a\}$ of the one-letter word $a$ and each nonterminal $B$ to $V(B)$, and concatenating these languages in order (the empty form is interpreted as $\{\varepsilon\}$). Then $V$ is a *valuation* of $g$ when, for…
nodes.title: Valuation of a grammar

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and $V$ a valuation of $g$. If a sentential form $u$ rewrites to $v$ by one production of $g$, then the language that $v$ denotes under $V$ is contained in the language that $u$ denotes under $V$.
nodes.title: A production step shrinks interpretations under a valuation

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and $V$ a valuation of $g$. If a sentential form $u$ derives $v$ in $g$ (in zero or more steps), then the language that $v$ denotes under $V$ is contained in the language that $u$ denotes under $V$.
nodes.title: Derivations shrink interpretations under a valuation

nodes.summary: For every context-free grammar $g$ and every valuation $V$ of $g$, the language generated by $g$ is contained in $V(S)$, where $S$ is the initial nonterminal of $g$.
nodes.title: Valuations bound the language of a grammar

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and let $u$, $u'$, $v$, $v'$ be sentential forms of $g$. If $u$ derives $u'$ and $v$ derives $v'$ in $g$ (each in zero or more steps), then the concatenation $uv$ derives $u'v'$ in $g$.
nodes.title: Concatenating derivations

nodes.summary: Given a map $f$ from nonterminals $N$ to nonterminals $N'$, renaming a grammar symbol by $f$ leaves a terminal $a$ unchanged and sends a nonterminal $A$ to the nonterminal $f(A)$.
nodes.title: Renaming the nonterminals of a symbol

nodes.summary: Given a map $f$ from nonterminals $N$ to nonterminals $N'$, the renaming by $f$ of a production $A \to u$ is the production $f(A) \to u'$, where $u'$ is obtained from $u$ by replacing each nonterminal $B$ with $f(B)$ and leaving each terminal unchanged.
nodes.title: Renaming the nonterminals of a production

nodes.summary: Let $f \colon N \to N'$ be a map of nonterminals, extended to sentential forms by renaming each nonterminal and keeping each terminal, and let $V$ assign a language to each nonterminal in $N'$. For every sentential form $u$ over $N$, the language that $f(u)$ denotes under $V$ equals the language that $u$ denotes under the assignment $V \circ f$.
nodes.title: Interpretation after renaming nonterminals

nodes.summary: Let $g$ and $G$ be context-free grammars over the same terminal alphabet, and let $f$ map the nonterminals of $g$ to those of $G$. Extend $f$ to symbols and sentential forms by renaming each nonterminal and keeping each terminal. Suppose that for every production $A \to \alpha$ of $g$, the renamed production $f(A) \to f(\alpha)$ is a production of $G$. Then whenever a sentential form $u$ derives $v$ in $g$ (in zero…
nodes.title: Derivations transfer along a renaming of nonterminals

nodes.summary: For a context-free grammar $g$ and a nonterminal $A$ of $g$, the language generated by $g$ from $A$ is the set of words $w$ over the terminals of $g$ such that $g$ derives $w$ from the one-symbol sentential form $A$. It is the language of $g$ with $A$ in place of the initial nonterminal.
nodes.title: Language generated from a nonterminal

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and assign to each nonterminal $A$ of $g$ the language of terminal words that $g$ derives from $A$. If a terminal word $w$ lies in the language that a sentential form $u$ of $g$ denotes under this assignment, then $u$ derives $w$ in $g$.
nodes.title: Words of the canonical interpretation are derivable

nodes.summary: For every context-free grammar $g$, the assignment that sends each nonterminal $A$ of $g$ to the language generated by $g$ from $A$ is a valuation of $g$.
nodes.title: The languages generated from each nonterminal form a valuation

nodes.summary: If $f$ is an injective map from nonterminals $N$ to nonterminals $N'$, then renaming grammar symbols by $f$, which fixes each terminal and sends each nonterminal $A$ to $f(A)$, is injective.
nodes.title: Injective renamings are injective on symbols

nodes.summary: If $f$ is an injective map from nonterminals $N$ to nonterminals $N'$, then renaming the nonterminals of productions over $N$ by $f$ is injective: two productions with the same renaming are equal.
nodes.title: Injective renamings are injective on productions

nodes.summary: Let $f$ map nonterminals $N$ to nonterminals $N'$, and let $w$ be a word over the terminals. Reading $w$ as a sentential form over $N$ and renaming its nonterminals by $f$ gives $w$ read as a sentential form over $N'$.
nodes.title: Renaming nonterminals fixes terminal words

nodes.summary: The empty language over any alphabet is context-free: take a grammar with no productions.
nodes.title: The empty language is context-free

nodes.summary: For every alphabet $T$, the language over $T$ whose only word is the empty word is context-free: a grammar with one nonterminal and a single production erasing it generates this language.
nodes.title: The language of the empty word is context-free

nodes.summary: For every word $w$ over an alphabet $T$, the language $\{w\}$ consisting of $w$ alone is context-free: one production spells the word out.
nodes.title: Singleton languages are context-free

nodes.summary: For a context-free grammar $g$ with terminal alphabet $T$, the relation "the sentential form $u$ yields the terminal word $w$" is the smallest relation such that: the empty form yields the empty word; if $u$ yields $w$, then for every terminal $a$ the form $a u$ yields $a w$; and if $A \to \alpha$ is a production of $g$, $\alpha$ yields $w_1$ and $u$ yields $w_2$, then the form $A u$ yields $w_1 w_2$.
nodes.title: Yield of a sentential form

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. If the sentential form $u$ yields the terminal word $w_1$ and the sentential form $v$ yields the terminal word $w_2$, then the concatenated form $u v$ yields $w_1 w_2$.
nodes.title: Concatenation of yields

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. If the concatenated sentential form $u v$ yields the terminal word $w$, then there are terminal words $w_1$ and $w_2$ with $w = w_1 w_2$ such that $u$ yields $w_1$ and $v$ yields $w_2$.
nodes.title: Splitting a yield over a concatenation

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and $A \to \alpha$ a production of $g$. If $\alpha$ yields the terminal word $w$, then the one-symbol sentential form $A$ yields $w$.
nodes.title: Yield through one production

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. If the sentential form $u$ yields the terminal word $w$, then $u$ derives $w$, read as a string of terminal symbols, in $g$: that is, $u \Rightarrow^* w$ in zero or more rewriting steps.
nodes.title: Yields are derivable

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. If the sentential form $u$ derives the terminal word $w$, read as a string of terminal symbols, in $g$, then $u$ yields $w$.
nodes.title: Derivable terminal words are yields

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar, $u$ a sentential form of $g$ and $w$ a word of terminals. Then $u$ yields $w$ in $g$ if and only if $u$ derives in $g$, by zero or more rewriting steps, the sentential form consisting of the letters of $w$ read as terminals.
nodes.title: Yields coincide with derivations of terminal words

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar with initial nonterminal $S$. A terminal word $w$ belongs to the language of $g$ if and only if the one-symbol sentential form $S$ yields $w$.
nodes.title: Language membership through yields
Ambiguity of context-free grammars

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar, $u$ a sentential form of $g$, $w$ a word of terminals and $r_1, \dots, r_n$ a list of rules over the terminals and nonterminals of $g$. The list $r_1, \dots, r_n$ is a leftmost derivation of $w$ from $u$ in $g$ when every $r_i$ is a production of $g$, and, starting from $u$ and for $i = 1, \dots, n$ in turn, the leftmost nonterminal of the current sentential form is the left-hand…
nodes.title: Leftmost derivation

nodes.summary: A context-free grammar $g$ is ambiguous if some word of terminals $w$ has two leftmost derivations from the start symbol of $g$ that use different lists of rules.
nodes.title: Ambiguous grammar

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. If a sentential form $u$ has a leftmost derivation in $g$ to a word of terminals $w$, then $u$ derives $w$ in $g$ (by zero or more rewriting steps).
nodes.title: Leftmost derivations are derivations

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. If a word of terminals $w$ has a leftmost derivation in $g$ from the start symbol of $g$, then $w$ belongs to the language of $g$.
nodes.title: Words with a leftmost derivation lie in the language

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and $u$ a word of terminals. If $u$ has a leftmost derivation in $g$ with list of rules $\rho$ to a word of terminals $w$, then $\rho$ is the empty list and $w = u$.
nodes.title: Leftmost derivations from a word of terminals are empty

nodes.summary: The language `{a ^ i b ^ j c ^ k | i = j or j = k}` over the alphabet `Fin 3` (`0, 1, 2` for `a, b, c`): the standard inherently ambiguous context-free language.
nodes.title: Canonical inherently ambiguous context-free language

nodes.summary: A language is inherently ambiguous when it is context-free and every grammar generating it is ambiguous.
nodes.title: Inherently ambiguous language

nodes.summary: The example language is the union of `a ^ n b ^ n c ^ *` and `a ^ * b ^ n c ^ n`.
nodes.title: Inherently ambiguous example as a union of two languages

nodes.summary: The example language is context-free.
nodes.title: The example language is context-free
Earley parser

nodes.summary: An Earley item: a production with a dot after `dot` symbols of its output, recognizing input that starts at the end of `pre` and whose recognized prefix is `consumed`. The full input is `pre ++ consumed ++ rest` for some `rest`.
nodes.title: Earley item

nodes.summary: The Earley chart for input `w`: the least set of items closed under initialization, prediction, scanning, and completion.
nodes.title: Earley chart

nodes.summary: The chart as a predicate on `EarleyItem`s.
nodes.title: Earley chart as a predicate on items

nodes.summary: Acceptance by the Earley recognizer: some completed item for a production of the initial nonterminal consumes the whole input.
nodes.title: Acceptance by the Earley recognizer

nodes.summary: The dot of a chart item never passes the end of its production.
nodes.title: Earley item dot stays within its production

nodes.summary: Soundness: the recognized prefix of a chart item yields the input it consumed.
nodes.title: Soundness of the Earley chart

nodes.summary: Completeness: if a chart item waits on a sentential form and that form yields a word fitting in the remaining input, the chart contains the item completed by that word.
nodes.title: Completeness of the Earley chart

nodes.summary: Inversion of a yield from a single nonterminal: it begins with one production of that nonterminal.
nodes.title: A yield from one nonterminal starts with one of its productions

nodes.summary: The Earley recognizer accepts exactly the grammar's language.
nodes.title: Correctness of the Earley recognizer
Elimination of empty and unit productions

nodes.summary: In a context-free grammar in which no production has an empty right-hand side, every nonempty sentential form yields only nonempty words.
nodes.title: No empty words without empty productions

nodes.summary: A nonterminal $A$ of a context-free grammar $g$ is nullable when $g$ derives the empty word from $A$.
nodes.title: Nullable nonterminal

nodes.summary: For a context-free grammar $g$ and a sentential form $u$, the nullable deletions of $u$ are the forms obtained from $u$ by deleting any selection of occurrences of nullable nonterminals, possibly none and possibly all, keeping the remaining symbols in order. They form a finite set.
nodes.title: Nullable deletions

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and $V$ an assignment of a language $V(A)$ to each nonterminal $A$ of $g$ such that the empty word belongs to $V(A)$ whenever $A$ is nullable (derives the empty word in $g$). If a sentential form $\alpha'$ is obtained from a sentential form $u$ by deleting some occurrences of nullable nonterminals, then the language denoted by $\alpha'$ under $V$ is contained in the language…
nodes.title: Deleting nullable nonterminals shrinks the denoted language

reading_title.source: Elimination of $\varepsilon$-productions

nodes.summary: For a context-free grammar $g$, the grammar obtained from $g$ by eliminating $\varepsilon$-productions has the same nonterminals and the same initial nonterminal as $g$. Its productions are the productions $A \to \alpha'$ such that $g$ has a production $A \to \alpha$, the form $\alpha'$ is obtained from $\alpha$ by deleting some (possibly no) occurrences of nullable nonterminals (those deriving the empty word in…
nodes.title: Elimination of $\varepsilon$-productions

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar with a production $A \to u$, and let $\alpha$ be a nonempty form obtained from $u$ by deleting some (possibly no) occurrences of nullable nonterminals. Then $A \to \alpha$ is a production of the grammar obtained from $g$ by eliminating ε-productions.
nodes.title: Productions of the ε-free grammar

reading_title.source: Productions of the $\varepsilon$-eliminated grammar come from productions of $g$

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. Every production $A \to \alpha'$ of the grammar obtained from $g$ by eliminating $\varepsilon$-productions arises from a production $A \to \alpha$ of $g$ with the same left-hand side $A$, such that $\alpha'$ is obtained from $\alpha$ by deleting some occurrences of nullable nonterminals and $\alpha'$ is nonempty.
nodes.title: Productions of the $\varepsilon$-eliminated grammar come from productions of $g$

reading_title.source: The $\varepsilon$-eliminated grammar has no empty productions

nodes.summary: For a context-free grammar $g$, no production of the grammar obtained from $g$ by eliminating $\varepsilon$-productions has empty right-hand side.
nodes.title: The $\varepsilon$-eliminated grammar has no empty productions

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and, for each nonterminal $A$, let $L_g(A)$ be the language of words $g$ derives from $A$. Then $L_g$ is a valuation of the grammar obtained from $g$ by eliminating ε-productions: for every production $A \to \alpha$ of that grammar, the language of $\alpha$ under $L_g$ (the concatenation of the languages of its symbols, a terminal $a$ denoting $\{a\}$) is contained in $L_g(A)$.
nodes.title: Soundness of ε-production elimination

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. If a sentential form $\alpha$ of $g$ yields a terminal word $w$ in $g$, then some form $\alpha'$ obtained from $\alpha$ by deleting some occurrences of nullable nonterminals yields $w$ in the grammar obtained from $g$ by eliminating $\varepsilon$-productions, and $w$ is empty if $\alpha'$ is empty.
nodes.title: Completeness of eliminating empty productions

parts: -eliminated grammar generates the nonempty words of
reading_title.source: The $\varepsilon$-eliminated grammar generates the nonempty words of $g$

nodes.summary: For a context-free grammar $g$ and every word $w$ over its terminals, $w$ is generated by the grammar obtained from $g$ by eliminating $\varepsilon$-productions if and only if $w$ is generated by $g$ and $w$ is nonempty.
nodes.title: The $\varepsilon$-eliminated grammar generates the nonempty words of $g$

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. A nonterminal $A$ of $g$ reaches a nonterminal $B$ by unit productions when there is a chain $A = A_0, A_1, \dots, A_n = B$ with $n \ge 0$ such that each $A_{i-1} \to A_i$ is a production of $g$. In particular, every nonterminal reaches itself.
nodes.title: Reachability by unit productions

nodes.summary: A sentential form is a unit output when it consists of a single nonterminal.
nodes.title: Unit output

nodes.summary: For a sentential form $u$, a finite word of terminal and nonterminal symbols, the nonterminals of $u$ form the finite set of all nonterminals that occur in $u$.
nodes.title: Nonterminals of a sentential form

nodes.summary: The nonterminals mentioned by a context-free grammar $g$ form the finite set consisting of the initial nonterminal of $g$, the left-hand side of every production of $g$, and every nonterminal occurring in the right-hand side of a production of $g$.
nodes.title: Set of nonterminals mentioned by a grammar

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and let $B$ be reachable from $A$ by a chain of zero or more unit productions of $g$. If $B$ is the left-hand side of some production of $g$, then $A$ is among the nonterminals mentioned by $g$ (its initial nonterminal, the left-hand sides of its productions, and the nonterminals in their right-hand sides).
nodes.title: Unit chains start at mentioned nonterminals

nodes.summary: A unit production is one whose output is a single nonterminal. For a context-free grammar $g$, the grammar obtained by eliminating unit productions has the same nonterminals and the same start symbol as $g$. Its productions are the $A \to \alpha$ such that $A$ is a nonterminal mentioned by $g$ (its start symbol or one occurring in a production of $g$), $g$ has a production $B \to \alpha$ that is not a unit…
nodes.title: Eliminating unit productions

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar, let $B$ be reachable from $A$ by a chain of zero or more unit productions of $g$, and let $B \to \beta$ be a production of $g$ whose right-hand side $\beta$ is not a single nonterminal. If $A$ is among the nonterminals mentioned by $g$, then $A \to \beta$ is a production of the grammar obtained from $g$ by eliminating unit productions.
nodes.title: Productions of the unit-free grammar

parts: Productions of the unit-eliminated grammar come from non-unit productions of
reading_title.source: Productions of the unit-eliminated grammar come from non-unit productions of $g$

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. For every production $A \to \beta$ of the grammar obtained from $g$ by eliminating unit productions, there are a nonterminal $B$ and a production $B \to \beta$ of $g$ such that $\beta$ is not a single nonterminal and $B$ is reachable from $A$ by a possibly empty chain of unit productions of $g$.
nodes.title: Productions of the unit-eliminated grammar come from non-unit productions of $g$

nodes.summary: For every context-free grammar $g$, no production of the grammar obtained from $g$ by eliminating unit productions has an output consisting of a single nonterminal.
nodes.title: Eliminating unit productions leaves no unit production

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. For every production of the grammar obtained from $g$ by eliminating unit productions, some production of $g$ has the same output.
nodes.title: Eliminating unit productions creates no new outputs

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and, for each nonterminal $A$, let $L_g(A)$ be the language of words $g$ derives from $A$. If $B$ is reachable from $A$ by a chain of zero or more unit productions $A \to A_1 \to \dots \to B$ of $g$, then $L_g(B) \subseteq L_g(A)$.
nodes.title: Languages along unit chains

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and, for each nonterminal $A$, let $L_g(A)$ be the language of words $g$ derives from $A$. Then $L_g$ is a valuation of the grammar obtained from $g$ by eliminating unit productions: for every production $A \to \alpha$ of that grammar, the language of $\alpha$ under $L_g$ (the concatenation of the languages of its symbols, a terminal $a$ denoting $\{a\}$) is contained in $L_g(A)$.

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and $A \to \alpha_1 B \alpha_2$ a production of $g$, where $B$ is a nonterminal and $\alpha_1$, $\alpha_2$ are sentential forms. If $\alpha_1$ yields the terminal word $l$ and $\alpha_2$ yields the terminal word $r$, then for every terminal word $w$ yielded by $B$ the word $l w r$ is yielded by $A$; that is, $(l, r)$ is a derivation context from $A$ to $B$.

Suppose that for every terminal word $w$ yielded by $A$ the word $l w r$ is also yielded by $A$, and that $A$ yields $x$. Then for every natural number $i$ the nonterminal $A$ yields $l^i x r^i$, where $l^i$ and $r^i$ denote the concatenations of $i$ copies of $l$ and of $r$.

nodes.summary: For an alphabet $T$, write $T \sqcup T$ for the disjoint union of a left and a right copy of $T$. This is the language over $T \sqcup T$ of the words obtained from a word $x$ over $T$ by replacing each letter with its left copy.

nodes.summary: For an alphabet $T$, write $T \sqcup T$ for the disjoint union of a left and a right copy of $T$. This is the deterministic automaton over $T \sqcup T$ with the two states true and false, whose start state and only accepting state are true, and which moves from state $b$ on a letter $c$ to true exactly when $b$ is true and $c$ lies in the left copy, and to false otherwise.

nodes.summary: An encoded context-free grammar over a terminal type $T$ consists of a start nonterminal, which is a natural number, and a list of productions. Each production is a pair of a left-hand side, a natural number, and a right-hand side, a list of elements of the disjoint union $\mathbb{N} \sqcup T$, in which a number $i$ from the left summand stands for nonterminal $i$ and an element $a$ of $T$ for terminal $a$.
nodes.title: Encoded context-free grammars

nodes.summary: Decoding sends an element of the disjoint union $\mathbb{N} \sqcup T$ to a grammar symbol with terminals $T$ and nonterminals $\mathbb{N}$: a natural number $i$ from the left summand goes to the nonterminal $i$, and an element $a$ of $T$ from the right summand goes to the terminal $a$.
nodes.title: Decoding a grammar symbol

nodes.summary: Encoding sends a grammar symbol with terminals $T$ and nonterminals $\mathbb{N}$ to an element of the disjoint union $\mathbb{N} \sqcup T$: the terminal $a$ goes to $a$ in the right summand $T$, and the nonterminal $i$ goes to $i$ in the left summand $\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: Encoding a grammar symbol

nodes.summary: Decoding a pair $(A, s)$ of a natural number $A$ and a list $s$ of elements of the disjoint union $\mathbb{N} \sqcup T$ gives the production, with terminals $T$ and nonterminals $\mathbb{N}$, whose left-hand side is the nonterminal $A$ and whose right-hand side is $s$ with each entry decoded as a symbol: a number $i$ from the left summand becomes the nonterminal $i$ and an element $a$ of $T$ becomes the terminal $a$.
nodes.title: Decoding a production

nodes.summary: Encoding a production with terminals $T$ and nonterminals $\mathbb{N}$ gives the pair $(A, s)$ where $A \in \mathbb{N}$ is its left-hand side and $s$ is its right-hand side with each symbol encoded as an element of the disjoint union $\mathbb{N} \sqcup T$: the terminal $a$ becomes $a$ in the right summand and the nonterminal $i$ becomes $i$ in the left summand.
nodes.title: Encoding a production

nodes.summary: For an encoded context-free grammar $g$ over $T$, the context-free grammar over $T$ whose nonterminals are the natural numbers, whose initial nonterminal is the start nonterminal of $g$, and whose productions are the decodings of the encoded productions of $g$: an encoded production $(i, u)$ becomes the production rewriting the nonterminal $i$ to the word obtained from $u$ by reading each entry $\mathrm{inl}\, j$…
nodes.title: Grammar denoted by an encoding

nodes.summary: The language of an encoded context-free grammar $g$ over $T$ is the language generated by the context-free grammar that $g$ denotes, whose nonterminals are the natural numbers, whose initial nonterminal is the start nonterminal of $g$ and whose productions are the decoded productions of $g$.

nodes.summary: The partial map from grammar symbols with terminals in $T$ and nonterminals in $N$ to $N$ that sends a nonterminal $A$ to $A$ and has no value on terminals.
nodes.title: Nonterminal of a symbol

nodes.summary: For a context-free grammar $G$, the list consisting of the initial nonterminal of $G$ followed, for each production of $G$ in turn (in some fixed order of its finite set of productions), by the left-hand side of the production and then the nonterminals of its right-hand side in order. Nonterminals may occur more than once.
nodes.title: List of nonterminals mentioned by a grammar

nodes.summary: For a context-free grammar $G$, the number of a nonterminal $A$ of $G$ is the position, counting from $0$, of the first occurrence of $A$ in the list of nonterminals that $G$ mentions (its initial nonterminal first); if $A$ does not occur in that list, its number is the length of the list.
nodes.title: Numbering of nonterminals

nodes.summary: For a context-free grammar $G$ and a natural number $n$, the nonterminal of $G$ with number $n$ is the entry at position $n$, counting from $0$, of the list of nonterminals that $G$ mentions (its initial nonterminal first); if the list has no entry at position $n$, it is the initial nonterminal of $G$.
nodes.title: Nonterminal with a given number

nodes.summary: For a context-free grammar $G$ over $T$, the encoded grammar whose start nonterminal is the number of the initial nonterminal of $G$ and whose productions are the productions of $G$, listed in some fixed order, with every nonterminal $A$ replaced by its number, the position, counting from $0$, of the first occurrence of $A$ in the list of nonterminals that $G$ mentions (its initial nonterminal first).

nodes.summary: Let $f$ map lists of natural numbers to lists of natural numbers and be monotone for list inclusion: $f(G) \subseteq f(G')$ whenever $G \subseteq G'$, where $G \subseteq G'$ means that every entry of $G$ is an entry of $G'$. If $B$ is a list with $f(G) \subseteq B$ for every list $G$, and $n$ is the length of $B$, then $f(f^n([\,])) \subseteq f^n([\,])$, where $f^n$ is the $n$-fold iterate of $f$ and $[\,]$ is the…

nodes.summary: Given a list $G$ of natural numbers and a symbol $s$ of an encoded grammar over an alphabet $T$, which is either a nonterminal $i \in \mathbb{N}$ or a terminal in $T$, $s$ is acceptable when it is a terminal or a nonterminal that occurs in $G$. The test returns a Boolean.
nodes.title: Acceptable symbols

nodes.summary: Given a list $G$ of nonterminals (natural numbers), the test accepts an encoded production $(A, \rho)$ when every symbol of $\rho$ is acceptable: a terminal always is, and a nonterminal is when it belongs to $G$. So the production is accepted exactly when every nonterminal occurring in $\rho$ belongs to $G$.
nodes.title: Acceptable productions

nodes.summary: Let a list of productions be given, each a pair of a nonterminal $A \in \mathbb{N}$ and a right-hand side made of nonterminals and terminals, together with a list $G$ of nonterminals. One round returns, in order, the left-hand sides of those productions in whose right-hand side every nonterminal belongs to $G$.
nodes.title: One round of the generating-nonterminal computation

nodes.summary: For an encoded grammar $g$, start from the empty list of nonterminals and, in each round, replace the current list $G$ by the list of left-hand sides of those productions of $g$ whose right-hand sides contain no nonterminal outside $G$. The generating nonterminals of $g$ are the list obtained after as many rounds as $g$ has productions.
nodes.title: Generating nonterminals

nodes.summary: For an encoded grammar $g$, the test returns true exactly when the start nonterminal of $g$ is not among the generating nonterminals of $g$.
nodes.title: The emptiness test for context-free grammars

nodes.summary: For an encoded grammar $g$, one more round of the generating-nonterminal computation, applied to the productions of $g$ and the generating nonterminals of $g$, yields only generating nonterminals of $g$: every left-hand side of a production of $g$ whose right-hand side has all its nonterminals among the generating nonterminals of $g$ is itself a generating nonterminal of $g$.

nodes.summary: In a context-free grammar $G$, if every nonterminal occurring in a sentential form $u$ derives some terminal word, then $u$ derives some terminal word.
nodes.title: Sentential forms of productive nonterminals derive terminal words

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be an encoded context-free grammar. A round sends a list $H$ of nonterminals to the left-hand sides of those productions of $g$ in whose right-hand side every nonterminal belongs to $H$. For every $k \ge 0$, every nonterminal obtained after $k$ rounds starting from the empty list derives some terminal word in the context-free grammar that $g$ denotes.

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an alphabet with decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding into the natural numbers. The predicate on encoded context-free grammars $g$ over $T$ that holds exactly when the language of $g$ is empty is a computable predicate.
nodes.title: Emptiness of context-free grammars is computable

nodes.summary: For every alphabet $T$ with decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding, the property of an encoded context-free grammar $g$ over $T$ that the language of $g$ is empty is decidable by a multi-stack machine. This is Sipser, Theorem 4.8: the problem $E_{\mathrm{CFG}}$ is decidable.

nodes.summary: For a word $w = w_0 w_1 \cdots w_{n-1}$ and natural numbers $i$ and $j$, the factor of $w$ from position $i$ to position $j$ is obtained by dropping the first $i$ letters of $w$ and keeping at most the first $j - i$ letters of the rest, where $j - i$ is $0$ when $j \le i$. nodes.summary: For every alphabet $T$ with decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding, the property of a pair $(g, w)$, where $g$ is an encoded context-free grammar over $T$ and $w$ is a word over $T$, that $w$ is in the language of $g$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine. nodes.summary: Let $g$ be an encoded grammar with pumping bound $N$. Every word $w$ generated by $g$ with $|w| \ge N$ can be written as $w = uvxyz$ with $vy$ nonempty and $|vxy| \le N$, such that $u v^i x y^i z$ is generated by $g$ for every natural number $i$, including $i = 0$.

nodes.summary: If the language of an encoded grammar $g$ contains a word whose length is at least the pumping bound of $g$, then the language of $g$ is infinite.

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be an encoded context-free grammar, let $L$ be the largest of $2$ and the lengths of the right-hand sides of the productions of $g$, let $K$ be the number of distinct left-hand sides of these productions, and let $N = L^{K+1}$ be the pumping bound of $g$. For every word $w$ in the language of $g$ with $|w| \ge N$, there is a word $v$ in the language of $g$ with $N \le |v| < 2N$.

If $\alpha$ yields the empty word in that grammar, then $\alpha$ also yields the empty word in the grammar denoted by the encoded grammar consisting of the productions of $g$ that contain no terminal.

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be an encoded context-free grammar and consider the grammar of its productions without terminals. If a sentential form $\alpha$ that contains no terminal yields a word $w$ in that grammar, then $w$ is the empty word.
nodes.title: Terminal-free productions yield only the empty word

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be an encoded context-free grammar, $\alpha$ a sentential form and $w$ a word. If $\alpha$ yields $w$ in the grammar denoted by the encoded grammar consisting of the productions of $g$ that contain no terminal, then $\alpha$ yields $w$ in the grammar $g$ denotes.
nodes.title: Yields in the terminal-free subgrammar are yields of the grammar
