nodes.summary: Let $N$ be a list of natural numbers and $u$ an encoded right-hand side, that is, a word whose letters are nonterminals $i \in \mathbb{N}$ or terminals. The result is the list of all words obtained from $u$ by deleting some of the occurrences of nonterminals that belong to $N$ (possibly none, possibly all) and keeping every other letter in order; each choice of deleted occurrences contributes one entry of the list.
nodes.title: Deleting nonterminals from an encoded right-hand side

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be an encoded context-free grammar. For every encoded word $u$ and every sentential form $\alpha$ of the grammar denoted by $g$, $\alpha$ is obtained from the decoding of $u$ by deleting some occurrences of nullable nonterminals of the grammar denoted by $g$ if and only if $\alpha$ is the decoding of a word obtained from $u$ by deleting some occurrences of nonterminals in the computed list of nullable…
nodes.title: Computed deletions agree with nullable deletions

nodes.summary: For an encoded context-free grammar $g$, the encoded grammar with the same start nonterminal whose productions are, for each production $A \to u$ of $g$, the productions $A \to v$ for every nonempty word $v$ obtained from $u$ by deleting some occurrences of nonterminals in the computed list of nullable nonterminals of $g$.
nodes.title: Removing empty productions from an encoded grammar

nodes.summary: For every encoded context-free grammar $g$, a production is a production of the grammar denoted by the encoded grammar obtained from $g$ by removing empty productions if and only if it is a production of the grammar obtained from the grammar denoted by $g$ by eliminating empty productions.
nodes.title: Productions of the computable removal of empty productions

nodes.summary: For every encoded context-free grammar $g$, the grammar denoted by the encoded grammar obtained from $g$ by removing empty productions is equal to the grammar obtained from the grammar denoted by $g$ by eliminating empty productions: from each production, all productions obtained by deleting some occurrences of nullable nonterminals from its output, except those with empty output.
nodes.title: Computable removal of empty productions agrees with the classical one

nodes.summary: For every encoded context-free grammar $g$, the language of the encoded grammar obtained from $g$ by removing empty productions consists of the nonempty words of the language of $g$.
nodes.title: Removing empty productions drops only the empty word

nodes.summary: For an encoded context-free grammar $g$, the list obtained by duplicate removal from the list made of the start nonterminal of $g$ followed, for each production of $g$ in order, by its left-hand side and then the nonterminals of its right-hand side in order. It lists without repetitions the nonterminals that $g$ mentions.
nodes.title: Nonterminals of an encoded grammar

nodes.summary: For an encoded right-hand side $u$, a list whose entries are nonterminals $i \in \mathbb{N}$ or terminals, the optional value is $B$ when $u$ consists of the single nonterminal $B$, and there is no value otherwise.
nodes.title: Target of a unit right-hand side

nodes.summary: For an encoded context-free grammar $g$, a natural number $A$ and a list $S$ of natural numbers, the list consisting of $A$ followed, for each production of $g$ in order whose left-hand side lies in $S$ and whose right-hand side is a single nonterminal $B$, by that nonterminal $B$.
nodes.title: One round of unit reachability

nodes.summary: For an encoded context-free grammar $g$ and a natural number $A$, let $n$ be the number of distinct nonterminals mentioned in $g$ (the start, the left-hand sides, and the nonterminals on right-hand sides). The list is obtained from the empty list by applying one round of unit reachability from $A$ exactly $n + 1$ times.
nodes.title: Nonterminals reachable by unit productions in an encoded grammar

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be an encoded context-free grammar and let $A$ and $B$ be natural numbers. Then $B$ belongs to the computed list of nonterminals reachable from $A$ by unit productions of $g$ if and only if there are $k \ge 0$ and nonterminals $A = C_0, C_1, \dots, C_k = B$ such that $C_{i-1} \to C_i$ is a production of the grammar denoted by $g$ for every $i$ with $1 \le i \le k$.
nodes.title: Unit reachability is computed

nodes.summary: For an encoded context-free grammar $g$, the encoded grammar with the start nonterminal of $g$ whose productions are listed as follows: for each nonterminal $A$ in the list of nonterminals of $g$, and for each production $B \to u$ of $g$ in order such that $B$ is in the computed list of nonterminals reachable from $A$ by unit productions and $u$ is not a single nonterminal, the production $A \to u$.
nodes.title: Unit elimination for encoded grammars

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be an encoded context-free grammar over terminals $T$ and let $r$ be a production with terminals in $T$ and nonterminals in $\mathbb{N}$. Then $r$ is a production of the grammar denoted by the encoded unit elimination of $g$ if and only if $r$ is a production of the grammar obtained from the grammar denoted by $g$ by eliminating unit productions.
nodes.title: Productions of the encoded unit elimination

nodes.summary: For every encoded context-free grammar $g$, the grammar denoted by the encoded unit elimination of $g$ is equal to the grammar obtained from the grammar denoted by $g$ by eliminating unit productions.
nodes.title: The encoded unit elimination denotes the unit-eliminated grammar

nodes.summary: For an encoded context-free grammar $g$, the encoded grammar obtained by first removing the empty productions of $g$ (encoded $\varepsilon$-elimination) and then removing the unit productions of the result (encoded unit elimination).
nodes.title: Reduction of an encoded grammar

nodes.summary: For every encoded context-free grammar $g$, the language of the reduction of $g$ (empty productions removed, then unit productions removed) consists of the nonempty words of the language of $g$.
nodes.title: The reduced grammar generates the language minus the empty word

nodes.summary: For every encoded context-free grammar $g$, every production of the grammar denoted by the reduction of $g$ (empty productions removed, then unit productions removed) has a nonempty output, and that output is not a single nonterminal.
nodes.title: The reduced grammar has no empty and no unit productions

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a type of terminals with a primitive recursive encoding. The map sending an encoded context-free grammar $g$ over $T$ to its reduction, the encoded grammar obtained from $g$ by removing empty productions and then unit productions, is primitive recursive, where encoded grammars are encoded as pairs of a start nonterminal and a list of productions.
nodes.title: Reduction is primitive recursive
Encoded finite automata

nodes.summary: An encoded deterministic finite automaton over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a deterministic finite automaton given as data with natural-number states: a start state in $\mathbb{N}$, a list of accepting states in $\mathbb{N}$, and a list of transitions $((s, a), t)$ with $s, t \in \mathbb{N}$ and $a \in \alpha$, read as "on letter $a$, state $s$ moves to $t$".
nodes.title: Encoded DFA

nodes.summary: For an encoded DFA $D$, a state $s \in \mathbb{N}$ and a letter $a$, the step of $D$ from $s$ on $a$ is the target of the first transition that $D$ lists from $s$ on $a$, or $s$ itself when $D$ lists no such transition.
nodes.title: Transition function of an encoded DFA

nodes.summary: An encoded DFA $D$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ denotes the deterministic automaton over $\alpha$ with state set $\mathbb{N}$ whose start state is the start state of $D$, whose transition function is the transition function of $D$, and whose accepting states are the states in the accepting list of $D$.
nodes.title: The automaton denoted by an encoded DFA

nodes.summary: The language of an encoded DFA $D$ is the set of words $w$ such that the state reached by running $D$ on $w$ from its start state, following its transition function, is one of its accepting states.
nodes.title: Language of an encoded DFA

nodes.summary: The letters of an encoded DFA $D$ form the list of the letters $a$ of its listed transitions $((s, a), t)$, in the order the transitions are listed.
nodes.title: Letters of an encoded DFA

nodes.summary: The states of an encoded DFA $D$ form the list consisting of its start state followed by the targets of its listed transitions, in the order they are listed.
nodes.title: States of an encoded DFA

nodes.summary: Let $D$ be an encoded DFA, $s \in \mathbb{N}$ a state and $a$ a letter. If $D$ lists no transition from $s$ on $a$, then the transition function of $D$ takes $s$ on $a$ to $s$.
nodes.title: Unlisted transitions fix the state

nodes.summary: Let $D$ be an encoded DFA, let $s, t \in \mathbb{N}$ be states and let $a$ be a letter. If $D$ lists at least one transition from $s$ on $a$, and every transition listed from $s$ on $a$ has target $t$, then the transition function of $D$ takes $s$ on $a$ to $t$.
nodes.title: A step determined by its listed transitions

nodes.summary: Let $D$ be an encoded DFA and let $a$ be a letter that is not among the letters of $D$, that is, no listed transition of $D$ is labelled $a$. Then for every state $s \in \mathbb{N}$ the transition function of $D$ takes $s$ on $a$ to $s$.
nodes.title: Letters without listed transitions fix every state

nodes.summary: For every encoded DFA $D$, state $s \in \mathbb{N}$ and letter $a$, the transition function of $D$ takes $s$ on $a$ either to the target of some listed transition of $D$ or to $s$ itself.
nodes.title: Where a step can lead

nodes.summary: Let $D$ be an encoded DFA and let $s$ be one of its states, that is, its start state or the target of one of its listed transitions. Then for every letter $a$ the transition function of $D$ takes $s$ on $a$ to one of the states of $D$.
nodes.title: The listed states are closed under transitions

nodes.summary: The complement of an encoded DFA $D$ has the same start state and the same transitions as $D$, and its accepting states are those states of $D$ (its start state and the targets of its listed transitions) that $D$ does not accept.
nodes.title: Complement of an encoded DFA

nodes.summary: For every encoded DFA $D$ and every word $w$, the complement of $D$ accepts $w$ if and only if $D$ does not accept $w$.
nodes.title: The complement DFA accepts the complement language

nodes.summary: A DFA over a finite alphabet with finitely many states has an encoded DFA with the same language.
nodes.title: Every finite DFA has an encoding

nodes.summary: Sending an encoded DFA over $\alpha$ to the triple of its start state, its list of accepting states and its list of transitions is an equivalence (a bijection with explicit inverse) between encoded DFAs over $\alpha$ and the set $\mathbb{N} \times \mathrm{List}\,\mathbb{N} \times \mathrm{List}((\mathbb{N} \times \alpha) \times \mathbb{N})$.
nodes.title: Encoded DFAs as triples

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with a primitive recursive encoding, and encode encoded DFAs over $\alpha$ through their start state, accepting states and transitions. The map sending a triple $(s, F, T)$, where $s \in \mathbb{N}$, $F$ is a list of natural numbers and $T$ is a list of pairs $((q, a), t)$ with $q, t \in \mathbb{N}$ and $a \in \alpha$, to the encoded DFA over $\alpha$ with start state $s$, accepting…
nodes.title: Assembling an encoded DFA is primitive recursive

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with a primitive recursive encoding and decidable equality, and encode encoded DFAs over $\alpha$ through their start state, accepting states and transitions. The map sending an encoded DFA $D$ over $\alpha$, a state $s \in \mathbb{N}$ and a letter $a \in \alpha$ to the state that $D$ moves to from $s$ on $a$ (the target of the first transition listed for $(s, a)$, or $s$ if there is…
nodes.title: The transition function of encoded DFAs is primitive recursive

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with a primitive recursive encoding and decidable equality, and encode encoded DFAs over $\alpha$ through their start state, accepting states and transitions. The map sending an encoded DFA $D$ and a word $w$ over $\alpha$ to the state reached by running $D$ on $w$ from its start state is primitive recursive.
nodes.title: Running an encoded DFA is primitive recursive

nodes.summary: An encoded NFA over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a nondeterministic finite automaton with ε-moves given as data, with natural numbers as states: a list of start states, a list of accepting states, a list of transitions $((s, a), t)$, meaning that on the letter $a$ the state $s$ may move to $t$, and a list of ε-moves $(s, t)$, meaning that the state $s$ may move to $t$ without reading a letter.
nodes.title: Encoded NFA

nodes.summary: An encoded NFA $N$ over $\alpha$ denotes the ε-NFA over $\alpha$ with state set $\mathbb{N}$ whose start states are the start states listed in $N$, whose accepting states are the accepting states listed in $N$, and in which a state $s$ may move to $t$ on a letter $a$ exactly when $((s, a), t)$ is a transition of $N$, and without reading a letter exactly when $(s, t)$ is an ε-move of $N$.
nodes.title: The ε-NFA of an encoded NFA

nodes.summary: The language of an encoded NFA $N$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ is the language accepted by the ε-NFA that $N$ denotes, whose states are the natural numbers: the words $w$ over $\alpha$ such that some accepting state of $N$ is among the states reached on $w$ from the start states of $N$, with ε-moves allowed before, between and after the letters.
nodes.title: Language of an encoded NFA

nodes.summary: For an encoded NFA $N$, this is the list of the start states of $N$, followed by the targets $t$ of its transitions $((s, a), t)$, followed by the targets $t$ of its ε-moves $(s, t)$.
nodes.title: States an encoded NFA mentions as start states or targets

nodes.summary: For an encoded NFA $N$, the ε-move relation holds between states $s$ and $t$ exactly when $(s, t)$ is one of the ε-moves of $N$.
nodes.title: ε-move relation

nodes.summary: For an encoded NFA $N$, a set $X$ of natural numbers and a natural number $t$, $t$ lies in the ε-closure of $X$ in the ε-NFA that $N$ denotes if and only if $t$ is reachable from some $u \in X$ by a sequence of zero or more ε-moves of $N$.
nodes.title: The ε-closure is reachability along ε-moves

nodes.summary: For an encoded NFA $N$ and a state $s$, the ε-successors of $s$ are the list of the targets $t$ of the ε-moves $(s, t)$ of $N$, in the order in which these ε-moves are listed.
nodes.title: ε-successors of a state

nodes.summary: For an encoded NFA $N$ and a list $S$ of states, the ε-closure of $S$ is a list whose members are exactly the states reachable from some state of $S$ by finitely many ε-moves of $N$ (zero moves included), computed by a search from each state of $S$.
nodes.title: ε-closure of a list of states

nodes.summary: For an encoded NFA $N$, a list $S$ of states and a letter $a$, the letter step lists the target $t$ of every transition $((s, a), t)$ of $N$ with $s \in S$, in the order of the transition list of $N$, without taking the ε-closure.
nodes.title: Letter step of an encoded NFA

nodes.summary: For an encoded NFA $N$, a list $S$ of states and a letter $a$, the list of states reached from $S$ on $a$: the ε-closure, computed as a list, of the list of states $t$ such that $((s, a), t)$ is a transition of $N$ for some $s$ in $S$.
nodes.title: One step of an encoded NFA on a list of states

nodes.summary: For an encoded NFA $N$ and a word $w = a_1 \cdots a_n$, the run of $N$ on $w$ is the list of states obtained by starting from the ε-closure of the start states of $N$ and, for each letter $a_i$ in turn, taking the letter step on $a_i$ and then the ε-closure.
nodes.title: Run of an encoded NFA

nodes.summary: For an encoded NFA $N$ and a word $w$, the membership test is the Boolean that is true exactly when some state reached on $w$ is an accepting state of $N$. The states reached on $w$ are computed from the ε-closure of the start states by, for each letter of $w$ in turn, following the transitions on that letter and taking the ε-closure.
nodes.title: Membership test for encoded NFAs

nodes.summary: For an encoded NFA $N$, a word $w$ and a natural number $t$, $t$ is among the states in the run of $N$ on $w$ if and only if $t$ is among the states that the ε-NFA denoted by $N$ reaches on $w$ from its start states, with ε-moves allowed before, between and after the letters.
nodes.title: The run of an encoded NFA agrees with ε-NFA evaluation

nodes.summary: For an encoded NFA $N$ and a word $w$, the membership test returns true on $w$ if and only if $w$ belongs to the language of $N$.
nodes.title: Correctness of the NFA membership test

nodes.summary: Let $N$ be an encoded NFA and $w$ a word. If $u$ is one of the states that the ε-NFA denoted by $N$ can be in after reading $w$, and $N$ has an ε-move from $u$ to $v$, then $v$ is also one of these states.
nodes.title: The states reached on a word are closed under ε-moves

nodes.summary: For an encoded NFA $N$ and a state $s$, this is the list of the targets $t$ of the transitions $((s, a), t)$ of $N$ on any letter $a$, followed by the targets $t$ of the ε-moves $(s, t)$ of $N$, each in the order of the corresponding list of $N$.
nodes.title: Successors of a state in an encoded NFA

nodes.summary: For an encoded NFA $N$, this is the list, found by a search from each start state of $N$ in turn through the start states of $N$ and the targets of its transitions and ε-moves, of the states reachable from a start state of $N$ by zero or more moves, each a transition of $N$ on some letter or an ε-move of $N$.
nodes.title: Reachable states of an encoded NFA

nodes.summary: For an encoded NFA $N$ and a natural number $t$, $t$ is among the reachable states of $N$ if and only if there is a word $w$ such that $t$ is among the states that the ε-NFA denoted by $N$ reaches on $w$ from its start states, with ε-moves allowed before, between and after the letters.
nodes.title: The reachable states are those some word can lead to

nodes.summary: For an encoded NFA $N$, the emptiness test is the Boolean that is true exactly when no state in the list of reachable states of $N$ is an accepting state of $N$; the reachable states are those reachable from a start state of $N$ by zero or more moves, each a transition on some letter or an ε-move.
nodes.title: Emptiness test for encoded NFAs

nodes.summary: An `εNFA` over a finite alphabet with finitely many states has an encoded NFA with the same language.
nodes.title: Every finite ε-NFA has an encoding

nodes.summary: An NFA over a finite alphabet with finitely many states has an encoded NFA with the same language.
nodes.title: Every finite NFA has an encoding

nodes.summary: The bijection between encoded NFAs over $\alpha$ and quadruples consisting of a list of natural numbers, a list of natural numbers, a list of elements of $(\mathbb{N} \times \alpha) \times \mathbb{N}$ and a list of pairs of natural numbers, which sends an encoded NFA to its start states, accepting states, transitions and ε-moves.
nodes.title: Encoded NFAs as tuples

nodes.summary: For every alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, the property of a pair $(N, w)$, where $N$ is an encoded NFA (with ε-moves) over $\alpha$ and $w$ is a word over $\alpha$, that $w$ is in the language of $N$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine. This is Sipser, Theorem 4.2: the problem $A_{\mathrm{NFA}}$ is decidable.
nodes.title: Membership for NFAs is decidable

nodes.summary: For every alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, the property of an encoded NFA $N$ (with ε-moves) over $\alpha$ that its language is empty is decidable by a multi-stack machine. This is the problem $E_{\mathrm{NFA}}$.
nodes.title: Emptiness of NFAs is decidable
Decision procedures for finite automata

nodes.summary: For DFAs $M$ and $N$ over the same alphabet, with sets of states $\sigma$ and $\sigma'$, this is the product DFA with set of states $\sigma \times \sigma'$ whose start state is the pair of the start states of $M$ and $N$, whose transition takes $(p, q)$ on a letter $a$ to the pair of the state to which $M$ moves from $p$ on $a$ and the state to which $N$ moves from $q$ on $a$, and whose accepting states are the…
nodes.title: Symmetric difference of two DFAs

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet $\alpha$. The round sends a finite set $S$ of states of $M$ to the set consisting of the start state of $M$ and of every state that the transition function of $M$ takes some $s \in S$ to on some letter $a \in \alpha$.
nodes.title: One round of the DFA reachability search

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet whose set of states $\sigma$ is finite and has decidable equality. The reachable states of $M$ form the finite set obtained from the empty set by applying one round of the DFA reachability search for $M$ exactly $|\sigma|$ times, where $|\sigma|$ is the number of states of $M$.
nodes.title: Reachable states of a DFA

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet with finitely many states. A state $s$ of $M$ is in the set of reachable states of $M$ if and only if there is a word $w$ such that running $M$ on $w$ from its start state ends in $s$.
nodes.title: A state is reachable exactly when some word leads to it

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, the start state of $M$ belongs to the reachable states of $M$.
nodes.title: The start state is reachable

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet whose set of states is finite and has decidable equality. If a state $s$ of $M$ is reachable from the start state, then for every letter $a$ the state to which $M$ moves from $s$ on $a$ is also reachable from the start state.
nodes.title: Reachable states are closed under transitions

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet whose set of states has decidable equality. For a natural number $n$ and a finite set $S$ of states of $M$, the reachability search from $S$ with at most $n$ rounds returns $S$ when $n = 0$. When $n = k + 1$, it returns $S$ if one round of the reachability search for $M$ sends $S$ to $S$ itself, and otherwise it returns the search from the image of $S$ under that round with…
nodes.title: Early-stopping DFA reachability search

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet with finitely many states. For every natural number $n$ at least the number of states of $M$, the early-stopping reachability search for $M$ from the empty set with at most $n$ rounds returns the set of reachable states of $M$.
nodes.title: The early-stopping search finds exactly the reachable states

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet $\alpha$ with a finite state set $\sigma$ with decidable equality, and let $n \ge |\sigma|$. The accessible part of $M$ found with $n$ rounds is the DFA over $\alpha$ whose states are the states found by the reachability search from the empty set with at most $n$ rounds, whose start state is the start state of $M$, whose transition function is that of $M$ restricted to these…
nodes.title: Accessible part of a DFA, by a bounded search

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet $\alpha$ with a finite state set $\sigma$ with decidable equality. The accessible part of $M$ is its accessible part found by the reachability search with $|\sigma|$ rounds: the DFA over $\alpha$ whose states are the states found by the reachability search from the empty set with at most $|\sigma|$ rounds (exactly the states that some word leads to from the start state of…
nodes.title: Accessible part of a DFA

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet $\alpha$ with a finite state set $\sigma$ with decidable equality, and let $n \ge |\sigma|$. For every state $p$ of the accessible part of $M$ found with $n$ rounds, some word $w$ leads the accessible part from its start state to $p$.
nodes.title: Every state of the accessible part is reached

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, the emptiness test returns true exactly when none of the reachable states of $M$ is an accepting state.
nodes.title: Emptiness test for DFAs

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet with finitely many states. The emptiness test applied to $M$ returns true if and only if the language accepted by $M$ is empty.
nodes.title: The emptiness test decides emptiness of DFAs

nodes.summary: For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, the universality test applied to $M$ is the emptiness test applied to the complement of $M$: the DFA with the same states, start state and transitions whose accepting states are the states that $M$ does not accept.
nodes.title: Universality test for DFAs

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet with finitely many states. The universality test applied to $M$ returns true if and only if $M$ accepts every word over the alphabet.
nodes.title: The universality test decides universality of DFAs

nodes.summary: Let $M$ and $N$ be DFAs over the same finite alphabet, with finite state sets with decidable equality and decidable sets of accepting states. Their symmetric difference is the product DFA on pairs of states that starts at the pair of start states, moves on a letter by moving both components, and accepts a pair $(p, q)$ when exactly one of the statements "$M$ accepts $p$" and "$N$ accepts $q$" holds. The equivalence…
nodes.title: Equivalence test for DFAs

nodes.summary: Let $M$ and $N$ be DFAs over the same finite alphabet, with finite state sets with decidable equality and decidable sets of accepting states. The equivalence test of $M$ and $N$ returns true if and only if $M$ and $N$ accept the same language.
nodes.title: Correctness of the equivalence test for DFAs

nodes.summary: For an encoded DFA $D$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ with decidable equality and a word $w$ over $\alpha$, the acceptance test is the Boolean that is true exactly when the state reached by running $D$ on $w$ from its start state is in the list of accepting states of $D$.
nodes.title: Acceptance test for encoded DFAs

nodes.summary: Let $s_0 \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\mathrm{next}$ assign to each $s \in \mathbb{N}$ a list $\mathrm{next}(s)$ of natural numbers, and let $B$ and $R$ be lists of natural numbers. The round from $s_0$ with successors $\mathrm{next}$ kept inside $B$ sends the list $R$ of states found so far to the following list: write $s_0$ followed, for each $s$ in $R$ in order, by $s$ and then the list $\mathrm{next}(s)$; keep the…
nodes.title: One round of the list reachability search

nodes.summary: Let $s_0 \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\mathrm{next}$ assign to each $s \in \mathbb{N}$ a list $\mathrm{next}(s)$ of natural numbers, and let $B$ be a list of natural numbers. One search round sends a list $R$ to the list obtained by writing $s_0$ followed, for each $s$ in $R$ in order, by $s$ and then the list $\mathrm{next}(s)$, keeping the entries that lie in $B$, and deleting every entry that occurs again later; its…
nodes.title: Bounded reachability search on lists of states

nodes.summary: Let $s_0 \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\mathrm{next}$ assign to every natural number a list of natural numbers, its successors, and let $B$ be a list of natural numbers that contains $s_0$ and is closed under successors: whenever $s$ is in $B$ and $t$ is a successor of $s$, then $t$ is in $B$. Then a natural number $t$ is in the list computed by the reachability search from $s_0$ through $\mathrm{next}$ within $B$ if and…
nodes.title: Correctness of the bounded reachability search

nodes.summary: For an encoded DFA $D$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ with decidable equality, the reachable states of $D$ form the list returned by the bounded reachability search on lists of states started at the start state of $D$, kept inside the states of $D$, in which the successors of a state $s$ are the states that the transition function of $D$ takes $s$ to on the letters of $D$, in the order of the letters.
nodes.title: Reachable states of an encoded DFA

nodes.summary: For an encoded DFA $D$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ with decidable equality, the emptiness test is the Boolean that is true exactly when no entry of the list of reachable states of $D$ is in the accepting list of $D$.
nodes.title: Emptiness test for encoded DFAs

nodes.summary: For encoded DFAs $D$ and $E$ over the same alphabet, code a pair $(s, t)$ of natural numbers by its image $\langle s, t \rangle \in \mathbb{N}$ under Mathlib's pairing function. This is the list of the numbers $\langle s, t \rangle$ with $s$ running over the states of $D$ in their listed order and, for each $s$, $t$ running over the states of $E$ in their listed order.
nodes.title: Coded pairs of states of two encoded DFAs

nodes.summary: Let $D$ and $E$ be encoded DFAs over the same alphabet, and let $p \in \mathbb{N}$ code the pair of states $(s, t)$ under the pairing bijection $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. The successors of $p$ form the list that has, for each letter $a$ in the letters of $D$ followed by the letters of $E$, the code of the pair made of the step of $D$ from $s$ on $a$ and the step of $E$ from $t$ on $a$.
nodes.title: Successors of a pair of states

nodes.summary: For encoded DFAs $D$ and $E$ over the same alphabet, code a pair $(s, t)$ of natural numbers by its image $\langle s, t \rangle \in \mathbb{N}$ under Mathlib's pairing function. The reachable pairs of $D$ and $E$ form the list returned by the bounded reachability search on lists of states started at $\langle s_D, s_E \rangle$, where $s_D$ and $s_E$ are the start states of $D$ and $E$, kept inside the list of coded…
nodes.title: Reachable pairs of states of two encoded DFAs

nodes.summary: Let $D$ and $E$ be encoded DFAs over an alphabet $\alpha$ with decidable equality. The equivalence test of $D$ and $E$ is the Boolean that is true exactly when, for every entry $p$ of the list of reachable pairs of states of $D$ and $E$, writing $p = \langle s, t \rangle$ with Mathlib's pairing function, $s$ is in the accepting list of $D$ if and only if $t$ is in the accepting list of $E$.
nodes.title: Equivalence test for encoded DFAs

nodes.summary: For an encoded DFA $D$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ with decidable equality, the universality test is the Boolean that is true exactly when every entry of the list of reachable states of $D$ is in the accepting list of $D$.
nodes.title: Universality test for encoded DFAs

nodes.summary: For an encoded DFA $D$, this is the DFA whose set of states is the finite set of states of $D$ (its start state and the targets of its listed transitions), whose start state is the start state of $D$, whose transition function is that of $D$ restricted to these states, and whose accepting states are those in the accepting list of $D$.
nodes.title: An encoded DFA on its listed states

nodes.summary: Let $D$ be an encoded DFA and let $N$ be the length of the list of states of $D$. If $D$ accepts a word of length at least $N$, then the language of $D$ is infinite.
nodes.title: A long accepted word makes the language of an encoded DFA infinite

nodes.summary: Let $D$ be an encoded DFA over an alphabet $\alpha$ with decidable equality, and let $N$ be the length of its list of states. For every natural number $n$ and every word $w$ of length $n$ in the language of $D$ with $N \le n$, the language of $D$ contains a word $v$ whose length $|v|$ satisfies $N \le |v| < 2N$.
nodes.title: Accepted words of length between the number of listed states and twice it

nodes.summary: For a finite alphabet $\alpha$ given with an enumeration of its letters and for $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the list of the words of length $n$ over $\alpha$: starting from the list whose only entry is the empty word, it replaces $n$ times each word $w$ of the current list by the words $a w$ for the letters $a$ of $\alpha$, in their enumeration order.
nodes.title: Words of a given length

nodes.summary: Let $D$ be an encoded DFA over a finite alphabet and let $N$ be the length of its list of states. The infiniteness test is the Boolean that is true exactly when the language of $D$ contains a word $w$ with $N \le |w| < 2N$; it checks every word of each length $N + i$ with $0 \le i < N$.
nodes.title: Infiniteness test for encoded DFAs

nodes.summary: For every encoded DFA $D$ over a finite alphabet, the infiniteness test returns true on $D$ if and only if the language of $D$ is infinite.
nodes.title: Correctness of the infiniteness test for encoded DFAs

nodes.summary: For every alphabet $\alpha$ with decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding, the property of a pair $(D, w)$ of an encoded DFA $D$ over $\alpha$ and a word $w$ over $\alpha$ that $w$ belongs to the language of $D$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine. This is the problem $A_{\mathrm{DFA}}$.
nodes.title: Acceptance for DFAs is decidable

nodes.summary: For every alphabet $\alpha$ with decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding, the property of an encoded DFA over $\alpha$ that its language is empty is decidable by a multi-stack machine. This is the problem $E_{\mathrm{DFA}}$.
nodes.title: Emptiness of DFAs is decidable

nodes.summary: For every alphabet $\alpha$ with decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding, the property of a pair of encoded DFAs over $\alpha$ that their languages are equal is decidable by a multi-stack machine. This is the problem $\mathrm{EQ}_{\mathrm{DFA}}$.
nodes.title: Equivalence of DFAs is decidable

nodes.summary: For every alphabet $\alpha$ with decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding, the property of an encoded DFA over $\alpha$ that its language is the set of all words over $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine. This is the problem $\mathrm{ALL}_{\mathrm{DFA}}$.
nodes.title: Universality of DFAs is decidable

nodes.summary: For every finite alphabet $\alpha$, given with an enumeration of its letters, decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding, the property of an encoded DFA over $\alpha$ that its language is infinite is decidable by a multi-stack machine. This is the problem $\mathrm{INFINITE}_{\mathrm{DFA}}$.
nodes.title: Infiniteness of DFAs is decidable
Emptiness of context-free and regular intersections

nodes.summary: Let $D$ be an encoded DFA, $R$ and $S$ lists of natural numbers (the items found so far and the states where the rest of a right-hand side can start), $X$ a grammar symbol and $p \in \mathbb{N}$. The test is true exactly when either $X$ is a terminal $a$ and the step of $D$ from $p$ on $a$ lies in $S$, or $X$ is a nonterminal $B$ and some $k$ in $S$ has $\langle B, \langle p, k \rangle \rangle$ in $R$, where…
nodes.title: Whether a symbol fits at a DFA state

nodes.summary: Let $D$ be an encoded DFA, $R$ a list of natural numbers (the items found so far) and $q \in \mathbb{N}$. The start states of a right-hand side $\beta$, a list of grammar symbols, for $q$ given $R$ are defined by recursion on $\beta$: for the empty right-hand side they are the one-element list $[q]$, and for a symbol $X$ followed by $\beta'$ they are the states of $D$, in order, at which $X$ fits given $R$ and the…
nodes.title: Start states of a right-hand side in a DFA

nodes.summary: For an encoded grammar $g$, an encoded DFA $D$ and a list $R$ of natural numbers (the items found so far), one round produces the list of the codes $\langle A, \langle p, q \rangle \rangle$, where $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is the natural-number pairing, for every production $A \to \beta$ of $g$, every state $q$ of $D$ and every start state $p$ of $\beta$ for $q$ given $R$.
nodes.title: One round of the item search against a DFA

nodes.summary: For an encoded grammar $g$ and an encoded DFA $D$, the candidate items form the list of the codes $\langle A, \langle p, q \rangle \rangle$, where $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is the natural-number pairing, for every left-hand side $A$ of a production of $g$ (listed once per production) and all states $p$ and $q$ of $D$.
nodes.title: Candidate items for a grammar and a DFA

nodes.summary: For an encoded grammar $g$ and an encoded DFA $D$, the found items are the list obtained from the empty list by applying one round of the item search of $g$ and $D$ as many times as the length of the list of candidate items of $g$ and $D$.
nodes.title: Items found for a grammar and a DFA

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be an encoded grammar with start nonterminal $S$, let $D$ be an encoded DFA with start state $s$, and write $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ for the natural-number pairing. The test of $g$ and $D$ is true exactly when there is no accepting state $f$ of $D$ that is also one of the states of $D$ and for which the code $\langle S, \langle s, f \rangle \rangle$ is among the found items of $g$ and $D$.
nodes.title: The intersection-emptiness test for a grammar and a DFA

nodes.summary: Let $D$ be an encoded DFA, $R$ a list of natural numbers and $q$ one of the states of $D$. Then for every right-hand side $\beta$, every start state of $\beta$ for $q$ given $R$ is one of the states of $D$.
nodes.title: Start states of a right-hand side are states of the DFA

nodes.summary: For an encoded grammar $g$ and an encoded DFA $D$, a natural number $x$ is a sound item when there are natural numbers $A$, $p$, $q$ and a word $w$ such that $x = \langle A, \langle p, q \rangle \rangle$, where $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is the natural-number pairing, the nonterminal $A$ yields $w$ in the grammar denoted by $g$, and the automaton denoted by $D$, run on $w$ from state $p$, ends in state $q$.
nodes.title: Sound items for a grammar and a DFA

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be an encoded context-free grammar and $D$ an encoded DFA over an alphabet $T$ with decidable equality, and let $\rho$ be an encoded right-hand side whose decoding yields a word $u$ in the grammar that $g$ denotes. If $p$ is one of the states of $D$ and the automaton that $D$ denotes, run on $u$ from state $p$, ends in state $q$, then $p$ is a start state of $\rho$ for $q$ given the items found for $g$ and…
nodes.title: Completeness of the start states in a DFA

nodes.summary: For every encoded grammar $g$ and every encoded DFA $D$, the intersection-emptiness test of $g$ and $D$ returns true if and only if the intersection of the language of $g$ and the language of $D$ is empty.
nodes.title: Correctness of the intersection-emptiness test

nodes.summary: For an encoded context-free grammar $g$ and an encoded DFA $D$ over the same alphabet $T$, where $T$ has decidable equality, the inclusion test on $g$ and $D$ is the Boolean value of the emptiness test on $g$ and the complement of $D$.
nodes.title: The inclusion test for a grammar and a DFA

nodes.summary: For every alphabet $T$ with decidable equality, every encoded context-free grammar $g$ over $T$ and every encoded DFA $D$ over $T$, the inclusion test on $g$ and $D$ returns true if and only if the language of $g$ is contained in the language of $D$.
nodes.title: Correctness of the inclusion test

nodes.summary: For every alphabet $T$ with decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding, the property of a pair $(g, D)$, where $g$ is an encoded context-free grammar over $T$ and $D$ is an encoded DFA over $T$, that the intersection of the language of $g$ and the language of $D$ is empty is decidable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: Emptiness of the intersection of a context-free and a regular language is decidable

nodes.summary: For every alphabet $T$ with decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding, the property of a pair $(g, D)$, where $g$ is an encoded context-free grammar over $T$ and $D$ is an encoded DFA over $T$, that the language of $g$ is contained in the language of $D$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: Inclusion of a context-free language in a regular language is decidable
Decision procedures for regular expressions

nodes.summary: A node of an encoded regular expression over an alphabet $\alpha$ is one of six kinds: zero, epsilon, a letter $a \in \alpha$, a sum with arguments $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$, a product (concatenation) with arguments $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$, or a star with argument $i \in \mathbb{N}$, where the arguments are indices of nodes.
nodes.title: Regular-expression node

nodes.summary: An encoded regular expression over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a list of regular-expression nodes, each a constant ($0$, $1$ or a letter) or an operator (sum, concatenation or star) whose arguments are node indices; the last node is the root. Any list is allowed: in the semantics, an argument that is not the index of an earlier node reads as $0$, and the empty list denotes $0$.
nodes.title: Encoded regular expressions

nodes.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$ and a natural number $k$, the node of $e$ at index $k$ is the entry at position $k$ (counting from $0$) of its list of nodes, or the zero node when $k$ is at least the length of the list.
nodes.title: Node at an index

nodes.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the regular expression at node $k$ is defined by recursion on $k$ from the node of $e$ at index $k$ (a zero node when $k$ is past the end): a zero node gives $0$, an epsilon node gives $1$, a node for a letter $a$ gives $a$, and a sum, product or star node gives the sum, product or star of the regular expressions at its arguments, where an argument that…
nodes.title: Regular expression at a node

nodes.summary: An encoded regular expression $e$ with $n$ nodes denotes the regular expression at its node $n - 1$, the last node. For $n = 0$ this is the expression at node $0$, which lies past the end of the list and is the empty expression $0$.
nodes.title: The regular expression denoted by an encoding

nodes.summary: Let $l$ and $m$ be lists of regular-expression nodes and let $k$ be smaller than the length of $l$. Then the regular expression at node $k$ of the encoding with nodes $l$ followed by $m$ equals the regular expression at node $k$ of the encoding with nodes $l$.
nodes.title: Appending nodes does not change earlier expressions

nodes.summary: For a regular expression $r$ and a list $l$ of nodes, the nodes of $r$ are appended after $l$ in postorder, by recursion on $r$. For $0$, $1$ and a letter $a$, append the single node $0$, $1$ or $a$. For a sum $s + t$ (respectively a concatenation $st$), append the nodes of $s$ after $l$, giving $l_1$, then the nodes of $t$ after $l_1$, giving $l_2$, then a sum (respectively concatenation) node with arguments…
nodes.title: Postorder encoding after a prefix

nodes.summary: The encoding of a regular expression $r$ is the list of nodes obtained by appending the nodes of $r$ in postorder after the empty list, so that the root of $r$ is the last node.
nodes.title: Encoding of a regular expression

nodes.summary: For every regular expression $r$ over an alphabet $\alpha$, the encoded regular expression obtained by flattening $r$ (listing the nodes of its subexpressions in postorder, so that the root of $r$ is the last node) denotes $r$.
nodes.title: Every regular expression has an encoding

nodes.summary: The flag triple of the empty language is $(\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false})$; the three flags of a language say whether it is nonempty, whether it has a nonempty word, and whether it is infinite. This triple is also read for an argument of a node that is not an earlier node.
nodes.title: Flags of the empty language

nodes.summary: For triples of booleans $b = (b_1, b_2, b_3)$ and $c = (c_1, c_2, c_3)$, the flags of the sum are $(b_1 \lor c_1, b_2 \lor c_2, b_3 \lor c_3)$.
nodes.title: Flags of a sum

nodes.summary: For triples of Booleans $b = (b_1, b_2, b_3)$ and $c = (c_1, c_2, c_3)$, the flags of the product are $(b_1 \land c_1,\ (b_2 \land c_1) \lor (b_1 \land c_2),\ (b_3 \land c_1) \lor (b_1 \land c_3))$.
nodes.title: Flags of a concatenation

nodes.summary: Given a triple of Booleans $(b_1, b_2, b_3)$, the flags of its star are $(\mathrm{true}, b_2, b_2)$. Read as the flags (nonempty, has a nonempty word, infinite) of a language, a star is always nonempty, and it has a nonempty word, and is infinite, exactly when the argument has a nonempty word.
nodes.title: Flags of a star

nodes.summary: Given the list $A$ of flag triples of the nodes before it, the flag triple of a node is $(\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false})$ for a zero node, $(\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false})$ for an epsilon node and $(\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false})$ for a letter node. For a sum, product or star node it is the flags of a sum, product or star applied to the entries of $A$ at its…
nodes.title: Flags of the next node

nodes.summary: For a list of nodes $n_0, \dots, n_{m-1}$, the flags $f_0, \dots, f_{m-1}$ are computed in one left-to-right pass: $f_k$ is the step flags of node $n_k$ computed from the flags $f_0, \dots, f_{k-1}$ of the nodes before it.
nodes.title: Flags of all nodes

nodes.summary: A triple of Booleans $(b_1, b_2, b_3)$ describes a language $L$ when $b_1$ is true exactly when $L$ is nonempty, $b_2$ is true exactly when $L$ contains a nonempty word, and $b_3$ is true exactly when $L$ is infinite.
nodes.title: Flags of a language

nodes.summary: For a list $l$ of nodes and a natural number $k$, let $f_k$ be the entry at position $k$ of the flags of $l$, or the zero flags $(\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false})$ if $k$ is at least the length of $l$. Then $f_k$ describes the language of the regular expression at node $k$ of the encoding $l$ when $k$ is less than the length of $l$, and describes the empty language otherwise.
nodes.title: Correctness of the flag pass

nodes.summary: Let $e$ be an encoded regular expression with nodes $n_0, \dots, n_{m-1}$, and let $f_0, \dots, f_{m-1}$ be the flags of all nodes of $e$, the triples of Booleans computed in one left-to-right pass over the nodes. The infiniteness test of $e$ is the third component of $f_{m-1}$, the flag triple of the last node (the root); when $e$ has no nodes it is false.
nodes.title: Infiniteness test for encoded regular expressions

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $k$, $i$ and $j$, the productions of a sum node $k$ with arguments $i$ and $j$ are the unit production $k \to i$ if $i < k$, followed by the unit production $k \to j$ if $j < k$ (and nothing else). Nonterminals are node indices.
nodes.title: Productions of a sum node

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $k$, $i$ and $j$, the productions of a concatenation node $k$ with arguments $i$ and $j$ are the single production $k \to i\,j$ (nonterminal $i$ followed by nonterminal $j$) when $i < k$ and $j < k$, and there are none otherwise.
nodes.title: Productions of a concatenation node

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $k$ and $i$, the productions of a star node $k$ with argument $i$ are $k \to \varepsilon$, followed by $k \to i\,k$ if $i < k$ (and nothing else). Nonterminals are node indices.
nodes.title: Productions of a star node

nodes.summary: For a natural number $k$ and a node $n$, the productions of node $k$ are the following encoded productions, all with left-hand side $k$, where nonterminal $i$ stands for node $i$: none if $n$ is the zero node; $k \to \varepsilon$ if $n$ is the empty-word node; $k \to a$ if $n$ is the character $a$; if $n$ is a sum with arguments $i$ and $j$, the unit production $k \to i$ when $i < k$ and the unit production…
nodes.title: Productions of a node

nodes.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$ with $n$ nodes, its grammar is the encoded context-free grammar with start nonterminal $n - 1$ (truncated subtraction, so $0$ when $n = 0$), in which nonterminal $k$ stands for node $k$. Its productions are, for each node $k < n$: none if node $k$ is $0$; $k \to \varepsilon$ if it is $\varepsilon$; if it is the letter $a$, the production $k \to a$; if it is the sum of nodes $i$…
nodes.title: The grammar of an encoded regular expression

nodes.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$, the language of a sentential form $X_1 \cdots X_n$ (terminals in $\alpha$, nonterminals in $\mathbb{N}$) is the product $L_1 \cdots L_n$, where $L_i$ is $\{a\}$, the language of the one-letter word $a$, when $X_i$ is the terminal $a$, and the language of the regular expression at node $k$ of $e$ when $X_i$ is the nonterminal $k$. The empty form has language $\{\varepsilon\}$.
nodes.title: Language of a sentential form

nodes.summary: Let $e$ be an encoded regular expression, $k$ a natural number and $x$ one of the productions of node $k$ built from the node of $e$ at index $k$. If a word $w$ belongs to the language of the right-hand side of $x$ (the concatenation, over its symbols, of $\{a\}$ for a terminal $a$ and of the language of the regular expression at node $i$ for a nonterminal $i$), then $w$ belongs to the language of the regular…
nodes.title: A production of a node only produces words of its language

nodes.summary: Let $e$ be an encoded regular expression. If a sentential form $u$ of the context-free grammar of $e$ yields a terminal word $w$, then $w$ belongs to the language of $u$: the concatenation, over the symbols of $u$, of $\{a\}$ for a terminal $a$ and of the language of the regular expression at node $k$ for a nonterminal $k$.
nodes.title: Soundness of the grammar of a regular expression

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with decidable equality, $e$ an encoded regular expression over $\alpha$ and $k$ a natural number. Every word in the language of the regular expression at node $k$ of $e$ is yielded by the sentential form consisting of the single nonterminal $k$ in the context-free grammar of $e$.
nodes.title: Completeness of the grammar of an encoded regular expression

nodes.summary: For every encoded regular expression $e$, the language of the context-free grammar of $e$ (one nonterminal per node, the root as start symbol) equals the language of the regular expression that $e$ denotes.
nodes.title: The grammar generates the language of the expression

nodes.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$ and a word $w$, the test returns the answer of the membership test for encoded context-free grammars on the word $w$ and the grammar of $e$, which has one nonterminal per node and the root as start symbol.
nodes.title: Membership test for regular expressions

nodes.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$, the test returns the answer of the emptiness test for encoded context-free grammars on the grammar of $e$, which has one nonterminal per node and the root as start symbol.
nodes.title: Emptiness test for regular expressions

nodes.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$ and an encoded DFA $D$, the inclusion test returns the Boolean computed by the CFG ⊆ DFA inclusion test on the grammar of $e$ and the automaton $D$.
nodes.title: Inclusion test

nodes.summary: The bijection between the nodes of encoded regular expressions over $\alpha$ and $1 \oplus 1 \oplus \alpha \oplus (\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}) \oplus (\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}) \oplus \mathbb{N}$, where $1$ is the one-point type, that sends the zero node and the empty-word node to the first and second copies of $1$, a character node $a$ to $a$, a sum node with arguments $i, j$ to $(i, j)$ in the first copy of…
nodes.title: Regex nodes as a sum type

nodes.summary: The map sending an encoded regular expression over $\alpha$ to its list of nodes is a bijection onto the lists of regular-expression nodes over $\alpha$; its inverse wraps a list of nodes as an encoding.
nodes.title: Encodings are lists of nodes

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with a primitive recursive coding by natural numbers. The set of pairs $(e, w)$ of an encoded regular expression $e$ over $\alpha$ and a word $w$ over $\alpha$ such that $w$ belongs to the language of the regular expression denoted by $e$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: Membership for regular expressions is decidable

nodes.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, the property of an encoded regular expression over $\alpha$ that the language it denotes is empty (E_REX) is decidable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: Emptiness of regular expressions is decidable

nodes.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, the property of an encoded regular expression over $\alpha$ that the language it denotes is infinite is decidable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: Infiniteness of regular expressions is decidable

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with decidable equality and a primitive recursive coding by natural numbers. The set of pairs $(e, D)$ of an encoded regular expression $e$ over $\alpha$ and an encoded DFA $D$ over $\alpha$ such that the language of the regular expression denoted by $e$ is contained in the language of $D$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: Inclusion of a regular language in a DFA language is decidable

nodes.summary: Two regular expressions $r$ and $s$ denote the same language if and only if every word of length less than $2^{n(r) + n(s)}$, where $n$ denotes the Thompson state count, is matched by $r$ exactly when it is matched by $s$.
nodes.title: Short distinguishing words

nodes.summary: Let $c = (c_0, \dots, c_{m-1})$ be a list of natural numbers, and read $c_i$ as $0$ when $i \ge m$. The Thompson state count of a regular-expression node from $c$ is $0$ for the node $0$, $1$ for the node $\varepsilon$, $2$ for a letter, $c_i + c_j$ for a sum node and for a concatenation node with arguments $i$ and $j$, and $c_i + 1$ for a star node with argument $i$.
nodes.title: One step of the Thompson state count

nodes.summary: For a list $l$ of regular-expression nodes, the list of Thompson state counts of $l$ is computed in one left-to-right pass: starting from the empty list, each node $n$ of $l$ in turn appends the count of $n$ computed from the list of counts built so far.
nodes.title: Thompson state counts of a node list

nodes.summary: The number of Thompson states of an encoded regular expression $e$ is the entry of the state counts of the nodes of $e$ at the last node, the root (read as $0$ when $e$ has no nodes).
nodes.title: Thompson state count of an encoding

nodes.summary: For every list $l$ of nodes of encoded regular expressions, the list of state counts of $l$ has the same length as $l$.
nodes.title: One state count per node

nodes.summary: For every list $l$ of regular-expression nodes and every node $n$, let $l'$ be the list $l$ with $n$ appended at the end. Then the list of Thompson state counts of $l'$ is the list of counts of $l$ followed by one more entry, the count of $n$ computed from the counts of $l$.
nodes.title: Appending a node appends its count

nodes.summary: For every list $l$ of nodes and every index $k$, the entry at index $k$ of the state counts of $l$ (read as $0$ past the end of the list) equals the Thompson state count of the regular expression at node $k$ of the encoding with nodes $l$ when $k$ is less than the length of $l$, and $0$ otherwise.
nodes.title: The pass computes the Thompson state count of every node

nodes.summary: For every encoded regular expression $e$, the number of Thompson states of $e$ computed by the pass over its nodes equals the Thompson state count of the regular expression that $e$ denotes.
nodes.title: The pass counts the states of Thompson's automaton

nodes.summary: For encoded regular expressions $e_1$ and $e_2$, the search bound is $2^{m + n}$, where $m$ and $n$ are the numbers of Thompson states of $e_1$ and $e_2$, each computed by one pass over the nodes of the encoding.
nodes.title: Search bound for equivalence

nodes.summary: Let $e_1$ and $e_2$ be encoded regular expressions over an alphabet $\alpha$, and let $B$ be their search bound for equivalence. The regular expressions denoted by $e_1$ and $e_2$ match the same language if and only if every word $w$ over $\alpha$ of length less than $B$ is matched by the expression denoted by $e_1$ exactly when it is matched by the expression denoted by $e_2$.
nodes.title: Short distinguishing words for encoded regular expressions

nodes.summary: Over a finite alphabet with decidable equality and a fixed enumeration of its letters, the equivalence test of two encoded regular expressions $e_1$ and $e_2$ returns true exactly when, for every length $n$ less than the search bound of $e_1$ and $e_2$ and every word $w$ of length $n$, the membership test gives the same answer for $e_1$ on $w$ as for $e_2$ on $w$.
nodes.title: Equivalence test

nodes.summary: Over a finite alphabet with decidable equality and a fixed enumeration of its letters, for all encoded regular expressions $e_1$ and $e_2$, the equivalence test returns true on $e_1$ and $e_2$ if and only if the regular expressions that $e_1$ and $e_2$ denote have the same language.
nodes.title: The equivalence test is correct

nodes.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, the map sending a list $c$ of natural numbers and a regular-expression node over $\alpha$ to the Thompson state count of the node computed from $c$ is primitive recursive.
nodes.title: One step of the Thompson state count is primitive recursive

nodes.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, the map sending a list of regular-expression nodes over $\alpha$ to the list of their Thompson state counts, computed in one left-to-right pass, is primitive recursive.
nodes.title: The pass of Thompson state counts is primitive recursive

nodes.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, the number of states of Thompson's automaton of an encoded regular expression over $\alpha$, computed by one pass over its nodes, is a primitive recursive function of the encoding.
nodes.title: The Thompson state count of an encoding is primitive recursive

nodes.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, the search bound $2^{m+n}$ for equivalence of two encoded regular expressions over $\alpha$, where $m$ and $n$ are the numbers of states of Thompson's automata of the two expressions, is a primitive recursive function of the pair of encoded expressions.
nodes.title: The equivalence search bound is primitive recursive

nodes.summary: Over a primitively encodable finite alphabet with decidable equality and a fixed enumeration of its letters, the equivalence test, as a function of two encoded regular expressions, is primitive recursive.
nodes.title: The equivalence test is primitive recursive

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite alphabet with a primitive recursive encoding. Equivalent tape representations

nodes.summary: A stack tape $s$ over an alphabet $\Gamma$ is a finite list of cells, each a symbol of $\Gamma$ or the blank cell, that does not end in a blank cell. Its half-tape view is the half-tape of cells (a sequence of cells taken up to trailing blanks, the blank cell being the default) whose cells are those of $s$ in order, followed by blank cells.
nodes.title: Half-tape view of a stack tape

nodes.summary: The half-tape view of the empty stack tape over $\Gamma$ is the half-tape all of whose cells are blank.
nodes.title: Half-tape view of the empty stack tape

nodes.summary: For every cell $c$ (a symbol of $\Gamma$ or the blank cell) and every stack tape $s$ over $\Gamma$, the half-tape view of the stack tape obtained by pushing $c$ onto $s$ is the half-tape view of $s$ with $c$ pushed onto its front.
nodes.title: Pushing a cell onto a stack tape

nodes.summary: For every stack tape $s$ over $\Gamma$ (a finite list of cells, each a symbol of $\Gamma$ or the blank, that does not end in a blank), the first cell of the half-tape view of $s$ (its cells followed by infinitely many blanks) is the first cell of $s$, which is the blank if $s$ is empty.
nodes.title: First cell of the half-tape view of a stack tape

nodes.summary: For every stack tape $s$ over $\Gamma$ (a list of cells, each a symbol of $\Gamma$ or the blank cell, not ending in a blank cell), the tail of the half-tape view of $s$ is the half-tape view of the tail of $s$: dropping the first cell of $s$ drops the first cell of its half-tape.
nodes.title: Tail of the half-tape view of a stack tape

nodes.summary: For every stack tape $s$ over $\Gamma$ (a finite list of cells, each a symbol of $\Gamma$ or the blank, that does not end in a blank) and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the cell at position $n$ of the half-tape view of $s$ (its cells followed by infinitely many blanks) is the $n$-th cell of $s$, counting from $0$, if $n$ is less than the length of $s$, and the blank otherwise.
nodes.title: Cells of the half-tape view of a stack tape

nodes.summary: For every word $a_1 \cdots a_n$ over $\Gamma$, the half-tape view of the stack tape whose cells are the non-blank cells $a_1, \dots, a_n$ is the half-tape whose first $n$ cells are $a_1, \dots, a_n$ and whose later cells are blank.
nodes.title: Half-tape view of a word

nodes.summary: If two stack tapes over $\Gamma$ have the same half-tape view, then they are equal.
nodes.title: The half-tape view of stack tapes is injective

Its cell view is the Mathlib tape over cells, with the blank as default symbol, whose head is the head cell of $t$ and whose left and right halves are the halves of $t$, blank past their ends. So the cell at position $i \in \mathbb{Z}$ of…
nodes.title: Cell view of a two-way tape

nodes.summary: For every two-way tape $t$ over $\Gamma$ (a head cell with a left and a right stack tape), the head cell of the view of $t$ as a tape of cells is the head cell of $t$.
nodes.title: Head cell of the view of a two-way tape

nodes.summary: For every two-way tape $t$ over $\Gamma$ (a head cell with a left and a right stack tape), the left half of the view of $t$ as a tape of cells is the half-tape view of the left stack tape of $t$.
nodes.title: Left half of the view of a two-way tape

nodes.summary: For every two-sided tape $t$ over $\Gamma$ (a head cell together with a left and a right stack tape), the right half of the tape view of $t$ is the half-tape view of the right half of $t$.
nodes.title: Right half of the tape view

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a two-way tape over $\Gamma$ with head cell $h$, left stack tape $(\ell_0, \dots, \ell_{p-1})$ and right stack tape $(r_0, \dots, r_{q-1})$. For every integer $i$, the cell at position $i$ of the view of $t$ as a tape of cells is $h$ if $i = 0$, $r_{i-1}$ if $0 < i \le q$, $\ell_{-i-1}$ if $-p \le i < 0$, and the blank otherwise.
nodes.title: The cells of the view

nodes.summary: For every tape $t$ and every cell $a$ (a symbol or the blank), the cell view of the tape obtained from $t$ by writing $a$ under the head equals the tape obtained from the cell view of $t$ by writing $a$ under its head.
nodes.title: The cell view commutes with writing

nodes.summary: For every tape $t$ and each direction $d$ (left or right), the cell view of the tape obtained from $t$ by moving the head one cell in direction $d$ equals the tape obtained from the cell view of $t$ by moving its head one cell in direction $d$.
nodes.title: The cell view commutes with head moves

nodes.summary: For every two-way tape $t$ over $\Gamma$ and every optional head move $d$, which is either no move or a move one cell in a direction, the cell view of the tape obtained from $t$ by the optional move $d$ is the cell view of $t$ when $d$ is no move, and the cell view of $t$ with its head moved one cell in direction $d$ when $d$ is a direction.

nodes.summary: The offset of an optional head move $d$ is $0$ if $d$ is no move, $-1$ if $d$ is a move to the left and $1$ if $d$ is a move to the right.
nodes.title: Offset of an optional head move

nodes.summary: For every optional head move $d$ (no move, a move to the left, or a move to the right), the offset of $d$ lies between $-1$ and $1$, that is, $-1 \le \mathrm{offset}(d) \le 1$.
nodes.title: The offset of an optional move is at most one

nodes.summary: For every two-way tape $t$ over $\Gamma$, every cell $a$ (a symbol of $\Gamma$ or the blank) and every integer $i$, the cell at position $i$ of the view of the tape obtained from $t$ by writing $a$ under the head is $a$ if $i = 0$, and the cell at position $i$ of the view of $t$ otherwise.

For every two-way tape $t$ over $\Gamma$ and every integer $i$, the cell at position $i$ of the view of the tape obtained from $t$ by the optional move $d$ is the cell at position $i + \delta(d)$ of the view of $t$.
nodes.title: Cells after an optional move

nodes.title: Cells after $n$ moves to the right

nodes.summary: For every word $w = w_0 w_1 \cdots w_{n-1}$ over $\Gamma$, the cell view of the input tape of $w$ is the Mathlib input tape of the list of non-blank cells $w_0, \dots, w_{n-1}$: the head is on $w_0$, the letters $w_1, \dots, w_{n-1}$ lie to its right in order, and every other cell is blank (for the empty word, every cell is blank).

nodes.summary: For an alphabet $\Gamma_0$ with a distinguished blank symbol $b$, the non-blank symbols of $\Gamma_0$ are the elements $x \in \Gamma_0$ with $x \ne b$. They form the tape alphabet of the single-tape machine that simulates a Post–Turing machine over $\Gamma_0$.
nodes.title: Non-blank symbols

nodes.summary: Let $\Gamma_0$ be an alphabet with blank symbol $b$. A tape cell over the non-blank symbols of $\Gamma_0$ is either blank or holds a symbol $x \ne b$ of $\Gamma_0$. Its cell symbol is $b$ for the blank cell and $x$ for the cell holding $x$. This map from cells to $\Gamma_0$ sends the blank cell to the blank symbol, so it is a pointed map.
nodes.title: Cell symbol

nodes.summary: For every cell $o$ over the non-blank symbols of an alphabet $\Gamma_0$ with blank symbol $b$, the cell symbol of $o$ is $b$ when $o$ is the blank cell and is $x$ when $o$ holds the non-blank symbol $x$.

nodes.summary: Let $\delta$ be a transition function of a multi-tape Turing machine with $k$ work tapes, assigning an action to each state, input symbol and tuple of $k$ work tape symbols, where a symbol may be blank. The successor of a configuration $c$ under $\delta$ is $c$ itself if $c$ is halted, and otherwise the configuration obtained by applying to $c$ the action $\delta(q, a, b)$, where $q$ is the state of $c$, $a$ the…

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be the deterministic multi-tape Turing machine with initial state $q_0$ and transition function $\delta$. For every configuration $c$, the step of $M$ from $c$ is the successor of $c$ under $\delta$: $c$ itself if $c$ is halted, and otherwise the result of applying to $c$ the action that $\delta$ selects for the state of $c$ and the symbols under its input and work tape heads.
nodes.title: Step of a machine given by a transition function

nodes.title: Step determinism

nodes.summary: For a configuration $c$ of a deterministic multi-tape Turing machine and every $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the run from $c$ after $t + 1$ steps is in the same configuration as the run from the successor of $c$ after $t$ steps.
nodes.title: Peeling off the first step of a run

nodes.summary: If a configuration $c$ of a deterministic multi-tape Turing machine is halted, then for every $t \in \mathbb{N}$ the run from $c$ is in configuration $c$ after $t$ steps.
nodes.title: Halted configurations are fixed

nodes.summary: For a configuration $c$ of a deterministic multi-tape Turing machine and steps $s \le t$, if the run from $c$ is halted after $s$ steps, then it is halted after $t$ steps.

nodes.summary: A deterministic multi-tape Turing machine started in a configuration $c$ halts at step $0$ if and only if $c$ is halted.

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a configuration of a deterministic multi-tape Turing machine and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$. If the run from $c$ is not halted after any $s < m$ steps, and the run from the configuration reached after $m$ steps halts at step $n$ (it is halted after $n$ steps and not halted after fewer), then the run from $c$ halts at step $m + n$.
nodes.title: Run composition for halting

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a deterministic multi-tape Turing machine, $c$ a configuration of $M$ and $m, n$ natural numbers. If $M$ started in $c$ halts at step $m + n$, that is, it is halted after $m + n$ steps and not halted after any fewer, then $M$ started in the configuration reached from $c$ after $m$ steps halts at step $n$.
nodes.title: Halting step after a run prefix

nodes.summary: If a deterministic multi-tape Turing machine runs in time $t$ on input $w$, then the run from the initial configuration on $w$ is halted after $t$ steps.
nodes.title: A time bound forces halting

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a deterministic multi-tape Turing machine, $w$ an input and $t$ a natural number. Then $M$ runs in time $t$ on $w$, that is, every computation path of $M$ on $w$ with at least $t$ steps ends in a halted configuration, if and only if $M$ started in its initial configuration on $w$ is halted after $t$ steps.

nodes.summary: A deterministic multi-tape Turing machine computes the output $o$ on input $w$ if and only if there is a step $t$ at which the run from the initial configuration on $w$ halts (it is halted after $t$ steps and not halted after any $s < t$ steps) and the configuration it reaches after $t$ steps has output tape $o$.
nodes.title: Computing an output means halting with it

nodes.summary: If a deterministic multi-tape Turing machine runs in time $t$ on input $w$, then for every word $o$ the machine computes $o$ on $w$ if and only if the configuration reached from the initial configuration on $w$ after $t$ steps has output tape $o$.

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a deterministic multi-tape Turing machine, $x$ an input and $t \in \mathbb{N}$. The number of work-tape cells visited along the computation path of $M$ on $x$ made of the first $t$ steps from the initial configuration equals the space used by the run of $M$ from the initial configuration on $x$ up to step $t$. Both count the visited cells on each work tape separately and sum over the work tapes.

Programming multi-stack machines

nodes.summary: A flag on a type $\sigma$ of machine states consists of a map $\mathrm{tag} : \mathrm{Bool} \to \sigma$ that stores a bit in a state and a map $\mathrm{untag} : \sigma \to \mathrm{Bool}$ that reads it back, such that $\mathrm{untag}(\mathrm{tag}(\beta)) = \beta$ for every bit $\beta$. The program primitives use it to branch on whether a pop found a symbol.
nodes.title: Flag bit of a machine state

nodes.summary: Let $f : \sigma \to \mathrm{Option}\,\sigma$ be a partial step function and let $\hat f$ be its lift to $\mathrm{Option}\,\sigma$, which sends $\mathrm{none}$ to $\mathrm{none}$ and $\mathrm{some}\,x$ to $f(x)$. Then $\hat f^{\,n}(\mathrm{none}) = \mathrm{none}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: A halted run stays halted

For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $M$ runs from $c$ to $d$ in exactly $n$ steps when applying the step function of $M$ $n$ times, starting at $c$, is defined at every step (no configuration before the last one has halted) and ends at $d$.

If executing the statement $M(l)$ from state $v$ and stacks $S$ yields $d$, then $M$ runs in exactly one step from the configuration with label $l$, state $v$ and stacks $S$ to $d$.

nodes.summary: Decode a head move: `0` moves left, `1` stays, anything else moves right.
nodes.title: Decoding a Turing machine head move

nodes.summary: A coded action for a machine with $k$ work tapes consists of a coded input-head move; for each of the $k$ work tapes, an optional symbol to write, the symbol being a bit or the blank (so a blank can be written), together with a coded head move; an optional output bit; and an optional next state in $\mathbb{N}$, where no next state means halting. A head move is coded by a natural number: $0$ moves left, $1$ stays,…
nodes.title: Coded actions

nodes.summary: The bijection between coded actions and tuples $(m, w, b, q)$ that sends an action to its coded input head move $m \in \mathbb{N}$, its work tape instructions $w$ (for each of the $k$ work tapes, an optional symbol to write and a coded head move), its optional output bit $b$ and its optional next state $q$.
nodes.title: Coded actions as tuples

nodes.summary: A coded action $a$ stands for the action of CSLib's multi-tape model that moves the input head by the decoded input move of $a$, on each work tape writes the optional symbol that $a$ gives for that tape and moves its head by the decoded move, emits the optional output bit of $a$, and enters the next state of $a$ (halting when there is none).
nodes.title: Decoding a coded action

nodes.summary: The default action of a missing table entry: halt without moving any head, writing any symbol or emitting an output bit.
nodes.title: Halting action

nodes.summary: A key of a table entry for a machine with $k$ work tapes is a triple $(q, a, w)$ of a state $q \in \mathbb{N}$, the symbol $a$ under the input head and the symbols $w = (w_i)_{i < k}$ under the $k$ work heads, where each symbol is a bit or the blank.
nodes.title: Keys of a code's table

nodes.summary: A code for a machine with $k$ work tapes over the binary alphabet, with states in $\mathbb{N}$, is a finite list of table entries, each a key (a state together with the symbols under the input head and the $k$ work heads) paired with a coded action. The table is looked up by key, the first matching entry wins, and a missing key halts the machine.
nodes.title: Codes for multi-tape machines

nodes.summary: The bijection between codes for machines with $k$ work tapes and finite lists of table entries, each a pair of a key and a coded action, that sends a code to its table.
nodes.title: Multi-tape codes as tables

nodes.summary: The natural number coding a code $c$: its encoding under the standard primitive recursive coding of codes, which identifies a code with its table, a list of pairs of a key and a coded action.
nodes.title: Numeric coding of codes

nodes.summary: The code coded by a natural number $n$, if any: decoding under the standard primitive recursive coding of codes, which identifies a code with its table, a list of pairs of a key and a coded action. The result is empty when $n$ codes no code.
nodes.title: Decoding numbers to codes

nodes.summary: For every code $c$ with $k$ work tapes, decoding the natural number $\operatorname{encode}(c)$ returns $c$: $\operatorname{decode}(\operatorname{encode}(c))$ is defined and equals $c$.
nodes.title: Code round-trip

nodes.summary: If two codes $c$ and $c'$ with the same number of work tapes have the same numeric code, then $c = c'$.
nodes.title: Injectivity of the numeric coding of codes

nodes.summary: For a code $c$ with $k$ work tapes, a state $q \in \mathbb{N}$, a symbol $a$ under the input head and symbols $w = (w_i)_{i < k}$ under the work heads (each symbol a bit or the blank), the action of $c$ at $(q, a, w)$ is the coded action of the first table entry of $c$ whose key is $(q, a, w)$, or, if there is no such entry, the halting action, which moves no head, writes and emits nothing, and has no next state.
nodes.title: Action of a code at a key

nodes.summary: The transition function of a code $c$ sends a state $q$, the symbol $a$ under the input head and the symbols $w$ under the work heads (each a bit or blank) to the action of CSLib's multi-tape model that the coded action of $c$ at $(q, a, w)$ stands for. That coded action is the one of the first table entry of $c$ with key $(q, a, w)$, or, if there is none, the one that halts without moving, writing or emitting.
nodes.title: Transition function of a code

nodes.summary: The machine of a code $c$ for $k$ work tapes is the machine of CSLib's multi-tape model with $k$ work tapes, the binary alphabet and states in $\mathbb{N}$ whose initial state is $0$ and whose transition function is the transition function of $c$.
nodes.title: The multi-tape machine of a code

nodes.summary: For a code $c$, a binary input $x$ and a configuration $C$ of the machine of $c$ on $x$, the step of the machine of $c$ sends $C$ to its successor under the transition function of $c$: $C$ itself if it has halted, and otherwise the result of applying to $C$ the action that the transition function of $c$ selects for the state of $C$ and the symbols under its heads.
nodes.title: Step of the machine of a code

nodes.summary: The states of a code $c$ for machines with $k$ work tapes form the finite set of natural numbers consisting of the initial state $0$ and the next state of every table entry of $c$ that does not halt.
nodes.title: States of a multi-tape code

nodes.summary: For a code $c$, a state $q$, an input symbol $a$ and work tape symbols $w$, if the action of $c$ at $(q, a, w)$ has a next state $q'$ (rather than halting), then $q'$ belongs to the set of states of $c$.
nodes.title: Next states of a code lie in its state set

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a code for a machine with $k$ work tapes. For every binary input $x$ and every number of steps $t$, if the machine of $c$, run for $t$ steps from its initial configuration on $x$, has not halted and is in state $q$, then $q$ lies in the finite set of states of $c$.
nodes.title: Codes denote finite-state machines

nodes.summary: A work tape is a pair of finite lists of cells, each cell a bit or blank: the cells left of the head, nearest first, and the cells from the head rightwards; cells beyond both lists are blank.
nodes.title: Work tapes as zippers

nodes.summary: The symbol read from a work tape given as a zipper $(l, r)$ is the first cell of $r$, or the blank if $r$ is empty.
nodes.title: Symbol under the head of a zipper tape

nodes.summary: Writing an optional symbol on a work tape leaves the tape unchanged when no symbol is given; given a symbol $s$ (a bit or blank), it replaces the cell under the head by $s$ and keeps all other cells.
nodes.title: Writing on a zipper tape

nodes.summary: For a coded move $m$ and a work tape given as a zipper $(l, r)$: if $m = 0$ the head moves one cell left, removing the first cell of $l$ (the blank if $l$ is empty) and putting it in front of $r$; if $m = 1$ the tape is unchanged; otherwise the head moves one cell right, removing the first cell of $r$ (the blank if $r$ is empty) and putting it in front of $l$.
nodes.title: Moving the head of a zipper tape

nodes.summary: For a work tape $t$ in zipper form and an integer $j$, the cell of $t$ at $j$ is the symbol at offset $j$ from the head: for $j = n \ge 0$ it is entry $n$ (counting from $0$) of the list of cells from the head rightwards, and for $j = -(n + 1)$ it is entry $n$ of the list of cells left of the head, nearest first; in either case it is the blank when the list has no entry $n$.
nodes.title: Cell of a zipper tape
