nodes.title: Explicit configurations of the code evaluator

nodes.summary: The bijection between explicit configurations and tuples $(q, p, t, o)$ that sends a configuration to its optional state $q$ (empty when halted), its shifted input head position $p \in \mathbb{N}$, its family $t$ of $k$ work tapes (each a zipper) and its output $o$ so far, a list of bits.
nodes.title: Explicit configurations as tuples

nodes.summary: The initial explicit configuration has state $0$, the input head on the first input cell (position $1$, positions being shifted by one), every work tape blank (both halves of its zipper empty), and empty output.
nodes.title: Initial configuration of the clocked evaluator

nodes.summary: For an input $x$ and a shifted input head position $p$, the input symbol is the blank if $p = 0$; otherwise it is the entry of $x$ at index $p - 1$ (counting from $0$) if $p - 1 < |x|$, and the blank if $p - 1 \ge |x|$.
nodes.title: Input symbol under the input head

nodes.summary: For an input of length $n$, a shifted input head position $p$ and a coded move $m$, the new position is $p - 1$ (truncated at $0$) if $m = 0$, $p$ if $m = 1$, and $\min(p + 1, n + 1)$ otherwise, so a move right never passes position $n + 1$, one cell beyond the input.

nodes.title: Applying a coded action

nodes.summary: One step of the evaluator for a code $c$ on a binary input $x$ leaves an explicit configuration $e$ unchanged if $e$ has halted; if $e$ is in state $q$, it applies to $e$ the coded action of $c$ at $q$, the input symbol at the input head position of $e$ and the symbols under the heads of the work tapes of $e$.
nodes.title: Evaluator step

nodes.summary: The clocked evaluator runs a code $c$ on a binary input $x$ for $T$ steps: it applies the evaluator's step $T$ times to the initial explicit configuration. If the resulting configuration is halted, it returns that configuration's output; otherwise it returns no result.
nodes.title: Clocked evaluator

nodes.summary: An explicit configuration $e$ represents a configuration $C$ of CSLib's multi-tape model on input $x$ when they have the same state, the same shifted input head position and the same output, and for every work tape $i$ and every cell $z \in \mathbb{Z}$, the content of cell $z$ of tape $i$ in $C$ equals the cell of tape $i$ of $e$ at offset $z - p_i$ from its head, where $p_i$ is the head position of tape $i$ in $C$.
nodes.title: Explicit configurations representing machine configurations

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a code and $x$ a binary input. If an explicit configuration $e$ represents a configuration $C$ of the machine of $c$ on $x$, then the evaluator's step of $e$ for $c$ on $x$ represents the successor of $C$ under the machine of $c$.
nodes.title: The evaluator simulates the machine step for step

nodes.summary: For a code $c$, an input $x$ and every $t$, the explicit configuration obtained from the initial one by $t$ steps of the evaluator for $c$ on $x$ represents the configuration that the machine of $c$ reaches after $t$ steps from its initial configuration on $x$.
nodes.title: The evaluator tracks the machine run

nodes.summary: For every code $c$, binary input $x$, clock $T \in \mathbb{N}$ and binary word $o$, the clocked evaluator of $c$ on $x$ with clock $T$ returns $o$ if and only if the machine of $c$, run for $T$ steps from its initial configuration on $x$, has halted and its output is $o$.
nodes.title: Evaluator agreement

nodes.summary: For a code $c$, an input $x$ and a clock $T$, the clocked evaluator of $c$ on $x$ with clock $T$ returns an output if and only if the machine of $c$ runs in time $T$ on $x$, that is, every computation path of that machine on $x$ with at least $T$ steps ends in a halted configuration.
nodes.title: The evaluator returns within the clock exactly when the machine runs in time

nodes.summary: For a code $c$ for machines with $k$ work tapes, a binary input $x$, a binary word $o$ and clocks $T \le T'$ in $\mathbb{N}$, if the clocked evaluator of $c$ on $x$ returns $o$ with clock $T$, then it also returns $o$ with clock $T'$.

nodes.summary: A code is a transition table: a finite list of rows, row $q$ belonging to the state $q \in \mathbb{N}$, each a finite list of entries, entry $a$ of a row belonging to the symbol $a \in \mathbb{N}$. nodes.title: Codes for single-tape machines

nodes.summary: A natural number codes a statement of a single-tape Turing machine with symbols in $\mathbb{N}$: $0$ moves the head left, $1$ moves the head right, and $a + 2$ writes the symbol $a$.
nodes.title: Decoding an action

nodes.summary: The tape symbol of a bit $b$ is $1$ if $b$ is false and $2$ if $b$ is true; the symbol $0$ is the blank.
nodes.title: Symbol of an input bit

nodes.summary: The input word of a list of bits $x$ is the list of natural numbers obtained from $x$ by replacing each bit by its symbol: $1$ for false and $2$ for true.
nodes.title: Input word of a list of bits

nodes.summary: Codes for single-tape machines correspond bijectively to transition tables, that is, to lists of rows, each a list of entries that are either empty or a pair of natural numbers: a code corresponds to its table.
nodes.title: Single-tape codes as tables

nodes.summary: For a code $c$ and numbers $q$ and $a$, the lookup of $c$ at state $q$ and symbol $a$ is the entry in row $q$, column $a$ of the table of $c$: either a pair $(q', s)$ of a next state and an action code, or no entry (halt). It is no entry when the table has no row $q$ or that row has no column $a$.
nodes.title: Table lookup of a code

nodes.summary: The machine of a code $c$ is the single-tape Turing machine with states and symbols in $\mathbb{N}$ that, in state $q$ reading symbol $a$, halts if the table lookup of $c$ at state $q$ and symbol $a$ has no entry, and otherwise, if the entry is $(q', s)$, enters state $q'$ and does the action coded by $s$: $0$ moves left, $1$ moves right and $a' + 2$ writes $a'$.
nodes.title: The machine of a single-tape code

nodes.summary: The set of states of a code $c$ is the finite set of natural numbers consisting of the initial state $0$ and every state $q'$ such that some entry of the table of $c$ is a pair $(q', s)$.
nodes.title: States of a single-tape code

nodes.summary: The decoded machine is supported by the finite set of states of its code.
nodes.title: Codes denote finite machines

nodes.summary: A configuration of the simulation consists of a state $q \in \mathbb{N}$, the list of the cells left of the head (nearest first), the symbol in the cell under the head, and the list of the cells right of the head (nearest first); states and symbols are natural numbers.
nodes.title: Explicit configurations

nodes.summary: Configurations correspond bijectively to tuples in $\mathbb{N} \times \mathrm{List}(\mathbb{N}) \times \mathbb{N} \times \mathrm{List}(\mathbb{N})$: a configuration corresponds to the tuple of its state, its cells left of the head, its cell under the head and its cells right of the head.
nodes.title: Configurations as tuples

nodes.summary: The TM0 configuration of a configuration $k$ of the simulation has the state of $k$, the cell under the head of $k$ as its head cell, and as the halves of its tape left and right of the head the cells of $k$ left and right of the head, nearest first, followed by infinitely many blanks.
nodes.title: TM0 configuration of a simulation configuration

nodes.summary: Let $k$ be a configuration with left cells $L$ (nearest first), head cell $h$ and right cells $R$ (nearest first), let $q'$ be a state and let $s$ be an action code. Acting on $k$ with $q'$ and $s$ gives a configuration with state $q'$, as follows. For $s = 0$ (move left), its head cell is the first entry of $L$, or the blank $0$ if $L$ is empty, its left cells are $L$ without its first entry, and its right cells…
nodes.title: Acting on a configuration

nodes.summary: The output of a configuration $k$ is the list consisting of the symbol under the head of $k$ followed by the cells right of the head (nearest first), with all trailing blanks $0$ removed.
nodes.title: Output of a configuration

nodes.summary: The initial configuration of the simulation on a list of bits $x$ has state $0$, an empty list of cells left of the head, the head on the first symbol of the input word of $x$ (the blank $0$ if $x$ is empty), and the remaining symbols of the input word, in order, right of the head.
nodes.title: Initial configuration of the code simulation

nodes.summary: For a code $c$ and a configuration $k$ of the simulation, look up the table entry of $c$ at the state of $k$ and the symbol under the head of $k$. If there is no entry, the step is undefined (the machine halts); if the entry is $(q', s)$, the step is the configuration obtained from $k$ by entering the state $q'$ and doing the action coded by $s$.
nodes.title: One step of a code

nodes.summary: For a code $c$ and a configuration $k$ of the simulation, the configuration after one step of $c$ from $k$ if that step is defined, and $k$ itself if $c$ halts at $k$.
nodes.title: One step of a code, or stay when halted

nodes.summary: For a code $c$, a list of bits $x$ and $T \in \mathbb{N}$, the configuration of $c$ on $x$ after $T$ steps is obtained from the initial configuration on $x$ by applying $T$ times the step of $c$, where a step leaves a halted configuration unchanged. It is the configuration after $T$ steps, or the halting configuration if the machine halts earlier.
nodes.title: Clocked configuration of a code

nodes.summary: Given a code $c$, a list of bits $x$ and a clock $T \in \mathbb{N}$, run the simulation of $c$ on $x$ for at most $T$ steps. If it halts within $T$ steps, the result is the output of the halting configuration: the tape from the head rightwards, with trailing blanks dropped. Otherwise there is no result.
nodes.title: The clocked evaluator

nodes.summary: For every code $c$ and every configuration $k$ of the simulation, the decoded TM0 machine of $c$ halts at the TM0 configuration of $k$ exactly when the step of $c$ from $k$ is undefined, and otherwise its step from the TM0 configuration of $k$ is the TM0 configuration of the step of $c$ from $k$.
nodes.title: Explicit steps agree with the decoded machine

nodes.summary: For a list of bits $x$, the initial configuration of the simulation on $x$, read as a configuration of a single-tape machine, is the initial configuration of a single-tape machine on the input word of $x$.
nodes.title: The explicit initial configuration is the machine's

nodes.summary: For every explicit configuration $k$, the half-tape of the Mathlib configuration of $k$ from the head rightwards (the cell under the head followed by the cells to its right) is the output of $k$, read with blanks beyond its end.
nodes.title: The output of a configuration as a Mathlib half-tape

Then the first run has a result exactly when the second does, and its result is the Mathlib…
nodes.title: Iterated steps of the decoded machine

nodes.summary: For a code $c$, a list of bits $x$ and $T \in \mathbb{N}$, the decoded machine of $c$ halts within $T$ steps on the input word of $x$ if and only if the explicit simulation of $c$, started from the initial configuration on $x$, reaches after some $j \le T$ steps a configuration that has no successor step.
nodes.title: Bounded halting of a decoded machine through its simulation

nodes.summary: For a code $c$, a list of bits $x$ and a clock $T \in \mathbb{N}$, the clocked evaluator of $c$ on $x$ with clock $T$ returns a value if and only if the simulation of $c$ has no step from the configuration after $T$ clocked steps on $x$ (the configuration after $T$ steps, or the halting configuration if the machine halts earlier).
nodes.title: Definedness of the clocked evaluator

nodes.summary: For a code $c$, a list of bits $x$ and a clock $T \in \mathbb{N}$, the clocked evaluator of $c$ on $x$ with clock $T$ returns a value if and only if the machine of $c$, started on the input word of $x$, halts within $T$ steps.
nodes.title: Clocked halting

nodes.summary: For a code $c$, a list of bits $x$, a clock $T \in \mathbb{N}$ and a list $l$ of natural numbers, the clocked evaluator returns $l$ on $c$, $x$ and $T$ if and only if the configuration of $c$ after $T$ clocked steps on $x$ has no successor step and its output is $l$.
nodes.title: Characterization of clocked results

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a code for a single-tape machine, $x$ a list of bits, $l$ a list of natural numbers and $T \le T'$ natural numbers. If the clocked evaluator returns $l$ on $c$ and $x$ with clock $T$, then it also returns $l$ with clock $T'$.
nodes.title: Monotonicity of the single-tape clocked evaluator

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a code, $x$ a list of bits, $T$ a natural number and $l$ a list of natural numbers. If the clocked evaluator, running $c$ on $x$ for at most $T$ steps, returns $l$, then the decoded machine of $c$, started on the input word of $x$, halts, and the tape from its head rightwards in the halting configuration is $l$ followed by blanks.
nodes.title: Clocked results agree with the machine's semantics

nodes.summary: For a code $c$ and a list of bits $x$, the machine decoded from $c$ halts on the input word of $x$ if and only if there is a clock $T \in \mathbb{N}$ for which the clocked evaluator of $c$ on $x$ with clock $T$ returns a result.

Clocked universal Turing machine

nodes.summary: The cell of a natural number $n$ is the list of bits consisting of $n$ copies of the bit true (units) followed by one bit false (a marker).
nodes.title: The cell of a number

nodes.summary: The cells of a list $(n_1, \ldots, n_m)$ of natural numbers are the concatenation of the cells of $n_1, \ldots, n_m$ in this order, so that the cell of $n_1$ comes first (on top of a stack).
nodes.title: The cells of a list of numbers

nodes.summary: The clocked universal machine has fifteen stacks: the state $Q$, the next state $N$, the action $A$ and the head cell $H$ (these four hold counters of units), the cells left ($L$) and right ($R$) of the head, the code $C$, the scan buffer $B$, the scratch counters $T$, $U$, $V$, the clock $\mathrm{Ck}$, and the parsing stacks: the encoded input $X$, the parse buffer $P$ and the output $O$.

nodes.summary: Every stack $k$ of the clocked universal machine holds bits: its alphabet is $\Gamma(k) = \mathrm{Bool}$.
nodes.title: Stack alphabet of the clocked universal machine

nodes.summary: The unit decoder sends the bit true (a unit) to the bit true, and sends the bit false (a marker) to no bit, which ends a block.
nodes.title: Decoding units

nodes.summary: For a label $\ell$, this instruction pops the top symbol of the code stack $C$ and discards it (doing nothing if $C$ is empty), pushes a marker (the bit false) onto the scan buffer $B$, and goes to $\ell$; the state bit is unchanged.
nodes.title: Moving a marker onto the scan buffer

nodes.summary: The program of the clocked universal machine gives an instruction for every label. Numbers sit on stacks as counters of units (the bit true), and a cell is a counter followed by a marker (the bit false).
nodes.title: The clocked universal program

nodes.summary: For a code $c$, the list of quadruples $(q, a, q', s)$, one for each state $q$ and symbol $a$ inside the table of $c$ whose table entry is a transition $(q', s)$ (enter the state $q'$ and do the action coded by $s$); halting positions are skipped. The quadruples are listed row by row, by increasing $q$, and within a row by increasing $a$.
nodes.title: Entries of a code

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $q$ and $a$ and a list of quadruples $(q_i, a_i, q'_i, s_i)$ of natural numbers, the result is the pair $(q'_i, s_i)$ of the first quadruple in the list with $q_i = q$ and $a_i = a$, and no result if no quadruple has the key $(q, a)$. This is the order in which the machine scans the code stack.
nodes.title: Looking up a key in a list of entries

nodes.summary: For every code $c$ and all natural numbers $q$ and $a$, looking up the key $(q, a)$ in the entries of $c$ gives the entry of the table of $c$ at state $q$ and symbol $a$: the pair $(q', s)$ if that position holds the transition $(q', s)$, and no result if it halts, including every position outside the table.

nodes.summary: For a list of quadruples of natural numbers, the list of natural numbers obtained by replacing each quadruple $(q, a, q', s)$ by the four numbers $q, a, q', s$ in this order, keeping the order of the quadruples.
nodes.title: Numbers of a list of entries

nodes.summary: The code stack of a code $c$ is the list of bits formed by the cells of the numbers $q, a, q', s$ of every entry $(q, a, q', s)$ of $c$ (a table position $(q, a)$ holding the transition $(q', s)$), with the entries ordered by $q$ and then by $a$, and the four numbers of an entry in the order $q, a, q', s$.

nodes.summary: A counter-machine instruction is one of: increment register $r$, decrement register $r$, or jump to instruction $q$ if register $r$ is zero, where the register index $r$ and the jump target $q$ are natural numbers.
nodes.title: Counter-machine instructions

nodes.summary: A counter-machine state consists of a program counter, which is a natural number, and the register contents, a function assigning a natural number to every register index $i \in \mathbb{N}$.

nodes.summary: For a counter-machine program $p$, a natural number $t$ and a state $s$, the execution of $p$ for $t$ steps from $s$ is the state obtained from $s$ by applying $t$ single steps of $p$.

nodes.summary: The output of a counter-machine program $p$ on a list of inputs is the partial natural number obtained as follows: run $p$ from the initial state on those inputs; if for some number $t$ of steps the program counter is at least the length of $p$ (the machine has halted), the output is the content of register $0$ after the least such $t$; if no such $t$ exists, the output is undefined.

nodes.title: Counter-machine execution is stable once halted

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a counter-machine program, $s$ a state, and $t_1 \le t_2$ natural numbers. If the state reached from $s$ after $t_1$ steps of $p$ has program counter at least the length of $p$, then the state reached from $s$ after $t_2$ steps equals the state reached after $t_1$ steps.

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a counter-machine program, let $x$ be a list of natural-number inputs, and let $t$ and $y$ be natural numbers. If the state reached after $t$ steps of $P$ from the initial state on $x$ has program counter at least the length of $P$ (so the machine has halted) and register $0$ holds $y$ in that state, then the output of $P$ on $x$ is defined and equals $y$.

Random-access machines

nodes.summary: An addressing mode of a random-access machine specifies an operand by a natural number $n$ in one of three ways: immediate (the operand is the value $n$ itself), direct (the operand is the contents of register $n$), or indirect (the operand is the contents of the register whose index is the contents of register $n$).
nodes.title: RAM addressing mode

nodes.summary: A store destination of a random-access machine names, by a natural number $n$, the register into which the accumulator is stored: either register $n$ itself (direct) or the register whose index is the contents of register $n$ (indirect).
nodes.title: RAM store destination

nodes.summary: An instruction of a random-access machine is one of the following: load an operand into the accumulator; store the accumulator into a store destination; add an operand to the accumulator; subtract an operand from the accumulator, truncating at $0$; jump to instruction $q$; jump to instruction $q$ if the accumulator is $0$; halt. Here an operand is given by a RAM addressing mode, a store destination is a RAM store…
nodes.title: RAM instruction

nodes.summary: A state of a random-access machine consists of a program counter in $\mathbb{N}$, an accumulator value in $\mathbb{N}$, and register contents, a function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ giving the contents of each register.
nodes.title: RAM state

nodes.summary: In a RAM state with register contents $r$, an operand resolves to a natural number: the immediate operand $n$ resolves to $n$ itself, the direct operand $n$ to the contents $r(n)$ of register $n$, and the indirect operand $n$ to $r(r(n))$.
nodes.title: Value of a RAM operand

nodes.summary: In a RAM state with register contents $r$, a store destination resolves to a register index: the direct destination $n$ resolves to $n$, and the indirect destination $n$ resolves to the contents $r(n)$ of register $n$.
nodes.title: Register written by a RAM store

If $p \ge \ell$, the step leaves $s$ unchanged. Otherwise it executes $P_p$, where $v$ denotes the value of the instruction's operand in $s$: a load sets the accumulator to $v$, an add sets it to $a + v$, a subtract sets it to $\max(a - v, 0)$, and a store writes $a$…

nodes.summary: The initial state on inputs $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ has program counter $0$ and accumulator $0$; register $i$ holds $x_i$ for $i < k$, and every other register holds $0$.
nodes.title: Initial RAM state

nodes.summary: For a program $P$, a natural number $t$ and a state $s$, the state after $t$ steps of $P$ from $s$ is obtained by applying one step of $P$ to $s$ exactly $t$ times.
nodes.title: Bounded execution of a RAM machine

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a program of length $\ell$ and $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ inputs. Run $P$ from the initial state on these inputs. If for some $t$ the program counter after $t$ steps is at least $\ell$, the output of $P$ on these inputs is the accumulator after the least such number of steps; otherwise the output is undefined.
nodes.title: Output of a RAM machine

nodes.summary: If the program counter of a state $s$ is at least the length of a program $P$, then one step of $P$ leaves $s$ unchanged.
nodes.title: A RAM step is sticky at halting states

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a program of length $\ell$, $s$ a state and $t$ a natural number. If the program counter after $t$ steps of $P$ from $s$ is at least $\ell$, then the state after $t + 1$ steps of $P$ from $s$ equals the state after $t$ steps.
nodes.title: RAM execution is stable once halted

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a program of length $\ell$, $s$ a state and $t_1 \le t_2$ natural numbers. If the program counter after $t_1$ steps of $P$ from $s$ is at least $\ell$, then the state after $t_2$ steps of $P$ from $s$ equals the state after $t_1$ steps.
nodes.title: RAM execution stays at its halted state

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a program of length $\ell$, let $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ be inputs and let $t$ and $y$ be natural numbers. If, after $t$ steps of $P$ from the initial state on these inputs, the program counter is at least $\ell$ and the accumulator equals $y$, then the output of $P$ on these inputs is defined and equals $y$.
nodes.title: Output membership for RAM machines

nodes.summary: For a symbol $c$, this is the single-tape machine with two states that, from its start state, writes back the symbol under the head, moves left and enters its second state, and from its second state writes $c$ and halts without moving.
nodes.title: The machine that prepends a symbol

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a symbol and $l$ a list of symbols, and consider the tape holding $l$ from the head rightwards, all other cells blank. Writing back the symbol under the head, moving the head one cell left, and then writing $c$ gives the tape holding the list $c$ followed by $l$ from the head rightwards, all other cells blank.
nodes.title: Prepending a symbol by stepping left

nodes.summary: For every symbol $c$ and every word $l$, the machine that prepends $c$, started on $l$, halts with output the word $c$ followed by $l$ within at most two steps.

nodes.summary: For every symbol $c$ and every word $l$, the machine that prepends $c$, started on $l$, halts with output the word $c$ followed by $l$.
nodes.title: Correctness of the prepending machine

nodes.summary: For a list of bits $w$, let $b_0, \dots, b_n$ be the reversal of $w$ followed by $\mathsf{true}$, reading $\mathsf{true}$ as $1$ and $\mathsf{false}$ as $0$. The input code of $w$ is the natural number $\sum_{i=0}^{n} b_i 2^i$. Its binary expansion, least significant bit first, is $b_0, \dots, b_n$: the input stack on which the single-tape emulation starts for the input word $w$.
nodes.title: Input code of a bit word

nodes.summary: For every list of bits $w$, reversing the binary encoding (least significant bit first) of the input code of $w$ and then dropping the first bit of the result gives back $w$.
nodes.title: Recovering a word from its input code

nodes.summary: For a natural number $m > 0$, let $b_0, \dots, b_n$ be its binary expansion, least significant bit first, without trailing zeros. The input decoding of $m$ is $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} b_{n-1-i} 2^i$, the value, least significant bit first, of the reversed expansion with its first bit dropped. The input decoding of $0$, whose expansion is empty, is $0$.

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a finite multi-stack machine whose input stack alphabet is identified with the bits. The bottom cell of the emulation's start tape is the cell flagged as the stack bottom that holds the symbol for $\mathrm{true}$ on the input stack and nothing on every other stack.

nodes.summary: For any type $\Sigma$, an element $x$ of $\Sigma \cup \{\bot\}$ (with $\bot$ the blank) and a finite list $l$ over $\Sigma \cup \{\bot\}$, the push of $x$ onto $l$ is the empty list when $x = \bot$ and $l$ is empty, and otherwise the list obtained by prepending $x$ to $l$.

nodes.title: The head of a stack tape is the first entry of its list

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a stack tape, a one-sided tape stored as its list of cells without trailing blanks. Then the cell list of the tail of $s$ is the tail of the cell list of $s$, the tail of the empty list being empty.
nodes.title: Tail of a stack tape, on cell lists

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a stack tape, a one-sided tape stored as its list of cells without trailing blanks, and $x$ a cell content, either a symbol or blank. Then the cell list of the tape obtained by pushing $x$ onto $s$ is the coded push of $x$ applied to the cell list of $s$: $x$ prepended to it, except that pushing a blank onto the empty tape gives the empty list.
nodes.title: Pushing onto a stack tape, on cell lists

nodes.summary: Let $\Sigma$ be a type with a primitive recursive coding, and let $x$ be a cell content, either a symbol of $\Sigma$ or blank. Then the coded push of $x$, the map on lists of cell contents that prepends $x$ to a list, except that it sends the empty list to the empty list when $x$ is blank, is primitive recursive.

nodes.summary: Let $\Sigma$ be a type with a primitive recursive coding and $\iota$ any map from the Booleans to $\Sigma$. nodes.summary: A single-tape machine $M$ halts on an input word $l$ if and only if iterating the step function of $M$ from the initial configuration on $l$, until a configuration with no successor is reached, terminates.

nodes.summary: A single-tape machine $M$ outputs the word $l'$ on the input word $l$ if and only if iterating the step function of $M$ from the initial configuration on $l$, until a configuration with no successor is reached, terminates at the halting configuration for $l'$: the halting state, with $l'$ written from the head rightwards and every other cell blank.

nodes.summary: For every configuration $c$ of a single-tape machine $M$, the code of $c$ has no successor under the coded step exactly when $c$ has no successor under the step function of $M$, and otherwise the coded step sends the code of $c$ to the code of the successor of $c$.

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, and fix primitive recursive codings of $\Sigma$ and of the states of $M$. Then the coded step of $M$, which maps a coded configuration to the coded configuration after one step of $M$ and has no value when the state is the halting state, is primitive recursive.
nodes.title: The coded step of a single-tape machine is primitive recursive

nodes.summary: For every configuration $c$ of a single-tape machine $M$, iterating the coded step from the code of $c$ until a coded configuration with no successor is reached terminates exactly when iterating the step function of $M$ from $c$ until a configuration with no successor is reached does, and then it ends at the code of the configuration where the run of $M$ from $c$ ends.

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, and fix primitive recursive codings of $\Sigma$ and of the states of $M$. Then the map sending an input word $w$ over $\Sigma$ to the code of the initial configuration of $M$ on $w$ is primitive recursive.

Then the predicate on words over $\Sigma$ that holds at a word exactly when $m$ accepts it is recognizable by a single-tape deterministic Turing machine.

nodes.summary: Let $m$ be a single-tape nondeterministic Turing machine with a finite set of states and a finite tape alphabet $\Sigma$ that has decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding. Let $\alpha$ be a primitively encodable type and $f$ a computable map from $\alpha$ to words over $\Sigma$. Then the predicate on $\alpha$ that holds at $a$ exactly when $m$ accepts $f(a)$ is recognizable by a single-tape…
nodes.title: Deterministic machines recognize NTM acceptance along a computable map

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$. A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is recognizable by a single-tape nondeterministic machine when there are a finite set of states, a finite tape alphabet $\Sigma$ with decidable equality, an injective map $\iota$ from the bits $\{0, 1\}$ to $\Sigma$ and a single-tape nondeterministic Turing machine $M$ with these states over $\Sigma$ such that…
nodes.title: Predicates recognizable by a single-tape nondeterministic machine

nodes.summary: A predicate recognized by a single-tape NTM is recognized by a deterministic single-tape machine (Sipser, Theorem 3.16, through recursion theory).
nodes.title: A predicate recognized by a single-tape NTM is recognized by a deterministic single-tape machine

reading_title.source: No single-tape NTM recognizes $n = 0$

nodes.summary: The predicate $n = 0$ on the natural numbers is not recognizable by any single-tape nondeterministic Turing machine.
nodes.title: No single-tape NTM recognizes $n = 0$

nodes.summary: There is a predicate $p$ on the natural numbers that is decidable by a single-tape deterministic Turing machine but is not recognizable by any single-tape nondeterministic Turing machine.
nodes.title: A decidable predicate that no single-tape NTM recognizes
Unlimited register machines

nodes.summary: Code of a URM instruction as a natural number: the instruction tag paired with the paired arguments, `Z n ↦ pair 0 n`, `S n ↦ pair 1 n`, `T m n ↦ pair 2 (pair m n)`, `J m n q ↦ pair 3 (pair m (pair n q))`.
nodes.title: Code of a URM instruction

nodes.summary: For every URM instruction $I$, unpairing the code of $I$ gives first component $0$ if $I$ is a zero instruction $Z\,n$, $1$ if it is a successor instruction $S\,n$, $2$ if it is a transfer $T\,m\,n$, and $3$ if it is a jump $J\,m\,n\,q$.
nodes.title: Tag of an instruction code

nodes.summary: Write $\langle a, b \rangle$ for the pairing of natural numbers $a$ and $b$. For every URM instruction $I$, unpairing the code of $I$ gives second component $n$ if $I$ is $Z\,n$ or $S\,n$, $\langle m, n \rangle$ if $I$ is $T\,m\,n$, and $\langle m, \langle n, q \rangle \rangle$ if $I$ is $J\,m\,n\,q$.
nodes.title: Payload of an instruction code

nodes.summary: A coded state is a program counter $k$ together with a list $r$ of register contents (in use, the contents of registers $0, \dots, R$, where $R$ is the register bound of the program), and a program is given by the list $c$ of its instruction codes. Write $c_k$ for entry $k$ of $c$, and $r_j$ for entry $j$ of $r$, read as $0$ when $j$ is past the end of $r$; setting an entry past the end of $r$ leaves $r$ unchanged.…
nodes.title: One coded URM step

nodes.summary: The coded step is primitive recursive, for any fixed list of instruction codes.
nodes.title: The coded step is primitive recursive

nodes.summary: The register bound $R$ of a URM program $p$ is the sum, over the instructions of $p$, of the largest register index each instruction refers to. Every register that an instruction of $p$ can read or write is at most $R$.
nodes.title: Register bound

nodes.summary: For a URM program $p$ with register bound $R$, the register list of a register state $\sigma$ is the list $(\sigma(0), \sigma(1), \dots, \sigma(R))$ of the contents of registers $0, \dots, R$.
nodes.title: Register list

nodes.summary: For a URM program $p$ with register bound $R$, the coded state of a machine state $s$ is the pair consisting of the program counter of $s$ and the register list $(r_0, \dots, r_R)$ of the contents of registers $0, \dots, R$ of $s$.
nodes.title: Coded machine state

nodes.summary: A coded state is a pair $(c, \ell)$ of a natural number $c$ and a list $\ell$ of natural numbers. Its machine state has program counter $c$, and register $n$ holds the $n$-th entry of $\ell$ (counting from $0$) when $n$ is less than the length of $\ell$, and $0$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Decoding a coded state

nodes.summary: For a URM program $p$ with register bound $R$ and a register state $\sigma$, the register list of $\sigma$ (the contents of registers $0, \dots, R$) has length $R + 1$.
nodes.title: Length of the register list

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a URM program with register bound $R$ and $\sigma$ a register state. For every $n$, the entry at position $n$ of the register list of $\sigma$, read with default $0$, is $\sigma(n)$ if $n \le R$ and $0$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Reading the register list

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a URM program with register bound $R$, let $\sigma$ be a register state, and let $n \le R$ and $v$ be natural numbers. The register list of the state obtained from $\sigma$ by setting register $n$ to $v$ equals the register list of $\sigma$ with its entry at position $n$ replaced by $v$.
nodes.title: Updating a register updates the register list

nodes.summary: For a URM program $p$ with register bound $R$ and every instruction $I$ of $p$, the largest register index referenced by $I$ is at most $R$.
nodes.title: Instructions stay within the register bound

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a URM program with register bound $R$. If an instruction of $p$ writes to register $n$, then $n \le R$.
nodes.title: Written registers lie within the register bound

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a URM program. If $n$ is a register read by some instruction of $p$, then $n$ is at most the register bound of $p$.
nodes.title: Registers read by a program lie within the register bound

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a URM program with register bound $R$, and let $c$ be a coded state: a program counter together with a list of register contents. If the list has length $R + 1$, then the coded state, with respect to $p$, of the machine state decoded from $c$ is $c$.
nodes.title: Decoding and re-encoding a coded state gives it back

nodes.summary: If a state $s$ of a URM program $p$ makes a step to some state, then the program counter of $s$ is less than the number of instructions of $p$.
nodes.title: A state that can step is running

nodes.summary: If the URM program $p$ has instruction $I$ at position $pc$, then the entry at position $pc$ of the list of instruction codes of $p$, read with default $0$, is the code of $I$.
nodes.title: Instruction codes by position

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a URM program, let $R$ be the sum over the instructions of $p$ of the largest register index each one mentions, and let $s'$ be a state that $p$ reaches from the state $s$ in one step. Then the coded step, run on the list of codes of the instructions of $p$, sends the coded state of $s$ (its program counter together with the list of the contents of its registers $0, \dots, R$) to the coded state of $s'$.
nodes.title: A machine step is a coded step

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a URM program and $s$ a machine state. If one coded URM step, run on the list of codes of the instructions of $p$ from the coded state of $s$, yields $c'$, then there is a machine state $s'$ such that $p$ steps from $s$ to $s'$ in one step and the coded state of $s'$ is $c'$.
nodes.title: A coded step is a machine step

nodes.summary: A predicate $P$ on the natural numbers is URM-decidable when some URM program computes its characteristic function: started on any input $n$ (register $0$ holding $n$, all other registers $0$), the program halts, and register $0$ then holds $1$ if $P(n)$ holds and $0$ otherwise.
nodes.title: URM-decidable predicate

nodes.summary: A predicate $P$ on the natural numbers is URM-recognizable when there is a URM program that, started with input $n$ in register $0$ and every other register $0$, halts if and only if $P(n)$ holds.
nodes.title: URM-recognizable predicates

nodes.summary: Given a list of instruction codes, the one-step function sends a coded state $s$ to the result of one coded URM step from $s$ when that step is defined, and leaves $s$ unchanged when it is not (in particular when $s$ is halted).
nodes.title: One-step function on coded states

nodes.summary: For every list of natural numbers, read as instruction codes, the function on coded states (pairs of a program counter and a register list) that sends a coded state to its successor under one coded step, and a coded state with no successor to itself, is primitive recursive.
nodes.title: The one-step function is primitive recursive

nodes.summary: For a list of instruction codes, a number $t$ and a coded state $s$, bounded execution applies the one-step function for these codes $t$ times, starting from $s$.
nodes.title: Bounded execution

nodes.summary: For a list of instruction codes, a number $t$ and a coded state $s$, bounded execution for $t + 1$ steps from $s$ is the one-step function applied to the result of bounded execution for $t$ steps from $s$.
nodes.title: Bounded execution unfolds by one step

nodes.summary: For a URM program $p$ with register bound $R$ and an input $x$, the initial coded state has program counter $0$ and register list $(x, 0, \dots, 0)$ of length $R + 1$: register $0$ holds $x$ and registers $1, \dots, R$ hold $0$.
nodes.title: Initial coded state

nodes.summary: The initial coded state is primitive recursive in the input.
nodes.title: The initial coded state is primitive recursive in the input

nodes.summary: For a URM program $p$, the bounded execution of $p$ for $t$ steps ($t$ iterations of the one-step function on the list of instruction codes of $p$), started from the initial coded state for input $x$, is a primitive recursive function of the pair $(x, t)$.
nodes.title: Bounded execution is primitive recursive in the input and the step bound

nodes.summary: For a URM program $p$ and an input $x$, the initial coded state for $x$ equals the coded state of the initial machine state with input list $[x]$.
nodes.title: The initial coded state codes the initial machine state

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a URM program, $x$ an input and $t$ a natural number. Then there is a machine state $s'$, reachable from the initial state with input list $[x]$ by steps of $p$, whose coded state equals the result of bounded execution for $t$ steps on the instruction codes of $p$ from the initial coded state for $x$.
nodes.title: Bounded execution only reaches codes of reachable states

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a URM program, $x$ an input and $t$ a number. If bounded execution for $t$ steps on the instruction codes of $p$ from the initial coded state for $x$ reaches a program counter at least the length of the list of instruction codes, then $p$ halts on the input list $[x]$.
nodes.title: A halted coded state gives a halting machine run

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a URM program and $x$ an input. If a machine state $s$ is reachable from the initial state with input list $[x]$ by steps of $p$, then for some number $t$, bounded execution for $t$ steps on the instruction codes of $p$ from the initial coded state for $x$ gives the coded state of $s$.
nodes.title: Every reachable state is reached by bounded execution

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a list of instruction codes, $s$ a coded state and $t$ a natural number. If after $t$ steps of bounded execution of $c$ from $s$ the program counter is at least the length of $c$, then $t + 1$ steps of bounded execution of $c$ from $s$ give the same coded state as $t$ steps.
nodes.title: Bounded URM execution is stable once halted

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a list of instruction codes, $s$ a coded state, and $t_1 \le t_2$ natural numbers. If after $t_1$ steps of bounded execution of $c$ from $s$ the program counter is at least the length of $c$, then $t_2$ steps of bounded execution of $c$ from $s$ give the same coded state as $t_1$ steps.
nodes.title: Bounded URM execution stays at its halted value

nodes.summary: For a URM program $p$, an input $x$ and a number $t$, run bounded execution for $t$ steps on the instruction codes of $p$ from the initial coded state for $x$. If the resulting program counter is less than the length of the list of instruction codes, the program is still running and there is no output; otherwise the output is the entry at position $0$ of the resulting register list, read with default $0$.
nodes.title: Output after a given number of steps

nodes.summary: For every URM program $p$, the function sending an input $x$ and a step count $t$ to the output of $p$ on $x$ after $t$ steps (nothing while $p$ is still running, the contents of register $0$ once it has halted) is a computable function of the pair $(x, t)$.
nodes.title: The URM output after a given number of steps is computable

nodes.summary: Let $f$ be a partial function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $\mathbb{N}$. Suppose some URM program has the following property for every natural number $x$: started with $x$ in register $0$ and all other registers $0$, it halts exactly when $f(x)$ is defined, and then it holds $f(x)$ in register $0$. Then $f$ is partial recursive.
nodes.title: A URM-computable partial function is partial recursive

nodes.summary: If a predicate $P$ on the natural numbers is URM-decidable, then it is a computable predicate: its Boolean decision function, sending $n$ to whether $P(n)$ holds, is computable.
nodes.title: A URM-decidable predicate is computable

nodes.summary: A URM-recognizable predicate is recursively enumerable.
nodes.title: A URM-recognizable predicate is recursively enumerable

nodes.summary: A URM-decidable predicate is decidable by a single-tape Turing machine.
nodes.title: A URM-decidable predicate is decidable by a single-tape Turing machine

nodes.summary: A URM-decidable predicate is decidable by a multi-stack Turing machine.
nodes.title: A URM-decidable predicate is decidable by a multi-stack Turing machine

nodes.summary: A URM-recognizable predicate is recognizable by a single-tape Turing machine.
nodes.title: A URM-recognizable predicate is recognizable by a single-tape Turing machine

nodes.summary: A URM-recognizable predicate is recognizable by a multi-stack Turing machine.
nodes.title: A URM-recognizable predicate is recognizable by a multi-stack Turing machine

nodes.summary: Let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. Suppose there is a URM program that, for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, started with $n$ in register $0$ and all other registers $0$, halts with $f(n)$ in register $0$. Then there is a multi-stack Turing machine that computes $f$ with input and output numbers written in binary: started on the binary word of $n$, it halts with the binary word of $f(n)$.
nodes.title: A URM-computable total function is computed by a multi-stack Turing machine

nodes.summary: Every predicate $P$ on $\mathbb{N}$ that is URM-decidable is decidable by a multi-stack Turing machine.
nodes.title: URM-decidability implies multi-stack decidability

nodes.summary: Every predicate $P$ on $\mathbb{N}$ that is URM-recognizable is recognizable by a multi-stack Turing machine.
nodes.title: URM-recognizability implies multi-stack recognizability

nodes.summary: Recursive and recursively enumerable predicates and their closure properties, the halting problem, Rice's and Rice–Shapiro theorems, the recursion and s-m-n theorems, enumerators, index sets such as totality, finiteness and minimal programs, and Busy Beaver functions.
nodes.title: Computability and undecidability

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a primitive recursive encoding into the natural numbers, and for each $a \in \alpha$ let $F_a$ be a partial function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $\mathbb{N}$, such that $(a, x) \mapsto F_a(x)$ is partial recursive. Then there is a computable map $g$ from $\alpha$ to codes of partial recursive functions such that for all $a \in \alpha$ and $x \in \mathbb{N}$, the partial function with code…

Busy beaver

nodes.summary: A head movement is one of exactly two directions: left or right.
nodes.title: Head movement

nodes.summary: The displacement of a head movement is $-1$ for a move to the left and $1$ for a move to the right.
nodes.title: Head displacement

nodes.summary: A Busy Beaver machine with $n$ working states is a transition table that assigns to each of the $n$ working states and each read symbol in $\{0, 1\}$ a symbol in $\{0, 1\}$ to write, a head movement (left or right), and a next state, which is either one of the $n$ working states or the halt state.
nodes.title: Busy Beaver machine

nodes.summary: A configuration of an $n$-state machine consists of a current state, which is either one of the $n$ working states or the halt state, an integer head position, and a tape assigning a symbol in $\{0, 1\}$ to every integer cell.
nodes.title: Busy Beaver machine configuration

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a machine with $n$ working states and let $c$ be a configuration with head position $h$. If $c$ is halted, the step leaves $c$ unchanged. Otherwise let $q$ be the current state, let $a$ be the symbol in cell $h$, and let $M(q, a) = (b, d, q')$. The step writes $b$ in cell $h$, leaving every other cell unchanged, moves the head to $h - 1$ if $d$ is left and to $h + 1$ if $d$ is right, and passes to the…
nodes.title: One step of a Busy Beaver machine

nodes.summary: For a machine with $n$ working states, the initial state is state $0$ when $n > 0$, and the halt state when $n = 0$.
nodes.title: Initial state

nodes.summary: The initial configuration of a machine with $n$ working states is in the initial state (state $0$, or the halt state when $n = 0$), with the head at position $0$ and every tape cell blank, that is, holding the symbol $0$.
nodes.title: Initial configuration of a Busy Beaver machine

reading_title.source: Configuration after $t$ steps

nodes.summary: For a Busy Beaver machine $M$ and $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the configuration of $M$ after $t$ steps is the result of applying the one-step map of $M$ $t$ times to the initial configuration on the blank tape.
nodes.title: Configuration after $t$ steps

reading_title.source: Halting within $t$ steps

nodes.summary: A Busy Beaver machine $M$ with $n$ working states halts within $t$ steps when the configuration reached after running $M$ for $t$ steps from the initial blank-tape configuration is in the halt state.
nodes.title: Halting within $t$ steps

nodes.summary: A Busy Beaver machine $M$ halts when there is a number of steps $t$ such that $M$ halts within $t$ steps, that is, when $M$ started from the initial blank-tape configuration eventually reaches the halt state.
nodes.title: Halting on the blank tape

nodes.summary: For an $n$-state machine $M$ that halts on the blank tape, its halting time is the least $t$ such that $M$, started on the blank tape, is in the halt state after $t$ steps.
nodes.title: Halting time

nodes.summary: For every $n$-state Busy Beaver machine $M$ and every $t \in \mathbb{N}$, if $h \in \mathbb{Z}$ is the head position after $M$ has run for $t$ steps from the initial configuration on the blank tape, then $|h| \le t$.
nodes.title: Head displacement bound

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a machine with $n$ working states, started in cell $0$ on the blank tape. For every $t \in \mathbb{N}$ and every cell $i \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $|i| > t$, the symbol in cell $i$ after $t$ steps is $0$.
nodes.title: Cells far from the origin stay blank

reading_title.source: Number of ones after $t$ steps

nodes.summary: For a Busy Beaver machine $M$ and $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the number of ones of $M$ after $t$ steps is the number of cells $i \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $-t \le i \le t$ that hold the symbol $1$ in the configuration of $M$ after $t$ steps, started on the blank tape.
nodes.title: Number of ones after $t$ steps

parts: steps, every one lies within distance
reading_title.source: After $t$ steps, every one lies within distance $t$ of the origin

nodes.summary: For every Busy Beaver machine $M$, every $t \in \mathbb{N}$ and every cell $i \in \mathbb{Z}$, if cell $i$ holds the symbol $1$ after $M$ runs for $t$ steps from the initial blank-tape configuration, then $-t \le i \le t$.
nodes.title: After $t$ steps, every one lies within distance $t$ of the origin

nodes.summary: For every Busy Beaver machine $M$ and every $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the number of ones of $M$ after $t + 1$ steps is at most the number of ones of $M$ after $t$ steps plus $1$.
nodes.title: The number of ones grows by at most one per step

reading_title.source: At most $t$ ones after $t$ steps

nodes.summary: For every Busy Beaver machine $M$ and every $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the number of ones of $M$ after $t$ steps is at most $t$.
nodes.title: At most $t$ ones after $t$ steps

nodes.summary: For a machine $M$ with $n$ working states, the runtime of $M$ is its halting time on the blank tape if $M$ halts, and $0$ if $M$ does not halt. This is the quantity whose maximum over all $n$-state machines is the shift function $S(n)$.
nodes.title: Runtime of a Busy Beaver machine

nodes.summary: For a Busy Beaver machine $M$: if $M$ halts on the blank tape, with halting time $T$, its score is the number of ones of $M$ after $T$ steps; if $M$ does not halt, its score is $0$.
nodes.title: Score of a machine

nodes.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, Rado's shift function $S(n)$ is the largest halting time of an $n$-state two-symbol machine that halts when started on the blank tape; machines that do not halt contribute $0$.
nodes.title: Busy Beaver shift function

nodes.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, Rado's score function $\Sigma(n)$ is the largest number of ones left on the tape, at its halting time, by an $n$-state two-symbol machine that halts when started on the blank tape; machines that do not halt contribute $0$.
nodes.title: Busy Beaver score function

nodes.summary: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, Rado's score function $\Sigma$ and Rado's shift function $S$ satisfy $\Sigma(n) \le S(n)$: the largest number of ones left on the tape by a halting $n$-state two-symbol machine started on the blank tape is at most the largest halting time of such a machine.
nodes.title: The Busy Beaver score is at most the shift

nodes.summary: Let $S(n)$ be Rado's shift function, the largest runtime of an $n$-state machine, where the runtime of a machine is its halting time on the blank tape if it halts and $0$ otherwise. For every $n$, some $n$-state machine $M$ has runtime equal to $S(n)$. Thus $S(n)$ is the halting time of a halting $n$-state machine, or $S(n) = 0$.
nodes.title: The shift function is attained

nodes.summary: Let $\Sigma(n)$ be the busy beaver score function, the largest score of an $n$-state machine, where the score of a machine is the number of ones on its final tape if it halts on the blank tape and $0$ otherwise. For every $n$, some $n$-state machine $M$ has score equal to $\Sigma(n)$. Thus $\Sigma(n)$ is the number of ones left by a halting $n$-state machine, or $\Sigma(n) = 0$.
nodes.title: The score function is attained

nodes.summary: An $n$-state machine $M$ is embedded into $n + 1$ states as follows. In a working state $q < n$ reading a symbol $s$, the new machine writes the symbol, makes the move and enters the next state that $M$ prescribes in state $q$ on $s$, halting when $M$ halts. In the new state $n$ it writes $0$, moves left and halts, whatever it reads.
nodes.title: Embedding a machine into one more state

nodes.summary: For a configuration $c$ of an $n$-state machine, its embedding is the configuration for $n + 1$ states with the same head position and the same tape as $c$. Its state is the state of $c$, where a working state $q \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ stays $q$ and the halt state stays the halt state.
nodes.title: Embedding a configuration into one more state

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a Busy Beaver machine with a single working state $0$. If the transition of $M$ from state $0$ on reading the blank symbol $0$ has next state $0$, then $M$ does not halt.
nodes.title: A one-state machine that stays in its state on a blank never halts

nodes.summary: Every halting one-state machine halts within one step.
nodes.title: One-state machines halt within one step

nodes.summary: The code of a machine $M$ with $n$ working states is the natural number that encodes the pair $(n, i)$ under a fixed pairing bijection $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, where $i$ is the index of $M$ in a fixed enumeration of the finitely many machines with $n$ working states.
nodes.title: Machine code

nodes.summary: The sentence code with tag $a$ and payload $p$ is the natural number $4p + a$. The tags in use are $0$ (the coded machine halts), $1$ (the coded machine does not halt), $2$ (the false sentence), and $3$ with payload the pairing code of $n$ and $B$ (every halting $n$-state machine halts within $B$ steps).
nodes.title: Sentence codes

nodes.summary: For an $n$-state machine $M$, the halting sentence of $M$ is the sentence code with tag $0$ and payload the code of $M$. It stands for "$M$ halts on the blank tape"; this meaning comes from soundness hypotheses on a theory, not from the code itself.
nodes.title: Halting sentence of a machine

nodes.summary: For a Busy Beaver machine $M$, the non-halting sentence of $M$ is the sentence code with tag $1$ whose payload is the code of $M$; it stands for "$M$ does not halt on the blank tape".
nodes.title: Non-halting sentence of a machine

nodes.summary: The false sentence is the sentence code with tag $2$ and payload $0$, that is, the natural number $2$.
nodes.title: The false sentence

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $B$, the runtime-bound sentence is the sentence code with tag $3$ and payload $\langle n, B \rangle$, the pairing of $n$ and $B$; as a number it equals $4 \langle n, B \rangle + 3$.
nodes.title: Runtime-bound sentence

nodes.summary: A formal theory is given by a provability predicate on sentence codes, which are natural numbers: for each natural number it specifies whether that sentence code is provable in the theory.
nodes.title: Formal theory

nodes.summary: A formal theory $T$ is consistent when $T$ does not prove the false sentence.
nodes.title: Consistent formal theory

nodes.summary: A formal theory $T$ is sound for halting sentences when, for every $n$ and every Busy Beaver machine $M$ with $n$ states, if $T$ proves the halting sentence of $M$ then $M$ halts on the blank tape, and if $T$ proves the non-halting sentence of $M$ then $M$ does not halt on the blank tape.
nodes.title: Soundness for halting sentences

nodes.summary: A formal theory $T$ decides halting for $n$-state machines when, for every $n$-state machine $M$, $T$ proves the halting sentence of $M$ or $T$ proves the non-halting sentence of $M$.
nodes.title: Theories deciding halting at a state count

nodes.summary: For a formal theory $T$, the first undecidable number of states is the least $n$ such that $T$ does not decide halting for all $n$-state machines, that is, there is an $n$-state machine $M$ for which $T$ proves neither the halting sentence nor the non-halting sentence of $M$. It is $0$ when there is no such $n$.
nodes.title: First undecidable number of states

nodes.summary: If a formal theory $T$ decides halting for $n$-state machines for every $n \le 5$, and fails to decide halting for $n$-state machines for some $n$, then the first undecidable size of $T$ is at least $6$.
nodes.title: Decidability through five states and the first undecidable size

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a formal theory and $M$ a Busy Beaver machine with $n$ working states. Suppose that $M$ halts if and only if $T$ proves the false sentence, that $M$ halts whenever $T$ proves the halting sentence of $M$, that $T$ is consistent, and that $T$ does not prove the non-halting sentence of $M$. Then $T$ does not decide halting for all machines with $n$ working states.
nodes.title: A consistency-search machine blocks decidability at its size

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a formal theory such that, for every $m$ and every Busy Beaver machine $M$ with $m$ working states, if $T$ proves the halting sentence of the embedding of $M$ into $m + 1$ states then $T$ proves the halting sentence of $M$, and if $T$ proves the non-halting sentence of the embedding of $M$ into $m + 1$ states then $T$ proves the non-halting sentence of $M$. Then for every $n$, if $T$ decides halting for…
nodes.title: Decidability of halting passes to fewer states

nodes.summary: A ZFC-like presentation consists of a formal theory $T$, given by a provability predicate on sentence codes in $\mathbb{N}$, together with a Boolean proof checker $\mathrm{check}(p, s)$ on pairs of natural numbers, such that the following hold. A sentence code $s$ is provable in $T$ if and only if $\mathrm{check}(p, s)$ is true for some $p \in \mathbb{N}$. $T$ is sound for halting: for every machine $M$, if $T$…
nodes.title: Proof-checker presentation of a ZFC-like theory

nodes.summary: For every ZFC-like presentation $Z$ and every $n \le 5$, the theory presented by $Z$ decides halting for $n$-state machines: for every $n$-state machine it proves the machine's halting sentence or its non-halting sentence.
nodes.title: ZFC-like theories decide halting through five states

nodes.summary: Rado's shift function $S$ satisfies $S(3) = 21$: among the two-symbol Busy Beaver machines with $3$ working states that halt when started on the blank tape, the largest halting time is $21$.
nodes.title: Three-state Busy Beaver shift value

nodes.summary: Rado's score function $\Sigma$ satisfies $\Sigma(3) = 6$: among the two-symbol Busy Beaver machines with $3$ working states that halt when started on the blank tape, the largest number of ones left on the tape at the halting time is $6$.
nodes.title: Three-state Busy Beaver score value

nodes.summary: Rado's shift function $S$ satisfies $S(4) = 107$: among the two-symbol Busy Beaver machines with $4$ working states that halt when started on the blank tape, the largest halting time is $107$.

nodes.summary: Rado's score function $\Sigma$ satisfies $\Sigma(4) = 13$: among the two-symbol Busy Beaver machines with $4$ working states that halt when started on the blank tape, the largest number of ones left on the tape at the halting time is $13$.

nodes.summary: Rado's shift function $S$ satisfies $S(5) = 47176870$: among the two-symbol Busy Beaver machines with $5$ working states that halt when started on the blank tape, the largest halting time is $47176870$.

nodes.summary: Rado's score function $\Sigma$ satisfies $\Sigma(5) = 4098$: among the two-symbol Busy Beaver machines with $5$ working states that halt when started on the blank tape, the largest number of ones left on the tape at the halting time is $4098$.
