Decidable and recognizable predicates

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$. If $p$ and $q$ are computable predicates on $\alpha$, then the predicate $a \mapsto p(a) \land q(a)$ is computable.
nodes.title: Computable predicates are closed under conjunction

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$. If $p$ and $q$ are computable predicates on $\alpha$, then the predicate $a \mapsto p(a) \lor q(a)$ is computable.
nodes.title: Computable predicates are closed under disjunction

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$. If $p$ and $q$ are recursively enumerable predicates on $\alpha$, then the predicate $a \mapsto p(a) \land q(a)$ is recursively enumerable.
nodes.title: Recursively enumerable predicates are closed under conjunction

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$. If $p$ and $q$ are recursively enumerable predicates on $\alpha$, then the predicate $a \mapsto p(a) \lor q(a)$ is recursively enumerable.
nodes.title: Recursively enumerable predicates are closed under disjunction

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be types with primitive recursive encodings into $\mathbb{N}$, let $R$ be a relation between $\alpha$ and $\beta$ that is recursively enumerable as a predicate on pairs $(a, b)$, and let $c$ be a primitive recursive function sending each $a \in \alpha$ to a finite list $c(a)$ of elements of $\beta$. Then the predicate $a \mapsto \exists b \in c(a),\ R(a, b)$ is recursively enumerable.
nodes.title: Bounded existential quantification preserves recursive enumerability

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be types with primitive recursive encodings into $\mathbb{N}$, let $R$ be a relation between $\alpha$ and $\beta$ that is recursively enumerable as a predicate on pairs $(a, b)$, and let $c$ be a primitive recursive function sending each $a \in \alpha$ to a finite list $c(a)$ of elements of $\beta$. Then the predicate $a \mapsto \forall b \in c(a),\ R(a, b)$ is recursively enumerable.
nodes.title: Bounded universal quantification preserves recursive enumerability

nodes.summary: Let $\gamma$ and $\beta$ be types with primitive recursive encodings into $\mathbb{N}$, let $l$ be a computable function sending each $x \in \gamma$ to a finite list $l(x)$ of elements of $\beta$, and let $g$ be a computable Boolean-valued function of $x \in \gamma$ and $b \in \beta$. Then the Boolean-valued function that sends $x$ to true exactly when $g(x, b)$ is true for some $b$ in $l(x)$ is computable.
nodes.title: Searching a computable list with a computable test is computable

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be types with primitive recursive encodings into $\mathbb{N}$, and let $R$ be a relation between $\alpha$ and $\beta$ that is recursively enumerable as a predicate on pairs $(a, b)$. Then there is a partial recursive function $g$ from $\alpha$ to $\beta$ such that, for every $a \in \alpha$, if $g(a)$ is defined then its value $b$ satisfies $R(a, b)$, and $g(a)$ is defined whenever some…
nodes.title: Selection for r.e. relations

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be types with primitive recursive encodings into $\mathbb{N}$, and let $R$ be a relation between $\alpha$ and $\beta$ that is recursively enumerable as a predicate on pairs $(a, b)$. Then the predicate $a \mapsto \exists b \in \beta,\ R(a, b)$ is recursively enumerable.
nodes.title: Existential projection preserves recursive enumerability

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine when there is a function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ computed by a multi-stack Turing machine, with input and output numbers written in binary, such that for every $a \in \alpha$, $f(\mathrm{encode}(a)) = 1$ if…
nodes.title: Decidability by multi-stack machines

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine when there are a multi-stack Turing machine $M$ and an identification of its input alphabet with the Booleans such that for every $a \in \alpha$, $p(a)$ holds if and only if $M$ halts when started on the binary…
nodes.title: Recognizability by multi-stack machines

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is co-recognizable by a multi-stack machine when its complement $\neg p$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: Co-recognizability by multi-stack machines

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine if and only if it is computable, that is, $p$ is decidable and its Boolean characteristic function $\alpha \to \mathrm{Bool}$ is computable.
nodes.title: Multi-stack decidable predicates are exactly the computable predicates

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine if and only if it is recursively enumerable, that is, the partial function on $\alpha$ that is defined, with a trivial value, exactly where $p$ holds is partial recursive.
nodes.title: Multi-stack recognizable predicates are exactly the r.e. predicates

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is co-recognizable by a multi-stack machine if and only if its complement $\neg p$ is recursively enumerable, that is, the partial function on $\alpha$ that is defined, with a trivial value, exactly where $\neg p$ holds is partial recursive.
nodes.title: Multi-stack co-recognizable predicates are exactly the co-r.e. predicates

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). If a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine, then $p$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: Decidable predicates are recognizable by multi-stack machines

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). If a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine, then so is its complement $\neg p$.
nodes.title: Decidability by multi-stack machines is closed under complement

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). If a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine, then $p$ is co-recognizable by a multi-stack machine, that is, its complement $\neg p$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: Decidable predicates are co-recognizable by multi-stack machines

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine if and only if it is both recognizable and co-recognizable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: Post's theorem for multi-stack machines

nodes.summary: Let $p$ and $q$ be predicates on a type $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding. If $p$ and $q$ are both decidable by multi-stack machines, then so is the predicate $a \mapsto p(a) \wedge q(a)$.
nodes.title: Decidable predicates are closed under conjunction

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a primitive recursive encoding. If $p$ and $q$ are predicates on $\alpha$ that are decidable by a multi-stack Turing machine, then so is the predicate $a \mapsto p(a) \lor q(a)$.
nodes.title: Decidable predicates are closed under disjunction

nodes.summary: Let $p$ and $q$ be predicates on a type $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding. If $p$ and $q$ are both recognizable by multi-stack machines, then so is the predicate $a \mapsto p(a) \wedge q(a)$.
nodes.title: Recognizable predicates are closed under conjunction

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a primitive recursive encoding. If $p$ and $q$ are predicates on $\alpha$ that are recognizable by a multi-stack Turing machine, then so is the predicate $a \mapsto p(a) \lor q(a)$.
nodes.title: Recognizable predicates are closed under disjunction

nodes.summary: For a Boolean-valued function $f$ on words over an alphabet $\sigma$, the language of $f$ is the set of words $u$ over $\sigma$ with $f(u) = \mathrm{true}$.
nodes.title: Language of a Boolean test

nodes.summary: For languages $L_1$ and $L_2$ over an alphabet $\sigma$ and a word $w$ over $\sigma$, $w$ lies in the concatenation $L_1 L_2$ if and only if there are words $u$ and $v$ with $w = uv$, $u \in L_1$ and $v \in L_2$.
nodes.title: Membership in a concatenation of languages

nodes.summary: Given Boolean tests $f$ and $g$ on words over $\sigma$, a word $w$ and a natural number $n$, the split test is the Boolean value that is true exactly when there is some $i < n$ such that $f$ is true on the prefix of $w$ of length $\min(i, |w|)$ and $g$ is true on the remaining suffix of $w$.
nodes.title: Bounded split test

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\sigma$ with a primitive recursive encoding. If membership in $L$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine, then there is a computable function $f$ from words over $\sigma$ to Booleans such that $L$ is the language of $f$, that is, the set of words $u$ with $f(u) = \mathrm{true}$.
nodes.title: Decidable languages have computable membership tests

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be an alphabet with a primitive recursive encoding. If $L_1$ and $L_2$ are languages over $\sigma$ whose membership predicates are decidable by a multi-stack Turing machine, then the membership predicate of their concatenation $L_1 L_2 = \{uv : u \in L_1, v \in L_2\}$ is also decidable by a multi-stack Turing machine.
nodes.title: Decidable languages are closed under concatenation

nodes.summary: For a word $w$ over $\sigma$ of length $n$, this is the list of the $n + 1$ pairs $(u, v)$ of words with $uv = w$, ordered by the length of $u$: for each $i = 0, 1, \dots, n$ it contains the prefix of $w$ of length $i$ paired with the remaining suffix.
nodes.title: Splits of a word

nodes.summary: Let $L_1$ and $L_2$ be languages over an alphabet $\sigma$ with a primitive recursive encoding. If membership in $L_1$ and membership in $L_2$ are recognizable by multi-stack machines, then so is membership in the concatenation $L_1 L_2$, the set of words $uv$ with $u \in L_1$ and $v \in L_2$.
nodes.title: Recognizable languages are closed under concatenation

nodes.summary: Given a letter $a$ and a list $\pi = [u_1, \dots, u_k]$ of words, the extensions of $\pi$ by $a$ are listed as follows: first $[[a], u_1, \dots, u_k]$, which starts a new piece $[a]$, and then, only when $k \ge 1$, also $[a u_1, u_2, \dots, u_k]$, which puts the letter $a$ in front of the first piece.
nodes.title: Extending a list of pieces by a letter

nodes.summary: For a word $w$ over $\sigma$, this is the list of all ways to write $w$ as a concatenation $w = u_1 u_2 \cdots u_k$ of nonempty words $u_1, \dots, u_k$, each recorded as the list $[u_1, \dots, u_k]$. The empty word has exactly one such partition, the empty list.
nodes.title: Partitions of a word into nonempty factors

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\sigma$ with a primitive recursive encoding. If membership in $L$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine, then so is membership in the Kleene star $L^*$, the set of all concatenations $u_1 \cdots u_k$ with $k \ge 0$ and $u_1, \dots, u_k \in L$.
nodes.title: Recognizable languages are closed under Kleene star

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\sigma$ with a primitive recursive encoding. If membership in $L$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine, then so is membership in the Kleene star $L^*$, the set of all concatenations $u_1 \cdots u_k$ with $k \ge 0$ and $u_1, \dots, u_k \in L$.
nodes.title: Decidable languages are closed under Kleene star

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ and $\tau$ be alphabets with primitive recursive encodings, let $f : \sigma \to \tau$ be primitive recursive, and let $L$ be a language over $\sigma$. If membership in $L$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine, then so is membership in the image language $f(L) = \{f(a_1) \cdots f(a_n) : a_1 \cdots a_n \in L\}$, obtained by applying $f$ letter by letter to the words of $L$.
nodes.title: Recognizable languages are closed under alphabet maps
Enumerators

nodes.summary: For a type $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, a function $e$ assigning to each natural number $n$ either an element $e(n)$ of $\alpha$ or nothing enumerates a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ when, for every $a \in \alpha$, $p(a)$ holds if and only if $e(n) = a$ for some natural number $n$.
nodes.title: Enumerating a predicate

nodes.summary: For every type $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding and every predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ that is recognizable by a multi-stack machine, there is a computable function $e$, assigning to each natural number either an element of $\alpha$ or nothing, that enumerates $p$.
nodes.title: Recognizable languages are enumerable

nodes.summary: For every type $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, every predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ and every computable function $e$, assigning to each natural number either an element of $\alpha$ or nothing, that enumerates $p$, the predicate $p$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: Enumerable languages are recognizable

nodes.summary: For every type $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine if and only if some computable function $e$, assigning to each natural number either an element of $\alpha$ or nothing, enumerates $p$. This is Sipser, Theorem 3.21: a language is Turing-recognizable if and only if some enumerator enumerates it.
nodes.title: Recognizable languages are exactly the enumerable ones
Halting problem and Rice's theorem

nodes.summary: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, no multi-stack machine decides whether a partial recursive code halts on input $n$.
nodes.title: The halting problem is undecidable by multi-stack machines

nodes.summary: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the set of partial recursive codes whose program halts on input $n$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: The halting problem is recognizable by multi-stack machines

nodes.summary: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the set of partial recursive codes whose program halts on input $n$ is not co-recognizable by a multi-stack machine: no multi-stack machine halts on exactly the codes whose program does not halt on input $n$.
nodes.title: The halting problem is not co-recognizable by multi-stack machines

nodes.summary: There is a multi-stack machine $M$, with a bijection between its input alphabet and the Booleans, such that no multi-stack machine decides, for $n \in \mathbb{N}$, whether $M$ halts when started on the binary representation of $n$ (written in $M$'s input alphabet through the bijection).
nodes.title: Some multi-stack machine has an undecidable halting set

nodes.summary: Let $C$ be a set of partial functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. If a multi-stack machine decides, for each partial recursive code, whether the function the code computes lies in $C$, then for all partial recursive functions $f$ and $g$, $f \in C$ implies $g \in C$.
nodes.title: Rice's theorem for multi-stack machines

nodes.summary: Let $p$ and $q$ be predicates on primitive recursively encodable types $\alpha$ and $\beta$, and write $\langle x \rangle \in \mathbb{N}$ for the code of $x$. Then $p$ is many-one reducible to $q$ if and only if there is a function $f : \alpha \to \beta$ with $p(a) \iff q(f(a))$ for all $a \in \alpha$, together with a function $F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that a multi-stack machine computes on binary…
nodes.title: Mapping reductions are computed by multi-stack machines

nodes.summary: Let $p$ and $q$ be predicates on primitive recursively encodable types $\alpha$ and $\beta$. If $p$ is many-one reducible to $q$ and $q$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine, then $p$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: Decidability transfers along mapping reductions

nodes.summary: Let $p$ and $q$ be predicates on primitive recursively encodable types $\alpha$ and $\beta$. If $p$ is many-one reducible to $q$ and $q$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine, then $p$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: Recognizability transfers along mapping reductions

nodes.summary: Let $C$ be a set of partial functions $\mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$, and suppose there are partial recursive functions $f \in C$ and $g \notin C$. Then the property of a partial recursive code $c$ that the partial function computed by $c$ belongs to $C$ is not decidable by a multi-stack Turing machine.
nodes.title: Rice's theorem for partial recursive codes

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a set of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$, and suppose there are partial recursive codes $c_1$ and $c_2$ such that the domain of $c_1$ (the set of inputs on which it halts) belongs to $P$ and the domain of $c_2$ does not. Then the property of a partial recursive code $c$ that the domain of $c$ belongs to $P$ is not decidable by a multi-stack Turing machine.
nodes.title: Rice's theorem for languages

nodes.summary: A partial recursive code $c$ accepts a natural number $n$ when $c$ halts on input $n$ with output $0$. Acceptance is a predicate on pairs $(c, n)$; it is the analogue of Sipser's $A_{\mathrm{TM}}$, where a machine may halt without accepting.
nodes.title: Acceptance by a code

nodes.summary: A partial recursive code $c$ halts on a natural number $n$ when its evaluation at $n$ is defined. Halting is a predicate on pairs $(c, n)$; it is the analogue of Sipser's $\mathrm{HALT}_{\mathrm{TM}}$.
nodes.title: Halting of a code on an input

nodes.summary: There is a partial recursive code $z$ that on input $0$ halts with output $0$ and on every input $x \ne 0$ does not halt.
nodes.title: A code that halts only on zero

nodes.summary: Say a partial recursive code $c$ accepts a natural number $n$ when $c$ halts on input $n$ with output $0$. Acceptance many-one reduces to halting: there is a computable map $f$ from pairs $(c, n)$ of a partial recursive code and a natural number to such pairs, such that for every pair $(c, n)$, the code $c$ accepts $n$ if and only if, writing $f(c, n) = (c', n')$, the code $c'$ halts on $n'$.
nodes.title: Acceptance reduces to halting

nodes.summary: Say a partial recursive code $c$ accepts a natural number $n$ when $c$ halts on input $n$ with output $0$. Halting many-one reduces to acceptance: there is a computable map $f$ from pairs $(c, n)$ of a partial recursive code and a natural number to such pairs, such that for every pair $(c, n)$, the code $c$ halts on $n$ if and only if, writing $f(c, n) = (c', n')$, the code $c'$ accepts $n'$.
nodes.title: Halting reduces to acceptance

nodes.summary: No multi-stack Turing machine decides, for pairs $(c, n)$ of a partial recursive code and a natural number, whether $c$ halts on $n$.
nodes.title: Halting is undecidable

nodes.summary: No multi-stack Turing machine decides, for pairs $(c, n)$ of a partial recursive code and a natural number, whether $c$ accepts $n$, that is, halts on $n$ with output $0$.
nodes.title: Acceptance is undecidable

nodes.summary: For a set $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, the unary language of $S$ is the language over the one-letter alphabet $\{\ast\}$ consisting of the words whose length lies in $S$.
nodes.title: Unary language of a set of naturals

nodes.summary: A partial recursive code $c$ has a regular halting set when the unary language of its domain (the set of inputs on which $c$ halts), that is, the language of the words over a one-letter alphabet whose length lies in the domain of $c$, is regular.
nodes.title: Codes with a regular halting set

nodes.summary: The unary language of the perfect squares, the set of words over a one-letter alphabet whose length is $m^2$ for some $m \in \mathbb{N}$, is not regular.
nodes.title: The unary squares are not regular

nodes.summary: For a partial recursive code $c$ and natural numbers $n$ and $x$, the value at $((c, n), x)$ is $0$ if $x$ is a perfect square; otherwise it is defined exactly when $c$ halts on input $n$, and then it is $0$.
nodes.title: Partial function of the halting-to-regularity reduction

nodes.summary: For a pair $q = (c, n)$ of a partial recursive code and a natural number, let $g_q$ be the partial function on $\mathbb{N}$ that on input $x$ halts with output $0$ if $x$ is a perfect square, and otherwise runs $c$ on $n$ and, if that halts, outputs $0$ (and is undefined if it does not). Write $\ulcorner q \urcorner$ for the standard encoding of $q$ as a natural number, and $\langle a, b \rangle$ for the standard…
nodes.title: A single code for the regularity reduction function

nodes.summary: There is a computable map $f$ from pairs $(c, n)$ of a partial recursive code and a natural number to partial recursive codes such that for every pair $(c, n)$, the code $c$ halts on $n$ if and only if the halting set of $f(c, n)$ (the set of inputs on which it halts), read as a unary language, is regular. That is, halting many-one reduces to regularity of halting sets.
nodes.title: Halting reduces to regularity of halting sets

nodes.summary: For a partial recursive code $c$, let $\operatorname{dom}(c) \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be the set of inputs on which $c$ halts. The property of $c$ that the unary language $\{w \in \{\ast\}^* : |w| \in \operatorname{dom}(c)\}$ is regular is not decidable by a multi-stack Turing machine.
nodes.title: Regularity of halting sets is undecidable
Emptiness and equivalence problems for programs

nodes.summary: The set $E$ consists of the codes $c$ of partial recursive functions on $\mathbb{N}$ that are defined on no input: for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the function computed by $c$ is undefined at $n$.
nodes.title: Codes with empty domain

nodes.summary: The set $E$ of codes of partial recursive functions on $\mathbb{N}$ that are defined on no input is not decidable by multi-stack machines.
nodes.title: Emptiness is undecidable

nodes.summary: The set of codes of partial recursive functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that are defined on at least one input is recognizable by multi-stack machines: some multi-stack machine halts on the binary encoding of a code $c$ exactly when the function coded by $c$ is defined on some input.
nodes.title: Nonemptiness is recognizable

nodes.summary: The set of codes of partial recursive functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that are defined on no input is co-recognizable by multi-stack machines: some multi-stack machine halts on the binary encoding of a code $c$ exactly when the function coded by $c$ is defined on at least one input.
nodes.title: Emptiness is co-recognizable

nodes.summary: The set $E$ of codes of partial recursive functions on $\mathbb{N}$ that are defined on no input is not recognizable by multi-stack machines: no multi-stack machine, started on the binary encoding of a code, halts exactly when the code is in $E$.
nodes.title: Emptiness is not recognizable

nodes.summary: The set $EQ$ consists of the pairs $(c_1, c_2)$ of codes of partial recursive functions on $\mathbb{N}$ that recognize the same language, that is, whose computed functions have the same domain: for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the function computed by $c_1$ is defined at $n$ if and only if the function computed by $c_2$ is.
nodes.title: Equivalent codes

nodes.summary: There is a code $e$ of a partial recursive function on $\mathbb{N}$ whose computed function is the empty partial function, undefined at every input.
nodes.title: A code defined nowhere

nodes.summary: The set $E$ of codes of partial recursive functions defined on no input is many-one reducible to the set $EQ$ of pairs of codes with the same domain: there is a computable map $f$ from codes to pairs of codes such that, for every code $c$, $c \in E$ if and only if $f(c) \in EQ$.
nodes.title: Emptiness reduces to equivalence

nodes.summary: The set $EQ$ of pairs of codes of partial recursive functions on $\mathbb{N}$ with the same domain is not recognizable by multi-stack machines: no multi-stack machine, started on the binary encoding of a pair of codes, halts exactly when the pair is in $EQ$.
nodes.title: Equivalence is not recognizable

nodes.summary: For a code $c$ of a partial recursive function on $\mathbb{N}$, the code $h(c)$ is the composition $k_0 \circ c \circ k_0$, where $k_0$ is the code of the constant function $0$: whatever its input, $h(c)$ runs $c$ on $0$ and, if this halts, outputs $0$.
nodes.title: Halting-on-zero code

nodes.summary: The set of codes $c$ of partial recursive functions on $\mathbb{N}$ that halt on input $0$ (are defined at $0$) is many-one reducible to the set $EQ$ of pairs of codes with the same domain: there is a computable map $f$ from codes to pairs of codes such that, for every code $c$, $c$ halts on $0$ if and only if $f(c) \in EQ$.
nodes.title: Halting on zero reduces to equivalence

nodes.summary: The set $EQ$ of pairs of codes of partial recursive functions on $\mathbb{N}$ with the same domain is not co-recognizable by multi-stack machines: no multi-stack machine, started on the binary encoding of a pair of codes, halts exactly when the pair is not in $EQ$.
nodes.title: Equivalence is not co-recognizable
Halting problem for single-tape Turing machines

nodes.summary: A single-tape Turing machine $M$ halts on an input word $l$ when its run, started in its start state with $l$ on the tape, reaches a halting configuration.
nodes.title: Halting of a single-tape machine

nodes.summary: A multi-stack machine halts on a word $l$ over the alphabet of its input stack if and only if the evaluation of its transition function, started at its main label and initial internal state with $l$ on the input stack and all other stacks empty, is defined.
nodes.title: Halting agrees with evaluation for multi-stack machines

nodes.summary: A finite type $\alpha$ with $n$ elements gets the primitive recursive coding transported from $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ along a fixed (noncanonically chosen) bijection between $\alpha$ and $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$.
nodes.title: Primitive recursive coding of a finite type

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a multi-stack machine together with a bijection $e$ from the alphabet of its input stack to the Booleans, and suppose the tape alphabet $\Gamma'$ of the single-tape emulation of $M$ is finite and carries a primitive recursive coding. Then the map sending $n \in \mathbb{N}$ to the initial tape of the emulation on the input word $e^{-1}(b_1) \cdots e^{-1}(b_m)$, where $b_1 \cdots b_m$ is the binary code of…
nodes.title: The input encoding of the single-tape emulation is primitive recursive

nodes.summary: There are a finite tape alphabet $\Gamma$ with a blank symbol, decidable equality and a primitive recursive coding, a type of states $\Lambda$ with a start state, a single-tape Turing machine $M$ with alphabet $\Gamma$ and states $\Lambda$, and a finite set $S$ of states that contains the start state and is closed under the transitions of $M$, such that the set of input words on which $M$ halts is not decidable by…
nodes.title: The halting problem for single-tape machines is undecidable
Kleene's recursion theorem

nodes.summary: There is a code $c$ of a partial recursive function on $\mathbb{N}$ that, on every input $n \in \mathbb{N}$, halts and outputs the number encoding $c$.
nodes.title: A quine

nodes.summary: There is a code $c$ of a partial recursive function on $\mathbb{N}$ such that, for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $c$ halts on input $n$ if and only if $n$ is the number encoding $c$.
nodes.title: A code that halts exactly on its own number
Minimal programs

nodes.summary: For a code $c$ of a partial recursive function, the description length of $c$ is the number of binary digits of the encoding of $c$ as a natural number, that is, the least $k$ such that this encoding is less than $2^k$ (so it is $0$ when the encoding is $0$).
nodes.title: Description length of a code

nodes.summary: A code $c$ of a partial recursive function is minimal when no code with a shorter description has the same domain: for every code $d$ whose description length is strictly less than that of $c$, the domain of $d$ (the set of inputs on which its evaluation is defined) differs from the domain of $c$. The set of minimal codes is denoted $\mathrm{MIN}$.
nodes.title: Minimal codes

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$ there is a code $c$ of a partial recursive function whose evaluation is defined exactly at $n$, that is, the domain of the partial function computed by $c$ is $\{n\}$.
nodes.title: Codes with singleton domain

nodes.summary: For every code $c$ of a partial recursive function there is a minimal code $D$ whose domain equals the domain of $c$, where the domain of a code is the set of inputs on which its evaluation is defined.
nodes.title: Every language of a code has a minimal code

nodes.summary: For every natural number $N$ there is a minimal code $D$ of a partial recursive function whose encoding as a natural number is greater than $N$.
nodes.title: Minimal codes are unbounded

nodes.summary: The set $\mathrm{MIN}$ of minimal codes of partial recursive functions is not recognizable by a multi-stack Turing machine: there is no finite multi-stack machine that, for every code $c$, halts on the binary encoding of the natural-number encoding of $c$ exactly when $c$ is minimal.
nodes.title: Minimal codes are not recognizable
Rice's theorem for acceptable numberings

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi$ assign to each natural number $e$ a partial function $\varphi_e : \mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$, and suppose that the universal function $(e, n) \mapsto \varphi_e(n)$ is partial computable, that every partial computable function $f : \mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$ equals $\varphi_e$ for some $e$, and that for every partial computable…
nodes.title: Rogers's fixed-point theorem for acceptable numberings

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi$ assign to each natural number $e$ a partial function $\varphi_e : \mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$, and suppose that every $\varphi_e$ is partial computable, that the universal function $(e, n) \mapsto \varphi_e(n)$ is partial computable, that every partial computable function $f : \mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$ equals $\varphi_e$ for some $e$, and that for every partial computable…
nodes.title: Rice's theorem for acceptable numberings
Rice–Shapiro theorem

nodes.summary: In a class with a recognizable index set, every partial recursive extension of a partial recursive member is a member.
nodes.title: Rice–Shapiro, upward closure

nodes.summary: Every partial recursive member of a class with a recognizable index set has a partial recursive finite subfunction in the class.
nodes.title: Rice–Shapiro, finite approximation

nodes.summary: For a finite list $\theta$ of pairs of natural numbers, the finite function of $\theta$ is the partial function $\mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$ whose value at $x$ is the second component of the first pair in $\theta$ with first component $x$, and which is undefined at $x$ when $\theta$ has no pair with first component $x$.
nodes.title: Finite function of a list of pairs

nodes.summary: A finite list $\theta$ of pairs of natural numbers is a graph when, for every pair $(x, y)$ in $\theta$, the finite function of $\theta$ takes the value $y$ at $x$; that is, the first pair in $\theta$ with first component $x$ is $(x, y)$.
nodes.title: Graphs of finite functions

nodes.summary: The set of finite lists of pairs of natural numbers that are graphs is recursively enumerable.
nodes.title: Being a graph is recursively enumerable

nodes.summary: For every partial function $g : \mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$ with finite domain there is a finite list $\theta$ of pairs of natural numbers such that the finite function of $\theta$ is $g$ and, for every pair $(x, y)$ in $\theta$, $g(x)$ is defined and equals $y$.
nodes.title: Finite-domain partial functions are finite functions

nodes.summary: The set of pairs $(c, \theta)$, where $c$ is a code of a partial recursive function and $\theta$ is a finite list of pairs of natural numbers, such that for every pair $(x, y)$ in $\theta$ the function computed by $c$ is defined at $x$ with value $y$, is recursively enumerable.
nodes.title: Extending a finite list of pairs is recursively enumerable

nodes.summary: Let $C$ be a class of partial functions $\mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$ and let $B$ be a recognizable set of finite lists of pairs of natural numbers. Suppose that a partial recursive function $f$ is in $C$ if and only if some $\theta \in B$ satisfies: for every pair $(x, y)$ in $\theta$, $f(x)$ is defined and equals $y$. Then the index set of $C$, the set of codes $c$ of partial recursive functions such…
nodes.title: Effective Rice–Shapiro, sufficiency

nodes.summary: Let $C$ be a class of partial functions $\mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$ whose index set, the set of codes $c$ of partial recursive functions such that the function computed by $c$ is in $C$, is recognizable. Then there is a recognizable set $B$ of finite lists of pairs of natural numbers, each of which is a graph, such that a partial recursive function $f$ is in $C$ if and only if some $\theta \in B$…
nodes.title: Effective Rice–Shapiro, necessity

nodes.summary: A class of partial functions has a recognizable index set iff, among partial recursive functions, its members are exactly the extensions of the finite functions in some recognizable set of graphs.
nodes.title: The effective Rice–Shapiro theorem
Totality problem for programs

nodes.summary: A code $c$ of a partial recursive function is total when it halts on every input: writing $\varphi_c$ for the partial function on $\mathbb{N}$ that $c$ computes, $\varphi_c(n)$ is defined for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: Total codes

nodes.summary: Writing $\varphi_c$ for the partial function on $\mathbb{N}$ computed by a code $c$ of a partial recursive function, the set of codes $c$ with $\varphi_c(0)$ defined is many-one reducible to the set of total codes, the codes that halt on every input: there is a computable function $f$ from codes to codes such that, for every code $c$, $\varphi_c(0)$ is defined if and only if $f(c)$ is total.
nodes.title: Halting on zero reduces to totality

nodes.summary: The set of total codes, the codes of partial recursive functions that halt on every input, is not co-recognizable by multi-stack machines: no multi-stack machine halts on the binary encoding of a code $c$ exactly when $c$ is not total.
nodes.title: Totality is not co-recognizable

nodes.summary: For a code $c$ of a partial recursive function, this is the partial function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that on input $k$ is undefined if $c$ halts on input $0$ within $k$ steps of bounded evaluation, and equals $0$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Diverging once a code halts on zero

nodes.summary: Writing $\varphi_c$ for the partial function on $\mathbb{N}$ computed by a code $c$ of a partial recursive function, the set of codes $c$ with $\varphi_c(0)$ undefined is many-one reducible to the set of total codes, the codes that halt on every input: there is a computable function $f$ from codes to codes such that, for every code $c$, $\varphi_c(0)$ is undefined if and only if $f(c)$ is total.
nodes.title: Non-halting on zero reduces to totality

nodes.summary: The set of total codes, the codes of partial recursive functions that halt on every input, is not recognizable by multi-stack machines: no multi-stack machine halts on the binary encoding of a code $c$ exactly when $c$ is total.
nodes.title: Totality is not recognizable

nodes.summary: The set of total codes, the codes of partial recursive functions that halt on every input, is not decidable by multi-stack machines: no multi-stack machine computes a total function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that takes the value $1$ at the number encoding a code $c$ exactly when $c$ is total.
nodes.title: Totality is undecidable
Finiteness problem for programs

nodes.summary: A code $c$ of a partial recursive function $\varphi_c$ on $\mathbb{N}$ is finite when the domain of $\varphi_c$, the set of inputs on which $c$ halts, is finite. The set of finite codes is denoted $\mathrm{FIN}$.
nodes.title: Codes with finite domain

nodes.summary: For a code $c$ of a partial recursive function, let $u_c$ be the partial function on $\mathbb{N}$ that on input $j$ is undefined if $c$ halts on input $0$ within $j$ steps (the step-bounded evaluation of $c$ on input $0$ with bound $j$ returns a value) and outputs $0$ otherwise. Then for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $u_c$ is defined at $k$ if and only if $c$ does not halt on input $0$ within $k$ steps.
nodes.title: Domain of the until-halts function

nodes.summary: The set of codes of partial recursive functions that halt on input $0$ is many-one reducible to the set of finite codes: there is a computable function $f$ from codes to codes such that, for every code $c$, $c$ halts on input $0$ if and only if the partial function of $f(c)$ has finite domain.
nodes.title: Halting reduces to finiteness

nodes.summary: The set of codes of partial recursive functions with finite domain is not co-recognizable by multi-stack Turing machines: no finite multi-stack machine whose input alphabet is identified with $\{0, 1\}$ halts on the binary encoding of the number of a code $c$ exactly when the partial function of $c$ has infinite domain.
nodes.title: Finiteness is not co-recognizable

nodes.summary: For a code $c$ of a partial recursive function, $h_c$ is the partial function on $\mathbb{N}$ that on input $k$ outputs $0$ if $c$ halts on input $0$ within $k$ steps (the step-bounded evaluation of $c$ on input $0$ with bound $k$ returns a value) and is undefined otherwise.
nodes.title: Halts-within function

nodes.summary: For a code $c$ of a partial recursive function, let $h_c$ be the partial function on $\mathbb{N}$ that on input $j$ outputs $0$ if $c$ halts on input $0$ within $j$ steps (the step-bounded evaluation of $c$ on input $0$ with bound $j$ returns a value) and is undefined otherwise. Then for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $h_c$ is defined at $k$ if and only if $c$ halts on input $0$ within $k$ steps.
nodes.title: Domain of the halts-within function

nodes.summary: The set of codes of partial recursive functions that do not halt on input $0$ is many-one reducible to the set of finite codes: there is a computable function $f$ from codes to codes such that, for every code $c$, $c$ does not halt on input $0$ if and only if the partial function of $f(c)$ has finite domain.
nodes.title: Non-halting reduces to finiteness

nodes.summary: The set of codes of partial recursive functions with finite domain is not recognizable by multi-stack Turing machines: no finite multi-stack machine whose input alphabet is identified with $\{0, 1\}$ halts on the binary encoding of the number of a code $c$ exactly when the partial function of $c$ has finite domain.
nodes.title: Finiteness is not recognizable

nodes.summary: The set of codes of partial recursive functions with finite domain is not decidable by multi-stack Turing machines: there is no total function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ computed by a finite multi-stack machine on binary encodings such that, for every code $c$ with number $n_c$, $f(n_c) = 1$ if and only if the partial function of $c$ has finite domain.
nodes.title: Finiteness is undecidable

nodes.summary: Specific undecidable problems and the reductions proving them undecidable: the Post correspondence problem and its variants, string rewriting, undecidable questions about context-free grammars (ambiguity, intersection, universality, regularity), and emptiness of linear bounded automata.
nodes.title: Undecidable problems
Diophantine sets and Hilbert's tenth problem

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi : A \to R$ be a ring homomorphism of commutative rings and let $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Polynomials with coefficients in $A$ are evaluated at points with coordinates in $R$ by first mapping their coefficients into $R$ by $\varphi$. A subset $S \subseteq R^k$ is Diophantine over $R$ with coefficients from $A$ through $\varphi$ when there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a finite set $P$ of polynomials with…
nodes.title: Diophantine sets

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi : A \to R$ be a ring homomorphism of commutative rings. A subset $S \subseteq R$ is Diophantine over $R$ with coefficients from $A$ through $\varphi$ when the set $\{(s) : s \in S\} \subseteq R^1$ of one-coordinate points with coordinate in $S$ is a Diophantine subset of $R^1$ over $R$ with coefficients from $A$ through $\varphi$.
nodes.title: Diophantine subsets of a ring

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi : A \to R$ be a ring homomorphism of commutative rings. For every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the whole space $R^k$ is Diophantine over $R$ with coefficients from $A$ through $\varphi$.
nodes.title: The whole space is Diophantine

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi : A \to R$ be a ring homomorphism of commutative rings, with $R$ nontrivial. For every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the empty subset of $R^k$ is Diophantine over $R$ with coefficients from $A$ through $\varphi$.
nodes.title: The empty set is Diophantine

nodes.summary: A set $S$ of natural numbers is recursively enumerable if and only if it is Diophantine, that is, there is a polynomial $p$ with integer coefficients such that $n \in S$ exactly when $p(n, t_1, \dots, t_k) = 0$ for some natural numbers $t_1, \dots, t_k$.
nodes.title: Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem
Emptiness problem for linear bounded automata

nodes.summary: For an alphabet $\Sigma$, the tape alphabet of the fenced machine consists of a symbol for each letter of $\Sigma$, two kinds of padding cells (left and right), which the simulated machine reads as blanks, and the wall, which marks the ends of the input.
nodes.title: Fenced alphabet

nodes.summary: For a set of states $Q$, the states of the fenced machine are two start states, a running state for each state $q \in Q$ of the simulated machine, and a trap state.
nodes.title: States of the fenced machine

nodes.summary: The simulated cell of a cell of the fenced machine is the cell of the simulated machine that it stands for: a symbol of the simulated machine stands for itself, and every other cell (a padding cell, a wall or a blank) stands for a blank.
nodes.title: Simulated cell of a fenced cell

nodes.summary: For a cell $o$ of the simulated machine, a symbol or a blank, the fenced cell of $o$ is the cell the fenced machine writes for a write of $o$: $o$ itself if $o$ is a symbol, and the padding cell $\mathrm{pad}$ if $o$ is a blank.
nodes.title: Fenced cell of a write

nodes.summary: For every cell $o$ of the simulated machine, a symbol or a blank, the simulated cell of the fenced cell of $o$ is $o$.
nodes.title: Reading back a fenced cell of a write

nodes.summary: Let $o$ be a cell of the simulated machine, a symbol or a blank, and copy it to the fenced machine, a symbol as itself and a blank as a blank. Then the simulated cell of the copy is $o$.
nodes.title: Reading back a copied cell

nodes.summary: For every cell $o$ of the simulated machine, a symbol or a blank, the fenced cell of $o$ is not a wall.
nodes.title: A fenced cell of a write is never a wall

nodes.summary: For a word $w$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$ and $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$, the fenced input of $w$ with $i$ padding cells on the left and $j$ on the right is the word over the fenced alphabet of $\Sigma$ made of a wall, $i$ left padding cells, the letters of $w$ as symbols, $j$ right padding cells and a wall, in this order.
nodes.title: Fenced input

nodes.summary: Let $w$ be a word of length $\ell$ and $i, j, n \in \mathbb{N}$. The cell at position $n$, counting from $0$, of the fenced input of $w$ with $i$ left and $j$ right padding cells is the wall if $n = 0$; a left padding cell if $1 \le n \le i$; the letter of $w$ at position $n - i - 1$, also counting from $0$, as a symbol, if $i < n \le i + \ell$; a right padding cell if $i + \ell < n \le i + \ell + j$; the wall if…
nodes.title: Cells of a fenced input

nodes.summary: For a word $w$ of length $n$ and natural numbers $i$ and $j$, the fenced input of $w$ with $i$ padding cells on the left and $j$ on the right has length $i + n + j + 2$: the word, the two paddings and the two walls.
nodes.title: Length of a fenced input

nodes.summary: A transition of a single-tape machine $M$, made of an optional symbol to write, an optional move and an optional next state, becomes the transition of the fenced machine of $M$ that writes the symbol, or a right padding cell where $M$ writes a blank, makes the same move, and goes to the running state of the next state $q$ of $M$, or halts where $M$ halts.
nodes.title: A transition lifted to the fenced machine

nodes.summary: In the running state of a state $q$ of a single-tape machine $M$, the fenced machine of $M$ acts on the cell under its head as follows: on a symbol $a$ it makes the lifted transition of $M$ in state $q$ on $a$; on a left or right padding cell it makes the lifted transition of $M$ in state $q$ on a blank; on a wall or a blank cell it leaves the cell unchanged, does not move, and enters the trap.
nodes.title: The running transition of the fenced machine

nodes.summary: For a single-tape machine $M$ over a finite inhabited alphabet $\Sigma$, the fenced machine of $M$ is the single-tape machine over the fenced alphabet of $\Sigma$ whose states are the states of the fenced machine for the states of $M$, which starts in the first start state and acts on the cell under its head as follows. In the first start state, on a wall it moves right into the second start state, and on any other…
nodes.title: The fenced machine

nodes.summary: For every single-tape Turing machine $M$, the fenced machine of $M$ is a linear bounded automaton.
nodes.title: The fenced machine is a linear bounded automaton

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape machine over a finite inhabited alphabet and $w$ a word over that alphabet. The fenced machine of $M$ halts on the fenced input of $w$ with $i$ padding cells on the left and $j$ on the right for some $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$ if and only if $M$ halts on $w$.
nodes.title: The fenced machine halts on some padding of a word iff the machine halts on it

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape machine over a finite inhabited alphabet and $w$ a word over that alphabet. The fenced machine of $M$ halts on none of the fenced inputs of $w$, with $i$ padding cells on the left and $j$ on the right for $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$, if and only if $M$ does not halt on $w$.
nodes.title: The fenced machine halts on no padding of a word iff the machine does not halt on it

nodes.summary: There exist a finite inhabited alphabet $\Gamma$ with a primitive recursive encoding, a linear bounded automaton $F$ over the fenced alphabet of $\Gamma$, and a primitive recursive map $e$ from codes of partial recursive functions to words over $\Gamma$, such that the set of codes $c$ for which $F$ halts on none of the fenced inputs of $e(c)$, with $i$ padding cells on the left and $j$ on the right for any…
nodes.title: Emptiness of a linear bounded automaton on computable input slices is undecidable
Post correspondence problem

nodes.summary: A domino over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a pair $(t, b)$ of words over $\alpha$: its top word $t$ and its bottom word $b$.
nodes.title: Domino (Post correspondence problem)

nodes.summary: For a sequence of dominoes $(t_1, b_1), \ldots, (t_n, b_n)$, its top word is the concatenation $t_1 t_2 \cdots t_n$ of their top words; the empty sequence has the empty top word.
nodes.title: Top word of a sequence of dominoes

nodes.summary: For a sequence $s = d_1, \dots, d_k$ of dominoes, the bottom word of $s$ is the concatenation $b_1 b_2 \cdots b_k$, where $b_i$ is the bottom word of $d_i$.
nodes.title: Bottom word of a domino sequence

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a finite list of dominoes. A solution of $P$ is a nonempty sequence $d_1, \dots, d_k$ of dominoes, each occurring in $P$ (repetitions allowed), such that the concatenation of the top words of $d_1, \dots, d_k$ equals the concatenation of their bottom words.
nodes.title: PCP solution

nodes.summary: A list $P$ of dominoes is a solvable instance of the Post correspondence problem when it has a PCP solution: a nonempty sequence of dominoes from $P$, repetitions allowed, whose top words and bottom words concatenate to the same word.
nodes.title: The Post correspondence problem

nodes.summary: A list $P$ of dominoes has an MPCP solution when $P$ is nonempty and some PCP solution of $P$ starts with the first domino of $P$.
nodes.title: The modified Post correspondence problem

nodes.summary: A list $P$ of dominoes has nonempty words when every domino of $P$ has a nonempty top word and a nonempty bottom word.
nodes.title: Instances with nonempty words

nodes.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$, the extended alphabet consists of the letters of $\alpha$ together with two new symbols: the star $\star$ and the end marker $\diamond$.
nodes.title: The extended alphabet of the MPCP-to-PCP reduction

nodes.summary: Each letter $a$ of the alphabet $\alpha$ is regarded as a symbol of the extended alphabet of the MPCP-to-PCP reduction, which consists of the letters of $\alpha$, the star $\star$ and the end marker $\diamond$.
nodes.title: The alphabet inside the extended alphabet

nodes.summary: The star $\star$ is the new symbol of the extended alphabet that is neither a letter of $\alpha$ nor the end marker $\diamond$.
nodes.title: The star symbol

nodes.summary: The end marker $\diamond$ is the symbol of the extended alphabet of the MPCP-to-PCP reduction that is neither a letter of $\alpha$ nor the star $\star$.
nodes.title: End marker

nodes.summary: Let $\star$ be the star of the extended alphabet. For a word $u = a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ over $\alpha$, the word $\star u$ over the extended alphabet is $\star a_1 \star a_2 \cdots \star a_n$, obtained by putting a star before every letter of $u$; the empty word gives the empty word.
nodes.title: A star before every letter

nodes.summary: Let $\star$ be the star of the extended alphabet. For a word $u = a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ over $\alpha$, the word $u\star$ over the extended alphabet is $a_1 \star a_2 \star \cdots a_n \star$, obtained by putting a star after every letter of $u$; the empty word gives the empty word.
nodes.title: A star after every letter

nodes.summary: For a word $w$ over the extended alphabet of the MPCP-to-PCP reduction, this is the word over $\alpha$ obtained from $w$ by deleting every star $\star$ and every end marker $\diamond$, keeping the letters of $\alpha$ in their order.
nodes.title: Erasing stars and end markers

nodes.summary: For a word $u$ over $\alpha$, write $\star u$ for the word over the extended alphabet obtained by putting a star $\star$ before every letter of $u$, and $u\star$ for the word obtained by putting a star after every letter. A domino $(t, b)$ over $\alpha$ is sent to the domino $(\star t, b\star)$ over the extended alphabet.
nodes.title: Starred image of a domino

nodes.summary: For a domino $(t, b)$ over an alphabet $\alpha$, its start domino is the domino $(\star t, \star b \star)$ over the extended alphabet, where $\star t$ puts the star $\star$ before every letter of $t$ and $b \star$ puts a star after every letter of $b$, so that the bottom word gets one extra star in front.
nodes.title: The start domino of the MPCP-to-PCP reduction

nodes.summary: Over the alphabet $\alpha$ extended with the star $\star$ and the end marker $\diamond$, the end domino is $(\star\diamond, \diamond)$: its top word is $\star$ followed by $\diamond$, and its bottom word is $\diamond$.
nodes.title: End domino of the MPCP-to-PCP reduction

nodes.summary: Write $\star$ for the star and $\diamond$ for the end marker of the extended alphabet; for a word $u$ over $\alpha$, $\star u$ puts a star before every letter of $u$ and $u \star$ puts a star after every letter of $u$. The empty list of dominoes is sent to the empty list. A list $P = [d_0, d_1, \ldots, d_n]$ of dominoes over $\alpha$, with $d_0 = (t_0, b_0)$, is sent to the following list of dominoes over the…
nodes.title: The reduction from MPCP to PCP

nodes.summary: For a domino $(t, b)$ over the extended alphabet, its unmapping is the domino over $\alpha$ obtained by deleting every star $\star$ and every end marker $\diamond$ from both $t$ and $b$, keeping the letters of $\alpha$ in order.
nodes.title: Erasing the markers from a domino

nodes.summary: If a list $P$ of dominoes has an MPCP solution, then the image of $P$ under the reduction from MPCP to PCP has a PCP solution.
nodes.title: An MPCP solution gives a PCP solution of the reduced instance

nodes.summary: On instances with nonempty words, a PCP solution of the reduced instance gives an MPCP solution. Let $P$ be a list of dominoes in which every domino has a nonempty top and a nonempty bottom. If the image of $P$ under the reduction from MPCP to PCP has a PCP solution, then $P$ has an MPCP solution.
nodes.title: On instances with nonempty words, a PCP solution of the reduced instance gives an MPCP solution

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a list of dominoes over an alphabet $\alpha$ in which every domino has a nonempty top and a nonempty bottom. Then $P$ has an MPCP solution if and only if the image of $P$ under the reduction from MPCP to PCP, an instance over $\alpha$ extended with a star and an end marker, has a PCP solution.
nodes.title: MPCP reduces to PCP on instances with nonempty words

nodes.summary: For a list $P$ of dominoes, this Boolean test returns true exactly when every domino of $P$ has a nonempty top and a nonempty bottom.
nodes.title: Boolean test for nonempty words

nodes.summary: For a list $P$ of dominoes, the total reduction sends $P$ to its image under the reduction from MPCP to PCP when every domino of $P$ has a nonempty top and a nonempty bottom, and to the empty instance, which has no PCP solution, otherwise.
nodes.title: The total reduction from MPCP to PCP

nodes.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive coding, the Boolean test of whether every domino of a list over $\alpha$ has a nonempty top and a nonempty bottom is a primitive recursive function of the list.
nodes.title: The nonempty-words test is primitive recursive

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with a primitive recursive coding, and let $\alpha'$ be $\alpha$ extended with two new symbols, the star and the end marker. There is a computable function $f$ from finite lists of dominoes over $\alpha$ to finite lists of dominoes over $\alpha'$ such that, for every list $P$ of dominoes over $\alpha$, $f(P)$ has a PCP solution if and only if both every domino of $P$ has a nonempty top…
nodes.title: MPCP many-one reduces to PCP

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with a primitive recursive coding and decidable equality, and let $P$ and $s$ be lists of dominoes over $\alpha$. The Boolean solution check of $s$ for $P$ is true exactly when $s$ is nonempty, every domino of $s$ occurs in $P$, and the top word of $s$ equals the bottom word of $s$, and it is false otherwise.
nodes.title: Boolean check for PCP solutions

nodes.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive coding, the set of lists of dominoes over $\alpha$ that have a PCP solution is recursively enumerable.
nodes.title: PCP is recursively enumerable

nodes.summary: For every alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, there is a multi-stack Turing machine that, started on the binary encoding of a list $P$ of dominoes over $\alpha$, halts exactly when $P$ has a PCP solution.
nodes.title: PCP is Turing-recognizable

nodes.summary: Write $|w|$ for the length of a word $w$. Let $s$ be a finite sequence of dominoes over an alphabet. If every domino $(t, b)$ in $s$ satisfies $|b| \le |t|$, then the concatenation of the bottom words of $s$ is no longer than the concatenation of the top words of $s$.
nodes.title: Total length of dominoes that are at least as long on top

nodes.summary: Write $|w|$ for the length of a word $w$. Let $s$ be a nonempty finite sequence of dominoes over an alphabet. If every domino $(t, b)$ in $s$ satisfies $|b| < |t|$, then the concatenation of the bottom words of $s$ is strictly shorter than the concatenation of the top words of $s$.
nodes.title: Total length of dominoes that are strictly longer on top

nodes.summary: For a finite sequence $s$ of dominoes, the swapped sequence is obtained from $s$ by exchanging the top and bottom word of every domino: each $(t, b)$ becomes $(b, t)$, and the order of the dominoes is unchanged.
nodes.title: Swapping top and bottom

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with at most one letter, and write $|w|$ for the length of a word $w$. A finite list $P$ of dominoes over $\alpha$ has a PCP solution if and only if either some domino $(t, b)$ in $P$ has $|t| = |b|$, or some domino $(t, b)$ in $P$ has $|t| < |b|$ and some domino $(t', b')$ in $P$ has $|b'| < |t'|$.
nodes.title: The unary PCP criterion

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with at most one letter, and write $|w|$ for the length of a word $w$. For a finite list $P$ of dominoes over $\alpha$, the unary test of $P$ is the Boolean value that is true exactly when some domino $(t, b)$ in $P$ has $|t| = |b|$, or some domino $(t, b)$ in $P$ has $|t| < |b|$ and some domino $(t', b')$ in $P$ has $|b'| < |t'|$.
nodes.title: The unary PCP test

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with at most one letter whose elements have a computable encoding. Then the Post correspondence problem over $\alpha$ is a computable predicate: some computable function decides, for every finite list $P$ of dominoes over $\alpha$, whether $P$ has a PCP solution.
nodes.title: PCP over a one-letter alphabet is decidable

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with at most one letter whose elements have a computable encoding. Then the Post correspondence problem over $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine: some multi-stack Turing machine decides, for every finite list $P$ of dominoes over $\alpha$, whether $P$ has a PCP solution.
nodes.title: Unary PCP is decidable by a multi-stack machine

nodes.summary: For a tape alphabet $\Gamma$ and a set of states $\Lambda$, the symbols of the rewriting system simulating a single-tape machine are a tape symbol $a$ for each $a \in \Gamma$, a state symbol $q$ for each $q \in \Lambda$, the left end marker $\vdash$, the right end marker $\dashv$ and the halting symbol $H$.
nodes.title: Symbols of the rewriting system of a single-tape machine

nodes.summary: A symbol of the rewriting system simulating a single-tape Turing machine is a control symbol if it is a state symbol or the halting symbol $H$; tape symbols and the end markers $\vdash$ and $\dashv$ are not control symbols.
nodes.title: Control symbols

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a property of the elements of a type $\alpha$, let $A$ and $B$ be lists over $\alpha$ none of whose elements satisfy $P$, and let $y \in \alpha$. If $C$ and $D$ are lists over $\alpha$ and $x \in \alpha$ satisfies $P$ with $C\,x\,D = A\,y\,B$ (concatenation), then $C = A$, $x = y$ and $D = B$.
nodes.title: Unique splitting at a marked letter

nodes.summary: Let $A$, $B$, $u$, $v$, $p$, $s$ be words over the symbols of the rewriting system simulating a single-tape machine, and let $x$ and $y$ be symbols. If no symbol of $A$ or of $B$ is a control symbol (a state symbol or the halting symbol), $x$ is a control symbol, and $u\,p\,x\,s\,v = A\,y\,B$, then $u\,p = A$, $x = y$ and $s\,v = B$.
nodes.title: Splitting a rewrite site at its control symbol

nodes.summary: For a state $q$, a tape symbol $h$ and words $L$, $R$ of tape symbols, the word of the configuration in state $q$ with head symbol $h$, left part $L$ (in reading order, from left to right) and right part $R$ is $\vdash L\,q\,h\,R \dashv$, where $\vdash$ and $\dashv$ are the end markers.
nodes.title: The word of a configuration

nodes.summary: The halting word is the word $\vdash H \dashv$ made of the left end marker, the halting symbol and the right end marker. It is the target word of the rewriting simulation of a single-tape machine.
nodes.title: The halting word

nodes.summary: A word $w$ spells a configuration $c$ of a single-tape Turing machine if there are a state $q$, a tape symbol $h$ and words $L$, $R$ of tape symbols such that $c$ is in state $q$, its head reads $h$, its tape reads $L$ immediately to the left of the head and $R$ immediately to the right of it, with blanks beyond, and $w = \vdash L\,q\,h\,R \dashv$.
nodes.title: Words spelling a configuration

nodes.summary: For an input $l$ of tape symbols, the start word is $\vdash q_0\, h\, R \dashv$, where $\vdash$ and $\dashv$ are the left and right end markers, $q_0$ is the default state, $h$ is the first symbol of $l$ (the default tape symbol if $l$ is empty) and $R$ is the rest of $l$. It spells the configuration in state $q_0$ with head symbol $h$, empty left part and right part $R$.
nodes.title: The start word

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine with finitely many states and tape symbols, let $\sqcup$ be its blank symbol, and write $\vdash$, $\dashv$ for the end markers and $H$ for the halting symbol. The rules for a state $q$ reading a tape symbol $a$ are: the rule $q\,a \to H$ if $M$ has no transition from $q$ reading $a$; the rule $q\,a \to q'\,b$ if $M$ writes $b$ and enters $q'$; the rules…
nodes.title: The rules for one transition

nodes.summary: For a finite tape alphabet $\Gamma$, let $H$ be the halting symbol of the rewriting system simulating a single-tape machine with tape alphabet $\Gamma$. The erasing rules are the rewriting rules $c\,H \to H$ and $H\,c \to H$ for every tape symbol $c \in \Gamma$: the halting symbol deletes the tape symbol on either side of it.
nodes.title: Erasing rules

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine with finitely many states and tape symbols, and write $H$ for the halting symbol. The rewriting system simulating $M$ is the finite list of rules consisting of the rules for every state $q$ reading every tape symbol $a$, followed by the erasing rules $c\,H \to H$ and $H\,c \to H$ for every tape symbol $c$.
nodes.title: The rewriting system simulating a Turing machine

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine with a finite tape alphabet $\Gamma$, a default (blank) symbol $\beta \in \Gamma$ and finitely many states. The symbols are the tape symbols, the states, the end markers $\vdash$ and $\dashv$, and the halting symbol $H$. Every rule $l \to r$ of the rewriting system simulating $M$ has one of the following eight forms, where $q, q'$ are states and $a, b, c$ are tape symbols.…
nodes.title: The eight kinds of rules of the machine-simulating rewriting system

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine with finitely many tape symbols and states. If the word $w$ spells the configuration $c$ and $M$ steps from $c$ to $c'$, then $w$ rewrites in one step of the rewriting system simulating $M$ to a word $w'$ that spells $c'$.
nodes.title: One machine step is one rewrite

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine with finitely many states and tape symbols, and let $\vdash$, $\dashv$ be the end markers and $H$ the halting symbol of the rewriting system simulating $M$. For all words $X$ and $Y$ of tape symbols, the word $\vdash X\,H\,Y \dashv$ rewrites in zero or more steps of this rewriting system to the halting word $\vdash H \dashv$.
nodes.title: The halting symbol erases the tape

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine with finitely many states and tape symbols, and let $\vdash$, $\dashv$ be the end markers and $H$ the halting symbol of the rewriting system simulating $M$. Let $c$ be a configuration of $M$ at which $M$ has no next step, and let $w$ be a word that spells $c$: for some state $q$, tape symbol $h$ and lists $L$, $R$ of tape symbols, $c$ is in state $q$ with $h$ under the head,…
nodes.title: A halted configuration rewrites to the halting word

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape machine with finitely many tape symbols and states, and $l$ an input. A word $w$ satisfies the invariant for $l$ when either $w$ spells a configuration that $M$ reaches from its initial configuration on $l$, or $M$ halts on $l$ and $w = \vdash X\, H\, Y \dashv$ for some words $X$ and $Y$ of tape symbols, where $\vdash$ and $\dashv$ are the left and right end markers and $H$ is the halting…
nodes.title: Invariant of the rewriting simulation of a single-tape machine

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape machine with finite tape alphabet and finite set of states, and let $l$ be an input word. Write $\vdash$ and $\dashv$ for the left and right end markers and $H$ for the halting symbol. A word $w$ satisfies the invariant for $M$ and $l$ when either $w$ spells a configuration that $M$ reaches from its initial configuration on $l$ (the configuration with state $q$, head symbol $h$, left part…
nodes.title: Every rewrite preserves the invariant of reachable words

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape machine with finite tape alphabet and finite set of states, and write $\vdash$ and $\dashv$ for the left and right end markers and $H$ for the halting symbol. For every input word $l$, $M$ halts on $l$ if and only if the start word ${\vdash}\,q_0\,h\,R\,{\dashv}$ of $l$ rewrites to the halting word ${\vdash}\,H\,{\dashv}$ in zero or more steps under the rules of $M$, where $q_0$ is the…
nodes.title: A single-tape machine halts iff its start word rewrites to the halting word

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine with finitely many states and tape symbols. Then the set of inputs on which $M$ halts is many-one reducible to the set of instances $(R, x, y)$, where $R$ is a list of rules and $x$, $y$ are words over the symbols of the rewriting system simulating $M$, such that every rule of $R$ has a nonempty left side and a nonempty right side and $x$ rewrites to $y$ in zero or more steps…
nodes.title: Single-tape halting many-one reduces to string rewriting reachability

nodes.summary: There is a finite alphabet $\alpha$, with a primitive recursive coding of its letters by natural numbers, such that no multi-stack Turing machine decides, for a finite list $R$ of rewriting rules over $\alpha$ and words $x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$, whether every rule of $R$ has a nonempty left side and a nonempty right side and $x$ rewrites to $y$ in zero or more steps of $R$.
nodes.title: Reachability for string rewriting is undecidable

nodes.summary: There is a finite alphabet $\alpha$, with a primitive recursive coding of its letters by natural numbers, such that no multi-stack Turing machine decides, for a finite list $P$ of dominoes over $\alpha$, whether every domino of $P$ has a nonempty top and a nonempty bottom and $P$ has a solution of the modified Post correspondence problem, that is, a nonempty sequence of dominoes of $P$, repetitions allowed, that…
nodes.title: MPCP is undecidable

nodes.summary: There is a finite alphabet $\alpha$, with a primitive recursive coding of its letters by natural numbers, such that no multi-stack Turing machine decides whether a finite list of dominoes over $\alpha$ has a solution, that is, a nonempty sequence of dominoes of the list, repetitions allowed, whose tops and bottoms concatenate to the same word.
nodes.title: The Post correspondence problem is undecidable

nodes.summary: The Boolean function on the symbols of the rewriting system simulating a single-tape Turing machine that is true on every state symbol and on the halting symbol $H$, and false on every tape symbol and on the end markers $\vdash$ and $\dashv$.
nodes.title: Boolean test for control symbols

nodes.summary: The number of control symbols of a word $w$ over the symbols of the rewriting system simulating a single-tape machine is the number of letters of $w$ that are states or the halting symbol $H$.
nodes.title: Number of control symbols

nodes.summary: If a word $w$ over the symbols of the rewriting system simulating a single-tape machine contains exactly one control symbol (a state symbol or the halting symbol), then $w = p\,x\,s$ for a control symbol $x$ and words $p$ and $s$ that contain no control symbol.
nodes.title: A word with one control symbol splits at it

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine with finitely many states and tape symbols, and let $\sqcup$ be its blank symbol. For words $u$, $v$ and a state $q$, the successor of $u\,q\,v$ is defined as follows. If $v$ does not begin with a tape symbol, there is none. If $v = a\,v'$ for a tape symbol $a$: when $M$ has no transition from $q$ reading $a$, it is $u\,H\,v'$, where $H$ is the halting symbol; when $M$ writes…
nodes.title: Rewriting at a state symbol

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape machine with finite tape alphabet and finite set of states. Let $x$ be a control symbol (a state symbol or the halting symbol $H$) and let $u$ and $v$ be words that contain no control symbol. If $u\,x\,v$ rewrites in one step to $w'$ under the rules of $M$, then either $x$ is a state symbol $q$ and the successor of $u\,q\,v$ under the rules for $q$ is defined and equals $w'$, or $x = H$ and…
nodes.title: A rewrite at the control symbol

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine with finitely many states and tape symbols, and call the states and the halting symbol $H$ control symbols. If a word $w$ rewrites to $w'$ in one step of the rewriting system simulating $M$, then $w$ and $w'$ contain the same number of control symbols.
nodes.title: Rewriting preserves the number of control symbols

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape machine with finite tape alphabet and finite set of states, and let $w$ be a word over the symbols of its rewriting system that contains exactly one control symbol (a state symbol or the halting symbol). If $w$ rewrites in one step to $w_1$ and in one step to $w_2$ under the rules of $M$, then there is a word $d$ such that $w_1$ rewrites to $d$ in at most one step and $w_2$ rewrites to $d$…
nodes.title: Local confluence on words with one control symbol

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine with finitely many states and tape symbols. There is no word $w$ such that the halting word $\vdash H \dashv$ rewrites to $w$ in one step of the rewriting system simulating $M$.
nodes.title: The halting word is irreducible

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine with finitely many states and tape symbols, and call the states and the halting symbol $H$ control symbols. A word $w$ rewrites to $w'$ by a controlled step when $w$ contains exactly one control symbol and $w$ rewrites to $w'$ in one step of the rewriting system simulating $M$.
nodes.title: Rewrites from words with one control symbol

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine with finitely many states and tape symbols, and call the states and the halting symbol $H$ control symbols. Suppose $w$ contains exactly one control symbol, and $w$ and $w'$ are equivalent under the equivalence relation generated by one-step rewriting in the rewriting system simulating $M$. Then $w$ and $w'$ are equivalent under the equivalence relation generated by the…
nodes.title: Thue equivalence from a word with one control symbol uses only controlled steps

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine with finitely many states and tape symbols, and call the states and the halting symbol $H$ control symbols. Consider the relation in which a word $w$ with exactly one control symbol rewrites to $w'$ by one step of the rewriting system simulating $M$. This relation is confluent: if $w$ rewrites in zero or more such steps to both $w_1$ and $w_2$, then $w_1$ and $w_2$ both…
nodes.title: The rewrites from words with one control symbol are confluent

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine with finitely many states and tape symbols, write $\vdash$ and $\dashv$ for the left and right end markers and $H$ for the halting symbol, and let $l$ be an input word of tape symbols. Then $M$ halts on $l$ if and only if the start word of $l$ and the halting word ${\vdash}\,H\,{\dashv}$ are equivalent under the reflexive, symmetric and transitive closure of one-step…
nodes.title: A single-tape machine halts iff its start word is Thue equivalent to the halting word

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine with finitely many states and tape symbols, and let $R_M$ be the rewriting system simulating $M$. Then the set of inputs on which $M$ halts is many-one reducible to the set of pairs $(x, y)$ of words over the symbols of $R_M$ that are equivalent under the reflexive, symmetric and transitive closure of one-step rewriting by $R_M$.
nodes.title: Single-tape halting many-one reduces to the word problem of a fixed Thue system

nodes.summary: (Post, Markov) There are a finite alphabet $\alpha$, with a primitive recursive coding of its letters by natural numbers, and a finite list $R$ of rewriting rules over $\alpha$ such that no multi-stack Turing machine decides, for words $x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$, whether $x$ and $y$ are equivalent under the reflexive, symmetric and transitive closure of one-step rewriting by $R$.
nodes.title: Some finite Thue system has an undecidable word problem

nodes.summary: There is a finite alphabet $\alpha$, with a primitive recursive coding of its letters by natural numbers, such that no multi-stack Turing machine decides, for a finite list $R$ of rewriting rules over $\alpha$ and words $x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$, whether $x$ and $y$ are equivalent under the reflexive, symmetric and transitive closure of one-step rewriting by $R$.
nodes.title: The uniform word problem for Thue systems is undecidable

nodes.summary: Given a map $f$ from words over $\alpha$ to words over $\beta$ and a list $P$ of dominoes over $\alpha$, the image of $P$ under $f$ is the list of dominoes over $\beta$ obtained by replacing each domino $(u, v)$ of $P$ by $(f(u), f(v))$, in the same order.
nodes.title: Image of a PCP instance under a word map

nodes.summary: Let $h$ map each letter of $\alpha$ to a word over $\beta$, and extend it to words by $h(a_1 \cdots a_n) = h(a_1) \cdots h(a_n)$. If this extension is injective on words over $\alpha$, then for every list $P$ of dominoes over $\alpha$, the list obtained from $P$ by replacing each domino $(u, v)$ by $(h(u), h(v))$ has a PCP solution if and only if $P$ has a PCP solution.
nodes.title: An injective word homomorphism preserves and reflects PCP solvability

nodes.summary: Given an indexing $e$ assigning a natural number to each letter of $\alpha$, the unary code of a letter $a$ is the Boolean word consisting of $e(a)$ copies of $\mathrm{true}$ followed by one $\mathrm{false}$; writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, it is $1^{e(a)} 0$.
nodes.title: Unary code of a letter

nodes.summary: Let $e$ be an injective map from $\alpha$ to the natural numbers, and let $c(a)$ be the unary code of a letter $a$: $e(a)$ copies of $\mathrm{true}$ followed by one $\mathrm{false}$. Then the map sending a word $a_1 \cdots a_n$ over $\alpha$ to the Boolean word $c(a_1) \cdots c(a_n)$ is injective.
nodes.title: The unary code of an injective indexing is uniquely decodable

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite alphabet with a primitive recursive encoding of its letters as natural numbers. Then the Post correspondence problem over $\alpha$ is many-one reducible to the Post correspondence problem over the two-letter alphabet of Booleans $\mathrm{true}$ and $\mathrm{false}$: there is a computable map $f$ sending each finite list $P$ of dominoes over $\alpha$ to a finite list $f(P)$ of dominoes over…
nodes.title: PCP over a finite alphabet many-one reduces to PCP over the binary alphabet

nodes.title: The Post correspondence problem is undecidable over the binary alphabet

nodes.title: The encoded letter terminal

nodes.summary: For $i \in \mathbb{N}$, this is the index $i$ as an encoded terminal over the alphabet $\alpha \oplus \mathbb{N}$: the element $\mathrm{inr}(\mathrm{inr}\, i)$ of $\mathbb{N} \oplus (\alpha \oplus \mathbb{N})$, whose left summand $\mathbb{N}$ holds the nonterminals and whose right summand holds the terminals.
nodes.title: The encoded index terminal

nodes.summary: For a natural number $A$, the nonterminal $A$ as a symbol of the right-hand side of an encoded production over the terminals $\alpha \sqcup \mathbb{N}$: the left injection of $A$ into $\mathbb{N} \sqcup (\alpha \sqcup \mathbb{N})$.

nodes.title: The $i$-th domino of a list

nodes.summary: For a list $P$ of dominoes, a map $\sigma$ assigning a word over $\alpha$ to each domino, a nonterminal $A \in \mathbb{N}$ and an index $i \in \mathbb{N}$, this is the production $A \to w_i\, A\, i$ in encoded form, where $w_i$ is $\sigma$ applied to the $i$-th domino of $P$ (the domino with both words empty when $i$ is past the end of $P$): its right-hand side is the letters of $w_i$ as terminals, then the…
nodes.title: The continuation production

nodes.summary: Let $P = (d_0, \dots, d_{k-1})$ be a list of dominoes over $\alpha$, set $d_i = (\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ for $i \ge k$, let $\sigma$ assign a word over $\alpha$ to each domino, and write $w_i = \sigma(d_i)$. For a nonterminal $A$ and a natural number $i$, this is the encoded production $A \to w_i \, i$, whose right-hand side is the letters of $w_i$ as terminals followed by the index terminal $i$.
nodes.title: The terminating production of a side grammar

nodes.summary: Let $P = (d_0, \dots, d_{k-1})$ be a list of dominoes over $\alpha$, let $\sigma$ assign a word over $\alpha$ to each domino, write $w_i = \sigma(d_i)$, and let $A$ be a nonterminal. The side productions are the list of encoded productions $A \to w_i \, A \, i$ and $A \to w_i \, i$ for $i = 0, 1, \dots, k - 1$, where the letters of $w_i$ are terminals and $i$ is an index terminal.
nodes.title: The productions of a side grammar

nodes.summary: Let $P = (d_0, \dots, d_{k-1})$ be a list of dominoes over $\alpha$, let $\sigma$ assign a word over $\alpha$ to each domino, and write $w_i = \sigma(d_i)$. The side word of a sequence $i_1, \dots, i_n$ of natural numbers is the word $w_{i_1} \cdots w_{i_n} \, i_n \cdots i_1$ over the letters of $\alpha$ and the index terminals $0, 1, 2, \dots$: the letters of…
nodes.title: The side word of an index sequence
