nodes.title: A terminal word derives only itself

nodes.summary: Let $N$ be a type of nonterminals, $u, v$ words over $\alpha \oplus \mathbb{N}$, $A, B \in N$, and $p, q$ strings of terminals in $\alpha \oplus \mathbb{N}$ and nonterminals in $N$. If $u\, A\, v = p\, B\, q$, where $u$ and $v$ are read as strings of terminals, then $p = u$, $B = A$ and $q = v$.

nodes.summary: A rewriting rule over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a pair $(l, r)$ of words over $\alpha$; applying it replaces an occurrence of $l$ by $r$.
nodes.title: Rewriting rules

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a string rewriting system, given as a list of rules. A word $w$ rewrites to a word $w'$ in one step of $R$ when there are a rule $(l, r)$ of $R$ and words $u$ and $v$ with $w = u l v$ and $w' = u r v$.
nodes.title: One-step rewriting

nodes.summary: For a list of rules $R$, a word $x$ derives a word $y$ when $x$ rewrites to $y$ in zero or more steps of $R$, that is, when $(x, y)$ lies in the reflexive-transitive closure of the one-step rewriting relation of $R$.

nodes.summary: An instance $(R, x, y)$ consists of a string rewriting system $R$, given as a list of rules, and two words $x$ and $y$; it is a yes-instance of the reachability problem when $x$ rewrites to $y$ in zero or more steps of $R$.
nodes.title: The reachability problem for string rewriting

nodes.summary: A string rewriting system $R$, given as a list of rules $(l, r)$, has nonempty sides when every rule of $R$ has a nonempty left side $l$ and a nonempty right side $r$.

Productive, creative, simple and immune sets

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $e$ and $n$, $n$ belongs to $W_e$, the $e$-th recursively enumerable set, when the partial recursive function $\varphi_e$ computed by the program with index $e$ in the standard numbering of partial recursive programs is defined at $n$; thus $W_e$ is the domain of $\varphi_e$.
nodes.title: Standard enumeration of the recursively enumerable sets

nodes.summary: A set $A$ of natural numbers is productive when there is a partial recursive function $f$ such that for every natural number $e$ with $W_e \subseteq A$, where $W_e$ is the $e$-th recursively enumerable set in the standard enumeration, $f(e)$ is defined, $f(e) \in A$ and $f(e) \notin W_e$.
nodes.title: Productive set

nodes.summary: A set $A$ of natural numbers is creative when it is recursively enumerable and its complement $\mathbb{N} \setminus A$ is productive.
nodes.title: Creative set

nodes.summary: A set $A$ of natural numbers is immune when it is infinite and every recursively enumerable set $B \subseteq A$ is finite.
nodes.title: Immune set

nodes.summary: A set $P$ of natural numbers is simple when it is recursively enumerable and its complement $\{n \mid \neg P(n)\}$ is immune.
nodes.title: Simple set

nodes.summary: No productive set of natural numbers is recursively enumerable: if it were the $e$-th recursively enumerable set $W_e$, its productive function would produce a member of it outside $W_e$.
nodes.title: A productive set is not recursively enumerable

nodes.summary: It would be an infinite RE subset of itself.
nodes.title: An immune set is not recursively enumerable

nodes.summary: Its complement would be an infinite RE set, contradicting immunity.
nodes.title: A simple set is not computable

nodes.summary: A simple set is recursively enumerable, by definition.
nodes.title: A simple set is recursively enumerable

nodes.summary: The complement of a simple set is immune, by definition.
nodes.title: The complement of a simple set is immune

nodes.summary: A creative set is recursively enumerable, by definition.
nodes.title: A creative set is recursively enumerable

nodes.summary: Its complement is productive, hence not RE, but the complement of a computable set is RE.
nodes.title: A creative set is not computable
Recursive isomorphism and 1-equivalence

nodes.summary: Two predicates $P$ and $Q$ on $\mathbb{N}$ are recursively isomorphic when there is a computable bijection $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that for every $n$, $P(n)$ holds if and only if $Q(f(n))$ holds.
nodes.title: Recursively isomorphic predicates

nodes.summary: Let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a computable bijection. Then its inverse function $f^{-1} : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is computable.
nodes.title: The inverse of a computable bijection is computable

nodes.summary: Let $P$ and $Q$ be predicates on $\mathbb{N}$. If $P$ and $Q$ are recursively isomorphic, then they are 1-equivalent: $P$ is one-one reducible to $Q$ and $Q$ is one-one reducible to $P$. Here $P$ is one-one reducible to $Q$ when there is a computable injective function $g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that for every $n$, $P(n)$ holds if and only if $Q(g(n))$ holds.
nodes.title: A recursive isomorphism gives a 1-equivalence
Turing reducibility

nodes.summary: The characteristic function of a set $p$ of natural numbers is the partial function $\mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$ that is defined at every $n$, with value $1$ if $n \in p$ and value $0$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Characteristic function of a set of naturals

nodes.summary: A set $p$ of natural numbers is decidable (computable as a predicate) if and only if its characteristic function is partial recursive.
nodes.title: A set is decidable iff its characteristic function is partial recursive

nodes.summary: Let $p$ and $q$ be sets of natural numbers such that the characteristic function of $p$ is Turing reducible to the characteristic function of $q$. If $q$ is decidable, then $p$ is decidable.
nodes.title: Decidability transfers down Turing reducibility

nodes.summary: Fix the standard bijective numbering $n \mapsto c_n$ of the codes of partial recursive functions $\mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$. The halting set is the set of natural numbers $n$ such that the partial recursive function with code $c_n$ is defined at $0$.
nodes.title: Halting set

nodes.summary: For every decidable set $q$ of natural numbers, the characteristic function of the halting set is not Turing reducible to the characteristic function of $q$.
nodes.title: The halting set is not Turing reducible to a decidable set

nodes.summary: If $p$ and $q$ are sets of natural numbers and $p$ is many-one reducible to $q$, that is, there is a computable $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $n \in p \iff f(n) \in q$ for all $n$, then the characteristic function of $p$ is Turing reducible to the characteristic function of $q$.
nodes.title: Many-one reducibility implies Turing reducibility

nodes.summary: For every set $p$ of natural numbers, the characteristic function of the complement $\mathbb{N} \setminus p$ and the characteristic function of $p$ are Turing equivalent: each is Turing reducible to the other.
nodes.title: Every set is Turing equivalent to its complement

nodes.summary: There is no computable function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that, for every $n$, $n$ is outside the halting set if and only if $f(n)$ is in the halting set.
nodes.title: The complement of the halting set is not many-one reducible to it

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number. A set $P$ of natural numbers is in $\Delta_n$ when it is in both classes $\Sigma_n$ and $\Pi_n$ of the arithmetical hierarchy.
nodes.title: The class Δₙ of the arithmetical hierarchy

nodes.summary: If $P$ is a decidable set of natural numbers and $g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is a computable function, then the set $\{w \in \mathbb{N} : g(w) \in P\}$ is decidable.
nodes.title: Computable predicates are closed under computable precomposition

nodes.summary: Let $\langle a, b \rangle$ denote the pairing bijection $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, $\langle a, b \rangle = b^2 + a$ if $a < b$ and $\langle a, b \rangle = a^2 + a + b$ otherwise. From $\mathsf{false}$ it may read any letter and move to either state; from $\mathsf{true}$ it may read only letters in $p$, and then it stays in $\mathsf{true}$.

nodes.summary: For a nondeterministic Büchi automaton, the transition graph has an edge from a state $s$ to a state $t$ exactly when the automaton has a transition from $s$ to $t$ reading some symbol.

nodes.summary: A nondeterministic Büchi automaton has a lasso if there are a start state $s_0$ and an accepting state $s$ such that the automaton can move from $s_0$ to $s$ by reading some finite word $u$, and from $s$ back to $s$ by reading some nonempty finite word $v$.

nodes.summary: A nondeterministic Büchi automaton accepts an infinite word $x = x_0 x_1 x_2 \cdots$ if and only if it has a run on $x$, that is, a sequence of states $s_0 s_1 s_2 \cdots$ with $s_0$ a start state and a transition from $s_k$ to $s_{k+1}$ reading $x_k$ for every $k$, such that $s_k$ is an accepting state for infinitely many $k$.

nodes.summary: Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a nondeterministic Büchi automaton over a nonempty alphabet. Suppose $s_0$ is a start state and $s$ an accepting state of $\mathcal{A}$, that reading the finite word $u$ the automaton can move from $s_0$ to $s$, and that reading a nonempty finite word $v$ it can move from $s$ back to $s$. Then $\mathcal{A}$ accepts the infinite word $u v^\omega = u v v v \cdots$.
nodes.title: Lassos give accepted ultimately periodic words

nodes.summary: If a nondeterministic Büchi automaton with finitely many states accepts some infinite word, then it has a lasso: some accepting state is visited twice along an accepting run, and the run between the two visits is the cycle.

nodes.summary: For finitely many states, the language of a nondeterministic Büchi automaton is nonempty iff some accepting state is reachable from a start state and lies on a nonempty cycle.

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be a nondeterministic Büchi automaton with finitely many states over a nonempty alphabet. If $A$ accepts some infinite word, then there are finite words $u$ and $v$ with $v$ nonempty such that $A$ accepts the ultimately periodic word $u v^\omega = u v v v \cdots$.

nodes.summary: For states $s$ and $t$ of a nondeterministic Büchi automaton, the automaton can move from $s$ to $t$ by reading some finite word (possibly empty) if and only if $t$ is reachable from $s$ in zero or more steps of the transition graph, which has an edge from $p$ to $q$ when some symbol takes $p$ to $q$.

nodes.summary: For states $s$ and $t$ of a nondeterministic Büchi automaton, the automaton can move from $s$ to $t$ by reading some nonempty finite word if and only if $t$ is reachable from $s$ in one or more steps of the transition graph, which has an edge from $p$ to $q$ when some symbol takes $p$ to $q$.

nodes.summary: A nondeterministic Büchi automaton has a lasso if and only if there are a start state $s_0$ and an accepting state $s$ such that $s$ is reachable from $s_0$ in zero or more steps of the transition graph and $s$ is reachable from itself in one or more steps; the transition graph has an edge from $p$ to $q$ when some symbol takes $p$ to $q$.

nodes.summary: For a nondeterministic Büchi automaton with finitely many states and a decidable start set, this is the set of its start states, viewed as a finite set.

nodes.summary: For a nondeterministic Büchi automaton with finitely many states, decidable equality of states, a finite alphabet, and decidable transitions, start set and accepting set, the lasso states form the finite set of accepting states $s$ that are reachable from some start state in zero or more transitions and lie on a nonempty cycle, that is, $s$ is reachable from itself in one or more transitions.

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be a nondeterministic Büchi automaton with finitely many states and finitely many symbols, with decidable equality of states, and whose transitions, start states and accepting states are decidable. Then $A$ has a lasso if and only if its set of lasso states, computed by finite reachability closures as the accepting states that are reachable from a start state and lie on a nonempty cycle, is nonempty.

nodes.summary: For a nondeterministic Büchi automaton with finitely many states and finitely many symbols, with decidable equality of states, and whose transitions, start states and accepting states are decidable, the emptiness test returns true exactly when the automaton has no lasso. It decides this by computing the set of lasso states; by the lasso characterization, it returns true iff no infinite word is accepted.
nodes.title: Büchi emptiness test

nodes.summary: For a nondeterministic Büchi automaton with finitely many states and finitely many symbols, with decidable equality of states, and whose transitions, start states and accepting states are decidable, the emptiness test returns true if and only if the automaton accepts no infinite word.

Generalized Büchi automata

nodes.summary: A generalized Büchi automaton with states $S$ and symbols $\Sigma$ is a nondeterministic automaton (a labelled transition relation on $S$ together with a set of start states) equipped with a natural number $k$ and $k$ acceptance sets $F_0, \dots, F_{k-1} \subseteq S$. A run is accepting when it visits every acceptance set infinitely often.
nodes.title: Generalized Büchi automaton

nodes.summary: An infinite word $x$ belongs to the language of a generalized Büchi automaton $g$ with acceptance sets $F_0, \dots, F_{k-1}$ iff there is a run $s$ of $g$ on $x$ such that for every $j < k$ there are infinitely many times $t$ with $s_t \in F_j$. Here a run of $g$ on $x$ is an infinite sequence of states $s_0, s_1, \dots$ with $s_0$ a start state and a transition from $s_i$ to $s_{i+1}$ labelled $x_i$ for every $i$.
nodes.title: Language of a generalized Büchi automaton

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a generalized Büchi automaton with acceptance sets $F_0, \dots, F_{k-1}$. The counter update takes a counter value $i \in \{0, \dots, k\}$ and a state $t$ of $g$ and returns a counter value in $\{0, \dots, k\}$: if $i < k$, it returns $i + 1$ when $t \in F_i$ and $i$ when $t \notin F_i$; if $i = k$, it returns $0$.
nodes.title: Counter update for degeneralization

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a generalized Büchi automaton with acceptance sets $F_0, \dots, F_{k-1}$ and counter update $\mathrm{next}$. If $i \in \{0, \dots, k\}$ satisfies $i < k$ and the state $t$ is not in $F_i$, then $\mathrm{next}(i, t) = i$.
nodes.title: The degeneralization counter stays when the awaited set is missed

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a generalized Büchi automaton with acceptance sets $F_0, \dots, F_{k-1}$, let $i \in \{0, \dots, k\}$ be a counter value and let $t$ be a state of $g$. If $i < k$ and $t \in F_i$, then the counter update of $i$ at $t$ is $i + 1$.
nodes.title: The degeneralization counter advances on a hit

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a generalized Büchi automaton with $k$ acceptance sets and let $i \in \{0, \dots, k\}$ be a counter value. If $i = k$, then for every state $t$ of $g$ the counter update of $i$ at $t$ is $0$.
nodes.title: The degeneralization counter resets at the top

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a generalized Büchi automaton with $k$ acceptance sets and let $s = (s_0, s_1, \dots)$ be an infinite sequence of states. The counter sequence $c_0, c_1, \dots$ of $s$, with values in $\{0, \dots, k\}$, is defined by $c_0 = 0$ and $c_{n+1} = \mathrm{next}(c_n, s_{n+1})$, where $\mathrm{next}$ is the counter update of $g$. So $c_n$ is the counter after reading the states $s_1, \dots, s_n$; the state $s_0$…
nodes.title: Counter sequence of a state sequence

nodes.summary: For every generalized Büchi automaton $g$ and every infinite sequence of states $s$, the counter sequence of $s$ has value $0$ at time $0$.
nodes.title: The counter sequence starts at zero

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a generalized Büchi automaton, $s$ an infinite sequence of states, and $c_0, c_1, \dots$ the counter sequence of $s$. For every $n$, $c_{n+1} = \mathrm{next}(c_n, s_{n+1})$, where $\mathrm{next}$ is the counter update of $g$.
nodes.title: Recursion step of the counter sequence

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a generalized Büchi automaton with acceptance sets $F_0, \dots, F_{k-1}$, let $s$ be an infinite sequence of states with counter sequence $c_0, c_1, \dots$, and let $i < k$ and $n$ satisfy $c_n = i$. If $m \ge n$ and $s_{j+1} \notin F_i$ for every $j$ with $n \le j < m$, then $c_m = i$.
nodes.title: The degeneralization counter waits for the awaited set

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a generalized Büchi automaton with acceptance sets $F_0, \dots, F_{k-1}$, and let $s$ be an infinite sequence of states that visits every $F_j$ infinitely often, with counter sequence $c_0, c_1, \dots$. Then for every time $n$ and every $j$ with $c_n \le j \le k$ there is a time $m \ge n$ with $c_m = j$.
nodes.title: The degeneralization counter reaches every higher value

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a generalized Büchi automaton with acceptance sets $F_0, \dots, F_{k-1}$ and counter update $\mathrm{next}$, let $s$ be an infinite sequence of states, and let $c_0, c_1, \dots$ be any sequence in $\{0, \dots, k\}$ with $c_{n+1} = \mathrm{next}(c_n, s_{n+1})$ for every $n$. Let $a \le b$ be times with $c_a = 0$ and $c_b = d \le k$, and suppose $c_t \ne k$ for every $t$ with $a < t < b$. Then for every…
nodes.title: The degeneralization counter crosses every value below its target

nodes.summary: Let $g$ be a generalized Büchi automaton with $k$ acceptance sets. Its degeneralization is the Büchi automaton over the same alphabet whose states are the pairs $(s, i)$ of a state $s$ of $g$ and a counter value $i \in \{0, \dots, k\}$. On a symbol $x$ there is a transition from $(s, i)$ to $(s', i')$ iff $g$ has a transition from $s$ to $s'$ on $x$ and $i'$ is the counter update of $i$ at the state $s'$. The start…
nodes.title: Degeneralization of a generalized Büchi automaton

nodes.summary: A word is accepted by the degeneralized Büchi automaton iff it is accepted by the generalized Büchi automaton.
nodes.title: Degeneralization preserves the language
Parity condition on infinite sequences

nodes.summary: Let $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of natural numbers and $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Then $n$ is the largest value occurring infinitely often in $(p_k)$ if $p_k = n$ for infinitely many $k$, and every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $p_k = m$ for infinitely many $k$ satisfies $m \le n$.
nodes.title: Largest infinitely occurring value

nodes.summary: A sequence $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ of natural numbers (priorities) satisfies the even max-parity condition if there is an even $n$ that is the largest value occurring infinitely often in $(p_k)$.
nodes.title: Even max-parity condition

nodes.summary: A sequence $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ of natural numbers (priorities) satisfies the odd max-parity condition if there is an odd $n$ that is the largest value occurring infinitely often in $(p_k)$.
nodes.title: Odd max-parity condition

nodes.summary: Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$. If a sequence $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ of natural numbers satisfies $p_k \le d$ for all $k$, then some natural number $n \le d$ is the largest value occurring infinitely often in $(p_k)$.
nodes.title: Bounded sequences have a largest infinitely occurring value

nodes.summary: Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$, let $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of natural numbers with $p_k \le d$ for all $k$, and let $n$ be the largest value occurring infinitely often in $(p_k)$. Then $p_k \le n$ for all sufficiently large $k$.
nodes.title: The tail of a bounded sequence is bounded by its largest infinitely occurring value

nodes.summary: Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$. If a sequence $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ of natural numbers satisfies $p_k \le d$ for all $k$, then it satisfies the odd max-parity condition if and only if it does not satisfy the even max-parity condition.
nodes.title: For bounded sequences the odd parity condition is the negation of the even one

nodes.summary: Let $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of natural numbers with $p_k \in \{1, 2\}$ for every $k$. Then $(p_k)$ satisfies the even max-parity condition if and only if $p_k = 2$ for infinitely many $k$.
nodes.title: Max-parity with priorities 1 and 2 is the Büchi condition

nodes.summary: Let $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of natural numbers and let $j, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Then $n$ is the largest value occurring infinitely often in the shifted sequence $(p_{j+k})_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ if and only if $n$ is the largest value occurring infinitely often in $(p_k)$.
nodes.title: Prefix independence of the largest infinitely occurring value
Parity automata

nodes.summary: A nondeterministic parity automaton with states in $Q$ and symbols in $\Sigma$ is a nondeterministic automaton (a transition relation labelled by symbols on $Q$, together with a set of start states) with a priority $p(q) \in \mathbb{N}$ assigned to each state $q \in Q$.
nodes.title: Nondeterministic parity automaton

nodes.summary: Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a nondeterministic parity automaton with finitely many states and priority function $p$. For every infinite sequence of states $s_0, s_1, s_2, \dots$, the priority sequence $p(s_0), p(s_1), p(s_2), \dots$ satisfies the even or the odd max-parity condition: the largest priority occurring infinitely often exists and is even, or it exists and is odd.
nodes.title: Every state sequence of a finite parity automaton has a parity winner

nodes.summary: A nondeterministic Büchi automaton is turned into the nondeterministic parity automaton with the same states, transitions and start states, in which every accepting state has priority $2$ and every other state has priority $1$.
nodes.title: Büchi automata as parity automata

nodes.summary: Every nondeterministic Büchi automaton accepts the same language of infinite words as its presentation as a parity automaton (priority $2$ on accepting states, $1$ elsewhere).
nodes.title: Büchi-to-parity conversion preserves the language
Parity games

nodes.summary: A parity game has exactly two players, the even player and the odd player.
nodes.title: Players of a parity game

nodes.summary: The opponent of a player of a parity game is the other player: the opponent of the even player is the odd player, and the opponent of the odd player is the even player.
nodes.title: Opponent

reading_title.source: Every player is $p$ or the opponent of $p$

nodes.summary: For all players $p$ and $q$ of a parity game, $q = p$ or $q$ is the opponent of $p$.
nodes.title: Every player is $p$ or the opponent of $p$

nodes.summary: A player wins an infinite sequence of natural-number priorities when the sequence satisfies that player's parity condition: the even player wins it when the largest priority occurring infinitely often exists and is even, and the odd player wins it when the largest priority occurring infinitely often exists and is odd.
nodes.title: Parity winning condition of a player

nodes.summary: A parity game on a type of positions consists of an owner for each position, which is one of the two players, a move relation between positions, where the owner of $v$ may move from $v$ to $w$ when $v$ is related to $w$, and a natural-number priority for each position, such that every position has at least one move (there are no dead ends).
nodes.title: Parity game

nodes.summary: An infinite sequence of positions $\pi_0, \pi_1, \dots$ of a parity game is a play if for every $i$ there is a move from $\pi_i$ to $\pi_{i+1}$.
nodes.title: Plays of a parity game

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, write $\Omega(v)$ for the priority of a position $v$, and let $p$ be a player. An infinite sequence $\pi = \pi_0 \pi_1 \pi_2 \dots$ of positions of $G$ is won by $p$ when its priority sequence $\Omega(\pi_0) \Omega(\pi_1) \Omega(\pi_2) \dots$ satisfies the parity condition of $p$: among the priorities occurring infinitely often there is a largest one, and it is even if $p$ is the even…
nodes.title: Winner of a play in a parity game

nodes.summary: A positional (memoryless) strategy for player `p`: a choice of successor at each position, legal at the positions `p` owns. Its values elsewhere are irrelevant.
nodes.title: Positional strategy in a parity game

nodes.summary: In a parity game, every player has a positional strategy, since every position has a move.
nodes.title: Positional strategies exist

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a positional strategy of player $p$ in a parity game. An infinite sequence of positions $\pi_0, \pi_1, \dots$ (not necessarily a play) conforms to $\sigma$ if $\pi_{i+1} = \sigma(\pi_i)$ for every $i$ such that $p$ owns $\pi_i$.
nodes.title: Plays conforming to a strategy

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a player of a parity game. A positional strategy $\sigma$ of $p$ wins from a position $v$ when every play starting at $v$ that conforms to $\sigma$ (at every position owned by $p$, the play moves to the successor chosen by $\sigma$) is won by $p$.
nodes.title: Winning strategy from a position

nodes.summary: The positions from which player `p` has a winning positional strategy.
nodes.title: Winning region of a parity game

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a player of a parity game in which every position has priority at most $d$, for some natural number $d$. Then every infinite sequence of positions, in particular every play, is won by $p$ or by the opponent of $p$.
nodes.title: Bounded priorities give every play a winner

nodes.summary: In a parity game, for every player $p$, no infinite sequence of positions (play or not) is won both by $p$ and by the opponent of $p$.
nodes.title: No play is won by both players

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a player of a parity game, $\pi = (\pi_0, \pi_1, \dots)$ an infinite sequence of positions and $j$ a natural number. Then the sequence $(\pi_j, \pi_{j+1}, \dots)$, obtained by dropping the first $j$ positions of $\pi$, is won by $p$ if and only if $\pi$ is won by $p$.
nodes.title: Winning is prefix independent

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a positional strategy of player $p$ and $\tau$ a positional strategy of the opponent of $p$ in a parity game. The joint successor of a position $v$ is $\sigma(v)$ if $p$ owns $v$, and $\tau(v)$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Joint successor of two strategies

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a player of a parity game, $\sigma$ a positional strategy of $p$ and $\tau$ a positional strategy of the opponent of $p$. The outcome of $\sigma$ and $\tau$ from a position $v$ is the infinite sequence of positions $v_0, v_1, v_2, \dots$ with $v_0 = v$ in which $v_{i+1}$ is the successor chosen by $\sigma$ at $v_i$ if $p$ owns $v_i$, and the successor chosen by $\tau$ at $v_i$ otherwise. It is the play…
nodes.title: Outcome of two positional strategies

nodes.summary: In a parity game, for every player $p$, no position lies both in the winning region of $p$ and in the winning region of the opponent of $p$.
nodes.title: The winning regions of the two players are disjoint

nodes.summary: In a parity game, let $\sigma$ be a positional strategy of player $p$ that wins from a position $v$, and let $w$ be a position with a move from $v$ to $w$ such that $w = \sigma(v)$ if $p$ owns $v$. Then $\sigma$ wins from $w$.
nodes.title: Winning strategies keep winning along allowed moves

nodes.summary: In a parity game, let $v$ be a position in the winning region of player $p$ that is owned by the opponent of $p$. Then every position $w$ with a move from $v$ to $w$ is in the winning region of $p$.
nodes.title: Opponent moves stay in the winning region

nodes.summary: In a parity game, let $\sigma$ be a positional strategy of player $p$ that wins from a position $v$ owned by $p$. Then the successor $\sigma(v)$ chosen by $\sigma$ is in the winning region of $p$.
nodes.title: A winning strategy's move stays in the winning region

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $X$ a set of positions. The controllable predecessor $\mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$ of $X$ for $p$ is the set of positions $v$ such that either $v$ is owned by $p$ and some move from $v$ leads into $X$, or $v$ is not owned by $p$ and every move from $v$ leads into $X$.
nodes.title: Controllable predecessor

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. The attractor operator of $T$ for $p$ is the monotone map on sets of positions sending $X$ to $T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p$ is the controllable predecessor for $p$.
nodes.title: Attractor operator

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. The attractor of $T$ for $p$ is the least fixed point of the attractor operator $X \mapsto T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$ on sets of positions, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p$ is the controllable predecessor for $p$.
nodes.title: Attractor

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player, $T$ a set of positions and $n$ a natural number. The $n$-th attractor stage $S_n$ of $T$ for $p$ is the set obtained by applying the attractor operator $X \mapsto T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$ $n$ times to $\emptyset$, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p$ is the controllable predecessor for $p$; thus $S_0 = \emptyset$ and $S_{n+1} = T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(S_n)$.
nodes.title: Attractor stages

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions, and let $A$ be the attractor of $T$ for $p$. Then $T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(A) = A$, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p(A)$ is the controllable predecessor of $A$ for $p$; that is, $A$ is a fixed point of the attractor operator $X \mapsto T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$.
nodes.title: The attractor is a fixed point

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. If a set $X$ of positions satisfies $T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X) \subseteq X$, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p$ is the controllable predecessor for $p$, then the attractor of $T$ for $p$ is contained in $X$.
nodes.title: The attractor lies in every closed set

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game with finitely many positions, $N$ of them, let $p$ be a player and $T$ a set of positions. Then the attractor of $T$ for $p$ equals the $N$-th attractor stage of $T$ for $p$, that is, the result of applying the attractor operator $X \mapsto T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$ $N$ times to $\emptyset$, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p$ is the controllable predecessor for $p$.
nodes.title: The attractor stabilizes after as many stages as there are positions

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. The attractor strategy of $p$ for $T$ is the positional strategy of $p$ that at a position $v$ moves to a successor of $v$ lying in the $n$-th attractor stage of $T$ for $p$, for the least $n$ for which $v$ has such a successor, and to an arbitrary successor of $v$ if no successor of $v$ lies in any attractor stage.
nodes.title: Attractor strategy

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player, $T$ a set of positions, $n$ a natural number and $S_n$ the $n$-th attractor stage of $T$ for $p$. If a position $v$ owned by $p$ lies in the controllable predecessor $\mathrm{cpre}_p(S_n)$ of $S_n$ for $p$, then the successor that the attractor strategy of $p$ for $T$ chooses at $v$ lies in $S_n$.
nodes.title: The attractor strategy moves into the stage from its controllable predecessor

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player, $T$ a set of positions and $n$ a natural number. If $\pi$ is a play of $G$ that conforms to the attractor strategy of $p$ for $T$ and whose initial position $\pi_0$ lies in the $n$-th attractor stage of $T$ for $p$, then $\pi_i \in T$ for some $i < n$.
nodes.title: The attractor strategy reaches the target from an attractor stage

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player, $\sigma$ a positional strategy of $p$, $T$ a set of positions and $v$ a position. The strategy $\sigma$ forces a visit to $T$ from $v$ when every play $\pi$ of $G$ with $\pi_0 = v$ that conforms to $\sigma$ visits $T$, that is, $\pi_i \in T$ for some $i \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: Forcing a visit to a set

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game with finitely many positions, $N$ of them, let $p$ be a player and $T$ a set of positions. If $\pi$ is a play of $G$ that conforms to the attractor strategy of $p$ for $T$ and whose initial position $\pi_0$ lies in the attractor of $T$ for $p$, then $\pi_i \in T$ for some $i < N$.
nodes.title: The attractor strategy reaches the target from the attractor

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game with finitely many positions, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. From every position $v$ of the attractor of $T$ for $p$, the attractor strategy of $p$ for $T$ forces a visit to $T$: every play from $v$ conforming to it visits $T$.
nodes.title: The attractor strategy forces a visit

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game and $p$ a player. A set $U$ of positions is a trap for $p$ when, for every position $v \in U$, every move from $v$ leads into $U$ if $v$ belongs to $p$, and some move from $v$ leads into $U$ if $v$ does not belong to $p$. Thus $p$ cannot force the play out of $U$.
nodes.title: Trap for a player

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. The complement of the attractor of $T$ for $p$ is a trap for $p$.
nodes.title: The complement of an attractor is a trap

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. If a set $U$ of positions is a trap for $p$ and is disjoint from $T$, then $U$ is disjoint from the attractor of $T$ for $p$.
nodes.title: Traps disjoint from a set avoid its attractor

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $U$ a set of positions. The trap strategy for $U$ is the positional strategy of the opponent of $p$ that, at each position $v$, moves to some position $w \in U$ with a move from $v$ to $w$ if there is one, and to an arbitrary position reachable from $v$ in one move otherwise.
nodes.title: Trap strategy

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $U$ a trap for $p$. If $\pi$ is a play with $\pi_0 \in U$ that conforms to the trap strategy of the opponent of $p$ for $U$, then $\pi_i \in U$ for every $i \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: The trap strategy stays in the trap

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player, $T$ a set of positions and $A$ the attractor of $T$ for $p$. If $\pi$ is a play starting at a position outside $A$ that conforms to the trap strategy of the opponent of $p$ for the complement of $A$, then $\pi_i \notin T$ for every $i \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: The trap strategy avoids the target

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. If a position $v$ is not in the attractor of $T$ for $p$, then no positional strategy of $p$ forces a visit to $T$ from $v$.
nodes.title: No strategy forces a visit from outside the attractor

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game with finitely many positions, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. A position $v$ lies in the attractor of $T$ for $p$ if and only if some positional strategy of $p$ forces a visit to $T$ from $v$.
nodes.title: Characterization of the attractor

nodes.summary: In a parity game $G$, the winning region of a player $p$, the set of positions from which $p$ has a winning positional strategy, is a trap for the opponent of $p$.
nodes.title: Winning regions are traps for the opponent

nodes.summary: An encoded finite parity game on the $n$ positions $0, \dots, n - 1$ consists of an owner for each position, given as a Boolean (false for the even player, true for the odd player), a move relation, given as a Boolean-valued $n \times n$ matrix, and a priority for each position, given as a natural number.
nodes.title: Encoded parity game

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game on the positions $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which every position has a move to some position. The associated parity game has the same positions, moves and priorities, and a position is owned by the odd player if $G$ assigns it to the odd player and by the even player otherwise; every position has a move by the hypothesis on $G$.
nodes.title: The parity game of a serial encoded game

nodes.summary: The dual of an encoded parity game $G$ is the encoded parity game with the same positions and moves in which every position is owned by the other player than in $G$ and has priority one more than in $G$.
nodes.title: Dual parity game

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game, $p$ a player (encoded as a Boolean: false for even, true for odd), and $U$, $X$ sets of positions. The controllable predecessor of $X$ for $p$ inside $U$ is the set of positions $v \in U$ such that either $v$ is owned by $p$ and some move of $G$ goes from $v$ to a position of $U \cap X$, or $v$ is not owned by $p$ and every move of $G$ from $v$ to a position of $U$ ends in $X$.
nodes.title: Controllable predecessor inside a set of positions

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game on $n$ positions, $p$ a player (encoded as a Boolean: false for even, true for odd), and $T$, $U$ sets of positions. The attractor of $T$ for $p$ inside $U$ is the set obtained from $\emptyset$ by applying $n$ times the map $X \mapsto (T \cap U) \cup \mathrm{CPre}_p^U(X)$, where $\mathrm{CPre}_p^U(X)$ is the controllable predecessor of $X$ for $p$ inside $U$.
nodes.title: Attractor inside a set of positions

nodes.summary: The rank of a priority `p` among the distinct priorities occurring in the game: the number of distinct priorities `q < p` that occur.
nodes.title: Rank of a priority in a parity game

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game on the positions $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. The compressed priority of a natural number $p$ is $2r + (p \bmod 2)$, where $r$ is the rank of $p$ in $G$: the number of distinct priorities $q < p$ that occur in $G$.
nodes.title: Compressed priority

nodes.summary: For an encoded parity game $G$ on $n$ positions, the compressed game has the same owners and moves as $G$ and gives each position $v$ the priority $2r + (q \bmod 2)$, where $q$ is the priority of $v$ in $G$ and $r$ is the number of distinct priorities occurring in $G$ that are smaller than $q$.
nodes.title: Priority compression

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game, and for a natural number $p$ let the rank of $p$ be the number of distinct priorities $q < p$ that occur in $G$. For every position $v$ of $G$, the rank of the priority of $v$ is strictly less than the number of distinct priorities that occur in $G$.
nodes.title: Priority ranks are below the number of priorities

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game, and for a natural number $p$ let the rank of $p$ be the number of distinct priorities $q < p$ that occur in $G$. If $v$ and $w$ are positions of $G$ and the priority of $w$ is strictly less than the priority of $v$, then the rank of the priority of $w$ is strictly less than the rank of the priority of $v$.
nodes.title: Strict monotonicity of priority ranks

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game, and for a natural number $p$ let the rank of $p$ be the number of distinct priorities $q < p$ that occur in $G$. If $v$ and $w$ are positions of $G$ and the priority of $w$ is at most the priority of $v$, then the rank of the priority of $w$ is at most the rank of the priority of $v$.
nodes.title: Monotonicity of priority ranks

nodes.summary: For an encoded parity game $G$ on $n$ positions, every priority of the priority-compressed game of $G$ is strictly less than $2n$.
nodes.title: Bound on compressed priorities

nodes.summary: For an encoded parity game $G$ and positions $v$, $w$, the priority of $v$ is smaller than the priority of $w$ in the priority-compressed game of $G$ if and only if it is smaller in $G$.
nodes.title: Priority compression preserves and reflects the order of priorities

nodes.summary: For an encoded parity game $G$ and every position $v$, the priority of $v$ in the priority-compressed game of $G$ has the same parity as the priority of $v$ in $G$.
nodes.title: Priority compression preserves parity

nodes.summary: For an encoded parity game $G$ and a set $U$ of positions, the maximal priority on $U$ is the largest priority of $G$ at a position of $U$, or $0$ if $U$ is empty.

Rabin and Streett automata

nodes.summary: A Rabin automaton is a nondeterministic automaton together with a set of Rabin pairs $(E, F)$, each a pair of sets of states. A run is accepting when some pair is hit: the run visits $E$ infinitely often and $F$ only finitely often.
nodes.title: Rabin automaton

nodes.summary: An infinite word $x$ is accepted by a Rabin automaton $r$ if and only if there is a run $s$ of $r$ on $x$ and a Rabin pair $(E, F)$ of $r$ such that $s$ visits $E$ infinitely often and visits $F$ only finitely often.
nodes.title: Membership in the language of a Rabin automaton

nodes.summary: Given a Rabin automaton with set of Rabin pairs $\mathcal{R}$, this is the Muller automaton with the same states, initial states and transitions whose accepting family consists of the sets $S$ of states for which some pair $(E, F) \in \mathcal{R}$ satisfies $S \cap E \neq \emptyset$ and $S \cap F = \emptyset$. A Muller automaton accepts a run when the set of states that the run visits infinitely often belongs to…
nodes.title: Muller presentation of a Rabin automaton

nodes.summary: If the state space is finite, then a Rabin automaton $r$ accepts the same language as its Muller presentation: the Muller automaton with the same transitions and initial states as $r$ whose acceptance sets are the sets $S$ of states such that, for some Rabin pair $(E, F)$ of $r$, $S$ meets $E$ and is disjoint from $F$.
nodes.title: Rabin-to-Muller conversion preserves the language

nodes.summary: A Streett automaton is a nondeterministic automaton together with a set of Streett pairs $(E, F)$, each a pair of sets of states. A run is accepting when every pair is respected: if the run visits $E$ infinitely often then it also visits $F$ infinitely often.
nodes.title: Streett automaton

nodes.summary: An infinite word $x$ is accepted by a Streett automaton $r$ if and only if there is a run $s$ of $r$ on $x$ such that for every Streett pair $(E, F)$ of $r$, if $s$ visits $E$ infinitely often then $s$ visits $F$ infinitely often.
nodes.title: Membership in the language of a Streett automaton

nodes.summary: Given a Streett automaton with set of Streett pairs $\mathcal{P}$, this is the Muller automaton with the same states, initial states and transitions whose accepting family consists of the sets $S$ of states such that every pair $(E, F) \in \mathcal{P}$ with $S \cap E \neq \emptyset$ also satisfies $S \cap F \neq \emptyset$. A Muller automaton accepts a run when the set of states that the run visits infinitely often…
nodes.title: Muller presentation of a Streett automaton

nodes.summary: If the state space is finite, then a Streett automaton $r$ accepts the same language as its Muller presentation: the Muller automaton with the same transitions and initial states as $r$ whose acceptance sets are the sets $S$ of states such that, for every Streett pair $(E, F)$ of $r$, if $S$ meets $E$ then $S$ meets $F$.
nodes.title: Streett-to-Muller conversion preserves the language

nodes.summary: Given a parity automaton with priority function $\Omega$ from states to natural numbers, this is the Rabin automaton with the same states, initial states and transitions whose Rabin pairs are the pairs $(E_i, F_i)$ for $i \in \mathbb{N}$, where $E_i = \{s : \Omega(s) = 2i\}$ and $F_i = \{s : \Omega(s) > 2i\}$.
nodes.title: Rabin presentation of a parity automaton

nodes.summary: If the state space is finite, then a parity automaton $a$ accepts the same language as its Rabin presentation: the Rabin automaton with the same transitions and initial states as $a$ whose Rabin pairs are the pairs $(E_i, F_i)$ for $i \in \mathbb{N}$, where $E_i$ is the set of states of priority $2i$ and $F_i$ the set of states of priority greater than $2i$.
nodes.title: Parity-to-Rabin conversion preserves the language

nodes.summary: Given a parity automaton with priority function $\Omega$ from states to natural numbers, this is the Streett automaton with the same states, initial states and transitions whose Streett pairs are the pairs $(E_i, F_i)$ for $i \in \mathbb{N}$, where $E_i = \{s : \Omega(s) = 2i + 1\}$ and $F_i = \{s : \Omega(s) > 2i + 1\}$.
nodes.title: Streett presentation of a parity automaton

nodes.summary: If the state space is finite, then a parity automaton $a$ accepts the same language as its Streett presentation: the Streett automaton with the same transitions and initial states as $a$ whose Streett pairs are the pairs $(E_i, F_i)$ for $i \in \mathbb{N}$, where $E_i$ is the set of states of priority $2i + 1$ and $F_i$ the set of states of priority greater than $2i + 1$.
nodes.title: Parity-to-Streett conversion preserves the language

nodes.summary: The Muller automaton of a parity automaton is the Muller presentation of its Rabin presentation. It has the same states, initial states and transitions, and its accepting family consists of the sets $S$ of states for which there is a natural number $i$ such that $S$ contains a state of priority $2i$ and no state of priority greater than $2i$. nodes.summary: If the state space is finite, then a parity automaton accepts the same language as its Muller presentation, the Muller automaton obtained by converting it to its Rabin presentation and that to a Muller automaton.
nodes.title: Parity-to-Muller conversion preserves the language

nodes.summary: Given a Rabin automaton, this is the Streett automaton with the same states, initial states and transitions and the same set of pairs.

nodes.summary: Let $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. A single-tape Turing machine $M$ runs in space $s$ when, for every input word $l$ of length $|l|$, every configuration reachable from the initial configuration of $M$ on $l$ uses at most $s(|l|)$ cells, whether or not the run halts. The cells used by a configuration are the head cell together with the cells on each side of it up to the outermost non-blank cell.
nodes.title: Space-bounded single-tape machines

nodes.summary: A single-tape machine is a linear bounded automaton when it runs in space $n + 1$ on inputs of length $n$: every configuration of its run on an input of length $n$ uses at most $n + 1$ cells, whether or not the run halts.
nodes.title: Linear bounded automaton

nodes.summary: If a single-tape machine runs in space $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and $s' : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfies $s(n) \le s'(n)$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then it runs in space $s'$.
nodes.title: Space bounds can be weakened

nodes.summary: If a single-tape machine runs in space $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, then $\max(1, n) \le s(n)$ for the length $n$ of every input word, since the initial configuration on an input of length $n$ uses $\max(1, n)$ cells.
nodes.title: A space bound is at least the space of the input

nodes.summary: A machine that, on a blank cell, writes a blank and does not move is a linear bounded automaton. Its head never leaves a blank cell, so it stays on the input or on the two blank cells next to it, and it writes non-blank symbols only on the input. The machine may change state on a blank cell, or halt there.
nodes.title: A machine that, on a blank cell, writes a blank and does not move is a linear bounded automaton

nodes.summary: For a single-tape machine with state set $Q$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the configuration bound at $k$ is the number $(|Q| + 1)(|\Sigma| + 1)(|\Sigma| + 2)^{2k}$.
nodes.title: Configuration bound

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape machine with state set $Q$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, where a configuration uses the cell under the head and the cells on either side of it up to the last non-blank one. For every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, at most $(|Q| + 1)(|\Sigma| + 1)(|\Sigma| + 2)^{2k}$ configurations of $M$ use at most $k$ cells.
nodes.title: Configurations of bounded space are finitely many

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape machine with state set $Q$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ that runs in space $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. If $M$ halts on an input word $w$ of length $n$, then from the initial configuration on $w$ it reaches a configuration in the halting state in at most $(|Q| + 1)(|\Sigma| + 1)(|\Sigma| + 2)^{2 s(n)}$ steps.
nodes.title: Space-bounded machines halt within the configuration bound

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape machine with state set $Q$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, fix any primitive recursive coding of $\Sigma$, and let $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be computable. If $M$ runs in space $s$, then the set of input words over $\Sigma$ on which $M$ halts is computable.
nodes.title: Halting of a machine running in computable space is computable

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape machine over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, and fix any primitive recursive coding of $\Sigma$. If $M$ is a linear bounded automaton, then the set of input words over $\Sigma$ on which $M$ halts is computable.
nodes.title: Halting of a linear bounded automaton is decidable

Evaluate the $n$-bit Kogge–Stone carry-lookahead adder with $K$ levels in the Boolean interpretation of the XOR/AND/OR basis, on the input made of the bits of $x$, the bits of $y$ and $c$. Then for every $i < n$, output $i$ of the adder is bit $i$ (the bit of weight $2^i$) of the sum $x + y + c$ taken modulo $2^n$.

nodes.summary: Let $n, K \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \le 2^K$, let $x, y$ be $n$-bit vectors and let $c$ be a carry-in bit. Evaluate the $n$-bit Kogge-Stone carry-lookahead adder with $K$ levels over the Boolean XOR/AND/OR basis on the input that lists the bits of $x$ from least to most significant, then those of $y$ in the same order, then $c$. nodes.summary: For all $n, K \in \mathbb{N}$, the $n$-bit Kogge-Stone carry-lookahead adder with $K$ levels has exactly $5n + 3nK$ gates: $2n$ in the first level, $3n$ in each of the $K$ Kogge-Stone levels, and $3n$ in the final level.
nodes.title: Gate count of the carry-lookahead adder

nodes.summary: For a signature $\sigma$, the depth interpretation is the interpretation of $\sigma$ in $\mathbb{N}$ that sends an operation symbol of arity $k$, applied to argument depths $d_0, \dots, d_{k-1}$, to $\max(0, d_0, \dots, d_{k-1}) + 1$: a gate is one deeper than its deepest argument, and a gate without arguments has depth $1$.
nodes.title: The depth interpretation

nodes.summary: For every program $p$ over a signature $\sigma$, the depth of each gate of $p$ equals the value of that gate when $p$ is evaluated under the depth interpretation of $\sigma$ with every input set to $0$.
nodes.title: Gate depths are evaluation in the depth interpretation

nodes.summary: For each gate of the arithmetic basis (XOR, AND or OR) and all argument depths $d_0, d_1 \in \mathbb{N}$, the depth interpretation of the arithmetic signature assigns the gate the depth $\max(d_0, d_1) + 1$.
nodes.title: Depth of an arithmetic gate

nodes.summary: In the program made of level $0$ and the first $k$ Kogge-Stone levels of the $n$-bit adder, where inputs have depth $0$ and a gate is one deeper than its deepest argument, for every bit $i < n$ the gate holding the generate signal of bit $i$ has depth $2k + 1$ and the gate holding its propagate signal has depth $k + 1$.
nodes.title: Depths after each level

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $n$, $K$ and $i < n$, in the gate program of the $n$-bit adder with $K$ Kogge–Stone levels, the carry gate of bit $i$ in the final level (gate $3i + 1$ of that level) has depth $\max(2K + 1, K + 2) + 1$, where inputs have depth $0$ and each gate is one deeper than its deepest argument.
nodes.title: Depth of the carry gates

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $n$, $K$ and $i < n$, in the gate program of the $n$-bit adder with $K$ Kogge–Stone levels, the sum gate of bit $i$ in the final level (gate $3i + 2$ of that level) has depth $2$ if $i = 0$ and depth $\max(2K + 1, K + 2) + 2$ otherwise, where inputs have depth $0$ and each gate is one deeper than its deepest argument.
nodes.title: Depth of the sum gates

nodes.summary: For all $K \ge 1$ and $n \ge 2$, the $n$-bit Kogge-Stone carry-lookahead adder with $K$ levels has depth exactly $2K + 3$, the depth being the largest depth of an output with the inputs at depth $0$.
nodes.title: Exact depth of the carry-lookahead adder

nodes.summary: For every $n \ge 2$, the $n$-bit Kogge-Stone carry-lookahead adder with $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$ levels has depth exactly $2 \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 5$, the depth being the largest depth of an output with the inputs at depth $0$.
nodes.title: Depth of the carry-lookahead adder with logarithmically many levels

nodes.summary: For $i \in \mathbb{N}$, the carry depth of bit $i$ is $0$ if $i = 0$ and $2i + 1$ if $i \ge 1$. It is used as the depth of the carry into bit $i$ of the ripple-carry adder, where the carry into bit $0$ is the carry-in input.
nodes.title: Carry depth in the ripple-carry adder

nodes.summary: Let $c(i)$ be the carry depth of bit $i$: $c(0) = 0$ and $c(i) = 2i + 1$ for $i \ge 1$. The formula assigns to gate $j$ of the ripple-carry adder, for every $j \in \mathbb{N}$, the depth $1$ when $j \bmod 5$ is $0$ or $2$, the depth $\max(1, c(\lfloor j/5 \rfloor)) + 1$ when $j \bmod 5$ is $1$ or $3$, and the depth $c(\lfloor j/5 \rfloor + 1)$ when $j \bmod 5 = 4$.

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$, $g \le 5n$ and $j < g$, evaluating the first $g$ gates of the $n$-bit ripple-carry adder in $\mathbb{N}$, with every input at depth $0$ and every gate one deeper than its deepest argument, gives gate $j$ the depth $d(j)$. nodes.summary: For every $n \ge 1$, the $n$-bit ripple-carry adder has depth $2n + 1$, the length of its carry chain.

nodes.summary: The wire count of a flat Boolean circuit on $n$ inputs, given as a list of gates, is the sum over its gates of the lengths of their predecessor lists: every reference of a gate to a gate index is counted, with multiplicity, while input variables and constants contribute nothing and the modulus of a mod gate is not counted.

Two's complement subtraction and overflow

nodes.summary: Let $x$ and $y$ be $n$-bit words and let $\bar y$ be the bitwise complement of $y$. Adding $x$ and $\bar y$ with carry in $1$ gives the $n$-bit result $x - y$ (the difference modulo $2^n$), and the carry out is $1$ exactly when there is no unsigned borrow, that is, when $y \le x$ as unsigned integers.
nodes.title: Subtraction by addition

nodes.summary: Let $x$ and $y$ be $n$-bit words and let $\bar y$ be the bitwise complement of $y$. Evaluate the $n$-bit ripple-carry adder, with XOR, AND and OR gates, on the bits of $x$, the bits of $\bar y$ and carry in $1$. Then for every $i < n$, output $i$ is bit $i$ (counting from the least significant bit $0$) of $x - y$ modulo $2^n$.
nodes.title: The ripple-carry adder subtracts

nodes.summary: Let $x$ and $y$ be $n$-bit words and let $\bar y$ be the bitwise complement of $y$. Evaluate the $n$-bit ripple-carry adder, with XOR, AND and OR gates, on the bits of $x$, the bits of $\bar y$ and carry in $1$. Its carry out (output $n$) is $1$ exactly when there is no unsigned borrow in $x - y$, that is, when $y \le x$ as unsigned integers.
nodes.title: Carry out of ripple-carry subtraction

nodes.summary: Let $x$ and $y$ be $n$-bit words, let $\bar y$ be the bitwise complement of $y$, and let $K$ satisfy $n \le 2^K$. Evaluate the $n$-bit carry-lookahead adder with $K$ levels, with XOR, AND and OR gates, on the bits of $x$, the bits of $\bar y$ and carry in $1$. Then for every $i < n$, output $i$ is bit $i$ (counting from the least significant bit $0$) of $x - y$ modulo $2^n$.
nodes.title: The carry-lookahead adder subtracts

nodes.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $x$ and $y$ be $n$-bit words. The two's complement addition $x + y$ overflows (the sum of the two's complement values of $x$ and $y$ is at least $2^{n-1}$ or less than $-2^{n-1}$) exactly when the carry into the sign bit $n - 1$ differs from the carry out of it, both carries taken when adding $x$ and $y$ with carry in $0$.
nodes.title: Signed overflow is the XOR of the last two carries

nodes.summary: The $n$-bit overflow adder is the $n$-bit ripple-carry adder with one extra XOR gate. It has the same $2n + 1$ inputs (the bits of the two summands, then the carry in) and $5n + 1$ gates: the $5n$ gates of the ripple-carry adder, followed by an XOR of the carry into bit $n - 1$ and the carry into bit $n$ (the carry out). Here the carry into bit $0$ is the carry in, and for $n = 0$ the index $n - 1$ is read as $0$.…
nodes.title: The overflow adder

nodes.summary: Let $x$ and $y$ be $n$-bit words and let $c$ be a carry-in bit. Evaluate the $n$-bit overflow adder and the $n$-bit ripple-carry adder, with XOR, AND and OR gates, on the bits of $x$, the bits of $y$ and $c$. Then for every $o < n + 1$, output $o$ of the overflow adder equals output $o$ of the ripple-carry adder: the first $n + 1$ outputs (the $n$ sum bits and the carry out) agree.
nodes.title: The overflow adder extends the ripple-carry adder

nodes.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $x$ and $y$ be $n$-bit words. Evaluate the $n$-bit overflow adder, with XOR, AND and OR gates, on the bits of $x$, the bits of $y$ and carry in $0$. Its last output (output $n + 1$) is $1$ exactly when the two's complement addition $x + y$ overflows, that is, when the sum of the two's complement values of $x$ and $y$ is at least $2^{n-1}$ or less than $-2^{n-1}$.
nodes.title: The overflow flag

nodes.summary: Let $x$ and $y$ be $n$-bit words. Evaluate the $n$-bit overflow adder, with XOR, AND and OR gates, on the bits of $x$, the bits of $y$ and carry in $0$. Then for every $i < n$, output $i$ is bit $i$ (counting from the least significant bit $0$) of $x + y$ modulo $2^n$.

nodes.summary: The binary encoding of a natural number $n$ is the list of its base-$2$ digits, least significant first, with the digit $1$ written as the Boolean value true and the digit $0$ as false. The list has no trailing zero digit, so $0$ is encoded by the empty list.

Arithmetic circuits for matrix multiplication

nodes.summary: For a type $F$ of scalars and $m, r, n \in \mathbb{N}$, a matrix arithmetic circuit is an arithmetic circuit over $F$ whose inputs are indexed by the entries $(i, k)$ of an $m \times r$ matrix together with the entries $(k, j)$ of an $r \times n$ matrix, and whose outputs are indexed by the entries $(i, j)$ of an $m \times n$ matrix.
nodes.title: Matrix arithmetic circuit

nodes.summary: For matrices $A \in F^{m \times r}$ and $B \in F^{r \times n}$, the input assignment of $(A, B)$ is the function on the entry positions $(i, k)$ of an $m \times r$ matrix together with the entry positions $(k, j)$ of an $r \times n$ matrix that sends $(i, k)$ to $A_{ik}$ and $(k, j)$ to $B_{kj}$. It supplies the inputs of a matrix arithmetic circuit.
nodes.title: Matrix input assignment

nodes.summary: A circuit $c$ over a field $F$ whose inputs are the entries of an $m \times r$ matrix and an $r \times n$ matrix computes matrix multiplication when, for all matrices $A \in F^{m \times r}$ and $B \in F^{r \times n}$ and all $i < m$, $j < n$, its output at $(i, j)$ on the entries of $A$ and $B$ equals $(AB)_{ij}$.
nodes.title: Circuits that compute the matrix product

nodes.summary: For a type $F$ of scalars and $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, the outer-product matrix circuit is the matrix arithmetic circuit for an $m \times 1$ matrix times a $1 \times n$ matrix with exactly $mn$ gates: for $i < m$ and $j < n$, the gate for $(i, j)$ multiplies the input at entry $(i, 0)$ of the first matrix by the input at entry $(0, j)$ of the second, and the output at $(i, j)$ is that gate.

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a semiring and $A$, $B$, $C$ types. An array $T : A \to B \to C \to F$ has trilinear rank at most $r$ when there are $s \le r$ and functions $u_i : A \to F$, $v_i : B \to F$, $w_i : C \to F$ for $i = 1, \dots, s$ such that $T(a, b, c) = \sum_{i=1}^{s} u_i(a)\,v_i(b)\,w_i(c)$ for all $a \in A$, $b \in B$, $c \in C$.
nodes.title: Trilinear rank at most $r$

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a semiring and $T : A \to B \to C \to F$ an array. If $T$ has trilinear rank at most $r$ and $r \le s$, then $T$ has trilinear rank at most $s$.
nodes.title: Monotonicity of trilinear rank bounds

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a semiring and $A$, $B$, $C$ finite types. Every array $T : A \to B \to C \to F$ has trilinear rank at most $|A| \cdot |B| \cdot |C|$.
nodes.title: Trivial upper bound on trilinear rank

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a semiring and let $A$, $B$, $C$ be finite types. The trilinear rank of a coefficient array $T : A \to B \to C \to F$ is the least $r \in \mathbb{N}$ for which there are $s \le r$ functions $u_i : A \to F$, $v_i : B \to F$, $w_i : C \to F$ with $T(a, b, c) = \sum_{i=1}^{s} u_i(a)\,v_i(b)\,w_i(c)$ for all $a \in A$, $b \in B$, $c \in C$.
nodes.title: Trilinear rank

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a semiring, let $A$, $B$, $C$ be finite types, let $T : A \to B \to C \to F$ be a coefficient array, and let $R(T)$ be its trilinear rank. Then there are $s \le R(T)$ functions $u_i : A \to F$, $v_i : B \to F$, $w_i : C \to F$ with $T(a, b, c) = \sum_{i=1}^{s} u_i(a)\,v_i(b)\,w_i(c)$ for all $a \in A$, $b \in B$, $c \in C$.
nodes.title: The trilinear rank is attained

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a semiring, let $A$, $B$, $C$ be finite types, and let $T : A \to B \to C \to F$ be a coefficient array. If there are $s \le r$ functions $u_i : A \to F$, $v_i : B \to F$, $w_i : C \to F$ with $T(a, b, c) = \sum_{i=1}^{s} u_i(a)\,v_i(b)\,w_i(c)$ for all $a \in A$, $b \in B$, $c \in C$, then the trilinear rank of $T$ is at most $r$.
nodes.title: Decompositions bound the trilinear rank

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a semiring and $A$, $B$, $C$ finite types. For every array $T : A \to B \to C \to F$ and every natural number $r$, $T$ has trilinear rank at most $r$ if and only if the trilinear rank of $T$ (the least length of a decomposition of $T$ into rank-one arrays) is at most $r$.
nodes.title: Rank bounds via the trilinear rank

nodes.summary: For a field $F$ and types $A$, $B$, $C$, write $F^X$ for the $F$-vector space of functions $X \to F$. The space of trilinear tensors over $F$ indexed by $A$, $B$, $C$ is the tensor product $(F^A \otimes_F F^B) \otimes_F F^C$ over $F$.
nodes.title: Trilinear tensors

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a field, let $A$ and $C$ be finite types, let $B$ be a type, and write $F^X$ for the space of functions $X \to F$. The coefficient map is the $F$-linear isomorphism from $(F^A \otimes_F F^B) \otimes_F F^C$ to the space of arrays $A \to B \to C \to F$ that sends each pure tensor $(u \otimes v) \otimes w$ to the array $(a, b, c) \mapsto u(a)\,v(b)\,w(c)$.
nodes.title: Coefficient array of a trilinear tensor

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a field, let $A$ and $C$ be finite types and let $B$ be a type. For $u : A \to F$, $v : B \to F$, $w : C \to F$ and $a \in A$, $b \in B$, $c \in C$, the coefficient array of the pure tensor $(u \otimes v) \otimes w$ takes the value $u(a)\,v(b)\,w(c)$ at $(a, b, c)$.
nodes.title: Coefficients of a pure tensor

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a field and $A$, $B$, $C$ types. A rank-one trilinear term with factors $u : A \to F$, $v : B \to F$ and $w : C \to F$ determines the pure tensor $(u \otimes v) \otimes w$ in the trilinear tensor space over $F$ indexed by $A$, $B$, $C$.
nodes.title: The pure tensor of a rank-one term

reading_title.source: Tensor rank at most $r$

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a field and $A$, $B$, $C$ types. An element $T$ of $(F^A \otimes_F F^B) \otimes_F F^C$ has tensor rank at most $r$ when there are $s \le r$ and functions $u_i : A \to F$, $v_i : B \to F$, $w_i : C \to F$ for $i = 1, \dots, s$ such that $T = \sum_{i=1}^{s} (u_i \otimes v_i) \otimes w_i$.
nodes.title: Tensor rank at most $r$

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a field and $A$, $B$, $C$ types with $A$ and $C$ finite, and let $T$ be an element of $(F^A \otimes_F F^B) \otimes_F F^C$. For every natural number $r$, $T$ has tensor rank at most $r$ if and only if its coefficient array $A \to B \to C \to F$, obtained by the canonical linear equivalence, has trilinear rank at most $r$.
nodes.title: Tensor rank bounds agree with coefficient rank bounds

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a field and let $A$, $B$, $C$ be finite types. The tensor rank of a trilinear tensor $T$ over $F$ indexed by $A$, $B$, $C$ is the least $r \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $T$ is a sum of at most $r$ pure tensors $(u \otimes v) \otimes w$ with $u : A \to F$, $v : B \to F$ and $w : C \to F$.
nodes.title: Tensor rank

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a field, let $A$, $B$, $C$ be finite types, let $T$ be a trilinear tensor over $F$ indexed by $A$, $B$, $C$, and let $R(T)$ be its tensor rank. Then $T$ is a sum of at most $R(T)$ pure tensors $(u \otimes v) \otimes w$ with $u : A \to F$, $v : B \to F$ and $w : C \to F$.
nodes.title: The tensor rank is attained

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a field, let $A$, $B$, $C$ be finite types, and let $T$ be a trilinear tensor over $F$ indexed by $A$, $B$, $C$. If $T$ is a sum of at most $r$ pure tensors $(u \otimes v) \otimes w$ with $u : A \to F$, $v : B \to F$ and $w : C \to F$, then the tensor rank of $T$ is at most $r$.
nodes.title: Decompositions bound the tensor rank

nodes.summary: The index set of an $m \times n$ matrix: pairs $(i, j)$ of a row index $i \in \{0, \dots, m-1\}$ and a column index $j \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$.

nodes.summary: For a field $F$ and natural numbers $m$, $n$, $p$, the matrix multiplication tensor is the array over $F$ indexed by triples $((i, j), (j', k), (k', i'))$ of an $m \times n$, an $n \times p$ and a $p \times m$ matrix coordinate, whose entry is $1$ if $j = j'$, $k = k'$ and $i' = i$, and $0$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Matrix multiplication tensor

nodes.summary: For a field $F$ and a natural number $n$, the square matrix multiplication tensor over $F$ is the matrix multiplication tensor for multiplying an $n \times n$ matrix by an $n \times n$ matrix. Its value at a triple of matrix coordinates $((i, j), (j', k), (k', i'))$ is $1$ when $j = j'$, $k = k'$ and $i = i'$, and $0$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Square matrix multiplication tensor

nodes.title: Coefficients of the matrix multiplication structure tensor

nodes.summary: For a field $F$ and a natural number $n$, the square matrix multiplication rank of $F$ at $n$ is the tensor rank of the structure tensor of multiplying two $n \times n$ matrices over $F$: the least number of pure tensors whose sum is that structure tensor.
nodes.title: Square matrix multiplication rank

nodes.summary: For every field $F$ and natural number $n$, the square matrix multiplication rank of $F$ at $n$ equals the trilinear rank of the square $n \times n$ matrix multiplication tensor over $F$.
nodes.title: Square matrix multiplication rank equals the coefficient tensor rank

Write $T$ for the matrix multiplication tensor over $F$ for $m, n, p$ and, for a natural number $q$, $[q] = \{0, \dots, q - 1\}$. The contraction of $T$ against $A$ and $B$ at output coordinate $(i, k)$ is
nodes.title: Matrix multiplication tensor contraction

nodes.summary: For a field $F$, matrices $A \in F^{m \times n}$ and $B \in F^{n \times p}$, and indices $i < m$ and $k < p$, the contraction of the matrix multiplication tensor against $A$ and $B$ at output coordinate $(i, k)$ equals the entry $(AB)_{ik}$ of the matrix product.
nodes.title: Contracting the matrix multiplication tensor gives the matrix product

nodes.summary: A real number $w$ is a matrix multiplication rank exponent over a field $F$ when $w \ge 0$ and there are a real $C > 0$ and a natural number $N_0 \ge 1$ such that for every $n \ge N_0$ the $n \times n$ matrix multiplication coefficient tensor over $F$ is a sum of at most $C n^w$ rank-one trilinear terms.
nodes.title: Matrix multiplication rank exponent

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a field and $w$ a real number. Then $w$ is a matrix multiplication rank exponent over $F$ if and only if $w \ge 0$ and there are a real $C > 0$ and a natural number $N_0 \ge 1$ such that for every $n \ge N_0$ the tensor rank of the $n \times n$ matrix multiplication structure tensor over $F$ is at most $C n^w$.
nodes.title: Rank exponents via the minimum tensor rank

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a field and let $w \le w'$ be real numbers. If $w$ is a matrix multiplication rank exponent for $F$, then so is $w'$.
nodes.title: Monotonicity of matrix multiplication rank exponents

nodes.summary: The matrix multiplication exponent $\omega(F)$ of a field $F$ is the infimum, taken in $[0, \infty]$, of the real numbers $w$ that are matrix multiplication rank exponents over $F$; it is $\infty$ when there is no such $w$.
nodes.title: Matrix multiplication exponent

nodes.summary: If a real number $w$ is a matrix multiplication rank exponent over a field $F$, then the matrix multiplication exponent $\omega(F)$ of $F$ satisfies $\omega(F) \le w$.
nodes.title: Rank exponents bound the matrix multiplication exponent

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a field and let $W$ be an element of $[0, \infty]$. If $W \le w$ for every real number $w$ that is a matrix multiplication rank exponent over $F$, then $W$ is at most the matrix multiplication exponent $\omega(F)$.
nodes.title: Lower bounds for the matrix multiplication exponent

nodes.summary: For every field $F$ and natural numbers $m, n, p$, the coefficient tensor of multiplying an $m \times n$ matrix by an $n \times p$ matrix over $F$ is a sum of at most $mnp$ rank-one trilinear terms.
nodes.title: Direct rank bound for the matrix multiplication tensor

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a field, let $m, n, p$ be natural numbers, and write $e_x$ for the standard basis vector with index $x$. The matrix multiplication structure tensor $\sum_{i < m,\, j < n,\, k < p} e_{(i,j)} \otimes e_{(j,k)} \otimes e_{(k,i)}$ in $F^{m \times n} \otimes F^{n \times p} \otimes F^{p \times m}$ is a sum of at most $mnp$ pure tensors $u \otimes v \otimes w$.

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a field, let $\omega(F)$ be its matrix multiplication exponent and let $w \ge 0$ be real. nodes.summary: A finite graph is a pair $(n, t)$ of a natural number $n$, the number of vertices, and a finite list $t$ of booleans, read as a row-major edge table. The length of $t$ is not required to be $n^2$.
nodes.title: Finite graphs as edge tables

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a graph with vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ and edge table $t$, a finite list of booleans. For vertices $a, b < n$, there is an edge from $a$ to $b$ exactly when the entry of $t$ at position $an + b$ (counting from $0$) is true; a position beyond the end of $t$ counts as false.

nodes.summary: Variables and relation symbols are indexed by natural numbers. nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a graph and let $(E_j)_{j \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a family of relations, each a predicate on finite lists of vertices of $G$. Relation symbol $0$ is interpreted as the edge relation of $G$: it holds of a list exactly when the list is $[a, b]$ for vertices $a, b$ with an edge from $a$ to $b$. For $i \ge 1$, relation symbol $i$ is interpreted as $E_{i-1}$.
