nodes.title: Satisfaction of an existential second-order sentence

nodes.summary: For a class $K$ of graphs, this is the decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of pairs of a natural number and a list of booleans, to a graph $G \in K$ with $n$ vertices whose edge table has length exactly $n^2$.
nodes.title: Encodings of a graph class as a decision problem

nodes.summary: Graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ are isomorphic if they have the same number of vertices and there is a bijection $\sigma$ from the vertices of $G_1$ to the vertices of $G_2$ such that for all vertices $a, b$ of $G_1$, there is an edge from $a$ to $b$ in $G_1$ if and only if there is an edge from $\sigma(a)$ to $\sigma(b)$ in $G_2$.
nodes.title: Isomorphic graphs

nodes.summary: A class $K$ of graphs is isomorphism-closed if for every $G_1 \in K$, every graph $G_2$ isomorphic to $G_1$ also belongs to $K$.
nodes.title: Isomorphism-closed graph classes

nodes.summary: A class $K$ of graphs is existential second-order definable if there are a natural number $k$, a first-order formula $\varphi$ and a boolean $e$ such that every graph $G$ with $n$ vertices whose edge table has length exactly $n^2$ satisfies the following: if $n > 0$, then $G \in K$ if and only if $G$ satisfies the existential second-order sentence $(k, \varphi)$; if $n = 0$, then $G \in K$ if and only if $e$ is true.
nodes.title: Existential second-order definable graph classes

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a class of finite graphs, each given as a pair $(n, t)$ of a number $n$ of vertices and a row-major edge table $t$ (a list of booleans), and suppose that $K$ is closed under graph isomorphism. Then the decision problem that accepts exactly the bitstrings decoding to a member $(n, t)$ of $K$ whose edge table has length $n^2$ is in NP if and only if $K$ is definable in existential second-order logic: there…
nodes.title: Fagin's theorem: NP is existential second-order logic
Immerman–Vardi theorem

nodes.summary: A finite ordered graph is a pair $(n, t)$ of a natural number $n$ and a finite list $t$ of booleans of any length. Here $n$ is the size of the domain $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, ordered numerically, and $t$ is read as a row-major edge table.
nodes.title: Finite ordered graphs

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an ordered graph with vertices $0, \dots, n - 1$ and edge table $t$, a list of booleans. There is an edge from $a$ to $b$ when the entry of $t$ at position $a n + b$ is true; positions beyond the end of $t$ count as false.
nodes.title: Edge relation of an ordered graph

nodes.summary: Variables and relation symbols are natural numbers. Formulas are built from equalities $x_a = x_b$ and atoms $R_i(x_{a_1}, \dots, x_{a_k})$ by negation, conjunction, disjunction, existential quantification and least-fixed-point formulas $\mathrm{lfp}(R, k, \varphi, (a_1, \dots, a_m))$, the least fixed point of the operator defined by $\varphi$ (with $R$ as the recursive relation, of arity $k$) applied to the tuple…
nodes.title: Formulas of first-order logic with least fixed points

nodes.summary: A relation symbol $R$ occurs only positively in a first-order formula with least fixed points over ordered graphs when every atomic formula with relation symbol $R$ in it, including those inside least-fixed-point subformulas whatever symbol they bind, lies under an even number of negations.
nodes.title: Positive occurrence of a relation symbol

nodes.summary: A relation symbol $R$ occurs only negatively in a formula $\varphi$ of first-order logic with least fixed points when every atomic formula $R(x_{a_1}, \dots, x_{a_k})$ in $\varphi$, including those inside least-fixed-point subformulas, lies under an odd number of negations.
nodes.title: Negative occurrence of a relation symbol

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi$ be a formula of first-order logic with least fixed points, whose relation symbols are natural numbers. All fixed points of $\varphi$ are positive when every least-fixed-point subformula of $\varphi$, nested ones included, binds a relation symbol $R \ge 2$ (so neither the order symbol $0$ nor the edge symbol $1$) and $R$ occurs only positively in the body of that subformula.
nodes.title: Formulas whose fixed points are all positive

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an ordered graph with vertices $0, \dots, n - 1$ and let $(E_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ be predicates on lists of vertices. Relation symbol $0$ holds of a list exactly when it is a pair $(a, b)$ with $a < b$, relation symbol $1$ holds of a list exactly when it is a pair $(a, b)$ with an edge from $a$ to $b$ in $G$, and relation symbol $i + 2$ is interpreted as $E_i$.
nodes.title: Interpretation of relation symbols in an ordered graph

nodes.summary: Let $e$ assign to each relation symbol (a natural number) either an arity or nothing. Whether a first-order formula with least fixed points over ordered graphs is well-formed relative to $e$ is defined by recursion on the formula. An equality of two variables is well-formed. An atomic formula $R(x_1, \dots, x_k)$ is well-formed when $k = a$ if $e(R) = a$; when $k = 2$ if $e$ assigns nothing to $R$ and $R$ is $0$…
nodes.title: Well-formed FO + LFP formulas

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an ordered graph with vertex set $V = \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, let $\rho$ assign a vertex to each variable $0, 1, 2, \dots$, and let $S$ assign to each relation symbol $i$ a predicate $S_i$ on lists of vertices. The truth of a formula is defined by recursion: $x_a = x_b$ holds when $\rho(a) = \rho(b)$; the atom $R_i(x_{a_1}, \dots, x_{a_k})$ holds when $S_i$ holds of $(\rho(a_1), \dots, \rho(a_k))$;…
nodes.title: Evaluation of FO + LFP formulas in an ordered graph

nodes.summary: An ordered graph $G$ with $n > 0$ vertices satisfies a formula $\varphi$ of first-order logic with least fixed points when $\varphi$ is well-formed in the environment where no relation symbol is bound, all fixed points of $\varphi$ are positive, and $\varphi$ is true in $G$ with every variable assigned the vertex $0$, relation symbol $0$ interpreted as the order $<$, relation symbol $1$ as the edge relation, and…
nodes.title: Satisfaction of an FO + LFP formula by an ordered graph

nodes.summary: For a class $K$ of ordered graphs, this is the decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of pairs of a natural number and a list of booleans, to some $G \in K$ whose edge table has length exactly $n^2$, where $n$ is the number of vertices of $G$.
nodes.title: Encodings of a class of ordered graphs

nodes.summary: A class $K$ of ordered graphs is definable in first-order logic with least fixed points when there are a formula $\varphi$ and a boolean $b$ such that every ordered graph $G$ with $n$ vertices whose edge table has length $n^2$ lies in $K$ exactly when either $n > 0$ and $G$ satisfies $\varphi$, or $n = 0$ and $b$ is true.
nodes.title: Definability in FO + LFP

nodes.summary: Source: N. Immerman, "Relational queries definable in polynomial time", Information and Control 68 (1986), 193-243 (STOC 1983); M. Y. Vardi, "The complexity of relational query languages", Proceedings of the Fourteenth Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC 1982), 137-146.
nodes.title: Immerman-Vardi: FO + least fixed point is P on ordered structures
Transitive closure logic and NL

nodes.summary: An ordered graph is encoded as a pair $(n, e)$ of a natural number $n$, the domain size, and a finite list $e$ of booleans of arbitrary length, the edge table in row-major order. It is read as the graph on $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, ordered numerically, with an edge from $a$ to $b$ when the entry of $e$ at position $an + b$ is true; a missing entry counts as false.
nodes.title: Ordered graphs for first-order logic with transitive closure

nodes.summary: For an ordered graph $(n, T)$ with edge table $T$ and elements $a, b < n$, there is an edge from $a$ to $b$ when the entry of $T$ at position $a n + b$ is true; positions beyond the end of $T$ count as false.
nodes.title: Edge relation of an ordered graph for FO + TC

nodes.summary: FO + TC formulas, with variables and relation symbols indexed by natural numbers, are built from equations between two variables and relation symbols applied to lists of variables by negation, conjunction, disjunction, existential quantification (which binds variable $0$, de Bruijn style) and transitive closure $\mathrm{TC}(\varphi; \bar u, \bar v)$ of a formula $\varphi$ applied to two lists $\bar u$, $\bar v$ of…
nodes.title: Formulas of first-order logic with transitive closure

nodes.summary: In an ordered graph with domain $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, relation symbol $0$ holds of a list of elements exactly when the list is $[a, b]$ with $a < b$, relation symbol $1$ holds exactly when the list is $[a, b]$ and there is an edge from $a$ to $b$, and every other relation symbol holds of no list.
nodes.title: Order and edge relations as FO + TC relation symbols

nodes.summary: Fix an ordered graph with domain $D = \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, an assignment $\rho$ of an element of $D$ to each variable index and an assignment $S$ of a relation on lists of elements of $D$ to each relation symbol. The truth value of a formula is defined by recursion. The equation between variables $i$ and $j$ holds when $\rho(i) = \rho(j)$. Relation symbol $i$ applied to variables $j_1, \dots, j_k$ holds when $S_i$…
nodes.title: Evaluation of FO + TC formulas

nodes.summary: The FO + TC formula $\mathrm{TC}(\varphi; (1), (2))$ of arity $1$ whose body $\varphi$ is $E(0, 1) \lor (E(0, 2) \land E(2, 1))$, where $E$ is relation symbol $1$ (the edge relation). In the body, variable $0$ is the source, variable $1$ the target, and variable $2$ is outer variable $0$, shifted by $2$; the endpoint arguments $1$ and $2$ are outer variables, not shifted. So the formula expresses that outer…
nodes.title: Example: parameterized transitive closure in FO + TC

nodes.summary: The FO + TC formula $\mathrm{TC}(\varphi; (0, 1), (2, 3))$ of arity $2$ whose body $\varphi$ states that relation symbol $1$ (the edge relation) holds of variables $0, 2$ and of variables $1, 3$. In the body, variables $0, 1$ are the source pair and $2, 3$ the target pair, so a step moves both components along an edge at the same time, and the formula expresses that the pair of outer variables $(2, 3)$ is reachable…
nodes.title: Example: simultaneous reachability of pairs in FO + TC

nodes.summary: An ordered graph with nonempty domain $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ satisfies an FO + TC formula $\varphi$ when $\varphi$ evaluates to true with every variable assigned the element $0$, relation symbol $0$ interpreted as the order $<$ and relation symbol $1$ as the edge relation (both only on two-element lists), and every other relation symbol interpreted as the empty relation.
nodes.title: Satisfaction of an FO + TC formula in an ordered graph

nodes.summary: For a set $K$ of ordered graphs, this is the decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of pairs of a natural number and a list of booleans, to some ordered graph $(n, T) \in K$ whose edge table $T$ has length exactly $n^2$.
nodes.title: Encodings of a class of ordered graphs

nodes.summary: A set $K$ of ordered graphs is FO + TC-definable when there are an FO + TC formula $\varphi$ and a boolean $b$ such that for every ordered graph $(n, T)$ whose edge table $T$ has length exactly $n^2$: if $n > 0$, then $(n, T) \in K$ exactly when $(n, T)$ satisfies $\varphi$, and if $n = 0$, then $(n, T) \in K$ exactly when $b$ is true.
nodes.title: Definability in FO + TC

nodes.summary: For every set $K$ of finite ordered graphs, the decision problem of the encodings of $K$ (the bitstrings that decode to a member $(n, T)$ of $K$ whose edge table $T$ has length exactly $n^2$) belongs to $\mathrm{NL}$ if and only if $K$ is definable in first-order logic with transitive closure.
nodes.title: Immerman: FO + transitive closure is NL on ordered structures

nodes.summary: Algorithmic information content of individual strings: universal description methods, incompressible strings, non-computability and upper semicomputability of Kolmogorov complexity.
nodes.title: Kolmogorov complexity

nodes.summary: For a code $c$ of a partial recursive function on the natural numbers and a binary string $w$, running $c$ on $w$ evaluates $c$ at the number encoding $w$; if this halts with output $m$, the result is the binary string encoded by $m$. The result is undefined when the evaluation does not halt or $m$ encodes no binary string.
nodes.title: Running a program on a binary string

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a code for a partial recursive function and let $n$ be its number in the standard encoding of codes as natural numbers. For a binary string $w$, the description of $c$ running on $w$ is the binary string $1^n 0 w$, that is, $n$ ones, then a zero, then $w$.
nodes.title: Description of a code running on an input

nodes.summary: A description `1ⁿ 0 w` runs code number `n` on `w`; a string of `1`s describes nothing.
nodes.title: The universal description method

nodes.summary: The Kolmogorov complexity $K(x)$ of a binary string $x$ is the least length of a binary string $p$ such that $U(p)$ is defined and equals $x$, where $U$ is the universal description method.
nodes.title: Kolmogorov complexity

nodes.summary: Let $x$ and $p$ be binary strings such that $U(p)$ is defined and equals $x$, where $U$ is the universal description method. Then the Kolmogorov complexity of $x$ is at most the length of $p$: $K(x) \le |p|$.
nodes.title: A description bounds the complexity

nodes.summary: For every binary string $x$ there is a binary string $p$ whose length is the Kolmogorov complexity $K(x)$ and such that $U(p)$ is defined and equals $x$, where $U$ is the universal description method.
nodes.title: Shortest descriptions exist

nodes.summary: There is a natural number $c$ such that every binary string $x$ satisfies $K(x) \le |x| + c$, where $K(x)$ is the Kolmogorov complexity of $x$ and $|x|$ is its length.
nodes.title: Complexity is at most the length plus a constant

nodes.summary: The universal description method, as a partial function from binary strings to binary strings, is partial recursive.
nodes.title: The universal description method is partial recursive

nodes.summary: Let $D$ be a partial recursive function from binary strings to binary strings. Then there is a code $c$ for a partial recursive function such that running $c$ equals $D$ as a partial function: for every binary string $w$, running $c$ on $w$ is defined exactly when $D(w)$ is, and then has the same value.
nodes.title: Every partial recursive description method has a code

nodes.summary: Let $D$ be a partial recursive function from binary strings to binary strings, viewed as a description method. Then there is a natural number $c$ such that for all binary strings $x$ and $p$ for which $D(p)$ is defined and equals $x$, the Kolmogorov complexity of $x$ satisfies $K(x) \le |p| + c$, where $|p|$ is the length of $p$.
nodes.title: Optimality (the invariance theorem)

nodes.summary: There is a natural number $c$ such that for every binary string $x$, the Kolmogorov complexity of the concatenation $xx$ of $x$ with itself satisfies $K(xx) \le K(x) + c$.
nodes.title: Doubling costs a constant

nodes.summary: For binary strings $p$ and $q$, the pair description of $p$ and $q$ is the binary string $1^{|p|} 0 p q$, that is, $|p|$ ones, where $|p|$ is the length of $p$, then a zero, then $p$, then $q$.
nodes.title: Pair description

nodes.summary: Write a binary string $s$ as $1^n s'$, where $n$ is the number of leading $1$s, and let $r$ be $s'$ without its first letter ($r$ is empty when $s'$ is). Let $r_1$ be the first $\min(n, |r|)$ letters of $r$ and $r_2$ the remaining ones. The pair reader maps $s$ to the concatenation $U(r_1)\,U(r_2)$, where $U$ is the universal description method, and is undefined when $U(r_1)$ or $U(r_2)$ is undefined. On a pair…
nodes.title: Reading pair descriptions

nodes.summary: There is a natural number $c$ such that for all binary strings $x$ and $y$, the Kolmogorov complexity of their concatenation $xy$ satisfies $K(xy) \le 2K(x) + K(y) + c$.
nodes.title: Concatenation costs at most twice the first part
Incompressible strings, and Kolmogorov complexity is not computable

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$ and a binary string $p$, the padding of $p$ to length $n$ is the string $0^k 1 p$ with $k = \max(n - 1 - |p|, 0)$; when $|p| < n$ it has length $n$.
nodes.title: Padding a string to a given length

nodes.summary: Fewer than `2 ^ m` strings have complexity below `m`. Padding their shortest descriptions to length `m` maps them injectively to strings of length `m` other than `0ᵐ`.
nodes.title: Few strings have small complexity

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, the finite set of all binary strings of length $n$.
nodes.title: Binary strings of a given length

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $n$ and $c$, fewer than $2^{n-c}$ binary strings of length $n$ have Kolmogorov complexity less than $n - c$, where $n - c$ is read as $0$ when $c > n$.
nodes.title: Most strings are incompressible

nodes.summary: Some string of length `n` has complexity at least `n`.
nodes.title: Incompressible strings exist at every length

nodes.summary: The function sending each binary string $x$ to its Kolmogorov complexity $K(x)$ is not computable: no partial recursive function, acting on binary strings through their encodings as natural numbers, halts on every binary string $x$ with output $K(x)$.
nodes.title: Kolmogorov complexity is not computable
Upper semicomputability of Kolmogorov complexity, and incompressible strings

nodes.summary: Let $U$ be the universal description method. The set of pairs $(x, p)$ of binary strings such that $U(p)$ is defined and equal to $x$ is recursively enumerable (recognizable).
nodes.title: The description relation is recognizable

nodes.summary: Let $K$ denote Kolmogorov complexity. The set of pairs $(x, n)$ of a binary string $x$ and a natural number $n$ with $K(x) \le n$ is recursively enumerable (recognizable).
nodes.title: Kolmogorov complexity is upper semicomputable

nodes.summary: Let $K$ denote Kolmogorov complexity and let $f$ be a partial recursive function from binary strings to binary strings. Then there is a natural number $c$ such that $K(y) \le K(x) + c$ for all binary strings $x$ and $y$ such that $f(x)$ is defined and equal to $y$.
nodes.title: A partial recursive map raises complexity by at most a constant

nodes.summary: Let $U$ be the universal description method, $K$ Kolmogorov complexity, and $|p|$ the length of a binary string $p$. There is a natural number $b$ such that for all binary strings $x$ and $p$, if $p$ is a shortest description of $x$, that is, $U(p)$ is defined and equal to $x$ and $|p| = K(x)$, then $|p| \le K(p) + b$.
nodes.title: Shortest descriptions are incompressible

nodes.summary: Let $K$ denote Kolmogorov complexity, and let $S$ be a recursively enumerable (recognizable) set of pairs $(x, n)$ of a binary string $x$ and a natural number $n$ such that $n \le K(x)$ for every $(x, n) \in S$. Then there is a natural number $B$ with $n \le B$ for every $(x, n) \in S$.
nodes.title: Chaitin's incompleteness theorem

nodes.summary: Let $K$ denote Kolmogorov complexity. If $f$ is a computable function from binary strings to natural numbers with $f(x) \le K(x)$ for every binary string $x$, then there is a natural number $B$ with $f(x) \le B$ for every binary string $x$.
nodes.title: A computable lower bound of Kolmogorov complexity is bounded

nodes.summary: Let $K$ denote Kolmogorov complexity. The set of pairs $(x, n)$ of a binary string $x$ and a natural number $n$ with $n \le K(x)$ is not recursively enumerable (recognizable).
nodes.title: Kolmogorov complexity is not lower semicomputable

nodes.summary: Let $K$ denote Kolmogorov complexity and $|x|$ the length of a binary string $x$. There is no recursively enumerable (recognizable) set $S$ of binary strings such that for every natural number $n$ some $x \in S$ has $|x| \ge n$, and every $x \in S$ satisfies $|x| \le K(x)$.
nodes.title: No recognizable set with arbitrarily long members consists of incompressible strings

nodes.summary: Let $K$ denote Kolmogorov complexity and $|x|$ the length of a binary string $x$. The set of incompressible binary strings, that is, of binary strings $x$ with $|x| \le K(x)$, is not recursively enumerable (recognizable).
nodes.title: The incompressible strings are not recognizable

nodes.summary: Let $K$ denote Kolmogorov complexity and $|x|$ the length of a binary string $x$. The set of incompressible binary strings, that is, of binary strings $x$ with $|x| \le K(x)$, is not decidable.
nodes.title: The incompressible strings are not decidable

nodes.summary: The PCP theorem and Dinur's gap amplification, optimization classes (NPO, APX, MAXSNP), and hardness of approximation results such as Håstad's MAX-3SAT bound and the absence of a PTAS for MAX-CUT.
nodes.title: Probabilistically checkable proofs and inapproximability

nodes.summary: A decision problem belongs to NP if and only if, for some natural numbers $c$ and $q$, it belongs to $\mathrm{PCP}(r, s)$, where the randomness bound is $r(n) = c \lfloor \log_2(n + 1) \rfloor$ and the query bound is the constant function $s(n) = q$.
nodes.title: The PCP theorem: NP = PCP(O(log n), O(1))
Approximability of MAX-3SAT

nodes.summary: A clause, given as a list of literals $(v, s)$ with variable index $v \in \mathbb{N}$ and polarity $s$, is nondegenerate if it has exactly three literals, its variable indices are pairwise distinct, and it contains no complementary pair, that is, no two literals $(v, s)$ and $(v, \lnot s)$.
nodes.title: Nondegenerate 3-clauses

nodes.summary: For bitstrings $x$ and $a$, read $a$ as the assignment giving variable $v$ the value $a_v$ if $v < |a|$ and false otherwise. If $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring decoding, to a pair $(u, \varphi)$ of a bitstring $u$ and a CNF formula $\varphi$ in which every variable index is less than $|u|$ and every clause is nondegenerate, then the MAX-3SAT value of $a$ on $x$ is the number of clauses of $\varphi$,…
nodes.title: Value of a MAX-3SAT assignment

nodes.summary: The MAX-3SAT optimum of a bitstring $x$ is the maximum, over all bitstrings $a$ of length $|x|$, of the MAX-3SAT value of $a$ on $x$.
nodes.title: Optimum of a MAX-3SAT instance

nodes.summary: If $\mathsf{P} \ne \mathsf{NP}$, then for every rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is no polynomial-time function $A$ from bitstrings to bitstrings such that, for every bitstring $x$, the bitstring $A(x)$ has the same length as $x$ and the MAX-3SAT value of the assignment $A(x)$ on $x$ is at least $(7/8 + \varepsilon)$ times the MAX-3SAT optimum of $x$.
nodes.title: Hastad: optimal inapproximability of MAX-3SAT

nodes.summary: The value of MAX-3SAT on an instance $x$ under an assignment $a$, both bitstrings, is defined as follows. Suppose $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a pair $(u, \varphi)$ of a bitstring $u$ and a CNF formula $\varphi$, and suppose moreover that $|a| \le |x|$, that every literal of $\varphi$ has variable index less than $|u|$ and that every clause of $\varphi$ has at most $3$ literals. Then the…
nodes.title: The MAX-3SAT objective

nodes.summary: An NPO (NP optimization) problem consists of a rational-valued value function $v$, a Boolean feasibility predicate $F$ and an objective encoding $e$, each taking an instance $x$ and a solution $s$ (both bitstrings), together with a polynomial $b$ with natural-number coefficients, such that the following hold. $F$ and $e$ are polynomial-time computable. For all $x$ and $s$, $e(x, s)$ is a triple $(\sigma, p, q)$ of…
nodes.title: NPO problems

nodes.summary: The optimum of an NPO problem $M$, with value function $v$ and solution length bound $b$, on an instance $x$ is the maximum of $v(x, s)$ over all bitstrings $s$ with $|s| \le b(|x|)$.
nodes.title: Optimum of an NPO problem

nodes.summary: An NPO problem $M$ is in APX when there are a rational number $\rho \ge 1$ and a polynomial-time computable map $A$ from bitstrings to bitstrings such that, for every instance $x$, the solution $A(x)$ is feasible for $x$ in $M$ and its value is at least $\mathrm{opt}_M(x) / \rho$, where $\mathrm{opt}_M(x)$ is the optimum of $M$ on $x$.
nodes.title: Membership in APX

nodes.summary: Write $\mathrm{opt}_M(x)$ for the optimum of an NPO problem $M$ on an instance $x$ and $v_M(x, s)$ for the value of a solution $s$ for $x$. An NPO problem $M_1$ L-reduces to an NPO problem $M_2$ when there are polynomial-time computable maps $f$, from bitstrings to bitstrings, and $g$, from pairs of bitstrings to bitstrings, and rational numbers $\alpha > 0$ and $\beta > 0$, such that for every instance $x$ the…
nodes.title: L-reductions

nodes.summary: A MAXSNP problem, in the normal form of Papadimitriou and Yannakakis, is an NPO problem $M$, with value function $v$ and solution length bound $b$, together with natural numbers $k$ and $N$, a polynomial-time computable map $W$ sending each instance $x$ to a list $W(x)$ of windows, each a pair $(w, j)$ of a list $w = (w_1, \dots, w_m)$ of natural numbers (variable indices) and a natural number $j$ (a pattern…
nodes.title: MAXSNP problems

nodes.summary: A MAXSNP problem $M$ is MAXSNP-complete when its underlying NPO problem is in APX and, for every MAXSNP problem $M'$, the underlying NPO problem of $M'$ L-reduces to the underlying NPO problem of $M$.
nodes.title: MAXSNP-completeness

nodes.summary: There is a MAXSNP problem whose value function is the MAX-3SAT value function and which is MAXSNP-complete: its underlying NPO problem is in APX, and the underlying NPO problem of every MAXSNP problem L-reduces to it.
nodes.title: MAX-3SAT is MAXSNP-complete
Dinur's gap amplification

nodes.summary: A 2CSP instance is a triple $(n, \Sigma, C)$ of a natural number $n$ (the number of variables), a natural number $\Sigma$ (the alphabet size) and a finite list $C$ of constraints, where each constraint is a triple $(u, v, P)$ of natural numbers $u$ and $v$ (the variables it mentions) and a finite list $P$ of pairs of natural numbers (the allowed label pairs).
nodes.title: 2CSP instances

nodes.summary: A 2CSP instance $(n, \Sigma, C)$ is well-formed when every constraint $(u, v, P)$ in $C$ satisfies $u < n$ and $v < n$, and every allowed pair $(a, b)$ in $P$ satisfies $a < \Sigma$ and $b < \Sigma$.
nodes.title: Well-formed 2CSP instances

nodes.summary: Let $I = (n, \Sigma, C)$ be a 2CSP instance and $\sigma$ an assignment of a label less than $\Sigma$ to each variable less than $n$. A constraint $(u, v, P)$ is satisfied by $\sigma$ when $u < n$, $v < n$ and the pair $(\sigma(u), \sigma(v))$ belongs to $P$.
nodes.title: Satisfied constraint of a 2CSP instance

nodes.summary: Let $I = (n, \Sigma, C)$ be a 2CSP instance and $\sigma$ an assignment of a label less than $\Sigma$ to each variable less than $n$. The value of $I$ under $\sigma$ is the rational number $1$ if $C$ is empty, and otherwise the number of entries of the list $C$ that are constraints satisfied by $\sigma$, divided by the length of $C$.
nodes.title: Value of a 2CSP instance under an assignment

nodes.summary: For a 2CSP instance $(n, \Sigma, C)$ and a natural number $v$, the degree of $v$ is the number of entries $(u, w, P)$ of the list $C$ with $u = v$ or $w = v$.

nodes.summary: Writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, the instance with source $s$, target $t$ and the digraph given by $n$ and the edge list $E$ is encoded as $s$ ones, a zero, $t$ ones, a zero, then $n$ ones and a zero, followed, for each pair $(u, v)$ of $E$ in order, by $u$ ones, a zero, $v$ ones and a zero.
nodes.title: Encoding of a PATH instance

nodes.summary: Writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, a bit string $x$ is parsed by reading a unary number $s$ (a run of ones ended by a zero), then a unary number $t$ from the rest, then a graph from what remains: a unary number $n$ followed by pairs $(u, v)$ of unary numbers until the input ends. The result is $(s, t, n, E)$, with $E$ the list of these pairs in order; there is no result unless the input ends right after $n$ or…
nodes.title: Decoding a PATH instance

nodes.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, there is an arc from $u$ to $v$ when the pair $(u, v)$ occurs in $E$, $u < n$ and $v < n$; listed pairs with an end at least $n$ give no arc.
nodes.title: Arcs of the PATH digraph

nodes.summary: PATH is the decision problem that accepts a bit string $x$ exactly when $x$ is the encoding of some instance $(s, t, n, E)$ with $s < n$, $t < n$ and a sequence $s = v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k = t$ with $k \ge 0$ such that each $(v_i, v_{i+1})$ is an arc, that is, a pair listed in $E$ with both ends below $n$.
nodes.title: The PATH problem

nodes.summary: For $n, s \in \mathbb{N}$, the initial marks are the list of $n$ booleans whose entry at position $i < n$ is true exactly when $i = s$; all entries are false when $s \ge n$.
nodes.title: Initial marks

nodes.summary: Given $n \in \mathbb{N}$, an edge list $E$ and a list $m$ of booleans (the marks), the pass scans the pairs $(u, v)$ of $E$ in order and, whenever $u < n$, $v < n$ and position $u$ of the current marks is true, sets position $v$ to true. A position beyond the end of the list counts as false and setting it changes nothing. Marks set earlier in the pass are seen by later pairs.
nodes.title: One marking pass

nodes.summary: For $n, s \in \mathbb{N}$ and an edge list $E$, the reach marks are obtained from the initial marks of $s$ among $0, \dots, n - 1$ by applying the marking pass over $E$ with bound $n$ exactly $n$ times.
nodes.title: Reach marks

nodes.summary: On a bit string $x$, the check decodes $x$ as a PATH instance. If decoding fails it returns false; if it yields $(s, t, n, E)$ it returns true exactly when $s < n$, $t < n$ and position $t$ of the marks after $n$ marking passes from $s$ over $E$ is true.
nodes.title: The marking algorithm for PATH

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $s, t, n$ and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, the PATH instance parser applied to the PATH instance encoding of $(s, t, n, E)$ succeeds and returns $(s, t, n, E)$.
nodes.title: Decoding inverts the PATH instance encoding

nodes.summary: For a bit string $x$, natural numbers $s, t, n$ and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, the PATH instance parser applied to $x$ succeeds with result $(s, t, n, E)$ if and only if $x$ is the PATH instance encoding of $(s, t, n, E)$.
nodes.title: The PATH instance parser succeeds exactly on encodings

nodes.summary: Let $s, t, n, s', t', n'$ be natural numbers and $E, E'$ lists of pairs of natural numbers. If the PATH instance encodings of $(s, t, n, E)$ and $(s', t', n', E')$ are equal, then $s = s'$, $t = t'$, $n = n'$ and $E = E'$.
nodes.title: The PATH instance encoding is injective

nodes.summary: Let $m$ be a list of booleans and $v, w$ natural numbers, and read a position at or beyond the end of a list as $\mathrm{false}$. Set the entry of $m$ at position $w$ to $\mathrm{true}$, leaving $m$ unchanged if $w$ is not less than the length of $m$. Then position $v$ of the result holds $\mathrm{true}$ if and only if position $v$ of $m$ holds $\mathrm{true}$, or $v = w$ and $w$ is less than the length of $m$.
nodes.title: Setting an entry of a boolean list to true

nodes.summary: Let $n, s, v$ be natural numbers, and read a position at or beyond the end of a list as $\mathrm{false}$. Position $v$ of the initial marks for $n$ vertices and source $s$ holds $\mathrm{true}$ if and only if $v < n$ and $v = s$.
nodes.title: The initial marks mark exactly the source, if it is a vertex

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number, $E$ a list of pairs of natural numbers and $m$ a list of booleans. A marking pass over $E$ for $n$ vertices, applied to $m$, gives a list of the same length as $m$.
nodes.title: A marking pass preserves the length

nodes.summary: Let $n, v \in \mathbb{N}$, let $E$ be a list of pairs of natural numbers and let $m$ be a list of booleans. If $v < |m|$ and the $v$-th entry of $m$ (counting from $0$) is true, then the same holds for the result of the marking pass of $E$ with bound $n$ on $m$.
nodes.title: Marks persist through a pass

nodes.summary: Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $P$ be a property of natural numbers and let $E$ be a list of pairs of natural numbers such that $P(u)$ implies $P(v)$ whenever $(u, v) \in E$, $u < n$ and $v < n$. If $m$ is a list of booleans such that $P(v)$ holds for every $v < |m|$ whose entry in $m$ is true, then $P(v)$ holds for every $v$ whose entry is true in the result of the marking pass of $E$ with bound $n$ on $m$.
nodes.title: Soundness of a pass

nodes.summary: Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $E$ be a list of pairs of natural numbers and let $m$ be a list of booleans, where $m$ marks $w$ when $w < |m|$ and the $w$-th entry of $m$ (counting from $0$) is true. If $(u, v) \in E$ with $u < n$ and $v < n$, $v < |m|$ and $m$ marks $u$, then the result of the marking pass of $E$ with bound $n$ on $m$ marks $v$.
nodes.title: A pass marks the heads of arcs with marked tails

nodes.summary: Let $l_1$ and $l_2$ be lists of booleans of the same length such that every position holding $\mathrm{true}$ in $l_1$ also holds $\mathrm{true}$ in $l_2$. Then $l_1$ has at most as many $\mathrm{true}$ entries as $l_2$, and strictly fewer if $l_1 \ne l_2$.
nodes.title: Counting true entries of pointwise dominated boolean lists

nodes.summary: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, every list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers and every list $m$ of booleans, let $m'$ be the result of the marking pass of $E$ with bound $n$ on $m$. Then $m' = m$, or $m'$ has strictly more entries equal to true than $m$.
nodes.title: A pass either changes nothing or adds a mark

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number, $E$ a list of pairs of natural numbers and $m$ a list of booleans. For every natural number $k$, applying $k$ marking passes over $E$ for $n$ vertices to $m$ gives a list of the same length as $m$.
nodes.title: Repeated marking passes preserve the length

nodes.summary: Let $n$ and $v$ be natural numbers, $E$ a list of pairs of natural numbers and $m$ a list of booleans whose position $v$ holds $\mathrm{true}$ (positions at or beyond the end read as $\mathrm{false}$). Then for every natural number $k$, position $v$ still holds $\mathrm{true}$ after $k$ marking passes over $E$ for $n$ vertices, starting from $m$.
nodes.title: Marks survive repeated passes

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n, s$ and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, the marks after $n$ marking passes over $E$ for $n$ vertices, starting from the initial marks for source $s$, form a list of length $n$.
nodes.title: The final marks have one entry per vertex

nodes.summary: Let $n, s \in \mathbb{N}$ with $s < n$ and let $E$ be a list of pairs of natural numbers. Let $r$ be the list obtained from the initial marks (only $s$ marked among $0, \dots, n - 1$) by $n$ marking passes of $E$ with bound $n$. Then one more marking pass of $E$ with bound $n$ leaves $r$ unchanged.
nodes.title: Repeated passes reach a fixpoint

nodes.summary: Let $n, s, t \in \mathbb{N}$ with $s < n$ and $t < n$, and let $E$ be a list of pairs of natural numbers. Start from the marks on $0, \dots, n - 1$ in which only $s$ is marked and apply $n$ marking passes of $E$ with bound $n$. Then $t$ is marked if and only if $t$ is reachable from $s$ in zero or more steps along the arcs of $E$ below $n$, the pairs $(u, v) \in E$ with $u < n$ and $v < n$.

nodes.title: Correctness of 2-3 tree insertion

nodes.summary: For a type $\alpha$, a 2-3 tree of unspecified height over $\alpha$ is a pair $(h, t)$ of a natural number $h$ and a height-indexed 2-3 tree $t$ over $\alpha$ of height $h$.
nodes.title: 2-3 trees of unspecified height

nodes.summary: An insertion result at height $h$ becomes a 2-3 tree of unspecified height as follows: a tree $t$ of height $h$ gives $t$ itself, of height $h$, and a split into trees $l$, $r$ of height $h$ around a key $k$ gives the 2-node with separator $k$, left child $l$ and right child $r$, of height $h + 1$.
nodes.title: Turning an insertion result into a 2-3 tree

nodes.summary: The empty 2-3 tree is the root of height $0$ whose underlying tree is the leaf.
nodes.title: Empty 2-3 tree

nodes.summary: The flattening of a 2-3 tree root is the flattening of its underlying tree, that is, the list of its keys in inorder.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal of a 2-3 tree root

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered key type, searching a root (a 2-3 tree packaged with its height) for a key $x$ returns the Boolean result of the 2-3 tree search for $x$ in the underlying height-indexed tree.
nodes.title: Search in a rooted 2-3 tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $<$. A 2-3 tree of unspecified height over $\alpha$ is ordered when its underlying height-indexed 2-3 tree satisfies the ordering invariant.
nodes.title: Ordering invariant for 2-3 trees of unspecified height

nodes.summary: To insert a key $x$ into a root, that is, a 2-3 tree together with its height $h$, insert $x$ into the underlying tree. If this returns a single tree of height $h$, that tree is the new root, of height $h$. If it returns a split into trees $l$ and $r$ around a key $k$, the new root is the 2-node with key $k$ and children $l$ and $r$, of height $h + 1$.
nodes.title: Insertion into a 2-3 tree root

nodes.summary: For every type $\alpha$ with a relation $<$, the empty 2-3 tree of unspecified height over $\alpha$ (the leaf, of height $0$) satisfies the ordering invariant.
nodes.title: The empty 2-3 tree is ordered

nodes.summary: For every root $t$, that is, a 2-3 tree together with its height index, the height of the underlying tree computed along its leftmost spine equals the stored height of $t$.
nodes.title: The stored height of a 2-3 tree root is its computed height

nodes.summary: For every root, that is, a 2-3 tree packaged with its height, the underlying height-indexed tree satisfies the balance invariant.
nodes.title: Every rooted 2-3 tree is balanced

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. If $t$ is an ordered 2-3 tree of unspecified height over $\alpha$ and $x \in \alpha$, then the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is ordered.
nodes.title: Insertion preserves the ordering of 2-3 trees

nodes.summary: Let the keys be linearly ordered, let $t$ be an ordered 2-3 tree root and let $x$ be a key. Then the flattening of the root obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ equals the ordered insertion of $x$ into the flattening of $t$.
nodes.title: Insertion into a 2-3 tree is ordered insertion into its traversal

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be linearly ordered and let $t$ be an ordered 2-3 tree root over $\alpha$. For all $x, y \in \alpha$, $y$ occurs in the inorder traversal of the root obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ occurs in the inorder traversal of $t$.
nodes.title: Keys after insertion into a 2-3 tree

nodes.summary: Let the keys be linearly ordered and let $t$ be a root (a 2-3 tree packaged with its height) whose underlying tree satisfies the ordering invariant. Then searching $t$ for a key $x$ returns true if and only if $x$ occurs in the inorder flattening of $t$.
nodes.title: Search in a rooted 2-3 tree is correct

nodes.summary: For linearly ordered keys, every key $x$ and every 2-3 tree root $t$, the stored height of the root obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is at most the stored height of $t$ plus one.
nodes.title: Insertion raises the height of a 2-3 tree by at most one

nodes.summary: For linearly ordered keys, the 2-3 tree root built from a list is defined by recursion: the empty list gives the empty 2-3 tree, and a list with head $x$ and tail $xs$ gives the result of inserting $x$ into the root built from $xs$. Thus the elements are inserted into the empty tree from the last to the first.
nodes.title: Building a 2-3 tree from a list

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every list $L$ of elements of $\alpha$, the 2-3 tree of unspecified height built from $L$, by inserting the elements of $L$ from right to left into the empty tree, is ordered.
nodes.title: Building a 2-3 tree from a list gives an ordered tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be linearly ordered. For every list $L$ over $\alpha$ and every $x \in \alpha$, $x$ occurs in the inorder traversal of the 2-3 tree built from $L$ (by inserting its elements from right to left into the empty tree) if and only if $x$ occurs in $L$.
nodes.title: Keys of a 2-3 tree built from a list
B-tree

nodes.summary: A raw B-tree with keys in a type $\alpha$ is either a leaf, holding a list of keys, or an internal node, holding a list of separator keys and a list of child raw B-trees. The type imposes no invariant: that an internal node with $k$ keys has $k + 1$ children, the bounds on key counts, the balance of the tree and the ordering of the keys are imposed separately by the structural and ordering invariants of B-trees.
nodes.title: Raw B-trees

nodes.summary: Given a raw B-tree $T$ and a list $s$, this returns the inorder traversal of $T$ followed by $s$. For a leaf it is the leaf's key list followed by $s$. For an internal node with separator keys $k_1, \dots, k_m$ and children $c_0, \dots, c_n$ it is the sequence $c_0, k_1, c_1, k_2, \dots$, in which children and keys alternate starting with a child until one of the two lists runs out, then the remaining keys or…
nodes.title: Accumulating flattening of a B-tree

nodes.summary: The flattening of a raw B-tree is the list of its keys defined recursively: for a leaf it is the leaf's key list, and for an internal node with keys $k_1, k_2, \dots$ and children $c_1, c_2, \dots$ it is the flattening of $c_1$, then $k_1$, then the flattening of $c_2$, then $k_2$, and so on, alternating while both lists last; whatever remains of the longer list is then appended in order, each surplus child…
nodes.title: Inorder flattening of a B-tree

nodes.summary: For every raw B-tree $T$ and every list $s$, the accumulating flattening of $T$ with suffix $s$ equals the inorder flattening of $T$ followed by $s$.
nodes.title: The accumulating B-tree flattening is correct

nodes.summary: For a raw B-tree $c$ and a list $C$ of raw B-trees, the flattening of the node with no keys and child list $c$ followed by $C$ is the flattening of $c$ followed by the flattening of the node with no keys and child list $C$.
nodes.title: Flattening a keyless node, one child at a time

nodes.summary: For a key $k$ and a list of keys $K$, the flattening of the node with key list $k$ followed by $K$ and no children is $k$ followed by the flattening of the node with key list $K$ and no children.
nodes.title: Flattening a childless node, one key at a time

nodes.summary: The flattening of the internal node with no keys and no children is the empty list.
nodes.title: Flattening of the empty node

nodes.summary: Let $K_1$ and $K_2$ be lists of keys, $m$ a key, and $C_1$ and $C_2$ lists of raw B-trees such that $C_1$ has exactly one more element than $K_1$. Then the flattening of the node whose key list is $K_1$ followed by $m$ followed by $K_2$ and whose child list is $C_1$ followed by $C_2$ equals the flattening of the node with keys $K_1$ and children $C_1$, followed by $m$, followed by the flattening of the node with…
nodes.title: Splitting a node's flattening at a separator

nodes.summary: A key $x$ belongs to a tree $T$ when $x$ occurs in the inorder flattening of $T$.
nodes.title: Membership in a B-tree

nodes.summary: A B-tree over a type with a relation $<$ is ordered when its inorder flattening is strictly increasing, that is, each key of the flattening is less than every key that comes after it. This single condition packages sortedness of the keys at each node and the separator bounds between a node's keys and the keys stored in its subtrees.
nodes.title: Ordered B-tree

nodes.summary: If an internal node with separator list $K$ is ordered, then $K$ is strictly increasing: every key of $K$ is smaller than every key that comes after it in $K$.
nodes.title: The separator keys of an ordered node are sorted

nodes.summary: Let $K_1$ and $K_2$ be lists of keys, $k$ a key, and $C_1$ and $C_2$ lists of B-trees such that $C_1$ has exactly one more tree than $K_1$ has keys. If the internal node whose key list is $K_1$ followed by $k$ followed by $K_2$, and whose child list is $C_1$ followed by $C_2$, is ordered, then every key in the flattening of the node with keys $K_1$ and children $C_1$ is less than $k$, and $k$ is less than every key…
nodes.title: Separator bounds in an ordered B-tree node

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered key type, the flattening of an ordered raw B-tree has no duplicate entries.
nodes.title: An ordered B-tree has no duplicate keys

nodes.summary: For a minimum degree $t$ and a minimum key count $m$ for the top node, the invariant is defined inductively over the height: a leaf with $k$ keys satisfies it at height $0$ when $m \le k \le 2t - 1$, and for every natural number $h$, an internal node with $k$ keys satisfies it at height $h + 1$ when $m \le k \le 2t - 1$, the node has exactly $k + 1$ children, and every child satisfies the invariant with minimum key…
nodes.title: Structural invariant of a B-tree

nodes.summary: For a minimum degree $t$ and a height $h$, a tree satisfies the root invariant when either $h = 0$ and the tree is a leaf with at most $2t - 1$ keys (possibly none, for the empty tree), or $h = h' + 1$ and the tree is an internal node with between $1$ and $2t - 1$ keys and exactly one more child than keys, every child satisfying the structural invariant for minimum degree $t$, minimum top-node key count $t - 1$ and…
nodes.title: Root invariant of a B-tree

nodes.summary: If a tree satisfies the root invariant for minimum degree $t$ at height $h$, then for some natural number $m$ it satisfies the structural invariant for minimum degree $t$, minimum top-node key count $m$ and height $h$.
nodes.title: Root-valid B-trees are valid

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered key type, the search for a key $x$ in a raw B-tree proceeds as follows. At a leaf, report whether $x$ is in the leaf's key list. At an internal node with separators $k_1, \dots, k_m$ and children $c_0, c_1, \dots$, scan the separators in order. On reaching $k_i$, report failure if the node has no child $c_{i-1}$; otherwise search $c_{i-1}$ if $x < k_i$, report success if $x = k_i$, and move…
nodes.title: B-tree search

nodes.summary: An insertion result over a key type $\alpha$ is either a single tree over $\alpha$, or a triple $(\ell, m, r)$ of two trees $\ell$ and $r$ over $\alpha$ and a key $m$ of $\alpha$. In insertion, the first form is a subtree that did not split, and the second form is an overflowing node split into two trees of the same height, with the median key $m$ promoted between them; the type itself does not record heights.
nodes.title: Result of inserting into a B-tree subtree

nodes.summary: The flattening of an insertion result that is a single tree is the flattening of that tree; for a result that splits into a left tree $\ell$, a promoted median key $m$ and a right tree $r$, it is the flattening of $\ell$, followed by $m$, followed by the flattening of $r$.
nodes.title: Flattening of a B-tree insertion result

nodes.summary: Over a linearly ordered key type, let $t$ be a natural number, $x$ a key, $K$ the key list of a leaf, and $K'$ the result of ordered insertion of $x$ into $K$. If $K'$ has at most $2t - 1$ keys, the insertion result is the single leaf with keys $K'$. Otherwise the leaf is split: the result consists of the leaf holding the first $t - 1$ keys of $K'$, the next key of $K'$ promoted as the median, and the leaf holding…
nodes.title: Insertion into a B-tree leaf

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a minimum degree, $s = t - 1$ (so $s = 0$ when $t = 0$), $k_1, \dots, k_m$ a list of keys and $c_1, \dots, c_n$ a list of B-trees. If $m > s$, splitting returns the pair of internal nodes formed by the keys $k_1, \dots, k_s$ with the first $t$ children (all of them if $n < t$) and by the keys $k_{s+2}, \dots, k_m$ with the children after the first $t$, together with the key $k_{s+1}$ promoted between…
nodes.title: Splitting a B-tree node

nodes.summary: For minimum degree $t$, a separator list $K$ and a child list $C$, the result is the internal node with separators $K$ and children $C$, kept as a single tree when $K$ has at most $2t - 1$ keys, and otherwise split by node splitting into two nodes and a promoted median key.
nodes.title: Rebuilding an internal node after insertion

nodes.summary: For minimum degree $t$ and a key $x$, insertion of $x$ into a tree returns an insertion result and is defined by recursion. At a leaf with key list $K$, it is leaf insertion of $x$ into $K$. At an internal node, the separator list and the child list are scanned together from the left. If $x$ is smaller than the current separator, or no separator is left but a child is, $x$ is inserted into the current child. If $x$…
nodes.title: Split-returning insertion into a B-tree subtree

nodes.summary: For minimum degree $t$, the tree obtained by inserting a key $x$ into a tree $T$ is computed from the split-returning insertion of $x$ into $T$: if that returns a single tree, this tree is the result; if it returns two trees $\ell$ and $r$ with a promoted median key $m$, the result is a new root node with the single separator $m$ and the two children $\ell$ and $r$.
nodes.title: B-tree insertion

nodes.summary: The empty B-tree is the leaf with no keys.
nodes.title: The empty B-tree

nodes.summary: A tree $T$ is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ when $t \ge 2$ (the CLRS Chapter 18 minimum-degree requirement), $T$ is ordered, and $T$ is root-valid at some height. This is the invariant preserved by insertion and by building a tree from a list.
nodes.title: B-trees of a given minimum degree

nodes.summary: If a tree is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$, then $t \ge 2$.
nodes.title: The minimum degree of a B-tree is at least two

nodes.summary: If a tree is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$, then it is ordered: each key of its inorder flattening is less than every key that comes after it.
nodes.title: B-trees are ordered

nodes.summary: If $T$ is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$, then there is a height $h$ such that $T$ satisfies the root structural invariant of minimum degree $t$ at height $h$.
nodes.title: B-trees satisfy the root invariant

nodes.summary: For every key type equipped with a binary relation $<$ and every natural number $t \ge 2$, the empty B-tree is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$.
nodes.title: The empty tree is a B-tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be linearly ordered, let $t \ge 2$, and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$. For every key $x \in \alpha$, the inorder flattening of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ with minimum degree $t$ equals the sorted insertion of $x$ into the inorder flattening of $T$.
nodes.title: B-tree insertion as sorted list insertion

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For all keys $x$ and $y$, $y$ belongs to the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ belongs to $T$.
nodes.title: Membership after B-tree insertion

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let the keys come from a linearly ordered type. If $T$ is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$, then for every key $x$ the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ is again a B-tree of minimum degree $t$: it is ordered and root-valid at some height.
nodes.title: Insertion preserves the B-tree invariant

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be linearly ordered and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$. For every key $x \in \alpha$, the search procedure returns true on $x$ and $T$ if and only if $x$ is a member of $T$, that is, $x$ occurs in the inorder flattening of $T$.
nodes.title: Correctness of B-tree search

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be linearly ordered, let $t \ge 2$, let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, and let $x \in \alpha$. Let $T'$ be the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ with minimum degree $t$. If $x$ occurs in the inorder flattening of $T$, then the flattening of $T'$ has the same length as that of $T$; otherwise it is one longer.
nodes.title: Size of a B-tree after insertion

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered key type and a natural number $t$, the tree built from the empty list is the empty tree, and the tree built from a list with head $x$ and tail $L$ is the result of inserting $x$, with minimum degree $t$, into the tree built from $L$. Thus the elements are inserted from right to left.
nodes.title: B-tree built from a list

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered key type, every natural number $t \ge 2$ and every list $L$ of keys, the tree obtained by inserting the elements of $L$ from right to left into the empty tree, each insertion with minimum degree $t$, is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$.
nodes.title: Building from a list yields a B-tree

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $xs$ be a list over a linearly ordered key type. A key $x$ belongs to the tree of minimum degree $t$ built from $xs$ (by inserting the elements of $xs$ into the empty tree, from right to left) if and only if $x$ is an element of $xs$.
nodes.title: Membership in a B-tree built from a list

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$. For every strictly increasing list $L$ of keys, the tree built from $L$ by inserting its keys from right to left into the empty tree with minimum degree $t$ has flattening exactly $L$.
nodes.title: Building a B-tree from a strictly increasing list

nodes.summary: For a minimum degree $t$, a key $x$ and a tree $T$, the rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ is the tree obtained by inserting the keys of the list $L$, from right to left, into the empty tree with B-tree insertion of minimum degree $t$, where $L$ is the inorder flattening of $T$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed ($L$ is the flattening itself when $x$ does not occur in it).
nodes.title: B-tree deletion by rebuilding

nodes.summary: For every minimum degree $t$, key $x$ and tree $T$, the rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ equals the tree built from the list obtained by removing the first occurrence of $x$ from the flattening of $T$, by inserting its keys from right to left into the empty tree with minimum degree $t$.
nodes.title: Rebuilding deletion unfolds to erase and rebuild

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$, let $T$ be an ordered tree and let $x$ be a key. The flattening of the rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ is the flattening of $T$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed (unchanged if $x$ does not occur).
nodes.title: Flattening after rebuilding deletion

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$. For every key $x$ and every tree $T$, whether or not $T$ is itself a B-tree, the rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$.
nodes.title: Rebuilding deletion yields a B-tree

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let keys come from a linearly ordered type. For every key $x$ and every tree $T$, not necessarily ordered, the tree obtained from $T$ by rebuild deletion of $x$ (removing the first occurrence of $x$, if any, from the inorder flattening of $T$ and rebuilding a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ from the remaining keys) is ordered: its inorder flattening is strictly increasing.
nodes.title: Rebuild deletion yields an ordered tree

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$. For every key $x$ and every tree $T$, there is a height $h$ such that the rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ is root-valid of minimum degree $t$ and height $h$: all leaves sit at depth $h$, every node holds at most $2t - 1$ keys, every non-root node holds at least $t - 1$ keys, an internal root holds at least one key, and an internal node with $k$ keys has $k + 1$ children.
nodes.title: Rebuilding deletion yields a root-valid tree

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered type. For all keys $x$ and $y$, the key $y$ lies in the tree obtained from $T$ by rebuild deletion of $x$ (erasing $x$ from the inorder flattening of $T$ and rebuilding a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ from the remaining keys) if and only if $y \ne x$ and $y$ lies in $T$.
nodes.title: Membership after rebuild deletion from a B-tree

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered type. For every key $x$, the tree obtained from $T$ by rebuild deletion of $x$ (erasing $x$ from the inorder flattening of $T$ and rebuilding a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ from the remaining keys) does not contain $x$.
nodes.title: The deleted key is absent after rebuild deletion

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$, let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$, and let $x$ and $y$ be keys. The B-tree search for $y$ in the rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ returns true if and only if $y \ne x$ and $y$ is stored in $T$.
nodes.title: Search after rebuilding deletion

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$, let $T$ be an ordered tree and let $x$ be a key that does not occur in the flattening of $T$. Then the rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ has the same flattening as $T$.
nodes.title: Rebuilding deletion of an absent key

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$, let $T$ be an ordered tree with flattening of length $n$, and let $x$ be a key. The flattening of the rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ has length $n - 1$ if $x$ occurs in the flattening of $T$, and length $n$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Key count after rebuilding deletion

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$, let $T$ be an ordered tree (its flattening is strictly increasing) and let $x$ be a key. Deleting $x$ twice by rebuilding with minimum degree $t$ gives a tree with the same flattening as deleting $x$ once.
nodes.title: Rebuilding deletion of the same key twice

nodes.summary: For a raw B-tree $T$, this is the length of the key list stored at the root of $T$: the number of keys of $T$ if $T$ is a leaf, and the number of separator keys of $T$ if $T$ is an internal node. Keys in the children are not counted.
nodes.title: Number of keys at the root of a B-tree

nodes.summary: For a nonempty list $l$, the result is the pair consisting of $l$ with its last element removed and the last element of $l$; for the empty list there is no result.
nodes.title: Splitting off the last element of a list

nodes.summary: For a tree $T$, the rightmost key of $T$ is an optional key defined by descending the rightmost spine: for a leaf it is the last of its keys (none if the leaf has no keys); for an internal node with at least one child it is the rightmost key of its last child; for an internal node with no children it is the last of its separator keys (none if there are none).
nodes.title: Rightmost key of a B-tree

nodes.summary: For a tree $T$, the leftmost key of $T$ is an optional key defined by descending the leftmost spine: for a leaf it is the first of its keys (none if the leaf has no keys); for an internal node with at least one child it is the leftmost key of its first child; for an internal node with no children it is the first of its separator keys (none if there are none).
nodes.title: Leftmost key of a B-tree

nodes.summary: Given a key $s$ and trees $L$ and $R$, the merge of $L$ and $R$ around $s$ is defined as follows. If $L$ and $R$ are leaves with key lists $k_1$ and $k_2$, it is the leaf with keys $k_1$, then $s$, then $k_2$. If $L$ and $R$ are internal nodes with key lists $k_1, k_2$ and child lists $c_1, c_2$, it is the internal node with keys $k_1$, then $s$, then $k_2$, and children $c_1$ followed by $c_2$. In every other case…
nodes.title: Merging two B-tree nodes around a separator

nodes.summary: Given a tree $c$ (the child), a separator key $k$ and a tree $s$ (the right sibling) such that $c$ and $s$ are both leaves or both internal nodes, $s$ has at least one key, and, when they are internal nodes, $s$ has at least one child: $k$ becomes the last key of $c$, the first key of $s$ is removed from $s$ and becomes the new separator, and, for internal nodes, the first child of $s$ is removed from $s$ and…
nodes.title: Borrowing a key from the right sibling

nodes.summary: Given a tree $s$ (the left sibling), a separator key $k$ and a tree $c$ (the child) such that $s$ and $c$ are both leaves or both internal nodes, $s$ has at least one key, and, when they are internal nodes, $s$ has at least one child: the last key of $s$ is removed from $s$ and becomes the new separator, $k$ becomes the first key of $c$, and, for internal nodes, the last child of $s$ is removed from $s$ and becomes…
nodes.title: Borrowing a key from the left sibling

nodes.summary: Let $D$ be an operation that deletes a key from a tree, let $t$ be a natural number, let $x$ be a key of a linearly ordered key type, and write $|c|$ for the number of keys stored at the root of a tree $c$. Deleting $x$ within a node with separator list $K$ and child list $C$, using $D$ on children, produces a new separator list and a new child list. Write $k$ for the first separator, $c$ for the first child, and…
nodes.title: Deletion within a B-tree node

nodes.summary: Given a height $h$, a minimum degree $t$, a key $x$ of a linearly ordered key type and a tree $T$, the result is defined as follows. If $T$ is a leaf, the result is the leaf whose key list is that of $T$ with the first occurrence of $x$ erased, whatever $h$ is. If $T$ is an internal node and $h = 0$, the result is $T$. If $T$ is an internal node and $h = n + 1$, the result is the internal node whose separator and…
nodes.title: Height-indexed B-tree deletion

nodes.summary: The height of a B-tree is computed by following first children: a leaf has height $0$, an internal node with no children has height $0$, and an internal node whose first child is $c$ has height one more than the height of $c$.
nodes.title: Height of a B-tree along first children

nodes.summary: Deleting a key $x$ of a linearly ordered key type from a tree $T$ with minimum degree $t$ applies height-indexed deletion of $x$ with minimum degree $t$ to $T$ at the height of $T$, where the height of a leaf, or of an internal node without children, is $0$, and the height of any other internal node is one more than the height of its first child. If the outcome is an internal node with no keys and exactly one…
nodes.title: Top-down B-tree deletion

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For every key $x$, the inorder flattening of the tree obtained from $T$ by top-down deletion of $x$ with minimum degree $t$ is the flattening of $T$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed (unchanged if $x$ does not occur).
nodes.title: Deletion from a B-tree erases the key from its flattening

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be an ordered tree over a linearly ordered key type (its inorder flattening is strictly increasing) that satisfies the root invariant of B-trees of minimum degree $t$ at height $h$. For every key $x$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ satisfies the root invariant of minimum degree $t$ at height $h$ or at height $h - 1$, where $h - 1$ is truncated…
nodes.title: Top-down deletion lowers the height by at most one

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For every key $x$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ is again a B-tree of minimum degree $t$.
nodes.title: Top-down deletion preserves the B-tree invariant

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For every key $x$, the tree obtained from $T$ by deleting $x$ (with minimum degree $t$) is ordered: its inorder flattening is strictly increasing.
nodes.title: Deletion from a B-tree yields an ordered tree

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For every key $x$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ satisfies the root invariant of B-trees of minimum degree $t$ at some height.
nodes.title: Top-down deletion yields a root-valid tree

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For all keys $x$ and $y$, $y$ belongs to the tree obtained from $T$ by deleting $x$ (with minimum degree $t$) if and only if $y \ne x$ and $y$ belongs to $T$.
nodes.title: Membership after deletion from a B-tree

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For every key $x$, $x$ does not belong to the tree obtained from $T$ by deleting $x$ (with minimum degree $t$).
nodes.title: The deleted key is absent after deletion from a B-tree

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For all keys $x$ and $y$, searching for $y$ in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ succeeds if and only if $y \ne x$ and $y$ is a key of $T$.
nodes.title: Search after top-down deletion

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$, let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type, and let $x$ be a key. If $x$ occurs in the inorder flattening of $T$, the flattening of the tree obtained from $T$ by deleting $x$ (with minimum degree $t$) has length one less than the flattening of $T$; otherwise the two flattenings have the same length.
nodes.title: Deletion shortens the flattening by one exactly when the key is present

nodes.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For every key $x$, deleting $x$ from $T$ twice with minimum degree $t$ gives a tree with the same inorder flattening as deleting $x$ from $T$ once.
nodes.title: Repeated top-down deletion
Binary search tree

nodes.summary: A key $x$ belongs to a binary tree $T$ when it is the key of some node of $T$: no key belongs to the empty tree, and $x$ belongs to a node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ exactly when $x$ belongs to $L$, $x = k$, or $x$ belongs to $R$.
nodes.title: Membership in a binary tree

nodes.summary: For a binary tree $t$ and a list $s$, the accumulated traversal of the empty tree onto $s$ is $s$, and the accumulated traversal of a node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ onto $s$ is the accumulated traversal of $L$ onto the list consisting of $k$ followed by the accumulated traversal of $R$ onto $s$.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal of a binary tree with an accumulator

nodes.summary: The inorder traversal of a binary tree $t$ is the accumulated inorder traversal of $t$ onto the empty list. Equivalently, the empty tree gives the empty list, and a node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ gives the inorder traversal of $L$, then $k$, then the inorder traversal of $R$.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal of a binary tree

nodes.summary: For a predicate $p$ on a type $\alpha$, the empty binary tree satisfies "every key satisfies $p$", and a node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ satisfies it exactly when $L$ satisfies it, $p(k)$ holds and $R$ satisfies it.
nodes.title: A predicate holding at every key of a binary tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $<$. The empty tree is ordered, and a binary tree with root key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ is ordered when $L$ and $R$ are ordered, every key of $L$ is less than $k$, and $k$ is less than every key of $R$.
nodes.title: Ordered binary trees

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, a key $x \in \alpha$ and a binary tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, the search for $x$ in $t$ returns a Boolean: false if $t$ is empty, and if $t$ is a node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$, the search for $x$ in $L$ when $x < k$, the search for $x$ in $R$ when $k < x$, and true otherwise.
nodes.title: Search in a binary search tree

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, a key $x \in \alpha$ and a binary tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, inserting $x$ into the empty tree gives the single node with key $x$ and empty subtrees; inserting $x$ into a node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ inserts $x$ into $L$ when $x < k$, inserts $x$ into $R$ when $k < x$, and returns the node unchanged when $x = k$.
nodes.title: Insertion into a binary search tree

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, a key $x \in \alpha$ and a binary tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, the rank of $x$ in $t$ is the number of positions of the inorder traversal of $t$ whose entry is strictly less than $x$.
nodes.title: Rank of a key in a binary tree

nodes.summary: For a binary tree $t$ and a natural number $i$, selecting index $i$ in $t$ returns the entry at zero-based position $i$ of the inorder traversal of $t$ when $i$ is less than the length of that traversal, and returns nothing otherwise.
nodes.title: Inorder selection in a binary tree

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, the binary tree built from a list $[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ of elements of $\alpha$ is obtained from the empty tree by inserting $x_n$, then $x_{n-1}$, and so on down to $x_1$, using binary search tree insertion; the empty list gives the empty tree.
nodes.title: Binary search tree built from a list

nodes.summary: For a type $\alpha$, a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ and a binary tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, every key of $t$ satisfies $p$ in the recursive sense (the empty tree qualifies, and a node qualifies when its left subtree qualifies, its key satisfies $p$ and its right subtree qualifies) if and only if $p(x)$ holds for every $x$ that is a member of $t$.
nodes.title: A predicate holds at all keys of a binary tree iff it holds at all its members

nodes.summary: For every binary tree $T$ and every key $x$, $x$ occurs in the inorder traversal of $T$ if and only if $x$ lies in $T$.
nodes.title: Membership in the inorder traversal of a binary tree

nodes.summary: Let the keys be linearly ordered. For all keys $x, y$ and every binary tree $T$, $y$ lies in the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ lies in $T$.
nodes.title: Membership after insertion into a binary search tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every key $x \in \alpha$ and every ordered binary tree $T$ over $\alpha$, the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ is ordered.
nodes.title: Binary search tree insertion preserves order

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, a key $x \in \alpha$ and a binary tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$ that is ordered (recursively, every key in the left subtree of a node is strictly smaller than the node's key and every key in its right subtree is strictly larger), the comparison search for $x$ in $t$ returns true if and only if $x$ is a member of $t$.
nodes.title: Search in a binary search tree is correct

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. If a binary tree $T$ over $\alpha$ is ordered, then in the inorder traversal of $T$ every key is less than every key that comes after it.
nodes.title: The inorder traversal of an ordered binary tree is strictly increasing

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ and a binary tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$ that is ordered (recursively, every key in the left subtree of a node is strictly smaller than the node's key and every key in its right subtree is strictly larger), the inorder traversal of $t$ is a list with no repeated entries.
nodes.title: The inorder traversal of a binary search tree has no duplicates

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every list $xs$ of elements of $\alpha$, the tree obtained from the empty tree by inserting the elements of $xs$ one at a time, from the last element to the first, is ordered.
nodes.title: Binary search trees built from a list are ordered

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, a key $x \in \alpha$ and a list $xs$ of elements of $\alpha$, $x$ is a member of the binary tree built from $xs$ by successive binary search tree insertion if and only if $x$ occurs in $xs$.
nodes.title: Members of the binary search tree built from a list

nodes.summary: For every binary tree $T$, the number of nodes of $T$ (each node carries one key, and the empty tree has none) equals the length of the inorder traversal of $T$.
nodes.title: The length of the inorder traversal of a binary tree is its number of nodes

nodes.summary: Let the keys be linearly ordered, and let $T$ be an ordered binary tree. If a key $x$ lies in $T$, then the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ has the same number of nodes as $T$.
nodes.title: Inserting a present key into a binary search tree leaves its size unchanged

nodes.summary: Let the keys be linearly ordered. For every binary tree $T$ and every key $x$ that does not lie in $T$, the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ has one more node than $T$.
nodes.title: Inserting an absent key into a binary search tree adds one node

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, a key $x \in \alpha$ and a binary tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, the rank of $x$ in $t$ equals the length of the list obtained from the inorder traversal of $t$ by keeping exactly the entries strictly less than $x$.
nodes.title: Rank counts the smaller inorder entries

nodes.summary: For a binary tree $t$ and a natural number $i$, selecting index $i$ in $t$ gives the same result as looking up zero-based position $i$ of the inorder traversal of $t$: the entry at that position when $i$ is less than the length of the traversal, and nothing otherwise.
nodes.title: Selection is indexing into the inorder traversal

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be a binary search tree with keys in $\alpha$, that is, at every node each key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and each key of the right subtree is strictly larger than the node's key. If $x$ is a key of $t$, then selecting, in $t$, the index equal to the rank of $x$ in $t$ returns $x$.
nodes.title: Selecting the rank of a key returns the key

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be a binary search tree with keys in $\alpha$, that is, at every node each key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and each key of the right subtree is strictly larger than the node's key. If selecting index $i$ in $t$ returns a key $x$, then the rank of $x$ in $t$ equals $i$.
nodes.title: The rank of a selected key is its index

nodes.summary: The join of the empty tree and a tree $R$ is $R$. The join of a tree with root key $k$, left subtree $L_1$ and right subtree $L_2$ and a tree $R$ is the tree with root key $k$, left subtree $L_1$ and right subtree the join of $L_2$ and $R$. Thus, when the first tree is nonempty, $R$ becomes the right subtree of its rightmost node.
nodes.title: Join of two binary trees

nodes.summary: Let $x$ be a key of a linearly ordered type. Deleting $x$ from the empty tree gives the empty tree. Deleting $x$ from a tree with root key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ gives the tree with root key $k$, left subtree $L$ with $x$ deleted and right subtree $R$ if $x < k$; the tree with root key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ with $x$ deleted if $k < x$; and the join of $L$ and $R$…
nodes.title: Deletion from a binary search tree

nodes.summary: For binary trees $L$ and $R$, a key $x$ occurs in the join of $L$ and $R$ if and only if $x$ occurs in $L$ or $x$ occurs in $R$.
nodes.title: Membership in a join

nodes.summary: For binary trees $L$ and $R$, the inorder traversal of the join of $L$ and $R$ is the inorder traversal of $L$ followed by the inorder traversal of $R$.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal of a join

nodes.summary: Let $L$ and $R$ be ordered binary search trees over a type with a relation $<$. If $a < b$ for every key $a$ of $L$ and every key $b$ of $R$, then the join of $L$ and $R$ is ordered.
nodes.title: Joining separated ordered trees

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree over a linearly ordered type, not necessarily ordered, and let $x$ and $y$ be keys with $y \ne x$. If $y$ occurs in $t$, then $y$ occurs in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$.
nodes.title: Deletion keeps the other keys

nodes.summary: If $t$ is an ordered binary search tree over a linearly ordered type and $x$ is a key, then $x$ does not occur in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$.
nodes.title: The deleted key is gone

nodes.summary: If $t$ is an ordered binary search tree over a linearly ordered type, then for all keys $x$ and $y$, the key $y$ occurs in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ if and only if $y$ occurs in $t$ and $y \ne x$.
nodes.title: Membership after deletion

nodes.summary: If $t$ is an ordered binary search tree over a linearly ordered type, then for every key $x$ the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ is ordered.
nodes.title: Deletion preserves the search-tree order

nodes.summary: If $t$ is an ordered binary search tree over a linearly ordered type and $x$ is a key, then the inorder traversal of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ is the inorder traversal of $t$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed (and is the inorder traversal of $t$ itself if $x$ does not occur in it).
nodes.title: Inorder traversal after deletion
AVL tree

nodes.summary: For a type $\alpha$, a tree with cached heights over $\alpha$ (the underlying type of AVL trees) is either empty, or a node made of a natural number $h$ (its cached height), a left subtree, a key in $\alpha$ and a right subtree.
nodes.title: Binary trees with cached heights

nodes.summary: The cached height of the empty tree is $0$, and the cached height of a node is the height value stored at that node, so it is read off the root in constant time.
nodes.title: Cached height of an AVL tree

nodes.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$, with $h$ of the empty tree equal to $0$. Given trees $L$ and $R$ and a key $k$, this is the node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$ whose cached height is $\max(h(L), h(R)) + 1$.
nodes.title: AVL node with computed height

nodes.summary: The empty tree has correct cached heights. A node storing the height $c$, with left subtree $\ell$ and right subtree $r$, has correct cached heights when $\ell$ and $r$ have correct cached heights and $c = \max(h(\ell), h(r)) + 1$, where $h$ denotes the height cached at the root of a tree (and $0$ for the empty tree).
nodes.title: Correct cached heights

nodes.summary: The empty tree is balanced. A node with left subtree $\ell$ and right subtree $r$ is balanced when $\ell$ and $r$ are balanced and $h(\ell) \le h(r) + 1$ and $h(r) \le h(\ell) + 1$, where $h$ denotes the height cached at the root of a tree (and $0$ for the empty tree). Equivalently, at every node the balance factor $h(\ell) - h(r)$ lies in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$.
nodes.title: AVL balance invariant

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type.
