Erasing the cached heights sends a tree with cached heights over $\alpha$ to a binary tree over $\alpha$: the empty tree goes to the empty binary tree, and a node with height $h$, left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$ goes to the binary-tree node with key $k$ whose left and right subtrees are the erasures of $L$ and $R$.
nodes.title: Erasing the cached heights of an AVL tree

nodes.summary: A key $x$ belongs to a tree $T$ when $x$ belongs to the binary tree obtained from $T$ by erasing the cached heights. Equivalently, no key belongs to the empty tree, and $x$ belongs to a node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$ exactly when $x$ belongs to $L$, $x = k$, or $x$ belongs to $R$.
nodes.title: Membership in an AVL tree

nodes.summary: For a predicate $p$ on keys and a tree $t$ with cached heights, $\mathrm{All}(p, t)$ holds when $p$ holds at the key of every node of $t$. It is defined as the corresponding predicate on the plain binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its cached heights.
nodes.title: Every key of an AVL tree satisfies a predicate

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $<$. A tree with cached heights over $\alpha$ is ordered when the binary tree obtained by erasing its cached heights is an ordered binary search tree: the empty tree is ordered, and a node with key $k$ is ordered when its left and right subtrees are ordered, every key of the left subtree is less than $k$, and every key of the right subtree is greater than $k$.
nodes.title: Ordered AVL trees

nodes.summary: Given a tree $t$ and a list $s$, this is the list of keys of $t$ in inorder (left subtree, root key, right subtree, recursively) followed by $s$. It is computed in linear time by the binary search tree traversal of $t$ with its cached heights erased.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal of an AVL tree onto a suffix

nodes.summary: The inorder traversal of a tree $t$ lists its keys with the left subtree first, then the root key, then the right subtree, recursively. It is the binary search tree inorder traversal of $t$ with its cached heights erased, computed in linear time.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal of an AVL tree

nodes.summary: A key $x$ lies in a tree $T$ if and only if $x$ lies in the binary tree obtained from $T$ by erasing the cached heights.
nodes.title: AVL membership is membership in the underlying binary tree

nodes.summary: For a predicate $p$ on keys and a tree $t$ with cached heights, $\mathrm{All}(p, t)$ holds if and only if $p$ holds at every key of the plain binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its cached heights. This holds by definition.
nodes.title: The all-keys predicate is unchanged by erasing height caches

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $<$. A tree $t$ with cached heights over $\alpha$ is ordered if and only if the binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing the cached heights is an ordered binary search tree.
nodes.title: Order of an AVL tree via its underlying binary tree

nodes.summary: For every AVL tree $t$, the inorder traversal of $t$ equals the binary search tree inorder traversal of the binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its cached heights; this holds by definition.
nodes.title: AVL inorder traversal agrees with the erased binary search tree

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ and a key $x$, the search for $x$ returns false on the empty tree; at a node with key $k$ it searches the left subtree if $x < k$, searches the right subtree if $k < x$, and returns true otherwise. The cached heights are ignored.
nodes.title: Membership search in an AVL tree

nodes.summary: For trees $l$, $r$ with cached heights and a key $x$, write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree) and $N(A, y, B)$ for the node with left subtree $A$, key $y$, right subtree $B$ and cached height $\max(h(A), h(B)) + 1$. The node $\mathrm{balance}(l, x, r)$ is defined by cases. If $h(l) > h(r) + 1$ and $l$ has left subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$, it is the…
nodes.title: AVL rebalancing

nodes.summary: Let the keys be linearly ordered, and write $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ for the AVL rebalancing of the node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$. Inserting $x$ into the empty tree gives the node with key $x$, two empty children and cached height $1$. Inserting $x$ into a node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$ gives $\mathrm{balance}(L', k, R)$, where $L'$ is the result of…
nodes.title: Insertion into an AVL tree

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, the tree built from the empty list is the empty tree, and the tree built from a list with head $x$ and tail $xs$ is obtained by AVL insertion of $x$ into the tree built from $xs$. Thus the list is inserted from right to left, starting from the empty tree.
nodes.title: Building an AVL tree from a list

nodes.summary: For a predicate $p$ on keys and a tree $t$ with cached heights, $\mathrm{All}(p, t)$ holds if and only if $p(x)$ holds for every $x \in t$, where $x \in t$ means that $x$ is the key of some node of $t$.
nodes.title: The all-keys predicate in terms of membership (AVL trees)

nodes.summary: A key $x$ occurs in the inorder traversal of a tree $T$ if and only if $x$ lies in $T$.
nodes.title: Membership in the inorder traversal of an AVL tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. If a tree $t$ with cached heights over $\alpha$ is ordered, then in the inorder traversal of $t$ every key is less than every key that comes after it.
nodes.title: The inorder traversal of an ordered AVL tree is strictly increasing

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, if an AVL tree is ordered, then its inorder traversal contains no key twice.
nodes.title: The inorder traversal of an ordered AVL tree has no duplicates

nodes.summary: If two AVL trees $\ell$ and $r$ have correct cached heights, then for every key $k$ the node built from $\ell$, $k$ and $r$ by the smart constructor, which stores the height $\max(h(\ell), h(r)) + 1$ where $h$ denotes the height cached at the root (and $0$ for the empty tree), also has correct cached heights.
nodes.title: The AVL node constructor preserves cached heights

nodes.summary: Let $\ell$ and $r$ be AVL trees that satisfy the AVL balance invariant, and write $h(\ell)$ and $h(r)$ for the heights cached at their roots (with height $0$ for the empty tree). If $h(\ell) \le h(r) + 1$ and $h(r) \le h(\ell) + 1$, then for every key $k$ the node built from $\ell$, $k$ and $r$ by the smart constructor, which stores the height $\max(h(\ell), h(r)) + 1$, satisfies the AVL balance invariant.
nodes.title: The AVL node constructor preserves balance

nodes.summary: Let $l$ and $r$ be trees with cached heights, let $x$ be a key, and write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree). If $h(l) \le h(r) + 1$ and $h(r) \le h(l) + 1$, then $\mathrm{balance}(l, x, r)$ is the node with left subtree $l$, key $x$, right subtree $r$ and cached height $\max(h(l), h(r)) + 1$; no rotation is performed.
nodes.title: Rebalancing when the heights of the children differ by at most one

nodes.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree), $\langle c; A, y, B \rangle$ for the node with cached height $c$, left subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$, and $N(A, y, B)$ for the node $\langle \max(h(A), h(B)) + 1; A, y, B \rangle$. Let $A$, $B$, $R$ be trees with cached heights, let $x$, $y$ be keys and let $c$ be a natural number. If $h(R) + 1 < c$ and…
nodes.title: Single right rotation in AVL rebalancing

nodes.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree), $\langle c; A, y, B \rangle$ for the node with cached height $c$, left subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$, and $N(A, y, B)$ for the node $\langle \max(h(A), h(B)) + 1; A, y, B \rangle$. Let $A$, $B$, $C$, $R$ be trees with cached heights, let $x$, $y$, $z$ be keys and let $c$, $c'$ be natural numbers. If $h(R) + 1 < c$…
nodes.title: Left-right double rotation in AVL rebalancing

nodes.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree), $\langle c; A, y, B \rangle$ for the node with cached height $c$, left subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$, and $N(A, y, B)$ for the node $\langle \max(h(A), h(B)) + 1; A, y, B \rangle$. Let $L$, $A$, $B$ be trees with cached heights, let $x$, $y$ be keys and let $c$ be a natural number. If $h(L) + 1 < c$ and…
nodes.title: Single left rotation in AVL rebalancing

nodes.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree), $\langle c; A, y, B \rangle$ for the node with cached height $c$, left subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$, and $N(A, y, B)$ for the node $\langle \max(h(A), h(B)) + 1; A, y, B \rangle$. Let $L$, $A$, $B$, $C$ be trees with cached heights, let $x$, $y$, $z$ be keys and let $c$, $c'$ be natural numbers. If $h(L) + 1 < c$…
nodes.title: Right-left double rotation in AVL rebalancing

nodes.summary: If two AVL trees $\ell$ and $r$ have correct cached heights, then for every key $k$ the tree produced by the rebalancing function from $\ell$, $k$ and $r$ also has correct cached heights.
nodes.title: AVL rebalancing preserves cached heights

nodes.summary: Let $l$ and $r$ be trees whose cached heights are correct at every node, and write $h$ for the cached height. Then for every key $k$, the rebalanced node $b$ built from $l$, $k$ and $r$ satisfies $h(b) \le \max(h(l), h(r)) + 1$.
nodes.title: Upper bound on height after AVL rebalancing

nodes.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$, with $h$ of the empty tree equal to $0$, and write $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ for the AVL rebalancing of the node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$. If $L$ and $R$ are trees whose cached heights are correct at every node, then for every key $k$ we have $\max(h(L), h(R)) \le h(\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R))$.
nodes.title: Rebalancing does not drop below the taller child

nodes.summary: Let $l$ and $r$ be trees whose cached heights are correct at every node and which are balanced (at every node the cached heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one), let $x$ be a key, and write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree). If $h(l) \le h(r) + 2$ and $h(r) \le h(l) + 2$, then $\mathrm{balance}(l, x, r)$ is balanced.
nodes.title: AVL rebalancing yields a balanced tree

nodes.summary: For all trees $l$ and $r$ and every key $k$, the inorder traversal of the rebalanced node built from $l$, $k$ and $r$ is the inorder traversal of $l$, followed by $k$, followed by the inorder traversal of $r$.
nodes.title: AVL rebalancing preserves the inorder traversal

nodes.summary: Write $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ for the AVL rebalancing of the node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$. For trees $L$ and $R$ and keys $k$ and $x$, the key $x$ lies in $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ if and only if $x$ lies in $L$, $x = k$, or $x$ lies in $R$.
nodes.title: Membership after AVL rebalancing

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, let $k \in \alpha$, and let $L$ and $R$ be ordered trees with cached heights over $\alpha$ such that every key of $L$ is less than $k$ and every key of $R$ is greater than $k$. Then the tree that rebalancing produces from left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$ is ordered.
nodes.title: Rebalancing an AVL node preserves the search-tree order

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. If an AVL tree $t$ over $\alpha$ has correct cached heights, then for every $x \in \alpha$ the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ also has correct cached heights.
nodes.title: AVL insertion preserves cached heights

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, if a tree $t$ has correct cached heights at every node, then for every key $x$ the cached height of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is at most the cached height of $t$ plus one.
nodes.title: Upper bound on height after AVL insertion

nodes.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$, with $h$ of the empty tree equal to $0$. Let the keys be linearly ordered, and let $T$ be a tree whose cached heights are correct at every node and which satisfies the AVL balance invariant at every node. Then for every key $x$, if $T'$ is the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$, we have $h(T) \le h(T')$.
nodes.title: Insertion does not lower the height

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, let $t$ be an AVL tree over $\alpha$ and let $x \in \alpha$. If $t$ has correct cached heights and satisfies the AVL balance invariant, then the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ also satisfies the AVL balance invariant.
nodes.title: AVL insertion preserves balance

nodes.summary: Let the keys be linearly ordered. A key $y$ lies in the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into a tree $T$ if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ lies in $T$.
nodes.title: Membership after insertion into an AVL tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every key $x \in \alpha$ and every ordered tree $t$ with cached heights over $\alpha$, the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is ordered.
nodes.title: AVL insertion preserves the search-tree order

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be an ordered AVL tree over $\alpha$. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, searching for $x$ in $t$ by following comparisons from the root returns true if and only if $x$ is a key of $t$.
nodes.title: Correctness of AVL search

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ over a linearly ordered type, the AVL tree built from $L$ by successive insertion has correct cached heights.
nodes.title: AVL trees built from a list have correct cached heights

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ over a linearly ordered type, the AVL tree built from $L$ by successive insertion satisfies the AVL balance invariant.
nodes.title: AVL trees built from a list are balanced

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every list $xs$ of elements of $\alpha$, the tree obtained from the empty tree by inserting the elements of $xs$ one at a time, from the last element to the first, is ordered.
nodes.title: AVL trees built from a list are ordered

nodes.summary: Let the keys be linearly ordered. A key lies in the tree obtained by inserting the entries of a list one at a time, from last to first, into the empty tree exactly when it is in the list.
nodes.title: Membership in an AVL tree built from a list

nodes.summary: Given a default value $d$ and a binary tree $T$ with cached heights, the leftmost key of $T$ with default $d$ is $d$ when $T$ is empty; when $T$ has left subtree $L$ and root key $k$, it is the leftmost key of $L$ with default $k$. Thus for a nonempty tree it is the key of the node reached from the root by following left children as far as possible, and it does not depend on $d$.
nodes.title: Leftmost key of a tree

nodes.summary: For a tree $t$ with cached heights, the tree obtained by removing the leftmost key of $t$ is defined by recursion on $t$. The empty tree stays empty. A node whose left subtree is empty is replaced by its right subtree. A node with nonempty left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$ is replaced by $\mathrm{balance}(l', k, r)$, where $l'$ is $l$ with its leftmost key removed and $\mathrm{balance}$ is the AVL…
nodes.title: Removing the leftmost key of an AVL tree

nodes.summary: Minimum deletion maps a binary tree with cached heights to the tree obtained by removing its leftmost key and rebalancing on the way back up. It is the operation of removing the minimum, under the name used for the successor step of deletion, where a deleted node with two children is replaced by the minimum of its right subtree.
nodes.title: Minimum deletion in an AVL tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $x \in \alpha$. Deleting $x$ from a tree with cached heights is defined by recursion on the tree, where $\mathrm{balance}$ denotes the AVL rebalancing function. The empty tree stays empty. For a node with left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$: if $x < k$, the result is $\mathrm{balance}(l', k, r)$, where $l'$ is $l$ with $x$ deleted; if $k < x$, the result is…
nodes.title: AVL tree deletion

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, a key $x \in \alpha$ and a tree $t$ with cached heights, $\mathrm{delete}(x, t)$ is defined to be $\mathrm{erase}(x, t)$, the AVL deletion of $x$ from $t$.
nodes.title: AVL tree deletion under its alternative name

nodes.summary: For every nonempty binary tree $T$ with cached heights and every default value $d$, the leftmost key of $T$ computed with default $d$ occurs in $T$.
nodes.title: The leftmost key lies in the tree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with a cached height at each node whose cached heights are correct: each node stores one more than the larger of the cached heights of its two subtrees, the empty tree having height $0$. Then the cached heights of the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its leftmost key, rebalancing on the way back up, are again correct.
nodes.title: Removing the minimum keeps cached heights correct

nodes.summary: If $t$ is a tree whose cached heights are correct, then the cached height of the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its leftmost key is at most the cached height of $t$.
nodes.title: Removing the leftmost key does not increase the height of an AVL tree

nodes.summary: If $t$ is a tree whose cached heights are correct and which is balanced, then the cached height of $t$ is at most one more than the cached height of the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its leftmost key.
nodes.title: Removing the leftmost key lowers the height of an AVL tree by at most one

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with a cached height at each node whose cached heights are correct, and which is balanced: at every node the cached heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one. Then the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its leftmost key, rebalancing on the way back up, is again balanced.
nodes.title: Removing the minimum preserves AVL balance

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights over a linearly ordered type. If $T$ is ordered as a search tree, then so is the tree obtained from $T$ by removing its leftmost key and rebalancing on the way back up.
nodes.title: Removing the leftmost key preserves search-tree order

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys from a linearly ordered type and a cached height at each node, and suppose $t$ is ordered: at every node, all keys in the left subtree are strictly smaller and all keys in the right subtree are strictly larger than the key at that node. Let $m$ be the leftmost key of $t$, or an arbitrary default value if $t$ is empty. Then every key of the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its…
nodes.title: Keys left after removing the minimum exceed it

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a nonempty tree with cached heights and $m$ its leftmost key. Then the inorder traversal of $t$ is $m$ followed by the inorder traversal of the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its leftmost key.
nodes.title: The inorder traversal begins with the leftmost key

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys from a linearly ordered type and a cached height at each node whose cached heights are correct: each node stores one more than the larger of the cached heights of its two subtrees, the empty tree having height $0$. Then for every key $x$, the cached heights of the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$, rebalancing along the search path, are again correct.
nodes.title: Deletion keeps cached heights correct

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$, and $t$ a tree whose cached heights are correct. Then the cached height of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ is at most the cached height of $t$.
nodes.title: Deletion does not increase the height of an AVL tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$, and $t$ a balanced tree whose cached heights are correct. Then the cached height of $t$ is at most one more than the cached height of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$.
nodes.title: Deletion lowers the height of an AVL tree by at most one

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys from a linearly ordered type and a cached height at each node, whose cached heights are correct, and which is balanced: at every node the cached heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one. Then for every key $x$, the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$, rebalancing along the search path, is again balanced.
nodes.title: Deletion preserves AVL balance

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights over a linearly ordered type, ordered as a search tree (every key in a left subtree is smaller, and every key in a right subtree is larger, than the key at the node). Then for every key $x$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ with rebalancing is again ordered as a search tree.
nodes.title: AVL deletion preserves search-tree order

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$, and $t$ an ordered tree. Then the inorder traversal of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ is the inorder traversal of $t$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed; if $x$ does not occur, the traversal is unchanged.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal after AVL deletion

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights whose keys come from a linearly ordered type, and let $x$ and $y$ be keys with $y \ne x$. If $y$ occurs in $T$, then $y$ occurs in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$. No search-tree ordering of $T$ is assumed.
nodes.title: AVL deletion keeps every other key

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights over a linearly ordered type, ordered as a search tree. Then for every key $x$, $x$ does not occur in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$.
nodes.title: Deletion removes the deleted key from an ordered AVL tree

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights over a linearly ordered type, ordered as a search tree (every key in a left subtree is smaller, and every key in a right subtree is larger, than the key at the node). Then for all keys $x$ and $y$, $y$ occurs in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ if and only if $y$ occurs in $T$ and $y \ne x$.
nodes.title: Keys of an ordered AVL tree after deletion

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys from a linearly ordered type and a cached height at each node whose cached heights are correct: each node stores one more than the larger of the cached heights of its two subtrees, the empty tree having height $0$. Then for every key $x$, the cached heights of the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$, rebalancing along the search path, are again correct.
nodes.title: Deleting a key keeps cached heights correct

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys from a linearly ordered type and a cached height at each node, whose cached heights are correct, and which is balanced: at every node the cached heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one. Then for every key $x$, the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$, rebalancing along the search path, is again balanced.
nodes.title: Deleting a key preserves AVL balance

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights over a linearly ordered type. If $T$ is ordered as a search tree, then for every key $x$ the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ with rebalancing is again ordered as a search tree.
nodes.title: Deleting a key from an ordered AVL tree keeps it ordered

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$, and $t$ an ordered tree. Then the inorder traversal of $\mathrm{delete}(x, t)$, the AVL deletion of $x$ from $t$ under its alternative name, is the inorder traversal of $t$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed; if $x$ does not occur, the traversal is unchanged.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal after AVL deletion, alternative name

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with a cached height at each node whose cached heights are correct: each node stores one more than the larger of the cached heights of its two subtrees, the empty tree having height $0$. Then the cached heights of the tree obtained from $t$ by minimum deletion (removing its leftmost key, rebalancing on the way back up) are again correct.
nodes.title: Minimum deletion keeps cached heights correct

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with a cached height at each node whose cached heights are correct, and which is balanced: at every node the cached heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one. Then the tree obtained from $t$ by minimum deletion (removing its leftmost key, rebalancing on the way back up) is again balanced.
nodes.title: Minimum deletion preserves AVL balance

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights over a linearly ordered type. If $T$ is ordered as a search tree, then so is the tree obtained by the minimum-removal step used for the successor in deletion, which removes the leftmost key of $T$ and rebalances on the way back up.
nodes.title: Successor-step minimum removal preserves search-tree order
Cartesian tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $\le$. A binary tree with keys in $\alpha$ is min-heap ordered when, at every node, the key $k$ of that node satisfies $k \le y$ for every key $y$ in its left subtree and every key $y$ in its right subtree. The empty tree is min-heap ordered.
nodes.title: Min-heap ordered binary tree

nodes.summary: For a binary tree $T$ with keys in $\alpha$, the root key of $T$ is an optional element of $\alpha$: it is absent (none) when $T$ is empty, and it is $k$ when the top node of $T$ holds the key $k$.
nodes.title: Optional root key of a binary tree

nodes.summary: For every predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ and every binary tree $T$ with keys in $\alpha$, every key of $T$ satisfies $p$ if and only if every element of the inorder traversal of $T$ satisfies $p$.
nodes.title: A predicate holds on every key iff it holds along the inorder traversal

nodes.summary: For every binary tree $T$ and every key $k$, if $T$ is nonempty with root key $k$, then $k$ is a key of $T$.
nodes.title: The root of a binary tree is one of its keys

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree over a preordered type that is heap-ordered (in min-heap order). If $T$ has root key $k$, then $k \le x$ for every key $x$ occurring in $T$.
nodes.title: The root of a heap-ordered tree is below every key

nodes.summary: For a value $m$ of a type with decidable equality and a list $xs$, the split of $xs$ at $m$ is the pair of the part of $xs$ before the first occurrence of $m$ and the part after it; that occurrence itself is dropped. If $m$ does not occur in $xs$, the split is the pair of $xs$ and the empty list.
nodes.title: Splitting a list at the first occurrence of a value

nodes.summary: Let $m$ be an element of a type with decidable equality and let $xs$ be a list in which $m$ occurs. When $xs$ is split at the first occurrence of $m$, the left part does not contain $m$.
nodes.title: Splitting at the first occurrence leaves the value out of the left part

nodes.summary: For an element $a$ and a list $as$ over a linear order, the left-fold minimum of $a$ and $as$ is the minimum of the list with head $a$ and tail $as$. It is computed from the head: it equals $a$ when $as$ is empty, and when $as$ has head $b$ and tail $bs$ it equals the left-fold minimum of $\min(a, b)$ and $bs$.
nodes.title: Minimum of a nonempty list

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linear order. For a natural number $n$ (the fuel) and a list $xs$ over $\alpha$, the tree built from $xs$ with fuel $n$ is the empty tree if $n = 0$ or $xs$ is empty. Otherwise $n = k + 1$ and $xs$ is nonempty; let $m$ be the minimum of $xs$, and let $L$ and $R$ be the parts of $xs$ before and after the first occurrence of $m$. Then the tree has root $m$, its left subtree is built from $L$ with…
nodes.title: Fuel-bounded Cartesian tree construction

nodes.summary: For a list $xs$ over a linear order, the Cartesian tree of $xs$ is the result of the fuel-bounded Cartesian tree construction on $xs$ with fuel equal to the length of $xs$. So the empty list gives the empty tree, and otherwise the root is the minimum $m$ of $xs$, the left subtree is built in the same way from the elements before the first occurrence of $m$, and the right subtree from the elements after that…
nodes.title: Cartesian tree of a list

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ over a linear order, the inorder traversal of the Cartesian tree of $xs$ is $xs$.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal of a Cartesian tree

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ over a linear order, the inorder traversal of the Cartesian tree of $xs$ is a permutation of $xs$.
nodes.title: The keys of a Cartesian tree permute its input

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ over a linear order and every element $x$, $x$ is a key of the Cartesian tree of $xs$ if and only if $x$ occurs in $xs$.
nodes.title: Keys of a Cartesian tree

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ over a linear order, the Cartesian tree of $xs$ is min-heap ordered.
nodes.title: Cartesian trees are heap-ordered

nodes.summary: For every nonempty list $xs$ over a linearly ordered type, the Cartesian tree of $xs$ has a root key $m$.
nodes.title: The Cartesian tree of a nonempty list has a root

nodes.summary: Let $xs$ be a list over a linearly ordered type. If the Cartesian tree of $xs$ has root key $m$, then $m$ occurs in $xs$ and $m \le y$ for every element $y$ of $xs$.
nodes.title: The root of a Cartesian tree is a minimum of the list
Order statistic tree

nodes.summary: A node entry of an order-statistic tree over a type $\alpha$ consists of a key in $\alpha$ and a natural number, the cached number of nodes in the subtree rooted at that node.
nodes.title: Order-statistic tree node entry

nodes.summary: An order-statistic tree with keys in a type $\alpha$ is a binary tree, possibly empty, each of whose nodes carries a key in $\alpha$ together with a natural number, meant as the cached number of nodes in the subtree rooted at that node. That these caches are correct is a separate condition.
nodes.title: Order-statistic tree

nodes.summary: The cached root size of an order-statistic tree is the subtree size stored in the entry of its root node, and is $0$ for the empty tree.
nodes.title: Cached root size

nodes.summary: The erasure of an order-statistic tree is the binary tree of the same shape whose node keys are the keys of the original nodes: the empty tree is sent to the empty tree, and a node is sent to the node with the same key whose left and right subtrees are the erasures of the original left and right subtrees, so every cached subtree size is dropped.
nodes.title: Erasing the size caches of an order-statistic tree

nodes.summary: An order-statistic tree has correct size caches when, at every node, the cached subtree size equals the number of nodes of the left subtree plus the number of nodes of the right subtree plus one, that is, the number of nodes of the subtree rooted at that node. The empty tree has correct size caches.
nodes.title: Correct size caches

nodes.summary: An order-statistic tree over a type equipped with a relation $<$ is ordered when the binary tree obtained by erasing its cached sizes is an ordered binary search tree: at every node, each key of the left subtree is $<$ the node's key, the node's key is $<$ each key of the right subtree, and both subtrees are ordered.
nodes.title: Ordered order-statistic tree

nodes.summary: The inorder traversal of an order-statistic tree is the inorder traversal of the binary tree obtained by erasing its cached subtree sizes: the traversal of the left subtree, then the root key, then the traversal of the right subtree, and the empty list for the empty tree.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal of an order-statistic tree

nodes.summary: Given a key $k$ and order-statistic trees $L$ and $R$, the node built from them has key $k$, left subtree $L$, right subtree $R$, and cached subtree size equal to the cached root size of $L$ plus the cached root size of $R$ plus one, where the empty tree has cached root size zero.
nodes.title: Order-statistic tree node with computed cache

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $q \in \alpha$. Searching for $q$ in the empty tree returns false. At a node with key $k$, the search continues in the left subtree if $q < k$, continues in the right subtree if $k < q$, and returns true otherwise.
nodes.title: Search in an order-statistic tree

nodes.summary: Inserting a key $k$ of a linearly ordered type into the empty tree gives a single node with key $k$ and cached size $1$. For a nonempty tree with root key $r$: if $k < r$, the key is inserted into the left subtree; if $r < k$, it is inserted into the right subtree; in both cases the root is rebuilt with key $r$ and cached size equal to the cached root sizes of its two subtrees plus one (an empty subtree counts as…
nodes.title: Insertion into an order-statistic tree

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered key type, the order-statistic tree built from a list of keys is obtained by inserting the keys into the empty tree from right to left: the empty list gives the empty tree, and a list with head $k$ and tail $l$ gives the insertion of $k$ into the tree built from $l$.
nodes.title: Order-statistic tree built from a list

nodes.summary: For a key $q$ of a linearly ordered type, the rank of $q$ in an order-statistic tree is computed by descending from the root. It is $0$ for the empty tree. At a node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$, it is the rank of $q$ in $L$ if $q < k$; it is $s(L) + 1$ plus the rank of $q$ in $R$ if $k < q$; and it is $s(L)$ if $q = k$. Here $s(L)$ is the subtree size cached at the root of $L$, and $0$ if…
nodes.title: Rank in an order-statistic tree

nodes.summary: For an order-statistic tree $T$ and a natural number $i$, select at index $i$ in $T$ is computed by descending from the root. It returns nothing for the empty tree. At a node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$, it is select at index $i$ in $L$ if $i < s(L)$; it returns $k$ if $i = s(L)$; and it is select at index $i - s(L) - 1$ in $R$ if $i > s(L)$. Here $s(L)$ is the subtree size cached at the…
nodes.title: Select in an order-statistic tree

nodes.summary: If an order-statistic tree $T$ has correct cached subtree sizes at every node, then the cached root size of $T$ (zero for the empty tree) equals the number of nodes of $T$.
nodes.title: Correct caches give the tree size

nodes.summary: Let $k$ be a key and let $L$ and $R$ be order-statistic trees whose cached subtree sizes are correct at every node. Then the node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$, whose root cache is the cached root size of $L$ plus the cached root size of $R$ plus one, also has correct cached subtree sizes at every node.
nodes.title: The cache-computing node constructor preserves correct size caches

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $k \in \alpha$ and $T$ an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$. Forgetting the cached sizes of the tree obtained by inserting $k$ into $T$ gives the same binary tree as inserting $k$, by ordinary binary-search-tree insertion, into $T$ with its cached sizes forgotten.
nodes.title: Insertion commutes with forgetting the size caches

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, let $k \in \alpha$, and let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ whose cached subtree sizes are correct at every node. Then the tree obtained by inserting $k$ into $T$ also has correct cached subtree sizes at every node.
nodes.title: Insertion preserves correct size caches

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over a linearly ordered key type that is ordered, meaning that after its cached sizes are erased, at every node each key of the left subtree is strictly smaller than the node's key and each key of the right subtree is strictly larger. Then for every key $k$, the tree obtained by inserting $k$ into $T$ is again ordered.
nodes.title: Insertion preserves ordering of order-statistic trees

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every list $\ell$ of elements of $\alpha$, the order-statistic tree obtained by inserting the elements of $\ell$ into the empty tree, from right to left, has correct cached subtree sizes at every node.
nodes.title: Order-statistic trees built from a list have correct size caches

nodes.summary: For every list $l$ of keys from a linearly ordered type, the order-statistic tree built from $l$ by successive insertion is ordered: after its cached sizes are erased, at every node each key of the left subtree is strictly smaller than the node's key and each key of the right subtree is strictly larger.
nodes.title: Order-statistic trees built from lists are ordered

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered key type, a key $k$ and a list $l$ of keys, $k$ is a key of some node of the order-statistic tree built from $l$ by successive insertion if and only if $k$ occurs in $l$.
nodes.title: Keys of an order-statistic tree built from a list

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $T$ an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ that is ordered: after forgetting the cached sizes, at every node all keys in the left subtree are smaller than the node's key and all keys in the right subtree are larger. Then for every $q \in \alpha$, comparison search for $q$ in $T$ returns true if and only if $q$ is the key of some node of $T$.
nodes.title: Search in an ordered order-statistic tree is correct

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over a linearly ordered key type whose cached subtree sizes are correct at every node and which is ordered. Then for every query $q$, the rank of $q$ computed by descending $T$ with cached left-subtree sizes equals the number of entries strictly smaller than $q$ in the inorder traversal of the binary tree obtained by erasing the caches of $T$.
nodes.title: Cached rank agrees with traversal rank

nodes.summary: For every order-statistic tree $T$ whose cached subtree sizes are correct and every natural number $i$, select at index $i$ in $T$ (descending with the cached sizes) returns the same result as taking the element at zero-based position $i$ of the inorder traversal of the binary tree obtained from $T$ by erasing the cached sizes; in particular both return nothing when that position does not exist.
nodes.title: Cached select agrees with inorder select

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over a linearly ordered type whose cached subtree sizes are correct and which satisfies the binary-search-tree ordering. For every key $k$ in $T$, select in $T$ at the index equal to the rank of $k$ in $T$ returns $k$.
nodes.title: Select inverts rank in an order-statistic tree

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over a linearly ordered type whose cached subtree sizes are correct and which satisfies the binary-search-tree ordering. If select at zero-based index $i$ in $T$ returns a key $k$, then the rank of $k$ in $T$ equals $i$.
nodes.title: Rank inverts select in an order-statistic tree

nodes.summary: The merge of order-statistic trees $A$ and $B$ is defined by recursion on $A$. If $A$ is empty, it is $B$. If $A$ has root key $x$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$, it is the node with key $x$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree the merge of $R$ and $B$, whose cached size is the sum of the cached root sizes of its children plus one, an empty child counting as zero. Thus $B$ is attached below the rightmost…
nodes.title: Merging order-statistic trees

nodes.summary: Deleting a key $k$ from an order-statistic tree over a linearly ordered type follows the comparison path from the root. The empty tree stays empty. At a node with key $x$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$: if $k < x$, the result is the node with key $x$, left subtree the deletion of $k$ from $L$ and right subtree $R$; if $x < k$, it is the node with key $x$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree the deletion of…
nodes.title: Deletion from an order-statistic tree

nodes.summary: Let $A$ and $B$ be order-statistic trees whose cached subtree size at every node equals the number of nodes in that node's subtree. Then the merge of $A$ and $B$ has the same property. No ordering between the keys of $A$ and $B$ is assumed.
nodes.title: Order-statistic merge preserves cache correctness

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $k \in \alpha$ a key and $T$ an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$. If the cached subtree size at every node of $T$ equals the number of nodes in that node's subtree, then the same holds for the tree obtained by deleting $k$ from $T$.
nodes.title: Order-statistic deletion preserves cache correctness

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and let $L$ and $R$ be ordered order-statistic trees over $\alpha$ such that $x < y$ for every key $x$ of $L$ and every key $y$ of $R$. Then the merge of $L$ and $R$ is ordered.
nodes.title: Merging separated ordered order-statistic trees preserves order

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ that is ordered, that is, after its cached sizes are removed, every key in a left subtree is strictly smaller than the key of its node and every key in a right subtree is strictly larger. Then for every key $k$, the tree obtained from $T$ by deleting $k$ is again ordered.
nodes.title: Deletion preserves order in an order-statistic tree

nodes.summary: For order-statistic trees $A$ and $B$, the inorder traversal of the merge of $A$ and $B$ is the inorder traversal of $A$ followed by the inorder traversal of $B$. No ordering between the keys of $A$ and $B$ is assumed.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal of an order-statistic merge

nodes.summary: For order-statistic trees $A$ and $B$ over a type $\alpha$ and any $x \in \alpha$, $x$ is a key of the merge of $A$ and $B$ if and only if $x$ is a key of $A$ or a key of $B$. No ordering between the keys of $A$ and $B$ is assumed.
nodes.title: Keys of an order-statistic merge

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $k \in \alpha$ and $T$ an ordered order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ (at every node, all keys of the left subtree are smaller and all keys of the right subtree are larger than the node's key). The inorder traversal of the tree obtained by deleting $k$ from $T$ is the inorder traversal of $T$ with every occurrence of $k$ removed.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal after order-statistic deletion

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $k \in \alpha$ and $T$ an ordered order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ (at every node, all keys of the left subtree are smaller and all keys of the right subtree are larger than the node's key). For every $y \in \alpha$, $y$ is a key of the tree obtained by deleting $k$ from $T$ if and only if $y$ is a key of $T$ and $y \ne k$.
nodes.title: Keys of an order-statistic tree after deletion

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $k \in \alpha$ and $T$ an ordered order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ (at every node, all keys of the left subtree are smaller and all keys of the right subtree are larger than the node's key). Then $k$ is not a key of the tree obtained by deleting $k$ from $T$.
nodes.title: Deleted key is absent from an order-statistic tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $k \in \alpha$ and $T$ an ordered order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ (at every node, all keys of the left subtree are smaller and all keys of the right subtree are larger than the node's key). Comparison search for $k$ in the tree obtained by deleting $k$ from $T$ returns false.
nodes.title: Search misses a key deleted from an order-statistic tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ that is ordered and whose cached subtree sizes are correct. Let $k$ and $q$ be keys and let $T'$ be the tree obtained from $T$ by deleting $k$. Then the rank of $q$ in $T'$, computed by navigation with cached sizes, equals the number of entries strictly smaller than $q$ in the inorder traversal of $T'$ with its cached sizes…
nodes.title: Rank after deletion in an order-statistic tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ whose cached subtree sizes are correct. Let $k$ be a key and let $T'$ be the tree obtained from $T$ by deleting $k$. Then for every natural number $i$, selecting position $i$ in $T'$ by navigation with cached sizes returns the entry at zero-based position $i$ of the inorder traversal of $T'$ with its cached sizes removed,…
nodes.title: Selection after deletion in an order-statistic tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ that is ordered and whose cached subtree sizes are correct, let $k$ be a key, and let $T'$ be the tree obtained from $T$ by deleting $k$. If $y$ is a key of $T'$, then selecting, with cached sizes, the position in $T'$ given by the cached rank of $y$ in $T'$ returns $y$.
nodes.title: Selecting the rank of a surviving key after deletion
Red–black tree

nodes.summary: The colors of red-black tree nodes are the two values red and black.
nodes.title: Red-black node colors

nodes.summary: A red-black tree with keys in a type $\alpha$ is either empty or a node consisting of a color (red or black), a left subtree, a key in $\alpha$, and a right subtree.
nodes.title: Red-black tree data type

nodes.summary: The color erasure of a red-black tree is the binary tree obtained by forgetting the node colors: the empty tree goes to the empty binary tree, and a node with key $k$ and subtrees $l$ and $r$ goes to the binary-tree node with key $k$ whose subtrees are the color erasures of $l$ and $r$.
nodes.title: Color erasure

nodes.summary: An element $x$ is a member of a red-black tree $t$ when $x$ is a member of the binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its colors, that is, when $x$ equals the key of some node of $t$.
nodes.title: Membership in a red-black tree

nodes.summary: For a red-black tree $t$ and a list $s$, this is the accumulator form of the binary-search-tree inorder traversal applied to the color erasure of $t$: for the empty tree it returns $s$, and for a node with key $k$ and subtrees $l$ and $r$ it returns the result for $l$ with suffix the list $k$ followed by $u$, where $u$ is the result for $r$ with suffix $s$.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal onto a suffix

nodes.summary: The inorder traversal of a red-black tree $t$ is the binary-search-tree inorder traversal of the color erasure of $t$, computed in linear time with an accumulator starting from the empty list. It lists the keys of $t$ from left to right: the empty tree gives the empty list, and a node with key $k$ and subtrees $l$ and $r$ gives the traversal of $l$, then $k$, then the traversal of $r$.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal of a red-black tree

nodes.summary: For a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ and a red-black tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, $p$ holds at every key of $t$ when $p$ holds at every key of the binary search tree obtained from $t$ by erasing colors.
nodes.title: Predicate holding at every key of a red-black tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $<$. A red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ is ordered when, at every node with key $k$, every key $y$ in the left subtree satisfies $y < k$ and every key $z$ in the right subtree satisfies $k < z$.
nodes.title: Ordered red-black tree

nodes.summary: For every red-black tree $t$ and every $x$, $x$ is a member of $t$ if and only if $x$ is a member of the binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its colors.
nodes.title: Red-black membership is membership in the underlying binary tree

nodes.summary: For every predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ and every red-black tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, $p$ holds at every key of $t$ if and only if $p$ holds at every key of the binary search tree obtained from $t$ by erasing colors. This holds by definition.
nodes.title: All keys of a red-black tree via its color erasure

nodes.summary: For keys with a relation $<$, a red-black tree $t$ is ordered if and only if the binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its colors is an ordered binary search tree.
nodes.title: A red-black tree is ordered exactly when its underlying binary tree is

nodes.summary: For every red-black tree $t$, the inorder traversal of $t$ equals the binary-search-tree inorder traversal of the color erasure of $t$; this holds by definition.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal ignores colors

nodes.summary: The root color of a red-black tree is the color of its root node; the empty tree has root color black.
nodes.title: Root color

nodes.summary: A red-black tree satisfies the red property when no red node has a red child, where empty subtrees count as black.
nodes.title: Red property of red-black trees

nodes.summary: A red-black tree satisfies the relaxed red invariant when it is empty, or when its left and right subtrees both satisfy the red invariant (no red node has a red child). The root itself is unconstrained, so a red root may have a red child.
nodes.title: Red invariant away from the root

nodes.summary: The black height of a red-black tree is the number of black nodes on its leftmost root-to-leaf path, counting the empty leaf as one black node: the empty tree has black height $1$, a red node has the black height of its left subtree, and a black node has the black height of its left subtree plus $1$.
nodes.title: Black height

nodes.summary: A red-black tree is balanced when every root-to-leaf path contains the same number of black nodes. Recursively: the empty tree is balanced, and a node is balanced when both of its subtrees are balanced and have the same black height (the number of black nodes on the leftmost root-to-leaf path, counting the leaf).
nodes.title: Black-height balanced red-black tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $<$. A red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ is valid when it is ordered, satisfies the red property (no red node has a red child), is balanced (every root-to-leaf path contains the same number of black nodes), and its root is black, where the empty tree counts as black.
nodes.title: Valid red-black tree

nodes.summary: Searching a red-black tree over a linearly ordered type for a key $x$ returns a Boolean, ignoring colors: the empty tree gives false, and at a node with key $k$ the search continues in the left subtree if $x < k$, continues in the right subtree if $k < x$, and returns true otherwise.
nodes.title: Search in a red-black tree

nodes.summary: Given a color $c$, red-black trees $l$ and $r$, and a key $k$, rebalancing produces a tree as follows. Suppose $c$ is black and one of these configurations occurs, taking the first that applies: $l$ is a red node with a red left child; $l$ is a red node with a red right child; $r$ is a red node with a red left child; $r$ is a red node with a red right child. The black root and the two red nodes then hold three keys…
nodes.title: Okasaki's rebalancing

nodes.summary: For keys from a linearly ordered type, the unchecked insertion of $x$ into a red-black tree is defined by recursion on the tree. Inserting $x$ into the empty tree gives a red node with key $x$ and two empty subtrees. Inserting $x$ into a node with color $c$, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$ gives: if $x < k$, Okasaki's rebalancing of color $c$, left subtree the insertion of $x$ into $l$, key $k$ and…
nodes.title: Unchecked red-black insertion

nodes.summary: Recoloring the root of a red-black tree black leaves the empty tree unchanged and turns a node with any color, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$ into the black node with left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$.
nodes.title: Blackening the root

nodes.summary: For every red-black tree $t$, the color erasure of the tree obtained from $t$ by recoloring its root black (the empty tree is left unchanged) equals the color erasure of $t$.
nodes.title: Recoloring the root black does not change the color erasure

nodes.summary: For keys from a linearly ordered type, inserting $x$ into a red-black tree $t$ gives the unchecked insertion of $x$ into $t$ with its root recolored black.
nodes.title: Red-black tree insertion

nodes.summary: The red-black tree built from a list over a linearly ordered type inserts the elements of the list into the empty tree from right to left: the empty list gives the empty tree, and a list with head $x$ and tail $xs$ gives the insertion of $x$ into the tree built from $xs$.
nodes.title: Red-black tree from a list

nodes.summary: For every predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ and every red-black tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, $p$ holds at every key of $t$ if and only if $p(x)$ holds for every $x \in \alpha$ that is a (structural) member of $t$.
nodes.title: All keys versus members of a red-black tree

nodes.summary: For every red-black tree $t$ and every $x$, $x$ occurs in the inorder traversal of $t$ if and only if $x$ is a member of $t$.
nodes.title: Membership in the inorder traversal of a red-black tree

nodes.summary: For keys from a linearly ordered type, if a red-black tree $t$ is ordered, then every entry of the inorder traversal of $t$ is strictly smaller than every later entry.
nodes.title: The inorder traversal of an ordered red-black tree is strictly increasing

nodes.summary: For keys from a linearly ordered type, a key $y$ is a member of the red-black tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ is a member of $t$.
nodes.title: Membership after insertion into a red-black tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$ a key, and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$. If $t$ is ordered (at every node with key $k$, every key in the left subtree is less than $k$ and every key in the right subtree is greater than $k$), then the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is ordered.
nodes.title: Red-black insertion preserves the search-tree order

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$ a key, and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$. If no red node of $t$ has a red child, then no red node of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ has a red child.
nodes.title: Red-black insertion preserves the red property

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. If a red-black tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$ is balanced (every root-to-leaf path contains the same number of black nodes), then for every $x \in \alpha$ the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is balanced.
nodes.title: Red-black insertion preserves black-height balance

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every red-black tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$ and every $x \in \alpha$, the black height of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ equals either the black height of $t$ or the black height of $t$ plus one.
nodes.title: Insertion raises the black height by at most one

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$ a key, and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ that is ordered, satisfies the red property (no red node has a red child), and is balanced (every root-to-leaf path contains the same number of black nodes). Then the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is valid.
nodes.title: Red-black insertion yields a valid tree from the invariants

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $x \in \alpha$. If $t$ is a valid red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$, then the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is also valid.
nodes.title: Red-black insertion preserves validity

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a red-black tree over a linearly ordered type that is ordered (every left key is smaller and every right key larger, recursively). Then for every key $x$, the search for $x$ in $t$ returns true if and only if $x$ is a key of some node of $t$.
nodes.title: Search in an ordered red-black tree is correct

nodes.summary: For a red-black tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type that is ordered (every left key is smaller and every right key larger, recursively), the inorder traversal of $t$ contains no key twice.
nodes.title: Ordered red-black trees have duplicate-free inorder traversals

nodes.summary: For every type $\alpha$ with a relation $<$, the empty red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ is a valid red-black tree.
nodes.title: The empty red-black tree is valid

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every list $l$ of elements of $\alpha$, the red-black tree obtained from the empty tree by inserting the elements of $l$ one at a time, from the last to the first, is valid.
nodes.title: Red-black trees built from a list are valid

nodes.summary: For keys from a linearly ordered type and every list $xs$, a key $x$ is a member of the red-black tree built from $xs$ by successive insertion if and only if $x$ occurs in $xs$.
nodes.title: Membership in a red-black tree built from a list

nodes.summary: The splice of a red-black tree $t$ with a red-black tree $s$ is defined by recursion on $t$. The splice of the empty tree with $s$ is $s$. The splice of the node with color $c$, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$ with $s$ is the node with color $c$, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree the splice of $r$ with $s$.
nodes.title: Splicing two red-black trees

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type, unbalanced deletion of $x$ from a red-black tree is defined by recursion on the tree. The empty tree stays empty. At a node with color $c$, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$: if $x < k$, the result is the node with color $c$, left subtree the unbalanced deletion of $x$ from $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$; if $k < x$, it is the node with color $c$, left…
nodes.title: Unbalanced red-black tree deletion

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered key type, the rebuild of a red-black tree $t$ is the tree obtained from the empty tree by inserting the keys of the inorder traversal of $t$ one at a time with Okasaki insertion, starting from the last key.
nodes.title: Rebuilding a red-black tree from its keys

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type and a red-black tree $t$, deleting $x$ from $t$ by rebuilding first forms the unbalanced deletion of $x$ from $t$, then rebalances it: starting from the empty tree, it inserts the keys of the inorder traversal of that tree one at a time, from the last key to the first.
nodes.title: Red-black tree deletion by rebuilding

nodes.summary: For red-black trees $t$ and $s$ with keys of any type, a key $x$ belongs to the splice of $t$ with $s$ if and only if $x$ belongs to $t$ or $x$ belongs to $s$.
nodes.title: Membership in a splice

nodes.summary: For red-black trees $t$ and $s$ with keys of any type, the inorder traversal of the splice of $t$ with $s$ is the inorder traversal of $t$ followed by the inorder traversal of $s$.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal of a splice

nodes.summary: Let $<$ be a relation on the keys, and let $L$ and $R$ be red-black trees that are ordered for $<$ such that $a < b$ for every key $a$ of $L$ and every key $b$ of $R$. Then the join of $L$ and $R$, obtained by putting $R$ in place of the empty right subtree of the rightmost node of $L$ (or $R$ itself if $L$ is empty) and keeping all colors, is ordered.
nodes.title: Joining separated ordered trees preserves order

nodes.summary: Let $x$ and $y$ be keys of a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be an ordered red-black tree. Then $y$ belongs to the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$ by rebuilding if and only if $y$ belongs to $t$ and $y \ne x$.
nodes.title: Membership after deletion by rebuilding

nodes.summary: Let $x$ be a key of a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be an ordered red-black tree. Then $x$ does not belong to the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$ by rebuilding.
nodes.title: The deleted key is absent after deletion by rebuilding

nodes.summary: Let $x$ be a key of a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be an ordered red-black tree. Then the inorder traversal of the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$ by rebuilding is the inorder traversal of $t$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed (it is unchanged if $x$ does not occur).
nodes.title: Inorder traversal after deletion by rebuilding

nodes.summary: For every linearly ordered key type, every key $x$ and every red-black tree $t$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ is a valid red-black tree: it is ordered, no red node has a red child, every root-to-leaf path contains the same number of black nodes, and its root is black (the empty tree counts as black). No hypothesis on $t$ is needed.
nodes.title: Red-black deletion yields a valid red-black tree

nodes.summary: For every linearly ordered key type, every key $x$ and every red-black tree $t$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ is ordered: at every node, all keys in the left subtree are strictly smaller than the node's key and all keys in the right subtree are strictly larger. No hypothesis on $t$ is needed.
nodes.title: Red-black deletion yields an ordered tree

nodes.summary: For every linearly ordered key type, every key $x$ and every red-black tree $t$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ satisfies the red invariant: no red node has a red child. No hypothesis on $t$ is needed.
nodes.title: Red-black deletion yields a tree with no red-red edge

nodes.summary: For every linearly ordered type of keys, every key $x$ and every red-black tree $t$, with no hypothesis on $t$, the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$ by rebuilding is black-height balanced.
nodes.title: Deletion by rebuilding is black-height balanced

nodes.summary: For every linearly ordered type of keys, every key $x$ and every red-black tree $t$, with no hypothesis on $t$, the root of the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$ by rebuilding is black, where the empty tree counts as having a black root.
nodes.title: Deletion by rebuilding gives a black root

nodes.summary: An extended color is one of three values: red, black or double black.
nodes.title: Extended root colors

nodes.summary: A tree with a possibly double-black root over a type $\alpha$ is one of the following: a genuine red-black tree over $\alpha$; the double-black empty tree; or a double-black node consisting of a left subtree, a key in $\alpha$ and a right subtree, where both subtrees are genuine red-black trees. Hence a double black can occur only at the root.
nodes.title: Trees with a possibly double-black root

nodes.summary: The inorder traversal of a red-black tree whose root may be double black ignores the double-black mark: a genuine tree gives its inorder traversal, the double-black empty tree gives the empty list, and a double-black node with left child $l$, key $k$ and right child $r$ gives the inorder traversal of $l$, followed by $k$, followed by the inorder traversal of $r$.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal of a possibly double-black tree

nodes.summary: The black height of a genuine red-black tree is its usual black height. The double-black empty tree has black height $2$, and a double-black node with left subtree $L$ has black height $h(L) + 2$, where $h(L)$ is the usual black height of $L$. Thus a double-black root counts as two black nodes, where the usual black height counts the empty tree as one.
nodes.title: Black height of a possibly double-black tree

nodes.summary: A tree whose root may be double black is balanced when it is a genuine red-black tree that is balanced, when it is the double-black empty tree, or when it is a double-black node whose left and right subtrees are both balanced and have the same black height.
nodes.title: Black-height balance of a possibly double-black tree

nodes.summary: A tree whose root may be double black satisfies the red invariant in the following cases: a genuine red-black tree satisfies it when it satisfies the usual red invariant (no red node has a red child); the double-black empty tree always satisfies it; and a double-black node with left subtree $l$ and right subtree $r$ satisfies it when both $l$ and $r$ satisfy the usual red invariant.
nodes.title: Red invariant for trees with a possibly double-black root

nodes.summary: The extended color of a tree whose root may be double black is the color of its root, red or black, when it is a genuine red-black tree, where the empty tree counts as black; it is double black for the double-black empty tree and for every double-black node.
nodes.title: Extended root color

nodes.summary: Add one black to the root of a red-black tree, producing a tree whose root may be double black: the empty tree becomes the double-black empty tree, a red root becomes black, and a black root becomes double black.
nodes.title: Adding a black to the root

nodes.summary: For a red-black tree $t$, this is the tree obtained from $t$ by coloring its root black: the empty tree stays empty, and a node with left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$, of either color, becomes the black node with left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$.
nodes.title: Recoloring the root black

nodes.summary: Blackening sends a tree whose root may be double black to a genuine red-black tree by changing only its root: a genuine tree has its root recolored black (the empty tree stays empty), the double-black empty tree becomes the empty tree, and a double-black node becomes the black node with the same subtrees and key.
nodes.title: Absorbing a double-black root

nodes.summary: For a red-black tree $t$ over a type $\alpha$, the leftmost key of $t$ is either a key in $\alpha$ or undefined. It is undefined when $t$ is empty. When $t$ is a node, of either color, with left subtree $l$ and key $k$, it is the leftmost key of $l$ if that is defined, and $k$ otherwise. Hence the leftmost key is defined exactly when $t$ is nonempty.
nodes.title: Leftmost key of a red-black tree

nodes.summary: Write $\mathrm{R}$ and $\mathrm{B}$ for red and black, and $N(c, T, y, T')$ for the node of color $c$ with left subtree $T$, key $y$ and right subtree $T'$. Given a color $c$, a tree $D$, a key $k$ and a tree $S$, the left repair returns a tree whose root may be double black, by the first case that applies. If $S = N(\mathrm{B}, T_1, y, N(\mathrm{R}, T_2, z, T_3))$ or, failing that,…
nodes.title: Left repair after double-black deletion

nodes.summary: Write $\mathrm{R}$ and $\mathrm{B}$ for red and black, and $N(c, T, y, T')$ for the node of color $c$ with left subtree $T$, key $y$ and right subtree $T'$. Given a color $c$, a tree $S$, a key $k$ and a tree $D$, the right repair returns a tree whose root may be double black, by the first case that applies. If $S = N(\mathrm{B}, N(\mathrm{R}, T_1, y, T_2), z, T_3)$ or, failing that,…
nodes.title: Right repair after double-black deletion

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a color, $L$ a tree whose root may be double black, $k$ a key and $R$ a red-black tree. If $L$ is a genuine red-black tree, the result is the genuine node with color $c$, left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$. Otherwise the double black of $L$ is absorbed first: a double-black empty tree becomes the empty tree, and a double-black node becomes the black node with the same children and key. The…
nodes.title: Rebalancing after deletion from the left subtree

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a color, $L$ a red-black tree, $k$ a key and $R$ a tree whose root may be double black. If $R$ is a genuine red-black tree, the result is the genuine node with color $c$, left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$. Otherwise the double black of $R$ is absorbed first: a double-black empty tree becomes the empty tree, and a double-black node becomes the black node with the same children and key. The…
nodes.title: Rebalancing after deletion from the right subtree

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type, deleting $x$ from a red-black tree returns a tree whose root may be double black, by recursion on the tree. The empty tree gives the empty tree. At a node of color $c$ with left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$: if $x < k$, the result is the left reassembly of color $c$, the deletion of $x$ from $l$, key $k$ and $r$; if $k < x$, it is the right reassembly of color…
nodes.title: Double-black deletion

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type and a red-black tree $t$, deleting $x$ from $t$ runs the double-black deletion of $x$ from $t$, which returns a tree whose root may be double black, and then absorbs a remaining double black at the root and recolors the root black.
nodes.title: Red-black tree deletion by the double-black method

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type and an ordered red-black tree $t$, the inorder traversal of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method is the inorder traversal of $t$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed (unchanged if $x$ does not occur).
nodes.title: Double-black deletion erases the key from the inorder traversal

nodes.summary: For keys $x$ and $y$ of a linearly ordered type and an ordered red-black tree $t$, $y$ is a key of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method if and only if $y$ is a key of $t$ and $y \ne x$.
nodes.title: Keys after double-black deletion

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ that is ordered, that is, at every node all keys of the left subtree are strictly smaller and all keys of the right subtree are strictly larger than the node's key. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the key $x$ does not occur in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method.
nodes.title: The deleted key is absent after double-black deletion

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ that is ordered, that is, at every node all keys of the left subtree are strictly smaller and all keys of the right subtree are strictly larger than the node's key. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method is again ordered.
nodes.title: Double-black deletion preserves the search-tree order

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ that is ordered, satisfies the red invariant (no red node has a red child), and is black-height balanced (all root-to-leaf paths contain the same number of black nodes). Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method is a valid red-black tree.
nodes.title: Double-black deletion yields a valid tree from the structural invariants

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $t$ a valid red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$: it is ordered, satisfies the red invariant, is black-height balanced, and has a black root. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method is again a valid red-black tree.
nodes.title: Double-black deletion preserves validity

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $t$ a valid red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$: it is ordered, satisfies the red invariant, is black-height balanced, and has a black root. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method satisfies the red invariant: no red node has a red child.
nodes.title: Double-black deletion from a valid tree keeps the red invariant

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$, and $T$ a valid red-black tree over $\alpha$. Then the tree obtained from $T$ by double-black deletion of $x$ is balanced.
nodes.title: Double-black deletion keeps a valid tree balanced

nodes.summary: For every key $x$ of a linearly ordered type and every red-black tree $t$, valid or not, the root of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method is black, where the empty tree counts as black.
nodes.title: Double-black deletion leaves a black root

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$, $T$ a valid red-black tree over $\alpha$, and $T'$ the tree obtained from $T$ by double-black deletion of $x$. Then the black height of $T'$ either equals the black height of $T$ or is one less than it.
nodes.title: Black height after double-black deletion
Skip list

nodes.summary: A skip-list node consists of a key, a value and a natural number, the height of its tower. The node itself does not require the height to be positive; positivity is part of the validity invariant of skip lists.
nodes.title: Skip-list node

nodes.summary: A deterministic skip list with keys in $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$ is represented by the list of its bottom-level nodes, each node an entry carrying a key in $\alpha$, a value in $\beta$ and a tower height, a natural number. No ordering or height condition is imposed by this structure.
nodes.title: Skip list

nodes.summary: The empty skip list is the skip list with no nodes.
nodes.title: Empty skip list

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. A skip list with keys in $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$ is valid when the keys of its bottom-level nodes are strictly increasing along the list and every node has a tower of positive height.
nodes.title: Valid skip list

nodes.summary: For a skip list and a level index $i$ (levels are numbered from $0$ at the bottom), level $i$ is the list of key-value pairs $(k, v)$ of the stored nodes whose tower height $h$ satisfies $i < h$, in the order in which these nodes appear in the bottom-level list of the skip list.
nodes.title: Level of a skip list

nodes.summary: The bottom-level abstraction of a skip list is the association list obtained from its bottom-level nodes, in order, by keeping the key-value pair $(k, v)$ of each node and forgetting its tower height.
nodes.title: Bottom-level abstraction of a skip list

nodes.summary: For a key $k$ and a skip list $S$, the stored tower height of $k$ in $S$ is the tower height of the first bottom-level node of $S$ whose key equals $k$ under the given Boolean equality test on keys; it is undefined when no node has key $k$.
nodes.title: Stored tower height of a key

nodes.summary: Let $k$ be a search key, $i$ a zero-based level and $L$ a list of skip-list nodes. Let $P$ be the longest prefix of $L$ whose nodes all have keys less than $k$. If some node of $P$ has tower height greater than $i$ (so it is visible at level $i$), advancing at level $i$ returns the part of $L$ after the last such node; otherwise it returns $L$ unchanged.
nodes.title: One level of skip-list search

nodes.summary: Let $k$ be a key and let $H$ be the greatest tower height in a skip list ($H = 0$ if the list is empty or every tower has height $0$). Start with the full list of bottom-level nodes, and for each level $i$ from $H - 1$ down to $0$ in turn (no levels when $H = 0$) replace the current list by the result of advancing at level $i$: within the longest initial segment of the current list whose keys are all less than $k$,…
nodes.title: Skip-list search window

nodes.summary: The lookup of a key $k$ in a skip list computes the search window for $k$, the suffix of the bottom-level nodes reached by descending from the highest level to level $0$, and returns the value of the first node in the window whose key is $k$, or no value if the window has no such node.
nodes.title: Skip-list lookup

nodes.summary: To insert key $k$ with value $v$ and requested height $h$ into a skip list, scan its bottom-level nodes in order, keeping every node whose key is less than $k$. At the first node whose key is not less than $k$: if its key equals $k$, its value is replaced by $v$ and its tower height is kept; if its key is greater than $k$, a new node with key $k$, value $v$ and tower height $\max(1, h)$ is placed before it. If…
nodes.title: Skip-list insertion

nodes.summary: For every linearly ordered type $\alpha$ and every type $\beta$, the empty skip list with keys in $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$ is valid.
nodes.title: The empty skip list is valid

nodes.summary: If a skip list is valid, then for every level index $i$ (levels are numbered from $0$ at the bottom), the keys in the list of key-value pairs visible at level $i$ are strictly increasing: every pair has a strictly smaller key than every pair after it.
nodes.title: Skip-list levels are sorted by key

nodes.summary: For every skip list and every level index $i$ (levels are numbered from $0$ at the bottom), the list of key-value pairs visible at level $i + 1$ is a subsequence, not necessarily contiguous, of the list of key-value pairs visible at level $i$.
nodes.title: Each skip-list level is a subsequence of the level below

nodes.summary: If a skip list is valid, then the keys of the pairs in its bottom-level abstraction, read in order, form a list without duplicates.
nodes.title: Keys of a valid skip list are distinct

nodes.summary: If a skip list is valid, then for every level index $i$ (levels are numbered from $0$ at the bottom), no key occurs twice in the list of key-value pairs visible at level $i$.
nodes.title: Keys on each skip-list level are distinct

nodes.summary: For every search key, every level $i$ and every list $L$ of skip-list nodes, advancing the search at level $i$ on $L$ returns a suffix of $L$.
nodes.title: One search step returns a suffix

nodes.summary: For every skip list and every key $k$, the search window for $k$ is a suffix of the list of the skip list's bottom-level nodes.
nodes.title: The search window is a suffix of the bottom level

nodes.summary: For every skip list and every key $k$, the top-down skip-list lookup of $k$ returns the same result as looking up $k$ in the bottom-level abstraction, the list of key-value pairs of all stored nodes in order: the value of the first pair with key $k$, or no value if there is none.
nodes.title: Skip-list search agrees with bottom-level lookup

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $\beta$ a type. If a skip list with keys in $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$ is valid, then for every key $k \in \alpha$, value $v \in \beta$ and requested height $h \in \mathbb{N}$ (including $h = 0$), inserting $k$ with value $v$ and requested height $h$ yields a valid skip list. This covers both a new key and a key already present, whose value is replaced.
nodes.title: Insertion preserves skip-list validity

nodes.summary: For every skip list, key $k$, value $v$ and requested height $h$, looking up $k$ after inserting $k$ with value $v$ and requested height $h$ returns $v$.
nodes.title: Lookup after insertion returns the inserted value

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every skip list $S$ with keys in $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$, all keys $k$ and $k'$ in $\alpha$ with $k' \ne k$, every value $v \in \beta$ and every requested height $h \in \mathbb{N}$, looking up $k'$ in the skip list obtained by inserting $k$ with value $v$ and requested height $h$ into $S$ gives the same result as looking up $k'$ in $S$.
nodes.title: Skip-list insertion does not change lookup of other keys
