nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a valid skip list in which the key $k$ has stored tower height $h_0$. Then after inserting $k$ into $S$ with any value and any requested height, the stored tower height of $k$ is still $h_0$.
nodes.title: Reinsertion preserves tower height

nodes.summary: If a key $k$ does not occur in a skip list $S$, then after inserting $k$ into $S$ with any value and requested height $h$, the stored tower height of $k$ is $\max(1, h)$.
nodes.title: Height of a newly inserted key

nodes.summary: Given a key $k$ from a linearly ordered type and a skip list $S$, the erasure of $k$ from $S$ is the skip list obtained by scanning the entries of $S$ in order: an entry whose key is less than $k$ is kept and the scan continues; at the first entry whose key is greater than $k$ the scan stops, and that entry and all later ones are kept; at the first entry whose key equals $k$ that entry is removed, the scan stops,…
nodes.title: Skip-list erasure

nodes.summary: For every key $k$, erasing $k$ from the empty skip list gives the empty skip list.
nodes.title: Erasing from the empty skip list

nodes.summary: Let $e$ be a skip-list entry and $L$ a list of entries. If a key $k$ is less than the key of $e$, then erasing $k$ from the skip list with entry list $e$ followed by $L$ leaves the entry list $e$ followed by $L$ unchanged.
nodes.title: Erasing a key below the first entry

nodes.summary: Let $e$ be a skip-list entry and $L$ a list of entries. If the key of $e$ is less than a key $k$, then erasing $k$ from the skip list with entry list $e$ followed by $L$ gives the entry list consisting of $e$ followed by the entry list obtained by erasing $k$ from the skip list with entry list $L$.
nodes.title: Erasing past a smaller first entry

nodes.summary: Let $e$ be a skip-list entry and $L$ a list of entries, and consider the skip list whose entry list is $e$ followed by $L$. If a key $k$ equals the key of $e$, then erasing $k$ from this skip list leaves the entry list $L$.
nodes.title: Erasing the key of the first entry

nodes.summary: If $S$ is a valid skip list and $k$ is a key, then the entry list of the skip list obtained by erasing $k$ from $S$ is the entry list of $S$ with every entry whose key equals $k$ removed, the remaining entries kept in their order.
nodes.title: Erasure on a valid skip list filters out the key

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a valid skip list, that is, its keys are strictly increasing and every stored tower has positive height. For every key $k$, the skip list obtained from $L$ by erasing $k$ is again valid.
nodes.title: Erasure preserves skip-list validity

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a valid skip list, that is, its keys are strictly increasing and every stored tower has positive height. For every key $k$, looking up $k$ in the skip list obtained from $L$ by erasing $k$ returns no value.
nodes.title: Erased keys are absent from a skip list

nodes.summary: If $S$ is a valid skip list and $k$, $k'$ are keys with $k' \ne k$, then looking up $k'$ in the skip list obtained by erasing $k$ from $S$ gives the same result as looking up $k'$ in $S$: the same value, or no value in both.
nodes.title: Erasure preserves lookups of other keys

nodes.summary: If $S$ is a valid skip list and $k$ is a key, then after erasing $k$ from $S$ the key $k$ has no stored tower height.
nodes.title: The erased key has no stored height

nodes.summary: If $S$ is a valid skip list and $k$, $k'$ are keys with $k' \ne k$, then the stored tower height of $k'$ in the skip list obtained by erasing $k$ from $S$ is the same as in $S$; in particular $k'$ has no stored height in one exactly when it has none in the other.
nodes.title: Erasure preserves the heights of other keys

nodes.summary: If $S$ is a valid skip list, $k$ is a key and $i$ is a natural number, then the level-$i$ list of key-value pairs (levels numbered from $0$) of the skip list obtained by erasing $k$ from $S$ is the level-$i$ list of $S$ with every pair whose key equals $k$ removed, the remaining pairs kept in their order.
nodes.title: Erasure removes the key from every level
Splay tree

nodes.summary: The optional root key of a binary tree is undefined (none) for the empty tree, and is the key $k$ for a tree whose root node holds $k$.
nodes.title: Root key of a splay tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and write $(k; L, R)$ for the binary tree with root key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$. For $x \in \alpha$, the splay $S_x(t)$ of a binary tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$ is defined by recursion on $t$. The empty tree splays to itself, and $t = (k; L, R)$ is left unchanged if $x = k$, if $x < k$ and $L$ is empty, or if $x > k$ and $R$ is empty. If $x < k$ and…
nodes.title: Splay operation

nodes.summary: For every key $x$ of a linearly ordered type, splaying $x$ in the empty binary tree gives the empty tree.
nodes.title: Splaying the empty tree

nodes.summary: For every key $x$ and every binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, the inorder traversal of the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ equals the inorder traversal of $t$. No search-tree ordering of $t$ is assumed.
nodes.title: Splaying preserves the inorder traversal

nodes.summary: For keys $x$ and $y$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, $y$ is a key of the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ if and only if $y$ is a key of $t$.
nodes.title: Splaying preserves membership

nodes.summary: For every binary tree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered type and every key $x$, the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ has the same number of nodes as $t$.
nodes.title: Splaying preserves the number of nodes

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys in a linearly ordered type and let $x$ be a key. If $t$ is a binary search tree (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), then the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ is again a binary search tree.
nodes.title: Splaying preserves the search-tree property

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary search tree with keys in a linearly ordered type (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), and let $x$ be a key that occurs in $t$. Then there are binary trees $l$ and $r$ such that splaying $x$ in $t$ gives the tree whose root holds $x$, with left subtree $l$ and right subtree $r$.
nodes.title: Splaying a present key brings it to the root

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary search tree with keys in a linearly ordered type (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), and let $x$ be a key that occurs in $t$. Then the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ is nonempty and its root key is $x$.
nodes.title: Root key after splaying a present key

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, let $x \in \alpha$, and write $(k; L, R)$ for the binary tree with root key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$. The split of a binary tree with keys in $\alpha$ at $x$ is the pair of trees defined by recursion: the empty tree splits into two empty trees; if $x < k$ and $L$ splits into $(L_1, L_2)$, then $(k; L, R)$ splits into $(L_1, (k; L_2, R))$; if $k < x$ and…
nodes.title: Search-path split at a key

nodes.summary: For keys $x$ and $y$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, if $y$ is a key of the left part or of the right part of the split of $t$ at $x$, then $y$ is a key of $t$.
nodes.title: Splay-tree split parts contain only original keys

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys in a linearly ordered type, and let $x$ and $y$ be keys with $y \ne x$. If $y$ occurs as a key of $t$, then $y$ occurs as a key of the left part or of the right part of the split of $t$ at $x$. The tree $t$ need not be a binary search tree.
nodes.title: Keys other than the split key survive a split

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be an ordered binary tree over a linearly ordered type and let $x$ be a key. When $t$ is split at $x$, every key of the left part is strictly less than $x$ and every key of the right part is strictly greater than $x$.
nodes.title: Splitting an ordered tree separates the keys around the split key

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys in a linearly ordered type and let $x$ be a key. If $t$ is a binary search tree (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), then the left part and the right part of the split of $t$ at $x$ are both binary search trees.
nodes.title: Both parts of a split search tree are search trees

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, inserting $x$ into $t$ splays $x$ in $t$, splits the resulting tree at $x$ into a left part and a right part, and returns the tree whose root key is $x$, whose left subtree is the left part and whose right subtree is the right part.
nodes.title: Splay-tree insertion

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, the access of $x$ in $t$ is the pair $(b, t')$, where $t'$ is the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ and $b$ is true exactly when $t'$ is nonempty and its root key is $x$.
nodes.title: Splay-tree access

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, the membership test of $x$ in $t$ is the Boolean component of the access of $x$ in $t$: it is true exactly when the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ is nonempty and its root key is $x$.
nodes.title: Splay-tree membership test

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, the tree component of the access of $x$ in $t$ is the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$.
nodes.title: The tree returned by a splay-tree access

nodes.summary: For keys $x$ and $y$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, $y$ is a key of the tree obtained by splay-tree insertion of $x$ into $t$ if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ is a key of $t$.
nodes.title: Keys after splay-tree insertion

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys in a linearly ordered type and let $x$ be a key. If $t$ is a binary search tree (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), then the splay-tree insertion of $x$ into $t$ is again a binary search tree.
nodes.title: Splay-tree insertion preserves the search-tree property

nodes.summary: For every binary tree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered type and every key $x$, the splay-tree insertion of $x$ into $t$ is a nonempty tree whose root key is $x$.
nodes.title: Splay-tree insertion puts the inserted key at the root

nodes.summary: For an ordered binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type and a key $x$, the splay-tree membership test of $x$ in $t$ returns true if and only if $x$ is a key of $t$.
nodes.title: Correctness of the splay-tree membership test
Treap

nodes.summary: For a type $\kappa$ of keys and a type $\nu$ of values, a treap tree is either empty or a node made of a left subtree, a key in $\kappa$, a value in $\nu$, a natural-number priority and a right subtree. Trees are finite, and no ordering of keys or priorities is imposed; the treap invariants are stated separately.
nodes.title: Treap trees

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a predicate on a key, a value and a natural-number priority. A tree satisfies $p$ at every node when $p(k, v, n)$ holds for the key $k$, value $v$ and priority $n$ of each of its nodes. By recursion, this holds for the empty tree, and holds for a node exactly when it holds for the left subtree, $p$ holds at the node's key, value and priority, and it holds for the right subtree.
nodes.title: Treap predicate holding at every node

nodes.summary: A key $k$, value $v$ and priority $p$ form an entry of a treap tree when some node stores exactly $k$, $v$ and $p$: the empty tree has no entries, and $(k, v, p)$ is an entry of a node with left subtree $L$, root key $r$, root value $w$, root priority $q$ and right subtree $R$ exactly when it is an entry of $L$, or $k = r$, $v = w$ and $p = q$, or it is an entry of $R$.
nodes.title: Entry membership in a treap tree

nodes.summary: A key $k$ is a key of a treap tree when it is stored at some node: no key belongs to the empty tree, and $k$ belongs to a node with left subtree $L$, root key $r$ and right subtree $R$ exactly when $k$ belongs to $L$, or $k = r$, or $k$ belongs to $R$.
nodes.title: Key membership in a treap tree

nodes.summary: For a tree $t$ and a list $s$ of key-value pairs, the traversal of $t$ onto $s$ is defined by recursion: for the empty tree it is $s$, and for a node with left subtree $l$, key $k$, value $v$ and right subtree $r$ it is the traversal of $l$ onto the list obtained by putting $(k, v)$ in front of the traversal of $r$ onto $s$. The result is the key-value pairs of $t$ in inorder, priorities dropped, followed by $s$.
nodes.title: Treap inorder traversal onto a suffix

nodes.summary: The contents of a tree $t$ is the list of its key-value pairs in inorder (left subtree, then node, then right subtree), with priorities dropped. It is defined as the inorder traversal of $t$ onto the empty list, which takes linear time.
nodes.title: Treap inorder contents

nodes.summary: For trees $l$ and $r$, a key $k$, a value $v$ and a natural-number priority $n$, the inorder list of key-value pairs of the node with left subtree $l$, key $k$, value $v$, priority $n$ and right subtree $r$ is the inorder list of $l$, followed by $(k, v)$, followed by the inorder list of $r$.
nodes.title: Treap inorder contents of a node

nodes.summary: The size of a tree is its number of nodes, computed recursively: the empty tree has size $0$, and a node with left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ has size equal to the size of $L$ plus one plus the size of $R$.
nodes.title: Size of a treap tree

nodes.summary: For a key type equipped with a relation $<$, a treap tree is ordered when it is empty, or when it is a node with key $k$ whose left and right subtrees are both ordered, every key $x$ in the left subtree satisfies $x < k$, and every key $y$ in the right subtree satisfies $k < y$.
nodes.title: Ordered treap tree

nodes.summary: A tree is heap-ordered when the priority of every node is at most the priority of every node below it. Recursively, the empty tree is heap-ordered, and a node with priority $p$ is heap-ordered when its left and right subtrees are heap-ordered and every node in them has priority at least $p$.
nodes.title: Heap order of treap priorities

nodes.summary: A binary tree whose nodes each carry a key, a value and a natural-number priority, with keys compared by a relation $<$ (any `LT` instance; no order axioms are assumed), is a valid treap when it satisfies both of the following at every node: every key in the left subtree is less than the node's key and the node's key is less than every key in the right subtree (search-tree order with respect to $<$), and the node's…
nodes.title: Valid treap

nodes.summary: Looking up a key $k$ in a tree with keys in a linearly ordered type follows the binary search tree comparisons. The empty tree gives no value. At a node with key $r$ and value $v$, the lookup continues in the left subtree if $k < r$, continues in the right subtree if $r < k$, and otherwise returns $v$.
nodes.title: Treap lookup

nodes.summary: The costed lookup of a key $k$ in a tree with keys in a linearly ordered type returns a possibly absent value together with a natural number counting the visited nodes. On the empty tree it returns no value and cost $0$. At a node with key $r$ and value $v$, if $k < r$ it returns the result of the costed lookup of $k$ in the left subtree with cost increased by $1$; if $r < k$ it does the same with the right…
nodes.title: Lookup with cost

nodes.summary: The root priority of a treap tree is an optional natural number: it is absent for the empty tree, and for a node it is the priority stored at that node.
nodes.title: Root priority of a treap tree

nodes.summary: The merge of two treap trees is defined recursively. Merging the empty tree with a tree $T$, or $T$ with the empty tree, gives $T$. If both trees are nodes, with root priorities $p$ for the first and $q$ for the second, then when $p \le q$ the result keeps the root of the first tree and its left subtree, and its right subtree is the merge of the first tree's right subtree with the second tree; otherwise the result…
nodes.title: Treap merge

nodes.summary:
For key type $\kappa$ and value type $
u$, a split result consists of a lower tree, an optional entry given by a value in $
u$ together with a natural-number priority, and an upper tree, where both trees are treap trees with keys in $\kappa$ and values in $
u$.
nodes.title: Result of a treap split

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linear order, and write $(L, k, v, q, R)$ for the node with left subtree $L$, key $k$, value $v$, priority $q$ and right subtree $R$. Splitting a tree at a pivot $p$ returns a split result, defined by recursion on the tree. The empty tree splits into two empty trees and no entry. For a node $(L, k, v, q, R)$: if $k < p$, split $R$ at $p$ into a lower tree $R_1$, an optional entry $e$ and an…
nodes.title: Treap split

nodes.summary: For a key $k$ of a linearly ordered key type, a value $v$, a priority $p$ and a tree $t$, inserting $k$ with value $v$ and priority $p$ into $t$ splits $t$ at $k$, drops the entry the split finds at $k$ if any, merges the part below $k$ with the single node $(k, v, p)$, and then merges the result with the part above $k$; all merges are priority-guided.
nodes.title: Treap insertion

nodes.summary: For a key $k$ of a linearly ordered key type and a tree $t$, deleting $k$ from $t$ splits $t$ at $k$ and returns the priority-guided merge of the part of the split below $k$ with the part above $k$; the entry the split finds at $k$, if any, is dropped.
nodes.title: Treap deletion

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a predicate on a key, a value and a natural-number priority, and let $t$ be a tree. Then $p$ holds at every node of $t$ if and only if $p(k, v, n)$ holds for every key $k$, value $v$ and priority $n$ such that the entry $(k, v, n)$ occurs as a node of $t$.
nodes.title: Treap all-nodes predicate via node membership

nodes.summary: If a key $k$, value $v$ and priority $p$ form an entry of a treap tree $t$, that is, some node of $t$ stores exactly $k$, $v$ and $p$, then $k$ is a key of $t$.
nodes.title: Entry membership implies key membership in a treap

nodes.summary: For every tree $t$, key $k$ and value $v$, the pair $(k, v)$ occurs in the inorder key-value list of $t$ if and only if $t$ has a node with key $k$ and value $v$, for some priority.
nodes.title: Inorder contents list the treap's entries

nodes.summary: For a key $k$ and a tree $t$, some pair $(k, v)$ occurs in the inorder list of key-value pairs of $t$ if and only if $k$ is the key of some node of $t$.
nodes.title: Keys occurring in the inorder contents

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a predicate on keys and let $t$ be a tree. Then the key of every node of $t$ satisfies $p$ if and only if $p(k)$ holds for every key $k$ that occurs in $t$.
nodes.title: Treap all-nodes predicate on keys via key membership

nodes.summary: The inorder key list of a tree $t$ is the list of first components of the inorder list of key-value pairs of $t$, that is, the keys of $t$ in inorder.
nodes.title: Inorder key list of a treap

nodes.summary: For trees $l$ and $r$, a key $k$, a value $v$ and a priority $p$, the inorder key list of the node with left subtree $l$, entry $(k, v, p)$ and right subtree $r$ is the inorder key list of $l$, followed by $k$, followed by the inorder key list of $r$.
nodes.title: Inorder keys of a node

nodes.summary: For every treap tree $t$ and key $k$, $k$ occurs in the inorder key list of $t$ if and only if $k$ is a key of $t$.
nodes.title: The inorder key list lists exactly the keys of a treap

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type. If a treap tree $t$ is ordered, then its inorder key list is strictly increasing: each key in the list is smaller than every key after it.
nodes.title: Inorder keys of an ordered treap are strictly increasing

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered key type, if a tree is ordered as a binary search tree (at every node, every key in the left subtree is smaller and every key in the right subtree is larger than the node's key), then its inorder key list has no duplicates.
nodes.title: Treap keys are distinct

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a tree with keys in a linearly ordered type that is ordered as a binary search tree (every key in a left subtree is smaller and every key in a right subtree is larger than the node's key). For every key $k$ and value $v$, looking up $k$ in $t$ returns $v$ if and only if $t$ has a node with key $k$ and value $v$, for some priority.
nodes.title: Treap lookup finds exactly the stored entries

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a tree with keys in a linearly ordered type that is ordered as a binary search tree (every key in a left subtree is smaller and every key in a right subtree is larger than the node's key). For every key $k$ and value $v$, looking up $k$ in $t$ returns $v$ if and only if the pair $(k, v)$ occurs in the inorder key-value list of $t$.
nodes.title: Treap lookup agrees with the inorder contents

nodes.summary: For every tree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered type and every key $k$, the value component of the costed lookup of $k$ in $t$ (ignoring the visit count) equals the result of looking up $k$ in $t$.
nodes.title: Costed lookup returns the ordinary lookup result

nodes.summary: For every tree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered type and every key $k$, the number of nodes visited by the costed lookup of $k$ in $t$ is at most the number of nodes of $t$.
nodes.title: Lookup cost is at most the tree size

nodes.summary: If a nonempty tree whose root has priority $p$ is heap-ordered, then every node of the tree, the root included, has priority at least $p$.
nodes.title: The root of a heap-ordered tree has minimal priority

nodes.summary: For all trees $l$ and $r$ and every key $k$, $k$ is the key of some node of the merge of $l$ and $r$ if and only if $k$ is the key of some node of $l$ or of some node of $r$.
nodes.title: Keys of a merged treap

nodes.summary: For trees $l$ and $r$, the inorder list of key-value pairs of the priority-guided merge of $l$ and $r$ is the inorder list of $l$ followed by the inorder list of $r$.
nodes.title: Treap merge concatenates inorder contents

nodes.summary: For keys equipped with a binary relation $<$, two trees $L$ and $R$ are separated when $a < b$ for every key $a$ occurring at a node of $L$ and every key $b$ occurring at a node of $R$.
nodes.title: Separated treap trees

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type. If treap trees $L$ and $R$ are both ordered and every key of $L$ is smaller than every key of $R$, then the merge of $L$ and $R$ is ordered.
nodes.title: Treap merge preserves search-tree order

nodes.summary: If two trees $l$ and $r$ are both heap-ordered in their priorities, then the priority-guided merge of $l$ and $r$ is heap-ordered.
nodes.title: Merging preserves heap order

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be an ordered treap tree. For every pivot key $k$, the lower tree and the upper tree produced by splitting $t$ at $k$ are both ordered.
nodes.title: Treap split preserves search-tree order

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be a heap-ordered treap tree. For every pivot key $k$, the lower tree and the upper tree produced by splitting $t$ at $k$ are both heap-ordered.
nodes.title: Treap split preserves heap order

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linear order and let $T$ be an ordered tree. For every pivot $p$, every key of the lower tree obtained by splitting $T$ at $p$ is strictly less than $p$, and every key of the upper tree is strictly greater than $p$.
nodes.title: Split bounds for an ordered treap

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linear order. If a tree is a valid treap, then for every pivot $p$, both the lower tree and the upper tree obtained by splitting it at $p$ are valid treaps.
nodes.title: Splitting a treap preserves validity

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linear order. If $L$ and $R$ are valid treaps and every key of $L$ is strictly less than every key of $R$, then the merge of $L$ and $R$ is a valid treap.
nodes.title: Merging separated treaps preserves validity

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linear order. If a tree is a valid treap, that is, its keys are in strict binary-search-tree order and its priorities are in min-heap order, then for every key $k$, value $v$ and natural-number priority $q$, the tree obtained by inserting $k$ with value $v$ and priority $q$ is again a valid treap.
nodes.title: Inserting into a treap preserves validity

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linear order. If a tree is a valid treap, that is, its keys are in strict binary-search-tree order and its priorities are in min-heap order, then for every key $k$ the tree obtained by erasing $k$ from it is again a valid treap.
nodes.title: Erasing from a treap preserves validity

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type, let $t$ be a tree and $k$ a pivot key, and let splitting $t$ at $k$ produce a lower tree $L$, an optional value-priority pair found at $k$, and an upper tree $G$. Then the inorder list of key-value pairs of $t$ is the inorder list of $L$, followed by $(k, v)$ if the split found a pair with value $v$ (and by nothing if it found none), followed by the inorder list of $G$.
nodes.title: Treap inorder contents split at a pivot

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type, let $t$ be a tree, $k$ a key, $v$ a value and $n$ a natural-number priority, and let $L$ and $G$ be the lower and upper trees produced by splitting $t$ at $k$. Then the inorder list of key-value pairs of the tree obtained by inserting $k$ with value $v$ and priority $n$ into $t$ is the inorder list of $L$, followed by $(k, v)$, followed by the inorder list of $G$.
nodes.title: Treap inorder contents after insertion

nodes.summary: Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type, let $t$ be a tree and $k$ a key, and let $L$ and $G$ be the lower and upper trees produced by splitting $t$ at $k$. Then the inorder list of key-value pairs of the tree obtained by erasing $k$ from $t$ is the inorder list of $L$ followed by the inorder list of $G$.
nodes.title: Treap inorder contents after erasure

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid treap with keys in a linearly ordered type, that is, $t$ is ordered as a binary search tree by key and as a min-heap by priority. For every key $k$, value $v$ and priority $p \in \mathbb{N}$, looking up $k$ in the tree obtained by inserting $k$ with value $v$ and priority $p$ into $t$ returns $v$.
nodes.title: Treap lookup after insertion

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid treap with keys in a linearly ordered type, that is, $t$ is ordered as a binary search tree by key and as a min-heap by priority. For every key $k$, looking up $k$ in the tree obtained by erasing $k$ from $t$ returns no value.
nodes.title: Erased keys are not found
Weight-balanced tree

nodes.summary: The empty binary tree has $0$ nodes.
nodes.title: Number of keys of the empty tree

nodes.summary: Write $|t|$ for the number of nodes of a binary tree $t$. For binary trees $l$ and $r$ and a key $k$, the node with key $k$, left subtree $l$ and right subtree $r$ has $|l| + |r| + 1$ nodes.
nodes.title: Number of keys of a node

nodes.summary: The Nievergelt–Reingold weight $w(t)$ of a binary tree $t$ is its number of keys plus one. Equivalently, it counts the external leaves: the empty tree has weight $1$, and the weight of a node is the sum of the weights of its two children.
nodes.title: Weight of a binary tree

nodes.summary: Write $|t|$ for the number of keys of a binary tree $t$ and $w(t) = |t| + 1$ for its weight. A binary tree is weight-balanced, or satisfies the invariant $\mathrm{BB}[1/4]$, when it is empty, or when it is a node with left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ such that $L$ and $R$ are weight-balanced, $4\,w(L) \le 3(w(L) + w(R))$ and $4\,w(R) \le 3(w(L) + w(R))$. Since the weight of a node is $w(L) + w(R)$, this says…
nodes.title: Weight-balanced trees

nodes.summary: For binary trees $L$, $R$ and a key $k$, write $|t|$ for the number of keys of a tree $t$, $w(t) = |t| + 1$ for its weight, $w = w(L) + w(R)$, and $\langle X, x, Y \rangle$ for the node with key $x$, left subtree $X$ and right subtree $Y$. The rebalanced node $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ is defined as follows. If $3w < 4\,w(L)$, then $L = \langle A, a, B \rangle$ is a node; if $|B| \le 2|A|$, the result is the…
nodes.title: Weight-balanced rebalancing

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type, the insertion $\mathrm{insert}(x, t)$ of $x$ into a binary tree $t$ is defined by recursion on $t$. Into the empty tree it gives the single node with key $x$. Into the node $N$ with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ it gives $\mathrm{balance}(\mathrm{insert}(x, L), k, R)$ if $x < k$, $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, \mathrm{insert}(x, R))$ if $k < x$, and $N$ itself if…
nodes.title: Weight-balanced insertion

nodes.summary: The tree built from a list $x_1, \dots, x_n$ of elements of a linearly ordered type is obtained from the empty tree by inserting $x_n, x_{n-1}, \dots, x_1$ in this order with weight-balanced insertion; the empty list gives the empty tree.
nodes.title: Weight-balanced tree from a list

nodes.summary: Let $L$ and $R$ be weight-balanced trees and $k$ a key, and write $|t|$ for the number of keys of a tree $t$. If $4(|L| + 1) \le 3(|L| + |R| + 2)$ and $4(|R| + 1) \le 3(|L| + |R| + 2)$, then the node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ is weight-balanced.
nodes.title: Building a weight-balanced node

nodes.summary: Write $|t|$ for the number of keys of a tree $t$ and $w(t) = |t| + 1$ for its weight. Let $N$ be the node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$. Then $N$ is weight-balanced if and only if $L$ and $R$ are weight-balanced, $4\,w(L) \le 3\,w(N)$ and $4\,w(R) \le 3\,w(N)$. This is the classical $\mathrm{BB}[1/4]$ invariant: each child has weight at most three quarters of the weight of the node.
nodes.title: Weight form of the balance condition at a node

nodes.summary: Write $|t|$ for the number of nodes of a binary tree $t$. For binary trees $l$ and $r$ and a key $k$, the weight-balanced rebalancing of $l$, $k$, $r$ has exactly $|l| + |r| + 1$ nodes.
nodes.title: Weight-balanced rebalancing preserves the number of keys

nodes.summary: Let $L$ and $R$ be weight-balanced trees and $k$ a key, and write $|t|$ for the number of keys of a tree $t$. If $4(|L| + 1) \le 3(|L| + |R| + 2) + 1$ and $4(|R| + 1) \le 3(|L| + |R| + 2) + 1$, then the rebalanced node $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ is weight-balanced.
nodes.title: Weight-balanced rebalancing restores balance

nodes.summary: For binary trees $l$ and $r$ and a key $k$, an element $x$ occurs in the weight-balanced rebalancing of $l$, $k$, $r$ exactly when $x$ occurs in $l$, $x = k$, or $x$ occurs in $r$. Membership is structural: $x$ is the key of some node.
nodes.title: Membership after weight-balanced rebalancing

nodes.summary: Let the keys carry a linear order, let $l$ and $r$ be ordered binary trees (strict binary search trees), and let $k$ be a key such that every key of $l$ is less than $k$ and every key of $r$ is greater than $k$. Then the weight-balanced rebalancing of $l$, $k$, $r$ is ordered.
nodes.title: Weight-balanced rebalancing preserves ordering

nodes.summary: Let the keys carry a linear order. For every key $x$ and every binary tree $t$, the tree obtained from $t$ by weight-balanced insertion of $x$ has at most one more node than $t$.
nodes.title: Weight-balanced insertion adds at most one key

nodes.summary: Let the keys carry a linear order. For every key $x$ and every binary tree $t$, the number of nodes of $t$ is at most the number of nodes of the tree obtained from $t$ by weight-balanced insertion of $x$.
nodes.title: Weight-balanced insertion does not decrease the number of keys

nodes.summary: For every key $x$ of a linearly ordered type and every weight-balanced tree $t$, the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ with weight-balanced insertion is weight-balanced.
nodes.title: Weight-balanced insertion preserves balance

nodes.summary: Let the keys carry a linear order. For all keys $x$, $y$ and every binary tree $t$, $y$ occurs in the tree obtained from $t$ by weight-balanced insertion of $x$ exactly when $y = x$ or $y$ occurs in $t$.
nodes.title: Membership after weight-balanced insertion

nodes.summary: Let the keys be linearly ordered. If a binary tree $t$ is ordered as a search tree (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key at the node), then the tree obtained from $t$ by weight-balanced insertion of any key $x$ is again ordered.
nodes.title: Weight-balanced insertion preserves the search-tree order

nodes.summary: For every list $x_1, \dots, x_n$ of elements of a linearly ordered type, the tree obtained from the empty tree by inserting $x_n, x_{n-1}, \dots, x_1$ in this order with weight-balanced insertion is weight-balanced.
nodes.title: Weight-balanced trees built by insertion are balanced

nodes.summary: Let the keys carry a linear order. For every list $xs$, the weight-balanced tree built from $xs$ by repeated insertion is ordered, that is, a strict binary search tree.
nodes.title: Weight-balanced trees built from a list are ordered

nodes.summary: Let the keys carry a linear order. For every key $x$ and every list $xs$, $x$ occurs in the weight-balanced tree built from $xs$ by repeated insertion exactly when $x$ is an element of $xs$.
nodes.title: Membership in a weight-balanced tree built from a list

nodes.summary: Write $w(t)$ for the weight of a binary tree $t$ (its number of keys plus one), and measure height so that the empty tree has height $0$ and a node has height one more than the taller of its children. If $t$ is weight balanced with parameter $1/4$ (at every node, each child has weight at most three quarters of the weight of the node) and has height $k + 1$ for a natural number $k$, then $w(t) \ge (4/3)^k$; in…
nodes.title: Exponential weight lower bound for weight-balanced trees

nodes.summary: Write $|t|$ for the number of keys of a binary tree $t$ and $h(t)$ for its height, where the empty tree has height $0$ and a node has height one more than the larger height of its two subtrees. If $t$ is weight-balanced, then $h(t) \le \lfloor \log_2 ((|t| + 1)^3) \rfloor + 1$.
nodes.title: Height of a weight-balanced tree is logarithmic

nodes.summary: Priority queues: binary, d-ary, binomial, Fibonacci and catenable heaps, indexed min-queues, and their sift, decrease-key and merge operations and costs.
nodes.title: Heaps and priority queues
Binary heap

nodes.summary: In a binary tree stored in level order in an array indexed from $0$, the parent index of a natural number $i$ is $\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$, where $i - 1$ is truncated subtraction of natural numbers, so the root index $0$ is sent to $0$.
nodes.title: Parent index in a level-order binary tree

nodes.summary: In a binary tree stored in level order in an array indexed from $0$, the left child of the node at index $i$ has index $2i + 1$.
nodes.title: Left child index in a level-order binary tree

nodes.summary: In the level-order layout of a binary tree in an array indexed from $0$, the right child of the node at index $i$ is at index $2i + 2$.
nodes.title: Right child index in an array-backed binary tree

nodes.summary: For an array $a$ of length $|a|$ and an index $i$ with $0 < i < |a|$, the parent index $\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$ of $i$ is also less than $|a|$.
nodes.title: The parent of a valid nonroot index is valid

nodes.summary: An array $a$ over a type with a relation $\le$, indexed from $0$, is heap ordered when every entry other than the root is at least its parent entry: for every index $i$ with $0 < i < |a|$, where $|a|$ is the length of $a$, we have $a_{\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor} \le a_i$.
nodes.title: Heap order on a level-order array

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array of length $|a|$ over a type with a relation $\le$, indexed from $0$, and for $j > 0$ let $p(j) = \lfloor (j - 1)/2 \rfloor$ be the parent of $j$. The array $a$ is ready for sift-up at an index $i$ when $i < |a|$, when $a_{p(j)} \le a_j$ for every $j \ne i$ with $0 < j < |a|$, and when, if $i > 0$, also $a_{p(i)} \le a_j$ for every $j$ with $0 < j < |a|$ and $p(j) = i$.
nodes.title: Arrays ready for sift-up

nodes.summary: For an array $a$ over a type ordered by $\le$, write $p(j) = \lfloor (j-1)/2 \rfloor$ for the parent of index $j$. The array $a$ is ready for sift-down at index $i$ when $i$ is a valid index of $a$; $a_{p(j)} \le a_j$ for every valid index $j > 0$ with $p(j) \ne i$; and, if $i > 0$, $a_{p(i)} \le a_j$ for every valid index $j > 0$ with $p(j) = i$.
nodes.title: Sift-down precondition

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array of length $|a|$ over a linearly ordered type, indexed from $0$, and let $i$ be an index with children $\ell = 2i + 1$ and $r = 2i + 2$. If $\ell \ge |a|$, then $i$ has no smaller child. Otherwise the smaller child of $i$ is $r$ when $r < |a|$ and $a_r < a_\ell$, and $\ell$ in every other case, so ties go to the left child.
nodes.title: Smaller child

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and all indices $i$ and $c$, if $c$ is the smaller child of $i$ in $a$, then $i < c$.
nodes.title: The smaller child has a larger index

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and all indices $i$ and $c$, if $c$ is the smaller child of $i$ in $a$, then $c$ is less than the length $|a|$ of $a$.
nodes.title: The smaller child is a valid index

nodes.summary: Given an array $a$ of length $|a|$ over a linearly ordered type, indexed from $0$, and an index $i$, the sift-up of $a$ from $i$ is defined by recursion on $i$. If $i = 0$ or $i \ge |a|$, the result is $a$. Otherwise let $p = \lfloor (i - 1)/2 \rfloor$ be the parent of $i$; if $a_i < a_p$, the result is the sift-up from $p$ of the array obtained from $a$ by exchanging the entries at positions $i$ and $p$, and…
nodes.title: Sift-up

nodes.summary: Sifting down an array $a$ over a linearly ordered type from index $i$ works as follows. If $i$ has a child in $a$, that is, if $2i+1$ is a valid index, let $c$ be the child of $i$ (among $2i+1$ and $2i+2$, if valid) holding the smaller value, preferring the left child $2i+1$ on ties. If $a_c < a_i$, swap the entries at $i$ and $c$ and continue sifting down from $c$; otherwise, or if $i$ has no child, return the…
nodes.title: Sift-down

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the array obtained by sifting up $a$ from $i$ is a permutation of $a$.
nodes.title: Sift-up permutes the array

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the array obtained by sifting down $a$ from $i$ is a permutation of $a$.
nodes.title: Binary-heap sift-down permutes the array

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the array obtained by sifting up $a$ from $i$ has the same multiset of entries as $a$.
nodes.title: Binary-heap sift-up preserves the multiset of entries

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the array obtained by sifting down $a$ from $i$ has the same multiset of entries as $a$.
nodes.title: Binary-heap sift-down preserves the multiset of entries

nodes.summary: If an array $a$ over a linearly ordered type is heap-ordered, then $a_0 \le a_i$ for every valid index $i$ of $a$.
nodes.title: The root of a heap-ordered binary-heap array is minimal

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and let $i$ be an index such that $a$ is ready for sift-up at $i$. Then the array obtained by sifting up $a$ from $i$ is heap ordered.
nodes.title: Sift-up restores heap order

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type that satisfies the sift-down precondition at a valid index $i$: the only edges that may violate heap order are those leaving $i$, and moving either child of $i$ up to position $i$ keeps the edge entering $i$ ordered. Then the array obtained by sifting down $a$ from $i$ is heap-ordered.
nodes.title: Sift-down restores heap order

nodes.summary: If an array $a$ of length $n$ over a linearly ordered type is heap-ordered and $x$ is any value, then the array obtained by appending $x$ to $a$ satisfies the sift-up precondition at index $n$, the position of $x$: the only edge that may violate heap order is the one entering index $n$.
nodes.title: Appending to a heap-ordered array prepares it for sift-up

nodes.summary: A binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ is an array $a$ of elements of $\alpha$ (its level-order storage), of length $|a|$ and with entries $a_0, \dots, a_{|a|-1}$, that is heap ordered: for every index $i$ with $0 < i < |a|$, the entry $a_{\lfloor (i - 1)/2 \rfloor}$ at the parent index of $i$ is at most $a_i$.
nodes.title: Binary min-heap

nodes.summary: The multiset of elements of a binary min-heap is the multiset of the entries of its level-order storage array, counted with multiplicity.
nodes.title: Elements of a binary min-heap

nodes.summary: The empty binary min-heap is the min-heap whose level-order storage array has no entries.
nodes.title: Empty binary min-heap

nodes.summary: To insert a value $x$ into a binary min-heap $h$, append $x$ at the end of the level-order array of $h$ and sift it up from its index (the old length of the array), repeatedly swapping it with its parent while it is smaller. The result is again a binary min-heap.
nodes.title: Insertion into a binary min-heap

nodes.summary: For a binary min-heap $h$, the minimum lookup returns the entry at index $0$ (the root) of the storage array of $h$ when that array is nonempty, and returns no value when it is empty.
nodes.title: Minimum lookup in a binary heap

nodes.summary: For a binary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type, looking up the minimum of $h$ returns no value if and only if the storage array of $h$ has size $0$.
nodes.title: Binary heap minimum lookup fails exactly when empty

nodes.summary: For a binary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type, looking up the minimum of $h$ returns a value if and only if the storage array of $h$ has positive size.
nodes.title: Binary heap minimum lookup succeeds exactly when nonempty

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If looking up the minimum of $h$ returns $x$, then $x$ belongs to the multiset of elements of $h$.
nodes.title: The binary heap minimum lookup returns a stored element

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If looking up the minimum of $h$ returns $x$, then $x \le y$ for every element $y$ of the multiset of elements of $h$.
nodes.title: The binary heap minimum lookup is a lower bound

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type and $x$ a value. The multiset of elements of the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $h$ is the multiset of elements of $h$ with one more copy of $x$ added.
nodes.title: Elements after binary heap insertion

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type and $x$ a value. The multiplicity of $x$ in the multiset of elements of the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $h$ is one more than its multiplicity in the multiset of elements of $h$.
nodes.title: Binary heap insertion adds one copy of the inserted value

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type, and let $x \ne y$ be values. Then $y$ occurs in the multiset of elements of the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $h$ exactly as many times as it occurs in the multiset of elements of $h$.
nodes.title: Binary heap insertion leaves other multiplicities unchanged

nodes.summary: For every binary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type and every value $x$, the level-order array of the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $h$ is heap-ordered: the entry at every nonroot index $i$ is at least the entry at its parent index $\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$.
nodes.title: Insertion into a binary min-heap preserves heap order

nodes.summary: For a nonempty array $a$ of length $n$, this operation swaps the entries at indices $0$ and $n - 1$ and then deletes the final entry. The result has length $n - 1$; when $n \ge 2$ its entry at index $0$ is $a_{n-1}$ and its entry at each index $0 < i < n - 1$ is $a_i$.
nodes.title: Moving the last entry to the root

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be a heap-ordered array over a linearly ordered type with at least two entries, and let $b$ be the array obtained from $a$ by moving its last entry to the root. Then $b$ is ready for sifting down at index $0$: index $0$ is valid in $b$, and for every index $j > 0$ of $b$ whose parent index $\lfloor (j - 1)/2 \rfloor$ is not $0$, the entry of $b$ at the parent index is at most $b_j$.
nodes.title: Moving the last entry to the root prepares a sift-down

nodes.summary: For a nonempty array $a$ over a linearly ordered type, the multiset of entries of the array obtained from $a$ by moving its last entry to the root equals the multiset of entries of $a$ with one occurrence of $a_0$ removed.
nodes.title: Moving the last entry to the root removes the old root

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type whose level-order array is nonempty. If the array has exactly one entry, the result is the empty heap. Otherwise the last entry of the array replaces the root, the array shrinks by one, and the result is the heap obtained by sifting this entry down from the root.
nodes.title: Removing the root of a nonempty binary min-heap

nodes.summary: For a binary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type, extraction returns nothing when the level-order array of $h$ is empty. Otherwise it returns the root entry (the first entry of the array) together with the heap obtained from $h$ by removing its root and restoring heap order.
nodes.title: Extracting the minimum of a binary min-heap

nodes.summary: For a binary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type, extracting the minimum of $h$ returns no result if and only if the level-order storage array of $h$ has size $0$.
nodes.title: Extraction from a binary min-heap fails exactly when it is empty

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds and returns a value $x$ together with a heap $r$, then $x$ belongs to the multiset of elements of $h$.
nodes.title: The value extracted from a binary min-heap is one of its elements

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds and returns a value $x$ together with a heap $r$, then $x \le y$ for every value $y$ in the multiset of elements of $h$.
nodes.title: The value extracted from a binary min-heap is minimal

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum of $h$ succeeds and returns the value $x$ and the heap $h'$, then the multiset of elements of $h'$ is obtained from the multiset of elements of $h$ by erasing one occurrence of $x$.
nodes.title: Elements after binary heap extraction

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum of $h$ succeeds and returns the value $x$ and the heap $h'$, then the multiset of elements of $h$ equals the multiset of elements of $h'$ with one copy of $x$ added.
nodes.title: Binary heap extraction splits off the minimum

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum of $h$ succeeds and returns the value $x$ and the heap $h'$, then the multiplicity of $x$ in the multiset of elements of $h'$ is its multiplicity in the multiset of elements of $h$ minus one.
nodes.title: Binary heap extraction removes one copy of the minimum

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum of $h$ succeeds and returns the value $x$ and the heap $h'$, then every value $y \ne x$ occurs in the multiset of elements of $h'$ exactly as many times as in the multiset of elements of $h$.
nodes.title: Binary heap extraction leaves other multiplicities unchanged

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type, and suppose extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds and returns a value $x$ together with a heap $r$. Then every value $y \ne x$ is an element of $r$ if and only if it is an element of $h$.
nodes.title: Membership after extraction from a binary min-heap

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds and returns a value $x$ together with a heap $r$, then the level-order array of $r$ is heap ordered: every entry other than the root is at least its parent entry.
nodes.title: Extraction from a binary min-heap leaves a heap-ordered array

nodes.summary: For every natural number $i > 0$, the parent index $p = \lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$ satisfies $\lfloor \log_2(p+1) \rfloor + 1 = \lfloor \log_2(i+1) \rfloor$; that is, in the level-order binary tree the parent of a nonroot index lies one level above it.
nodes.title: The heap parent is one level up

nodes.summary: Given an array $a$ of length $|a|$ over a linearly ordered type and an index $i$, this computes the sift-up of $a$ at $i$ together with a cost $(c, s) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, where $c$ counts value comparisons and $s$ counts swaps. If $i \ge |a|$ or $i = 0$, the result is $a$ with cost $(0, 0)$. Otherwise let $p = \lfloor (i - 1)/2 \rfloor$ be the parent of $i$. If $a_i < a_p$, the result is this sift-up…
nodes.title: Sift-up with comparison and swap counts

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $i$, the array returned by sift-up with comparison and swap counts on $a$ at index $i$ equals the array returned by the plain sift-up of $a$ at $i$.
nodes.title: Counting does not change the result of sift-up

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $i$, the number of value comparisons counted by sift-up with comparison and swap counts on $a$ at index $i$ is at most $\lfloor \log_2(i+1) \rfloor$, the depth of index $i$ in the level-order binary tree.
nodes.title: Comparison bound for sift-up

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $i$, the number of swaps counted by sift-up with comparison and swap counts on $a$ at index $i$ is at most $\lfloor \log_2(i+1) \rfloor$, the depth of index $i$ in the level-order binary tree.
nodes.title: Swap bound for sift-up

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $i$, if sift-up with comparison and swap counts on $a$ at index $i$ counts $c$ comparisons and $s$ swaps, then $c + s \le 2 \lfloor \log_2(i+1) \rfloor$.
nodes.title: Combined comparison and swap bound for sift-up

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type, sift-up with comparison and swap counts on $a$ at index $0$ has cost $(0, 0)$: it counts no comparisons and no swaps.
nodes.title: Sift-up at the root costs nothing

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ of length $|a|$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $i$ with $i \ge |a|$, sift-up with comparison and swap counts on $a$ at index $i$ has cost $(0, 0)$: it counts no comparisons and no swaps.
nodes.title: Sift-up at an out-of-range index costs nothing

nodes.summary: Given a binary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type, with level-order array $a$, an index $i < |a|$ and a value $x \le a_i$, decrease-key returns the heap whose array is obtained from $a$ by replacing the entry at position $i$ with $x$ and then sifting position $i$ up, repeatedly swapping the entry with its parent while it is strictly smaller than the parent.
nodes.title: Decrease-key in a binary min-heap

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type, with level-order array $a$, let $i < |a|$ and let $x \le a_i$. The array of the heap obtained by decreasing the key at position $i$ to $x$ equals the result of sifting up position $i$ in the array obtained from $a$ by replacing its entry at position $i$ with $x$.
nodes.title: Array of a binary heap after decrease-key

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type, with level-order array $a$, let $i < |a|$ and let $x \le a_i$. The array of the heap obtained by decreasing the key at position $i$ to $x$ is heap-ordered: the entry at every nonroot position is at least the entry at its parent position.
nodes.title: Decrease-key yields a heap-ordered array

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type, with level-order array $a$, let $i < |a|$ and let $x \le a_i$. The array of the heap obtained by decreasing the key at position $i$ to $x$ has the same length as $a$.
nodes.title: Decrease-key preserves the heap size

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type, with level-order array $a$, let $i < |a|$ and let $x \le a_i$. The multiset of elements of the heap obtained by decreasing the key at position $i$ to $x$ is obtained from the multiset of elements of $h$ by removing one occurrence of $a_i$ and adding one occurrence of $x$.
nodes.title: Multiset of a binary heap after decrease-key

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and let $i$ and $c$ be natural numbers. If $c$ is the smaller child of $i$ in $a$, then $\lfloor \log_2 (c+1) \rfloor = \lfloor \log_2 (i+1) \rfloor + 1$; that is, in the level-order binary tree stored in $a$, the node $c$ lies exactly one level below $i$.
nodes.title: The smaller child lies one level below its parent

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type, of size $|a|$, and let $i$ and $c$ be natural numbers. If $c$ is the smaller child of $i$ in $a$, then $\lfloor \log_2 (c+1) \rfloor \le \lfloor \log_2 |a| \rfloor$.
nodes.title: The smaller child's level is bounded by the array size

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and $i$ an index, with left child $2i + 1$ and right child $2i + 2$; cost is counted as the pair (value comparisons, array swaps). If both children are valid indices of $a$, the selection costs $(1, 0)$ and returns the right child when its value is strictly less than the value at the left child, and the left child otherwise. If only the left child is a valid index,…
nodes.title: Timed smaller-child selection

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the value returned by timed child selection at $i$, with its cost discarded, is the smaller child of $i$ in $a$ (an optional index, absent when $i$ has no valid child).
nodes.title: Timed child selection returns the smaller child

nodes.summary: For an array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and an index $i$, timed sift-down returns an array together with a cost pair (value comparisons, array swaps), where costs add componentwise. If the left child index $2i+1$ is not a valid index of $a$, it returns $a$ at cost $(0, 0)$. Otherwise let $c$ be the smaller child of $i$: the left child $2i+1$, unless the right child $2i+2$ is a valid index and…
nodes.title: Sift-down with comparison and swap counts

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the array returned by timed sift-down from $i$, with its cost discarded, equals the array returned by sift-down from $i$.
nodes.title: Timed sift-down returns the sift-down result

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and $i$ an index, and count cost as the pair (value comparisons, array swaps). The timed child selection at $i$ in $a$ has cost $(1, 0)$ if the right child index $2i + 2$ is less than the size of $a$, and cost $(0, 0)$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Cost of child selection

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and $i$ an index. If the smaller-child selection at $i$ in $a$ returns no child, then the timed child selection at $i$, with cost counted as the pair (value comparisons, array swaps), has cost $(0, 0)$.
nodes.title: Child selection at a node without children costs nothing

nodes.summary: Write $|a|$ for the size of an array $a$, and let $\ell(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ for $n \ge 1$ and $\ell(0) = 0$. For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the number of array swaps counted by timed sift-down from $i$ is at most $\max(0, \ell(|a|) - \ell(i+1))$.
nodes.title: Sift-down performs at most one swap per remaining level

nodes.summary: Write $|a|$ for the size of an array $a$, and let $\ell(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ for $n \ge 1$ and $\ell(0) = 0$. For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the number of value comparisons counted by timed sift-down from $i$ is at most $2 \max(0, \ell(|a|) - \ell(i+1))$.
nodes.title: Sift-down makes at most two comparisons per remaining level

nodes.summary: Write $|a|$ for the size of an array $a$, and let $\ell(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ for $n \ge 1$ and $\ell(0) = 0$. For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the number of value comparisons plus the number of array swaps counted by timed sift-down from $i$ is at most $3 \max(0, \ell(|a|) - \ell(i+1))$.
nodes.title: Total sift-down cost is at most three per remaining level

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and $i$ an index. If the smaller-child selection at $i$ in $a$ returns no child, then sift-down from $i$, with cost counted as the pair (value comparisons, array swaps), has cost $(0, 0)$: it makes no value comparisons and no array swaps.
nodes.title: Sift-down from a node without children costs nothing

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type, of size $|a|$, and let $i$ be an index with $|a| \le 2i+1$, so that the left child of $i$ is not a valid index (this includes invalid indices $i$). Then timed sift-down from $i$ has cost pair $(0, 0)$: it counts no comparisons and no swaps.
nodes.title: Sift-down from a leaf costs nothing

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type, of size $|a|$, and let $i$ be a natural number with $|a| \le i$. Then timed sift-down from $i$ has cost pair $(0, 0)$: it counts no comparisons and no swaps.
nodes.title: Sift-down from an invalid index costs nothing
Binomial heap

nodes.summary: A binomial tree over a type $\alpha$ is a node that stores a rank, which is a natural number, a root value in $\alpha$, and a list of binomial trees over $\alpha$ as its children. The type imposes no invariant; the binomial-tree shape and heap order are expressed by a separate validity predicate.
nodes.title: Binomial tree

nodes.summary: The rank of a binomial tree is the natural number stored at its root node.
nodes.title: Rank of a binomial tree

nodes.summary: The root of the binomial tree with rank $r$, root value $a$ and list of children $c$ is $a$.
nodes.title: Root of a binomial tree

nodes.summary: The children of a binomial tree are the binomial trees in the list stored at its root node, in their stored order.
nodes.title: Children of a binomial tree

nodes.summary: The multiset of elements of a binomial tree with root value $x$ and children $t_1, \dots, t_k$ is defined recursively as $\{x\}$ added to the multiset sum of the multisets of elements of $t_1, \dots, t_k$; the stored rank plays no role.
nodes.title: Elements of a binomial tree

nodes.summary: For every binomial tree $t$, the root of $t$ occurs in the multiset represented by $t$.
nodes.title: The root of a binomial tree is one of its elements

nodes.summary: For a type $\alpha$ with a relation $\le$, validity of binomial trees over $\alpha$ is defined inductively: the tree with stored rank $r$, root $a$ and list of children $c_1, \dots, c_k$ is valid when every child $c_i$ is valid, the ranks of $c_1, \dots, c_k$ are exactly $r - 1, r - 2, \dots, 0$ in this order, the multiset of elements of the tree (its root together with the elements of all its children) has exactly…
nodes.title: Valid binomial tree

nodes.summary: For a value $a$ in a linear order, the binomial heap whose list of trees consists of exactly one tree: the tree of rank $0$ with root $a$ and no children.
nodes.title: Singleton binomial heap

nodes.summary: Over a linear order, the link of binomial trees $s$ and $t$ is defined as follows. If the root of $s$ is at most the root of $t$, it is the tree whose rank is one more than the rank of $s$, whose root is the root of $s$, and whose children are $t$ followed by the children of $s$. Otherwise it is the tree whose rank is one more than the rank of $s$, whose root is the root of $t$, and whose children are $s$ followed…
nodes.title: Linking two binomial trees

nodes.summary: For any two binomial trees $s$ and $t$ over a linearly ordered type, the multiset of elements of the tree obtained by linking $s$ and $t$ is the sum of the multisets of elements of $s$ and $t$.
nodes.title: Linking binomial trees adds their elements

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ and any $a \in \alpha$, the singleton binomial tree with rank $0$, root $a$ and no children is valid.
nodes.title: Singleton binomial trees are valid

nodes.summary: For a type $\alpha$ with a relation $\le$, every child of a valid binomial tree over $\alpha$ is itself a valid binomial tree.
nodes.title: Children of a valid binomial tree are valid

nodes.summary: For a type $\alpha$ with a relation $\le$, if a valid binomial tree over $\alpha$ has rank $r$, then the ranks of its children, listed in their stored order, are $r - 1, r - 2, \dots, 1, 0$; there are no children when $r = 0$.
nodes.title: Child ranks of a valid binomial tree

nodes.summary: For a type $\alpha$ with a relation $\le$, every valid binomial tree of rank $r$ over $\alpha$ represents a multiset of exactly $2^r$ elements, counted with multiplicity.
nodes.title: Size of a valid binomial tree

nodes.summary: A valid binomial tree of rank $r$ holding $n$ elements, counted with multiplicity, satisfies $r \le \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$.
nodes.title: The rank of a valid binomial tree is logarithmic

nodes.summary: For a type $\alpha$ with a relation $\le$ and a valid binomial tree $t$ over $\alpha$, the root $a$ of $t$ satisfies $a \le v$ for every element $v$ of the multiset represented by $t$.
nodes.title: The root of a valid binomial tree is a lower bound

nodes.summary: If $s$ and $t$ are valid binomial trees of equal rank, then the tree obtained by linking $s$ with $t$ is valid.
nodes.title: Linking preserves binomial-tree validity

nodes.summary: For a type $\alpha$ with a relation $\le$, a list of binomial trees over $\alpha$ is a valid forest when every tree in it is a valid binomial tree and the ranks of its trees are strictly increasing along the list.
nodes.title: Valid binomial forest

nodes.summary: The multiset of elements of a list of binomial trees $t_1, \dots, t_k$ is the multiset sum of the multisets of elements of $t_1, \dots, t_k$; for the empty list it is the empty multiset.
nodes.title: Elements of a binomial forest

nodes.summary: For a natural number $r$, a list of binomial trees has ranks at least $r$ when every tree in it has rank at least $r$.
nodes.title: Rank lower bound for a forest

nodes.summary: For every type $\alpha$ with a relation $\le$, the empty list of binomial trees over $\alpha$ is a valid binomial forest.
nodes.title: The empty forest is valid

nodes.summary: For a type $\alpha$ with a relation $\le$ and lists $L$, $R$ of binomial trees over $\alpha$, if $L$ is a sublist of $R$ (obtained by deleting entries while keeping the order of the rest) and $R$ is a valid forest, then $L$ is a valid forest.
nodes.title: Validity of binomial forests passes to sublists

nodes.summary: If $F$ is a valid binomial forest and $T$ is a tree of $F$ of rank $r$, then $r \le \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$, where $n$ is the number of elements, counted with multiplicity, represented by $F$.
nodes.title: Tree ranks in a valid forest are logarithmic

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $\le$. If a valid binomial forest over $\alpha$ has $n$ elements, counted with multiplicity, then it consists of at most $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$ trees, where $\lfloor \log_2 0 \rfloor$ is taken to be $0$.
nodes.title: A valid binomial forest has logarithmically many trees

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $\le$. If a list of binomial trees over $\alpha$ is a valid binomial forest and its multiset of elements has cardinality $0$, then the list has length $0$.
nodes.title: A valid binomial forest with no elements has no trees

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type, the carry of a binomial tree $t$ into a list $F$ of binomial trees is defined by recursion on $F$. If $F$ is empty, the result is the one-tree list $[t]$. If $F$ starts with a tree $u$ followed by a list $F'$ and the rank of $t$ is less than the rank of $u$, the result is $F$ with $t$ prepended. Otherwise the result is the carry of the link of $t$ and $u$ into $F'$.
nodes.title: Carry insertion into a binomial forest

nodes.summary: Over a linear order, the meld of two lists of binomial trees is defined by recursion on their total length. For every list $L$, the meld of the empty list with $L$ is $L$, and the meld of $L$ with the empty list is $L$. For nonempty lists with first trees $s$ and $t$ and remaining lists $F$ and $G$: if the rank of $s$ is less than the rank of $t$, the meld is $s$ followed by the meld of $F$ with the second list; if…
nodes.title: Melding binomial forests

nodes.summary: For any two lists $L$ and $R$ of binomial trees over a linearly ordered type, the multiset of elements of the meld of $L$ and $R$ is the sum of the multisets of elements of $L$ and $R$.
nodes.title: Melding binomial forests adds their elements

nodes.summary: Let $r$ be a natural number and let $F$ and $G$ be valid binomial forests in which every tree has rank at least $r$. Then the meld of $F$ and $G$ is a valid binomial forest in which every tree has rank at least $r$.
nodes.title: Melding preserves forest validity and rank lower bounds

nodes.summary: For a list $T$ of binomial trees over a linear order, the result is nothing when $T$ is empty. Otherwise it is the first tree $m$ of $T$ whose root is minimal among the roots of the trees of $T$, together with the list obtained from $T$ by deleting that occurrence of $m$, the remaining trees keeping their order.
nodes.title: Removing a minimum-root tree from a forest

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a list of binomial trees over a linear order, and suppose that removing a minimum tree from $T$ returns the tree $m$ and the list $R$. Then the multiset represented by $m$ plus the multiset represented by the forest $R$ equals the multiset represented by the forest $T$; $m$ is a member of $T$; $R$ is a sublist of $T$; and the root of $m$ is at most the root of every tree in $T$.
nodes.title: Removing a minimum-root tree

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ and a valid binomial tree $t$ over $\alpha$, the children of $t$ listed in reverse order form a valid binomial forest: every tree in the list is valid and the ranks strictly increase along the list.
nodes.title: Reversed children of a valid binomial tree form a valid forest

nodes.summary: A binomial min-heap over a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ consists of a list of binomial trees over $\alpha$ together with a proof that this list is a valid binomial forest: every tree in it is a valid binomial tree and the tree ranks are strictly increasing along the list.
nodes.title: Binomial heap

nodes.summary: Over a linearly ordered type, the multiset of elements of a binomial heap is the multiset of elements of its list of binomial trees, that is, the multiset sum of the multisets of elements of its trees.
nodes.title: Elements of a binomial heap

nodes.summary: Every tree in a binomial heap holding $n$ elements, counted with multiplicity, has rank at most $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$.
nodes.title: Tree ranks in a binomial heap are logarithmic

nodes.summary: If a binomial heap over a linearly ordered type has $n$ elements, counted with multiplicity, then its number of trees is at most $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$, where $\lfloor \log_2 0 \rfloor$ is taken to be $0$.
nodes.title: A binomial heap has logarithmically many trees

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, the empty binomial heap over $\alpha$ is the binomial heap whose list of trees is empty.
nodes.title: Empty binomial heap

nodes.summary: Over a linear order, the meld of two binomial heaps is the binomial heap whose forest is the meld of the forests of the two heaps.
nodes.title: Melding binomial heaps

nodes.summary: For a value $a$ in a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, the one-element binomial heap of $a$ is the binomial heap whose list of trees consists of exactly one tree: the binomial tree of rank $0$ with root $a$ and no children.
nodes.title: One-element binomial heap

nodes.summary: Inserting a value $x$ into a binomial heap $H$ over a linearly ordered type gives the meld of the one-element binomial heap containing $x$ with $H$.
nodes.title: Insertion into a binomial heap

nodes.summary: The minimum lookup of a binomial heap over a linearly ordered type returns no value when the heap has no trees, and otherwise returns the least of the root values of its trees, leaving the heap unchanged.
nodes.title: Minimum of a binomial heap

nodes.summary: Given a list of binomial trees over a linearly ordered type, if the list is empty there is no result. Otherwise, remove the first tree whose root is minimal among the roots of the list; the result is the root of that tree together with the forest obtained by melding its children, in reversed order, with the remaining trees.
nodes.title: Minimum deletion on a binomial forest

nodes.summary: If the binomial heap $H$ has no trees, there is no result. Otherwise, remove from the list of trees of $H$ the first tree whose root is minimal; the result is that root together with the binomial heap whose list of trees is obtained by melding the children of the removed tree, in reversed order, with the remaining trees.
nodes.title: Deleting the minimum of a binomial heap

nodes.summary: For every binomial heap $H$ over a linearly ordered type, deleting the minimum of $H$ and then replacing the remaining heap by its list of trees gives the same result as minimum deletion on the list of trees of $H$: both have no result, or both return the same minimum value and the same list of trees.
nodes.title: Binomial heap deletion agrees with forest deletion

nodes.summary: For any two binomial heaps $H_1$ and $H_2$ over a linearly ordered type, the multiset of elements of the meld of $H_1$ and $H_2$ is the sum of the multisets of elements of $H_1$ and $H_2$.
nodes.title: Melding binomial heaps adds their elements

nodes.summary: For every binomial heap $H$ over a linearly ordered type and every value $v$, the multiset of elements of the heap obtained by inserting $v$ into $H$ is the multiset of elements of $H$ with one more occurrence of $v$.
nodes.title: Insertion into a binomial heap adds one occurrence

nodes.summary: For a binomial heap $H$ over a linearly ordered type, the minimum lookup of $H$ returns no value if and only if the list of trees of $H$ is empty.
nodes.title: The minimum lookup fails exactly on the empty binomial heap

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a binomial heap over a linearly ordered type. If the minimum lookup of $H$ returns $m$, then $m$ is an element of $H$.
nodes.title: The minimum lookup of a binomial heap returns one of its elements

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a binomial heap over a linearly ordered type. If the minimum lookup of $H$ returns $m$, then $m \le v$ for every element $v$ of $H$.
nodes.title: The minimum lookup of a binomial heap returns a lower bound

nodes.summary: For a binomial heap $H$ over a linearly ordered type, deleting the minimum of $H$ returns no result if and only if the list of trees of $H$ is empty.
nodes.title: Deleting the minimum fails only on the empty binomial heap

nodes.summary: For a binomial heap $H$ over a linearly ordered type, if deleting the minimum of $H$ succeeds and returns a value $m$ and a heap $H'$, then the multiset of elements of $H'$ is the multiset of elements of $H$ with one occurrence of $m$ removed.
nodes.title: Deleting the minimum of a binomial heap removes one occurrence

nodes.summary: For a binomial heap $H$ over a linearly ordered type, if deleting the minimum of $H$ succeeds and returns a value $m$ and a heap $H'$, then the multiset of elements of $H$ equals the multiset of elements of $H'$ with one more occurrence of $m$.
nodes.title: Deleting the minimum of a binomial heap splits its multiset

nodes.summary: If deleting the minimum of a binomial heap $H$ over a linearly ordered type succeeds and returns a value $m$ together with a remaining heap, then $m \le v$ for every value $v$ in the multiset of elements of $H$.

reading_title.source: Smallest child among the offsets from $s$

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type, of length $|a|$, let $d$, $i$ and $s$ be natural numbers, and call $d i + k + 1$ the child of $i$ at offset $k$. Scanning the offsets $s, s + 1, \dots, d - 1$, this returns the index of a scanned child of $i$ below $|a|$ whose entry in $a$ is least among those, taking the smallest offset among ties, or nothing if no scanned child index is below $|a|$.
nodes.title: Smallest child among the offsets from $s$

reading_title.source: Smallest child in a $d$-ary heap array

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array of length $|a|$ over a linearly ordered type and let $d$ and $i$ be natural numbers. The children of $i$ are the indices $d i + k + 1$ for $0 \le k < d$, and a child is valid when it is below $|a|$. The smallest child of $i$ is the valid child of $i$ with the least entry, taking the smallest offset $k$ among ties, or nothing if $i$ has no valid child.

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array of length $|a|$ over a linearly ordered type and let $d$, $i$ and $c$ be natural numbers. If the smallest valid child of $i$ in the $d$-ary heap array $a$ is $c$, then $c < |a|$.

nodes.summary: Let $d \ge 2$, let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and let $i$ and $c$ be natural numbers. If the smallest valid child of $i$ in the $d$-ary heap array $a$ is $c$, then $i < c$.

reading_title.source: Insertion into a $d$-ary heap preserves other multiplicities

reading_title.source: Removing the root of a $d$-ary min-heap

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a $d$-ary min-heap whose storage array $a$ is nonempty. Removing the root of $h$ gives the heap of arity $d$ whose storage array is empty if $a$ has one entry. Otherwise the last entry of $a$ replaces the root, the last position is dropped, and the new root is repeatedly swapped with its smallest $d$-ary child while that child is smaller.

reading_title.source: Removing the root of a $d$-ary heap preserves its arity

nodes.summary: For a $d$-ary min-heap $h$ with nonempty storage array, the heap obtained from $h$ by removing its root has the same arity $d$ as $h$.
nodes.title: Removing the root of a $d$-ary heap preserves its arity

The min-heap built from the empty list is the empty min-heap of arity $d$, and the min-heap built from a list with head $x$ and tail $xs$ of elements of $\alpha$ is obtained by inserting $x$ into the min-heap built from $xs$. Thus the min-heap built from $[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ starts from the empty min-heap…
nodes.title: Building a $d$-ary min-heap from a list

nodes.summary: For every requested arity $r$ and every list $xs$ over a linearly ordered type, the multiset of elements of the min-heap of arity $\max(2, r)$ built from $xs$ by successive insertions equals the multiset of entries of $xs$.
nodes.title: Building a heap from a list keeps its elements

reading_title.source: Arity of a $d$-ary heap built from a list

nodes.summary: For every requested arity $r \in \mathbb{N}$ and every list $xs$ over a linearly ordered type, the $d$-ary min-heap built from $xs$ with requested arity $r$ has arity equal to the normalized arity of $r$, namely $\max(2, r)$.

reading_title.source: Extracting the minimum of a $d$-ary min-heap

nodes.summary: For a $d$-ary min-heap $h$, extracting the minimum returns nothing if the storage array of $h$ is empty. Otherwise it returns the root entry (the entry at index $0$) together with the heap obtained from $h$ by removing its root: the last entry moves to the root and sifts down along a single $d$-ary child path.
nodes.title: Extracting the minimum of a $d$-ary min-heap

nodes.summary: For a $d$-ary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type, extracting the minimum from $h$ returns no result if and only if the storage array of $h$ is empty.
nodes.title: Extracting the minimum of a d-ary heap fails exactly on the empty heap

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a $d$-ary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds, returning a value $x$ and a heap $h'$, then the multiset of elements of $h$ is the multiset of elements of $h'$ with one more occurrence of $x$.
nodes.title: Extracted minimum and remaining d-ary heap recover the original elements

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a $d$-ary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds, returning a value $x$ and a heap $h'$, then the multiset of elements of $h'$ is obtained from the multiset of elements of $h$ by removing one occurrence of $x$.
nodes.title: Extracting the minimum of a d-ary heap removes one occurrence

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a $d$-ary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds, returning a value $x$ and a heap $h'$, then the multiplicity of $x$ in the multiset of elements of $h'$ is its multiplicity in the multiset of elements of $h$ minus one.
nodes.title: Extracting the minimum of a d-ary heap lowers its multiplicity by one

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a $d$-ary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds, returning a value $x$ and a heap $h'$, then $x$ belongs to the multiset of elements of $h$.
nodes.title: The extracted minimum of a d-ary heap is one of its elements

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a $d$-ary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds, returning a value $x$ and a heap $h'$, then $x \le y$ for every element $y$ of the multiset of elements of $h$.
nodes.title: The extracted minimum of a d-ary heap is a lower bound

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a $d$-ary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds, returning a value $x$ and a heap $h'$, then $h'$ has the same arity as $h$.
nodes.title: Extracting the minimum preserves the arity of a d-ary heap
