reading_title.source: Extracting the minimum leaves a heap-ordered $d$-ary heap

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a $d$-ary min-heap. If extracting the minimum of $h$ returns a value $x$ and a heap $h'$ of arity $d'$, then $d' \ge 2$ and the storage array $a$ of $h'$ is heap-ordered: for every index $i$ with $0 < i < |a|$, the entry $a_{\lfloor (i-1)/d' \rfloor}$ is at most $a_i$.
nodes.title: Extracting the minimum leaves a heap-ordered $d$-ary heap

reading_title.source: Size of a $d$-ary min-heap

nodes.summary: For every $d$-ary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type, the number of elements of $h$, counted with multiplicity, equals the length of its backing array.

Fibonacci heap

nodes.summary: A Fibonacci tree over a type $\alpha$ is a rose tree: a node carrying a stored degree $d \in \mathbb{N}$, a root value in $\alpha$, and a finite list of child Fibonacci trees.
nodes.title: Fibonacci tree

nodes.summary: The degree of the Fibonacci tree with stored degree $d$, root value $r$ and list of children $c$ is the stored natural number $d$; it is not computed from the children.
nodes.title: Degree of a Fibonacci tree

nodes.summary: The root of a Fibonacci tree is the value stored at its top node.
nodes.title: Root of a Fibonacci tree

nodes.summary: The children of the Fibonacci tree with stored degree $d$, root value $r$ and list of subtrees $c$ are the trees of the list $c$, in order.
nodes.title: Children of a Fibonacci tree

nodes.summary: The multiset $M(t)$ of values stored in a Fibonacci tree $t$, defined recursively: if $t$ has root value $r$ and children $t_1, \dots, t_k$, then $M(t) = \{r\} + M(t_1) + \cdots + M(t_k)$. The stored degree plays no role.
nodes.title: Multiset of a Fibonacci tree

nodes.summary: For every Fibonacci tree, its root value belongs to the multiset of elements the tree represents.
nodes.title: The root of a Fibonacci tree is one of its elements

nodes.summary: Every Fibonacci tree represents at least one element: the multiset of elements of any Fibonacci tree has positive size.
nodes.title: Fibonacci trees are nonempty

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ carry a relation $\le$. A Fibonacci tree with stored degree $d$, root $r \in \alpha$ and list of children $c$ is valid when every tree in $c$ is valid, $d$ equals the length of $c$, and $r \le x$ for every element $x$ of the multiset represented by the tree (the root together with the elements of all children).
nodes.title: Valid Fibonacci trees

nodes.summary: For a value $x$ of a linearly ordered type, the one-element Fibonacci heap on $x$ has as its only tree the single-node tree with root $x$, and its cached minimum is $x$.
nodes.title: One-element Fibonacci heap

nodes.summary: Let $s$ and $t$ be Fibonacci trees over a linearly ordered type. If the root of $s$ is at most the root of $t$, the link of $s$ and $t$ is the tree with the root of $s$, stored degree one more than that of $s$, and children $t$ followed by the children of $s$. Otherwise it is the tree with the root of $t$, stored degree one more than that of $t$, and children $s$ followed by the children of $t$.
nodes.title: Linking two Fibonacci trees

nodes.summary: If two Fibonacci trees $s$ and $t$ over a linearly ordered type have the same degree $d$, then their link has degree $d + 1$.
nodes.title: Degree of the link of two trees of equal degree

nodes.summary: For any two Fibonacci trees $S$ and $T$ over a linearly ordered type, the tree obtained by linking $S$ and $T$ represents the sum of the multisets represented by $S$ and by $T$.
nodes.title: Linking adds the elements

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every $v \in \alpha$, the Fibonacci tree of degree $0$ with root $v$ and no children is valid.
nodes.title: Singleton Fibonacci trees are valid

nodes.summary: Every child of a valid Fibonacci tree is itself a valid Fibonacci tree.
nodes.title: Children of a valid Fibonacci tree are valid

nodes.summary: For every valid Fibonacci tree, its stored degree equals the number of its children.
nodes.title: The degree of a valid Fibonacci tree is its number of children

nodes.summary: The root of a valid Fibonacci tree is no greater than every element of the multiset the tree represents.
nodes.title: Roots of valid Fibonacci trees are lower bounds

nodes.summary: For every valid Fibonacci tree over a type with a relation $\le$, the degree of the tree is strictly less than the number of elements, counted with multiplicity, of the multiset the tree represents, since every child contributes at least one element.
nodes.title: The degree of a valid Fibonacci tree is less than its size

nodes.summary: If $s$ and $t$ are valid Fibonacci trees over a linearly ordered type, then the link of $s$ and $t$ is a valid Fibonacci tree.
nodes.title: Linking preserves validity of Fibonacci trees

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ carry a relation $\le$. A Fibonacci forest, a list of Fibonacci trees with values in $\alpha$, is valid when every tree in it is a valid Fibonacci tree.
nodes.title: Valid Fibonacci forests

nodes.summary: Write $M(t)$ for the multiset of values stored in a Fibonacci tree $t$. The multiset represented by a Fibonacci forest, a list of Fibonacci trees $t_1, \dots, t_k$, is the sum $M(t_1) + \cdots + M(t_k)$; the empty forest represents the empty multiset.
nodes.title: Multiset of a Fibonacci forest

nodes.summary: A Fibonacci forest, a list of Fibonacci trees $t_1, \dots, t_k$, has sorted degrees when the stored degrees of its trees strictly increase along the list: $\deg t_i < \deg t_j$ whenever $i < j$.
nodes.title: Forests with strictly increasing degrees

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ carry a relation $\le$. The empty forest, containing no Fibonacci trees with values in $\alpha$, is valid.
nodes.title: The empty Fibonacci forest is valid

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ carry a relation $\le$. If $F$ and $G$ are valid Fibonacci forests with values in $\alpha$, then the forest consisting of the trees of $F$ followed by the trees of $G$ is valid.
nodes.title: Concatenation preserves validity of Fibonacci forests

nodes.summary: If a list of Fibonacci trees is a valid forest, then every sublist of it (a subsequence, not necessarily contiguous) is a valid forest.
nodes.title: Sublists of valid Fibonacci forests are valid

nodes.summary: For any two lists $L$ and $R$ of Fibonacci trees, the forest made of the trees of $L$ followed by the trees of $R$ represents the sum of the multisets represented by $L$ and by $R$.
nodes.title: Elements of a concatenated forest

nodes.summary: The minimum root of a forest of Fibonacci trees over a linearly ordered type is an optional value: it is absent for the empty forest, and for a nonempty forest it is the least of the roots of its trees.
nodes.title: Minimum root of a forest

nodes.summary: For optional values $x$ and $y$ of a linearly ordered type, their combined minimum is defined as follows: if $x$ and $y$ are both present, with values $a$ and $b$, it is $\min(a, b)$; if exactly one of $x$ and $y$ is present, it is that value; and if both are absent, it is absent.
nodes.title: Minimum of two optional values

nodes.summary: A forest of Fibonacci trees over a linearly ordered type has no minimum root exactly when it is empty.
nodes.title: Only the empty forest has no minimum root

nodes.summary: If a forest $F$ of Fibonacci trees over a linearly ordered type has minimum root $m$, then $m$ is the root of some tree of $F$ and $m$ is at most the root of every tree of $F$.
nodes.title: The minimum root is a least root

nodes.summary: For forests $F$ and $G$ of Fibonacci trees over a linearly ordered type, the minimum root of $F$ followed by $G$ is the combined minimum of the optional minimum roots of $F$ and of $G$: their minimum if both exist, the one that exists if only one does, and absent if neither does.
nodes.title: Minimum root of a concatenated forest

nodes.summary: Given a Fibonacci tree $t$ and a list of Fibonacci trees, the insertion of $t$ into the list is defined recursively. Inserting $t$ into the empty list gives the one-tree list $[t]$. For a list with first tree $s$ and remaining list $L$: if the stored degree of $t$ is less than the stored degree of $s$, the result is $t$ followed by $s$ and then $L$; if the two stored degrees are equal, the result is the insertion…
nodes.title: Inserting a tree into a forest

nodes.summary: The consolidation of a list of Fibonacci trees is defined recursively: the consolidation of the empty list is the empty list, and the consolidation of a list with first tree $t$ and remaining list $L$ is the insertion of $t$ into the consolidation of $L$.
nodes.title: Consolidation of a forest

nodes.summary: For every list of Fibonacci trees over a linearly ordered type, its consolidation represents the same multiset as the original list.
nodes.title: Consolidation preserves the elements

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. If a Fibonacci forest with values in $\alpha$ is valid, then its consolidation is valid.
nodes.title: Consolidation preserves validity

nodes.summary: For every list of Fibonacci trees, the stored degrees of the trees in its consolidation are strictly increasing in list order.
nodes.title: Consolidation sorts root degrees

nodes.summary: For every list of Fibonacci trees, the trees in its consolidation have pairwise distinct stored degrees.
nodes.title: Consolidation yields distinct root degrees

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a valid forest of Fibonacci trees whose degrees are strictly increasing along the list. Then the number of trees in $F$ is at most the number of elements, counted with multiplicity, that $F$ represents.
nodes.title: Degree-sorted forests have at most as many trees as elements

nodes.summary: For a list of Fibonacci trees over a linearly ordered type, this returns nothing on the empty list. Otherwise it returns the first tree whose root is minimal among all roots in the list, so earlier trees win ties, together with the list of the remaining trees in their original order.
nodes.title: Removing a minimum tree from a Fibonacci forest

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a list of Fibonacci trees over a linearly ordered type. If removing a minimum tree from $T$ returns a tree $m$ and a list $R$, then the multiset of elements of $m$ plus the multiset of elements of $R$ equals the multiset of elements of $T$, the tree $m$ belongs to $T$, the list $R$ is a sublist of $T$, and the root of $m$ is at most the root of every tree in $T$.
nodes.title: Minimum-tree removal in a Fibonacci forest

nodes.summary: A Fibonacci min-heap over a linearly ordered type consists of a list of Fibonacci trees, each valid (heap-ordered, and at every node the stored degree equals the number of children), together with a cached minimum equal to the least root value of these trees, absent when the list is empty.
nodes.title: Fibonacci heap

nodes.summary: The multiset represented by a Fibonacci heap over a linearly ordered type is the multiset of its list of trees: the sum, over the trees in the list, of the multisets of values stored in them. The cached minimum plays no role.
nodes.title: Multiset of a Fibonacci heap

nodes.summary: The Fibonacci heap over a linearly ordered type whose list of trees is empty and whose cached minimum is absent.
nodes.title: Empty Fibonacci heap

nodes.summary: For a value $x$ of a linearly ordered type, the singleton Fibonacci heap on $x$ has as its only tree the single-node tree with root $x$, stored degree $0$ and no children, and its cached minimum is $x$.
nodes.title: Singleton Fibonacci heap

nodes.summary: The meld of Fibonacci heaps $H_1$ and $H_2$ is the Fibonacci heap whose root list is the root list of $H_1$ followed by that of $H_2$, and whose cached minimum is the smaller of the two cached minima when both heaps have one, and otherwise the cached minimum of whichever heap has one (none if neither does).
nodes.title: Melding Fibonacci heaps

nodes.summary: The union of Fibonacci heaps $H_1$ and $H_2$ is their meld: the heap whose trees are those of $H_1$ followed by those of $H_2$, and whose cached minimum is the smaller of the two cached minima (the one that exists if a heap is empty, none if both are).
nodes.title: Union of Fibonacci heaps

nodes.summary: Inserting a value $x$ into a Fibonacci heap $H$ gives the meld of the one-element Fibonacci heap containing $x$ with $H$, the one-element heap coming first.
nodes.title: Insertion into a Fibonacci heap

nodes.summary: Find-min on a Fibonacci heap returns its cached minimum without modifying the heap: the least root value of its trees, or no value when the heap has no trees.
nodes.title: Find-min for Fibonacci heaps

nodes.summary: Given a list of Fibonacci trees over a linearly ordered type, the result is nothing if the list is empty. Otherwise the first tree whose root is minimal is removed, and the result is its root value together with the consolidation of the forest made of the removed tree's children followed by the remaining trees.
nodes.title: Minimum deletion on a forest

nodes.summary: If the root list of the heap is empty, the result is nothing. Otherwise the first tree of the root list whose root is minimal is removed, and the result is its root value together with the heap whose root list is the consolidation of the removed tree's children followed by the remaining trees, and whose cached minimum is the minimum root of this consolidated forest.
nodes.title: Deleting the minimum of a Fibonacci heap

nodes.summary: For every Fibonacci heap $H$, deleting the minimum of $H$ and keeping only the returned value and the root list of the resulting heap gives the same result as the root-list minimum deletion applied to the root list of $H$: either both fail, or both return the same value and the same list of trees.
nodes.title: Fibonacci heap minimum deletion agrees with its root-list version

nodes.summary: The empty Fibonacci heap represents the empty multiset.
nodes.title: The empty Fibonacci heap has no elements

nodes.summary: For every value $x$ of a linearly ordered type, the singleton Fibonacci heap on $x$, whose only tree is the single-node tree with root $x$, represents the multiset $\{x\}$.
nodes.title: Multiset of a singleton Fibonacci heap

nodes.summary: For any two Fibonacci heaps $H_1$ and $H_2$ over a linearly ordered type, the meld of $H_1$ and $H_2$ represents the sum of the multisets represented by $H_1$ and by $H_2$.
nodes.title: Melding adds the elements

nodes.summary: For Fibonacci heaps $H_1$ and $H_2$ over a linearly ordered type, the multiset represented by the union of $H_1$ and $H_2$ is the sum of the multisets represented by $H_1$ and by $H_2$.
nodes.title: The union of Fibonacci heaps adds their multisets

nodes.summary: For every Fibonacci heap $H$ over a linearly ordered type and every value $x$, the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $H$ represents the multiset of $H$ with one more occurrence of $x$.
nodes.title: Insertion adds one occurrence

nodes.summary: For Fibonacci heaps $H_1$ and $H_2$, the number of elements of the meld of $H_1$ and $H_2$, counted with multiplicity, is the number of elements of $H_1$ plus the number of elements of $H_2$.
nodes.title: Melding adds the sizes of Fibonacci heaps

nodes.summary: For every Fibonacci heap $H$ and every value $x$, the number of elements of the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $H$, counted with multiplicity, is the number of elements of $H$ plus one.
nodes.title: Insertion increases the size of a Fibonacci heap by one

nodes.summary: For a Fibonacci heap $H$ over a linearly ordered type, find-min on $H$ returns no value if and only if $H$ has no trees.
nodes.title: Find-min fails exactly on the empty Fibonacci heap

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a Fibonacci heap over a linearly ordered type. If find-min on $H$ returns $m$, then $m$ belongs to the multiset represented by $H$.
nodes.title: Find-min returns an element of the Fibonacci heap

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a Fibonacci heap over a linearly ordered type. If find-min on $H$ returns $m$, then $m \le v$ for every value $v$ in the multiset represented by $H$.
nodes.title: Find-min returns a lower bound of the Fibonacci heap

nodes.summary: Deleting the minimum of a Fibonacci heap fails if and only if the heap's list of root trees is empty.
nodes.title: Fibonacci heap minimum deletion fails exactly on the empty heap

nodes.summary: If deleting the minimum of a Fibonacci heap $H$ succeeds and returns the value $m$ and the heap $H'$, then the multiset of elements of $H'$ is the multiset of elements of $H$ with one occurrence of $m$ removed.
nodes.title: Fibonacci heap minimum deletion removes one copy of the minimum

nodes.summary: If deleting the minimum of a Fibonacci heap $H$ succeeds and returns the value $m$ and the heap $H'$, then the multiset of elements of $H$ is the multiset of elements of $H'$ with one copy of $m$ added.
nodes.title: Fibonacci heap minimum deletion splits off the minimum

nodes.summary: If deleting the minimum of a Fibonacci heap $H$ succeeds and returns the value $m$, then $m \le v$ for every element $v$ of $H$.
nodes.title: Fibonacci heap minimum deletion returns a lower bound

nodes.summary: If deleting the minimum of a Fibonacci heap succeeds and returns the heap $H'$, then the degrees of the root trees of $H'$, in list order, are strictly increasing; consolidation is what makes them so.
nodes.title: Minimum deletion leaves a Fibonacci heap with strictly increasing root degrees

nodes.summary: If deleting the minimum of a Fibonacci heap succeeds and returns the heap $H'$, then the number of root trees of $H'$ is at most the number of elements of $H'$, counted with multiplicity.
nodes.title: After minimum deletion a Fibonacci heap has at most as many roots as elements

nodes.summary: For a list $p = (i_1, \dots, i_n)$ of natural numbers and a Fibonacci tree $t$, the subtree of $t$ at $p$ is found by starting at the root and moving to the child with zero-based index $i_1$, then to its child with index $i_2$, and so on. The result is absent when some index is at least the number of children of the current node. The empty path addresses the whole tree $t$.
nodes.title: Subtree of a Fibonacci tree at a path

nodes.summary: For a path $p$ of child indices and a Fibonacci tree $t$, the cut of $t$ at $p$ is either undefined or a pair of an extracted subtree and an optional remainder tree. For the empty path, the extracted subtree is $t$ and there is no remainder. For a path consisting of an index $i$ followed by a path $q$, where $t$ has root $r$ and children $c_0, \dots, c_{k-1}$, the cut is undefined if $i \ge k$ or if the cut of…
nodes.title: Cutting a subtree out of a Fibonacci tree

nodes.summary: For a Fibonacci tree $t$ and a key $k$, this is the tree whose root value is $k$ and whose stored degree and list of children are those of $t$.
nodes.title: Replacing the root key of a Fibonacci tree

nodes.summary: For a Fibonacci tree $t$ and any key $k$, the multiset of elements represented by the tree obtained from $t$ by replacing its root value with $k$ equals the multiset of elements of $t$ with one occurrence of the root of $t$ removed and $k$ added.
nodes.title: Elements after replacing the root key

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a valid Fibonacci tree over a preordered type and let $k$ be a key that is at most the root of $T$. Then the tree obtained from $T$ by replacing its root by $k$, keeping its degree and children, is valid: the new root is still no greater than every represented element.
nodes.title: Lowering the root keeps a Fibonacci tree valid

nodes.summary: If a Fibonacci tree $t$ is valid and a path $p$ of child indices addresses a subtree $s$ of $t$, then $s$ is valid.
nodes.title: Subtrees of a valid Fibonacci tree are valid

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a Fibonacci tree and $p$ a path of child indices. If cutting $t$ at $p$ extracts a subtree $s$ (with or without a remainder), then $s$ is the subtree of $t$ at $p$.
nodes.title: A cut extracts the addressed subtree

nodes.summary: If a path $p$ of child indices addresses a subtree $s$ of a Fibonacci tree $t$, then cutting $t$ at $p$ succeeds and extracts exactly $s$, together with some remainder, which may be absent.
nodes.title: Every addressed subtree can be cut out

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a Fibonacci tree and $p$ a path of child indices. If cutting $t$ at $p$ extracts a subtree $s$ and leaves no remainder, then $s = t$.
nodes.title: A cut without remainder extracts the whole tree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a Fibonacci tree and $p$ a path of child indices. If cutting $t$ at $p$ extracts a subtree $s$ and leaves a remainder tree $t'$, then the multiset of elements of $t$ is the sum of the multisets of elements of $t'$ and of $s$.
nodes.title: Cutting a subtree splits the elements of a Fibonacci tree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid Fibonacci tree over a type with a relation $\le$, and $p$ a path of child indices. If cutting $t$ at $p$ extracts a subtree $s$ (with or without a remainder), then $s$ is valid.
nodes.title: The subtree extracted by a cut from a valid tree is valid

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid Fibonacci tree over a type with a relation $\le$, and $p$ a path of child indices. If cutting $t$ at $p$ extracts a subtree and leaves a remainder tree $t'$, then $t'$ is valid: its children are valid, its stored degree equals its number of children, and its root is $\le$ every element of $t'$.
nodes.title: The remainder of a cut from a valid tree is valid

nodes.summary: For a forest given as a list of Fibonacci trees, an index $i$ and a path $p$ of child indices, the cut is undefined if the list has no tree at position $i$ (counting from $0$) or if cutting that tree $t$ at $p$ is undefined. Otherwise, if cutting $t$ at $p$ extracts the subtree $s$, the result is $s$ together with the list in which the tree at position $i$ is removed (if the cut of $t$ left no remainder) or…
nodes.title: Cutting a subtree out of a Fibonacci forest

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a forest of Fibonacci trees, $i$ an index and $p$ a path of child indices. If cutting $F$ at the $i$-th tree and path $p$ extracts a subtree $s$ and leaves the forest $F'$, then the multiset of elements of $F$ is the sum of the multisets of elements of $F'$ and of $s$.
nodes.title: Cutting a subtree splits the elements of a Fibonacci forest

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a valid forest of Fibonacci trees over a type with a relation $\le$, $i$ an index and $p$ a path of child indices. If cutting $F$ at index $i$ and path $p$ extracts a subtree $s$ and leaves the forest $F'$, then $s$ is a valid tree and $F'$ is a valid forest.
nodes.title: Cutting a valid forest leaves valid parts

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a forest of Fibonacci trees whose tree at position $i$ is $t$, and let $p$ be a path of child indices such that the subtree of $t$ at $p$ is $s$. Then cutting $F$ at index $i$ and path $p$ is defined and extracts $s$, together with some remaining forest.
nodes.title: Every addressed subtree of a forest can be cut out

nodes.summary: Given a Fibonacci heap $H$ over a linearly ordered type, a root index $i$, a path $p$ of child indices and a key $k$, decrease-key cuts the subtree $S$ at path $p$ out of the $i$-th tree of the root list of $H$, replaces the root of $S$ by $k$, and puts the resulting tree in front of the remaining forest (the root list with the $i$-th tree replaced by what is left of it after the cut, or removed when $S$ is that…
nodes.title: Decrease-key in a Fibonacci heap

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a Fibonacci heap, $i$ a root index, $p$ a path of child indices and $k$ a key. Suppose that cutting the subtree at path $p$ out of the $i$-th tree of the root list of $H$ succeeds, extracting the subtree $S$ and leaving the forest $R$, and that $k$ is at most the root of $S$. Then the root list of the heap obtained from $H$ by decreasing the key at root index $i$ and path $p$ to $k$ consists of $S$ with…
nodes.title: Root list after decrease-key

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a Fibonacci heap, $i$ a root index and $p$ a path of child indices. If cutting the subtree at path $p$ out of the $i$-th tree of the root list of $H$ fails, then for every key $k$, decreasing the key at root index $i$ and path $p$ to $k$ returns $H$ unchanged.
nodes.title: Decrease-key at an unresolved address does nothing

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a Fibonacci heap, $i$ a root index, $p$ a path of child indices and $k$ a key. Suppose that cutting the subtree at path $p$ out of the $i$-th tree of the root list of $H$ succeeds and extracts the subtree $S$, and that $k$ is not at most the root of $S$ (keys are linearly ordered, so $k$ is greater than that root). Then decreasing the key at root index $i$ and path $p$ to $k$ returns $H$ unchanged.
nodes.title: Decrease-key with a larger key does nothing

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a Fibonacci heap, $i$ a root index, $p$ a path of child indices and $k$ a key. Suppose that cutting the subtree at path $p$ out of the $i$-th tree of the root list of $H$ succeeds and extracts the subtree $S$, and that $k$ is at most the root of $S$. Then the multiset represented by the heap obtained from $H$ by decreasing the key at root index $i$ and path $p$ to $k$ is the multiset represented by $H$…
nodes.title: Decrease-key replaces one key

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a Fibonacci heap, let $T$ be the $i$-th tree of its root list, and let $S$ be the subtree of $T$ at the path $p$ of child indices. If the key $k$ is at most the root of $S$, then the multiset represented by the heap obtained from $H$ by decreasing the key at root index $i$ and path $p$ to $k$ is the multiset represented by $H$ with one occurrence of the root of $S$ removed and one occurrence of $k$ added.
nodes.title: Decrease-key replaces one key, stated by address

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a Fibonacci heap, $i$ a root index, $p$ a path of child indices and $k$ a key. Suppose that cutting the subtree at path $p$ out of the $i$-th tree of the root list of $H$ succeeds and extracts the subtree $S$, and that $k$ is at most the root of $S$. Then the multiset represented by the heap obtained from $H$ by decreasing the key at root index $i$ and path $p$ to $k$ has the same number of elements,…
nodes.title: Decrease-key preserves the number of elements

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a Fibonacci heap whose minimum, as returned by find-min, is $m$, and let $i$ be a root index, $p$ a path of child indices and $k$ a key. Suppose that cutting the subtree at path $p$ out of the $i$-th tree of the root list of $H$ succeeds and extracts the subtree $S$, and that $k$ is at most the root of $S$. Then find-min on the heap obtained from $H$ by decreasing the key at root index $i$ and path $p$…
nodes.title: Minimum after decrease-key

nodes.summary: For every Fibonacci heap $H$, root index $i$, path $p$ of child indices and key $k$, the root list of the heap obtained from $H$ by decreasing the key at root index $i$ and path $p$ to $k$ is a valid forest, that is, every tree in it is valid.
nodes.title: Decrease-key yields a valid forest
Indexed minimum priority queue

An indexed minimum queue over the identities $0, \dots, n-1$ consists of a binary min-heap whose entries are pairs $(k, v)$ of a key $k \in W \cup \{\top\}$ and an identity $v < n$, ordered lexicographically (first by key, then by identity), together with a position vector…
nodes.title: Indexed minimum queue

nodes.summary: For every linearly ordered type $W$ and every natural number $n$, the empty indexed minimum queue over the identities $0, \dots, n-1$, with keys in $W$ with a new greatest element adjoined, has the empty min-heap and a position vector that assigns nothing to each of the $n$ identities, so no identity is present.
nodes.title: Empty indexed minimum queue

nodes.summary: Costs are counted as five event counts: comparisons, swaps, reads of the position vector, writes to the position vector, and entry appends, pops or replacements. For an indexed minimum queue $q$ over the identities $0, \dots, n-1$ and an identity $v < n$, the membership test returns true exactly when the position vector of $q$ assigns an index to $v$, and its cost is one position read and no other event.
nodes.title: Membership test in an indexed minimum queue

nodes.summary: Let $W$ be a linearly ordered type and let $W \cup \{\top\}$ be $W$ with a new greatest element $\top$ adjoined. Costs are counted as five event counts: comparisons, swaps, reads of the position vector, writes to the position vector, and entry appends, pops or replacements. Costs are counted as five event counts: comparisons, swaps, reads of the position vector, writes to the position vector, and entry appends, pops or replacements. Given an indexed minimum queue $q$, extract-min fails (returns nothing) exactly when the heap of $q$ is empty, at zero cost. Otherwise let $(k, v)$ be the root entry of the heap. If the heap has one entry, extract-min returns $(k, v)$ together with the…
nodes.title: Extract-min in an indexed minimum queue

nodes.summary: Let $W$ be a linearly ordered type and let $q$ be an indexed min-queue over $W$ with identities in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. If the position table of $q$ records slot $i$ for an identity $v$, then $i$ is less than the number of entries currently stored in the heap array of $q$.
nodes.title: Recorded positions lie inside the heap

nodes.summary: Let $q$ be an indexed min queue over a linear order $W$ with identities in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $v$ be an identity. The position vector of $q$ records no slot for $v$ if and only if no entry of the heap array of $q$ has identity $v$.
nodes.title: Absent identities carry no heap entry

nodes.summary: For every linear order $W$, every $n$ and every identity $v \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the position vector of the empty indexed min queue over $W$ with identities in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ records no slot for $v$.
nodes.title: The empty indexed min queue has no present identity

nodes.summary: Let $q$ be an indexed min queue over a linear order $W$ with identities in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $v$ be an identity and let $k \in W \cup \{\top\}$. Inserting $v$ with key $k$ into $q$ returns no queue if and only if the position vector of $q$ records a slot for $v$.
nodes.title: Insertion fails exactly on present identities

nodes.summary: Let $q$ be an indexed min queue over a linear order $W$ with identities in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Extracting the minimum of $q$ returns no result if and only if the heap array of $q$ has size $0$.
nodes.title: Extraction from an indexed min queue fails exactly when it is empty

nodes.summary: Let $q$ be an indexed min queue over a linear order $W$ with identities in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $v$ be an identity. The membership test for $v$ in $q$ returns true if and only if the position vector of $q$ records a slot for $v$.
nodes.title: Membership reads the position vector

nodes.summary: Let $q$ be an indexed min queue over a linear order $W$ with identities in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $v$ be an identity. The cost of the membership test for $v$ in $q$, counted in five event classes (comparisons, swaps, position-vector reads, position-vector writes, and entry appends, pops or replacements), is exactly one position-vector read and no event of any other class.
nodes.title: Membership costs one position read

nodes.summary: Let $q$ be an indexed min queue over a linear order $W$ with identities in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $v$ be an identity and let $k \in W \cup \{\top\}$, and suppose that inserting $v$ with key $k$ into $q$ returns the queue $q'$. Then the heap of $q'$ is the binary min-heap push of the entry $(k, v)$ onto the heap of $q$; the position vector of $q'$ records a slot $i$ for $v$, with $i$ less than the size of the heap…
nodes.title: Successful insertion into an indexed min queue

nodes.summary: Let $q$ be an indexed min queue over a linear order $W$ with identities in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $v$ be an identity and let $k \in W$. Decreasing the key of $v$ to $k$ in $q$ returns no queue if and only if either the position vector of $q$ records no slot for $v$, or it records a slot $i$ for $v$ with $i$ less than the size of the heap array of $q$ and $k$ is not strictly less, in $W \cup \{\top\}$, than the…
nodes.title: Decrease-key fails exactly on absent identities and non-decreases

nodes.title: Successful decrease-key

nodes.summary: Given a type $K$ of keys, a type $V$ of values, a number $m$ of slots, and two hash functions $h_1, h_2 : K \to \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$, a cuckoo hash table consists of two tables, each a vector of $m$ slots; every slot is either empty or holds a key–value pair $(k, v)$ with $k \in K$ and $v \in V$. The structure itself does not require a pair $(k, v)$ to sit at slot $h_1(k)$ of the first table or at slot $h_2(k)$ of…

nodes.summary: The empty cuckoo hash table has every slot of both tables vacant.
nodes.title: Empty cuckoo hash table

nodes.summary: A cuckoo hash table with hash functions $h_1, h_2$ satisfies the placement invariant when every pair $(k, v)$ in slot $i$ of the first table has $i = h_1(k)$, and every pair $(k, v)$ in slot $i$ of the second table has $i = h_2(k)$.
nodes.title: Placement invariant of a cuckoo hash table

nodes.summary: A key $k$ is stored with value $v$ in a cuckoo hash table when the pair $(k, v)$ occupies some slot of the first table or some slot of the second table.

nodes.summary: A cuckoo hash table is key-deterministic when each key is stored with at most one value: for every key $k$ and values $v_1, v_2$, if the bindings $k \mapsto v_1$ and $k \mapsto v_2$ are both stored in the table, then $v_1 = v_2$. Duplicate copies of the same pair are allowed.

nodes.summary: For any hash functions $h_1, h_2$ into $m$ slots, the empty cuckoo hash table, with every slot of both tables vacant, satisfies the placement invariant.

nodes.summary: No key is stored with two different values in the empty cuckoo hash table, vacuously.
nodes.title: The empty cuckoo hash table is key-deterministic

nodes.summary: For a cuckoo hash table $T$ with hash functions $h_1$ and $h_2$ and a key $k$, the lookup of $k$ in $T$ returns $v$ if slot $h_1(k)$ of the first table holds a pair $(k, v)$; otherwise it returns $v$ if slot $h_2(k)$ of the second table holds a pair $(k, v)$; otherwise it returns nothing. No other slot is examined.

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a cuckoo hash table that satisfies the placement invariant and is key-deterministic. For every key $k$ and value $v$, if the binding $k \mapsto v$ is stored in $T$, then looking up $k$ in $T$ returns $v$.

nodes.summary: A slot of a cuckoo hash table is either empty or holds a pair $(k, v)$ of a key and a value. For a slot $s$ and a key $k'$, this test is true when $s$ holds a pair whose key is $k'$, and false when $s$ is empty or holds a pair with a different key.

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a cuckoo hash table that satisfies the placement invariant and is key-deterministic. Then for every key $k' \ne k$ and every value $v'$, the binding $k' \mapsto v'$ is stored in $T'$ if and only if it is stored in $T$.

Hash table with separate chaining

nodes.summary: For a key type $\alpha$, a value type $\beta$ and a hash function $h : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$, a hash table with hash function $h$ consists of a positive number $m$ of buckets and, for each bucket index $i < m$, a chain stored at bucket $i$: an association list of key–value pairs whose keys are pairwise distinct. The structure itself does not require keys to lie in their hash-selected bucket.
nodes.title: Hash table with separate chaining

nodes.summary: For a hash function $h$ and a positive integer $m$, the empty hash table with hash function $h$ has $m$ buckets, each holding the empty chain.

nodes.summary: For a hash table with hash function $h$ and $m$ buckets, looking up a key $k$ searches only the bucket with index $h(k) \bmod m$: the result is the value bound to $k$ in that bucket's association list, or nothing if $k$ has no binding there.

nodes.summary: Inserting a key $k$ with value $v$ into a hash table with $m$ buckets and hash function $h$ keeps the bucket count and every bucket other than bucket $h(k) \bmod m$, and replaces the chain at bucket $h(k) \bmod m$ by that chain with $k$ bound to $v$: any earlier binding of $k$ in that chain is removed and the binding of $k$ to $v$ is added.

nodes.summary: A hash table with hash function $h$ and $m$ buckets is valid when every binding lies in its hash-selected bucket: for every bucket index $i < m$ and every key $k$, if $k$ has a binding in bucket $i$, then $h(k) \bmod m = i$.

nodes.summary: The finite map represented by a hash table with $m$ buckets is built from the list of all bindings of buckets $0, 1, \dots, m - 1$, concatenated in this order: it binds exactly the keys occurring in this list, and binds each such key to the value of its first binding in the list.

nodes.summary: For every hash function $h$, every positive bucket count $m$ and every key $k$, looking up $k$ in the empty hash table with hash function $h$ and $m$ buckets finds no value.

nodes.summary: For every hash function $h$ and every positive bucket count $m$, the finite map represented by the empty hash table with hash function $h$ and $m$ buckets is the empty finite map.

Open addressing

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a type of keys, $V$ a type of values, $m$ a natural number, and $p$ a probe sequence assigning to each key $k$ and each $i \in \mathbb{N}$ a slot $p(k, i) \in \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$. An open-addressing hash table with $m$ slots and probe sequence $p$ consists of $m$ slots, each either empty or holding a single pair $(k, v)$ with $k \in K$ and $v \in V$.
nodes.title: Open-addressing hash table

nodes.summary: Given a hash function $h : K \to \mathbb{N}$ and a number of slots $m > 0$, the $i$-th probe of a key $k$ is the slot $(h(k) + i) \bmod m$ in $\{0, \dots, m - 1\}$.
nodes.title: Linear-probing probe sequence

nodes.summary: Given hash functions $h_1, h_2 : K \to \mathbb{N}$ and a number of slots $m > 0$, the $i$-th probe of a key $k$ is the slot $(h_1(k) + i \cdot h_2(k)) \bmod m$ in $\{0, \dots, m - 1\}$.
nodes.title: Double-hashing probe sequence

nodes.summary: The open-addressing table with $m$ slots and a given probe sequence in which every slot is empty.
nodes.title: Empty open-addressing table

nodes.summary: Given a table with $m$ slots and probe sequence $p$, a key $k$, a starting index $s$ and a budget $f$ of probes, examine the slots $p(k, s), p(k, s + 1), \dots$ in order, for at most $f$ probes. The scan returns the value bound to $k$ in the first examined slot that holds a binding for $k$, and returns no value if it first reaches an empty slot or exhausts the budget.
nodes.title: Bounded lookup scan

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an open-addressing hash table with $m$ slots and probe sequence $p$, and let $k$ be a key. The lookup of $k$ in $T$ inspects the slots $p(k, 0), p(k, 1), \dots, p(k, m - 1)$ in this order. It returns the value $v$ of the first inspected slot that holds a pair $(k, v)$, and returns nothing if an empty slot is inspected first or if none of the $m$ inspected slots holds the key $k$.
nodes.title: Lookup in an open-addressing table

nodes.summary: Given a table with $m$ slots and probe sequence $p$, a key $k$, a value $v$, a starting index $s$ and a budget $f$ of probes, examine the slots $p(k, s), p(k, s + 1), \dots$ in order, for at most $f$ probes. At the first examined slot that is empty or holds a binding for $k$, the scan returns the table with that slot overwritten by the binding $k \mapsto v$ and every other slot unchanged; if all $f$ examined slots…
nodes.title: Bounded insertion scan

nodes.summary: To insert the binding $k \mapsto v$ into a table with $m$ slots and probe sequence $p$, examine the slots $p(k, 0), p(k, 1), \dots, p(k, m - 1)$ in order. At the first one that is empty or already holds a binding for $k$, write $k \mapsto v$ there, leaving every other slot unchanged, and return the updated table. If all $m$ examined slots hold bindings for other keys, the insertion fails and returns no table.
nodes.title: Insertion into an open-addressing table

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an open-addressing table with $m$ slots and probe sequence $p$, where $p(k, i) \in \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$ is the slot visited by the $i$-th probe of key $k$. Then $T$ is valid when it satisfies two conditions. Probe-closedness: whenever slot $j$ holds a binding $k \mapsto v$, there is an $i < m$ with $p(k, i) = j$ such that the slots $p(k, i')$ are occupied for all $i' < i$; this is what lets a lookup stop…
nodes.title: Valid open-addressing tables

nodes.summary: An open-addressing hash table $T$ stores the binding $k \mapsto v$ when some slot of $T$ holds the pair $(k, v)$.
nodes.title: Stored binding in an open-addressing table

nodes.summary: For all types $K$ and $V$, every number of slots $m$ and every probe sequence $p$, which assigns to each key $k$ and each $i \in \mathbb{N}$ a slot $p(k, i) \in \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$, the empty table with $m$ slots and probe sequence $p$, in which every slot is vacant, is valid: it is probe-closed and no key is stored in two different slots.
nodes.title: The empty open-addressing table is valid

nodes.summary: For every key $k$, looking up $k$ in the empty open-addressing table returns no value.
nodes.title: Lookup in the empty open-addressing table

nodes.summary: If inserting the binding $k \mapsto v$ into an open-addressing hash table $T$ succeeds and yields the table $T'$, then looking up $k$ in $T'$ returns $v$. No validity assumption on $T$ is needed.
nodes.title: Lookup after a successful open-addressing insertion

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a valid table with $m$ slots and probe sequence $p$, whose keys have decidable equality. If inserting the binding $k \mapsto v$ into $T$ (adding it, or replacing the binding already stored for $k$) succeeds and returns the table $T'$, then $T'$ is valid: it is probe-closed and no key is stored in two different slots.
nodes.title: Insertion preserves validity of an open-addressing table

nodes.summary: If looking up a key $k$ in an open-addressing hash table $T$ returns the value $v$, then $T$ stores the binding $k \mapsto v$. No validity assumption is needed.
nodes.title: Open-addressing lookup returns only stored bindings

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an open-addressing table and $k$ a key such that no slot of $T$ stores a binding $k \mapsto v$ for any value $v$. Then looking up $k$ in $T$ returns no value. No validity assumption on $T$ is needed.
nodes.title: Lookup of an absent key fails

nodes.summary: If a valid open-addressing hash table $T$ stores the binding $k \mapsto v$, then looking up $k$ in $T$ returns some value.
nodes.title: Valid open-addressing tables find every stored key

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a valid open-addressing hash table and $k$ a key. Looking up $k$ in $T$ returns a value if and only if $T$ stores a binding $k \mapsto v$ for some value $v$.
nodes.title: Open-addressing lookup succeeds exactly on stored keys

nodes.summary: If a valid open-addressing hash table $T$ stores both $k \mapsto v_1$ and $k \mapsto v_2$, then $v_1 = v_2$.
nodes.title: Bindings in a valid open-addressing table are unique

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a valid open-addressing table, $k$ a key and $v$ a value. Then looking up $k$ in $T$ returns $v$ if and only if the binding $k \mapsto v$ is stored in some slot of $T$.
nodes.title: Lookup in a valid table returns exactly the stored binding

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an open-addressing hash table, and suppose that inserting the binding $k \mapsto v$ into $T$ succeeds and yields the table $T'$. Then for every key $k' \neq k$ and every value $v'$, the table $T'$ stores $k' \mapsto v'$ if and only if $T$ stores $k' \mapsto v'$.
nodes.title: Open-addressing insertion leaves other keys' bindings unchanged

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a valid open-addressing table and suppose inserting the binding $k \mapsto v$ into $T$ succeeds with result $T'$. Then for every key $k' \ne k$, looking up $k'$ in $T'$ gives the same result as looking up $k'$ in $T$.
nodes.title: Insertion does not affect lookups of other keys

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an open-addressing hash table with $m$ slots and probe sequence $p$. If inserting a binding $k \mapsto v$ into $T$ fails, then for every $i < m$ the slot $p(k, i)$ holds a pair $(k', v')$ with $k' \neq k$.
nodes.title: Failed open-addressing insertion finds every probed slot taken
Perfect hashing

nodes.summary: Fix a type $\alpha$ of keys, a type $\beta$ of values and a primary hash function $h : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$. A two-level (FKS) perfect hash table consists of a number $b > 0$ of buckets and, for each bucket $i < b$, a secondary size $m_i \in \mathbb{N}$, a secondary hash function $h_i : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ and a secondary table of $m_i$ slots, each of which is empty or holds one binding $(k, v)$ with…
nodes.title: Two-level perfect hash table

nodes.summary: To look up a key $k$ in a two-level perfect hash table with $b$ buckets, primary hash $h$, secondary sizes $m_i$ and secondary hashes $h_i$, let $i = h(k) \bmod b$. If $m_i = 0$, the lookup returns nothing. Otherwise it inspects the single slot $h_i(k) \bmod m_i$ of the secondary table of bucket $i$: if that slot holds a binding $(k, v)$, the lookup returns $v$; if the slot is empty or holds a binding with a…
nodes.title: Lookup in a perfect hash table

nodes.summary: Given a primary hash function $h$ from keys to natural numbers, a number of buckets $b > 0$, and for each bucket $i < b$ a secondary table size $m_i$ and a secondary hash function $h_i$, the empty table is the two-level perfect hash table with primary hash $h$, $b$ buckets, secondary sizes $m_i$ and secondary hashes $h_i$ in which every slot of every secondary table is vacant.
nodes.title: Empty perfect hash table

nodes.summary: A key $k$ and a value $v$ are stored in a two-level perfect hash table $T$ when some secondary slot, in some bucket of $T$, holds the binding $(k, v)$.
nodes.title: Bindings stored in a perfect hash table

nodes.summary: The entries of a two-level perfect hash table form the list of the bindings $(k, v)$ held in its occupied secondary slots, listed bucket by bucket in increasing bucket order and, within each bucket, in increasing slot order.
nodes.title: Entries of a perfect hash table

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a two-level perfect hash table with primary hash $h$, $b$ buckets, secondary table sizes $m_i$ and secondary hashes $g_i$. Then $T$ is valid when two conditions hold. Placement: whenever slot $j$ of bucket $i$ holds a binding $(k, v)$, we have $i = h(k) \bmod b$ and $j = g_i(k) \bmod m_i$. Injectivity: for every bucket $i$, if keys $k_1$ and $k_2$ both occur in bindings stored in bucket $i$ and…
nodes.title: Valid perfect hash table

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a two-level perfect hash table with $b$ buckets and primary hash $h$, and for each bucket $i$ let $m_i$ be its secondary table size and $h_i$ its secondary hash. Suppose every binding $(k, v)$ held in slot $j$ of bucket $i$ satisfies $h(k) \bmod b = i$ and $j = h_i(k) \bmod m_i$. Then for every bucket $i$ and all keys $k_1, k_2$ that are each held, with some value, in some slot of bucket $i$, if…
nodes.title: Placement implies secondary injectivity

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a two-level perfect hash table with $b$ buckets, primary hash $h$, secondary sizes $m_i$ and secondary hashes $h_i$. If, whenever slot $j$ of the secondary table of bucket $i$ holds a binding $(k, v)$, we have $h(k) \bmod b = i$ and $j = h_i(k) \bmod m_i$, then $T$ is valid.
nodes.title: Placement suffices for validity of a perfect hash table

nodes.summary: For every two-level perfect hash table, every key $k$ and every value $v$, the pair $(k, v)$ belongs to the list of entries of the table (the contents of its occupied secondary slots, bucket by bucket) if and only if some secondary slot of the table holds the binding $(k, v)$.
nodes.title: Entries of a perfect hash table are its stored bindings

nodes.summary: For every primary hash function, every positive number of buckets, and every choice of secondary table sizes and secondary hash functions, the empty two-level perfect hash table with these parameters is valid: no slot is occupied, so both conditions of validity hold vacuously.
nodes.title: The empty perfect hash table is valid

nodes.summary: For every primary hash function, every number $b > 0$ of buckets, every choice of secondary sizes and secondary hash functions, every key $k$ and every value $v$, no secondary slot of the empty two-level perfect hash table with these data holds the binding $(k, v)$.
nodes.title: The empty perfect hash table stores nothing

nodes.summary: For a two-level perfect hash table with decidable equality on keys, and with no validity hypothesis, if looking up a key $k$ returns a value $v$, then some secondary slot of the table holds the binding $(k, v)$.
nodes.title: Soundness of perfect-hash lookup

nodes.summary: For a valid two-level perfect hash table, if the binding $(k, v)$ is held in some slot of the table, then looking up $k$ returns $v$.
nodes.title: Lookup finds every stored binding

nodes.summary: In a valid two-level perfect hash table, if some secondary slots hold bindings $(k, v_1)$ and $(k, v_2)$ with the same key $k$, then $v_1 = v_2$.
nodes.title: Stored values in a valid perfect hash table are unique

nodes.summary: For a valid two-level perfect hash table and any key $k$, looking up $k$ returns no value if and only if there is no value $v$ such that the binding $(k, v)$ is held in some slot of the table.
nodes.title: Lookup fails exactly on unstored keys

nodes.summary: For a valid two-level perfect hash table, if the pair $(k, v)$ belongs to the list of entries of the table, then looking up $k$ returns $v$.
nodes.title: Lookup finds every entry

nodes.summary: For a two-level perfect hash table with decidable equality on keys, if looking up a key $k$ returns a value $v$, then $(k, v)$ belongs to the list of entries of the table. No validity hypothesis is needed.
nodes.title: Successful perfect-hash lookups return entries

nodes.summary: For every primary hash function, every number of buckets $b > 0$, all secondary table sizes and secondary hash functions, and every key $k$, looking up $k$ in the empty table returns no value.
nodes.title: Lookup in the empty perfect hash table fails

nodes.summary: For every primary hash function, every number of buckets $b > 0$, and all secondary table sizes and secondary hash functions, the list of entries of the empty table is the empty list.
nodes.title: The empty perfect hash table has no entries

nodes.summary: For a two-level perfect hash table and a bucket $i$, the occupancy $n_i$ of bucket $i$ is the number of slots of the secondary table of bucket $i$ that hold a binding. It is the $n_i$ of the Fredman–Komlós–Szemerédi analysis.
nodes.title: Occupancy of a perfect-hashing bucket

nodes.summary: For a two-level perfect hash table, write $n_i$ for the number of occupied secondary slots of bucket $i$. The total number of keys of the table is $\sum_i n_i$, the number of occupied secondary slots over all buckets.
nodes.title: Total number of keys of a perfect hash table

nodes.summary: For a two-level perfect hash table, write $m_i$ for the number of slots of the secondary table of bucket $i$. The total secondary space of the table is $\sum_i m_i$, the number of secondary slots over all buckets.
nodes.title: Total secondary space of a perfect hash table

nodes.summary: A two-level perfect hash table with $b$ buckets is square-sized when, for every bucket $i < b$, the size $m_i$ of its secondary table equals $n_i^2$, where $n_i$ is the number of occupied slots of that secondary table.
nodes.title: FKS square sizing rule

nodes.summary: For every two-level perfect hash table and every bucket $i$, the number $n_i$ of occupied slots of bucket $i$ is at most the number $m_i$ of slots of the secondary table of bucket $i$.
nodes.title: Bucket occupancy is at most the secondary table size

nodes.summary: In a two-level perfect hash table with $b$ buckets and secondary sizes $m_0, \dots, m_{b-1}$, every bucket $i < b$ satisfies $m_i \le \sum_{j < b} m_j$, the total secondary space.
nodes.title: Each secondary table fits in the total secondary space

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a two-level perfect hash table satisfying the FKS sizing rule, and write $n_i$ for the number of occupied secondary slots of bucket $i$. Then the total secondary space of $T$ equals $\sum_i n_i^2$, the sum over all buckets $i$.
nodes.title: Total secondary space under square sizing

nodes.summary: If a two-level perfect hash table satisfies the FKS sizing rule, then its total secondary space is at most the square of its total number of keys.
nodes.title: Quadratic space bound under square sizing
Universal hashing

nodes.summary: For a finite family $H$ of functions from a set $\alpha$ to $\{0, 1, \dots, m - 1\}$ and keys $x, y \in \alpha$, the collision count of $x$ and $y$ in $H$ is the number of functions $h \in H$ with $h(x) = h(y)$.
nodes.title: Collision count

nodes.summary: A finite family $H$ of functions from a set $\alpha$ to $\{0, 1, \dots, m - 1\}$ is universal if $m > 0$, $H$ is nonempty, and for all distinct keys $x \ne y$ in $\alpha$ the number of functions $h \in H$ with $h(x) = h(y)$, multiplied by $m$, is at most $|H|$; that is, $x$ and $y$ collide under at most a $1/m$ fraction of the members of $H$.
nodes.title: Universal hash family

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a finite set of indices from a type $\iota$, and let $h$ assign to each index $i \in \iota$ a function $h_i$ from a set $\alpha$ to $\{0, 1, \dots, m - 1\}$. The family $h$ is universal on $s$ if $m > 0$, $s$ is nonempty, and for all distinct keys $x \ne y$ in $\alpha$ the number of indices $i \in s$ with $h_i(x) = h_i(y)$, multiplied by $m$, is at most $|s|$.
nodes.title: Indexed universal hash family

nodes.summary: For every finite family $H$ of functions from a set $\alpha$ to $\{0, 1, \dots, m - 1\}$ and all keys $x, y \in \alpha$, the number of functions $h \in H$ with $h(x) = h(y)$ is at most $|H|$.
nodes.title: Collision count is at most the family size

nodes.summary: For every finite family $H$ of functions from a set $\alpha$ to $\{0, 1, \dots, m - 1\}$ and every key $x \in \alpha$, the collision count of $x$ with itself in $H$ equals $|H|$: $x$ collides with itself under every function in $H$.
nodes.title: A key collides with itself under the whole family

nodes.summary: For every type of keys $\alpha$ and every natural number $m$, the empty family of functions $\alpha \to \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$ is not universal: universality includes nonemptiness, since its meaning is a bound on the collision probability for a uniformly chosen member.
nodes.title: The empty hash family is not universal

nodes.summary: For every index type $\iota$, every type of keys $\alpha$, every natural number $m$ and every family $(h_i)_{i \in \iota}$ of functions $h_i \colon \alpha \to \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$, the family is not universal over the empty index set: indexed universality includes nonemptiness of the index set, since there is no uniform random choice from an empty family.
nodes.title: The empty indexed family is not universal

nodes.summary: For every natural number $m$ and all distinct keys $x \ne y$ in a set $\alpha$, the collision count of $x$ and $y$ in the empty family of functions from $\alpha$ to $\{0, 1, \dots, m - 1\}$, multiplied by $m$, is at most the size of the empty family, which is $0$.
nodes.title: The empty family satisfies the collision bound

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $p$ and $m$ with $m > 0$ and elements $a, b$ of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, the mod-prime hash function $h_{a,b} \colon \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} \to \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$ is $h_{a,b}(x) = \operatorname{val}(ax + b) \bmod m$, where $ax + b$ is computed in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and $\operatorname{val}(z)$ is the canonical natural-number representative of $z$ (the residue in $\{0, \dots, p - 1\}$…
nodes.title: Mod-prime hash function

nodes.summary: For a natural number $p$, the index set of the mod-prime family is the set of pairs $(a, b)$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and $a \neq 0$.
nodes.title: Mod-prime index set

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $p$ and $m$ with $m > 0$, the indexed mod-prime family assigns to each index $(a, b)$, with $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and $a \neq 0$, the mod-prime hash function $h_{a,b} \colon \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} \to \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$.
nodes.title: Indexed mod-prime family

nodes.summary: For $p > 0$ and $m > 0$, the mod-prime family is the finite set of all functions $h_{a,b}$ from $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ to $\{0, 1, \dots, m - 1\}$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and $a \ne 0$, where $h_{a,b}$ is the mod-prime hash function with index $(a, b)$.
nodes.title: Mod-prime family of distinct functions

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $p$ and $m$ with $m > 0$ and elements $a, b, x$ of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, the mod-prime hash value $h_{a,b}(x) \in \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$, read as a natural number, equals $\operatorname{val}(ax + b) \bmod m$. Here $ax + b$ is computed in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, and $\operatorname{val}(z)$ is the canonical natural-number representative of $z$: the residue in $\{0, \dots, p - 1\}$ when…
nodes.title: Value of the mod-prime hash

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a natural number, $m > 0$ and $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, and write $\operatorname{val}(z)$ for the canonical natural-number representative of $z \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ (for $p = 0$, where $\mathbb{Z}/0\mathbb{Z} = \mathbb{Z}$, its absolute value), so that the mod-prime hash function is $h_{a,b}(x) = \operatorname{val}(ax + b) \bmod m$. For all keys $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, we have…
nodes.title: Collisions of a mod-prime hash function

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a natural number and fix two keys $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. The pair map at $x$ and $y$ sends an index $(a, b)$ of the mod-prime family, that is, $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ with $a \ne 0$, to the pair $(ax + b, ay + b) \in (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^2$ of inner hash values at $x$ and $y$.
nodes.title: The pair map of the mod-prime family

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a natural number, let $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, and let $(a, b)$ be an index of the mod-prime family, so that $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and $a \ne 0$. Then the pair map at $x$ and $y$ sends $(a, b)$ to $(ax + b, ay + b)$.
nodes.title: Evaluating the pair map

nodes.summary:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $x

nodes.title: The two values of the pair map differ

nodes.summary:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $x 
eq y$ be elements of the field $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. The pair bijection for $x, y$ is the bijection from the indices $(a, b)$, with $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and $a

nodes.title: Pair bijection of the CLRS counting argument

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a prime and let $x \neq y$ be elements of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. For every index $(a, b)$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and $a \neq 0$, the image of $(a, b)$ under the pair bijection for $x, y$, viewed as an element of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, is the value of the pair map at $(a, b)$, namely $(ax + b, ay + b)$.
nodes.title: The pair bijection is given by the pair map

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a prime and let $x \ne y$ be keys in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. Then the pair map at $x$ and $y$, which sends an index $(a, b)$ of the mod-prime family (so $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and $a \ne 0$) to $(ax + b, ay + b)$, is injective.
nodes.title: The pair map is injective

nodes.summary:
Let $p$ be a prime and $m > 0$, and for $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ with $a 
e 0$ let $h_{a,b}(x) = ((ax + b)  mod p)  mod m$ be the mod-prime hash function. For distinct keys $x 
e y$ in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, the number of index pairs $(a, b)$ with $a 
e 0$ and $h_{a,b}(x) = h_{a,b}(y)$, multiplied by $m$, is at most $p(p - 1)$, the total number of index pairs.
nodes.title: Collision bound for the mod-prime hash functions

nodes.summary: For every positive natural number $p$, the set of pairs $(a, b)$ of elements of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ with $a \neq 0$ has exactly $p(p - 1)$ elements.
nodes.title: Number of mod-prime indices

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a prime and $m$ a positive natural number. The indexed mod-prime family, whose member at the index $(a, b)$, with $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and $a \neq 0$, is the mod-prime hash function $h_{a,b}$, is universal over the set of all such indices: this set is nonempty, and for all distinct keys $x \neq y$ in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, the number of indices $(a, b)$ with $h_{a,b}(x) = h_{a,b}(y)$,…
nodes.title: Universality of the mod-prime family

nodes.summary: Let $p > 0$ and $m > 0$. A function $h$ from $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ to $\{0, 1, \dots, m - 1\}$ belongs to the mod-prime family of distinct functions exactly when $h = h_{a,b}$ for some index $(a, b)$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and $a \ne 0$, where $h_{a,b}$ is the mod-prime hash function with index $(a, b)$.
nodes.title: Members of the mod-prime family

nodes.summary: Sequential containers and their amortized costs: linked lists (singly, doubly, sentinel), stacks with multipop, queues, deques, dynamic tables, binary counters, LRU caches, and generic list operations (ordered insertion, splitting, chunking, inclusive prefixes) that support them.
nodes.title: Lists, stacks, queues and dynamic arrays
Binary counter

nodes.summary: A $k$-bit counter is a vector $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{k-1})$ of bits stored lowest bit first. Incrementing $b$ changes the initial run of $1$ bits $b_0, \dots, b_{t-1}$ to $0$ and then changes the first $0$ bit $b_t$, if there is one, to $1$; if every bit is $1$, all bits become $0$ and no new bit is added. The result is again a $k$-bit counter, and the cost of the increment is the number of bits changed, one unit per…
nodes.title: Binary counter increment

nodes.summary: Let $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{k-1})$ be a $k$-bit counter stored lowest bit first, with bits $b_i \in \{0, 1\}$ and unsigned value $v(b) = \sum_{i < k} b_i 2^i$. If $b'$ is the counter returned by incrementing $b$, then $v(b') = (v(b) + 1) \bmod 2^k$.
nodes.title: Increment adds one with wraparound

nodes.summary: Let $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{k-1})$ be a $k$-bit counter stored lowest bit first, and let $t$ be the length of its initial run of $1$ bits, that is, the largest $t \le k$ with $b_0 = \dots = b_{t-1} = 1$. The cost of incrementing $b$ is $t + 1$ if $t < k$, and $t$ if $t = k$.
nodes.title: Exact cost of an increment

nodes.summary: For every $k$-bit counter $b$ (a vector of $k$ bits, lowest bit first), the cost of incrementing $b$ is at most $k$.
nodes.title: Increment costs at most the width

nodes.summary: For a width $k$, a $k$-bit counter $b$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the run of $n$ increments from $b$ is defined recursively. The run of $0$ increments returns $b$ at cost zero. The run of $n + 1$ increments performs the run of $n$ increments, then increments the counter it returned and returns the result; its cost is the cost of the $n$-step run plus the cost of that increment.
nodes.title: Running the binary counter

nodes.summary: For every width $k$ and every $k$-bit counter $b$, running zero increments from $b$ returns $b$ unchanged at cost zero.
nodes.title: Running zero increments

nodes.summary: For every bit vector $b$ and every natural number $n$, the bit vector returned by running $n + 1$ increments from $b$ is the increment of the bit vector returned by running $n$ increments from $b$.
nodes.title: One more increment

nodes.summary: For every width $k$, every $k$-bit counter $b$ and every $n$, the cost of running $n + 1$ successive increments from $b$ equals the cost of running $n$ increments from $b$ plus the cost of incrementing the counter that the $n$-step run returns.
nodes.title: Cost recurrence for the binary counter run

nodes.summary: For every width $k$, every $k$-bit counter $b$ and every $n$, let $v$ be the value of $b$ read as an unsigned binary number with the least significant bit first. After $n$ successive increments starting from $b$, the counter read the same way has value $(v + n) \bmod 2^k$.
nodes.title: Counter value after successive increments

nodes.summary: Let $k$, $i$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $i < k$, and for each $t$ let $c_t$ be the bit vector returned by running $t$ increments from the all-false bit vector of width $k$. Then the number of $t < n$ such that the bit at position $i$ of $c_t$ (counting from the low-order bit, starting at $0$) differs from the bit at position $i$ of $c_{t+1}$ is $\lfloor n / 2^i \rfloor$.
nodes.title: Flip counts of the individual bits

nodes.summary: For every $k$, the cost of incrementing the $k$-bit counter whose $k$ bits are all $1$ is exactly $k$.
nodes.title: Incrementing the all-ones counter costs the full width

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $k$ and $n$, running $n$ increments from the all-false bit vector of width $k$ costs exactly $\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \lfloor n / 2^i \rfloor$.
nodes.title: Exact cost of increments from zero

nodes.summary: For every width $k$ and every $n > 0$, performing $n$ successive increments on the $k$-bit counter that starts with all bits zero costs strictly fewer than $2n$ bit changes in total.
nodes.title: Aggregate cost bound for the binary counter

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $k$ and $n$ with $k > 0$, running $n$ increments from the all-false bit vector of width $k$ costs at least $n$.
nodes.title: Lower bound on the cost of increments from zero

nodes.summary: Resetting a bit vector $b$ of width $k$ returns the all-false bit vector of width $k$ and charges cost $1$ for each position of $b$ that holds true, that is, for each bit it changes from true to false.
nodes.title: Resetting a binary counter

nodes.summary: For every bit vector $b$ of width $k$, the bits returned by resetting $b$ are, in order, $k$ copies of false.
nodes.title: Reset returns the all-false counter

nodes.summary: For every bit vector $b$ of width $k$, the bits returned by resetting $b$, read low-order bit first as an unsigned binary numeral, have value $0$.
nodes.title: Reset yields the value zero

nodes.summary: For every bit vector $b$ of width $k$, the cost of resetting $b$ equals the number of positions of $b$ that hold true.
nodes.title: Cost of resetting a binary counter

nodes.summary: Let $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{k-1})$ be a $k$-bit counter and $b' = (b'_0, \dots, b'_{k-1})$ the counter returned by resetting $b$. The cost of resetting $b$ equals the number of indices $i < k$ with $b_i \ne b'_i$.
nodes.title: Reset cost is the Hamming distance

nodes.summary: For every $k$-bit counter $b$ (a vector of $k$ bits), the cost of resetting $b$ is at most $k$.
nodes.title: Reset costs at most the width

nodes.summary: Resetting a bit vector of width $0$ has cost $0$.
nodes.title: Resetting a width-zero counter costs nothing

nodes.summary: For every width $k$, resetting the all-false bit vector of width $k$ has cost $0$.
nodes.title: Resetting the all-false counter costs nothing

nodes.summary: For every $k$-bit counter $b$, resetting the counter returned by resetting $b$ returns the same counter as resetting $b$ once.
nodes.title: Reset is idempotent

nodes.summary: For every $k$-bit counter $b$, resetting the counter returned by resetting $b$ has cost $0$.
nodes.title: A second reset costs nothing

nodes.summary: For every $k$-bit counter $b$ (a vector of $k$ bits), the cost of resetting $b$ plus the number of $1$ bits in the returned counter equals the number of $1$ bits in $b$.

nodes.summary: A deque with elements in a type $\alpha$ consists of two lists of elements of $\alpha$, the front list and the back list. The front list holds the front part of the sequence in order and the back list holds the back part in reverse order.
nodes.title: Two-list deque

nodes.summary: The sequence represented by a deque with front list $f$ and back list $b$ is $f$ followed by the reverse of $b$; it lists the elements from front to back.
nodes.title: Represented sequence of a deque

nodes.summary: The empty deque is the deque whose front list and back list are both empty.
nodes.title: The empty deque

nodes.summary: The emptiness test of a deque returns true exactly when both its front list and its back list are empty.
nodes.title: Emptiness test for a deque

nodes.summary: For every deque $d$, the emptiness test of $d$ returns true if and only if the sequence represented by $d$ is empty.
nodes.title: Correctness of the deque emptiness test

nodes.summary: Let $d$ be a deque with front list $f$ and back list $b$, where $b$ is stored in reverse order. Pushing an element $x$ at the front of $d$ gives the deque with front list consisting of $x$ followed by the entries of $f$, and back list $b$.
nodes.title: Push at the front of a deque

nodes.summary: For every deque $d$ and element $x$, the sequence represented by the deque obtained by pushing $x$ at the front of $d$ is $x$ followed by the sequence represented by $d$.
nodes.title: Pushing at the front of a deque

nodes.summary: Let $d$ be a deque with front list $f$ and back list $b$, where $b$ is stored in reverse order. Pushing an element $x$ at the back of $d$ gives the deque with front list $f$ and back list consisting of $x$ followed by the entries of $b$.
nodes.title: Push at the back of a deque

nodes.summary: For every deque $d$ and element $x$, the sequence represented by the deque obtained by pushing $x$ at the back of $d$ is the sequence represented by $d$ followed by $x$.
nodes.title: Pushing at the back of a deque

nodes.summary: Let $d$ be a deque with front list $f$ and back list $b$, where $b$ is stored in reverse order. Peeking at the front of $d$ returns, without removing it, the first element of $f$ when $f$ is nonempty, and otherwise the last element of $b$; when both lists are empty it returns no element.
nodes.title: Peek at the front of a deque

nodes.summary: For every deque $d$, peeking at the front of $d$ returns the first element of the sequence represented by $d$, and returns no element when that sequence is empty.
nodes.title: Peeking at the front gives the first element

nodes.summary: Let $d$ be a deque with front list $f$ and back list $b$, where $b$ is stored in reverse order. Peeking at the back of $d$ returns, without removing it, the first element of $b$ when $b$ is nonempty, and otherwise the last element of $f$; when both lists are empty it returns no element.
nodes.title: Peek at the back of a deque

nodes.summary: For every deque $d$, peeking at the back of $d$ returns the last element of the sequence represented by $d$ when that sequence is nonempty, and returns nothing when it is empty.
nodes.title: Peeking at the back of a deque

nodes.summary: If popping the back of a deque $d$ succeeds and returns an element $x$ and a deque $d'$, then the sequence represented by $d$ is the sequence represented by $d'$ followed by $x$.
