nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each empty or holding a node, in which the cells $x$ and $y$ are allocated, the next pointer of $y$ is not NIL, and the cell $w$ it points to is allocated; write $S[c]$ for the node at an allocated cell $c$. Then the store returned by sentinel insertion of $x$ after $y$ is obtained from $S$ by three updates, each applied to the result of the previous one: replace the content of $x$…
nodes.title: The store after sentinel insertion

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each empty or holding a node, in which the cells $x$ and $y$ are allocated, the next pointer of $y$ is not NIL, and the cell it points to is allocated; write $S[c]$ for the node at an allocated cell $c$. Let $S'$ be the store returned by sentinel insertion of $x$ after $y$. Then for every cell $z$, the content of $z$ in $S'$ is obtained from its content in $S$ by three steps in…
nodes.title: Sentinel insertion, cell by cell

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each empty or holding a node, in which the cells $x$ and $y$ are allocated, the next pointer of $y$ is not NIL, and the cell it points to is allocated. Let $S'$ be the store returned by sentinel insertion of $x$ after $y$. If a cell $z$ differs from $x$ and from $y$, and the next pointer of $y$ in $S$ is not $z$, then $z$ has the same content in $S'$ as in $S$.
nodes.title: Sentinel insertion leaves other cells unchanged

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each empty or holding a node, in which the cells $x$ and $y$ are allocated, the next pointer of $y$ is not NIL, and the cell it points to is allocated. Let $S'$ be the store returned by sentinel insertion of $x$ after $y$. Then every cell $z$ is allocated in $S'$ if and only if it is allocated in $S$.
nodes.title: Sentinel insertion preserves allocation

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each empty or holding a node, in which the cells $x$ and $y$ are allocated, the next pointer of $y$ is not NIL, and the cell it points to is allocated. Let $S'$ be the store returned by sentinel insertion of $x$ after $y$. Then for every cell $z$, either $z$ is empty in both $S$ and $S'$, or it holds a node in both and the two nodes have the same payload, including keys and…
nodes.title: Sentinel insertion preserves payloads

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each empty or holding a node, in which the cells $x$ and $y$ are allocated, the next pointer of $y$ is not NIL, and the cell it points to is allocated. Suppose $S$ circularly represents the list $L$ of cells with sentinel $s$, that $L$ is the concatenation of lists $B$ and $A$, and that $y$ is the last element of $B$, or $y = s$ if $B$ is empty. If $x \ne s$ and $x$ does not occur…
nodes.title: Sentinel insertion preserves the circular list

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each empty or holding a node, in which the cells $x$ and $y$ are allocated, the next pointer of $y$ is not NIL, and the cell it points to is allocated. Suppose $S$ circularly represents the list $L$ with sentinel $s$, that $L$ is the concatenation of lists $B$ and $A$, and that $y$ is the last element of $B$, or $y = s$ if $B$ is empty. Suppose $S$ also circularly represents the…
nodes.title: Sentinel insertion preserves a disjoint circular list

nodes.summary: Let a store have cells indexed by $\{0, \dots, m-1\}$, each empty or holding a node that carries a key, satellite data and optional next and prev links, and let the cell $s$ be the sentinel of some list of data nodes that the store circularly represents. Sentinel search for a key $k$ first overwrites the key of the sentinel with $k$, keeping its satellite data and links, then starts at the successor of $s$ and…
nodes.title: Search in a circular list with a sentinel

nodes.summary: If a store circularly represents the list $L$ of data nodes with sentinel $s$, then sentinel search for a key $k$ returns the first node of $L$ (in list order, which starts at the successor of $s$) whose key in the input store is $k$, and returns no node if no node of $L$ has key $k$. In particular, the sentinel is never returned.
nodes.title: Sentinel search returns the first matching node

nodes.summary: If a store circularly represents the list $L$ of $n$ data nodes with sentinel $s$, then sentinel search for a key $k$ costs exactly $2i + 4$, where $i$ is the position, counting from $0$, of the first node of $L$ whose key is $k$, and $i = n$ if no node of $L$ has key $k$.
nodes.title: Cost of sentinel search

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be the sentinel of some list of data nodes that a store circularly represents, and let $k$ be a key. In the store returned by sentinel search for $k$, the cell $s$ holds the original sentinel node with its key replaced by $k$ and its satellite data and next and prev links unchanged, and every cell $z \ne s$ holds exactly what it held in the input store.
nodes.title: Sentinel search changes only the sentinel's key

nodes.summary: If a store circularly represents the list $L$ of data nodes with sentinel $s$, then for every key $k$ the store returned by sentinel search for $k$ still circularly represents $L$ with sentinel $s$.
nodes.title: Sentinel search preserves the circular list
Dynamic table

nodes.summary: A dynamic table with items of type $\alpha$ consists of an array of slots $s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$, each either empty or holding an item of type $\alpha$, together with an item count $n$ satisfying $n \le m$. The number $m$ of slots is the capacity of the table.
nodes.title: Dynamic table

nodes.summary: A dynamic table with slots $s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$ and item count $n$ is well formed when, for every $i < m$, slot $s_i$ is occupied if and only if $i < n$; that is, the occupied slots are exactly the first $n$.
nodes.title: Well-formed dynamic table

nodes.summary: A dynamic table with slots $s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$ and item count $n$ is well formed if and only if, for every $i < m$, slot $s_i$ is occupied exactly when $i < n$.
nodes.title: Characterization of well-formed dynamic tables

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a dynamic table with slots $s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$, each empty or holding an item, and item count $n \le m$. The contents of $T$ is the array of the items held by the occupied slots among $s_0, \dots, s_{n-1}$, in order; empty slots in this prefix are skipped.
nodes.title: Contents of a dynamic table

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a dynamic table with slots $s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$, each empty or holding an item, and item count $n \le m$. The contents of $T$ is the array obtained from the prefix $s_0, \dots, s_{n-1}$ by skipping the empty slots and keeping the items of the occupied ones, in order.
nodes.title: Formula for the contents of a dynamic table

nodes.summary: The empty dynamic table is the table with no slots (capacity $0$) and item count $0$. It models a table before its first allocation.
nodes.title: Empty dynamic table

nodes.summary: The empty dynamic table has an empty slot array, so capacity $0$, and item count $0$.
nodes.title: The empty dynamic table has no slots and no items

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a dynamic table with slots $s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$ and item count $n \le m$, and let $x$ be an item. Inserting $x$ into $T$ proceeds as follows. If $m = 0$, first replace the slots by a single empty slot. Then, if the table is full, that is, $n$ equals the current capacity $c$, allocate $2c$ empty slots and copy the $c$ old slots into the first $c$ of them, at cost $1$ per copied slot. Finally write $x$…
nodes.title: TABLE-INSERT

nodes.summary: Given a dynamic table $T$ and an array $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ of items, the result of inserting the array into $T$ is obtained by starting from $T$ and inserting $x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{k-1}$ one at a time with TABLE-INSERT, in array order. Its cost is the sum of the costs of the $k$ insertions; for an empty array the result is $T$ at cost $0$.
nodes.title: Inserting an array of items into a dynamic table

nodes.summary: For every dynamic table $T$ with item count $n$ and every item $x$, the table returned by inserting $x$ into $T$ with TABLE-INSERT has item count $n + 1$.
nodes.title: Insertion increases the item count by one

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a dynamic table with item count $n$ and capacity (number of slots) $m$, and let $x$ be an item. The table returned by inserting $x$ into $T$ with TABLE-INSERT has capacity $1$ if $m = 0$, capacity $2m$ if $m > 0$ and $n = m$, and capacity $m$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Capacity after an insertion

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a dynamic table with item count $n$ and capacity $m$, and let $x$ be an item. Inserting $x$ into $T$ with TABLE-INSERT costs $1 + n$ if $m > 0$ and $n = m$, and costs $1$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Cost of an insertion

nodes.summary: For a dynamic table $T$ with item count $n$ and capacity (number of slots) $m$, let $\Phi(T) = 2n - m$, an integer that may be negative. If inserting an item $x$ into $T$ has cost $c$ and returns the table $T'$, then $c + \Phi(T') - \Phi(T) \le 3$. Here the cost of an insertion is one unit for writing $x$ plus one unit for each old slot copied when a full table is doubled.
nodes.title: Amortized cost of dynamic-table insertion

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a well-formed dynamic table with slots $s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$ and item count $n$, let $x$ be an item, and let $T'$ be the table returned by inserting $x$ into $T$ with TABLE-INSERT, with capacity $m'$. Then the slots of $T'$ are $s_0, \dots, s_{n-1}$, followed by a slot holding $x$, followed by $m' - (n + 1)$ empty slots.
nodes.title: Slots after an insertion

nodes.summary: If $T$ is a well-formed dynamic table and $x$ is an item, then the table returned by inserting $x$ into $T$ with TABLE-INSERT is well formed.
nodes.title: Insertion preserves well-formedness

nodes.summary: If $T$ is a well-formed dynamic table and $x$ is an item, then the contents of the table obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ are the contents of $T$ followed by $x$.
nodes.title: Insertion appends to the contents

nodes.summary: Call a dynamic table with item count $n$ well formed when, for every slot index $i$, slot $i$ is occupied exactly when $i < n$. If a dynamic table $T$ is well formed, then for every array $xs$, the table obtained from $T$ by inserting the entries of $xs$ one at a time with TABLE-INSERT, in array order, is again well formed.
nodes.title: Repeated insertion preserves well-formedness of a dynamic table

nodes.summary: If $T$ is a well-formed dynamic table and $x_1, \dots, x_k$ is an array of items, then inserting $x_1, \dots, x_k$ into $T$ one at a time, in this order, gives a table whose contents are the contents of $T$ followed by $x_1, \dots, x_k$.
nodes.title: Inserting an array appends it to the contents

nodes.summary: Starting from the empty dynamic table and inserting the items of an array of length $k$ one at a time, the resulting table has capacity (number of slots) at most $2k$.
nodes.title: Capacity after inserting into the empty table

nodes.summary: Starting from the empty dynamic table and inserting the items of an array of length $k$ one at a time, the total cost is at most $3k$, where each insertion costs one unit for writing the new item plus one unit for each old slot copied when a full table is doubled.
nodes.title: Total cost of insertions into the empty table

nodes.summary: Starting from the empty dynamic table and inserting the items of a nonempty array of length $k$ one at a time, the total cost is less than $3k$.
nodes.title: Strict cost bound for nonempty insertion sequences

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a dynamic table with slots $s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$, each empty or holding an item, and item count $n \le m$. The lookup at logical position $i$ returns the item held by $s_i$ when $i < n$ and $s_i$ is occupied; it returns no value when $i < n$ and $s_i$ is empty, and when $i \ge n$.
nodes.title: Lookup in a dynamic table

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a dynamic table with item count $n$. For every natural number $i \ge n$, the lookup at logical position $i$ in $T$ returns no value.
nodes.title: Lookup beyond the item count returns nothing

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a well-formed dynamic table holding $n$ items. For every natural number $i$, the lookup at logical position $i$ in $T$ returns a value if and only if $i < n$.
nodes.title: Lookup succeeds exactly below the item count

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a dynamic table with slots $s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$, each empty or holding an item, and item count $n \le m$. Deleting the last item of $T$ gives the following table. If $n = 0$, the result is $T$ itself. Otherwise, if $4(n-1) < m$, that is, the load factor after deletion is strictly below $1/4$, the table contracts: the result has slots $s_0, \dots, s_{n-2}$ followed by $\lfloor m/2 \rfloor - (n-1)$ empty…
nodes.title: Deletion from a dynamic table

nodes.summary: Applying deletion to a dynamic table with item count $n$ gives a table with item count $n - 1$ when $n \ge 1$, and item count $0$ when $n = 0$.
nodes.title: Item count after deletion

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a dynamic table with capacity $m$ and item count $n$, and apply deletion to $T$. If $n = 0$, the capacity stays $m$. If $n \ge 1$ and $4(n-1) < m$, the new capacity is $\lfloor m/2 \rfloor$. Otherwise the capacity stays $m$.
nodes.title: Capacity after deletion

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a well-formed dynamic table with slots $s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$ holding $n \ge 1$ items, and let $m'$ be the capacity of the table obtained by applying deletion to $T$. The slots of that table are the first $n - 1$ slots $s_0, \dots, s_{n-2}$ of $T$ followed by $m' - (n - 1)$ empty slots.
nodes.title: Slots after deletion

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a well-formed dynamic table, that is, its occupied slots are exactly its first $n$ slots, where $n$ is its item count. Then the table obtained by applying deletion to $T$ is again well-formed.
nodes.title: Deletion preserves well-formedness

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a well-formed dynamic table. The contents of the table obtained by applying deletion to $T$ is the contents of $T$ with its last entry removed; when the contents of $T$ is empty, it stays empty.
nodes.title: Deletion removes the last item from the contents

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a well-formed dynamic table holding $n$ items, and let $i$ be a natural number with $i < n - 1$. After applying deletion to $T$, the lookup at logical position $i$ returns the same result as the lookup at position $i$ in $T$.
nodes.title: Deletion preserves lookups below the last position

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a dynamic table with item count $n$, where $n - 1$ is read as $0$ when $n = 0$. After applying deletion to $T$, the lookup at logical position $n - 1$ returns no value.
nodes.title: Lookup at the vacated position after deletion
Join list (catenable heap)

nodes.summary: A catenable heap over a type $\alpha$ is a persistent unsorted heap, represented as a join list (catenation tree): it is either the empty heap, an element of $\alpha$ added in front of a catenable heap, or the join of two catenable heaps.
nodes.title: Catenable heap

nodes.summary: The naive flattening of a catenable heap is defined by recursion: the empty heap flattens to the empty list, the heap with an element $x$ added in front of a heap $t$ flattens to $x$ followed by the naive flattening of $t$, and the join of heaps $l$ and $r$ flattens to the naive flattening of $l$ followed by that of $r$.
nodes.title: Naive flattening of a catenable heap

nodes.summary: Given a catenable heap $h$ and a list $s$, the accumulating flattening of $h$ onto $s$ is defined by recursion on $h$: for the empty heap it is $s$; for the heap with an element $x$ added in front of a heap $t$ it is $x$ followed by the accumulating flattening of $t$ onto $s$; for the join of heaps $l$ and $r$ it is the accumulating flattening of $l$ onto the accumulating flattening of $r$ onto $s$.
nodes.title: Accumulating flattening of a catenable heap

nodes.summary: The flattening of a catenable heap $h$ is the list of its elements from left to right, computed as the accumulating flattening of $h$ onto the empty list.
nodes.title: Flattening of a catenable heap

nodes.summary: The multiset of elements of a catenable heap $h$ is the multiset of the entries of the left-to-right list of elements of $h$.
nodes.title: Multiset of elements of a catenable heap

nodes.summary: The size of a catenable heap is the length of its left-to-right list of elements, that is, the number of its elements counted with multiplicity.
nodes.title: Size of a catenable heap

nodes.summary: For every catenable heap $h$ and list $a$, flattening $h$ from left to right in front of the accumulator $a$ gives the naive left-to-right flattening of $h$ followed by $a$.
nodes.title: Accumulator flattening of a catenable heap

nodes.summary: For every catenable heap $h$, the flattening of $h$ equals the naive flattening of $h$.
nodes.title: Flattening of a catenable heap equals its naive flattening

nodes.summary: The flattening of the empty catenable heap is the empty list.
nodes.title: Flattening the empty catenable heap

nodes.summary: For an element $x$ and a catenable heap $t$, the flattening of the heap with $x$ added in front of $t$ is $x$ followed by the flattening of $t$.
nodes.title: Flattening a front node of a catenable heap

nodes.summary: For catenable heaps $l$ and $r$, the flattening of the join of $l$ and $r$ is the flattening of $l$ followed by the flattening of $r$.
nodes.title: Flattening a join of catenable heaps

nodes.summary: The multiset of elements of the empty catenable heap is the empty multiset.
nodes.title: The empty catenable heap has no elements

nodes.summary: For every element $a$ and every catenable heap $t$, the multiset of elements of the heap obtained by adding $a$ in front of $t$ is the multiset of elements of $t$ with one more copy of $a$.
nodes.title: Multiset of a front node

nodes.summary: For all catenable heaps $L$ and $R$, the multiset of elements of the join node with left child $L$ and right child $R$ is the multiset sum of the multisets of elements of $L$ and $R$ (multiplicities add).
nodes.title: Multiset of a join node

nodes.summary: The empty catenable heap has size $0$.
nodes.title: The empty catenable heap has size zero

nodes.summary: For every element $a$ and catenable heap $t$, the size of the heap obtained by adding $a$ in front of $t$ is the size of $t$ plus one.
nodes.title: Size of a heap with an element added in front

nodes.summary: For catenable heaps $\ell$ and $r$, the size of the join node with left child $\ell$ and right child $r$ is the size of $\ell$ plus the size of $r$.
nodes.title: Size of a catenable heap join

nodes.summary: For every catenable heap $h$, the size of $h$ equals the cardinality of the multiset of its elements.
nodes.title: Size of a catenable heap as a multiset cardinality

nodes.summary: The operation that creates a catenable heap returns the empty heap and charges cost $0$, since it allocates no node.
nodes.title: Creating an empty catenable heap

nodes.summary: For an element $x$ and a catenable heap $h$, inserting $x$ into $h$ returns the heap with $x$ added in front of $h$ and charges cost $1$, for the one front node it allocates.
nodes.title: Insertion into a catenable heap

nodes.summary: The union of catenable heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$ allocates one join node, at cost $1$, and returns that join node, whose left child is $h_1$ and whose right child is $h_2$; neither operand is traversed or changed.
nodes.title: Union of catenable heaps

nodes.summary: Creating a catenable heap returns the empty heap, at cost $0$.
nodes.title: Cost and result of creating a catenable heap

nodes.summary: For every element $x$ and catenable heap $h$, inserting $x$ into $h$ returns the heap with $x$ added in front of $h$, at cost exactly $1$.
nodes.title: Cost and result of insertion into a catenable heap

nodes.summary: For all catenable heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$, the union of $h_1$ and $h_2$ returns the join node whose left child is $h_1$ and whose right child is $h_2$, at cost $1$.
nodes.title: Union allocates one join node

nodes.summary: The heap returned by the operation that creates a catenable heap is the empty heap.
nodes.title: Result of creating a catenable heap

nodes.summary: The operation that creates an empty catenable heap has time cost $0$.
nodes.title: Creating an empty catenable heap costs nothing

nodes.summary: For every element $x$ and catenable heap $h$, the heap returned by inserting $x$ into $h$ is the heap with $x$ added in front of $h$.
nodes.title: Result of insertion into a catenable heap

nodes.summary: For every element $x$ and catenable heap $h$, inserting $x$ into $h$ has time cost exactly $1$.
nodes.title: Insertion into a catenable heap costs one

nodes.summary: For all catenable heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$, the heap returned by their union is the join of $h_1$ and $h_2$, with $h_1$ as left child and $h_2$ as right child, both unchanged.
nodes.title: Result of the union of catenable heaps

nodes.summary: For all catenable heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$, the union of $h_1$ and $h_2$ has time cost exactly $1$, independently of $h_1$ and $h_2$.
nodes.title: Union of catenable heaps costs one

nodes.summary: The flattening of the heap returned by the operation that creates a catenable heap is the empty list.
nodes.title: A newly created catenable heap flattens to the empty list

nodes.summary: For an element $x$ and a catenable heap $h$, the flattening of the heap returned by inserting $x$ into $h$ is $x$ followed by the flattening of $h$.
nodes.title: Flattening after insertion into a catenable heap

nodes.summary: For catenable heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$, the flattening of the heap returned by the union of $h_1$ and $h_2$ is the flattening of $h_1$ followed by the flattening of $h_2$.
nodes.title: Flattening a union of catenable heaps

nodes.summary: The multiset of elements of the heap returned by the make operation is the empty multiset.
nodes.title: A newly made catenable heap has no elements

nodes.summary: For every element $x$ and every catenable heap $h$, the multiset of elements of the heap returned by inserting $x$ into $h$ is the multiset of elements of $h$ with one more copy of $x$.
nodes.title: Insertion adds one copy of the element

nodes.summary: For all catenable heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$, the multiset of elements of the heap returned by the union of $h_1$ and $h_2$ is the multiset sum of the multisets of elements of $h_1$ and $h_2$ (multiplicities add).
nodes.title: Union adds the multisets of elements

nodes.summary: The heap returned by the operation that creates an empty catenable heap has size $0$.
nodes.title: A newly made catenable heap has size zero

nodes.summary: For every element $x$ and catenable heap $h$, the heap returned by inserting $x$ into $h$ has size one more than the size of $h$.
nodes.title: Insertion into a catenable heap increases its size by one

nodes.summary: For catenable heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$, the heap returned by the union of $h_1$ and $h_2$ has size equal to the size of $h_1$ plus the size of $h_2$.
nodes.title: Size of a catenable heap union
Least-recently-used cache

nodes.summary: For a type $K$ of keys, a type $V$ of values and a natural number $c$, an LRU cache of capacity $c$ is a list of key-value pairs in $K \times V$, ordered from most to least recently used, whose keys are pairwise distinct and whose length is at most $c$.
nodes.title: Least-recently-used cache

nodes.summary: Two LRU caches with the same key type, value type and capacity are equal if their lists of entries are equal.
nodes.title: Extensionality of LRU caches

nodes.summary: Given a key $k$ and a list of key–value pairs, erasing $k$ deletes every pair whose key is $k$ and keeps the other pairs in their original order. When the keys in the list are pairwise distinct, at most one pair is deleted.
nodes.title: Erasing a key from a list of entries

nodes.summary: For every capacity $c$, the empty LRU cache of capacity $c$ is the cache with no entries.
nodes.title: Empty LRU cache

nodes.summary: The key list of an LRU cache is the list of the keys of its entries in the order of the cache, so the most recently used key comes first.
nodes.title: Key list of an LRU cache

nodes.summary: The size of an LRU cache is the number of entries it stores.
nodes.title: Size of an LRU cache

nodes.summary: Looking up a key $k$ in an LRU cache returns an optional value together with a cache. If the cache stores a binding $(k, v)$, the result is $v$ together with the cache in which that binding is moved to the front and the other entries keep their order; otherwise the result is no value together with the unchanged cache.
nodes.title: LRU cache lookup

nodes.summary: Putting the binding $(k, v)$ into an LRU cache of capacity $c$ removes any entry with key $k$, places $(k, v)$ at the front as the most recently used entry, and then keeps only the first $c$ entries, so the least recently used entries beyond the capacity are evicted.
nodes.title: Insertion into an LRU cache

nodes.summary: The keys stored in any LRU cache are pairwise distinct.
nodes.title: Keys of an LRU cache are distinct

nodes.summary: Every LRU cache of capacity $c$ has size at most $c$.
nodes.title: An LRU cache never exceeds its capacity

nodes.summary: If the key $k$ is not stored in an LRU cache, then looking up $k$ returns no value and leaves the cache unchanged.
nodes.title: A lookup of an absent key misses

nodes.summary: If an LRU cache stores the pair $(k, v)$, then looking up $k$ returns $v$.
nodes.title: A lookup of a stored key returns its value

nodes.summary: If an LRU cache stores the pair $(k, v)$, then after looking up $k$ the most recently used (first) entry of the cache is $(k, v)$.
nodes.title: A successful lookup moves the entry to the front

nodes.summary: For every LRU cache of positive capacity, every key $k$ and every value $v$, looking up $k$ in the cache obtained by putting the binding $(k, v)$ returns $v$.
nodes.title: Lookup after insertion into an LRU cache

nodes.summary: For every LRU cache $C$ of capacity $c$, key $k$ and value $v$, the cache obtained by putting the binding $(k, v)$ into $C$ has size at most $c$.
nodes.title: Insertion respects the capacity of an LRU cache

nodes.summary: For every LRU cache $C$, key $k$ and value $v$, the keys of the cache obtained by putting the binding $(k, v)$ into $C$ are pairwise distinct.
nodes.title: Insertion keeps the keys of an LRU cache distinct

nodes.summary: For every LRU cache of capacity $c$ and every key $k$, the cache after looking up $k$ holds at most $c$ entries.
nodes.title: Lookup respects the capacity

nodes.summary: For every LRU cache and every key $k$, the keys of the cache obtained by looking up $k$ are pairwise distinct.
nodes.title: Lookups keep keys distinct

nodes.summary: For every LRU cache, key $k$ and value $v$, every key-value pair $p$ stored in the cache after putting the binding $(k, v)$ either equals $(k, v)$, or was stored before and has a key different from $k$.
nodes.title: Entries after insertion

nodes.summary: For every LRU cache and every key $k$, a key-value pair is stored in the cache after looking up $k$ if and only if it was stored in the cache before the lookup.
nodes.title: Lookup preserves the stored bindings

nodes.summary: For every LRU cache and every key $k$, the list of entries of the cache after looking up $k$ is a permutation of the list of entries before.
nodes.title: A lookup permutes the entries

nodes.summary: For every LRU cache and every key $k$, the cache after looking up $k$ holds exactly as many entries as before.
nodes.title: Lookup preserves the size

nodes.summary: Let an LRU cache of capacity $c$ hold fewer than $c$ entries or already store a binding for the key $k$, and let $v$ be a value. Then a key-value pair $p$ is stored in the cache after putting the binding $(k, v)$ if and only if $p = (k, v)$, or $p$ was stored before and the key of $p$ differs from $k$.
nodes.title: Insertion without eviction

nodes.summary: Let $C$ be an LRU cache of positive capacity, $k$ a key and $v$ a value. After the binding $(k, v)$ is put into $C$, the first entry of the resulting cache, its most recently used entry, is $(k, v)$.
nodes.title: With positive capacity, the inserted binding becomes the most recent entry

nodes.summary: Let $C$ be an LRU cache of capacity $c$ that holds fewer than $c$ entries or already stores the key $k$. Then for every key $k' \ne k$ and every value $v$, looking up $k'$ in the cache obtained by putting the binding $(k, v)$ into $C$ returns the same optional value as looking up $k'$ in $C$.
nodes.title: A put without eviction preserves lookups of other keys

nodes.summary: Let $C$ be an LRU cache of capacity $c$, let $k'$ be a key not stored in $C$, and let $k$ be a key stored in $C$. If $k$ is no longer stored after putting $k'$ with any value $v$ into $C$, then $C$ held exactly $c$ entries and $k$ is the last key of $C$, that is, the least recently used one.
nodes.title: The evicted key is the least recently used one

For a list with head $a$ and tail $\ell$, it is $x$ followed by the whole list if $x < a$; it is $a$ followed by the ordered insertion of $x$ into $\ell$ if $a < x$; and it is the list unchanged if $a = x$.

nodes.summary: Over a linearly ordered type, if every element of a list $\ell$ is smaller than every later element of $\ell$ and $x$ belongs to $\ell$, then the ordered insertion of $x$ into $\ell$ is $\ell$ itself.
nodes.title: Inserting a present element into a strictly increasing list

nodes.summary: Fix a capacity $n$, let $s$ be a store assigning to each identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, and let $\mathrm{head}$ be an identity below $n$ or NIL. Otherwise $h$ is an identity $i$: the search returns nothing if cell $i$ is unallocated, returns $i$ if the node in cell $i$ has payload $t$, and otherwise continues…

It follows next pointers from $h$ and returns the first visited identity whose node has payload $t$, returning nothing if it reaches NIL or an unallocated cell first, or if $n$ steps run out.

Stack with multipop

nodes.summary: Stacks over a type $\alpha$ are lists of elements of $\alpha$, with the first element as the top. Pushing $v \in \alpha$ onto a stack $s$ returns the stack with top $v$ followed by the elements of $s$, at cost $1$ (one successful push event).
nodes.title: Stack push

nodes.summary: Stacks over a type $\alpha$ are lists of elements of $\alpha$, with the first element as the top. Popping the empty stack returns underflow (no value) at cost $0$. Popping a stack with top $v$ and remaining stack $t$ returns the pair $(v, t)$ at cost $1$ (one successful pop event).
nodes.title: Stack pop

nodes.summary: Stacks over a type $\alpha$ are lists of elements of $\alpha$, with the first element as the top. Reading the top of the empty stack returns underflow (no value) at cost $0$. Reading the top of a stack with top $v$ returns $v$ at cost $1$ (one successful top event); the stack itself is not returned or changed.
nodes.title: Stack top

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a stack over a type $\alpha$ (a list of elements of $\alpha$ whose first element is the top). If $s$ is empty, popping $s$ returns underflow (no value) at cost $0$. If $s$ has top $h$ and remaining stack $t$, popping $s$ returns the pair $(h, t)$ at cost $1$.
nodes.title: Result and cost of stack pop

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a stack over a type $\alpha$ (a list of elements of $\alpha$ whose first element is the top). If $s$ is empty, reading the top of $s$ returns underflow (no value) at cost $0$. If $s$ has top $h$, reading the top of $s$ returns $h$ at cost $1$.
nodes.title: Result and cost of reading the stack top

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type, let $s$ be a stack over $\alpha$ (a list of elements of $\alpha$ whose first element is the top) and let $v \in \alpha$. Pushing $v$ onto $s$ returns the stack with top $v$ followed by the elements of $s$, at cost $1$. Popping $s$ returns underflow (no value) at cost $0$ if $s$ is empty, and returns the pair $(h, t)$ at cost $1$ if $s$ has top $h$ and remaining stack $t$. Reading the top of…
nodes.title: Result and cost of the stack operations

nodes.summary: For a stack $S$, stored as a list with its top first, and a natural number $k$, MULTIPOP of $S$ with count $k$ repeatedly removes the top element while the stack is nonempty and fewer than $k$ elements have been removed, and returns the remaining stack. Each removed element costs one unit, and nothing else is charged.
nodes.title: MULTIPOP

nodes.summary: For every stack $S$, stored as a list with its top first, and every natural number $k$, the stack returned by MULTIPOP of $S$ with count $k$ is $S$ with its top $k$ elements removed, or the empty stack if $S$ has fewer than $k$ elements.
nodes.title: Result of MULTIPOP

nodes.summary: For every stack $S$ and every natural number $k$, the cost of MULTIPOP of $S$ with count $k$ is $\min(|S|, k)$, where $|S|$ is the number of elements of $S$.
nodes.title: Cost of MULTIPOP

nodes.summary: For a stack $S$ and an integer $k$, MULTIPOP with integer count $k$ is MULTIPOP of $S$ with the natural count $\max(k, 0)$, with the same result and cost. In particular, a count $k \le 0$ removes nothing.
nodes.title: MULTIPOP with an integer count

nodes.summary: For every stack $S$ and every integer $k \le 0$, MULTIPOP with integer count $k$ applied to $S$ returns $S$ at cost $0$.
nodes.title: MULTIPOP with a nonpositive count does nothing

nodes.summary: For a type $\alpha$ of stack entries, a stack operation is one of the following: $\mathrm{PUSH}(x)$ for an element $x \in \alpha$, $\mathrm{POP}$, or $\mathrm{MULTIPOP}(k)$ for an integer count $k$.
nodes.title: Stack operations for the MULTIPOP aggregate analysis

nodes.summary: Given a stack $S$ and a finite sequence of operations, each a PUSH of a value, a POP or a MULTIPOP with an integer count, the operations are applied to $S$ in order. PUSH of $x$ puts $x$ on top at cost $1$; POP removes the top element at cost $1$; MULTIPOP with count $k$ is MULTIPOP with an integer count, costing one unit per element removed. If a POP meets an empty stack, the run stops and reports an error, that…
nodes.title: Running a sequence of stack operations

nodes.summary: For every stack $S$, every value $x$ and every finite sequence $\sigma$ of stack operations, running PUSH $x$ followed by $\sigma$ on $S$ has the same result and cost as first performing the standalone PUSH of $x$ on $S$ and then running $\sigma$ on the resulting stack, the two costs being added.
nodes.title: Running a PUSH agrees with the standalone PUSH

nodes.summary: For every stack $S$ and every finite sequence $\sigma$ of stack operations, running POP followed by $\sigma$ on $S$ has the same result and cost as first performing the standalone POP on $S$ and then, if it reports underflow, stopping with an error at no further cost, or, if it removes the top element and leaves the stack $S'$, running $\sigma$ on $S'$, the two costs being added.
nodes.title: Running a POP agrees with the standalone POP

nodes.summary: For every stack $S$ and every finite sequence $\sigma$ of stack operations, if running $\sigma$ on $S$ succeeds with final stack $F$, then the cost of the run plus the number of elements of $F$ equals the number of elements of $S$ plus twice the number of PUSH operations in $\sigma$.
nodes.title: Cost balance for stack operation sequences

nodes.summary: For every stack $S$ and every sequence of $n$ stack operations (PUSH, POP and MULTIPOP), if running the sequence on $S$ succeeds, that is, no POP meets an empty stack, then its cost is at most $|S| + 2n$, where $|S|$ is the number of elements of $S$.
nodes.title: Aggregate cost of stack operation sequences
Two-list queue

nodes.summary: For a queue stored as an enqueue list and a dequeue list, the potential is the length of the enqueue list: the number of elements that will be reversed when they are moved to the dequeue list.
nodes.title: Potential of a two-list queue

nodes.summary: For a queue stored as an enqueue list and a dequeue list, the modeled cost of dequeueing is $1$ when the dequeue list is nonempty, and $m + 1$ when the dequeue list is empty, where $m$ is the length of the enqueue list (the number of elements reversed when they are moved to the dequeue list).
nodes.title: Modeled cost of a dequeue

nodes.summary: Enqueueing a value $v$ onto a two-list queue $q$ returns the queue obtained from $q$ by adding $v$ at the back, that is, by prepending $v$ to the enqueue list, together with a recorded cost of $1$.
nodes.title: Timed enqueue

nodes.summary: For every two-list queue $q$ and every value $v$, the modeled cost of enqueueing $v$ onto $q$ plus the potential of the resulting queue equals the potential of $q$ plus $2$.
nodes.title: Amortized cost of enqueueing

nodes.summary: Dequeueing from a two-list queue $q$ returns the next element in first-in, first-out order together with the remaining queue, or returns no element together with $q$ itself when $q$ is empty. In both cases the recorded cost is the modeled dequeue cost of $q$.
nodes.title: Timed dequeue

nodes.summary: For every two-list queue $q$, the modeled cost of dequeueing from $q$ plus the potential of the resulting queue equals the potential of $q$ plus $1$. This includes the case where $q$ is empty.
nodes.title: Amortized cost of dequeueing

nodes.summary: A queue operation over a type $\alpha$ is either a request to enqueue a value $v \in \alpha$ or a request to dequeue. Sequences of such operations are used to state aggregate cost bounds.
nodes.title: Queue operation

nodes.summary: The potential-method charge of a queue operation is $2$ for an enqueue and $1$ for a dequeue.
nodes.title: Amortized charge of a queue operation

nodes.summary: For a queue $q$, an enqueue operation with value $v$ performs the costed enqueue of $v$ onto $q$. A dequeue operation performs the costed dequeue of $q$ and keeps the remaining queue and the cost, discarding the removed value; on an empty queue the remaining queue is $q$ itself.
nodes.title: One step of a queue operation

nodes.summary: For every queue $q$ and every queue operation $o$, the modeled cost of performing $o$ on $q$ plus the potential of the resulting queue equals the potential of $q$ plus the charge of $o$.
nodes.title: Amortized cost of one queue operation

nodes.summary: Running a list of queue operations from a queue $q$ performs the operations one step at a time from left to right, starting at $q$. The result is the final queue, and the cost is the sum of the costs of the individual steps; running the empty list returns $q$ at cost $0$.
nodes.title: Running a sequence of queue operations

nodes.summary: For a list of queue operations, the total charge is the sum of the amortized charges of its operations, where an enqueue is charged $2$ and a dequeue is charged $1$.
nodes.title: Total charge of a sequence of queue operations

nodes.summary: For every list of queue operations and every two-list queue $q$, the modeled cost of running the operations from left to right starting at $q$, plus the potential of the final queue, equals the potential of $q$ plus the total charge of the operations.
nodes.title: Amortized cost of a sequence of queue operations

nodes.summary: For every list of $n$ queue operations and every two-list queue $q$, the modeled cost of running the operations from left to right starting at $q$ is at most the potential of $q$ plus $2n$.
nodes.title: Linear bound on the cost of queue operations

nodes.summary: A queue is stored as a dequeue list and an enqueue list whose most recently enqueued element comes first. Its contents are its elements in FIFO order: the dequeue list followed by the reverse of the enqueue list.
nodes.title: Contents of a two-list queue

nodes.summary: For every queue $q$, the array obtained from $q$, read as a list, equals the contents of $q$.
nodes.title: Array conversion lists the contents

nodes.summary: For every queue $q$ and value $v$, the contents of the queue obtained by enqueueing $v$ onto $q$ are the contents of $q$ followed by $v$.
nodes.title: Enqueueing appends to the contents

nodes.summary: For every queue $q$, the emptiness test of $q$ returns true if and only if the contents of $q$ are empty.
nodes.title: The queue emptiness test matches the contents

nodes.summary: For every queue $q$, dequeueing $q$ returns nothing if and only if the contents of $q$ are empty.
nodes.title: Dequeueing fails exactly on empty queues

nodes.summary: If dequeueing a queue $q$ succeeds and returns an element $a$ and a queue $r$, then the contents of $q$ are $a$ followed by the contents of $r$.
nodes.title: A successful dequeue splits off the first element

nodes.summary: Structures answering range, interval or nearest-point queries: segment trees, Fenwick trees, sparse tables, interval trees, range trees, kd-trees, ball trees and fractional cascading.
nodes.title: Range-query and spatial structures
Ball tree

nodes.summary: For a dimension $d$, a ball tree over the integer points $\mathbb{Z}^d$ (functions $\{0, \dots, d-1\} \to \mathbb{Z}$) is either empty, a leaf holding one point, or a node holding a center point $c \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, a natural number $b$ (the squared-radius bound of the node's sphere) and two child ball trees.
nodes.title: Ball tree

nodes.summary: For a ball tree $T$ and a list $A$ of points, the accumulating traversal returns $A$ when $T$ is empty, the point $p$ followed by $A$ when $T$ is a leaf holding $p$, and, when $T$ is a node with children $L$ and $R$, the accumulating traversal of $L$ whose accumulator is the accumulating traversal of $R$ with accumulator $A$.
nodes.title: Accumulating traversal of a ball tree

nodes.summary: The point list of a ball tree is the list of the points held at its leaves, from left to right: the empty tree gives the empty list, a leaf holding $p$ gives the list $[p]$, and a node gives the point list of its left subtree followed by the point list of its right subtree. The centers stored at nodes are not included.
nodes.title: Point list of a ball tree

nodes.summary: The size of a ball tree is the number of points held in its leaves: it is $0$ for the empty tree, $1$ for a leaf, and the sum of the sizes of the two children for a node; the center of a node is not counted.
nodes.title: Size of a ball tree

nodes.summary: For every ball tree $t$, the list of points stored in $t$, read from left to right, has length equal to the size of $t$.
nodes.title: Number of points of a ball tree

nodes.summary: For points $p, q \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, the squared distance from $p$ to $q$ is the natural number $\sum_{i=0}^{d-1} (p_i - q_i)^2$, computed in $\mathbb{Z}$ and then converted to $\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: Squared Euclidean distance

nodes.summary: For all points $p, q \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, the squared distance from $p$ to $q$ equals the squared distance from $q$ to $p$.
nodes.title: Symmetry of squared distance

nodes.summary: For all points $a, b, c \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, writing $\delta(x, y)$ for the squared distance from $x$ to $y$, we have $\delta(a, c) \le 2\,(\delta(a, b) + \delta(b, c))$.
nodes.title: Relaxed triangle inequality for squared distance

nodes.summary: For a center $c \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ and a list $P$ of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, the squared covering radius of $P$ about $c$ is the largest squared distance from $c$ to a point of $P$, or $0$ if $P$ is empty.
nodes.title: Squared covering radius

nodes.summary: Let $c \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ and let $L$ be a list of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$. For every point $p$ of $L$, the squared distance from $c$ to $p$ is at most the squared radius of $L$ around $c$, the largest squared distance from $c$ to a point of $L$.
nodes.title: Points lie within the squared radius

nodes.summary: Let $d$ be a dimension and write $\delta(x, y)$ for the squared distance from $x$ to $y$ in $\mathbb{Z}^d$. For a ball tree $T$ over $\mathbb{Z}^d$, a query point $q \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, a squared radius $r \in \mathbb{N}$ and a list $A$ of points, the accumulating search of $T$ for $q$ and $r$ with accumulator $A$ is $A$ when $T$ is empty; when $T$ is a leaf holding $p$, it is $p$ followed by $A$ if…
nodes.title: Accumulating ball-tree search

nodes.summary: The search of a ball tree $T$ for a query point $q \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ and a squared radius $r \in \mathbb{N}$ is the accumulating search of $T$ for $q$ and $r$ started with the empty accumulator.
nodes.title: Ball-tree similarity search

nodes.summary: Validity of a ball tree is defined inductively: the empty tree and every leaf are valid, and a node with center $c$ and squared-radius bound $b$ is valid when both of its subtrees are valid and every point in the point list of either subtree lies within squared Euclidean distance $b$ of $c$.
nodes.title: Bounding-sphere invariant of a ball tree

nodes.summary: For every ball tree $T$ over $\mathbb{Z}^d$ satisfying the bounding-sphere invariant, every query point $q \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ and every $r \in \mathbb{N}$, the search of $T$ for $q$ and $r$ equals the list of points of $T$, from left to right, filtered to the points $p$ whose squared distance from $q$ is at most $r$, in their order. Pruning against the bounding spheres loses no point.
nodes.title: Ball-tree search is exact

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a ball tree satisfying the bounding-sphere invariant. For all $q, p \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ and every natural number $r$, $p$ is returned by the similarity search of $t$ with query $q$ and squared radius $r$ if and only if $p$ is one of the points stored in $t$ and the squared distance from $q$ to $p$ is at most $r$.
nodes.title: Search of a valid ball tree

nodes.summary: The ball tree built from a list of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ is defined by recursion on the list. The empty list gives the empty tree and a one-point list $[p]$ gives the leaf $p$. A list $L = [x_1, \dots, x_n]$ with $n \ge 2$ gives a node whose center is $x_1$, whose bound is the squared radius of $L$ around $x_1$ (the largest squared distance from $x_1$ to a point of $L$), whose left child is the tree built from…
nodes.title: Building a ball tree by halving

nodes.summary: For every list of points in $\mathbb{Z}^d$, the ball tree built from it by recursive halving satisfies the bounding-sphere invariant.
nodes.title: Ball trees built by halving are valid

nodes.summary: For every list $P$ of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, the list of points of the ball tree built from $P$, from left to right, is a permutation of $P$.
nodes.title: A built ball tree stores a permutation of its input

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and every point $p \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, $p$ is one of the points stored in the ball tree built from $L$ if and only if $p$ occurs in $L$.
nodes.title: Points of a built ball tree

nodes.summary: For every list $P$ of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, the size of the ball tree built from $P$ equals the length of $P$, that is, the number of entries of $P$ counted with repetition.
nodes.title: Size of a built ball tree

nodes.summary: For every list $P$ of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, every query point $q \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ and every $r \in \mathbb{N}$, let $T$ be the ball tree built from $P$. The search of $T$ for $q$ and $r$ equals the list of points of $T$, from left to right, filtered to the points $p$ whose squared distance from $q$ is at most $r$, in their order.
nodes.title: Ball-tree search of a built tree

nodes.summary: For every list $P$ of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, every query point $q \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ and every $r \in \mathbb{N}$, the search of the ball tree built from $P$ for $q$ and $r$ is a permutation of the sublist of $P$ consisting of the points $p$ whose squared distance from $q$ is at most $r$, kept with their multiplicities.
nodes.title: Ball-tree search of a built tree, up to order

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, let $q, p \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ and let $r$ be a natural number. Then $p$ is returned by the similarity search with query $q$ and squared radius $r$ on the ball tree built from $L$ if and only if $p$ occurs in $L$ and the squared distance from $q$ to $p$ is at most $r$.
nodes.title: Search of a built ball tree
Fenwick tree

nodes.summary: A Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) over a commutative additive monoid $\alpha$ is an array of elements of $\alpha$, read as one-indexed interval sums with an unused dummy entry at index $0$. The structure itself imposes no condition on the entries, and the underlying array it represents is not stored; the relation saying that a tree represents a given array is defined separately.
nodes.title: Fenwick tree

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n > 0$, $\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is the largest power of two dividing $n$; for $n = 0$ it is defined as $\operatorname{lowbit}(0) = 0$.
nodes.title: Lowest set bit

nodes.summary: By convention, $\operatorname{lowbit}(0) = 0$.
nodes.title: Lowbit of zero

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n > 0$, $\operatorname{lowbit}(n) > 0$, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is the value of the lowest set bit of $n$ in binary.
nodes.title: The lowest set bit of a positive number is positive

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$, $\operatorname{lowbit}(n) \le n$, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is the value of the lowest set bit of $n$ in binary (with $\operatorname{lowbit}(0) = 0$).
nodes.title: The lowest set bit is at most the number

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n > 0$, $\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ divides $n$, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is the value of the lowest set bit of $n$ in binary.
nodes.title: The lowest set bit divides the number

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n > 0$, $\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is a power of two: $\operatorname{lowbit}(n) = 2^k$ for some natural number $k$.
nodes.title: The lowest set bit is a power of two

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n > 0$, the quotient $n / \operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is odd, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is the value of the lowest set bit of $n$ in binary.
nodes.title: Dividing out the lowest set bit leaves an odd number

nodes.summary: For a list $a$ of elements of a commutative additive monoid $\alpha$ and a natural number $j$, the interval sum at the one-indexed position $j$ is the sum of the $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ entries of $a$ ending at zero-indexed position $j - 1$, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ is the largest power of two dividing $j$ (with $\operatorname{lowbit}(0) = 0$) and entries past the end of $a$ count as $0$.
nodes.title: Fenwick-tree interval sum of a list

nodes.summary: For an array $a$ of elements of a commutative additive monoid $\alpha$ and a natural number $j$, this is the sum of the $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ entries of $a$ ending at zero-indexed position $j - 1$, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ is the largest power of two dividing $j$ (with $\operatorname{lowbit}(0) = 0$) and entries past the end of $a$ count as $0$.
nodes.title: Interval sum read from an array

nodes.summary: A Fenwick tree $t$ over an additive commutative monoid represents a list $a$ of length $n$ when its stored array has length $n + 1$ (a dummy entry at index $0$ plus one entry per element of $a$) and, for every $j$ with $1 \le j \le n$, the stored entry at index $j$ equals the block sum of $a$ at $j$: the sum of the $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ entries of $a$ ending at position $j - 1$ (positions counted from $0$),…
nodes.title: Fenwick tree representing a list

nodes.summary: The size of a Fenwick tree is the length of its stored array minus one, truncated at $0$; the one accounts for the dummy entry at index $0$. It is read off the stored array in constant time.
nodes.title: Size of a Fenwick tree

nodes.summary: If a Fenwick tree $t$ over an additive commutative monoid represents a list $a$, then the size of $t$ equals the length of $a$.
nodes.title: A Fenwick tree has the length of the list it represents

nodes.summary: For a list $a$ of length $n$ over a commutative additive monoid $\alpha$, the Fenwick tree built from $a$ stores the array of length $n + 1$ whose entry at index $0$ is $0$ and whose entry at each one-indexed position $j$ with $1 \le j \le n$ is the sum of the $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ entries of $a$ ending at zero-indexed position $j - 1$, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ is the largest power of two dividing $j$.
nodes.title: Building a Fenwick tree from a list

nodes.summary: For every list $a$ over an additive commutative monoid, the Fenwick tree built from $a$ has size equal to the length of $a$.
nodes.title: Size of a built Fenwick tree

nodes.summary: For every list $a$ over an additive commutative monoid, the Fenwick tree built from $a$ represents $a$.
nodes.title: Building a Fenwick tree yields a valid representation

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a Fenwick tree over an additive commutative monoid with $n$ underlying entries, let $k$ be a natural number and let $m = \min(k, n)$. The prefix sum of length $k$ of $t$ is the sum of the stored entries of $t$ at the positions $j_0 = m$, $j_{r+1} = j_r - \operatorname{lowbit}(j_r)$, taken for as long as $j_r > 0$.
nodes.title: Fenwick tree prefix sum

nodes.summary: For every Fenwick tree $t$ over an additive commutative monoid, the prefix sum of length $0$ of $t$ is $0$.
nodes.title: The empty prefix sum is zero

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a Fenwick tree representing a list $a$ of elements of an additive commutative monoid. Then for every natural number $k$, including $k > |a|$, the prefix sum of length $k$ of $t$ equals the sum of the first $\min(k, |a|)$ entries of $a$.
nodes.title: Correctness of Fenwick tree prefix sums

nodes.summary: For every list $a$ of elements of an additive commutative monoid and every natural number $k$, the prefix sum of length $k$ of the Fenwick tree built from $a$ equals the sum of the first $\min(k, |a|)$ entries of $a$.
nodes.title: Prefix sums of a built Fenwick tree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a Fenwick tree over a commutative additive monoid $\alpha$, let $n$ be its size (the length of its stored array minus one), let $i$ be a natural number and let $\delta \in \alpha$. Adding $\delta$ at underlying position $i$ adds $\delta$ to the stored entries at the one-indexed positions $j_1 = i + 1$ and $j_{k+1} = j_k + \operatorname{lowbit}(j_k)$, for as long as $j_k \le n$, where…
nodes.title: Point update of a Fenwick tree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a Fenwick tree over a commutative additive monoid $\alpha$, and let $n$ be its size (the length of its stored array minus one). For every natural number $i \ge n$ and every $\delta \in \alpha$, the point update of $t$ adding $\delta$ at position $i$ returns $t$ itself.
nodes.title: Out-of-range point updates leave a Fenwick tree unchanged

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a Fenwick tree over an additive commutative monoid that represents a list $a$ of length $n$. For every index $i < n$ (counting from $0$) and every element $\delta$, the tree obtained from $t$ by adding $\delta$ at position $i$ represents the list obtained from $a$ by replacing its entry $a_i$ with $a_i + \delta$.
nodes.title: Point update preserves representation

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a Fenwick tree representing a list $a$ of elements of an additive commutative monoid, let $i < |a|$ be a position, let $\delta$ be an element of the monoid, and let $k$ be any natural number, possibly larger than $|a|$. Then the prefix sum of length $k$ of the tree obtained from $t$ by adding $\delta$ at position $i$ equals the prefix sum of length $k$ of $t$ plus $\delta$ if $i < k$, and equals the…
nodes.title: Prefix sums after a point update

nodes.summary: For a Fenwick tree $t$ over an additive commutative group and natural numbers $\mathit{lo}$ and $\mathit{hi}$, the range sum of $t$ over $[\mathit{lo}, \mathit{hi})$ is $0$ if $\mathit{hi} \le \mathit{lo}$, and otherwise the prefix sum of length $\mathit{hi}$ of $t$ minus the prefix sum of length $\mathit{lo}$ of $t$.
nodes.title: Fenwick tree range sum

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a Fenwick tree representing a list $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ of elements of an additive commutative group. Then for all natural numbers $\mathit{lo}$ and $\mathit{hi}$, the range sum of $t$ over $[\mathit{lo}, \mathit{hi})$ equals $\sum_{\mathit{lo} \le i < \min(\mathit{hi}, n)} a_i$; in particular it is $0$ when $\mathit{hi} \le \mathit{lo}$.
nodes.title: Correctness of Fenwick tree range sums
Fractional cascading

nodes.summary: For a flag $b$ (true or false) and a list $\ell$, the alternating selection of $\ell$ with initial flag $b$ is defined by recursion on $\ell$: the empty list gives the empty list; for a list with head $a$ and tail $\ell'$, if $b$ is true it keeps $a$ and continues on $\ell'$ with flag false, and if $b$ is false it drops $a$ and continues on $\ell'$ with flag true.
nodes.title: Alternating selection with a flag

nodes.summary: The sample of a list $[x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots]$ is the list $[x_0, x_2, x_4, \dots]$ of every other element, starting with the first, in their original order.
nodes.title: Sample of a catalog

nodes.summary: For every flag $b$ (true or false) and every list $\ell$, the alternating selection of $\ell$ with initial flag $b$ is a sublist of $\ell$: it is obtained from $\ell$ by deleting some elements and keeping the rest in order.
nodes.title: Alternating selection gives a sublist

nodes.summary: For every list $\ell$, the sample of $\ell$ is a sublist of $\ell$: it is obtained from $\ell$ by deleting some elements and keeping the rest in order.
nodes.title: The sample is a sublist

nodes.summary: For a catalog (finite list) $L$, every entry of the sample of $L$ (every other entry of $L$, starting with the first) is an entry of $L$.
nodes.title: Entries of a sample are entries of the catalog

nodes.summary: For every catalog $L$, twice the length of the sample of $L$ is at most the length of $L$ plus one.
nodes.title: Doubled sample length bound

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ (over any type), the sample of $xs$ has length at most $\lfloor (|xs| + 1)/2 \rfloor$, half the length of $xs$ rounded up: for an even length $2m$ the bound is $m$, and for an odd length $2m + 1$ it is $m + 1$.
nodes.title: The sample has at most half the length, rounded up

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ (over any type), the sample of $xs$, every other element starting with the first, has length at most the length of $xs$.
nodes.title: The sample is no longer than the list

nodes.summary: If a list over a linear order is sorted in nondecreasing order, then so is its sample.
nodes.title: The sample of a sorted list is sorted

nodes.summary: For lists $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ over a linearly ordered type, their sorted merge is the result of merge sort, with respect to $\le$, applied to the concatenation of $\ell_1$ followed by $\ell_2$.
nodes.title: Sorted merge of two catalogs

nodes.summary: For any lists $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ over a linear order, the sorted merge of $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ is a permutation of the concatenation of $\ell_1$ followed by $\ell_2$.
nodes.title: A sorted merge rearranges the concatenation

nodes.summary: For catalogs (finite lists) $L$ and $M$ over a linearly ordered type, the sorted merge of $L$ and $M$ has length equal to the length of $L$ plus the length of $M$.
nodes.title: Length of a sorted merge

nodes.summary: For any lists $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ over a linear order, sorted or not, their sorted merge is sorted in nondecreasing order.
nodes.title: A sorted merge is sorted

nodes.summary: For lists $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ over a linear order and any element $v$, $v$ belongs to the sorted merge of $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ if and only if $v$ belongs to $\ell_1$ or to $\ell_2$.
nodes.title: Elements of a sorted merge

nodes.summary: For a value $x$ of a linearly ordered type and a catalog (finite list) $L$, the lower bound of $x$ in $L$ is the number of entries of $L$ that are less than $x$, counted with multiplicity. For a sorted catalog this is the first index whose entry is not less than $x$, or the length of $L$ if there is none.
nodes.title: Lower bound of a value in a catalog

nodes.summary: For a value $x$ and a catalog $L$ over a linearly ordered type, the lower bound of $x$ in $L$ (the number of entries of $L$ less than $x$) is at most the length of $L$.
nodes.title: Lower bound is at most the catalog length

nodes.summary: For a value $x$ and catalogs $L$ and $M$ over a linearly ordered type, the lower bound of $x$ in the sorted merge of $L$ and $M$ equals the lower bound of $x$ in $L$ plus the lower bound of $x$ in $M$, where the lower bound of $x$ in a catalog is the number of its entries less than $x$.
nodes.title: Lower bound in a sorted merge splits

nodes.summary: For a value $x$ and a catalog $L$ over a linearly ordered type, the number of entries less than $x$ in the sample of $L$ (every other entry of $L$, starting with the first) is at most the number of entries of $L$ less than $x$.
nodes.title: Lower bound in a sample is at most the lower bound in the catalog

nodes.summary: For a value $x$ and a catalog $L$, the scan count of $x$ in $L$ is the number of elements of $L$ that are $< x$, computed by a direct scan: it is $0$ for the empty catalog, and for a catalog with head $a$ and tail $L'$ it is the scan count of $x$ in $L'$, plus $1$ if $a < x$.
nodes.title: Scan count of smaller elements

nodes.summary: For every value $x$ and every catalog $L$, the scan count of elements of $L$ that are $< x$ equals the lower bound of $x$ in $L$.
nodes.title: The scan count equals the lower bound

nodes.summary: For catalogs $c$ and $a$, the augmentation of $c$ by $a$ is the sorted merge of $c$ with the sample of $a$ (every other element of $a$, starting with the first). In fractional cascading, $a$ is the next augmented catalog.
nodes.title: Augmenting a catalog by the next one

nodes.summary: For any lists $c$ and $a$ over a linear order, sorted or not, the augmented catalog obtained by merging $c$ with the sample of $a$ is sorted in nondecreasing order.
nodes.title: One augmentation step yields a sorted list

nodes.summary: For lists $c$ and $a$ over a linearly ordered type, the augmented catalog obtained by merging $c$ with the sample $s(a)$ of $a$ has length $|c| + |s(a)|$.
nodes.title: Length of one augmented catalog

nodes.summary: For lists $c$ and $a$ over a linearly ordered type, the augmented catalog obtained by merging $c$ with the sample of $a$ has length at most $|c| + \lfloor (|a| + 1)/2 \rfloor$, the length of $c$ plus half the length of $a$ rounded up.
nodes.title: Length bound for one augmented catalog

nodes.summary: For catalogs $c$ and $a$ over a linearly ordered type, a value $v$ is an entry of the augmented catalog of $c$ with $a$ (the sorted merge of $c$ with the sample of $a$) if and only if $v$ is an entry of $c$ or an entry of the sample of $a$.
nodes.title: Membership in an augmented catalog

nodes.summary: For catalogs $c$ and $a$ over a linearly ordered type, every entry $v$ of the augmented catalog of $c$ with $a$ (the sorted merge of $c$ with the sample of $a$) is an entry of $c$ or an entry of $a$.
nodes.title: Entries of an augmented catalog come from the two catalogs

nodes.summary: For a value $x$ and catalogs $c$ and $a$ over a linearly ordered type, the lower bound of $x$ in the augmented catalog of $c$ with $a$ (the sorted merge of $c$ with the sample of $a$) equals the lower bound of $x$ in $c$ plus the lower bound of $x$ in the sample of $a$, where the lower bound of $x$ in a catalog is the number of its entries less than $x$.
nodes.title: Lower bound in an augmented catalog splits

nodes.summary: For a value $x$ and catalogs $c$ and $a$ over a linearly ordered type, the lower bound of $x$ in the augmented catalog of $c$ with $a$ (the sorted merge of $c$ with the sample of $a$) is at most the lower bound of $x$ in $c$ plus the lower bound of $x$ in $a$, where the lower bound of $x$ in a catalog is the number of its entries less than $x$.
nodes.title: Lower bound in an augmented catalog is at most the sum

nodes.summary: Given a catalog $c$ and a list $L$ of catalogs, the result is $c$ itself if $L$ is empty, and otherwise the sorted merge of $c$ with the sample (every other element, starting with the first) of the first catalog of $L$.
nodes.title: Augmenting a catalog by the head of a list

nodes.summary: For a list of catalogs $c_1, \dots, c_k$, the augmented catalogs $A_1, \dots, A_k$ are built from the last one backwards: $A_k = c_k$, and for $i < k$, $A_i$ is the sorted merge of $c_i$ with the sample (every other element, starting with the first) of $A_{i+1}$. The empty list of catalogs has no augmented catalogs.
nodes.title: Augmented catalogs

nodes.summary: For every list $cs$ of catalogs over a linearly ordered type, the list of augmented catalogs built from $cs$ has the same length as $cs$: there is one augmented catalog per catalog.
nodes.title: Number of augmented catalogs

nodes.summary: For every catalog $c$, the list of augmented catalogs of the one-element list $[c]$ is $[c]$: the only augmented catalog is $c$ itself.
nodes.title: Augmenting a single catalog

nodes.summary: If every catalog in a list of catalogs over a linear order is sorted in nondecreasing order, then every augmented catalog built from that list is sorted in nondecreasing order.
nodes.title: The augmented catalogs of sorted catalogs are sorted

nodes.summary: For every list $cs = [c_1, \dots, c_k]$ of catalogs over a linearly ordered type, every augmented catalog built from $cs$ has length at most $|c_1| + \dots + |c_k|$.
nodes.title: Augmented catalogs are bounded by the total input size

nodes.summary: For a catalog $L$ and a value $v$, the bridge pointer of $v$ into $L$ is the number of elements of $L$ that are $\le v$.
nodes.title: Bridge pointer

nodes.summary: For every catalog $L$ and value $v$, the bridge pointer of $v$ into $L$ is at most the length of $L$.
nodes.title: Bridge pointers are at most the catalog length

nodes.summary: For catalogs $C$ and $L$, the bridge pointers of $C$ into $L$ form the list obtained by replacing each entry $v$ of $C$, in order, by the bridge pointer of $v$ into $L$.
nodes.title: Bridge pointer list

nodes.summary: For lists $c$ and $d$ over a linearly ordered type, the list of bridge pointers of $c$ into $d$ has the same length as $c$: there is one bridge pointer per entry of $c$.
nodes.title: Number of bridge pointers

nodes.summary: For lists $c$ and $d$ over a linearly ordered type, every entry $p$ of the list of bridge pointers of $c$ into $d$ satisfies $p \le |d|$, where $|d|$ is the length of $d$; so every recorded bridge pointer is a boundary index of $d$.
nodes.title: Bridge pointers are at most the next catalog's length

nodes.summary: For a value $x$ and a list of catalogs, the search returns, for each catalog in order, the number of its elements that are $< x$, computed by a direct scan of that catalog. This is the lower-bound position of $x$ in each catalog.
nodes.title: Searching every catalog

nodes.summary: Searching the empty list of catalogs for any value $x$ gives the empty list of positions.
nodes.title: Searching no catalogs

nodes.summary: For a value $x$, a catalog $c$ and a list of catalogs $cs$, searching $c$ followed by $cs$ for $x$ gives first the direct-scan count of the elements of $c$ that are $< x$, followed by the positions obtained by searching $cs$ for $x$.
nodes.title: Searching a nonempty list of catalogs

nodes.summary: For every value $x$ and every list $cs$ of catalogs over a linearly ordered type, searching each catalog of $cs$ for $x$ gives a list of positions of the same length as $cs$.
nodes.title: One search position per catalog

nodes.summary: For a value $x$ and a list of catalogs $c_1, \dots, c_k$, searching every catalog for $x$ returns the list whose $i$-th entry is the lower bound of $x$ in $c_i$, that is, the number of elements of $c_i$ that are $< x$.
nodes.title: Correctness of searching every catalog

nodes.summary: For every value $x$, list of catalogs $C_0, \dots, C_{k-1}$ and index $i$: if $i < k$, the $i$-th position returned by searching all catalogs for $x$ is the lower bound of $x$ in $C_i$; if $i \ge k$, the search result has no $i$-th entry.
nodes.title: Search positions are lower bounds, index by index

nodes.summary: Let $x$ be a value and let $cs$ be a list of catalogs whose entry at index $i$ is the catalog $c$. Then searching every catalog of $cs$ for $x$ gives, at index $i$, the lower bound of $x$ in $c$ (the number of elements of $c$ that are $< x$), and this lower bound is at most the length of $c$.
nodes.title: Search positions are boundary indices

nodes.summary: For a value $x$ and a list of catalogs, the augmented search builds the augmented catalogs and returns, for each augmented catalog in order, the number of its elements that are $< x$, computed by a direct scan of that catalog.
nodes.title: Searching every augmented catalog

nodes.summary: For every value $x$ and every list $cs$ of catalogs over a linearly ordered type, searching each augmented catalog built from $cs$ for $x$ gives a list of positions of the same length as $cs$.
nodes.title: One augmented search position per catalog

nodes.summary: For a value $x$ and a list of catalogs $cs$, searching every augmented catalog of $cs$ for $x$ returns, for each augmented catalog in order, the lower bound of $x$ in it, that is, the number of its elements that are $< x$.
nodes.title: Correctness of augmented search
Interval tree

nodes.summary: An interval is a pair of integers, its low endpoint and its high endpoint, read as the closed interval from the low to the high endpoint. The structure itself imposes no order on the endpoints; the public update operations accept an interval only when its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint.
nodes.title: Interval

nodes.summary: A closed interval with integer endpoints $a$ (low) and $b$ (high) is valid when its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint, $a \le b$.
nodes.title: Valid interval

nodes.summary: For an interval $[a, b]$ with integer endpoints, the Boolean validity test returns true exactly when $a \le b$.
nodes.title: Boolean interval validity test

nodes.summary: An interval $I$ with low endpoint $a$ and high endpoint $b$ overlaps an interval $J$ with low endpoint $c$ and high endpoint $d$ when $a \le d$ and $c \le b$; in particular, intervals that share only an endpoint overlap.
nodes.title: Overlapping closed intervals

nodes.summary: For an interval $I$ with low endpoint $a$ and high endpoint $b$ and an interval $J$ with low endpoint $c$ and high endpoint $d$, the overlap test of $I$ against $J$ returns true exactly when $a \le d$ and $c \le b$; it compares $a$ with $d$ first and returns false without the second comparison when $a > d$.
nodes.title: Overlap test for closed intervals

nodes.summary: For an interval $I$ with low endpoint $a$ and high endpoint $b$ and an interval $J$ with low endpoint $c$ and high endpoint $d$, the instrumented overlap test of $I$ against $J$ returns the pair (false, $1$) when $a > d$, the pair (false, $2$) when $a \le d$ and $c > b$, and the pair (true, $2$) when $a \le d$ and $c \le b$; the number is the count of endpoint comparisons evaluated.
nodes.title: Overlap test with comparison count

nodes.summary: For intervals $I$ and $J$, the Boolean component of the instrumented overlap test of $I$ against $J$ equals the overlap test of $I$ against $J$.
nodes.title: The instrumented overlap test returns the plain result

nodes.summary: For intervals $I$ and $J$, the instrumented overlap test of $I$ against $J$ reports $2$ endpoint comparisons when the low endpoint of $I$ is at most the high endpoint of $J$, and $1$ comparison otherwise.
nodes.title: Comparison count of the overlap test

nodes.summary: An entry of the interval tree consists of an identifier, which is a natural number, and an interval with integer low and high endpoints.
nodes.title: Interval tree entry

nodes.summary: The key of an entry is the pair $(\ell, i) \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$, where $\ell$ is the low endpoint of the entry's interval and $i$ is the entry's identifier.
nodes.title: Search key of an interval entry

nodes.summary: For keys $(a, i)$ and $(b, j)$ in $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ (a low endpoint and an occurrence identifier), the comparison returns less-than if $a < b$, or if $a = b$ and $i < j$; greater-than if $a > b$, or if $a = b$ and $i > j$; and equal if $a = b$ and $i = j$.
nodes.title: Lexicographic comparison of keys

nodes.summary: A cost record for the interval tree consists of seven natural-number counters, each defaulting to $0$: node visits, key comparisons, endpoint comparisons, cached-maximum reads, cache writes, rotations, and identifier-index operations.
nodes.title: Operation cost counters for interval trees

nodes.summary: An interval tree is either empty or a node consisting of a left subtree, an entry, a right subtree and three cached fields: a height and a size (natural numbers) and a maximum high endpoint (an integer). The type imposes no balance or consistency condition on these fields; it is the carrier on which the AVL interval-tree operations act.
nodes.title: Interval tree

nodes.summary: The cached maximum of an interval tree is no value when the tree is empty, and when the tree is a node it is the integer stored in the node's cached maximum-high-endpoint field.
nodes.title: Cached maximum of an interval tree

nodes.summary: For an integer $a$ and an optional integer $v$, the value is $a$ when $v$ is absent and $\max(a, v)$ when $v$ is present. It combines a value with an optional subtree maximum without using a sentinel value.
nodes.title: Maximum with an optional value

nodes.summary: For subtrees $L$ and $R$ and an entry $e$, the node maximum is the largest of the high endpoint of the interval of $e$, the cached maximum high endpoint stored at the root of $L$, and the one stored at the root of $R$, where an empty subtree stores no cached maximum and contributes nothing.
nodes.title: Maximum high endpoint at a node

nodes.summary: For an interval tree $T$ write $h(T)$ and $|T|$ for its cached height and size, both $0$ for the empty tree. Given interval trees $L$ and $R$ and an entry $e$, this builds the node with left subtree $L$, entry $e$ and right subtree $R$ whose cached height is $\max(h(L), h(R)) + 1$, whose cached size is $|L| + |R| + 1$, and whose cached maximum high endpoint is the largest of the high endpoint of $e$ and the cached…
nodes.title: Node construction with repaired metadata

nodes.summary: An interval tree satisfies the cache invariant when every cached field is exact, recursively. The empty tree satisfies it. A node with stored height $h$, stored size $s$, stored maximum $m$, left subtree $L$, entry $e$ and right subtree $R$ satisfies it when $L$ and $R$ satisfy it, $m$ is at least the high endpoint of every entry of $L$, of $e$ and of every entry of $R$, $m$ equals the high endpoint of one of these…
nodes.title: Cache invariant of an interval tree

nodes.summary: The empty tree is low-endpoint ordered, and a node is low-endpoint ordered when both of its subtrees are low-endpoint ordered, every interval in the left subtree has low endpoint at most the low endpoint of the node's interval, and the node's low endpoint is at most the low endpoint of every interval in the right subtree.
nodes.title: Low-endpoint ordered interval tree

nodes.summary: A tree satisfies the validity invariant when every interval stored in it is valid, that is, its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint. Recursively, the empty tree satisfies it, and a node satisfies it when its left subtree does, the interval of its entry is valid, and its right subtree does.
nodes.title: Validity invariant of an interval tree

nodes.summary: Write $\langle L, x, R\rangle$ for a node with left subtree $L$, entry $x$ and right subtree $R$. The right rotation sends $\langle\langle a, x, b\rangle, y, c\rangle$ to $\langle a, x, \langle b, y, c\rangle\rangle$, where both nodes of the result get freshly recomputed height, size and maximum high endpoint. Every tree not of this shape is returned unchanged.
nodes.title: Right rotation

nodes.summary: Write $\langle L, x, R\rangle$ for a node with left subtree $L$, entry $x$ and right subtree $R$. The left rotation sends $\langle a, x, \langle b, y, c\rangle\rangle$ to $\langle\langle a, x, b\rangle, y, c\rangle$, where both nodes of the result get freshly recomputed height, size and maximum high endpoint. Every tree not of this shape is returned unchanged.
nodes.title: Left rotation

nodes.summary: Write $\langle L, x, R\rangle$ for a node with left subtree $L$, entry $x$ and right subtree $R$. The left-right rotation sends $\langle\langle a, x, \langle b, y, c\rangle\rangle, z, d\rangle$ to $\langle\langle a, x, b\rangle, y, \langle c, z, d\rangle\rangle$, where all three nodes of the result get freshly recomputed height, size and maximum high endpoint. Every tree not of this shape is returned unchanged.
nodes.title: Left-right double rotation

nodes.summary: Write $\langle L, x, R\rangle$ for a node with left subtree $L$, entry $x$ and right subtree $R$. The right-left rotation sends $\langle a, x, \langle\langle b, y, c\rangle, z, d\rangle\rangle$ to $\langle\langle a, x, b\rangle, y, \langle c, z, d\rangle\rangle$, where all three nodes of the result get freshly recomputed height, size and maximum high endpoint. Every tree not of this shape is returned unchanged.
nodes.title: Right-left double rotation

nodes.summary: Rebalancing a tree $T$ returns a tree and a cost, where heights are the stored heights. If $T$ is empty, or neither subtree of its root is more than one taller than the other, it returns $T$ unchanged with zero cost. If the left subtree $L$ is more than one taller than the right subtree, it applies a right rotation, costing $2$ cache writes and one rotation, when the left child of $L$ is at least as tall as the…
nodes.title: AVL rebalancing step with cost

nodes.summary: Inserting an entry $x$ into a tree returns a new tree together with an operation cost; keys (low endpoint, then identifier) are compared lexicographically. Into the empty tree, $x$ is inserted as a single node, at a cost of one node visit and one cache write. At a node with entry $y$: if the key of $x$ equals the key of $y$, then $y$ is replaced by $x$, at a cost of one node visit, one key comparison and one cache…
nodes.title: Keyed insertion with cost

nodes.summary: Removing the leftmost entry of an interval tree $T$ returns nothing when $T$ is empty. When the root's left subtree is empty, it returns the root entry, the right subtree, and a cost of one node visit. Otherwise it removes the leftmost entry $m$ of the left subtree recursively (returning nothing if that fails), rebuilds the root node over the new left subtree with recomputed height, size and maximum high endpoint,…
nodes.title: Removing the leftmost entry, with its cost

nodes.summary: Erasing a key $k \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ from an interval tree returns a new tree together with its cost; the key of an entry is the pair of its low endpoint and identifier, and keys are compared lexicographically. The empty tree is returned unchanged at a cost of one node visit. At a node with entry $x$, the key $k$ is compared with the key of $x$. If $k$ is smaller, $k$ is erased from the left subtree;…
nodes.title: Keyed erasure with cost
