nodes.summary: Given a query interval $q = [c, d]$ and an interval tree $T$, the instrumented overlap search returns an optional entry together with a cost record, defined by recursion on $T$. On the empty tree it returns no entry and records one node visit. At a node with left subtree $L$, entry $e$ with interval $[a, b]$ and right subtree $R$, it first tests overlap by evaluating $a \le d$ and, only if that holds, $c \le b$;…
nodes.title: Instrumented overlap search

nodes.summary: For every query interval $q$, the instrumented overlap search of $q$ in the empty interval tree returns no entry, and its cost record counts one node visit and zero for every other counter (key comparisons, endpoint comparisons, cached-maximum reads, cache writes, rotations and index operations).
nodes.title: Instrumented search in the empty tree

nodes.summary: Let $e$ be an entry whose interval is $[a, b]$, let $q = [c, d]$ be a query interval, and let $k = 2$ if $a \le d$ and $k = 1$ otherwise. Consider the single-node tree built from $e$ with empty subtrees and exact cached fields. If $[a, b]$ and $[c, d]$ overlap (that is, $a \le d$ and $c \le b$), the instrumented overlap search of $q$ in this tree returns $e$ with a cost record of one node visit and $k$ endpoint…
nodes.title: Instrumented search in a one-entry tree

nodes.summary: The overlap search of a query interval $q$ in an interval tree $T$ returns the optional entry produced by the instrumented overlap search of $q$ in $T$, discarding its cost record.
nodes.title: Interval-tree overlap search

nodes.summary: For a tree $T$ and a query interval $q$, the oracle search returns the first entry, in the in-order list of entries of $T$, whose interval overlaps $q$ as closed intervals, and returns nothing when no entry's interval overlaps $q$.
nodes.title: Linear-scan overlap search

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree whose cached height, size and maximum high endpoint are exact at every node, and whose low endpoints respect the search order (at every node, low endpoints in the left subtree are at most the node's, and those in the right subtree at least the node's). If some entry stored in $T$ has an interval that overlaps the query interval $Q$ (each interval's low endpoint is at most the other's…
nodes.title: Completeness of interval-tree search

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree whose cached height, size and maximum high endpoint are exact at every node, and whose low endpoints respect the search order (at every node, low endpoints in the left subtree are at most the node's, and those in the right subtree at least the node's). Then searching $T$ for a query interval $Q$ returns nothing if and only if no entry stored in $T$ has an interval that overlaps $Q$ (each…
nodes.title: Interval-tree search fails exactly when nothing overlaps

nodes.summary: The Boolean cache check returns true on the empty tree. On a node with stored height $h$, stored size $s$, stored maximum $m$, left subtree $L$, entry $e$ and right subtree $R$ it returns true exactly when $h = \max(\operatorname{height} L, \operatorname{height} R) + 1$, $s = \operatorname{size} L + \operatorname{size} R + 1$, $m$ is the largest of the high endpoint of $e$ and the cached maxima of those of $L$ and…
nodes.title: Executable cache check for interval trees

nodes.summary: Given an optional lower bound, an optional upper bound and a key $k$ (a pair of an integer and a natural number), this test returns true exactly when the lower bound is absent or strictly below $k$, and the upper bound is absent or strictly above $k$. Keys are compared lexicographically: first by the integer, then by the natural number.
nodes.title: Key between optional bounds

nodes.summary: Keys of entries are pairs (low endpoint, identifier), ordered lexicographically. Given optional lower and upper key bounds $\ell$ and $u$, the check accepts the empty tree, and accepts a node with left subtree $L$, entry $e$ and right subtree $R$ exactly when the key $k$ of $e$ is strictly greater than $\ell$ if $\ell$ is present and strictly less than $u$ if $u$ is present, the interval of $e$ has low endpoint at…
nodes.title: Ordered-and-valid check for interval trees

nodes.summary: The balance check returns true on the empty tree. On a node whose left and right subtrees have stored heights $h_L$ and $h_R$ (the empty tree has height $0$), it returns true exactly when the node's stored height equals $\max(h_L, h_R) + 1$, $h_L \le h_R + 1$, $h_R \le h_L + 1$, and the check returns true on both subtrees.
nodes.title: Boolean AVL balance check for interval trees

nodes.summary: An interval tree is AVL balanced with exact stored heights when it is empty, or when it is a node such that, writing $h_L$ and $h_R$ for the stored heights of its left and right subtrees (the empty tree has height $0$), the node's stored height equals $\max(h_L, h_R) + 1$, $h_L \le h_R + 1$, $h_R \le h_L + 1$, and both subtrees are again AVL balanced with exact stored heights.
nodes.title: AVL balance of an interval tree

nodes.summary: The empty tree is key-ordered, and a node is key-ordered when both of its subtrees are key-ordered, the key of every entry in the left subtree is strictly less than the key of the node's entry, and the key of the node's entry is strictly less than the key of every entry in the right subtree. Keys are compared lexicographically: low endpoint first, then identifier.
nodes.title: Key-ordered interval tree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be an interval tree and let $\ell$ and $u$ be optional keys in $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$. If the executable ordering check of $t$ with lower bound $\ell$ and upper bound $u$ succeeds, then $t$ is key-ordered, and every entry $e$ stored in $t$ satisfies $\ell < \operatorname{key}(e)$ when $\ell$ is present and $\operatorname{key}(e) < u$ when $u$ is present, where $<$ is the lexicographic order on keys…
nodes.title: The executable ordering check implies key ordering

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be an interval tree and let $\ell$ and $u$ be optional keys in $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$. If the executable ordering check of $t$ with lower bound $\ell$ and upper bound $u$ succeeds, then $t$ is low-endpoint ordered, and every entry $e$ stored in $t$ satisfies $\ell < \operatorname{key}(e)$ when $\ell$ is present and $\operatorname{key}(e) < u$ when $u$ is present, where $<$ is the lexicographic order…
nodes.title: The executable ordering check implies low-endpoint ordering

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree and let $\ell$ and $u$ be optional lower and upper key bounds. If the executable check of $T$ with bounds $\ell$ and $u$, which tests that every key lies strictly between its bounds and that every stored interval passes the Boolean validity test, returns true, then every interval stored in $T$ is valid, that is, its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint.
nodes.title: The ordering check implies interval validity

nodes.summary: If removing the leftmost entry of a tree $T$ returns an entry $m$, a tree $T'$ and a cost, then the list consisting of $m$ followed by the in-order entries of $T'$ is a permutation of the in-order entries of $T$.
nodes.title: Removing the minimum preserves the other entries

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a tree whose entries are strictly ordered by key, and let $x$ be an entry. The in-order list of entries of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ by key is a permutation of the list consisting of $x$ followed by those entries of $t$ whose key differs from the key of $x$.
nodes.title: Entries after keyed insertion

nodes.summary: The key of an entry is the pair $(\ell, i) \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ of its low endpoint $\ell$ and identifier $i$; keys are compared lexicographically. Let $T$ be an interval tree whose keys are strictly ordered (every key in a left subtree is lexicographically below its node's key and every key in a right subtree is above it), and let $k \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ be a key. Then the in-order list…
nodes.title: Keyed erasure removes exactly the entries with that key

nodes.summary: If a tree is strictly ordered by key, then the keys of its stored entries are pairwise distinct.
nodes.title: Strictly key-ordered trees have distinct keys

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a key-ordered interval tree: at every node, the keys in the left subtree are strictly smaller and those in the right subtree strictly larger than the node's key, where the key of an entry is the pair (low endpoint, identifier) compared lexicographically. If removing the leftmost entry of $T$ returns the entry $m$ (together with the remaining tree and a cost record), then every entry $e$ stored in $T$ is…
nodes.title: The removed minimum has the least key

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a key-ordered interval tree and let $e$ be an entry. Then the tree returned by the cost-instrumented keyed insertion of $e$ into $t$ (which replaces the entry with the same key, if there is one; the reported cost is discarded) is again key-ordered.
nodes.title: Insertion into an interval tree preserves key ordering

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a key-ordered interval tree. If the cost-instrumented removal of the leftmost entry of $t$ succeeds, returning that entry, a remaining tree $t'$ and a cost, then $t'$ is key-ordered.
nodes.title: Removing the minimum from an interval tree preserves key ordering

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a key-ordered interval tree and let $k \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ be a key. Then the tree returned by the cost-instrumented keyed deletion of $k$ from $t$ (the reported cost is discarded) is again key-ordered.
nodes.title: Deletion from an interval tree preserves key ordering

nodes.summary: Let $L$ and $R$ be interval trees that are AVL balanced with exact stored heights, with heights $h_L$ and $h_R$ satisfying $h_L \le h_R + 2$ and $h_R \le h_L + 2$. Let $N$ be a node with left subtree $L$, entry $e$ and right subtree $R$ whose stored height is $\max(h_L, h_R) + 1$ (its stored size and stored maximum are arbitrary), and let $B$ be the tree obtained by rebalancing $N$ (the tree component of the…
nodes.title: Rebalancing an interval-tree node with exact stored height restores AVL balance

nodes.summary: Let $L$ and $R$ be interval trees that are AVL balanced with exact stored heights, with heights $h_L$ and $h_R$ satisfying $h_L \le h_R + 2$ and $h_R \le h_L + 2$, and let $e$ be an entry. Let $B$ be the tree obtained by rebalancing the node that the smart constructor builds from $L$, $e$ and $R$ (the tree component of the result; the cost is ignored). Then $B$ is AVL balanced with exact stored heights, the height…
nodes.title: Rebalancing a rebuilt interval-tree node restores AVL balance

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree that is AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and let $e$ be an entry. The tree $T'$ returned by keyed insertion of $e$ into $T$ (which replaces an entry with the same key, if there is one; we take the tree component of the result and ignore the cost) is again AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and the height of $T'$ is either the height of $T$ or one more.
nodes.title: Keyed insertion preserves AVL balance in an interval tree

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree that is AVL balanced with exact stored heights. If removing the leftmost entry of $T$ succeeds and returns an entry $m$, a remaining tree $R$ and a cost $c$, then $R$ is AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and the height of $R$ is either the height of $T$ or one less.
nodes.title: Removing the minimum preserves AVL balance in an interval tree

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree that is AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and let $k$ be a key (a pair of an integer low endpoint and a natural-number identifier). The tree $T'$ returned by keyed deletion of $k$ from $T$ (the tree component of the result; the cost is ignored) is again AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and the height of $T'$ is either the height of $T$ or one less.
nodes.title: Keyed deletion preserves AVL balance in an interval tree

nodes.summary: If $L$ and $R$ are interval trees satisfying the validity invariant and $e$ is an entry whose interval $[a, b]$ satisfies $a \le b$, then the node with left subtree $L$, entry $e$ and right subtree $R$, built by the node constructor that recomputes the cached fields, satisfies the validity invariant.
nodes.title: Node construction preserves interval validity

nodes.summary: If an interval tree $T$ satisfies the validity invariant, then every entry stored in $T$ has an interval $[a, b]$ with $a \le b$.
nodes.title: Stored intervals of a valid tree are valid

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree in which every stored interval $[a, b]$ satisfies $a \le b$, and let $e$ be an entry whose interval $[a, b]$ satisfies $a \le b$. Then the tree returned by keyed insertion of $e$ into $T$ also has every stored interval $[a, b]$ satisfying $a \le b$.
nodes.title: Keyed insertion preserves interval validity

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree in which every stored interval is valid (its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint). If the instrumented removal of the leftmost entry of $T$ succeeds, returning that entry $m$, the remaining tree $T'$ and a cost record $c$, then every interval stored in $T'$ is valid.
nodes.title: Removing the minimum preserves interval validity

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree in which every stored interval $[a, b]$ satisfies $a \le b$. Then for every key $(\ell, i)$ with $\ell$ an integer and $i$ a natural number, the tree returned by keyed erasure of $(\ell, i)$ from $T$ also has every stored interval $[a, b]$ satisfying $a \le b$.
nodes.title: Keyed erasure preserves interval validity

nodes.summary: An indexed interval tree consists of a root interval tree together with an identifier index: a finite map, implemented as a balanced search tree, from natural-number identifiers to integer low endpoints.
nodes.title: Indexed interval tree

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an indexed interval tree and let $e$ be an entry with identifier $i$ and interval $[a, b]$. Inserting $e$ into $T$ first tests $a \le b$. If $a > b$, it returns no tree, at a cost of one endpoint comparison. Otherwise, if the identifier index of $T$ maps $i$ to a low endpoint $\ell$, the entry with key $(\ell, i)$ is erased from the root tree of $T$ by keyed erasure; if $i$ is not in the index, the root…
nodes.title: Insertion by identifier with cost

nodes.summary: To erase identifier $i$ from an indexed interval tree, look $i$ up in the identifier index. If it is absent, the tree is returned unchanged at a cost of one index operation. If the index maps $i$ to a low endpoint $\ell$, the entry with key $(\ell, i)$ is erased from the underlying interval tree, $i$ is removed from the index, and the cost is the cost of the keyed erasure plus two index operations.
nodes.title: Erasure by identifier with cost

nodes.summary: For an indexed interval tree, the forward index check returns true exactly when the identifier index maps the identifier of every stored entry to the low endpoint of that entry's interval.
nodes.title: Forward identifier-index check

nodes.summary: For an indexed interval tree, the backward index check returns true exactly when, for every identifier $i$ that the identifier index maps to a low endpoint $\ell$, some stored entry has identifier $i$ and an interval with low endpoint $\ell$.
nodes.title: Backward identifier-index check

nodes.summary: For an indexed interval tree, the check returns true exactly when all of the following hold: at every node the cached height and size agree with the values recomputed from its children's cached heights and sizes, and the cached maximum high endpoint equals the largest of the node's own high endpoint and its children's cached maxima; the tree is AVL-balanced (sibling heights differ by at most one) with exact stored…
nodes.title: Representation check for the indexed interval tree

nodes.summary: An indexed interval tree $T$ satisfies the representation invariant when its root tree has exact cached metadata (heights, sizes, and attained maximum high endpoints), is strictly ordered by the composite key (low endpoint, then identifier), is AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and stores only valid intervals; the identifiers of the stored entries are pairwise distinct; the identifier index maps the…
nodes.title: Representation invariant of an indexed interval tree

nodes.summary: If interval trees $L$ and $R$ satisfy the cache invariant (every cached maximum high endpoint, height and size is exact), then for every entry $e$ the node that the smart constructor builds from $L$, $e$ and $R$ also satisfies the cache invariant.
nodes.title: The interval-tree smart constructor preserves the cache invariant

nodes.summary: If the executable cache check returns true on an interval tree $t$, then $t$ satisfies the cache invariant.
nodes.title: The executable cache check implies the cache invariant

nodes.summary: If an interval tree $t$ satisfies the cache invariant, then so does the right rotation of $t$, which leaves $t$ unchanged when $t$ is empty or has an empty left subtree.
nodes.title: Right rotation preserves the interval-tree cache invariant

nodes.summary: If an interval tree $t$ satisfies the cache invariant, then so does the left rotation of $t$, which leaves $t$ unchanged when $t$ is empty or has an empty right subtree.
nodes.title: Left rotation preserves the interval-tree cache invariant

nodes.summary: If an interval tree $t$ satisfies the cache invariant, then so does the left-right double rotation of $t$, which leaves $t$ unchanged unless $t$ has a nonempty left subtree whose right subtree is nonempty.
nodes.title: Left-right rotation preserves the interval-tree cache invariant

nodes.summary: If an interval tree $t$ satisfies the cache invariant, then so does the right-left double rotation of $t$, which leaves $t$ unchanged unless $t$ has a nonempty right subtree whose left subtree is nonempty.
nodes.title: Right-left rotation preserves the interval-tree cache invariant

nodes.summary: If an interval tree $t$ satisfies the cache invariant, then the tree returned by the rebalancing step at the root of $t$ also satisfies the cache invariant.
nodes.title: Rebalancing preserves the interval-tree cache invariant

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree satisfying the cache invariant (every cached maximum high endpoint, height and size is exact), and let $e$ be an entry. The tree returned by keyed insertion of $e$ into $T$ (the tree component of the result; the cost is ignored) also satisfies the cache invariant. This includes the case where an entry with the same key is replaced.
nodes.title: Keyed insertion preserves the interval-tree cache invariant

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be an interval tree that satisfies the cache invariant. If removing the leftmost entry of $t$ succeeds and returns an entry, a tree $t'$ and an operation cost, then $t'$ satisfies the cache invariant.
nodes.title: Removing the minimum preserves the interval-tree cache invariant

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree satisfying the cache invariant (every cached maximum high endpoint, height and size is exact), and let $k$ be a key (a pair of an integer low endpoint and a natural-number identifier). The tree returned by keyed deletion of $k$ from $T$ (the tree component of the result; the cost is ignored) also satisfies the cache invariant. This includes keys that do not occur in $T$.
nodes.title: Keyed deletion preserves the interval-tree cache invariant

nodes.summary: If the executable checker returns true on an indexed interval tree $T$, then $T$ satisfies the representation invariant.
nodes.title: Soundness of the invariant checker

nodes.summary: The search of an indexed interval tree $T$ for a query interval $q = [c, d]$ returns nothing when $c > d$, and otherwise returns the entry, if any, found by the instrumented overlap search of $q$ in the root tree of $T$. For every indexed interval tree $T$, every query interval $q$ and every entry $e$, if this search returns $e$, then $e$ is one of the entries stored in the root tree of $T$ and the interval of $e$…
nodes.title: Soundness of indexed interval-tree search

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an indexed interval tree satisfying its representation invariant, and let $Q$ be a valid query interval (low endpoint at most high endpoint). If some entry stored in $T$ has an interval that overlaps $Q$ (each interval's low endpoint is at most the other's high endpoint), then searching $T$ for $Q$ returns some entry.
nodes.title: Completeness of indexed interval search

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an indexed interval tree satisfying the representation invariant, and let $x$ be an entry whose interval is valid (its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint). If inserting $x$ into $T$ succeeds with result $T'$, then $T'$ satisfies the representation invariant, $x$ is stored in the root tree of $T'$, and an entry $e$ is stored in the root tree of $T'$ if and only if either $e = x$, or $e$ is stored…
nodes.title: Correctness of insertion into an indexed interval tree

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an indexed interval tree satisfying the representation invariant, and let $i$ be a natural number. Then the tree obtained by erasing identifier $i$ from $T$ again satisfies the invariant, and an entry is stored in it if and only if it is stored in $T$ and its identifier differs from $i$.
nodes.title: Correctness of erasure from the indexed interval tree
k-d tree

nodes.summary: A kd-tree over points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ is either empty, a leaf holding one point of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, or a split node holding a split axis $a \in \{0, \dots, d-1\}$, a split value $s \in \mathbb{Z}$ and two kd-trees, its left and right subtrees.
nodes.title: Kd-trees

nodes.summary: For a kd-tree $t$ over points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and a list $\mathit{acc}$ of such points, the accumulator traversal of $t$ onto $\mathit{acc}$ is $\mathit{acc}$ when $t$ is empty, the point $p$ followed by $\mathit{acc}$ when $t$ is a leaf holding $p$, and, when $t$ is a split node with left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$, the traversal of $L$ onto the traversal of $R$ onto $\mathit{acc}$.
nodes.title: Kd-tree point traversal with an accumulator

nodes.summary: The point list of a kd-tree is the list of the points stored at its leaves, from left to right.
nodes.title: Point list of a kd-tree

nodes.summary: For every kd-tree $t$ over $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and every list $acc$ of points, the accumulator traversal of $t$ onto $acc$ equals the list of points of $t$ in left-to-right order followed by $acc$.
nodes.title: Accumulator traversal of a kd-tree

nodes.summary: For a split node with axis $a$, split value $s$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$, the point list of the node is the point list of $L$ followed by the point list of $R$.
nodes.title: Point list of a kd-tree split node

nodes.summary: The size of a kd-tree is defined by recursion: the empty tree has size $0$, a leaf has size $1$, and a split node has the sum of the sizes of its two children. Since points are stored only at leaves, this is the number of points stored in the tree, counted with multiplicity.
nodes.title: Size of a kd-tree

nodes.summary: For every kd-tree $t$, the list of the points stored in $t$, read from left to right, has length equal to the size of $t$, the number of points stored in $t$.
nodes.title: Length of the point list of a kd-tree

nodes.summary: For a dimension $d \ge 1$ and an axis $a \in \{0, \dots, d - 1\}$, the next split axis is $(a + 1) \bmod d$, so the axes are visited cyclically.
nodes.title: Next split axis of a kd-tree

nodes.summary: For $lo, hi, p \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, the point $p$ lies in the closed axis-aligned box $[lo, hi]$ when $lo_i \le p_i \le hi_i$ for every coordinate $i \in \{0, \dots, d-1\}$.
nodes.title: Membership in an axis-aligned box

nodes.summary: Points are vectors in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ with coordinates $p_0, \dots, p_{d-1}$; the box $[lo, hi]$ consists of the points $p$ with $lo_i \le p_i \le hi_i$ for every $i$. For a kd-tree $t$ and a list $acc$ of points, the accumulator report of $t$ for $[lo, hi]$ onto $acc$ is defined by recursion on $t$. For the empty tree it is $acc$. For a leaf $p$ it is $p$ followed by $acc$ if $p$ lies in the box, and $acc$…
nodes.title: Accumulator range report of a kd-tree

nodes.summary: For a kd-tree $t$ over $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and $lo, hi \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, the range report of $t$ for the box $[lo, hi]$ is the accumulator range report of $t$ for $[lo, hi]$ onto the empty list.
nodes.title: Orthogonal range report of a kd-tree

nodes.summary: A kd-tree satisfies the kd invariant when at every split node, with axis $a$ and split value $s$, every point of the left subtree has $a$-coordinate at most $s$ and every point of the right subtree has $a$-coordinate at least $s$.
nodes.title: Kd invariant

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid kd-tree over $\mathbb{Z}^d$, let $lo, hi \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, and let $acc$ be a list of points. The accumulator range report of $t$ for the box $[lo, hi]$ onto $acc$ equals the list of points of $t$, in left-to-right order, that lie in the box (the points $p$ with $lo_i \le p_i \le hi_i$ for every coordinate $i$), followed by $acc$.
nodes.title: Accumulator range report of a valid kd-tree

nodes.summary: For every valid kd-tree $t$ over $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and all $lo, hi \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, the range report of $t$ for the box $[lo, hi]$ equals the list of points of $t$, in left-to-right order, that lie in the box, that is, the points $p$ with $lo_i \le p_i \le hi_i$ for every coordinate $i$.
nodes.title: Correctness of the kd-tree range report

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a kd-tree over $\mathbb{Z}^d$ that satisfies the kd invariant, and let $lo, hi, p \in \mathbb{Z}^d$. Then $p$ occurs in the range report of $t$ for the box $[lo, hi]$ if and only if $p$ is one of the points stored in $t$ and $lo_i \le p_i \le hi_i$ for every coordinate $i$.
nodes.title: Range report of a valid kd-tree

nodes.summary: For an axis $a \in \{0, \dots, d-1\}$ and a list of points in $\mathbb{Z}^d$, this is the $a$-coordinate of the first point of the list, or $0$ if the list is empty.
nodes.title: First-point coordinate

nodes.summary: Let $d \ge 1$, let $a \in \{0, \dots, d-1\}$ be an axis and let $P$ be a list of points in $\mathbb{Z}^d$. The kd-tree built from $P$ starting at axis $a$ is the empty tree if $P$ is empty and the leaf holding $p$ if $P = [p]$. If $P$ has $n \ge 2$ points, sort $P$ by $a$-coordinate with merge sort, let $L$ be the first $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ points of the sorted list and $R$ the remaining ones. The result is the…
nodes.title: Kd-tree construction by median splits

nodes.summary: For $d \ge 1$, every axis $a$ and every list of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, the kd-tree built from the list by median splits starting at axis $a$ satisfies the kd invariant.
nodes.title: Median-split kd-trees satisfy the kd invariant

nodes.summary: For $d \ge 1$, every axis $a$ and every list of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, the point list of the kd-tree built from the list by median splits starting at axis $a$ is a permutation of the list.
nodes.title: Building a kd-tree preserves its points

nodes.summary: Let $d \ge 1$, let $a \in \{0, \dots, d-1\}$ and let $P$ be a list of points in $\mathbb{Z}^d$. A point $p \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ is stored in the kd-tree built from $P$ by median splits starting at axis $a$ if and only if $p$ occurs in $P$.
nodes.title: A built kd-tree holds the same points as its input

nodes.summary: Let $d \ge 1$. For every starting axis $a$ and every list $P$ of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, the size of the kd-tree built from $P$ starting at axis $a$ equals the length of $P$ (repeated points counted with multiplicity).
nodes.title: Size of a built kd-tree

nodes.summary: For $d \ge 1$ and a list of points in $\mathbb{Z}^d$, this is the kd-tree built from the list by alternating-axis median splits, starting with split axis $0$.
nodes.title: Kd-tree construction from the first axis

nodes.summary: For $d \ge 1$ and every list of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, the kd-tree built from the list by median splits starting at axis $0$ satisfies the kd invariant.
nodes.title: Kd-trees built from axis 0 satisfy the kd invariant

nodes.summary: For $d \ge 1$ and every list of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, the point list of the kd-tree built from the list by median splits starting at axis $0$ is a permutation of the list.
nodes.title: Building a kd-tree from axis 0 preserves its points

nodes.summary: Let $d \ge 1$. For every starting axis $a$, every list $P$ of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and all $lo, hi \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, let $T$ be the kd-tree built from $P$ starting at axis $a$. The range report of $T$ for the box $[lo, hi]$ equals the list of points of $T$, in left-to-right order, that lie in the box, that is, the points $p$ with $lo_i \le p_i \le hi_i$ for every coordinate $i$.
nodes.title: Range report of a built kd-tree as a filter

nodes.summary: Let $d \ge 1$. For every starting axis $a$, every list $P$ of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and all $lo, hi \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, the range report for the box $[lo, hi]$ of the kd-tree built from $P$ starting at axis $a$ is a permutation of the list of entries of $P$ that lie in the box, that is, the points $p$ with $lo_i \le p_i \le hi_i$ for every coordinate $i$.
nodes.title: Range report of a built kd-tree up to order

nodes.summary: Let $d \ge 1$, let $a \in \{0, \dots, d-1\}$, let $P$ be a list of points in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and let $lo, hi, p \in \mathbb{Z}^d$. Then $p$ occurs in the range report, for the box $[lo, hi]$, of the kd-tree built from $P$ by median splits starting at axis $a$ if and only if $p$ occurs in $P$ and $lo_i \le p_i \le hi_i$ for every coordinate $i$.
nodes.title: Membership in the range report of a built kd-tree

nodes.summary: Let $d \ge 1$, let $P$ be a list of points in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and let $lo, hi, p \in \mathbb{Z}^d$. Then $p$ occurs in the range report, for the box $[lo, hi]$, of the kd-tree built from $P$ by median splits starting at axis $0$ if and only if $p$ occurs in $P$ and $lo_i \le p_i \le hi_i$ for every coordinate $i$.
nodes.title: Range report of a kd-tree built from the first axis
Range tree

nodes.summary: A one-dimensional range tree over the integers is either empty, a single leaf holding an integer, or a binary node made of two integers $l$ and $h$ together with a left and a right subtree. The integers $l$ and $h$ are meant to cache the interval $[l, h]$ spanned by the leaf values of the node's subtree; the type does not enforce this, the bounds-correctness predicate does.
nodes.title: Range tree

nodes.summary: For a range tree $t$ and a list $a$ of integers, $\operatorname{aux}(t, a)$ is $a$ if $t$ is empty, the list $x$ followed by $a$ if $t$ is a single leaf with value $x$, and $\operatorname{aux}(L, \operatorname{aux}(R, a))$ if $t$ is a node with left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$.
nodes.title: Leaf traversal of a range tree with an accumulator

nodes.summary: The leaf list of a range tree $t$ is the list of the integers stored at its leaves, read from left to right and with repetitions.
nodes.title: Leaf list of a range tree

nodes.summary: For every range tree $t$ and every list $a$ of integers, the accumulator leaf traversal of $t$ started from $a$ equals the leaf list of $t$ followed by $a$.
nodes.title: Range-tree leaf traversal appends to its accumulator

nodes.summary: For all integers $lo$, $hi$ and range trees $L$, $R$, the leaf list of the node with stored bounds $lo$, $hi$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ is the leaf list of $L$ followed by the leaf list of $R$.
nodes.title: Leaf list of a range-tree node

nodes.summary: The size of a range tree is its number of leaves: $0$ for the empty tree, $1$ for a leaf, and the sum of the sizes of the two children for a node.
nodes.title: Number of leaves of a range tree

nodes.summary: For every range tree $t$, the list of leaf values of $t$ read from left to right has length equal to the number of leaves of $t$.
nodes.title: Length of the leaf list of a range tree

nodes.summary: For a range tree $t$, $\operatorname{tmin}(t)$ is $0$ if $t$ is empty, $x$ if $t$ is a single leaf with value $x$, and the stored lower bound $lo$ if $t$ is a node with stored bounds $lo$, $hi$ and two subtrees.
nodes.title: Cached lower bound of a range tree

nodes.summary: For a range tree $t$, $\operatorname{tmax}(t)$ is $0$ if $t$ is empty, $x$ if $t$ is a single leaf with value $x$, and the stored upper bound $hi$ if $t$ is a node with stored bounds $lo$, $hi$ and two subtrees.
nodes.title: Cached upper bound of a range tree

nodes.summary: For a range tree $s$, write $s_{\min}$ and $s_{\max}$ for its cached lower and upper bounds: the stored interval endpoints at a node, the value itself at a leaf, and $0$ for the empty tree. Bounds-validity is defined inductively: the empty tree and every leaf are bounds-valid, and a node with cached interval $[a, b]$, left child $\ell$ and right child $r$ is bounds-valid when $\ell$ and $r$ are bounds-valid, each…
nodes.title: Bounds-valid range trees

nodes.summary: A range tree $t$ is valid when it has correct cached bounds (every node has two subtrees with nonempty leaf lists, and its stored lower and upper bounds are the minimum of the lower bounds and the maximum of the upper bounds of its two subtrees, recursively) and its leaf list is sorted in nondecreasing order.
nodes.title: Valid range tree

nodes.summary: If a range tree $t$ is valid, then its list of leaf values, read from left to right, is sorted in nondecreasing order.
nodes.title: Valid range trees have sorted leaves

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a bounds-valid range tree, and write $t_{\min}$ and $t_{\max}$ for its cached lower and upper bounds. Then every leaf value $x$ of $t$ satisfies $t_{\min} \le x \le t_{\max}$.
nodes.title: Leaf values of a bounds-valid tree lie between the cached bounds

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a bounds-valid range tree with at least one leaf. Then the cached lower bound of $t$ and the cached upper bound of $t$ are both leaf values of $t$.
nodes.title: The cached bounds of a nonempty bounds-valid range tree are leaf values

nodes.summary: For integers $a$, $b$ and a list $\mathit{acc}$ of integers, the accumulator range report of a range tree for $[a, b]$ starting from $\mathit{acc}$ is defined by recursion on the tree. The empty tree returns $\mathit{acc}$. A leaf with value $x$ returns $x$ followed by $\mathit{acc}$ if $a \le x \le b$, and $\mathit{acc}$ otherwise. A node with cached interval $[l, h]$ returns $\mathit{acc}$ if $h < a$ or $b < l$;…
nodes.title: Accumulator range report

nodes.summary: The range report of a range tree $t$ for integers $a$ and $b$ is the accumulator range report of $t$ for $[a, b]$ starting from the empty list.
nodes.title: Range report

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a bounds-valid range tree, let $a$ and $b$ be integers and let $\mathit{acc}$ be a list of integers. Then the accumulator range report of $t$ for $[a, b]$ starting from $\mathit{acc}$ is the list of the leaf values $x$ of $t$ with $a \le x \le b$, in left-to-right order and with repetitions, followed by $\mathit{acc}$.
nodes.title: Accumulator range report of a bounds-valid range tree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a range tree satisfying the bounds-correctness predicate: every node has two subtrees with at least one leaf each and caches the least and the greatest leaf value of its subtree. For all integers $a$ and $b$, the range report of $t$ for $[a, b]$ equals the list of leaf values $x$ of $t$ with $a \le x \le b$, in left-to-right order.
nodes.title: Correctness of the range report

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a range tree satisfying the bounds-correctness predicate: every node has two subtrees with at least one leaf each and caches the least and the greatest leaf value of its subtree. For all integers $a$, $b$ and $x$, the value $x$ occurs in the range report of $t$ for $[a, b]$ if and only if $x$ is a leaf value of $t$ and $a \le x \le b$.
nodes.title: Membership in a range report

nodes.summary: For a range tree $t$ and integers $a$ and $b$, the range count of $t$ over $[a, b]$ is the length of the range report of $t$ for $[a, b]$.
nodes.title: Range count

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a bounds-valid range tree and let $a$ and $b$ be integers. Then the range count of $t$ over $[a, b]$ equals the number of leaves of $t$ whose value lies in $[a, b]$.
nodes.title: Range count of a bounds-valid tree

nodes.summary: For a range tree $s$, write $s_{\min}$ and $s_{\max}$ for its cached lower and upper bounds. The range tree built from a list $L$ of integers of length $n$ is defined by recursion on $n$: the empty list gives the empty tree, a one-element list $[x]$ gives the leaf $x$, and for $n \ge 2$ it is the node whose left child $\ell$ is the tree built from the first $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ entries of $L$, whose right child…
nodes.title: Building a range tree from a list

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ of integers, the leaf list of the range tree built from $xs$ is $xs$.
nodes.title: Building a range tree preserves the list

nodes.summary: For every list $\mathit{xs}$ of integers, the range tree built from $\mathit{xs}$ has exactly as many leaves as $\mathit{xs}$ has elements.
nodes.title: Size of a built range tree

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ of integers, the range tree built from $L$ by recursive halving is bounds-valid.
nodes.title: Built range trees are bounds-valid

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ of integers that is sorted in nondecreasing order, the range tree built from $xs$ is valid.
nodes.title: Building from a sorted list gives a valid range tree

nodes.summary: For every list $\mathit{xs}$ of integers and all integers $a$ and $b$, the range report for $[a, b]$ on the range tree built from $\mathit{xs}$ equals the list of elements $x$ of $\mathit{xs}$ with $a \le x \le b$, in their original order.
nodes.title: Range report on a built tree

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ of integers and all integers $a$ and $b$, the range count over $[a, b]$ of the range tree built from $L$ equals the number of entries of $L$, counted with multiplicity, that lie in $[a, b]$.
nodes.title: Range counting on a built tree

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ of integers and all integers $a$, $b$ and $x$, the value $x$ occurs in the range report for $[a, b]$ on the range tree built from $L$ if and only if $x$ is an entry of $L$ and $a \le x \le b$.
nodes.title: Range report membership on a built tree
Region quadtree
Quadtree carrier and structural invariants

nodes.summary: A finite region quadtree with a value leaf or four ordered quadrants.
nodes.title: Region quadtree

nodes.summary: The maximum number of branches from the root to a leaf.
nodes.title: Height of a quadtree

nodes.summary: Every subtree is compressed and no branch has four identical leaves. Identical nonleaf children are allowed: they need not represent a constant.
nodes.title: Compressed quadtree

nodes.summary: Selects low/low, low/high, high/low, or high/high, respectively, when `(x, y)` is `(true, true)`, `(true, false)`, `(false, true)`, or `(false, false)`. In lookup, `true` means that the corresponding coordinate is below the split.
nodes.title: Quadrant selection by coordinate flags

nodes.summary: A bound on branch height bounds all four child heights one level lower.
nodes.title: Height bound for the children of a quadtree branch
Boolean region quadtree operations

nodes.summary: A branch constructor that collapses four identical Boolean leaves. This is local compression, not recursive normalization of its arguments.
nodes.title: Compressing branch constructor for Boolean quadtrees

nodes.summary: Boolean lookup with `false` on a nonleaf at scale zero. Leaves ignore coordinates; positive scales use the shared quadrant order.
nodes.title: Boolean quadtree lookup

nodes.summary: Complements every leaf, compressing the rebuilt branches.
nodes.title: Complement of a Boolean quadtree

nodes.summary: Boolean union, short-circuiting constant regions and compressing branches when both inputs are branches.
nodes.title: Union of Boolean quadtrees

nodes.summary: Ordered Boolean difference: cells in the first region but not the second. A full first region complements the second; an empty second returns the first.
nodes.title: Difference of Boolean quadtrees

nodes.summary: Local compression never increases a branch's height.
nodes.title: Local compression does not increase quadtree height

nodes.summary: Four compressed children produce a compressed result.
nodes.title: Local compression of compressed children is compressed

nodes.summary: Compression preserves positive-scale lookup. Scale zero is excluded: collapsing four `true` leaves changes a branch's zero-scale default.
nodes.title: Local compression preserves lookup at positive scales

nodes.summary: Complementation does not increase height.
nodes.title: Quadtree complementation does not increase height

nodes.summary: Complementation preserves compression of the input.
nodes.title: Quadtree complementation preserves compression

nodes.summary: Complementation negates each lookup whenever the scale bounds height.
nodes.title: Quadtree complementation negates lookup at sufficient scale

nodes.summary: Union height is bounded by the maximum input height.
nodes.title: Height bound for quadtree union

nodes.summary: Difference height is bounded by the maximum input height.
nodes.title: Height bound for quadtree difference

nodes.summary: Union preserves compression when both inputs are compressed.
nodes.title: Quadtree union preserves compression

nodes.summary: Difference preserves compression when both inputs are compressed.
nodes.title: Quadtree difference preserves compression

Segment tree

nodes.summary: A segment tree with values in $\alpha$ is either empty, a leaf holding a value in $\alpha$, or an internal node holding a cached segment aggregate in $\alpha$, a cached segment length in $\mathbb{N}$, a left child and a right child, both segment trees.
nodes.title: Segment tree

nodes.summary: The aggregate of a segment tree with values in an additive monoid is $0$ for the empty tree, $x$ for a single leaf with value $x$, and the aggregate cached at the root for an internal node.
nodes.title: Aggregate of a segment tree

nodes.summary: The size of a segment tree is $0$ for the empty tree, $1$ for a leaf, and, for an internal node, the segment length cached at that node.
nodes.title: Size of a segment tree

nodes.summary: Given a segment tree and a list $acc$, the accumulator traversal returns $acc$ for the empty tree, the list $acc$ with $x$ prepended for a leaf with value $x$, and, for an internal node with left child $L$ and right child $R$, the traversal of $L$ starting from the result of the traversal of $R$ starting from $acc$.
nodes.title: Accumulator traversal of a segment tree

nodes.summary: The leaf list of a segment tree is the list of its leaf values from left to right: the empty list for the empty tree, $[x]$ for a leaf with value $x$, and the leaf list of the left child followed by the leaf list of the right child for an internal node.
nodes.title: Leaf list of a segment tree

nodes.summary: For every segment tree $t$ and every list $acc$, the accumulator traversal of $t$ starting from $acc$ returns the leaf list of $t$ followed by $acc$.
nodes.title: Accumulator traversal prepends the leaf list

nodes.summary: For every internal node of a segment tree, with any cached aggregate, any cached length, left child $L$ and right child $R$, its leaf list is the leaf list of $L$ followed by the leaf list of $R$.
nodes.title: Leaf list of an internal node

nodes.summary: Validity of a segment tree over an additive monoid is defined inductively: the empty tree and every leaf are valid, and an internal node with valid left child $L$ and valid right child $R$ is valid when its cached aggregate is the aggregate of $L$ plus the aggregate of $R$ and its cached length is the size of $L$ plus the size of $R$. Here the aggregate and size of the empty tree are $0$ and $0$, of a leaf with…
nodes.title: Valid segment trees

nodes.summary: If $t$ is a valid segment tree with values in an additive monoid, then the length of the list of leaf values of $t$, read from left to right, equals the size of $t$.
nodes.title: Size of a valid segment tree

nodes.summary: If $t$ is a valid segment tree with values in an additive monoid, then the aggregate of $t$ equals the sum of the leaf values of $t$, taken from left to right.
nodes.title: Aggregate of a valid segment tree

nodes.summary: The segment tree built from a list $L$ with entries in an additive monoid is the empty tree if $L$ is empty, and a single leaf with value $x$ if $L = (x)$. If $L$ has length $n \ge 2$, it is the internal node whose left child is the tree built from the first $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ entries of $L$, whose right child is the tree built from the remaining entries, and which caches the aggregate of the left child plus the…
nodes.title: Building a segment tree from a list

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ over an additive monoid, the segment tree built from $xs$ is valid.
nodes.title: Built segment trees are valid

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ with entries in an additive monoid, the leaf list of the segment tree built from $xs$ is $xs$.
nodes.title: Building a segment tree preserves the list

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ with entries in an additive monoid, the segment tree built from $xs$ has size equal to the length of $xs$.
nodes.title: Size of a built segment tree

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ with entries in an additive monoid, the aggregate of the segment tree built from $L$ equals the sum of the entries of $L$, taken from left to right.
nodes.title: Aggregate of a built segment tree

nodes.summary: For a segment tree $t$ with values in an additive monoid and natural numbers $l, r$, the range query over $[l, r)$, with positions counted from the start of the segment of $t$, is defined recursively. On the empty tree it is $0$. On a leaf with value $x$ it is $x$ if $l = 0 < r$, and $0$ otherwise. On an internal node with cached aggregate $a$, cached size $s$ and children $t_1, t_2$, it is $0$ if $r \le l$ or…
nodes.title: Range query on a segment tree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid segment tree with values in an additive monoid, let $(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ be its leaf values from left to right, and let $l, r$ be natural numbers. The range query over $[l, r)$ on $t$ returns $\sum_{l \le k < \min(r, n)} x_k$, the sum taken in increasing order of $k$; it is $0$ when $\min(r, n) \le l$.
nodes.title: Correctness of range queries on a valid segment tree

nodes.summary: Let $L = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ be a list with entries in an additive monoid and let $l, r$ be natural numbers. The range query over $[l, r)$ on the segment tree built from $L$ returns $\sum_{l \le k < \min(r, n)} x_k$, the sum taken in increasing order of $k$; it is $0$ when $\min(r, n) \le l$.
nodes.title: Range queries on a built segment tree

nodes.summary: The point update of a segment tree over an additive monoid at an index $i \in \mathbb{N}$, relative to the tree's segment, with a value $y$ is defined recursively. The empty tree stays empty. A leaf becomes a leaf with value $y$ if $i = 0$ and is unchanged otherwise. At an internal node with left child $L$ and right child $R$: if $i$ is less than the size of $L$, then $L$ is replaced by its point update at $i$ with…
nodes.title: Point update of a segment tree

nodes.summary: For every segment tree $t$ over an additive monoid, every index $i$ and every value $y$, the point update of $t$ at $i$ with $y$ has the same size as $t$.
nodes.title: Point update preserves the size of a segment tree

nodes.summary: If $t$ is a valid segment tree over an additive monoid, then for every natural number $i$ and every value $y$, the point update of $t$ at $i$ with $y$ is valid.
nodes.title: Point update preserves validity

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid segment tree over an additive monoid and let $i$ be a natural number less than the size of $t$. Then for every value $y$, the leaf list of the point update of $t$ at $i$ with $y$ is the leaf list of $t$ with its entry at position $i$ (counting from $0$) replaced by $y$.
nodes.title: Leaf list after an in-range point update

nodes.summary: For every valid segment tree $t$ over an additive monoid, every index $i$ at least the size of $t$ and every value $y$, the point update of $t$ at $i$ with $y$ has the same leaf list as $t$.
nodes.title: Out-of-range point update leaves the leaf list unchanged

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ with entries in an additive monoid, every index $i$ smaller than the length of $xs$ and every value $y$, the leaf list of the segment tree built from $xs$, after the point update at $i$ with $y$, is $xs$ with its entry at position $i$ (counting from $0$) replaced by $y$.
nodes.title: Point update of a built segment tree

nodes.summary: Let $L = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ be a list with entries in an additive monoid, let $i < n$, and let $y$ be an element of the monoid. Applying the point update at index $i$ with value $y$ to the segment tree built from $L$ gives a tree whose aggregate is the sum, taken from left to right, of the list obtained from $L$ by replacing $x_i$ with $y$.
nodes.title: Aggregate after a point update of a built segment tree

nodes.summary: Let $L = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ be a list with entries in an additive monoid, let $i < n$, let $y$ be an element of the monoid, and let $L'$ be the list obtained from $L$ by replacing $x_i$ with $y$, with entries $x'_0, \dots, x'_{n-1}$. Apply the point update at index $i$ with value $y$ to the segment tree built from $L$. For all natural numbers $l, r$, the range query over $[l, r)$ on the result returns…
nodes.title: Range queries after a point update of a built segment tree
Sparse table

nodes.summary: A sparse table over a type $\alpha$ consists of an array of elements of $\alpha$, called its data, and an array of arrays of elements of $\alpha$, called its levels.
nodes.title: Sparse table

nodes.summary: For a type $\alpha$ with a minimum operation, the option minimum extends $\min$ to optional values (elements of $\alpha$ or none): on two elements $a, b$ of $\alpha$ it returns $\min(a, b)$, and none is a neutral element on either side.
nodes.title: Option minimum

nodes.summary: For every linearly ordered type $\alpha$ and every optional value $a$ (an element of $\alpha$ or none), the option minimum of $a$ with itself is $a$.
nodes.title: Idempotence of the option minimum

nodes.summary: For a list $a$ over a type with a minimum operation $\min$, the levels of $a$ are defined recursively: level $0$ is $a$, and if level $k$ is $\ell = (\ell_0, \dots, \ell_{m-1})$, then level $k + 1$ is the list of the values $\min(\ell_i, \ell_{i+2^k})$ for $0 \le i < m - 2^k$ (empty when $m \le 2^k$).
nodes.title: Levels of a sparse table

nodes.summary: For a list $a$ of length $n$ over a type with a minimum operation and a natural number $k$, level $k$ of $a$ has length $\max(n + 1 - 2^k, 0)$: one element for each start index $i$ with $i + 2^k \le n$.
nodes.title: Length of a level

nodes.summary: Let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be a list over a linearly ordered type, and let $k$ and $i$ be natural numbers with $i + 2^k \le n$. Then level $k$ of $a$ has an element at index $i$, and it equals $\min(a_i, a_{i+1}, \dots, a_{i+2^k-1})$.
nodes.title: Levels hold interval minima

nodes.summary: For a type with a minimum operation, an array $(r_0, \dots, r_{n-1})$ and a natural number $k$, the next level is the array of length $n - 2^k$ (empty when $2^k \ge n$) whose entry $i$ is $\min(r_i, r_{i + 2^k})$.
nodes.title: Next level of a sparse table row

nodes.summary: Work over a type with a minimum operation $\min$. Given a pair $(r, L)$ of a current row $r$ (an array of length $|r|$) and an array $L$ of the rows recorded so far, and a natural number $k$, the build step returns the pair $(r', L')$, where $L'$ is $L$ with $r$ appended at the end, and $r'$ is the array whose entry $i$ is $\min(r_i, r_{i+2^k})$ for each $i$ with $i + 2^k < |r|$.
nodes.title: One step of the sparse-table construction

nodes.summary: For a list $a$ of length $n$ over a type with a minimum operation $\min$, the sparse table built from $a$ has data $a$ and $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$ stored rows, where $\lfloor \log_2 0 \rfloor$ is taken to be $0$. The rows are produced by iterating the build step for $k = 0, 1, \dots, \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$, starting from the current row $a$ and no recorded rows. So row $0$ is $a$, and entry $i$ of row…
nodes.title: Building a sparse table

nodes.summary: A sparse table over a type with a minimum operation, whose data is a list $a$ of length $n$, is valid when it has exactly $m + 1$ levels, where $m = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ for $n \ge 1$ and $m = 0$ for $n = 0$, and for each $k \le m$ its level $k$ is the list $L_k$ defined by $L_0 = a$ and, for $x = L_j$, $L_{j+1}$ is the list of length $|x| - 2^j$ (empty when $2^j \ge |x|$) whose entry $i$ is…
nodes.title: Valid sparse table

nodes.summary: For every list $a$ over a type with a minimum operation, the sparse table built from $a$ is valid: its stored rows are exactly the levels $0, 1, \dots, \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ of $a$, in this order, where $n$ is the length of $a$ and $\lfloor \log_2 0 \rfloor$ is taken to be $0$.
nodes.title: Built sparse tables are valid

nodes.summary: For a sparse table $t$ and natural numbers $k$ and $i$, the entry of $t$ at row $k$ and index $i$ is element $i$ of the $k$-th stored row of $t$ (both counted from $0$) when $t$ has a $k$-th row and that row has an element at index $i$; otherwise the entry is undefined. Both lookups are random-access array lookups.
nodes.title: Sparse-table entries

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid sparse table over a type with a minimum operation, with data $d$ of length $n$, and let $k \le \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$, where $\lfloor \log_2 0 \rfloor$ is taken to be $0$. Then for every index $i$, the entry of $t$ at row $k$ and index $i$ is defined exactly when level $k$ of $d$ has an element at index $i$, and in that case the two are equal.
nodes.title: Rows of a valid sparse table are its levels

nodes.summary: Let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be a list over a linearly ordered type, and let $k$ and $i$ be natural numbers with $i + 2^k \le n$. Then the entry of the sparse table built from $a$ at row $k$ and index $i$ is defined and equals $\min(a_i, a_{i+1}, \dots, a_{i+2^k-1})$.
nodes.title: Entries of a built sparse table are interval minima

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid sparse table over a linearly ordered type, with data $d = (d_0, \dots, d_{n-1})$, and let $k$ and $i$ be natural numbers with $i + 2^k \le n$. Then the entry of $t$ at row $k$ and index $i$ is defined and equals $\min(d_i, d_{i+1}, \dots, d_{i+2^k-1})$.
nodes.title: Entries of a valid sparse table are interval minima

nodes.summary: For a sparse table $t$ over a type with a minimum operation and natural numbers $l, r$, the query over $[l, r)$ returns none when $r \le l$. Otherwise, with $k = \lfloor \log_2 (r - l) \rfloor$, it returns the option minimum (the minimum, with none as a neutral element on either side) of the entries of $t$ at level $k$ and indices $l$ and $r - 2^k$, in this order, where an entry not stored in $t$ counts as none.
nodes.title: Sparse table range-minimum query

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid sparse table over a linearly ordered type whose data is the list $(a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$, and let $l, r$ be natural numbers with $r \le n$. Then the range-minimum query over $[l, r)$ on $t$ returns the minimum of the slice $(a_l, \dots, a_{r-1})$ (none when $r \le l$, where the slice is empty).
nodes.title: Correctness of queries on valid sparse tables

nodes.summary: Let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be a list over a linearly ordered type and let $l, r$ be natural numbers with $r \le n$. Then the range-minimum query over $[l, r)$ on the sparse table built from $a$ returns the minimum of the slice $(a_l, \dots, a_{r-1})$ (none when $r \le l$, where the slice is empty).
nodes.title: Correctness of sparse table queries

nodes.summary: For every list $a$ of length $n$ over a linearly ordered type, the range-minimum query over $[0, n)$ on the sparse table built from $a$ returns the minimum of $a$ (none when $a$ is empty).
nodes.title: Whole-range sparse table query

nodes.summary: Prefix- and bit-indexed structures: tries, radix (Patricia) tries, suffix arrays and suffix trees, van Emde Boas trees, x-fast and y-fast tries.
nodes.title: Tries, suffix structures and integer dictionaries
Radix trie

nodes.summary: For types $\alpha$ and $\beta$, a radix trie with keys that are lists over $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$ is a node made of an optional value in $\beta$ and a finite list of child edges, each a pair of a label, which is a list over $\alpha$, and a radix trie (the subtree at the end of the edge).
nodes.title: Radix trie

nodes.summary: The empty radix trie is the single node that stores no value and has no child edges; it contains no key-value entries.
nodes.title: Empty radix trie

nodes.summary: For lists $s$ and $t$ over a type with decidable equality, the longest common prefix of $s$ and $t$ is defined by recursion: it is empty if $s$ or $t$ is empty; if $s$ has first element $a$ and rest $s'$, and $t$ has first element $b$ and rest $t'$, it is $a$ followed by the longest common prefix of $s'$ and $t'$ when $a = b$, and empty when $a \ne b$.
nodes.title: Longest common prefix

nodes.summary: For every list $s$ over a type with decidable equality, the longest common prefix of $s$ and $s$ is $s$.
nodes.title: Longest common prefix of a list with itself

nodes.summary: Write $uv$ for the list $u$ followed by the list $v$. For lists $p$, $s$ and $t$ over a type with decidable equality, the longest common prefix of $ps$ and $pt$ is $p$ followed by the longest common prefix of $s$ and $t$.
nodes.title: A shared prefix factors out of the longest common prefix

nodes.summary: Let $s$ and $t$ be lists over a type with decidable equality, with longest common prefix $p$. Then there are lists $s'$ and $t'$ such that $s$ is $p$ followed by $s'$, $t$ is $p$ followed by $t'$, and either $s'$ is empty, or $t'$ is empty, or $s'$ and $t'$ are both nonempty with different first elements.
nodes.title: Characterization of the longest common prefix

nodes.summary: Let $s$ and $t$ be lists over a type with decidable equality, and let $p$ be the longest common prefix of $s$ and $t$. Then $s$ is $p$ followed by the list obtained by dropping the first $|p|$ elements of $s$, where $|p|$ is the length of $p$.
nodes.title: A list is its common prefix with another list followed by the rest

nodes.summary: Let $s$ and $t$ be lists over a type with decidable equality, let $p$ be their longest common prefix, of length $n$, and let $s'$ and $t'$ be the lists obtained from $s$ and $t$ by dropping their first $n$ elements. Then $s$ is $p$ followed by $s'$, $t$ is $p$ followed by $t'$, and either $s'$ is empty, or $t'$ is empty, or $s'$ and $t'$ are both nonempty with different first elements.
nodes.title: Longest common prefix in terms of dropped remainders

nodes.summary: Let $s$ and $t$ be lists over a type with decidable equality. If the longest common prefix of $s$ and $t$ is $t$, then $s$ is $t$ followed by the list obtained by dropping the first $|t|$ elements of $s$, where $|t|$ is the length of $t$.
nodes.title: When the common prefix is the second list, the first list extends it

nodes.summary: Let $s$, $t$ and $u$ be lists over a type with decidable equality. If $s$ is $t$ followed by $u$, then the longest common prefix of $s$ and $t$ is $t$.
nodes.title: The longest common prefix of a list and its prefix

nodes.summary: Given a symbol $c$ and a list of edges, each a pair of a label (a list of symbols) and a subtree, this returns the first edge in the list whose label starts with $c$, or nothing if no label starts with $c$.
nodes.title: Edge search by first symbol

nodes.summary: Given a symbol $c$, an edge $e$ (a pair of a label and a radix trie) and a list of child edges, this operation replaces the first edge of the list whose label starts with $c$ by $e$ and keeps all other edges in order. If no label in the list starts with $c$, it appends $e$ at the end of the list.
nodes.title: Replacing the child edge for a symbol

nodes.summary: Looking up a key, a list over $\alpha$, in a radix trie returns an optional value. At a node, the empty key returns the value stored at the node, if any. A nonempty key $k$ with first symbol $c$ goes to the first child edge whose label starts with $c$. If there is no such edge, or its label $\ell$ is not a prefix of $k$, the lookup returns no value; otherwise it continues in the subtree of that edge with $k$ minus…
nodes.title: Radix trie lookup

nodes.summary: Let $k$ be a nonempty key with first symbol $c$, and consider a node with children $C$ (a list of edges, each a label with a subtree), whatever value the node stores. If no edge of $C$ has a label starting with $c$, looking up $k$ at the node returns no value. Otherwise let $(\ell, T')$ be the first such edge of $C$: if the longest common prefix of $k$ and $\ell$ is $\ell$, the lookup returns the lookup in $T'$ of…
nodes.title: Radix trie lookup of a nonempty key at a node

nodes.summary: For every key $k$, looking up $k$ in the empty radix trie returns no value.
nodes.title: Lookup in the empty radix trie

nodes.summary: Inserting a value $v$ at a key $k$ (a list of symbols) into a radix trie works as follows. If $k$ is empty, the root's value becomes $v$. Otherwise let $c$ be the first symbol of $k$. If no child edge of the root has a label starting with $c$, a new edge labelled $k$ leading to a leaf storing $v$ is added after the existing edges. Otherwise take the first such edge, with label $\ell$ and subtree $s$, let $q$ be the…
nodes.title: Insertion into a radix trie

nodes.summary: For every radix trie $T$, key $k$ and value $v$, looking up $k$ in the trie obtained from $T$ by inserting $v$ at $k$ returns $v$.
nodes.title: Lookup of a key just inserted into a radix trie

nodes.summary: For every radix trie $T$, all keys $k \ne k'$ and every value $v$, looking up $k$ in the trie obtained from $T$ by inserting $v$ at $k'$ gives the same result as looking up $k$ in $T$.
nodes.title: Insertion into a radix trie leaves lookups of other keys unchanged

nodes.summary: A radix trie is path-compressed at its root when its root node stores a value or has at least two child edges.
nodes.title: Path-compressed root

nodes.summary: Validity of radix tries is defined inductively: a node is valid when every label of its child edges is nonempty, the first symbols of the labels of its child edges are pairwise distinct, and for each child edge the subtree at its end is valid and path-compressed at its root (its root stores a value or has at least two child edges).
nodes.title: Valid radix trie

nodes.summary: For all types $\alpha$ and $\beta$, the empty radix trie whose keys are lists over $\alpha$ and whose values lie in $\beta$ is valid.
nodes.title: The empty radix trie is valid

nodes.summary: If a radix-trie node with child edges $(\ell_1, t_1), \dots, (\ell_n, t_n)$ is valid, then the first symbols of the labels $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_n$ are pairwise distinct.
nodes.title: Sibling edge labels start with distinct symbols

nodes.summary: If a radix-trie node is valid, then for each of its child edges, the subtree at the end of that edge is path-compressed at its root: its root stores a value or has at least two child edges.
nodes.title: Children of a valid node are path-compressed

nodes.summary: If $t$ is a valid radix trie, then for every key $k$ and value $v$, the trie obtained by inserting $v$ at $k$ in $t$ is valid.
nodes.title: Insertion preserves validity of radix tries

nodes.summary: The entries of a radix trie are its key-value pairs, listed recursively. For a node with child edges $(\ell_1, t_1), \dots, (\ell_n, t_n)$ in stored order, the list starts with the pair $(\varepsilon, v)$, where $\varepsilon$ is the empty key, if the node stores a value $v$; it continues with the entries of $t_1$ with $\ell_1$ prepended to every key, then the entries of $t_2$ with $\ell_2$ prepended, and so on up…
nodes.title: Entries of a radix trie

nodes.summary: The stored keys of a radix trie form the list of the keys of its entries, in the same order.
nodes.title: Stored keys of a radix trie

nodes.summary: For a valid radix trie $T$, every key $k$ and every value $v$, looking up $k$ in $T$ returns $v$ if and only if the pair $(k, v)$ occurs in the list of entries of $T$.
nodes.title: Lookup agrees with the entries of a valid radix trie

nodes.summary: For a valid radix trie $T$ and every key $k$, $k$ is a stored key of $T$ if and only if looking up $k$ in $T$ returns some value.
nodes.title: Stored keys of a valid radix trie are the keys with a successful lookup

nodes.summary: If $t$ is a valid radix trie, then its list of stored keys has no duplicates.
nodes.title: Stored keys of a valid radix trie are distinct

nodes.summary: For a radix trie $t$ and a pattern $p$ (a list of symbols), prefix search returns a boolean computed as follows. If $p$ is empty, it is true exactly when $t$ stores at least one key. Otherwise let $c$ be the first symbol of $p$ and take the first child edge of the root whose label starts with $c$; if there is none, the answer is false. If that edge has label $\ell$ and subtree $s$, then: when $p$ is a prefix of…
nodes.title: Prefix search in a radix trie

nodes.summary: For a valid radix trie $t$ and a list $p$ of symbols, prefix search for $p$ in $t$ succeeds if and only if some stored key $k$ of $t$ has $p$ as a prefix.
nodes.title: Prefix search is correct on valid radix tries

nodes.summary: The trie built from the empty list is the empty trie, and the trie built from a list with head $(k, v)$ and tail $L$ is the trie built from $L$ with the value $v$ inserted at the key $k$. Later pairs in the list are thus inserted first, so on duplicate keys the head-most value wins.
nodes.title: Radix trie built from a list of key-value pairs

nodes.summary: For a list $L$ of key-value pairs, if $(k, v)$ belongs to $L$, then looking up $k$ in the radix trie built from $L$ returns some value.
nodes.title: Every listed key is present in the built radix trie

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ of key-value pairs, if looking up a key $k$ in the radix trie built from $L$ returns a value $v$, then the pair $(k, v)$ occurs in $L$.
nodes.title: Lookups in a radix trie built from a list come from the list

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ of key-value pairs and every key $k$, $k$ is a stored key of the radix trie built from $L$ if and only if the pair $(k, v)$ occurs in $L$ for some value $v$.
nodes.title: Keys of a radix trie built from a list

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list of key-value pairs, whose keys are lists over $\gamma$, in which no key occurs twice. If the pair $(k, v)$ occurs in $L$, then looking up $k$ in the radix trie built from $L$ returns $v$.
nodes.title: Lookup in a radix trie built from a list with distinct keys
Suffix array

nodes.summary: For a list $s = (s_0, \dots, s_{n-1})$ over a linearly ordered alphabet and a natural number $i$, the suffix of $s$ at $i$ is the list obtained from $s$ by dropping its first $i$ entries: it is $(s_i, \dots, s_{n-1})$ when $i < n$ and the empty list when $i \ge n$.
nodes.title: Suffix of a list at an index

nodes.summary: For a list $s$ of length $n$ over a linearly ordered alphabet, the list of suffixes of $s$ is the list, for $i = 0, 1, \dots, n$ in this order, of the lists obtained from $s$ by dropping its first $i$ entries. It starts with $s$ itself and ends with the empty list.
nodes.title: Suffixes of a list

nodes.summary: For a list $s$ of length $n$ over a linearly ordered alphabet, the suffix array of $s$ is the list of the indices $0, 1, \dots, n - 1$, sorted so that the suffixes of $s$ starting at them appear in lexicographic order.
nodes.title: Suffix array

nodes.summary: For a list $s$ of length $n$ over a linearly ordered alphabet, the suffix array of $s$ is a permutation of the list $0, 1, \dots, n - 1$ of all indices below $n$.
nodes.title: The suffix array is a permutation of the indices

nodes.summary: For a list $s$ over a linearly ordered alphabet, the suffixes of $s$ taken in suffix-array order are sorted lexicographically: whenever an index $i$ comes before an index $j$ in the suffix array of $s$, the suffix of $s$ starting at $i$ is lexicographically less than or equal to the suffix of $s$ starting at $j$.
nodes.title: The suffix array sorts the suffixes

nodes.summary: For lists $x$ and $y$, $\mathrm{lcp}(x, y)$ is the length of the longest common prefix of $x$ and $y$: the number of positions, counted from the start, at which $x$ and $y$ agree before they first differ or one of them ends.
nodes.title: Longest common prefix length

nodes.summary: For lists $x$ and $y$ over a type with decidable equality, let $\operatorname{lcp}(x, y)$ be the length of their longest common prefix. Then the first $\operatorname{lcp}(x, y)$ elements of $x$ and the first $\operatorname{lcp}(x, y)$ elements of $y$ form the same list.
nodes.title: Two lists agree on their longest common prefix

nodes.summary: Let $x$ and $y$ be lists and let $\mathrm{lcp}(x, y)$ be the length of their longest common prefix. For every natural number $q \le \mathrm{lcp}(x, y)$, the first $q$ elements of $x$ and of $y$ agree.
nodes.title: Common prefixes of every shorter length

nodes.summary: For lists $x$ and $y$, let $\mathrm{lcp}(x, y)$ be the length of the longest common prefix of $x$ and $y$. For every natural number $q$, we have $q \le \mathrm{lcp}(x, y)$ if and only if $q$ is at most the lengths of both $x$ and $y$ and the first $q$ elements of $x$ and of $y$ agree.
nodes.title: Characterization of the longest common prefix length

nodes.summary: For a list $s$ and a list of indices $i_0, i_1, \dots, i_k$, this is the list of length $k$ whose $t$-th entry, for $t < k$, is the length of the longest common prefix of the suffixes of $s$ starting at $i_t$ and at $i_{t+1}$, where the suffix starting at an index at or past the end of $s$ is the empty list. It has one entry per adjacent pair of indices, and it is empty for an empty index list.
nodes.title: Longest-common-prefix lengths of adjacent suffixes

nodes.summary: For a list $s$ over a linearly ordered alphabet, the LCP array of $s$ is the list of longest-common-prefix lengths of adjacent suffixes in suffix-array order: if the suffix array of $s$ is $i_0, i_1, \dots, i_k$, then the LCP array has length $k$ and its $t$-th entry, for $t < k$, is the length of the longest common prefix of the suffixes of $s$ starting at $i_t$ and at $i_{t+1}$. It is empty when $s$ is empty.
nodes.title: The LCP array

nodes.summary: If `x ≤ y ≤ z` and `P` is a prefix of both `x` and `z`, then `P` is a prefix of `y`.
nodes.title: Prefix classes are lexicographic intervals

nodes.summary: Truncation is monotone for the lexicographic order: `x ≤ y → x.take m ≤ y.take m`.
nodes.title: Truncation is monotone for the lexicographic order

nodes.summary: If rows `r₁ ≤ r₂ ≤ r₃` of the suffix array of `s` are in range and the suffixes of rows `r₁` and `r₃` start with `P`, so does the suffix of row `r₂`.
nodes.title: The occurrences of a pattern are contiguous in the suffix array

nodes.summary: Binary search for the boundary of a predicate on `[lo, hi)`: the first index at which `p` is false, assuming `p` holds on an initial segment of `[lo, hi)` (`lowerBound_spec`). Each call probes the midpoint and recurses on one half.
nodes.title: Binary search for the boundary of a predicate

nodes.summary: The number of probes `lowerBound p lo hi` makes.
nodes.title: Number of probes made by the binary search

nodes.summary: If `p` holds on an initial segment of `[lo, hi)` (whenever it holds at `j`, it holds at every `i` with `lo ≤ i ≤ j`), then `lowerBound p lo hi` is the end `k` of that segment: `lo ≤ k ≤ hi`, `p` holds on `[lo, k)` and fails on `[k, hi)`.
nodes.title: Binary search is correct

nodes.summary: At most `⌊log₂ (hi - lo)⌋ + 1` probes, for any predicate.
nodes.title: Binary search is logarithmic

nodes.summary: The suffix of row `r` of the (precomputed) suffix array `sa` of `s`, truncated to `m` letters: the key compared with the pattern during the search. `sa` is computed once by `saSearch` and passed in, so probes do not rebuild the suffix array.
nodes.title: Truncated suffix of a suffix-array row

nodes.summary: Suffix-array search (Manber and Myers 1993): the row interval `[sp, ep)` of the suffixes of `s` that start with `P`, found by two binary searches over the rows `[0, |s|)`. The suffix array is computed once and shared by both searches.
nodes.title: Suffix-array search for a pattern's row interval

nodes.summary: The search returns a genuine interval of rows: `sp ≤ ep ≤ |s|`.
nodes.title: Suffix-array search returns a valid row interval

nodes.summary: A row `r < |s|` lies in `[sp, ep)` exactly when the suffix of row `r` starts with `P`.
nodes.title: Suffix-array search is correct
Suffix tree

nodes.summary: For a list $s = (s_0, \dots, s_{n-1})$ over $\alpha$, the terminated string of $s$ is the list $(\mathrm{some}\,s_0, \dots, \mathrm{some}\,s_{n-1}, \mathrm{none})$ over $\mathrm{Option}\,\alpha$: every symbol of $s$ tagged $\mathrm{some}$, followed by the terminator $\mathrm{none}$.
nodes.title: Terminated string

nodes.summary: For a list $s$ over $\alpha$ and a natural number $i \le |s|$, removing the first $i$ entries of the terminated string of $s$ gives the suffix of $s$ starting at index $i$ with every symbol tagged $\mathrm{some}$, followed by $\mathrm{none}$.
nodes.title: Suffixes of the terminated string

nodes.summary: For a list $s = (s_0, \dots, s_{n-1})$ over $\alpha$, let $\hat s = (\mathrm{some}\,s_0, \dots, \mathrm{some}\,s_{n-1}, \mathrm{none})$ be its terminated string. The suffix entries of $s$ are the list of pairs $(\hat s_{\ge i}, i)$ for $i = 0, 1, \dots, n$ in increasing order, where $\hat s_{\ge i}$ is $\hat s$ with its first $i$ entries removed: each nonempty suffix of $\hat s$ paired with its starting index.
nodes.title: Suffix entries of a string

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a list over $\alpha$. The lists obtained from the terminated string of $s$ by removing its first $i$ symbols, for $i$ ranging over $0, 1, \ldots, |s|$, are pairwise distinct.
nodes.title: Terminated suffixes are distinct

nodes.summary: For a list $s = (s_0, \dots, s_{n-1})$ over $\alpha$, let $\hat s = (\mathrm{some}\,s_0, \dots, \mathrm{some}\,s_{n-1}, \mathrm{none})$ be its terminated string over $\mathrm{Option}\,\alpha$. The suffix tree of $s$ is the radix trie with keys over $\mathrm{Option}\,\alpha$ and natural-number values obtained from the empty trie by inserting, for $i = n, n - 1, \dots, 0$ in this order, the suffix of $\hat s$…
nodes.title: Suffix tree

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a list over $\alpha$ and $i$ a natural number with $i \le |s|$. Looking up, in the suffix tree of $s$, the terminated string of $s$ with its first $i$ symbols removed returns $i$.
nodes.title: Lookup of a suffix returns its starting index

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a list over $\alpha$, let $k$ be a list over $\alpha$ extended by a fresh terminator symbol, and let $i$ be a natural number. If looking up $k$ in the suffix tree of $s$ returns $i$, then $i \le |s|$ and $k$ is the terminated string of $s$ with its first $i$ symbols removed.
nodes.title: Lookup in the suffix tree returns starting indices

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a list over $\alpha$. A key $k$ is stored in the suffix tree of $s$ if and only if there is a natural number $i \le |s|$ such that $k$ is the terminated string of $s$ with its first $i$ symbols removed.
nodes.title: The stored keys of a suffix tree are its terminated suffixes

nodes.summary: For a list $s$ over $\alpha$, the stored keys of $s$ form the list of keys stored in the suffix tree of $s$, in stored sibling order.
nodes.title: Stored keys of the suffix tree

nodes.summary: For a list $s$ over $\alpha$, the list of stored keys of the suffix tree of $s$ has length $|s| + 1$.
nodes.title: The suffix tree stores one key per suffix

nodes.summary: For lists $p$ and $q$ over $\alpha$, view their symbols in $\alpha$ extended by a fresh terminator symbol. If $p$ is a prefix of $q$ followed by the terminator, then $p$ is a prefix of $q$.
nodes.title: A tagged pattern cannot reach past the terminator

nodes.summary: For lists $s$ and $p$, $p$ is an infix (a contiguous sublist) of $s$ if and only if there is a natural number $i$ such that $p$ is a prefix of the list obtained from $s$ by removing its first $i$ symbols.
nodes.title: Infixes are prefixes of suffixes

nodes.summary: For lists $s$ and $p$ over $\alpha$, prefix search for $p$ (each symbol viewed in the alphabet extended by the terminator) in the suffix tree of $s$ succeeds if and only if there is a natural number $i$ such that $p$ is a prefix of the list obtained from $s$ by removing its first $i$ symbols.
nodes.title: Suffix-tree search finds exactly the prefixes of suffixes

nodes.summary: For lists $s$ and $p$ over $\alpha$, prefix search for $p$ (each symbol viewed in the alphabet extended by the terminator) in the suffix tree of $s$ succeeds if and only if $p$ occurs in $s$ as a contiguous sublist (an infix).
nodes.title: Suffix-tree search finds exactly the infixes
Trie

nodes.summary: A trie with keys that are lists over $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$ is a node consisting of an optional value in $\beta$ and a finite list of children, each child being a pair of a letter in $\alpha$ and a trie. The letters labelling the children need not be distinct.
nodes.title: Trie

nodes.summary: The empty trie is the trie consisting of a single root node that stores no value and has no children, so it contains no key-value entries.
nodes.title: Empty trie

nodes.summary: The lookup of a key (a list over $\alpha$) in a trie returns an optional value in $\beta$, by recursion on the key. For the empty key it is the optional value stored at the root. For a key with first letter $a$ followed by the key $k$, it fails if no child of the root is labelled $a$, and otherwise it is the lookup of $k$ in the first child labelled $a$.
nodes.title: Trie lookup

nodes.summary: Inserting a value $v$ at a key $k$ (a list of letters) in a trie stores $v$ at the node reached by following $k$ from the root, replacing any value stored there. Along the way, a missing child is created as an empty trie and appended after its siblings, an existing child is updated in place, and all other values and children are unchanged.
nodes.title: Trie insertion

nodes.summary: Validity of tries is defined inductively: a trie node with optional value $v$ and child list $c$ is valid when the letters labelling the children in $c$ are pairwise distinct and every child trie in $c$ is valid.
nodes.title: Valid trie

nodes.summary: The entries of a trie are the list of its key-value pairs, where a key is a list of letters. If the root stores a value $v$, the list begins with the pair consisting of the empty key and $v$; it continues, for each child in the stored sibling order, with the entries $(k, w)$ of that child, in order, each rewritten as $(a k, w)$, where $a$ is the letter labelling the child and $a k$ is the key $k$ with $a$ prepended.
nodes.title: Entries of a trie
