nodes.summary: For every key $k$, looking up $k$ in the empty trie returns no value.
nodes.title: Lookup in the empty trie

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with decidable equality. For every trie $T$ with keys that are lists over $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$, every key $k$ and every value $v \in \beta$, looking up $k$ in the trie obtained from $T$ by inserting $v$ at $k$ returns $v$.
nodes.title: Lookup after insertion in a trie

nodes.summary: For every trie $T$, all keys $k \ne k'$ and every value $v$, looking up $k$ in the trie obtained by inserting $v$ at $k'$ in $T$ gives the same result as looking up $k$ in $T$.
nodes.title: Trie insertion leaves other keys unchanged

nodes.summary: If a trie node with optional value $v$ and child list $c$ is valid, then the letters labelling the children in $c$ are pairwise distinct.
nodes.title: Valid trie nodes have distinct child keys

nodes.summary: The empty trie is valid.
nodes.title: Validity of the empty trie

nodes.summary: If a trie $T$ is valid, then for every key $k$ (a list of letters) and every value $v$, the trie obtained by inserting $v$ at $k$ in $T$ is valid.
nodes.title: Insertion preserves trie validity

nodes.summary: For every valid trie $T$, every key $k$ and every value $v$, looking up $k$ in $T$ returns $v$ if and only if $(k, v)$ is one of the entries of $T$.
nodes.title: Trie lookup agrees with the entries

nodes.summary: Two tries $T$ and $T'$ are lookup-equivalent when, for every key $k$, looking up $k$ in $T$ gives the same result as looking up $k$ in $T'$.
nodes.title: Lookup equivalence of tries

nodes.summary: Every trie is lookup-equivalent to itself.
nodes.title: Reflexivity of trie lookup equivalence

nodes.summary: If a trie $T$ is lookup-equivalent to a trie $T'$, then $T'$ is lookup-equivalent to $T$.
nodes.title: Symmetry of trie lookup equivalence

nodes.summary: If a trie $T_1$ is lookup-equivalent to a trie $T_2$ and $T_2$ is lookup-equivalent to a trie $T_3$, then $T_1$ is lookup-equivalent to $T_3$.
nodes.title: Transitivity of trie lookup equivalence

nodes.summary: Let $T$ and $T'$ be valid tries with keys that are lists over $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$, and suppose $T$ and $T'$ are lookup-equivalent. Then for every key $k$ and every value $v \in \beta$, the pair $(k, v)$ occurs in the entry list of $T$ if and only if it occurs in the entry list of $T'$.
nodes.title: Lookup-equivalent valid tries have the same entries

nodes.summary: For every trie $T$, all keys $k_1 \ne k_2$ and all values $v_1, v_2$, inserting $v_1$ at $k_1$ and then $v_2$ at $k_2$ gives a trie that is lookup-equivalent to the one obtained by inserting $v_2$ at $k_2$ and then $v_1$ at $k_1$.
nodes.title: Insertions at distinct keys commute in a trie

nodes.summary: The empty-node test is true on a trie node exactly when the node carries no value and has no children; when deletion leaves a child in this state, the child is removed from its parent.
nodes.title: Empty trie nodes

nodes.summary: The empty-node test is true on a trie $t$ exactly when $t$ is the node with no value and no children, that is, the empty trie.
nodes.title: Characterization of empty nodes

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list of pairs $(k, c)$ of a key $k$ in $\alpha$ and a trie $c$ (the children of a trie node), let $a$ be a key and $t$ a trie, and call $t$ empty when it carries no value and has no children. Setting the child at $a$ to $t$ in $L$ gives the following list. If no entry of $L$ has key $a$, the result is $L$ itself when $t$ is empty, and $L$ with $(a, t)$ appended at the end otherwise. If some entry of…
nodes.title: Setting a child in a trie's child list

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list of letter–trie pairs, $a$ a letter and $c$ a trie, and let $L'$ be obtained from $L$ by setting the child at $a$ to $c$ (removing the entries at $a$ instead when $c$ has neither value nor children). Looking up $a$ in $L'$ finds nothing when $c$ has neither value nor children, and finds $c$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Looking up a child just set

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list of letter–trie pairs, $c$ a trie and $a \ne b$ letters, and let $L'$ be obtained from $L$ by setting the child at $b$ to $c$ (removing the entries at $b$ instead when $c$ has neither value nor children). Then looking up $a$ in $L'$ gives the same result as looking up $a$ in $L$.
nodes.title: Setting a child leaves the other children unchanged

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list of letter–trie pairs whose letters are pairwise distinct and whose tries are all valid, let $c$ be a valid trie and $a$ a letter. Then the list obtained from $L$ by setting the child at $a$ to $c$ (removing the entries at $a$ instead when $c$ has neither value nor children) again has pairwise distinct letters, and every trie in it is valid.
nodes.title: Setting a child preserves the child-list part of validity

nodes.summary: Let a trie node with value $v$ and child list $L$ be valid, let $c$ be a valid trie and $a$ a letter. Then the node with value $v$ whose child list is obtained from $L$ by setting the child at $a$ to $c$ (removing the entries at $a$ instead when $c$ has neither value nor children) is valid.
nodes.title: Setting a child preserves validity

nodes.summary: Deleting a key $k$ (a list of letters) from a trie $t$ works by recursion on $k$. If $k$ is empty, the root of $t$ loses its value and keeps its children. If $k$ consists of a first letter $a$ followed by a key $k'$ and the root of $t$ has no child at $a$, then $t$ is unchanged. Otherwise $k'$ is deleted from the first child at $a$. If the result has neither value nor children, every entry at $a$ is removed from…
nodes.title: Deletion from a trie

nodes.summary: For every trie $t$ and every key $k$, looking up $k$ in the trie obtained from $t$ by deleting $k$ finds no value.
nodes.title: A deleted key is absent

nodes.summary: For every trie $t$ and all keys $k \ne k'$, looking up $k$ in the trie obtained from $t$ by deleting $k'$ gives the same result as looking up $k$ in $t$.
nodes.title: Deletion does not affect other keys

nodes.summary: If a trie $t$ is valid, that is, every node has distinct child keys and valid child tries, then for every key $k$ the trie obtained from $t$ by deleting $k$ is valid.
nodes.title: Deletion preserves trie validity
Van Emde Boas tree

nodes.summary: For a natural number $m$, a two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ consists of a summary bit vector of length $m$ and, for each $i < m$, a cluster bit vector of length $m$; bit $j$ of cluster $i$ records whether the element $im + j$ is stored. Unlike the fully recursive van Emde Boas tree over universes of size $2^{2^k}$, the summary and the clusters here are plain bit vectors, not…
nodes.title: Two-level van Emde Boas tree

nodes.summary: For a natural number $m$, the empty van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ is the tree in which all $m$ summary bits and all $m^2$ cluster bits ($m$ clusters of $m$ bits each) are unset.
nodes.title: Empty van Emde Boas tree

nodes.summary: An element $x$ of the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ is a member of a two-level van Emde Boas tree $t$ when bit $x \bmod m$ of cluster $\lfloor x / m \rfloor$ of $t$ is set. The summary bits are not consulted.
nodes.title: Membership in a van Emde Boas tree

nodes.summary: Let $m$ be a natural number, let $t$ be a van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and let $x$ be an element of the universe. Inserting $x$ into $t$ gives the tree obtained from $t$ by setting bit $x \bmod m$ of cluster $\lfloor x / m \rfloor$ and summary bit $\lfloor x / m \rfloor$, leaving every other bit unchanged.
nodes.title: Insertion into a van Emde Boas tree

nodes.summary: A two-level van Emde Boas tree $t$ with $m$ clusters is valid when, for every cluster index $i < m$, summary bit $i$ of $t$ is set exactly when cluster $i$ of $t$ is nonempty, that is, when some bit $j < m$ of cluster $i$ is set.
nodes.title: Summary invariant of a van Emde Boas tree

nodes.summary: Let $m$ be a natural number. For a van Emde Boas tree $t$ over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, the set of stored elements of $t$ is the finite set of those elements of the universe that are members of $t$.
nodes.title: Set of stored elements of a van Emde Boas tree

nodes.summary: For every $m$ and every $x$ in the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, $x$ is not a member of the empty two-level van Emde Boas tree over that universe.
nodes.title: The empty van Emde Boas tree has no members

nodes.summary: For every two-level van Emde Boas tree $t$ over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and every $x$ in that universe, $x$ is a member of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$.
nodes.title: An inserted element is a member of a van Emde Boas tree

nodes.summary: For every two-level van Emde Boas tree $t$ over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and all $x \ne y$ in that universe, $y$ is a member of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ if and only if $y$ is a member of $t$.
nodes.title: Insertion into a van Emde Boas tree leaves other elements unchanged

nodes.summary: For every two-level van Emde Boas tree $t$ over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and all $x, y$ in that universe, $y$ is a member of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ is a member of $t$.
nodes.title: Membership after insertion into a van Emde Boas tree

nodes.summary: For every two-level van Emde Boas tree $t$ over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and all $x, y$ in that universe, if $y$ is a member of $t$, then $y$ is a member of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$.
nodes.title: Insertion into a van Emde Boas tree keeps existing members

nodes.summary: For every natural number $m$, the empty two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ satisfies the summary invariant: each summary bit is set exactly when its cluster is nonempty.
nodes.title: The empty van Emde Boas tree is valid

nodes.summary: For every natural number $m$, every element $x$ of the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and every two-level van Emde Boas tree $t$ over that universe that satisfies the summary invariant (each summary bit is set exactly when its cluster is nonempty), the tree obtained from $t$ by inserting $x$ also satisfies the summary invariant.
nodes.title: Insertion preserves validity of van Emde Boas trees

nodes.summary: For every two-level van Emde Boas tree $t$ over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and every $x$ in that universe, $x$ belongs to the finite set of stored elements of $t$ if and only if $x$ is a member of $t$.
nodes.title: The contents of a van Emde Boas tree are its members

nodes.summary: For every natural number $m$, the set of stored elements of the empty van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ is empty.
nodes.title: Contents of the empty van Emde Boas tree

nodes.summary: Let $m$ be a natural number, let $t$ be a van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and let $x$ be an element of the universe. The set of stored elements of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is the set of stored elements of $t$ together with $x$. No validity assumption on $t$ is needed.
nodes.title: Contents after insertion into a van Emde Boas tree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$. If some summary bit of $t$ is set, let $h$ be the least cluster index whose summary bit is set; if cluster $h$ has a set position, let $\ell$ be the least one. The minimum query on $t$ then returns the element $h \cdot m + \ell$. If no summary bit is set, or cluster $h$ has no set position, it returns no element.
nodes.title: Minimum query of a van Emde Boas tree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$. If the minimum query on $t$ returns $x$, then $x$ is stored in $t$.
nodes.title: The van Emde Boas minimum is stored

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$. If the minimum query on $t$ returns $x$, then $x \le y$ for every $y$ stored in $t$.
nodes.title: The van Emde Boas minimum is a lower bound

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$. The minimum query on $t$ returns no element if and only if no element of the universe is stored in $t$.
nodes.title: Empty minimum query in a van Emde Boas tree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, and let $x$ be in the universe. The minimum query on $t$ returns $x$ if and only if $x$ is stored in $t$ and $x \le y$ for every $y$ stored in $t$.
nodes.title: Characterization of the van Emde Boas minimum

nodes.summary: For every $m$, the minimum query of the empty two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ returns no element.
nodes.title: The empty van Emde Boas tree has no minimum

nodes.summary: For every $x$ in the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, the minimum query on the two-level van Emde Boas tree obtained by inserting $x$ into the empty tree returns $x$.
nodes.title: Minimum of a one-element van Emde Boas tree

nodes.summary: For a two-level van Emde Boas tree $t$ over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, the maximum query first finds the greatest index $i < m$ whose summary bit is set, and then the greatest index $j < m$ whose bit is set in cluster $i$; it returns the element $i m + j$. It returns no element if no summary bit is set, or if no bit of cluster $i$ is set. When the summary bits record exactly the nonempty clusters,…
nodes.title: Maximum query of a van Emde Boas tree

nodes.summary: For every two-level van Emde Boas tree $t$ over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and every $x$ in that universe, if the maximum query of $t$ returns $x$, then $x$ is a member of $t$. No validity hypothesis on $t$ is needed.
nodes.title: The maximum query of a van Emde Boas tree returns a member

nodes.summary: Let $m$ be a natural number and let $t$ be a valid van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$. If the maximum query on $t$ returns $x$, then $y \le x$ for every member $y$ of $t$.
nodes.title: The van Emde Boas maximum query bounds every member

nodes.summary: Let $m$ be a natural number and let $t$ be a valid van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$. The maximum query on $t$ returns no element if and only if no element of the universe is a member of $t$.
nodes.title: When the van Emde Boas maximum query returns nothing

nodes.summary: Let $m$ be a natural number, let $t$ be a valid van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and let $x$ be an element of the universe. The maximum query on $t$ returns $x$ if and only if $x$ is a member of $t$ and $y \le x$ for every member $y$ of $t$.
nodes.title: Correctness of the van Emde Boas maximum query

nodes.summary: For every natural number $m$, the maximum query on the empty van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ returns no element.
nodes.title: Maximum query on the empty van Emde Boas tree

nodes.summary: Let $m$ be a natural number and let $x$ be an element of the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$. The maximum query on the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into the empty van Emde Boas tree over this universe returns $x$.
nodes.title: Maximum query on a one-element van Emde Boas tree

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and let $x = hm + \ell$ with $0 \le h, \ell < m$, so that $x$ sits at position $\ell$ of cluster $h$. If cluster $h$ has a set position after $\ell$, the successor of $x$ in $T$ is $hm + \ell'$ for the least such position $\ell'$. Otherwise, let $h'$ be the least cluster index with $h < h'$ whose summary bit is set; the successor is…
nodes.title: Successor query in a two-level van Emde Boas tree

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, not necessarily valid, and let $x$ and $y$ be elements of the universe. If the successor of $x$ in $T$ is $y$, then $y$ is a member of $T$.
nodes.title: The van Emde Boas successor is stored

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, not necessarily valid, and let $x$ and $y$ be elements of the universe. If the successor of $x$ in $T$ is $y$, then $x < y$.
nodes.title: The van Emde Boas successor is strictly larger than its argument

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a valid two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and let $x$, $y$, $z$ be elements of the universe. If the successor of $x$ in $T$ is $y$ and $z$ is a member of $T$ with $x < z$, then $y \le z$.
nodes.title: No member lies strictly between an element and its van Emde Boas successor

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a valid two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and let $x$ be an element of the universe. Then $x$ has no successor in $T$ if and only if every member $z$ of $T$ satisfies $z \le x$.
nodes.title: A van Emde Boas successor is missing exactly when nothing larger is stored

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a valid two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and let $x$ and $y$ be elements of the universe. Then the successor of $x$ in $T$ is $y$ if and only if $y$ is a member of $T$, $x < y$, and $y \le z$ for every member $z$ of $T$ with $x < z$.
nodes.title: The van Emde Boas successor is the least larger member

nodes.summary: For every $m$ and every element $x$ of the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, $x$ has no successor in the empty two-level van Emde Boas tree over that universe.
nodes.title: The empty van Emde Boas tree has no successors

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and let $x = hm + \ell$ with $0 \le h, \ell < m$, so that $x$ sits at position $\ell$ of cluster $h$. If cluster $h$ has a set position before $\ell$, the predecessor of $x$ in $T$ is $hm + \ell'$ for the greatest such position $\ell'$. Otherwise, let $h'$ be the greatest cluster index with $h' < h$ whose summary bit is set; the…
nodes.title: Predecessor query in a two-level van Emde Boas tree

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, not necessarily valid, and let $x$ and $y$ be elements of the universe. If the predecessor of $x$ in $T$ is $y$, then $y$ is a member of $T$.
nodes.title: The van Emde Boas predecessor is stored

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, not necessarily valid, and let $x$ and $y$ be elements of the universe. If the predecessor of $x$ in $T$ is $y$, then $y < x$.
nodes.title: The van Emde Boas predecessor is strictly smaller than its argument

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, and let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be in the universe. If the predecessor query for $x$ in $t$ returns $y$, and $z$ is stored in $t$ with $z < x$, then $z \le y$.
nodes.title: Maximality of the van Emde Boas predecessor

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, and let $x$ be in the universe. The predecessor query for $x$ in $t$ returns no element if and only if $x \le z$ for every $z$ stored in $t$.
nodes.title: Empty predecessor query in a van Emde Boas tree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, and let $x$ and $y$ be in the universe. The predecessor query for $x$ in $t$ returns $y$ if and only if $y$ is stored in $t$, $y < x$, and $z \le y$ for every $z$ stored in $t$ with $z < x$.
nodes.title: Characterization of the van Emde Boas predecessor

nodes.summary: For every $x$ in the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, the predecessor query for $x$ in the empty two-level van Emde Boas tree returns no element.
nodes.title: Predecessor queries in the empty van Emde Boas tree
X-fast trie

nodes.summary: An x-fast trie over $w$-bit keys consists of a finite set of stored keys in $\{0, \dots, 2^w - 1\}$ together with, for each level $l \in \{0, \dots, w\}$, a finite set of natural numbers, intended to hold the $l$-bit prefixes of the stored keys.
nodes.title: x-fast trie

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $l$ and $w$ and a $w$-bit key $x < 2^w$, the length-$l$ prefix of $x$ is the natural number $\lfloor x / 2^{w-l} \rfloor$, where $w - l$ is truncated subtraction (it is $0$ when $l > w$). For $l \le w$ these are the top $l$ bits of $x$, a number below $2^l$.
nodes.title: Bit prefix of a key

nodes.summary: For every $w$-bit key $x < 2^w$, the length-$0$ prefix of $x$ (the trie root) is $0$.
nodes.title: The empty prefix is zero

nodes.summary: For every $w$-bit key $x < 2^w$, the length-$w$ prefix of $x$ equals $x$.
nodes.title: The full-length prefix of a key is the key

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $l \le w$ and a $w$-bit key $x < 2^w$, the length-$l$ prefix of $x$ is less than $2^l$.
nodes.title: A prefix fits in its length

nodes.summary: An x-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys is valid when, for every level $l \in \{0, \dots, w\}$, the level-$l$ set of $t$ equals the set of $l$-bit prefixes (top $l$ bits) of the stored keys of $t$.
nodes.title: Valid x-fast trie

nodes.summary: The empty x-fast trie over $w$-bit keys stores no keys, and the prefix set at each of its levels $0, 1, \dots, w$ is empty.
nodes.title: The empty x-fast trie

nodes.summary: Inserting a $w$-bit key $x$ into an x-fast trie $t$ adds $x$ to the keys stored in $t$ and, for each level $0 \le l \le w$, adds the $l$-bit prefix of $x$ to the prefix set at level $l$.
nodes.title: Insertion into an x-fast trie

nodes.summary: For every $w$, the empty x-fast trie over $w$-bit keys, which has no stored keys and every level empty, is valid.
nodes.title: The empty x-fast trie is valid

nodes.summary: If $t$ is a valid x-fast trie over $w$-bit keys and $x \in \{0, \dots, 2^w - 1\}$, then the x-fast trie obtained from $t$ by inserting $x$ is valid.
nodes.title: Insertion preserves validity of an x-fast trie

nodes.summary: For every x-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys and every $w$-bit key $x$, the set of keys stored in the trie obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is the set of keys stored in $t$ with $x$ added.
nodes.title: Keys of an x-fast trie after insertion

nodes.summary: For an x-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys, a level $0 \le l \le w$ and a $w$-bit key $x$, the probe of level $l$ of $t$ at $x$ returns true exactly when the $l$-bit prefix of $x$ belongs to the prefix set stored at level $l$ of $t$.
nodes.title: Level probe of an x-fast trie

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid x-fast trie over $w$-bit keys, let $0 \le l \le w$ and let $x$ be a $w$-bit key. The probe of level $l$ of $t$ at $x$ succeeds if and only if some key $y$ stored in $t$ has the same $l$-bit prefix as $x$.
nodes.title: Level probes of a valid x-fast trie

nodes.summary: For an x-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys and a key $x < 2^w$, the membership query of $x$ in $t$ answers true exactly when the length-$w$ prefix of $x$, which is $x$ itself, lies in the prefix set that $t$ stores for level $w$: a single probe of the deepest level, as in the classical structure.
nodes.title: Membership query in an x-fast trie

nodes.summary: For a valid x-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys and a $w$-bit key $x$, the membership test of $t$ at $x$, which probes the deepest level $w$, returns true if and only if $x$ is stored in $t$.
nodes.title: The membership test of a valid x-fast trie is exact

nodes.summary: For every x-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys and every $w$-bit key $x$, the membership test at $x$ of the trie obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ returns true.
nodes.title: An inserted key passes the membership test

nodes.summary: For an x-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys and a key $x \in \{0, \dots, 2^w - 1\}$, the successor of $x$ in $t$ is the least stored key of $t$ that is greater than $x$ when some stored key is greater than $x$; otherwise $x$ has no successor in $t$.
nodes.title: Successor in an x-fast trie

nodes.summary: For an x-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys and a key $x < 2^w$, the predecessor of $x$ in $t$ is the greatest key stored in $t$ that is smaller than $x$, if such a key exists; otherwise the query returns no key.
nodes.title: Predecessor query in an x-fast trie

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be an x-fast trie over $w$-bit keys and let $x$ and $y$ be keys in $\{0, \dots, 2^w - 1\}$. The successor of $x$ in $t$ exists and equals $y$ if and only if $y$ is a stored key of $t$, $x < y$, and $y \le z$ for every stored key $z$ of $t$ with $x < z$.
nodes.title: Characterization of the x-fast trie successor

nodes.summary: For an x-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys and a key $x < 2^w$, the successor query of $x$ in $t$ returns no key if and only if no key stored in $t$ is greater than $x$.
nodes.title: When an x-fast trie has no successor

nodes.summary: For an x-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys and keys $x, y < 2^w$, the predecessor query of $x$ in $t$ returns $y$ if and only if $y$ is stored in $t$, $y < x$, and every key $z$ stored in $t$ with $z < x$ satisfies $z \le y$.
nodes.title: Characterization of the x-fast trie predecessor

nodes.summary: For an x-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys and a key $x < 2^w$, the predecessor query of $x$ in $t$ returns no key if and only if no key stored in $t$ is smaller than $x$.
nodes.title: When an x-fast trie has no predecessor

nodes.summary: A y-fast trie skeleton over $w$-bit keys consists of an x-fast trie over $w$-bit keys, whose stored keys are the representatives, together with a bucket $B_r$, a finite set of keys, for every key $r \in \{0, \dots, 2^w - 1\}$.
nodes.title: y-fast trie skeleton

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a y-fast trie over $w$-bit keys, let $R$ be the set of keys stored in the representative x-fast trie of $t$, and for each $r \in R$ let $B(r)$ be the bucket owned by $r$. The set of keys stored in $t$ is the union of the buckets of its representatives, $\bigcup_{r \in R} B(r)$.
nodes.title: Keys of a y-fast trie

nodes.summary: For every y-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys and every $w$-bit key $x$, $x$ is stored in $t$ if and only if $x$ lies in the bucket owned by some representative of $t$, that is, by some key stored in the representative x-fast trie of $t$.
nodes.title: Membership in a y-fast trie via representatives' buckets

nodes.summary: A y-fast trie skeleton $t$ over $w$-bit keys, with bucket $B_r$ owned by each key $r$, is valid when its representative x-fast trie is valid, a key $r$ is stored in the representative x-fast trie exactly when its bucket $B_r$ is nonempty, and every key $r$ stored in the representative x-fast trie lies in its own bucket $B_r$.
nodes.title: Valid y-fast trie skeleton

nodes.summary: If a y-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys is valid, then every key of the representative x-fast trie of $t$ is a stored key of $t$.
nodes.title: Representatives of a valid y-fast trie are stored keys

nodes.summary: If $t$ is a valid y-fast trie over $w$-bit keys, then a $w$-bit key $x$ is stored in $t$ if and only if $x$ lies in the bucket owned by some $w$-bit key $r$ (such an owner $r$ is then necessarily a representative).
nodes.title: Keys of a valid y-fast trie are the keys in buckets
Y-fast trie

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $w$ and $B$, a grouped y-fast trie over $w$-bit keys with group bound $B$ consists of an x-fast trie over $w$-bit keys, which holds the representatives, and a list of groups, each a list of $w$-bit keys. The structure itself imposes no condition on these fields; the intended invariants (the representative trie is a valid x-fast trie whose keys are exactly the group maxima, every group is…
nodes.title: Grouped y-fast trie

nodes.summary: The key set of a grouped y-fast trie $t$ is the finite set of all keys that occur in some group of $t$.
nodes.title: Keys of a grouped y-fast trie

nodes.summary: For every grouped y-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys and every key $x$, $x$ lies in the contents of $t$ if and only if $x$ belongs to some group of $t$.
nodes.title: Stored keys are the keys of the groups

nodes.summary: A list of groups, each a list of $w$-bit keys, is group ordered when every key of an earlier group is smaller than every key of a later group.
nodes.title: Ordered list of groups

nodes.summary: A grouped y-fast trie $t$ over keys in $\{0, \dots, 2^w - 1\}$ with group bound $B$ is valid when its representative trie is a valid x-fast trie; a key $r$ is stored in the representative trie exactly when $r$ is the last element of some group of $t$; every group of $t$ is nonempty, has at most $B$ keys, and is strictly increasing; and the groups of $t$ are ordered, that is, every key of an earlier group is smaller…
nodes.title: Validity of a grouped y-fast trie

nodes.summary: For a grouped y-fast trie $t$ and a key $r$, the group of $r$ is the first group of $t$, in the order of the groups, whose last element is $r$, or the empty list if no group of $t$ ends with $r$.
nodes.title: Group of a representative

nodes.summary: For a grouped y-fast trie $t$ and a key $x$, the result is $x$ itself if the membership test of the representative x-fast trie of $t$ (a single probe of its deepest level) reports $x$ as present. Otherwise it is the successor of $x$ in the representative x-fast trie, that is, the least representative greater than $x$, or nothing if there is none.
nodes.title: Least representative at or above a key

nodes.summary: Given a grouped y-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys and a key $x$, the query first finds a representative $r$: $r = x$ if the membership probe of the representative x-fast trie accepts $x$, and otherwise $r$ is the successor of $x$ in the representative trie. If there is no such $r$, the query returns false. Otherwise it returns whether $x$ belongs to the group owned by $r$, namely the first group of $t$ whose last…
nodes.title: Membership query of a grouped y-fast trie

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid grouped y-fast trie over $w$-bit keys. Then for every key $x$, the membership query on $t$ (locate the least representative at least $x$, then scan its group) returns true at $x$ if and only if $x$ lies in the contents of $t$.
nodes.title: Correctness of the y-fast trie membership query

nodes.summary: For a grouped y-fast trie $t$ and a key $x$, let $r$ be the least key greater than $x$ stored in the representative x-fast trie of $t$; if there is none, the query returns nothing. Otherwise let $g$ be the first group of $t$ whose last element is $r$, or the empty list if no group has last element $r$. The query then returns the first key of $g$ greater than $x$, or nothing if $g$ has no such key.
nodes.title: Successor query in a grouped y-fast trie

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid grouped y-fast trie and let $x$, $y$ be keys. The successor query for $x$ in $t$ returns $y$ if and only if $y$ is stored in $t$, $x < y$, and $y \le z$ for every key $z$ stored in $t$ with $x < z$.
nodes.title: Successor query returns the least larger stored key

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a valid grouped y-fast trie and $x$ a key. The successor query for $x$ in $t$ returns nothing if and only if no key stored in $t$ is greater than $x$.
nodes.title: Successor query fails exactly when no larger key is stored

nodes.summary: For every key length $w$ and group bound $B$, the empty grouped y-fast trie has the empty x-fast trie as its trie of representatives and has no groups.
nodes.title: The empty grouped y-fast trie

nodes.summary: For every key width $w$ and group bound $B$, the empty grouped y-fast trie satisfies the grouped y-fast trie invariant.
nodes.title: The empty grouped y-fast trie is valid

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $w$ and $B$ and every $w$-bit key $x$, the membership query on the empty grouped y-fast trie over $w$-bit keys with group bound $B$ returns false at $x$.
nodes.title: The empty grouped y-fast trie has no members

nodes.summary: For every key $x$, the successor query for $x$ in the empty grouped y-fast trie returns nothing.
nodes.title: The empty grouped y-fast trie has no successors

nodes.summary: For a list $rs$ of $w$-bit keys, the representative x-fast trie of $rs$ is obtained from the empty x-fast trie over $w$-bit keys by inserting the elements of $rs$ one at a time, from first to last.
nodes.title: Representative trie of a list

nodes.summary: For every list of $w$-bit keys, the x-fast trie obtained from the empty x-fast trie by inserting the keys of the list one at a time satisfies the x-fast trie invariant: each level holds exactly the prefixes of that length of the stored keys.
nodes.title: Inserting a list of keys into the empty x-fast trie gives a valid trie

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ of $w$-bit keys, the x-fast trie obtained by inserting the elements of $L$ one by one into the empty x-fast trie stores exactly the elements of $L$: its key set is the set of elements of $L$.
nodes.title: Keys of the trie of representatives

nodes.summary: For a list of groups $g_1, \dots, g_k$, each a list of $w$-bit keys, and any group-size bound $B$, this is the grouped y-fast trie whose groups are $g_1, \dots, g_k$ in this order and whose representative x-fast trie is obtained from the empty x-fast trie by inserting the last element of each nonempty group, in order. No condition on the groups is checked here; when a group is sorted, its last element is its maximum.
nodes.title: Grouped y-fast trie from a list of groups

nodes.summary: Let $w$ and $B$ be natural numbers and let $g_1, \dots, g_k$ be a list of groups, each a list of keys in $\{0, \dots, 2^w - 1\}$. Suppose every group is nonempty, has at most $B$ keys, and is strictly increasing, and the groups are ordered: every key of an earlier group is smaller than every key of a later group. Then the grouped y-fast trie with group bound $B$ assembled from these groups, whose representatives…
nodes.title: Assembling a valid grouped y-fast trie from groups

nodes.summary: Given a bound $B$, a fuel $n$ and a list $l$ of $w$-bit keys, the fuel-bounded chunking is the empty list of chunks when $n = 0$ or $l$ is empty; otherwise it is the chunk formed by the first $\min(B, |l|)$ elements of $l$, followed by the fuel-bounded chunking with bound $B$ and fuel $n - 1$ of the remaining elements of $l$.
nodes.title: Fuel-bounded chunking

nodes.summary: Given a bound $B$ and a list $l$ of $w$-bit keys, when $B > 0$ the chunking of $l$ cuts $l$ from the left into consecutive chunks of exactly $B$ elements each, except that the last chunk holds the remaining one to $B$ elements; there are no chunks when $l$ is empty. When $B = 0$, the chunking has no chunks if $l$ is empty and is the single chunk $l$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Chunking a list into groups

nodes.summary: For every nonempty list $l$ of $w$-bit keys, the chunking of $l$ with bound $B = 0$ consists of the single chunk $l$.
nodes.title: Chunking with bound zero

nodes.summary: For every bound $B$ (including $B = 0$) and every list $l$ of $w$-bit keys, concatenating the chunks of the chunking of $l$ with bound $B$, in order, gives back $l$.
nodes.title: Chunking preserves the list

nodes.summary: Let $B > 0$ and let $l$ be a strictly increasing list of $w$-bit keys. Then every chunk of the chunking of $l$ into groups of at most $B$ keys is nonempty, has at most $B$ elements, and is strictly increasing.
nodes.title: Chunks of a sorted list

nodes.summary: Let $B$ be a natural number and let $l$ be a strictly increasing list of $w$-bit keys. Then the chunk groups of $l$ with bound $B$ are group ordered: every key of an earlier chunk is smaller than every key of a later chunk.
nodes.title: Chunks of a sorted list are ordered

nodes.summary: For a group bound $B$ and a list $l$ of $w$-bit keys, this is the grouped y-fast trie whose groups, in order, are consecutive pieces of $l$ that together make up $l$, and whose representative x-fast trie is obtained from the empty x-fast trie by inserting the last element of each group, in order. If $B > 0$, the groups are obtained by repeatedly cutting off the first $B$ keys, so every group has exactly $B$ keys…
nodes.title: Grouped y-fast trie from a sorted list

nodes.summary: Let $w$ and $B$ be natural numbers with $0 < B$, and let $l$ be a strictly increasing list of keys in $\{0, \dots, 2^w - 1\}$. Then the grouped y-fast trie with group bound $B$ built from $l$ by cutting it into consecutive groups of at most $B$ keys is valid.
nodes.title: Building from a sorted list gives a valid grouped y-fast trie

nodes.summary: For every natural number $w$ and every nonempty list $l$ of $w$-bit keys, the grouped y-fast trie with group bound $B = 0$ built from $l$ is not valid.
nodes.title: Building from a nonempty list with group bound zero gives an invalid trie

nodes.summary: For every group bound $B$ (including $B = 0$) and every list $l$ of $w$-bit keys, sorted or not, the key set of the grouped y-fast trie built from $l$ with group bound $B$ is exactly the set of elements of $l$.
nodes.title: Keys of the grouped y-fast trie built from a list

nodes.summary: Let $B > 0$ and let $l$ be a strictly increasing list of $w$-bit keys. Then for every key $x$, the membership query on the grouped y-fast trie built from $l$ with group bound $B$ returns true at $x$ if and only if $x$ belongs to $l$.
nodes.title: Membership in a trie built from a sorted list

nodes.summary: Let $B > 0$, let $l$ be a strictly increasing list of $w$-bit keys, and let $x$, $y$ be keys. The successor query for $x$ in the grouped y-fast trie built from $l$ with group bound $B$ returns $y$ if and only if $y$ belongs to $l$, $x < y$, and $y \le z$ for every $z$ in $l$ with $x < z$.
nodes.title: Successor in the trie built from a sorted list

nodes.summary: Union-find with rank and path compression (including its connected-components application), link-cut trees and Euler-tour trees.
nodes.title: Disjoint sets and dynamic trees
Disjoint-set data structure

nodes.summary: A parent forest on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ consists of a parent map $p$ from the vertices to themselves (a vertex $x$ with $p(x) = x$ is a root) and a depth certificate $d$ assigning a natural number to every vertex, such that every non-root edge strictly decreases the certificate: if $p(x) \ne x$, then $d(p(x)) < d(x)$.
nodes.title: Parent forest with a depth certificate

nodes.summary: For a parent forest $F$ with parent map $p$ and a vertex $x$, the root of $x$ is found by following parent pointers from $x$: it is $x$ itself if $p(x) = x$, and otherwise it is the root of $p(x)$.
nodes.title: Root of a vertex in a parent forest

nodes.summary: For a parent forest $F$ with parent map $p$ and a vertex $x$, the path length of $x$ is the number of parent edges followed from $x$ to its root: it is $0$ if $p(x) = x$, and otherwise one more than the path length of $p(x)$.
nodes.title: Path length to the root

nodes.summary: For a vertex $x$ of a parent forest $F$, find with cost returns the root that find returns for $x$, together with the cost $\ell(x) + 1$, where $\ell(x)$ is the path length of $x$ (the number of non-root parent edges that find traverses from $x$). That is, it charges one unit for every visited vertex, including the root.
nodes.title: Find with cost

nodes.summary: Two vertices $x$ and $y$ of a parent forest $F$ are equivalent when find returns the same root for $x$ as for $y$ in $F$.
nodes.title: Equivalent vertices of a parent forest

nodes.summary: For every vertex $x$ of a parent forest $F$, the vertex $r$ that find returns for $x$ is a root of $F$: the parent of $r$ in $F$ is $r$ itself.
nodes.title: Find returns a root

nodes.summary: For every vertex $x$ of a parent forest $F$, find returns the same root for the parent of $x$ in $F$ as for $x$.
nodes.title: Find is unchanged along a parent pointer

nodes.summary: For every vertex $x$ of a parent forest $F$, the vertex $x$ is equivalent in $F$ to the root that find returns for $x$.
nodes.title: Every vertex is equivalent to its representative

nodes.summary: For every vertex $x$ of a parent forest $F$, the cost that find with cost charges on $x$ equals $\ell(x) + 1$, where $\ell(x)$ is the path length of $x$: the number of non-root parent edges that find traverses from $x$.
nodes.title: The cost of find is the path length plus one

nodes.summary: For every vertex $x$ of a parent forest $F$ with depth certificate $d$, the cost that find with cost charges on $x$ is at most $d(x) + 1$.
nodes.title: The cost of find is at most the depth certificate plus one

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a parent forest with parent map $p$, and let $r$ and $s$ be vertices. The linked parent map sends $r$ to $s$ and agrees with $p$ on every other vertex: it maps $z$ to $s$ if $z = r$, and to $p(z)$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Parent map after linking two roots

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a parent forest with depth certificate $d$, and let $r$ and $s$ be vertices. The linked depth certificate assigns to a vertex $z$ the number $d(z) + d(s) + 1$ if $z$ is equivalent to $r$ in $F$ (that is, $z$ and $r$ have the same root), and $d(z)$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Depth certificate after linking two roots

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a parent forest with parent map $p$ and depth certificate $d$, and let $r \ne s$ be two distinct roots of $F$. Linking $r$ to $s$ gives the parent forest whose parent map is the linked parent map (the parent of $r$ becomes $s$ and all other parents are unchanged) and whose depth certificate is the linked depth certificate (the certificate of every vertex equivalent to $r$ grows by $d(s) + 1$ and all…
nodes.title: Linking two roots of a parent forest

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a union-find forest on $n$ vertices: each vertex $z$ has a parent $p(z)$, where roots are their own parents, and a depth certificate $d(z) \in \mathbb{N}$ with $d(p(z)) < d(z)$ whenever $p(z) \ne z$. Let $x$ and $y$ be vertices, and let $r_x$ and $r_y$ be the roots reached from $x$ and $y$ by following parent pointers. If $r_x = r_y$, the union of $x$ and $y$ in $F$ is $F$ itself. Otherwise it is the…
nodes.title: Union in a union-find forest

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a parent forest, let $x, y, z$ be vertices of $F$, and let $F'$ be the forest obtained from $F$ by the union of $x$ and $y$. If $z$ is equivalent to $x$ in $F$, then find returns for $z$ in $F'$ the root that find returns for $y$ in $F$; otherwise find returns the same root for $z$ in $F'$ as in $F$.
nodes.title: Representatives after a union

nodes.summary: For every parent forest $F$ and vertices $x$ and $y$, the vertices $x$ and $y$ are equivalent in the forest obtained from $F$ by the union of $x$ and $y$.
nodes.title: Union makes its arguments equivalent

nodes.summary: If $x$ and $y$ are equivalent vertices of a parent forest $F$, then the union of $x$ and $y$ in $F$ is $F$ itself.
nodes.title: Union of equivalent vertices changes nothing

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a parent forest and let $x, y, a, b$ be vertices of $F$. Then $a$ and $b$ are equivalent in the forest obtained from $F$ by the union of $x$ and $y$ if and only if $a$ and $b$ are equivalent in $F$, or $a$ is equivalent to $x$ and $b$ is equivalent to $y$ in $F$, or $a$ is equivalent to $y$ and $b$ is equivalent to $x$ in $F$.
nodes.title: Equivalence after a union

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a parent forest and let $x, y, z$ be vertices of $F$. If $z$ is not equivalent to $x$ in $F$, then find returns the same root for $z$ in the forest obtained from $F$ by the union of $x$ and $y$ as in $F$.
nodes.title: Union preserves the representatives of unrelated classes

nodes.summary: For a parent forest $F$ and vertices $x$ and $y$, the costed union returns the union of $x$ and $y$ in $F$ together with a cost equal to the cost of finding the root of $x$ plus the cost of finding the root of $y$ (each one unit per visited vertex, including the root), plus one more unit when the roots of $x$ and $y$ are distinct; when they coincide, union performs no link and none is charged.
nodes.title: Union in a parent forest with cost

nodes.summary: For every parent forest $F$ with depth certificate $d$ and vertices $x$ and $y$, the cost charged for the union of $x$ and $y$ in $F$ (two root searches at one unit per visited vertex, plus one unit for the link when the roots differ) is at most $d(x) + d(y) + 3$.
nodes.title: Cost bound for union in a parent forest

nodes.summary: Call two natural numbers $a$ and $c$ equivalent in a union-find structure when they have the same root, where a number that is not a node is its own root. Let $U$ be a union-find structure with nodes $0, \dots, N-1$ and let $x, y < N$. The equivalence query on $x$ and $y$, which runs FIND-SET with path compression on $x$ and then on $y$, returns a union-find structure $U'$ and a boolean $b$ such that $U'$ has $N$…
nodes.title: Correctness of the union-find equivalence query

nodes.summary: Given a natural number $n$ and a list $E$ of pairs of vertices in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, CONNECTED-COMPONENTS first builds the union-find structure with $n$ singleton nodes $0, \dots, n-1$ by $n$ MAKE-SET calls. It then processes the pairs $(u, v)$ of $E$ in list order: it asks whether $u$ and $v$ are equivalent using two FIND-SET calls, keeping the path compression done by the query, and if they are not equivalent…
nodes.title: Connected components via union-find

reading_title.source: Connected components allocates $n$ nodes

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$ and every list $E$ of pairs of vertices in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the union-find structure returned by CONNECTED-COMPONENTS on $n$ and $E$ has exactly $n$ nodes.
nodes.title: Connected components allocates $n$ nodes

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number and let $E$ be a list of pairs of vertices in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. For all vertices $a, b < n$, $a$ and $b$ are equivalent in the union-find structure returned by CONNECTED-COMPONENTS on $n$ and $E$ if and only if $a$ and $b$ are joined by a path in the simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ whose edges are the unordered pairs $\{u, v\}$ with $(u, v)$ in $E$ and $u \ne v$.
nodes.title: Connected components computes reachability

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number, let $E$ be a list of pairs of vertices in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $m$ be the length of $E$. Let $G$ be the simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ whose edges are the unordered pairs $\{u, v\}$ with $(u, v)$ in $E$ and $u \ne v$, and let $k$ be the number of connected components of $G$. Running CONNECTED-COMPONENTS on $n$ and $E$ makes exactly $n$ MAKE-SET calls, $2m$ FIND-SET calls and…
nodes.title: Operation counts of connected components

nodes.summary: For a union-find structure $S$ with node array $A$ and a node $x < |S|$, this is the recursive path-compression routine of FIND, paired with a cost in $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$. It charges $(1, 0)$ for testing whether $x$ is a root. If the parent $y$ of $x$ in $A$ equals $x$, it returns $A$ and the root $x$. Otherwise it runs on $y$, obtaining an array $A'$ and a root $r$, charges $(0, 1)$ for one parent…
nodes.title: Cost-counted FIND auxiliary

nodes.summary: For a union-find structure $S$ and a node $x < |S|$, the value returned by the cost-counted FIND auxiliary on $x$ (the compressed node array together with the root of $x$), with its cost discarded, equals the result of the Batteries path-compression auxiliary routine of FIND on $x$.
nodes.title: The cost-counted FIND auxiliary returns the uncounted result

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a union-find structure and $x < |S|$ a node. If the parent of $x$ in $S$ is $x$ itself, then the cost-counted FIND auxiliary on $x$ has cost $(1, 0)$: one root test and no parent writes.
nodes.title: Cost of the FIND auxiliary at a root

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a union-find structure and $x < |S|$ a node whose parent $y$ in $S$ differs from $x$. If $c_x$ and $c_y$ are the costs of the cost-counted FIND auxiliary on $x$ and on $y$, then $c_x = (1, 0) + (c_y + (0, 1))$: one root test at $x$, then the run on $y$, then one parent write.
nodes.title: Cost recurrence of the FIND auxiliary at a non-root

nodes.summary: For a union-find structure $S$ and a node $x < |S|$, if the cost-counted FIND auxiliary on $x$ has cost $(t, w)$, where $t$ counts root tests and $w$ counts parent writes, then $t = w + 1$.
nodes.title: Root tests exceed parent writes by one

nodes.summary: For a union-find structure $S$ and a node $x < |S|$, this runs the cost-counted FIND auxiliary on $x$, obtaining a node array $A'$, a root $r$ and a cost $(t, w)$. It returns the union-find structure with node array $A'$, together with $r$ as a node of that structure (whose size equals $|S|$), at cost $(t, w)$.
nodes.title: Cost-counted FIND

nodes.summary: For a union-find structure $S$ and a node $x < |S|$, the value returned by the cost-counted FIND on $x$ (the compressed union-find structure together with the root of $x$), with its cost discarded, equals the result of the Batteries FIND with path compression on $x$.
nodes.title: The cost-counted FIND returns the FIND result

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a union-find structure, let $R$ be one more than the maximum rank of a node of $S$, and let $x < |S|$ be a node. The number of parent writes performed by the cost-counted FIND auxiliary on $x$ (the second coordinate of its cost) is at most $R - \operatorname{rank}(x)$.
nodes.title: Parent writes are bounded by the rank gap

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a union-find structure with parent map $p$ (where $p(i) = i$ for $i \ge |S|$), let $x < |S|$, and let $p'$ be the parent map of the structure produced by FIND with path compression on $x$. Then for every natural number $i$, $p'(i)$ is the root of $x$ if $i = p^k(x)$ for some $k \ge 0$, and $p'(i) = p(i)$ otherwise.
nodes.title: FIND compresses exactly the original path to the root

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a union-find structure on the indices $0, \dots, n-1$ with parent function $p$, let $x < n$, and let $r$ be the root of $x$ in $s$. After find with path compression is run on $x$, for every index $i < n$ the node at $i$ in the resulting array keeps its rank from $s$, and its parent is $r$ if $i = p^k(x)$ for some $k \ge 0$, and is its original parent $p(i)$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Effect of path-compressing find on each node

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a union-find structure with $n$ nodes and parent map $p$, and let $x < n$. Then there is $d < n$ such that $p^d(x)$ is the root of $x$ and $p^k(x)$ is not the root of $x$ for every $k < d$.
nodes.title: The root is reached in fewer parent steps than there are nodes

nodes.summary: For an array $A$ of union-find nodes, write $\rho_A(i)$ for the rank stored at index $i$ of $A$, or $0$ if $i$ is not an index of $A$. Let $x, y$ be indices of $A$ and let $A'$ be the array obtained from $A$ by the Batteries link by rank of $x$ and $y$. Then for every natural number $i$, $\rho_{A'}(i) = \rho_A(y) + 1$ if $x \ne y$, $\rho_A(x) = \rho_A(y)$ and $i = y$, and $\rho_{A'}(i) = \rho_A(i)$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Ranks after linking two nodes of an array

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a union-find structure, write $\rho(i)$ for the rank of $i$ in $S$ ($0$ if $i$ is not a node of $S$), and let $x, y$ be nodes of $S$ such that $y$ is a root, that is, the parent of $y$ is $y$. Let $S'$ be the result of linking $x$ and $y$ by rank. Then for every natural number $i$, the rank of $i$ in $S'$ is $\rho(y) + 1$ if $x \ne y$, $\rho(x) = \rho(y)$ and $i = y$, and is $\rho(i)$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Ranks after linking in a union-find structure

nodes.summary: Let $U$ be a union-find structure on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $x, y < n$ be roots of $U$, i.e. each is its own parent. Let $U'$ be obtained by linking $x$ and $y$ by rank: nothing changes if $x = y$; otherwise, if $\operatorname{rank}(y) < \operatorname{rank}(x)$ then $y$ gets parent $x$, and if not then $x$ gets parent $y$ and, when the two ranks are equal, the rank of $y$ increases by one. Then for every…
nodes.title: Linking two roots by rank

nodes.summary: Let $U$ be a union-find structure on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $x, y < n$. Run find with path compression on $x$ in $U$, giving a structure $U_1$ and a root $r_x$; then run find on $y$ in $U_1$ (not in $U$), giving a structure $U_2$ and a root $r_y$. Then the node array of the union of $x$ and $y$ in $U$ equals the array obtained from the node array of $U_2$ by linking $r_x$ and $r_y$ by rank: nothing changes if…
nodes.title: Union unfolds to two finds and a link

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a union-find structure and $x$ a node of $S$, and let $S'$ be the structure returned by FIND on $x$ with path compression. For every natural number $i$, the rank of $i$ in $S'$ equals the rank of $i$ in $S$, where the rank of an index that is not a node is $0$.
nodes.title: Path compression preserves ranks

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a union-find structure, write $\rho(i)$ for the rank of $i$ in $S$ ($0$ if $i$ is not a node of $S$) and $r(i)$ for the root of $i$ in $S$. For nodes $x, y$ of $S$ and every natural number $i$, the rank of $i$ in the union of $x$ and $y$ in $S$ (union by rank with path compression) is $\rho(r(y)) + 1$ if $r(x) \ne r(y)$, $\rho(r(x)) = \rho(r(y))$ and $r(y) = i$, and is $\rho(i)$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Ranks after a union

nodes.summary: Given an array $A$ of union-find nodes, each storing a parent index and a rank, and indices $x, y$ of $A$, this computation returns an array together with a count $(t, p, w)$ of rank tests $t$, parent writes $p$ and rank writes $w$. If $x = y$ it returns $A$ with count $(0, 0, 0)$. Otherwise it makes one rank test; if the rank of $y$ is less than the rank of $x$, it sets the parent of $y$ to $x$ (one parent write).…
nodes.title: Linking by rank with operation counts

nodes.summary: For an array $A$ of union-find nodes and indices $x, y$ of $A$, the array returned by counted linking of $x$ and $y$ in $A$ is exactly the array produced by the uncounted Batteries link by rank of $x$ and $y$ in $A$.
nodes.title: Counted linking returns the linked array

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be an array of union-find nodes, let $x, y$ be indices of $A$, and write $r_x$ and $r_y$ for the ranks stored at $x$ and $y$. Counted linking of $x$ and $y$ in $A$ makes $(t, p, w)$ rank tests, parent writes and rank writes, where $(t, p, w)$ is $(0, 0, 0)$ if $x = y$, is $(1, 1, 0)$ if $x \ne y$ and $r_y < r_x$, is $(2, 1, 1)$ if $x \ne y$ and $r_x = r_y$, and is $(2, 1, 0)$ otherwise, that is, if…
nodes.title: Operation counts of linking by rank

nodes.summary: For a union-find structure $S$ and indices $x, y$ of $S$, this computation runs counted FIND on $x$ in $S$, giving a structure $S_1$ and a root $r_x$; then counted FIND on $y$ in $S_1$, giving a structure $S_2$ and a root $r_y$; then counted linking of $r_x$ and $r_y$ in the node array of $S_2$. It returns the array produced by the linking, with cost $((a, b), (t, p, w))$, where $a$ and $b$ are the total numbers of…
nodes.title: Union by rank with operation counts

nodes.summary: For a union-find structure $S$ and indices $x, y$ of $S$, the array returned by the counted union of $x$ and $y$ in $S$ equals the node array of the Batteries union of $x$ and $y$ in $S$ (union by rank with path compression).
nodes.title: Counted union returns the union's array

nodes.summary: For a union-find structure $S$ and indices $x, y$ of $S$, in the counted union of $x$ and $y$ in $S$ the total number of root tests made by its two FIND calls equals the total number of parent writes they make plus $2$.
nodes.title: The FIND phases of a union make two more root tests than parent writes
Euler tour tree

nodes.summary: A rooted ordered tree with vertices in a type $V$ consists of a root vertex in $V$ together with an ordered list of child subtrees, each a rooted ordered tree with vertices in $V$.
nodes.title: Rooted ordered tree

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a property of trees. Suppose that for every vertex $r$ and all trees $c_1, \dots, c_k$ (with $k \ge 0$), if $P$ holds for each $c_i$, then $P$ holds for the tree with root $r$ and child subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_k$. Then $P$ holds for every tree.
nodes.title: Induction principle for rooted trees

nodes.summary: The root of the tree with root vertex $r$ and child subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_k$ is the vertex $r$.
nodes.title: Root of a rooted tree

nodes.summary: The children of a tree are the child subtrees of its root, as a list in their given order.
nodes.title: Children of a rooted tree

nodes.summary: The size of a tree is its number of nodes, counting repeated vertex labels with multiplicity: the tree with root $r$ and child subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_k$ has size $1 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \operatorname{size}(c_i)$.
nodes.title: Size of a rooted tree

nodes.summary: For a rooted ordered tree $t$ with root $r$ and child subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_k$ (in order) and a list $a$, the accumulator traversal $T(t, a)$ is the list whose first entry is $r$ and whose remaining entries are $T(c_1, T(c_2, \dots, T(c_k, a) \dots))$; when $k = 0$ the remaining entries are $a$.
nodes.title: Accumulator preorder traversal

nodes.summary: The preorder vertex list of a rooted ordered tree $t$ is the accumulator preorder traversal of $t$ started from the empty list.
nodes.title: Preorder vertex list of a rooted tree

nodes.summary: For every rooted ordered tree $t$ and every list $a$, the accumulator preorder traversal of $t$ started from $a$ equals the preorder vertex list of $t$ followed by $a$.
nodes.title: Accumulator preorder traversal is append

nodes.summary: For a vertex $r$ and rooted ordered trees $c_1, \dots, c_k$, the preorder vertex list of the tree with root $r$ and child subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_k$ (in order) is $r$ followed by the concatenation of the preorder vertex lists of $c_1, \dots, c_k$, in this order.
nodes.title: Preorder vertex list of a node

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a tree with root $r$ and child subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_k$ in order, and let $a$ be a list of vertices. For a list $L$ of vertices, write $r \cdot L$ for the list $L$ with $r$ put in front. The Euler tour of $t$ with accumulator $a$, written $T(t, a)$, is $r \cdot L_1$, where $L_{k+1} = a$ and $L_i = T(c_i, r \cdot L_{i+1})$ for $i = k, \dots, 1$.
nodes.title: Euler tour with an accumulator

nodes.summary: The Euler tour of a tree $t$ with root $r$ and child subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_k$ in order is the list of vertices consisting of $r$, followed, for each $i = 1, \dots, k$ in turn, by the Euler tour of $c_i$ and then $r$. It is the vertex sequence of the depth-first walk that returns to the parent vertex after each child subtree.
nodes.title: Euler tour

nodes.summary: For every tree $t$ and every list $a$ of vertices, the Euler tour of $t$ with accumulator $a$ equals the Euler tour of $t$ followed by $a$.
nodes.title: Accumulator lemma for the Euler tour

nodes.summary: For a vertex $r$ and a list of trees $c_1, \dots, c_k$, the Euler tour of the tree with root $r$ and child subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_k$ in order is $r$, followed, for each $i = 1, \dots, k$ in turn, by the Euler tour of $c_i$ and then $r$.
nodes.title: Recursive formula for the Euler tour

nodes.summary: The arc sequence of a tree $t$ is the list of consecutive pairs of its Euler tour: if the Euler tour of $t$ is $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k$, then the arc sequence of $t$ is $(v_0, v_1), (v_1, v_2), \dots, (v_{k-1}, v_k)$.
nodes.title: Arc sequence of the Euler tour

nodes.summary: For every tree $t$, the arc sequence of $t$ is the Euler tour of $t$ zipped with its own tail: if the Euler tour of $t$ is $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k$, then the arc sequence of $t$ is $(v_0, v_1), (v_1, v_2), \dots, (v_{k-1}, v_k)$.
nodes.title: Arc sequence as the zipped Euler tour

nodes.summary: For every tree $t$ and every $v$, $v$ occurs in the Euler tour of $t$ if and only if $v$ is a vertex of $t$.
nodes.title: The Euler tour visits exactly the vertices of the tree

nodes.summary: A rooted ordered tree is valid when its list of vertices in preorder has no duplicates, that is, every vertex label occurs at most once in the tree.
nodes.title: Valid Euler-tour tree

nodes.summary: A tree $t$ is valid if and only if its list of vertices in preorder has no repeated entries.
nodes.title: Valid trees have distinct vertices

nodes.summary: For every vertex $r$, the tree with root $r$ and no child subtrees is valid.
nodes.title: A single-vertex tree is valid

nodes.summary: Let $t_1$ be a tree with root $r$ and child subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_k$, and let $t_2$ be a tree. The link of $t_1$ and $t_2$ is the tree with root $r$ and child subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_k, t_2$, so $t_2$ becomes the new last child subtree of the root of $t_1$.
nodes.title: Linking two rooted trees

nodes.summary: Let $t_1$ and $t_2$ be valid trees such that no vertex of $t_1$ is a vertex of $t_2$. Then the link of $t_1$ and $t_2$, that is, $t_1$ with $t_2$ added as the last child subtree of its root, is valid.
nodes.title: Linking valid trees with disjoint vertices gives a valid tree

nodes.summary: For every vertex $r$, the link of the single-vertex tree with root $r$ and another single-vertex tree with root $r$ is not valid, since the vertex $r$ occurs twice in it. Hence the link of two valid trees need not be valid when their vertex sets are not disjoint.
nodes.title: Linking two copies of a single vertex is not valid

nodes.summary: For lists $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ of vertices and a vertex $r$, the splice of $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ at $r$ is the list consisting of the entries of $\tau_1$, followed by the entries of $\tau_2$, followed by $r$.
nodes.title: Splicing two Euler tours

nodes.summary: For trees $t_1$ and $t_2$, let $t$ be the link of $t_1$ and $t_2$, that is, $t_1$ with $t_2$ added as the last child subtree of its root. The Euler tour of $t$ is the Euler tour of $t_1$, followed by the Euler tour of $t_2$, followed by the root of $t_1$.
nodes.title: Euler tour of a linked tree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a tree with root $r$ and child subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_k$. Cutting the last child subtree of $t$ gives no result when $k = 0$; when $k \ge 1$ it gives the pair consisting of the tree with root $r$ and child subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_{k-1}$, together with the removed subtree $c_k$.
nodes.title: Cutting the last child subtree
Link-cut tree

nodes.summary: For a vertex $r$ and a list of vertices $c_1, \dots, c_k$, the spine is the rooted tree $r \to c_1 \to \cdots \to c_k$: its root is $r$, each vertex has the next one in the list as its only child, and the last vertex ($c_k$, or $r$ when $k = 0$) is a leaf.
nodes.title: Path tree on a vertex list

nodes.summary: The forest built from the empty list is empty; the forest built from a list $r, c_1, \dots, c_k$ consists of the single spine $r \to c_1 \to \cdots \to c_k$, the rooted tree in which each vertex has the next one as its only child.
nodes.title: Forest from a vertex list

nodes.summary: For a vertex $x$ and a forest given as a list of trees, the first tree whose vertices contain $x$, or nothing when no tree contains $x$.
nodes.title: Tree of a forest containing a vertex

nodes.summary: Given a vertex $x$ and a forest, given as a list of rooted ordered trees, removing the trees containing $x$ deletes from the list every tree that has $x$ among its vertices and keeps the remaining trees in their original order.
nodes.title: Removing the trees that contain a vertex

nodes.summary: Let $f$ be a forest of rooted ordered trees whose concatenated vertex lists have no duplicates, let $x$ be a vertex, and let $t$ be the first tree of $f$ containing $x$. Then the concatenated vertex list of the forest obtained from $f$ by removing every tree containing $x$, followed by the vertex list of $t$, is a permutation of the concatenated vertex list of $f$.
nodes.title: Removing the tree containing a vertex splits the forest's vertices

nodes.summary: For a vertex $x$ and a tree $T$, the subtree of $T$ rooted at the first occurrence of $x$ in preorder, or nothing when $x$ does not occur in $T$.
nodes.title: Subtree rooted at a vertex

nodes.summary: Two vertices $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in a rooted tree $t$ when they are joined by a parent-child edge of $t$ in either direction: some node of $t$ labelled $a$ has a child labelled $b$, or some node of $t$ labelled $b$ has a child labelled $a$.
nodes.title: Adjacency in a rooted tree

nodes.summary: If $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in a tree $t$, that is, joined by a parent-child edge in either direction, then $a$ is a vertex of $t$.
nodes.title: The first endpoint of a tree edge is a vertex

nodes.summary: For every rooted ordered tree $T$ and vertices $a$ and $b$, if $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $T$ (joined by a parent-child edge in either direction), then $b$ and $a$ are adjacent in $T$.
nodes.title: Adjacency in a tree is symmetric

nodes.summary: If $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in a tree $t$, that is, joined by a parent-child edge in either direction, then $b$ is a vertex of $t$.
nodes.title: The second endpoint of a tree edge is a vertex

nodes.summary: For vertices $a$, $b$ and a rooted tree $t$ with root $r$ and child subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_k$, the adjacency test of $a$ and $b$ in $t$ returns true exactly when $r = a$ and some $c_i$ has root $b$, or $r = b$ and some $c_i$ has root $a$, or the adjacency test of $a$ and $b$ returns true in some $c_i$.
nodes.title: Adjacency test

nodes.summary: For a vertex $y$ and trees $N$ and $T$, grafting $N$ at $y$ in $T$ attaches $N$ as a new last child of the first node of $T$ labelled $y$ in preorder, keeping every existing node and edge; it returns nothing when $y$ does not occur in $T$. This is the tree surgery behind linking two trees: it adds exactly the edge from $y$ to the root of $N$.
nodes.title: Grafting a tree below a vertex

nodes.summary: Let $t$ and $C$ be trees and $y$ a vertex. If grafting $C$ at $y$ in $t$, that is, attaching $C$ as a new last child of a node labelled $y$, produces the tree $t'$, then for every $v$, $v$ is a vertex of $t'$ if and only if $v$ is a vertex of $t$ or a vertex of $C$.
nodes.title: Vertices after grafting

nodes.summary: Let $T$ and $N$ be rooted ordered trees and $y$ a vertex. If grafting $N$ into $T$ at $y$ is defined and yields the tree $T'$, then the root of $T'$ equals the root of $T$.
nodes.title: Grafting keeps the root

nodes.summary: Let $t$ and $u$ be rooted trees and $y$ a vertex, and suppose that grafting $u$ as a new child under $y$ in $t$ succeeds and yields the tree $t'$. Then for all vertices $a$ and $b$, the vertices $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t'$ if and only if they are adjacent in $t$, or adjacent in $u$, or $a = y$ and $b$ is the root of $u$, or $a$ is the root of $u$ and $b = y$.
nodes.title: Edges after grafting

nodes.summary: Let $t$ and $s$ be rooted ordered trees and $y$ a vertex. If grafting $s$ as a new child at $y$ in $t$ succeeds and yields the tree $t'$, then the vertex list of $t'$ is a permutation of the vertex list of $t$ followed by the vertex list of $s$.
nodes.title: Grafting adds the new subtree's vertices

nodes.summary: For a vertex $x$ and a rooted ordered tree $T$ with root $r$, rerooting $T$ at $x$ is defined recursively. If $r = x$, the result is $T$ itself. Otherwise let $C$ be the first child subtree of $r$ that contains $x$, let $p$ be the root of $C$, and let $C'$ be $C$ rerooted at $x$. The result is $C'$ with the tree formed by $r$ and its remaining children (in their original order) attached as a new last child of the…
nodes.title: Rerooting a tree at a vertex

nodes.summary: For every rooted ordered tree $T$ and every vertex $x$ that is not a vertex of $T$, rerooting $T$ at $x$ is undefined (it returns no tree).
nodes.title: Rerooting fails at an absent vertex

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted tree and $x$ a vertex. If rerooting $t$ at $x$ yields the tree $t'$, then a vertex lies in $t'$ if and only if it lies in $t$.
nodes.title: Rerooting preserves the vertex set

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted tree with no repeated vertex, and suppose that rerooting $t$ at a vertex $x$ yields the tree $t'$. Then for all vertices $a$ and $b$, the vertices $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t'$ if and only if they are adjacent in $t$.
nodes.title: Rerooting keeps every edge

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted ordered tree and $x$ a vertex. If rerooting $t$ at $x$ yields the tree $t'$, then the vertex list of $t'$ is a permutation of the vertex list of $t$.
nodes.title: Rerooting preserves the vertices

nodes.summary: For a vertex $x$ and a rooted ordered tree $T$, pruning $T$ at $x$ removes every subtree of $T$ whose root is labelled $x$, keeping every other node and edge and the order of children. If the root of $T$ is $x$, nothing remains and pruning is undefined. Otherwise the result is the tree with the same root whose children are, in their original order, the pruned children of the root, with the children labelled $x$…
nodes.title: Pruning the subtrees rooted at a vertex

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted ordered tree and $x$ a vertex that does not occur in $t$. Then pruning the subtrees rooted at $x$ from $t$ succeeds and returns $t$ itself.
nodes.title: Pruning at an absent vertex changes nothing

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted tree and $x$ a vertex. If pruning $t$ at $x$ leaves the tree $t'$, then every vertex of $t'$ is a vertex of $t$ and is different from $x$.
nodes.title: Vertices of a pruned tree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted tree whose preorder vertex list has no repeated vertex, and let $x$ be a vertex. Suppose the subtree search finds the subtree $s$ of $t$ rooted at $x$, and pruning $t$ at $x$ leaves the tree $t'$. Then every vertex of $t$ that is not a vertex of $s$ is a vertex of $t'$.
nodes.title: Pruning keeps the vertices outside the detached subtree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted ordered tree whose vertex list has no duplicates and let $x$ be a vertex. If $x$ occurs in $t$, with $s$ the subtree of $t$ rooted at $x$, and pruning at $x$ leaves a tree $t'$ (that is, $x$ is not the root of $t$), then the vertex list of $t$ is a permutation of the vertex list of $t'$ followed by the vertex list of $s$.
nodes.title: Pruning a subtree splits the vertex list

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a rooted ordered tree and $x$ a vertex. If pruning $T$ at $x$ yields a tree $T'$ (that is, the root of $T$ is not $x$), then the root of $T'$ equals the root of $T$.
nodes.title: Pruning keeps the root

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted tree with no repeated vertex and $x$ a vertex, and suppose that removing every subtree rooted at $x$ from $t$ leaves the tree $t'$ (that is, the root of $t$ is not $x$). If $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t$ and both are vertices of $t'$, then $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t'$.
nodes.title: Pruning keeps surviving edges

nodes.summary: For a vertex $x$ and a rooted ordered tree $T$, the root path of $x$ is defined exactly when $x$ is a vertex of $T$. It is then the list of vertices on the path from the root of $T$ down to $x$, root first and ending with $x$; if $x$ occurs more than once, the path leads to its first occurrence in preorder.
nodes.title: Root-to-vertex path

nodes.summary: If $p$ is the path from the root of a tree $T$ down to a vertex $x$ of $T$, then $p$ is nonempty and its last (deepest) vertex is $x$.
nodes.title: A root path ends at its target

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a tree and $x$ a vertex. If the root path of $x$ in $t$ (the path from the root of $t$ down to $x$) is defined and equals $p$, then $p$ is nonempty and its first vertex is the root of $t$.
nodes.title: The root path starts at the root

nodes.summary: If $p$ is the path in a tree $t$ from the root down to a vertex $x$, then every vertex of $p$ is a vertex of $t$.
nodes.title: Root paths stay inside the tree

nodes.summary: If the preorder vertex list of a rooted tree $t$ has no repeated vertex and $p$ is the path from the root of $t$ down to a vertex $x$, then $p$ has no repeated vertex.
nodes.title: Root paths have distinct vertices

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a tree and $x$ a vertex. If the root path of $x$ in $t$ is defined and equals $p = (p_0, \dots, p_k)$, then for every $i < k$ the vertices $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ are adjacent in $t$, that is, joined by a parent-child edge of $t$ in one direction or the other.
nodes.title: Consecutive vertices of a root path are adjacent

nodes.summary: For vertices $a$ and $b$ and a rooted ordered tree $t$, $a$ is a parent of $b$ in $t$ when some node of $t$ labelled $a$ has a child subtree whose root is $b$. Preferred edges of a link-cut tree are directed this way, from a node to its preferred child.
nodes.title: Parent-child relation in a rooted tree

nodes.summary: For every rooted tree $t$ and all vertices $a$ and $b$, if $a$ is the parent of $b$ somewhere in $t$, then $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t$.
nodes.title: Parent-child edges are edges

nodes.summary: If $a$ is the parent of $b$ somewhere in a tree $t$, then $a$ is a vertex of $t$.
nodes.title: The parent endpoint of a tree edge is a vertex

nodes.summary: If $a$ is the parent of $b$ somewhere in a tree $t$, then $b$ is a vertex of $t$.
nodes.title: The child endpoint of a tree edge is a vertex

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a tree and $x$ a vertex. If the root path of $x$ in $t$ is defined and equals $p = (p_0, \dots, p_k)$, then for every $i < k$ the vertex $p_i$ is the parent of $p_{i+1}$ somewhere in $t$.
nodes.title: A root path follows parent-child edges downward

nodes.summary: For a list of vertices $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_n$, its path edges are the ordered pairs $(v_0, v_1), (v_1, v_2), \dots, (v_{n-1}, v_n)$ of consecutive vertices, in this order; a list with at most one vertex has no path edges. For a path listed from the root downward each pair is (parent, child), and the preferred edges installed by an access to a vertex $x$ are the path edges of the root-to-$x$ path.
nodes.title: Consecutive edges of a vertex path

nodes.summary: Given a list $E$ of preferred edges, each a pair (parent, preferred child), the decomposition of a tree $T$ is a pair (down, rest): down is the preferred path that starts at the root of $T$ and follows edges of $E$ downward, and rest is the list of all other preferred paths of $T$. When a node has several children joined to it by edges of $E$ (excluded in valid states, where each vertex has at most one preferred…
nodes.title: Preferred-path decomposition of a tree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted ordered tree and let $E$ be a list of preferred edges, each a pair (parent, child). The preferred paths of $t$ under $E$ are listed as follows: first the downward path of the preferred-path decomposition of $t$ under $E$, which starts at the root of $t$ and follows preferred edges downward, and then all other paths of that decomposition, in the order the decomposition returns them.
nodes.title: Preferred paths of a tree

nodes.summary: For every list of preferred edges, the downward preferred path in the preferred-path decomposition of a tree is nonempty and its first vertex is the root of the tree.
nodes.title: The downward preferred path starts at the root

nodes.summary: For every list of preferred edges, the downward preferred path of a tree followed by the concatenation of the other paths of its preferred-path decomposition is a permutation of the vertex list of the tree.
nodes.title: Preferred paths permute the vertex list

nodes.summary: For every list $E$ of directed edges and every rooted ordered tree $t$, the concatenation of the preferred paths of $t$ under $E$ is a permutation of the preorder vertex list of $t$.
nodes.title: The preferred paths of a tree rearrange its vertex list

nodes.summary: For every list of preferred edges, in the preferred-path decomposition of a tree $T$, the downward preferred path and every other path are paths of $T$: any two consecutive vertices are joined by a parent-child edge of $T$, in either direction.
nodes.title: Decomposition paths are paths of the tree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a tree and $E$ any list of pairs of vertices, read as preferred (parent, child) edges. For every path $p = (p_0, \dots, p_k)$ in the preferred-path decomposition of $t$ under $E$ and every $i < k$, the vertices $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ are adjacent in $t$, that is, joined by a parent-child edge of $t$ in one direction or the other.
nodes.title: Preferred paths of a tree follow tree edges

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a tree whose vertex list is duplicate-free, let $x$ be a vertex of $T$ with root path $p$ (the path from the root of $T$ down to $x$), and let $E$ be a list of directed edges such that every consecutive pair of $p$, parent first, lies in $E$, and every edge of $E$ whose first vertex lies on $p$ is such a consecutive pair. Then the downward preferred path of the preferred-path decomposition of $T$ under…
nodes.title: Access edges make the root path the downward preferred path

nodes.summary: A state of a link-cut tree over a vertex type $V$ consists of the represented forest, a list of rooted ordered trees with vertices in $V$, and a list of preferred (solid) edges, each a pair $(u, v)$ of vertices meant as the edge from a node $u$ to its preferred child $v$ in the represented forest; the structure itself does not require these pairs to be edges of the forest. The preferred-path decomposition is…
nodes.title: Link-cut tree state

nodes.summary: A vertex $x$ belongs to a link-cut tree state $s$ when $x$ is a vertex of some tree of the represented forest of $s$.
nodes.title: Vertex of a link-cut tree state

nodes.summary: Two vertices $x$ and $y$ are connected in a link-cut tree state $s$ when some tree of the represented forest of $s$ has both $x$ and $y$ among its vertices.
nodes.title: Connectivity in a link-cut tree state

nodes.summary: For a link-cut tree state $s$ and vertices $x$ and $y$, $x$ and $y$ are connected in $s$ if and only if some tree of the represented forest of $s$ contains both $x$ and $y$ in its Euler tour.
nodes.title: Connectivity via Euler tours

nodes.summary: A link-cut tree state $s$ is valid when four conditions hold: the concatenation of the vertex lists of the trees of its represented forest has no duplicates (so the trees are vertex-disjoint); its list of preferred edges has no duplicates; every preferred edge $(a, b)$ is a parent-child edge of some tree of the represented forest, with $a$ the parent of $b$; and any two preferred edges with the same parent are…
nodes.title: Valid link-cut tree states

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state whose list of preferred edges is empty. If the concatenation of the vertex lists of the trees of the represented forest of $s$ has no duplicates, then $s$ is valid.
nodes.title: Validity of states with no preferred edges

nodes.summary: For a link-cut tree state $s$, its preferred paths are obtained by taking, for each represented tree of $s$ in forest order, the preferred paths of that tree under the preferred edges of $s$, and concatenating these lists. Within a tree these are its maximal chains of preferred edges when each vertex has at most one preferred child, each listed from its shallowest to its deepest vertex; a vertex incident to no…
nodes.title: Preferred-path decomposition of a link-cut tree state
