nodes.summary: For every link-cut tree state $s$ and every vertex $v$, $v$ lies on some path of the preferred-path decomposition of $s$ if and only if $v$ is a vertex of some tree of the represented forest of $s$. No validity hypothesis on $s$ is needed.
nodes.title: Preferred paths cover exactly the vertices of the forest

nodes.summary: In a valid link-cut tree state, the concatenation of all preferred paths of the decomposition has no repeated vertex: no vertex occurs twice on one path or on two different paths.
nodes.title: Preferred paths cover each vertex at most once

nodes.summary: In a valid link-cut tree state, any two preferred paths at different positions of the preferred-path decomposition have no vertex in common.
nodes.title: Preferred paths are pairwise vertex-disjoint

nodes.summary: Every preferred path of a valid state has distinct vertices.
nodes.title: Preferred paths have distinct vertices

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state. For every path $p = (p_0, \dots, p_k)$ in the preferred-path decomposition of $s$ and every $i < k$, some represented tree of $s$ has $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ adjacent, that is, joined by a parent-child edge in one direction or the other.
nodes.title: Preferred paths of a link-cut tree state follow represented edges

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and $x$ a vertex. If $x$ is a vertex of some tree of the represented forest of $s$, let $T$ be the first such tree and let $p$ be the path in $T$ from its root down to $x$. Accessing $x$ keeps the represented forest and replaces the preferred edges by those preferred edges of $s$ whose parent endpoint is not on $p$, followed by the edges of $p$, each directed from parent to child.…
nodes.title: Access in a link-cut tree

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state, $x$ a vertex, and $(u, w)$ a preferred edge of $s$, directed from the parent $u$ to the child $w$. Suppose that, if some tree of the represented forest of $s$ contains $x$, then $u$ does not lie on the path in the first such tree from its root down to the first occurrence of $x$ in preorder. Then $(u, w)$ is still a preferred edge after accessing $x$.
nodes.title: Access keeps off-path preferred edges

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and $x$ a vertex, let $t$ be the first tree of the represented forest of $s$ that contains $x$, and let $p$ be the path in $t$ from the root down to the first occurrence of $x$ in preorder. Then every edge of $p$, taken as the pair (parent, child) of consecutive vertices of $p$, is a preferred edge of the state obtained from $s$ by accessing $x$.
nodes.title: Access makes the root path preferred

nodes.summary: For every link-cut tree state $s$ and every vertex $x$, accessing $x$ changes only the preferred edges: the represented forest of the resulting state equals the represented forest of $s$.
nodes.title: Access leaves the represented forest unchanged

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a valid link-cut tree state and let $x$ be a vertex of its represented forest. Then, after accessing $x$, the preferred-path decomposition of the new state contains a path $p$ whose last vertex is $x$, and $p$ is the path from the root down to $x$ in some tree of the represented forest of $s$.
nodes.title: After access, the accessed vertex ends its preferred path

nodes.summary: If a link-cut tree state $s$ is valid, then for every vertex $x$ the state obtained from $s$ by accessing $x$ is again valid.
nodes.title: Access preserves validity

nodes.summary: Given a vertex $x$ and a state $s$, the state $\operatorname{makeRoot}(x, s)$ has no preferred edges (all edges dashed), and its forest is defined as follows. If $x$ is not a vertex of the forest, the forest is unchanged. Otherwise the first represented tree containing $x$ is rerooted at $x$: the edges on the path from its old root to $x$ are reversed, and when the tree has distinct vertices every undirected edge…
nodes.title: Making a vertex the root in a link-cut tree state

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and $x$ a vertex of its represented forest. After making $x$ the root, some represented tree has root $x$ and contains $x$ as a vertex.
nodes.title: Making a vertex the root installs a tree rooted there

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a valid link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be connected in $s$. Then $x$ and $y$ are still connected in the state obtained from $s$ by making $x$ the root of its represented tree.
nodes.title: Making a vertex the root keeps its connections

nodes.summary: For every valid link-cut tree state $s$ and every vertex $x$, the state obtained from $s$ by making $x$ the root of its represented tree is valid.
nodes.title: Rerooting a link-cut tree state preserves validity

nodes.summary: Given vertices $x$ and $y$ and a state $s$, the state $\operatorname{link}(x, y, s)$ has no preferred edges (all edges dashed), and its forest is defined as follows. If $x$ or $y$ is not a vertex of the forest, the forest is unchanged. Otherwise let $t_x$ and $t_y$ be the first represented trees containing $x$ and $y$. If $x$ is a vertex of $t_y$, the forest is unchanged. Otherwise $t_x$ is rerooted at $x$ (the…
nodes.title: Linking two trees of a link-cut tree state

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be vertices of its represented forest. Then in the state obtained from $s$ by linking $x$ to $y$, the vertices $x$ and $y$ are connected, that is, some represented tree contains both. No invariant on the state is needed.
nodes.title: Linking connects the endpoints

nodes.summary: For every valid link-cut tree state $s$ and all vertices $x$ and $y$, the state obtained from $s$ by linking $x$ and $y$ is valid.
nodes.title: Linking in a link-cut tree preserves validity

nodes.summary: Cutting at a vertex $x$ resets the preferred edges of the state to the empty list and changes its forest as follows. If no tree of the forest contains $x$, the forest is unchanged. Otherwise let $T$ be the first tree containing $x$ and $S$ the first subtree of $T$ rooted at $x$ in preorder. Every tree containing $x$ is removed from the forest, and two trees are appended at the end: first the remainder of $T$ with…
nodes.title: Cutting off the subtree at a vertex

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state, let $t$ be the first tree of its represented forest containing the vertex $x$, and let $u$ be the first subtree of $t$ in preorder whose root is $x$. After cutting $s$ at $x$, the vertex $x$ is not connected to any vertex $y$ that is not a vertex of $u$.
nodes.title: A cut disconnects a vertex from everything outside its subtree

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state, let $x$ and $y$ be vertices, and let $t$ be the first tree of the represented forest of $s$ that contains $x$. Suppose no vertex occurs twice in $t$, and let $T_x$ be the subtree of $t$ rooted at $x$. If $y$ is a vertex of $t$ but not of $T_x$, then after cutting $s$ at $x$ both $x$ and $y$ are vertices of the represented forest.
nodes.title: Both sides of a cut remain in the forest

nodes.summary: If $s$ is a valid link-cut tree state, then for every vertex $x$ the state obtained from $s$ by cutting off the subtree rooted at $x$ is again valid.
nodes.title: Cutting preserves validity

nodes.summary: For vertices $x$ and $y$ and a link-cut tree state $s$, cutting the edge between $x$ and $y$ works as follows. If $x$ and $y$ are adjacent in some tree of the represented forest of $s$, the result is obtained from $s$ by first making $x$ the root of its represented tree and then cutting off the subtree rooted at $y$. Otherwise the represented forest is left unchanged. In both cases the list of preferred edges…
nodes.title: Cutting an edge of a link-cut tree

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be adjacent in some tree of the represented forest of $s$. Then cutting the edge between $x$ and $y$ in $s$ gives the same state as first making $x$ the root of its represented tree and then cutting off the subtree rooted at $y$.
nodes.title: Edge cut on an adjacent pair

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be adjacent in no tree of the represented forest of $s$. Then cutting the edge between $x$ and $y$ in $s$ leaves the represented forest unchanged and makes the list of preferred edges empty.
nodes.title: Edge cut on a non-adjacent pair

nodes.summary: If $s$ is a valid link-cut tree state, then for all vertices $x$ and $y$ the state obtained from $s$ by cutting the edge between $x$ and $y$ is again valid.
nodes.title: Edge cutting preserves validity

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a valid link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be adjacent in some tree of the represented forest of $s$. After the edge cut of $x$ and $y$ in $s$, the vertices $x$ and $y$ are not connected: no represented tree contains both.
nodes.title: Cutting an edge separates its endpoints

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a valid link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be adjacent in some tree of its represented forest. If $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in some tree of the represented forest of $s$, and neither $a = x$ and $b = y$ nor $a = y$ and $b = x$, then $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in some tree of the represented forest obtained from $s$ by cutting the edge between $x$ and $y$.
nodes.title: An edge cut keeps every other edge

nodes.summary: Algorithms computing properties of explicit graphs (traversal, connectivity, shortest paths, spanning trees, flows, matchings, Euler circuits) with correctness and cost proofs; pure graph theory belongs to GraphTheory, and verifiers or reductions for NP problems belong to TheoryOfComputation.
nodes.title: Graph algorithms

nodes.summary: Graph representations as adjacency lists and adjacency matrices, breadth-first and depth-first search with predecessor trees, strongly connected components, topological sorting, transitive closure and Hierholzer's Euler circuits.
nodes.title: Graph traversal and connectivity
Adjacency list

nodes.summary: A directed adjacency graph on a type $V$ consists of a list of vertices that has no duplicates and contains every element of $V$ (so $V$ is finite), together with, for each vertex $v$, an ordered list of the out-neighbors of $v$, in which entries may repeat.
nodes.title: Directed adjacency graph

nodes.summary: For a directed adjacency graph $G$ on $V$ and vertices $s, t \in V$, there is an edge from $s$ to $t$ in $G$ when $t$ occurs in the adjacency list of $s$.
nodes.title: Edge of a directed adjacency graph

nodes.summary: For a directed adjacency graph $G$, a natural number $n$ and vertices $s$ and $t$, there is a walk of length $n$ from $s$ to $t$ in $G$ when there are vertices $v_0, \dots, v_n$ with $v_0 = s$ and $v_n = t$ such that $(v_i, v_{i+1})$ is an edge of $G$ for every $i < n$.
nodes.title: Walks of a given length

nodes.summary: The digraph associated with a directed adjacency graph $G$ on a vertex type $V$ is the directed graph on $V$ in which $s$ is adjacent to $t$ exactly when $G$ has an edge from $s$ to $t$. It forgets the order of the adjacency lists and the multiplicity of their entries.
nodes.title: The digraph of a directed adjacency graph

nodes.summary: For a directed adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$ and $t$, $s$ is adjacent to $t$ in the digraph associated with $G$ if and only if $G$ has an edge from $s$ to $t$, that is, $t$ occurs in the adjacency list of $s$.
nodes.title: Adjacency in the associated digraph

nodes.summary: In a directed adjacency graph, there is a walk of length $0$ from a vertex $s$ to a vertex $t$ if and only if $s = t$.
nodes.title: Walks of length zero

nodes.summary: In a directed adjacency graph $G$, for every natural number $n$ and all vertices $s$ and $t$, there is a walk of length $n + 1$ from $s$ to $t$ if and only if there is a vertex $v$ such that $(s, v)$ is an edge of $G$ and there is a walk of length $n$ from $v$ to $t$.
nodes.title: Splitting off the first edge of a walk

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph on $V$ and let $s, m, t \in V$. If $G$ has a walk of length exactly $a$ from $s$ to $m$ and a walk of length exactly $b$ from $m$ to $t$, then $G$ has a walk of length exactly $a + b$ from $s$ to $t$.
nodes.title: Concatenation of walks

nodes.summary: For a directed adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$ and $t$, $t$ is reachable from $s$ when the pair $(s, t)$ lies in the reflexive-transitive closure of the edge relation of $G$: either $s = t$, or a finite sequence of edges of $G$ leads from $s$ to $t$.
nodes.title: Reachability in a directed graph

nodes.summary: In a directed adjacency graph $G$, a vertex $t$ is reachable from a vertex $s$ if and only if there is a natural number $n$ such that $G$ has a walk of length exactly $n$ from $s$ to $t$.
nodes.title: Reachability by walks

nodes.summary: In a directed adjacency graph $G$, a vertex $t$ is reachable from a vertex $s$ if and only if $(s, t)$ lies in the reflexive-transitive closure of the edge relation of $G$.
nodes.title: Reachability is the reflexive-transitive closure of the edge relation

nodes.summary: The labelled transition system of a directed adjacency graph $G$ has the vertices of $G$ as states and a single label, and it has a transition from $s$ to $t$ exactly when $G$ has an edge from $s$ to $t$.
nodes.title: The transition system of a directed adjacency graph

nodes.summary: In a directed adjacency graph $G$, a vertex $t$ is reachable from a vertex $s$ if and only if, in the unit-labelled labelled transition system of $G$, there is a finite list of labels along which $s$ reaches $t$ by a multistep transition.
nodes.title: Reachability in the associated transition system

nodes.summary: For a directed adjacency graph $G$ on a vertex type with decidable equality, the transpose of $G$ has the same vertex enumeration as $G$, and the adjacency list of a vertex $v$ consists of the vertices $u$ such that $v$ occurs in the adjacency list of $u$ in $G$, each listed once and in the order of the vertex enumeration.
nodes.title: Transpose of a directed adjacency graph

nodes.summary: Let $V$ have decidable equality and let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph on $V$. For all $s, t \in V$, the transpose of $G$ has an edge from $s$ to $t$ if and only if $G$ has an edge from $t$ to $s$.
nodes.title: Edges of the transpose graph

nodes.summary: For a directed adjacency graph $G$ on a vertex type with decidable equality, every natural number $n$ and all vertices $s$ and $t$, there is a walk of length $n$ from $s$ to $t$ in the transpose of $G$ if and only if there is a walk of length $n$ from $t$ to $s$ in $G$.
nodes.title: Walks in the transpose are reversed walks

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph on a vertex type with decidable equality, and let $G^{\mathsf{T}}$ be its transpose. For all vertices $s$ and $t$, $t$ is reachable from $s$ in $G^{\mathsf{T}}$ if and only if $s$ is reachable from $t$ in $G$.
nodes.title: Reachability in the transpose graph

nodes.summary: Two directed adjacency graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ on the same vertex type are semantically equivalent when they have the same edges: for all vertices $s$ and $t$, $G_1$ has an edge from $s$ to $t$ if and only if $G_2$ does.
nodes.title: Semantic equivalence of directed adjacency graphs

nodes.summary: Every directed adjacency graph $G$ is semantically equivalent to itself.
nodes.title: Semantic equivalence of directed adjacency graphs is reflexive

nodes.summary: If a directed adjacency graph $G_1$ is semantically equivalent to a directed adjacency graph $G_2$, then $G_2$ is semantically equivalent to $G_1$.
nodes.title: Semantic equivalence of directed adjacency graphs is symmetric

nodes.summary: If a directed adjacency graph $G_1$ is semantically equivalent to $G_2$, and $G_2$ is semantically equivalent to $G_3$, then $G_1$ is semantically equivalent to $G_3$.
nodes.title: Semantic equivalence of directed adjacency graphs is transitive

nodes.summary: If two directed adjacency graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ are semantically equivalent, then for every natural number $n$ and all vertices $s$ and $t$, there is a walk of length $n$ from $s$ to $t$ in $G_1$ if and only if there is a walk of length $n$ from $s$ to $t$ in $G_2$.
nodes.title: Semantically equivalent graphs have the same walks

nodes.summary: If two directed adjacency graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ on $V$ are semantically equivalent, then for all $s, t \in V$, $t$ is reachable from $s$ in $G_1$ if and only if $t$ is reachable from $s$ in $G_2$.
nodes.title: Semantically equivalent graphs have the same reachability

nodes.summary: For directed adjacency graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ on a vertex type with decidable equality, if $G_1$ and $G_2$ are semantically equivalent, then their transposes are semantically equivalent.
nodes.title: Transposition preserves semantic equivalence

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph on a vertex type with decidable equality. The transpose of the transpose of $G$ is semantically equivalent to $G$, that is, it has exactly the same edges as $G$.
nodes.title: Transposing twice gives a semantically equivalent graph

nodes.summary: For a type $V$ with decidable equality, a directed adjacency graph $G$ on $V$ and vertices $s, t \in V$, the edge test of $G$ at $(s, t)$ is the Boolean value that is true exactly when $t$ occurs in the adjacency list of $s$.
nodes.title: Boolean edge test

nodes.summary: For a type $V$ with decidable equality, a directed adjacency graph $G$ on $V$ and vertices $s, t \in V$, the Boolean edge test of $G$ at $(s, t)$ returns true if and only if $G$ has an edge from $s$ to $t$.
nodes.title: The Boolean edge test is correct

nodes.summary: Given a directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$ and $t$, erasing the edge $s \to t$ gives the directed-adjacency graph with the same vertex enumeration as $G$ whose out-neighbour list at $s$ is the out-neighbour list of $s$ in $G$ with every occurrence of $t$ removed (the remaining entries keep their order), and whose out-neighbour list at every other vertex is the same as in $G$.
nodes.title: Erasing a directed edge

nodes.summary: For every directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$ and $t$, the graph obtained from $G$ by erasing the edge $s \to t$ has the same vertex enumeration as $G$: the same list of vertices, in the same order.
nodes.title: Erasing an edge keeps the vertex enumeration

nodes.summary: For every directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$ and $t$, the out-neighbour list of $s$ in the graph obtained from $G$ by erasing the edge $s \to t$ is the out-neighbour list of $s$ in $G$ with every occurrence of $t$ removed, the remaining entries kept in their original order.
nodes.title: Out-neighbours of the source after erasing an edge

nodes.summary: For every directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$, $t$ and $u$ with $u \ne s$, the out-neighbour list of $u$ in the graph obtained from $G$ by erasing the edge $s \to t$ equals the out-neighbour list of $u$ in $G$.
nodes.title: Erasing an edge leaves the other out-neighbour lists unchanged

nodes.summary: For every directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$, $t$, $u$ and $v$, there is an edge from $u$ to $v$ in the graph obtained from $G$ by erasing the edge $s \to t$ if and only if there is an edge from $u$ to $v$ in $G$ and it is not the case that both $u = s$ and $v = t$.
nodes.title: Edges after erasing an edge

nodes.summary: For every directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$ and $t$, the Boolean edge lookup for $s \to t$ in the graph obtained from $G$ by erasing the edge $s \to t$ returns false.
nodes.title: The erased edge is absent

nodes.summary: For every directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$ and $t$, erasing the edge $s \to t$ from $G$ and then erasing it again gives, at every vertex, the same out-neighbour list as erasing it once.
nodes.title: Erasing an edge twice gives the same out-neighbour lists

nodes.summary: For every directed-adjacency graph $G$, vertices $s$, $t$, $u$ and $v$, and natural number $n$, if there is a walk of length $n$ from $u$ to $v$ in the graph obtained from $G$ by erasing the edge $s \to t$, then there is a walk of length $n$ from $u$ to $v$ in $G$.
nodes.title: Walks after erasing an edge are walks in the original graph

nodes.summary: For every directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$, $t$, $u$ and $v$, if $v$ is reachable from $u$ in the graph obtained from $G$ by erasing the edge $s \to t$, then $v$ is reachable from $u$ in $G$.
nodes.title: Reachability after erasing an edge implies reachability in the original graph
Adjacency matrix

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, an adjacency matrix on $n$ vertices is a directed graph on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ given by a Boolean-valued function $\mathrm{adj}$ on ordered pairs of vertices: $\mathrm{adj}(i, j)$ is true exactly when there is a directed edge from $i$ to $j$.
nodes.title: Adjacency matrix

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$, the empty adjacency matrix on $n$ vertices is the directed graph on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with no edges: its adjacency function is false on every ordered pair of vertices.
nodes.title: Empty adjacency matrix

nodes.summary: For an adjacency matrix $m$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and vertices $i, j$, the edge query of $m$ at $(i, j)$ is the Boolean value that is true exactly when $m$ has a directed edge from $i$ to $j$.
nodes.title: Edge query of an adjacency matrix

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$ and all vertices $i$ and $j$ among the $n$ vertices, the empty adjacency matrix on $n$ vertices has no edge from $i$ to $j$.
nodes.title: The empty adjacency matrix has no edges

nodes.summary: For an adjacency matrix $m$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and vertices $i$ and $j$, adding the edge from $i$ to $j$ gives the adjacency matrix that has an edge from $i$ to $j$ and agrees with $m$ on every other ordered pair of vertices.
nodes.title: Edge insertion in an adjacency matrix

nodes.summary: For an adjacency matrix $m$ on $n$ vertices and vertices $i$ and $j$, the matrix obtained from $m$ by adding the edge from $i$ to $j$ has an edge from $i$ to $j$.
nodes.title: An inserted edge is present

nodes.summary: For an adjacency matrix $m$ on $n$ vertices and vertices $i$, $j$, $a$, $b$ with $a \ne i$ or $b \ne j$, the matrix obtained from $m$ by adding the edge from $i$ to $j$ has an edge from $a$ to $b$ if and only if $m$ does.
nodes.title: Inserting an edge leaves other pairs unchanged

nodes.summary: For an adjacency matrix $m$ on $n$ vertices and vertices $i$, $j$, $a$, $b$, the matrix obtained from $m$ by adding the edge from $i$ to $j$ has an edge from $a$ to $b$ if and only if $a = i$ and $b = j$, or $m$ has an edge from $a$ to $b$.
nodes.title: Edges after inserting an edge

nodes.summary: For an adjacency matrix $m$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and vertices $i$ and $j$, removing the edge from $i$ to $j$ gives the adjacency matrix that has no edge from $i$ to $j$ and agrees with $m$ on every other ordered pair of vertices.
nodes.title: Edge deletion in an adjacency matrix

nodes.summary: Let $m$ be an adjacency matrix on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $i, j$ be vertices. Then the graph obtained from $m$ by deleting the edge from $i$ to $j$ has no edge from $i$ to $j$.
nodes.title: Deleting an edge removes it

nodes.summary:
Let $m$ be an adjacency matrix on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $i, j, a, b$ be vertices with $(a, b) 
e (i, j)$, that is, $a 
e i$ or $b 
e j$. Then the graph obtained from $m$ by deleting the edge from $i$ to $j$ has an edge from $a$ to $b$ if and only if $m$ has an edge from $a$ to $b$.
nodes.title: Deleting an edge leaves the other entries unchanged

nodes.summary: For an adjacency matrix $m$ on $n$ vertices and vertices $i$, $j$, $a$, $b$, the matrix obtained from $m$ by removing the edge from $i$ to $j$ has an edge from $a$ to $b$ if and only if $(a, b) \ne (i, j)$ and $m$ has an edge from $a$ to $b$.
nodes.title: Edges after deleting an edge

nodes.summary: Two adjacency matrices $m$ and $m'$ on the same $n$ vertices are equal if, for all vertices $i$ and $j$, $m$ has an edge from $i$ to $j$ exactly when $m'$ does.
nodes.title: Extensionality of adjacency matrices

nodes.summary: For an adjacency matrix $m$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and a vertex $i$, the out-neighbor list of $i$ is the list of all vertices $j$ such that $m$ has a directed edge from $i$ to $j$, in increasing order.
nodes.title: Out-neighbor list

nodes.summary: Let $m$ be an adjacency matrix on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $i, j$ be vertices. Then $j$ belongs to the out-neighbor list of $i$ if and only if $m$ has a directed edge from $i$ to $j$.
nodes.title: The out-neighbor list matches the edge query

nodes.summary: For an adjacency matrix $m$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and a vertex $i$, no vertex occurs twice in the out-neighbor list of $i$.
nodes.title: Out-neighbor lists have no duplicates

nodes.summary: For an adjacency matrix $m$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and a vertex $i$, the out-neighbor list of $i$ is strictly increasing: every vertex in it is smaller than every vertex that comes after it.
nodes.title: Out-neighbor lists are strictly increasing

nodes.summary: In the graph with no edges on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the out-neighbor list of every vertex $i$ is the empty list.
nodes.title: Out-neighbor lists of the empty graph

nodes.summary: Let $m$ be an adjacency matrix on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $i, j$ be vertices. Then $j$ belongs to the out-neighbor list of $i$ in the graph obtained from $m$ by adding the edge from $i$ to $j$.
nodes.title: Adding an edge makes its target an out-neighbor

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, given by its adjacency matrix, and let $i$ and $j$ be vertices. After the edge from $i$ to $j$ is deleted from $G$ (whether or not $G$ had that edge), $j$ is not an out-neighbor of $i$.
nodes.title: Deleting an edge removes the out-neighbor

nodes.summary: Let $m$ be an adjacency matrix on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $i, j, b$ be vertices. Then $b$ belongs to the out-neighbor list of $i$ in the graph obtained from $m$ by adding the edge from $i$ to $j$ if and only if $b = j$ or $b$ belongs to the out-neighbor list of $i$ in $m$.
nodes.title: Out-neighbors after adding an edge

nodes.summary: The out-degree of a vertex $i$ of a directed graph given by an adjacency matrix is the number of its out-neighbors, that is, the number of vertices $j$ such that there is an edge from $i$ to $j$.
nodes.title: Out-degree

nodes.summary: For every $n$, every vertex of the empty directed graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ has out-degree $0$.
nodes.title: Vertices of the empty graph have out-degree zero
Breadth-first search

nodes.summary: A breadth-first search result on a vertex type $V$ consists of a distance function, assigning to each vertex either a natural number or none, and a list of vertices. They are meant to record the shortest distance from the source (none when the vertex is unreachable) and the vertices in first-discovery order.
nodes.title: Result of breadth-first search

nodes.summary: Given a finite directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and a source vertex $s$, the list model keeps a list of processed pairs and a queue of pairs $(v, d)$ of a vertex and a distance, starting with no processed pairs and the queue $[(s, 0)]$. It performs one round per vertex of $G$: if the queue is empty, nothing changes; otherwise the front pair $(u, d)$ is removed from the queue and recorded as…
nodes.title: List model of breadth-first search

nodes.summary: Given a finite directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and a source vertex $s$, breadth-first search keeps a FIFO queue of pairs $(v, d)$ of a vertex and a distance and a table of discovered vertices with their distances, starting with the queue $[(s, 0)]$ and $s$ discovered at distance $0$. It performs one round per vertex of $G$: if the queue is empty, nothing changes; otherwise it dequeues the front pair…
nodes.title: Breadth-first search

nodes.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and every source vertex $s$, the result of the executable breadth-first search from $s$ equals the result of the list model of breadth-first search from $s$: both report the same distance (or none) for every vertex and the same first-discovery order.
nodes.title: The executable BFS agrees with the list model

reading_title.source: Breadth-first search on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$

nodes.summary: Given a natural number $n$, an adjacency function assigning to each vertex $i < n$ an ordered list of vertices among $0, \dots, n-1$, and a source vertex $s < n$, this is the result of breadth-first search from $s$ on the finite directed graph with vertex enumeration $0, 1, \dots, n-1$ and these adjacency lists.
nodes.title: Breadth-first search on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$

nodes.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and all vertices $s$ and $v$, breadth-first search from $s$ reports some distance for $v$ (rather than none) if and only if $v$ is reachable from $s$ in $G$.
nodes.title: BFS reports a distance exactly for the reachable vertices

nodes.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and all vertices $s$ and $v$, the vertex $v$ occurs in the first-discovery order of breadth-first search from $s$ if and only if $v$ is reachable from $s$ in $G$.
nodes.title: BFS lists exactly the reachable vertices

nodes.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and every vertex $s$, no vertex occurs twice in the first-discovery order of breadth-first search from $s$.
nodes.title: BFS discovers each vertex at most once

nodes.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists, all vertices $s$ and $v$, and every natural number $d$, breadth-first search from $s$ reports distance $d$ for $v$ if and only if there is a walk of exactly $d$ edges from $s$ to $v$ in $G$ and $d \le k$ for every natural number $k$ such that there is a walk of exactly $k$ edges from $s$ to $v$.
nodes.title: BFS reports exactly the shortest walk length

nodes.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ given by ordered adjacency lists and every vertex $s$ of $G$, breadth-first search in $G$ from $s$ reports a distance for $s$ itself, and that distance is $0$ edges.
nodes.title: Breadth-first search places the source at distance zero

nodes.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and every vertex $s$, the distances reported by breadth-first search from $s$, listed along its first-discovery order, form a nondecreasing sequence, where a vertex without a reported distance counts as $0$.
nodes.title: BFS discovers vertices in nondecreasing distance

nodes.summary: A breadth-first search forest on a vertex type $V$ consists of a breadth-first search result, namely a partial distance function from $V$ to the natural numbers and a list of vertices, together with a partial predecessor function from $V$ to $V$. For a search from a source vertex $s$, these are meant to give the distance from $s$ of each reachable vertex, the reachable vertices in first-discovery order, and the…
nodes.title: Breadth-first search forest

nodes.summary: Given a finite directed graph $G$ on a vertex type $V$, with ordered adjacency lists, and a source vertex $s$, this runs first-in-first-out breadth-first search from $s$ for $|V|$ rounds. The queue starts with $s$ at distance $0$. Each round tries to dequeue a vertex $u$; if it succeeds, it scans the neighbors of $u$ in adjacency-list order, and each neighbor not yet discovered gets distance one more than $u$,…
nodes.title: Breadth-first search with parent pointers

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be the predecessor function of a breadth-first search forest, let $n$ be the length of its discovery order, and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices. Starting from $v_k = t$, this walks back along $p$, setting $v_{i-1} = p(v_i)$, until it reaches a vertex $v_0$ that tests equal to $s$, and returns the list $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k$. It returns no list if the walk meets a vertex that does not test equal to $s$ and has…
nodes.title: Path reconstruction from BFS parents

nodes.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and every source vertex $s$, the output of breadth-first search with parents from $s$ in $G$, with its cost and its predecessor table forgotten, equals the result of ordinary FIFO breadth-first search from $s$ in $G$: the same distance table and the same first-discovery order.
nodes.title: Breadth-first search with parents returns the ordinary BFS result

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph with ordered adjacency lists, $s$ a vertex, and $F$ the predecessor forest computed by breadth-first search with parents from $s$ in $G$. A vertex $v$ has no recorded predecessor in $F$ if and only if $v = s$ or $v$ is not reachable from $s$ along directed edges of $G$.
nodes.title: Exactly the source and the unreachable vertices have no BFS parent

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph with ordered adjacency lists, $s$ a vertex, and $F$ the predecessor forest computed by breadth-first search with parents from $s$ in $G$. If $F$ records $p$ as the predecessor of a vertex $v$, then $G$ has a directed edge from $p$ to $v$, that is, $v$ occurs in the adjacency list of $p$.
nodes.title: BFS parents are joined by graph edges

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph with ordered adjacency lists, $s$ a vertex, and $F$ the predecessor forest computed by breadth-first search with parents from $s$ in $G$. If $F$ records $p$ as the predecessor of a vertex $v$, then there is a natural number $d$ such that $F$ records distance $d$ for $p$ and distance $d + 1$ for $v$.
nodes.title: A BFS parent is one step closer to the source

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph with ordered adjacency lists, $s$ a vertex, and $F$ the predecessor forest computed by breadth-first search with parents from $s$ in $G$. For every vertex $v \ne s$, the predecessor that $F$ records for $v$ is the first vertex $u$, in the first-discovery order of ordinary FIFO breadth-first search from $s$ in $G$, whose adjacency list contains $v$; if no vertex in that order has…
nodes.title: The BFS parent is the first discovered in-neighbour

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by adjacency lists, and let $s$ and $v$ be vertices with $v$ reachable from $s$ in $G$. There is exactly one list of vertices that starts at $s$, ends at $v$, and in which each vertex after the first has the preceding vertex as its saved parent in the breadth-first search forest of $G$ from $s$.
nodes.title: Each reachable vertex has a unique saved-parent chain

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by adjacency lists and let $s$ and $v$ be vertices. If a list of vertices starts at $s$, ends at $v$, and each of its vertices after the first has the preceding vertex as its saved parent in the breadth-first search forest of $G$ from $s$, then no vertex occurs twice in the list.
nodes.title: Saved-parent chains are simple

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by adjacency lists and let $s$ and $v$ be vertices. In the breadth-first search forest of $G$ from $s$, there is no sequence $v = x_0, x_1, \dots, x_k = v$ with $k \ge 1$ in which each $x_i$ is the saved parent of $x_{i+1}$.
nodes.title: The saved-parent relation is acyclic

nodes.summary: For every breadth-first search forest $F$ and every vertex $s$, following the saved parents of $F$ from $s$ back to $s$ returns the one-vertex path $[s]$. This holds for every forest, including one whose discovery order is empty.
nodes.title: Path reconstruction at the source

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by adjacency lists, and let $s$ and $v$ be vertices. Following the saved parents of the breadth-first search forest of $G$ from $s$ back from $v$ towards $s$ returns no path if and only if $v$ is not reachable from $s$ in $G$.
nodes.title: Path reconstruction fails exactly at unreachable vertices

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by adjacency lists, let $s$ and $v$ be vertices, and suppose that following the saved parents of the breadth-first search forest of $G$ from $s$ back from $v$ returns a list $P$ of vertices. Then $P$ starts at $s$ and ends at $v$, each vertex of $P$ after the first has the preceding vertex as its saved parent, $G$ has an edge from each vertex of $P$ to the next, no vertex…
nodes.title: Reconstructed BFS paths are shortest paths

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by adjacency lists, let $s$ and $v$ be vertices, and suppose breadth-first search from $s$ reports distance $d$ for $v$. Following the saved parents of the breadth-first search forest of $G$ from $s$ back from $v$ costs exactly $3d + 2$, counting one unit for each comparison with $s$, each parent lookup and each vertex prepended to the path.
nodes.title: Cost of path reconstruction for a reachable vertex

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by adjacency lists, and let $s$ and $v$ be vertices with $v$ not reachable from $s$ in $G$. Following the saved parents of the breadth-first search forest of $G$ from $s$ back from $v$ costs exactly $2$, counting one unit for each comparison with $s$, each parent lookup and each vertex prepended to the path: one comparison of $v$ with $s$ and one lookup of the missing parent…
nodes.title: Cost of path reconstruction for an unreachable vertex

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph with vertex list $V$ and adjacency lists $\mathrm{adj}(u)$, let $s$ be a vertex, and let $L$ be the list of vertices in the order in which breadth-first search from $s$ discovers them. The cost of breadth-first search with parents from $s$, counting dequeue attempts, adjacency checks, enqueues and parent writes, equals $|V| + \sum_{u \in L} |\mathrm{adj}(u)| + |L| + (|L| - 1)$,…
nodes.title: Exact cost of BFS with parents

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph with vertex list $V$ and adjacency lists $\mathrm{adj}(u)$, and let $s$ be a vertex. The cost of breadth-first search with parents from $s$, counting dequeue attempts, adjacency checks, enqueues and parent writes, is at most $3|V| + \sum_{u \in V} |\mathrm{adj}(u)|$, where adjacency lists are counted with repetitions.
nodes.title: Linear bound on the cost of BFS with parents
Depth-first search

nodes.summary: A traversal over a vertex type $V$ consists of three lists: a preorder (discovery order) list of vertices, a postorder (finish order) list of vertices, and a list of parent pairs in $V \times V$, each stored as $(\text{child}, \text{parent})$.
nodes.title: Depth-first traversal record

nodes.summary: Given a directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and an ordered list of roots, depth-first search processes the roots from left to right, skipping roots already visited. Visiting an unvisited vertex $v$ marks it visited and records its discovery, then processes the out-neighbours of $v$ in adjacency-list order, visiting each one not yet visited at that moment and recording $v$ as its parent, and finally…
nodes.title: Left-first depth-first search

nodes.summary: Zero or more independent DFS machine steps.
nodes.title: Sequences of depth-first search machine steps

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists and let $r = (r_1, \dots, r_k)$ be a list of root vertices. A traversal $T$ is a left-first DFS of $G$ from $r$ when some finite run of the following machine ends with an empty work list and with recorded preorder, postorder and (child, parent) list equal to those of $T$.
nodes.title: Left-first depth-first traversals

nodes.summary: For every directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and every ordered list of roots, the traversal computed by left-first depth-first search of $G$ from these roots conforms to left-first DFS for $G$ and these roots.
nodes.title: Executable DFS meets the left-first specification

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a directed graph with ordered adjacency lists, fix an ordered list of roots, and let $T$ be a traversal. If $T$ conforms to left-first DFS for $G$ and these roots, then $T$ equals the traversal computed by left-first depth-first search of $G$ from these roots.
nodes.title: The left-first DFS specification determines the traversal

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists and let $R$ be a list of roots. Every vertex in the preorder (discovery order) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$ is reachable in $G$ from some root in $R$ by a directed path (possibly of length zero).
nodes.title: Depth-first search discovers only reachable vertices

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists and let $R$ be a list of roots. If a vertex $v$ is reachable in $G$ from some root in $R$ by a directed path (possibly of length zero), then $v$ occurs in the preorder (discovery order) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$.
nodes.title: Depth-first search discovers every reachable vertex

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices. A vertex $v$ occurs in the discovery order (preorder) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$ if and only if there is a root $r$ in $R$ from which $v$ is reachable in $G$ by a directed path of length zero or more.
nodes.title: Depth-first search discovers exactly the reachable vertices

nodes.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ given by ordered adjacency lists and every list $R$ of roots, the preorder (discovery order) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$ contains no vertex twice.
nodes.title: Depth-first search discovers each vertex at most once

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices. A vertex $v$ occurs in the finish order (postorder) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$ if and only if there is a root $r$ in $R$ from which $v$ is reachable in $G$ by a directed path of length zero or more.
nodes.title: Depth-first search finishes exactly the reachable vertices

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices. The finish order (postorder) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$ contains no vertex twice.
nodes.title: DFS finishes each vertex at most once

nodes.summary: For elements $x$ and $y$ and a list $xs$, $x$ occurs before $y$ in $xs$ when there are lists $a$, $b$ and $c$ such that $xs$ is the concatenation of $a$, the element $x$, $b$, the element $y$ and $c$; that is, some occurrence of $x$ lies at a strictly earlier position than some occurrence of $y$.
nodes.title: Occurring before in a list

nodes.summary: Given a list $P$ of (child, parent) pairs, $p$ is a parent of $c$ in $P$ when the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in $P$.
nodes.title: Parent relation of a list of pairs

nodes.summary: The forest roots of a traversal $T$ are the vertices of the preorder of $T$ that do not occur as the child in any (child, parent) pair recorded by $T$, listed in the order in which they occur in the preorder.
nodes.title: Roots of a DFS forest

nodes.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ given by ordered adjacency lists and every list $r$ of root vertices, the list of forest roots of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from $r$ contains no vertex twice.
nodes.title: DFS forest roots are distinct

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists, let $r$ be a list of root vertices, and let $v$ and $p$ be vertices. If $v$ is a forest root of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from $r$, then $(v, p)$ is not among the (child, parent) pairs recorded by that search.
nodes.title: A DFS forest root has no parent

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. If the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search, then $G$ has a directed edge from $p$ to $c$.
nodes.title: DFS parent pairs are graph edges

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. In the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search, no vertex occurs as the child of more than one entry; that is, the list of children has no repeated entries.
nodes.title: No vertex is recorded twice as a DFS child

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists, let $r$ be a list of root vertices, and let $v$ be a vertex in the preorder of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from $r$. Then $v$ is a forest root of that search, or there is exactly one vertex $p$ such that $(v, p)$ is among the (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search.
nodes.title: Every discovered vertex is a forest root or has a unique parent

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. If the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search, then $p$ occurs strictly before $c$ in the discovery order (preorder) of the search.
nodes.title: In preorder, a DFS parent precedes its child

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a directed graph with ordered adjacency lists and fix an ordered list of roots. If $(c, p)$ is one of the (child, parent) pairs recorded by the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from these roots, then $c$ occurs before $p$ in the postorder (finish order) of that search.
nodes.title: A DFS child finishes before its parent

nodes.summary: For a directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and an ordered list of roots, the decreasing finish order is the reverse of the postorder of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from those roots: the vertices that search visits, listed from the latest finished to the earliest finished.
nodes.title: Decreasing finish order

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. If the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search, then $p$ occurs strictly before $c$ in the decreasing finish order, the reverse of the finish order.
nodes.title: In decreasing finish order, a DFS parent precedes its child

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists, let $r$ be a list of root vertices, and let $v$ be a vertex. Then $v$ occurs in the decreasing finish order of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from $r$ if and only if $v$ is reachable in $G$ from some vertex of $r$.
nodes.title: Decreasing finish order lists exactly the vertices reachable from the roots

nodes.summary: For every directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and every ordered list of roots, the decreasing finish order of the depth-first search of $G$ from those roots contains no vertex twice.
nodes.title: Decreasing finish order has no repeated vertices

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. Say that $p$ is a recorded parent of $c$ when the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search, and call a discovered vertex with no recorded parent a forest root. Then for every vertex $v$ in the discovery order (preorder) there are $k \ge 0$ and vertices…
nodes.title: Parent chains in a DFS forest end at a forest root

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. Say that $p$ is a recorded parent of $c$ when the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search. Then there are no $k \ge 1$ and vertices $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k$ with $v_k = v_0$ such that each $v_{i+1}$ is a recorded parent of $v_i$.
nodes.title: The DFS parent relation is acyclic

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists, let $r$ be a list of root vertices, and let $v$ be a vertex. If $v$ is a forest root of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from $r$, then $v$ occurs in $r$.
nodes.title: DFS forest roots are scheduled roots

nodes.summary: For a directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists, the whole-graph traversal is the left-first depth-first search of $G$ whose roots are all vertices of $G$, taken in the graph's fixed vertex enumeration order.
nodes.title: Depth-first search of the whole graph

nodes.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ given by ordered adjacency lists and every vertex $v$ of $G$, $v$ occurs in the preorder of the whole-graph depth-first search of $G$, that is, the left-first depth-first search of $G$ whose roots are all vertices of $G$ in the graph's vertex order.
nodes.title: Whole-graph DFS discovers every vertex

nodes.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ given by ordered adjacency lists and every vertex $v$ of $G$, $v$ occurs in the postorder of the whole-graph depth-first search of $G$, that is, the left-first depth-first search of $G$ whose roots are all vertices of $G$ in the graph's vertex order.
nodes.title: Whole-graph DFS finishes every vertex

nodes.summary: For a directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists, the whole-graph decreasing finish order is the decreasing finish order of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ whose roots are all vertices of $G$, taken in the graph's vertex enumeration order; its vertices are listed from the latest finished to the earliest finished.
nodes.title: Whole-graph decreasing finish order

nodes.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ given by ordered adjacency lists and every vertex $v$ of $G$, $v$ occurs in the whole-graph decreasing finish order of $G$, that is, the decreasing finish order of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ whose roots are all vertices of $G$ in the graph's vertex order.
nodes.title: Whole-graph decreasing finish order contains every vertex

nodes.summary: For every directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists, the whole-graph decreasing finish order of $G$ contains no vertex twice.
nodes.title: Whole-graph decreasing finish order has no repeated vertices

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph with ordered adjacency lists $N(v)$, whose entries may repeat, and let $R$ be a list of roots, possibly with repetitions. Run the depth-first search machine from $R$ (each transition drops a pending vertex that is already visited, discovers a new vertex, or finishes a vertex). Let $v_1, \dots, v_k$ be the preorder of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$. Then there is a terminal…
nodes.title: Exact transition count of depth-first search

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph whose vertices are listed without repetition as $v_1, \dots, v_n$, with ordered adjacency lists $N(v)$ whose entries may repeat. Run the depth-first search machine with roots $v_1, \dots, v_n$ in this order (each transition drops a pending vertex that is already visited, discovers a new vertex, or finishes a vertex). Then there is a terminal machine state, with no work left, whose…
nodes.title: Exact transition count of whole-graph depth-first search
Hierholzer's algorithm for Euler circuits

nodes.summary: Given a directed adjacency graph $G$ and a function $R$ assigning to each vertex $u$ a list $R(u)$ of vertices, the edge list of $R$ is the list of pairs $(u, w)$, one for each entry $w$ of $R(u)$, taken over the vertices $u$ in the order of the vertex enumeration of $G$ and, for each $u$, in the order of $R(u)$. A repeated entry gives a repeated pair.
nodes.title: Edge list of an adjacency function

nodes.summary: The edge list of a directed adjacency graph $G$ is the list of pairs $(u, w)$, one for each entry $w$ of the adjacency list of $u$, taken over the vertices $u$ in the order of the vertex enumeration of $G$ and, for each $u$, in adjacency-list order. A repeated adjacency entry gives a repeated pair, so $G$ is read as a multigraph with one edge occurrence per entry.
nodes.title: Edge list of a directed graph

nodes.summary: For a finite sequence of vertices $W = (w_0, w_1, \dots, w_n)$, the steps of $W$ are the list of consecutive pairs $((w_0, w_1), (w_1, w_2), \dots, (w_{n-1}, w_n))$, in order. A sequence with at most one vertex has no steps.
nodes.title: Steps of a walk

nodes.summary: A finite directed multigraph, read from its adjacency lists with each entry $w$ in the list of $u$ counted as one occurrence of the edge $u \to w$, is balanced when every vertex is the source of as many edge occurrences as it is the target of.
nodes.title: Balanced directed multigraph

nodes.summary: A finite directed multigraph is semi-balanced for vertices $s$ and $t$ when, for every vertex $x$, the number of edge occurrences leaving $x$ plus $[x = t]$ equals the number entering $x$ plus $[x = s]$, where $[P]$ is $1$ if $P$ holds and $0$ otherwise. So for $s \ne t$, one more edge occurrence leaves $s$ than enters it, one more enters $t$ than leaves it, and every other vertex is balanced; for $s = t$ every…
nodes.title: Semi-balanced directed multigraph

nodes.summary: In a finite directed multigraph, a list of vertices $W = (w_0, \dots, w_k)$ is an Euler path from $s$ to $t$ when $w_0 = s$, $w_k = t$, and its list of steps $(w_0, w_1), \dots, (w_{k-1}, w_k)$ is a permutation of the list of edge occurrences of the graph, so that each edge occurrence, counted with multiplicity, is traversed exactly once.
nodes.title: Euler path in a directed multigraph

nodes.summary: In a finite directed multigraph, a list of vertices $W$ is an Euler circuit from a vertex $s$ when it is an Euler path from $s$ to $s$: it starts and ends at $s$, and its list of consecutive pairs is a permutation of the list of edge occurrences of the graph.
nodes.title: Euler circuit in a directed multigraph

nodes.summary: Given a fuel $n$, a vertex $v$, an assignment $R$ of a list of remaining out-neighbours to each vertex, and a list $\mathit{acc}$ of vertices, the recursion returns a list of vertices and a new assignment, with a cost. With fuel $0$ it returns $(\mathit{acc}, R)$ at cost $0$. With fuel $n + 1$: if $R(v)$ is empty, it returns $v$ followed by $\mathit{acc}$ together with $R$, at cost $0$; otherwise $R(v)$ is $w$…
nodes.title: Hierholzer's recursion

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph, read as a multigraph with one edge occurrence per adjacency entry, let $s$ be a vertex, and let $m$ be the number of edge occurrences of $G$, that is, the length of its edge list. Hierholzer's algorithm on $G$ from $s$ runs Hierholzer's recursion from $s$ with fuel $m + 1$, with the adjacency list of each vertex as its list of remaining out-neighbours and the empty list as…
nodes.title: Hierholzer's algorithm

nodes.summary: Let $A$ and $B$ be nonempty vertex sequences, where $A$ ends at the vertex $a$ and $B$ starts at the vertex $b$. Then the steps of the concatenation $A B$ are the steps of $A$, followed by the step $(a, b)$, followed by the steps of $B$.
nodes.title: Steps of a concatenated walk

nodes.summary: For an element $e$ and lists $A$, $B$, $C$ of the same type, the list $e \cdot A \cdot B \cdot C$ is a permutation of $B \cdot e \cdot A \cdot C$, where $\cdot$ denotes concatenation and $e$ stands for the one-element list.
nodes.title: Moving a block of a list in front of an element is a permutation

nodes.summary: A list $E$ of ordered pairs of vertices is semi-balanced for vertices $v$ and $t$ when, for every vertex $x$, the number of pairs in $E$ with first component $x$ plus $[x = t]$ equals the number with second component $x$ plus $[x = v]$, where $[P]$ is $1$ if $P$ holds and $0$ otherwise. So for $v \ne t$, $v$ has one more outgoing than incoming occurrence, $t$ one more incoming than outgoing, and every other vertex…
nodes.title: Semi-balanced edge list

nodes.summary: A list $E$ of ordered pairs of vertices, read as directed edge occurrences, is balanced when every vertex $x$ occurs as the first component of exactly as many entries of $E$ as it occurs as the second component, counted with multiplicity.
nodes.title: Balanced edge list

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed multigraph, let $R$ assign to each vertex $u$ a list $R(u)$ of remaining out-neighbours, and let $E(R)$ be the list of remaining edge occurrences, one pair $(u, w)$ for each entry $w$ of $R(u)$. Let $v$ and $t$ be vertices, $\mathit{acc}$ a list of vertices and $n$ a natural number with $|E(R)| < n$, and suppose $E(R)$ is semi-balanced for $v$ and $t$: for every vertex $x$, the number…
nodes.title: Contract of Hierholzer's recursion

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph, read as a multigraph with one edge per adjacency entry, and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices such that $G$ is semi-balanced for $s$ and $t$. Then the vertex sequence $W$ returned by Hierholzer's algorithm on $G$ from $s$ starts at $s$ and ends at $t$, and the edge list of $G$ is a permutation of the list of consecutive pairs of $W$ followed by some further list of pairs. So $W$ is…
nodes.title: Hierholzer's algorithm returns a trail in a directed multigraph

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph, read as a multigraph with one edge per adjacency entry, and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices such that $G$ is semi-balanced for $s$ and $t$ (at $s$ one more edge occurrence leaves than enters, at $t$ one more enters than leaves, and at every other vertex as many leave as enter; at every vertex when $s = t$) and the source of every edge of $G$ is reachable from $s$. Then the vertex…
nodes.title: Hierholzer's algorithm finds Euler paths in directed multigraphs

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph, read as a multigraph with one edge per adjacency entry, that is balanced (every vertex is the source of exactly as many edge occurrences as it is the target of), and let $s$ be a vertex such that the source of every edge of $G$ is reachable from $s$. Then the vertex sequence returned by Hierholzer's algorithm on $G$ from $s$ is an Euler circuit of $G$ from $s$.
nodes.title: Hierholzer's algorithm finds Euler circuits in directed multigraphs

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph, read as a multigraph with one edge per adjacency entry, and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices such that $G$ is semi-balanced for $s$ and $t$ and the source of every edge of $G$ is reachable from $s$. Then Hierholzer's algorithm on $G$ from $s$ costs exactly $|E|$ units, where $|E|$ is the number of edge occurrences of $G$, that is, the length of its edge list.
nodes.title: Running time of Hierholzer's algorithm

nodes.summary: If a finite directed multigraph has an Euler path from $s$ to $t$, then it is semi-balanced for $s$ and $t$: counting edge occurrences, $s$ has one more outgoing than incoming edge, $t$ one more incoming than outgoing, and every other vertex is balanced (every vertex, when $s = t$).
nodes.title: A directed multigraph with an Euler path is semi-balanced

nodes.summary: If a finite directed multigraph has an Euler circuit from some vertex $s$, then it is balanced: every vertex is the source of as many edge occurrences as it is the target of.
nodes.title: A directed multigraph with an Euler circuit is balanced

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph, read as a multigraph with one edge per adjacency entry, and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices such that the source of every edge of $G$ is reachable from $s$. Then $G$ has an Euler path from $s$ to $t$ if and only if $G$ is semi-balanced for $s$ and $t$: at $s$ one more edge occurrence leaves than enters, at $t$ one more enters than leaves, and every other vertex is the source of…
nodes.title: Euler path criterion for directed multigraphs

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph, read as a multigraph with one edge per adjacency entry, and let $s$ be a vertex such that the source of every edge of $G$ is reachable from $s$. Then $G$ has an Euler circuit from $s$ if and only if $G$ is balanced, that is, every vertex is the source of exactly as many edge occurrences as it is the target of.
nodes.title: Euler circuit criterion for directed multigraphs

nodes.summary: The ordered pair $(a, b)$ of vertices, viewed as the unordered pair $\{a, b\}$, so that $(a, b)$ and $(b, a)$ give the same unordered edge.
nodes.title: Unordered edge of an ordered pair

nodes.summary: For a finite list $R$ of edges of an undirected multigraph, each given as a pair $(a, b)$, the degree of a vertex $x$ is the number of edges in $R$ whose first component is $x$ plus the number whose second component is $x$; parallel edges count separately and a loop $(x, x)$ counts twice.
nodes.title: Degree in an undirected edge list

nodes.summary: For a finite list $R$ of edges of an undirected multigraph and vertices $v$, $t$, the condition holds when for every vertex $x$ the number $\deg_R(x) + [x = v] + [x = t]$ is even, where $\deg_R$ is the degree in $R$ (a loop counts twice) and $[P]$ is $1$ if $P$ holds and $0$ otherwise. Thus if $v \ne t$, exactly $v$ and $t$ have odd degree, and if $v = t$, every degree is even.
nodes.title: Degree parity condition for two endpoints

nodes.summary: For a list $E$ of edges (ordered pairs of vertices), a vertex $x$ is reachable from a vertex $s$ when there are vertices $s = v_0, v_1, \dots, v_n = x$ with $n \ge 0$ such that for each $i < n$, $(v_i, v_{i+1})$ or $(v_{i+1}, v_i)$ belongs to $E$.
nodes.title: Reachability in an undirected multigraph

nodes.summary: For a finite list $E$ of edges of an undirected multigraph and vertices $s$, $t$, a sequence of vertices $W = (w_0, \dots, w_n)$ is an Euler path of $E$ from $s$ to $t$ when $w_0 = s$, $w_n = t$, and the multiset of unordered pairs $\{w_{i-1}, w_i\}$ for $1 \le i \le n$ equals the multiset of the edges of $E$ taken as unordered pairs. Thus every edge is traversed exactly once, in either direction.
nodes.title: Euler path in an undirected multigraph

nodes.summary: For an edge $e = (a, b)$ and a vertex $v$, the other endpoint of $e$ at $v$ is $b$ if $a = v$, and $a$ otherwise; in particular a loop $(v, v)$ gives $v$.
nodes.title: Other endpoint of an edge

nodes.summary: The recursion takes a fuel $f \in \mathbb{N}$, a vertex $v$, a list $R$ of remaining edges and an accumulator list $A$ of vertices, and returns a list of vertices and a list of remaining edges. With fuel $0$ it returns $A$ and $R$ unchanged. With fuel $f + 1$: if no edge of $R$ has $v$ as an endpoint, it returns $v$ prepended to $A$, together with $R$; otherwise, with $e$ the first such edge, it removes $e$ from…
nodes.title: Undirected Hierholzer recursion

nodes.summary: Given a list $E$ of undirected edges (ordered pairs of vertices) and a start vertex $s$, run the undirected Hierholzer recursion from $s$ on $E$ with an empty accumulator and fuel $|E| + 1$, and return the list of emitted vertices; its cost is the cost of that recursion.
nodes.title: Undirected Hierholzer's algorithm

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a finite list of edges of an undirected multigraph, each an ordered pair of vertices, let $e = (a, b)$ be an edge in $R$, and let $x$ be a vertex. Then the degree of $x$ in $R$ equals the degree of $x$ in the list obtained from $R$ by removing the first occurrence of $e$, plus $[x = a] + [x = b]$, where $[P]$ is $1$ if $P$ holds and $0$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Degree after removing an edge

nodes.summary: If an ordered pair $e = (a, b)$ of vertices has $a = v$ or $b = v$, then the unordered pair $\{a, b\}$ equals $\{v, w\}$, where $w$ is the other endpoint of $e$ at $v$.
nodes.title: An edge at a vertex joins it to its other endpoint

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a list of edges, $v$, $t$ vertices such that exactly $v$ and $t$ have odd degree in $R$ (no vertex when $v = t$), $A$ a list of vertices, and $f > |R|$ a fuel bound. Run the undirected Hierholzer recursion with fuel $f$ from $v$ on $R$ with accumulator $A$, and let $R'$ be the remaining edge list it returns and $c$ its cost. Then there is a vertex sequence $W$ starting at $v$ and ending at $t$ such that…
nodes.title: Invariant of the undirected Hierholzer recursion

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a list of undirected edges and $s$, $t$ vertices such that exactly $s$ and $t$ have odd degree in $E$ (no vertex has odd degree when $s = t$). Then the vertex sequence $W$ returned by the undirected Hierholzer algorithm on $E$ from $s$ starts at $s$ and ends at $t$, and the consecutive pairs of $W$, as unordered pairs, form a sub-multiset of the edges of $E$ as unordered pairs: no edge is traversed more…
nodes.title: Undirected Hierholzer's algorithm returns a trail

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a list of undirected edges (ordered pairs of vertices) and $s$, $t$ vertices such that exactly $s$ and $t$ have odd degree in $E$ (no vertex has odd degree when $s = t$), and suppose the first endpoint of every edge of $E$ is reachable from $s$ through edges of $E$. Then the vertex sequence returned by the undirected Hierholzer algorithm on $E$ from $s$ is an Euler path of $E$ from $s$ to $t$.
nodes.title: Undirected Hierholzer's algorithm finds Euler paths

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a list of undirected edges (ordered pairs of vertices) in which every vertex has even degree, and let $s$ be a vertex such that the first endpoint of every edge of $E$ is reachable from $s$ through edges of $E$. Then the vertex sequence returned by the undirected Hierholzer algorithm on $E$ from $s$ is an Euler path of $E$ from $s$ to $s$, that is, an Euler circuit at $s$.
nodes.title: Undirected Hierholzer's algorithm finds Euler circuits

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a list of undirected edges and $s$, $t$ vertices such that exactly $s$ and $t$ have odd degree in $E$ (no vertex has odd degree when $s = t$), and suppose the first endpoint of every edge of $E$ is reachable from $s$ through edges of $E$. Then the undirected Hierholzer algorithm on $E$ from $s$ costs exactly $|E|$, the number of edges of $E$, in the cost model that charges one unit per removed edge.
nodes.title: Cost of the undirected Hierholzer algorithm

nodes.summary: For a vertex $x$, this assigns to an unordered pair $\{a, b\}$ the number $[x = a] + [x = b]$ of its endpoints equal to $x$, where $[P]$ is $1$ if $P$ holds and $0$ otherwise; in particular a loop $\{x, x\}$ gives $2$.
nodes.title: Multiplicity of a vertex in an unordered edge

nodes.summary: Let $A$ and $B$ be finite lists of edges of an undirected multigraph such that the multiset of edges of $A$, taken as unordered pairs, equals that of $B$. Then every vertex has the same degree in $A$ as in $B$.
nodes.title: Degrees depend only on the unordered edges

nodes.summary: Let $W = (w_0, \dots, w_n)$ be a nonempty sequence of vertices with $w_0 = s$ and $w_n = t$, and consider the multigraph whose edges are the consecutive pairs $(w_{i-1}, w_i)$ for $1 \le i \le n$. In it every vertex other than $s$ and $t$ has even degree (a loop counts twice); if $s \ne t$, then $s$ and $t$ have odd degree, and if $s = t$, every vertex has even degree.
nodes.title: Degrees along a walk

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a finite list of edges of an undirected multigraph and let $W$ be an Euler path of $E$ from $s$ to $t$. Then every vertex other than $s$ and $t$ has even degree in $E$ (a loop counts twice); if $s \ne t$, then $s$ and $t$ have odd degree, and if $s = t$, every vertex has even degree.
nodes.title: Degrees of an undirected Euler path

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a finite list of edges of an undirected multigraph (parallel edges and loops allowed), each given as a pair $(a, b)$, and let $s$, $t$ be vertices such that the first endpoint $a$ of every edge is reachable from $s$ along edges of $E$ traversed in either direction. Then $E$ has an Euler path from $s$ to $t$ if and only if, when $s \ne t$, exactly $s$ and $t$ have odd degree, and, when $s = t$, every…
nodes.title: Euler's theorem for undirected multigraphs
Strongly connected components

nodes.summary: In a directed adjacency graph $G$, vertices $u$ and $v$ are strongly connected when $v$ is reachable from $u$ and $u$ is reachable from $v$ in $G$.
nodes.title: Strongly connected vertices

nodes.summary: In a directed graph $G$, every vertex is strongly connected to itself.
nodes.title: Strong connectivity is reflexive

nodes.summary: In a directed graph $G$, if $u$ is strongly connected to $v$, then $v$ is strongly connected to $u$.
nodes.title: Strong connectivity is symmetric

nodes.summary: In a directed graph $G$, if $u$ is strongly connected to $v$ and $v$ is strongly connected to $w$, then $u$ is strongly connected to $w$.
nodes.title: Strong connectivity is transitive

nodes.summary: For a directed graph $G$, the relation on the vertices of $G$ that holds between $u$ and $v$ exactly when $u$ and $v$ are strongly connected in $G$, packaged as an equivalence relation.
nodes.title: Strong connectivity as an equivalence relation

nodes.summary: For a directed graph $G$ and vertices $u$ and $v$, the test returns true exactly when $v$ occurs in the preorder of the depth-first search of $G$ from the single root $u$, and $u$ occurs in the preorder of the depth-first search of $G$ from the single root $v$.
nodes.title: Executable mutual-reachability test

nodes.summary: For a directed graph $G$ and vertices $u$ and $v$, the executable mutual-reachability test on $u$ and $v$ returns true if and only if $u$ and $v$ are strongly connected in $G$.
nodes.title: The mutual-reachability test is correct

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a directed graph and let $v_1, \dots, v_n$ be its vertices in decreasing order of finishing time in a depth-first search of the whole graph that takes its roots in the vertex order of $G$. For each $i$, let $C_i$ be the list of those $v_j$, in increasing order of $j$, such that $v_i$ and $v_j$ are strongly connected (tested by two depth-first searches). The output is the list $C_1, \dots, C_n$ with…
nodes.title: Strongly connected components algorithm

nodes.summary: For every directed graph $G$, each block returned by the strongly connected components algorithm on $G$ contains at least one vertex.
nodes.title: Computed components are nonempty

nodes.summary: For every directed graph $G$, each block returned by the strongly connected components algorithm on $G$ contains no vertex more than once.
nodes.title: Computed components have no repeated vertices

nodes.summary: For every directed graph $G$, any two blocks at different positions of the list returned by the strongly connected components algorithm on $G$ have no vertex in common.
nodes.title: Computed components are pairwise disjoint

nodes.summary: For a directed graph $G$ and a vertex $v$, $v$ belongs to some block of the computed strongly connected components of $G$ if and only if $v$ occurs in the vertex enumeration of $G$.
nodes.title: The computed components cover the vertex list

nodes.summary: For a directed graph $G$ and vertices $u$ and $v$, some block of the computed strongly connected components of $G$ contains both $u$ and $v$ if and only if $u$ and $v$ are strongly connected in $G$.
nodes.title: Vertices share a computed component exactly when strongly connected

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a directed graph, let $B$ be one of the blocks returned by the strongly connected components algorithm on $G$, and let $m$ be a vertex of $B$. Then for every vertex $v$ of $G$, the vertices $m$ and $v$ are strongly connected (each is reachable from the other) if and only if $v$ lies in $B$.
nodes.title: Each computed component is a full mutual-reachability class

nodes.summary: A list $\mathcal{B}$ of vertex lists is an SCC partition of a directed graph $G$ when every block of $\mathcal{B}$ is nonempty and contains no vertex twice, blocks at different positions of $\mathcal{B}$ are disjoint, a vertex lies in some block exactly when it is a vertex of $G$, two vertices lie in a common block exactly when they are strongly connected (each is reachable from the other), and for every block $B$,…
nodes.title: SCC partition

nodes.summary: For every directed graph $G$, the list of blocks returned by the strongly connected components algorithm on $G$ is an SCC partition of $G$: every block is nonempty and contains no vertex twice, blocks at different positions of the list are disjoint, every vertex of $G$ lies in some block, two vertices lie in a common block exactly when they are strongly connected, and for every vertex $m$ of a block $B$ and every…
nodes.title: The computed components form the SCC partition

nodes.summary: In a directed graph $G$, a list $S$ of vertices reaches a list $T$ of vertices when some vertex of $S$ reaches some vertex of $T$ by a directed path in $G$, possibly of length zero.
nodes.title: Reachability between components

nodes.summary: A list $\mathcal{B}$ of vertex lists of a directed graph $G$ has an acyclic condensation when, for all $S, T \in \mathcal{B}$, if some vertex of $S$ reaches some vertex of $T$ in $G$ and some vertex of $T$ reaches some vertex of $S$, then $S = T$. That is, reachability between the blocks is antisymmetric.
nodes.title: Acyclic condensation

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a directed graph and let $S$ and $T$ be blocks returned by the strongly connected components algorithm on $G$. If some vertex of $S$ reaches some vertex of $T$ and some vertex of $T$ reaches some vertex of $S$, then $S = T$.
nodes.title: The condensation of the computed components is acyclic
Topological sorting

nodes.summary: For a finite directed graph $G$, a list $R$ of vertices and a vertex $v$, the indegree of $v$ within $R$ is the number of entries $u$ of $R$, counted with multiplicity, such that $G$ has an edge from $u$ to $v$.
nodes.title: Indegree within a vertex list

nodes.summary: The indegree of a vertex $v$ in a finite directed graph $G$ is the number of vertices $u$ such that $G$ has an edge from $u$ to $v$; repeated entries in adjacency lists count once.
nodes.title: Indegree

nodes.summary: The result of Kahn's topological sorting algorithm on a graph with vertices of type $\alpha$ is either a success, carrying a list of vertices, or a failure, carrying the list of vertices processed before the queue emptied and the list of vertices that remain.
nodes.title: Outcome of Kahn's topological sort

nodes.summary: Run Kahn's algorithm with a first-in first-out queue on a finite directed graph $G$ whose vertices are enumerated as $v_1, \dots, v_n$. Initially every vertex is remaining, the counter of each vertex is its number of in-neighbours, and the queue holds the vertices with no in-neighbours in enumeration order. At each of $n$ steps, if the queue is nonempty, its front vertex $x$ is removed from the queue and from the…
nodes.title: Kahn's topological sort

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of vertices. A list $c = [c_1, \dots, c_k]$ of vertices is a directed cycle of $G$ in $R$ when $k \ge 1$, the vertices $c_1, \dots, c_k$ are pairwise distinct, $G$ has an edge from $c_i$ to $c_{i+1}$ for each $1 \le i < k$ and an edge from $c_k$ to $c_1$, and every $c_i$ lies in $R$.
nodes.title: Directed cycle within a vertex list

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and let $R$ and $c = [c_1, \dots, c_k]$ be lists of vertices. Then $c$ is a directed cycle of $G$ in $R$ if and only if $k \ge 1$, the vertices $c_1, \dots, c_k$ are pairwise distinct, $G$ has an edge from $c_i$ to $c_{i+1}$ for every $1 \le i < k$, $G$ has an edge from $c_k$ to $c_1$, and every $c_i$ lies in $R$.
nodes.title: Characterization of directed cycles within a vertex list

nodes.summary: A finite directed graph $G$ is acyclic when it has no directed cycle, that is, no nonempty list $[c_1, \dots, c_k]$ of pairwise distinct vertices such that $G$ has an edge from $c_i$ to $c_{i+1}$ for each $1 \le i < k$ and an edge from $c_k$ to $c_1$.
nodes.title: Acyclic directed graph

nodes.summary: A finite directed graph $G$ is acyclic if and only if there is no directed cycle of $G$ in its vertex list, that is, no nonempty list of pairwise distinct vertices in which each vertex has an edge to the next and the last vertex has an edge to the first.
nodes.title: Acyclicity means having no directed cycle

nodes.summary: A list $L$ of vertices of a finite directed graph $G$ is a topological order of $G$ when $L$ has no duplicates, a vertex lies in $L$ exactly when it lies in the vertex enumeration of $G$, and for every edge $u \to v$ of $G$ the first position of $u$ in $L$ is strictly smaller than the first position of $v$ in $L$.
nodes.title: Topological order

nodes.summary: If Kahn's topological sort on a finite directed graph $G$ returns a success with list $L$, then $L$ has no duplicates.
nodes.title: A successful topological sort has no repeated vertex

nodes.summary: If Kahn's topological sort on a finite directed graph $G$ returns a success with list $L$, then a vertex lies in $L$ if and only if it lies in the vertex enumeration of $G$.
nodes.title: A successful topological sort lists every vertex

nodes.summary: If Kahn's topological sort on a finite directed graph $G$ returns a success with list $L$, then for every edge $u \to v$ of $G$ the first position of $u$ in $L$ is strictly smaller than the first position of $v$ in $L$.
nodes.title: A successful topological sort points every edge forward

nodes.summary: If Kahn's topological sort on a finite directed graph $G$ returns a success with list $L$, then $L$ is a topological order of $G$.
nodes.title: A successful topological sort is a topological order

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph. If deterministic FIFO Kahn topological sorting of $G$ fails after processing the vertex list $P$ and leaving the vertex list $R$ unprocessed, then $R$ is nonempty, neither $P$ nor $R$ has repeated entries, a vertex lies in the vertex list of $G$ if and only if it lies in $P$ or in $R$, and no vertex lies in both $P$ and $R$.
nodes.title: A failed Kahn run splits the vertices into processed and unprocessed ones

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph. If deterministic FIFO Kahn topological sorting of $G$ fails after processing the vertex list $P$ and leaving the vertex list $R$ unprocessed, then for every vertex $v$ in $R$ the indegree of $v$ within $R$, the number of entries $u$ of $R$ such that $G$ has an edge from $u$ to $v$, is positive.
nodes.title: Unprocessed vertices of a failed Kahn run have positive indegree among the unprocessed

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph. If deterministic FIFO Kahn topological sorting of $G$ fails after processing the vertex list $P$ and leaving the vertex list $R$ unprocessed, then $G$ has a directed cycle in $R$: a nonempty list of pairwise distinct vertices of $R$ in which each vertex has an edge to the next and the last vertex has an edge to the first.
nodes.title: A failed Kahn run leaves a directed cycle

nodes.summary: If Kahn's topological sort on a finite directed graph $G$ returns a success, then $G$ is acyclic.
nodes.title: Success of Kahn's algorithm implies acyclicity

nodes.summary: If a finite directed graph $G$, given by a vertex enumeration and adjacency lists, is acyclic, then deterministic FIFO Kahn topological sorting of $G$ returns success with some vertex order.
nodes.title: Kahn's algorithm succeeds on acyclic graphs

nodes.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$, Kahn's topological sort on $G$ returns a success if and only if $G$ is acyclic.
