nodes.title: Kahn's algorithm succeeds exactly on acyclic graphs

nodes.title: Transition recurrence of the transitive-closure stages

Traversal of implicit binary trees

nodes.summary: The frontier below `s`, left to right, cut at depth `k`. At depth zero it is `[s]`, even when `step s` branches. Duplicate occurrences are retained.
nodes.title: Depth-cut frontier of a binary branching step

nodes.summary: One depth-first round on `(stack, output)`. Terminal states are prepended to the output; a branching state is replaced by its left child followed by its right child.
nodes.title: One depth-first round of binary branching

nodes.summary: Every depth-cut frontier is nonempty.
nodes.title: Depth-cut frontiers are nonempty

nodes.summary: An empty work stack is fixed by any number of rounds.
nodes.title: An empty work stack is fixed by every round

nodes.summary: If every frontier occurrence is terminal, exactly `2 * length - 1` rounds process the tree below `s`, preserving the tail `r` and prepending its reversed frontier to `out`. The terminal-frontier hypothesis is essential: a depth cut may contain branching states.
nodes.title: Exact round count for traversing a terminal frontier

nodes.summary: After at least `2 * length - 1` rounds from `[s]`, the stack is empty and all terminal frontier occurrences have been collected in reverse order.
nodes.title: Enough rounds empty the stack and collect the frontier

nodes.summary: A natural-valued weight additive across each branch equals the sum of the frontier weights, even when the frontier is cut before termination.
nodes.title: Additive weight of the root is the sum over the frontier

nodes.summary: A map commuting with both steps transports the ordered frontier, preserving multiplicity.
nodes.title: Commuting maps transport the ordered frontier

nodes.summary: A commuting node map transports one stack round and its accumulated output.
nodes.title: Commuting maps transport one depth-first round

nodes.summary: A commuting node map transports any number of rounds. No injectivity is required.
nodes.title: Commuting maps transport any number of rounds

nodes.summary: One stack round accumulating natural weights rather than a list of terminal states. The previous count is retained, and each terminal occurrence contributes its weight.
nodes.title: Weight-counting depth-first round

nodes.summary: Counting rounds are the projection of list-output rounds to the sum of output weights.
nodes.title: Counting rounds project list-output rounds

nodes.summary: With a terminal frontier and enough rounds, the final count is its total weight.
nodes.title: Final count of counting rounds is the frontier weight

nodes.summary: With at most `d` further depth steps and `h` further heavy steps, the frontier has at most `∑ j ∈ range (h + 1), d.choose j` occurrences. The source budget hypotheses are retained, including the strict heavy-budget inequality.
nodes.title: Binomial bound on the frontier size under depth and heavy budgets

nodes.summary: A depth allowance covering the remaining depth budget produces only terminal states.
nodes.title: A large enough depth cut yields only terminal states

nodes.summary: Every frontier occurrence satisfies the resource invariant at some budgets.
nodes.title: Frontier occurrences satisfy the resource invariant

nodes.summary: A property split by branches holds at the root iff it holds at some frontier occurrence.
nodes.title: Branch-split properties hold at the root iff at some leaf

nodes.summary: The depth budget bounds the stack by `D + 1` at every round; each pending state satisfies the resource invariant. This is a list-size bound, not a machine-space model.
nodes.title: Depth budget bounds the depth-first stack size

nodes.summary: Step transport restricted to a preserved invariant transports the frontier and records that all its occurrences satisfy the invariant.
nodes.title: Invariant-restricted step transport of the frontier

nodes.summary: One round does not decrease the combined number of pending and collected occurrences.
nodes.title: A round does not decrease pending plus collected occurrences

nodes.summary: With a terminal frontier, pending and collected occurrences together never exceed its length, including before traversal is complete.
nodes.title: Pending plus collected occurrences are bounded by the frontier length

nodes.summary: A property of every state ever on the stack holds of each collected leaf.
nodes.title: Stack invariants hold for every collected leaf

nodes.summary: Increasing a depth cut beyond a terminal frontier leaves the list unchanged.
nodes.title: Deepening the cut past a terminal frontier changes nothing

Bellman–Ford algorithm

nodes.summary: A weighted directed edge on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ consists of a source vertex, a target vertex and an integer weight.
nodes.title: Weighted directed edge

nodes.summary: For a list of weighted edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the associated ordered directed graph enumerates its vertices as $0, 1, \dots, n-1$, and the outgoing neighbor list of a vertex $u$ is the list of targets of the edges of the list with source $u$, in the order in which they occur and with repetitions.
nodes.title: Weight-forgetting directed graph

nodes.summary: For a vertex $s$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and a list of weighted edges $e_1, \dots, e_k$ on these vertices, the vertices of the path from $s$ along this list are the list $s, t_1, \dots, t_k$, where $t_i$ is the target of $e_i$.
nodes.title: Vertices of a path

nodes.summary: The weight of a list of integer-weighted edges is the sum of the weights of its entries, an edge occurring several times being counted each time.
nodes.title: Bellman–Ford path weight

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a list of weighted directed edges on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$. A list $P = (e_1, \dots, e_k)$ of weighted directed edges is a weighted path in $E$ from $s$ to $t$ when every $e_i$ belongs to $E$, the target of $e_i$ is the source of $e_{i+1}$ for every $i < k$, and either $k = 0$ and $s = t$, or $k \ge 1$, the source of $e_1$ is $s$ and the target of $e_k$ is $t$.
nodes.title: Weighted path in an edge list

nodes.summary: For a list $E$ of weighted directed edges on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ and vertices $u$, $v$, the graph obtained from $E$ by forgetting weights has an edge from $u$ to $v$ if and only if some edge in $E$ has source $u$ and target $v$.
nodes.title: Edges of the weight-forgetting graph

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a list of weighted directed edges on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices. If the list consisting of an edge $e$ followed by a list $R$ of edges is a weighted path in $E$ from $s$ to $t$, then $R$ is a weighted path in $E$ from the target of $e$ to $t$.
nodes.title: Tail of a weighted path

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a list of weighted directed edges on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ and let $s$, $m$ and $t$ be vertices. If $P$ is a weighted path in $E$ from $s$ to $m$ and $e$ is an edge belonging to $E$ with source $m$ and target $t$, then the list $P$ followed by $e$ is a weighted path in $E$ from $s$ to $t$.
nodes.title: Appending an edge to a weighted path

nodes.summary: For every list $P$ of weighted directed edges on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ and every weighted directed edge $e$ on these vertices, the weight of the list $P$ followed by $e$ is the weight of $P$ plus the weight of $e$.
nodes.title: Weight of a path with an edge appended

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a list of weighted directed edges on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices. If a list $P$ of $k$ edges is a weighted path in $E$ from $s$ to $t$, then there is a walk of length $k$ from $s$ to $t$ in the directed graph obtained from $E$ by forgetting the weights.
nodes.title: Weighted paths give walks of the same length

nodes.summary: For a list of weighted edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and vertices $s$ and $t$, the vertex $t$ is reachable from $s$ in the directed graph obtained from the list by forgetting the weights if and only if there is a weighted path from $s$ to $t$ using edges of the list.
nodes.title: Reachability by weighted paths

nodes.summary: For a list of weighted edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and a source vertex $s$, a reachable negative cycle consists of a base vertex $b$, a weighted path $p$ from $s$ to $b$ using edges of the list whose vertices along $p$ from $s$ are pairwise distinct, and a nonempty weighted path $c$ from $b$ to $b$ using edges of the list whose edges have pairwise distinct sources and whose weight is negative.
nodes.title: Reachable negative cycle witness

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a list of weighted directed edges on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ and $s$ a vertex. Then $E$ has a negative cycle reachable from $s$ when there is a reachable negative cycle witness for $E$ and $s$: a base vertex $b$, a weighted path in $E$ from $s$ to $b$ that visits no vertex twice, and a nonempty weighted path in $E$ from $b$ to $b$ whose edge sources are pairwise distinct and whose total weight is…
nodes.title: Existence of a reachable negative cycle

nodes.summary: For a graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, the output of a successful Bellman-Ford run consists of a source vertex $s$, for every vertex a distance that is either an integer or $\infty$, and for every vertex an optional predecessor edge (a weighted directed edge, or none).
nodes.title: Bellman-Ford distance table

The path to a vertex $t$ is built backwards from $t$: at a vertex $v \ne s$, take the recorded predecessor edge $e$ of $v$, put it in front of the edges collected so far, and continue from the source of $e$. nodes.title: Bellman-Ford path reconstruction

nodes.summary: The cost of a Bellman-Ford run is a pair of natural numbers: the number of edge occurrences checked by relaxation passes, and the number of predecessor edges read or emitted while reconstructing a negative-cycle witness.
nodes.title: Bellman-Ford cost counters

nodes.summary: The total of a Bellman–Ford cost record is its number of edge relaxation checks plus its number of negative-cycle witness reconstruction steps.
nodes.title: Total Bellman–Ford cost

nodes.summary: For a list of weighted edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and a source vertex $s$, a Bellman–Ford result is either a distance record (a source vertex, an optional integer distance for each vertex and an optional predecessor edge for each vertex) or a reachable negative cycle witness for the list and $s$.

nodes.title: Bellman–Ford algorithm

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $s$ be a vertex. Bellman-Ford run on $E$ from $s$ returns distances if and only if there is no negative cycle reachable from $s$, that is, no simple path from $s$ to a vertex $b$ together with a nonempty cycle through $b$ along edges of $E$ whose edge sources are pairwise distinct and whose total weight is negative.
nodes.title: Bellman-Ford succeeds exactly when no negative cycle is reachable

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $s$ be a vertex. nodes.title: Bellman-Ford reports a negative cycle exactly when one is reachable

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $s$ be a vertex. If Bellman-Ford run on $E$ from $s$ returns distances $d$ and the distance $d(t)$ of a vertex $t$ is a finite integer $\delta$, then there is a walk from $s$ to $t$ along edges of $E$ whose total weight is $\delta$.
nodes.title: Bellman-Ford distances are realized by walks

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $s$ be a vertex. If Bellman-Ford run on $E$ from $s$ returns distances $d$, the distance $d(t)$ of a vertex $t$ is a finite integer $\delta$, and $P$ is a walk from $s$ to $t$ along edges of $E$ (vertices may repeat), then $\delta$ is at most the total weight of $P$.
nodes.title: Bellman-Ford distances are lower bounds on walk weights

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $s$ be a vertex. If Bellman-Ford run on $E$ from $s$ returns distances $d$, with $\infty$ marking a vertex that has no finite distance, then for every vertex $t$, $d(t) = \infty$ if and only if $t$ is not reachable from $s$ in the directed graph obtained from $E$ by forgetting the weights.
nodes.title: Bellman-Ford leaves exactly the unreachable vertices at infinite distance

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $s$ be a vertex. Suppose Bellman-Ford run on $E$ from $s$ returns distances $d$ together with predecessor edges, and the predecessor edge of a vertex $t$ is an edge $e$ from $u$ to $v$ of weight $w$. Then $e$ belongs to $E$, $v = t$, and $d(u)$ and $d(t)$ are both finite with $d(t) = d(u) + w$.
nodes.title: Bellman-Ford predecessor edges are tight

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $s$ be a vertex. If Bellman-Ford run on $E$ from $s$ returns distances together with predecessor edges, then $s$ has no predecessor edge.
nodes.title: Bellman-Ford gives the source no predecessor

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $s$ be a vertex. If Bellman-Ford run on $E$ from $s$ returns distances $d$, with $\infty$ marking a vertex that has no finite distance, together with predecessor edges, then for every vertex $t$, reconstructing a path to $t$ (following predecessor edges back from $t$ for at most $n$ steps until $s$ is reached) fails if…

nodes.summary: For every capacity matrix $c$ with natural-number entries on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and all vertices $s$ and $t$, the flow $f$ returned by the Edmonds–Karp algorithm on $c$, $s$, $t$ is feasible for $c$, $s$, $t$: it is skew-symmetric, satisfies $f(u, v) \le c(u, v)$ for all vertices $u, v$, and has zero net outflow at every vertex other than $s$ and $t$.
nodes.title: The Edmonds–Karp flow is feasible

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a capacity matrix with natural-number entries on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, let $s$ and $t$ be vertices, and let $f$ be a flow (an integer-valued matrix on pairs of vertices). If the breadth-first shortest-path search finds no path from $s$ to $t$ in the residual graph of $f$ with respect to $c$, then for every fuel bound $k$, the augmenting-path iteration started at $f$ with fuel $k$ returns $f$.
nodes.title: The iteration stops when there is no augmenting path

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a capacity function, $s$ and $t$ vertices, and $f$ a flow that is feasible for $c$, $s$ and $t$. Then the net flow leaving $s$ under $f$ is at most $\sum_v c(s, v)$, the total capacity leaving $s$.
nodes.title: The flow value is at most the source capacity

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a capacity matrix with natural-number entries on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $s$ and $t$ be distinct vertices. Then $t$ is not reachable from $s$ in the residual graph of the flow returned by the Edmonds–Karp algorithm on $c$, $s$, $t$.
nodes.title: No augmenting path remains after Edmonds–Karp

nodes.summary: For a capacity matrix $c$ with natural-number entries on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and a set $S$ of vertices, the capacity of the cut $S$ is the integer $\sum_{u \in S} \sum_{v \notin S} c(u, v)$.
nodes.title: Cut capacity

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a capacity function, $s$ and $t$ vertices, and $f$ a flow that is feasible for $c$, $s$ and $t$. For every set $S$ of vertices with $s \in S$ and $t \notin S$, the net flow leaving $s$ under $f$ is at most the capacity of the cut $S$, namely $\sum_{u \in S} \sum_{v \notin S} c(u, v)$.
nodes.title: Weak max-flow min-cut duality

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a capacity matrix assigning a natural number $c(u, v)$ to each ordered pair of vertices among $0, \dots, n - 1$, let $f$ be a flow on these vertices, and let $s$ be a vertex. The residual cut of $c$, $f$ and $s$ is the set of vertices visited by breadth-first search from $s$ in the residual graph of $c$ and $f$, that is, the set of vertices reachable from $s$ in that residual graph.
nodes.title: Residual cut

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a capacity matrix with natural-number entries on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $s$ and $t$ be distinct vertices, and let $f$ be the flow returned by the Edmonds–Karp algorithm on $c$, $s$, $t$. Then the net flow of $f$ out of $s$ equals the capacity of the cut formed by the vertices reachable from $s$ in the residual graph of $f$.
nodes.title: The Edmonds–Karp flow value equals its residual cut capacity

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a capacity matrix with natural-number entries on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $s$ and $t$ be distinct vertices, and let $f$ be the flow returned by the Edmonds–Karp algorithm on $c$, $s$, $t$. Then every integer flow $g$ that is feasible for $c$, $s$, $t$ has value at $s$ at most the value of $f$ at $s$, where the value of a flow at $s$ is its net flow out of $s$.
nodes.title: Maximality of the Edmonds–Karp flow

nodes.summary: For a capacity function $c$ on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ with natural-number values, the real capacities are the same values viewed as real numbers, $(u, v) \mapsto c(u, v) \in \mathbb{R}$.
nodes.title: Real capacities

nodes.summary: For an integer flow matrix $f$ on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, its arc flow is the natural-number matrix whose entry at $(u, v)$ is the positive part $\max(f(u, v), 0)$ of $f(u, v)$.
nodes.title: Arc flow of an integer flow

nodes.summary: For an integer flow matrix $f$ on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, its real arc flow is the function $(u, v) \mapsto \max(f(u, v), 0)$, the arc flow of $f$, viewed as real numbers.
nodes.title: Real arc flow

nodes.summary: Let $f$ be an integer flow matrix on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ that is skew-symmetric, $f(u, v) = -f(v, u)$ for all $u, v$, and let $a(u, v) = \max(f(u, v), 0)$ be its arc flow. Then $f(u, v) = a(u, v) - a(v, u)$ for all vertices $u$ and $v$.
nodes.title: A skew flow is the difference of its arc flows

nodes.summary: Let $f$ be a skew-symmetric integer flow matrix on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, so $f(u, v) = -f(v, u)$ for all $u, v$, and let $a(u, v) = \max(f(u, v), 0)$ be its arc flow, viewed as real numbers. Then for every vertex $v$, $\sum_w a(v, w) - \sum_u a(u, v) = \sum_w f(v, w)$, the net flow leaving $v$.
nodes.title: Net outflow in the arc representation

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a capacity function on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ with natural-number values and let $s, t$ be vertices. If an integer flow matrix $f$ is a feasible skew-symmetric $s$-$t$ flow for $c$, then its arc flow $(u, v) \mapsto \max(f(u, v), 0)$, viewed as a real function, is a feasible $s$-$t$ flow for $c$ viewed as real capacities.
nodes.title: A feasible skew flow gives a feasible flow

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a capacity function on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ with natural-number values and let $s \ne t$ be vertices. The set of vertices reachable from $s$ in the residual graph of the flow computed by the Edmonds-Karp algorithm on $c$, $s$, $t$ is an $s$-$t$ cut: it contains $s$ and not $t$.
nodes.title: The Edmonds-Karp residual cut separates source and sink

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a capacity function on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ with natural-number values, viewed as real capacities, and let $s \ne t$ be vertices. Let $f$ be the real arc flow of the flow computed by the Edmonds-Karp algorithm on $c$, $s$, $t$ (its positive part, viewed as real numbers), and let $S_0$ be the set of vertices reachable from $s$ in the residual graph of that flow. Then $f$ is a feasible $s$-$t$ flow…
nodes.title: Edmonds-Karp computes a maximum flow and a minimum cut

parts: cut is smaller than the Edmonds–Karp residual cut
reading_title.source: No $s$-$t$ cut is smaller than the Edmonds–Karp residual cut

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a capacity function on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ with natural-number values, viewed as real capacities, and let $s \ne t$ be vertices. Let $S_0$ be the set of vertices reachable from $s$ in the residual graph of the flow computed by the Edmonds–Karp algorithm on $c$, $s$, $t$. Then for every $s$-$t$ cut $S$, the capacity of $S_0$ is at most the capacity of $S$.
nodes.title: No $s$-$t$ cut is smaller than the Edmonds–Karp residual cut

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a capacity function on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ with natural-number values, viewed as real capacities, and let $s \ne t$ be vertices. Then there is a natural-number valued function $f$ on pairs of vertices which, viewed as a real function, is a feasible $s$-$t$ flow for $c$ whose value is at least the value of every feasible real-valued $s$-$t$ flow for $c$.
nodes.title: Integral flow theorem
Gale–Shapley algorithm

nodes.summary: A permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, read as a ranking ($\sigma(k)$ is the $k$-th choice, $\sigma(0)$ the best), gives the strict total order on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which $a$ is preferred to $b$ when $\sigma^{-1}(a) < \sigma^{-1}(b)$.
nodes.title: Preference order of a ranking

nodes.summary: Given for each proposer $m$ a ranking $\sigma_m$ of the $n$ receivers ($\sigma_m(k)$ is the choice of $m$ of rank $k$, rank $0$ the best), the proposers' preference profile assigns to $m$ the strict total order in which $m$ prefers $w$ to $w'$ when $\sigma_m^{-1}(w) < \sigma_m^{-1}(w')$.
nodes.title: Proposers' preferences from rankings

nodes.summary: Given for each receiver $w$ a ranking $\sigma_w$ of the $n$ proposers (a permutation of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, with $\sigma_w(0)$ her first choice), the receivers' preference profile assigns to $w$ the preference order of $\sigma_w$: $w$ prefers $a$ to $b$ when $\sigma_w^{-1}(a) < \sigma_w^{-1}(b)$.
nodes.title: Receivers' preference profile from rankings

nodes.summary: A state of deferred acceptance with $n$ proposers and $n$ receivers, both numbered $0, \dots, n-1$, records for each proposer a natural number, the number of proposals he has made (his next proposal goes to his choice of that rank), and for each receiver either the proposer she currently holds or that she holds nobody.
nodes.title: Deferred-acceptance state

nodes.summary: The initial state with $n$ proposers and $n$ receivers: every proposer has made $0$ proposals and no receiver holds anyone.
nodes.title: Initial state of deferred acceptance

nodes.summary: A proposer $m$ is free in a state $s$ of deferred acceptance when no receiver holds $m$ in $s$.
nodes.title: Free proposer

nodes.summary: In a state $s$ of deferred acceptance, the proposer whom receiver $w$ holds after proposer $m$ proposes to her is $m$ if she holds nobody in $s$ or ranks $m$ strictly better than her current holder $m'$ in her ranking, and $m'$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Receiver's holder after a proposal

nodes.summary: Fix, for each proposer, a ranking of the $n$ receivers and, for each receiver, a ranking of the $n$ proposers (rank $0$ is the first choice). Let $s$ be a state of deferred acceptance in which proposer $m$ has made $k$ proposals. If $k < n$, then $m$ proposes to the receiver $w$ of rank $k$ in his ranking: his number of proposals becomes $k + 1$, and $w$ now holds $m$ if she held nobody or ranks $m$ strictly above…
nodes.title: A proposal

nodes.summary: In a state $s$ of deferred acceptance with proposers $0, 1, \dots, n-1$, the chooser returns the least proposer $m$ who is free in $s$ and has made fewer than $n$ proposals in $s$, or no proposer if there is none.
nodes.title: Choosing the next proposer

nodes.summary: Fix rankings for $n$ proposers and $n$ receivers, both numbered $0, \dots, n-1$. Starting from a state $s$ with a budget of $f$ proposals: if $f = 0$, or if no proposer is both free (held by no receiver) and has made fewer than $n$ proposals, the run returns $s$; otherwise the lowest-numbered such proposer makes a proposal, and the run continues from the resulting state with budget $f - 1$.
nodes.title: Running deferred acceptance

nodes.summary: Let each of $n$ proposers rank the $n$ receivers, and each receiver rank the $n$ proposers, with rank $0$ the best. Deferred acceptance is the state reached from the initial state, in which no one has proposed and no receiver holds anyone, by repeating the following step at most $n^2$ times, stopping early once no proposer is both free and has made fewer than $n$ proposals: the least such proposer, having made $p$…
nodes.title: Deferred acceptance

nodes.summary: Let each proposer $m$ have a ranking $\sigma_m$ of the $n$ receivers and each receiver $w$ a ranking $\tau_w$ of the $n$ proposers, where $\sigma_m(k)$ is the choice of $m$ of rank $k$ (rank $0$ is the best) and $\tau_w^{-1}(x)$ is the rank of $x$ for $w$. A state $s$ of deferred acceptance satisfies the invariant when: every proposer has made at most $n$ proposals; if $w$ holds $m$, then $m$ has made $k + 1$…
nodes.title: Invariant of deferred acceptance

nodes.summary: Let each proposer $m$ have a ranking $\sigma_m$ of the $n$ receivers and each receiver $w$ a ranking $\tau_w$ of the $n$ proposers, where $\sigma_m^{-1}(x)$ and $\tau_w^{-1}(x)$ are ranks ($0$ the best). If $\nu$ is a perfect matching that is stable for the preferences given by these rankings, there are no proposer $m$ and receiver $w$ with $\sigma_m^{-1}(w) < \sigma_m^{-1}(\nu(m))$ and…
nodes.title: A stable matching has no blocking pair

nodes.summary: Let each proposer $m$ have a ranking $\sigma_m$ of the $n$ receivers ($\sigma_m(k)$ is the choice of $m$ of rank $k$, rank $0$ the best), and each receiver a ranking of the $n$ proposers. Let $s$ be a state of deferred acceptance satisfying the invariant, let $\nu$ be a perfect matching that is stable for the preferences given by the rankings, let $m$ be a proposer, and let $b$ be a natural number at most the…
nodes.title: Rejected proposals bound stable partners

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a state of deferred acceptance, $m$ a proposer and $w$ a receiver with ranking $\tau_w$ of the proposers ($\tau_w^{-1}(x)$ is the rank of $x$, rank $0$ the best). Then one of the following holds: $w$ holds nobody in $s$ and holds $m$ after $m$ proposes to her; or $w$ holds some $y$ in $s$ with $\tau_w^{-1}(m) < \tau_w^{-1}(y)$ and holds $m$ after $m$ proposes to her; or $w$ holds some $y$ in $s$ with…
nodes.title: Cases of the receiver's new holder

nodes.summary: For a state $s$ of deferred acceptance with $n$ proposers and $n$ receivers, in which each proposer $m$ has made $k_m$ proposals, the number of proposals still available is $\sum_{m} \max(n - k_m, 0)$, the sum running over all $n$ proposers.
nodes.title: Remaining proposals

nodes.summary: Fix rankings for $n$ proposers and $n$ receivers. If proposer $m$ has made fewer than $n$ proposals in a state $s$ of deferred acceptance, then after $m$ proposes, the total number of proposals made by all proposers is one more than in $s$.
nodes.title: A proposal adds one to the proposal count

nodes.summary: For any rankings of the $n$ receivers by each of the $n$ proposers and of the proposers by each receiver, in the final state of deferred acceptance the numbers of proposals made by the proposers sum to at most $n \cdot n$.
nodes.title: Deferred acceptance makes at most n² proposals

nodes.summary: Fix rankings of the $n$ receivers by each of $n$ proposers and of the proposers by each receiver. Let $s$ be a state of deferred acceptance that satisfies the invariant of deferred acceptance for these rankings, and suppose that no proposer is both free in $s$ and has made fewer than $n$ proposals in $s$. Then every proposer is held by some receiver in $s$.
nodes.title: When deferred acceptance stops, every proposer is held

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a state of deferred acceptance with $n$ proposers and $n$ receivers. If every proposer is held by some receiver in $s$, then every receiver holds some proposer in $s$.
nodes.title: Every receiver holds someone once every proposer is held

nodes.summary: In a state $s$ of deferred acceptance with $n$ proposers and $n$ receivers, both numbered $0, \dots, n-1$, the partner of a receiver $w$ is the proposer she holds in $s$; if she holds nobody, it is the proposer numbered $w$ (a default value).
nodes.title: Receiver's partner

nodes.summary: In a state $s$ of deferred acceptance with $n$ proposers and $n$ receivers, both numbered $0, \dots, n-1$, the partner of a proposer $m$ is the lowest-numbered receiver that holds $m$ in $s$; if no receiver holds $m$, it is the receiver numbered $m$ (a default value).
nodes.title: Proposer's partner

nodes.summary: Each proposer with the receiver who holds him at the end.
nodes.title: The Gale-Shapley matching

nodes.summary: Let each proposer $m$ rank the $n$ receivers by a permutation $\sigma_m$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, where $\sigma_m(k)$ is his choice of rank $k$, let each receiver rank the $n$ proposers, and let $p_m$ be the number of proposals $m$ has made in the final state of deferred acceptance. Then $p_m \ge 1$, and the Gale-Shapley partner $\mu(m)$ of $m$ has rank $p_m - 1$ in his ranking, that is,…
nodes.title: A proposer's final partner is his last proposal

nodes.summary: For $n$ proposers and $n$ receivers, each with a ranking of the other side, the perfect matching computed by deferred acceptance is stable for the strict preferences given by these rankings.
nodes.title: The Gale-Shapley matching is stable

nodes.summary: No stable matching gives a proposer a partner he prefers to his Gale-Shapley partner.
nodes.title: Proposer-optimality

nodes.summary: No stable matching gives a receiver a partner she likes less than her Gale-Shapley partner.
nodes.title: Receiver-pessimality

nodes.summary: For a strict total order $<$ on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the rank of an element $a$ is the number of elements $b$ with $b < a$ (the elements preferred to $a$), as an element of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$.
nodes.title: Rank under a strict total order

reading_title.source: Every strict total order on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is given by a ranking

nodes.summary: For every strict total order $\prec$ on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ there is a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ such that, for all $a$ and $b$, $a \prec b$ holds exactly when $\sigma^{-1}(a) < \sigma^{-1}(b)$.

nodes.summary: Let the $n$ proposers and the $n$ receivers both be numbered $0, \dots, n-1$. Let each proposer $m$ have a strict total order $\lt _m$ of preference on the receivers and each receiver $w$ a strict total order $\lt _w$ of preference on the proposers, where $x \lt _m y$ means that $m$ prefers $x$ to $y$, and likewise for $\lt _w$. Then there are permutations $\sigma_m$ (one for each proposer $m$) and $\tau_w$ (one…

Kruskal's algorithm

nodes.summary: A raw edge is an undirected weighted input edge given by three natural numbers: two endpoints, which are not yet checked to be vertices of the graph, and a weight.
nodes.title: Raw input edge

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, an input graph on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ consists of a list of raw edges, kept in input order; the same pair of endpoints may occur on several edges.
nodes.title: Kruskal input graph

nodes.summary: A weighted edge on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ consists of an ordinal, a natural number recording its zero-based position in the original input list, two endpoints in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, and a natural-number weight.
nodes.title: Weighted edge

nodes.summary: The sorting key of a weighted edge $e$ is the pair $(w(e), i(e)) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ of its weight $w(e)$ and its input ordinal $i(e)$, the zero-based position of $e$ in the original input edge list.
nodes.title: Sorting key of a weighted edge

nodes.summary: For pairs of natural numbers $(w, i)$ and $(w', i')$, $(w, i) \preceq (w', i')$ holds when $w < w'$, or $w = w'$ and $i \le i'$. This is the non-strict lexicographic order on $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$; Kruskal's algorithm applies it to keys (weight, input ordinal).
nodes.title: Lexicographic order on edge keys

nodes.summary: Given natural numbers $n$ and $i$ and a raw edge with source $s$, target $t$ and weight $w$, decoding at ordinal $i$ returns the validated edge on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with ordinal $i$, source $s$, target $t$ and weight $w$ when $s < n$ and $t < n$, and returns no edge otherwise.
nodes.title: Decoding a raw edge at an ordinal

nodes.summary: Given $n$, a starting ordinal $o$ and a list of raw edges $e_0, e_1, \dots, e_{m-1}$, this returns, in input order, the weighted edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ obtained from those $e_k$ whose two endpoints are both less than $n$; each keeps the endpoints and weight of $e_k$ and carries the ordinal $o + k$. Edges with an endpoint at least $n$ are omitted, but they still count towards the ordinals of later…
nodes.title: Validating an edge list from a given ordinal

nodes.summary: For a graph $G$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ given by its list of raw edges $e_0, e_1, \dots, e_{m-1}$, the valid edges of $G$ are, in input order, the weighted edges obtained from those $e_k$ whose two endpoints are both less than $n$; each keeps the endpoints and weight of $e_k$ and carries its zero-based input ordinal $k$. Edges with an endpoint at least $n$ are omitted.
nodes.title: Valid edges of an input graph

nodes.summary: Sorting a list of validated edges is merge sort with the comparison $(w, i) \preceq (w', i')$ if $w < w'$, or $w = w'$ and $i \le i'$, applied to the pairs (weight, input position) of the edges.
nodes.title: Sorting edges by weight and input position

nodes.summary: For a finite weighted multigraph $G$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the ordered edges of $G$ are its valid input edges (those whose endpoints are both less than $n$), sorted by merge sort in lexicographic order of (weight, input position): by nondecreasing weight, with edges of equal weight in input order.
nodes.title: Valid edges in Kruskal order

nodes.summary: The initial forest on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is the parent forest in which every vertex is its own parent, so every vertex is a root, and whose depth certificate is $0$ at every vertex.
nodes.title: Discrete parent forest

nodes.summary: Connectivity of vertices $u$ and $v$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ by a list of validated edges, read newest first, is defined by recursion on the list. By the empty list, $u$ and $v$ are connected exactly when $u = v$. By a list whose first edge $e$ has source $a$ and target $b$ and whose remaining edges form the list $L$, the vertices $u$ and $v$ are connected when $u$ and $v$ are connected by $L$, or $u$ is connected…
nodes.title: Connectivity by a newest-first edge list

nodes.summary: Vertices $u$ and $v$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ are connected by a list $e_1, \dots, e_k$ of validated edges when they are connected by the reversed list $e_k, \dots, e_1$ in the sense of connectivity by a newest-first edge list.
nodes.title: Connectivity by an edge list

nodes.summary: A list $e_1, \dots, e_k$ of validated edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, read newest first, is newest-first acyclic when, for every $i$, the endpoints of $e_i$ are not connected by the later list $e_{i+1}, \dots, e_k$ in the sense of connectivity by a newest-first edge list.
nodes.title: Acyclicity of a newest-first edge list

nodes.summary: A list $e_1, \dots, e_k$ of validated edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is acyclic when, for every $i$, the endpoints of $e_i$ are not connected by the preceding edges $e_1, \dots, e_{i-1}$, in the sense of connectivity by an edge list.
nodes.title: Acyclic edge list

nodes.summary: A list $L$ of validated edges spans a finite weighted multigraph $G$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ when, for every valid input edge of $G$ (one whose endpoints are both less than $n$), the two endpoints of that edge are connected using the edges of $L$.
nodes.title: Edge lists spanning a graph

nodes.summary: For an input graph $G$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, a list $F$ of validated edges is a spanning forest of $G$ when every edge of $F$ is a valid edge of $G$, $F$ is acyclic, and $F$ spans $G$: for every valid edge of $G$, its endpoints are connected by $F$.
nodes.title: Spanning forest of an input graph

nodes.summary: For an input graph $G$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, a list $e_1, \dots, e_k$ of validated edges is an ordered spanning forest of $G$ when it is a spanning forest of $G$ and its keys are nondecreasing: for all $i < j$, the key of $e_i$ is at most the key of $e_j$, where the key of an edge with weight $w$ and input ordinal $o$ is the pair $(w, o)$ and keys are compared lexicographically.
nodes.title: Ordered spanning forest

nodes.summary: The total weight of a list of validated edges is the sum of the weights of its entries, each entry counted once, so parallel edges and repeated entries each contribute their weight.
nodes.title: Total weight of a Kruskal edge list

nodes.summary: A state of the Kruskal scan on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ consists of a union-find parent forest on these vertices, which records the current partition, and the list of edges accepted so far, newest first.
nodes.title: Kruskal scan state

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a Kruskal scan state and $e$ a validated edge with endpoints $u$ and $v$. If $u$ and $v$ are equivalent in the union-find forest of $s$, processing $e$ leaves $s$ unchanged. Otherwise $e$ is accepted: the new forest is the union of $u$ and $v$ in the forest of $s$, and $e$ is put at the front of the list of accepted edges.
nodes.title: One Kruskal step

nodes.summary: Starting from a Kruskal scan state $s$, scanning a list of validated edges $e_1, \dots, e_k$ applies one Kruskal step to each edge in list order: the scan of the empty list returns $s$, and the scan of $e_1, \dots, e_k$ is the scan of $e_2, \dots, e_k$ from the state obtained by processing $e_1$ in $s$.
nodes.title: Scanning a list of edges

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an input graph on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, give each valid edge with weight $w$ and input ordinal $o$ the key $(w, o)$, and compare keys lexicographically. The graph $G$ has the greedy cut property when the following holds for every way of splitting the valid edges of $G$, sorted by key, into an initial segment, an edge $e$ and a final segment. Let $P$ be the union-find partition obtained by…
nodes.title: Greedy cut property of Kruskal's scan

nodes.summary: For a finite weighted multigraph $G$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, Kruskal's algorithm starts from the partition of the vertices into singletons and processes the valid input edges of $G$ (those whose endpoints are both less than $n$) in lexicographic order of (weight, input position). An edge whose endpoints lie in different classes of the current partition is accepted and its two classes are merged; an…
nodes.title: Kruskal's algorithm

nodes.summary: For every graph $G$ on $n$ vertices, every edge in the list returned by Kruskal's algorithm on $G$ is a valid edge of $G$: an input edge whose two endpoints are both below $n$, carrying its input ordinal.
nodes.title: Kruskal selects only valid input edges

nodes.summary: For every graph $G$, the edge list returned by Kruskal's algorithm on $G$ is acyclic: each edge in it joins two vertices that are not connected by the edges before it in the list.
nodes.title: Kruskal's output is acyclic

nodes.summary: For every finite weighted multigraph $G$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, given by its list of input edges, and every valid input edge of $G$ (one whose endpoints are both less than $n$), the two endpoints of that edge are connected by the edges that Kruskal's algorithm selects on $G$.
nodes.title: Kruskal's selected edges span the graph

nodes.summary: For every graph $G$, if an edge $e$ comes before an edge $f$ in the list returned by Kruskal's algorithm on $G$, then $e$ has smaller weight than $f$, or the same weight as $f$ and input ordinal at most that of $f$.

Bisimulation

nodes.summary: Let $s$ and $t$ be bisimilar states of a labelled transition system, and suppose $s$ reaches a state $s'$ by a multistep transition along a finite (possibly empty) list of labels $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_n$. Then there is a state $t'$ such that $t$ reaches $t'$ by a multistep transition along the same list of labels, and $s'$ and $t'$ are bisimilar.
nodes.title: Bisimilarity transfers multistep transitions

nodes.summary: Let $s$ and $t$ be bisimilar states of a labelled transition system. Then for every label $\mu$, $s$ has a transition labelled $\mu$ if and only if $t$ has a transition labelled $\mu$.
nodes.title: Bisimilar states enable the same labels

nodes.summary: Let $s$ and $t$ be bisimilar states of a labelled transition system. Then the set of labels $\mu$ for which $s$ has a transition labelled $\mu$ equals the set of labels $\mu$ for which $t$ has a transition labelled $\mu$.
nodes.title: Bisimilar states have equal sets of outgoing labels

Calculus of communicating systems

nodes.summary: For a type $A$ of actions, the finite CCS processes over $A$ are built from the inactive process $\mathbf{0}$ by action prefix $a.P$ (an action $a \in A$ followed by a process $P$), nondeterministic choice $P + Q$, and parallel composition $P \mid Q$.
nodes.title: Finite CCS processes

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a partial function that assigns to some pairs of actions $(a, b)$ an action $\sigma(a, b)$. The transition relation $P \xrightarrow{a} P'$ on finite CCS processes (built from prefix $a.P$, choice $P + Q$ and parallel composition $P \mid Q$) determined by $\sigma$ is the least relation such that $a.P \xrightarrow{a} P$; if $P \xrightarrow{a} P'$ then $P + Q \xrightarrow{a} P'$,…
nodes.title: Operational semantics of finite CCS with a synchronization function

nodes.summary: The transition relation $P \xrightarrow{a} P'$ on finite CCS processes is the operational semantics of finite CCS whose synchronization function is undefined on every pair of actions. Thus prefix and choice move as usual, and a parallel composition $P \mid Q$ moves only by letting one of $P$ and $Q$ move; there are no communication steps.
nodes.title: Transitions of finite CCS without communication

nodes.summary: The labelled transition system whose states are the finite CCS processes, whose labels are the actions, and whose transitions $P \xrightarrow{a} P'$ are those of the communication-free operational semantics of finite CCS.
nodes.title: Labelled transition system of finite CCS

nodes.summary: Given relations $R$ and $S$ on finite CCS processes, write $P_1 + P_2$ for the nondeterministic choice of $P_1$ and $P_2$. The choice lift of $R$ and $S$ relates $P$ to $Q$ exactly when $R(P, Q)$ holds, or $S(P, Q)$ holds, or $P = P_1 + P_2$ and $Q = Q_1 + Q_2$ with $R(P_1, Q_1)$ and $S(P_2, Q_2)$.
nodes.title: Lifting relations through choice

nodes.summary: For every action $a$ and all finite CCS processes $P$ and $Q$, if $P$ and $Q$ are strongly bisimilar in the labelled transition system of finite CCS, then the prefixed processes $a.P$ and $a.Q$ are strongly bisimilar there as well.
nodes.title: Prefix preserves strong bisimilarity

nodes.summary: Given a relation $E$ on finite CCS processes, its equation closure relates $P$ to $Q$ exactly when $P = Q$ or $E(P, Q)$; that is, it is the reflexive closure of $E$.
nodes.title: Reflexive closure of a relation on processes

nodes.summary: For a set of names, a CCS label is either the silent action $\tau$, the input on a name $a$, or the output on a name $a$.
nodes.title: CCS labels

nodes.summary: Two CCS labels are complementary when one is the input on a name $a$ and the other is the output on the same name $a$, in either order. No other pair of labels is complementary; in particular the silent label $\tau$ has no complement.
nodes.title: Complementary labels

nodes.summary: Let the names form a type with decidable equality. For labels $a$ and $b$, the synchronization of $a$ with $b$ is the silent action $\tau$ when $a$ is the input on a name $n$ and $b$ is the output on the same name $n$, or when $a$ is the output on $n$ and $b$ is the input on $n$. For every other pair of labels, including any pair involving $\tau$, there is no result.
nodes.title: Synchronization of CCS labels

nodes.summary: The transition relation on CCS processes with labels over a set of names given by the raw step relation for the synchronization function under which an input and an output on the same name, in either order, synchronize to the silent label $\tau$, and no other pair of labels synchronizes.
nodes.title: CCS transition relation with communication

nodes.summary: The labelled transition system whose states are CCS processes with labels over a set of names, whose labels are CCS labels over those names, and whose transition relation is the CCS transition relation with communication.
nodes.title: Labelled transition system of CCS with communication

nodes.summary: For CCS processes $P$, $Q$, $R$ and a CCS label $a$, the parallel composition $P \mid Q$ has a transition labelled $a$ to $R$ in the CCS transition relation with communication if and only if one of the following holds: $P$ has a transition labelled $a$ to some $P'$ and $R = P' \mid Q$; or $Q$ has a transition labelled $a$ to some $Q'$ and $R = P \mid Q'$; or $a = \tau$ and there are processes $P'$, $Q'$ and…
nodes.title: Transitions of a parallel composition

nodes.summary: Given two relations $R$ and $S$ on CCS processes with labels over a set of names, their parallel lift relates a process $U$ to a process $V$ exactly when $R$ relates $U$ to $V$, or $S$ relates $U$ to $V$, or $U = P_1 \mid Q_1$ and $V = P_2 \mid Q_2$ where $R$ relates $P_1$ to $P_2$ and $S$ relates $Q_1$ to $Q_2$.
nodes.title: Parallel lift of two relations

nodes.summary: For CCS processes $P_1$, $P_2$, $Q_1$, $Q_2$ with labels over a set of names: if $P_1$ and $P_2$ are strongly bisimilar and $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ are strongly bisimilar in the labelled transition system of CCS with communication, then the parallel compositions $P_1 \mid Q_1$ and $P_2 \mid Q_2$ are strongly bisimilar there.
nodes.title: Parallel composition preserves strong bisimilarity

nodes.summary: For every CCS label $a$ and all CCS processes $P$ and $Q$: if $P$ and $Q$ are strongly bisimilar in the labelled transition system of CCS with communication, then so are the prefixed processes $a.P$ and $a.Q$.
nodes.title: Prefix preserves strong bisimilarity in CCS with communication

nodes.summary: For CCS processes $P_1$, $P_2$, $Q_1$, $Q_2$ with labels over a set of names: if $P_1$ and $P_2$ are strongly bisimilar and $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ are strongly bisimilar in the labelled transition system of CCS with communication, then the choices $P_1 + Q_1$ and $P_2 + Q_2$ are strongly bisimilar there.
nodes.title: Choice preserves strong bisimilarity in CCS with communication

nodes.summary: For all CCS processes $P$ and $Q$ with labels over a set of names, $P \mid Q$ and $Q \mid P$ are strongly bisimilar in the labelled transition system of CCS with communication.
nodes.title: Parallel composition is commutative up to strong bisimilarity

nodes.summary: Let the names form a type with decidable equality. For every CCS process $P$ over input, output and silent labels on these names, the parallel composition $0 \mid P$ of the inactive process $0$ with $P$ is strongly bisimilar to $P$ in the communication labelled transition system.
nodes.title: The inactive process is a left unit for parallel composition

nodes.summary: Let the names form a type with decidable equality. For every CCS process $P$ over input, output and silent labels on these names, the parallel composition $P \mid 0$ of $P$ with the inactive process $0$ is strongly bisimilar to $P$ in the communication labelled transition system.
nodes.title: The inactive process is a right unit for parallel composition

nodes.summary: A visible CCS label, excluding the silent action.
nodes.title: Visible CCS label

nodes.summary: The complement of the input label on a channel $a$ is the output label on $a$, and the complement of the output label on $a$ is the input label on $a$.
nodes.title: Complement of a visible label

nodes.summary: The inclusion of visible labels into CCS labels sends the input on a channel $a$ to the input on $a$, and the output on $a$ to the output on $a$.
nodes.title: Visible labels as CCS labels

nodes.summary: A finite CCS relabelling over channel names is a finite list of entries $(a, \ell)$, each pairing a channel name $a$ with a visible label $\ell$, that is, an input or an output on some channel. The entry $(a, \ell)$ gives $\ell$ as the image of the input on $a$; the image of the output on $a$ is then the complement of $\ell$. The first entry with name $a$ is used, and a name occurring in no entry is mapped to itself.
nodes.title: Relabelling

nodes.summary: Let $f$ be a finite relabelling whose table lists the entries $(a_1, \ell_1), \dots, (a_k, \ell_k)$, where each $a_i$ is a channel name and each $\ell_i$ a visible label. The image of a channel name $a$ under $f$ is $\ell_i$ for the first index $i$ with $a_i = a$, and the input label on $a$ when no entry has name $a$.
nodes.title: Applying a relabelling to a channel name

nodes.summary: Finite CCS processes with the static operators, over a type of channel names, are built from the inactive process $0$ by the prefix $\alpha.P$ of a CCS action $\alpha$ (silent, an input or an output) and a process $P$, the choice $P + Q$, the parallel composition $P \mid Q$, the restriction $P \setminus L$ of $P$ by a finite list $L$ of names, and the relabelling $P[f]$ of $P$ by a finite relabelling $f$.
nodes.title: Static CCS processes

nodes.summary: Each finite CCS process over CCS labels is sent to the process with static operators of the same shape: the inactive process goes to the inactive process, the prefix of an action $\alpha$ to a process $P$ goes to the prefix of $\alpha$ to the image of $P$, and a choice or a parallel composition of $P$ and $Q$ goes to the choice or the parallel composition of the images of $P$ and $Q$.
nodes.title: Embedding finite CCS into CCS with static operators

nodes.summary: For a relabelling $f$, the silent action $\tau$ is relabelled to $\tau$, an input on a channel $a$ is relabelled to the image of $a$ under $f$, and an output on $a$ is relabelled to the complement of the image of $a$ under $f$, each viewed as a CCS label.
nodes.title: Relabelling an action

nodes.summary: For every relabelling $f$ and all CCS labels $\alpha$ and $\beta$, if $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are complementary, then the actions obtained by relabelling $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with $f$ are complementary.
nodes.title: Relabelling preserves complementary actions

nodes.summary: Given a finite list $L$ of blocked channel names, the silent action $\tau$ is always permitted, and an input or an output on a channel $a$ is permitted exactly when $a \notin L$.
nodes.title: Actions permitted by a restriction

nodes.summary: The labelled transition relation $P \xrightarrow{\alpha} P'$ on static CCS processes, with actions $\alpha$ the CCS labels (silent $\tau$, inputs and outputs), is the least relation closed under the following rules, where $\alpha.P$ is the prefix, $P + Q$ the choice, $P \mid Q$ the parallel composition, $P \setminus L$ the restriction of $P$ by a finite list $L$ of channel names, and $P[f]$ the relabelling of $P$…
nodes.title: Transitions of static CCS

nodes.summary: The labelled transition system of finite CCS with static operators has the finite CCS processes with restriction and relabelling as states and the CCS labels as labels, and its transitions are the steps of the structural operational semantics of these processes.
nodes.title: Transition system of CCS with restriction and relabelling

nodes.summary: Given a finite list $L$ of channel names and a relation $R$ on static CCS processes, the lifted relation relates $P$ to $Q$ exactly when either $R$ relates $P$ to $Q$, or $P = P' \setminus L$ and $Q = Q' \setminus L$ for some processes $P'$ and $Q'$ that $R$ relates.
nodes.title: Lifting a relation through a restriction

nodes.summary: For every finite list $L$ of channel names and all static CCS processes $P$ and $Q$, if $P$ and $Q$ are strongly bisimilar in the labelled transition system of finite CCS with static operators, then so are the restricted processes $P \setminus L$ and $Q \setminus L$.
nodes.title: Restriction preserves strong bisimilarity

nodes.summary: Given a relabelling $f$ and a relation $R$ on finite CCS processes with static operators, the lifted relation is the least relation that relates $P$ to $Q$ and relates the relabelling of $P$ by $f$ to the relabelling of $Q$ by $f$ whenever $R$ relates $P$ to $Q$.
nodes.title: Closure of a relation under one relabelling

nodes.summary: For every relabelling $f$ and all finite CCS processes $P$ and $Q$ with static operators, if $P$ and $Q$ are strongly bisimilar in the labelled transition system of finite CCS with static operators, then the relabellings of $P$ and of $Q$ by $f$ are strongly bisimilar there.
nodes.title: Relabelling preserves strong bisimilarity

nodes.summary: Given a set of names and a set of process constants, the recursive CCS processes are generated by the following constructors: the inactive process $\mathbf{0}$; a process constant $A$; a prefix $\alpha.P$ for a CCS label $\alpha$ and a process $P$; a choice $P + Q$; a parallel composition $P \mid Q$; a restriction $P \setminus L$ for a finite list $L$ of names; and a relabelling $P[f]$ for a CCS relabelling $f$.
nodes.title: Recursive CCS processes

nodes.summary: Given a type of channel names and a type of process constants, a recursive specification assigns to each process constant $A$ a defining body: a CCS process expression over those names, which may itself mention process constants (including $A$).
nodes.title: Recursive CCS specification

nodes.summary: Let the channel names have decidable equality and let $\Delta$ be a recursive specification, assigning to each process constant $A$ its defining body $\Delta(A)$. The labelled transition relation $P \xrightarrow{\alpha} P'$ relative to $\Delta$ on recursive CCS processes, with actions $\alpha$ the CCS labels (silent $\tau$, inputs and outputs), is the least relation closed under the following rules, where…
nodes.title: Transitions of recursive CCS

nodes.summary: Assuming equality of names is decidable, for a recursive specification $\Delta$ the labelled transition system generated by $\Delta$ has the recursive CCS processes as states and the CCS labels as labels, and its transitions $P \xrightarrow{\alpha} P'$ are exactly the steps of the structural operational semantics relative to $\Delta$.
nodes.title: Labelled transition system of a recursive specification

nodes.title: Guardedness under a prefix flag

nodes.summary: A recursive CCS process is guarded when all of its constant occurrences lie beneath an action prefix.
nodes.title: Guarded process

nodes.summary: Every recursive CCS process $P$ is guarded under the flag $\mathrm{true}$: once an action prefix has been crossed, every constant occurrence counts as guarded.
nodes.title: Every process is guarded beneath a prefix

nodes.summary: The constant occurrences of a recursive CCS process $P$ are the list of the process constants occurring in $P$, from left to right and with repetitions: the inactive process $\mathbf{0}$ has none; a constant $A$ has the single occurrence $A$; a prefix $\alpha.Q$, a restriction $Q \setminus L$ and a relabelling $Q[f]$ have the occurrences of $Q$; and a choice $Q + R$ or a parallel composition $Q \mid R$ has the…
nodes.title: Constant occurrences of a process

nodes.summary: Assuming equality of process constants is decidable, the constants of a recursive CCS process $P$ are the list obtained from the constant occurrences of $P$ by removing duplicates, so that every process constant occurring in $P$ appears in it exactly once.
nodes.title: Constants of a process

nodes.summary: Given a map $\rho$ from one set of process constants to another, renaming the constants of a recursive CCS process $P$ by $\rho$ replaces each occurrence of a constant $A$ by $\rho(A)$ and leaves $P$ otherwise unchanged: the inactive process, prefixes, choices, parallel compositions, restrictions and relabellings are kept as they are.
nodes.title: Renaming process constants

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a recursive CCS process, let $\rho$ be a map from its process constants to another set of constants, and let $P\rho$ be the process obtained from $P$ by renaming its constants by $\rho$. Then for each Boolean flag $b$, $P\rho$ is guarded under $b$ if and only if $P$ is guarded under $b$.
nodes.title: Renaming constants preserves guardedness

nodes.summary: A recursive specification $\Delta$, which assigns to each process constant $A$ a body $\Delta(A)$, is guarded when for every constant $A$ the body $\Delta(A)$ is a guarded process.
nodes.title: Guarded recursive specification
Labelled transition systems

nodes.summary: In a labelled transition system, say that a state $s$ can reach a state $t$ when there is a finite list of labels along which $s$ makes a multistep transition to $t$. If $s$ can reach $m$ and $m$ can reach $t$, then $s$ can reach $t$.
nodes.title: Reachability in a labelled transition system is transitive

nodes.summary: For a sequence $s_0, s_1, s_2, \dots$ and a natural number $k$, the shift of the sequence by $k$ is the sequence whose $i$-th term is $s_{i+k}$; that is, the suffix starting at index $k$, re-indexed from $0$.
nodes.title: Shifted sequence

nodes.summary: In a labelled transition system, a sequence of states $s_0, s_1, s_2, \dots$ is a finite run of length $k$ when for every $i < k$ there is a label $a$ such that there is a transition from $s_i$ to $s_{i+1}$ labelled $a$.
nodes.title: Finite run

nodes.summary: In a labelled transition system, a sequence of states $s_0, s_1, s_2, \dots$ is an infinite run when for every $i$ there is a label $a$ such that there is a transition from $s_i$ to $s_{i+1}$ labelled $a$.
nodes.title: Infinite run

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a predicate on the states of a labelled transition system such that, whenever $P(s)$ holds and there is a transition from $s$ to $t$ with some label, $P(t)$ holds. Then for every infinite run $s_0, s_1, s_2, \dots$ with $P(s_0)$, the predicate $P(s_k)$ holds for every $k$.
nodes.title: Invariant principle for infinite runs

nodes.summary: Select a witnessing label at each step of an infinite state run.
nodes.title: Infinite state runs lift to labeled executions

nodes.summary: Forget the labels of a canonical infinite execution.
nodes.title: Labeled infinite executions give state runs

Observational congruence

nodes.summary: In a labelled transition system whose labels include a silent label $\tau$, there is a rooted weak transition from $s$ to $t$ with label $\mu$ when there are states $s_1$ and $s_2$ such that $s$ reaches $s_1$ by zero or more $\tau$-transitions, $s_1 \xrightarrow{\mu} s_2$ is a transition, and $s_2$ reaches $t$ by zero or more $\tau$-transitions. In particular, a rooted weak transition with label $\tau$ contains at…
nodes.title: Rooted weak transition

nodes.summary: In a labelled transition system with a silent label $\tau$, every transition $s \xrightarrow{\mu} t$ is a rooted weak transition from $s$ to $t$ with label $\mu$.
nodes.title: Transitions are rooted weak transitions

nodes.summary: In a labelled transition system with a silent label $\tau$, every rooted weak transition from $s$ to $t$ with label $\mu$ is a weak transition from $s$ to $t$ with label $\mu$, where a weak transition with label $\mu$ is either the trivial step from a state to itself with label $\tau$, or a transition with label $\mu$ preceded and followed by zero or more $\tau$-transitions.
nodes.title: Rooted weak transitions are weak transitions

nodes.summary: In a labelled transition system with a silent label $\tau$, if $s$ reaches $m$ by zero or more $\tau$-transitions and there is a rooted weak transition from $m$ to $t$ with label $\mu$, then there is a rooted weak transition from $s$ to $t$ with label $\mu$.
nodes.title: Silent steps before a rooted weak transition

nodes.summary: In a labelled transition system with silent action $\tau$, if there is a rooted weak transition from $s$ to $m$ with label $a$, and $t$ is reachable from $m$ by zero or more $\tau$-transitions, then there is a rooted weak transition from $s$ to $t$ with label $a$.
nodes.title: Appending silent steps to a rooted weak transition

nodes.summary: In a labelled transition system with a silent label $\tau$, if there is a rooted weak transition from $s$ to $m$ with label $\tau$ and a weak transition from $m$ to $t$ with label $\mu$, then there is a rooted weak transition from $s$ to $t$ with label $\mu$. Here a weak transition with label $\mu$ is either the trivial step from a state to itself with label $\tau$, or a transition with label $\mu$ preceded and…
nodes.title: A rooted silent step followed by a weak transition is rooted

nodes.summary: In a labelled transition system with a silent label $\tau$, states $p$ and $q$ are rooted weakly bisimilar (observation congruent) when every transition $p \xrightarrow{\mu} p'$ is matched by a rooted weak transition from $q$ to some $q'$ with label $\mu$ such that $p'$ and $q'$ are weakly bisimilar, and every transition $q \xrightarrow{\mu} q'$ is matched by a rooted weak transition from $p$ to some $p'$ with…
nodes.title: Rooted observation congruence

nodes.summary: In a labelled transition system with a silent label $\tau$, if $p$ and $q$ are rooted weakly bisimilar and there is a rooted weak transition from $p$ to $p'$ with label $\mu$, then there is a state $q'$ with a rooted weak transition from $q$ to $q'$ with label $\mu$ such that $p'$ and $q'$ are weakly bisimilar.
nodes.title: Observation congruence matches rooted weak transitions

nodes.summary: In a labelled transition system with silent action $\tau$, if $p$ is rooted observationally congruent to $q$ and $q$ is rooted observationally congruent to $r$, then $p$ is rooted observationally congruent to $r$.
nodes.title: Transitivity of rooted observational congruence

nodes.summary: In every labelled transition system with a silent label $\tau$, rooted weak bisimilarity (observation congruence) is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
nodes.title: Observation congruence is an equivalence relation

nodes.summary: In a labelled transition system with a silent label $\tau$, any two strongly bisimilar states are rooted weakly bisimilar.
nodes.title: Strong bisimilarity implies observation congruence

nodes.summary: In a labelled transition system with a silent label $\tau$, any two rooted weakly bisimilar states are weakly bisimilar.
nodes.title: Observation congruence implies weak bisimilarity
Finite-state CCS agents

nodes.summary: For a list $l$ of pairs $(a, q)$ of a label and a process, the process that chooses among the prefixes $a.q$ listed in $l$: the empty list gives the inactive process $\mathbf{0}$, and the list with head $(a, q)$ and tail $r$ gives the choice $a.q + P$ between the prefix $a.q$ and the process $P$ built in the same way from $r$.
nodes.title: Sum of prefixes

nodes.summary: For every recursive specification, every list $l$ of pairs of a label and a process, every label $a$ and every process $q$, the sum of the prefixes listed in $l$ has a transition labelled $a$ to $q$ exactly when $(a, q)$ belongs to $l$.
nodes.title: Transitions of a sum of prefixes

nodes.summary: Fix a recursive specification. A family of processes $P_x$ indexed by codes $x$ realizes a function $s$ that lists, for each code $x$, labelled transitions $(a, y)$ with $a$ a label and $y$ a code, when for every code $x$, every label $a$ and every process $q$, the process $P_x$ has a transition with label $a$ to $q$ exactly when $s(x)$ contains an entry $(a, y)$ with $P_y = q$.
nodes.title: Realization of a code-level transition system

nodes.summary: Fix a recursive specification, a map $\iota$ from codes to process constants and a function $s$ listing labelled transitions for each code. Suppose that for every code $x$, writing $(a_1, y_1), \dots, (a_n, y_n)$ for the entries of $s(x)$ in order, the body of the constant $\iota(x)$ is $a_1.\iota(y_1) + (a_2.\iota(y_2) + \dots + (a_n.\iota(y_n) + 0))$, which is $0$ when $n = 0$. Then the processes $\iota(x)$,…
nodes.title: Constants listing their transitions realize them

nodes.summary: Given functions $s$ and $t$ listing the labelled transitions of codes $x$ and $y$, the transitions of the pair $(x, y)$ are listed in three blocks: $(a, (x', y))$ for each entry $(a, x')$ of $s(x)$; then $(a, (x, y'))$ for each entry $(a, y')$ of $t(y)$; then $(\tau, (x', y'))$ for each entry $(a, x')$ of $s(x)$ and each entry $(b, y')$ of $t(y)$ whose labels are complementary, that is, one is the input and the…
nodes.title: Code-level parallel composition

nodes.summary: Fix a recursive specification. If the processes $P_x$ realize $s$ and the processes $Q_y$ realize $t$, then the parallel compositions $P_x \mid Q_y$, indexed by pairs $(x, y)$, realize the code-level parallel composition of $s$ and $t$.
nodes.title: Parallel composition preserves realization

nodes.summary: For a list $L$ of blocked names, the test returns true on a label exactly when the label is the silent action $\tau$, or an input or an output on a name that does not occur in $L$. It is the Boolean form of the condition that restriction by $L$ allows the label.
nodes.title: Boolean restriction test

nodes.summary: For a list $L$ of blocked names and a function $s$ listing the labelled transitions of each code, the restricted transitions of a code $x$ are the entries $(a, y)$ of $s(x)$, in order, whose label $a$ is the silent action $\tau$ or an input or an output on a name that does not occur in $L$.
nodes.title: Code-level restriction

nodes.summary: Fix a recursive specification and a list $L$ of blocked names. If the processes $P_x$ realize $s$, then the restricted processes $P_x \setminus L$ realize the code-level restriction of $s$ by $L$.
nodes.title: Restriction preserves realization

nodes.summary: Let $s$ list the labelled transitions $(a, x')$ of each implementation code $x$, let $t$ list those of each specification code $y$, and let $R$ be a finite list of code pairs. The forward check succeeds when for every pair $(x, y)$ in $R$ and every entry $(a, x')$ of $s(x)$, either $a = \tau$ and $(x', y)$ is in $R$, or some entry $(a, y')$ of $t(y)$ with the same label has $(x', y')$ in $R$.
nodes.title: Forward certificate check

nodes.summary: Let $s$ list the labelled transitions $(a, x')$ of each implementation code $x$, let $t$ list those of each specification code $y$, and let $R$ be a finite list of code pairs. The backward check succeeds when for every pair $(x, y)$ in $R$ and every entry $(a, y')$ of $t(y)$, at least one of the following holds: $a = \tau$ and $(x, y')$ is in $R$; some entry $(a, x')$ of $s(x)$ with the same label has $(x', y')$ in…
nodes.title: Backward certificate check

nodes.summary: For transition lists $s$ of implementation codes and $t$ of specification codes and a finite list $R$ of code pairs, the certificate check succeeds when both the forward check and the backward check succeed on $s$, $t$ and $R$.
nodes.title: Weak-bisimulation certificate check

nodes.summary: Let $f$ realize the code-level transition function $s$ and $g$ realize $t$ for a recursive specification, and let $R$ be a list of code pairs on which the certificate check of $s$, $t$ and $R$ succeeds. Then for every pair $(x, y)$ in $R$, the processes $f(x)$ and $g(y)$ are weakly bisimilar in the labelled transition system of the specification.
nodes.title: Certificate checks give weak bisimilarity

nodes.summary: Given code-level transition functions $s$ on codes $\alpha$ and $t$ on codes $\beta$, each listing labelled steps to codes, a relation $R$ given as a list of code pairs, and codes $x$ and $y$, the root check succeeds exactly when every listed step $(a, x')$ of $s(x)$ is matched by some listed step $(a, y')$ of $t(y)$ with the same label and $(x', y') \in R$, and every listed step $(a, y')$ of $t(y)$ is matched by…
nodes.title: Direct check of the root condition

nodes.summary: Let $f$ realize the code-level transition function $s$ and $g$ realize $t$ for a recursive specification, and let $R$ be a list of code pairs on which the certificate check of $s$, $t$ and $R$ succeeds. If the root check of $s$, $t$ and $R$ succeeds at codes $x$ and $y$, then the processes $f(x)$ and $g(y)$ are rooted weakly bisimilar (observation congruent) in the labelled transition system of the specification…
nodes.title: Certificate checks give rooted observation congruence
π-calculus
The π-calculus: syntax, substitution, structural congruence, reduction

nodes.summary: A channel name: a free channel `const n`, or the `i`-th enclosing binder `var i`.
nodes.title: Channel name in the π-calculus

nodes.summary: Processes of the π-calculus. `inp a p` binds variable `0` in `p`; `nu p` binds variable `0` in `p` as a fresh channel.
nodes.title: Processes of the π-calculus

nodes.summary: Shift free variables at or above `cutoff` up by one, e.g. when pushing a process under a binder.
nodes.title: Lifting free de Bruijn indices of a π-calculus name

nodes.summary: Shift free variables of a process, entering binders with an increased cutoff.
nodes.title: Lifting free de Bruijn indices of a π-calculus process

nodes.summary: Substitute the name `n` for the variable at `cutoff`: variables below the cutoff are bound by inner binders and untouched, the variable at the cutoff is replaced by `n`, and variables above shift down by one.
nodes.title: Substitution of a name into a π-calculus name

nodes.summary: Substitute the name `n` for the variable at `cutoff` in a process. Under a binder, `n` is lifted by one at cutoff `0` so it keeps referring to the same outer names: every free index of `n` refers to a binder above the substitution point, so all of them shift. Lifting at the current cutoff would leave indices below the cutoff captured by the new binder.
nodes.title: Substitution of a name into a π-calculus process at a cutoff

nodes.summary: Substitute the name `n` for the innermost bound variable of `p`.
nodes.title: Substitution for the innermost bound variable of a process

nodes.summary: Swap the two de Bruijn indices `cutoff` and `cutoff + 1` in a name: the two binders at that depth exchange places.
nodes.title: Swapping adjacent de Bruijn indices in a name

nodes.summary: Swap the two binders at depth `cutoff` throughout a process, incrementing the cutoff under binders.
nodes.title: Swapping adjacent binders throughout a process

nodes.summary: Substitution leaves a process with no `var 0` untouched: a constant channel stays constant, and the empty process stays empty.
nodes.title: Substitution leaves constant channels and the empty process unchanged

nodes.summary: Structural congruence: `|` is commutative and associative with unit `nil`, `ν` extrudes over `|` (lifting the other side, which cannot mention the fresh name), restriction of `nil` is `nil`, nested restrictions commute (swapping the two bound indices), and replication unfolds.
nodes.title: Structural congruence of π-calculus processes

nodes.summary: Guarded-choice resolution: discard sum branches to reach a guarded process. Transitivity handles nested sums.
nodes.title: Guarded-choice resolution in the π-calculus

nodes.summary: Reduction: communication (substituting the sent channel for the input variable) between any selected output and input guards, reduction under `|` and `ν`, and reduction up to structural congruence.
nodes.title: Reduction relation of the π-calculus

nodes.summary: Structural congruence preserves immediate barbs.
nodes.title: Structural congruence preserves immediate barbs

nodes.summary: Every structural law of `Basic` is sound for strong barbed bisimilarity, including scope extrusion and replication unfolding.
nodes.title: Structurally congruent processes are barbed bisimilar

nodes.summary: An output not behind a prefix, on any subject (including bound names). This is an overapproximation for arbitrary unguarded sums, not a barb.

nodes.summary: Structural rearrangement cannot expose an output from an input-guarded process. This includes arbitrary uses of replication and scope laws.
nodes.title: Structural congruence preserves unguarded outputs
