Operational semantics of the simply typed lambda calculus

nodes.summary: A term of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$ is a value exactly when it is a lambda abstraction.
nodes.title: Values of STLC

nodes.summary: One-step reduction on terms of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$ is the least relation closed under three left-to-right call-by-value rules: if $f$ reduces to $f'$, then the application $f\,a$ reduces to $f'\,a$; if $f$ is a value and $a$ reduces to $a'$, then $f\,a$ reduces to $f\,a'$; and if $a$ is a value, then the application of the abstraction of $b$ to $a$ reduces to $b[a]$, the result of substituting $a$ for…
nodes.title: Small-step call-by-value reduction in STLC

nodes.summary: If a term $t$ of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$ is a value, then there is no term $t'$ to which $t$ reduces in one call-by-value step.
nodes.title: Values are irreducible

nodes.summary: If a term $f$ of function type $A \Rightarrow B$ in the empty context is a value, then $f$ is a lambda abstraction: there is a term $b$ of type $B$ in the one-variable context $[A]$ such that $f$ is the abstraction of $b$.
nodes.title: Canonical forms for closed function values

nodes.summary: Every term $t$ of type $A$ in the empty context is either a value or reduces in one call-by-value step to some term $t'$.
nodes.title: Progress for closed STLC terms

nodes.summary: For terms $t$, $t_1$, $t_2$ of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$, if $t$ reduces in one call-by-value step both to $t_1$ and to $t_2$, then $t_1 = t_2$.
nodes.title: Small-step call-by-value reduction in STLC is deterministic

nodes.summary: A term $t$ of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$ is in normal form when there is no term $t'$ such that $t$ reduces to $t'$ in one call-by-value step.
nodes.title: Normal forms for call-by-value reduction in STLC

nodes.summary: A term $t$ of type $A$ in the empty context is in normal form, that is, has no call-by-value reduction step, if and only if it is a value.
nodes.title: Closed normal forms are exactly the values

nodes.summary: For terms of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$, multi-step reduction is the reflexive transitive closure of one-step call-by-value reduction.
nodes.title: Multi-step call-by-value reduction in STLC

nodes.summary: Fix a typing context $\Gamma$. For terms $t$ and $v$ of the same type in context $\Gamma$, the big-step evaluation relation $t \Downarrow v$ is the least relation such that every lambda abstraction $\lambda.\,b$ evaluates to itself, and an application $f\,a$ evaluates to $v$ whenever $f \Downarrow \lambda.\,b$, $a \Downarrow u$ and $b[u] \Downarrow v$, where $b[u]$ is the body $b$ with its newest free variable…
nodes.title: Big-step call-by-value evaluation in the simply typed lambda calculus

nodes.summary: In the call-by-value simply typed lambda calculus, if a term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ evaluates by big-step evaluation to a term $v$, written $t \Downarrow v$, then $v$ is a value, that is, a lambda abstraction.
nodes.title: Big-step evaluation produces values

nodes.summary: Every value $v$, that is, every lambda abstraction, of any type in any typing context evaluates to itself in the big-step semantics: $v \Downarrow v$.
nodes.title: Values evaluate to themselves

nodes.summary: Let $t$ and $v$ be terms of the same type in the same typing context. If $t$ evaluates to $v$ in the big-step semantics, written $t \Downarrow v$, then $t$ reduces to $v$ in finitely many (possibly zero) left-to-right call-by-value steps.
nodes.title: Big-step evaluation implies small-step evaluation

nodes.summary: Let $t$, $t'$ and $v$ be terms of the same type $A$ in the same typing context $\Gamma$. If $t$ reduces to $t'$ in one left-to-right call-by-value step and $t'$ evaluates to $v$ in the big-step semantics, written $t' \Downarrow v$, then $t \Downarrow v$.
nodes.title: Big-step evaluation is closed under backward reduction steps

nodes.summary: Let $t$, $t'$ and $v$ be terms of the same type $A$ in the same typing context $\Gamma$. If $t$ reduces to $t'$ in finitely many (possibly zero) left-to-right call-by-value steps and $t'$ evaluates to $v$ in the big-step semantics, written $t' \Downarrow v$, then $t \Downarrow v$.
nodes.title: Big-step evaluation is closed under backward multi-step reduction

nodes.summary: Let $t$ and $v$ be terms of the same type in the same typing context. If $t$ reduces to $v$ in finitely many (possibly zero) left-to-right call-by-value steps and $v$ is a value, then $t$ evaluates to $v$ in the big-step semantics, written $t \Downarrow v$.
nodes.title: Small-step evaluation to a value implies big-step evaluation

nodes.summary: For terms $t$ and $v$ of the same type in the same typing context, $t$ evaluates to $v$ in the big-step semantics, written $t \Downarrow v$, if and only if $t$ reduces to $v$ in finitely many (possibly zero) left-to-right call-by-value steps and $v$ is a value, that is, a lambda abstraction.
nodes.title: Big-step evaluation is small-step evaluation to a value

nodes.summary: For every typing context $\Gamma$ and type $A$, if a term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ evaluates in the big-step call-by-value semantics both to $v$ and to $w$, written $t \Downarrow v$ and $t \Downarrow w$, then $v = w$.
nodes.title: Determinism of big-step evaluation in the simply typed lambda calculus

nodes.summary: For every type $A$ and every closed term $t$ of type $A$, that is, a term in the empty typing context, there is a term $v$ such that $t$ evaluates to $v$ in the big-step call-by-value semantics, written $t \Downarrow v$.
nodes.title: Closed simply typed terms have a big-step evaluation

nodes.summary: For every closed term $t$ of type $A$, that is, a term in the empty typing context, $t$ terminates (it reduces to a value in finitely many left-to-right call-by-value steps) if and only if there is a term $v$ such that $t$ evaluates to $v$ in the big-step semantics, written $t \Downarrow v$.
nodes.title: Termination in terms of big-step evaluation
Denotational semantics of the simply typed lambda calculus

nodes.summary: Given an interpretation $I$ assigning a type $I(b)$ to each base type $b$, the denotation $[\![A]\!]_I$ of a simple type $A$ is defined by recursion on $A$: a base type $b$ denotes $I(b)$, and a function type $A \Rightarrow B$ denotes the type of all functions from $[\![A]\!]_I$ to $[\![B]\!]_I$.
nodes.title: Denotation of simple types

nodes.summary: Given an interpretation $I$ assigning a type to each base type and a typing context $\Gamma$ (a list of simple types), an environment for $\Gamma$ assigns to every variable $x$ of $\Gamma$, of any simple type $A$, an element of the denotation $[\![A]\!]_I$.
nodes.title: Semantic environments for the denotational semantics of STLC

nodes.summary: Given an interpretation $I$ of the base types, a value $a$ in the denotation of a type $A$ and an environment $\eta$ for a context $\Gamma$, the extended environment for the context $A :: \Gamma$ sends the newest variable to $a$ and the successor $\mathrm{succ}\,x$ of each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to $\eta(x)$.
nodes.title: Extending a semantic environment in STLC

nodes.summary: Given a renaming $\rho$ from context $\Gamma$ to context $\Delta$ (a type-preserving map from the variables of $\Gamma$ to those of $\Delta$) and an environment $\eta$ for $\Delta$, the renamed environment for $\Gamma$ sends each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to $\eta(\rho(x))$; that is, it is the composite $\eta \circ \rho$.
nodes.title: Renaming an environment

nodes.summary: Given an interpretation $I$ of the base types, the denotation of a well-typed term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ in an environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$ is the element of the denotation of $A$ defined by recursion on $t$: a variable $x$ denotes $\eta(x)$, an application $f\,a$ denotes the denotation of $f$ applied to the denotation of $a$ (both in $\eta$), and an abstraction $\lambda.\,b$ denotes the function…
nodes.title: Denotation of an STLC term

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types, every type-preserving renaming $\rho$ from context $\Gamma$ to context $\Delta$, every term $t$ in context $\Gamma$ and every environment $\eta$ for $\Delta$, the denotation in $\eta$ of the term obtained by renaming the variables of $t$ along $\rho$ equals the denotation of $t$ in the environment that sends each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to $\eta(\rho(x))$.
nodes.title: Renaming lemma for STLC denotation

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types, every term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, every type $B$, every value $a$ in the denotation of $B$ and every environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$, the weakening of $t$ to the context $B :: \Gamma$ has, in the environment that extends $\eta$ by $a$ for the newest variable, the same denotation as $t$ in $\eta$.
nodes.title: Weakening preserves STLC denotation

nodes.summary: Given an interpretation $I$ of the base types, a type-preserving substitution $\sigma$ mapping each variable of a context $\Gamma$ to a term in a context $\Delta$, and an environment $\eta$ for $\Delta$, this is the environment for $\Gamma$ that sends each variable $x$ to the denotation of $\sigma(x)$ in $\eta$.
nodes.title: Denotation of an STLC substitution

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types, every type-preserving substitution $\sigma$ mapping each variable of a context $\Gamma$ to a term in a context $\Delta$, every term $t$ in context $\Gamma$ and every environment $\eta$ for $\Delta$, the denotation in $\eta$ of $t$ with $\sigma$ applied simultaneously to its variables equals the denotation of $t$ in the environment that sends each variable $x$ of…
nodes.title: Substitution lemma for STLC denotation

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types, every term $b$ of type $B$ in context $A :: \Gamma$, every term $a$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ and every environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$, the denotation in $\eta$ of $b$ with its newest variable replaced by $a$ equals the denotation of $b$ in the environment that extends $\eta$ by the denotation of $a$ in $\eta$ for the newest variable.
nodes.title: Denotation of an instantiated STLC body

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types, if a term $t$ reduces to $t'$ in one step of call-by-value reduction, then $t$ and $t'$ have the same denotation in every environment $\eta$ for their context.
nodes.title: One reduction step preserves STLC denotation

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types, if a term $t$ reduces to $t'$ in zero or more steps of call-by-value reduction, then $t$ and $t'$ have the same denotation in every environment $\eta$ for their context.
nodes.title: Multi-step reduction preserves STLC denotation

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types, if a term $t$ evaluates to $v$ under call-by-value big-step evaluation, then $t$ and $v$ have the same denotation in every environment $\eta$ for their context.
nodes.title: Big-step evaluation preserves STLC denotation

nodes.summary: Fix an interpretation $I$ of the base types as types. Two terms $t$ and $u$ of the same type $A$ in the same context $\Gamma$ are semantically equal in $I$ when, for every semantic environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$, the denotation of $t$ in $I$ at $\eta$ equals the denotation of $u$ in $I$ at $\eta$.
nodes.title: Semantic equality of terms in a model

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types, every term $t$ is semantically equal to itself in $I$: it has the same denotation as itself in every environment.
nodes.title: Semantic equality is reflexive

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types and all terms $t$ and $u$ of the same type in the same context, if $t$ and $u$ are semantically equal in $I$, then $u$ and $t$ are semantically equal in $I$.
nodes.title: Symmetry of semantic equality of terms

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types and all terms $t$, $u$ and $w$ of the same type in the same context, if $t$ and $u$ are semantically equal in $I$ and $u$ and $w$ are semantically equal in $I$, then $t$ and $w$ are semantically equal in $I$.
nodes.title: Transitivity of semantic equality of terms

nodes.summary: Fix an interpretation $I$ of the base types. If terms $f$ and $g$ of type $A \Rightarrow B$ in a context $\Gamma$ are semantically equal in $I$ (they have the same denotation in every environment), and terms $a$ and $b$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$ are semantically equal in $I$, then the applications $f\,a$ and $g\,b$ are semantically equal in $I$.
nodes.title: Semantic equality is a congruence for application

nodes.summary: Fix an interpretation $I$ of the base types. If two terms of type $B$ in the context $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$ are semantically equal in $I$ (they have the same denotation in every environment), then their lambda abstractions, terms of type $A \Rightarrow B$ in $\Gamma$, are semantically equal in $I$.
nodes.title: Semantic equality is a congruence for lambda abstraction

nodes.summary: Fix an interpretation $I$ of the base types. If terms $t$ and $u$ of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$ are semantically equal in $I$ (they have the same denotation in every environment), then for every type-preserving renaming $\rho$ of the variables of $\Gamma$ into a context $\Delta$, the renamed terms $\rho(t)$ and $\rho(u)$ are semantically equal in $I$.
nodes.title: Renaming preserves semantic equality

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types, if two terms $t$ and $u$ of the same type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$ are semantically equal in $I$, then for every simultaneous substitution $\sigma$ from $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$, the result of applying $\sigma$ to $t$ and the result of applying $\sigma$ to $u$ are semantically equal in $I$.
nodes.title: Substitution preserves semantic equality

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types, if a term $t$ reduces to a term $u$ in one call-by-value evaluation step, then $t$ and $u$ are semantically equal in $I$: they have the same denotation in every environment.
nodes.title: Single-step evaluation is a semantic equation

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types, if a term $t$ reduces to a term $u$ in zero or more call-by-value evaluation steps, then $t$ and $u$ are semantically equal in $I$: they have the same denotation in every environment.
nodes.title: Multi-step evaluation is a semantic equation

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types, every term $t$ of type $B$ in the context $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$, and every term $a$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$, the redex $(\lambda.\,t)\,a$ is semantically equal in $I$ (has the same denotation in every environment) to the instantiation $t[a]$, which replaces the newest free variable of $t$ by $a$.
nodes.title: Beta is sound for the denotational semantics

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types and every term $f$ of type $A \Rightarrow B$ in a context $\Gamma$, let $f'$ be the weakening of $f$ to the context $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable $x$ of type $A$. Then the term $\lambda x.\, f'\,x$, which binds $x$, is semantically equal to $f$ in $I$ (has the same denotation in every environment).
nodes.title: Eta is sound for the denotational semantics

nodes.summary: Fix an interpretation $I$ of the base types as types. Two simultaneous substitutions $\sigma$ and $\tau$ from a context $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$ are pointwise semantically equal in $I$ when, for every variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ (of any type) and every semantic environment $\eta$ for $\Delta$, the denotation of the term $\sigma(x)$ in $I$ at $\eta$ equals the denotation of the term $\tau(x)$ in $I$ at $\eta$.
nodes.title: Pointwise semantic equality of substitutions

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types and every simultaneous substitution $\sigma$ that replaces each variable of a context $\Gamma$ by a term of the same type in a context $\Delta$, $\sigma$ is pointwise semantically equal to itself in $I$: for every variable $x$ of $\Gamma$, the term $\sigma(x)$ has the same denotation as itself in every environment for $\Delta$.
nodes.title: Pointwise semantic equality of substitutions is reflexive

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types and all simultaneous substitutions $\sigma$ and $\tau$ from a context $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$, if $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are pointwise semantically equal in $I$, then $\tau$ and $\sigma$ are pointwise semantically equal in $I$.
nodes.title: Symmetry of pointwise semantic equality of substitutions

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types and all simultaneous substitutions $\sigma$, $\tau$ and $\upsilon$ from a context $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$, if $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are pointwise semantically equal in $I$ and $\tau$ and $\upsilon$ are pointwise semantically equal in $I$, then $\sigma$ and $\upsilon$ are pointwise semantically equal in $I$.
nodes.title: Transitivity of pointwise semantic equality of substitutions

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types, every term $t$ of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$, and all simultaneous substitutions $\sigma$ and $\tau$ from $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$ that are pointwise semantically equal in $I$, the result of applying $\sigma$ to $t$ and the result of applying $\tau$ to $t$ are semantically equal in $I$.
nodes.title: Semantically equal substitutions give semantically equal results

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types, every context $\Gamma$ and every type $A$, semantic equality in $I$ of terms of type $A$ in $\Gamma$ (having the same denotation in every environment) is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
nodes.title: Semantic equality is an equivalence relation

nodes.summary: Fix simple types over a type of base types. A one-hole context whose hole has type $A$ in variable context $\Gamma$, and which produces a term of type $B$ in variable context $\Delta$, is built by four rules. The hole itself is such a context, with $\Delta = \Gamma$ and $B = A$. If $C$ produces type $S \Rightarrow T$ in $\Delta$ and $a$ is a term of type $S$ in $\Delta$, then the application $C\,a$ produces type…
nodes.title: Typed one-hole contexts

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a typed one-hole context whose hole has type $A$ in variable context $\Gamma$ and which produces a term of type $B$ in variable context $\Delta$. For a term $t$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$, the plugged term $E[t]$ of type $B$ in $\Delta$ is defined by recursion on $E$: $[\,][t] = t$, $(E\,a)[t] = E[t]\,a$, $(f\,E)[t] = f\,E[t]$ and $(\lambda.\,E)[t] = \lambda.\,E[t]$, where $[\,]$ is the bare hole, $E\,a$…
nodes.title: Plugging a term into an STLC context

nodes.summary: Let $E_2$ be a typed one-hole context whose hole has type $B$ in variable context $\Delta$ and which produces a term of type $C$ in context $\Theta$, and let $E_1$ be one whose hole has type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ and which produces a term of type $B$ in $\Delta$. The composite $E_2 \circ E_1$, with hole of type $A$ in $\Gamma$ and result of type $C$ in $\Theta$, replaces the hole of $E_2$ by $E_1$; by recursion…
nodes.title: Composition of STLC contexts

nodes.summary: Let $E_2$ be a typed one-hole context whose hole has type $B$ in variable context $\Delta$ and which produces a term of type $C$ in context $\Theta$, and let $E_1$ be one whose hole has type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ and which produces a term of type $B$ in $\Delta$. Then for every term $t$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$, $(E_2 \circ E_1)[t] = E_2[E_1[t]]$.
nodes.title: Plugging into a composite STLC context

nodes.summary: Let $E_1$ be a typed one-hole context whose hole has type $A$ in variable context $\Gamma$ and which produces a term of type $B$ in context $\Delta$, $E_2$ one with hole of type $B$ in $\Delta$ producing type $C$ in $\Theta$, and $E_3$ one with hole of type $C$ in $\Theta$ producing type $D$ in $\Xi$. Then $(E_3 \circ E_2) \circ E_1 = E_3 \circ (E_2 \circ E_1)$.
nodes.title: Associativity of composition of STLC contexts

nodes.summary: Fix an interpretation $I$ of the base types. Let $t$ and $u$ be terms of type $A$ in variable context $\Gamma$ that denote the same value in $I$ under every semantic environment. Then for every typed one-hole context $C$ whose hole has type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ and which produces a term of type $B$ in context $\Delta$, the terms $C[t]$ and $C[u]$ obtained by plugging $t$ and $u$ into the hole also denote the…
nodes.title: Semantic equality is a congruence for typed contexts

nodes.summary: Two terms $t$ and $u$ of type $A$ in variable context $\Gamma$ are model-equal when, for every interpretation $I$ of the base types by types in the same universe as the type of base types, they are semantically equal in $I$: with function types interpreted as full function spaces, the denotations of $t$ and $u$ agree at every semantic environment for $\Gamma$.
nodes.title: Model equality of STLC terms

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a typed one-hole context whose hole has type $A$ in variable context $\Gamma$ and which produces a term of type $B$ in context $\Delta$. If two terms $t$ and $u$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$ are model-equal, then $E[t]$ and $E[u]$ are model-equal.
nodes.title: Model equality is a congruence for STLC contexts

nodes.summary: For every term $b$ of type $B$ in the variable context $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$, and every term $a$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$, the application $(\lambda.\,b)\,a$ is model-equal to $b[a]$, the result of substituting $a$ for the newest variable of $b$.
nodes.title: Model-independent beta equality

nodes.summary: For every term $f$ of type $A \Rightarrow B$ in variable context $\Gamma$, the term $\lambda.\,(f^{\uparrow}\,x_0)$ is model-equal to $f$, where $f^{\uparrow}$ is $f$ weakened by a newest variable of type $A$ and $x_0$ is that variable.
nodes.title: Model-independent eta equality

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a typed one-hole context whose hole has type $B$ in variable context $\Gamma$ and which produces a term of type $C$ in context $\Delta$. For every term $b$ of type $B$ in $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$, and every term $a$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$, the term $E[(\lambda.\,b)\,a]$ is model-equal to $E[b[a]]$, where $b[a]$ is the result of substituting $a$ for the newest variable of $b$.
nodes.title: Beta equality inside an STLC context

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a typed one-hole context whose hole has type $A \Rightarrow B$ in variable context $\Gamma$ and which produces a term of type $C$ in context $\Delta$. For every term $f$ of type $A \Rightarrow B$ in $\Gamma$, the term $E[\lambda.\,(f^{\uparrow}\,x_0)]$ is model-equal to $E[f]$, where $f^{\uparrow}$ is $f$ weakened by a newest variable of type $A$ and $x_0$ is that variable.
nodes.title: Eta equality inside an STLC context
Normalization by evaluation

nodes.summary: For a context $\Gamma$, the semantic values of a simple type in $\Gamma$ are defined by recursion on the type. At a base type $b$ they are the neutral terms of type $b$ in $\Gamma$ (variables applied to zero or more normal arguments). At an arrow type $A \Rightarrow B$ a semantic value is a family that, for every context $\Delta$ and every renaming from $\Gamma$ to $\Delta$, maps semantic values of type $A$ in…
nodes.title: Kripke semantic values

nodes.summary: Given a renaming $\rho$ from a context $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$, a simple type $A$ and a semantic value $v$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$, the renamed value is the semantic value of type $A$ in $\Delta$ defined by cases on $A$. At a base type it is the neutral term $v$ with its free variables renamed by $\rho$. At an arrow type $A = B \Rightarrow C$ it sends a renaming $\sigma$ from $\Delta$ to a context $\Theta$…
nodes.title: Renaming a semantic value

nodes.summary: For contexts $\Delta$ and $\Gamma$, a semantic environment for $\Gamma$ in $\Delta$ assigns to every variable of $\Gamma$, of any type $A$, a Kripke semantic value of type $A$ in $\Delta$.
nodes.title: Semantic environments for normalization by evaluation

nodes.summary: Given a renaming $\rho$ from a context $\Delta$ to a context $\Theta$ and a semantic environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$ in $\Delta$, the renamed environment is the semantic environment for $\Gamma$ in $\Theta$ that sends each variable $x$ of type $A$ to the semantic value $\eta(x)$ renamed along $\rho$ at type $A$.
nodes.title: Renaming a semantic environment

nodes.summary: Given a semantic value $a$ of type $A$ in a context $\Delta$ and a semantic environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$ in $\Delta$, the extended environment is the semantic environment for the context $A :: \Gamma$ (the context $\Gamma$ with a new innermost variable of type $A$) in $\Delta$ that sends the new innermost variable to $a$ and sends the successor of each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to $\eta(x)$.
nodes.title: Extending a semantic environment by one variable

nodes.summary: For a context $\Gamma$, the identity environment is the semantic environment for $\Gamma$ in $\Gamma$ that sends each variable $x$ of type $A$ to the reflection at type $A$ of the neutral term $x$. Reflection turns a neutral term into a semantic value of the same type in the same context.
nodes.title: The identity semantic environment

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a term of type $T$ in context $\Gamma$ and let $\eta$ be a semantic environment interpreting every variable of $\Gamma$ as a semantic value in context $\Delta$. The evaluation $\operatorname{ev}(t, \eta)$ is the semantic value of type $T$ in context $\Delta$ defined by recursion on $t$: a variable $x$ evaluates to $\eta(x)$; an application $f\,a$ evaluates to the semantic function…
nodes.title: Evaluation into the Kripke semantic domain

nodes.summary: For a term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, its normal form is the beta-normal, eta-long term of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ obtained by reifying, at type $A$, the evaluation of $t$ in the identity semantic environment of $\Gamma$, which interprets each variable as the reflection of that variable.
nodes.title: Normalization by evaluation

nodes.summary: For a term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, its normalized term is the term of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ underlying the beta-normal, eta-long normal form of $t$ computed by normalization by evaluation.
nodes.title: Normalization of terms

nodes.summary: For every type $A$, every renaming $\rho$ from a context $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$, and every neutral term $n$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, transporting the semantic value obtained by reflecting $n$ at type $A$ along $\rho$ gives the reflection at type $A$ of the neutral term $n$ renamed by $\rho$.
nodes.title: Reflection commutes with renaming

nodes.summary: Let $\Gamma$ be a context, $A$ a type, and $\Gamma, A$ the context $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$. Transport the identity semantic environment of $\Gamma$ (which reflects each variable as a neutral value) along the weakening renaming from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma, A$ that sends each variable to its successor, and extend the result by the reflection at type $A$ of the newest variable of $\Gamma, A$.…
nodes.title: The identity environment under a binder

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a term of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, and let $\xi$ and $\zeta$ be semantic environments interpreting the variables of $\Gamma$ in a context $\Delta$. If $\xi(x) = \zeta(x)$ for every variable $x$ of $\Gamma$, of any type, then evaluating $t$ in $\xi$ and evaluating $t$ in $\zeta$ give the same semantic value.
nodes.title: Evaluation respects pointwise equal environments

nodes.summary: For every neutral term $n$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, evaluating the underlying term of $n$ in the identity semantic environment of $\Gamma$ gives the reflection of $n$ at type $A$.
nodes.title: Evaluating a neutral term reflects it

nodes.summary: For every beta-normal, eta-long normal form $n$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, normalizing the underlying term of $n$ by evaluation returns the normal form $n$ itself.
nodes.title: Normal forms are fixed points of normalization

nodes.summary: For every term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, normalizing the underlying term of the normal form that normalization by evaluation computes from $t$ gives the same term as normalizing $t$.
nodes.title: Renormalizing a computed normal form

nodes.summary: For every term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, normalizing the normalized term of $t$ by evaluation gives the normalized term of $t$ again.
nodes.title: Normalization by evaluation is idempotent

nodes.summary: For every eta-long normal form $n$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, normalizing the underlying term of $n$ returns that term unchanged.
nodes.title: Normalization fixes the terms of normal forms

nodes.summary: For every context $\Gamma$ and type $A$, two eta-long normal forms of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ with the same underlying term are equal.
nodes.title: Erasing normal forms is injective

nodes.summary: A term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ is canonical when it is the underlying term of some beta-normal, eta-long normal form of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$.
nodes.title: Canonical terms

nodes.summary: A term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ is canonical if and only if normalization by evaluation maps $t$ to itself, that is, the term underlying the normal form computed for $t$ is $t$.
nodes.title: Canonical terms are the fixed points of normalization

nodes.summary: For every term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, the term obtained by normalizing $t$ by evaluation is canonical.
nodes.title: Normalized terms are canonical

nodes.summary: If a term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ is canonical, then for every renaming $\rho$ from $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$, the term obtained by renaming $t$ along $\rho$ is canonical.
nodes.title: Renaming preserves canonical terms

nodes.summary: For a context $\Gamma$ and a type $A$, a certified canonical term of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ is a term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ together with a proof that $t$ is a fixed point of normalization by evaluation: the term underlying the normal form computed for $t$ is $t$ itself.
nodes.title: Certified canonical terms

nodes.summary: The canonical term of an eta-long normal form $n$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ is the underlying term of $n$, certified to be a fixed point of normalization.
nodes.title: Normal forms as canonical terms

nodes.summary: For a canonical term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, that is, a term that normalization returns unchanged, its normal form is the eta-long normal form that normalization by evaluation computes from $t$.
nodes.title: The normal form of a canonical term

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a term of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$. If $t$ is canonical, then there is exactly one beta-normal, eta-long normal form of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ whose underlying term is $t$.
nodes.title: Canonical terms have a unique normal form

nodes.summary: Fix an interpretation $I$ of the base types. For a context $\Gamma$, an environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$ in $I$, a type $A$, a Kripke semantic value $v$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$ and an element $d$ of the denotation of $A$ under $I$, the relation "$v$ realizes $d$ at $\eta$" is defined by recursion on $A$. At a base type, $v$ is a neutral term, and $v$ realizes $d$ when the denotation of $v$, read as a term, in $\eta$…
nodes.title: Kripke realization relation for NbE

nodes.summary: Fix an interpretation $I$ of the base types. Let $v$ be a Kripke semantic value of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ that realizes an element $d$ of the denotation of $A$ at an environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$. If $\rho : \Gamma \to \Delta$ is a renaming and $\theta$ is an environment for $\Delta$ with $\theta \circ \rho = \eta$, then the transport of $v$ along $\rho$ realizes $d$ at $\theta$.
nodes.title: Realization is stable under renaming

nodes.summary: Fix an interpretation $I$ of the base types, contexts $\Delta$ and $\Gamma$, an environment $\theta$ for $\Delta$ in $I$, a Kripke semantic environment $\xi$ assigning to each variable of $\Gamma$ a semantic value in $\Delta$, and an environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$ in $I$. Then $\xi$ realizes $\eta$ at $\theta$ when for every type $A$ and every variable $x$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$, the semantic value $\xi(x)$…
nodes.title: Realization of environments

nodes.summary: Fix an interpretation $I$ of the base types. Let $t$ be a term of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, let $\xi$ be a Kripke semantic environment assigning to each variable of $\Gamma$ a semantic value in context $\Delta$, and let $\eta$ and $\theta$ be environments in $I$ for $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$. If $\xi$ realizes $\eta$ at $\theta$, then the NbE evaluation of $t$ in $\xi$ realizes the denotation of $t$ in $\eta$ at…
nodes.title: Fundamental lemma for NbE evaluation

nodes.summary: Fix an interpretation $I$ of the base types and an environment $\eta$ for a context $\Gamma$ in $I$. Then the identity Kripke semantic environment on $\Gamma$, which reflects each variable as a neutral value, realizes $\eta$ at $\eta$.
nodes.title: The identity semantic environment realizes every environment

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types, every term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ and every environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$ in $I$, the NbE normal form of $t$ has the same denotation in $\eta$ as $t$.
nodes.title: NbE preserves denotation

nodes.summary: For every interpretation $I$ of the base types and every term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, $t$ and its NbE normal form are semantically equal in $I$: they have the same denotation in every environment for $\Gamma$ in $I$.
nodes.title: Every term is semantically equal to its NbE normal form in each model

nodes.summary: Every term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ is model-equal to its NbE normal form.
nodes.title: Every term is model-equal to its NbE normal form

nodes.summary: If two terms $t$ and $u$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ have the same NbE normal form, then $t$ and $u$ are model-equal.
nodes.title: Equal NbE normal forms imply model equality
Normalization of the simply typed lambda calculus

nodes.summary: Let $f$ and $f'$ be terms of type $A \Rightarrow B$ and let $a$ be a term of type $A$, all in the same context. If $f$ evaluates to $f'$ in zero or more call-by-value steps, then the application $f\,a$ evaluates to $f'\,a$ in zero or more steps.
nodes.title: Multi-step evaluation is a congruence in function position

nodes.summary: Let $f$ be a term of type $A \Rightarrow B$ and let $a$, $a'$ be terms of type $A$, all in the same context. If $f$ is a value and $a$ evaluates to $a'$ in zero or more call-by-value steps, then the application $f\,a$ evaluates to $f\,a'$ in zero or more steps.
nodes.title: Evaluating the argument of a value function is a multi-step congruence

nodes.summary: Let $t$, $t'$ and $v$ be terms of the same type in the same context, with $v$ a value. If $t$ evaluates to $v$ and $t$ evaluates to $t'$, each in finitely many call-by-value steps, then $t'$ evaluates to $v$ in finitely many steps.
nodes.title: Evaluation to a value passes through every reduct

nodes.summary: A closed term $t$ terminates when it evaluates, in finitely many call-by-value steps, to a value.
nodes.title: Termination of closed terms

nodes.summary: Every closed term of the simply typed lambda calculus that is a value terminates.
nodes.title: Values terminate

nodes.summary: Let $t$ and $t'$ be closed terms of the same type. If $t$ evaluates to $t'$ in zero or more call-by-value steps and $t'$ terminates, then $t$ terminates.
nodes.title: Termination is closed under backward evaluation

nodes.summary: Let $t$ and $t'$ be closed terms of the same type. If $t$ terminates and $t$ evaluates to $t'$ in zero or more call-by-value steps, then $t'$ terminates.
nodes.title: Termination is closed under forward evaluation

nodes.summary: Reducibility of a closed term $t$ is defined by recursion on its simple type. At a base type, $t$ is reducible when it terminates. At a function type $A \Rightarrow B$, $t$ is reducible when it terminates and, for every reducible closed term $a$ of type $A$, the application $t\,a$ is reducible.
nodes.title: Tait reducibility for closed terms

nodes.summary: Every reducible closed term of the simply typed lambda calculus terminates.
nodes.title: Reducible terms terminate

nodes.summary: Let $t$ and $t'$ be closed terms of the same type. If $t$ is reducible and $t$ evaluates to $t'$ in zero or more call-by-value steps, then $t'$ is reducible.
nodes.title: Reducibility is closed under forward evaluation

nodes.summary: Let $t$ and $t'$ be closed terms of the same type. If $t$ evaluates to $t'$ in zero or more call-by-value steps and $t'$ is reducible, then $t$ is reducible.
nodes.title: Reducibility is closed under backward evaluation

nodes.summary: Let $t$ and $t'$ be closed terms of the same type. If $t$ evaluates to $t'$ in zero or more call-by-value steps, then $t$ is reducible if and only if $t'$ is reducible.
nodes.title: Reducibility is invariant under evaluation

nodes.summary: A substitution $\sigma$ that replaces each variable of a context $\Gamma$ by a closed term of the same type is reducible when $\sigma(x)$ is reducible for every variable $x$ of $\Gamma$.
nodes.title: Reducible substitutions

nodes.summary: Every substitution from the empty context to closed terms is reducible, since the empty context has no variables.
nodes.title: Substitutions on the empty context are reducible

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution that sends each variable of a context $\Gamma$ to a closed term of the same type, and let $a$ be a closed term of type $A$. If $\sigma$ and $a$ are reducible, then so is the substitution on the context $A, \Gamma$ that sends the newest variable to $a$ and each older variable $x$ to $\sigma(x)$.
nodes.title: Extending a reducible substitution by a reducible term keeps it reducible

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a term of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$, and let $\sigma$ be a reducible substitution sending each variable of $\Gamma$ to a closed term of the same type. Then the closed term obtained by applying $\sigma$ to $t$ is reducible.
nodes.title: Fundamental theorem of the reducibility relation

nodes.summary: Every closed well-typed term of the simply typed lambda calculus is reducible.
nodes.title: Closed terms are reducible

nodes.summary: Every closed well-typed term evaluates, in finitely many call-by-value steps, to a value.
nodes.title: Termination of the call-by-value simply typed lambda calculus

nodes.summary: Let $v$ and $t$ be terms of the same type in the same context. If $v$ is a value and $v$ reduces to $t$ in zero or more call-by-value steps, then $v = t$.
nodes.title: Values reduce only to themselves

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a term in any context. If $t$ reduces in zero or more call-by-value steps to a value $v$ and also to a value $w$, then $v = w$.
nodes.title: Uniqueness of the value reached by evaluation

nodes.summary: A closed term $t$ of the simply typed lambda calculus normalizes when it reduces, in zero or more call-by-value steps, to a term in normal form, that is, a term with no further call-by-value reduction step.
nodes.title: Normalizing closed terms

nodes.summary: A closed well-typed term $t$ normalizes, that is, reduces in zero or more call-by-value steps to a normal form (a term with no further reduction step), if and only if it terminates, that is, reduces in zero or more call-by-value steps to a value.
nodes.title: Normalization and termination coincide

nodes.summary: Every closed well-typed term normalizes: it reduces in zero or more call-by-value steps to a normal form.
nodes.title: Normalization of closed terms

nodes.summary: If a closed term $t$ reduces in zero or more call-by-value steps to a normal form $n$ and also to a normal form $m$, then $n = m$.
nodes.title: Uniqueness of normal forms

nodes.summary: For every closed term $f$ of a function type $A \Rightarrow B$ there is a term $b$ of type $B$ in the context with a single variable of type $A$ such that $f$ reduces, in zero or more call-by-value steps, to the lambda abstraction with body $b$.
nodes.title: Closed functions evaluate to lambda abstractions

nodes.summary: In the pure, constant-free calculus there is no closed term whose type is a base type.
nodes.title: No closed terms of base type

nodes.summary: Two closed terms $t$ and $u$ of the same type have the same result when there is a value $v$ such that both $t$ and $u$ reduce to $v$ in zero or more call-by-value steps.
nodes.title: Closed terms with the same result

nodes.summary: Every closed term has the same result as itself.
nodes.title: Reflexivity of having the same result

nodes.summary: If closed terms $t$ and $u$ have the same result, then $u$ and $t$ have the same result.
nodes.title: Symmetry of having the same result

nodes.summary: If closed terms $t$ and $u$ have the same result, and $u$ and a closed term $v$ have the same result, then $t$ and $v$ have the same result.
nodes.title: Transitivity of having the same result

nodes.summary: If a closed term $t$ reduces to a term $u$ in zero or more call-by-value steps, then $t$ and $u$ have the same result.
nodes.title: Evaluation preserves the result of a closed term

nodes.summary: Let $t$, $t'$ and $u$ be closed terms of the same type. If $t$ reduces to $t'$ in zero or more call-by-value steps, and $t'$ and $u$ have the same result, then $t$ and $u$ have the same result.
nodes.title: Left expansion preserves having the same result

nodes.summary: Let $t$, $u$ and $u'$ be closed terms of the same type. If $u$ reduces to $u'$ in zero or more call-by-value steps, and $t$ and $u'$ have the same result, then $t$ and $u$ have the same result.
nodes.title: Right expansion preserves having the same result

nodes.summary: Let $f$ and $g$ be closed terms of a function type $A \Rightarrow B$, and let $a$ and $b$ be closed terms of type $A$. If $f$ and $g$ have the same result and $a$ and $b$ have the same result, then the applications $f\,a$ and $g\,b$ have the same result.
nodes.title: Application preserves having the same result

nodes.summary: For every simple type $A$, the relation of having the same result is an equivalence relation on the closed terms of type $A$.
nodes.title: Having the same result is an equivalence relation
Type checking for the simply typed lambda calculus

nodes.summary: Raw terms are extrinsic de Bruijn syntax over a given type of base types: a raw term is either a variable given by a natural-number index $n$, an application $f\,a$ of two raw terms $f$ and $a$, or a lambda abstraction $\lambda A.\,t$ consisting of a simple type $A$ over the base types (the parameter type) and a raw term $t$ (the body). Variables and applications carry no type information.
nodes.title: Raw lambda terms

nodes.summary: Writing $|t|$ for the size of a raw term $t$, the size counts the syntax nodes of $t$: a variable has size $1$, an application $f\,a$ has size $|f| + |a| + 1$, and a lambda abstraction $\lambda A.\,t$ has size $|t| + 1$, so the type annotation $A$ is not counted.
nodes.title: Size of a raw term

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $k$ (the amount) and $c$ (the cutoff, $0$ by default), shifting a raw term by $k$ at cutoff $c$ replaces a variable index $n$ by $n + k$ if $c \le n$ and leaves it unchanged otherwise, shifts both sides of an application by $k$ at cutoff $c$, and sends $\lambda A.\,t$ to $\lambda A.\,t'$, where $t'$ is $t$ shifted by $k$ at cutoff $c + 1$.
nodes.title: Shifting raw terms

nodes.summary: Given a context $\Gamma$, a list of types, and a natural number $n$, looking up the de Bruijn index $n$ in $\Gamma$ either fails or returns a type $A$ together with an intrinsic variable of type $A$ in $\Gamma$. It is defined by recursion: lookup fails in the empty context; index $0$ in the context $A :: \Gamma$, obtained by adding $A$ at the front of $\Gamma$, returns $A$ with the zero variable; and index $n + 1$…
nodes.title: Variable lookup

nodes.summary: For a context $\Gamma$ and a type $A$, a well-typed de Bruijn variable of type $A$ in $\Gamma$ is sent to its natural-number index, forgetting its type: the variable for the first entry of the context has index $0$, and the successor of a variable $x$ has the index of $x$ plus $1$.
nodes.title: Index of a typed variable

nodes.summary: For every context $\Gamma$, type $A$ and intrinsic variable $x$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$, looking up the de Bruijn index of $x$ in $\Gamma$ succeeds and returns the type $A$ together with $x$.
nodes.title: Lookup recovers an intrinsic variable from its index

nodes.summary: For every context $\Gamma$ and natural number $n$, if looking up the de Bruijn index $n$ in $\Gamma$ succeeds with a type $A$ and an intrinsic variable $x$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$, then the de Bruijn index of $x$ is $n$.
nodes.title: Lookup returns a variable with the queried index

nodes.summary: The erasure of an intrinsically typed term in a context $\Gamma$ is the raw term defined by recursion: a variable becomes the raw variable whose index is its position in $\Gamma$ (counting from $0$ at the front); an application of $f$ to $a$ becomes the raw application of the erasure of $f$ to the erasure of $a$; and a lambda with parameter type $B$ becomes the raw lambda annotated with $B$ whose body is the…
nodes.title: Erasure of intrinsically typed terms

nodes.summary: For a context $\Gamma$ of simple types, a checked term in $\Gamma$ is a pair $(A, t)$ of a simple type $A$ and an intrinsically typed term $t$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$.
nodes.title: Checked terms

nodes.summary: Assume equality of base types is decidable. Elaboration in a context $\Gamma$ of simple types sends a raw term either to failure or to a checked term in $\Gamma$ (a simple type together with an intrinsically typed term of that type in $\Gamma$), by recursion on the raw term. A variable with de Bruijn index $n$ elaborates to the variable at position $n$ of $\Gamma$ (counting from $0$ at the front), with the type…
nodes.title: Elaboration of raw STLC terms

nodes.summary: Assume equality of base types is decidable. For every intrinsically typed term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, elaborating the erasure of $t$ in $\Gamma$ succeeds and returns exactly the pair $(A, t)$. In other words, erasure is a section of elaboration.
nodes.title: Elaboration inverts erasure

nodes.summary: Assume equality of base types is decidable. If elaborating a raw term $r$ in context $\Gamma$ succeeds with type $A$ and intrinsically typed term $t$, then the erasure of $t$ is exactly $r$.
nodes.title: Elaboration preserves the input syntax

nodes.summary: For a fixed context $\Gamma$ and type $A$, erasure is injective on intrinsically typed terms of type $A$ in $\Gamma$: two such terms with the same erasure are equal.
nodes.title: Erasure is injective

nodes.summary: For a context $\Gamma$ (a list of simple types), a raw term $t$ and a type $A$, the judgment $\Gamma \vdash t : A$ is the least relation closed under three rules. A variable with de Bruijn index $n$ has type $A$ in $\Gamma$ whenever looking up $n$ in $\Gamma$ succeeds with the type $A$ and some intrinsic variable of type $A$. If $\Gamma \vdash f : A \Rightarrow B$ and $\Gamma \vdash a : A$, then the application…
nodes.title: Declarative typing of raw terms

nodes.summary: For every intrinsically typed term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, the erasure of $t$ has type $A$ in $\Gamma$ under the declarative typing judgment for raw terms.
nodes.title: Erasure preserves typing

nodes.summary: Let $\Gamma$ be a context of simple types and $r$ a raw term. If $r$ has type $A$ in $\Gamma$ and $r$ has type $B$ in $\Gamma$ under the declarative typing judgment for raw terms, then $A = B$.
nodes.title: Uniqueness of types for raw terms

nodes.summary: Assume equality of base types is decidable. If a raw term $r$ has type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ under the declarative typing judgment, then elaborating $r$ in $\Gamma$ succeeds and returns the type $A$ together with some intrinsically typed term of type $A$ in $\Gamma$.
nodes.title: Completeness of elaboration

nodes.summary: Assume equality of base types is decidable. If elaborating a raw term $r$ in context $\Gamma$ succeeds with type $A$ (and some intrinsically typed term of type $A$ in $\Gamma$), then $r$ has type $A$ in $\Gamma$ under the declarative typing judgment.
nodes.title: Soundness of elaboration

nodes.summary: Assume equality of base types is decidable. For every context $\Gamma$, raw term $t$ and type $A$, the declarative typing judgment $\Gamma \vdash t : A$ holds if and only if there is an intrinsically typed term $u$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ such that elaborating $t$ in $\Gamma$ succeeds and returns the type $A$ together with $u$.
nodes.title: Declarative typing agrees with elaboration

nodes.summary: Assume equality of base types is decidable. Given a context $\Gamma$ and a raw term $t$, type inference elaborates $t$ in $\Gamma$; if elaboration succeeds, it returns the type component of the result and forgets the intrinsically typed term, and if elaboration fails, inference fails.
nodes.title: Type inference for raw terms

nodes.summary: Assume equality of base types is decidable. For every context $\Gamma$, raw term $t$ and type $A$, type inference for $t$ in $\Gamma$ returns $A$ if and only if the declarative typing judgment $\Gamma \vdash t : A$ holds.
nodes.title: Type inference is sound and complete

nodes.summary: Assume equality of base types is decidable. Given a context $\Gamma$ (a list of simple types), a raw term $r$ and a simple type $A$, the type checker returns true exactly when type inference for $r$ in $\Gamma$ returns the type $A$, and false otherwise.
nodes.title: Type checking for raw STLC terms

nodes.summary: Let the base types have decidable equality. Given a context $\Gamma$ of simple types and a raw term $r$, raw normalization elaborates $r$ in $\Gamma$. If elaboration fails, raw normalization fails. If elaboration returns a type $A$ and an intrinsically typed term $t$ of type $A$, raw normalization returns $A$ together with the erasure to a raw term of the normal form of $t$ computed by normalization by evaluation.
nodes.title: Normalization of raw terms

nodes.summary: Assume equality of base types is decidable. For every intrinsically typed term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, raw normalization of the erasure of $t$ in $\Gamma$ succeeds and returns the type $A$ together with the erasure of the normal form of $t$ computed by normalization by evaluation.
nodes.title: Raw normalization of an erased term

nodes.summary: Let the base types have decidable equality, let $\Gamma$ be a context of simple types and let $r$ be a raw term. If normalizing $r$ in $\Gamma$ succeeds and returns a type $A$ together with a raw term, then type inference for $r$ in $\Gamma$ returns $A$.
nodes.title: Raw normalization reports the inferred type

nodes.summary: Assume equality of base types is decidable. For every context $\Gamma$ and raw term $t$, if raw normalization of $t$ in $\Gamma$ succeeds with a type $A$ and a raw term $t'$, then the declarative typing judgment $\Gamma \vdash t' : A$ holds.
nodes.title: Raw normalization produces well-typed terms

nodes.summary: Assume equality of base types is decidable. For every context $\Gamma$ and raw term $t$, if raw normalization of $t$ in $\Gamma$ succeeds with a type $A$ and a raw term $t'$, then raw normalization of $t'$ in $\Gamma$ succeeds with the same type $A$ and the same term $t'$.
nodes.title: Raw normalization is idempotent

nodes.summary: Given a renaming $\rho : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ of de Bruijn indices, its lift through one binder is the map $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ sending $0$ to $0$ and $n + 1$ to $\rho(n) + 1$.
nodes.title: Lifting a numerical renaming

nodes.summary: Given a map $\rho : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ on de Bruijn indices, renaming a raw term by $\rho$ replaces each variable $n$ by $\rho(n)$, renames both parts of an application by $\rho$, and renames the body of a lambda abstraction, keeping its parameter type, by the lifted map $\rho'$ given by $\rho'(0) = 0$ and $\rho'(n + 1) = \rho(n) + 1$.
nodes.title: Renaming of raw terms

nodes.summary: For maps $\rho, \sigma : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, the lift of $\sigma \circ \rho$ through one binder equals the lift of $\sigma$ composed after the lift of $\rho$.
nodes.title: Lifting commutes with composition of numerical renamings

nodes.summary: For all maps $\rho, \sigma : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and every raw term $t$, renaming $t$ by $\rho$ and then renaming the result by $\sigma$ gives the same raw term as renaming $t$ by the composite $\sigma \circ \rho$.
nodes.title: Composition of renamings of raw terms

nodes.summary: For every map $\rho : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and every raw term $t$, the renaming of $t$ by $\rho$ has the same number of syntax nodes as $t$.
nodes.title: Renaming preserves the size of a raw term

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $k$ and $c$ and every raw term $t$, shifting $t$ by $k$ at cutoff $c$ (adding $k$ to each variable index that is at least the cutoff, which grows by one under each binder) gives a raw term with the same number of syntax nodes as $t$.
nodes.title: Shifting preserves the size of a raw term

nodes.summary: The list of de Bruijn indices of a raw term, read from left to right with repetitions: a variable with index $n$ gives $[n]$, an application gives the indices of the function followed by those of the argument, and a lambda abstraction gives the indices of its body, unshifted.
nodes.title: Indices occurring in a raw term

nodes.summary: For a binder depth $d$ and a raw term $t$, the free indices of $t$ at depth $d$ form a list defined by recursion on $t$: a variable with index $n$ contributes $[n - d]$ if $d \le n$ and the empty list otherwise; an application contributes the free indices of the function followed by those of the argument, both at depth $d$; and a lambda abstraction contributes the free indices of its body at depth $d + 1$.
nodes.title: Free indices of a raw term

nodes.summary: A raw term $t$ is closed when its list of free indices at binder depth $0$ is empty.
nodes.title: Closed raw terms

nodes.summary: A typed renaming $\rho$ from context $\Gamma$ to context $\Delta$ agrees with a map $r : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ when, for every type $A$ and every variable $x$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$, the de Bruijn index of $\rho(x)$ equals $r$ applied to the de Bruijn index of $x$.
nodes.title: Agreement of a typed and a numerical renaming

nodes.summary: Let $\rho$ be a typed renaming from context $\Gamma$ to $\Delta$ and let $r : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a numerical renaming that agrees with $\rho$. Then for every type $A$, the lift of $\rho$ under a binder of type $A$ agrees with the lift of $r$ through one binder.
nodes.title: Agreement of renamings is preserved by lifting

nodes.summary: Let $\rho$ be a typed renaming from context $\Gamma$ to $\Delta$, let $\sigma$ be a typed renaming from $\Delta$ to $\Xi$, and let $r, s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. If $\rho$ agrees with $r$ and $\sigma$ agrees with $s$, then the composite renaming that applies $\rho$ and then $\sigma$ agrees with $s \circ r$.
nodes.title: Agreement of renamings is preserved by composition

nodes.summary: Let $\rho$ be a typed renaming from context $\Gamma$ to $\Delta$ and let $r : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a numerical renaming that agrees with $\rho$. Then for every intrinsically typed term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, the erasure of the renamed term $\rho(t)$ equals the raw renaming by $r$ (lifted at every binder) of the erasure of $t$.
nodes.title: Erasure commutes with renaming

nodes.summary: For every intrinsically typed term $t$ in context $\Gamma$ and every type $B$, the erasure of the weakening of $t$ to the context $\Gamma$ extended by $B$ equals the raw renaming by the successor map $n \mapsto n + 1$ (lifted at every binder) of the erasure of $t$. Thus every free index is incremented by one.
nodes.title: Erasure of a weakened term

nodes.summary: Let $\rho$ be a type-preserving renaming of variables from context $\Gamma$ to context $\Delta$, and let $r, s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ both agree with $\rho$: for every variable $x$ of $\Gamma$, the de Bruijn index of $\rho(x)$ is the image of the index of $x$ under $r$, and also under $s$. nodes.title: Multi-step evaluation with references

nodes.summary: If $v$ is a value, then there are no stores $\mu$, $\mu'$ and term $t'$ such that the configuration $(v, \mu)$ steps to $(t', \mu')$: values are normal forms.

Operational semantics of IMP

nodes.summary: A state of an IMP program is a function $\sigma : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ assigning a natural-number value $\sigma(i)$ to each variable, where variables are identified by natural numbers $i$.
nodes.title: IMP program states

nodes.summary: The arithmetic expressions of IMP are built inductively from the constants $n$, one for each natural number $n$, and the variables $x_i$, one for each natural number $i$: if $a_1$ and $a_2$ are arithmetic expressions, then so are $a_1 + a_2$, $a_1 - a_2$ and $a_1 \cdot a_2$.
nodes.title: Arithmetic expressions of IMP

nodes.summary: The Boolean expressions of IMP are built inductively from the constants true and false and the comparisons $a_1 = a_2$ and $a_1 \le a_2$ of arithmetic expressions $a_1, a_2$: if $b$, $b_1$ and $b_2$ are Boolean expressions, then so are the negation $\neg b$ and the conjunction $b_1 \wedge b_2$.
nodes.title: Boolean expressions of IMP

nodes.summary: The commands of the while-language IMP are built inductively from skip and the assignments $x_i := a$ of an arithmetic expression $a$ to the variable $x_i$ with index $i \in \mathbb{N}$: if $c$, $c_1$ and $c_2$ are commands and $b$ is a Boolean expression, then so are the sequential composition $c_1 ; c_2$, the conditional if $b$ then $c_1$ else $c_2$, and the loop while $b$ do $c$.
nodes.title: Commands of IMP

nodes.summary: The value of an arithmetic expression in a state $\sigma : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is the natural number defined by recursion on the expression: a constant $n$ has value $n$, the variable $x_i$ with index $i$ has value $\sigma(i)$, and for arithmetic expressions $a_1$ and $a_2$, the expressions $a_1 + a_2$, $a_1 - a_2$ and $a_1 \cdot a_2$ have as value the sum, the truncated difference and the product of the…
nodes.title: Evaluation of IMP arithmetic expressions

nodes.summary: The truth value of a Boolean expression in a state $\sigma : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is defined by recursion on the expression: the constants true and false have values true and false; for arithmetic expressions $a_1$ and $a_2$, the comparison $a_1 = a_2$ is true exactly when the values of $a_1$ and $a_2$ in $\sigma$ are equal, and $a_1 \le a_2$ is true exactly when the value of $a_1$ is at most the value of…
nodes.title: Evaluation of IMP Boolean expressions

nodes.summary: The big-step relation says when running a command $c$ from a state $s$ terminates in a state $t$; we then say that $c$ takes $s$ to $t$. It is the least relation satisfying the following rules. The command $\mathtt{skip}$ takes $s$ to $s$. The assignment $x := a$ takes $s$ to the state $s[x \mapsto a(s)]$, which agrees with $s$ except that $x$ has the value $a(s)$ of the arithmetic expression $a$ in $s$. If $c_1$…
nodes.title: Big-step semantics of IMP

nodes.summary: For every command $c$ and every state $s$, if $c$ run from $s$ terminates in a state $t_1$ and also in a state $t_2$ under the big-step semantics, then $t_1 = t_2$.
nodes.title: Determinism of IMP big-step semantics

nodes.summary: A configuration of IMP is a pair $(c, \sigma)$ of a command $c$ and a state $\sigma$.
nodes.title: IMP configuration

nodes.summary: The single-step relation $\to$ on IMP configurations is the smallest relation satisfying the following rules, for all variables $x$, arithmetic expressions $a$, Boolean expressions $b$, commands $c, c_1, c_1', c_2$ and states $\sigma, \sigma'$. Assignment: $(x := a, \sigma) \to (\mathtt{skip}, \sigma[x \mapsto v])$, where $v$ is the value of $a$ in $\sigma$. Sequencing:…
nodes.title: IMP small-step relation

nodes.summary: The relation $\to^*$ on IMP configurations is the reflexive, transitive closure of the small-step relation: $x \to^* y$ when $y$ is reached from $x$ by a finite sequence of zero or more small steps.
nodes.title: IMP multi-step relation

nodes.summary: A command $c$ terminates from an initial state $\sigma$ in a final state $\tau$ when the configuration $(c, \sigma)$ reaches $(\mathtt{skip}, \tau)$ in finitely many small steps.
nodes.title: Termination of an IMP command

nodes.summary: For all IMP configurations $x$, $y$, $z$, if $x$ steps to $y$ and $x$ steps to $z$ in one small step, then $y = z$.
nodes.title: Determinism of IMP small-step semantics

nodes.summary: For every IMP command $c$ and states $s$ and $s'$, if $c$ evaluates from $s$ to $s'$ in the big-step semantics, then $c$ started in $s$ terminates by small steps in $s'$: finitely many small steps lead from the configuration $(c, s)$ to $(\mathrm{skip}, s')$.
nodes.title: Big-step executions terminate in small steps

nodes.summary: Let $x = (c, s)$ and $y = (d, t)$ be configurations and $s'$ a state. If $x$ moves to $y$ in one small step and $d$ evaluates from $t$ to $s'$ in the big-step semantics, then $c$ evaluates from $s$ to $s'$ in the big-step semantics.
nodes.title: Prepending one small step to a big-step execution

nodes.summary: Let $x = (c, s)$ and $y = (d, t)$ be configurations and $s'$ a state. If $x$ reaches $y$ in finitely many (possibly zero) small steps and $d$ evaluates from $t$ to $s'$ in the big-step semantics, then $c$ evaluates from $s$ to $s'$ in the big-step semantics.
nodes.title: Prepending finitely many small steps to a big-step execution

nodes.summary: For every IMP command $c$ and states $s$ and $s'$, if $c$ started in $s$ terminates by small steps in $s'$, then $c$ evaluates from $s$ to $s'$ in the big-step semantics.
nodes.title: Small-step termination implies big-step evaluation

nodes.summary: For every IMP command $c$ and states $s$ and $s'$, $c$ started in $s$ terminates by small steps in $s'$ if and only if $c$ evaluates from $s$ to $s'$ in the big-step semantics.
nodes.title: Equivalence of small-step and big-step semantics

nodes.summary: For every IMP command $c$ and states $s$, $s_1$, $s_2$, if $c$ started in $s$ terminates by small steps in $s_1$ and also terminates by small steps in $s_2$, then $s_1 = s_2$.
nodes.title: Small-step termination is deterministic

nodes.summary: For assertions $P$ and $Q$ on states and an IMP command $c$, the partial-correctness Hoare triple with precondition $P$, command $c$ and postcondition $Q$ is valid if and only if, for all states $s$ and $s'$, whenever $P$ holds in $s$ and $c$ started in $s$ terminates by small steps in $s'$, $Q$ holds in $s'$.
nodes.title: Hoare validity via small-step termination

nodes.summary: A configuration of the stack machine is a triple $(pc, \sigma, s)$ of a program counter $pc \in \mathbb{N}$, a stack $\sigma$, which is a finite list of natural numbers whose head is the top of the stack, and a state $s$ assigning a natural number to each variable.
nodes.title: Stack machine configurations

A configuration $(pc, \sigma, s)$ steps to a configuration $c'$ under $P$ exactly when $pc < |P|$ and, for the instruction at position $pc$ of $P$ (counted from $0$), one of the following holds, where $s[x \mapsto v]$ is the state $s$ with variable $x$ set to $v$.
nodes.title: Step relation of the stack machine

nodes.summary: For a program $P$, the multi-step relation on configurations is the reflexive transitive closure of the step relation of the stack machine running $P$: it relates $c$ to $c'$ when $c'$ is obtained from $c$ by zero or more steps.
nodes.title: Multi-step execution of the stack machine

nodes.summary: For every program $P$, the step relation of the stack machine running $P$ is deterministic: if a configuration $x$ steps to $y$ and to $z$, then $y = z$. The fetched instruction and the shape of the stack determine the next configuration.
nodes.title: Determinism of the stack machine

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a program, that is a list of instructions, and let $(pc, \sigma, s)$ be a configuration with $|P| \le pc$. Then the stack machine running $P$ has no step from $(pc, \sigma, s)$ to any configuration, since there is no instruction at position $pc$ to fetch.
nodes.title: No step past the end of the program

nodes.summary: The instruction count $\ell(a)$ of an arithmetic expression $a$ is defined by recursion on $a$: a constant or a variable has count $1$, and if $a$ is the sum, difference or product of $a_1$ and $a_2$, then $\ell(a) = \ell(a_1) + \ell(a_2) + 1$.
nodes.title: Instruction count of an arithmetic expression

nodes.summary: The instruction count $\ell(b)$ of a Boolean expression $b$ is defined by recursion on $b$, using the instruction count $\ell(a)$ of arithmetic expressions $a$: a truth value has count $1$; the tests $a_1 = a_2$ and $a_1 \le a_2$ have count $\ell(a_1) + \ell(a_2) + 1$; the negation of $b_1$ has count $\ell(b_1) + 1$; and the conjunction of $b_1$ and $b_2$ has count $\ell(b_1) + \ell(b_2) + 1$.
nodes.title: Instruction count of a Boolean expression

nodes.summary: The compiled code of an arithmetic expression is the list of stack-machine instructions defined by recursion: a constant $n$ compiles to the single instruction push $n$, a variable $x$ to the single instruction load $x$, and the sum, difference or product of $a_1$ and $a_2$ to the code of $a_1$, then the code of $a_2$, then the single instruction add, sub or mul respectively.
nodes.title: Compilation of arithmetic expressions

nodes.summary: The compiled code of a Boolean expression is the list of stack-machine instructions defined by recursion, using the compiled code of arithmetic expressions: the truth value true compiles to the single instruction push $1$ and false to push $0$; the test $a_1 = a_2$ (respectively $a_1 \le a_2$) compiles to the code of $a_1$, then the code of $a_2$, then the equality (respectively order) test instruction; the…

Let $C_0(c)$ be the compiled code of $c$ at base program counter $0$ and $\ell(c)$ the instruction count of $c$.
