Denotational semantics of IMP

nodes.summary: Given a Boolean expression $b$ (the guard) and a binary relation $B$ on states (the body relation), the functional sends a relation $R$ on states to the relation that relates $s$ to $s'$ exactly when either $b$ evaluates to false in $s$ and $s' = s$, or $b$ evaluates to true in $s$ and there is a state $m$ with $B$ relating $s$ to $m$ and $R$ relating $m$ to $s'$.
nodes.title: One-step unfolding functional of a while loop

nodes.summary: Let $b$ be a Boolean expression, $B$ a binary relation on states, and $\Phi$ the one-step unfolding functional of a while loop with guard $b$ and body relation $B$. Then $\Phi$ is monotone for inclusion of relations: for all relations $R_1$ and $R_2$ on states with $R_1 \subseteq R_2$, we have $\Phi(R_1) \subseteq \Phi(R_2)$.
nodes.title: Monotonicity of the while-loop unfolding functional

nodes.summary: For a boolean guard $b$ and a relation $B$ between states (the body denotation), this is the map $\Phi$ on relations between states, ordered by inclusion, where $\Phi(R)$ relates $s$ to $s'$ exactly when either $b$ is false in $s$ and $s' = s$, or $b$ is true in $s$ and there is a state $m$ with $B(s, m)$ and $R(m, s')$. The map $\Phi$ is monotone: $R_1 \subseteq R_2$ implies $\Phi(R_1) \subseteq \Phi(R_2)$.
nodes.title: The while-loop functional as a monotone map

nodes.summary: The denotation of an IMP command is a binary relation on states, defined by recursion on the command. The command $\mathtt{skip}$ relates $s$ to $s'$ iff $s' = s$. For a variable identifier $x$ and an arithmetic expression $a$, the assignment $x := a$ relates $s$ to $s'$ iff $s'$ is $s$ with $x$ updated to the value of $a$ in $s$. The sequence $c_1; c_2$ relates $s$ to $s'$ iff there is a state $m$ such that $c_1$…
nodes.title: Relational denotational semantics of IMP

nodes.summary: Let $b$ be a Boolean expression and $c$ an IMP command, let $W$ be the relational denotation of $\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$, and let $\Phi$ be the one-step unfolding functional of a while loop with guard $b$ and body relation the denotation of $c$. Then $W = \Phi(W)$.
nodes.title: The while denotation is a fixed point

nodes.summary: For every Boolean expression $b$, IMP command $c$ and states $s$ and $s'$, the relational denotation of $\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$ relates $s$ to $s'$ if and only if either $b$ evaluates to false in $s$ and $s' = s$, or $b$ evaluates to true in $s$ and there is a state $m$ such that the denotation of $c$ relates $s$ to $m$ and the denotation of the loop relates $m$ to $s'$.
nodes.title: Unfolding equation for the while denotation

nodes.summary: Let $b$ be a Boolean expression, $c$ an IMP command and $P$ a binary relation on states, and let $\Phi$ be the one-step unfolding functional of a while loop with guard $b$ and body relation the denotation of $c$. If $\Phi(P) \subseteq P$, then for all states $s$ and $s'$ related by the relational denotation of $\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$, $P$ relates $s$ to $s'$.
nodes.title: Park induction for while loops

nodes.summary: For every IMP command $c$ and all states $s$ and $s'$, if the relational denotation of $c$ relates $s$ to $s'$, then executing $c$ from $s$ terminates in $s'$ according to the big-step semantics.
nodes.title: Denotational executions are big-step executions

nodes.summary: For every IMP command $c$ and all states $s$ and $s'$, if executing $c$ from $s$ terminates in $s'$ according to the big-step semantics, then the relational denotation of $c$ relates $s$ to $s'$.
nodes.title: Big-step executions are denotational executions

nodes.summary: For every IMP command $c$ and all states $s$ and $s'$, the relational denotation of $c$ relates $s$ to $s'$ if and only if executing $c$ from $s$ terminates in $s'$ according to the big-step semantics.
nodes.title: Agreement of the denotational and big-step semantics of IMP

nodes.summary: For every IMP command $c$ and all states $s$, $s_1$ and $s_2$, if the relational denotation of $c$ relates $s$ to $s_1$ and $s$ to $s_2$, then $s_1 = s_2$.
nodes.title: The denotational semantics of IMP is deterministic
Heap semantics of IMP

nodes.summary: A heap is a finite partial map from addresses to values, where addresses and values are natural numbers: it stores a value $v \in \mathbb{N}$ at each address of a finite set of addresses in $\mathbb{N}$, called the addresses allocated in the heap.
nodes.title: Heap

nodes.summary: Two heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$ are disjoint when no address is allocated in both: every address allocated in $h_1$ is not allocated in $h_2$.
nodes.title: Disjoint heaps

nodes.summary: For heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$, if $h_1$ and $h_2$ are disjoint, then $h_2$ and $h_1$ are disjoint.
nodes.title: Symmetry of heap disjointness

nodes.summary: For every heap $h$, the empty heap is disjoint from $h$ (with the empty heap as the first heap).
nodes.title: The empty heap is disjoint from every heap

nodes.summary: For every heap $h$, $h$ is disjoint from the empty heap (with the empty heap as the second heap).
nodes.title: Every heap is disjoint from the empty heap

nodes.summary: For heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$, let $h_1 \cup h_2$ be their left-biased union (at an address allocated in both it keeps the value from $h_1$). If the address $a$ is not allocated in $h_2$, then erasing $a$ from $h_1 \cup h_2$ gives the union of $h_2$ with the heap obtained from $h_1$ by erasing $a$, taken with that heap on the left.
nodes.title: Erasing an address that the right heap of a union lacks

nodes.summary: If heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$ are disjoint and the address $a$ is not allocated in $h_2$, then for every value $v$, the heap obtained from $h_1$ by inserting $a$ with value $v$ (overwriting any value $h_1$ stores at $a$) is disjoint from $h_2$.
nodes.title: Inserting an address the other heap lacks preserves disjointness

nodes.summary: If heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$ are disjoint, then for every address $a$, the heap obtained from $h_1$ by erasing $a$ (removing the address $a$ and its value) is disjoint from $h_2$.
nodes.title: Erasing an address preserves disjointness

nodes.summary: For every address $a$, value $v$ and heap $h$, the singleton heap that stores $v$ at $a$ and allocates no other address is disjoint from $h$ if and only if $a$ is not allocated in $h$.
nodes.title: Disjointness from a singleton heap

nodes.summary: If a heap $h$ stores the value $v$ at the address $a$, then erasing $a$ from $h$ and then inserting $a$ with value $v$ gives back $h$.
nodes.title: Reinserting an erased value restores the heap

nodes.summary: For every heap $h$ there is an address that is not allocated in $h$.
nodes.title: Every heap has a free address

nodes.summary: Heap commands extend the commands of IMP with heap operations. A heap command is one of: $\mathbf{skip}$; an assignment $x := a$; a sequence $c_1; c_2$; a conditional $\mathbf{if}\ b\ \mathbf{then}\ c_1\ \mathbf{else}\ c_2$; a loop $\mathbf{while}\ b\ \mathbf{do}\ c$; a heap read $x := [a]$; a heap write $[a] := e$; an allocation $x := \mathbf{alloc}(e)$; or a deallocation $\mathbf{free}(a)$. Here $x$ is a variable…
nodes.title: Heap commands

nodes.summary: A heap configuration is a triple $(c, s, h)$ of a heap command $c$, a store $s$ and a heap $h$.
nodes.title: Heap configurations

nodes.summary: The single-step relation $(c, s, h) \to (c', s', h')$ on heap configurations is the least relation closed under the rules below. Here $a(s)$ is the value of an expression $a$ in the store $s$, $s[x \mapsto n]$ is $s$ with variable $x$ set to $n$, $h[\ell \mapsto n]$ is $h$ with address $\ell$ set to $n$, and $h \setminus \ell$ is $h$ with address $\ell$ removed.
nodes.title: Small-step semantics of heap commands

nodes.summary: The relation $(c, s, h) \to^* (c', s', h')$ on heap configurations is the reflexive-transitive closure of the small-step relation: it holds when the first configuration reaches the second by a finite, possibly empty, sequence of small steps.
nodes.title: Multi-step heap execution

nodes.summary: A heap configuration, consisting of a heap command, a store and a heap, is safe when every heap configuration reachable from it in zero or more heap steps either has command $\mathtt{skip}$ or can take a further heap step.
nodes.title: Safe heap configurations

nodes.summary: If a heap configuration is safe and reaches a second configuration by finitely many (possibly zero) small steps, then the second configuration is safe.
nodes.title: Safety is preserved along executions

nodes.summary: Let $h$ and $h_f$ be disjoint heaps, $c$ a heap command and $s$ a store. If the configuration $(c, s, h)$ can take a small step, then so can $(c, s, h \cup h_f)$.
nodes.title: Adding a frame heap preserves the ability to step

nodes.summary: Let $h$ and $h_f$ be disjoint heaps, $c$ a heap command and $s$ a store, and suppose that the configuration $(c, s, h)$ can take a small step. If $(c, s, h \cup h_f)$ takes a small step to $(c', s', h'')$, then there is a heap $h_1$, disjoint from $h_f$, such that $(c, s, h)$ takes a small step to $(c', s', h_1)$ and $h'' = h_1 \cup h_f$.
nodes.title: Frame decomposition of a single heap step

nodes.summary: Let $h$ and $h_f$ be disjoint heaps, $c$ a heap command and $s$ a store, and suppose that the configuration $(c, s, h)$ is safe. If $(c, s, h \cup h_f)$ reaches $(c'', s'', h'')$ by finitely many (possibly zero) small steps, then there is a heap $h_2$, disjoint from $h_f$, such that $(c, s, h)$ reaches $(c'', s'', h_2)$ by finitely many small steps, $h'' = h_2 \cup h_f$, and $(c'', s'', h_2)$ is safe.
nodes.title: Frame decomposition of heap executions

nodes.summary: The embedding sends each plain IMP command to the heap command of the same shape: $\mathtt{skip}$ goes to $\mathtt{skip}$, an assignment of an arithmetic expression to a variable goes to the same assignment, a sequence goes to the sequence of the embeddings of its parts, and a conditional or while loop goes to the conditional or while loop with the same guard and with each subcommand replaced by its embedding.
nodes.title: Embedding of IMP into the heap language

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a plain IMP command, $s$ a store and $h$ a heap, and write $\overline{d}$ for the embedding of a plain command $d$ into the heap language. Then $(\overline{c}, s, h)$ takes a heap step to a heap configuration $K$ if and only if there are a plain command $c'$ and a store $s'$ such that $(c, s)$ takes a plain small step to $(c', s')$ and $K = (\overline{c'}, s', h)$.
nodes.title: Heap steps of embedded commands are plain steps

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a plain IMP command, $s$ a store and $h$ a heap, and write $\overline{d}$ for the embedding of a plain command $d$ into the heap language. If $(\overline{c}, s, h)$ reaches a heap configuration $(c_2, s_2, h_2)$ in zero or more heap steps, then $h_2 = h$ and there is a plain command $c_2'$ with $c_2 = \overline{c_2'}$ such that $(c, s)$ reaches $(c_2', s_2)$ in zero or more plain small steps.
nodes.title: Executions of embedded commands are plain executions

nodes.summary: Let $c, c_2$ be plain IMP commands, $s, s_2$ stores and $h$ a heap, and write $\overline{d}$ for the embedding of a plain command $d$ into the heap language. If $(c, s)$ reaches $(c_2, s_2)$ in zero or more plain small steps, then $(\overline{c}, s, h)$ reaches $(\overline{c_2}, s_2, h)$ in zero or more heap steps.
nodes.title: Plain executions lift to the heap language

nodes.summary: For every plain IMP command $c$ with embedding $\overline{c}$ into the heap language, every store $s$ and every heap $h$, the heap configuration $(\overline{c}, s, h)$ is safe.
nodes.title: Embedded plain commands are safe

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a plain IMP command with embedding $\overline{c}$ into the heap language, let $s, s'$ be stores and let $h$ be a heap. Then $c$ terminates from $s$ with final store $s'$ if and only if $(\overline{c}, s, h)$ reaches $(\mathtt{skip}, s', h)$ in zero or more heap steps.
nodes.title: Embedding preserves termination

nodes.summary: The set $\mathrm{mod}(c)$ of variables a heap command $c$ may assign to is defined by recursion on $c$. It is empty for $\mathbf{skip}$, a heap write $[a] := e$ and a deallocation $\mathbf{free}(a)$; it is $\{x\}$ for an assignment $x := a$, a heap read $x := [a]$ and an allocation $x := \mathbf{alloc}(e)$; it is $\mathrm{mod}(c_1) \cup \mathrm{mod}(c_2)$ for a sequence $c_1; c_2$ and for a conditional…
nodes.title: Modified variables of a heap command

nodes.summary: Write $\mathrm{mod}(c)$ for the set of variables a heap command $c$ may assign to. If the configuration $(c, s, h)$ takes a small step to $(c', s', h')$, then $\mathrm{mod}(c') \subseteq \mathrm{mod}(c)$.
nodes.title: Steps do not enlarge the modified variables

nodes.summary: If a heap configuration $(c, s, h)$ takes one heap step to $(c', s', h')$, then $s'(x) = s(x)$ for every variable $x$ outside the set of variables that $c$ may assign to.
nodes.title: A heap step only changes assignable variables

nodes.summary: If a heap configuration $(c, s, h)$ reaches a heap configuration $(c', s', h')$ in zero or more heap steps, then $s'(x) = s(x)$ for every variable $x$ outside the set of variables that $c$ may assign to.
nodes.title: Heap executions only change assignable variables
PCF and computational adequacy

nodes.summary: PCF types are the simple types over a single ground type, the type of natural numbers.
nodes.title: PCF types

nodes.summary: The ground type $\mathsf{nat}$ of natural numbers is the unique base type of PCF, whose types are the simple types over a single base type.
nodes.title: Natural number type of PCF

nodes.summary: PCF uses the typed de Bruijn variables of the simply typed $\lambda$-calculus over a single base type: a variable of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$ is a position in the list $\Gamma$ at which $A$ occurs.
nodes.title: PCF variables

nodes.summary: Write $\mathsf{nat}$ for the ground type of natural numbers and $A \Rightarrow B$ for the type of functions from $A$ to $B$. The intrinsically typed PCF terms of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$ (a list of PCF types) are generated by the following rules: every variable of type $A$ in $\Gamma$ is a term of type $A$; if $t$ has type $B$ in the context $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$, then $\lambda t$…
nodes.title: PCF terms

nodes.summary: For contexts $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ (lists of PCF types), a renaming from $\Gamma$ to $\Delta$ is a map sending each variable of $\Gamma$ of type $A$, for every type $A$, to a variable of $\Delta$ of the same type $A$; it is the STLC notion of renaming at PCF types.
nodes.title: PCF renamings

nodes.summary: A substitution from a context $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$ (lists of PCF types) assigns to every variable of $\Gamma$, of any type $A$, a PCF term of type $A$ in context $\Delta$.
nodes.title: Parallel substitutions for PCF

nodes.summary: For every context $\Gamma$ and natural number $n$, the numeral of $n$ is the term $\mathsf{succ}^n(\mathsf{zero})$ of type $\mathsf{nat}$ in $\Gamma$: the numeral of $0$ is $\mathsf{zero}$, and the numeral of $n + 1$ is $\mathsf{succ}$ applied to the numeral of $n$.
nodes.title: PCF numerals

nodes.summary: In every context, the map sending a natural number $n$ to the numeral $\mathsf{succ}^n(\mathsf{zero})$ of type $\mathsf{nat}$ is injective: distinct natural numbers give distinct numerals.
nodes.title: Injectivity of PCF numerals

nodes.summary: Given a renaming $\rho$ from a context $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$, the renaming along $\rho$ of a PCF term of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ is the term of type $A$ in context $\Delta$ obtained by replacing each variable $x$ by $\rho(x)$. Under a $\lambda$-binder, $\rho$ is replaced by its lift, which sends the bound variable to itself and the successor of each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to the successor of…
nodes.title: Renaming of PCF terms

nodes.summary: Let $\Gamma$ be a context and $A$, $B$ types. Weakening sends a PCF term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ to the term of type $A$ in the context obtained by prepending a new variable of type $B$ to $\Gamma$, by renaming every free variable of $t$ to its successor, that is, by shifting each de Bruijn index up by one.
nodes.title: Weakening of PCF terms

nodes.summary: For every context $\Gamma$, type $A$ and term $t$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$, renaming $t$ along the identity renaming of $\Gamma$ gives $t$.
nodes.title: Renaming a PCF term by the identity

nodes.summary: For every context $\Gamma$, the identity substitution from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma$ sends each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to the term consisting of $x$ alone.
nodes.title: Identity PCF substitution

nodes.summary: Given a substitution $\sigma$ from a context $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$ and a type $A$, the lift of $\sigma$ is the substitution from $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$ to $\Delta$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$ that sends the newest variable to the newest variable and every older variable $x$ to the weakening of $\sigma(x)$ by one variable.
nodes.title: Lifting a PCF substitution under a binder

nodes.summary: For a PCF term $a$ of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$, this is the substitution from the context $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$ to $\Gamma$ that sends the newest variable to $a$ and each older variable $x$ to the variable $x$ of $\Gamma$.
nodes.title: Single-variable substitution in PCF

nodes.summary: Given a substitution $\sigma$ from a context $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$ and a term $a$ of type $A$ in $\Delta$, the extended substitution goes from $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$ to $\Delta$: it sends the newest variable to $a$ and every older variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to $\sigma(x)$.
nodes.title: Extending a PCF substitution by a term

nodes.summary: Given a substitution $\sigma$ from a context $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$, applying $\sigma$ to a PCF term of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ gives the term of type $A$ in context $\Delta$ obtained by replacing each variable $x$ by $\sigma(x)$. Under a $\lambda$-binder, $\sigma$ is replaced by its lift, which sends the bound variable to itself and the successor of each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to the weakening of…
nodes.title: Substitution in PCF terms

nodes.summary: Given a term $b$ of type $B$ in a context $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$, and a term $a$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$, the instantiation of $b$ with $a$ is the term of type $B$ in $\Gamma$ obtained by applying to $b$ the substitution that sends the newest variable to $a$ and every older variable to itself.
nodes.title: Instantiating the newest variable of a PCF term

nodes.summary: Let $\rho$ be a renaming from a context $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$ and $\sigma$ a substitution from $\Delta$ to a context $\Xi$. For every PCF term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, applying $\sigma$ to the renaming of $t$ along $\rho$ gives the result of applying to $t$ the substitution from $\Gamma$ to $\Xi$ that sends each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to $\sigma(\rho(x))$.
nodes.title: Substitution after renaming in PCF

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution from a context $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$ and $\rho$ a renaming from $\Delta$ to a context $\Xi$. For every PCF term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, renaming along $\rho$ the result of applying $\sigma$ to $t$ gives the result of applying to $t$ the substitution from $\Gamma$ to $\Xi$ that sends each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to the renaming of $\sigma(x)$ along $\rho$.
nodes.title: Renaming after substitution in PCF

nodes.summary: Write $t[\sigma]$ for the result of applying a substitution $\sigma$ to a PCF term $t$. Let $\sigma$ be a substitution from a context $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$ and $\tau$ a substitution from $\Delta$ to a context $\Xi$. For every PCF term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, $t[\sigma][\tau] = t[\sigma']$, where $\sigma'$ is the substitution from $\Gamma$ to $\Xi$ that sends each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to…
nodes.title: Composition of PCF substitutions

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution from a context $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$, let $b$ be a term of type $B$ in $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$, and let $a$ be a term of type $A$ in $\Delta$. Applying the lift of $\sigma$ to $b$ and then instantiating the newest variable with $a$ gives the same term as applying to $b$ the extension of $\sigma$ by $a$, which sends the newest variable to $a$ and…
nodes.title: Instantiation after substitution under a binder

nodes.summary: A closed PCF term is a value when it is a $\lambda$-abstraction or the numeral $\mathsf{succ}^n\,\mathsf{zero}$ for some natural number $n$.
nodes.title: Values of PCF

nodes.summary: If a closed PCF term $v$ of the ground type of natural numbers is a value, then $v$ is the numeral $\mathsf{succ}^n\,\mathsf{zero}$ for some natural number $n$.
nodes.title: Closed values of ground type are numerals

nodes.summary: Write $\underline{n}$ for the numeral $\mathsf{succ}^n\,\mathsf{zero}$. For closed PCF terms $t$ and $v$ of the same type, $t \Downarrow v$ ($t$ evaluates to $v$) is the least relation closed under the following rules, where all terms are closed and $n$ ranges over natural numbers. Every $\lambda$-abstraction evaluates to itself, and $\mathsf{zero} \Downarrow \mathsf{zero}$. If $t \Downarrow \underline{n}$, then…
nodes.title: Big-step call-by-name evaluation of PCF

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$, the closed PCF numeral $\underline{n} = \mathsf{succ}^n\,\mathsf{zero}$ evaluates to itself under big-step call-by-name evaluation: $\underline{n} \Downarrow \underline{n}$.
nodes.title: Numerals evaluate to themselves

nodes.summary: For every type $A$ and every closed PCF term $v$ of type $A$ that is a value, $v \Downarrow v$ under big-step call-by-name evaluation.
nodes.title: PCF values evaluate to themselves

nodes.summary: For closed PCF terms $t$ and $v$ of the same type, if $t \Downarrow v$ under big-step call-by-name evaluation, then $v$ is a value.
nodes.title: PCF evaluation results are values

nodes.summary: For closed PCF terms $t$, $v$, $w$ of the same type, if $t \Downarrow v$ and $t \Downarrow w$ under big-step call-by-name evaluation, then $v = w$.
nodes.title: Determinism of PCF big-step evaluation

nodes.summary: The ω-complete partial order denoted by a PCF type is defined by recursion on the type: the ground type denotes the flat domain of partial natural numbers, and a function type $A \to B$ denotes the ω-complete partial order of Scott-continuous maps from the domain of $A$ to the domain of $B$.
nodes.title: Domain of a PCF type

nodes.summary: For every PCF type $A$, the domain denoted by $A$ has a least element, defined by recursion on $A$: at the ground type it is the undefined element of the flat domain of partial natural numbers, and at a function type $B \to C$ it is the continuous map that sends every argument to the least element of the domain denoted by $C$.
nodes.title: Least elements of PCF domains

nodes.summary: The ω-complete partial order of environments for a context $\Gamma$ (a list of PCF types) is defined by recursion on $\Gamma$: the empty context has the one-point order, and the environments for $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$ are the pairs $(\eta, a)$ of an environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$ and an element $a$ of the domain of $A$, ordered componentwise.
nodes.title: Semantic environments for PCF

nodes.summary: For a variable $x$ of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$, the lookup of $x$ is the Scott-continuous map from environments for $\Gamma$ to the domain of $A$ defined by recursion on $x$: if $x$ is the newest variable, it sends an environment $(\eta, a)$ to $a$; if $x$ is the shift of a variable $y$ of the older context, it sends $(\eta, a)$ to the lookup of $y$ at $\eta$.
nodes.title: Variable lookup in a PCF environment

nodes.summary: Let $\Gamma$ be a context, that is, a list of PCF types, and suppose that for every type $A$ and every variable $x$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$ we are given a value $f(x)$ in the domain denoted by $A$. The environment built from $f$ is the environment for $\Gamma$ defined by recursion on $\Gamma$: for the empty context it is the unique element of the one-point domain, and for the context obtained from $\Gamma'$ by…
nodes.title: Environment from a family of values

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an ω-complete partial order and let $t$, $s_1$, $s_2$ be Scott-continuous maps from $\alpha$ to the flat domain of partial natural numbers. Their strict zero test is the Scott-continuous map sending $x \in \alpha$ to $s_1(x)$ if $t(x)$ is defined and equal to $0$, to $s_2(x)$ if $t(x)$ is defined and nonzero, and to the undefined value if $t(x)$ is undefined.
nodes.title: Strict zero test as a continuous map

nodes.summary: The denotation of a PCF term $t$ of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$ is the Scott-continuous map $[\![t]\!]$ from environments for $\Gamma$ to the domain of $A$, defined by recursion on $t$: a variable denotes its lookup map; $[\![\lambda t]\!]$ is the currying of $[\![t]\!]$; $[\![f\,a]\!]\eta = [\![f]\!]\eta\,([\![a]\!]\eta)$; $[\![\mathsf{zero}]\!]$ is constantly the defined value $0$;…
nodes.title: Denotation of PCF terms

nodes.summary: For every PCF term $t$ of type $A \to A$ in a context $\Gamma$ and every environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$, the denotation of $\mathsf{fix}\,t$ at $\eta$ equals the denotation of the application $t\,(\mathsf{fix}\,t)$ at $\eta$.
nodes.title: Fixed-point equation for the PCF denotation of fix

nodes.summary: Let $\rho$ be a type-preserving renaming of the variables of a context $\Gamma$ into a context $\Delta$, let $t$ be a PCF term of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, and let $\eta$ be an environment for $\Delta$. Then the denotation at $\eta$ of the renaming of $t$ along $\rho$ equals the denotation of $t$ at the environment for $\Gamma$ that gives each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ the value of the variable $\rho(x)$ in…
nodes.title: PCF denotation of a renamed term

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a PCF term of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$, let $\eta$ be an environment for $\Gamma$, and let $b$ be an element of the domain of a type $B$. The denotation of the weakening of $t$ (the same term in the context $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $B$) at the extended environment $(\eta, b)$ equals the denotation of $t$ at $\eta$.
nodes.title: Weakening preserves the PCF denotation

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a type-preserving substitution assigning to each variable of a context $\Gamma$ a PCF term in a context $\Delta$, let $t$ be a term of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, and let $\eta$ be an environment for $\Delta$. Then the denotation at $\eta$ of the term obtained by applying $\sigma$ to $t$ equals the denotation of $t$ at the environment for $\Gamma$ that gives each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ the value…
nodes.title: PCF denotation of a substituted term

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a PCF term of type $B$ in the context $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$, let $a$ be a term of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, and let $\eta$ be an environment for $\Gamma$. Writing $[\![s]\!]\eta$ for the denotation of a term $s$ at $\eta$, the denotation at $\eta$ of the term obtained from $t$ by substituting $a$ for the newest variable equals $\![t]\!$, the denotation of $t$ at the…
nodes.title: PCF denotation of instantiation

nodes.summary: Write $\underline{n}$ for the numeral $\mathrm{succ}^n\,\mathrm{zero}$, and $b[a]$ for the result of substituting the closed term $a$ for the bound variable of an abstraction body $b$. One-step call-by-name reduction $t \to t'$ between closed PCF terms of the same type is the least relation closed under these rules: $f\,a \to f'\,a$ whenever $f \to f'$; $(\lambda b)\,a \to b[a]$, without evaluating $a$;…
nodes.title: Call-by-name reduction step of PCF

nodes.summary: For closed PCF terms $t$ and $t'$ of the same type, $t \to^* t'$ holds when $t$ reduces to $t'$ in finitely many, possibly zero, one-step call-by-name reductions; that is, $\to^*$ is the reflexive transitive closure of one-step reduction.
nodes.title: Multi-step call-by-name reduction of PCF

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$, the closed numeral $\mathrm{succ}^n\,\mathrm{zero}$ of type nat does not reduce: there is no closed term $t'$ such that $\mathrm{succ}^n\,\mathrm{zero}$ reduces to $t'$ in one call-by-name step.
nodes.title: PCF numerals are normal forms

nodes.summary: If $v$ is a closed PCF value of type $A$ (an abstraction or a numeral), then there is no closed term $t'$ such that $v$ reduces to $t'$ in one call-by-name step.
nodes.title: PCF values are normal forms

nodes.summary: One-step call-by-name reduction of closed PCF terms is deterministic: if a closed term $t$ of type $A$ reduces in one step to $t_1$ and also reduces in one step to $t_2$, then $t_1 = t_2$.
nodes.title: Determinism of PCF call-by-name reduction

nodes.summary: Let $t$ and $v$ be closed PCF terms of type $A$. If $t$ evaluates to $v$ in the big-step call-by-name semantics, then $t$ reduces to $v$ in finitely many (possibly zero) call-by-name steps.
nodes.title: Big-step evaluation implies reduction in PCF

nodes.summary: Let $t$, $t'$ and $v$ be closed PCF terms of type $A$. If $t$ reduces to $t'$ in one call-by-name step and $t'$ evaluates to $v$ in the big-step call-by-name semantics, then $t$ evaluates to $v$.
nodes.title: Backward reduction preserves evaluation in PCF

nodes.summary: Let $t$ and $v$ be closed PCF terms of type $A$. If $t$ reduces to $v$ in finitely many (possibly zero) call-by-name steps and $v$ is a value, then $t$ evaluates to $v$ in the big-step call-by-name semantics.
nodes.title: Reduction to a value implies big-step evaluation in PCF

nodes.summary: For closed PCF terms $t$ and $v$ of type $A$, $t$ evaluates to $v$ in the big-step call-by-name semantics if and only if $t$ reduces to $v$ in finitely many (possibly zero) call-by-name steps and $v$ is a value.
nodes.title: Big-step evaluation agrees with small-step reduction in PCF

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be a PCF type and let $t$ and $v$ be closed terms of type $A$. If $t$ evaluates to $v$ under big-step call-by-name evaluation, then for every environment $\eta$ of the empty context, the denotations of $t$ and $v$ at $\eta$ are equal.
nodes.title: Soundness of the PCF denotational semantics

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a closed PCF term of the ground type of natural numbers and let $n$ be a natural number. If $t$ evaluates to the numeral for $n$, then for every environment $\eta$ of the empty context, the denotation of $t$ at $\eta$ is the defined element $n$ of the flat domain of partial natural numbers.
nodes.title: Closed PCF terms that evaluate to a numeral denote its value

nodes.summary: For each PCF type $A$, the relation "$d$ formally approximates $t$" between an element $d$ of the domain of $A$ and a closed term $t$ of type $A$ is defined by recursion on $A$. At the ground type, whose domain is the flat domain of partial natural numbers, $d$ formally approximates $t$ when, for every natural number $n$ such that $d$ is defined with value $n$, the term $t$ evaluates to the numeral $n$. At a…
nodes.title: Formal approximation relation

nodes.summary: For every PCF type $A$ and every closed term $t$ of type $A$, the least element $\bot$ of the domain of $A$ formally approximates $t$.
nodes.title: The least element approximates every term

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be a PCF type, $t$ a closed term of type $A$ and $(c_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ a chain in the domain of $A$. If every $c_i$ formally approximates $t$, then the supremum $\bigsqcup_i c_i$ formally approximates $t$.

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a field with a linear order. Given weights in $K$ on $n$ experts and a binary advice (true or false) from each expert, the weighted majority vote is true when the total weight of the experts advising false is at most the total weight of the experts advising true, and false otherwise. In particular ties go to true.

If $W$ is the total weight of $w$ and $W'$ is the total weight after updating $w$ on $r$ with penalty $\beta$, then $2 W' \le (1 + \beta) W$.

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a joint probability law on $\alpha \times \beta$ with $\alpha$ and $\beta$ finite, the law of an attribute $X$ (first coordinate) and a label $Y$ (second coordinate). The information gain of splitting on $X$ for predicting $Y$ is the real number $H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)$, where $H(Y)$ is the Shannon entropy in bits of the marginal law of $Y$ and $H(Y \mid X)$ is the conditional entropy in bits of $Y$ given…
nodes.title: Information gain of a split

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a joint probability law on $\alpha \times \beta$ with $\alpha$ and $\beta$ finite, and let $p_X$ and $p_Y$ be its marginal laws on $\alpha$ and on $\beta$. Writing $H$ for Shannon entropy in bits, the information gain of $p$ equals $H(p_X) + H(p_Y) - H(p)$.
nodes.title: Information gain in terms of entropies

nodes.summary: For every joint probability law $p$ on $\alpha \times \beta$ with $\alpha$ and $\beta$ finite, the information gain of $p$ is at least $0$.
nodes.title: No split has negative information gain

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be finite sets carrying σ-algebras in which singletons are measurable, and let $p$ be a joint probability law on $\alpha \times \beta$. The information gain of $p$, regarded as an element of $[0, \infty]$, equals the mutual information in bits of $p$ viewed as a probability measure on $\alpha \times \beta$.
nodes.title: Information gain is mutual information

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be finite sets carrying σ-algebras in which singletons are measurable, and let $p$ be a joint probability law on $\alpha \times \beta$. The information gain of $p$ is zero if and only if $p$, as a measure, equals the product of its marginal law on $\alpha$ and its marginal law on $\beta$; that is, exactly when the attribute (first coordinate) and the label (second coordinate) are independent.
nodes.title: Zero information gain means independence

It describes the Gaussian distribution $N(m, P)$ when $P$ is positive semidefinite (the belief is valid); for other matrices Mathlib's multivariate Gaussian is a junk value. Prediction with positive semidefinite process noise, update with positive definite…

nodes.summary: A belief is valid when its covariance matrix is positive semidefinite.
nodes.title: Valid Gaussian beliefs

nodes.summary: The law of a belief with mean $m$ and covariance $P$ is Mathlib's multivariate Gaussian measure $N(m, P)$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. It is the Gaussian distribution with mean $m$ and covariance $P$ when $P$ is positive semidefinite (the belief is valid); otherwise it is the point mass at $m$.
nodes.title: Law of a belief

nodes.summary: Given real $n \times n$ matrices $F$ and $Q$, the prediction of a belief with mean $m$ and covariance $P$ is the belief with mean $F m$ and covariance $F P F^\top + Q$. It models the dynamics $x' = F x + w$ with process noise $w \sim N(0, Q)$.
nodes.title: Kalman prediction

nodes.summary: For a real $p \times n$ matrix $H$, a real $p \times p$ matrix $R$ and a belief with covariance $P$, the Kalman gain is the real $n \times p$ matrix $K = P H^\top (H P H^\top + R)^{-1}$, where the inverse is taken to be $0$ when $H P H^\top + R$ is singular.
nodes.title: Kalman gain

nodes.summary: Given a real $p \times n$ observation matrix $H$, a real $p \times p$ matrix $R$, an observation $y \in \mathbb{R}^p$ and a belief with mean $m$ and covariance $P$, the updated belief has mean $m + K (y - H m)$ and covariance $(I - K H) P$, where $K = P H^\top (H P H^\top + R)^{-1}$ is the Kalman gain and the matrix inverse is taken to be $0$ when $H P H^\top + R$ is singular.
nodes.title: Kalman filter update

nodes.summary: Given real $n \times n$ matrices $F$ and $Q$, a real $p \times n$ matrix $H$, a real $p \times p$ matrix $R$ and an observation $y \in \mathbb{R}^p$, one filter step sends a belief to the update, with $H$, $R$ and $y$, of its prediction with $F$ and $Q$.
nodes.title: Kalman filter step

nodes.summary: Let $F$ and $Q$ be real $n \times n$ matrices with $Q$ positive semidefinite. If a belief is valid, that is, its covariance $P$ is positive semidefinite, then the predicted belief, with covariance $F P F^\top + Q$, is valid.
nodes.title: Prediction preserves validity

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a real $p \times n$ matrix, $R$ a real $p \times p$ matrix and $y \in \mathbb{R}^p$, and let a belief have covariance $P$. Then the covariance of the belief updated with $H$, $R$ and $y$ equals $P - P H^\top (H P H^\top + R)^{-1} H P$. Here $M^{-1}$ is the matrix inverse, taken to be $0$ when $M$ is singular, so no invertibility is assumed.
nodes.title: Schur form of the updated covariance

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a real $p \times n$ matrix, $R$ a symmetric positive definite real $p \times p$ matrix and $y \in \mathbb{R}^p$. If a belief is valid, then the belief updated with $H$, $R$ and $y$ is valid.

nodes.summary: Let $F$ and $Q$ be real $n \times n$ matrices with $Q$ positive semidefinite, $H$ a real $p \times n$ matrix, $R$ a positive definite real $p \times p$ matrix and $y \in \mathbb{R}^p$. nodes.title: Chain of conditional distributions

nodes.summary: For a chain of conditional distributions with values in a type $\alpha$, write $p_k(\cdot \mid x_0, \dots, x_{k-1})$ for the conditional distribution of variable $k$ given the earlier ones. The joint distribution $P_n : \alpha^n \to \mathbb{R}$ of the first $n$ variables is defined by the chain rule: $P_0 = 1$ and $P_{n+1}(x_0, \dots, x_n) = P_n(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}) \, p_n(x_n \mid x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$.

For every $n$ and every $y = (y_0, \dots, y_{n-1}) \in \alpha^n$, $\sum_{a \in \alpha} P_{n+1}(y_0, \dots, y_{n-1}, a) = P_n(y)$.

Then for every $n$ and every $x \in \alpha^n$ we have $P_n(x) = \prod_{k < n} p_k(x_k \mid x_0, \dots, x_{k-1})$.

nodes.summary: Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. If two chains of conditional distributions $c$ and $c'$ with values in a type $\alpha$ have the same conditional distribution of variable $k$ given the earlier variables for every $k < n$, then they have the same joint distribution of the first $n$ variables.
nodes.title: Joint distribution determined by the first conditionals

nodes.summary: Given a chain $c$ of conditional distributions with values in $\alpha$, an index $n$ and a family $f$ assigning to each $y \in \alpha^n$ a probability distribution $f(y)$ on $\alpha$, the updated chain has conditional distribution $f$ for variable $n$ and the same conditional distribution as $c$ for every other variable.
nodes.title: Replacing one conditional of a chain

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite nonempty type and $n \in \mathbb{N}$. For every function $P : \alpha^n \to \mathbb{R}$ with $P(x) \ge 0$ for all $x$ and $\sum_x P(x) = 1$, there is a chain of conditional distributions with values in $\alpha$ whose joint distribution of the first $n$ variables equals $P$.
nodes.title: The chain rule

nodes.summary: A Bayesian network with values in a type $\alpha$ on the nodes $0, \dots, n - 1$, listed in a topological order, assigns to each node $k$ a finite set of parents among the earlier nodes $0, \dots, k - 1$, and a conditional probability table: for each assignment of values in $\alpha$ to the parents of $k$, a finitely supported probability distribution on $\alpha$ for the value of node $k$.
nodes.title: Bayesian network

nodes.summary: A Bayesian network $b$ on nodes $0, \dots, n - 1$ with values in a nonempty type $\alpha$ defines a chain of conditional distributions. For $k < n$, the conditional distribution of variable $k$ given values $y_0, \dots, y_{k-1}$ of the earlier variables is the table of node $k$ applied to the values $y_j$ of its parents $j$. For $k \ge n$ it is the point mass at a fixed arbitrary element of $\alpha$.
nodes.title: The chain of a Bayesian network

nodes.summary: Let $B$ be a Bayesian network on the nodes $0, \dots, n - 1$ with values in a nonempty type $\alpha$. The joint distribution of $B$ is the function $P : \alpha^n \to \mathbb{R}$ given by $P(x) = P_n(x)$ for $x \in \alpha^n$, where $P_n$ is the joint distribution of the first $n$ variables of the chain of conditional distributions of $B$.
nodes.title: Joint distribution of a Bayesian network

nodes.summary: The joint is the product over nodes of the probability of the node's value given the values of its parents.
nodes.title: Factorization of a Bayesian network

nodes.summary: Let $B$ be a Bayesian network on the nodes $0, \dots, n - 1$ with values in a finite nonempty type $\alpha$, and let $P$ be its joint distribution. Then $\sum_{x \in \alpha^n} P(x) = 1$.
nodes.title: The joint distribution of a Bayesian network sums to one

nodes.summary: Let $B$ be a Bayesian network on the nodes $0, \dots, n - 1$ with values in a nonempty type $\alpha$, and let $P_m$ be the joint distribution of the first $m$ nodes of $B$ viewed as a chain of conditional distributions. For a node $k < n$, write $p_k(\cdot \mid z)$ for its conditional probability table at values $z$ of its parents. Let $y = (y_0, \dots, y_{k-1}) \in \alpha^k$ with $P_k(y) \ne 0$, and write…

nodes.summary: `FiniteWeight.marginal` on a `Finset` of nodes, as a sum over a decidable filter.

nodes.summary: `marginal P S x'` depends only on the values of `x'` on `S`.

nodes.summary: Fixing more variables decreases the probability.
nodes.title: Fixing more variables decreases the marginal

nodes.summary: Summing out one more variable `i ∉ S`.

nodes.summary: Conditional independence is symmetric.

nodes.summary: If `X ⫫ Y | Z` then `X' ⫫ Y | Z` for `X' ⊆ X`.
nodes.title: Decomposition

nodes.summary: If `X ∪ W ⫫ Y | Z` then `X ⫫ Y | Z ∪ W` (for a nonnegative law).
nodes.title: Weak union

nodes.summary: A set of nodes is ancestral if it contains the parents of each of its nodes.
nodes.title: Ancestral set of nodes

nodes.summary: The product of the tables of the nodes in `A`, with the uniform distribution on the other nodes. For an ancestral `A` it has the same marginals on `A` as the joint (`marginal_joint_eq_ancProd`).
nodes.title: Product of the tables of an ancestral set

nodes.summary: On all nodes, `ancProd` is the joint.
nodes.title: The ancestral product on all nodes is the joint

nodes.summary: For an ancestral set `A` and `S ⊆ A`, the marginals of the joint on `S` are those of `ancProd A`.
nodes.title: The law of an ancestral set depends only on its tables

nodes.summary: The global Markov property for `Finset`s of nodes; `condIndep_of_dSeparated` is the statement for arbitrary sets of nodes.
nodes.title: Global Markov property for finite sets of nodes

nodes.summary: The global Markov property (soundness of d-separation: Geiger, Verma & Pearl 1990; Lauritzen, Dawid, Larsen & Leimer 1990): if `Z` d-separates `X` from `Y` in the graph of a Bayesian network, then `X` and `Y` are conditionally independent given `Z` under its joint law. nodes.summary: The values of the parents of node `k` in a full assignment `x`.

(The new table of `k` is the point mass on the empty parent set; the tables of the other nodes are transported along the equality of their parent sets.)

nodes.summary: The parents of the intervened node are deleted.
nodes.title: Intervention deletes the parents of the intervened node

nodes.summary: The parents of every other node are unchanged by the intervention.
nodes.title: Intervention leaves the parents of other nodes unchanged

nodes.title: The truncated factorization

nodes.summary: The intervention `do(X_k = a)` does not change the law of the parents of node `k`.

nodes.summary: Adjustment for the direct causes (Pearl 2009, Theorem 3.2.2; the case `Z = pa(X)` of the back-door adjustment): for every function `f` of the variables, `E[f | do(X_k = a)] = ∑_z P(pa_k = z) E[f | X_k = a, pa_k = z]`, assuming `P(X_k = a, pa_k = z) > 0` whenever `P(pa_k = z) > 0`.
nodes.title: Adjustment for the direct causes

nodes.summary: The table of node `k` is the conditional law of `X_k` given its parents: `P(X_k = a, pa_k = z) = p_k (a | z) P(pa_k = z)`.
nodes.title: A node's table is its conditional law given its parents

nodes.summary: Adjustment for the direct causes when the table of node `k` gives the value `a` positive probability at every value of the parents.
nodes.title: Adjustment for the direct causes under table positivity

nodes.summary: Let `Z` be a set of nodes preceding `k` in the topological order (so `Z` contains no descendant of `k`) that contains the parents of `k`. Then `Z` meets the back-door criterion for every outcome node `y ∉ Z` (a path from `k` to `y` that starts with an arrow into `k` starts `k ← p` with `p ∈ pa(k) ⊆ Z`, an interior non-collider, so it is blocked), and for every function `f` of the variables…
nodes.title: Back-door adjustment for a set of predecessors containing the parents

nodes.summary: For a set `Z` of predecessors of `k` containing its parents, the table of `k` is its conditional law given `Z`: `P(X_k = a, Z = z) = p_k (a | z_{pa k}) P(Z = z)`.
nodes.title: A node's table is its conditional law given a predecessor set

nodes.summary: Back-door adjustment for a set of predecessors containing the parents, when the table of node `k` gives the value `a` positive probability at every value of the parents.
nodes.title: Back-door adjustment for a set of predecessors

nodes.summary: The edge `i → j` of the network's graph: `i` is a parent of `j`.
nodes.title: Edge of a Bayesian network

nodes.summary: `j` is a descendant of `i` (every node is its own descendant).
nodes.title: Descendant relation in a Bayesian network

nodes.summary: `i` and `j` are adjacent in the skeleton of the graph.
nodes.title: Adjacency in the skeleton of a Bayesian network

nodes.summary: A path of the skeleton from `x` to `y`: a list of distinct nodes, consecutive ones adjacent, starting at `x` and ending at `y`.
nodes.title: Path in the skeleton of a Bayesian network

nodes.summary: The consecutive nodes `u, m, w` of a path are blocked by `Z` (Pearl 2009, Definition 1.2.3): either `m` is a collider `u → m ← w` none of whose descendants is in `Z`, or `m` is not a collider (a chain or a fork) and `m ∈ Z`.

nodes.summary: A path is blocked by `Z` if some three consecutive nodes of it are.
nodes.title: Blocked path

nodes.summary: d-separation (Pearl 1988; Pearl 2009, Definition 1.2.3): `Z` d-separates `X` from `Y` if every path between a node of `X` and a node of `Y` is blocked by `Z`.
nodes.title: d-separation

nodes.summary: Blocking at a node does not depend on the direction in which the path is read.
nodes.title: Blocking at a node is independent of path direction

nodes.summary: The reverse of a path from `x` to `y` is a path from `y` to `x`.

nodes.summary: If a path is blocked by `Z`, so is its reverse.
nodes.title: Reversal preserves blocked paths

nodes.summary: Symmetry of d-separation. d-separation is symmetric.
nodes.title: Symmetry of d-separation

nodes.summary: The network of the intervention `do(X_W = w)` with the arrows into `W` removed: every node `j ∈ W` has no parents and the point mass at `w j` as its table.

nodes.summary: After `do(X_W = w)`, the joint is the product of the tables of the nodes outside `W` on assignments agreeing with `w` on `W`.
nodes.title: The truncated factorization for a set of nodes

nodes.summary: The arrows of `b.mutilateSet W w` are those of `b` not pointing into `W`.
nodes.title: Arrows of the mutilated network

nodes.summary: A descendant after removing the arrows into `W` is a descendant in `b`.
nodes.title: Descendants in the mutilated network are descendants in the original

nodes.summary: After removing the arrows into `W`, a node of `W` is a descendant only of itself.
nodes.title: Intervened nodes descend only from themselves

nodes.summary: After `do(X_k = a)`, assignments with `x k ≠ a` have probability `0`.
nodes.title: Assignments contradicting an intervention have probability zero

nodes.summary: For `x k = a`, `P(x) = P(x | do(X_k = a)) · p_k(a | x_{pa k})`.
nodes.title: Joint law as interventional law times the node's table

nodes.summary: The intervention `do(X_k = a)` does not change the law of the non-descendants of `k`.
nodes.title: The intervention `do(X_k = a)` does not change the law of the non-descendants of `k`

nodes.summary: The back-door adjustment (Pearl 1995; Pearl 2009, Theorem 3.3.2): if the set `Z` contains no descendant of the treatment node `k` and blocks every path between `k` and the outcome node `y` that begins with an arrow into `k`, then `P(X_y = v | do(X_k = a)) = ∑_z P(Z = z) P(X_y = v | X_k = a, Z = z)`, assuming `P(X_k = a, Z = z) > 0` whenever `P(Z = z) > 0`.
nodes.title: The back-door adjustment

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be finite and consider a pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$ with unary factors $\varphi_i$ and pairwise factors $\psi_k$. The message from the last vertex $n + 1$ to its parent is the function $\mu : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ given by $\mu(a) = \sum_{b \in \alpha} \psi_n(b, a) \, \varphi_{n+1}(b)$, where $\psi_n$ is the factor of the edge between vertex $n + 1$ and its parent.

nodes.title: One step of variable elimination

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be finite. The root message of a pairwise tree model $m$ on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ is the function $r_m : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by recursion on $n$: if $n = 0$, it is the unary factor of the root $0$; if $m$ is a model on the vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$, it is $r_{m'}$, where $m'$ is the model on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ obtained from $m$ by eliminating the last vertex.
nodes.title: Root message of a tree model

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be finite and let $m$ be a pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ with weight $w$ and root message $r : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$. Then for every function $g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ of the root value, $\sum_x w(x) \, g(x_0) = \sum_{a \in \alpha} r(a) \, g(a)$, where $x$ ranges over all assignments $\{0, \dots, n\} \to \alpha$.
nodes.title: Variable elimination is exact

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be finite and let $m$ be a pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ with weight $w$ and root message $r : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$. Then the partition function of $m$ is the total root message: $\sum_x w(x) = \sum_{a \in \alpha} r(a)$, where $x$ ranges over all assignments $\{0, \dots, n\} \to \alpha$.
nodes.title: Variable elimination computes the partition function

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be finite and let $m$ be a pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ with weight $w$ and root message $r : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$. Then for every $a \in \alpha$ the unnormalized marginal of the root at $a$ equals $r(a)$, that is, $\sum_x w(x) = r(a)$, where $x$ ranges over the assignments $\{0, \dots, n\} \to \alpha$ with $x_0 = a$.

nodes.summary: Comparison and distribution sorting algorithms (including their expected-cost analyses), and searching and selection in lists and arrays (binary and linear search, quickselect, median of medians, simultaneous min-max). Comparator sorting networks, their depth and the 0-1 principle form the Sorting networks subfield.
nodes.title: Sorting and searching

nodes.summary: Comparator networks that sort: the bubble network, Batcher's bitonic and odd–even merge networks, depth bounds, and the zero-one and permutation principles.
nodes.title: Sorting networks
Sorting networks and the zero-one principle

nodes.summary: A comparator network on $n$ wires is a finite list of pairs $(i, j)$ of wires $i, j \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, each pair standing for the comparator $(i, j)$; the comparators are applied in list order.
nodes.title: Comparator network

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linear order, let $n$ be a natural number, and let $v$ assign a value $v(k) \in \alpha$ to each wire $k \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$. For wires $i$ and $j$, the comparator $(i, j)$ sends $v$ to the assignment that has $\min(v(i), v(j))$ on wire $i$, $\max(v(i), v(j))$ on wire $j$ when $j \ne i$, and $v(k)$ on every other wire $k$.
nodes.title: Comparator

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linear order. The output of a comparator network on an assignment $v$ of a value in $\alpha$ to each of its $n$ wires is obtained by starting from $v$ and applying the comparators of the network one after another, in list order.
nodes.title: Running a comparator network

nodes.summary: A comparator network on $n$ wires sorts inputs over a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ if, for every input $v$ assigning a value in $\alpha$ to each wire, the output of running the network on $v$ is monotone in the wire order: for all wires $i \le j$, the output value on wire $i$ is at most the output value on wire $j$.
nodes.title: Networks that sort

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be linear orders, let $f : \alpha \to \beta$ be monotone, and let $n$ be a natural number. For all wires $i, j \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ and every assignment $v$ of a value in $\alpha$ to each wire, the comparator $(i, j)$ applied to $f \circ v$ gives $f \circ w$, where $w$ is the output of the comparator $(i, j)$ on $v$.
nodes.title: Comparators commute with monotone maps

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be linear orders and let $f : \alpha \to \beta$ be monotone. For every comparator network on $n$ wires and every assignment $v$ of a value in $\alpha$ to each wire, the output of the network on $f \circ v$ is $f \circ w$, where $w$ is the output of the network on $v$.
nodes.title: Networks commute with monotone maps

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linear order and let $n$ be a natural number. For all wires $i, j \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ and every assignment $v$ of a value in $\alpha$ to each wire, there is a permutation $\sigma$ of the wires such that the output of the comparator $(i, j)$ on $v$ is $v \circ \sigma$.
nodes.title: A comparator permutes its inputs

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linear order. For every comparator network on $n$ wires and every assignment $v$ of a value in $\alpha$ to each wire, there is a permutation $\sigma$ of the wires such that the output of the network on $v$ is $v \circ \sigma$.
nodes.title: The output of a comparator network is a permutation of its input

nodes.summary: The 0-1 principle (CLRS Theorem 27.2): a network that sorts every Boolean input sorts every input over every linear order.
nodes.title: The 0-1 principle

nodes.summary: The Boolean sorting test of a comparator network on $n$ wires returns true exactly when, for every assignment $v$ of a Boolean value to each wire, the output $w$ of the network on $v$ satisfies $w(i) \le w(j)$ for all wires $i \le j$, where $\mathrm{false} < \mathrm{true}$.
nodes.title: Boolean sorting test

nodes.summary: A comparator network passes the Boolean sorting test if and only if it sorts inputs over the Booleans, that is, for every assignment of a Boolean value to each wire, the output of the network is monotone in the wire order.
nodes.title: The Boolean sorting test is correct

nodes.summary: If a comparator network on $n$ wires passes the Boolean sorting test, then for every linear order $\alpha$ it sorts inputs over $\alpha$: for every assignment $v$ of a value in $\alpha$ to each wire, the output of the network on $v$ is monotone in the wire order.
nodes.title: A network that passes the Boolean sorting test sorts over every linear order

nodes.summary: For a Boolean input $v$ on $n$ wires, the spread of $v$ is the input with natural-number values whose value on wire $i < n$ is $n + i$ if $v(i)$ is true and $i$ if $v(i)$ is false.
nodes.title: Spread of a Boolean input

nodes.summary: For every Boolean input $v$ on $n$ wires, applying the threshold map that sends a natural number $k$ to true if $n \le k$ and to false otherwise to the spread of $v$ gives back $v$: for every wire $i$, the spread of $v$ at $i$ is at least $n$ exactly when $v(i)$ is true.
nodes.title: A Boolean input is a threshold of its spread

nodes.summary: A network that sorts every input with distinct natural values sorts every input over every linear order.
nodes.title: Sorting distinct inputs suffices

nodes.summary: For a map $w$ from $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ to the natural numbers and an index $i < n$, the rank of $w(i)$ among the values of $w$ is the number of indices $j < n$ with $w(j) < w(i)$. It is less than $n$, so it is again an index in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$.
nodes.title: Rank among the values of an input

nodes.summary: For an injective map $w$ from $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ to the natural numbers, the ranking permutation of $w$ is the permutation of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ that sends each $i$ to the rank of $w(i)$ among the values of $w$, that is, to the number of indices $j$ with $w(j) < w(i)$. Since $w$ is injective, this map is a bijection.
nodes.title: The ranking permutation

nodes.summary: A comparator network on $n$ wires that sorts each of the $n!$ permutations $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, viewed as the input whose value on wire $i$ is $\sigma(i)$, sorts every input over every linear order.
nodes.title: The permutation principle
Bitonic sorter

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linear order. For wires $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$ and an assignment $f$ of values in $\alpha$ to the wires $x \in \mathbb{N}$, the comparator $(i, j)$ applied to $f$ puts $\min(f(i), f(j))$ on wire $i$, puts $\max(f(i), f(j))$ on wire $j$ when $j \ne i$, and leaves every other wire unchanged.
nodes.title: Comparator on natural-number-indexed wires

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linear order. Given a list $ps$ of comparators, each a pair $(i, j)$ of natural numbers, and an input $f : \mathbb{N} \to \alpha$ giving the value on each wire, running $ps$ on $f$ applies the comparators of $ps$ to the wire values one after another, from first to last. The comparator $(i, j)$ puts the minimum of the values on wires $i$ and $j$ on wire $i$ and their maximum on wire $j$, and leaves…
nodes.title: Running a comparator network on natural-number-indexed wires

nodes.summary: A list $ps$ of comparators, each a pair $(i, j)$ of natural numbers, lies within $[l, h)$ if every comparator $(i, j)$ in $ps$ satisfies $l \le i < h$ and $l \le j < h$.
nodes.title: Comparators within an interval

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linear order and let $ps$ be a list of comparators $(i, j)$ on $\mathbb{N}$-indexed wires that all lie within $[l, h)$, that is, $l \le i < h$ and $l \le j < h$ for every $(i, j)$ in $ps$. Then for every input $f : \mathbb{N} \to \alpha$ and every wire $x$ with $x < l$ or $h \le x$, the value of wire $x$ after running $ps$ on $f$ is $f(x)$.
nodes.title: Locality of comparator networks

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linear order, let $l, h \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $c$ be a list of comparators on $\mathbb{N}$-indexed wires each of which joins two wires $x$ with $l \le x < h$. If an input $f : \mathbb{N} \to \alpha$ takes the same value $a$ on every wire $x$ with $l \le x < h$, then running $c$ on $f$ gives an output that also takes the value $a$ on every such wire.
nodes.title: Constant blocks stay constant

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $m$ and $b$, the half-cleaner on the block of wires $[b, b + 2m)$ is the list of comparators $(b + i, b + m + i)$ for $i = 0, 1, \dots, m - 1$, in this order: it compares wire $b + i$ with wire $b + m + i$.
nodes.title: Half-cleaner

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linear order, let $m, b \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \alpha$ be an input on $\mathbb{N}$-indexed wires. Running the half-cleaner on $[b, b + 2m)$ on $f$ puts $\min(f(b + i), f(b + m + i))$ on wire $b + i$ and $\max(f(b + i), f(b + m + i))$ on wire $b + m + i$ for every $i < m$, and leaves the value $f(x)$ on every wire $x$ outside $[b, b + 2m)$ unchanged.
nodes.title: Output of the half-cleaner

nodes.summary: A sequence $s : \mathbb{N} \to \{0, 1\}$ is an interval indicator of length $L$ if there are natural numbers $a \le e \le L$ such that for every $i < L$, $s(i) = 1$ exactly when $a \le i < e$.
nodes.title: Interval indicators

nodes.summary: A sequence $s : \mathbb{N} \to \{0, 1\}$ is bitonic of length $L$ if either $s$ or its complement $1 - s$ is an interval indicator of length $L$; that is, on the positions $0, \dots, L - 1$ it has the form $0^a 1^b 0^c$ or $1^a 0^b 1^c$. Values of $s$ at positions $i \ge L$ are unconstrained.
nodes.title: Bitonic 0-1 sequences

nodes.summary: Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $s_0, s_1, \dots, s_{2m-1}$ be a bitonic sequence of Booleans, ordered by $\mathrm{false} < \mathrm{true}$. For $i < m$ put $\ell_i = \min(s_i, s_{i+m})$ and $u_i = \max(s_i, s_{i+m})$. Then either $\ell_i = \mathrm{false}$ for every $i < m$ and $u_0, \dots, u_{m-1}$ is bitonic, or $u_i = \mathrm{true}$ for every $i < m$ and $\ell_0, \dots, \ell_{m-1}$ is bitonic.
nodes.title: The half-cleaner lemma

nodes.summary: A Boolean sequence $g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathrm{Bool}$ is sorted on the block $[b, b + L)$ if $g(b + i) \le g(b + j)$ for all $i \le j < L$, where Booleans are ordered by $\mathrm{false} < \mathrm{true}$.
nodes.title: Sorted on a block

nodes.summary: The bitonic merger on the block of wires $[b, b + 2^k)$ is the list of comparators defined by recursion on $k$. For $k = 0$ it is empty. On the block $[b, b + 2^{k+1})$ it is the half-cleaner on $[b, b + 2^{k+1})$, followed by the bitonic merger on $[b, b + 2^k)$, followed by the bitonic merger on $[b + 2^k, b + 2^{k+1})$.
nodes.title: Bitonic merger

nodes.summary: Let $k, b \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $f$ assign a Boolean value to each wire $x \in \mathbb{N}$, with Booleans ordered by $\mathrm{false} < \mathrm{true}$. If the sequence $f(b), f(b + 1), \dots, f(b + 2^k - 1)$ is bitonic, then running the bitonic merger on the block $[b, b + 2^k)$ on $f$ gives an assignment $g$ that is sorted on that block: $g(b + i) \le g(b + j)$ whenever $i \le j < 2^k$.
nodes.title: The bitonic merger sorts every bitonic `0`-`1` input

nodes.summary: Let $ps$ be a list of comparators on $\mathbb{N}$-indexed wires and let $ps'$ be obtained by replacing each comparator $(i, j)$ in $ps$ by $(j, i)$. For every input $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathrm{Bool}$ and every wire $x$, the value of wire $x$ after running $ps'$ on $f$ is the negation of the value of wire $x$ after running $ps$ on the complemented input $y \mapsto \lnot f(y)$.
nodes.title: Reversing the comparators conjugates the network by complement on Booleans

nodes.summary: A comparator $(i, j)$ puts the minimum of the values on wires $i$ and $j$ on wire $i$ and the maximum on wire $j$. Batcher's bitonic sorter on the block of wires $[b, b + 2^k)$ is the list of comparators defined by recursion on $k$. For $k = 0$ it is empty. On the block $[b, b + 2^{k+1})$ it is Batcher's bitonic sorter on $[b, b + 2^k)$, followed by Batcher's bitonic sorter on $[b + 2^k, b + 2^{k+1})$ with every…
nodes.title: Batcher's bitonic sorter on a block of wires

nodes.summary: Let $k, b \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $f$ assign a Boolean value to each wire $x \in \mathbb{N}$, with Booleans ordered by $\mathrm{false} < \mathrm{true}$. Running Batcher's bitonic sorter on the block $[b, b + 2^k)$ on $f$ gives an assignment $g$ that is sorted on that block: $g(b + i) \le g(b + j)$ whenever $i \le j < 2^k$.
nodes.title: The bitonic sorter sorts every `0`-`1` input

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $m$ and $b$, the half-cleaner on the block of wires $[b, b + 2m)$ has exactly $m$ comparators.
nodes.title: Size of the half-cleaner

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $k$ and $b$, the bitonic merger on the block of wires $[b, b + 2^k)$ has $k \cdot 2^{k-1}$ comparators; precisely, twice its number of comparators equals $k \cdot 2^k$.
nodes.title: Size of the bitonic merger

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $k$ and $b$, the bitonic sorter on the block of $\mathbb{N}$-indexed wires $[b, b + 2^k)$ has $k(k+1)2^k/4$ comparators; precisely, four times its number of comparators equals $k(k+1)2^k$.
nodes.title: Size of the bitonic sorter on a block of wires

nodes.summary: For a natural number $N$ and a list of comparators on wires indexed by $\mathbb{N}$, this is the network on the $N$ wires $0, \dots, N - 1$ that keeps, in their original order, the comparators $(i, j)$ with $i < N$ and $j < N$, and drops all the others.
nodes.title: Restricting comparators to finitely many wires

nodes.summary: For $N \in \mathbb{N}$ and a Boolean vector $v = (v_0, \dots, v_{N-1})$, its extension by $\mathrm{false}$ is the function on $\mathbb{N}$ that takes the value $v_j$ at each $j < N$ and the value $\mathrm{false}$ at each $j \ge N$.
nodes.title: Extension of a Boolean vector by false

nodes.summary: Let $N \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $P$ be a list of comparators on natural-number-indexed wires, each of which joins two wires below $N$. For every Boolean input $v$ on the wires $0, \dots, N - 1$, run the network on $N$ wires obtained from $P$ on $v$ and extend its output by $\mathrm{false}$ to all wires in $\mathbb{N}$; the result equals the result of running $P$ on the extension of $v$ by $\mathrm{false}$.
nodes.title: Transported comparator lists agree with the original on Boolean inputs

nodes.summary: For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, Batcher's bitonic sorting network on $2^k$ wires is the comparator network on the wires $0, 1, \dots, 2^k - 1$ made of the comparators of Batcher's bitonic sorter on the block $[0, 2^k)$ that join two wires below $2^k$ (in fact all of them), applied in the same order.
nodes.title: Batcher's bitonic sorting network

nodes.summary: For every $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and every linearly ordered type $\alpha$, Batcher's bitonic sorting network on $2^k$ wires sorts inputs over $\alpha$: for every assignment $v$ of elements of $\alpha$ to the wires $0, 1, \dots, 2^k - 1$, the output of the network on $v$ is monotone in the wire order.
nodes.title: Batcher's bitonic sorter sorts every input over every linear order

nodes.summary: For every natural number $k$, Batcher's bitonic sorting network on $2^k$ wires has $k(k+1)2^k/4$ comparators; precisely, four times its number of comparators equals $k(k+1)2^k$.
nodes.title: Comparator count of Batcher's bitonic sorter
Bubble sorting network

nodes.summary: For $n$ wires and an index $i$, this is the comparator on wires $i$ and $i + 1$ when $i + 1 < n$, and nothing when wire $i + 1$ does not exist.
nodes.title: Adjacent comparator

nodes.summary: On $n$ wires, the bubble pass ending at wire $m$ is the comparator network $(0, 1), (1, 2), \ldots, (m - 1, m)$, applied in this order, where a comparator $(i, i + 1)$ is left out when wire $i + 1$ does not exist (that is, when $i + 1 \ge n$).
nodes.title: Bubble pass

nodes.summary: On $n$ wires and for a number $m$, this is the comparator network obtained by concatenating the bubble passes ending at wires $m - 1, m - 2, \ldots, 0$, in this order; for $m = 0$ it is empty.
nodes.title: Successive bubble passes

nodes.summary: The bubble sorting network on $n$ wires is the comparator network obtained by concatenating the bubble passes ending at wires $n - 1, n - 2, \ldots, 0$, in this order, where the bubble pass ending at wire $k$ consists of the comparators $(0, 1), (1, 2), \ldots, (k - 1, k)$.
nodes.title: Bubble sorting network

nodes.summary: Let $w$ be an input on $n$ wires with values in a linearly ordered type, let $m < n$, and let $w'$ be the output of the bubble pass ending at wire $m$ (the comparators $(0, 1), \ldots, (m - 1, m)$) run on $w$. Then $w'_i = w_i$ for every wire $i > m$; $w'_i \le w'_m$ for every wire $i \le m$; and for every wire $i \le m$ there is a wire $j \le m$ with $w'_i = w_j$.
nodes.title: Effect of one bubble pass

nodes.summary: Let $w$ assign to each of $n$ wires a value in a linearly ordered type, and let $m$ be a natural number. Then $w$ is settled from $m$ when $w_i \le w_j$ for all wires $m \le i \le j$ (the wires $m, \ldots, n - 1$ are sorted) and $w_i \le w_j$ for all wires $i < m \le j$ (they hold the largest values). This is the invariant before the bubble pass ending at wire $m - 1$.
nodes.title: Settled top wires

nodes.summary: Let $ps$ be a list of comparators all of whose wires lie in $[a, b)$. Then for all initial levels $\ell : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and every wire $x$ with $x < a$ or $b \le x$, the level of $x$ after $ps$ starting from $\ell$ is $\ell(x)$.

nodes.summary: Let $ps$ be a list of comparators all of whose wires lie in $[a, b)$, and let $\ell, \ell' : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be initial levels that agree on every wire in $[a, b)$. Then for every wire $x$ in $[a, b)$, the level of $x$ after $ps$ starting from $\ell$ equals the level of $x$ after $ps$ starting from $\ell'$.
nodes.title: Levels inside a block depend only on initial levels inside it

nodes.summary: Let $a$, $m$, $b$, $d$ be natural numbers, and let $p$ and $q$ be lists of comparators on wires indexed by $\mathbb{N}$, where every comparator of $p$ joins two wires in $[a, m)$ and every comparator of $q$ joins two wires in $[m, b)$. If $p$ and $q$ both have depth at most $d$, then the concatenation of $p$ followed by $q$ also has depth at most $d$: the two lists run in parallel.
nodes.title: Parallel composition of comparator lists on adjacent blocks

nodes.summary: For every list $ps$ of comparators and all initial levels $\ell : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, the levels after the list obtained from $ps$ by replacing each comparator $(i, j)$ with $(j, i)$, starting from $\ell$, equal the levels after $ps$ starting from $\ell$.
nodes.title: Swapping the wires of every comparator does not change levels

nodes.summary: Given a list $ps$ of comparators and a table $t$ of natural numbers $t_0, \dots, t_{N-1}$, the tabulated levels are computed by processing the comparators in order: a comparator $(i, j)$ sets both entries $t_i$ and $t_j$ to $\max(t_i, t_j) + 1$, where an entry outside the table reads as $0$ and a write outside the table is ignored.
nodes.title: Tabulated levels

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a list of natural numbers of length $N$ and let $ps$ be a list of comparators all of whose wires lie in $[0, N)$. Extend $t$ to all wires by setting $t_y = 0$ for $y \ge N$. Then for every wire $x$, the entry at position $x$ of the tabulated levels of $ps$ starting from the table $t$ (read as $0$ when $x \ge N$) equals the level of wire $x$ after $ps$, starting from the initial levels $y \mapsto t_y$.

For $k + 1$ it is the sorter for $k$ (sorting wires $0, \dots, 2^k - 1$), followed by the sorter for $k$ with each wire $i$ renamed to $2^k + i$ (sorting wires $2^k, \dots, 2^{k+1} - 1$), followed by Batcher's odd-even merger on $2^{k+1}$ wires.

nodes.summary: Given an array $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ over a linearly ordered type and a key $k$, lower-bound search maintains a half-open interval $[l, h)$ of indices, starting from $[0, n)$. While $l < h$, it compares $a_m$ with $k$ at the midpoint $m = l + \lfloor (h - l)/2 \rfloor$, charging one unit for this comparison, and continues with $[m + 1, h)$ if $a_m < k$ and with $[l, m)$ otherwise. When $l = h$ it returns $l$.
nodes.title: Lower-bound search

nodes.summary: Let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be an array over a linearly ordered type, sorted in nondecreasing order, let $k$ be a key, and let $\ell$ be the index returned by lower-bound search for $k$ in $a$. Then $\ell \le n$, $a_j < k$ for every $j < \ell$, and $k \le a_j$ for every $j$ with $\ell \le j < n$.
nodes.title: Correctness of lower-bound search

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ of length $n$ over a linearly ordered type and every key $k$, lower-bound search for $k$ in $a$ makes at most $\lceil \log_2 (n + 1) \rceil$ element comparisons.

nodes.summary: Given an array $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ over a linearly ordered type and a key $k$, binary search for the first occurrence of $k$ in $a$ runs lower-bound search for $k$ in $a$, obtaining an index $\ell$. If $\ell < n$, it makes one further comparison, charged one unit, and returns $\ell$ when $a_\ell = k$ and no index otherwise; if $\ell \ge n$, it returns no index without further cost.
nodes.title: Binary search for the first occurrence

nodes.summary: Let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be an array over a linearly ordered type, sorted in nondecreasing order, let $k$ be a key and let $i$ be a natural number. Binary search for the first occurrence of $k$ in $a$ returns the index $i$ if and only if $i < n$, $a_i = k$, and $a_j < k$ for every $j < i$.
nodes.title: Binary search returns the first occurrence of the key

nodes.summary: Let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be an array over a linearly ordered type, sorted in nondecreasing order, and let $k$ be a key. Binary search for the first occurrence of $k$ in $a$ returns no index if and only if $a_i \ne k$ for every $i < n$.
nodes.title: Binary search reports absence exactly when the key is absent

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array of length $n$ over a linearly ordered type, let $k$ be a key, and let $\ell$ be the index returned by lower-bound search for $k$ in $a$. The number of element comparisons made by binary search for the first occurrence of $k$ in $a$ equals the number made by lower-bound search for $k$ in $a$, plus $1$ if $\ell < n$ and plus $0$ otherwise.

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ of length $n$ over a linearly ordered type and every key $k$, binary search for the first occurrence of $k$ in $a$ makes at most $\lceil \log_2 (n + 1) \rceil + 1$ element comparisons.
nodes.title: Comparison bound for binary search for the first occurrence
