nodes.summary: Let $k$ be a natural number and let $\mathrm{key}$ assign to each record a key in $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$. Counting sort of an array $A$ of records returns an array together with a count of charged operations. It starts $k$ counters at zero, counts the records of $A$ with each key, replaces the counters by cumulative counts so that the counter of key $q$ holds the number of records with key at most $q$, and then scans…
nodes.title: Counting sort

nodes.summary: Let $k$ be a natural number, let $\mathrm{key}$ assign to each record a key in $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$, and let $A$ be an array of records. The array that counting sort returns on $A$ lists its records in nondecreasing order of key, is a permutation of $A$, and is stable: for every key $q < k$, the records of the output with key $q$, read from left to right, form the same sequence as the records of $A$ with key $q$.
nodes.title: Correctness of counting sort

nodes.summary: Let $k$ be a natural number, let $\mathrm{key}$ assign to each record a key in $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$, and let $A$ be an array of $n$ records. Counting sort on $A$ with this key is charged at most $7n + 3k$ operations, where one operation is charged for each counter initialization, key evaluation, counter read, counter write and output write.
nodes.title: Running time of counting sort
Heapsort

nodes.summary: For a list $xs$ of elements of a linearly ordered type, heap sort inserts the entries of $xs$ one at a time, from first to last, into the empty binary min-heap, and then extracts the minimum of the heap as many times as the heap has entries, each time continuing with the remaining heap. The output is the list of the extracted minima in the order in which they were extracted.
nodes.title: Heap sort

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ of elements of a linearly ordered type, the output of heap sort on $xs$ and $xs$ itself are equal as multisets: every value occurs in both lists the same number of times.
nodes.title: Heap sort preserves multiplicities

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ of elements of a linearly ordered type, heap sort returns a permutation of $xs$.
nodes.title: Heap sort permutes its input

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ of elements of a linearly ordered type, heap sort returns a list sorted in nondecreasing order.
nodes.title: Heap sort output is sorted

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ of elements of a linearly ordered type, heap sort returns a list that is sorted in nondecreasing order and is a permutation of $xs$.
nodes.title: Correctness of heap sort
Insertion sort

nodes.summary: For elements $x$ and $y$ of a linearly ordered type, this computation returns the truth value of $x \le y$ and charges one unit of time.
nodes.title: Charged comparison

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an element of a linearly ordered type. Inserting $a$ into the empty list returns $[a]$ at no cost. Inserting $a$ into a list with head $b$ and tail $l$ first charges one unit for comparing $a \le b$; if $a \le b$ it returns $a$ followed by $b$ and $l$, and otherwise it inserts $a$ into $l$, adding that cost, and returns $b$ followed by the result.
nodes.title: Costed insertion into a list

nodes.summary: On a list over a linearly ordered type, insertion sort returns the empty list at no cost when the input is empty. On a list with head $a$ and tail $l$, it sorts $l$ and then inserts $a$ into the result by costed insertion; its cost is the cost of sorting $l$ plus the cost of that insertion. Exactly one unit is charged for each order comparison.
nodes.title: Insertion sort with comparison cost

nodes.summary: For an element $a$ and a list $l$ over a linearly ordered type, the list returned by costed insertion of $a$ into $l$ is the ordered insertion of $a$ into $l$ with respect to $\le$: $a$ is placed immediately before the first element $b$ of $l$ with $a \le b$, or at the end of $l$ if there is no such element.
nodes.title: Costed insertion returns the ordered insertion

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ over a linearly ordered type, the list returned by insertion sort with comparison costs equals the standard insertion sort of $xs$ with respect to $\le$, which inserts the head into the sorted tail.
nodes.title: Cost-annotated insertion sort returns the standard insertion sort

nodes.summary: For a list $l$ over a linearly ordered type in the lowest universe, the costed insertion sort of $l$ equals CSLib's generic monadic insertion sort run in the time-counting monad with the charged comparison: the returned lists agree and the numbers of charged comparisons agree.
nodes.title: Agreement with CSLib's monadic insertion sort

nodes.summary: For every list $l$ over a linearly ordered type, the list returned by insertion sort on $l$ is nondecreasing.
nodes.title: Insertion sort returns a sorted list

nodes.summary: For every list $l$ over a linearly ordered type, the list returned by insertion sort is a permutation of $l$; in particular every element occurs in it exactly as often as in $l$.
nodes.title: Insertion sort permutes its input

nodes.summary: For every list $l$ over a linearly ordered type, the list returned by insertion sort is nondecreasing and is a permutation of $l$.
nodes.title: Correctness of insertion sort

nodes.summary: For an element $a$ and a list $l$ over a linearly ordered type, costed insertion of $a$ into $l$ charges at most $n$ comparisons, where $n$ is the length of $l$.
nodes.title: Cost of a single insertion

nodes.summary: On a list of length $n$ over a linearly ordered type, insertion sort charges at most $n(n-1)/2$ comparisons.
nodes.title: Comparison bound for insertion sort
Bucket sort

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function and let $x_1, \dots, x_n$ be an array of elements of $R$ that all lie in $[0, 1)$. If $n = 0$, bucket sort returns the empty array at zero cost. Otherwise it creates $n$ empty buckets indexed by $0, \dots, n - 1$, visits the entries in order and prepends each entry $x$ to bucket $\lfloor n x \rfloor$, sorts each bucket with insertion sort, and concatenates…
nodes.title: Bucket sort

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function and let $x_1, \dots, x_n$ be an array of elements of $R$ that all lie in $[0, 1)$. For $0 \le i < n$ let $B_i$ be the list of the entries $x_j$ with $\lfloor n x_j \rfloor = i$, in decreasing order of $j$, and let $T(B_i)$ be the number of comparisons insertion sort makes on $B_i$. Then the cost of bucket sort on this array equals…
nodes.title: Exact cost of bucket sort

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function. For every array of $n$ elements of $R$ that all lie in $[0, 1)$, the cost of bucket sort on this array is at least $5n$.
nodes.title: Linear lower bound on the cost of bucket sort

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function and let $x_1, \dots, x_n$ be an array of elements of $R$ that all lie in $[0, 1)$. For $0 \le i < n$ let $c_i$ be the number of indices $j$ with $\lfloor n x_j \rfloor = i$. Then the cost of bucket sort on this array is at most $5n + \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} c_i^2$.
nodes.title: Bound on the cost of bucket sort via squared bucket sizes

nodes.summary: For every linearly ordered field $R$ with a floor function, bucket sort applied to the empty array of elements of $R$ returns the empty array at zero cost.
nodes.title: Bucket sort on the empty array

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function. For every array of elements of $R$ that all lie in $[0, 1)$, the array returned by bucket sort is a permutation of the input: every element occurs in the output exactly as many times as in the input.
nodes.title: Bucket sort permutes its input

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function. For every array of elements of $R$ that all lie in $[0, 1)$, the array returned by bucket sort is nondecreasing: each entry is at most every entry after it.
nodes.title: Bucket sort sorts

nodes.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1}$ be independent random variables, each uniformly distributed on $[0, 1)$. For $i < n$, let $N_i$ be the number of indices $j < n$ with $\lfloor n \omega_j \rfloor = i$. Then $\mathbb{E}[N_i] = 1$.
nodes.title: Expected occupancy of a bucket in bucket sort

nodes.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1}$ be independent random variables, each uniformly distributed on $[0, 1)$. For $i < n$, let $N_i$ be the number of indices $j < n$ with $\lfloor n \omega_j \rfloor = i$. Then $\operatorname{Var}(N_i) = 1 - 1/n$.
nodes.title: Variance of a bucket's occupancy in bucket sort

nodes.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1}$ be independent random variables, each uniformly distributed on $[0, 1)$. For $i < n$, let $N_i$ be the number of indices $j < n$ with $\lfloor n \omega_j \rfloor = i$. Then $\mathbb{E}[N_i^2] = 2 - 1/n$.
nodes.title: Second moment of a bucket's occupancy in bucket sort

nodes.summary: For every $n$, the function $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ that maps $\omega = (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ to the number of time steps that bucket sort charges on the array $(\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ if every $\omega_j$ lies in $[0, 1)$, and to $0$ otherwise, is measurable.
nodes.title: The running time of bucket sort is measurable

nodes.summary: For every $n$, let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ map $\omega = (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ to the number of time steps that bucket sort charges on the array $(\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ if every $\omega_j$ lies in $[0, 1)$, and to $0$ otherwise. Then $T$ is integrable with respect to the product of $n$ copies of the uniform distribution on $[0, 1)$.
nodes.title: The running time of bucket sort is integrable

nodes.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $\omega = (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ have independent coordinates, each uniformly distributed on $[0, 1)$. Let $T(\omega)$ be the number of time steps that bucket sort charges on the array $(\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ if every $\omega_j$ lies in $[0, 1)$, and $T(\omega) = 0$ otherwise. Then $5n \le \mathbb{E}[T]$.
nodes.title: Lower bound on the expected time of bucket sort

nodes.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $\omega = (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ have independent coordinates, each uniformly distributed on $[0, 1)$. Let $T(\omega)$ be the number of time steps that bucket sort charges on the array $(\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ if every $\omega_j$ lies in $[0, 1)$, and $T(\omega) = 0$ otherwise. Then $\mathbb{E}[T] \le 5n + (n - 1)/2$.
nodes.title: Upper bound on the expected time of bucket sort

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be the number of time steps that bucket sort charges on the empty array, the only input of length $n = 0$. Its expectation under the product of zero copies of the uniform distribution on $[0, 1)$ is $0$.
nodes.title: Bucket sort on the empty input has expected time zero

nodes.summary: Let $\omega_0$ be uniformly distributed on $[0, 1)$, and let $T(\omega_0)$ be the number of time steps that bucket sort charges on the one-element array $(\omega_0)$ if $\omega_0 \in [0, 1)$, and $T(\omega_0) = 0$ otherwise. Then $\mathbb{E}[T] = 5$.
nodes.title: Expected time of bucket sort on one input

nodes.summary: For each $n$, let $\omega = (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ have independent coordinates, each uniformly distributed on $[0, 1)$. Let $T_n(\omega)$ be the number of time steps that bucket sort charges on the array $(\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ if every $\omega_j$ lies in $[0, 1)$, and $T_n(\omega) = 0$ otherwise. Then $\mathbb{E}[T_n] = \Theta(n)$ as $n \to \infty$.
nodes.title: Bucket sort runs in expected linear time
Linear search

nodes.summary: Given a predicate $p$ on a type $\alpha$ and a list $L$ of elements of $\alpha$, linear search scans $L$ from the front and returns the index of the first element of $L$ that satisfies $p$, or no index if no element does, together with a cost that counts one unit for each evaluation of $p$. On the empty list it returns no index at cost $0$. On a list with head $x$ and tail $T$ it evaluates $p(x)$ at a cost of one…
nodes.title: Linear search

nodes.summary: For every predicate $p$ on a type $\alpha$ and every list $L = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ over $\alpha$, the index returned by linear search for $p$ on $L$ (ignoring its cost) equals the result of the standard library's first-index search: the least $i < n$ with $p(x_i)$ true, or no index if $p(x_i)$ is false for every $i < n$.
nodes.title: Linear search returns the first satisfying index

nodes.summary: For every predicate $p$ on a type $\alpha$, every list $L = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ over $\alpha$ and every natural number $i$, linear search for $p$ on $L$ returns the index $i$ if and only if $i < n$, $p(x_i)$ is true, and $p(x_j)$ is false for every $j < i$.
nodes.title: Characterization of a successful linear search

nodes.summary: For every predicate $p$ on a type $\alpha$ and every list $L$ over $\alpha$, linear search for $p$ on $L$ returns no index if and only if $p(x)$ is false for every element $x$ of $L$.
nodes.title: Linear search fails exactly when no element satisfies the predicate

nodes.summary: For every predicate $p$ on a type $\alpha$, linear search for $p$ on the empty list has cost $0$: it evaluates $p$ zero times.
nodes.title: Cost of linear search on the empty list

nodes.summary: For every predicate $p$ on a type $\alpha$, every $x \in \alpha$ and every list $T$ over $\alpha$, the cost of linear search for $p$ on the list with head $x$ and tail $T$ is $1$ if $p(x)$ is true, and $1$ plus the cost of linear search for $p$ on $T$ if $p(x)$ is false. The head costs one evaluation of $p$, and the tail is searched only when the head fails.
nodes.title: Cost recurrence for linear search

nodes.summary: For every predicate $p$ on a type $\alpha$, every list $L$ over $\alpha$ and every natural number $i$, if linear search for $p$ on $L$ returns the index $i$, then its cost is $i + 1$: it evaluates $p$ exactly $i + 1$ times.
nodes.title: Cost of a successful linear search

nodes.summary: For every predicate $p$ on a type $\alpha$ and every list $L$ over $\alpha$, if linear search for $p$ on $L$ returns no index, then its cost is the length of $L$: it evaluates $p$ once for every element of $L$.
nodes.title: Cost of an unsuccessful linear search

nodes.summary: For every predicate $p$ on a type $\alpha$ and every list $L$ over $\alpha$, the cost of linear search for $p$ on $L$ is at most the length of $L$: it evaluates $p$ at most once for every element of $L$.
nodes.title: Linear search costs at most the list length
Radix sort

nodes.summary: Let $b \ge 2$ and let every record carry a key that is a vector of $d$ digits in $\{0, \dots, b-1\}$, most significant digit first, at positions $0, \dots, d-1$. Radix sort runs $d$ passes of stable counting sort on the array, the pass for position $i$ sorting by the digit of the key at position $i$, for $i = d-1, d-2, \dots, 0$, that is, from the least to the most significant digit. Its cost is the total cost of…
nodes.title: Radix sort

nodes.summary: Let $b \ge 2$ and let every record carry a key that is a vector $(k_0, \dots, k_{d-1})$ of $d$ digits in $\{0, \dots, b-1\}$, most significant digit first. For every input array, the output of radix sort is a permutation of the input, is in nondecreasing lexicographic order of keys, and is in nondecreasing order of the numbers $\sum_{i < d} k_i b^{d-1-i}$ whose base-$b$ digits are the keys. Moreover it is stable:…
nodes.title: Correctness of radix sort

nodes.summary: Let $b \ge 2$ and let every record carry a key that is a vector of $d$ digits in $\{0, \dots, b-1\}$. On an array of $n$ records, radix sort uses at most $d(7n + 3b)$ charged operations, where each counting-sort pass charges one unit for every counter initialization, key evaluation, counter read, counter write and output write.
nodes.title: Cost bound for radix sort
Rearranging a permutation into unimodal order

nodes.summary: An array $a$ of natural numbers is unimodal if it is the concatenation of a strictly increasing array $b$ followed by a strictly decreasing array $b'$, where either part may be empty.
nodes.title: Unimodal arrays

nodes.summary: For two vectors $a, b \in \mathbb{N}^n$, this is the number of indices $i < n$ with $a_i \neq b_i$, that is, the Hamming distance between $a$ and $b$.
nodes.title: Number of differing positions

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array of length $n$ that is a permutation of $1, \dots, n$, and let $m(a)$ be the value that the program $\mathrm{minRearrange}$ computes on $a$. Then some unimodal permutation $x$ of $1, \dots, n$ differs from $a$ in exactly $m(a)$ positions, and every unimodal permutation of $1, \dots, n$ differs from $a$ in at least $m(a)$ positions. So $m(a)$ is the minimum number of positions in which $a$ differs…
nodes.title: Correctness of the unimodal rearrangement algorithm
Selection sort

nodes.summary: Given an initial candidate $c$ in a linearly ordered type and a list $L$, minimum extraction returns a pair $(m, r)$ together with a cost. If $L$ is empty, it returns $c$ with the empty list at cost $0$. If $L$ has head $x$ and tail $L'$, it compares $x$ with $c$ at cost one: if $x < c$, it extracts from $L'$ with candidate $x$, obtaining $(m, r)$, and returns $m$ with the list $c$ followed by $r$; otherwise it…
nodes.title: Minimum extraction

nodes.summary: Selection sort of a list $L$ over a linearly ordered type is defined recursively. If $L$ is empty, the result is the empty list at cost $0$. If $L$ has head $x$ and tail $L'$, minimum extraction from $L'$ with initial candidate $x$ yields a minimum $m$ and the list $r$ of remaining elements, and the result is $m$ followed by the selection sort of $r$. The cost is the sum of the costs of all these minimum extractions.
nodes.title: Selection sort

nodes.summary: For every element $c$ of a linearly ordered type and every list $L$ over it, minimum extraction from $L$ with initial candidate $c$ has cost exactly $|L|$, the length of $L$; that is, it performs exactly $|L|$ order comparisons.
nodes.title: Cost of minimum extraction

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be an element of a linearly ordered type and $L$ a list over it, and let $(m, r)$ be the pair returned by minimum extraction from $L$ with initial candidate $c$. Then the list $m$ followed by $r$ is a permutation of the list $c$ followed by $L$, $m \le c$, and $m \le x$ for every element $x$ of $L$.
nodes.title: Correctness of minimum extraction

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ over a linearly ordered type, the list returned by selection sort on $L$ is sorted in nondecreasing order (each entry is $\le$ every later entry) and is a permutation of $L$, so it preserves duplicate multiplicities.
nodes.title: Correctness of selection sort

nodes.summary: For every list of length $n$ over a linearly ordered type, selection sort has cost exactly $n(n-1)/2$ in the model that charges one unit per order comparison; that is, it performs exactly $n(n-1)/2$ comparisons.
nodes.title: Comparison count of selection sort
Simultaneous minimum and maximum

nodes.summary: Given a list $xs$ over a linearly ordered type, the paired algorithm returns no result when $xs$ is empty and otherwise returns a pair (a candidate minimum and a candidate maximum), counting one unit of time for each comparison of elements. On a one-element list $[a]$ it returns $(a, a)$ without a comparison. On a longer list of odd length both candidates start at the first element without a comparison; on a list…
nodes.title: Simultaneous minimum and maximum

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ over a linearly ordered type, the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm returns no result on $xs$ when $xs$ is empty, and returns the pair $(\min xs, \max xs)$ of the least and greatest elements of $xs$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Correctness of the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ over a linearly ordered type, the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm returns no result on $xs$ if and only if $xs$ is empty.
nodes.title: The min–max algorithm returns no result exactly on the empty list

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ over a linearly ordered type and all elements $lo$ and $hi$ of that type, the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm returns the pair $(lo, hi)$ on $xs$ if and only if $lo$ and $hi$ both belong to $xs$, $lo \le x$ for every $x$ in $xs$, and $x \le hi$ for every $x$ in $xs$.
nodes.title: Characterization of the min–max output

nodes.summary: On the empty list, the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm returns no result and makes no comparisons.
nodes.title: The min–max algorithm on the empty list

nodes.summary: For every element $a$ of a linearly ordered type, on the list $[a]$ the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm returns the pair $(a, a)$ and makes no comparisons.
nodes.title: The min–max algorithm on a one-element list

nodes.summary: For every natural number $k$ and every list of length $2k + 1$ over a linearly ordered type, the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm makes exactly $3k$ comparisons.
nodes.title: Comparisons of the min–max algorithm on odd-length lists

nodes.summary: For every natural number $k \ge 1$ and every list of length $2k$ over a linearly ordered type, the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm makes exactly $3k - 2$ comparisons.
nodes.title: Comparisons of the min–max algorithm on even-length lists

nodes.summary: For every list of length $n$ over a linearly ordered type, the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm makes no comparisons when $n = 0$ and exactly $\lceil 3n/2 \rceil - 2$ comparisons when $n \ge 1$.
nodes.title: Comparison count of the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm
Three-way partitioning

nodes.summary: A three-way partition over a type $\alpha$ consists of three lists over $\alpha$, called below, equal and above. They are meant to hold the elements strictly below, equal to, and strictly above a pivot; the record itself imposes no condition on them.
nodes.title: Three-way partition record

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be an element of a linearly ordered type $\alpha$. The three-way partition of a list over $\alpha$ around $p$, together with the time it is charged, is defined by recursion on the list. The empty list gives three empty lists at no cost. For a list with head $x$ and tail $xs$, one unit of time is charged for comparing $x$ with $p$, the tail $xs$ is partitioned, and $x$ is put at the front of its below list…
nodes.title: Stable three-way partition

nodes.summary: For every element $p$ of a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ and every list $xs$ over $\alpha$, the time charged by the stable three-way partition of $xs$ around $p$ equals the length of $xs$: one unit for each comparison, one comparison per element.
nodes.title: Cost of the stable three-way partition

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be an element of a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, let $xs$ be a list over $\alpha$, and let $B$, $E$ and $A$ be the below, equal and above lists of the stable three-way partition of $xs$ around $p$. Then the concatenation $B$, $E$, $A$ is a permutation of $xs$, every element $x$ of $B$ satisfies $x < p$, every element of $E$ equals $p$, and every element $x$ of $A$ satisfies $p < x$.
nodes.title: Correctness of the stable three-way partition

nodes.summary: For every element $p$ of a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ and every list $xs$ over $\alpha$, the below list of the stable three-way partition of $xs$ around $p$ is the list of the elements $x$ of $xs$ with $x < p$, in their order in $xs$ and with their multiplicities.
nodes.title: The below list of a three-way partition is a filter

nodes.summary: For every element $p$ of a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ and every list $xs$ over $\alpha$, the equal list of the stable three-way partition of $xs$ around $p$ is the list of the elements $x$ of $xs$ with $x = p$, in their order in $xs$ and with their multiplicities.
nodes.title: The equal list of a three-way partition is a filter

nodes.summary: For every element $p$ of a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ and every list $xs$ over $\alpha$, the above list of the stable three-way partition of $xs$ around $p$ is the list of the elements $x$ of $xs$ with $p < x$, in their order in $xs$ and with their multiplicities.
nodes.title: The above list of a three-way partition is a filter

nodes.summary: For every element $p$ of a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ and every list $xs$ over $\alpha$, the lengths of the below, equal and above lists of the stable three-way partition of $xs$ around $p$ add up to the length of $xs$.
nodes.title: Sizes of the three parts of a three-way partition
Quickselect

nodes.summary: Deterministic quickselect takes a list $L$ over a linear order and a zero-based rank $k$ and returns an element or no element, together with its cost, the number of element comparisons it makes. If $k \ge |L|$, it returns no element at no cost. Otherwise it runs the following recursion, starting from the list $L$ and the rank $k$. On an empty list it returns no element. On a list with first entry $p$ and remaining…
nodes.title: Quickselect

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list over a linear order and let $k$ be a natural number. Quickselect on $L$ with zero-based rank $k$ returns no element if and only if $|L| \le k$.
nodes.title: Quickselect fails exactly out of range

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list over a linear order, let $p$ be an element, let $q$ be a Boolean predicate on the elements, and let $B$, $E$, $A$ be the blocks of entries below, equal to and above $p$ in the three-way partition of $L$ around $p$. If $q$ is false on every entry of $E$ and on every entry of $A$, then the number of entries of $L$ satisfying $q$ equals the number of entries of $B$ satisfying $q$, both counted with…
nodes.title: Counting through the below block

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list over a linear order, let $p$ be an element, let $q$ be a Boolean predicate on the elements, and let $B$, $E$, $A$ be the blocks of entries below, equal to and above $p$ in the three-way partition of $L$ around $p$. If $q$ is true on every entry of $B$ and on every entry of $E$, then the number of entries of $L$ satisfying $q$ equals $|B| + |E|$ plus the number of entries of $A$ satisfying $q$, all…
nodes.title: Counting through the above block

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list over a linear order, let $p$ be an element, and let $B$ be the block of entries below $p$ in the three-way partition of $L$ around $p$. Then the number of entries of $L$ that are strictly less than $p$, counted with multiplicity, equals $|B|$.
nodes.title: Entries below the pivot

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list over a linear order, let $p$ be an element, and let $B$ and $E$ be the blocks of entries below and equal to $p$ in the three-way partition of $L$ around $p$. Then the number of entries of $L$ that are at most $p$, counted with multiplicity, equals $|B| + |E|$.
nodes.title: Entries at most the pivot

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list over a linear order and let $k$ be a natural number. If quickselect on $L$ with zero-based rank $k$ returns an element $x$, then $x$ is an entry of $L$, and, counting entries of $L$ with multiplicity, the number of entries less than $x$ is at most $k$ and $k$ is less than the number of entries at most $x$.
nodes.title: Correctness of quickselect

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list over a linear order, let $S$ be the insertion sort of $L$ in nondecreasing order, and let $k$ be a natural number. If $k < |L|$, quickselect on $L$ with zero-based rank $k$ returns the entry of $S$ at zero-based position $k$; if $k \ge |L|$, it returns no element.
nodes.title: Quickselect agrees with sorting

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list over a linear order, let $k$ be a natural number and let $x$ be an element. Counting entries of $L$ with multiplicity, if the number of entries less than $x$ is at most $k$ and $k$ is less than the number of entries at most $x$, then quickselect on $L$ with zero-based rank $k$ returns $x$.
nodes.title: Rank inequalities determine the quickselect value

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ over a linear order, of length $n$, and every natural number $k$, quickselect on $L$ with rank $k$ makes at most $n(n-1)/2$ comparisons.
nodes.title: Worst-case comparison bound for quickselect
Median of medians

nodes.summary: Given a list $xs$ over a linear order, split $xs$ into consecutive blocks of five elements, the last of which may be shorter. Sort each block $g$ by insertion sort and return, in block order, the entry at position $\lfloor (|g| - 1)/2 \rfloor$ (counting from $0$) of each sorted block, that is, its lower median. The cost is the total number of comparisons made by these insertion sorts.
nodes.title: Group medians for median-of-medians selection

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ of length $n$ over a linear order, computing the group medians of $xs$ takes at most $2n$ comparisons.
nodes.title: Comparison cost of the group medians

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ over a linear order, every entry of the list of group medians of $xs$ is an element of $xs$.
nodes.title: Group medians come from the input

nodes.summary: Let $xs$ be a list over a linear order, and let $g_1, \dots, g_m$ be its consecutive blocks of five elements, the last of which may be shorter. Then the list of group medians of $xs$ has the same length $m$, say $x_1, \dots, x_m$, and for each $i$, writing $k_i = \lfloor (|g_i| - 1)/2 \rfloor$ and counting elements of $g_i$ with multiplicity: $x_i$ belongs to $g_i$, at most $k_i$ elements of $g_i$ are less than…
nodes.title: Group medians are lower medians of their blocks

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ of length $n$ over a linear order, the list of group medians of $xs$ has exactly $\lfloor (n + 4)/5 \rfloor = \lceil n/5 \rceil$ entries.
nodes.title: Number of group medians

nodes.summary: Given a list $L$ over a linear order and a zero-based rank $k$, median-of-medians selection returns either an element of $L$ or nothing, charging one unit of cost per order comparison. If $k \ge |L|$, where $|L|$ is the length of $L$, it returns nothing at no cost. Otherwise it runs the following recursive procedure on $(L, k)$ with a budget of $|L|$ nested calls, returning nothing if the budget runs out. A list of…
nodes.title: Median-of-medians selection

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ of length at most $140$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $k$, median-of-medians selection of rank $k$ in $L$ coincides with timed quickselect of rank $k$ in $L$: both return the same result and are charged the same number of comparisons.
nodes.title: Median-of-medians selection is quickselect on short lists

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $k$ at least the length of $L$, median-of-medians selection of rank $k$ in $L$ returns nothing and is charged zero comparisons.
nodes.title: Out-of-range ranks cost no comparisons

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ of length $n \le 140$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $k$, median-of-medians selection of rank $k$ in $L$ is charged at most $80n$ comparisons.
nodes.title: Comparison bound for median-of-medians selection on short lists

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list of length at most $140$ over a linearly ordered type and let $k$ be a natural number. If median-of-medians selection of rank $k$ in $L$ returns an element $x$, then $x$ occurs in $L$, the number of entries of $L$ less than $x$, counted with multiplicity, is at most $k$, and $k$ is less than the number of entries of $L$ that are at most $x$.
nodes.title: Correctness of median-of-medians selection on short lists

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list over a linearly ordered type and let $k$ be a natural number. If median-of-medians selection of rank $k$ in $L$ returns an element $x$, then $x$ occurs in $L$, the number of entries of $L$ less than $x$, counted with multiplicity, is at most $k$, and $k$ is less than the number of entries of $L$ that are at most $x$.
nodes.title: Correctness of median-of-medians selection

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $k$ less than the length of $L$, median-of-medians selection of rank $k$ in $L$ returns some element.
nodes.title: Median-of-medians selection succeeds on valid ranks

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $k$, median-of-medians selection of rank $k$ in $L$ returns nothing if and only if $k$ is at least the length of $L$.
nodes.title: Median-of-medians selection fails exactly on out-of-range ranks

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $k$, median-of-medians selection of rank $k$ in $L$ returns the entry at zero-based position $k$ of the insertion sort of $L$ by $\le$ when $k$ is less than the length of $L$, and returns nothing otherwise.
nodes.title: Median-of-medians selection agrees with sorting

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list without repeated entries over a linear order and let $k \in \mathbb{N}$. If median-of-medians selection on $L$ at zero-based rank $k$ returns an element $x$, then the set $\{y \in L : y \le x\}$ has exactly $k + 1$ elements.
nodes.title: Set rank of a median-of-medians result

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list without repeated entries over a linear order and let $i \ge 1$. If median-of-medians selection on $L$ at zero-based rank $i - 1$ returns an element $x$, then the set $\{y \in L : y \le x\}$ has exactly $i$ elements.
nodes.title: One-based rank of a median-of-medians result

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list without repeated entries over a linear order, of length $n$, and let $1 \le i \le n$. Then median-of-medians selection on $L$ at zero-based rank $i - 1$ returns an element $x$ of $L$, and the set $\{y \in L : y \le x\}$ has exactly $i$ elements.
nodes.title: Median of medians selects every one-based rank

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a nonempty list of length $n$ over a linear order, and let $k = \lfloor (n - 1)/2 \rfloor$. Then median-of-medians selection on $L$ at zero-based rank $k$ returns an element $x$ of $L$ such that at most $k$ entries of $L$ are less than $x$ and more than $k$ entries of $L$ are at most $x$, where entries are counted with repetition.
nodes.title: Median of medians finds the lower median

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a nonempty list of length $n$ over a linear order, and let $k = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$. Then median-of-medians selection on $L$ at zero-based rank $k$ returns an element $x$ of $L$ such that at most $k$ entries of $L$ are less than $x$ and more than $k$ entries of $L$ are at most $x$, where entries are counted with repetition.
nodes.title: Median of medians finds the upper median

nodes.summary: Let $n$, $m$ and $p$ be natural numbers with $n \ge 140$, $m \le \lfloor (n + 4)/5 \rfloor$ and $p \le \lfloor 7n/10 \rfloor + 6$. Then $20m + 20p + n \le 20n$.
nodes.title: Size budget for the two median-of-medians recursive calls

nodes.summary: Let $n$, $m$, $p$, $a$, $c_1$ and $c_2$ be natural numbers with $n \ge 140$, $m \le \lfloor (n + 4)/5 \rfloor$, $p \le \lfloor 7n/10 \rfloor + 6$, $c_1 \le 20am$ and $c_2 \le 20ap$. Then $c_1 + c_2 + an \le 20an$.
nodes.title: Cost budget for one median-of-medians step

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ of length $n$ over a linear order and every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, median-of-medians selection on $L$ at rank $k$ charges at most $80n$ comparisons, where $n$ counts repeated entries.
nodes.title: Median of medians makes linearly many comparisons

nodes.summary: Let $T : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and $a \in \mathbb{N}$. Suppose that $T(n) \le 20an$ for every $n \le 140$, and that for every $n > 140$ there are $m, p \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \le \lfloor (n + 4)/5 \rfloor$, $p \le \lfloor 7n/10 \rfloor + 6$ and $T(n) \le T(m) + T(p) + an$. Then $T(n) \le 20an$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: Linear solution of the median-of-medians recurrence
Quicksort

nodes.summary: Deterministic quicksort on lists over a linear order, using the first entry as pivot and counting comparisons. The empty list is returned unchanged at no cost. On a list with first entry $p$ and tail $t$, the algorithm stably splits $t$ into the entries less than $p$, equal to $p$ and greater than $p$, using one comparison per entry of $t$; it then recursively sorts the lesser and greater parts and returns the…
nodes.title: Quicksort

nodes.summary: For every list $\ell$ over a linear order, the output of quicksort on $\ell$ is sorted in nondecreasing order and is a permutation of $\ell$; in particular every value occurs in the output exactly as often as in $\ell$.
nodes.title: Correctness of quicksort

nodes.summary: For every list of length $n$ over a linear order, quicksort performs at most $n(n-1)/2$ comparisons.
nodes.title: Worst-case comparison bound for quicksort

nodes.summary: For a list $\ell$ over a linear order and elements $a$ and $b$, this is the number of entries $x$ of $\ell$, counted with multiplicity, such that $a < x < b$.
nodes.title: Number of list entries strictly between two values

nodes.summary: Let $\ell$ be a list without repeated entries over a linear order. nodes.title: Expected comparisons of quicksort on a random permutation

Take the expected number of comparisons made by quicksort on the list obtained by rearranging the entries of $\ell$ by a uniformly random permutation of their positions, which is an element of $[0, \infty]$, and convert it to a real number. nodes.summary: Optimization problems solved by tabulated recurrences: knapsack variants, subset sum, rod cutting, matrix-chain ordering, optimal binary search trees, longest common and longest increasing subsequences (including patience sorting) and maximum subarray (Kadane and divide-and-conquer); string edit distance goes to String algorithms.

Longest common subsequence

nodes.summary: Given lists $x = x_1 \cdots x_m$ and $y = y_1 \cdots y_n$ over a type with a boolean equality test, fill a table $c_{i,j}$ for $0 \le i \le m$ and $0 \le j \le n$ by $c_{i,0} = c_{0,j} = 0$, by $c_{i,j} = c_{i-1,j-1} + 1$ when the test reports $x_i = y_j$, and by $c_{i,j} = \max(c_{i-1,j}, c_{i,j-1})$ otherwise. Then build a witness $w$ by walking back from $(m, n)$ until $i = 0$ or $j = 0$: when the test reports…
nodes.title: Longest common subsequence by dynamic programming

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type whose boolean equality test agrees with equality, let $x$ and $y$ be lists over $\alpha$, and let $(k, w)$ be the pair returned by the dynamic-programming longest common subsequence algorithm on $x$ and $y$. Then $w$ has length $k$, $w$ is a subsequence (not necessarily contiguous) of both $x$ and $y$, and every common subsequence of $x$ and $y$ has length at most the length of $w$.
nodes.title: Correctness of the longest common subsequence algorithm

nodes.summary: For lists $x$ and $y$ of lengths $m$ and $n$ over a type with a boolean equality test, the abstract time of the dynamic-programming longest common subsequence algorithm on $x$ and $y$ (its number of table and reconstruction transitions) is at most $mn + (m + n)$.
nodes.title: Running time of the longest common subsequence algorithm
Longest increasing subsequence

nodes.summary: For a list $xs$ over a preorder and a natural number $k$, $k$ is the length of a longest strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$ when some strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$ has length $k$ and every strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$ has length at most $k$. Here a subsequence need not be contiguous, and strictly increasing means that each element is strictly less than every later one.
nodes.title: Length of a longest increasing subsequence

nodes.title: Table cell of the LIS dynamic program

nodes.summary: Given a value $x$ and a list $t$ of entries $(y, k, zs)$, where $y$ is a value, $k$ a natural number and $zs$ a list of values, this timed computation returns the pair of $k$ and the list $y$ followed by $zs$ for an entry of $t$ with $x < y$ whose $k$ is largest among such entries, provided that $k$ is positive; if no entry with $x < y$ has $k > 0$, it returns $0$ and the empty list. It costs one unit per entry of…
nodes.title: Best table entry above a value

Building the table costs the total cost of these scans.
nodes.title: Table of the quadratic LIS program

nodes.summary: Given a list $t$ of entries $(y, k, zs)$, where $k$ is a natural number and $zs$ is a list with elements of the same type as $y$, this timed computation returns the pair of $k$ and the list $y$ followed by $zs$ for an entry of $t$ whose $k$ is largest, provided that this $k$ is positive, and returns $0$ and the empty list otherwise (in particular when $t$ is empty). It costs one unit per entry of $t$.
nodes.title: Table entry of largest length

nodes.title: Longest increasing subsequence by dynamic programming

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a preorder with decidable $<$. For every value $x \in \alpha$ and every list $t$ of entries $(y, k, zs)$, where $y \in \alpha$, $k$ is a natural number and $zs$ is a list over $\alpha$, the scan of $t$ for the best table entry above $x$ costs exactly the length of $t$.
nodes.title: Cost of the scan for the best entry above a value

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ of length $n$ over a preorder, twice the cost of the quadratic longest-increasing-subsequence program on $xs$ equals $n(n + 1)$, so the program costs exactly $n(n + 1)/2$.

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ over a preorder, the list returned by the quadratic longest-increasing-subsequence program on $xs$ is a subsequence of $xs$, is strictly increasing (each element strictly less than every later one), and is at least as long as every strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$.
nodes.title: Correctness of the quadratic LIS program

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ over a preorder, the length of the list returned by the quadratic longest-increasing-subsequence program on $xs$ is the length of a longest strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$.
nodes.title: The quadratic LIS program attains the optimal length

nodes.title: Correctness of the quadratic LIS program, by length

nodes.summary: Given an array $t$ of tails and an element $x$ over a linear order, let $i$ be the index returned by the lower-bound binary search for $x$ in $t$. If $i$ is less than the size of $t$, the step replaces the entry of $t$ at index $i$ by $x$; otherwise it appends $x$ to $t$. Its cost is the number of comparisons made by the binary search.
nodes.title: Patience step

nodes.summary: Given an array of tails and a list over a linear order, the patience scan applies the patience step to the elements of the list in order: on the empty list it returns the tails unchanged, and on a list $x$ followed by $xs$ it applies the patience step for $x$ to the tails and then runs the patience scan of $xs$ from the result. Its cost is the total cost of the steps.
nodes.title: Patience scan

nodes.summary: Given a list $xs$ over a linear order, patience sorting runs the patience scan of $xs$ starting from the empty array of tails and returns the size of the resulting array. Its cost is the number of comparisons made by the scan.
nodes.title: Patience sorting

nodes.title: The patience scan preserves the invariant

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ over a linear order, the value returned by patience sorting on $xs$ is the length of a longest strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$: some strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$ has this length, and no strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$ is longer.
nodes.title: Correctness of patience sorting

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ over a linear order, the value returned by patience sorting on $xs$ equals the length of the list returned on $xs$ by the quadratic dynamic program for a longest strictly increasing subsequence.
nodes.title: Patience sorting agrees with the quadratic dynamic program

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linear order. For every array $t$ over $\alpha$ and every element $x \in \alpha$, the array returned by the patience step for $x$ on $t$ has size at most the size of $t$ plus $1$.
nodes.title: A patience step grows the tails by at most one

nodes.summary: For every list $xs$ of length $n$ over a linear order, patience sorting on $xs$ uses at most $n \lceil \log_2 (n + 1) \rceil$ comparisons.

Matrix chain multiplication

nodes.summary: A parenthesization of $n$ matrices is a full binary tree whose leaves are labeled by indices in $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$: either a single leaf naming matrix $i$, or a product node with a left and a right parenthesization as factors. Labels may be repeated, omitted, or out of order.
nodes.title: Parenthesization

nodes.summary: The leaf indices of a parenthesization of $n$ matrices form the list of indices in $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ obtained by reading its leaves from left to right: $[i]$ for a single leaf naming matrix $i$, and the concatenation of the lists of the left and right factors for a product node.
nodes.title: Leaf indices of a parenthesization

nodes.summary: Let $p = (p_0, \dots, p_n)$ be a vector of natural numbers, regarding matrix $i$ (for $0 \le i < n$) as having $p_i$ rows and $p_{i+1}$ columns. The row count of a parenthesization of $n$ matrices with respect to $p$ is $p_i$ for a single leaf naming matrix $i$, and the row count of the left factor for a product node.
nodes.title: Row count of a parenthesization

nodes.summary: Let $p = (p_0, \dots, p_n)$ be a vector of natural numbers, regarding matrix $i$ (for $0 \le i < n$) as having $p_i$ rows and $p_{i+1}$ columns. The column count of a parenthesization of $n$ matrices with respect to $p$ is $p_{i+1}$ for a single leaf naming matrix $i$, and the column count of the right factor for a product node.
nodes.title: Column count of a parenthesization

nodes.summary: Let $p = (p_0, \dots, p_n)$ be a vector of natural numbers, regarding matrix $i$ (for $0 \le i < n$) as having $p_i$ rows and $p_{i+1}$ columns. A parenthesization of $n$ matrices is dimension-compatible with $p$ when, at every product node, the column count of the left factor equals the row count of the right factor, where row and column counts are taken with respect to $p$. A single leaf is always…
nodes.title: Dimension-compatible parenthesization

nodes.summary: Let $p = (p_0, \dots, p_n)$ be a vector of natural numbers, regarding matrix $i$ (for $0 \le i < n$) as having $p_i$ rows and $p_{i+1}$ columns. A parenthesization of $n$ matrices is valid for $p$ when its leaf indices, read left to right, are exactly $0, 1, \dots, n - 1$, and it is dimension-compatible with $p$.
nodes.title: Valid parenthesization

nodes.summary: Let $p = (p_0, \dots, p_n)$ be a vector of natural numbers, regarding matrix $i$ (for $0 \le i < n$) as having $p_i$ rows and $p_{i+1}$ columns, and let $r(T)$ and $c(T)$ be the row and column counts of a parenthesization $T$ with respect to $p$. The scalar multiplication count of a single leaf is $0$, and that of a product node with factors $L$ and $R$ is the sum of the counts of $L$ and $R$ plus $r(L)\,c(L)\,c(R)$.
nodes.title: Scalar multiplication count of a parenthesization

nodes.summary: A matrix-chain cost is a pair of natural numbers counting the abstract events charged by matrix-chain ordering and reconstruction: the number of split candidates evaluated by the dynamic program, and the number of tree nodes emitted during reconstruction.
nodes.title: Matrix-chain cost

nodes.summary: The total of a matrix-chain cost is its number of candidate evaluations plus its number of reconstruction nodes.
nodes.title: Total matrix-chain cost

nodes.summary: A matrix-chain result for $n$ matrices pairs a natural number, the reported optimal scalar multiplication count, with a parenthesization of $n$ matrices, the reported optimal parenthesization. The structure itself does not require the count to be minimal or to be attained by the parenthesization.

nodes.title: Matrix-chain ordering returns a valid parenthesization

nodes.summary: For every $n \ge 1$ and all natural numbers $p_0, \dots, p_n$, the scalar-multiplication cost of the parenthesization returned by the matrix-chain ordering algorithm on the dimensions $p_0, \dots, p_n$ equals the optimal cost it reports.
nodes.title: Matrix-chain ordering reports the cost of its parenthesization

nodes.summary: For every $n \ge 1$, all natural numbers $p_0, \dots, p_n$ and every parenthesization $T$ of $n$ matrices that is valid for these dimensions, the optimal cost reported by the matrix-chain ordering algorithm on the dimensions $p_0, \dots, p_n$ is at most the scalar-multiplication cost of $T$.

nodes.title: Split candidates evaluated by matrix-chain ordering

nodes.title: Reconstruction size in matrix-chain ordering

nodes.summary: For every $n \ge 1$ and all natural numbers $p_0, \dots, p_n$, the total number of events charged by the matrix-chain ordering algorithm run on the dimensions $p_0, \dots, p_n$ is $\binom{n+1}{3} + (2n - 1)$.

nodes.summary: For every $n \ge 1$ and all natural numbers $p_0, \dots, p_n$, the total number of events charged by the matrix-chain ordering algorithm run on the dimensions $p_0, \dots, p_n$ is at most $3n^3$.
nodes.title: Cubic bound for matrix-chain ordering
Maximum subarray problem

nodes.summary: For a list $L$ over an additive monoid $\alpha$ with a linear order, an element $m \in \alpha$ is the maximum subarray sum of $L$ when some nonempty contiguous sublist of $L$ has sum $m$ and every nonempty contiguous sublist of $L$ has sum at most $m$.
nodes.title: Being the maximum subarray sum

nodes.summary: For a list $L$ over an additive monoid $\alpha$ with a linear order, an element $e \in \alpha$ is the maximum suffix sum of $L$ when some nonempty suffix of $L$ has sum $e$ and every nonempty suffix of $L$ has sum at most $e$. A nonempty suffix is a contiguous run ending at the last element of $L$.
nodes.title: Being the maximum suffix sum

nodes.summary: Given accumulators $e, b$ in an additive monoid $\alpha$ with a linear order, the scan over the empty list returns $b$ at cost $0$. Over a list with first element $x$ and remaining elements $L$, it sets $e' = \max(x, e + x)$ and returns the result of the scan of $L$ from the accumulators $e'$ and $\max(b, e')$, at cost $3$ plus the cost of that scan.

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type with an additive monoid structure. On the empty list, Kadane's algorithm returns no value. On a list $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ of elements of $\alpha$ with $n \ge 1$, it sets $e = b = x_1$; then for $i = 2, \dots, n$ in turn it replaces $e$ by $\max(x_i, e + x_i)$ and then $b$ by $\max(b, e)$; finally it returns $b$. If $c$ is a composition of $k$ and $d$ is a composition of $l$ with $k + l \le n$, then the revenue of their concatenation, a composition of $k + l$, is the revenue of $c$ plus the revenue of $d$.

Subset sum

nodes.summary: Given a list $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ of natural numbers and a target $t \in \mathbb{N}$, this timed procedure starts from the list $L_0 = (0)$ and, for $i = 1, \dots, n$ in order, forms $L_i$ from $L_{i-1}$ in four steps: add $x_i$ to every entry of $L_{i-1}$; merge $L_{i-1}$ with this shifted list (the standard merge of two lists, comparing entries with $\le$); delete adjacent repeated values; and keep only the…
nodes.title: Attainable sums in exact subset sum

nodes.summary: Let $x$ be a list of natural numbers, $t$ a natural number, and $L$ the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal on $x$ with target $t$. A natural number $z$ belongs to $L$ if and only if $z \le t$ and $z$ is the sum of some sublist of $x$ (a subsequence, not necessarily contiguous).
nodes.title: Characterization of the exact subset sum list

nodes.summary: For every list $x$ of natural numbers and every natural number $t$, the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal on $x$ with target $t$ contains $0$.
nodes.title: Zero is always a computed sum

nodes.summary: For every list $x$ of natural numbers and every natural number $t$, the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal on $x$ with target $t$ is strictly increasing; in particular it has no repeated entries.
nodes.title: The exact subset sum list is strictly increasing

nodes.summary: For every list $x$ of natural numbers, of length $n$, and every natural number $t$, the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal on $x$ with target $t$ has length at most $2^n$.
nodes.title: The number of computed sums is at most two to the power of the input length

nodes.summary: For every list $x$ of natural numbers and every natural number $t$, the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal on $x$ with target $t$ has length at most $t + 1$.
nodes.title: The number of computed sums is at most the target plus one

nodes.summary: For every list $x$ of natural numbers with sum $S$ and every natural number $t$, the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal on $x$ with target $t$ has length at most $S + 1$.
nodes.title: The number of computed sums is at most the input total plus one

nodes.summary: Let $i \le n$ be natural numbers. On the list $1, 2, 4, \dots, 2^{i-1}$ (the first $i$ entries of $1, 2, \dots, 2^{n-1}$) with target $2^n - 1$, the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal is exactly $0, 1, 2, \dots, 2^i - 1$ in increasing order.
nodes.title: Prefixes of the powers of two attain every sum

nodes.summary: Given a list $x$ of natural numbers and a target $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the procedure first computes the list $L = (\ell_1, \dots, \ell_m)$ of attainable sums of $x$ with target $t$, then scans it from left to right, keeping a running maximum that starts at $0$, and returns $\max(0, \ell_1, \dots, \ell_m)$. Its counted events are those of computing $L$ plus one per entry of $L$.
nodes.title: Exact subset sum procedure

nodes.summary: For every list $x$ of natural numbers and every natural number $t$, the value returned by the exact subset sum algorithm on $x$ with target $t$ equals $\max(\cdots\max(\max(0, s_1), s_2)\cdots, s_k)$, where $s_1, \dots, s_k$ is the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal on $x$ with target $t$.
nodes.title: Exact subset sum returns the maximum of the computed sums

nodes.summary: Let $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ be a list of natural numbers and $t \in \mathbb{N}$ a target. For $0 \le i \le n$ let $L_i$ be the list of attainable sums of the prefix $(x_1, \dots, x_i)$ with target $t$. For $i < n$ let $M_i$ be the merge of $L_i$ with the list obtained by adding $x_{i+1}$ to every entry of $L_i$, let $c_i$ be the number of comparisons this merge makes, and let $D_i$ be $M_i$ with adjacent repeated…
nodes.title: Event count of exact subset sum

nodes.summary: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the exact subset-sum procedure on the list $(2^0, 2^1, \dots, 2^{n-1})$ (empty when $n = 0$) with target $2^n - 1$ makes at least $2^n - 1$ counted events.
nodes.title: Exponential lower bound for exact subset sum on powers of two

nodes.summary: For every list $x$ of $n$ natural numbers and every target $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the exact subset-sum procedure on $x$ and $t$ makes at most $1 + n + 7(2^n - 1) + 2^n$ counted events.
nodes.title: Exponential upper bound for exact subset sum

nodes.summary: For every list $x$ of $n$ natural numbers with sum $s$ and every target $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the exact subset-sum procedure on $x$ and $t$ makes at most $1 + n + (7n + 1)\min(t + 1, s + 1)$ counted events.
nodes.title: Pseudo-polynomial bound for exact subset sum

nodes.summary: Let $x$ be a list of $n$ natural numbers and let $t, d \in \mathbb{N}$ with $t \le n^d$. Then the exact subset-sum procedure on $x$ and $t$ makes at most $1 + n + (7n + 1)(n^d + 1)$ counted events.
nodes.title: Polynomial event bound for exact subset sum with a polynomially bounded target

nodes.summary: Let $x$ be a list of $n$ natural numbers and let $d \in \mathbb{N}$ be such that every entry of $x$ is at most $n^d$. Then for every target $t \in \mathbb{N}$ the exact subset-sum procedure on $x$ and $t$ makes at most $1 + n + (7n + 1)(n \cdot n^d + 1)$ counted events.
nodes.title: Polynomial event bound for exact subset sum with polynomially bounded inputs

nodes.summary: Let $x$ be a list of natural numbers, $t$ a natural number, and $r$ the value returned by the exact subset sum algorithm on $x$ with target $t$. Then $r$ is the sum of some sublist of $x$ (a subsequence, not necessarily contiguous), $r \le t$, and every sublist of $x$ whose sum is at most $t$ has sum at most $r$.
nodes.title: Optimality of exact subset sum

nodes.summary: Let $x$ be a list of distinct positive natural numbers, $t$ a positive natural number, and $r$ the value returned by the exact subset sum algorithm on $x$ with target $t$. Then $r$ is the sum of some sublist of $x$ (a subsequence, not necessarily contiguous), $r \le t$, and every sublist of $x$ whose sum is at most $t$ has sum at most $r$.

nodes.title: Total value of a knapsack selection

nodes.title: Bottom-up zero-one knapsack algorithm

Then $S$ is feasible for $W$, $v$ is the total value of $S$, and every feasible set $T$ of item indices has total value at most $v$.
nodes.title: Correctness of the zero-one knapsack algorithm

nodes.summary: For every list of $n$ knapsack items and every capacity $W \in \mathbb{N}$, the bottom-up knapsack algorithm costs exactly $n(W + 1) + n$ ticks: one for each of the $n(W + 1)$ table cells it computes and one for each of the $n$ item rows it inspects during reconstruction.

nodes.summary: For every list of $n$ knapsack items and every capacity $W \in \mathbb{N}$ with $W \ge 1$, the bottom-up knapsack algorithm costs at most $3nW$ ticks.

Interval scheduling

nodes.summary: Let each activity $a$ have a start time $s(a)$ and a finish time $f(a)$ in a linearly ordered type, thought of as the closed-open interval $[s(a), f(a))$. Two activities $a$ and $b$ are compatible when $f(a) \le s(b)$ or $f(b) \le s(a)$; in particular, activities whose intervals only touch at an endpoint are compatible.
nodes.title: Compatible activities

nodes.summary: For any start and finish times and any activities $a$ and $b$, if $a$ is compatible with $b$, then $b$ is compatible with $a$.
nodes.title: Symmetry of interval compatibility

The result is the list of selected activities in sorted order, together with a cost that counts one for each…

Then $S$ is a subpermutation of $L$ (each activity occurs in $S$ at most as often as in $L$), any two entries of $S$ at distinct positions are compatible, and every subpermutation $M$ of $L$…

Matroid greedy algorithm

nodes.summary: Given an oracle $O$ that accepts or rejects each finite subset of a type $\alpha$, a finite set $S \subseteq \alpha$ and a list $e_1, \dots, e_n$ of elements of $\alpha$, the greedy scan processes $e_1, \dots, e_n$ in order, starting with $S$ as the current set: it replaces the current set $T$ by $T \cup \{e_i\}$ if $O$ accepts $T \cup \{e_i\}$, and leaves it unchanged otherwise. It returns the final current set…
nodes.title: Greedy scan with an independence oracle

nodes.summary: Given an oracle $O$ that accepts or rejects each finite subset of a type $\alpha$ and a list $L$ of elements of $\alpha$, the greedy algorithm starts from the empty set, processes the elements of $L$ in order, adds an element $e$ to the current set $T$ when $O$ accepts $T \cup \{e\}$ and leaves $T$ unchanged otherwise, and returns the final set. It charges one unit of time per element processed.
nodes.title: Greedy algorithm on a matroid

nodes.summary: For every oracle $O$ on finite subsets of a type $\alpha$, every finite set $S \subseteq \alpha$ and every list $L$ of elements of $\alpha$, the greedy scan with oracle $O$ from $S$ over $L$ takes time exactly the length of $L$.

nodes.summary: For every oracle $O$ on finite subsets of a type $\alpha$ and every list $L$ of elements of $\alpha$, the greedy algorithm with oracle $O$ on $L$ takes time exactly the length of $L$, one oracle query per element.
nodes.title: Running time of the matroid greedy algorithm

nodes.summary: For every oracle $O$ on finite subsets of a type $\alpha$, every finite set $S \subseteq \alpha$ and all lists $P$ and $Q$ of elements of $\alpha$, the set returned by the greedy scan with oracle $O$ from $S$ over $P$ followed by $Q$ equals the set returned by the greedy scan with oracle $O$ over $Q$ starting from the set that the scan with oracle $O$ from $S$ over $P$ returns.

For every list $L$ of elements of $\alpha$, the set returned by the greedy algorithm with oracle $O$ on $L$ is independent in $M$, and each of its elements occurs in $L$.
nodes.title: The matroid greedy result is independent

nodes.title: The matroid greedy result is a base

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type, let $\mathrm{indep}$ be an independence system on the finite subsets of $\alpha$ and let $I$ be an independent set. For every list $L$ of elements of $I$ and every finite set $S \subseteq I$, the greedy scan of $L$ starting from $S$ returns $S$ together with all elements of $L$.

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type, let $\mathrm{indep}$ be an independence oracle on the finite subsets of $\alpha$, let $S$ be a finite subset of $\alpha$ and let $L$ be a list of elements of $\alpha$ such that $\mathrm{indep}$ rejects $S \cup \{e\}$ for every $e$ in $L$. Then the greedy scan of $L$ starting from $S$ returns $S$.

nodes.title: Greedy optimality

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite type and let $\mathrm{indep}$ be an independence system on the finite subsets of $\alpha$ for which the greedy algorithm is optimal. If $I$ and $J$ are independent sets with $|I| < |J|$, then some element $e \in J$ with $e \notin I$ makes $I \cup \{e\}$ independent.
nodes.title: Greedy optimality gives the augmentation axiom

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite type and let $\mathrm{indep}$ be an independence system on the finite subsets of $\alpha$ for which the greedy algorithm is optimal. Then there is a matroid $M$ on $\alpha$ whose ground set is all of $\alpha$ such that a finite set $S \subseteq \alpha$ is independent in $M$ exactly when $S$ is independent under $\mathrm{indep}$.
nodes.title: Greedy-optimal independence systems are matroids
