The greedy algorithm is optimal for $\mathrm{indep}$ if and only if there is a matroid $M$ on $\alpha$ whose ground set is all of $\alpha$ such that a finite set $S \subseteq \alpha$ is independent in $M$ exactly when $S$ is independent under $\mathrm{indep}$.
nodes.title: Rado–Edmonds theorem
Graphic matroid

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set and let $ab$ be an edge of $H$. If $a$ and $b$ are not connected in the graph obtained from $H$ by deleting the edge $ab$, then that graph has exactly one more connected component than $H$.
nodes.title: Deleting a bridge adds one component

nodes.summary: Let $V$ be a finite vertex set. For every natural number $n$ and every forest (acyclic simple graph) $F$ on $V$ with exactly $n$ edges, the number of edges of $F$ plus the number of connected components of $F$ equals $|V|$. So a forest on $V$ with $e$ edges has $|V| - e$ connected components.
nodes.title: Edges plus components of a forest

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set, and let $I$ and $J$ be sets of edges of $G$ that each form an acyclic graph. If $|I| < |J|$, then there is an edge $e \in J$ with $e \notin I$ such that $I \cup \{e\}$ still forms an acyclic graph.
nodes.title: Augmentation property of forests

nodes.summary: A set $I$ of unordered pairs of vertices is a forest of a simple graph $G$ when every element of $I$ is an edge of $G$ and the graph with edge set $I$ has no cycles.
nodes.title: Forests of a graph

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set, the graphic matroid of $G$ is the matroid on unordered pairs of vertices whose ground set is the edge set of $G$ and whose independent sets are the forests of $G$, that is, the sets of edges of $G$ that form an acyclic graph.
nodes.title: Graphic matroid

nodes.summary: The graph of a finite edge set, with decidable adjacency.
nodes.title: Graph of a finite edge set

nodes.summary: On a finite vertex set, for a finite set $S$ of unordered pairs of vertices and a pair $e = \{u, v\}$, the bridge test returns true exactly when $u$ and $v$ are not connected by a path in the graph whose edges are the non-loop pairs of $S \setminus \{e\}$. When $e \in S$ is not a loop, this says that $e$ is a bridge of $S$: deleting it disconnects its endpoints.
nodes.title: Bridge test for an edge set

nodes.summary: On a finite vertex set, let $S$ be a finite set of unordered pairs of vertices and let $u$, $v$ be vertices. The bridge test of $S$ on the pair $\{u, v\}$ returns true if and only if $u$ and $v$ are not connected by a path in the graph whose edges are the non-loop pairs of $S \setminus \{\{u, v\}\}$.
nodes.title: Characterization of the bridge test

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set, the forest oracle accepts a finite set $S$ of unordered pairs of vertices exactly when every $e \in S$ is an edge of $G$ and passes the bridge test in $S$: its endpoints are not connected in the graph formed by the other pairs of $S$. It serves as the independence oracle of the graphic matroid of $G$, since a graph is a forest if and only if every edge is a bridge.
nodes.title: Forest oracle

nodes.summary: For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set and a finite set $S$ of unordered pairs of vertices, the forest oracle of $G$ accepts $S$ if and only if $S$ is independent in the graphic matroid of $G$.
nodes.title: The forest oracle decides graphic-matroid independence

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex type $V$. For every list $L$ of unordered pairs of vertices, the matroid greedy algorithm run on $L$ with the forest oracle of $G$ returns a forest of $G$: a set of edges of $G$ without cycles.
nodes.title: Kruskal's algorithm returns a forest

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex type $V$, let $w$ assign a natural number to each unordered pair of vertices, and let $L$ be a list of unordered pairs of vertices in nonincreasing order of $w$ (each entry weighs at least as much as every later one). Let $T$ be the set returned by the matroid greedy algorithm run on $L$ with the forest oracle of $G$. Then every forest $I$ of $G$ all of whose edges occur…
nodes.title: Optimality of Kruskal's algorithm

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set and let $L$ be a list of unordered pairs of vertices such that a pair is an edge of $G$ if and only if it occurs in $L$. Then the matroid greedy algorithm run with the forest oracle of $G$ on $L$ returns a base of the graphic matroid of $G$, that is, a maximal forest of $G$.
nodes.title: Kruskal's algorithm returns a maximal forest

nodes.summary: Polynomial-time algorithms with proved approximation ratios for NP-hard optimization: vertex cover, set cover, metric TSP, list scheduling, maximum coverage.
nodes.title: Approximation algorithms
Double-tree approximation for metric TSP

nodes.summary: A cost function $d$ assigning to each pair of vertices a value in a linearly ordered additive commutative monoid is metric when, for all vertices $x$, $y$, $z$, it is symmetric, $d(x, y) = d(y, x)$, zero on the diagonal, $d(x, x) = 0$, nonnegative, $0 \le d(x, y)$, and satisfies the triangle inequality $d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)$.
nodes.title: Metric cost function

nodes.summary: Let $d$ be a cost function on the vertices with values in an additive commutative monoid. For a vertex $x$ and a list $L = [y_1, \dots, y_n]$ of vertices, the cost of the walk from $x$ through $L$ is $d(x, y_1) + d(y_1, y_2) + \dots + d(y_{n-1}, y_n)$, and $0$ when $L$ is empty.
nodes.title: Cost of a walk

nodes.summary: For a cost function $d$ on the vertices with values in an additive commutative monoid, the cost of the closed tour that visits $x_0, x_1, \dots, x_k$ in order and returns to its first vertex is $\sum_{i=1}^{k} d(x_{i-1}, x_i) + d(x_k, x_0)$. The empty tour costs $0$.
nodes.title: Cost of a closed tour

nodes.summary: A rooted forest with vertices in $\alpha$ is either empty, or consists of a first tree with root $v$, whose subtrees form a forest (the children of $v$), followed by a forest of the remaining trees (the siblings of $v$).
nodes.title: Rooted forest in left-child right-sibling form

nodes.summary: The list of the vertices of a forest in preorder: empty for the empty forest, and for a forest with first root $v$, children forest $C$ and sibling forest $S$, the vertex $v$, followed by the preorder of $C$, followed by the preorder of $S$.
nodes.title: Preorder of a forest

nodes.summary: For a cost function $d$ and a vertex $p$, the weight of a forest hanging below $p$ is the total cost of its tree edges: each top-level vertex $v$ is joined to $p$ by an edge of cost $d(p, v)$, and each vertex $u$ is joined to each of its children $c$ by an edge of cost $d(u, c)$. The empty forest has weight $0$.
nodes.title: Weight of a forest below a vertex

nodes.summary: The forest of a list $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ of vertices is the path $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$: $x_1$ is its only top-level vertex and each $x_{i+1}$ is the only child of $x_i$. The empty list gives the empty forest.
nodes.title: Path as a forest

nodes.summary: For a forest $F$ and a list $a$ of vertices, this is the timed computation defined as follows. On the empty forest it returns $a$ at no cost. On a forest with first root $v$, children forest $C$ and sibling forest $S$, it charges one time unit, walks $S$ with accumulator $a$ to get a list $b$, walks $C$ with accumulator $b$ to get a list $c$, and returns $v$ followed by $c$. It thus returns the vertices of $F$ in…
nodes.title: Preorder walk with an accumulator

nodes.summary: For a forest $F$, the preorder walk of $F$ is the preorder walk of $F$ with the empty list as accumulator: a timed computation that returns the vertices of $F$ in preorder, at one time unit per vertex.
nodes.title: Preorder walk

nodes.summary: CLRS `APPROX-TSP-TOUR`, steps 3 and 4: given a root $r$ and a forest $F$ (the subtrees of a spanning tree with root $r$), return the tour that lists $r$ followed by the vertices of $F$ in preorder. As a timed computation it charges one unit for $r$ and one unit for each vertex visited by the preorder walk of $F$.
nodes.title: The APPROX-TSP-TOUR algorithm

nodes.summary: For every forest $F$ and every list $a$ of vertices, the preorder walk of $F$ with accumulator $a$ returns the vertices of $F$ in preorder followed by $a$.
nodes.title: Result of the preorder walk with an accumulator

nodes.summary: For every root $r$ and forest $F$, the running time of `APPROX-TSP-TOUR` on $r$ and $F$ equals the length of the list of $r$ followed by the vertices of $F$ in preorder: one unit per vertex of the returned tour.
nodes.title: Running time of `APPROX-TSP-TOUR`

nodes.summary: Let $d$ be a cost function on the vertices with values in a linearly ordered additive commutative monoid, which is symmetric, zero on the diagonal, nonnegative, and satisfies the triangle inequality. For vertices $q$, $p$ and a list $L$ of vertices, the cost of the walk from $q$ through $L$ is at most $d(q, p)$ plus the cost of the walk from $p$ through $L$.
nodes.title: Changing the starting vertex of a walk

nodes.summary: Let $d$ be a cost function on the vertices with values in a linearly ordered additive commutative monoid, which is symmetric, zero on the diagonal, nonnegative, and satisfies the triangle inequality. For a vertex $p$ and lists $A$, $B$ of vertices, the cost of the walk that starts at $p$, visits $A$ and then $B$ in order and returns to $p$ is at most the cost of the walk from $p$ through $A$ back to $p$ plus the…
nodes.title: Shortcutting a closed walk through its base point

nodes.summary: Let $d$ be a cost function on the vertices with values in a linearly ordered additive commutative monoid, which is symmetric, zero on the diagonal, nonnegative, and satisfies the triangle inequality. For vertices $v$, $p$ and a list $C$ of vertices, the cost of the walk from $v$ through $C$ ending at $p$ is at most the cost of the walk from $v$ through $C$ ending back at $v$, plus $d(v, p)$.
nodes.title: Rerouting the end of a walk

nodes.summary: Let $d$ be a cost function on the vertices with values in a linearly ordered additive commutative monoid, which is symmetric, zero on the diagonal, nonnegative, and satisfies the triangle inequality. For a forest $F$ and a vertex $p$, let $w$ be the weight of $F$ hanging below $p$: the total cost of the edges joining $p$ to the top-level vertices of $F$ and each vertex of $F$ to its children. Then the cost of the…
nodes.title: The closed preorder walk below a vertex costs at most twice the forest

nodes.summary: Let $d$ be a cost function on the vertices with values in a linearly ordered additive commutative monoid that is symmetric, zero on the diagonal, nonnegative and satisfies the triangle inequality. Let $T$ be a rooted tree with root $r$, given by the forest $F$ of the subtrees of $r$, and let $w(T)$ be its weight, the total cost of its edges. Then the closed tour that visits $r$, then the vertices of $F$ in…
nodes.title: The preorder tour costs at most twice the tree

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ of vertices, the preorder of the forest of $L$ (the path through the vertices of $L$ in order) is $L$ itself.
nodes.title: Preorder of a path

nodes.summary: The tree with root $r$ and subtree forest $F$ is a spanning tree of a list $V$ of vertices when the vertices of $V$ are distinct and the list of $r$ followed by the vertices of $F$ in preorder is a permutation of $V$: the vertices of the tree are those of $V$, each exactly once.
nodes.title: Rooted spanning tree of a vertex list

nodes.summary: Let $d$ be a cost function on the vertices with values in a linearly ordered additive commutative monoid. The tree with root $r$ and subtree forest $F$ is a minimum spanning tree of a list $V$ of vertices for $d$ when it is a spanning tree of $V$ (the vertices of $V$ are distinct and the list of $r$ followed by the vertices of $F$ in preorder is a permutation of $V$) and, for every vertex $r'$ and forest $F'$ such…
nodes.title: Minimum spanning tree of a vertex list

nodes.summary: A list $H$ is a tour of a list $V$ of vertices when the vertices of $V$ are distinct and $H$ is a permutation of $V$: $H$ lists each vertex of $V$ exactly once and nothing else.
nodes.title: Tour of a vertex list

nodes.summary: Let $d$ be a cost function on the vertices with values in a linearly ordered additive commutative monoid that is symmetric, zero on the diagonal, nonnegative and satisfies the triangle inequality. Let $V$ be a list of distinct vertices. Let $T$ be a minimum spanning tree of $V$ for $d$: a rooted tree whose vertices are the elements of $V$, each once, whose weight (the total cost of its edges) is at most that of…
nodes.title: A minimum spanning tree costs at most any tour

nodes.summary: Let $V$ be a list of distinct vertices, and let $r$ and $F$ be such that $r$ followed by the vertices of the forest $F$ in preorder is a permutation of $V$ (the tree with root $r$ and subtree forest $F$ spans $V$). Then the list returned by `APPROX-TSP-TOUR` on $r$ and $F$ is a tour of $V$: it is a permutation of $V$.
nodes.title: The approximate TSP tour is a tour

nodes.summary: Let $d$ be a cost function on vertices with values in a linearly ordered additive commutative monoid that is symmetric, zero on the diagonal, nonnegative and satisfies the triangle inequality. Let $V$ be a list of vertices, let the tree with root $r$ and subtree forest $F$ be a minimum spanning tree of $V$ for $d$, and let $H$ be a tour of $V$. Then the cost under $d$ of the closed tour returned by…
nodes.title: APPROX-TSP-TOUR on a given minimum spanning tree costs at most twice any tour

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a parent array on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, assigning to each vertex $v$ either a parent $p(v)$ or no parent. Then $\operatorname{up}(v)$ is the parent $p(v)$ when $v$ has one, and $v$ itself otherwise, so a root stays put.
nodes.title: One step up a parent array

nodes.summary: Let $p$ assign to each vertex of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ either a parent or nothing. The children of a vertex $v$ are the vertices $c$ whose parent $p(c)$ is $v$, listed in increasing order.
nodes.title: Children in a parent array

nodes.summary: Let $p$ assign to each vertex of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ either a parent or nothing. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and a vertex $v$, the forest below $v$ of depth $k$ is empty when $k = 0$. For depth $k + 1$ it has one tree for each child $c$ of $v$ (each vertex whose parent is $v$), in increasing order of $c$, namely $c$ with the forest below $c$ of depth $k$ as its subtrees.
nodes.title: Forest of a parent array below a vertex

nodes.summary: Let $p$ assign to each vertex of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ either a parent or nothing, and let a step up move a vertex to its parent, leaving a vertex without parent in place. The parent array $p$ is a parent tree with root $r$ when $r$ has no parent and every vertex reaches $r$ after finitely many steps up.
nodes.title: Parent tree

reading_title.source: Descendant within $k$ levels

nodes.summary: Let $p$ assign to each vertex of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ either a parent or nothing, and let a step up move a vertex to its parent, leaving a vertex without parent in place. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, a vertex $u$ lies strictly below a vertex $v$, at most $k$ levels down, when for some $j < k$ the vertex reached from $u$ after $j$ steps up has parent $v$.
nodes.title: Descendant within $k$ levels

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a parent array on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $d$ be a cost on ordered pairs of vertices with values in an additive commutative monoid, and let $\operatorname{up}(u)$ be the parent of $u$, or $u$ itself if $u$ has no parent. For every $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and every vertex $v$, let $F$ be the forest of the subtrees of the children of $v$ in $p$, cut off $k$ levels below $v$. Then the weight under…
nodes.title: Weight of the forest built from a parent array

nodes.summary: Let $p$ assign to each vertex of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ either a parent or nothing, forming a parent tree with root $r$, and let a step up move a vertex to its parent, leaving a vertex without parent in place. Then every vertex $u \ne r$ lies strictly below $r$, at most $n$ levels down: for some $j < n$, the vertex reached from $u$ after $j$ steps up has parent $r$.
nodes.title: Every non-root vertex lies below the root

nodes.summary: Let $p$ assign to each vertex of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ either a parent or nothing, forming a parent tree with root $r$. Then $r$ together with the forest below $r$ of depth $n$ built from $p$ is a spanning tree of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$: $r$ followed by the vertices of the forest in preorder lists every vertex exactly once.
nodes.title: The forest of a parent tree spans all vertices

nodes.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the complete graph on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ as a directed adjacency: the vertices are listed in increasing order, and the neighbours of each vertex $u$ are all vertices other than $u$, in increasing order.
nodes.title: Complete graph as an ordered adjacency

nodes.summary: Given costs $d(u,v)$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with values in a type with commutative addition, the weight of an unordered pair $\{u, v\}$ is $d(u,v) + d(v,u)$, which does not depend on the order of $u$ and $v$. When $d$ is symmetric this is twice the cost, which leaves minimum spanning trees unchanged.
nodes.title: Symmetrized edge weights

nodes.summary: Given costs $d(u,v)$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with values in a linearly ordered type with a zero and commutative addition, and a root $r$, this is the parent array returned by Prim's algorithm run from $r$ on the complete graph on these vertices, with the weight of the edge $\{u, v\}$ equal to $d(u,v) + d(v,u)$: it sends each vertex to its parent, or to no parent.
nodes.title: Prim's parent array on the complete graph

nodes.summary: Given costs $d(u,v)$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with values in a linearly ordered type with a zero and commutative addition, and a root $r$, take Prim's parent array for $d$ and $r$ (Prim's algorithm run from $r$ on the complete graph with edge weights $d(u,v) + d(v,u)$). This forest is the forest of the subtrees below $r$ in that parent array, cut off $n$ levels below $r$, in left-child right-sibling…
nodes.title: Forest of Prim's tree

nodes.summary: Given costs $d(u,v)$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with values in a linearly ordered type with a zero and commutative addition, and a root $r$, the tour is $r$ followed by the vertices of the forest of Prim's tree below $r$ in preorder. Its running time counts one unit per vertex of the tour; running Prim's algorithm and building the forest are not counted.
nodes.title: APPROX-TSP-TOUR with Prim's tree

nodes.summary: For all vertices $u, v$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, $v$ is listed among the neighbours of $u$ in the complete graph as an ordered adjacency if and only if $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in the complete simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, that is, $u \ne v$.
nodes.title: Neighbours in the complete adjacency

nodes.summary: Given costs $d(u,v)$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with values in a linearly ordered type with a zero and commutative addition, and a root $r$, Prim's tree is the simple graph on these vertices in which distinct vertices $u$ and $v$ are adjacent when one of them is the parent of the other in Prim's parent array for $d$ and $r$.
nodes.title: Prim's tree

nodes.summary: For costs $d(u,v)$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with values in any linearly ordered type with a zero and commutative addition, and any root $r$, Prim's tree for $d$ and $r$ is a tree on all of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, that is, a spanning tree of the complete graph.
nodes.title: Prim's tree is a spanning tree

nodes.summary: Let $d(u,v)$ be real costs on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $r$ be a vertex, and weigh each edge $\{u, v\}$ by $d(u,v) + d(v,u)$. Then Prim's tree for $d$ and $r$ is a tree, and for every tree $H$ on these vertices the total weight of the edges of Prim's tree is at most the total weight of the edges of $H$.
nodes.title: Prim's tree is a minimum spanning tree

nodes.summary: Let $W$ be a linearly ordered type with a zero and a commutative addition, let $d$ assign a weight in $W$ to each ordered pair of vertices of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, and let $r$ be a vertex. Then Prim's parent array for $d$ from $r$ is a parent tree with root $r$: $r$ has no parent, and every vertex reaches $r$ after finitely many steps up, where a step up moves a vertex to its parent and leaves a vertex without…
nodes.title: Prim's parent array is a parent tree

nodes.summary: Let $W$ be a linearly ordered type with a zero and a commutative addition, let $d$ assign a weight in $W$ to each ordered pair of vertices of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, and let $r$ be a vertex. Then $r$ together with Prim's forest for $d$ and $r$ is a spanning tree of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$: $r$ followed by the vertices of the forest in preorder lists every vertex exactly once.
nodes.title: Prim's forest spans all vertices

nodes.summary: For costs $d(u,v)$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with values in a linearly ordered type with a zero and commutative addition, and any root $r$, the list returned by APPROX-TSP-TOUR with Prim's tree for $d$ and $r$ is a permutation of $0, 1, \dots, n-1$: it visits every vertex exactly once.
nodes.title: The tour from Prim's tree is a tour

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a parent array on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which the root $r$ has no parent and every chain of parents reaches $r$, and let $w$ assign to each unordered pair $\{u, v\}$ of vertices (possibly $u = v$) a value in a commutative additive monoid. Write $\hat p(u)$ for the parent of $u$, or $u$ itself if $u$ has no parent. Then the sum of $w(e)$ over the edges $e$ of the parent graph (distinct $u$…
nodes.title: Edge sums over a parent tree

nodes.summary: Let $d$ be a real metric cost on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ (symmetric, zero on the diagonal, nonnegative, and satisfying the triangle inequality), and let $r$ be a vertex. Then the cost of the closed tour through the list returned by APPROX-TSP-TOUR with Prim's tree for $d$ and $r$ is at most twice the cost of the closed tour through $H$, for every list $H$ that visits each of $0, 1, \dots, n-1$ exactly once.

Greedy set cover

nodes.summary: Given a list $F$ of finite sets and a finite set $U$, the best set of $F$ for $U$ is the first set $S$ in the list $F$ that maximizes $|S \cap U|$, or $\emptyset$ when $F$ is empty.
nodes.title: Greedy choice of a set

Let $T$ be the first $S_i$ in the list that maximizes $|S_i \cap U|$, or $T = \emptyset$ when $n = 0$. nodes.title: Greedy set cover

nodes.summary: For every list $F$ of finite sets and every finite set $U$, every set in the list returned by the greedy set cover algorithm on $F$ and $U$ is a member of $F$.
nodes.title: The greedy set cover draws its sets from the family

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a list of finite sets and $U$ a finite set such that every element of $U$ lies in some set of $F$. Then every element of $U$ lies in some set of the list returned by the greedy set cover algorithm on $F$ and $U$.
nodes.title: The greedy set cover is a cover

nodes.summary: For every list $F$ of finite sets and every finite set $U$, the list returned by the greedy set cover algorithm on $F$ and $U$ has length at most $|U|$.
nodes.title: The greedy set cover has at most as many sets as elements

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a list of finite sets and $U$ a finite set. The running time of greedy set cover of $U$ from $F$ is at most $(|U| + 1)(|F| + \sum_{S \in F} |S|)$, where $|F|$ is the length of the list and the sum runs over the entries of $F$, counted with repetition.
nodes.title: Running time of greedy set cover

nodes.summary: Write $H(n) = 1 + \frac12 + \dots + \frac1n$ for the $n$-th harmonic number, so $H(0) = 0$. For natural numbers $d \le a \le k$, we have $\frac{d}{k} \le H(a) - H(a - d)$, where $\frac{d}{k}$ is read as $0$ when $k = 0$.
nodes.title: Lower bound for a difference of harmonic numbers

nodes.summary: Let $L$ be a list of finite sets and $T$ a finite set such that every element of $T$ lies in some member of $L$. Then $|T| \le \sum_{S \in L} |S \cap T|$, where the sum runs over the list $L$ with repetitions.
nodes.title: Covering bound by intersections

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a list of finite sets, $U$ a finite set, and $H(n) = 1 + \frac12 + \dots + \frac1n$ the $n$-th harmonic number. For every list $C^*$ of members of $F$ that together cover $U$, the list of sets returned by the greedy set cover algorithm on $F$ and $U$ has length at most $\sum_{S \in C^*} H(|S \cap U|)$, where the sum runs over the list $C^*$ with repetitions.
nodes.title: Potential bound for greedy set cover

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a list of finite sets each with at most $d$ elements, $U$ a finite set, and $H(n) = 1 + \frac12 + \dots + \frac1n$ the $n$-th harmonic number. For every list $C^*$ of members of $F$ that together cover $U$, the list of sets returned by the greedy set cover algorithm on $F$ and $U$ has length at most $|C^*| \cdot H(d)$, where $|C^*|$ is the length of $C^*$.
nodes.title: Harmonic bound in the largest set size for greedy set cover

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a list of finite sets, $U$ a finite set, and $H(n) = 1 + \frac12 + \dots + \frac1n$ the $n$-th harmonic number. For every list $C^*$ of members of $F$ that together cover $U$, the list of sets returned by the greedy set cover algorithm on $F$ and $U$ has length at most $|C^*| \cdot H(|U|)$, where $|C^*|$ is the length of $C^*$.
nodes.title: Harmonic bound in the universe size for greedy set cover

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a list of finite sets and $U$ a finite set. For every list $C^*$ of members of $F$ that together cover $U$, the list of sets returned by the greedy set cover algorithm on $F$ and $U$ has length at most $|C^*| \cdot (\ln |U| + 1)$, where $|C^*|$ is the length of $C^*$ and $\ln 0 = 0$.
nodes.title: Greedy set cover is a logarithmic approximation

nodes.summary: Given a list $F$ of finite sets, a finite set $U$ and a rational cost $w(S)$ for each finite set $S$, this is the first set $S$ in $F$ with $S \cap U \ne \emptyset$ that minimizes the ratio $w(S) / |S \cap U|$ among the sets of $F$ meeting $U$, or nothing when no set of $F$ meets $U$.

nodes.summary: Let $F = [S_1, \dots, S_n]$ be a list of finite sets, $U$ a finite set and $w$ a function giving each finite set $S$ a rational cost $w(S)$. The weighted greedy set cover of $U$ from $F$ with costs $w$ is computed as follows. If no $S_i$ meets $U$, the result is the empty list. nodes.title: Weighted greedy set cover

nodes.summary: For every list $F$ of finite sets, finite set $U$ and rational cost function $w$ on finite sets, every set chosen by the weighted greedy set cover of $U$ from $F$ with costs $w$ belongs to $F$.
nodes.title: The weighted greedy set cover uses sets of the family

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be a list of finite sets, $U$ a finite set and $w$ any rational cost function on finite sets. If every element of $U$ lies in some set of $F$, then every element of $U$ lies in some set chosen by the weighted greedy set cover of $U$ from $F$ with costs $w$.
nodes.title: The weighted greedy set cover is a cover

nodes.summary: Let $F = [S_1, \dots, S_m]$ be a list of finite sets, $U$ a finite set and $w$ a rational cost function on finite sets. The weighted greedy set cover of $U$ from $F$ with costs $w$ runs in time at most $(|U| + 1)\,(m + |S_1| + \dots + |S_m|)$: at most $|U| + 1$ searches for a best set, each costing $m$ plus the total size of the sets of $F$.

List scheduling on identical machines

nodes.summary: Let $m$ be a natural number. An assignment $\sigma$ of a list $\sigma(i)$ of natural numbers (processing times) to each machine $i \in \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$ is a schedule of a list $J$ of natural numbers when the sum over all machines $i$ of the multisets of entries of $\sigma(i)$ equals the multiset of entries of $J$, that is, every number occurs in the lists $\sigma(i)$ together exactly as often as it occurs in $J$.
nodes.title: Schedule of a list of jobs

List update problem

nodes.summary: The cost of accessing an item $x$ in a list $L$ is its position in $L$, counting from $1$: one more than the index of the first occurrence of $x$ in $L$. If $x$ does not occur in $L$, the cost is the length of $L$ plus one.
nodes.title: Access cost

nodes.summary: For a list $L$ and an item $x$, moving $x$ to the front gives the list consisting of $x$ followed by $L$ with its first occurrence of $x$ removed; if $x$ does not occur in $L$, this is $x$ followed by $L$.
nodes.title: Move-to-front

nodes.summary: Starting from a list $L$, move-to-front serves a request sequence $\sigma$ one request at a time: a request $x$ costs the position of $x$ in the current list, counting from $1$ (an item not in the list costs its length plus one), and then $x$ is moved to the front (inserted at the front if absent). The cost of move-to-front on $\sigma$ from $L$ is the sum of these access costs.
nodes.title: Cost of move-to-front

nodes.summary: Starting from a list $L$ and serving a request sequence $\sigma$, move-to-front moves each request $x$ in turn to the front of the current list (inserting it at the front if it is absent). The final list of move-to-front on $\sigma$ from $L$ is the list it ends with.

nodes.summary: A deterministic online bipartite matching algorithm with $a$ offline (left) vertices $0, \dots, a - 1$ is given by a proposal rule: on each arrival it receives the neighbour lists (lists of left vertices) of all earlier arrivals, in order, and the neighbour list of the current arrival, and proposes a left vertex to match the arrival to, or none.
nodes.title: Deterministic online bipartite matching algorithm

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be an online matcher with $a$ left vertices, $h$ a history (the neighbour lists of earlier arrivals), $U$ a list of left vertices already matched, and $\sigma$ a sequence of arrivals, each given by its list of left neighbours. nodes.summary: A list $m$ of left vertices is a perfect matching of a sequence $\sigma$ of arrivals (neighbour lists) when $m$ and $\sigma$ have the same length, the entries of $m$ are pairwise distinct, and for each $j$ the $j$-th entry of $m$ lies in the $j$-th neighbour list of $\sigma$.

nodes.summary: For a sequence $\sigma = (\sigma_0, \dots, \sigma_{k-1})$ of arrivals, each a list of left vertices in $\{0, \dots, a - 1\}$, the bipartite graph of $\sigma$ is given by adjacency lists: left vertex $i$ is sent to the list, in increasing order, of the arrivals $j < k$ with $i \in \sigma_j$.
nodes.title: Graph of a sequence of arrivals

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a sequence of arrivals (neighbour lists) and $m$ a perfect matching of $\sigma$. Then the bipartite graph of $\sigma$, in which left vertex $i$ is adjacent to arrival $j$ when $i$ lies in the $j$-th neighbour list, has a matching with as many edges as $\sigma$ has arrivals.
nodes.title: Perfect matchings of the arrivals are matchings of their graph

Ski rental problem

nodes.summary: A deterministic strategy is either a day $t \in \mathbb{N}$ on which to buy the skis, after renting on the days before it, or the choice to rent forever. Days are numbered from $1$; the value $t = 0$ is also a strategy, and the cost treats it as renting forever.
nodes.title: Deterministic ski-rental strategy

nodes.summary: Renting skis costs $1$ per day and buying them costs a natural number $B$. The cost $\mathrm{cost}_B(s, d) \in \mathbb{N}$ of a strategy $s$ for a season of $d \in \mathbb{N}$ days is $(t - 1) + B$ if $s$ buys on a day $t$ with $1 \le t \le d$ (rent for $t - 1$ days, then buy), and $d$ otherwise, that is, if $s$ rents forever or buys on a day $t$ with $t = 0$ or $t > d$ (rent every day).
nodes.title: Cost of a ski-rental strategy

nodes.summary: For a purchase price $B \in \mathbb{N}$ and a season of $d \in \mathbb{N}$ days, the offline optimum is $\mathrm{opt}_B(d) = \min(d, B)$: rent every day or buy on day one, whichever is cheaper.
nodes.title: Offline optimum for ski rental

nodes.summary: For a purchase price $B$, the break-even strategy is the deterministic strategy that buys on day $B$.
nodes.title: Break-even strategy

nodes.summary: For every purchase price $B$, every deterministic strategy $s$ and every season length $d$, the offline optimum $\mathrm{opt}_B(d)$ is at most the cost $\mathrm{cost}_B(s, d)$ of $s$ for a season of $d$ days.
nodes.title: The offline optimum bounds every strategy's cost

nodes.summary: For every purchase price $B \ge 1$ and every season length $d$, the break-even strategy $\mathrm{breakEven}_B$ pays at most $2 - 1/B$ times the offline optimum $\mathrm{opt}_B(d)$: its cost $\mathrm{cost}_B(\mathrm{breakEven}_B, d)$ for a season of $d$ days satisfies $B \cdot \mathrm{cost}_B(\mathrm{breakEven}_B, d) \le (2B - 1) \cdot \mathrm{opt}_B(d)$.
nodes.title: Ski-rental upper bound for the break-even strategy

nodes.summary: For every purchase price $B \ge 1$ and every season length $d \in \mathbb{N}$, the cost $\mathrm{cost}_B(\mathrm{breakEven}_B, d)$ of the break-even strategy for a season of $d$ days is at most $2 \cdot \mathrm{opt}_B(d)$, twice the offline optimum $\mathrm{opt}_B(d)$. In particular, the break-even strategy is $2$-competitive.
nodes.title: The break-even strategy pays at most twice the optimum

nodes.summary: Every deterministic strategy pays at least `(2 - 1/B)` times the optimum on some season, `(2 B - 1) * opt ≤ B * cost`.
nodes.title: Lower bound

nodes.title: Randomized algorithms and probabilistic analysis
Average-case running time

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be an algorithm on inputs of a type $\gamma$ whose running time $T_A(x)$ on each input $x$ is a natural number, and let $D$ be a probability mass function on $\gamma$. The expected running time of $A$ under $D$ is the extended nonnegative expectation $\sum_{x \in \gamma} D(x)\, T_A(x) \in [0, \infty]$ of the running time, the sum taken over all inputs.
nodes.title: Expected running time

nodes.summary: For a list $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$, the uniform permutation of $x$ is the probability distribution on lists obtained by choosing a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ uniformly at random and outputting $(x_{\sigma(0)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(n-1)})$.
nodes.title: Uniformly random rearrangement of a list

nodes.summary: For a list $x$, every list in the support of the uniform permutation of $x$ has the same length as $x$.
nodes.title: Rearrangements preserve length

nodes.summary: For a list $x$, every list in the support of the uniform permutation of $x$ is a permutation of $x$, that is, it has the same entries with the same multiplicities.
nodes.title: Rearrangements are permutations

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be an algorithm on lists whose running time $T_A(y)$ on each list $y$ is a natural number, and let $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ be a list of length $n$. The expected running time of $A$ when its input is $x$ rearranged by a uniformly random permutation equals
nodes.title: Average formula for the expected time over random orderings

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be an algorithm on inputs of a type $\gamma$ whose running time $T_A(x)$ on each input $x$ is a natural number, let $D$ be a probability mass function on $\gamma$, and let $c$ be a natural number. If $T_A(x) = c$ for every input $x$ in the support of $D$, then the expected running time of $A$ under $D$ equals $c$.
nodes.title: Constant running time on the support gives that expected time

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be an algorithm on lists whose running time $T_A(y)$ on each list $y$ is a natural number, let $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ be a list of length $n$, and let $c$ be a natural number. If $T_A(x_{\sigma(0)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(n-1)}) = c$ for every permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, then the expected running time of $A$ when its input is $x$ rearranged by a uniformly random permutation equals $c$.
nodes.title: Constant running time on all rearrangements gives that expected time

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be an algorithm on lists whose running time $T_A(y)$ on each list $y$ is a natural number, and let $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ be a list of length $n$. The expected running time of $A$ when its input is $x$ rearranged by a uniformly random permutation, converted from $[0, \infty]$ to a real number, equals
nodes.title: Average formula for the expected time over random orderings, in the reals
Fisher–Yates shuffle

nodes.summary: Given a vector $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ and a draw history $d$, which assigns to each position $i < n$ a number $d_i$ with $0 \le d_i < n - i$, the Fisher–Yates computation processes the positions $i = 0, 1, \dots, n - 1$ in increasing order and at position $i$ swaps the entries at positions $i$ and $i + d_i$ of the current vector. It returns the final vector together with a cost pair in…
nodes.title: Fisher–Yates shuffle with supplied draws

nodes.summary: For every vector $x$ of length $n$ and every draw history $d$, which assigns to each position $i < n$ a number $d_i$ with $0 \le d_i < n - i$, the Fisher–Yates computation on $x$ and $d$ has cost pair $(n, n)$: it retrieves exactly $n$ draws and performs exactly $n$ swaps.
nodes.title: Cost of the Fisher–Yates shuffle

nodes.summary: For every vector $x$ of length $n$ and every draw history $d$, which assigns to each position $i < n$ a number $d_i$ with $0 \le d_i < n - i$, the list of entries of the vector returned by the Fisher–Yates computation on $x$ and $d$ is a permutation of the list of entries of $x$. In particular every value occurs equally often in both, even when values of $x$ repeat.
nodes.title: Fisher–Yates output is a rearrangement of its input

nodes.summary: For the empty vector $x$ (of length $0$) and its empty draw history, the Fisher–Yates computation returns $x$ with cost pair $(0, 0)$: it retrieves no draws and performs no swaps.
nodes.title: Fisher–Yates on the empty vector

nodes.summary: For every vector $x$ of length $1$ and every draw history $d$, the Fisher–Yates computation returns $x$ unchanged with cost pair $(1, 1)$: it still retrieves the single draw $d_0 = 0$ and performs the self-swap at position $0$.
nodes.title: Fisher–Yates on a one-element vector

nodes.summary: For a vector $x$ of length $n$, this is the probability distribution on outcomes (a vector of length $n$ together with a cost pair in $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$) obtained by choosing a draw history $d$ uniformly at random among all assignments of a number $d_i$ with $0 \le d_i < n - i$ to each position $i < n$, and returning the result of the Fisher–Yates computation on $x$ and $d$.
nodes.title: Output distribution of the Fisher–Yates shuffle

nodes.summary: Let $x$ be a vector of length $n$, and consider the draw histories $d$, which assign to each position $i < n$ a number $d_i$ with $0 \le d_i < n - i$. For every outcome $o$ (a vector of length $n$ together with a cost pair), the probability that the Fisher–Yates output distribution of $x$ assigns to $o$ equals the sum, over all draw histories $d$ for which the Fisher–Yates computation on $x$ and $d$ yields exactly…
nodes.title: Probability of a Fisher–Yates outcome

nodes.summary: Let $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ be a vector and let $\sigma$ be a permutation of $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ chosen uniformly at random. Then the Fisher–Yates output distribution of $x$ equals the distribution of the outcome consisting of the vector $(x_{\sigma(0)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(n-1)})$ with cost pair $(n, n)$.
nodes.title: Fisher–Yates produces a uniformly random permutation

nodes.summary: Let $k \le n$ and let $a_0, \dots, a_{k-1}$ be distinct elements of $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$. Run the Fisher–Yates computation on the vector $(0, 1, \dots, n - 1)$ with every draw history $d$, which assigns to each position $i < n$ a number $d_i$ with $0 \le d_i < n - i$, and give each history weight $1/n!$. Then the total weight of the histories whose output vector has entry $a_p$ at position $p$ for every $p < k$…
nodes.title: Prefix probabilities of the Fisher–Yates shuffle
Freivalds' algorithm

nodes.summary: Given $n \times n$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $\mathbb{F}_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2$, stored as arrays of rows, and a seed $r \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$, the trial computes the column vectors $Br$, $A(Br)$ and $Cr$, each by accumulating matrix products into a zero column, and returns true exactly when $A(Br) = Cr$. Its cost is the pair (number of scalar multiplications, number of scalar additions), each multiply-add step counting…
nodes.title: Freivalds trial

nodes.summary: For $n \times n$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and every seed $r \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$, the Freivalds trial performs exactly $3n^2$ scalar multiplications and exactly $3n^2$ scalar additions.
nodes.title: Cost of the Freivalds trial

nodes.summary: An $n \times n$ array $A$ of rows over $\mathbb{F}_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2$ determines the $n \times n$ matrix over $\mathbb{F}_2$ whose $(i, j)$ entry is entry $j$ of row $i$ of $A$.
nodes.title: Matrix of a Freivalds input

nodes.summary: For $n \times n$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and every seed $r \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$, the Freivalds trial on $A$, $B$, $C$, $r$ returns true if and only if $A(Br) = Cr$.
nodes.title: Acceptance criterion of the Freivalds trial

nodes.summary: For $n \times n$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and every seed $r \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$, the Freivalds trial on $A$, $B$, $C$, $r$ returns true if and only if $(AB - C)r = 0$.
nodes.title: Acceptance via the product discrepancy

nodes.summary: Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_2$ with $AB = C$. Then for every seed $r \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$ the Freivalds trial on $A$, $B$, $C$, $r$ returns true. This includes the case $n = 0$.
nodes.title: Completeness of the Freivalds trial

nodes.summary: For $0 \times 0$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and the empty seed $r$, the Freivalds trial returns true at zero cost: it performs no scalar multiplications and no scalar additions.
nodes.title: Freivalds trial on empty matrices

nodes.summary: Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_2$ with $AB \ne C$. Then twice the number of seeds $r \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$ on which the Freivalds trial returns true is at most the number of all seeds in $\mathbb{F}_2^n$; that is, at most half of the seeds accept.
nodes.title: Soundness of the Freivalds trial

nodes.summary: For $n \times n$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $\mathbb{F}_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, given as arrays, the Freivalds trial law is the probability distribution on $\{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$ of the value returned by the Freivalds trial on $A$, $B$, $C$ with seed $r$, where $r$ is drawn uniformly from $\mathbb{F}_2^n$.
nodes.title: Freivalds trial law

nodes.summary: Let $\mathbb{F}_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. For every $n$ and every vector $r \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$, the uniform probability distribution on $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ assigns to $r$ the probability $(2^n)^{-1}$.
nodes.title: Uniform mass of a Freivalds seed

nodes.summary: Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, given as arrays. The probability that the Freivalds trial law of $A$, $B$, $C$ returns true equals the number of seeds $r \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$ on which the Freivalds trial on $A$, $B$, $C$ with seed $r$ accepts, divided by the number $|\mathbb{F}_2^n|$ of all seeds.
nodes.title: Acceptance probability of the Freivalds trial as a seed count

nodes.summary: Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, given as arrays. If $AB = C$, then the Freivalds trial law of $A$, $B$, $C$ returns true with probability $1$. This includes the case $n = 0$ of empty matrices.
nodes.title: The Freivalds trial accepts a correct product with probability one

nodes.summary: Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, given as arrays. If $AB \ne C$, then the Freivalds trial law of $A$, $B$, $C$ returns true with probability at most $1/2$.
nodes.title: The Freivalds trial accepts a wrong product with probability at most one half

nodes.summary: Given $n \times n$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $\mathbb{Z}/2$ and seeds $r_0, \dots, r_{k-1} \in (\mathbb{Z}/2)^n$, run the Freivalds trial on $A$, $B$, $C$ with each seed $r_0, \dots, r_{k-1}$ in order, including the trials after a rejection, and return the conjunction of their results (true when $k = 0$). The arithmetic cost of the run is the sum of the costs of the $k$ trials.
nodes.title: Repeated Freivalds test on fixed seeds

nodes.summary: For $n \times n$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $\mathbb{Z}/2$ and seeds $r_0, \dots, r_{k-1} \in (\mathbb{Z}/2)^n$, the repeated Freivalds test on these seeds performs exactly $3kn^2$ scalar multiplications and $3kn^2$ scalar additions.
nodes.title: Cost of the repeated Freivalds test on fixed seeds

nodes.summary: For $n \times n$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $\mathbb{Z}/2$ and seeds $r_0, \dots, r_{k-1} \in (\mathbb{Z}/2)^n$, the repeated Freivalds test on these seeds accepts if and only if, for every $i < k$, the Freivalds trial on $A$, $B$, $C$ with seed $r_i$ accepts.
nodes.title: Acceptance of the repeated Freivalds test on fixed seeds

nodes.summary: Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{Z}/2$ with $AB = C$. Then for every $k$, including $k = 0$, and all seeds $r_0, \dots, r_{k-1} \in (\mathbb{Z}/2)^n$, the repeated Freivalds test on these seeds accepts.
nodes.title: Completeness of the repeated Freivalds test on fixed seeds

nodes.summary: For $n \times n$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $\mathbb{Z}/2$, the repeated Freivalds test on the empty list of seeds ($k = 0$) accepts and performs no scalar multiplications or additions.
nodes.title: Repeated Freivalds test with no trials

nodes.summary: For $0 \times 0$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $\mathbb{Z}/2$ and any number $k$ of seeds (each the empty vector), the repeated Freivalds test accepts and performs no scalar multiplications or additions.
nodes.title: Repeated Freivalds test on empty matrices

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n, k$ and $n \times n$ matrices $A, B, C$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$, this is the probability distribution on $\{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$ of the result returned by the repeated Freivalds executor on $A, B, C$ when its history of $k$ seeds is drawn uniformly from $(\mathbb{F}_2^n)^k$.
nodes.title: Output distribution of repeated Freivalds trials

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $n$ and $k$, under the uniform distribution on histories of $k$ seeds, that is, on $(\mathbb{F}_2^n)^k$, every history has probability exactly $(2^{nk})^{-1}$. This includes the cases $k = 0$ and $n = 0$.
nodes.title: Uniform mass of a Freivalds seed history

nodes.summary: Let $n, k$ be natural numbers and let $A, B, C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_2$. The number of histories $(r_1, \dots, r_k)$ of seeds $r_i \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$ on which the repeated Freivalds executor accepts equals $a^k$, where $a$ is the number of seeds $r \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$ on which a single Freivalds trial accepts.
nodes.title: Counting accepted histories of repeated Freivalds trials

nodes.summary: Let $n, k$ be natural numbers and let $A, B, C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_2$. If the history of $k$ seeds is drawn uniformly from $(\mathbb{F}_2^n)^k$, the probability that the repeated Freivalds executor accepts is $p^k$, where $p$ is the probability that a single Freivalds trial accepts on a seed drawn uniformly from $\mathbb{F}_2^n$.
nodes.title: Acceptance probability of repeated Freivalds trials

nodes.summary: Let $n, k$ be natural numbers and let $A, B, C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_2$ with $AB = C$. If the history of $k$ seeds is drawn uniformly from $(\mathbb{F}_2^n)^k$, then the repeated Freivalds executor accepts with probability $1$.
nodes.title: Completeness of repeated Freivalds trials

nodes.summary: Let $n, k$ be natural numbers and let $A, B, C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_2$ with $AB \ne C$. If the history of $k$ seeds is drawn uniformly from $(\mathbb{F}_2^n)^k$, then the repeated Freivalds executor accepts with probability at most $(2^k)^{-1}$.
nodes.title: Soundness of repeated Freivalds trials

nodes.summary: Let $A = B = (1)$ and $C = (0)$ be $1 \times 1$ matrices over $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. Then $AB \neq C$.
nodes.title: The sharp Freivalds example has a wrong product

nodes.summary: Let $A = B = (1)$ and $C = (0)$ be $1 \times 1$ matrices over $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. For every seed $r \in (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^1$, the Freivalds trial on $A$, $B$, $C$ with seed $r$, which compares $A(Br)$ with $Cr$, accepts if and only if the single entry $r_0$ of $r$ is $0$.
nodes.title: The sharp Freivalds example accepts exactly the zero seed

nodes.summary: Let $A = B = (1)$ and $C = (0)$ be $1 \times 1$ matrices over $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. Exactly one seed $r \in (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^1$ is accepted by the Freivalds trial on $A$, $B$, $C$.
nodes.title: The sharp Freivalds example has exactly one accepted seed

nodes.summary: Let $A = B = (1)$ and $C = (0)$ be $1 \times 1$ matrices over $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. When the seed is drawn uniformly from $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^1$, the Freivalds trial on $A$, $B$, $C$ accepts with probability exactly $1/2$.
nodes.title: The sharp Freivalds example is accepted with probability one half

nodes.summary: Let $A = B = (1)$ and $C = (0)$ be $1 \times 1$ matrices over $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, and let $k$ be a natural number. Run $k$ Freivalds trials on $A$, $B$, $C$ with seeds drawn independently and uniformly from $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^1$, accepting exactly when every trial accepts. Then the run accepts with probability exactly $2^{-k}$.
nodes.title: Exact acceptance probability of repeated trials on the sharp Freivalds example
Hiring problem

nodes.summary: Given candidates $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ in a linearly ordered type, the scan interviews them in order while keeping a current manager, initially none, which counts as below every candidate. Candidate $i$ is hired exactly when $x_i$ is strictly greater than the value of the current manager, and then becomes the new manager; ties keep the earlier manager. The scan returns the zero-based index of the final manager…
nodes.title: The hire-assistant scan

nodes.summary: For every list $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ in a linearly ordered type, the manager returned by the hire-assistant scan is none when the list is empty, and otherwise is the smallest index $i$ such that $x_i$ is a maximum of the list.
nodes.title: The hire-assistant scan returns the earliest best candidate

nodes.summary: For every list $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ in a linearly ordered type, the list of indices hired by the hire-assistant scan, in chronological order, is the increasing list of all indices $i < n$ such that $x_j < x_i$ for every $j < i$.
nodes.title: The hire-assistant scan hires exactly the strict prefix maxima

nodes.summary: For every list of $n$ candidates in a linearly ordered type, the cost pair of the hire-assistant scan is $(n, h)$, where $h$ is the length of the list of hired indices that the scan returns.
nodes.title: Cost of the hire-assistant scan

nodes.summary: On the empty list, the hire-assistant scan returns no manager and an empty list of hires, with cost pair $(0, 0)$.
nodes.title: Hire-assistant scan on no candidates

nodes.summary: For every element $a$ of a linearly ordered type, on the one-element list $[a]$ the hire-assistant scan returns manager index $0$ and hire list $[0]$, with cost pair $(1, 1)$: the single candidate is hired regardless of its quality.
nodes.title: Hire-assistant scan on one candidate

nodes.summary: For every nonempty list of $n$ candidates in a linearly ordered type, the number of hires $h$ recorded in the cost pair of the hire-assistant scan satisfies $1 \le h \le n$.
nodes.title: Hire-count bounds for the hire-assistant scan

nodes.summary: For every strictly increasing list $x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_{n-1}$ in a linearly ordered type, including the empty list, the hire-assistant scan hires the indices $0, 1, \dots, n - 1$ in that order, and its cost pair is $(n, n)$.
nodes.title: Strictly increasing input hires every candidate

nodes.summary: Let $x$ be a list of $n$ pairwise distinct elements of a linearly ordered type, and rearrange its entries by a uniformly random permutation of the indices. The expected number of hires, valued in $[0, \infty]$, that the hire-assistant procedure (interview the entries in order, hiring each one strictly better than every earlier one) makes on the rearranged list equals $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{1}{i+1}$.
nodes.title: Expected number of hires under a random permutation

nodes.summary: Let $x$ be a list of $n$ pairwise distinct elements of a linearly ordered type, and rearrange its entries by a uniformly random permutation of the indices. The expected number of hires that the hire-assistant procedure (interview the entries in order, hiring each one strictly better than every earlier one) makes on the rearranged list, an element of $[0, \infty]$, converted to a real number, equals…
nodes.title: Expected number of hires as a real harmonic sum

nodes.summary: Let $x$ be a list of $n$ pairwise distinct elements of a linearly ordered type, and rearrange its entries by a uniformly random permutation of the indices. The expected number of hires that the hire-assistant procedure (interview the entries in order, hiring each one strictly better than every earlier one) makes on the rearranged list, an element of $[0, \infty]$, converted to a real number, equals the harmonic…

Karger's algorithm

nodes.summary: A state over a vertex type $V$ consists of a list of current (super-)vertices in $V$ and a list of edges, each an ordered pair of elements of $V$; repeated pairs are parallel edges.
nodes.title: Multigraph state of Karger's algorithm

nodes.summary: A multigraph, given by a list of vertices and a list of edges (pairs of vertices, with multiplicity), is valid when its vertex list has no repeated entries and every edge joins two distinct vertices of the list.
nodes.title: Valid multigraph

nodes.summary: For a list of edges (pairs of vertices, repeated pairs counted with multiplicity) and a map $X$ from vertices to booleans, the size of the cut $X$ is the number of edges $(u, v)$ in the list with $X(u) \ne X(v)$.
nodes.title: Size of a cut

nodes.summary: A map $X$ from vertices to booleans is a cut of a multigraph state $G$ when some vertex $v$ of $G$ has $X(v) = \mathrm{true}$ and some vertex $w$ of $G$ has $X(w) = \mathrm{false}$.
nodes.title: Cuts of a multigraph

nodes.summary: A natural number $k$ is the minimum cut size of a multigraph state $G$ when some cut of $G$ has size $k$ and every cut of $G$ has size at least $k$.
nodes.title: Minimum cut size

nodes.summary: For vertices $a$ and $b$, renaming $b$ to $a$ is the map on vertices that sends $b$ to $a$ and fixes every other vertex.
nodes.title: Renaming a vertex

nodes.summary: For a multigraph state $G$ and a pair of vertices $e = (a, b)$, the contraction of $G$ along $e$ deletes the first occurrence of $b$ from the vertex list, replaces $b$ by $a$ in both endpoints of every edge, and then deletes every edge whose two endpoints are equal.
nodes.title: Edge contraction

nodes.summary: For a natural number $k$, a number $f$ of allowed contractions and a multigraph $G$ with edge list $E_G$, the probability $P_k(f, G)$ that the contraction process on $G$ returns $k$ is defined by recursion on $f$. If $f = 0$, or $G$ has at most two vertices, or $G$ has no edges, then $P_k(f, G)$ is $1$ when $G$ has exactly $k$ edges and $0$ otherwise. Otherwise…
nodes.title: Success probability of the contraction process

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a multigraph state, $e = (a, b)$ a pair of vertices and $Y$ a map from vertices to booleans, and let $\rho$ send $b$ to $a$ and fix every other vertex. The size of the cut $Y$ in the contraction of $G$ along $e$ equals the size of the cut $Y \circ \rho$ in $G$.
nodes.title: Cut sizes under contraction

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a valid multigraph state with minimum cut size $k$, and let $X$ be a cut of $G$ of size $k$. If $e = (a, b)$ is an edge of $G$ with $X(a) = X(b)$, then the contraction of $G$ along $e$ also has minimum cut size $k$.
nodes.title: Contraction preserves the minimum cut size

nodes.summary: If a multigraph $G$ is valid and $e$ is one of its edges, then the contraction of $G$ along $e$ is valid and has exactly one vertex fewer than $G$.
nodes.title: Contraction preserves validity and removes one vertex

nodes.summary: For a valid multigraph $G$, the sum over the vertices $v$ of $G$ of the number of edges crossing the singleton cut $\{v\}$ equals twice the number of edges of $G$.
nodes.title: Handshake lemma

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a valid multigraph state with $n \ge 2$ vertices, $m$ edges (counted with multiplicity) and minimum cut size $k$. Then $n k \le 2m$: every vertex has degree at least $k$, since its singleton is a cut.
nodes.title: Minimum cut size bounds the number of edges

nodes.summary: For every natural number $k$, every number $f$ of allowed contractions and every multigraph state $G$, the probability $P_k(f, G)$ that the contraction process on $G$ returns $k$ satisfies $0 \le P_k(f, G)$.
nodes.title: The success probability is nonnegative

nodes.summary: For every natural number $k$, every number of allowed contractions and every multigraph $G$, the probability that the contraction process on $G$ returns $k$ is at most $1$.
nodes.title: The success probability is at most one

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a valid multigraph with $n \ge 2$ vertices and minimum cut size $k$. Then the contraction process on $G$, with $n$ contractions allowed, returns $k$ with probability at least $2 / (n(n-1))$.
nodes.title: Karger's bound

nodes.summary: For a multigraph $G$ with $n$ vertices and natural numbers $k$ and $t$, let $p$ be the probability that one run of the contraction process on $G$, with $n$ contractions allowed, returns $k$. The repeated success probability is $1 - (1 - p)^t$, the probability that at least one of $t$ independent runs returns $k$.
nodes.title: Success probability of repeated runs

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a valid multigraph state with $n \ge 2$ vertices and minimum cut size $k$, and let $t$ be a natural number with $n(n-1) \le 2t$. Then the probability that at least one of $t$ independent runs of the contraction process returns $k$ is at least $1/2$.
nodes.title: Repeating Karger's algorithm succeeds with probability at least one half

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a valid multigraph with $n \ge 2$ vertices and minimum cut size $k$, and let $c$ and $t$ be natural numbers with $c \cdot n(n-1) \le 2t$. Then the probability that at least one of $t$ independent runs of the contraction process on $G$ returns $k$ is at least $1 - (1/2)^c$.
nodes.title: Amplification with high probability

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a valid multigraph with $n \ge 2$ vertices and minimum cut size $k$, and let $t$ be a natural number with $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil \cdot n(n-1) \le 2t$. Then the probability that at least one of $t$ independent runs of the contraction process on $G$ returns $k$ is at least $1 - 1/n$.
nodes.title: Karger's algorithm succeeds with high probability

nodes.summary: For a map $X$ from vertices to booleans, a fuel bound $f$ and a multigraph $G$, this is the probability that the contraction process on $G$ (contract an edge chosen uniformly at random, counted with multiplicity, while more than two vertices and at least one edge remain, making at most $f$ contractions) never contracts an edge whose endpoints $X$ separates and ends with exactly two vertices on which $X$ takes both…
nodes.title: Probability that a run outputs a given cut

nodes.summary: Two maps $X, Y$ from vertices to booleans are distinct on a list of vertices $S$ when some $v \in S$ has $X(v) \ne Y(v)$ and some $w \in S$ has $X(w) = Y(w)$; so on $S$ neither cut is the other or its complement.
nodes.title: Cuts distinct as partitions

reading_title.source: Each minimum cut survives with probability at least $2/(n(n-1))$

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a valid multigraph with $n \ge 2$ vertices whose minimum cut size $k$ is at least $1$, and let $X$ be a cut of $G$ with exactly $k$ crossing edges. Then the probability that the contraction process on $G$, allowed up to $n$ contractions, outputs the cut $X$ is at least $2/(n(n-1))$.
nodes.title: Each minimum cut survives with probability at least $2/(n(n-1))$

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a valid multigraph with vertex list $S$, let $f$ be a number of allowed contractions, and let $X_1, \dots, X_m$ be Boolean functions on the vertex type that are pairwise distinct as partitions of $S$. Then the probabilities that the contraction process on $G$, with $f$ contractions allowed, outputs $X_1, \dots, X_m$ add up to at most $1$.
nodes.title: Survival probabilities of distinct cuts sum to at most one

reading_title.source: At most $n(n-1)/2$ minimum cuts

nodes.summary: At most $n(n-1)/2$ minimum cuts (Karger; Kleinberg and Tardos, Section 13.2). Let $G$ be a valid multigraph with $n \ge 2$ vertices whose minimum cut size $k$ is at least $1$. If $X_1, \dots, X_m$ are cuts of $G$, each with exactly $k$ crossing edges, that are pairwise distinct as partitions of the vertices of $G$, then $2m \le n(n-1)$, that is, $m \le n(n-1)/2$.
nodes.title: At most $n(n-1)/2$ minimum cuts
MinHash and Jaccard similarity

nodes.summary: The min-hash of `A` under the permutation `π`: the least element of `π(A)`, or `⊤` if `A` is empty.
nodes.title: Min-hash of a set under a permutation

nodes.summary: The number of permutations of `U` under which `A` and `B` have the same min-hash, times `|A ∪ B|`, equals `|A ∩ B|` times the number of all permutations.
nodes.title: MinHash, counting form

nodes.summary: MinHash collision probability (Broder 1997): for a uniformly random permutation `π` of the finite universe `U` (`uniformOn Set.univ` on `Equiv.Perm U`, for any measurable structure in which singletons are measurable, e.g. `⊤`) and sets `A`, `B` with `A ∪ B` nonempty, `P(min π(A) = min π(B)) = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|`, the Jaccard similarity of `A` and `B`.
nodes.title: MinHash collision probability

List ranking by pointer jumping

nodes.summary: For a successor map $\mathrm{succ}$ on the nodes $0, \dots, n-1$, where $\mathrm{succ}(v)$ is either a node or undefined, the $k$-step jump from $v$ is the node reached by applying $\mathrm{succ}$ $k$ times starting at $v$, and is undefined if some step is undefined: the $0$-step jump from $v$ is $v$, and the $(k+1)$-step jump is $\mathrm{succ}$ of the $k$-step jump.
nodes.title: Iterated successor

nodes.summary: A successor function $\mathrm{succ}$ on the nodes $0, \dots, n - 1$, mapping each node to its successor or to nothing, terminates when from every node $v$ the walk of $n$ steps along $\mathrm{succ}$ runs off the end, that is, there is no node $n$ steps down the list from $v$.
nodes.title: Terminating successor functions

nodes.summary: Let $\mathrm{succ}$ be a successor map on the nodes $0, \dots, n-1$ whose lists terminate. The rank of a node $v$ is the least $k$ such that following $\mathrm{succ}$ for $k + 1$ steps from $v$ runs off the end of the list, that is, the number of nodes after $v$ in its list.
nodes.title: Rank of a node in a linked list

nodes.summary: Let $\mathrm{succ}$ be a successor map on the nodes $0, \dots, n-1$ whose lists terminate. For every node $v$ and every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, following $\mathrm{succ}$ for $k$ steps from $v$ runs off the end of the list if and only if $k > \operatorname{rank}(v)$.
nodes.title: The characteristic property of the rank

nodes.summary: Let $\mathrm{succ}$ be a successor map on the nodes $0, \dots, n-1$ whose lists terminate. If following $\mathrm{succ}$ for $a$ steps from a node $v$ reaches the node $u$, then $a \le \operatorname{rank}(v)$ and $\operatorname{rank}(u) = \operatorname{rank}(v) - a$.
nodes.title: Rank decreases along jumps

nodes.summary: A pointer-jumping state on the nodes $0, \dots, n - 1$ assigns to each node a pointer, which is either a node or empty (once it points past the end of the list), and a distance in $\mathbb{N}$, the distance covered by the pointer.
nodes.title: Pointer-jumping state for list ranking

nodes.summary: For a successor map $\mathrm{succ}$ on the nodes $0, \dots, n-1$, where $\mathrm{succ}(v)$ is either a node or undefined (at the end of a list), the initial pointer-jumping state gives each node $v$ the pointer $\mathrm{succ}(v)$ and the distance $0$ if $\mathrm{succ}(v)$ is undefined and $1$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Initial state of pointer jumping

nodes.summary: In one parallel round, every node $v$ whose pointer is a node $u$ adds the distance of $u$ to its own distance and moves its pointer to the pointer of $u$ (undefined if that of $u$ is); a node whose pointer is undefined keeps its distance and its undefined pointer.
nodes.title: One round of pointer jumping

reading_title.source: The list-ranking state after $t$ rounds

nodes.summary: For a successor function $\mathrm{succ}$ on the nodes $0, \dots, n - 1$, the pointer-jumping state after $t$ rounds is defined by recursion on $t$: after $0$ rounds it is the initial state of $\mathrm{succ}$, and after $t + 1$ rounds it is one round of pointer jumping applied to the state after $t$ rounds.
nodes.title: The list-ranking state after $t$ rounds

nodes.summary: Let $\mathrm{succ}$ map each of the nodes $0, \dots, n - 1$ to its successor or to nothing, and suppose the lists terminate: from every node, $n$ steps run off the end. Write $\mathrm{rank}(v)$ for the number of nodes after $v$. nodes.summary: Let $\mathrm{succ}$ be a successor map on the nodes $0, \dots, n-1$ whose lists terminate, and let $t$ be a natural number with $n \le 2^t$. Then after $t$ rounds of pointer jumping from the initial state, the distance of every node $v$ is the rank of $v$.
nodes.title: After enough rounds, the distances are the ranks

nodes.summary: The tabulation of a pointer-jumping state $s$ on the nodes $0, \dots, n - 1$ is the pair of arrays of length $n$ whose entries at $v$ are the pointer and the distance of $v$ in $s$.
nodes.title: Tabulating a list-ranking state

nodes.summary: Given an array $P$ of pointers (each a node among $0, \dots, n-1$ or undefined) and an array $D$ of natural-number distances, one round returns arrays $P'$ and $D'$ of length $n$ where, for each node $v$, $P'[v]$ is $P[u]$ if $P[v] = u$ and is undefined if $P[v]$ is undefined, and $D'[v] = D[v] + D[u]$ if $P[v] = u$ and $D'[v] = D[v]$ if $P[v]$ is undefined. Entries missing from the input arrays are read as…
nodes.title: One pointer-jumping round on arrays

nodes.summary: For a successor function $\mathrm{succ}$ on the nodes $0, \dots, n - 1$ and $t \ge 0$, the arrays after $t$ rounds are a pair of arrays (pointers and distances) defined by recursion on $t$: after $0$ rounds they are the tabulation of the initial state of $\mathrm{succ}$, and after $t + 1$ rounds they are one round on arrays applied to the arrays after $t$ rounds.
nodes.title: List-ranking rounds on arrays

nodes.summary: For a successor map $\mathrm{succ}$ on the nodes $0, \dots, n-1$, list ranking by pointer jumping runs $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ rounds of pointer jumping on arrays, starting from the initial state, and returns the resulting array of distances, whose entry $v$ is the distance of node $v$.
nodes.title: List ranking by pointer jumping

nodes.summary: Let $\mathrm{succ}$ be a successor map on the nodes $0, \dots, n-1$ whose lists terminate. Then for every node $v$, entry $v$ of the table returned by list ranking by pointer jumping, which runs $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ rounds, is the rank of $v$.

For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and a node $v$, this is $x_u$ where $u$ is the node $k$ steps after $v$ along its list, and $0$ if the list ends before $k$ steps.

nodes.summary: Let $n$ nodes be linked into lists by a partial successor function, and let each node $v$ carry a value $x_v$ in an additive monoid $M$ (not necessarily commutative). For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and a node $v$, the segment sum of length $k$ from $v$ is the sum, in list order, of the values of the first $k$ nodes of the list starting at $v$ (fewer if the list ends sooner); for $k = 0$ it is $0$.

nodes.summary: Let $n$ nodes be linked into lists by a partial successor function, each node $v$ carrying a value $x_v$ in an additive monoid $M$. The suffix sum of a node $v$ is the segment sum of length $n$ from $v$: the sum, in list order, of the values of the first $n$ nodes of the list starting at $v$ (fewer if it ends sooner).
nodes.title: Suffix sums

nodes.summary: Let $n$ nodes be linked into lists by a partial successor function such that, starting from any node, $n$ steps run off the end of its list, and let each node $v$ carry a value $x_v$ in an additive monoid $M$. Then for every node $v$, the suffix sum of $v$ is $x_v$ plus the suffix sum of the successor of $v$, or just $x_v$ if $v$ has no successor.

nodes.summary: Let $n$ nodes be linked into lists by a partial successor function such that, starting from any node, $n$ steps run off the end of its list. If every node has value $1 \in \mathbb{N}$, then the suffix sum of every node $v$ is $\operatorname{rank}(v) + 1$, where $\operatorname{rank}(v)$ is the number of nodes after $v$ in its list.

nodes.summary: Given a state in which each node $v$ has a pointer $p(v)$, either a node or undefined, and a sum $s(v)$ in an additive monoid $M$, one round produces a new state as follows.
