nodes.summary: For a sequence $x : \mathbb{N} \to M$ in a monoid $M$ and $a, b \in \mathbb{N}$, the window product is the ordered product $x_a x_{a+1} \cdots x_{b-1}$ of the terms with indices $a \le j < b$; it is the empty product $1$ when $b \le a$.
nodes.title: Window product

nodes.summary: For a sequence $x_0, x_1, \dots$ in a monoid $M$ and a natural number $i$, the prefix product at $i$ is $x_0 x_1 \cdots x_i$, the factors taken in increasing order of index.
nodes.title: Prefix product

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a monoid and $x : \mathbb{N} \to M$ a sequence, and for $a, b \in \mathbb{N}$ let $x_{[a, b)}$ be the ordered product $x_a x_{a+1} \cdots x_{b-1}$ (equal to $1$ if $b \le a$). For all $a \le b \le c$, $x_{[a, b)} \, x_{[b, c)} = x_{[a, c)}$.
nodes.title: Products of adjacent windows

nodes.summary: Given a sequence $x_0, x_1, \dots$ in a monoid $M$, the value $s_k(i)$ at position $i$ after $k$ rounds is defined by $s_0(i) = x_i$ and, for each $k$, $s_{k+1}(i) = s_k(i - 2^k) \, s_k(i)$ if $2^k \le i$ and $s_{k+1}(i) = s_k(i)$ otherwise.
nodes.title: The Kogge–Stone scan

nodes.summary: Let $x_0, x_1, \dots$ be a sequence in a monoid $M$, let $k$ and $i$ be natural numbers, and let $m = \min(i + 1, 2^k)$. After $k$ rounds of the Kogge–Stone scan, position $i$ holds the product $x_{i+1-m} \cdots x_i$ of the $m$ consecutive inputs ending at $i$, taken in increasing order of index.
nodes.title: What the scan holds after each round

nodes.summary: Let $x_0, x_1, \dots$ be a sequence in a monoid $M$ and let $n$ and $K$ be natural numbers with $n \le 2^K$. After $K$ rounds of the Kogge–Stone scan, every position $i < n$ holds the prefix product $x_0 x_1 \cdots x_i$.
nodes.title: The scan computes all prefix products

nodes.summary: The work of round $k$ on $n$ positions is $\max(n - 2^k, 0)$, the number of positions $i < n$ with $i \ge 2^k$, each of which performs one multiplication.
nodes.title: Work of a scan round

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the work of round $k$ on $n$ positions equals the number of positions $i$ with $2^k \le i < n$.
nodes.title: The work of a round counts its combining positions

nodes.summary: The total work of $K$ rounds on $n$ positions is $\sum_{k=0}^{K-1} \max(n - 2^k, 0)$, the sum over the rounds $k < K$ of the work $\max(n - 2^k, 0)$ of round $k$.
nodes.title: Work of the Kogge–Stone scan

nodes.summary: For all $n, K \in \mathbb{N}$, the total work of $K$ rounds of the scan on $n$ positions is at most $nK$.
nodes.title: Work bound for the Kogge–Stone scan

nodes.summary: The span of $K$ rounds of the scan is $K$: each round is one parallel step.
nodes.title: Span of the Kogge–Stone scan

nodes.summary: Let $x_0, x_1, \dots$ be a sequence in a monoid $M$ and let $n$ be a natural number. After $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ rounds of the Kogge–Stone scan (the least $K$ with $n \le 2^K$), every position $i < n$ holds the prefix product $x_0 x_1 \cdots x_i$.
nodes.title: The scan computes all prefixes in logarithmically many rounds

nodes.summary: Given a list $y_0, \dots, y_{n-1}$ in a monoid $M$ and a natural number $k$, one round produces the list of length $n$ whose entry $i$ is $y_{i - 2^k} \, y_i$ when $2^k \le i$ and $y_i$ when $i < 2^k$.
nodes.title: One round of the scan on a list

nodes.summary: For a list $y = (y_0, \dots, y_{n-1})$ in a monoid $M$, the list after $K$ rounds is defined by recursion on $K$: after $0$ rounds it is $y$, and after $K + 1$ rounds it is round $K$ applied to the list after $K$ rounds. Here round $k$ sends a list $(z_0, \dots, z_{n-1})$ to the list of length $n$ whose entry $i$ is $z_i$ for $i < 2^k$ and $z_{i - 2^k} z_i$ for $2^k \le i < n$.
nodes.title: Tabulated Kogge–Stone scan

nodes.summary: Let $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ be a list of elements of a monoid $M$, extended to a sequence by $x_j = 1$ for $j \ge n$. For every number of rounds $K$ and every position $i < n$, entry $i$ of the list produced by $K$ rounds of the tabulated scan equals the value at position $i$ after $K$ rounds of the Kogge–Stone scan applied to the sequence $x$.
nodes.title: The tabulated scan agrees with the round recursion

nodes.summary: Let $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ be a list of elements of a monoid $M$ and let $K$ be a natural number with $n \le 2^K$. Then for every $i < n$, entry $i$ of the list produced by $K$ rounds of the tabulated scan equals the prefix product $x_0 x_1 \cdots x_i$.
nodes.title: The tabulated scan computes all prefix products

nodes.summary: For a sequence $x \colon \mathbb{N} \to M$ in a monoid $M$, the sequence of adjacent pair products is the sequence whose term at $i$ is $x(2i) \cdot x(2i+1)$.
nodes.title: Adjacent pair products of a sequence

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a monoid. For a natural number $k$ and a sequence $x = (x_0, x_1, \dots)$ in $M$, the scan $B_k(x)$ is the sequence in $M$ defined by recursion on $k$: $B_0(x)$ is constantly $1$, and $B_{k+1}(x)$ is obtained from the scan $y = B_k(p)$ of the pair products $p_i = x_{2i} x_{2i+1}$ by setting $B_{k+1}(x)_{2i} = y_i$ and $B_{k+1}(x)_{2i+1} = y_i x_{2i}$ for every $i$.
nodes.title: Blelloch's scan

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a monoid, $k$ a natural number and $x = (x_0, x_1, \dots)$ a sequence in $M$. For every $j < 2^k$, the value at position $j$ of Blelloch's scan of $x$ on $2^k$ positions is the exclusive prefix product $x_0 x_1 \cdots x_{j-1}$ (equal to $1$ when $j = 0$).
nodes.title: Blelloch's scan computes the exclusive prefix products

nodes.summary: The number $W(k)$ of monoid multiplications Blelloch's scan performs on $2^k$ positions is defined by $W(0) = 0$ and $W(k+1) = 2^k + W(k) + 2^k$: on $2^{k+1}$ positions, $2^k$ pair products, the recursive scan on the $2^k$ pair products, and $2^k$ products for the odd positions.
nodes.title: Work of Blelloch's scan

nodes.summary: The span $S(k)$ of Blelloch's scan on $2^k$ positions is defined by $S(0) = 0$ and $S(k+1) = S(k) + 2$: one parallel step for the pair products, the recursive scan, and one parallel step for the odd positions.
nodes.title: Parallel steps of Blelloch's scan

nodes.summary: For every natural number $k$, the number $W(k)$ of monoid multiplications Blelloch's scan performs on $n = 2^k$ positions satisfies $W(k) + 2 = 2^{k+1}$, so $W(k) = 2^{k+1} - 2 < 2n$.
nodes.title: Blelloch's scan is work-efficient

nodes.summary: For every natural number $k$, the span of Blelloch's scan on $n = 2^k$ positions is $2k = 2 \log_2 n$.
nodes.title: Blelloch's scan has logarithmic span

nodes.summary: For a list $[a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{n-1}]$ of elements of a monoid $M$, the list of adjacent pair products is $[a_0 a_1, a_2 a_3, \ldots]$: it has length $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, its $i$-th entry is $a_{2i} a_{2i+1}$, and when $n$ is odd the last element $a_{n-1}$ is dropped.
nodes.title: Adjacent pair products of a list

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a monoid. For lists $z = (z_0, z_1, \dots)$ and $x = (x_0, x_1, \dots)$ in $M$, the expansion of $z$ along $x$ is the list $(z_0, z_0 x_0, z_1, z_1 x_2, z_2, z_2 x_4, \dots)$: each $z_i$ is followed by $z_i x_{2i}$, and the list stops at the first $i$ for which $z_i$ or $x_{2i+1}$ does not exist.
nodes.title: Interleaving step of Blelloch's list scan

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a monoid. For a natural number $k$ and a list $xs = (x_0, x_1, \dots)$ in $M$, the list scan $L_k(xs)$ is defined by recursion on $k$: $L_0(xs)$ is the one-element list $(1)$, and $L_{k+1}(xs)$ is obtained from the list scan $z = L_k(p)$ of the pair products $p = (x_0 x_1, x_2 x_3, \dots)$ of $xs$ (a trailing unpaired entry is dropped) by interleaving: $L_{k+1}(xs) = (z_0, z_0 x_0, z_1, z_1 x_2, \dots)$,…
nodes.title: Blelloch's scan on lists

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a monoid, $k$ a natural number and $xs = (x_0, \dots, x_{2^k - 1})$ a list in $M$ of length $2^k$. For every $j < 2^k$, the entry at position $j$ of Blelloch's list scan of $xs$ in $k$ rounds equals the value at position $j$ of Blelloch's scan on $2^k$ positions of the sequence $x_0, \dots, x_{2^k - 1}, 1, 1, \dots$ obtained by extending $xs$ by $1$.
nodes.title: The list implementation computes Blelloch's scan

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a monoid, $k$ a natural number and $xs = (x_0, \dots, x_{2^k - 1})$ a list in $M$ of length $2^k$. For every $j < 2^k$, the entry at position $j$ of Blelloch's list scan of $xs$ in $k$ rounds is the exclusive prefix product $x_0 x_1 \cdots x_{j-1}$ (equal to $1$ when $j = 0$).
nodes.title: The list implementation computes the exclusive prefix products
Work–span model and Brent's theorem

nodes.summary: A computation DAG on $n$ unit-time tasks, numbered $0, \dots, n - 1$, assigns to each task $v$ a list of predecessors (the tasks $v$ waits for), each numbered below $v$; so the numbering is a topological order.
nodes.title: Computation DAG

nodes.summary: The depth of a task $v$ is the number of tasks on a longest path ending at $v$: it is $1$ plus the largest depth of a predecessor of $v$, or $1$ if $v$ has no predecessors.
nodes.title: Depth of a task in a computation DAG

nodes.summary: The span of a computation DAG is the number of tasks on a longest path, that is, the largest depth of a task, and $0$ when there are no tasks.
nodes.title: Span of a computation DAG

nodes.summary: In a computation DAG, if $u$ is a predecessor of $v$, then the depth of $u$ is strictly less than the depth of $v$.
nodes.title: Predecessors have smaller depth

nodes.summary: For $k \le n$, the list of the depths of tasks $0, \dots, k - 1$ of a computation DAG on $n$ tasks, computed in topological order: the empty list for $k = 0$, and for $k + 1$ the list for $k$ followed by $1$ plus the largest entry of that list at a predecessor of task $k$ (or $1$ if task $k$ has no predecessors).
nodes.title: Depths of an initial segment of tasks

nodes.summary: The list of the depths of tasks $0, \dots, n - 1$ of a computation DAG on $n$ tasks, computed once each in topological order: the entry for task $k$ is $1$ plus the largest entry at a predecessor of $k$, or $1$ if $k$ has no predecessors.
nodes.title: Table of depths

nodes.summary: For every task $v$ of a computation DAG, the entry of the table of depths at position $v$ equals the depth of $v$.
nodes.title: The table of depths is correct

nodes.summary: A schedule of a computation DAG on $n$ tasks on $p$ processors assigns to each task $v$ a step $t(v) \in \mathbb{N}$ in which it runs, such that $t(u) < t(v)$ whenever $u$ is a predecessor of $v$, and for every step $s$ at most $p$ tasks $v$ have $t(v) = s$.
nodes.title: Schedule of a computation DAG

nodes.summary: The length of a schedule is the number of steps it takes: one more than the latest step in which a task runs (steps are numbered from $0$), or $0$ if there are no tasks.
nodes.title: Length of a schedule

nodes.summary: For a computation DAG on $n$ tasks, every schedule of it on $p$ processors that takes $T$ steps satisfies $n \le p T$. In particular, for $p > 0$ the schedule takes at least $n / p$ steps.
nodes.title: The work law

nodes.summary: For every schedule of a computation DAG on $p$ processors, with steps numbered from $0$, every task $v$ runs in a step $t$ with $\operatorname{depth}(v) \le t + 1$.
nodes.title: Depth bounds the step of a task

nodes.summary: No schedule is shorter than the span.
nodes.title: The span law

nodes.summary: For a computation DAG and a natural number $d$, the size of level $d$ is the number of tasks of depth $d$.
nodes.title: Level size

nodes.summary: For a computation DAG and natural numbers $p$ and $d$, let $L_d$ be the number of tasks of depth $d$. The number of steps of level $d$ on $p$ processors is $\lceil L_d / p \rceil$ if $p \ge 1$, and $0$ if $p = 0$.
nodes.title: Steps of a level

nodes.summary: For a computation DAG and natural numbers $p$ and $d$, let $s_e$ be the number of steps of level $e$ on $p$ processors: $\lceil L_e / p \rceil$ if $p \ge 1$ and $0$ if $p = 0$, where $L_e$ is the number of tasks of depth $e$. The first step of level $d$ is $\sum_{e < d} s_e$.
nodes.title: First step of a level

nodes.summary: In a computation DAG, the rank of a task $v$ is the number of tasks of the same depth as $v$ with a smaller number than $v$. Taken in numbering order, the tasks of a level have ranks $0, 1, 2, \dots$
nodes.title: Rank within a level

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a computation DAG and $p$ a natural number. If $p \ge 1$, for each $d$ let $L_d$ be the number of tasks of depth $d$ and $o_d = \sum_{e < d} \lceil L_e / p \rceil$, and for each task $v$ let $r(v)$ be the number of tasks of the same depth as $v$ with a smaller number; the step of a task $v$ is $o_{\operatorname{depth}(v)} + \lfloor r(v) / p \rfloor$. If $p = 0$, the step of every task is $0$.
nodes.title: Step of a task in Brent's schedule

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a computation DAG and $p \ge 1$. If two tasks $u$ and $v$ run in the same step of Brent's level-by-level schedule on $p$ processors, then $u$ and $v$ have the same depth.
nodes.title: No step of Brent's level schedule mixes levels

nodes.summary: In a computation DAG, if tasks $u$ and $v$ have the same depth and $u$ has a smaller number than $v$, then the rank of $u$ is smaller than the rank of $v$, where the rank of a task is the number of tasks of the same depth with a smaller number. In particular, ranks are distinct within a level.
nodes.title: Ranks increase within a level

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a computation DAG and $p \ge 1$. For each $d$ let $L_d$ be the number of tasks of depth $d$ and $o_d = \sum_{e < d} \lceil L_e / p \rceil$, and for each task $v$ let $r(v)$ be the number of tasks of the same depth as $v$ with a smaller number. Brent's level schedule is the schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors that runs each task $v$ at step $o_{\operatorname{depth}(v)} + \lfloor r(v) / p \rfloor$.
nodes.title: Brent's level schedule

reading_title.source: Level $0$ is empty

nodes.summary: In every computation DAG no task has depth $0$, so the number of tasks of depth $0$ is $0$.
nodes.title: Level $0$ is empty

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a computation DAG with $n$ tasks and span $D$, and let $p \ge 1$. If Brent's level schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors takes $T$ steps, then $pT \le n + (p - 1) D$, that is, $T \le (n - D)/p + D$.
nodes.title: Brent's theorem

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a computation DAG on $n$ unit-time tasks with span $D$, and let $p \ge 1$. Then some schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors has length $T$ with $pT \le n + (p - 1)D$, and every schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors has a length $T'$ with $n \le pT'$ (the work law) and $D \le T'$ (the span law).
nodes.title: Brent's theorem with the work and span laws

nodes.summary: The load of step $t$ in a schedule $S$ of a computation DAG is the number of tasks that $S$ runs in step $t$.
nodes.title: Load of a step

nodes.summary: In a schedule $S$ of a task graph, a task $v$ is ready at step $t$ if $v$ runs in a step later than $t$ and every predecessor of $v$ runs in a step earlier than $t$.
nodes.title: Ready task

nodes.summary: A schedule $S$ of a computation DAG on $p$ processors is greedy if, for every step $t$ and every task that is ready at step $t$, exactly $p$ tasks run in step $t$: a step leaves a ready task waiting only when all $p$ processors are busy.
nodes.title: Greedy schedule

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a schedule of a computation DAG on $p$ processors taking $T$ steps. Then $S$ is greedy if and only if, for every step $t < T$ and every task $v$ that is ready at step $t$, exactly $p$ tasks run in step $t$.
nodes.title: Greediness need only be checked at the steps of the schedule

nodes.summary: For a schedule $S$ of a computation DAG on $p$ processors and a natural number $t$, the number of incomplete steps before step $t$ is the number of steps $s < t$ in which $S$ runs fewer than $p$ tasks.
nodes.title: Number of incomplete steps

nodes.summary: In a greedy schedule, fewer than `depth v` incomplete steps precede the step of task `v`.
nodes.title: Each incomplete step advances the critical path

nodes.summary: For a schedule $S$ of a task graph with $n$ tasks that takes $T$ steps, the numbers of tasks run in the steps $0, 1, \dots, T - 1$ add up to $n$.
nodes.title: The step loads add up to the number of tasks

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a computation DAG with $n$ tasks, and let $S$ be a schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors taking $T$ steps. If $C$ is the number of steps $t < T$ in which $S$ runs at least $p$ tasks (the complete steps, where all $p$ processors are busy), then $pC \le n$.
nodes.title: Complete steps are bounded by the work

reading_title.source: A greedy schedule has at most $D$ incomplete steps

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a computation DAG with span $D$, and let $S$ be a greedy schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors taking $T$ steps. Then at most $D$ of the steps $t < T$ are incomplete, that is, run fewer than $p$ tasks.
nodes.title: A greedy schedule has at most $D$ incomplete steps

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a schedule of a computation DAG on $p$ processors taking $T$ steps, numbered from $0$. For every step $t < T$ there is a task that $S$ runs at step $t$ or later.
nodes.title: Every step of a schedule has a task running at or after it

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a greedy schedule of a task graph on $p$ processors that takes $T$ steps, numbered $0, \dots, T - 1$. Then every step $t < T$ of $S$ runs at least one task.
nodes.title: A greedy schedule never idles

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a computation DAG with $n$ tasks and span $D$, and let $S$ be a greedy schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors taking $T$ steps. Then $pT \le n + (p - 1)D$.
nodes.title: The greedy scheduling bound

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a computation DAG with $n$ tasks and span $D$, and let $S$ be a greedy schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors taking $T$ steps. Then $pT \le n + pD$, that is, $T \le n/p + D$ when $p \ge 1$.
nodes.title: The work-span bound for greedy schedules

nodes.summary: For a commutative ring $R$, a natural number $m$ and a vector $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{2m-1}) \in R^{2m}$, the split returns the pair of vectors $(x_0, x_2, \dots, x_{2m-2})$ and $(x_1, x_3, \dots, x_{2m-1})$ in $R^m$ of the entries of $x$ at even and at odd indices, in order, at a time cost of $4m$ (the charged reads and writes).
nodes.title: Even–odd split for the FFT

nodes.summary: For a commutative ring $R$, an element $\omega \in R$, vectors $q, r \in R^m$, a state $(w, y)$ with $w \in R$ and $y \in R^{2m}$, and an index $k < m$, the butterfly at $k$ returns the state $(w \omega, y')$, where $y'$ is obtained from $y$ by setting entry $k$ to $q_k + w r_k$ and entry $k + m$ to $q_k - w r_k$, at a time cost of $8$.
nodes.title: One FFT butterfly

nodes.summary: For a commutative ring $R$, an element $\omega \in R$ and vectors $q, r \in R^m$ and $y \in R^{2m}$, the butterfly pass starts from the state $(1, y)$, applies the FFT butterfly with $\omega$, $q$ and $r$ at the indices $k = 0, 1, \dots, m - 1$ in increasing order, and returns the final state; its time cost is the sum of the costs of these $m$ butterflies.
nodes.title: FFT butterfly pass

nodes.summary: For a commutative ring $R$, a natural number $d$, an element $\omega \in R$ and a vector $x \in R^{2^d}$, the FFT of $x$ with root $\omega$ is defined by recursion on $d$. For $d = 0$ it returns $x$ at cost $0$. For $d + 1$ it splits $x$ into its even- and odd-indexed subvectors $e, o \in R^{2^d}$ (cost $4 \cdot 2^d$), computes $\omega^2$ (cost $1$), computes the FFTs $q$ of $e$ and $r$ of $o$ with root $\omega^2$,…
nodes.title: Radix-two fast Fourier transform

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $\omega \in R$ and $x$ an array over $R$ of length $n$, and let $d = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ (with $d = 0$ when $n = 0$). If $n = 2^d$, the array FFT runs the radix-two FFT with root $\omega$ on $x$, viewed as a vector of length $2^d$, and returns its output as an array, with the cost of that run. Otherwise it returns no result, at cost $0$; the length check itself is free.
nodes.title: Radix-two FFT on arrays

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $\omega \in R$ and $x$ an array over $R$. The array FFT of $x$ with root $\omega$ returns no result if and only if the length of $x$ is different from $2^d$ for every natural number $d$.
nodes.title: The array FFT rejects exactly the non-powers of two

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $\omega \in R$, $m$ a natural number, $q, r$ vectors over $R$ of length $m$, $w \in R$ a twiddle, $o$ an output vector over $R$ of length $2m$, and $k < m$. Then the butterfly step at index $k$ applied to the state $(w, o)$ produces an output vector whose entry at index $k$ is $q_k + w r_k$.
nodes.title: Lower write of a butterfly step

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $\omega \in R$, $m$ a natural number, $q, r$ vectors over $R$ of length $m$, $w \in R$ a twiddle, $o$ an output vector over $R$ of length $2m$, and $k < m$. Then the butterfly step at index $k$ applied to the state $(w, o)$ produces an output vector whose entry at index $k + m$ is $q_k - w r_k$.
nodes.title: Upper write of a butterfly step

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $\omega \in R$, $m$ a natural number, $q, r$ vectors over $R$ of length $m$, $w \in R$ a twiddle, $o$ an output vector over $R$ of length $2m$, and $k < m$. Then for every index $i < 2m$ with $i \ne k$ and $i \ne k + m$, the butterfly step at index $k$ applied to the state $(w, o)$ produces an output vector whose entry at index $i$ is $o_i$.
nodes.title: A butterfly step leaves other entries unchanged

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $\omega \in R$, $m$ a natural number, $q = (q_0, \dots, q_{m-1})$ and $r = (r_0, \dots, r_{m-1})$ vectors over $R$, and $o$ a vector over $R$ of length $2m$. The butterfly loop with root $\omega$ on $q$ and $r$, started from twiddle $1$ and output vector $o$, ends with twiddle $\omega^m$ and an output vector $y$ such that $y_k = q_k + \omega^k r_k$ and $y_{k+m} = q_k - \omega^k r_k$…
nodes.title: Result of the butterfly loop

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a type, $m$ a natural number and $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{2m-1})$ a vector of length $2m$ over $R$. For every $k < m$, entry $k$ of the first (even) vector returned by the FFT split of $x$ is $x_{2k}$.
nodes.title: The FFT split extracts the even-indexed entries

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a type, $m$ a natural number and $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{2m-1})$ a vector of length $2m$ over $R$. For every $k < m$, entry $k$ of the second (odd) vector returned by the FFT split of $x$ is $x_{2k+1}$.
nodes.title: The FFT split extracts the odd-indexed entries

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For every $\omega \in R$ and every vector $x \in R^{2^0}$, the vector returned by the radix-two FFT of depth $0$ with root $\omega$ on $x$ is $x$ itself.
nodes.title: The FFT of depth zero returns its input

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $d$ a natural number, $\omega \in R$ and $x \in R^{2^{d+1}}$, with entries indexed from $0$. Let $e, o \in R^{2^d}$ be the even- and odd-indexed subsequences of $x$ returned by the FFT split, and let $E$ and $O$ be the vectors returned by the radix-two FFT of depth $d$ with root $\omega \cdot \omega$ on $e$ and on $o$. Then for every $k < 2^d$, entry $k$ of the vector returned by the…
nodes.title: Low half of the FFT butterfly recurrence

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $d$ a natural number, $\omega \in R$ and $x \in R^{2^{d+1}}$, with entries indexed from $0$. Let $e, o \in R^{2^d}$ be the even- and odd-indexed subsequences of $x$ returned by the FFT split, and let $E$ and $O$ be the vectors returned by the radix-two FFT of depth $d$ with root $\omega \cdot \omega$ on $e$ and on $o$. Then for every $k < 2^d$, entry $k + 2^d$ of the vector returned…
nodes.title: High half of the FFT butterfly recurrence

nodes.summary: For every natural number $m$ and every vector $x$ of length $2m$, splitting $x$ into its even-indexed and its odd-indexed subsequences costs exactly $4m$ charged operations: two reads and two writes for each of the $m$ even/odd pairs.
nodes.title: Cost of the FFT even/odd split

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $m$ a natural number. For every $\omega \in R$, all vectors $q, r \in R^m$, every current twiddle $w \in R$ and output vector of length $2m$ over $R$, and every index $k < m$, one butterfly step costs exactly $8$ charged operations: two reads, four scalar operations and two writes.
nodes.title: Cost of one FFT butterfly

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $m$ a natural number. For every $\omega \in R$, all vectors $q, r \in R^m$ and every output vector of length $2m$ over $R$, the pass that, starting from twiddle $1$, applies one butterfly for each index $k < m$ in increasing order costs exactly $8m$ charged operations.
nodes.title: Cost of the FFT butterfly pass

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For every natural number $d$, every $\omega \in R$ and every vector $x \in R^{2^d}$, the radix-two FFT of $x$ with root $\omega$ costs $T$ charged operations, where $T + 1 = (7d + 1) \cdot 2^d$; that is, $T = (7d + 1) \cdot 2^d - 1$.
nodes.title: Exact cost of the radix-two FFT

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For every natural number $d$, every $\omega \in R$ and every vector $x$ over $R$ of length $n = 2^d$, the radix-two FFT of $x$ with root $\omega$ costs $T$ charged operations, where $T + 1 = (7 \log_2 n + 1) \cdot n$.
nodes.title: Exact cost of the radix-two FFT in terms of the input length

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For every natural number $d$, every $\omega \in R$ and every vector $x \in R^{2^d}$, the radix-two FFT of $x$ with root $\omega$ costs at most $8 \cdot 2^d \cdot d$ charged operations, that is, at most eight per entry per recursion level.
nodes.title: Cost bound for the radix-two FFT

nodes.summary: For every natural number $d$, every primitive $2^d$-th root of unity $\omega \in \mathbb{C}$, every vector $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{2^d - 1})$ in $\mathbb{C}^{2^d}$ and every $k < 2^d$, the $k$-th entry of the radix-two FFT of $x$ with root $\omega$ equals the discrete Fourier sum $\sum_{j=0}^{2^d - 1} \omega^{jk} x_j$.
nodes.title: Correctness of the radix-two FFT

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $d$ a natural number, $\omega \in R$ and $x$ a vector over $R$ of length $2^d$. Then the array FFT of $x$, viewed as an array, with root $\omega$ returns a result, namely the output of the radix-two FFT of the length-$2^d$ vector $x$ with root $\omega$, viewed as an array.
nodes.title: The array FFT agrees with the vector FFT

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $d$ a natural number, $\omega \in R$ and $x$ a vector over $R$ of length $2^d$. Then the cost of the array FFT of $x$, viewed as an array, with root $\omega$ equals the cost of the radix-two FFT of the length-$2^d$ vector $x$ with root $\omega$.
nodes.title: The array FFT costs the same as the vector FFT

nodes.summary: Let $d$ be a natural number, $\omega \in \mathbb{C}$ a primitive $2^d$-th root of unity, $x_0, \dots, x_{2^d - 1}$ complex numbers and $k < 2^d$. Then the array FFT of the array $(x_0, \dots, x_{2^d - 1})$ with root $\omega$ returns an array $y$ of length $2^d$ whose entry at index $k$ is the discrete Fourier sum $\sum_{j=0}^{2^d - 1} \omega^{jk} x_j$.
nodes.title: The array FFT computes the discrete Fourier transform

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $d$ a natural number, $\omega \in R$ and $x$ a vector over $R$ of length $2^d$. Then the cost $T$ of the array FFT of $x$, viewed as an array, with root $\omega$ satisfies $T + 1 = (7d + 1) \cdot 2^d$.
nodes.title: Exact cost of the array FFT

nodes.title: The radix-two FFT with root $e^{2\pi i/n}$, divided by $n$, computes the inverse DFT

nodes.summary: For a type with a star operation $z \mapsto \bar z$ and a vector $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ of length $n$ over it, this costed computation returns $(\bar x_0, \dots, \bar x_{n-1})$ and charges $3n$ operations: one read, one conjugation and one write per entry.
nodes.title: Charged entrywise conjugation

nodes.summary: For a type with a multiplication, a scalar $c$ and a vector $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ of length $n$ over it, this costed computation returns $(c x_0, \dots, c x_{n-1})$ and charges $3n$ operations: one read, one multiplication and one write per entry.
nodes.title: Charged entrywise scaling

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a field that is a star ring, with star operation $z \mapsto \bar z$. For a natural number $d$, an element $\omega \in R$ and a vector $x \in R^{2^d}$, the inverse FFT conjugates every entry of $x$, applies the radix-two FFT with root $\omega$, conjugates every entry of the result, and multiplies every entry by the inverse $(2^d)^{-1}$ of $2^d$ in $R$ (which is $0$ when $2^d = 0$ in $R$). It charges…
nodes.title: Inverse FFT by conjugation

nodes.summary: For a type $R$ with a multiplication and vectors $x, y$ of length $n$ over $R$, the pointwise product returns the vector of length $n$ whose $i$-th entry is $x_i \cdot y_i$ for every $i < n$, and charges $4n$ time units: two reads, one multiplication and one write per entry.
nodes.title: Timed pointwise product

nodes.summary: For a type $R$ with a zero, a natural number $d$ and a vector $x$ of length $2^d$ over $R$, padding returns the vector of length $2^{d+1}$ whose $i$-th entry is $x_i$ for $i < 2^d$ and $0$ for $2^d \le i < 2^{d+1}$, and charges $3 \cdot 2^d$ time units.
nodes.title: Zero padding to twice the length

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a field that is a star ring, $d$ a natural number, $\omega \in R$, and $x, y$ vectors of length $2^d$ over $R$. Circular convolution runs the timed radix-two FFT of length $2^d$ with root $\omega$ on $x$ and then on $y$, multiplies the two transforms pointwise, and applies the timed inverse FFT of length $2^d$ with root $\omega$ to the product. It returns the result of the inverse transform, and its cost…
nodes.title: FFT circular convolution

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a field that is a star ring, $d$ a natural number, $\omega \in R$, and $x, y$ vectors of length $2^d$ over $R$. Linear convolution zero-pads $x$ and $y$ to length $2^{d+1}$ and returns the FFT circular convolution of the two padded vectors at length $2^{d+1}$ with root $\omega$. Its cost is the cost of the two paddings plus the cost of the circular convolution.
nodes.title: FFT linear convolution

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a field that is a star ring, $\omega \in R$, and $x, y$ arrays over $R$, where $x$ has length $n$. If $n = 2^d$ for some natural number $d$ and $y$ also has length $n$, the procedure returns the FFT circular convolution of $x$ and $y$ (read as vectors of length $2^d$) with root $\omega$, converted to an array, at the cost of that convolution. Otherwise it returns no result, at cost $0$.
nodes.title: FFT circular convolution on arrays

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a field that is a star ring, $\omega \in R$, and $x, y$ arrays over $R$, where $x$ has length $n$. If $n = 2^d$ for some natural number $d$ and $y$ also has length $n$, the procedure returns the FFT linear convolution of $x$ and $y$ (read as vectors of length $2^d$) with root $\omega$, an array of length $2n$, at the cost of that convolution. Otherwise it returns no result, at cost $0$.
nodes.title: FFT linear convolution on arrays

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a type with a multiplication, let $n$ be a natural number and let $x$ and $y$ be vectors of length $n$ over $R$. For every index $i < n$, entry $i$ of the pointwise product of $x$ and $y$ equals $x_i y_i$.
nodes.title: Entries of the pointwise product

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a type with a zero, let $d$ be a natural number and let $x$ be a vector of length $2^d$ over $R$. For every index $i < 2^d$, entry $i$ of the zero-padded vector of length $2^{d+1}$ produced from $x$ equals $x_i$.
nodes.title: Zero padding keeps the input prefix

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a type with a zero, let $d$ be a natural number and let $x$ be a vector of length $2^d$ over $R$. For every index $i$ with $2^d \le i < 2^{d+1}$, entry $i$ of the zero-padded vector of length $2^{d+1}$ produced from $x$ is $0$.
nodes.title: Zero padding fills the second half with zeros

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a field with a star-ring structure, let $\omega \in R$, and let $x$ and $y$ be arrays over $R$. The array circular-convolution procedure with root $\omega$ returns no result on $x$ and $y$ if and only if it is not the case that the length of $x$ is a power of two $2^k$ with $k \ge 0$ and $y$ has the same length as $x$.
nodes.title: Rejection by array circular convolution

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a field with a star-ring structure, let $\omega \in R$, and let $x$ and $y$ be arrays over $R$. The array zero-padded linear-convolution procedure with root $\omega$ returns no result on $x$ and $y$ if and only if it is not the case that the length of $x$ is a power of two $2^k$ with $k \ge 0$ and $y$ has the same length as $x$.
nodes.title: Rejection by array linear convolution

nodes.summary: Let $N = 2^d$, let $\omega \in \mathbb{C}$ be a primitive $N$-th root of unity and let $x \in \mathbb{C}^N$. Conjugating every entry of $x$, running the FFT procedure with root $\omega$ and conjugating every entry of the result gives the same vector as running the FFT procedure on $x$ with root $\overline{\omega}$.
nodes.title: Conjugating around the FFT conjugates the root

nodes.summary: Let $N = 2^d$, let $\omega \in \mathbb{C}$ be a primitive $N$-th root of unity and let $x \in \mathbb{C}^N$. The output of the inverse FFT procedure on $x$ with root $\omega$ is the output of the FFT procedure on $x$ with root $\overline{\omega}$ with every entry multiplied by $N^{-1}$.
nodes.title: The inverse FFT is a normalized FFT at the conjugate root

For every $k < N$, entry $k$ of the output of the inverse FFT procedure on $x$ with root $\omega$ equals $N^{-1}$ times the discrete Fourier sum of length $N$ with root $\overline{\omega}$ at frequency $k$ of the sequence $j \mapsto x_j$ (set to $0$ for $j \ge N$), that is,…

For every $k < N$, entry $k$ of its output equals the canonical inverse discrete Fourier transform of the function on $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ sending the class of $j < N$ to $x_j$, evaluated at the class of $k$; that is, it…
nodes.title: Inverse FFT at the negative-sign root computes the inverse DFT

For every $k < N$, entry $k$ of its output equals $N^{-1}$ times the canonical discrete Fourier transform of the function on $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ sending the class of $j < N$ to $x_j$, evaluated at the class of $k$; that is,…
nodes.title: Inverse FFT at the positive-sign root computes the normalized forward DFT

nodes.summary: Let $N = 2^d$ and let $\omega = e^{-2\pi i/N}$, the value at $-1$ of the standard additive character of $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$. For every $x \in \mathbb{C}^N$, running the FFT procedure on $x$ with root $\omega$ and then the inverse FFT procedure on its output with root $\omega$ returns $x$.
nodes.title: Inverse FFT after FFT is the identity at the negative-sign root

nodes.summary: Let $N = 2^d$ and let $\omega = e^{-2\pi i/N}$, the value at $-1$ of the standard additive character of $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$. For every $x \in \mathbb{C}^N$, running the inverse FFT procedure on $x$ with root $\omega$ and then the FFT procedure on its output with root $\omega$ returns $x$.
nodes.title: FFT after inverse FFT is the identity at the negative-sign root

The vector returned by FFT circular convolution of $x$ and $y$ with root $\omega$ equals the vector returned by the inverse FFT with root $\omega$ applied to the vector returned by pointwise multiplication of $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{y}$, where $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{y}$ are the vectors returned by the radix-two FFT of $x$…
nodes.title: Output of FFT circular convolution

The vector returned by FFT linear convolution of $x$ and $y$ with root $\omega$ equals the vector returned by FFT circular convolution, at length $2^{d+1}$ with root $\omega$, of the vectors returned by zero-padding $x$ and $y$ to length $2^{d+1}$.

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a field with a star-ring structure, let $d$ be a natural number, let $\omega \in R$, and let $x$ and $y$ be vectors of length $2^d$ over $R$. The cost charged by circular convolution of $x$ and $y$ with root $\omega$, plus $2$, equals $(21d + 16) \cdot 2^d$.

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a field with a star-ring structure, let $d$ be a natural number, let $\omega \in R$, and let $x$ and $y$ be vectors of length $2^d$ over $R$. Floating-point rounding

nodes.summary: For $m$ in a linearly ordered field $K$ with a floor function, $\operatorname{rne}(m)$ is the integer $\lfloor m \rfloor$ if $m - \lfloor m \rfloor < 1/2$, the integer $\lfloor m \rfloor + 1$ if $m - \lfloor m \rfloor > 1/2$, and, when $m - \lfloor m \rfloor = 1/2$, whichever of $\lfloor m \rfloor$ and $\lfloor m \rfloor + 1$ is even.
nodes.title: Nearest-integer rounding with ties to even

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function. For every $m \in K$, the integer $\operatorname{rne}(m)$ obtained by rounding $m$ to the nearest integer, ties to even, satisfies $|\operatorname{rne}(m) - m| \le m - \lfloor m \rfloor$ and $|\operatorname{rne}(m) - m| \le \lfloor m \rfloor + 1 - m$.
nodes.title: Rounding error bounded by the distances to neighbouring integers

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function. For every $m \in K$ and every integer $k$, the integer $\operatorname{rne}(m)$ obtained by rounding $m$ to the nearest integer, ties to even, satisfies $|\operatorname{rne}(m) - m| \le |k - m|$: no integer is closer to $m$ than $\operatorname{rne}(m)$.
nodes.title: Round to nearest integer

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function. For every $m \in K$, the integer $\operatorname{rne}(m)$ obtained by rounding $m$ to the nearest integer, ties to even, satisfies $|\operatorname{rne}(m) - m| \le 1/2$.
nodes.title: Rounding to the nearest integer is within one half

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function, let $m \in K$, and let $\operatorname{rne}(m)$ be the integer obtained by rounding $m$ to the nearest integer, ties to even. If $|\operatorname{rne}(m) - m| = 1/2$, that is, $m$ is halfway between two consecutive integers, then $\operatorname{rne}(m)$ is even.
nodes.title: Ties to even for the nearest integer

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function, let $m \in K$ and let $k$ be an integer. If $m \le k$, then $\operatorname{rne}(m) \le k$, where $\operatorname{rne}(m)$ is $m$ rounded to the nearest integer with ties to even.
nodes.title: Rounding to nearest preserves integer upper bounds

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function, let $m \in K$ and let $k$ be an integer. If $k \le m$, then $k \le \operatorname{rne}(m)$, where $\operatorname{rne}(m)$ is $m$ rounded to the nearest integer with ties to even.
nodes.title: Rounding to nearest preserves integer lower bounds

nodes.summary: For a natural number $p$, an element $x$ of a linearly ordered field with a floor function is a binary floating-point number with a $p$-bit significand and unbounded exponent when $x = m \cdot 2^e$ for some integers $m$ and $e$ with $|m| < 2^p$.
nodes.title: Binary floating-point numbers

nodes.summary: For a natural number $p$ and integers $q_{\min}$ and $q_{\max}$, an element $x$ of a linearly ordered field with a floor function is a number of the binary format with $p$-bit significands and last-place exponents in $[q_{\min}, q_{\max}]$ when $x = m \cdot 2^e$ for some integers $m$ and $e$ with $|m| < 2^p$ and $q_{\min} \le e \le q_{\max}$. These are zero, the subnormal numbers and the normal numbers of the format.
nodes.title: Floating-point numbers of a bounded format

nodes.summary: For a natural number $p$ (the significand length) and $x$ in a linearly ordered field $K$ with a floor function, the exponent of the last place of $x$ is the integer $\lfloor \log_2 |x| \rfloor - (p - 1)$. Here $\lfloor \log_2 |x| \rfloor$ is the integer logarithm: the largest integer $n$ with $2^n \le |x|$ when $x \ne 0$, and $0$ when $x = 0$.
nodes.title: Exponent of the last place

nodes.summary: For a natural number $p$ and an element $x$ of a linearly ordered field with a floor function, let $e$ be the exponent of the last place of $x$ at precision $p$, and let $\operatorname{rne}$ round to the nearest integer with ties to the even one. The rounding of $x$ to nearest, ties to even, is $\mathrm{fl}_p(x) = \operatorname{rne}(x / 2^e) \cdot 2^e$: scale $x$ so that its last place is the units digit, round to…
nodes.title: Round to nearest, ties to even

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function, let $p \ge 1$ be a natural number and let $x \in K$ be nonzero. Let $e = \lfloor \log_2 |x| \rfloor - (p - 1)$ be the exponent of the last place of $x$ for $p$-bit significands. Then $2^{p-1} \le |x / 2^e|$ and $|x / 2^e| < 2^p$.
nodes.title: Bounds on the scaled significand

nodes.summary: Let $x$ be an element of a linearly ordered field with a floor function, let $p$ be a natural number, and let $e$ be the exponent of the last place of $x$ at precision $p$. Writing $\operatorname{rne}$ for rounding to the nearest integer with ties to even, the rounding $\mathrm{fl}_p(x)$ of $x$ to nearest, ties to even, at precision $p$ has the error…
nodes.title: The rounding error at the scale of the last place

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function and let $p$ be a natural number. For every $x \in K$, the rounding $\mathrm{fl}(x)$ of $x$ to nearest, ties to even, with $p$-bit significands satisfies $|\mathrm{fl}(x) - x| \le u\,|x|$, where $u = 2^{-p}$ is the unit roundoff.
nodes.title: The relative error bound

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function and let $p \ge 1$. For every $x \in K$ and every binary floating-point number $f \in K$ with a $p$-bit significand (and unbounded exponent), the rounding $\mathrm{fl}(x)$ of $x$ to nearest, ties to even, with $p$-bit significands satisfies $|\mathrm{fl}(x) - x| \le |f - x|$: no floating-point number is closer to $x$ than $\mathrm{fl}(x)$.
nodes.title: Round to nearest for floating-point numbers

nodes.summary: Let $p \ge 1$ and let $x$ be an element of a linearly ordered field with a floor function. If $x$ is a binary floating-point number with a $p$-bit significand, that is, $x = m \cdot 2^e$ for some integers $m$ and $e$ with $|m| < 2^p$, then rounding $x$ to nearest, ties to even, at precision $p$ returns $x$: $\mathrm{fl}_p(x) = x$.
nodes.title: Floating-point numbers round to themselves

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function, let $p$ be a natural number, let $x \in K$, and let $e$ be the exponent of the last place of $x$, which is $\lfloor \log_2 |x| \rfloor - (p - 1)$ for $x \ne 0$. If the rounding $\mathrm{fl}(x)$ of $x$ to nearest, ties to even, with $p$-bit significands satisfies $|\mathrm{fl}(x) - x| = 2^e / 2$, then the integer $\operatorname{rne}(x / 2^e)$, the…
nodes.title: Ties to even for floating-point rounding

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function, let $p \ge 1$, let $x \in K$ be nonzero, and let $e = \lfloor \log_2 |x| \rfloor - (p - 1)$ be the exponent of the last place of $x$. Then $|\operatorname{rne}(x / 2^e)| \le 2^p$, where $\operatorname{rne}$ rounds to the nearest integer, ties to even.
nodes.title: Bound on the rounded significand

nodes.summary: Let $p \ge 1$. For every element $x$ of a linearly ordered field with a floor function, the rounding $\mathrm{fl}_p(x)$ of $x$ to nearest, ties to even, is a binary floating-point number with a $p$-bit significand: $\mathrm{fl}_p(x) = m \cdot 2^e$ for some integers $m$ and $e$ with $|m| < 2^p$.
nodes.title: Rounding gives a floating-point number

nodes.summary: Let $p \ge 1$, let $q_{\min}$ and $q_{\max}$ be integers, and let $x$ be an element of a linearly ordered field with a floor function. If $2^{q_{\min} + p - 1} \le |x|$ ($x$ is at least the smallest normal number) and $|x| \le (2^p - 1) \cdot 2^{q_{\max}}$ ($x$ is at most the largest finite number), then the rounding $\mathrm{fl}_p(x)$ of $x$ to nearest, ties to even, is a number of the binary format with $p$-bit…
nodes.title: In the normal range, rounding stays in the format

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function, let $p \ge 1$, and let $q_{\min}$ and $q_{\max}$ be integers. For every $x \in K$ and every number $f$ of the binary format with $p$-bit significands and last-place exponents in $[q_{\min}, q_{\max}]$, the rounding $\mathrm{fl}(x)$ of $x$ to nearest, ties to even, with $p$-bit significands satisfies $|\mathrm{fl}(x) - x| \le |f - x|$.
nodes.title: Round to nearest in a bounded format

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function and let $p$ be a natural number. Let $x, y \in K$ and let $m_x, m_y, e_x, e_y$ be integers with $|m_x| < 2^p$, $|m_y| < 2^p$, $x = m_x 2^{e_x}$ and $y = m_y 2^{e_y}$. If $y / 2 \le x \le 2y$, then there is an integer $k$ with $|k| < 2^p$ and $x - y = k \cdot 2^{\min(e_x, e_y)}$.
nodes.title: The difference of floating-point numbers within a factor of two

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a natural number and let $x$ and $y$ be binary floating-point numbers with $p$-bit significands (and unbounded exponent) in a linearly ordered field with a floor function. If $y / 2 \le x \le 2y$, then $x - y$ is also a binary floating-point number with a $p$-bit significand.
nodes.title: Sterbenz's lemma

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a natural number, let $q_{\min}$ and $q_{\max}$ be integers, and let $x$ and $y$ be numbers of the binary format with $p$-bit significands whose last place has exponent in $[q_{\min}, q_{\max}]$ (subnormal numbers included), in a linearly ordered field with a floor function. If $y / 2 \le x \le 2y$, then $x - y$ is also a number of this format.
nodes.title: Sterbenz's lemma in a bounded format

nodes.summary: Let $p \ge 1$ and let $x$ and $y$ be binary floating-point numbers with $p$-bit significands in a linearly ordered field with a floor function. If $y / 2 \le x \le 2y$, then rounding $x - y$ to nearest, ties to even, at precision $p$ returns it exactly: $\mathrm{fl}_p(x - y) = x - y$.

Horner's method

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative semiring, let $x \in R$, and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1} \in R$ be coefficients listed in ascending order of degree. Horner evaluation starts with the accumulator $v = 0$ and, for $i = n-1, \dots, 0$ in turn, replaces $v$ by $a_i + x v$, charging two operations (one multiplication and one addition) for each step. It returns the final accumulator together with the total number of operations…

nodes.summary: For every commutative semiring $R$, every $x \in R$ and all coefficients $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1} \in R$, Horner evaluation of $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ at $x$ charges exactly $2n$ operations, one multiplication and one addition per coefficient.
nodes.title: Horner evaluation uses $2n$ operations

nodes.summary: For every commutative semiring $R$, every $x \in R$ and all coefficients $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1} \in R$, the value returned by Horner evaluation of $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ at $x$ is $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} a_i x^i$.
nodes.title: Horner evaluation computes the coefficient sum

nodes.summary: For every commutative semiring $R$, every $x \in R$ and all coefficients $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1} \in R$, the value returned by Horner evaluation of $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ at $x$ equals $p(x)$, where $p = a_0 + a_1 X + \dots + a_{n-1} X^{n-1} \in R[X]$ is the polynomial with these coefficients.
nodes.title: Horner evaluation is polynomial evaluation

nodes.summary: For every commutative semiring $R$ and every $x \in R$, Horner evaluation at $x$ with no coefficients ($n = 0$) returns $0$ and charges $0$ operations.

nodes.summary: For every commutative semiring $R$, every $x \in R$ and every single coefficient $a_0 \in R$ ($n = 1$), Horner evaluation of $a_0$ at $x$ returns $a_0$ and charges $2$ operations.
nodes.title: Horner evaluation of a constant polynomial

nodes.summary: For every commutative semiring $R$ and all coefficients $a_0, \dots, a_n \in R$ (at least one coefficient), the value returned by Horner evaluation of $a_0, \dots, a_n$ at $x = 0$ is $a_0$.

If $n \le 1$, it returns $xy$ at cost $1$. If $n \ge 2$, let $m = \lceil n/2 \rceil$, let $a$ and $b$ be the natural-number quotient and remainder of $x$ by $B^m$, and let $c$ and $d$ be those of $y$ by $B^m$. It runs itself with digit count $m$ on the…

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $a, b, c, d$, write $P = |a - b| \cdot |c - d|$. If $b \le a$ holds exactly when $d \le c$, then $ac + bd - P = ad + bc$, where the subtraction is truncated at $0$; otherwise $ac + bd + P = ad + bc$.
nodes.title: Karatsuba's middle coefficient

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $B$, $n$, $x$ and $y$, Karatsuba multiplication of $x$ and $y$ as $n$-digit numbers in base $B$ returns $xy$.
nodes.title: Correctness of Karatsuba multiplication

nodes.summary: Let $B \ge 1$ and $n$ be natural numbers, let $m = \lceil n/2 \rceil$, and let $x < B^n$ be a natural number. Then the high part $\lfloor x / B^m \rfloor$, the low part $x \bmod B^m$, and their distance $|\lfloor x / B^m \rfloor - x \bmod B^m|$ are all less than $B^m$.
nodes.title: Size bound for Karatsuba's recursive operands

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $B$, $n$, $x$ and $y$, the cost of Karatsuba multiplication of $x$ and $y$ as $n$-digit numbers in base $B$ equals $T(n)$, where $T$ is the Karatsuba cost recurrence, $T(n) = 1$ for $n \le 1$ and $T(n) = 3\,T(\lceil n/2 \rceil) + n$ for $n \ge 2$.
nodes.title: Cost of Karatsuba multiplication

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be the Karatsuba cost recurrence, $T(n) = 1$ for $n \le 1$ and $T(n) = 3\,T(\lceil n/2 \rceil) + n$ for $n \ge 2$. For every natural number $k$, $T(2^k) + 2^{k+1} = 3^{k+1}$.
nodes.title: Karatsuba cost at powers of two

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be the Karatsuba cost recurrence, $T(n) = 1$ for $n \le 1$ and $T(n) = 3\,T(\lceil n/2 \rceil) + n$ for $n \ge 2$, and let $\ell(n)$ be the least natural number $k$ with $n \le 2^k$ (so $\ell(n) = \lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ for $n \ge 1$). For every natural number $n$, $T(n) \le 3^{\ell(n) + 1}$.
nodes.title: Power-of-three bound on the Karatsuba cost recurrence

nodes.summary: Let $\ell(n)$ be the least natural number $k$ with $n \le 2^k$ (so $\ell(n) = \lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ for $n \ge 1$). For all natural numbers $B$, $n$, $x$ and $y$, the cost of Karatsuba multiplication of $x$ and $y$ as $n$-digit numbers in base $B$ is at most $3^{\ell(n) + 1}$.

Rectangular matrix accumulation adds the product $AB$ to the accumulator $C$: for $i < p$, then $j < r$, then $k < q$, each in increasing order, it replaces $C_{ij}$ by $C_{ij} + A_{ik} B_{kj}$. It returns the final matrix together with…

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with an addition and a multiplication, and let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\alpha$, stored as vectors of rows. Square matrix accumulation on $A$, $B$, $C$ is rectangular matrix accumulation on $A$, $B$, $C$ with all three dimensions equal to $n$: it adds $AB$ to the accumulator $C$ and returns the result with its cost pair (scalar multiplications, scalar additions).
nodes.title: Square matrix accumulation

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a commutative additive monoid with a multiplication, and let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $p \times q$, $q \times r$ and $p \times r$ matrices over $\alpha$, stored as vectors of rows. For all $i < p$ and $j < r$, the $(i, j)$ entry of the matrix returned by rectangular matrix accumulation on $A$, $B$, $C$ is $C_{ij} + \sum_{k < q} A_{ik} B_{kj}$.

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a commutative additive monoid with a multiplication, and let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $p \times q$, $q \times r$ and $p \times r$ matrices over $\alpha$, stored as vectors of rows. The matrix returned by rectangular matrix accumulation on $A$, $B$, $C$ equals $C + AB$, where $AB$ is the matrix product, $(AB)_{ij} = \sum_{k < q} A_{ik} B_{kj}$.
nodes.title: Rectangular matrix accumulation computes $C + AB$

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with an addition and a multiplication, and let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $p \times q$, $q \times r$ and $p \times r$ matrices over $\alpha$. Rectangular matrix accumulation on $A$, $B$, $C$ has cost $(pqr, pqr)$: it charges exactly $pqr$ scalar multiplications and exactly $pqr$ scalar additions.
nodes.title: Operation count of rectangular matrix accumulation

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with an addition and a multiplication. If $A$ is a $p \times 0$ matrix, $B$ a $0 \times r$ matrix and $C$ a $p \times r$ matrix over $\alpha$, then rectangular matrix accumulation on $A$, $B$, $C$ returns $C$ unchanged at cost $(0, 0)$.

The matrix returned by square matrix accumulation on $A$, $B$, $C$ equals $C + AB$, where $AB$ is the matrix product, $(AB)_{ij} = \sum_{k < n} A_{ik} B_{kj}$.

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with an addition and a multiplication, and let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\alpha$. Square matrix accumulation on $A$, $B$, $C$ has cost $(n^3, n^3)$: it charges exactly $n^3$ scalar multiplications and exactly $n^3$ scalar additions.

The procedure adds the product of $A$ and $B$ to the accumulator $C$ by the eight-call recursion of CLRS. The recursive multiply-accumulate procedure on $A$, $B$, $C$ performs exactly $8^k$ scalar multiplications and exactly $8^k$ accumulator additions. Since $8^k = n^3$, each count is the cube of the dimension.

Modular exponentiation

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $n$, modular exponentiation with base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ is the recursive procedure that returns $1$ if $b = 0$. If $b > 0$ is even, it computes the result $d$ for exponent $b/2$ (same base and modulus) and returns $d \cdot d \bmod n$. If $b$ is odd, it computes the result $d$ for exponent $b - 1$ and returns $a \cdot d \bmod n$. Each even or odd step performs one…
nodes.title: Modular exponentiation

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $a$ and $n$, modular exponentiation with base $a$, exponent $0$ and modulus $n$ returns $1$ and performs no multiplications.
nodes.title: Base case of modular exponentiation

nodes.summary: Let $a$, $b$, $n$ be natural numbers with $b > 0$ and $b$ even. If modular exponentiation on base $a$, exponent $b/2$ and modulus $n$ returns the value $d$ using $t$ multiplications, then on base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ it returns the value $(d \cdot d) \bmod n$ using $t + 1$ multiplications.
nodes.title: Even step of modular exponentiation

nodes.summary: Let $a$, $b$, $n$ be natural numbers with $b$ odd. If modular exponentiation on base $a$, exponent $b - 1$ and modulus $n$ returns the value $d$ using $t$ multiplications, then on base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ it returns the value $(a \cdot d) \bmod n$ using $t + 1$ multiplications.
nodes.title: Odd step of modular exponentiation

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $a$ and $n$, modular exponentiation with base $a$, exponent $0$ and modulus $n$ returns $1$.
nodes.title: Modular exponentiation returns 1 at exponent zero

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $a$ and $n$, modular exponentiation with base $a$, exponent $0$ and modulus $n$ performs no multiplications.
nodes.title: No multiplications at exponent zero

nodes.summary: Let $a$, $b$, $n$ be natural numbers with $b > 0$ and $b$ even, and let $d$ be the value returned by modular exponentiation on base $a$, exponent $b/2$ and modulus $n$. Then the value returned on base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ is $(d \cdot d) \bmod n$.
nodes.title: Value of the even step of modular exponentiation

nodes.summary: Let $a$, $b$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $b$ positive and even. Modular exponentiation with base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ performs exactly one more multiplication than it does with base $a$, exponent $b/2$ and modulus $n$.
nodes.title: Multiplication count in the even case

nodes.summary: Let $a$, $b$, $n$ be natural numbers with $b$ odd, and let $d$ be the value returned by modular exponentiation on base $a$, exponent $b - 1$ and modulus $n$. Then the value returned on base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ is $(a \cdot d) \bmod n$.
nodes.title: Value of the odd step of modular exponentiation

nodes.summary: Let $a$, $b$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $b$ odd. Modular exponentiation with base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ performs exactly one more multiplication than it does with base $a$, exponent $b - 1$ and modulus $n$.
nodes.title: Multiplication count in the odd case

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $a$, $b$, $n$ with $n > 0$, including $b = 0$, the value $r$ returned by modular exponentiation on base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ satisfies $r \bmod n = a^b \bmod n$.
nodes.title: Modular exponentiation is correct up to reduction

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $a$, $b$, $n$ with $n > 0$, the value $r$ returned by modular exponentiation on base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ satisfies $r \bmod n = (a \bmod n)^b \bmod n$.
nodes.title: Modular exponentiation with a reduced base

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $a$, $b$, $n$ with $b > 0$, the value $r$ returned by modular exponentiation on base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ satisfies $r \bmod n = r$ (with the convention $r \bmod 0 = r$).
nodes.title: Modular exponentiation returns a reduced value

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $a$, $b$, $n$ with $b > 0$ and $n > 0$, the value returned by modular exponentiation on base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ equals $a^b \bmod n$.
nodes.title: Correctness of modular exponentiation

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $a$, $b$, $n$ with $b > 0$ and $n > 0$, the value returned by modular exponentiation on base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ is less than $n$.
nodes.title: Modular exponentiation returns a value below the modulus

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $a$, $b$, $n$ with $b > 0$ and $n > 0$, the value $r$ returned by modular exponentiation on base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ satisfies $r = a^b \bmod n$ and $r < n$.
nodes.title: Modular exponentiation returns the least residue

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $a$ and $n$ with $n > 1$, the value returned by modular exponentiation with base $a$, exponent $0$ and modulus $n$ equals $a^0 \bmod n$ and is less than $n$.
nodes.title: Least residue at exponent zero

nodes.summary: For every natural number $a$, modular exponentiation with base $a$, exponent $0$ and modulus $1$ returns $1$, whereas $a^0 \bmod 1 = 0$.
nodes.title: Unreduced result at modulus one

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $a$, $a'$, $b$, $n$ and $n'$, modular exponentiation performs the same number of multiplications with base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ as with base $a'$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n'$.
nodes.title: The multiplication count depends only on the exponent

nodes.summary: Let $a$, $b$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $b > 0$, and let $\beta = \lfloor \log_2 b \rfloor + 1$ be the number of binary digits of $b$. The number of multiplications performed by modular exponentiation with base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ is at least $\beta$ and at most $2\beta - 1$.
nodes.title: Multiplication count of modular exponentiation
Miller–Rabin primality test

nodes.summary: For a natural number $m > 0$, the two-adic split of $m$ is the pair $(t, u)$ of natural numbers with $m = 2^t u$ and $u$ odd. For $m = 0$ it is $(0, 0)$.
nodes.title: Splitting off the power of two

nodes.summary:
Fix a modulus $n$. With no squarings remaining, the loop at the current value $x$ reports a witness exactly when $x 
e 1$, at no cost. With $k + 1$ squarings remaining, it costs one modular multiplication and computes $y = x^2  mod n$; it reports a witness if $y = 1$, $x 
e 1$ and $x 
e n - 1$, and otherwise continues at $y$ with $k$ squarings remaining.
nodes.title: The Miller–Rabin squaring loop

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $a$ and $n$, write $n - 1 = 2^t u$ with $u$ odd (here $n - 1$ is truncated at $0$, and $t = u = 0$ when $n \le 1$). The test sets $x_0$ to the result of modular exponentiation of $a$ to the power $u$ modulo $n$, which is $a^u \bmod n$ when $u > 0$ and $1$ when $u = 0$. For $i = 1, \dots, t$ it computes $x_i = x_{i-1}^2 \bmod n$ and returns true as soon as $x_i = 1$, $x_{i-1} \ne 1$ and…
nodes.title: Miller–Rabin witness test

nodes.summary: Given a natural number $n$ and a list of bases $a_1, \dots, a_s$, the test runs the witness test for $n$ on each base in turn. It answers *composite* as soon as some base $a_i$ is a witness to the compositeness of $n$, and *prime* if none is (in particular on the empty list). Its cost is the sum of the costs of the witness tests it runs.
nodes.title: The Miller–Rabin test

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $n$, $k$ and $x$, the cost of the squaring loop modulo $n$ started at $x$ with $k$ squarings remaining is at most $k$.
nodes.title: Cost bound for the Miller–Rabin squaring loop

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $a$ and $n$, write $n - 1 = 2^t u$ with $u$ odd (here $n - 1$ is truncated at $0$, and $t = u = 0$ when $n \le 1$). The cost of the witness test on base $a$ and modulus $n$ is at most the cost of the modular exponentiation of $a$ to the power $u$ modulo $n$ plus $t$: at most one multiplication for each of the $t$ squarings.
nodes.title: Cost of the Miller–Rabin witness test

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a prime and let $k$ and $x$ be natural numbers with $x < p$ and $x^{2^k} \bmod p = 1$. Then the squaring loop modulo $p$ started at $x$ with $k$ squarings remaining reports no witness.
nodes.title: The squaring loop modulo a prime finds no witness when it ends at 1

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a prime and $a$ a natural number with $0 < a < n$. Then the witness test does not report $a$ as a witness to the compositeness of $n$.
nodes.title: A prime has no Miller–Rabin witnesses in range

nodes.summary: Let $n$ and $a$ be natural numbers with $0 < a < n$. If the witness test reports $a$ as a witness to the compositeness of $n$, then $n$ is not prime.
nodes.title: A Miller–Rabin witness in range proves compositeness

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a prime. For every list of bases $a_1, \dots, a_s$ (possibly empty) with $0 < a_i < n$ for each $i$, the Miller–Rabin test run on $n$ with these bases answers *prime*.
nodes.title: The Miller–Rabin test never rejects a prime when its bases lie in range

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number and $a_1, \dots, a_s$ a list of bases with $0 < a_i < n$ for each $i$. If the Miller–Rabin test run on $n$ with these bases answers *composite*, then $n$ is not prime.
nodes.title: With bases in range, a composite answer of the Miller–Rabin test is correct

nodes.summary: Let $n$, $k$ and $x$ be natural numbers with $n > 0$, $x < n$ and $x^{2^k} \bmod n \ne 1$. Then the squaring loop modulo $n$ started at $x$ with $k$ squarings remaining reports a witness.
nodes.title: The squaring loop reports a witness when it does not end at 1

nodes.summary: Let $a$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $n > 1$. If $a^{n-1} \bmod n \ne 1$, that is, $a^{n-1} \not\equiv 1 \pmod{n}$, then the Miller–Rabin witness test on base $a$ and modulus $n$ returns true.
nodes.title: Fermat witnesses are Miller–Rabin witnesses

nodes.summary: Let $n$, $k$ and $x$ be natural numbers with $x < n$. If the Miller–Rabin squaring loop modulo $n$, started at $x$ with $k$ squarings to perform, reports no witness, then $x = 1$ or $x^{2^i} \equiv -1 \pmod n$ for some $i < k$.
nodes.title: When the squaring loop finds no witness

nodes.summary: Let $n > 1$ and write $n - 1 = 2^t u$ with $u$ odd. If $a$ is a natural number for which the Miller–Rabin witness test $\mathrm{WITNESS}(a, n)$ returns false, then $a^u \equiv 1 \pmod n$, or $a^{2^i u} \equiv -1 \pmod n$ for some $i < t$.
nodes.title: What a non-witness satisfies

nodes.summary: Let $n > 1$ and let $a$ be a natural number such that the witness test $\mathrm{WITNESS}(a, n)$ returns false. Then $a^{n-1} \equiv 1 \pmod n$ and $a$ is coprime to $n$.
nodes.title: Non-witnesses pass Fermat's test and are units

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, the non-witnesses of $n$ form the finite set of bases $a$ with $0 < a < n$ for which the Miller–Rabin witness test $\mathrm{WITNESS}(a, n)$ returns false, that is, the bases that do not witness the compositeness of $n$.
nodes.title: Non-witnesses of a number

nodes.summary: Let $n > 1$, and suppose some $x$ coprime to $n$ has $x^{n-1} \not\equiv 1 \pmod n$. Then at most $(n - 1)/2$ of the bases $1, \dots, n - 1$ are non-witnesses for $n$.
nodes.title: At most half the bases are non-witnesses when some unit fails Fermat's test

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a Carmichael number: $n > 2$, $n$ is not prime, and $b^{n-1} \equiv 1 \pmod n$ for every $b$ coprime to $n$. Then at most $(n - 1)/2$ of the bases $1, \dots, n - 1$ are non-witnesses for $n$.
nodes.title: At most half the bases are non-witnesses for a Carmichael number

nodes.summary: Let $n > 1$ be odd and not prime. Then at most $(n - 1)/2$ of the bases $1, \dots, n - 1$ are non-witnesses for $n$; equivalently, at least $(n - 1)/2$ of them are witnesses to the compositeness of $n$.
nodes.title: At most half the bases are non-witnesses

nodes.summary: For every natural number $n$ and every list of bases, the Miller–Rabin test on $n$ with these bases answers *prime* if and only if, for every base $a$ in the list, the witness test $\mathrm{WITNESS}(a, n)$ returns false, that is, $a$ is not a witness to the compositeness of $n$.
nodes.title: Miller–Rabin answers prime exactly when no base is a witness

nodes.summary: Let $n > 1$ be odd and not prime, and let $s$ be a natural number. Among the $(n - 1)^s$ lists $(b_1, \dots, b_s)$ of bases with $0 < b_i < n$, at most $((n - 1)/2)^s$ make the Miller–Rabin test of $n$ with bases $b_1, \dots, b_s$ answer *prime*.
nodes.title: Half error bound for Miller–Rabin with several bases

nodes.summary: At most a quarter of the bases are non-witnesses when some unit fails Fermat's test and the modulus is not a prime power. Let $n > 1$ be odd and not prime, and not of the form $p^e$ with $p$ prime and $e \ge 2$. Suppose some $z$ coprime to $n$ has $z^{n-1} \not\equiv 1 \pmod n$. Then at most $(n - 1)/4$ of the bases $1, \dots, n - 1$ are non-witnesses for $n$.
nodes.title: At most a quarter of the bases are non-witnesses when some unit fails Fermat's test and the modulus is not a prime power

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a Carmichael number: $n > 2$, $n$ is not prime, and $b^{n-1} \equiv 1 \pmod n$ for every $b$ coprime to $n$. Then at most $(n - 1)/4$ of the bases $1, \dots, n - 1$ are non-witnesses for $n$.
nodes.title: At most a quarter of the bases are non-witnesses for a Carmichael number

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a prime and $k \ge 2$ with $p^k$ odd. Then at most $(p^k - 1)/4$ of the bases $1, \dots, p^k - 1$ are non-witnesses for $p^k$.
nodes.title: At most a quarter of the bases are non-witnesses for an odd prime power

nodes.summary: Let $n > 1$ be odd and not prime. Then at most $(n - 1)/4$ of the bases $1, \dots, n - 1$ are non-witnesses for $n$, so one uniformly random base fails to expose $n$ as composite with probability at most $1/4$.
nodes.title: At most a quarter of the bases are non-witnesses

nodes.summary: Let $n > 1$ be odd and not prime, and let $s$ be a natural number. Among the $(n - 1)^s$ lists $(b_1, \dots, b_s)$ of bases with $0 < b_i < n$, at most $\lfloor (n - 1)/4 \rfloor^s$ make the Miller–Rabin test of $n$ with bases $b_1, \dots, b_s$ answer *prime*.
nodes.title: Quarter error bound for Miller–Rabin with several bases

If $d \mid b$, it returns the array $[x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{d-1}]$, where…
nodes.title: Modular linear equation solver

nodes.summary: Let $a > 0$ and $n > 0$ be natural numbers, $b$ an integer, $d = \gcd(a, n)$, and $y$ the coefficient of $a$ in the Bézout identity $d = n u + a y$ computed by the extended Euclidean algorithm on $(n, a)$. If $d \mid b$, the list returned by the modular linear equation solver on $a$, $b$, $n$ is $[x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{d-1}]$ with $x_i = \bigl((y \cdot (b / d)) \bmod n + i \cdot (n / d)\bigr) \bmod n$, where…
nodes.title: Output of the modular linear equation solver

parts: The solver returns exactly the solutions below
reading_title.source: The solver returns exactly the solutions below $n$

nodes.summary: Let $a > 0$ and $n > 0$ be natural numbers and $b$ an integer. A natural number $x$ occurs in the output of the modular linear equation solver on $a$, $b$, $n$ if and only if $x < n$ and $a x \equiv b \pmod{n}$.
nodes.title: The solver returns exactly the solutions below $n$

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $a > 0$ and $n > 0$ and an integer $b$, the entries of the output of the modular linear equation solver on $a$, $b$, $n$ are pairwise distinct.
nodes.title: The solver returns no repeated residues

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $a > 0$ and $n > 0$ and an integer $b$, the output of the modular linear equation solver on $a$, $b$, $n$ has $\gcd(a, n)$ entries if $\gcd(a, n)$ divides $b$, and no entries otherwise.
nodes.title: Number of residues returned by the solver

parts: The solver returns nothing exactly when
reading_title.source: The solver returns nothing exactly when $\gcd(a, n) \nmid b$

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $a > 0$ and $n > 0$ and an integer $b$, the modular linear equation solver on $a$, $b$, $n$ returns the empty array if and only if $\gcd(a, n)$ does not divide $b$.
nodes.title: The solver returns nothing exactly when $\gcd(a, n) \nmid b$

nodes.summary: Let $a > 0$ and $n > 0$ be natural numbers, $b$ an integer and $d = \gcd(a, n)$, and put $c = 4 + 3d$ if $d \mid b$ and $c = 0$ otherwise. The cost $T$ of the modular linear equation solver on $a$, $b$, $n$ satisfies $1 + c \le T \le 6(2 \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 2) + 1 + c$.
nodes.title: Cost bounds for the modular linear equation solver
Strassen algorithm

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a type with a zero, an addition, a subtraction and a multiplication (no ring axioms are assumed). For $k \ge 0$ and $2^k \times 2^k$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $R$, this procedure runs Strassen's seven-product recursion for adding $AB$ to $C$. It returns a $2^k \times 2^k$ matrix together with a pair of counts: the number of scalar multiplications and the number of scalar additions and subtractions it…
nodes.title: Strassen's matrix accumulator

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a non-unital, non-associative ring. For every $k \ge 0$ and all $2^k \times 2^k$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $R$, the matrix returned by Strassen's accumulator on $A$, $B$, $C$ equals $C + AB$, where $AB$ is the usual matrix product, $(AB)_{ij} = \sum_t A_{it} B_{tj}$.
nodes.title: Correctness of Strassen's matrix accumulator

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a non-unital, non-associative ring. For every $k \ge 0$, all $2^k \times 2^k$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $R$ and all indices $i, j$, the $(i, j)$ entry of the matrix returned by Strassen's accumulator on $A$, $B$, $C$ is $C_{ij} + \sum_{t} A_{it} B_{tj}$, the sum running over all $2^k$ indices $t$.
nodes.title: Entries of Strassen's matrix accumulator

nodes.summary: Let $R$ be a type with a zero, an addition, a subtraction and a multiplication. For every $k \ge 0$ and all $2^k \times 2^k$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $R$, Strassen's accumulator on $A$, $B$, $C$ performs exactly $7^k$ scalar multiplications and exactly $(25 \cdot 7^k - 22 \cdot 4^k)/3$ scalar additions and subtractions.

Closest pair of points problem

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field. The squared distance between points $p = (p_1, p_2)$ and $q = (q_1, q_2)$ of $K^2$ is $(p_1 - q_1)^2 + (p_2 - q_2)^2$.
nodes.title: Squared distance in the plane

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field, and write $d(p, q) = (p_1 - q_1)^2 + (p_2 - q_2)^2$ for the squared distance between points $p = (p_1, p_2)$ and $q = (q_1, q_2)$ of $K^2$. For a list $c_1, \dots, c_n$ of points of $K^2$, an element $\delta$ of $K$ is the least pairwise squared distance of the list when $\delta = d(c_i, c_j)$ for some $i < j$ and $\delta \le d(c_i, c_j)$ for all $i < j$.
nodes.title: Least pairwise squared distance

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field, and write $d(p, q) = (p_1 - q_1)^2 + (p_2 - q_2)^2$ for the squared distance between points $p = (p_1, p_2)$ and $q = (q_1, q_2)$ of $K^2$. For a point $p$ and a list $c_1, \dots, c_m$ of points of $K^2$, the least squared distance from $p$ to the list is no value if $m = 0$ and $\min_{1 \le k \le m} d(p, c_k)$ otherwise. Computing it is charged one unit of cost per point of the…
nodes.title: Least squared distance from a point to a list

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a field with a linear order, and write $d(p, q) = (x - x')^2 + (y - y')^2$ for the squared distance between points $p = (x, y)$ and $q = (x', y')$ of $K^2$. On a list $c_1, \dots, c_n$ of points in $K^2$, the brute-force scan returns no value if $n < 2$, and otherwise returns $\min_{i < j} d(c_i, c_j)$: for each $i$ it computes the least squared distance from $c_i$ to the later points…
nodes.title: Brute-force closest pair

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field, and write $d(p, q) = (p_1 - q_1)^2 + (p_2 - q_2)^2$ for the squared distance between points $p = (p_1, p_2)$ and $q = (q_1, q_2)$ of $K^2$. Let $\delta \in K$, let $p = (p_1, p_2)$ be a point of $K^2$ and $c_1, \dots, c_m$ a list of points $c_l = (x_l, y_l)$ of $K^2$, and let $k \le m$ be largest such that $(y_l - p_2)^2 < \delta$ for all $1 \le l \le k$. The scan from $p$ with…
nodes.title: Strip scan from a point

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field, $\delta \in K$ and $c_1, \dots, c_n$ a list of points of $K^2$. For each $i$, the strip scan runs the strip scan from $c_i$ with threshold $\delta$ on the later points $c_{i+1}, \dots, c_n$. It returns the least of the values these scans return, or no value if none of them returns a value, and its cost is the sum of their costs.

Otherwise let $m = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, and run the recursion on $c_1, \dots, c_m$ and on $c_{m+1}, \dots, c_n$. If neither call returns a value, it returns no value. Otherwise let $\delta$ be the least of the returned values, let $T$ be the…
nodes.title: Closest-pair recursion

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a field with a linear order. Given a list of points in $K^2$, the closest-pair algorithm sorts the points by first coordinate (merge sort, at no cost) and runs the closest-pair recursion on the sorted list. It returns a squared distance or no value, and is charged one unit of cost per squared distance computed.

nodes.title: The closest-pair algorithm returns the answer

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and let $ps$ be a list of at least two points in $K^2$. Then the divide-and-conquer closest-pair algorithm returns a value $\delta$, and $\delta$ is the least squared distance between two entries of $ps$ at different positions: some two entries at different positions have squared distance $\delta$, and any two entries at different positions have squared distance at least $\delta$.
nodes.title: Correctness of divide-and-conquer closest pair

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field. For every list of points in $K^2$, the divide-and-conquer closest-pair algorithm returns no value if and only if the list has fewer than two entries.

nodes.title: Divide and conquer agrees with brute force

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a field with a linear order and let $ps$ be a list of $n$ points in $K^2$. Counting one unit of cost per squared distance computed, twice the cost of the brute-force scan on $ps$ equals $n(n-1)$; that is, the scan computes exactly $n(n-1)/2$ squared distances.

nodes.summary: A tagged point is a pair $(p, s)$ of a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and a Boolean $s$, read as the side of the dividing line on which $p$ lies: false for left, true for right.
nodes.title: Side-tagged points

nodes.summary: For a real $\delta$, two tagged points $a$ and $b$ are same-side far apart when, if $a$ and $b$ carry the same side, the squared distance between their points is at least $\delta$.
nodes.title: Same-side points far apart

The cost of the scan from $q$ over $L$ with threshold $\delta$, one unit per squared distance computed, equals the length of the longest initial segment of $L$ all of whose points $r = (r_1, r_2)$ satisfy $(r_2 - q_2)^2 < \delta$.

nodes.summary: For every list of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, the closest-pair algorithm computes at most $7 n \lceil \log_2 n \rceil + n$ squared distances, where $\lceil \log_2 0 \rceil$ is read as $0$. In particular it computes $O(n \log n)$ distances.

Orientation and segment intersection tests

nodes.summary: For $p = (x_p, y_p)$ and $q = (x_q, y_q)$ in $K^2$, where $K$ is a linearly ordered field, the cross product is $p \times q = x_p y_q - x_q y_p$ (CLRS equation (33.1)).
nodes.title: Cross product of plane vectors

nodes.summary: For points $p_i, p_j, p_k \in K^2$, where $K$ is a linearly ordered field, CLRS's DIRECTION$(p_i, p_j, p_k)$ is the cross product $(p_k - p_i) \times (p_j - p_i)$.
nodes.title: Direction of three points

nodes.summary: For points $p_i = (x_i, y_i)$, $p_j = (x_j, y_j)$ and $p_k = (x_k, y_k)$ in $K^2$, where $K$ is a linearly ordered field, CLRS's ON-SEGMENT$(p_i, p_j, p_k)$ is the Boolean that is true exactly when $p_k$ lies in the bounding box of $p_i$ and $p_j$, that is, $\min(x_i, x_j) \le x_k \le \max(x_i, x_j)$ and $\min(y_i, y_j) \le y_k \le \max(y_i, y_j)$.
nodes.title: The ON-SEGMENT test

nodes.summary: Two elements $d$ and $e$ of a field with a linear order straddle zero when $d > 0$ and $e < 0$, or $d < 0$ and $e > 0$; that is, $d$ and $e$ are nonzero with opposite signs.
nodes.title: Values of opposite sign

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field, $d \in K$ and $p_i, p_j, p_k \in K^2$. When $d = 0$, this step costs one unit and returns the value of ON-SEGMENT$(p_i, p_j, p_k)$; when $d \neq 0$, it costs nothing and returns false.
nodes.title: Collinear-endpoint step of SEGMENTS-INTERSECT

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and $p, q, r \in K^2$. If $r$ lies on the closed segment from $p$ to $q$, then ON-SEGMENT$(p, q, r)$ is true, that is, $r$ lies in the bounding box of $p$ and $q$.
nodes.title: Points of a segment lie in its bounding box

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and $p, q, r \in K^2$. If $r$ lies on the closed segment from $p$ to $q$, then the direction $(r - p) \times (q - p)$ is zero, that is, $r$ is collinear with $p$ and $q$.

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field, write $(u_1, u_2) \times (v_1, v_2) = u_1 v_2 - v_1 u_2$ for the cross product on $K^2$, and let $p, q, r \in K^2$. If $r$ is collinear with $p$ and $q$, that is, the direction $(r - p) \times (q - p)$ is zero, and ON-SEGMENT$(p, q, r)$ is true, that is, $r$ lies in the bounding box of $p$ and $q$, then $r$ lies on the closed segment from $p$ to $q$.
