nodes.summary: If $d$ and $e$ are elements of a linearly ordered field that straddle zero, that is, they are nonzero with opposite signs, then $0 \le d / (d - e) \le 1$.
nodes.title: Zero-crossing parameter of values of opposite sign

nodes.summary: Let $d$ and $e$ be nonzero elements of a linearly ordered field. If $a d + b e = 0$ for some $a, b \ge 0$ in the field with $a + b = 1$, then $d$ and $e$ have opposite signs.
nodes.title: A vanishing convex combination of nonzero values forces opposite signs

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and $p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4 \in K^2$. Suppose the directions $(p_1 - p_3) \times (p_4 - p_3)$ and $(p_2 - p_3) \times (p_4 - p_3)$ are nonzero with opposite signs, and so are $(p_3 - p_1) \times (p_2 - p_1)$ and $(p_4 - p_1) \times (p_2 - p_1)$. Then the closed segments $p_1 p_2$ and $p_3 p_4$ have a common point.
nodes.title: Properly crossing segments meet

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and $p, q, r \in K^2$ with $p \neq q$. If $(r - p) \times (q - p) = 0$, then $r = p + \mu (q - p)$ for some $\mu \in K$.
nodes.title: Points with direction zero lie on the line

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and $p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4 \in K^2$. Suppose the directions $(p_1 - p_3) \times (p_4 - p_3)$ and $(p_2 - p_3) \times (p_4 - p_3)$ are both zero and the closed segments $p_1 p_2$ and $p_3 p_4$ have a common point. Then $p_1$ or $p_2$ lies on the segment $p_3 p_4$, or $p_3$ or $p_4$ lies on the segment $p_1 p_2$.
nodes.title: Collinear case of segment intersection

nodes.title: Lower chain

nodes.summary: Let $\Bbbk$ be a field with a linear order. For a list $P$ of points of $\Bbbk^2$, sort $P$ by merge sort into nondecreasing lexicographic $(x, y)$ order and return the lower chain of the sorted list. Only the orientation tests of the lower chain are counted; sorting costs nothing.
nodes.title: Lower chain of unsorted points

nodes.summary: Let $\Bbbk$ be a linearly ordered field and let $p_1, \dots, p_n$ be points of $\Bbbk^2$ that are strictly increasing in lexicographic $(x, y)$ order. Then the lower chain of $p_1, \dots, p_n$ is a sublist of $p_1, \dots, p_n$: it is $p_{i_1}, \dots, p_{i_m}$ for some indices $i_1 < \dots < i_m$.

nodes.summary: Let $\Bbbk$ be a linearly ordered field and let $p_1, \dots, p_n$ be points of $\Bbbk^2$ that are strictly increasing in lexicographic $(x, y)$ order. If $n \ge 1$, the lower chain of $p_1, \dots, p_n$ starts at $p_1$; if $n = 0$, the lower chain is empty.
nodes.title: The lower chain starts at the first point

nodes.summary: Let $\Bbbk$ be a linearly ordered field and let $p_1, \dots, p_n$ be points of $\Bbbk^2$ that are strictly increasing in lexicographic $(x, y)$ order. If $n \ge 1$, the lower chain of $p_1, \dots, p_n$ ends at $p_n$; if $n = 0$, the lower chain is empty.

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a field with a linear order. The upper chain of a list of points $p_1, \dots, p_n \in K^2$ is the lower chain of the reversed list $p_n, \dots, p_1$, together with its cost: the same scan, counting the same orientation tests. For points sorted by $(x, y)$ it runs from the last point back to the first.

nodes.summary: Let $\Bbbk$ be a field with a linear order. The convex hull of a list $P$ of points of $\Bbbk^2$ is the lower chain of $P$ followed by the upper chain of $P$ with its first and last points removed, together with its cost: the cost of computing the lower chain plus the cost of computing the upper chain.

nodes.summary: Let $p_1, \dots, p_n$ be points of $\Bbbk^2$, for an ordered field $\Bbbk$, strictly increasing in the lexicographic order on $(x, y)$. If $n = 0$ the upper chain is empty; otherwise its last vertex is $p_1$.

Then $\mathrm{DIRECTION}(p, q, r) = (q_x - p_x)\,(y_{pq}(r_x) - r_y)$.

If $[p, q] \cap [p', q']$ is nonempty, then it contains a point $m$ with $m_1 \le w_1$ for every $w \in [p, q] \cap [p', q']$.

Burrows–Wheeler transform and FM-index

nodes.summary: The text `t` with the sentinel `⊥` appended: `t.map (↑) ++ [⊥]`. The sentinel is the unique occurrence of `⊥` and is smaller than every letter.
nodes.title: Text with an appended sentinel

nodes.summary: The starting positions `0, …, |t|` of the rotations of `withSentinel t`, sorted by their rotations in lexicographic order: row `r` of the Burrows–Wheeler matrix is `(withSentinel t).rotate ((sortedRotations t)[r])`.
nodes.title: Sorted rotations of a sentinel-terminated text

nodes.summary: The Burrows–Wheeler transform: the last column of the sorted rotation matrix.
nodes.title: Burrows–Wheeler transform

nodes.summary: `C[c]`: the number of letters of `L` smaller than `c`.
nodes.title: Count of smaller letters in the FM-index

nodes.summary: `rank_c(L, r)`: the number of occurrences of `c` among the first `r` letters of `L`.
nodes.title: Rank of a letter in a prefix of the last column

nodes.summary: The LF-mapping computed from the last column alone: `LF(r) = C[L[r]] + rank_{L[r]}(L, r)`.
nodes.title: LF-mapping from the last column

nodes.summary: `k` steps of the inversion walk from row `r`: the letters `L[r], L[LF r], …`.
nodes.title: Steps of the Burrows–Wheeler inversion walk

nodes.summary: Inversion of the Burrows–Wheeler transform: walk the LF-mapping `|L| - 1` times from row `0` (the rotation that starts with the sentinel) and reverse the letters read.
nodes.title: Inversion of the Burrows–Wheeler transform

nodes.summary: The Burrows–Wheeler transform of `t` has length `|t| + 1` (the sentinel adds one letter).
nodes.title: Length of the Burrows–Wheeler transform

nodes.summary: A sentinel-free word `P` is a prefix of `u ++ ⊥ :: v` (letters lifted to `WithBot α`) exactly when it is a prefix of `u`: the sentinel `⊥` stops every match.
nodes.title: The sentinel stops every prefix match

nodes.summary: The rows of the Burrows–Wheeler matrix are sorted: the rotations listed by `sortedRotations t` are in lexicographically nondecreasing order.
nodes.title: Rows of the Burrows–Wheeler matrix are sorted

nodes.summary: For every row `r`, row `lf (bwt t) r` holds the rotation of row `r` rotated right by one position, i.e. starting one position earlier in the text.
nodes.title: The LF-mapping property

nodes.summary: The Burrows–Wheeler transform is inverted by the LF-mapping walk.
nodes.title: Inversion

nodes.summary: FM-index backward search: the half-open row interval `[sp, ep)` for a pattern, computed from the last column alone, processing the pattern from its last letter to its first. The interval for the suffix and `C[c]` are each computed once per letter, so a pattern of length `m` makes `m` recursive calls.
nodes.title: FM-index backward search

nodes.summary: Backward search always returns a genuine interval of rows, `sp ≤ ep ≤ |L|`, on any list `L` (so the difference in `backwardSearch_count` involves no truncated subtraction).
nodes.title: Backward search returns a genuine row interval

nodes.summary: After processing `P`, the interval `[sp, ep)` is exactly the set of rows whose rotation starts with `P`.
nodes.title: Backward search is correct

nodes.summary: `ep - sp` is the number of positions `i ≤ |t|` at which `P` occurs in `t`.
nodes.title: Counting occurrences

nodes.summary: For `i, j ≤ |t|`, rotation `i` of `withSentinel t` is smaller than rotation `j` exactly when suffix `i` is smaller than suffix `j`.
nodes.title: Rotations of `t$` compare as suffixes

nodes.summary: Sorting the rotations of `withSentinel t` orders the starting positions exactly as sorting its suffixes.
nodes.title: The Burrows–Wheeler matrix is the suffix array of `t$`

nodes.summary: `bwt[r] = t$[SA[r] - 1]`, the letter cyclically before the suffix of row `r` (the sentinel for the row of the whole text, `SA[r] = 0`).
nodes.title: The transform from the suffix array

nodes.summary: Row `r ≤ |t|` lies in the interval `[sp, ep)` computed by backward search on `bwt t` exactly when `P` is a prefix of the suffix of `t` at position `SA[r]`.
nodes.title: Backward-search intervals are suffix-array intervals

nodes.summary: The occurrences of `P` reported by the FM-index: the suffix-array entries `SA[sp], …, SA[ep - 1]` of the backward-search interval. The BWT and the interval are bound once with `let` and reused, so one query builds the BWT and runs the backward search once, not three times.
nodes.title: Occurrences of a pattern reported by the FM-index

nodes.summary: `i` is reported for `P` exactly when `i ≤ |t|` and `P` is a prefix of `t.drop i` (the empty pattern occurs at all `|t| + 1` positions).
nodes.title: The reported positions are exactly the occurrences

nodes.summary: Each occurrence is reported once.
nodes.title: FM-index reports each occurrence once

nodes.summary: The number of reported positions is the length `ep - sp` of the backward-search interval.
nodes.title: Number of FM-index occurrences equals the interval length

nodes.summary: For a row `r ≤ |t|`, `LF r` is a row and `SA[LF r] = SA[r] - 1` cyclically (`SA[LF r] = |t|` when `SA[r] = 0`).
nodes.title: LF in suffix-array terms

nodes.summary: `SA[r] = SA[LF r] + 1` when `SA[r] > 0`.
nodes.title: The LF step moves one position left in the text

nodes.summary: `k` steps of sampled-suffix-array locate from row `r`: return the stored value of the first sampled row reached along the LF-mapping, plus the number of LF steps taken. `sample r` is the stored value `SA[r]` of row `r`, if any.
nodes.title: Step-bounded sampled-suffix-array locate

nodes.summary: Sampled-suffix-array locate (Ferragina and Manzini 2000): the text position of row `r` from the last column `L` and the samples, with at most `|L|` LF steps.

nodes.summary: The number of LF steps `locateAux L sample k r` takes.

nodes.summary: If every stored value is correct (`sample r = some v → v = SA[r]` for rows `r ≤ |t|`) and every row of text position `0` is sampled, then `locate` returns `SA[r]` for every row `r ≤ |t|`.

nodes.summary: For `0 < s`, if every row whose text position is a multiple of `s` is sampled, then from row `r ≤ |t|` locate makes at most `SA[r] mod s` LF steps (for any amount of fuel `k`). At `s = 0` the `s - 1` bound would be `0` while the proof only gives `SA[r] mod 0 = SA[r]` steps.

nodes.summary: An edit step over a type $\alpha$ is one of four operations, for $a, b \in \alpha$: keep $a$ (consume the input value $a$ and reproduce it), delete $a$ (consume $a$), insert $a$ (produce $a$ without consuming input), or substitute $a$ by $b$ (consume $a$ and produce $b$).
nodes.title: Edit step

nodes.summary: An edit script over a type $\alpha$ is a finite list of edit steps over $\alpha$, applied from left to right.
nodes.title: Edit script

nodes.summary: The cost of an edit step is $0$ for a keep step and $1$ for a deletion, an insertion or a substitution.
nodes.title: Unit cost of an edit step

nodes.summary: The cost of an edit script is the sum of the unit costs of its steps; the empty script has cost $0$.
nodes.title: Cost of an edit script

nodes.summary: Over a type $\alpha$ with a boolean equality test, running an edit script on an input list processes the steps from left to right and either fails or returns an output list. A keep step with value $a$ consumes the next input value $b$ and outputs $a$; a deletion of $a$ consumes $b$ and outputs nothing; a substitution of $a$ by $c$ consumes $b$ and outputs $c$. Each of these three fails if the input is exhausted or…

nodes.summary: Over a type with a boolean equality test, an edit script transforms a list $x$ into a list $y$ when running the script on $x$ succeeds and outputs $y$.
nodes.title: An edit script transforming one list into another

nodes.summary: An edit-distance result over a type $\alpha$ consists of a natural number, the reported distance, and an edit script over $\alpha$.

nodes.summary: An edit-distance cost record is a pair of natural numbers: the number of dynamic-programming table cells initialized or transitioned, and the number of operations emitted while reconstructing an edit script.
nodes.title: Edit-distance cost counters

nodes.summary: The total of an edit-distance cost record is the number of table cells initialized or transitioned plus the number of operations emitted during reconstruction.

nodes.summary: For lists $s$ and $t$ over a type whose Boolean equality test agrees with equality, the edit script returned by the edit distance algorithm on $s$ and $t$ transforms $s$ into $t$.
nodes.title: Correctness of the returned edit script

nodes.summary: Let $s$ and $t$ be lists over a type whose Boolean equality test agrees with equality. Every edit script that transforms $s$ into $t$ has unit cost at least the distance returned by the edit distance algorithm on $s$ and $t$.
nodes.title: Minimality of the computed edit distance

nodes.summary: For every list $t$ over a type with a Boolean equality test, the distance returned by the edit distance algorithm from the empty list to $t$ is the length of $t$.
nodes.title: Edit distance from the empty list

nodes.summary: For every list $s$ over a type with a Boolean equality test, the distance returned by the edit distance algorithm from $s$ to the empty list is the length of $s$.
nodes.title: Edit distance to the empty list

nodes.summary: For every list $s$ over a type whose Boolean equality test agrees with equality, the distance returned by the edit distance algorithm from $s$ to $s$ is $0$.
nodes.title: Edit distance of a list to itself

nodes.summary: For lists $s$ and $t$ over a type whose Boolean equality test agrees with equality, the distance returned by the dynamic-programming edit distance algorithm on $s$ and $t$ is $0$ if and only if $s = t$.
nodes.title: Edit distance vanishes only on equal lists

nodes.summary: For lists $s$ and $t$ over a type with a Boolean equality test, write $|s|$ and $|t|$ for their lengths. The number of table-cell transitions charged by the dynamic-programming edit distance algorithm on $s$ and $t$ is exactly $(|s| + 1)(|t| + 1)$, one per pair of a prefix of $s$ and a prefix of $t$.
nodes.title: Table cost of the edit distance algorithm

nodes.summary: For lists $s$ and $t$ over a type with a Boolean equality test, the number of reconstruction steps charged by the edit distance algorithm on $s$ and $t$ equals the length of the edit script it returns.
nodes.title: Reconstruction cost of the edit distance algorithm

nodes.summary: For lists $s$ and $t$ over a type with a Boolean equality test, write $|s|$ and $|t|$ for their lengths. The number of reconstruction steps charged by the edit distance algorithm on $s$ and $t$ is at most $|s| + |t|$.
nodes.title: Reconstruction cost bound for edit distance

nodes.summary: For lists $s$ and $t$ over a type with a Boolean equality test, the total number of events charged by the edit distance algorithm on $s$ and $t$, that is its cell transitions plus its reconstruction steps, equals $(|s| + 1)(|t| + 1) + k$, where $k$ is the length of the edit script it returns.

String matching problem

nodes.summary: For lists $p$ (the pattern) and $t$ (the text) over a type $\alpha$ and a natural number $k$, the pattern $p$ matches the text $t$ at the zero-based offset $k$ when $k$ is at most the length of $t$ and $p$ is a prefix of the list obtained from $t$ by dropping its first $k$ entries.
nodes.title: Pattern match at an offset

nodes.summary: For lists $p$ and $t$ and a natural number $k$, the pattern $p$ matches the text $t$ at the zero-based offset $k$ if and only if $k$ is at most the length of $t$ and $p$ is a prefix of the list obtained from $t$ by dropping its first $k$ entries.
nodes.title: Characterization of a match at an offset

nodes.summary: For lists $p$ and $t$, there is an offset $k$ such that the pattern $p$ matches the text $t$ at $k$ if and only if $p$ is an infix of $t$, that is, $t$ is the concatenation of some list $u$, then $p$, then some list $v$.
nodes.title: A pattern occurs in a text iff it matches at some offset
Knuth–Morris–Pratt algorithm

nodes.summary: For lists $p$ (the pattern) and $t$ (the text) over a type with a boolean equality, KMP search for $p$ in $t$ returns either a zero-based offset or no offset, together with a cost: the number of symbol comparisons it makes. If $p$ is empty, it returns the offset $0$ at cost $0$. Otherwise it first builds the prefix table of $p$, a list of entries each pairing a symbol with a failure value. The transition of a table…
nodes.title: Knuth–Morris–Pratt search

nodes.summary: For every pattern $p$, the KMP prefix table of $p$ has exactly as many entries as $p$ has symbols, one for each symbol of $p$.
nodes.title: Size of the KMP prefix table

nodes.summary: Each entry of the Knuth–Morris–Pratt prefix table is a pair consisting of a symbol and a failure length. For every type with a Boolean equality test and every list $p$ over it, the list of first components of the entries of the prefix table built from $p$, read in order, equals $p$.
nodes.title: The KMP prefix table stores the pattern

nodes.summary: Let $p$ and $t$ be lists over a type with a lawful boolean equality, and write $|t|$ for the length of $t$. For every natural number $i$, KMP search for $p$ in $t$ returns the offset $i$ if and only if $p$ matches $t$ at $i$ and at no $j < i$, where $p$ matches $t$ at $i$ when $i \le |t|$ and $p$ is a prefix of the list obtained from $t$ by dropping its first $i$ elements.
nodes.title: KMP returns the first match

nodes.summary: For lists $p$ and $t$ over a type with a lawful boolean equality, write $|t|$ for the length of $t$. KMP search for $p$ in $t$ returns no offset if and only if there is no natural number $i$ at which $p$ matches $t$, where $p$ matches $t$ at $i$ when $i \le |t|$ and $p$ is a prefix of the list obtained from $t$ by dropping its first $i$ elements.
nodes.title: KMP finds no match exactly when no offset matches

nodes.summary: For lists $p$ (the pattern) and $t$ (the text) over a type with a lawful boolean equality, KMP search for $p$ in $t$ returns no offset if and only if $p$ is not a contiguous sublist of $t$, that is, there are no lists $u$, $v$ with $t = u \, p \, v$ (concatenation).
nodes.title: KMP finds no match exactly when the pattern does not occur

nodes.summary: Let $p$ and $t$ be lists over a type with a lawful boolean equality, with $p$ nonempty. Let the first-infix split of $t$ by $p$ be the pair $(u, v)$ with $t = u \, p \, v$ (concatenation) and $u$ as short as possible, or nothing if $p$ does not occur in $t$. Then the value returned by KMP search for $p$ in $t$ is the length of $u$ if the split exists, and no offset otherwise.
nodes.title: KMP search agrees with the first-infix split

nodes.summary: For any pattern $p$ and text $t$, lists over a type with a boolean equality, KMP search for $p$ in $t$ makes at most $2|p| + 2|t|$ symbol comparisons in total, those made while building the prefix table included, where $|p|$ and $|t|$ are the lengths of $p$ and $t$.
nodes.title: KMP search makes linearly many comparisons

nodes.title: The KMP failure function

Let $c$ be a list, $x$ a symbol, and $cx$ the list $c$ followed by $x$. Suppose the state $s \le n$ is the length of the longest prefix of $p$ that is a suffix of $c$: $p_{\lt s}$ is a suffix of $c$, and every $k \le n$ such that $p_{\lt k}$ is a suffix of $c$ satisfies $k \le s$. Then…
nodes.title: Correctness of the KMP transition

nodes.summary: For every text $t$, KMP search for the empty pattern in $t$ returns offset $0$ at cost $0$, that is, without any symbol comparisons.

Naive string matching

nodes.summary: Let $p = p_0 \cdots p_{m-1}$ be a pattern and $t = t_0 \cdots t_{n-1}$ a text over an alphabet with a Boolean equality test. If $m \le n$, the naive matcher handles the shifts $s = 0, 1, \dots, n - m$ in turn: it compares $p_i$ with $t_{s+i}$ for $i = 0, 1, \dots$ until a comparison fails or all $m$ symbols are compared, and it reports $s$ if no comparison failed. It returns the reported shifts in the order found,…
nodes.title: Naive string matcher

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a pattern of length $m$ and $t$ a text of length $n$. If $m \le n$, the list of shifts reported by the naive matcher on $p$ and $t$ is the increasing list of all $s \in \{0, \dots, n - m\}$ such that $p$ is a prefix of the suffix of $t$ starting at the zero-based position $s$, with symbols compared by the Boolean equality of the alphabet. If $m > n$, the list is empty.
nodes.title: Output of naive matching

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type whose Boolean equality agrees with equality, and write $|t|$ for the length of a list $t$. For every pattern $p$ and text $t$ over $\alpha$ and every natural number $s$, the naive matcher run on $p$ and $t$ reports the shift $s$ if and only if $p$ matches $t$ at $s$, that is, $s \le |t|$ and $p$ is a prefix of the suffix of $t$ obtained by dropping its first $s$ symbols.
nodes.title: Correctness of naive string matching

nodes.summary: For every pattern $p$ and text $t$, the list of shifts reported by the naive matcher on $p$ and $t$ is strictly increasing; in particular, no shift is reported twice.
nodes.title: Naive matching reports shifts in increasing order

nodes.summary: Let $p = p_0 \cdots p_{m-1}$ be a pattern and $t = t_0 \cdots t_{n-1}$ a text. If $m \le n$, the number of symbol comparisons performed by the naive matcher on $p$ and $t$ is
nodes.title: Exact comparison count of naive matching

nodes.summary: For a pattern of length $m$ and a text of length $n$, the naive matcher performs at most $(n - m + 1) \cdot m$ symbol comparisons if $m \le n$, and no comparisons if $m > n$.
nodes.title: Upper bound on the comparisons of naive matching

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type whose Boolean equality is reflexive, let $x \in \alpha$, and let $m \le n$ be natural numbers. On the pattern consisting of $m$ copies of $x$ and the text consisting of $n$ copies of $x$, the naive matcher reports exactly the shifts $0, 1, \dots, n - m$ in increasing order, so all overlapping occurrences are reported.
nodes.title: Naive matching on a repeated symbol reports every shift

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type whose Boolean equality is reflexive, let $x \in \alpha$, and let $m \le n$ be natural numbers. On the pattern consisting of $m$ copies of $x$ and the text consisting of $n$ copies of $x$, the naive matcher performs exactly $(n - m + 1) \cdot m$ symbol comparisons.
nodes.title: Comparison count of naive matching on a repeated symbol

nodes.summary: For every text $t$ of length $n$, the naive matcher run on the empty pattern and $t$ reports exactly the shifts $0, 1, \dots, n$ in increasing order and performs no symbol comparisons.
nodes.title: Naive matching with the empty pattern

nodes.summary: If the pattern $p$ is longer than the text $t$, then the naive matcher run on $p$ and $t$ reports no shifts and performs no symbol comparisons.
nodes.title: Naive matching with a pattern longer than the text

Let $B$ be the number of offsets $s < r$ with…
nodes.title: Exact cost of Rabin–Karp matching

nodes.summary: For every base $d$, every modulus $q > 0$, all lists of natural numbers $P$ (the pattern) and $T$ (the text) and every natural number $s$, Rabin–Karp matching of $P$ in $T$ with base $d$ and modulus $q$ reports the offset $s$ if and only if $P$ matches $T$ at $s$, that is, $s \le |T|$ and $P$ is a prefix of the suffix of $T$ that starts at position $s$ (counting from $0$).
nodes.title: Correctness of Rabin–Karp matching

nodes.summary: For every base $d$, modulus $q > 0$ and lists of natural numbers $P$ and $T$, the offsets returned by Rabin–Karp matching of $P$ in $T$ form a strictly increasing list; in particular no offset is reported twice.
nodes.title: Rabin–Karp reports offsets in increasing order

nodes.summary: For every base $d$, modulus $q > 0$ and list of natural numbers $T$, Rabin–Karp matching of the empty pattern in $T$ returns the list $[0, 1, \dots, |T|]$ of all offsets from $0$ to $|T|$ in increasing order, at counted cost $0$.

Index lists from $0$, write $T_{s..}$ for the suffix of $T$ starting at position $s$, and for a list $S$ with at least $m$ entries put $h(S) = \bigl(\sum_{i\lt m} S_i\, d^{m-1-i}\bigr) \bmod q$. nodes.summary: For every base $d$, modulus $q > 0$ and lists of natural numbers $P$ and $T$ with $|T| < |P|$, Rabin–Karp matching of $P$ in $T$ returns no offsets, at counted cost exactly $1 + 2(|P| - 1) + 6|T|$.

nodes.title: Rabin–Karp offsets on repeated-symbol words

Let $C$ be the counted cost of Rabin–Karp matching with base $d$ and modulus $q$ of the pattern $a^m$ in the text $a^n$ (the lists of $m$ and of $n$ copies of $a$), minus $8m - 1$, with subtraction truncated at $0$. Then $m(n - m + 1) \le C \le 10\,m(n - m + 1)$.

This timed computation returns a table of $(m+1)A$ entries in $\{0, \dots, m\}$, stored row by row: for each state $q \le m$ and symbol $a < A$, the entry at index $qA + a$ is found by trying $k = \min(m, q+1)$ and then each smaller value in turn, and is the first $k$ for which $P_k$ is a suffix of…
nodes.title: Transition table of the string-matching automaton

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a pattern of length $m$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$ and write $P_k$ for its prefix of length $k$. For every state $q \le m$ and symbol $a < A$, the entry at index $qA + a$ of the transition table of $P$ is the greatest $k \le m$ such that $P_k$ is a suffix of the word $P_q a$.
nodes.title: Correctness of the string-matching transition table

nodes.summary: For every pattern of length $m$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$, the cost of computing its transition table is at most $2A(m+1)^3$.
nodes.title: Cost bound for the string-matching transition table

nodes.summary: For a pattern $P$ of length $m$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$, the string-matching automaton of $P$ is the deterministic finite automaton with states $\{0, \dots, m\}$, input symbols $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$, start state $0$, accepting set $\{m\}$, and transition from state $q$ on symbol $a$ given by the entry at index $qA + a$ of the transition table of $P$.
nodes.title: String-matching automaton

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a pattern of length $m$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$ and write $P_k$ for its prefix of length $k$. For every word $w$ over this alphabet, the state that the string-matching automaton of $P$ reaches from its start state after reading $w$ is the greatest $k \le m$ such that $P_k$ is a suffix of $w$.
nodes.title: The string-matching automaton tracks the longest matched prefix

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a pattern of length $m$ and $T$ a text over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$. This timed computation first computes the transition table of $P$, then runs through $T$ starting in state $0$: on reading the $i$-th symbol $a$ of $T$ in state $q$ it moves to the state given by the table entry at index $qA + a$, and if that state is $m$ it reports the shift $i - m$. If $m = 0$, the shift $0$ is also reported…
nodes.title: Finite-automaton string matcher

nodes.summary: For every pattern $P$ and text $T$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$, where $T$ has length $n$, the cost of the finite-automaton matcher on $P$ and $T$ equals the cost of computing the transition table of $P$, plus $2n$, plus the number of shifts the matcher returns.
nodes.title: Exact cost of the finite-automaton matcher

nodes.summary: For every pattern $P$ and text $T$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$, the list of shifts returned by the finite-automaton matcher equals the list returned by the naive string matcher.

Z algorithm

nodes.summary: Given a word $s = s_0 \dots s_{n-1}$ over a type $\alpha$ with a Boolean equality test, Gusfield's Z-box algorithm returns an array $Z$ of $n$ natural numbers with $Z_0 = n$. It visits $i = 1, \dots, n - 1$ in turn, keeping a box $[\ell, r)$, initially empty, that is the rightmost match of a prefix of $s$ found so far. If $\ell \le i < r$ and $Z_{i - \ell} < r - i$, it sets $Z_i = Z_{i - \ell}$. Otherwise it finds…
nodes.title: Z-algorithm

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a Boolean equality test. For every nonempty word of length $n$ over $\alpha$, the Z-array $Z$ computed by the Z-algorithm has $Z_0 = n$.
nodes.title: The first Z-value is the word length

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a lawful Boolean equality test, let $s = s_0 \dots s_{n-1}$ be a word over $\alpha$, and let $Z$ be the Z-array computed by the Z-algorithm on $s$. For every position $i < n$ and every natural number $q$, $q \le Z_i$ holds if and only if $q \le n - i$ and $s_k = s_{i+k}$ for all $k < q$. Hence $Z_i$ is the length of the longest common prefix of $s$ and its suffix $s_i \dots s_{n-1}$.
nodes.title: Z-values are longest common prefix lengths

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a Boolean equality test, not necessarily lawful, and let $s$ be a word of length $n$ over $\alpha$. For every position $i < n$, the entry at $i$ of the Z-array computed by the Z-algorithm on $s$ is at most $n - i$.
nodes.title: Z-values are at most the suffix length

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a Boolean equality test, not necessarily lawful. On every word of length $n$ over $\alpha$, the Z-algorithm has cost at most $3(n - 1)$, read as $0$ when $n = 0$, where the cost counts one unit for each visited position $i \ge 1$ and one unit for each symbol comparison.
nodes.title: Linear upper bound for the Z-algorithm

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a Boolean equality test, not necessarily lawful. On every word of length $n$ over $\alpha$, the Z-algorithm has cost at least $n - 1$, where the cost counts one unit for each visited position $i \ge 1$ and one unit for each symbol comparison.
nodes.title: Linear lower bound for the Z-algorithm

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a lawful Boolean equality test, let $a \in \alpha$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$. The Z-array computed by the Z-algorithm on the word $a^n$ has entry $n - i$ at every position $i < n$.
nodes.title: Z-array of a repeated symbol

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a lawful Boolean equality test, let $a \in \alpha$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$. The Z-algorithm run on the word $a^n$ has cost exactly $2(n - 1)$, read as $0$ when $n = 0$, where the cost counts one unit for each visited position $i \ge 1$ and one unit for each symbol comparison. Thus it makes $n - 1$ visits and $n - 1$ comparisons.
nodes.title: Z-algorithm cost on a repeated symbol

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a lawful Boolean equality test and let $a \ne b$ be elements of $\alpha$. For every $n \ge 1$, the Z-algorithm run on the word $a^n b$ has cost exactly $3n - 1$, where the cost counts one unit for each visited position $i \ge 1$ and one unit for each symbol comparison. In terms of the input length $N = n + 1$, this is $3N - 4$.
nodes.title: Z-algorithm cost on a repeated symbol followed by a distinct one

nodes.title: Boyer–Moore matcher for all occurrences

nodes.summary: For every text $t$ of length $n$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$, the Boyer–Moore matcher with the empty pattern and text $t$ returns the list $0, 1, \dots, n$ of all offsets from $0$ to $n$ in increasing order, at cost $n + 1$.
nodes.title: Boyer–Moore with the empty pattern

nodes.summary: Let $p$ and $t$ be words over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$. If $t$ is strictly shorter than $p$, then the Boyer–Moore matcher with pattern $p$ and text $t$ returns the empty list at cost $0$: no preprocessing or search events are charged.
nodes.title: Boyer–Moore with a pattern longer than the text

nodes.summary: For all words $p$ and $t$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$ and every natural number $k$, the offset $k$ belongs to the list returned by the Boyer–Moore matcher with pattern $p$ and text $t$ if and only if $p$ occurs in $t$ at offset $k$, that is, $k \le |t|$ and $p$ is a prefix of the word obtained from $t$ by deleting its first $k$ letters. In particular, overlapping occurrences are all returned.
nodes.title: Boyer–Moore returns exactly the occurrences

nodes.summary: For all words $p$ and $t$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$, the list of offsets returned by the Boyer–Moore matcher with pattern $p$ and text $t$ is strictly increasing: each entry is smaller than every entry after it.
nodes.title: Boyer–Moore returns offsets in strictly increasing order

nodes.summary: For all words $p$ and $t$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$, the list of offsets returned by the Boyer–Moore matcher with pattern $p$ and text $t$ equals the list returned by the naive matcher with pattern $p$ and text $t$, entry by entry and in the same order. Only the returned lists are compared, not the costs.
nodes.title: Boyer–Moore agrees with the naive matcher

nodes.summary: Let $p$ and $t$ be words over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$ of lengths $m$ and $n$. The cost of the Boyer–Moore matcher with pattern $p$ and text $t$ is at most $n + 1$ if $m = 0$, at most $0$ if $n < m$, and at most $\sigma + n + 11m - 6 + (m + 4)(n - m + 1)$ if $1 \le m \le n$.
nodes.title: Worst-case cost of Boyer–Moore matching

nodes.summary: Let $x$ be a letter of the alphabet $\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$, let $m$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $0 < m \le n$, and write $x^k$ for the word of $k$ copies of $x$. The cost of the Boyer–Moore matcher with pattern $x^m$ and text $x^n$ equals $m + n + P + (m + 4)(n - m + 1)$, where $P$ is the cost of the Boyer–Moore preprocessing of the pattern $x^m$.
nodes.title: Exact Boyer–Moore cost when pattern and text repeat the same letter

nodes.summary: Exact Boyer–Moore cost when the pattern repeats one letter and ends in another, which alone makes up the text. Let $a \ne b$ be letters of the alphabet $\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$ and let $m$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $2 \le m \le n$. Write $a^{m-1}b$ for the word of $m - 1$ copies of $a$ followed by one $b$, and $b^n$ for the word of $n$ copies of $b$. The cost of the Boyer–Moore matcher with pattern…
nodes.title: Exact Boyer–Moore cost when the pattern repeats one letter and ends in another, which alone makes up the text

nodes.summary: Search and decision procedures from artificial intelligence: A* search, game-tree search with alpha-beta pruning, arc consistency for constraint satisfaction, and value and policy iteration for Markov decision processes.
nodes.title: Heuristic search and planning
A* search algorithm

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $w$ assign a natural number $w(u, v)$ to each pair of vertices. A heuristic $h$ assigning a natural number to each vertex is consistent (monotone) if $h(u) \le w(u, v) + h(v)$ for every edge $u \to v$ of $G$.
nodes.title: Consistent heuristic

nodes.summary: For a directed graph $G$ with natural edge weights $w$, a heuristic $h$ with natural values is admissible for a goal vertex $t$ when it never overestimates the weight of a path to $t$: $h(v) \le d$ for every vertex $v$ and every weight $d$ of a path in $G$ from $v$ to $t$.
nodes.title: Admissible heuristic

nodes.summary: Let $w$ assign a natural number $w(u, v)$ to each pair of vertices and let $h$ assign a natural number to each vertex. The reduced weight of the pair $(u, v)$ is the natural number $w(u, v) + h(v) - h(u)$, computed with truncated subtraction, so it is $0$ when $h(u) > w(u, v) + h(v)$.
nodes.title: Reduced weight

nodes.summary: An A* result on $n$ vertices consists of a Dijkstra result on $n$ vertices (the underlying search, with its source, final keys and predecessor pointers) and a vector that assigns to each vertex $v$ a value $g(v) \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$. In the output of A* from a source $s$ with a consistent heuristic $h$, the underlying search runs on the reduced weights, its keys are $f(v) - h(s)$ where $f = g + h$, and…
nodes.title: Output of A-star search

nodes.summary: Given an A* result $r$ on $n$ vertices and a vertex $v$, follow the predecessor pointers of the underlying Dijkstra search backward from $v$, at most $n$ times, until the source is reached, and return the visited vertices in order from the source to $v$. There is no result if a vertex without a predecessor is met before the source, or if the source is not reached within $n$ steps.
nodes.title: Path recovered from an A-star result

nodes.summary: A* search. Given a directed graph $G$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with natural edge weights $w$, a heuristic $h$ with natural values and a source vertex $s$, A* runs Dijkstra's algorithm from $s$ on the reduced weights $w(u, v) + h(v) - h(u)$ at Dijkstra's cost, and returns Dijkstra's result (its distances $g'$ and predecessor pointers) together with the path weights $g(v) = g'(v) + h(s) - h(v)$, where…
nodes.title: A* search

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with natural edge weights $w$, let $h$ be a consistent heuristic with natural values, and let $w_h(x, y) = w(x, y) + h(y) - h(x)$ be the reduced weight, with the subtraction truncated at $0$. For all vertices $u$ and $v$ and every nonempty list of vertices $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k$ with $v_0 = u$, $v_k = v$ and an edge of $G$ from each $v_i$ to $v_{i+1}$,…
nodes.title: Reduced weights telescope along paths

nodes.summary: A consistent heuristic that vanishes at the goal is admissible.
nodes.title: A consistent heuristic that vanishes at the goal is admissible

nodes.summary: The final keys of A*. Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with natural edge weights $w$, let $h$ be a consistent heuristic with natural values and let $s$ be a source vertex. If the path weight $g(v)$ that A* from $s$ returns for a vertex $v$ is finite, then the distance $g'(v)$ that Dijkstra's algorithm from $s$ computes for $v$ on the reduced weights $w(x, y) + h(y) - h(x)$…
nodes.title: The final keys of A*

nodes.summary: A*'s finite path weights are realized by paths. Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with natural edge weights $w$, let $h$ be a consistent heuristic with natural values and let $s$ be a source vertex. If the path weight $g(v)$ that A* from $s$ returns for a vertex $v$ is finite, then some path in $G$ from $s$ to $v$ has weight exactly $g(v)$.
nodes.title: A*'s finite path weights are realized by paths

nodes.summary: A* with a consistent heuristic is optimal. Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with natural edge weights $w$, let $h$ be a consistent heuristic with natural values and let $s$ be a source vertex. If the path weight $g(v)$ that A* from $s$ returns for a vertex $v$ is finite, then $g(v) \le d$ for every weight $d$ of a path in $G$ from $s$ to $v$.
nodes.title: A* with a consistent heuristic is optimal

nodes.summary: A* leaves exactly the unreachable vertices at infinity. Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with natural edge weights $w$, let $h$ be any heuristic with natural values and let $s$ be a source vertex. The path weight $g(v)$ that A* from $s$ returns for a vertex $v$ is infinite if and only if $v$ is not reachable from $s$ in $G$.
nodes.title: A* leaves exactly the unreachable vertices at infinity

nodes.summary: A*'s predecessor paths are simple and realize its path weights. Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with natural edge weights $w$, let $h$ be a consistent heuristic with natural values and let $s$ be a source vertex. If following the predecessor pointers that A* from $s$ returns, back from a vertex $v$, yields the vertex list $p$ (listed from $s$ to $v$), then the path weight $g(v)$…
nodes.title: A*'s predecessor paths are simple and realize its path weights

nodes.summary: A*'s predecessor edges are tight. Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with natural edge weights $w$, let $h$ be a consistent heuristic with natural values and let $s$ be a source vertex. If A* from $s$ records $u$ as the predecessor of a vertex $v$, then $G$ has an edge from $u$ to $v$, the path weights $g(u)$ and $g(v)$ that A* returns are both finite, and $g(v) = g(u) + w(u, v)$.
nodes.title: A*'s predecessor edges are tight

nodes.summary: Cost of A*. Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with natural edge weights $w$, let $h$ be any heuristic with natural values and let $s$ be a source vertex. In Dijkstra's dense cost model, which counts the vertex entries inspected by minimum selection and the adjacency entries inspected by relaxation, A* from $s$ charges exactly $n^2 + m$ events in total, where $m$ is the number of…
nodes.title: Cost of A*
AC-3 algorithm

nodes.summary: A binary constraint satisfaction problem with variables in $X$ and values in $D$ consists of a finite list of directed arcs $(x, y)$ with $x, y \in X$, and, for all variables $x, y$ and values $a, b \in D$, a Boolean saying whether the arc $(x, y)$ allows $x = a$ together with $y = b$.
nodes.title: Binary constraint satisfaction problem

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction problem with variables $X$ and values $D$, and give each variable $x$ a finite domain $\mathrm{dom}(x) \subseteq D$. An assignment $\sigma : X \to D$ is a solution of $P$ within $\mathrm{dom}$ when $\sigma(x) \in \mathrm{dom}(x)$ for every variable $x$ and, for every arc $(x, y)$ of $P$, the arc $(x, y)$ allows the pair $(\sigma(x), \sigma(y))$.
nodes.title: Solution of a binary CSP within given domains

nodes.summary: Given a binary CSP $P$ and domains $\mathrm{dom}$, an arc $(x, y)$ is consistent when for every value $a \in \mathrm{dom}(x)$ there is a value $b \in \mathrm{dom}(y)$ such that the arc $(x, y)$ allows $x = a$ together with $y = b$.
nodes.title: Arc consistency

nodes.summary: A binary constraint satisfaction problem is symmetric when, for all variables $x, y$ and values $a, b$, the constraint on the ordered pair $(x, y)$ allows $x = a$ together with $y = b$ exactly when the constraint on $(y, x)$ allows $y = b$ together with $x = a$.
nodes.title: Symmetric binary CSP

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction problem with values $D$, $\mathrm{dom}$ finite domains for its variables, and $x$, $y$ variables. The revision of the arc $(x, y)$ is the set of values $a \in \mathrm{dom}(x)$ that have a support in the domain of $y$: some $b \in \mathrm{dom}(y)$ such that the arc $(x, y)$ allows the pair $(a, b)$.
nodes.title: Revision of an arc

nodes.summary: For a binary constraint satisfaction problem $P$ and a variable $x$, the in-degree of $x$ is the number of arcs $(z, x)$ of $P$ ending at $x$, counted with multiplicity in the list of arcs of $P$.
nodes.title: In-degree of a variable

nodes.summary: For a binary constraint satisfaction problem $P$ and variables $x$ and $y$, the arcs requeued after revising $(x, y)$ are the arcs $(z, x)$ of $P$ with $z \neq y$, in their order in the list of arcs of $P$.
nodes.title: Arcs requeued after a revision

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction problem with finitely many variables, $\mathrm{dom}$ finite domains for its variables and $q$ a queue of arcs. The potential of $\mathrm{dom}$ and $q$ is
nodes.title: Termination potential of AC-3

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction problem with finitely many variables, $\mathrm{dom}$ finite domains for its variables, $x$ and $y$ variables and $q$ a queue of arcs. Suppose the revision $R$ of the arc $(x, y)$ with respect to $\mathrm{dom}$ differs from $\mathrm{dom}(x)$, and let $\mathrm{dom}'$ agree with $\mathrm{dom}$ except that $\mathrm{dom}'(x) = R$. Then the potential of $\mathrm{dom}'$ with the…
nodes.title: A shrinking revision lowers the potential

nodes.summary: Given a binary CSP $P$ with finitely many variables, domains $\mathrm{dom}$ and a queue $q$ of pairs of variables, AC-3 returns $\mathrm{dom}$ when $q$ is empty. Otherwise it removes the first pair $(x, y)$ of $q$ and revises it: the revised domain of $x$ consists of the values $a \in \mathrm{dom}(x)$ for which some $b \in \mathrm{dom}(y)$ has the arc $(x, y)$ allowing $x = a$ together with $y = b$. If the revised…
nodes.title: The AC-3 algorithm

nodes.summary: For a binary CSP $P$ with finitely many variables and domains $\mathrm{dom}$, AC-3 on the whole problem is AC-3 run from $\mathrm{dom}$ with the queue initialized to the arc list of $P$; it returns the final domains together with the number of revisions performed.
nodes.title: AC-3 on the whole problem

nodes.summary: For a binary CSP $P$ with finitely many variables, domains $\mathrm{dom}$, a queue $q$ of pairs of variables and a variable $v$, the domain of $v$ returned by AC-3 run from $\mathrm{dom}$ with queue $q$ is a subset of $\mathrm{dom}(v)$.
nodes.title: AC-3 only shrinks domains

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction problem, $\mathrm{dom}$ finite domains for its variables and $\sigma$ a solution of $P$ within $\mathrm{dom}$. For every arc $(x, y)$ of $P$, the value $\sigma(x)$ lies in the revision of the arc $(x, y)$ with respect to $\mathrm{dom}$.
nodes.title: Revision keeps solution values

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction problem with finitely many variables, $\mathrm{dom}$ finite domains for its variables, and $q$ a queue of arcs each of which is an arc of $P$. Then every solution $\sigma$ of $P$ within $\mathrm{dom}$ is also a solution of $P$ within the domains returned by AC-3 started from $\mathrm{dom}$ with queue $q$.
nodes.title: No solution is lost

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction problem with finitely many variables and $\mathrm{dom}$ finite domains for its variables. If $\sigma$ is a solution of $P$ within $\mathrm{dom}$, then for every variable $v$ the value $\sigma(v)$ lies in the domain of $v$ returned by AC-3 run from $\mathrm{dom}$ with all arcs of $P$ queued.
nodes.title: Solutions survive AC-3

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction problem with finitely many variables and $\mathrm{dom}$ finite domains for its variables. If AC-3, run from $\mathrm{dom}$ with all arcs of $P$ queued, returns the empty domain for some variable $v$, then no assignment $\sigma$ is a solution of $P$ within $\mathrm{dom}$.
nodes.title: An emptied domain rules out solutions

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a binary CSP whose constraints are symmetric, that is the arc $(x, y)$ allows $(a, b)$ exactly when the arc $(y, x)$ allows $(b, a)$. Let $\mathrm{dom}$ be domains, let $x \ne y$ be variables, let $R$ be the set of values $a \in \mathrm{dom}(x)$ for which some $b \in \mathrm{dom}(y)$ has the arc $(x, y)$ allowing $x = a$ together with $y = b$, and let $\mathrm{dom}'$ be $\mathrm{dom}$ with the domain of…
nodes.title: Arc consistency after one AC-3 revision

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a binary CSP with finitely many variables whose constraints are symmetric, that is the arc $(x, y)$ allows $(a, b)$ exactly when the arc $(y, x)$ allows $(b, a)$, and whose arcs all join two distinct variables. Let $\mathrm{dom}$ be domains and $q$ a queue whose entries are arcs of $P$, such that every arc of $P$ not in $q$ is consistent with respect to $\mathrm{dom}$. Then every arc of $P$ is consistent…
nodes.title: Arc consistency invariant of AC-3

nodes.summary: AC-3 makes every arc consistent, for constraints given symmetrically on both orientations of an arc and arcs between distinct variables.
nodes.title: AC-3 makes every arc consistent

nodes.summary: For a binary CSP $P$ with finitely many variables, domains $\mathrm{dom}$ and a queue $q$ of pairs of variables, the number of revisions AC-3 performs from $\mathrm{dom}$ with queue $q$ is at most the potential $\ell + \sum_x |\mathrm{dom}(x)| \cdot \mathrm{indeg}(x)$, where $\ell$ is the length of $q$ and $\mathrm{indeg}(x)$ is the number of entries of the arc list of $P$ ending at $x$.
nodes.title: AC-3 revisions are bounded by the potential

nodes.summary: For a binary CSP $P$ with finitely many variables and initial domains $\mathrm{dom}$, AC-3 run from $\mathrm{dom}$ with every arc of $P$ queued performs at most $m + \sum_x |\mathrm{dom}(x)| \cdot \mathrm{indeg}(x)$ revisions, where $m$ is the length of the arc list of $P$ and $\mathrm{indeg}(x)$ is the number of entries of that list ending at $x$.
nodes.title: Bound on the number of AC-3 revisions
Alpha–beta pruning

nodes.summary: A game tree with values in a type $\alpha$ is either a leaf, which carries a value in $\alpha$ (the value of a terminal position), or an inner node, which carries a finite list of game trees (the positions reachable in one move; the list may be empty). Game trees are built inductively, so every game tree is finite.
nodes.title: Game tree

nodes.summary: The number of leaves of a game tree is defined recursively: a leaf counts $1$, and an inner node counts the total number of leaves of its children (so an inner node without children counts $0$).
nodes.title: Number of leaves

nodes.summary: The number of leaves of a finite list of game trees is the sum of the numbers of leaves of its members ($0$ for the empty list).
nodes.title: Number of leaves of a list of game trees

nodes.summary: For a player $p$ to move and values $a$ and $b$ in a linear order, alpha-beta pruning with window $[a, b]$ returns the value of a leaf at a cost of one unit (one leaf evaluation), and on an inner node runs the alpha-beta scan of its children for $p$ with window $[a, b]$.
nodes.title: Alpha-beta pruning

nodes.summary: Given the player $p$ to move, values $a$ and $b$ in a linear order and a list of game trees (the children of a position), the scan runs alpha-beta pruning for the other player on the children in order, each time with the current bounds $a$ and $b$. The maximizer replaces $a$ by $\max(a, v)$, where $v$ is the child's returned value, and stops as soon as $b \le a$, returning the new $a$; if it never stops early it…
nodes.title: Alpha-beta scan of the children

nodes.summary: Let values lie in a linear order. For all values $a$ and $b$ and every finite list of game trees, the value returned by the alpha-beta scan of the list with the maximizer to move and window $[a, b]$ is at least $a$.
nodes.title: Lower bound for the maximizer's scan

nodes.summary: For all values $a, b$ in a linear order and every list $ts$ of game trees, the value returned by the alpha-beta scan of $ts$ for the minimizer with lower bound $a$ and upper bound $b$ is at most $b$.
nodes.title: The minimizer's alpha-beta scan stays at or below its upper bound

nodes.summary: For either player $p$ to move and all values $a, b$ in a linear order, alpha-beta pruning run on a game tree $t$ for $p$ with window $[a, b]$ evaluates at most as many leaves as $t$ has, each leaf evaluation costing one unit.
nodes.title: Alpha-beta never evaluates more leaves than the tree has

nodes.summary: For either player $p$, all values $a, b$ in a linear order and every list $ts$ of game trees, the alpha-beta scan of $ts$ for $p$ with lower bound $a$ and upper bound $b$ evaluates at most as many leaves as the trees in $ts$ have in total, each leaf evaluation costing one unit.
nodes.title: Cost of the alpha-beta scan

nodes.summary: Let values lie in a bounded linear order. The minimax value of a game tree with player $p$ to move (the maximizer or the minimizer) is defined recursively: a leaf is worth the value it carries; an inner node is worth, for the maximizer, the maximum of the minimax values of its children with the minimizer to move, and for the minimizer, the minimum of the minimax values of its children with the maximizer to move. An…
nodes.title: Minimax value

nodes.summary: Let values lie in a bounded linear order. For a player $p$ and a finite list of game trees, the value for $p$ is the best of their minimax values with the other player to move: for the maximizer, the maximum of these values, or $\bot$ if the list is empty; for the minimizer, the minimum of these values, or $\top$ if the list is empty.
nodes.title: Minimax value of a list of positions

nodes.summary: Alpha-beta is correct (Knuth and Moore 1975, Theorem 1): for `a ≤ b`, the result of alpha-beta agrees with the minimax value after clamping both to the window `[a, b]`.
nodes.title: Alpha-beta is correct

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be the player to move, $ts$ a list of game trees with values in a bounded linear order, and $a \le b$. Let $r$ be the value returned by the alpha-beta scan of $ts$ for $p$ with window $[a, b]$, and let $m$ be the best value for $p$ among $ts$: the maximum of the minimax values of the trees in $ts$ for the minimizer ($\bot$ if $ts$ is empty) when $p$ is the maximizer, and the minimum of their minimax values…
nodes.title: Correctness of the alpha-beta scan

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a game tree with values in a bounded linear order, $p$ the player to move and $a < b$ values. If the minimax value of $t$ for $p$ is at most $a$, then alpha-beta pruning run on $t$ for $p$ with the window $[a, b]$ returns a value at most $a$.
nodes.title: Alpha-beta fails low when the minimax value is at most the lower bound

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a game tree with values in a bounded linear order, $p$ the player to move and $a, b$ values. If the minimax value $v$ of $t$ for $p$ satisfies $a < v < b$, then alpha-beta pruning run on $t$ for $p$ with the window $[a, b]$ returns exactly $v$.
nodes.title: Alpha-beta is exact inside the window

nodes.summary: Let values lie in a bounded linear order, let $t$ be a game tree, let $p$ be a player, and let $a < b$. If the minimax value of $t$ with $p$ to move is at least $b$, then the value returned by alpha-beta pruning on $t$ with $p$ to move and window $[a, b]$ is at least $b$.
nodes.title: Alpha-beta at or above the top of the window

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a game tree whose values lie in a bounded linear order with least element $\bot$ and greatest element $\top$. For either player $p$ to move, alpha-beta pruning run on $t$ for $p$ with the window $[\bot, \top]$ returns exactly the minimax value of $t$ for $p$.
nodes.title: Alpha-beta with the full window returns the minimax value
Value iteration

nodes.summary: A Markov decision process with states in $S$, actions in $A$ and values in $K$ consists of a reward $r(s, a) \in K$ for taking action $a$ in state $s$ and, for all states $s, s'$ and actions $a$, a value $p(s, a, s') \in K$, the probability of moving from $s$ to $s'$ under action $a$.
nodes.title: Markov decision process

nodes.summary: A Markov decision process with finitely many states and transition probabilities $P(s,a,s')$ in a field $K$ with a linear order is stochastic when $0 \le P(s,a,s')$ for all states $s, s'$ and actions $a$, and $\sum_{s'} P(s,a,s') = 1$ for every state $s$ and action $a$.
nodes.title: Stochastic Markov decision process

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with a finite set of states $S$ and with rewards $r(s,a)$ and transition probabilities $P(s,a,s')$ in a field $K$, and let $\gamma \in K$. The Q-value of action $a$ in state $s$ against a value estimate $V : S \to K$ is $r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s,a,s') \, V(s')$.

Birthday bound

nodes.summary: For a nonempty finite set $\alpha$ and a natural number $q$, the collision experiment is the probability distribution on $\{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$ obtained by drawing a function $s \colon \{0, \dots, q - 1\} \to \alpha$ uniformly at random (equivalently, $q$ independent uniform samples $s(0), \dots, s(q - 1)$ from $\alpha$) and outputting true exactly when $s$ is not injective, that is, when $s(i) = s(j)$…
nodes.title: The collision experiment

nodes.summary: For a nonempty finite set $\alpha$ and a natural number $q$, the collision probability is the probability, as a real number, that the collision experiment with $q$ samples from $\alpha$ outputs true, that is, that $q$ independent uniform samples from $\alpha$ contain two equal samples at distinct positions.
nodes.title: Collision probability

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite set with $N$ elements and $q$ a natural number. The probability that $q$ independent uniform samples from $\alpha$ contain a collision equals $1 - N (N - 1) \cdots (N - q + 1) / N^q$, where the product $N (N - 1) \cdots (N - q + 1)$ has $q$ factors (it is $1$ for $q = 0$ and $0$ for $q > N$).
nodes.title: The exact collision probability

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite set with $N$ elements and $q$ a natural number. The probability that $q$ independent uniform samples from $\alpha$ contain a collision is at most $q (q - 1) / (2 N)$.
nodes.title: Birthday upper bound

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite set with $N$ elements and $q$ a natural number. The probability that $q$ independent uniform samples from $\alpha$ contain a collision is at least $1 - \exp(-q (q - 1) / (2 N))$.
nodes.title: Birthday lower bound, exponential form

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite set with $N$ elements, $q$ a natural number, and $x = q (q - 1) / (2 N)$. The probability that $q$ independent uniform samples from $\alpha$ contain a collision is at least $x / (1 + x)$.
nodes.title: Birthday lower bound, rational form

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite set with $N$ elements and $q$ a natural number with $q (q - 1) \le 2 N$. The probability that $q$ independent uniform samples from $\alpha$ contain a collision is at least $q (q - 1) / (4 N)$.
nodes.title: Birthday lower bound

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite set with $N$ elements and $q$ a natural number with $q \le \sqrt{2 N}$. The probability that $q$ independent uniform samples from $\alpha$ contain a collision is at least $q (q - 1) / (4 N)$.
nodes.title: Birthday lower bound as stated in Katz and Lindell

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite set with $N$ elements and $q$ a natural number with $q \le \sqrt{N}$. The probability that $q$ independent uniform samples from $\alpha$ contain a collision is at least $q (q - 1) / (4 N)$.
nodes.title: Birthday lower bound for at most square-root many samples

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite set with $N$ elements and $q$ a natural number with $2 N \le q (q - 1)$. The probability that $q$ independent uniform samples from $\alpha$ contain a collision is at least $1/2$.

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a group, $q$ a natural number, $g \in G$ and $a \in \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$. Then $g^a$ is defined as $g^n$, where $n$ is the natural-number value of $a$: its representative in $\{0, \dots, q-1\}$ when $q > 0$, and $|a|$ when $q = 0$ (in which case $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z} = \mathbb{Z}$).
nodes.title: Group exponentiation with modular exponents

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a group, $q$ a natural number and $g \in G$. For $x \in G$ and $c \in \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ write $x^c$ for $x^n$, where $n$ is the natural-number value of $c$: its representative in $\{0, \dots, q-1\}$ when $q > 0$, and $|c|$ when $q = 0$ (in which case $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z} = \mathbb{Z}$). Then $(g^b)^a = (g^a)^b$ for all $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group of order $q$, with $q \neq 0$, and let $g \in G$ generate $G$, that is, every element of $G$ is an integer power of $g$. Then $a \mapsto g^a$ is a bijection from $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ to $G$, where $g^a = g^n$ for the representative $n \in \{0, \dots, q-1\}$ of $a$. Its inverse is the discrete logarithm to base $g$.

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a commutative group with a fixed element $g$ and let $q$ be a natural number. nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a commutative group and $q$ a natural number. For $a \in \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ and $c \in G$ write $c^a$ for $c^{\operatorname{val}(a)}$, where $\operatorname{val}(a) \in \mathbb{N}$ is the representative of $a$ in $\{0, \dots, q-1\}$ if $q \ge 1$ and $|a|$ if $q = 0$. Decrypting a ciphertext $(c_1, c_2) \in G \times G$ with the secret key $x \in \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ gives $c_2 \cdot (c_1^x)^{-1}$.

nodes.summary: For a function $f : X \to Y$ and a secret key $sk : \{0, \dots, \ell - 1\} \times \{0, 1\} \to X$, the public key is the map $pk : \{0, \dots, \ell - 1\} \times \{0, 1\} \to Y$ with $pk(i, b) = f(sk(i, b))$.
nodes.title: Lamport public key

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group. The group one-time pad on $G$ is the private-key encryption scheme with messages, keys and ciphertexts in $G$ whose key $k$ is drawn uniformly from $G$, which encrypts a message $m$ as $k m$, and which decrypts a ciphertext $c$ as $k^{-1} c$.
nodes.title: The group one-time pad

nodes.title: Group one-time pad ciphertexts are uniform

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group.
