nodes.summary: Suppose there are at least two possible orders and the set of generals is finite with $n$ elements, where $3 \le n \le 3m$. Then for every oral-message protocol, every commander $c$ and every number of rounds $T$, the protocol does not solve the Byzantine generals problem with commander $c$ and at most $m$ traitors in $T$ rounds: there are an order, a set of at most $m$ traitors and a behaviour of the traitors for…
nodes.title: No protocol for $n$ generals tolerates $m$ traitors when $3 \le n \le 3m$

nodes.summary: The majority of a finite multiset $s$ of values is the value $x$ such that more than half of the elements of $s$ are equal to $x$ (counted with multiplicity), if there is one (there is at most one), and a fixed default value (retreat) otherwise.
nodes.title: Majority of a multiset

nodes.summary: If more than half of the elements of a multiset $s$ of values are equal to $x$ (counted with multiplicity), then the majority of $s$ is $x$.
nodes.title: A value filling more than half of a multiset is its majority

nodes.summary: If, for every value $x$, at most half of the elements of a multiset $s$ of values are equal to $x$ (counted with multiplicity), then the majority of $s$ is the default value (retreat).
nodes.title: Majority falls back to the default value

nodes.summary: Fix a predicate saying which generals are loyal and an adversary $\mathrm{adv}$ that assigns a value to each pair of a finite sequence of generals and a recipient. The value that lieutenant $p$ receives from commander $c$, who holds the value $v$ and whose superiors form the sequence $\sigma$, is $v$ if $c$ is loyal, and is $\mathrm{adv}(\sigma c, p)$ if $c$ is a traitor, where $\sigma c$ is $\sigma$ followed by $c$.
nodes.title: Value received from a commander

nodes.summary: Fix which generals are loyal and a strategy for the traitors, which assigns a value to each list of generals and each recipient. Let $c$ be a commander holding the value $v$, let $\sigma$ be the list of the commanders above $c$, and let $S$ be a finite set of lieutenants. For a general $q$, let $r_q$ be the value $q$ receives from $c$: $v$ if $c$ is loyal, and otherwise the value the strategy assigns to the list…
nodes.title: The oral messages algorithm

nodes.summary: If the commander $c$ is loyal, then for every value $v$, every list of superiors of $c$ and every general $p$, the value $p$ receives from $c$ is $v$.
nodes.title: A loyal commander sends its value

nodes.summary: Fix which generals are loyal and an adversary $\mathrm{adv}$ that assigns a value to each pair of a list of generals and a recipient. If the commander $c$ is a traitor, then for every value $v$, every list $\sigma$ of superiors of $c$ and every general $p$, the value $p$ receives from $c$ is $\mathrm{adv}(\sigma c, p)$, where $\sigma c$ is $\sigma$ followed by $c$.
nodes.title: A traitorous commander sends the adversary's value

nodes.summary: Let $m$ and $k$ be natural numbers, and let a loyal commander $c$ run $\mathrm{OM}(m)$ with a value $v$ and any list of superiors, sending to a finite set $S$ of lieutenants. If $2k + m < |S| + 1$ (more than $2k + m$ generals when $c \notin S$) and at most $k$ of the generals in $S \cup \{c\}$ are traitors, then, whatever the traitors send, every loyal lieutenant $p \in S$ decides $v$.
nodes.title: A loyal commander is obeyed under oral messages

nodes.summary: Let a loyal commander $c$ run $\mathrm{OM}(m)$ with a value $v$ and any list of superiors, sending to a finite set $S$ of lieutenants. If $3m < |S| + 1$ (more than $3m$ generals when $c \notin S$) and at most $m$ of the generals in $S \cup \{c\}$ are traitors, then, whatever the traitors send, every loyal lieutenant $p \in S$ decides $v$.
nodes.title: Validity under oral messages (IC2)

nodes.summary: Let a commander $c$ run $\mathrm{OM}(m)$ with a value $v$ and any list of superiors, sending to a finite set $S$ of lieutenants with $c \notin S$. If there are more than $3m$ generals, that is $3m < |S| + 1$, and at most $m$ of the generals in $S \cup \{c\}$ are traitors, then, whatever the traitors send, any two loyal lieutenants $p, p' \in S$ decide the same value.
nodes.title: Agreement under oral messages (IC1)

nodes.summary: Let a commander $c$ run $\mathrm{OM}(m)$ with a value $v$ and any list of superiors, sending to a finite set $S$ of lieutenants with $c \notin S$. If there are more than $3m$ generals, that is $3m < |S| + 1$, and at most $m$ of the generals in $S \cup \{c\}$ are traitors, then, whatever the traitors send, any two loyal lieutenants in $S$ decide the same value (IC1), and if $c$ is loyal, every loyal lieutenant in…
nodes.title: Oral messages achieve interactive consistency

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite set of more than $3m$ generals, at most $m$ of whom are traitors, and let the commander $c \in G$ run $\mathrm{OM}(m)$ with the value $v$, with no superiors and with all the other generals as lieutenants. Then, whatever the traitors send, any two loyal lieutenants decide the same value, and if $c$ is loyal, every loyal lieutenant decides $v$.
nodes.title: The oral messages algorithm solves the Byzantine generals problem
Chang–Roberts leader election

nodes.summary: For a ring of $n + 1$ processes $0, \dots, n$, a global state assigns to each process $k$ the FIFO channel of messages waiting at $k$, oldest first, where each message is the index of the process whose identifier it carries, and records for each process whether it has declared itself leader.
nodes.title: Chang–Roberts global states

nodes.summary: On the ring of $n + 1$ processes $0, \dots, n$, the successor of process $k$ is $k + 1$ when $k < n$, and $0$ when $k = n$.
nodes.title: Successor on the Chang–Roberts ring

nodes.summary: On a ring of $n + 1$ processes numbered $0, \dots, n$, the predecessor of $k$ is $k - 1$ if $k \ne 0$, and $n$ if $k = 0$.
nodes.title: Predecessor on the ring

nodes.summary: On a ring of $n + 1$ processes with identifiers $\mathrm{id}$, process $k$ receives the oldest message in its channel in state $s$. If the channel of $k$ is empty there is no step. Otherwise let $j$ be the origin of that message, which is removed from the channel: if $\mathrm{id}(k) < \mathrm{id}(j)$, process $k$ forwards it by appending $j$ to the end of the channel of its successor on the ring; otherwise, if…
nodes.title: Delivering a message in the Chang–Roberts ring

nodes.summary: For identifiers $\mathrm{id}$, the algorithm is the labelled transition system whose states are the global states and whose labels are processes: there is a transition from $s$ to $t$ labelled $k$ exactly when delivering the oldest message in the channel of process $k$ in state $s$ gives $t$.
nodes.title: The Chang–Roberts transition system

nodes.summary: In the initial state the channel into each process $k$ holds exactly one message, whose origin is the predecessor of $k$ on the ring (so every process has sent its identifier to its successor), and no process is leader.
nodes.title: Initial state of the Chang–Roberts ring

nodes.summary: Given a natural-number identifier $\mathrm{id}(k)$ for each process $k$ of the ring of $n + 1$ processes, a global state $s$ is reachable when the Chang–Roberts transition system with these identifiers leads from the initial state to $s$ by a multistep transition along some finite list of labels, that is, of receiving processes.
nodes.title: Reachable states of Chang–Roberts

nodes.summary: For processes $j$ and $m$ on a ring of $n + 1$ processes numbered $0, \dots, n$, the gap from $j$ to $m$ is the number of successor steps from $j$ to $m$: it is $m - j$ if $j \le m$, and $m + (n + 1) - j$ otherwise. It lies in $[0, n]$.
nodes.title: Forward distance on the ring

nodes.summary: For processes $j, k$ of the ring of $n + 1$ processes, the distance travelled by a message from $j$ waiting at $k$ is $n + 1$, the whole ring, when $k = j$, and otherwise the ring distance from $j$ to $k$, the number of links from $j$ forward to $k$.
nodes.title: Distance travelled by a message

nodes.summary: Given identifiers $\mathrm{id}$ on a ring of $n + 1$ processes, a state satisfies the invariant when two conditions hold. First, for every message from origin $j$ waiting in the channel of process $k$, every process $m \ne j$ that the message has already passed has a smaller identifier, $\mathrm{id}(m) < \mathrm{id}(j)$; here $m$ has been passed when its forward distance from $j$ is less than the distance the…
nodes.title: The Chang–Roberts invariant

nodes.summary: For processes $j$ and $k$ of the ring with $k \ne j$, the distance travelled by a message from $j$ waiting at the successor of $k$ is the number of links from $j$ forward to $k$, plus one.
nodes.title: Forwarding adds one link

nodes.summary: For every process $k$ of the ring, the distance travelled by a message from the predecessor of $k$ waiting at $k$ is $1$.
nodes.title: The initial messages have travelled one link

nodes.summary: For every assignment of identifiers, if the invariant holds in a state $s$ and the state $t$ is reached from $s$ by delivering messages along some schedule of receiving processes (a multistep transition of the algorithm's labelled transition system), then the invariant holds in $t$.
nodes.title: The Chang–Roberts invariant is preserved along runs

nodes.summary: For every assignment of identifiers, every state reachable from the initial state satisfies the invariant.
nodes.title: The Chang–Roberts invariant holds in every reachable state

nodes.summary: Let $\mathrm{id}$ assign a natural-number identifier, not necessarily distinct, to each process $0, \dots, n$ of the Chang–Roberts ring. In every state reachable with these identifiers, if process $i$ has declared itself leader, then $\mathrm{id}(m) < \mathrm{id}(i)$ for every process $m \ne i$.
nodes.title: Only the maximum is elected

nodes.summary: In every state of the Chang–Roberts algorithm reachable from the initial state, any two processes that have declared themselves leader are equal.
nodes.title: There is at most one leader

nodes.summary: Given a natural-number identifier $\mathrm{id}(k)$ for each process $k$ of the ring, a global state $s$ and a list $k_1, \dots, k_r$ of processes, the run applies the Chang–Roberts delivery step at $k_1$, then at $k_2$, and so on. It returns the final state, or no state as soon as some $k_i$ has an empty channel at its turn; on the empty list it returns $s$.
nodes.title: Running a delivery schedule

nodes.summary: Given a natural-number identifier $\mathrm{id}(k)$ for each process $k$ of the ring, for all global states $s, t$ and every list $\kappa$ of processes, running the schedule $\kappa$ from $s$ returns $t$ if and only if the Chang–Roberts transition system with identifiers $\mathrm{id}$ has a multistep transition from $s$ to $t$ labelled by $\kappa$.
nodes.title: Runs are multistep transitions
Deadlock and circular wait

nodes.summary: A resource-allocation snapshot, for a type $P$ of processes and a type $R$ of resources, records for each resource the process holding it, if any (so each resource has at most one holder), and for each process $p$ and resource $r$ whether $p$ has an outstanding request for $r$. A process never requests a resource it holds.
nodes.title: Resource-allocation snapshot

nodes.summary: In a resource-allocation snapshot $s$, a process $p$ waits for a process $q$ when there is a resource $r$ that $p$ requests in $s$ and that $q$ holds in $s$.
nodes.title: Wait-for relation

nodes.summary: In a resource-allocation snapshot $s$, a set $D$ of processes is deadlocked when $D$ is nonempty and every process $p \in D$ waits in $s$ for some process $q \in D$, that is, $p$ requests in $s$ a resource that $q$ holds in $s$.
nodes.title: Deadlocked set of processes

nodes.summary: A resource-allocation snapshot $s$ has circular wait when some process $p$ waits for itself through a chain of one or more wait-for edges in $s$, that is, there are processes $p = p_0, p_1, \dots, p_k = p$ with $k \ge 1$ such that $p_{i-1}$ waits for $p_i$ in $s$ for each $1 \le i \le k$.
nodes.title: Circular wait

nodes.summary: In a resource-allocation snapshot, no process $p$ waits for itself, that is, there is no resource that $p$ both requests and holds.
nodes.title: No process waits for itself directly

nodes.summary: In a resource-allocation snapshot, if no resource requested by a process $p$ has a holder, then $p$ waits for no process $q$.
nodes.title: A process whose requests are all free waits for no one

nodes.summary: If a resource-allocation snapshot has circular wait, that is, some process $p$ waits for itself through a chain of one or more wait-for edges, then some set of processes is deadlocked.
nodes.title: Circular wait yields a deadlocked set

nodes.summary: In a resource-allocation snapshot with finitely many processes, if some set of processes is deadlocked, then the snapshot has circular wait: some process waits for itself through a chain of one or more wait-for edges.
nodes.title: A deadlocked set forces circular wait

nodes.summary: In a resource-allocation snapshot with finitely many processes, some set of processes is deadlocked if and only if the snapshot has circular wait, that is, some process waits for itself through a chain of one or more wait-for edges.
nodes.title: Deadlock is circular wait

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a resource-allocation snapshot and let $\mathrm{rank}$ assign a natural number to each resource. The snapshot $s$ is ordered by $\mathrm{rank}$ when, for every process $p$, every resource $r$ that $p$ requests in $s$ and every resource $r'$ that $p$ holds in $s$, we have $\mathrm{rank}(r') < \mathrm{rank}(r)$: each process requests only resources ranked strictly above every resource it holds.
nodes.title: Havender's resource ordering

nodes.summary: Let $\mathrm{rank}$ assign a natural number to each resource. If a resource-allocation snapshot is ordered by $\mathrm{rank}$ (Havender's discipline), that is, $\mathrm{rank}(r') < \mathrm{rank}(r)$ whenever some process requests $r$ and holds $r'$, then the snapshot has no circular wait: no process waits for itself through a chain of one or more wait-for edges.
nodes.title: Resource ordering prevents circular wait

nodes.summary: Let $\mathrm{rank}$ assign a natural number to each resource. If a resource-allocation snapshot with finitely many processes is ordered by $\mathrm{rank}$ (Havender's discipline), that is, $\mathrm{rank}(r') < \mathrm{rank}(r)$ whenever some process requests $r$ and holds $r'$, then no set of processes is deadlocked.
nodes.title: Resource ordering prevents deadlock
Deadlock detection

nodes.summary: For a type $P$ of processes and a type $R$ of resource types, a state consists of two functions $\mathrm{alloc}, \mathrm{request} : P \to R \to \mathbb{N}$: $\mathrm{alloc}(p)(r)$ is the number of instances of resource type $r$ that process $p$ holds, and $\mathrm{request}(p)(r)$ is the number of instances of $r$ that $p$ is waiting for.
nodes.title: Resource-allocation state

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a type of processes and $R$ a type of resource types, and let $S$ be a state that gives each process $p$ an allocation $\mathrm{alloc}(p)$ and a request $\mathrm{request}(p)$, both functions $R \to \mathbb{N}$ ordered componentwise. A list of processes $p_1, \dots, p_k$ is a reduction sequence of $S$ from the free vector $w : R \to \mathbb{N}$ when, for every $1 \le i \le k$, we have…
nodes.title: Reduction sequences

nodes.summary: Let $w$ be a resource vector and $p$ a process whose request is at most $w$. If $\sigma$ is a reduction sequence from $w$, then the list obtained from $\sigma$ by removing the first occurrence of $p$, if any, is a reduction sequence from $w$ plus the allocation of $p$.
nodes.title: Letting a process that fits finish first preserves reduction sequences

nodes.summary: Let $w$ be a resource vector. If $\sigma$ is a reduction sequence from $w$ and no process of $\sigma$ has a request at most $w$, then $\sigma$ is empty.
nodes.title: A reduction sequence in which no process fits is empty

nodes.summary: Given the fuel, a number of steps, together with the free resource vector $w$ and a list of pending processes, the algorithm returns two lists: the processes that finished, in order, and the processes left over. With fuel $0$, or when no pending process has a request at most $w$, no process finishes and all the pending processes are left over. Otherwise the fuel is $n + 1$ for some $n$; take the first pending…
nodes.title: The detection algorithm with fuel

nodes.summary: Given the free resource vector $w$ and a list of pending processes, run the detection algorithm: repeatedly take the first pending process whose request is at most what is free, let it finish, remove that entry from the list and add its allocation to what is free, until no pending process has a request at most what is free. This is the list of the processes taken, in the order they were taken.
nodes.title: The processes the detection algorithm lets finish

nodes.summary: Given the free resource vector $w$ and a list of pending processes, repeatedly take the first pending process whose request is at most what is free, let it finish, remove that entry from the list and add its allocation to what is free, until no pending process has a request at most what is free. The processes still pending then are the ones reported as deadlocked.
nodes.title: The detection algorithm

nodes.summary: Let $w$ be the free resource vector, let the list of pending processes contain no duplicates, and let the fuel be at least the number of pending processes. If $\sigma$ is a duplicate-free reduction sequence from $w$ all of whose processes are pending, then no process of $\sigma$ is among the processes that the detection algorithm with that fuel leaves over.
nodes.title: The algorithm with fuel leaves over no process of a reduction sequence

nodes.summary: Let $w$ be the free resource vector. For every process $q$ that the detection algorithm reports, the request of $q$ is not at most $w$ plus the sum of the allocations of the processes that the algorithm lets finish: for at least one resource type, $q$ requests more than is free even after all those processes have released their allocations.
nodes.title: Every reported process is stuck

nodes.summary: For every free resource vector $w$ and every list of pending processes, the processes that the detection algorithm lets finish, in the order it lets them finish, form a reduction sequence from $w$.
nodes.title: The processes the algorithm lets finish form a reduction sequence

nodes.summary: Let $w$ be the free resource vector and let the list of pending processes contain no duplicates. A process $p$ is reported by the detection algorithm if and only if $p$ is pending and no duplicate-free reduction sequence $\sigma$ from $w$ made of pending processes contains $p$.
nodes.title: Correctness of deadlock detection

nodes.summary: Let $w$ be the free resource vector and let the list of pending processes contain no duplicates. The detection algorithm, started with $w$ free, reports no process if and only if some reordering of the pending processes is a reduction sequence from $w$.
nodes.title: No deadlock is reported exactly when all the processes can finish
Dining philosophers problem

nodes.summary: A state of the three dining philosophers is a triple $(s_0, s_1, s_2)$ with each $s_i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ the phase of philosopher $i$: $0$ thinking, $1$ holding the first fork, $2$ eating (holding both forks).
nodes.title: Dining-philosophers state

nodes.summary: For a state $s = (s_0, s_1, s_2)$ of the three dining philosophers and a philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, the phase of philosopher $i$ in $s$ is the component $s_i$.
nodes.title: Phase of a philosopher

nodes.summary: For a state $s = (s_0, s_1, s_2)$ of the three dining philosophers, a philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ and a phase $p \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, setting the phase of philosopher $i$ to $p$ gives the state obtained from $s$ by replacing the component $s_i$ by $p$ and keeping the other two components.
nodes.title: Updating the phase of a philosopher

nodes.summary: A protocol for three philosophers $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ sitting between forks $0, 1, 2$ consists of two maps $\mathrm{first}, \mathrm{second}$ from $\{0, 1, 2\}$ to itself, the fork philosopher $i$ picks up first and the one it picks up second, such that for every $i$ these are its two neighbouring forks $i$ and $i + 1$ (modulo $3$) in some order: either $\mathrm{first}(i) = i$ and $\mathrm{second}(i) = i + 1$, or…
nodes.title: Dining-philosophers protocol

nodes.summary: Given a protocol and a state, fork $f$ is held exactly when some philosopher $i$ either has $f$ as its first fork and is in phase $1$ or $2$, or has $f$ as its second fork and is in phase $2$ (eating).
nodes.title: Held forks

nodes.summary: Given a protocol and a state, philosopher $i$ can move exactly when it is thinking (phase $0$) and its first fork is not held by any philosopher, or it holds its first fork (phase $1$) and its second fork is not held by any philosopher, or it is eating (phase $2$), in which case its move puts both forks down.
nodes.title: When a philosopher can move

nodes.summary: The state obtained from $s$ when philosopher $i$ moves: the phase of $i$ advances from thinking ($0$) to holding its first fork ($1$), from $1$ to eating ($2$), and from eating back to thinking; the phases of the other philosophers are unchanged. Whether the move is allowed is not checked here.
nodes.title: Move of a philosopher

nodes.summary: For a protocol $P$, the labelled transition system on the states whose labels are the philosophers: there is a transition from $s$ to $t$ labelled $i$ exactly when philosopher $i$ can move in $s$ under $P$ and $t$ is the state obtained from $s$ by the move of philosopher $i$.
nodes.title: Transition system of a dining-philosophers protocol

nodes.summary: The valuation of the atoms $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ on the states of the dining philosophers: atom $i$ holds at a state exactly when philosopher $i$ is eating there, that is, when its phase is $2$.
nodes.title: The eating valuation

nodes.summary: The state in which all three philosophers are thinking, that is, every phase is $0$.
nodes.title: Initial state of the dining philosophers

nodes.summary: The protocol in which every philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ picks up fork $i$ (its left fork) first and fork $i + 1$ (modulo $3$) second.
nodes.title: Naive dining-philosophers protocol

nodes.summary: The protocol in which every philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ picks up the lower-numbered of its two forks $i$ and $i + 1$ (modulo $3$) first and the higher-numbered one second: philosophers $0$ and $1$ take fork $i$ first, and philosopher $2$ takes fork $0$ first and fork $2$ second.
nodes.title: Resource-ordered dining-philosophers protocol

nodes.summary: The CTL formula $\neg\,\mathsf{EX}\,\top$ over the philosophers as atoms. It holds at a state exactly when the state has no successor; in the transition system of a protocol, exactly when no philosopher can move.
nodes.title: The deadlock formula

nodes.summary: For a philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, the CTL formula $\neg(p_i \wedge p_{i+1})$ over the atoms $p_0, p_1, p_2$ (one per philosopher), with indices modulo $3$. Under the valuation in which $p_j$ holds when philosopher $j$ eats, it says that the neighbouring philosophers $i$ and $i + 1$ do not eat at the same time.
nodes.title: Neighbours-apart formula

nodes.summary: Consider the transition system of the naive protocol, in which every philosopher $i$ picks up fork $i$ first and fork $i + 1$ second (indices modulo $3$), with atom $i$ read as "philosopher $i$ is eating". Its initial state, where all philosophers are thinking, satisfies the CTL formula $\mathsf{EF}$ applied to the deadlock formula: from it, a state in which no philosopher can move is reachable.
nodes.title: The naive protocol can deadlock

nodes.summary: In the transition system of the naive protocol, with atom $i$ read as "philosopher $i$ is eating", the state in which every philosopher holds its first fork (every phase is $1$) satisfies the deadlock formula: no philosopher can move there.
nodes.title: A deadlock state of the naive protocol

nodes.summary: In the transition system of the three dining philosophers under the resource-ordered protocol, the initial state, in which everybody thinks, satisfies the CTL formula $\mathrm{AG}\,\mathrm{EX}\,\top$: every state reachable from it has a successor, that is, some philosopher can move.
nodes.title: Resource ordering prevents deadlock for the dining philosophers

nodes.summary: In the transition system of the three dining philosophers under the resource-ordered protocol, with the atom $p_j$ holding when philosopher $j$ eats, the initial state, in which everybody thinks, satisfies the CTL formula $\mathrm{AG}\,\mathrm{EF}\,p_i$ for every philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$: from every state reachable from the initial state, some state in which philosopher $i$ eats is reachable.
nodes.title: Every philosopher can still eat under resource ordering

nodes.summary: For every philosopher $i$, in the transition system of the naive protocol, with atom $j$ read as "philosopher $j$ is eating", the initial state satisfies $\mathsf{AG}$ applied to the formula that philosophers $i$ and $i + 1$ (indices modulo $3$) do not both eat: in no state reachable from the initial state, where all philosophers are thinking, are philosophers $i$ and $i + 1$ both eating.
nodes.title: Mutual exclusion under the naive protocol

nodes.summary: In the transition system of the three dining philosophers under the resource-ordered protocol, with the atom $p_j$ holding when philosopher $j$ eats, the initial state, in which everybody thinks, satisfies the CTL formula $\mathrm{AG}\,\neg(p_i \wedge p_{i+1})$ for every philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, with indices modulo $3$: in no state reachable from the initial state do philosophers $i$ and $i + 1$ both eat.
nodes.title: Neighbours never eat together under resource ordering

nodes.summary: Philosopher $i$ can move in state $s$ when it thinks and neither of its forks $i$ and $i + 1$ (modulo $3$) is held in $s$, or when it eats (it then puts both forks down); a philosopher holding only its first fork cannot move. A fork is held as in the naive protocol: philosopher $j$ holds fork $j$ when it holds its first fork or eats, and holds fork $j + 1$ when it eats.
nodes.title: Enabled moves under atomic acquisition

nodes.summary: In a state $s$ (the phases of the three philosophers), the move of philosopher $i$ changes only the phase of $i$: if $i$ is thinking, it starts eating, picking up both forks at once; otherwise it goes back to thinking. The phases of the other two philosophers are unchanged.
nodes.title: Move of a philosopher under atomic acquisition

nodes.summary: The labelled transition system on the states of the three philosophers, labelled by the philosopher that moves: there is a step labelled $i$ from $s$ to $t$ exactly when either philosopher $i$ thinks in $s$, neither of its forks $i$ and $i + 1$ (modulo $3$) is held in $s$, and $t$ is $s$ with philosopher $i$ eating; or philosopher $i$ eats in $s$ and $t$ is $s$ with philosopher $i$ thinking. A fork is held as in…
nodes.title: Dining philosophers with atomic fork acquisition

nodes.summary: The number of seated philosophers in a state $s$ is the number of philosophers that hold at least one fork in $s$, that is, whose phase is either holding the first fork or eating.
nodes.title: Number of seated philosophers

nodes.summary: Philosopher $i$ can move in state $s$ when it can move in $s$ under the naive protocol and, if it is thinking, fewer than two philosophers hold at least one fork in $s$. Under the naive protocol each philosopher $i$ picks up the left fork $i$ first and then the right fork $i + 1$ (modulo $3$), each only when no philosopher holds it, and an eating philosopher can always put both forks down.
nodes.title: Enabled moves under a butler

nodes.summary: The labelled transition system on the states of the three philosophers, labelled by the philosopher that moves: there is a step labelled $i$ from $s$ to $t$ exactly when philosopher $i$ can move in $s$ under the naive protocol, if philosopher $i$ is thinking then fewer than two philosophers hold a fork in $s$, and $t$ is $s$ with philosopher $i$ advanced one phase (thinking to holding its first fork, to eating, to…
nodes.title: Dining philosophers with a butler

nodes.summary: In the dining philosophers transition system with atomic acquisition of both forks, every state reachable from the initial state (all three philosophers thinking) has a successor: some philosopher can move.
nodes.title: Atomic acquisition prevents deadlock

nodes.summary: In the dining philosophers transition system with atomic acquisition of both forks, for each philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, from every state reachable from the initial state (all three philosophers thinking) a state in which philosopher $i$ eats is reachable, in zero or more steps.
nodes.title: Under atomic acquisition every philosopher can always still eat

nodes.summary: In the dining philosophers transition system with atomic acquisition of both forks, for each philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, in no state reachable from the initial state (all three philosophers thinking) do philosopher $i$ and its neighbour $i + 1$ (modulo $3$) both eat.
nodes.title: Mutual exclusion under atomic acquisition

nodes.summary: In the dining philosophers transition system of the naive protocol under a butler, every state reachable from the initial state (all three philosophers thinking) has a successor: some philosopher can move.
nodes.title: A butler prevents deadlock

nodes.summary: In the dining philosophers transition system of the naive protocol under a butler, for each philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, from every state reachable from the initial state (all three philosophers thinking) a state in which philosopher $i$ eats is reachable, in zero or more steps.
nodes.title: Under a butler every philosopher can always still eat

nodes.summary: In the dining philosophers transition system of the naive protocol under a butler, for each philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, in no state reachable from the initial state (all three philosophers thinking) do philosopher $i$ and its neighbour $i + 1$ (modulo $3$) both eat.
nodes.title: Mutual exclusion under a butler
Go-back-N protocol

nodes.summary: The channel names of the go-back-N protocol are $\mathsf{acc}$ (accept a message from the user), $\mathsf{del}$ (deliver a message to the user) and, for every natural number $k$: $\mathsf{send}\,k$ (sender to data channel, a frame with sequence number $k$), $\mathsf{recv}\,k$ (data channel to receiver), $\mathsf{ack}\,k$ (receiver to sender, the cumulative acknowledgement naming $k$ as the next expected frame) and…
nodes.title: Channel names of go-back-N

nodes.summary: A state of the go-back-N sender is a triple of natural numbers: the base of the window (the sequence number of the oldest unacknowledged frame), the number of outstanding messages (accepted but not yet acknowledged), and the offset from the base of the next frame to transmit.
nodes.title: Go-back-N sender state

nodes.summary: A receiver state is one of the following, for a natural number $e$ or $k$: expecting the frame with sequence number $e$; about to deliver $e$, having received the expected frame $e$; or about to acknowledge $k$, the next expected sequence number.
nodes.title: Receiver states of go-back-N

nodes.summary: For a go-back-N sender with window base $b$, $c$ outstanding messages and next-frame offset $o$, and an acknowledgement $k$, let $d = \max(k + 3 - b, 0) \bmod 3$. If $1 \le d \le c$, the window slides: the new sender has base $k$, $c - d$ outstanding messages and next-frame offset $\max(o - d, 0)$. Otherwise the sender is unchanged.
nodes.title: Sender update on an acknowledgement

nodes.summary: The transitions of a sender with window base $b$, $n$ outstanding messages and next offset $o$, as pairs of a label and a successor state, in this order: if $n < 2$, an input on $\mathsf{acc}$ to $(b, n + 1, o)$; if $o < n$, an output on $\mathsf{send}\,((b + o) \bmod 3)$ to $(b, n, o + 1)$; if $0 < n$, a silent timeout step to $(b, n, 0)$; and, for each $k = 0, 1, 2$, an input on $\mathsf{ack}\,k$ to the state…
nodes.title: Sender transitions of go-back-N

nodes.summary: The data channel holds at most one frame. When empty, for each sequence number $k \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ it can input on channel $\mathrm{send}_k$ and then hold frame $k$. When holding frame $k$, it can either output on channel $\mathrm{recv}_k$ or silently lose the frame by a $\tau$ step; in both cases it becomes empty.
nodes.title: Transitions of the go-back-N data channel

nodes.summary: The transitions of the receiver, as pairs of a label and a successor state. Expecting $e$, for each $k = 0, 1, 2$ it can input on $\mathsf{recv}\,k$ and then is about to deliver $e$ if $k = e$, and about to acknowledge $e$ otherwise. About to deliver $e$, it outputs on $\mathsf{del}$ and is then about to acknowledge $(e + 1) \bmod 3$. About to acknowledge $k$, it outputs on $\mathsf{ack}\,k$ and then expects $k$.
nodes.title: Receiver transitions of go-back-N

nodes.summary: The transitions of the go-back-N two-place buffer at occupancy $n \in \mathbb{N}$: if $n < 2$ it inputs on $\mathsf{acc}$ and moves to occupancy $n + 1$, and if $n > 0$ it outputs on $\mathsf{del}$ and moves to occupancy $n - 1$. It has no other transitions.
nodes.title: Transitions of the two-place buffer

nodes.summary: The lossy one-place acknowledgement channel of the lossy go-back-N variant, given by its transitions in each state. When empty, it inputs on $\mathsf{reply}_k$ and then holds $k$, for each $k \in \{0, 1, 2\}$. When it holds $k$, it either outputs on $\mathsf{ack}_k$ or silently loses $k$, and in both cases it becomes empty. It has no other transitions.
nodes.title: Transitions of the lossy acknowledgement channel

nodes.summary: The transitions of the receiver of the lossy variant, as pairs of a label and a successor state, are those of the receiver of the reliable protocol, except in the state about to acknowledge $k$: there the only transition is an output on $\mathsf{reply}\,k$, to the acknowledgement channel, after which the receiver expects $k$.
nodes.title: Receiver transitions of lossy go-back-N

nodes.summary: The process constants of the go-back-N specification, one for each state of each component: a sender constant for each sender state, a data-channel constant for each channel content (empty or a natural number), a receiver constant for each receiver state, a buffer constant for each occupancy $n \in \mathbb{N}$, an acknowledgement-channel constant for each channel content (empty or a natural number), and a constant…
nodes.title: Process constants of the go-back-N model

nodes.summary: The specification assigns to every process constant the choice, over the transitions listed for its state, of the prefixes $a.K$, where $a$ is the label of the transition and $K$ is the process constant for its target state; an empty list gives the inactive process. The constants are those of the sender, the data channel, the receiver, the two-place buffer, the acknowledgement channel and the receiver of the lossy…
nodes.title: Recursive CCS specification of go-back-N

nodes.summary: The labelled transition system whose states are the CCS processes over the go-back-N channel names and process constants, whose labels are the CCS labels over the channel names, and whose transitions are those generated by the go-back-N recursive specification.
nodes.title: Labelled transition system of go-back-N

nodes.summary: The internal channels of the go-back-N protocol are $\mathrm{send}_k$ (sender to data channel), $\mathrm{recv}_k$ (data channel to receiver) and $\mathrm{ack}_k$ (receiver to sender) for $k \in \{0, 1, 2\}$; all of them are restricted.
nodes.title: Internal channels of go-back-N

nodes.summary: A configuration of the go-back-N protocol consists of a sender state, the content of the data channel (either empty or a single frame with sequence number $k \in \mathbb{N}$), and a receiver state.
nodes.title: Go-back-N configurations

nodes.summary: For a configuration consisting of a sender state $s$, a data channel content $d$ (empty or one frame) and a receiver state $r$, the protocol process is the parallel composition $(S_s \mid D_d) \mid R_r$ of the process constants for the sender in state $s$, the data channel holding $d$ and the receiver in state $r$, with the internal channels restricted: the send, receive and acknowledgement channels for the…
nodes.title: Go-back-N protocol process in a configuration

nodes.summary: The transitions of a go-back-N configuration (sender, data channel, receiver) are those of the parallel composition of the three components, in which one component moves alone or two components synchronize on complementary labels in a silent step, restricted to the silent steps and the steps whose label is not on an internal channel ($\mathsf{send}_k$, $\mathsf{recv}_k$ or $\mathsf{ack}_k$ for $k \in \{0, 1, 2\}$).
nodes.title: Transitions of go-back-N configurations

nodes.summary: For an occupancy $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the process constant of the go-back-N specification for the two-place buffer holding $n$ messages.
nodes.title: The two-place buffer process

nodes.summary: The initial configuration of the go-back-N protocol consists of the sender with window base $0$, no outstanding messages and next-frame offset $0$; the empty data channel; and the receiver expecting sequence number $0$.
nodes.title: Initial configuration of go-back-N

nodes.summary: The go-back-N protocol with window size $2$ and sequence numbers modulo $3$ is the recursive CCS process in its initial configuration: the parallel composition of the sender with an empty window based at $0$, the empty lossy one-place data channel, and the receiver expecting $0$, with the internal channels $\mathrm{send}_k$, $\mathrm{recv}_k$ and $\mathrm{ack}_k$ for $k \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ restricted.
nodes.title: The go-back-N protocol

nodes.summary: The two-place buffer process of the go-back-N model with occupancy $0$.
nodes.title: The empty two-place buffer

nodes.summary: A list of $147$ pairs, each a go-back-N configuration together with the occupancy of the two-place buffer it simulates, namely the number of accepted but undelivered messages. It contains every reachable configuration, and it is ordered so that every pair can reach the visible actions of its buffer state through pairs listed earlier.
nodes.title: Weak-bisimulation certificate for go-back-N

nodes.summary: Over a lossy one-place data channel, with timeouts and cumulative acknowledgements, the protocol is weakly bisimilar to the empty two-place buffer.
nodes.title: Go-back-N with window 2 implements a two-place buffer

nodes.summary: The go-back-N protocol is observation congruent (rooted weakly bisimilar) to the empty two-place buffer: every transition of either process is matched by a rooted weak transition of the other with the same label (silent steps, a step with that label, silent steps), and the resulting processes are weakly bisimilar.
nodes.title: Go-back-N with window 2 is observation congruent to a two-place buffer

nodes.summary: The list of channels restricted in the lossy variant: the internal channels of the reliable protocol, namely $\mathsf{send}\,k$, $\mathsf{recv}\,k$ and $\mathsf{ack}\,k$ for $k = 0, 1, 2$, followed by the channels $\mathsf{reply}\,0$, $\mathsf{reply}\,1$ and $\mathsf{reply}\,2$ from the receiver to the acknowledgement channel.
nodes.title: Internal channels of lossy go-back-N

nodes.summary: A configuration of the lossy go-back-N variant is a go-back-N configuration (sender state, data channel content, receiver state) together with the content of the acknowledgement channel, either empty or a single acknowledgement $k \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: Configurations of lossy go-back-N

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a configuration of the lossy variant, and let $S$, $D$, $R$ and $A$ be the process constants for its sender state, its data-channel content, its receiver state (as a receiver of the lossy variant) and its acknowledgement-channel content. The process of the lossy variant in $c$ is $((S \mid D) \mid R) \mid A$ with the internal channels of the lossy variant restricted.
nodes.title: The lossy go-back-N process in a configuration

nodes.summary: The transitions of a configuration of the lossy go-back-N variant come from the parallel composition of the sender, the data channel, the lossy-variant receiver and the acknowledgement channel (in each composition either side moves alone, or the two sides synchronize on complementary input and output labels in a silent step), keeping only the silent transitions and those whose label is not on an internal channel…
nodes.title: Transitions of lossy go-back-N configurations

nodes.summary: The process of the lossy variant of go-back-N in its initial configuration: the sender's window is based at $0$ with no outstanding messages and next offset $0$, the data channel and the acknowledgement channel are empty, and the receiver expects frame $0$.
nodes.title: Go-back-N with a lossy acknowledgement channel

nodes.summary: Let $c$ and $c'$ be configurations of the lossy variant and $a$ a label. If $(a, c')$ is one of the configuration-level transitions of $c$, then in the labelled transition system of the go-back-N specification the lossy process in configuration $c$ has a transition labelled $a$ to the lossy process in configuration $c'$.
nodes.title: Configuration transitions are process transitions in lossy go-back-N

nodes.summary: For every occupancy $n$, every process reachable from the go-back-N buffer with occupancy $n$ by zero or more silent steps is that buffer itself.
nodes.title: The silent closure of the buffer is trivial

nodes.summary: For every occupancy $n$ and every visible label $a$, if the go-back-N buffer with occupancy $n$ reaches a process $Q$ by a weak transition labelled $a$ (silent steps, one $a$-step, silent steps), then $Q$ is the buffer with some occupancy $m$ such that the buffer at occupancy $n$ has a transition labelled $a$ to occupancy $m$.
nodes.title: Visible weak steps of the buffer

nodes.summary: The list of the seven configurations of go-back-N with a lossy acknowledgement channel in which the sender's window has base $0$ with two outstanding messages, the receiver holds frame $1$ about to deliver it, and the acknowledgement channel is empty, while the sender's offset of the next frame to transmit and the data channel are, in order: offset $2$ and empty, offset $0$ and empty, offset $1$ holding frame $0$,…
nodes.title: Silent closure of the stuck lossy go-back-N configuration

nodes.summary: Consider go-back-N with a lossy acknowledgement channel in the configuration where the sender's window has base $0$ with two outstanding messages, both transmitted (offset of the next frame $2$), the data channel and the acknowledgement channel are empty, and the receiver holds frame $1$ about to deliver it. This process has no weak transition labelled by accepting a message: no sequence of silent steps followed by…
nodes.title: The stuck lossy go-back-N configuration refuses new messages

nodes.summary: With a lossy acknowledgement channel and the deliver-then-acknowledge receiver, go-back-N is not weakly bisimilar to the two-place buffer. Accept two messages, deliver the first and lose its acknowledgement, and let the receiver take the second frame: the buffer now holds one message and accepts another, but the protocol cannot accept before it delivers.
nodes.title: Lossy acknowledgements break the buffer specification
Lamport clocks

nodes.summary: An event of an execution, for a type $P$ of processes, consists of the process in $P$ it belongs to and, if it is a receipt, a natural number: the position in the execution of the event whose message it receives. The structure does not require that position to be earlier than the event itself.
nodes.title: Event

nodes.summary: An execution $e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ is well formed when every receipt names an earlier event: whenever $e_j$ receives the message sent by the event at position $i$, then $i < j$.
nodes.title: Well-formed executions

nodes.summary: In an execution, position $i$ precedes position $j$ by one step when $i < j$, both positions hold events, and either the two events belong to the same process or the event at $j$ receives the message of the event at $i$.
nodes.title: One step of happened-before

nodes.summary: Lamport's happened-before relation on the positions of an execution is the transitive closure of one step of happened-before: $a$ happened before $b$ when there is a chain $a = i_0, i_1, \dots, i_k = b$ with $k \ge 1$ in which each $i_m$ precedes $i_{m+1}$ by one step.
nodes.title: Happened-before

nodes.summary: If position $a$ happened before position $b$ in an execution, then $a < b$.
nodes.title: Happened-before goes forward in the execution

nodes.summary: The state is a counter $c(p) \in \mathbb{N}$ for each process $p$ together with the timestamps assigned so far. An event $e$ of process $p$ gets the timestamp $t = \max(c(p), s) + 1$, where $s$ is the timestamp already assigned at the position that $e$ receives from; $s = 0$ if $e$ is not a receipt or if no timestamp has been assigned at that position. The step sets $c(p)$ to $t$ and appends $t$ to the timestamps.
nodes.title: One step of the Lamport clock algorithm

nodes.summary: The clock algorithm over an execution applies one step of the algorithm to each event in order, starting from all process counters $0$ and no timestamps. The result is the final counters together with the timestamps assigned to the events, in order.
nodes.title: Running the Lamport clock algorithm

nodes.summary: The Lamport timestamps $t_0, \dots, t_{n-1}$ of an execution $e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ are computed by Lamport's clock algorithm. Every process keeps a counter, initially $0$. For $k = 0, \dots, n-1$ in turn, let $c$ be the current counter of the process of $e_k$, and let $m = t_i$ if $e_k$ receives the message sent by the event at position $i$ with $i < k$, and $m = 0$ otherwise. Then $t_k = \max(c, m) + 1$, and the…
nodes.title: Lamport timestamps

nodes.summary: Let $e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ be an execution, and extend it by appending further events. For every $i < n$, the Lamport timestamp of the event at position $i$ is the same in the extended execution as in the original one.
nodes.title: Appending events does not change earlier timestamps

nodes.summary: After the Lamport clock algorithm has run over an execution, the counter of each process is at least the timestamp of every event of that process in the execution.
nodes.title: Process counters dominate their timestamps

nodes.summary: Let $e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ be an execution and let $i < k \le n$. The Lamport timestamp of $e_i$ in the whole execution equals its Lamport timestamp in the prefix $e_0, \dots, e_{k-1}$.
nodes.title: A timestamp depends only on a prefix containing its event

nodes.summary: If position $i$ precedes position $j$ by one step of happened-before in an execution, then the Lamport timestamp of $i$ is smaller than the Lamport timestamp of $j$.
nodes.title: One step of happened-before raises the timestamp

nodes.summary: Let $e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ be a well-formed execution and let $t_k$ be the Lamport timestamp of $e_k$. If $j < n$ and $e_j$ receives the message sent by the event at position $i$, then $t_i < t_j$.
nodes.title: A receipt is stamped later than its send

nodes.summary: Let $e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ be an execution and let $t_k$ be the Lamport timestamp of $e_k$. If $i < j < n$ and $e_i$ and $e_j$ belong to the same process, then $t_i < t_j$.
nodes.title: Lamport timestamps increase along each process

nodes.summary: In every execution, if the event at position $a$ happened before the event at position $b$, then the Lamport timestamp of $a$ is smaller than the Lamport timestamp of $b$ (Lamport 1978).
nodes.title: The clock condition

nodes.summary: If position $a$ happened before position $b$ in an execution, then the execution has an event at position $a$ and an event at position $b$.
nodes.title: Happened-before relates positions of the execution

nodes.summary: Fix a linear order on the processes. In an execution $e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ with Lamport timestamps $t_0, \dots, t_{n-1}$, position $a$ precedes position $b$ when $a < n$, $b < n$, and either $t_a < t_b$, or $t_a = t_b$ and the process of $e_a$ is smaller than the process of $e_b$.
nodes.title: Lamport's total order

nodes.summary: In every execution, if the event at position $a$ happened before the event at position $b$, then position $a$ precedes position $b$ in Lamport's total order.
nodes.title: Lamport's total order extends happened-before

nodes.summary: In every execution, for any two distinct positions $a \ne b$ that both hold events, $a$ precedes $b$ or $b$ precedes $a$ in Lamport's total order.
nodes.title: Lamport's order is total
Two-phase commit

nodes.summary: In two-phase commit the coordinator is in one of three states: waiting (collecting votes), committed (it has decided commit) or aborted (it has decided abort).
nodes.title: Coordinator states

nodes.summary: A participant is in one of four states: working (it has not voted), prepared (it voted yes and waits for the decision), committed, or aborted (it voted no, or learned of an abort).
nodes.title: Participant states in two-phase commit

nodes.summary: For a set $P$ of participants, a global state consists of a coordinator state together with a participant state for each participant $p \in P$.
nodes.title: Global states of two-phase commit

nodes.summary: The actions of the two-phase commit protocol over a set $P$ of participants are: a participant $p \in P$ votes yes; a participant $p$ votes no; the coordinator decides commit; the coordinator decides abort; a participant $p$ learns the commit decision; and a participant $p$ learns the abort decision.
nodes.title: Two-phase commit actions

nodes.summary: For a global state $s$, a participant $p$ and a participant state $x$, the updated state has the same coordinator state as $s$, gives participant $p$ the state $x$, and leaves the state of every other participant unchanged.
nodes.title: Updating one participant's state

nodes.summary: The protocol steps from a global state $s$ to a global state $t$ by an action exactly in the following cases. A working participant $p$ may vote yes, after which $p$ is prepared, or vote no, after which $p$ is aborted. If the coordinator is waiting and every participant is prepared, the coordinator may decide commit, after which it is committed. If the coordinator is waiting, it may decide abort, after which it is…
nodes.title: Transitions of two-phase commit

nodes.summary: For a set $P$ of participants, the labelled transition system whose states are the global states of the protocol, whose labels are the protocol actions, and whose transitions are the protocol steps.
nodes.title: Two-phase commit as a transition system

nodes.summary: The initial state of the two-phase commit protocol: the coordinator is waiting and every participant is working.
nodes.title: Initial state of two-phase commit

nodes.summary: A global state $s$ is reachable when some finite sequence of protocol actions leads by protocol steps from the initial state, in which the coordinator is waiting and every participant is working, to $s$.
nodes.title: Reachable states of two-phase commit

nodes.summary: If a global state $s$ of the two-phase commit protocol is reachable and some action takes $s$ to $t$ in one protocol step, then $t$ is reachable.
nodes.title: Reachable states are closed under steps

nodes.summary: A global state $s$ of the two-phase commit protocol satisfies the invariant when two conditions hold: if the coordinator has committed, then every participant is prepared or committed; and every committed participant has a committed coordinator.
nodes.title: Two-phase commit invariant

nodes.summary: If a state $s$ of the two-phase commit protocol satisfies the inductive invariant and a state $t$ is reached from $s$ by a finite sequence of transitions, then $t$ satisfies the invariant.
nodes.title: Multistep transitions preserve the two-phase commit invariant

nodes.summary: For every set $P$ of participants, every global state of the two-phase commit protocol that is reachable from the initial state satisfies the inductive invariant, that is, both of the following hold: if the coordinator has committed, then every participant is prepared or committed; and every committed participant has a committed coordinator.
nodes.title: The two-phase commit invariant holds in reachable states

nodes.summary: For every set $P$ of participants, in every reachable state of the two-phase commit protocol, if some participant $p$ has committed, then no participant $q$ has aborted.
nodes.title: Atomicity between participants

nodes.summary: In every reachable state of the two-phase commit protocol, if the coordinator has decided commit, then every participant voted yes, that is, every participant is prepared or committed.
nodes.title: Validity for the coordinator

nodes.summary: In every reachable state of the two-phase commit protocol, if some participant has committed, then every participant voted yes, that is, every participant is prepared or committed.
nodes.title: Validity for participants

nodes.summary: In every reachable state of the two-phase commit protocol, if some participant has aborted, then the coordinator has not decided commit.
nodes.title: An aborted participant rules out a coordinator commit

nodes.summary: In every reachable state of the two-phase commit protocol, if some participant has committed, then the coordinator has committed.
nodes.title: A committed participant has a committed coordinator

nodes.summary: In every reachable state of the two-phase commit protocol, if the coordinator has decided commit, then no participant has aborted.
nodes.title: A committed coordinator has no aborted participant

nodes.summary: In every reachable state of the two-phase commit protocol, if the coordinator has decided abort, then no participant has committed.
nodes.title: An aborted coordinator has no committed participant
Vector clocks

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be the set of processes. Given the current vectors $V_q \in \mathbb{N}^P$ of the processes $q$ and the timestamps $T_0, T_1, \dots$ assigned so far, the vector clock algorithm stamps an event $e$ of process $p$ as follows. Let $m = T_i$ if $e$ receives the message sent by the event at position $i$ and $T_i$ has been assigned, and $m = 0$ otherwise. The stamp of $e$ is the pointwise maximum of $V_p$ and $m$,…
nodes.title: Vector clock stamp of an event

nodes.summary: The state of the algorithm holds a vector $V_q \in \mathbb{N}^P$ for each process $q$, where $P$ is the set of processes, and the timestamps assigned so far, kept in an array for constant-time append and lookup. On an event $e$ of process $p$, the step replaces $V_p$ by the stamp $s$ of $e$ computed from the current state, leaves the other vectors unchanged, and appends $s$ to the timestamps.
nodes.title: One step of the vector clock algorithm

nodes.summary: The state of the vector clock algorithm after an execution is obtained by starting from the state in which every process's vector is $0$ and no timestamps have been assigned, and applying one step of the algorithm to each event of the execution in order.
nodes.title: Running the vector clock algorithm

nodes.summary: The vector timestamps of an execution are the list of vectors that the vector clock algorithm, run over the execution, assigns to its events, in order.
nodes.title: Vector timestamps of an execution

nodes.summary: For every execution and every natural number $i$, the entry at index $i$ of the array of timestamps built by the vector clock algorithm on the execution equals the $i$-th vector timestamp of the execution, where an index out of range gives the zero vector in both lookups.
nodes.title: Array lookup agrees with the timestamp list

nodes.summary: For every execution and every position $j$ of an event $e$ of it, the vector timestamp of $j$ equals the stamp of $e$ computed from the state of the vector clock algorithm after the first $j$ events of the execution.
nodes.title: Timestamps are stamps from the preceding state

nodes.summary: For every execution and every position $i$ of an event of it, the vector timestamp of $i$ is pointwise at most the vector of that event's process in the state of the vector clock algorithm after the whole execution.
nodes.title: Each process's vector dominates its events' timestamps

nodes.summary: Run the vector clock algorithm over an execution, starting from all vectors $0$. For every process $p$, the vector held by $p$ at the end is either the zero vector or the vector timestamp of some event of $p$ in the execution.
nodes.title: A process's final vector is zero or one of its timestamps

nodes.summary: For every position $j$ of an event of an execution, if $p$ is the process of that event, then the $p$-entry of the vector timestamp of $j$ is at least $1$.
nodes.title: An event's own entry is positive

nodes.summary: In an execution, write $V_i$ for the vector timestamp that the vector clock algorithm gives to the event at position $i$. If the event at position $j$ follows the event at position $i$ by one step of happened-before, then $V_i(q) \le V_j(q)$ for every process $q$.
nodes.title: Vector timestamps are monotone along one step of happened-before

nodes.summary: In an execution, write $V_i$ for the vector timestamp that the vector clock algorithm gives to the event at position $i$. If the event at position $a$ happened before the event at position $b$, then $V_a(q) \le V_b(q)$ for every process $q$.
nodes.title: Vector timestamps are monotone along happened-before

nodes.summary: Let $a$ and $b$ be positions of events of an execution, and let $p$ be the process of the event at $a$. If the $p$-entry of the vector timestamp of $a$ is at most the $p$-entry of the vector timestamp of $b$, then $a = b$ or $a$ happened before $b$.
nodes.title: Own-entry comparison detects happened-before

nodes.summary: For two events of an execution, `a` happened before `b` exactly when `a`'s timestamp is smaller than `b`'s in the pointwise order.
nodes.title: Vector clocks characterize happened-before

nodes.summary: Logics for proving programs correct: Hoare logic for partial and total correctness with soundness and relative completeness, weakest preconditions, verification-condition generation, and separation logic.
nodes.title: Program logics and verification
Hoare logic

nodes.summary: An assertion is a predicate on program states: it assigns a proposition to each state. Assertions serve as the preconditions and postconditions of Hoare triples.
nodes.title: Assertion

nodes.summary: An assertion $P$ entails an assertion $Q$ when every state that satisfies $P$ also satisfies $Q$.
nodes.title: Entailment of assertions

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be an assertion, $x$ a variable and $e$ an arithmetic expression. The assertion $P[e/x]$ holds in a state $s$ exactly when $P$ holds in the state obtained from $s$ by setting the value of $x$ to the value of $e$ in $s$.
nodes.title: Substitution in an assertion

nodes.summary: For assertions $P$ and $Q$ and a command $c$, the partial-correctness Hoare triple $\lbrace P \rbrace\ c\ \lbrace Q \rbrace$ is valid when, for all states $s$ and $t$, if $s$ satisfies $P$ and executing $c$ from $s$ terminates in $t$ under the big-step semantics, then $t$ satisfies $Q$.
nodes.title: Validity of a Hoare triple

nodes.summary: Let $I$ be an assertion, $b$ a Boolean expression and $c$ a command. Write $I \wedge b$ for the assertion that $I$ holds and $b$ evaluates to true, and $I \wedge \neg b$ for the assertion that $I$ holds and $b$ evaluates to false. If the partial-correctness Hoare triple $\lbrace I \wedge b \rbrace\ c\ \lbrace I \rbrace$ is valid, then so is the triple…
nodes.title: Invariant rule for while loops

nodes.summary: For a command $c$ and an assertion $Q$, the weakest liberal precondition of $c$ with respect to $Q$ is the assertion that holds in a state $s$ exactly when every state $t$ in which an execution of $c$ from $s$ terminates, under the big-step semantics, satisfies $Q$.
nodes.title: Weakest liberal precondition

nodes.summary: Let $b$ be a Boolean expression, $c$ a command and $Q$ an assertion. Write $\mathrm{wlp}(d, R)$ for the weakest liberal precondition of a command $d$ with respect to an assertion $R$, and let $W$ be the loop $\mathbf{while}\ b\ \mathbf{do}\ c$. Then $\mathrm{wlp}(W, Q)$ is the assertion that holds in a state $s$ exactly when both of the following hold: if $b$ evaluates to false in $s$, then $Q$ holds in $s$; and if…
nodes.title: Weakest liberal precondition unfolding of a while loop

nodes.summary: Let $I$ and $Q$ be assertions, $b$ a Boolean expression and $c$ a command. Suppose that every state satisfying $I$ in which $b$ evaluates to true satisfies the weakest liberal precondition of $c$ with respect to $I$, and that every state satisfying $I$ in which $b$ evaluates to false satisfies $Q$. Then $I$ entails the weakest liberal precondition of the loop $\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$ with respect to $Q$.
nodes.title: Loop invariants entail the weakest liberal precondition of the loop

nodes.summary: For assertions $P$ and $Q$ on states and a command $c$, the total-correctness Hoare triple with precondition $P$, command $c$ and postcondition $Q$ is valid when every state $s$ satisfying $P$ has a terminating big-step execution of $c$ from $s$ ending in a state $t$ that satisfies $Q$.
nodes.title: Validity of total-correctness Hoare triples

nodes.summary: Let $I$ be an assertion (the invariant), $V$ a function from states to natural numbers (the variant), $b$ a Boolean guard and $c$ a command. Suppose that for every state $s$ satisfying $I$ in which $b$ evaluates to true, there is a terminating big-step execution of $c$ from $s$ ending in a state $s'$ that satisfies $I$ with $V(s') < V(s)$. Then the total-correctness Hoare triple with precondition $I$, command…
nodes.title: Variant rule for while loops

nodes.summary: For assertions $P$, $Q$ and a command $c$, if the total-correctness Hoare triple with precondition $P$, command $c$ and postcondition $Q$ is valid, then the partial-correctness Hoare triple with the same precondition, command and postcondition is valid.
nodes.title: Total correctness implies partial correctness

nodes.summary: If the total-correctness Hoare triple with precondition $P$, command $c$ and postcondition $Q$ is valid and a state $s$ satisfies $P$, then there is a state $t$ such that $c$, started in $s$, reaches $\mathtt{skip}$ with state $t$ in finitely many small steps, and $t$ satisfies $Q$.
nodes.title: Total correctness gives a terminating small-step run

nodes.summary: For a command $c$ and a postcondition $Q$, the weakest precondition $\mathrm{wp}(c, Q)$ is the assertion that holds at a state $s$ exactly when there is a terminating big-step execution of $c$ from $s$ ending in a state that satisfies $Q$.
nodes.title: Weakest precondition for total correctness

nodes.summary: For a Boolean guard $b$, a loop body $c$, a postcondition $Q$ and a state $s$, the state $s$ satisfies the total-correctness weakest precondition $\mathrm{wp}(\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c, Q)$ if and only if either $b$ evaluates to false in $s$ and $s$ satisfies $Q$, or $b$ evaluates to true in $s$ and $s$ satisfies $\mathrm{wp}(c, \mathrm{wp}(\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c, Q))$.
nodes.title: Weakest-precondition unfolding of a while loop

nodes.summary: For every command $c$, postcondition $Q$ and state $s$, if $s$ satisfies the total-correctness weakest precondition $\mathrm{wp}(c, Q)$, then $s$ satisfies the weakest liberal precondition $\mathrm{wlp}(c, Q)$.
nodes.title: Total-correctness weakest precondition implies the weakest liberal precondition

nodes.summary: Here an assertion is a predicate on states, and an assertion $P$ entails an assertion $P'$ when every state satisfying $P$ satisfies $P'$. For an assertion $P$ and a Boolean expression $b$, the assertion $P \land b$ holds in a state when $P$ holds there and $b$ evaluates to true in it, and the assertion $P \land \lnot b$ holds in a state when $P$ holds there and $b$ evaluates to false in it. Derivability of…
nodes.title: Derivability in Hoare logic for partial correctness

nodes.summary: Every partial-correctness Hoare triple $\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}$ that is derivable in the partial-correctness proof system is valid: for all states $s$ and $s'$, if $s$ satisfies $P$ and $c$ has a terminating big-step execution from $s$ to $s'$, then $s'$ satisfies $Q$.
nodes.title: Soundness of Hoare logic for partial correctness

nodes.summary: Let $P$, $P'$ and $Q$ be assertions and $c$ a command. If $P$ entails $P'$ (every state satisfying $P$ satisfies $P'$) and the partial-correctness triple $\{P'\}\,c\,\{Q\}$ is derivable in the partial-correctness proof system, then so is $\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}$.
nodes.title: Precondition strengthening for partial correctness

nodes.summary: For every command $c$ and every assertion $Q$, the triple whose precondition is the weakest liberal precondition of $c$ with respect to $Q$, whose command is $c$ and whose postcondition is $Q$ is derivable in partial-correctness Hoare logic.
nodes.title: The weakest liberal precondition gives a derivable triple

nodes.summary: For all assertions $P$ and $Q$ and every command $c$, if the total-correctness triple with precondition $P$, command $c$ and postcondition $Q$ is valid, then it is derivable in total-correctness Hoare logic.
nodes.title: Relative completeness of total-correctness Hoare logic

nodes.summary: A Hoare triple, given by a precondition $P$, a command $c$ and a postcondition $Q$, is derivable in the default inference system on Hoare triples, which is partial-correctness Hoare logic, if and only if it is valid for partial correctness.
nodes.title: Partial-correctness Hoare logic as an inference system

nodes.summary: For all assertions $P$ and $Q$ and every command $c$, the partial-correctness triple with precondition $P$, command $c$ and postcondition $Q$ is derivable if and only if, for all states $s$ and $t$ such that $P$ holds at $s$ and the pair $(s, t)$ lies in the relational denotation of $c$, $Q$ holds at $t$.
nodes.title: Partial-correctness Hoare logic matches the denotational semantics

nodes.summary: Let $b$ be a Boolean expression and $c$ a command. For a natural number $n$ and states $s$, $s'$, the loop $\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$ runs from $s$ to $s'$ in $n$ iterations when, started in $s$, it exits in $s'$ after exactly $n$ executions of the body $c$. This is the least relation such that the loop runs from $s$ to $s$ in $0$ iterations whenever $b$ evaluates to false in $s$, and the loop runs from…
nodes.title: Loop runs with a given number of iterations

nodes.summary: Let $b$ be a boolean expression, $c$ a command, $n$ a natural number and $s$, $t$ states. If the loop $\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$, started in $s$, exits in $t$ after exactly $n$ executions of the body $c$, then the loop $\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$ runs from $s$ to $t$ in the big-step semantics.
nodes.title: Counted loop runs are big-step executions

nodes.summary: Let $b$ be a Boolean expression, $c$ a command and $s$, $s'$ states. If the loop $\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$ has a terminating big-step execution from $s$ to $s'$, then there is a natural number $n$ such that the loop, started in $s$, exits in $s'$ after exactly $n$ executions of the body $c$.
nodes.title: Every terminating loop run has an iteration count

nodes.summary: Let $b$ be a boolean expression, $c$ a command and $s$ a state. If the loop $\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$, started in $s$, exits in a state $t$ after exactly $n$ executions of the body and also exits in a state $t'$ after exactly $m$ executions of the body, then $n = m$.
nodes.title: Uniqueness of the loop iteration count

nodes.summary: Let $b$ be a Boolean expression, $c$ a command and $s$ a state. If there are a natural number $n$ and a state $s'$ such that the loop $\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$, started in $s$, exits in $s'$ after exactly $n$ executions of the body $c$, then the iteration count of the loop from $s$ is such an $n$; otherwise it is $0$.
nodes.title: Loop iteration count

nodes.summary: Let $b$ be a Boolean expression, $c$ a command, $n$ a natural number and $s$, $s'$ states. If the loop $\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$, started in $s$, exits in $s'$ after exactly $n$ executions of the body $c$, then the iteration count of the loop from $s$ is $n$.
nodes.title: The iteration count of a terminating loop run

nodes.summary: Let $b$ be a Boolean expression, $c$ a command and $s$ a state. If the loop $\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$ has no terminating big-step execution from $s$ to any state, then the iteration count of the loop from $s$ is $0$.
nodes.title: The iteration count of a nonterminating loop is zero

nodes.summary: Derivability of total-correctness Hoare triples $\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}$, for assertions $P$, $Q$ (predicates on states) and IMP commands $c$, is the least relation closed under the following rules. In an assertion, $b$ for a boolean expression means that $b$ evaluates to true and $\neg b$ that it evaluates to false. Skip: $\{Q\}\,\mathtt{skip}\,\{Q\}$. Assignment: for a variable $x$ and an arithmetic expression $a$,…
nodes.title: Total-correctness Hoare logic

nodes.summary: For all assertions $P$ and $Q$ and every command $c$, if the triple $\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}$ is derivable in total-correctness Hoare logic, then it is valid for total correctness: every state satisfying $P$ has a terminating big-step execution of $c$ ending in a state that satisfies $Q$.
nodes.title: Soundness of total-correctness Hoare logic

nodes.summary: Let $P$, $P'$ and $Q$ be assertions and $c$ a command. If $P$ entails $P'$ (every state satisfying $P$ satisfies $P'$) and the triple $\{P'\}\,c\,\{Q\}$ is derivable in total-correctness Hoare logic, then so is $\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}$.
nodes.title: Precondition strengthening for total correctness

nodes.summary: For every IMP command $c$ and every assertion $Q$ (a predicate on states), the triple $\{\mathrm{wp}(c, Q)\}\,c\,\{Q\}$ is derivable in the total-correctness Hoare logic. Here $\mathrm{wp}(c, Q)$ is the semantic weakest precondition: it holds in a state $s$ exactly when there is a terminating execution of $c$ from $s$ ending in a state satisfying $Q$.
nodes.title: The weakest-precondition triple is derivable in total-correctness Hoare logic

nodes.summary: For all assertions $P$ and $Q$ and every command $c$, if the total-correctness Hoare triple $\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}$ is valid, then it is derivable in total-correctness Hoare logic.
nodes.title: Total-correctness Hoare logic is relatively complete

nodes.summary: For all assertions $P$ and $Q$ and every command $c$, if the triple with precondition $P$, command $c$ and postcondition $Q$ is derivable in total-correctness Hoare logic, then it is derivable in partial-correctness Hoare logic.
nodes.title: Total-correctness derivations give partial-correctness derivations

nodes.summary: For all assertions $P$, $Q$ (predicates on states) and every IMP command $c$, the triple $\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}$ is derivable in the total-correctness Hoare logic if and only if it is totally valid.
nodes.title: Soundness and relative completeness of total-correctness Hoare logic

nodes.summary: For all assertions $P$, $Q$ (predicates on states) and every IMP command $c$, the triple $\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}$ is derivable in the total-correctness Hoare logic if and only if for every state $s$ satisfying $P$ there is a state $s'$ such that $(s, s')$ lies in the relational denotation of $c$ and $s'$ satisfies $Q$.
nodes.title: Total-correctness Hoare logic is sound and complete for the denotational semantics

nodes.summary: A Hoare triple $\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}$ consists of a precondition $P$ and a postcondition $Q$, both assertions (predicates on states), and an IMP command $c$. It is the judgement form of both the partial-correctness and the total-correctness Hoare logic.
nodes.title: Hoare triples

nodes.summary: An empty type used only as a label: derivability of Hoare triples in the total-correctness Hoare logic is registered as an inference system under this tag, while partial-correctness derivability is the default inference system on Hoare triples.
nodes.title: Total-correctness tag for Hoare triples

nodes.summary: For every Hoare triple $\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}$, the triple is derivable in the default inference system on Hoare triples, which is partial-correctness Hoare logic, if and only if it is valid for partial correctness.
nodes.title: Derivability in the default inference system on Hoare triples is validity

nodes.summary: A Hoare triple, given by a precondition $P$, a command $c$ and a postcondition $Q$, is derivable in the inference system on Hoare triples tagged total correctness, which is total-correctness Hoare logic, if and only if it is valid for total correctness.
nodes.title: Total-correctness Hoare logic as an inference system

nodes.summary: A one-step simulation lifts to arbitrary finite iteration. The simulator `p` need not be invertible or a test.
nodes.title: A one-step simulation lifts to finite iteration

nodes.summary: An idempotent subidentity preserved by one step is preserved by iteration. This is a corollary of `star_simulation`; the test assumptions are explicit, with no additional algebraic structure.
nodes.title: Tests preserved by one step are preserved by iteration

nodes.title: Diagonal test relation of an assertion

nodes.title: Membership in a diagonal test relation

nodes.title: Diagonal tests are subidentities

nodes.title: Composing diagonal tests conjoins their assertions

nodes.summary: The verification inequality is precisely universal partial correctness: every execution from `P` ends in `Q`.
nodes.title: Verification inequality characterizes partial correctness

nodes.summary: A postcondition can be absorbed on the right exactly when it holds on every execution starting in the precondition.
nodes.title: Postcondition absorption characterizes partial correctness

nodes.title: Partial correctness as unreachability of the negated postcondition
