nodes.summary: A finite joint law consists of positive integers $n_X$ and $n_Y$ and a probability distribution on $\{0, \dots, n_X - 1\} \times \{0, \dots, n_Y - 1\}$.
nodes.title: Finite joint law

nodes.summary: The input law of a finite joint law $p$ on $\{0, \dots, n_X - 1\} \times \{0, \dots, n_Y - 1\}$ is its first marginal: the law on $\{0, \dots, n_X - 1\}$ that is the image of $p$ under $(x, y) \mapsto x$.
nodes.title: Input law

nodes.summary: The output law of a finite joint law $p$ of an input $X$ and an output $Y$ is the law of $Y$: the marginal of $p$ on the output alphabet, obtained by pushing $p$ forward along the projection onto the second coordinate.
nodes.title: Output law

nodes.summary: The mutual information of a finite joint law $p$ of $(X, Y)$ is $I(X; Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X, Y)$, where $H(X)$ and $H(Y)$ are the Shannon entropies in bits of the input and output laws of $p$, and $H(X, Y)$ is the Shannon entropy in bits of $p$.
nodes.title: Mutual information

nodes.summary: A finite extension of a finite joint law $p$ on $\{0, \dots, n_X - 1\} \times \{0, \dots, n_Y - 1\}$ consists of a positive integer $n_S$ and a probability law on triples $(x, y, s)$ with $s \in \{0, \dots, n_S - 1\}$ whose marginal on the pairs $(x, y)$ is exactly $p$.
nodes.title: Finite extension of a joint law

nodes.summary: The trivial extension of a finite joint law $p$ of an input $X$ and an output $Y$ has the one-letter auxiliary alphabet $\{0\}$ and, as its law, the law of $((X, Y), 0)$ for $(X, Y)$ distributed according to $p$; its $(X, Y)$ marginal is $p$.
nodes.title: Trivial extension

nodes.summary: For a finite extension $q$ of a finite joint law $p$, viewed as the law of a triple $(X, Y, S)$ with $S$ taking values in $\{0, \dots, n_S - 1\}$, the auxiliary law is the marginal law of $S$ under $q$.
nodes.title: Auxiliary marginal of an extension

nodes.summary: Let $q$ be a finite extension of a finite joint law of $(X, Y)$, that is, a law of $((X, Y), S)$ with an auxiliary variable $S$. Its input-auxiliary law is the joint law of $(X, S)$: the image of the law of $q$ under $((x, y), s) \mapsto (x, s)$.
nodes.title: Input-auxiliary law

nodes.summary: Let $q$ be a finite extension of a finite joint law of $(X, Y)$, that is, a law of $((X, Y), S)$ with an auxiliary variable $S$. Its output-auxiliary law is the joint law of $(Y, S)$: the image of the law of $q$ under $((x, y), s) \mapsto (y, s)$.
nodes.title: Output-auxiliary law

nodes.summary: For a finite extension $q$ of a finite joint law $p$, viewed as the law of a triple $(X, Y, S)$ whose $(X, Y)$ marginal is $p$, this is $I(X; S) = H(X) + H(S) - H(X, S)$, where $H(X)$ is the Shannon entropy in bits of the $X$ marginal of $p$, and $H(S)$ and $H(X, S)$ are the Shannon entropies in bits of the $S$ and $(X, S)$ marginals of $q$.
nodes.title: Mutual information between the input and the auxiliary

nodes.summary: For a finite extension $q$ of a finite joint law $p$, viewed as the law of a triple $(X, Y, S)$ whose $(X, Y)$ marginal is $p$, this is $H(Y \mid S) = H(Y, S) - H(S)$, where $H(Y, S)$ and $H(S)$ are the Shannon entropies in bits of the $(Y, S)$ and $S$ marginals of $q$.
nodes.title: Conditional entropy of the output given the auxiliary

nodes.summary: For a finite extension of a finite joint law, with input $X$, output $Y$ and auxiliary $S$, the conditional entropy of $Y$ given $(X, S)$ is $H(Y \mid X, S) = H(X, Y, S) - H(X, S)$, where $H$ denotes Shannon entropy in bits, $H(X, Y, S)$ is the entropy of the law of the extension and $H(X, S)$ is the entropy of its $(X, S)$ marginal.
nodes.title: Conditional entropy of the output given the input and the auxiliary

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a finite joint law of an input $X$ and an output $Y$ whose output alphabet has exactly one letter. Then for every finite extension of $p$ by an auxiliary $S$, the conditional entropy $H(Y \mid X, S)$ of the output given the input and the auxiliary is $0$.
nodes.title: Zero output entropy given input and auxiliary for a one-letter output

nodes.summary: For every finite joint law $p$, the auxiliary law of the trivial extension of $p$ is the point mass at $0$, the only letter of its one-letter auxiliary alphabet $\{0\}$.

nodes.summary: For every finite joint law $p$, the mutual information $I(X; S)$ between the input $X$ and the auxiliary $S$ in the trivial extension of $p$, whose auxiliary alphabet has a single letter, is $0$.

nodes.summary: The losing and the winning states of the Accelerated Zeckendorf Game are defined by simultaneous induction: a state is losing when every move from it leads to a winning state, and a state is winning when some move from it leads to a losing state. nodes.summary: A state $s$ is winning (the player to move has a winning strategy) if some move takes $s$ to a losing state. Winning and losing states are defined by simultaneous induction: a state is losing if every move from it reaches a winning state.

nodes.summary: A function $h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ has the *NS property* if it is monotone (weakly increasing) and, for all $z, z' \in \mathbb{N}$ and every natural number $i \ge 1$, $\lfloor z / 2^i \rfloor = \lfloor z' / 2^i \rfloor$ implies $\lfloor h(z) / 2^{i-1} \rfloor = \lfloor h(z') / 2^{i-1} \rfloor$.

nodes.summary: The identity function on the natural numbers does not have the NS property: $\lfloor 0/2 \rfloor = \lfloor 1/2 \rfloor$, but $0 \ne 1$.

nodes.summary: Let $z \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $h(a) \le h(b)$ whenever $a \le b \le z$, and $\lfloor h(a) / 2^{i-1} \rfloor = \lfloor h(b) / 2^{i-1} \rfloor$ whenever $a, b \le z$, $i \ge 1$ and $\lfloor a / 2^i \rfloor = \lfloor b / 2^i \rfloor$. Then the function sending $x$ to $h(x)$ for $x \le z$ and to $h(z)$ for $x > z$ has the NS property.

Snort

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph, let $k$ be a natural number, and let $A$ and $B$ be finite sets of vertices of $G$, the vertices coloured so far by the player to move and by the opponent. A legal move colours a vertex $v$ that lies in neither $A$ nor $B$ and has no neighbour in $B$. With move bound $0$ the player to move loses. With move bound $k + 1$ the player to move wins at $(A, B)$ exactly when some legal…
nodes.title: Snort positions with a move bound

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph. In Snort on $G$ the two players alternately colour a vertex that is not yet coloured and is not adjacent to any vertex coloured by the opponent, and a player with no legal move loses. The first player wins Snort on $G$ when the player who moves first has a winning strategy from the position in which no vertex is coloured.
nodes.title: First player wins Snort

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph. In Snort on $G$, two players alternately colour a vertex of $G$ that is not yet coloured, each with their own colour, and a player may not colour a vertex adjacent to a vertex of the opponent's colour; a player with no legal move loses. The second player wins Snort on $G$ if, starting from the position in which no vertex is coloured, the player who moves first has no winning…
nodes.title: Second-player win in Snort

nodes.summary: In Snort on a finite graph $G$, a pair $(u, v)$ of vertices is a response pair if $u \neq v$, $u$ and $v$ are not adjacent (so the first player colouring $u$ and the second answering $v$ is legal), and the first player, now to move, loses from the position in which the first player has coloured $u$ and the second player has coloured $v$.
nodes.title: Snort response pairs

nodes.summary: An opposition of a graph $G$ is an automorphism $f$ of $G$ such that for every vertex $v$, $f(f(v)) = v$, $f(v) \neq v$, and $f(v)$ is not adjacent to $v$; that is, an involutive automorphism moving every vertex outside its closed neighbourhood.
nodes.title: Oppositions

nodes.summary: A graph $G$ is opposable if it has an opposition: an automorphism $f$ of $G$ such that for every vertex $v$, $f(f(v)) = v$, $f(v) \neq v$, and $f(v)$ is not adjacent to $v$.
nodes.title: Opposable graphs

nodes.summary: A graph $G$ is almost opposable if there are a vertex $u$ and a set $S$ of vertices with $u \in S \subseteq N[u]$, where $N[u]$ is the closed neighbourhood of $u$ ($u$ together with its neighbours), such that the subgraph $G - S$ induced on the vertices outside $S$ is opposable.
nodes.title: Almost opposable graph

nodes.summary: A graph $G$ is compatibly almost opposable if there are a vertex $u$, a set $S$ of vertices with $u \in S \subseteq N[u]$ (the closed neighbourhood of $u$), an automorphism $\alpha$ of $G$ with $\alpha(\alpha(v)) = v$ for every vertex $v$, and an opposition $f$ of the subgraph $G - S$ induced on the vertices outside $S$, such that $\alpha(x) = f(x)$ for every vertex $x \notin S$.
nodes.title: Compatibly almost opposable graphs

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a graph. A subgraph $M$ of $K$ is an opposition matching of $K$ if it is a perfect matching of $K$ and for any two distinct edges $ab$ and $cd$ of $M$, $ac \in E(K) \iff bd \in E(K)$ and $ad \in E(K) \iff bc \in E(K)$.
nodes.title: Opposition matchings

nodes.summary: Let $G$ and $H$ be graphs with vertex sets $V$ and $W$, and let $\varphi$ be a Boolean function of four Boolean arguments. The product $G \varphi H$ is the graph on $V \times W$ in which two distinct vertices $(g_1, h_1)$ and $(g_2, h_2)$ are adjacent exactly when $\varphi(g_1 g_2 \in E(G), h_1 h_2 \in E(H), g_1 = g_2, h_1 = h_2)$ is true.
nodes.title: Graph product given by a Boolean formula

nodes.summary: For simple graphs $G$ on $V$ and $H$ on $W$, the strong product $G \boxtimes H$ is the simple graph on $V \times W$ in which $(g_1, h_1)$ and $(g_2, h_2)$ are adjacent if and only if $g_1 = g_2$ and $h_1 h_2$ is an edge of $H$, or $g_1 g_2$ is an edge of $G$ and $h_1 = h_2$, or $g_1 g_2$ is an edge of $G$ and $h_1 h_2$ is an edge of $H$.
nodes.title: Strong product of graphs

nodes.summary: For a graph $G$, vertices $u$ and $v$ of $G$ and a natural number $n$, the $n$-firework of $G$ at $(u, v)$ is the graph obtained from $G$ by adding $2n$ new vertices, $n$ of which are adjacent only to $u$ and the other $n$ adjacent only to $v$.
nodes.title: Firework of a graph

nodes.summary: For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and natural numbers $n_0, \dots, n_{k-1}$, the $k$-dimensional strong grid $P_{n_0} \boxtimes \cdots \boxtimes P_{n_{k-1}}$ is the simple graph whose vertices are the tuples $(x_0, \dots, x_{k-1})$ of integers with $0 \le x_i < n_i$ for each $i$, in which two vertices $x$ and $y$ are adjacent if and only if $x \ne y$ and $|x_i - y_i| \le 1$ for every $i$.
nodes.title: Strong grid

nodes.summary: For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and side lengths $n_1, \dots, n_k \in \mathbb{N}$, the $k$-dimensional Cartesian grid has as vertices the tuples $(x_1, \dots, x_k)$ of integers with $0 \le x_i < n_i$ for each $i$, and two tuples are adjacent when they differ in exactly one coordinate, and there by exactly one. It is the Cartesian product $P_{n_1} \square \cdots \square P_{n_k}$ of the paths $P_{n_i}$ on $n_i$ vertices.
nodes.title: Cartesian grid

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, the king's graph of the $n \times m$ board is the simple graph whose vertices are the pairs $(i, j)$ with $0 \le i < n$ and $0 \le j < m$, in which two distinct pairs $(i, j)$ and $(i', j')$ are adjacent when $|i - i'| \le 1$ and $|j - j'| \le 1$.
nodes.title: King's graph

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, the knight's graph of the $n \times m$ board is the simple graph whose vertices are the pairs $(i, j)$ with $0 \le i < n$ and $0 \le j < m$, in which two pairs $(i, j)$ and $(i', j')$ are adjacent when either $|i - i'| = 1$ and $|j - j'| = 2$, or $|i - i'| = 2$ and $|j - j'| = 1$.
nodes.title: Knight's graph

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, the bishop's graph on the $n \times m$ board has as vertices the cells $(i, j)$ with $0 \le i < n$ and $0 \le j < m$, and two distinct cells $(i, j)$ and $(i', j')$ are adjacent when they lie on a common diagonal, that is, when $|i - i'| = |j - j'|$.
nodes.title: Bishop's graph

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, the queen's graph of the $n \times m$ board is the simple graph whose vertices are the pairs $(i, j)$ with $0 \le i < n$ and $0 \le j < m$, in which two distinct pairs $(i, j)$ and $(i', j')$ are adjacent when $i = i'$, or $j = j'$, or $|i - i'| = |j - j'|$; that is, when they share a row, a column or a diagonal.
nodes.title: Queen's graph

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph and let $(u, v)$ be a response pair of $G$ whose distance in $G$ is at least $3$ (infinite distance, when $u$ and $v$ lie in different components, is allowed). If the second player wins Snort on $G$, then for every natural number $n$ at least the number $|V(G)|$ of vertices of $G$, the second player wins Snort on the $n$-firework of $G$ at $(u, v)$.

nodes.summary: Let $G$ and $H$ be graphs. If $G$ is almost opposable and $H$ has a universal vertex, that is, a vertex adjacent to every other vertex of $H$, then the strong product $G \boxtimes H$ is almost opposable.
nodes.title: Strong products with a graph that has a universal vertex

nodes.summary: Let $G$ and $H$ be compatibly almost opposable graphs. Suppose that for some vertex $u$ of $G$ there are an involutive automorphism $\alpha$ of $G$ and an opposition $f$ of the induced subgraph $G - u$ on the vertices other than $u$ such that $\alpha(x) = f(x)$ for every vertex $x \neq u$. Then the Cartesian product $G \square H$ is compatibly almost opposable.
nodes.title: Cartesian products of compatibly almost opposable graphs

nodes.summary: Let $k \ge 1$ and $n_1, \dots, n_k \ge 1$. Then the $k$-dimensional strong grid $P_{n_1} \boxtimes \cdots \boxtimes P_{n_k}$, the strong product of the paths $P_{n_i}$ on $n_i$ vertices, is almost opposable.
nodes.title: Almost opposability of strong grids

nodes.summary: Let $k \ge 1$ and $n_1, \dots, n_k \ge 1$, and let $G = P_{n_1} \square \cdots \square P_{n_k}$ be the $k$-dimensional Cartesian grid, the Cartesian product of the paths $P_{n_i}$ on $n_i$ vertices. Then $G$ is almost opposable if and only if at most one of $n_1, \dots, n_k$ is even, and $G$ is opposable if more than one of them is even.
nodes.title: Opposability of Cartesian grids

Sprague–Grundy theorem

nodes.summary: Write $x \to y$ when there is a move from position $x$ to position $y$, and assume there is no infinite sequence of moves $x_0 \to x_1 \to x_2 \to \cdots$. Call a set $P$ of positions stable if no move leads from a position in $P$ to a position in $P$, and absorbing if from every position outside $P$ some move leads to a position in $P$. Then any two stable and absorbing sets of positions are equal.
nodes.title: Uniqueness of the P-positions of a terminating impartial game

nodes.summary: An impartial game consists of a type of positions, a starting position, for each position $p$ a finite set of positions reachable from $p$ in one move, and a rank function assigning a natural number to each position such that every move strictly decreases the rank: if $q$ is reachable from $p$ in one move, then $\mathrm{rank}(q) < \mathrm{rank}(p)$.
nodes.title: Impartial game

nodes.summary: In an impartial game $G$, the P-positions are defined by well-founded recursion along moves: a position $p$ is a P-position if and only if no position reachable from $p$ in one move is a P-position. Positions that are not P-positions are called N-positions.
nodes.title: P-positions

nodes.summary: The sum $G + H$ of two impartial games $G$ and $H$ is the impartial game whose positions are the pairs $(a, b)$ of a position $a$ of $G$ and a position $b$ of $H$, and in which a move changes exactly one component: from $(a, b)$ one may move to $(a', b)$ for any move from $a$ to $a'$ in $G$, or to $(a, b')$ for any move from $b$ to $b'$ in $H$. Its starting position is the pair of the starting positions of $G$ and…
nodes.title: Sum of impartial games

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, the Nim heap of size $n$ is the impartial game whose positions are $0, 1, \dots, n$, whose starting position is $n$, and in which a move from $k$ goes to any $j < k$; the rank of a position is its value.
nodes.title: Nim heap

nodes.summary: Two impartial games $G$ and $H$ are equivalent when no third game tells them apart as summands: for every impartial game $K$, the starting position of the sum $G + K$ is a P-position if and only if the starting position of the sum $H + K$ is a P-position. The starting position of a sum is the pair of the starting positions of its summands.
nodes.title: Equivalence of impartial games

nodes.summary: In an impartial game $G$, a position $p$ is a P-position if and only if every position reachable from $p$ in one move is not a P-position.
nodes.title: Recursive characterization of P-positions

nodes.summary: Every impartial game $G$ is equivalent to a Nim heap: there is a natural number $n$ such that $G$ is equivalent to the Nim heap of size $n$.

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ and let $k$ be a natural number. In the $(k+1:k)$-pebbling game on $G$, a move removes $k+1$ pebbles from a vertex and adds $k$ pebbles to an adjacent vertex. This is the set of natural numbers $m$ such that every position with $m$ pebbles in total (a number of pebbles on each vertex, summing to $m$) is an N-position, that is, not a P-position.
nodes.title: Totals at which every pebbling game is an N-game

nodes.summary: For every simple graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the number $0$ does not belong to the set of totals $m$ such that every $(k+1:k)$-pebbling game on $G$ with $m$ pebbles is an N-game. Indeed, the empty position admits no move, so it is a P-game.

reading_title.source: Winning positions of $(2:1)$-pebbling on $K_2$

nodes.summary: Let $a = (a_0, a_1)$ be a position of the $(2:1)$-pebbling game on the complete graph $K_2$, with $a_0$ and $a_1$ pebbles on its two vertices. If $a_0 + a_1$ is even, then $a$ is an N-position (that is, not a P-position) if and only if $a_0 \not\equiv a_1 \pmod 3$. If $a_0 + a_1$ is odd, then $a$ is an N-position if and only if $a_0 \equiv a_1 \pmod 3$.

Let $a = (a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3)$ be a position, with $a_i$ pebbles on $v_i$, that lies in $Y_{aabc}$: for some $i$, $a_{i+2} \equiv a_i + 2$ and $a_{i+1} \equiv a_{i-1} + 1 \pmod 4$. Then $a$ is an N-position, that is, not a P-position.

Impartial placement games

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite set of cells and let $E$ be a predicate on subsets of $\alpha$, the condition under which play has ended. A position $S \subseteq \alpha$ (the set of occupied cells) is terminal when $E(S)$ holds or $S = \alpha$: play has ended, or every cell is occupied. These are the positions with no options.
nodes.title: Terminal positions of a placement game

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite set of cells and let $E$ be a predicate on subsets of $\alpha$, the condition under which play has ended. A position $S \subseteq \alpha$ is an ult when it is not terminal but has a terminal option: $S$ is not terminal, and there is a cell $c \notin S$ such that $S \cup \{c\}$ is terminal.
nodes.title: Ults of a placement game

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite set of cells and let $E$ be a predicate on subsets of $\alpha$, the condition under which play has ended. A position $S \subseteq \alpha$ is a penult when it is not terminal and all of its options are ults: $S$ is not terminal, and $S \cup \{c\}$ is an ult for every cell $c \notin S$.
nodes.title: Penults of a placement game

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite set of cells and $E$ a predicate on subsets of $\alpha$ saying when play has ended. In the placement game on $\alpha$ with end predicate $E$, a position $T$ is a move from a position $S$ if and only if $E(S)$ fails and $T = S \cup \{c\}$ for some cell $c \notin S$.
nodes.title: Moves of a placement game

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite set of cells and $E$ a predicate on subsets of $\alpha$ saying when play has ended. The player to move from a position $S \subseteq \alpha$ wins the placement game on $\alpha$ with end predicate $E$ when $S$ is not a P-position of that game under normal play, in which the player unable to move loses.

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite set of cells and $E$ a predicate on subsets of $\alpha$ saying when play has ended. In the placement game on $\alpha$ with end predicate $E$, the player to move from a position $S \subseteq \alpha$ wins if and only if $E(S)$ fails and there is a cell $c \notin S$ such that the player to move from $S \cup \{c\}$ does not win.
nodes.title: Normal-play recursion for placement games

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite set of cells. For every predicate $E$ on subsets of $\alpha$, the full board $\alpha$ is a terminal position of the placement game with ending condition $E$.

nodes.summary: For a finite set $s$ of natural numbers, $\operatorname{mex}(s)$ is the least natural number that does not belong to $s$.
nodes.title: Minimum excludant of a finite set

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a finite set of natural numbers and $m$ a natural number. Then $\operatorname{mex}(s)$, the least natural number not in $s$, equals $m$ if and only if $m \notin s$ and every natural number $n < m$ lies in $s$.
nodes.title: Characterization of the minimum excludant

nodes.summary: For a rule function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, the Grundy number $G_f(x)$ of a pile of $x$ stones in Maximum Nim is defined by recursion on $x$ as the mex (least natural number not in the set) of $\{G_f(x - u) : 1 \le u \le \min(f(x), x)\}$, the Grundy numbers of the positions reachable from $x$ by removing $u$ stones.
nodes.title: Grundy numbers of Maximum Nim

nodes.summary: For every rule function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and every pile size $x \in \mathbb{N}$, the Grundy number $G_f(x)$ of a pile of $x$ stones in Maximum Nim with rule function $f$ equals the mex (least natural number not in the set) of $\{G_f(x - u) : 1 \le u \le \min(f(x), x)\}$.
nodes.title: Recursive formula for Maximum Nim Grundy numbers

nodes.summary: For a rule function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, the Maximum Nim game with rule $f$ is the impartial game whose positions are the pile sizes $x \in \mathbb{N}$, in which the moves from $x$ go to $x - u$ for each $u$ with $1 \le u \le \min(f(x), x)$. The rank of a position is the pile size itself, and the starting position is the empty pile $0$.
nodes.title: The Maximum Nim game

nodes.summary: Let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a rule function and let $x$ be a pile size. The position $x$ of the Maximum Nim game with rule $f$ is a P-position if and only if, for every $u$ with $1 \le u \le \min(f(x), x)$, the position $x - u$ is not a P-position.

Smith's remoteness function

nodes.summary: For an impartial game $G$, the remoteness $R(p)$ of a position $p$ of $G$ is defined by well-founded recursion along moves; the options of $p$ are the positions reachable from $p$ in one move. If $p$ has no options, then $R(p) = 0$. Otherwise, if some option $q$ of $p$ has $R(q)$ even, then $R(p)$ is $1$ plus the least even value of $R(q)$ over the options $q$ of $p$; if every option $q$ of $p$ has $R(q)$ odd, then…
nodes.title: Smith's remoteness function

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an impartial game, $p$ a position of $G$, and $R$ the set of remotenesses of the options of $p$ (the positions reachable from $p$ in one move). If $R$ contains an even number, the remoteness of $p$ is $1$ plus the least even element of $R$; otherwise, if $R$ is nonempty, it is $1$ plus the largest element of $R$; and if $R$ is empty, it is $0$.

nodes.title: Euclid P-position test

nodes.summary: The moves of Euclid from a pair $(a, b)$ of natural numbers are as follows. If $a = b$, $a = 0$ or $b = 0$, there are none. If $0 < a < b$, the moves are to the pairs $(a, b - ja)$ for every integer $j \ge 1$ with $ja < b$; if $0 < b < a$, the moves are to the pairs $(a - jb, b)$ for every integer $j \ge 1$ with $jb < a$.

Slow Nim

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a position of Slow$A$-Nim on $n$ stacks, with $p_i$ tokens on stack $i$, and let $S$ be a set of stacks. The position after playing on $S$ is obtained by removing one token from each stack of $S$: its stack $i$ holds $p_i - 1$ if $i \in S$ and $p_i$ otherwise, where an empty stack of $S$ stays empty.

The options of $p$ in Slow$A$-Nim are the positions obtained from $p$ by choosing a nonempty set $S$ of stacks with $|S| \in A$, each holding at least one token, and removing one token from each stack of $S$.

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be a finite set of natural numbers and let $p$ be a position of Slow$A$-Nim on $n$ stacks. For each stack $i$, let $u_i(p)$ be the least height of stack $i$ over all terminal positions (positions with no moves) reachable from $p$ by a sequence of zero or more moves. The reduction of $p$ is the position $r(p)$ with $r(p)_i = p_i - u_i(p)$ for every stack $i$.

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be a finite set of natural numbers and $p$ a position of Slow$A$-Nim on $n$ stacks. A finite sequence $S_1, \dots, S_m$ of sets of stacks is legal from $p$ when it is empty, or when $S_1$ is nonempty, $|S_1| \in A$, every stack in $S_1$ holds at least one token in $p$, and $S_2, \dots, S_m$ is legal from the position obtained from $p$ by removing one token from each stack of $S_1$.

nodes.title: Terminal positions of exact slow $k$-NIM

nodes.summary: Let $k$ and $f$ be natural numbers and let $x$ be a position on $k + 1$ piles. Call $x$ terminal when $k = 0$ or fewer than $k$ of its piles are nonempty. The value at $f$ and $x$ is $0$ when $f = 0$ or $x$ is terminal; otherwise it is $1$ plus the value at $f - 1$ and the position reached from $x$ by the M-move. Thus it counts the M-moves played from $x$, stopping at a terminal position or after $f$ moves.
nodes.title: Fuel-bounded length of M-rule play

nodes.summary: Let $k, f \in \mathbb{N}$ and $x \in \mathbb{N}^{k+1}$, and write $M_f(x)$ for the number of M-rule steps from $x$ in Slow$\{k\}$-Nim on $k + 1$ stacks, counted for at most $f$ steps. Then $M_{f+1}(x) = 0$ if $x$ has no options, and otherwise $M_{f+1}(x) = 1 + M_f(x')$, where $x'$ is the position obtained from $x$ by the M-move.

Sylver coinage

nodes.summary: For a set $M$ of natural numbers (a position of Sylver Coinage), the set $L(M)$ of legal moves consists of the natural numbers that are not finite sums of elements of $M$, repetitions allowed, i.e. the natural numbers outside the additive submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$ generated by $M$. Since $0$ is the empty sum, every legal move is positive.
nodes.title: Legal moves in Sylver Coinage

nodes.summary: A set $M$ of natural numbers is a P-position of Sylver Coinage when $1 \notin M$ and, for every legal move $q$ of $M$, the position $M \cup \{q\}$ is an N-position. P-positions and N-positions are defined together, as a mutual inductive definition. In particular a position whose only legal move is $1$ is a P-position (the player to move must name $1$ and loses).
nodes.title: P-positions of Sylver Coinage

nodes.summary: A position $M$ of Sylver Coinage is an N-position (the player to move wins) when either $1 \in M$, so that the previous player named $1$ and lost, or some legal move $q$ of $M$ leads to a P-position $M \cup \{q\}$. N-positions and P-positions are defined together inductively by these rules.
nodes.title: N-positions of Sylver Coinage

nodes.summary: For every set $M$ of natural numbers, $0$ is not a legal move of the Sylver Coinage position $M$.
nodes.title: Zero is never a legal move

reading_title.source: The position $\{2, 3\}$ is a P-position

nodes.summary: In Sylver Coinage, the position $\{2, 3\}$ is a P-position: its only legal move is $1$.
nodes.title: The position $\{2, 3\}$ is a P-position

nodes.summary: The position $\{2\}$ of Sylver Coinage is an N-position: the player to move wins by naming $3$, which leaves the P-position $\{2, 3\}$.
nodes.title: Opening with 2 loses

nodes.summary: For every prime $p > 3$, the position $\{p\}$ of Sylver Coinage is a P-position: a first player who opens with $p$ wins.
nodes.title: Hutchings' theorem

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a position of Sylver Coinage with set of legal moves $L(M)$. A natural number $x$ is an end of $M$ if $x \in L(M)$ and every $y \in L(M)$ with $y \ne x$ is still a legal move of the position $M \cup \{x\}$; that is, naming $x$ eliminates no other legal move.
nodes.title: Ends of a Sylver Coinage position

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a position of Sylver Coinage whose set of legal moves $L(M)$ has a greatest element $F$. Then $F$ is an end of $M$.
nodes.title: The largest legal move is an end

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a set of natural numbers whose set of legal moves $L(M)$ has a greatest element $F > 1$, and suppose that $F$ is the only end of $M$ (so $M$ is an ender). Then for every legal move $x$ of $M$ with $x < F$, the number $F$ is not a legal move of $M \cup \{x\}$.
nodes.title: In an ender, every smaller move eliminates the largest legal move

nodes.summary: Let $M$ be a position of Sylver Coinage whose set of legal moves $L(M)$ has a greatest element $F$ with $F > 1$. If every end of $M$ equals $F$ (that is, $M$ is an ender), then $M$ is an N-position.

If $F \notin S$ and every natural number $n > F$ lies in $S$ (so $F$ is the Frobenius number of $S$), then $x \in S \iff F - x \notin S$ for every natural number $x \le F$.

nodes.summary: Fix a natural number $\ell$. The sequence $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ is defined recursively: $a_n$ is the least natural number greater than $\ell$ that differs from $a_i$ and from $a_i + i + \ell + 1$ for every $i < n$. Writing $b_i = a_i + i + \ell + 1$, this says that $a_n$ is the least natural number outside $\{0, 1, \dots, \ell\} \cup \{a_i, b_i : i < n\}$; in particular $a_0 = \ell + 1$ and $b_0 = 2\ell + 2$.

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio. The sequence $g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ of Komak et al. is defined by recursion on $n$: if some $m < n$ satisfies $\lfloor n\varphi \rfloor = \lfloor m\varphi^2 \rfloor + 1$, then $g(n) = 1 - g(m)$ for the least such $m$; otherwise $g(n) = 1$.

nodes.summary: Social choice theory studies rules that aggregate individual preferences into a collective ranking or choice, and the impossibility theorems that limit them.
nodes.title: Social choice theory
Arrow's impossibility theorem

nodes.summary: A strict total order on a type $\alpha$ consists of a relation $<$ on $\alpha$ that is irreflexive ($a < a$ holds for no $a$), transitive ($a < b$ and $b < c$ imply $a < c$) and total on distinct elements ($a \ne b$ implies $a < b$ or $b < a$). Here it models a strict preference over alternatives.
nodes.title: Strict preference orders for Arrow's theorem

nodes.summary: A relation $<$ on a type $\alpha$ that is irreflexive ($a < a$ holds for no $a$), transitive ($a < b$ and $b < c$ imply $a < c$) and total on distinct elements ($a \ne b$ implies $a < b$ or $b < a$) defines a strict total order on $\alpha$.
nodes.title: Strict total order from a relation (Arrow's theorem)

nodes.summary: For a strict total order $T$ on a type $\alpha$, this is its underlying binary relation $\lt _T$ on $\alpha$.
nodes.title: Preference relation of a strict total order (Arrow's theorem)

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a strict total order on a type $\alpha$, and write $a \lt _T b$ for its relation. Then for every $a \in \alpha$, $a \lt _T a$ does not hold.
nodes.title: Irreflexivity of strict preference (Arrow's theorem)

nodes.summary: If $<$ is a strict total order on a type $\alpha$ and $a, b, c \in \alpha$ satisfy $a < b$ and $b < c$, then $a < c$.
nodes.title: Strict preference orders for Arrow's theorem are transitive

nodes.summary: If $<$ is a strict total order on a type $\alpha$ and $a, b \in \alpha$ are distinct, then $a < b$ or $b < a$.
nodes.title: Strict preference orders for Arrow's theorem are total

nodes.summary: A profile assigns to each voter a strict total order on the alternatives.
nodes.title: Preference profile (Arrow's theorem)

nodes.summary: A social welfare function maps each unrestricted profile to a social strict total order.
nodes.title: Social welfare function

nodes.summary: A social welfare function $F$ satisfies the Pareto condition if for every profile $p$ and all alternatives $a, b$, whenever every voter strictly prefers $a$ to $b$ in $p$, the social order $F(p)$ also strictly prefers $a$ to $b$.
nodes.title: Pareto condition

nodes.summary: A social welfare function $F$ satisfies independence of irrelevant alternatives if for all profiles $p_1, p_2$ and all alternatives $a, b$ the following holds: if every voter strictly prefers $a$ to $b$ in $p_1$ exactly when that voter strictly prefers $a$ to $b$ in $p_2$, then $F(p_1)$ strictly prefers $a$ to $b$ exactly when $F(p_2)$ does.
nodes.title: Independence of irrelevant alternatives

nodes.summary: A voter $d$ is a dictator for a social welfare function $F$ if for every profile $p$ and all alternatives $a, b$, whenever $d$ strictly prefers $a$ to $b$ in $p$, the social order $F(p)$ also strictly prefers $a$ to $b$.
nodes.title: Dictator of a social welfare function

nodes.summary: A social welfare function $F$ is dictatorial if some voter $d$ is a dictator for $F$: for every profile $p$ and all alternatives $a, b$, whenever $d$ strictly prefers $a$ to $b$ in $p$, the social order $F(p)$ also strictly prefers $a$ to $b$.
nodes.title: Dictatorial social welfare function

nodes.summary: Suppose there are finitely many alternatives, at least three of them, and finitely many voters, at least one. Then every social welfare function, which assigns a strict total order of the alternatives to each profile of strict total orders (one per voter), that satisfies the Pareto condition and independence of irrelevant alternatives is dictatorial.
nodes.title: Arrow's impossibility theorem for strict preferences, general form

nodes.summary: Suppose there are finitely many alternatives, at least three of them, and finitely many voters, at least one. Then every social welfare function, which assigns a strict total order of the alternatives to each profile of strict total orders (one per voter), that satisfies the Pareto condition and independence of irrelevant alternatives is dictatorial.
nodes.title: Arrow's impossibility theorem for strict preferences

For a relation $R$ on $A$, say $R$ strictly ranks $a$ above $b$ if $R(a, b)$ holds and…

Suppose that each vote is correct with probability $p$, that is $\mu(X_i = \text{true}) = p$ for every $i$. For…

Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem

nodes.summary: A strict total order on a type $\alpha$ is a binary relation $<$ on $\alpha$ that is irreflexive ($a < a$ holds for no $a$), transitive ($a < b$ and $b < c$ imply $a < c$) and total on distinct elements ($a \ne b$ implies $a < b$ or $b < a$). In the Gibbard–Satterthwaite development it models a voter's strict preference over alternatives.
nodes.title: Strict preference orders for the Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem

nodes.summary: A binary relation $<$ on a type $\alpha$ that is irreflexive ($a < a$ holds for no $a$), transitive ($a < b$ and $b < c$ imply $a < c$) and total on distinct elements ($a \ne b$ implies $a < b$ or $b < a$) defines a strict total order on $\alpha$ whose relation is $<$.
nodes.title: Building a strict preference order in the Gibbard–Satterthwaite setting

nodes.summary: The relation of a strict total order $T$ on a type $\alpha$ is its underlying binary relation $\lt _T$ on $\alpha$, which is irreflexive, transitive, and relates any two distinct elements in one direction or the other.
nodes.title: Relation of a strict preference order

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a strict total order on a type $\alpha$, with relation $\lt _T$. Then $a \lt _T a$ fails for every $a \in \alpha$.
nodes.title: Irreflexivity of strict preference

nodes.summary: Let $<$ be the relation of a strict total order on a type $\alpha$. If $a, b, c \in \alpha$ satisfy $a < b$ and $b < c$, then $a < c$.
nodes.title: Transitivity of strict preferences in the Gibbard–Satterthwaite setting

nodes.summary: Let $<$ be the relation of a strict total order on a type $\alpha$. If $a, b \in \alpha$ and $a \ne b$, then $a < b$ or $b < a$.
nodes.title: Strict preferences in the Gibbard–Satterthwaite setting are total

nodes.summary: For a type $A$ of alternatives and a type $V$ of voters, a profile is a function assigning to each voter $i \in V$ a strict total order $\lt _i$ on $A$, the strict preference of voter $i$.
nodes.title: Preference profiles for the Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem

nodes.summary: For a type $A$ of alternatives and a type $V$ of voters, a resolute social choice function is a function $F$ sending each profile $p$ (an assignment of a strict total order on $A$ to each voter in $V$) to a single chosen alternative $F(p) \in A$.
nodes.title: Social choice functions

nodes.summary: For a strict total order $o$ on the alternatives, write $x \succ_o y$ when $x$ is related to $y$ by $o$ ($o$ ranks $x$ above $y$). An alternative $t$ is top-ranked by $o$ when $t \succ_o b$ for every alternative $b \ne t$.
nodes.title: Top-ranked alternative

nodes.summary: A resolute social choice function $F$ is onto when every alternative $a$ is chosen at some profile, that is, $F(p) = a$ for some profile $p$.
nodes.title: Onto social choice function

nodes.summary: Let $p_1$ and $p_2$ be profiles, each assigning a strict total order on the alternatives to every voter, and let $i$ be a voter. Then $p_2$ differs from $p_1$ at most at voter $i$ when $p_1(j) = p_2(j)$ for every voter $j \ne i$.
nodes.title: Profiles differing only at one voter

nodes.summary: For a strict total order $P$, write $x \succ_P y$ when $x$ is related to $y$ by $P$ ($P$ ranks $x$ above $y$). A resolute social choice function $F$ is strategy-proof when, for all profiles $p_1$, $p_2$ and every voter $i$ such that $p_1(j) = p_2(j)$ for all voters $j \ne i$, it is not the case that $F(p_2) \succ_{p_1(i)} F(p_1)$: no voter gains by misreporting alone, judged by the true order $p_1(i)$.
nodes.title: Strategy-proof social choice function

nodes.summary: For a resolute social choice function $F$, a voter $d$ is a dictator when, for every profile $p$, the chosen alternative $F(p)$ is top-ranked in the preference order $p(d)$ of voter $d$.
nodes.title: Dictator of a social choice function

nodes.summary: A resolute social choice function $F$ is dictatorial when some voter is a dictator for $F$: there is a voter $d$ such that, for every profile $p$, the chosen alternative $F(p)$ is top-ranked in the preference order $p(d)$ of voter $d$.
nodes.title: Dictatorial social choice function

nodes.summary: Let the set of alternatives be finite and the set of voters be finite and nonempty, and suppose there are at least three distinct alternatives. Then every resolute social choice function on profiles of strict preference orders that is onto and strategy-proof is dictatorial.
nodes.title: Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem, finiteness form

nodes.summary: Let the set of alternatives be finite and the set of voters be finite and nonempty, and suppose there are at least three distinct alternatives. Then every resolute social choice function on profiles of strict preference orders that is onto and strategy-proof is dictatorial.
nodes.title: Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem

nodes.summary: Cooperative game theory studies games in which coalitions of players can make binding agreements, and solution concepts such as the core and the Shapley value for dividing a coalition's worth.
nodes.title: Cooperative game theory
Shapley value

nodes.summary: Given a set $N$ of players, a cooperative game on $N$ is a function $v$ that assigns to every coalition $S \subseteq N$ a real number $v(S)$, the worth of $S$, such that $v(\emptyset) = 0$.
nodes.title: Cooperative game with transferable utility

nodes.summary: Let $v$ be a cooperative game on a finite set $N$ of players. A player $i \in N$ is a null player of $v$ if $v(S \cup \{i\}) = v(S)$ for every coalition $S \subseteq N$ with $i \notin S$.
nodes.title: Null player

nodes.summary: Let $N$ be a finite set of players and $\varphi$ an $\mathbb{R}$-linear map from cooperative games on $N$ (added and scaled pointwise) to payoff vectors in $\mathbb{R}^N$. Then $\varphi$ is efficient if for every game $v$ the payoffs add up to the worth of the grand coalition: $\sum_{i \in N} \varphi(v)_i = v(N)$.
nodes.title: Efficient value

nodes.summary: Let $N$ be a finite set of players and $\varphi$ an $\mathbb{R}$-linear map from cooperative games on $N$ (added and scaled pointwise) to payoff vectors in $\mathbb{R}^N$. Then $\varphi$ is symmetric if for every game $v$ and every permutation $\sigma$ of $N$ with $v(\sigma(S)) = v(S)$ for all coalitions $S \subseteq N$, every player $i$ satisfies $\varphi(v)_{\sigma(i)} = \varphi(v)_i$.
nodes.title: Symmetric value

nodes.summary: Let $N$ be a finite set of players and $\varphi$ an $\mathbb{R}$-linear map from cooperative games on $N$ (added and scaled pointwise) to payoff vectors in $\mathbb{R}^N$. Then $\varphi$ satisfies the null player axiom if $\varphi(v)_i = 0$ for every game $v$ and every null player $i$ of $v$.
nodes.title: Null player axiom
Bondareva–Shapley theorem

nodes.summary: A payoff vector $x \colon N \to \mathbb{R}$ is a core allocation of a cooperative game $v$ on a finite set $N$ of players if it is efficient, $\sum_{i \in N} x_i = v(N)$, and coalitionally rational, $v(S) \le \sum_{i \in S} x_i$ for every coalition $S \subseteq N$.
nodes.title: Core allocation

nodes.summary: A cooperative game $v$ on a finite set $N$ of players is balanced if for every family of real weights $(\lambda_S)_{S \subseteq N}$ with $\lambda_S \ge 0$ for every coalition $S \subseteq N$ and $\sum_{S \subseteq N,\, i \in S} \lambda_S = 1$ for every player $i \in N$, one has $\sum_{S \subseteq N} \lambda_S \, v(S) \le v(N)$.
nodes.title: Balanced cooperative game

nodes.summary: Let $v$ be a cooperative game with transferable utility on a finite set $N$ of players. Then $v$ has a core allocation $x \colon N \to \mathbb{R}$, that is, the core of $v$ is nonempty, if and only if $v$ is balanced.
nodes.title: Bondareva–Shapley theorem

nodes.summary: Mathematical biology models populations, genomes, and biochemical networks, from coalescents and reaction dynamics to the algorithms that read biological sequences.
nodes.title: Mathematical Biology

nodes.summary: Mathematical models of allele frequencies in populations under random mating, selection, mutation, migration and genetic drift, including the Wright–Fisher and Moran models and their diffusion limits.
nodes.title: Population genetics

nodes.summary: The Wright–Fisher diffusion as the continuum limit of allele-frequency dynamics: generator and semigroup, fixation probabilities, absorption and sojourn times, mutation and stationary laws, allele age and the Poisson random field.
nodes.title: Diffusion theory
Wright–Fisher diffusion

nodes.summary: The backward generator of the Wright–Fisher diffusion with genic selection, time in units of `2N` generations and scaled selection coefficient `σ = 2Ns`: `(L_σ u)(x) = x (1 - x) / 2 · u''(x) + σ x (1 - x) · u'(x)`.
nodes.title: Backward generator of the Wright–Fisher diffusion with selection

nodes.summary: Kimura's fixation probability of an allele at initial frequency `x` with scaled selection coefficient `σ = 2Ns`: `(1 - e^{-2σx}) / (1 - e^{-2σ})`, and `x` in the neutral case.
nodes.title: Kimura's fixation probability

nodes.summary: Kimura–Ohta mean time to absorption (loss or fixation) of a neutral allele at frequency `x`, in units of `2N` generations: `-2 (x log x + (1 - x) log (1 - x))`. In generations this is `-4N (x ln x + (1 - x) ln (1 - x))`.
nodes.title: Kimura–Ohta mean absorption time of a neutral allele

nodes.summary: Wright's (unnormalized) stationary density of the Wright–Fisher diffusion with scaled mutation rates `α` (towards the allele) and `β` (away from it): `x ^ (2α - 1) (1 - x) ^ (2β - 1)` (real powers).
nodes.title: Wright's stationary density of the Wright–Fisher diffusion

nodes.summary: The constant `K σ` such that `(kimuraFixation σ)' x = K σ · e^{-2σx}`: `1` if `σ = 0`, and `2σ / (1 - e^{-2σ})` otherwise.
nodes.title: Slope constant of Kimura's fixation probability

nodes.summary: For `σ ≠ 0` the denominator `1 - e^{-2σ}` of Kimura's formula does not vanish.
nodes.title: Denominator of Kimura's formula is nonzero

nodes.summary: An allele that is absent is never fixed.
nodes.title: Kimura's fixation probability vanishes at frequency zero

nodes.summary: An allele that is already fixed stays fixed.
nodes.title: Kimura's fixation probability equals one at frequency one

nodes.summary: Neutral case: the fixation probability equals the initial frequency.
nodes.title: Neutral fixation probability equals the initial frequency

nodes.summary: The slope constant of Kimura's formula never vanishes.
nodes.title: Slope constant of Kimura's formula is nonzero

nodes.summary: The derivative of Kimura's fixation probability: `u'(x) = K σ · e^{-2σx}`.
nodes.title: Derivative of Kimura's fixation probability at a point

nodes.summary: Kimura's fixation probability is continuous in the initial frequency.
nodes.title: Continuity of Kimura's fixation probability

nodes.summary: The derivative of Kimura's fixation probability, as a function.
nodes.title: Derivative of Kimura's fixation probability as a function

nodes.summary: The fixation probability solves the backward equation `x (1 - x) / 2 · u'' + σ x (1 - x) · u' = 0` (everywhere).
nodes.title: Kimura (1962)

nodes.summary: If `u` is continuous on `[0, 1]`, differentiable on `(0, 1)` with derivative `u'` differentiable on `(0, 1)`, solves the backward equation `L_σ u = 0` on `(0, 1)`, and satisfies `u 0 = 0`, `u 1 = 1`, then `u` is Kimura's fixation probability on `[0, 1]`.
nodes.title: Uniqueness of the fixation probability (Kimura 1962)

nodes.summary: Uniqueness of the fixation probability, `C²` form: a function continuous on `[0, 1]`, `C²` on `(0, 1)`, solving `L_σ u = 0` on `(0, 1)` with `u 0 = 0`, `u 1 = 1` equals Kimura's fixation probability on `[0, 1]`.
nodes.title: Uniqueness of the fixation probability

nodes.summary: Kimura's fixation probability is nonnegative at nonnegative frequencies, for every selection coefficient `σ`.
nodes.title: Nonnegativity of Kimura's fixation probability

nodes.summary: Kimura's fixation probability is at most `1` at frequencies `y ≤ 1`, for every selection coefficient `σ`.
nodes.title: Kimura's fixation probability is at most one

nodes.summary: Kimura's fixation probability is a probability on `[0, 1]`.
nodes.title: Kimura's fixation probability lies in the unit interval

nodes.summary: Advantageous alleles (`σ > 0`) are fixed with probability strictly larger than their initial frequency `x ∈ (0, 1)`.
nodes.title: Advantageous alleles fix more often than their initial frequency

nodes.summary: The neutral mean absorption time vanishes at `x = 0`.
nodes.title: Neutral mean absorption time vanishes at frequency zero

nodes.summary: The neutral mean absorption time vanishes at `x = 1`.
nodes.title: Neutral mean absorption time vanishes at frequency one
Derivative of the neutral mean absorption time

nodes.summary: The neutral mean absorption time solves `L_0 T = -1` on `(0, 1)`.
nodes.title: Kimura–Ohta (1969)

nodes.summary: `H(x) = 2x(1 - x)` is an eigenfunction of the neutral generator with eigenvalue `-1`, so `E[H_t] = H_0 e^{-t}` (time in units of `2N` generations).
nodes.title: Decay of heterozygosity

nodes.summary: Moment duality with Kingman's coalescent at generator level: the neutral generator maps `y ↦ y ^ n` to `C(n, 2) (x ^ (n - 1) - x ^ n)`, which is the generator of the block-counting process (jumps `n → n - 1` at rate `C(n, 2)`) applied to `n ↦ x ^ n`.
nodes.title: Moment duality with Kingman's coalescent

nodes.summary: On `(0, 1)`, with infinitesimal variance `a(x) = x (1 - x)` and mutation drift `b(x) = α (1 - x) - β x`, Wright's density `π(x) = x ^ (2α - 1) (1 - x) ^ (2β - 1)` satisfies `(a π)' = 2 b π`, i.e. the stationary forward (Fokker–Planck) equation `½ (a π)' - b π = 0` with zero probability flux.
nodes.title: Wright's stationary density (zero-flux form)

nodes.summary: For `α, β > 0` the stationary density integrates to the Beta function `B(2α, 2β) = Γ(2α) Γ(2β) / Γ(2α + 2β)`, so `wrightDensity α β x / B(2α, 2β)` is the Beta`(2α, 2β)` probability density on `(0, 1)`.
nodes.title: Normalization of Wright's density

nodes.summary: For `α, β > 0` Wright's density has a finite, positive total mass on `(0, 1)`.
nodes.title: Wright's density has finite positive total mass

nodes.summary: For `α, β > 0` Wright's density is integrable on `[0, 1]`.
nodes.title: Integrability of Wright's density on the unit interval

nodes.summary: If the number `X` of copies of an allele among `M` gene copies (`M = 2N` for diploids) is `Binomial(M, x)`, then the new frequency `p' = X / M` satisfies `E[2 p' (1 - p')] = (1 - 1/M) · 2x(1 - x)`.
nodes.title: Heterozygosity decay in one Wright–Fisher generation
Diffusion limit of the Wright–Fisher model

nodes.summary: For `M` gene copies and current frequency `x`, the expected value of `f` at the next frequency, `∫ k, f (k / M) ∂Bin(M, x)`, is the `M`-th Bernstein approximation of `f` on `[0, 1]` evaluated at `x`.
nodes.title: One Wright–Fisher generation as a Bernstein approximation

nodes.summary: For `f` of class `C²` and `x ∈ [0, 1]`, the one-generation generator of the neutral Wright–Fisher chain with `M` gene copies, sped up by the factor `M` (time in units of `M` generations), converges to the neutral Wright–Fisher diffusion generator `(L_0 f)(x) = x (1 - x) / 2 · f''(x)`.
nodes.title: Wright–Fisher diffusion limit, generator form (Feller 1951; Voronovskaya 1932)
Fixation and absorption in the Wright–Fisher diffusion

nodes.summary: `X` solves the martingale problem for the Wright–Fisher diffusion with scaled genic selection coefficient `σ = 2Ns` (time in units of `2N` generations) with respect to the filtration `ℱ` and the measure `μ`: `X` takes values in `[0, 1]`, has continuous paths, is adapted to `ℱ`, and for every `C²` function `f` the process `f (X t) - f (X 0) - ∫₀ᵗ generator σ f (X s) ds` is an `ℱ`-martingale.
nodes.title: Martingale problem for the Wright–Fisher diffusion

nodes.summary: The absorption time of a `[0, 1]`-valued path: the first time it is at `0` or `1` (the infimum of the empty set is `0` in `ℝ≥0`; the path is absorbed almost surely, see `ae_exists_absorbed`).
nodes.title: Absorption time of a frequency path

nodes.summary: Kimura's fixation probability is a `C²` function of the initial frequency on all of `ℝ`.
nodes.title: Kimura's fixation probability is twice continuously differentiable

nodes.summary: The slope constant of Kimura's formula is positive.
nodes.title: Positivity of Kimura's slope constant

nodes.summary: Kimura's fixation probability is strictly increasing in the initial frequency.
nodes.title: Strict monotonicity of Kimura's fixation probability

nodes.summary: A solution of the Wright–Fisher martingale problem is almost surely absorbed: from some time on it is constantly `0` or constantly `1`.
nodes.title: Absorption in finite time

nodes.summary: For a solution of the Wright–Fisher martingale problem with scaled selection coefficient `σ = 2Ns` started at frequency `x`, the probability that the allele is eventually fixed is `(1 - e^{-2σx}) / (1 - e^{-2σ})` (`x` when `σ = 0`).
nodes.title: Kimura's fixation probability, process form

nodes.summary: For a solution of the neutral Wright–Fisher martingale problem started at frequency `x`, the expected time to loss or fixation, in units of `2N` generations, is `-2 (x log x + (1 - x) log (1 - x))`.
nodes.title: Kimura–Ohta mean absorption time, process form
Sojourn times of the Wright–Fisher diffusion

nodes.summary: The neutral Wright–Fisher Green's function (sojourn density), time in units of `2N` generations (Ewens 2004, Chapter 4): `G(p, x) = 2 (1 - p) / (1 - x)` for `x ≤ p` and `G(p, x) = 2 p / x` for `p < x`. In the diffusion reading, for `0 < x < 1`, `G(p, x) dx` is the expected time a neutral allele started at frequency `p` spends at frequencies in `(x, x + dx)` before loss or fixation.
nodes.title: Neutral Wright–Fisher Green's function

nodes.summary: For continuous `g` and `p ∈ (0, 1)`, the function `u(q) = ∫ x in 0..1, G(q, x) g(x)` solves the neutral backward equation `L_0 u = -g` at `p`. In the diffusion reading, `u(p)` is the expected value of `∫₀^T g(X_t) dt` up to the absorption time `T`.
nodes.title: Green's representation (Ewens 2004, Chapter 4)

nodes.summary: Boundary value at `0`: an allele that is absent spends no time in `(0, 1)`, so `∫ x in 0..1, G(0, x) g(x) = 0`.
nodes.title: Sojourn integral vanishes for an absent allele

nodes.summary: Boundary value at `1`: a fixed allele spends no time in `(0, 1)`, so `∫ x in 0..1, G(1, x) g(x) = 0`.
nodes.title: Sojourn integral vanishes for a fixed allele

nodes.summary: For `p ∈ [0, 1]`, the total expected sojourn time `∫ x in 0..1, G(p, x)` is the Kimura–Ohta mean absorption time `-2 (p log p + (1 - p) log (1 - p))` (units of `2N` generations).
nodes.title: Mean absorption time as a sojourn integral
Poisson random field model

nodes.summary: The Sawyer–Hartl (1992) Poisson-random-field density: the expected number of sites per unit frequency at which the derived allele has frequency `x`, for scaled mutation rate `θ = 4Nu` and scaled genic selection `σ = 2Ns`: `θ · u_σ(1 - x) / (x (1 - x))` with `u_σ = kimuraFixation σ`, i.e. `θ (1 - e^{-2σ(1 - x)}) / ((1 - e^{-2σ}) x (1 - x))`, and `θ / x` when `σ = 0`. The model domain is `θ > 0` and `x ∈ (0, 1)`; at…
nodes.title: Sawyer–Hartl Poisson random field density

nodes.summary: The Poisson-random-field density with selection, explicitly: `θ (1 - e^{-2σ(1 - x)}) / ((1 - e^{-2σ}) x (1 - x))` for `σ ≠ 0`.
nodes.title: Closed form of the Poisson random field density with selection

nodes.summary: The neutral Poisson-random-field density is `θ / x` (for `x ≠ 1`).
nodes.title: Neutral Poisson random field density

nodes.summary: A new neutral mutation enters at a small frequency `p`; with mutations arriving at rate `θ / (2p)` per unit time (so that the mutational input of frequency is `θ / 2`), the expected sojourn density at `x ≥ p` is `θ / (2p) · G(p, x) = θ / x`, the neutral Poisson-random-field density.
nodes.title: The neutral density from the Green's function

nodes.summary: On `(0, 1)` the weighted density `F(x) = x (1 - x) φ(x)` of the Poisson-random-field density solves the stationary Fokker–Planck equation `½ F'' - σ F' = 0` of the Wright–Fisher diffusion with genic selection `σ` (the forward equation `½ (x (1 - x) φ)'' - (σ x (1 - x) φ)' = 0`).
nodes.title: Stationary forward equation (Sawyer–Hartl 1992)

nodes.summary: On `(0, 1)` the current `J = σ F - F' / 2` of the stationary forward equation, for the weighted density `F(x) = x (1 - x) φ(x)`, is the constant `θ · u_σ'(0) / 2` (`u_σ'(0) = kimuraSlope σ = 2σ / (1 - e^{-2σ})`, and `1` for `σ = 0`), so `J = θ σ / (1 - e^{-2σ})`, and `J = θ / 2` in the neutral case: the mutational input of frequency at `0`, carried through `(0, 1)` to fixation at `1`.
nodes.title: Probability current

nodes.summary: As `x → 0⁺` the weighted density `x (1 - x) φ(x)` tends to `θ`. (This is not the probability current, which is `current_prfDensity`.)
nodes.title: Boundary normalization at `0`

nodes.summary: As `x → 1⁻` the weighted density `x (1 - x) φ(x)` tends to `0`.
nodes.title: Boundary normalization at `1`

nodes.summary: Let `θ ≠ 0` and let `φ` be a density on `(0, 1)` whose weighted density `x (1 - x) φ(x)` extends to a function `F` continuous on `[0, 1]`, twice differentiable on `(0, 1)`, solving the stationary forward equation `½ F'' - σ F' = 0` there, with boundary normalizations `F(0) = θ` and `F(1) = 0`. Then `φ` is the Sawyer–Hartl density on `(0, 1)`.
nodes.title: ODE characterization of the Poisson-random-field density

nodes.summary: The expected unfolded site-frequency spectrum of a sample of `n` gene copies under the Poisson random field: the expected number of sites where exactly `i` of the `n` sampled copies carry the derived allele, `E ξ_i = ∫ x in 0..1, C(n, i) x ^ i (1 - x) ^ (n - i) φ(x)`. The site-frequency spectrum consists of the segregating classes `1 ≤ i < n`. The value at `i = n` is the expected number of sites at which every…
nodes.title: Expected site frequency spectrum under the Poisson random field

nodes.summary: With `σ = 0`, for the segregating classes `1 ≤ i < n` the expected number of sites with `i` derived copies in a sample of `n` is `θ / i`.
nodes.title: Neutral site-frequency spectrum (Fu 1995)

nodes.summary: With `σ = 0` the expected number of sites at which all `n ≥ 1` sampled copies carry the derived allele is `θ / n`. These sites are monomorphic in the sample, so this is not a class of the site-frequency spectrum.
nodes.title: Expected number of sites derived in the whole neutral sample
Selection duality and general one-dimensional diffusions

nodes.summary: The generator of the line-counting process of the ancestral selection graph with scaled selection coefficient `σ` (time in units of `2N` generations, the scaling of `generator`): from `n` lines, branching `n → n + 1` at rate `n σ` and coalescence `n → n - 1` at rate `C(n, 2)`.
nodes.title: Generator of the ancestral selection graph line-counting process

nodes.summary: Selection duality (Mano 2009) at generator level, with the line-counting process of the ancestral selection graph (Krone–Neuhauser 1997) as the dual: the Wright–Fisher generator with genic selection maps `y ↦ (1 - y) ^ n` to `C(n, 2) ((1 - x)^(n-1) - (1 - x)^n) + n σ ((1 - x)^(n+1) - (1 - x)^n)`. This identity holds for every real `σ`; the dual is a Markov chain only for `σ ≥ 0`.
nodes.title: Selection duality (Mano 2009)

nodes.summary: The selection duality in operator form: `L_σ` applied to `y ↦ (1 - y) ^ n` equals the ancestral-selection-graph generator applied to `k ↦ (1 - x) ^ k` at `n`.
nodes.title: Selection duality in operator form

nodes.summary: The stationary law of the ancestral-selection-graph line-counting process with `σ > 0`: `π_k = (2σ)^k / k! / (e^{2σ} - 1)` for `k ≥ 1` and `π_0 = 0`, a Poisson`(2σ)` law conditioned to be positive. For `σ = 0` the stationary law is `δ₁`: branching vanishes, coalescence reaches state `1`, and state `1` is absorbing, so `π_1 = 1` and `π_k = 0` otherwise (the limit of the `σ > 0` formula as `σ → 0`).
nodes.title: Stationary law of the ancestral selection graph line counts

nodes.summary: Detailed balance of the ancestral-selection-graph chain: `π_k · (k σ) = π_{k+1} · C(k + 1, 2)` for every `k` (the flux `k → k + 1` equals the flux `k + 1 → k`). This is an identity for every real `σ`.
nodes.title: Detailed balance

nodes.summary: Global balance (stationarity `π Q = 0`) of the ancestral-selection-graph chain at state `k + 1`: the outflow `π_{k+1} ((k + 1) σ + C(k + 1, 2))` equals the inflow `π_k (k σ) + π_{k+2} C(k + 2, 2)` (for `k = 0` the inflow from the unreachable state `0` vanishes).
nodes.title: Global balance

nodes.title: Stationary weights under selection are nonnegative

nodes.summary: The probability generating function of the stationary law: for `σ > 0` and every real `y`, `∑ₖ π_k y^k = (e^{2σy} - 1) / (e^{2σ} - 1)`.

nodes.summary: One generation of the Wright–Fisher chain on `M` gene copies (`M = 2N`): mutation moves the frequency `x` to `p' = mutatedFreq u₁ u₂ x`, then the new count is `Binomial(M, p')`. With `u₁ = θ₁ / (2M)`, `u₂ = θ₂ / (2M)` (`θᵢ = 4N uᵢ`), the expected change of frequency per `2N = M` generations is exactly the drift coefficient of `mutationGenerator`: `M · (E[k / M] - x) = (θ₁ (1 - x) - θ₂ x) / 2`, for every `M`.

nodes.summary: In the setting of `integral_binomial_mutatedFreq_drift`, the scaled second moment of the frequency change is `M · E[(k / M - x) ^ 2] = p' (1 - p') + (θ₁ (1 - x) - θ₂ x) ^ 2 / (4M)` with `p' = mutatedFreq u₁ u₂ x = x + (θ₁ (1 - x) - θ₂ x) / (2M)`. As `M → ∞` with `θ₁, θ₂, x` fixed this tends to `x (1 - x)`, the diffusion coefficient of `mutationGenerator` (the limit itself is not stated here).

nodes.summary: The neutral Wright–Fisher diffusion semigroup on polynomials, defined by moment duality on the monomial basis: `polySemigroup t (X ^ n) = dualMomentPoly t n`. It is meaningful for `t ≥ 0`; the formula is defined, and the group law holds, for every real `t`.

Ewens sampling formula and the Chinese restaurant process

nodes.summary: The Ewens sampling formula: the probability, under the neutral infinite-alleles model with scaled mutation rate `θ = 4Nu`, that a sample of `n` genes has allelic partition `π` (`π.parts.count j` alleles carried by exactly `j` genes each): `n! * (∏ j, (θ / j) ^ (a j) / (a j)!) / θ^{(n)}` (Ewens 1972), for `θ > 0`.
nodes.title: Ewens sampling formula

nodes.summary: The Ewens sampling formula is a probability distribution on the partitions of `n` (Ewens 1972; equivalently, Cauchy's cycle-type formula `∑_{σ ∈ S_n} θ^{#cycles σ} = θ^{(n)}`).
nodes.title: The Ewens sampling formula is a probability distribution

nodes.summary: The Ewens sampling formula is nonnegative for `θ > 0`; with `sum_ewensProb` it is a probability distribution on the partitions of `n`.
nodes.title: Nonnegativity of the Ewens sampling formula

nodes.summary: Expected number of alleles in a sample of `n` genes under the Ewens sampling formula: `E[K_n] = ∑_{i < n} θ / (θ + i)` (Ewens 1972).
nodes.title: Expected number of alleles

nodes.summary: One step of Hoppe's urn on allelic partitions (Hoppe 1984): from a partition `π` of `k`, the next gene carries a new allele with probability `θ / (θ + k)` (target parts `1 ::ₘ π.parts`), and copies an allele carried by `j` genes with probability `j * a j / (θ + k)`, where `a j = π.parts.count j` (target parts `(j + 1) ::ₘ π.parts.erase j`). The value is the transition probability from `π` to `π'`.
nodes.title: One step of Hoppe's urn

nodes.summary: The law of the allelic partition after `n` draws from Hoppe's urn, started from the empty sample: `hoppeLaw θ (n + 1) π' = ∑ π, hoppeLaw θ n π * hoppeStep θ π π'`.
nodes.title: Law of the allelic partition from Hoppe's urn

nodes.summary: Hoppe-urn transition probabilities are nonnegative.
nodes.title: Hoppe urn transition probabilities are nonnegative

nodes.summary: The Hoppe-urn transition is stochastic: from every partition of `k` the probabilities of the partitions of `k + 1` sum to one.
nodes.title: Hoppe urn transition is stochastic

nodes.summary: Hoppe's urn generates the Ewens sampling formula (Hoppe 1984): after `n` draws, the allelic partition has law `ewensProb θ`.
nodes.title: Hoppe's urn generates the Ewens sampling formula

nodes.summary: The law of Hoppe's urn after `n` draws is nonnegative for `θ > 0`.
nodes.title: Nonnegativity of the Hoppe urn law

nodes.summary: Seat customer `n` at a new table: the partition of `Fin (n + 1)` whose blocks are the blocks of `π` (relabeled into `Fin (n + 1)`) together with the singleton `{n}`.
nodes.title: Seating a customer at a new table

nodes.summary: Seat customer `n` at the occupied table `B` of `π`: the block `B` becomes `B ∪ {n}` and the other blocks are unchanged.
nodes.title: Seating a customer at an occupied table

nodes.summary: The blocks of `newTable π`.
nodes.title: Blocks of the partition after opening a new table

nodes.summary: The blocks of `joinTable π B hB`.
nodes.title: Blocks of the partition after joining a table

nodes.summary: Seat customer `n` according to the choice `c`: `none` opens a new table, `some B` joins the occupied table `B`.
nodes.title: Seating a customer by a seating choice

nodes.summary: The probability of each seating choice for customer `n` given the partition `π` of the first `n` customers: `θ / (n + θ)` for a new table, `|B| / (n + θ)` for the table `B`.
nodes.title: Seating probabilities in the Chinese restaurant process

nodes.summary: The seating probabilities are nonnegative for `θ > 0`.
nodes.title: Nonnegativity of seating probabilities

nodes.summary: The seating probabilities sum to one for `θ > 0`.
nodes.title: Seating probabilities sum to one

nodes.summary: The seating choice of customer `n`, as a probability distribution.
nodes.title: Seating choice distribution of a customer

nodes.summary: One step of the Chinese restaurant process: the law of the partition of `Fin (n + 1)` given the partition `π` of the first `n` customers.
nodes.title: One step of the Chinese restaurant process

nodes.summary: The Chinese restaurant process with parameter `θ > 0`: the law of the random partition of the customers `Fin n` into tables, built one customer at a time by `crpStep` (Aldous 1985, §11; Pitman 2006, ch. 3).
nodes.title: Chinese restaurant process

nodes.summary: The closed-form law of the Chinese restaurant process, `θ^{|π|} ∏_{B ∈ π} (|B| - 1)! / θ^{(n)}` (Pitman 2006, §3.1). Every block is nonempty, so `|B| - 1` is never a truncated natural subtraction.
nodes.title: Closed-form law of the Chinese restaurant process

nodes.summary: Removing the last customer undoes every seating: restricting `seat π c` to the first `n` customers gives back `π`.
nodes.title: Removing the last customer undoes a seating

nodes.summary: Different seating choices give different partitions.
nodes.title: Injectivity of seating

nodes.summary: Every partition of `Fin (n + 1)` arises by seating customer `n` into its restriction to the first `n` customers.
nodes.title: Every partition arises from seating the last customer

nodes.summary: One seating multiplies the closed-form law by the seating probability.
nodes.title: Seating multiplies the closed-form law by the seating probability

nodes.summary: Law of the Chinese restaurant process (Pitman 2006, §3.1): `P(π) = θ^{|π|} ∏_{B ∈ π} (|B| - 1)! / θ^{(n)}`.
nodes.title: Law of the Chinese restaurant process

nodes.summary: The law of the Chinese restaurant process as a real number.
nodes.title: Chinese restaurant process law as a real number

nodes.summary: Exchangeability, pointwise: relabeling the customers by a permutation `σ` does not change the probability of a partition.
nodes.title: Exchangeability

nodes.summary: Exchangeability of the Chinese restaurant process (Aldous 1985, §11): the law of the partition relabeled by any permutation of the customers is the law of the partition.
nodes.title: Exchangeability of the Chinese restaurant process

nodes.summary: Restricting the random partition of `Fin (n + 1)` to the first `n` customers gives the process with `n` customers.
nodes.title: Consistency of the Chinese restaurant process

nodes.summary: Restricting the random partition of `Fin n` to the first `m ≤ n` customers gives the process with `m` customers.
nodes.title: Consistency for every sample size

nodes.summary: The allelic partition of a set partition of `Fin n`: the multiset of its block sizes, a partition of the integer `n`.
nodes.title: Allelic partition of a set partition

nodes.summary: The law of the multiset of block sizes after `n` customers is the law `Ewens.hoppeLaw` of Hoppe's urn on allelic partitions after `n` draws.
nodes.title: The block sizes follow Hoppe's urn

nodes.summary: The allelic partition of the Chinese restaurant process follows the Ewens sampling formula (Ewens 1972; Hoppe 1984): the multiset of block sizes after `n` customers has law `Ewens.ewensProb θ`.
nodes.title: The allelic partition of the Chinese restaurant process follows the Ewens sampling formula

nodes.title: Expected number of tables

nodes.summary: Haldane's survival probability `π(s) = 1 - q(s)` of a mutant with selective advantage `s` per generation, whose number of copies in the next generation is Poisson with mean `1 + s`. The model needs `s ≥ -1`; for `s < -1` the mean is truncated to `0` (`Real.toNNReal`), the mutant leaves no copies, and `π(s) = 0`.

Hardy–Weinberg law

nodes.summary: Mendel's law of segregation: a parent with genotype `g` transmits its maternal allele `g.1` or its paternal allele `g.2`, each with probability `1/2`.
nodes.title: Mendel's law of segregation

nodes.summary: The law of a random gamete of a generation with genotype law `G`: pick a parent from `G`, then one of its two alleles by `transmit`. Its mass at `a` is the frequency of allele `a` (`gamete_apply`).
nodes.title: Law of a random gamete

nodes.summary: The offspring genotype law under random union of gametes: the maternal and paternal alleles are independent gametes of the parental generation.
nodes.title: Offspring genotype law under random union of gametes

nodes.summary: `transmit g` puts mass `1/2` on each of the two alleles of `g` (mass `1` on `a` for a homozygote `g = (a, a)`).
nodes.title: Allele transmission law of a parental genotype

nodes.summary: The gamete law is the allele frequency: `gamete G a = ½ ∑ b, G (a, b) + ½ ∑ b, G (b, a)`, half the expected number of copies of `a` in a parental genotype.
nodes.title: Gamete law equals the allele frequency

nodes.summary: Hardy–Weinberg proportions (Hardy 1908, Weinberg 1908): after one generation of random mating the genotype law is the product `p ⊗ p` of the parental allele frequencies `p = gamete G`.
nodes.title: Hardy–Weinberg proportions

nodes.summary: Allele frequencies are conserved under random mating: the gamete law of the offspring equals that of the parents.
nodes.title: Allele frequencies are conserved

nodes.summary: The Hardy–Weinberg proportions reached after one generation of random mating are a fixed point of random mating.
nodes.title: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium

nodes.summary: The two allele frequencies sum to one: `p + q = 1`.
nodes.title: The two allele frequencies sum to one

Infinite-alleles model and homozygosity

nodes.summary: One generation of drift and mutation in the infinite-alleles model with `M` gene copies and mutation probability `u` per copy: `F' = (1 - u)² (1/M + (1 - 1/M) F)`. The model domain is `2 ≤ M` (two distinct copies must exist) and `0 ≤ u ≤ 1`; the theorems below assume only `1 ≤ M`, and `M = 1` is an algebraic extension with no biological meaning. For `M = 0` the definition uses the junk value `1/0 = 0`.
nodes.title: Homozygosity recursion in the infinite-alleles model

nodes.summary: The equilibrium homozygosity `F* = (1 - u)² / (M - (M - 1)(1 - u)²)`. Biologically meaningful for `2 ≤ M`; its denominator is positive for `1 ≤ M` and `0 < u ≤ 1`, the hypotheses of the theorems below (`M = 1` being an algebraic extension).
nodes.title: Equilibrium homozygosity in the infinite-alleles model

nodes.summary: `F*` is a fixed point of the homozygosity recursion.
nodes.title: Equilibrium homozygosity is a fixed point of the recursion

nodes.summary: For `0 < u ≤ 1`, `F*` is the unique fixed point of the homozygosity recursion.
nodes.title: Uniqueness of the equilibrium homozygosity

nodes.summary: For `0 < u ≤ 1` the homozygosity converges to `F*` from every initial value `F₀`.
nodes.title: Convergence of homozygosity to equilibrium

nodes.summary: With `M = 2N` gene copies and mutation probability `u = θ/(4N)` (so that `θ = 4Nu`), the equilibrium homozygosity tends to `1/(1 + θ)` as `N → ∞`.
nodes.title: Kimura–Crow limit

reading_title.source: Limit $\theta/(1+\theta)$ of the equilibrium heterozygosity

nodes.summary: The equilibrium heterozygosity `H* = 1 - F*` tends to `θ/(1 + θ)` as `N → ∞` with `M = 2N` and `u = θ/(4N)`.
nodes.title: Limit $\theta/(1+\theta)$ of the equilibrium heterozygosity

nodes.summary: Linkage disequilibrium tends to `0` whenever `0 < r ≤ 1`; this contains the biological range `0 < r ≤ 1/2`. For `r = 0` (complete linkage) `D` is constant.
nodes.title: Linkage disequilibrium tends to zero

nodes.summary: Haldane's map function `r(d) = (1 - e^{-2d}) / 2`: the recombination fraction between two loci at map distance `d` Morgans when crossovers form a Poisson process (no interference).
nodes.title: Haldane's map function

nodes.summary: The probability that a Poisson count of mean `d` is odd, as a series: `∑_{k odd} e^{-d} d^k / k! = (1 - e^{-2d}) / 2` (Haldane 1919). The series identity holds for every real `d`; it is a probability for `0 ≤ d`.
nodes.title: Series for the probability of an odd Poisson count

nodes.summary: Haldane's map function (Haldane 1919): if the number of crossovers in an interval of map length `d` Morgans is Poisson with mean `d`, the probability of an odd number of crossovers, i.e. of recombination between the ends of the interval, is `(1 - e^{-2d}) / 2`.
nodes.title: Haldane's map function from Poisson crossovers

nodes.summary: Haldane's map function is nonnegative at nonnegative distances.
nodes.title: Nonnegativity of Haldane's map function

nodes.summary: The recombination fraction is always below `1/2` (for every real `d`).
nodes.title: Haldane's recombination fraction is below one half

nodes.summary: Loci far apart are unlinked in the limit: `r → 1/2` as `d → ∞`.
nodes.title: Distant loci are unlinked in the limit

nodes.summary: The inverse map function `d = -½ log(1 - 2r)` recovers the map distance.
nodes.title: Inverse Haldane map function recovers map distance

nodes.summary: Every `r < 1/2` is the recombination fraction at the distance `-½ log(1 - 2r)`. The hypothesis keeps `log` on positive arguments: at `r = 1/2` the right side would use the junk value `log 0 = 0`. The distance is nonnegative exactly when `0 ≤ r`.
nodes.title: Every recombination fraction below one half is attained

nodes.summary: The Lea–Coulson clone-size law `P(size = j) = 1 / (j (j + 1))` for `j ≥ 1` (`P(size = 0) = 0`).

nodes.summary: The `k`-fold convolution power of a sequence on `ℕ`: `p^{*0} = δ₀` and `p^{*(k+1)}(n) = ∑_{i ≤ n} p(i) p^{*k}(n - i)`.

nodes.summary: The Luria–Delbrück probability of `n` mutants with expected mutation number `m`: the compound-Poisson law `∑_k e^{-m} m^k / k! · cloneProb^{*k}(n)`. Since clones have size at least `1`, only `k ≤ n` contribute.
nodes.title: Luria–Delbrück distribution

nodes.summary: Probability that one step of the Moran process with `N` individuals and mutant relative fitness `r` takes the mutant count from `i` to `i + 1`: a mutant is chosen to reproduce (probability `r i / (r i + N - i)`) and a wild type is chosen to die (probability `(N - i) / N`). Meaningful for `0 < r` and `i ≤ N` (the real subtraction `N - i` is negative for `i > N`).
nodes.title: Up-step probability of the Moran process

nodes.summary: Probability that one step of the Moran process takes the mutant count from `i` to `i - 1`: a wild type is chosen to reproduce (probability `(N - i) / (r i + N - i)`) and a mutant is chosen to die (probability `i / N`). Meaningful for `0 < r` and `i ≤ N`.

nodes.summary: The fixation probability of the Moran process started from `i` mutants out of `N`: `(1 - r⁻¹ ^ i) / (1 - r⁻¹ ^ N)` for `r ≠ 1`, and `i / N` in the neutral case `r = 1`. The model's domain is `0 < r`, `N ≥ 1`, `i ≤ N`; outside it the value is the closed formula evaluated with Lean's total division (e.g. `x / 0 = 0`) and carries no meaning.
nodes.title: Fixation probability of the Moran process

nodes.summary: One-step transition probabilities of the Moran process on the states `Fin (N + 1)`: `a_i` to `i + 1`, `b_i` to `i - 1`, `1 - a_i - b_i` to `i`, and `0` elsewhere.

nodes.summary: One generation of Wright's island-model identity-by-descent recursion for a deme of `M` gene copies (`M = 2N` for `N` diploids) receiving a fraction `m` of migrants from an infinite pool: `F' = (1 - m) ^ 2 * (1 / M + (1 - 1 / M) * F)`. Biologically meaningful for `M ≥ 2` and `0 ≤ m ≤ 1`; `M = 1` is an algebraic extension (no pair of distinct copies exists), and at `M = 0` Lean's `1 / 0 = 0` gives a junk value.

nodes.summary: `π'` arises from `π` by merging two blocks: `π` refines `π'` and has exactly one more block (so exactly two blocks of `π` lie in one block of `π'`, and the others are blocks of `π'`).

nodes.summary: The transition matrix of the jump chain of Kingman's coalescent: from a partition with `k ≥ 2` blocks, move to each of the `k.choose 2` partitions obtained by merging two blocks with probability `1 / k.choose 2`; a partition with at most one block is absorbing.

nodes.summary: The law of the jump chain after `m` jumps, started from the partition into singletons: `jumpLaw n m π` is the probability that the partition after `m` coalescences is `π`.

nodes.summary: The probability `(n - k)! k! (k - 1)! ∏_{B ∈ π} |B|! / (n! (n - 1)!)` of a partition `π` with `k` blocks of a sample of size `n` (meaningful for `1 ≤ k ≤ n`; for the empty sample it gives `1` to the empty partition).

nodes.summary: The rate matrix of Kingman's partition-valued coalescent: each pair of blocks merges at rate `1`, so a partition with `k` blocks is left at total rate `k.choose 2` (time in units of `2N` generations).

nodes.summary: The time-`t` marginal of Kingman's `n`-coalescent started from singletons: `timeLaw n t π = exp (t • partitionRate n) ⊥ π` is the probability that the ancestral partition of the sample at time `t ≥ 0` (in units of `2N` generations) is `π`. The matrix exponential is defined for every real `t`; the identities below hold for every real `t`.

nodes.summary: Kingman's formula (Kingman 1982; Durrett 2008, ch. 1). For `m < n`, after `m` coalescences the jump chain started from singletons is at a partition `π` with probability `kingmanProb n π = (n - k)! k! (k - 1)! ∏_{B ∈ π} |B|! / (n! (n - 1)!)` if `π` has `k = n - m` blocks, and `0` otherwise. (For `m ≥ n - 1` the chain has been absorbed at the one-block partition.)

nodes.summary: Kingman's formula is a probability distribution on the partitions with `k` blocks, for `1 ≤ k ≤ n`. Equivalently, `∑_{π, k blocks} ∏_{B ∈ π} |B|! = n! (n - 1)! / ((n - k)! k! (k - 1)!)`, the Lah number `L(n, k)`.

nodes.summary: A piecewise-constant population-size history with `K` pieces: piece `j < K` starts at time `start j` (backward from the present, `start 0 = 0`, strictly increasing) and has relative size `size j > 0`; the last piece extends to infinity. nodes.summary: The population-size function of a piecewise-constant history: at time `s ≥ 0` it is the size of the piece `j` with `start j ≤ s < start (j + 1)` (the last piece has no end). Equal to `0` for `s < 0` (junk; only `s ≥ 0` is meaningful).

nodes.summary: For a history with `K ≥ 1` pieces and `m ≥ 2`, writing `a = C(m,2)` and `R = cumRate h.sizeFn`, `a c_m = size 0 + ∑_{j=1}^{K-1} (size j - size (j-1)) exp(-a R(start j))`. In particular the integral defining `c_m` converges.

nodes.summary: Bhaskar–Song identifiability (Bhaskar & Song 2014, Corollary 7, "determined" half, stated for the first-coalescence times): two piecewise-constant histories with `K` pieces whose expected first-coalescence times `c_m` agree for `2 ≤ m ≤ n`, with `n ≥ 2K`, have the same population size at every time `s ≥ 0`. The proof writes `C(m,2) c_m` as an exponential sum in `C(m,2)` over at most `2K - 1` rates…
nodes.title: Bhaskar–Song identifiability

nodes.summary: Tightness of `n ≥ 2K` (Bhaskar & Song 2014, Corollary 7): for every `K ≥ 2` there are two piecewise-constant histories with `K` pieces whose sizes differ at some time `s ≥ 0` but whose first-coalescence times `c_m` agree for `2 ≤ m ≤ 2K - 1`; so `sizeFn_eq_of_firstCoalMean_eq` fails for `n = 2K - 1`. The construction is explicit: with `z = 2^{-C(m,2)}`, the two histories have coalescent-time breakpoints…

nodes.summary: At each transient state `s` the exit rate is positive and the mean coalescence time is the mean holding time `1 / qₛ` plus the mean time from the next state, `h s = 1 / qₛ + ∑ₜ (q(s, t) / qₛ) h t`.
