Λ-coalescents

nodes.summary: Pitman's merger rate `λ_{b,k} = ∫ x ^ (k - 2) (1 - x) ^ (b - k) Λ(dx)`: while there are `b` blocks, the rate at which a given set of `k` of them merges into one block, for `2 ≤ k ≤ b` (Pitman 1999, Theorem 1; Sagitov 1999). Powers are natural-number powers, so `0 ^ 0 = 1`. Outside `2 ≤ k ≤ b` no such merger exists, and the rate is defined to be `0`.
nodes.title: Pitman's merger rate

nodes.summary: The total merger rate `λ_b = ∑_{k=2}^b (b.choose k) λ_{b,k}` while there are `b` blocks (Pitman 1999; Berestycki 2009, §3.1).
nodes.title: Total merger rate of a Λ-coalescent

nodes.summary: The generator of the block-counting process of the Λ-coalescent on the states `0, …, n` (state `b` means `b` blocks): from `b` blocks the process jumps to `j < b` blocks at rate `(b.choose (b + 1 - j)) λ_{b, b + 1 - j}` (a `(b + 1 - j)`-merger), and the diagonal is `-λ_b`. States `0` and `1` are absorbing (state `0` is never reached from `b ≥ 1`).
nodes.title: Generator of the Λ-coalescent block-counting process

nodes.title: Merger rates are bounded by the total mass of Λ

nodes.summary: Pitman's consistency relation `λ_{b,k} = λ_{b+1,k} + λ_{b+1,k+1}` for `2 ≤ k ≤ b` (Pitman 1999; Berestycki 2009, §3.1): a given `k`-set of `b` blocks merges, with an extra block present, either without it or together with it.
nodes.title: Pitman's consistency relation

nodes.summary: The polynomial identity behind the closed form of the total merger rate: `x ^ 2 ∑_{k=2}^b (b.choose k) x ^ (k - 2) (1 - x) ^ (b - k) = 1 - (1 - x) ^ b - b x (1 - x) ^ (b - 1)` for every real `x` and every `b` (binomial theorem).
nodes.title: Binomial identity behind the total merger rate

nodes.summary: The total merger rate in closed form (Berestycki 2009, §3.1): `λ_b = (b.choose 2) Λ {0} + ∫_{(0,1]} (1 - (1 - x) ^ b - b x (1 - x) ^ (b - 1)) / x ^ 2 Λ(dx)`. The atom at `0` (the Kingman part) is split off, so no division by `0` occurs.
nodes.title: The total merger rate in closed form

nodes.summary: Adding a block raises the total merger rate by `b λ_{b+1,2}`: `λ_{b+1} = λ_b + b λ_{b+1,2}`. The new events are exactly the binary mergers of the new block with one of the `b` old ones (a consequence of the consistency relation).
nodes.title: Recursion for the total merger rate

nodes.summary: The total merger rate `λ_b` is nondecreasing in the number of blocks `b`.
nodes.title: Monotonicity of the total merger rate

nodes.summary: A finite measure on `[0, 1]` is determined by its merger rates; indeed by the rates `λ_{k,k} = ∫ x ^ (k - 2) Λ(dx)` of complete mergers, which are its moments (Pitman 1999, Theorem 1).
nodes.title: Uniqueness in Pitman's representation

nodes.summary: Kingman's coalescent is the Λ-coalescent with `Λ = δ₀`: only binary mergers occur, each pair merging at rate `1` (Pitman 1999; Berestycki 2009, §3.1).
nodes.title: Kingman's coalescent

nodes.summary: For Kingman's coalescent the total merger rate is the number of pairs, `λ_b = b.choose 2`.
nodes.title: Total merger rate of Kingman's coalescent

nodes.summary: The Bolthausen–Sznitman coalescent (`Λ` = Lebesgue measure on `[0, 1]`) has merger rates given by the Beta integral `λ_{b,k} = (k - 2)! (b - k)! / (b - 1)!` for `2 ≤ k ≤ b` (Bolthausen–Sznitman 1998; Pitman 1999; Berestycki 2009, §3.1).
nodes.title: Merger rates of the Bolthausen–Sznitman coalescent

nodes.summary: For the Bolthausen–Sznitman coalescent the total merger rate is `λ_b = b - 1` (`b ≥ 1`).
nodes.title: Total merger rate of the Bolthausen–Sznitman coalescent

(Uniqueness of `Λ` is `LambdaCoalescent.eq_of_mergerRate_eq`.)

nodes.summary: An alignment over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a finite list of columns, where each column is a pair $(u, v)$ and each of $u$ and $v$ is either a letter of $\alpha$ or a gap.
nodes.title: Alignment

nodes.summary: A list $A$ of columns, each a pair of optional letters, is an alignment of sequences $x$ and $y$ when no column has both entries empty, the letters present in the first entries of the columns, read in order, form $x$, and the letters present in the second entries, read in order, form $y$.
nodes.title: Valid alignment of two sequences

nodes.summary: Given a substitution score $\sigma$, which assigns an integer $\sigma(a, b)$ to all letters $a, b \in \alpha$, and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$, a column pairing letters $a$ and $b$ scores $\sigma(a, b)$, a column pairing a letter with a gap (on either side) scores $g$, and a column with a gap on both sides scores $0$.
nodes.title: Score of an alignment column

nodes.summary: Given a substitution score $\sigma$, which assigns an integer $\sigma(a, b)$ to all letters $a, b \in \alpha$, and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$, the score of an alignment $A$ over $\alpha$ is the sum, over all columns of $A$, of the score of the column with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$.
nodes.title: Score of an alignment

nodes.summary: If $A_1$ is an alignment of sequences $x_1$ and $y_1$, and $A_2$ is an alignment of sequences $x_2$ and $y_2$, then the concatenation of $A_1$ and $A_2$ is an alignment of the concatenation of $x_1$ and $x_2$ and the concatenation of $y_1$ and $y_2$.
nodes.title: Concatenation of alignments

nodes.summary: Fix a substitution score $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$, and write $|x|$ for the length of a sequence $x$ and $ax$ for the sequence with first element $a$ followed by $x$. For a fuel $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sequences $x, y$ over $\alpha$, the value $N_n(x, y) \in \mathbb{Z}$ is defined by $N_0(x, y) = 0$, by $N_{n+1}(x, y) = g\,|y|$ if $x$ is empty and…
nodes.title: Fuel-bounded Needleman–Wunsch recursion

nodes.summary: Given a type $\alpha$, a substitution score $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$, the Needleman–Wunsch score $\mathrm{NW}(xs, ys)$ of two lists over $\alpha$ is defined by recursion on their total length: if one of the lists is empty, it is $g$ times the length of the other; and for lists $a\,xs$ and $b\,ys$ with heads $a$, $b$ and tails $xs$, $ys$,
nodes.title: Needleman–Wunsch score

nodes.summary: For every substitution score $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$, gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ and sequence $y$ over $\alpha$ of length $|y|$, the Needleman–Wunsch score of the empty sequence and $y$ with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$ is $g\,|y|$: one gap per letter.
nodes.title: Aligning the empty sequence with a sequence

nodes.summary: For every substitution score $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$, gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ and sequence $x$ over $\alpha$ of length $|x|$, the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ and the empty sequence with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$ is $g\,|x|$: one gap per letter.
nodes.title: Aligning a sequence with the empty sequence

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a substitution score and $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ a gap score, and write $N(x, y)$ for the Needleman–Wunsch score of sequences $x, y$ over $\alpha$ with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$. For all letters $a, b \in \alpha$ and sequences $x, y$, writing $ax$ for the sequence with first element $a$ followed by $x$,
nodes.title: The Needleman–Wunsch recurrence

nodes.summary: Given a fuel $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sequences $x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$, this lists alignments column by column from the front. With fuel $0$ the list is empty. With fuel $n + 1$: two empty sequences give the single empty alignment; if only $y$ is nonempty, with first letter $b$ and rest $y'$, each alignment of $x$ and $y'$ with fuel $n$ is preceded by the column pairing a gap with $b$; if only $x$ is nonempty,…
nodes.title: Fuel-bounded enumeration of alignments

nodes.summary: For sequences $x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$, this is the list produced by the fuel-bounded enumeration of alignments of $x$ and $y$ with fuel $|x| + |y| + 1$.
nodes.title: The list of all alignments

nodes.summary: For sequences $x$ and $y$ and a list $A$ of columns, $A$ occurs in the enumerated list of all alignments of $x$ and $y$ if and only if $A$ is an alignment of $x$ and $y$.
nodes.title: The enumerated alignments are exactly the valid ones

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a substitution score and $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ a gap score. For all sequences $x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$ and every valid alignment $A$ of $x$ and $y$, the score of $A$ with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$ is at most the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ and $y$.
nodes.title: Needleman–Wunsch is optimal

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a substitution score and $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ a gap score. For all sequences $x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$ there is a valid alignment $A$ of $x$ and $y$ whose score with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$ equals the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ and $y$.
nodes.title: Needleman–Wunsch is attained

nodes.summary: Fix a substitution score $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$, and write $ax$ for the sequence with first element $a$ followed by $x$. For a fuel $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sequences $x, y$ over $\alpha$, the value $F_n(x, y) \in \mathbb{Z}$ is defined by $F_0(x, y) = 0$, by $F_{n+1}(x, y) = 0$ if $x$ or $y$ is empty, and by
nodes.title: Fuel-bounded Smith–Waterman recursion

nodes.summary: Given a substitution score $\sigma(a, b) \in \mathbb{Z}$ for letters $a, b$ and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$, and writing $sc$ for a sequence $s$ followed by a letter $c$, the terminal Smith–Waterman cell $H(x, y)$ of two sequences $x$ and $y$ is the integer defined by $H(x, y) = 0$ when $x$ or $y$ is empty, and
nodes.title: The terminal Smith–Waterman cell

nodes.summary: For every substitution score $\sigma$, every gap score $g$ and all sequences $x$ and $y$, the terminal Smith–Waterman cell $H(x, y)$ satisfies $H(x, y) \ge 0$.
nodes.title: The terminal Smith–Waterman cell is nonnegative

nodes.summary: For a substitution score $\sigma$, a gap score $g$ and every sequence $y$, the terminal Smith–Waterman cell of the empty sequence and $y$ is $0$.
nodes.title: The terminal cell vanishes when the first sequence is empty

nodes.summary: For a substitution score $\sigma$, a gap score $g$ and every sequence $x$, the terminal Smith–Waterman cell of $x$ and the empty sequence is $0$.
nodes.title: The terminal cell vanishes when the second sequence is empty

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and $g$ a gap score, and for a sequence $s$ and a letter $c$ write $sc$ for $s$ followed by $c$. For all sequences $x$ and $y$ and all letters $a$ and $b$, the terminal Smith–Waterman cell $H$ satisfies
nodes.title: The Smith–Waterman recurrence

nodes.summary: If $s$ is a suffix of the list obtained by appending an element $a$ at the end of a list $xs$, then either $s$ is empty, or there is a suffix $s'$ of $xs$ such that $s$ is $s'$ with $a$ appended at the end.
nodes.title: Suffixes of a list with an element appended

nodes.summary: If a list $s$ is a suffix of a list $xs$, then for every element $a$, the list $s$ with $a$ appended at the end is a suffix of $xs$ with $a$ appended at the end.
nodes.title: Appending an element preserves suffixes

nodes.summary: For a list of columns $A$ and sequences $x$ and $y$, $A$ is an alignment of the reversal of $x$ and the reversal of $y$ if and only if the reversal of $A$ (its columns in reverse order) is an alignment of $x$ and $y$.
nodes.title: Reversing an alignment

nodes.summary: For every substitution score $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$, gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ and alignment $A$, the alignment obtained by listing the columns of $A$ in reverse order has the same score as $A$.
nodes.title: Reversal preserves alignment score

nodes.summary: Reversing both sequences preserves the optimal global score.
nodes.title: Needleman–Wunsch is reversal-invariant

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a substitution score and $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ a gap score, and write $N(x, y)$ for the Needleman–Wunsch score of sequences $x, y$ over $\alpha$ with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$. For all sequences $x, y$ and letters $a, b \in \alpha$, writing $xa$ for the sequence $x$ followed by the letter $a$,
nodes.title: The Needleman–Wunsch recurrence, end-peeling

nodes.summary: For a list $l$ of integers, this is the largest of $0$ and the entries of $l$; in particular the empty list gives $0$.
nodes.title: Maximum of an integer list with floor zero

nodes.summary: For lists $xs$ and $ys$, the list of all pairs $(u, v)$ where $u$ is a suffix of $xs$ and $v$ is a suffix of $ys$, the empty lists and $xs$, $ys$ themselves included.
nodes.title: Pairs of suffixes

nodes.summary: Given a substitution score $\sigma$ and an integer gap score $g$, the suffix maximum of lists $xs$ and $ys$ is the maximum of the Needleman–Wunsch scores of all pairs $(u, v)$ with $u$ a suffix of $xs$ and $v$ a suffix of $ys$.
nodes.title: Suffix maximum of Needleman–Wunsch scores

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a substitution score and $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ a gap score. If $(x', y')$ is a suffix pair of sequences $x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$, that is, $x'$ is a suffix of $x$ and $y'$ is a suffix of $y$, then the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x'$ and $y'$ is at most the suffix maximum of $x$ and $y$, both with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$.
nodes.title: Suffix pairs score at most the suffix maximum

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score, $g$ an integer gap score, $xs$ and $ys$ lists and $y$ an integer. If every pair $(u, v)$ with $u$ a suffix of $xs$ and $v$ a suffix of $ys$ has Needleman–Wunsch score at most $y$, then the maximum Needleman–Wunsch score over all such suffix pairs is at most $y$.
nodes.title: Upper bounds on the suffix maximum

nodes.summary: For a substitution score $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$, a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ and sequences $x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$, there is a suffix pair $(x', y')$ of $x$ and $y$, that is, a suffix $x'$ of $x$ and a suffix $y'$ of $y$, whose Needleman–Wunsch score equals the suffix maximum of $x$ and $y$.
nodes.title: The suffix maximum is attained

nodes.summary: For every scoring function $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$, every gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ and all lists $x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$, the suffix maximum of $x$ and $y$ (the largest Needleman–Wunsch score, under $\sigma$ and $g$, of a suffix of $x$ against a suffix of $y$) is at least $0$, since the pair of empty suffixes scores $0$.
nodes.title: The suffix maximum is nonnegative

nodes.summary: If $A$ is an alignment of sequences $x$ and $y$ and $a$ is a letter, then $A$ followed by the column with $a$ in the first row and a gap in the second row is an alignment of $x$ followed by $a$ and of $y$.
nodes.title: Extending an alignment by a letter of the first sequence

nodes.summary: If $A$ is an alignment of sequences $x$ and $y$ and $b$ is a letter, then $A$ followed by the column with a gap in the first row and $b$ in the second row is an alignment of $x$ and of $y$ followed by $b$.
nodes.title: Extending an alignment by a letter of the second sequence

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a substitution score, $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ a gap score, and write $N(x, y)$ for the Needleman–Wunsch score of sequences $x, y$ over $\alpha$ with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$. For all sequences $x, y$ and every letter $a \in \alpha$, writing $xa$ for $x$ with $a$ appended at the end, $N(x, y) + g \le N(xa, y)$.
nodes.title: Appending to the first sequence loses at most one gap

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a substitution score, $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ a gap score, and write $N(x, y)$ for the Needleman–Wunsch score of sequences $x, y$ over $\alpha$ with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$. For all sequences $x, y$ and every letter $b \in \alpha$, writing $yb$ for $y$ with $b$ appended at the end, $N(x, y) + g \le N(x, yb)$.
nodes.title: Appending to the second sequence loses at most one gap

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a substitution score and $g \le 0$ a gap score. If $x'$ is a suffix of a sequence $x$ and $y'$ is a suffix of a sequence $y$ over $\alpha$, then the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x'$ and $y'$ is at most the terminal Smith–Waterman cell score of $x$ and $y$, both with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$.
nodes.title: Suffix pairs score at most the terminal Smith–Waterman cell

nodes.summary: For every substitution score $\sigma$, every gap score $g$ of either sign and all sequences $x$ and $y$, the terminal Smith–Waterman cell $H(x, y)$ is at most the maximum Needleman–Wunsch score over all pairs of a suffix of $x$ and a suffix of $y$.
nodes.title: The terminal cell is at most the suffix maximum

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and $g \le 0$ an integer gap score. For all lists $xs$ and $ys$, the maximum Needleman–Wunsch score over all pairs of a suffix of $xs$ and a suffix of $ys$ is at most the terminal Smith–Waterman cell score of $xs$ and $ys$.
nodes.title: The suffix maximum is at most the terminal Smith–Waterman cell

nodes.summary: For a substitution score $\sigma$, a gap score $g \le 0$ and all sequences $x$ and $y$, the terminal Smith–Waterman cell $H(x, y)$ equals the maximum Needleman–Wunsch score over all pairs of a suffix of $x$ and a suffix of $y$ (the empty suffixes included).
nodes.title: For nonpositive gaps, the terminal Smith–Waterman cell is the best suffix-pair score

nodes.summary: For lists $xs$ and $ys$, the list of all pairs $(p, q)$ where $p$ is a prefix of $xs$ and $q$ is a prefix of $ys$, the empty lists and $xs$, $ys$ themselves included.
nodes.title: Pairs of prefixes

nodes.summary: For sequences $x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$, the list of infix pairs of $x$ and $y$ is obtained by going through each prefix $p$ of $x$ and each prefix $q$ of $y$ and, for each such $(p, q)$, listing all pairs $(x', y')$ of a suffix $x'$ of $p$ and a suffix $y'$ of $q$.
nodes.title: Infix pairs

nodes.summary: For an integer substitution score $\sigma$, an integer gap score $g$ and sequences $x$ and $y$, the local score of $x$ and $y$ is the maximum of the Needleman–Wunsch score of $(x', y')$ over all pairs of an infix $x'$ of $x$ and an infix $y'$ of $y$ (contiguous and possibly empty).
nodes.title: Local alignment score

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a substitution score and $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ a gap score. If $(x', y')$ is an infix pair of sequences $x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$, that is, $x'$ is a suffix of a prefix of $x$ and $y'$ is a suffix of a prefix of $y$, then the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x'$ and $y'$ is at most the local score of $x$ and $y$, both with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$.
nodes.title: Infix pairs score at most the local score

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be an integer substitution score, $g$ an integer gap score, $x$ and $y$ sequences and $c$ an integer. If the Needleman–Wunsch score of every pair $(x', y')$ with $x'$ an infix of $x$ and $y'$ an infix of $y$ is at most $c$, then the local score of $x$ and $y$ is at most $c$.
nodes.title: Upper bounds on the local score

nodes.summary: Given a substitution score $\sigma$ and a gap score $g$, the Smith–Waterman score of two sequences $x$ and $y$ is the maximum of the terminal Smith–Waterman cell $H(p, q)$ over all pairs of a prefix $p$ of $x$ and a prefix $q$ of $y$ (the empty prefixes included).
nodes.title: The Smith–Waterman score

nodes.summary: For a substitution score $\sigma$, a gap score $g$, sequences $x$ and $y$, a prefix $p$ of $x$ and a prefix $q$ of $y$, the terminal Smith–Waterman cell $H(p, q)$ is at most the Smith–Waterman score of $x$ and $y$.
nodes.title: Each prefix-pair cell is at most the Smith–Waterman score

nodes.summary: For a substitution score $\sigma$, a gap score $g$, sequences $x$ and $y$ and an integer $c$, if the terminal Smith–Waterman cell $H(p, q)$ is at most $c$ for every prefix $p$ of $x$ and every prefix $q$ of $y$, then the Smith–Waterman score of $x$ and $y$ is at most $c$.
nodes.title: Bounding the Smith–Waterman score by its cells

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be an integer-valued substitution score on letters and let $g$ be an integer gap score with $g \le 0$. Then for all sequences $x$ and $y$, the local score of $x$ and $y$ (the maximum Needleman–Wunsch score over pairs of infixes) equals their Smith–Waterman score (the maximum terminal-cell score over pairs of prefixes).
nodes.title: The local score equals the Smith–Waterman score

nodes.summary: The cells `F[i+1][j+1], F[i+1][j+2], …` of a row from the remaining letters `b :: ys` of the second sequence, the remaining cells `up :: prev` of the previous row, the previous row's cell `diag` to the upper left and the cell `left` just computed. A previous row that is too short ends the row early (this does not happen for rows of the table, `nextRow_eq`).
nodes.title: Remaining cells of a Needleman–Wunsch table row

nodes.summary: The row of the table for the prefix extended by `a`, from the previous row: the first cell is one more gap than the previous row's first cell, then the recurrence left to right.
nodes.title: Next row of the Needleman–Wunsch table

nodes.summary: The rows of the table, filled top to bottom over the letters of the first sequence; the result is the last row. Row `0` is `F[0][j] = j * gap`.
nodes.title: Row-by-row filling of the Needleman–Wunsch table

nodes.summary: The last row `F[|xs|][·]` of the Needleman–Wunsch table.
nodes.title: Last row of the Needleman–Wunsch table

nodes.summary: Its last cell `F[|xs|][|ys|]`.
nodes.title: The Needleman–Wunsch table

nodes.summary: From the row of the prefix `px`, `nextRow` computes the row of `px ++ [a]`: the cells `nwScore (px ++ [a]) py` for the prefixes `py` of `ys`, shortest first.
nodes.title: One row of the table

nodes.summary: The last row of the table is `F[|xs|][j] = nwScore xs (ys.take j)`: the cells `nwScore xs py` over the prefixes `py` of `ys`, shortest first.
nodes.title: The last row of the table

nodes.summary: The table computes the optimal global alignment score (Needleman–Wunsch 1970), for every substitution score `σ` and gap score `gap`.
nodes.title: The table computes the optimal global alignment score
Banded sequence alignment

nodes.summary: Let $w \in \mathbb{N}$ be a band width. For natural numbers $i$, $j$ and an alignment $A$, the band check of $A$ with width $w$ from offset $(i, j)$ is true exactly when every prefix $P$ of $A$ (including the empty prefix and $A$ itself) satisfies $|(i + p) - (j + q)| \le w$, where $p$ and $q$ are the numbers of columns of $P$ whose first, respectively second, entry is present.
nodes.title: Band check from a starting offset

nodes.summary: Let $w \in \mathbb{N}$. An alignment $A$ is banded with width $w$ when, for every prefix of $A$ (including the empty prefix and $A$ itself), the number of columns of that prefix with a letter in the first row and the number with a letter in the second row differ by at most $w$.
nodes.title: Banded alignments

nodes.summary: For integers $a$, $d$, $t$ and $w$, if $|a| \le w$, $|a - d| \le w$ and $0 \le t \le d$, then $|a - t| \le w$.
nodes.title: Bound at an intermediate point, difference form

nodes.summary: For integers $a$, $d$, $t$ and $w$, if $|a| \le w$, $|a + d| \le w$ and $0 \le t \le d$, then $|a + t| \le w$.
nodes.title: Bound at an intermediate point, sum form

nodes.summary: Let $w, i, j \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $A$ be an alignment. If the band check of $A$ with width $w$ from offset $(i, j)$ is true, then $|(i + p) - (j + q)| \le w$, where $p$ and $q$ are the numbers of columns of $A$ whose first, respectively second, entry is present.
nodes.title: A passing band check bounds the final offset

nodes.summary: Let $w \in \mathbb{N}$. If $A$ is a valid alignment of sequences $x$ and $y$ and $A$ is banded with width $w$, then the lengths of $x$ and $y$ differ by at most $w$, that is $\bigl| |x| - |y| \bigr| \le w$.
nodes.title: Banded alignments force close lengths

nodes.summary: For sequences $x = x_1 \dots x_m$ and $y = y_1 \dots y_n$, let $k = \min(m, n)$. The diagonal alignment of $x$ and $y$ consists of the columns $(x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_k, y_k)$, which pair letters by position whether or not they are equal, followed by one column for each remaining letter of the longer sequence, in order, pairing that letter with a gap.
nodes.title: Diagonal alignment

nodes.summary: For all sequences $x$ and $y$, the diagonal alignment of $x$ and $y$ is a valid alignment of $x$ and $y$: none of its columns consists of two gaps, and deleting the gaps from its first and second rows gives $x$ and $y$ respectively.
nodes.title: The diagonal alignment is a valid alignment

nodes.summary: Let $w, i, j \in \mathbb{N}$, let $y$ be a list of length $n$, and let $A$ be the alignment with one column for each element $b$ of $y$, in order, with empty first entry and second entry $b$. If $|i - j| \le w$ and $|i - (j + n)| \le w$, then the band check of $A$ with width $w$ from offset $(i, j)$ is true.
nodes.title: Columns using only the second sequence stay in the band

nodes.summary: Let $w, i, j \in \mathbb{N}$, let $x$ be a list of length $n$, and let $A$ be the alignment with one column for each element $a$ of $x$, in order, with first entry $a$ and empty second entry. If $|i - j| \le w$ and $|(i + n) - j| \le w$, then the band check of $A$ with width $w$ from offset $(i, j)$ is true.
nodes.title: Columns using only the first sequence stay in the band

nodes.summary: Let $w, i, j \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x$, $y$ be lists of lengths $m$ and $n$. If $|i - j| \le w$ and $|(i + m) - (j + n)| \le w$, then the band check of the diagonal alignment of $x$ and $y$ with width $w$ from offset $(i, j)$ is true.
nodes.title: The diagonal alignment stays in the band

nodes.summary: Let $w \in \mathbb{N}$. If two sequences $x$ and $y$ have lengths differing by at most $w$, that is $\bigl| |x| - |y| \bigr| \le w$, then the diagonal alignment of $x$ and $y$ is banded with width $w$.
nodes.title: The diagonal alignment is banded

nodes.summary: Fix a substitution score $\sigma$, assigning an integer $\sigma(a, b)$ to each pair of letters $a$, $b$, an integer gap score $g$ and a band width $w \in \mathbb{N}$. The banded alignment score of two sequences $x$ and $y$ is the maximum, over all valid alignments of $x$ and $y$ that are banded with width $w$, of the (integer) alignment score with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$. It has no value (it is the empty…
nodes.title: Banded alignment score

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be an integer substitution score on an alphabet, $g$ an integer gap score and $w \in \mathbb{N}$ a band width. For sequences $x$ and $y$ over the alphabet and an integer $s$, if the banded score of $x$ and $y$ (under $\sigma$, $g$ and width $w$) is defined and equals $s$, then $s$ is at most the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ and $y$.
nodes.title: The banded score is at most the Needleman–Wunsch score

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be an integer substitution score on an alphabet, $g$ an integer gap score and $w \in \mathbb{N}$ a band width. For sequences $x$ and $y$ over the alphabet, if some alignment of $x$ and $y$ is banded with width $w$ and has score (under $\sigma$ and $g$) equal to the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ and $y$, then the banded score of $x$ and $y$ (under $\sigma$, $g$ and width $w$) is defined and equals their…
nodes.title: Banded alignment is exact when some optimal alignment is banded

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be an integer substitution score on an alphabet, $g$ an integer gap score and $w \in \mathbb{N}$ a band width. For sequences $x$ and $y$ over the alphabet, of lengths $m$ and $n$, with $w < |m - n|$, the banded score of $x$ and $y$ (under $\sigma$, $g$ and width $w$) is undefined: no alignment of $x$ and $y$ is banded with width $w$.
nodes.title: No banded score when the lengths differ by more than the band width

nodes.summary: Fix a substitution score $\sigma$, assigning an integer $\sigma(a, b)$ to each pair of letters $a$, $b$, an integer gap score $g$ and a band width $w \in \mathbb{N}$. If two sequences $x$ and $y$ have lengths differing by at most $w$, that is $\bigl| |x| - |y| \bigr| \le w$, then the banded alignment score of $x$ and $y$ (for $\sigma$, $g$ and $w$) is defined: it equals some integer $s$.
nodes.title: The banded score is defined when the lengths are close

nodes.summary: The number of gap columns of an alignment: columns with exactly one letter.
nodes.title: Number of gap columns of an alignment

nodes.summary: Along every prefix, the offset difference is at most the starting difference plus the number of gap columns: an alignment starting at `(i, j)` stays in the band of width `w` as soon as `|i - j| + gapColumns A ≤ w`.
nodes.title: An alignment with few gap columns stays in the band from its start

nodes.summary: An alignment with at most `w` gap columns is `w`-banded.
nodes.title: An alignment with at most w gap columns is w-banded

nodes.summary: With nonpositive substitution scores and gap score at most `-1`, an alignment scores at most minus its number of gap columns.
nodes.title: Alignment score is at most minus the number of gap columns

nodes.summary: The band lemma (Ukkonen 1985): with nonpositive substitution scores and gap score at most `-1`, every alignment scoring at least `-w` (cost at most `w`) is `w`-banded.
nodes.title: The band lemma

nodes.summary: The banded optimum is exact when the optimal score is at least `-w` (optimal cost at most `w`), for nonpositive substitution scores and gap score at most `-1`: some optimal alignment exists and, by the band lemma, it is `w`-banded.
nodes.title: The banded optimum is exact
Gotoh affine-gap alignment

nodes.summary: A gap state is one of three values: $\mathrm{none}$, $\mathrm{gapX}$ and $\mathrm{gapY}$. The affine-gap score and the Gotoh recursion carry one as the kind of the previous column: $\mathrm{gapX}$ after a column pairing an element of the first sequence with a gap, $\mathrm{gapY}$ after a column pairing a gap with an element of the second sequence, and $\mathrm{none}$ otherwise, including before the first column.

nodes.title: Gotoh score

nodes.summary: Given an integer gap-open cost $o$, an integer gap-extend cost $e$, gap states $p$ (of the column before the run) and $c$ (of the run's columns) and a length $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the cost of a run of $k$ gap columns is $k e$ if $p = c$ (the run continues an open run); otherwise it is $0$ for $k = 0$ and $o + (k - 1) e$ for $k \ge 1$.

Multiple sequence alignment

nodes.summary: A multiple alignment with $k$ rows over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a finite list of columns, each of which assigns to every row $i \in \{0, \dots, k-1\}$ either a letter of $\alpha$ or a gap. No condition ties the rows to given sequences.
nodes.title: Multiple alignments

nodes.summary: A multiple alignment $A$ of $k$ rows is a valid multiple alignment of sequences $s_0, \dots, s_{k-1}$ when no column of $A$ consists only of gaps and, for every $i < k$, deleting the gaps from row $i$ of $A$ gives $s_i$.
nodes.title: Valid multiple alignment

nodes.summary: Given a multiple alignment $A$ of $k$ sequences and rows $i, j < k$, the pairwise alignment induced by $A$ on rows $i$ and $j$ is obtained by keeping, for each column $c$ of $A$ in order, the pair $(c_i, c_j)$, and dropping the columns in which both $c_i$ and $c_j$ are gaps.

nodes.summary: For a multiple alignment $A$ of $k$ sequences and rows $i, j < k$, no column of the pairwise alignment induced by $A$ on rows $i$ and $j$ is a gap in both rows.

Semi-global and overlap alignment

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ of integers, the maximum of $L$ with floor $0$ (which is $0$ for the empty list) is at least $0$.
nodes.title: The floored list maximum is nonnegative

nodes.summary: The overlap pairs of sequences $x$ and $y$ are the pairs $(x', y')$ in which $x'$ is a suffix of $x$ and $y'$ is a prefix of $y$, or $x'$ is a prefix of $x$ and $y'$ is a suffix of $y$. Prefixes and suffixes include the empty sequence and the whole sequence; the pairs are listed with the suffix–prefix pairs first, and the list can contain repetitions.
nodes.title: Overlap pairs

nodes.summary: Given a substitution score $\sigma$ and a gap score $g$, the overlap score of sequences $s$ and $t$ is the maximum, with floor $0$, of the Needleman–Wunsch scores of the overlap pairs of $s$ and $t$: the pairs $(s', t')$ where $s'$ is a suffix of $s$ and $t'$ a prefix of $t$, or $s'$ is a prefix of $s$ and $t'$ a suffix of $t$.
nodes.title: Overlap alignment score

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and $g$ a gap score. If $(x', y')$ is an overlap pair of sequences $x$ and $y$, then the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x'$ against $y'$ is at most the overlap score of $x$ and $y$, both taken with $\sigma$ and $g$.
nodes.title: Overlap-pair scores are at most the overlap score

nodes.summary: Fix a substitution score $\sigma$ and a gap score $g$, and sequences $s$ and $t$. If an integer $b$ is at least the Needleman–Wunsch score of every overlap pair of $s$ and $t$ (a suffix of $s$ with a prefix of $t$, or a prefix of $s$ with a suffix of $t$), then the overlap score of $s$ and $t$ is at most $b$.
nodes.title: Upper bounds for the overlap score

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and $g$ a gap score. For all sequences $x$ and $y$ there is an overlap pair $(x', y')$ of $x$ and $y$ such that the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x'$ against $y'$ (with $\sigma$ and $g$) equals the overlap score of $x$ and $y$.
nodes.title: The overlap score is attained

nodes.summary: For every substitution score $\sigma$, gap score $g$ and sequences $s$ and $t$, the overlap score of $s$ and $t$ is at least $0$.
nodes.title: The overlap score is nonnegative

nodes.summary: The infixes of a sequence $y$ are its contiguous substrings: the sequences $l$ such that $y$ is the concatenation of $s$, $l$ and $t$ for some sequences $s$ and $t$, including the empty sequence and $y$ itself. They are listed as the suffixes of the prefixes of $y$, so the list can contain repetitions.
nodes.title: Infixes

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and $g$ a gap score. The fitting score of a sequence $x$ against a sequence $y$ is the maximum, over all infixes $l$ of $y$ (including the empty one), of the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ against $l$ with $\sigma$ and $g$: the best global alignment score of $x$ against a substring of $y$.
nodes.title: Fitting score

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and $g$ a gap score. If $l$ is an infix of a sequence $y$, then for every sequence $x$ the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ against $l$ is at most the fitting score of $x$ against $y$, both taken with $\sigma$ and $g$.
nodes.title: Infix scores are at most the fitting score

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score, $g$ a gap score, $x$ and $y$ sequences and $b$ an integer. If the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ against every infix of $y$ (with $\sigma$ and $g$) is at most $b$, then the fitting score of $x$ against $y$ is at most $b$.
nodes.title: Upper bounds on the fitting score

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and $g$ a gap score. For all sequences $x$ and $y$ there is an infix $l$ of $y$ such that the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ against $l$ (with $\sigma$ and $g$) equals the fitting score of $x$ against $y$.
nodes.title: The fitting score is attained

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and $g$ a gap score. For all sequences $x$ and $y$, the overlap score of $x$ and $y$ is at most the local score of $x$ and $y$, both taken with $\sigma$ and $g$.
nodes.title: The overlap score is at most the local score

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a substitution score and $g$ a gap score. For all sequences $x$ and $y$, the fitting score of $x$ against $y$ is at most the local score of $x$ and $y$, both taken with $\sigma$ and $g$.
nodes.title: The fitting score is at most the local score

ARACNE gene network reconstruction

nodes.summary: The network ARACNE reconstructs from symmetric pairwise mutual informations `I` with independence threshold `I₀` and DPI tolerance zero (Margolin et al. 2006): `{i, k}` is an edge iff `i ≠ k`, `I₀ < I i k`, and no third gene `j` with `I₀ < I i j` and `I₀ < I j k` has `I i k < min (I i j) (I j k)`.
nodes.title: ARACNE gene network reconstruction

nodes.summary: If the true network `T` is a forest whose edges all carry mutual information above `I₀`, and `I a b ≤ min (I a c) (I c b)` whenever `c` separates `a` from `b` in `T` (every walk from `a` to `b` visits `c`), then ARACNE keeps every edge of `T`.
nodes.title: No false negatives

nodes.summary: If the true network `T` is a tree and `I a b < min (I a c) (I c b)` whenever `c` separates `a` from `b` in `T`, then every edge ARACNE keeps is an edge of `T`.
nodes.title: No false positives

nodes.summary: ARACNE recovers tree networks exactly (Margolin et al. 2006, Theorem 1): if the true network `T` is a tree whose edges all carry mutual information above `I₀`, and the strict data-processing inequality holds on every separated triple, then ARACNE returns `T`. Strictness is the explicit form of the paper's exclusion of exact cancellations; with equality ARACNE can keep an indirect edge (see the tests).
nodes.title: ARACNE recovers tree networks exactly

nodes.summary: Chow–Liu trees survive ARACNE (Margolin et al. 2006, Theorem 2): a spanning tree `T` of maximum total weight `∑_{{i, k} ∈ T} I i k` among all spanning trees, whose edges all carry mutual information above `I₀`, is a subnetwork of the ARACNE network.
nodes.title: Chow–Liu trees survive ARACNE

nodes.summary: The `k`-mers of `s` in order of position: the length-`k` windows `(s.drop i).take k` for `i + k ≤ |s|`.

nodes.summary: Executable form of `kmers`: the suffixes of `s` are generated once by `List.tails`, so the cost is `O(|s| · k)` rather than the `Θ(|s|²)` of recomputing `s.drop i` for every `i`. The compiler uses it in place of `kmers` (`kmers_eq_kmersImpl`).
nodes.title: Efficient executable computation of k-mers

nodes.summary: The edge of the de Bruijn multigraph contributed by a `k`-mer `w`: from its prefix `(k-1)`-mer `w.dropLast` to its suffix `(k-1)`-mer `w.tail`.
nodes.title: De Bruijn edge of a k-mer

nodes.summary: The de Bruijn multigraph of `s` (Pevzner–Tang–Waterman 2001) as its list of edge occurrences: one edge per `k`-mer occurrence, in order of position.

nodes.summary: The string spelled by a walk of `(k-1)`-mers: the first vertex followed by the last letter of each later vertex.

nodes.summary: Its steps are exactly the edges contributed by the `k`-mers of `s`, one per occurrence, in order of position.

nodes.summary: The `k`-mer walk of `s` is an Eulerian trail of its de Bruijn multigraph: its steps are a permutation of the edge occurrences, each traversed once.
nodes.title: The `k`-mer walk of `s` is an Eulerian trail

nodes.summary: The `(k-1)`-mer walk of `s` spells `s` back (`2 ≤ k`, `k - 1 ≤ |s|`).
nodes.title: The (k-1)-mer walk of a string spells the string

nodes.summary: Every Eulerian trail spells a string with the same `k`-mer multiset (`2 ≤ k`): if `W` is a walk of `(k-1)`-mers whose steps are a permutation of the edge occurrences of the de Bruijn multigraph of `s`, then the `k`-mers of the spelled string are a permutation of those of `s`. (The empty walk is allowed: it is a trail only when `s` has no `k`-mers, and spells `[]`.)

Lander–Waterman coverage model

nodes.summary: A read of length `L` starting at position `s` of a circular genome of length `G` covers base `x` when `x` is one of `s, s + 1, …, s + L - 1 (mod G)`, i.e. `(x - s) mod G < L`.
nodes.title: Read covering a base of a circular genome

nodes.summary: The depth of coverage of base `x`: the number of reads covering it.
nodes.title: Depth of coverage of a base

nodes.summary: The totalized normalized count `|E| / G ^ N` of a set of start tuples. For `0 < G`, this is the probability when the `N` start positions are independent and uniform on `Fin G`. If `G = 0` and `N > 0`, the sample space is empty and this value is zero, so it is not a probability law. For `N = 0`, there is one empty start tuple, even when `G = 0`.
nodes.title: Normalized count of read start tuples

nodes.summary: `normalizedCount` agrees with Mathlib's totalized uniform measure on all start tuples. This measure is a probability law only when the sample space is nonempty.
nodes.title: Normalized count agrees with the totalized uniform measure

nodes.summary: For `L ≤ G`, base `x` is uncovered by all `N` reads for exactly `(G - L) ^ N` of the `G ^ N` start tuples.
nodes.title: Exact coverage count

nodes.summary: For `L ≤ G`, base `x` is covered by exactly `k` reads for `N.choose k * L ^ k * (G - L) ^ (N - k)` of the start tuples.
nodes.title: Exact depth law (count form)

nodes.summary: Exact uncovered probability (Clarke–Carbon, Lander–Waterman, circular genome): `(1 - L / G) ^ N` for `L ≤ G`.
nodes.title: Exact uncovered probability

nodes.summary: The depth at a fixed base is binomial with `N` trials and success probability `L / G`, for `L ≤ G`.
nodes.title: Exact depth law

nodes.summary: With read length `L` fixed, genome lengths `G N ≥ L`, and coverage `N L / G_N → c` as the number of reads `N → ∞`, the probability that a given base is uncovered tends to `e^{-c}`.
nodes.title: Lander–Waterman limit for the uncovered fraction

nodes.summary: Under the hypotheses of `tendsto_normalizedCount_uncovered`, the probability that a given base is covered by exactly `k` reads tends to `e^{-c} c^k / k.factorial`.
nodes.title: The coverage depth tends to Poisson(`c`)

nodes.summary: Read `j` has no successor when no other read starts in the `L - 1` positions after it, `starts j + 1, …, starts j + L - 1 (mod G)` (reads starting at the same position are not successors of each other). In Lander and Waterman's terms such a read is counted as ending an island, but several no-successor reads can lie in one island, so this is not the island count.
nodes.title: Read with no successor

nodes.summary: For `L ≤ G`, summed over the reads, the number of start tuples in which read `j` has no successor is `N * G * (G - (L - 1)) ^ (N - 1)`. This counts no-successor reads, not island ends: a start tuple can have several no-successor reads in one island.
nodes.title: Count of no-successor reads (exact)

nodes.summary: For `0 < G` and `L ≤ G`, the expected number of reads with no successor is `N (1 - (L - 1) / G) ^ (N - 1)`. The `0 < G` hypothesis is essential: at `G = 0` and `N > 0`, the right-hand expression is `N` while the sum of totalized normalized counts is zero.
nodes.title: Expected number of no-successor reads (exact)
Nussinov algorithm for RNA secondary structure

nodes.summary: A secondary structure on `s` (Nussinov et al. 1978): a finite set of base pairs `(i, j)`, each closing a hairpin with at least `m` unpaired positions strictly inside (`i + m < j`), joining complementary bases (`pair s[i] s[j]`, which also puts both positions inside `s`), with every position in at most one pair and no two pairs crossing (`i < k < j < l`).
nodes.title: RNA secondary structure

nodes.summary: The largest of a list of naturals (`0` for the empty list).
nodes.title: Maximum of a list of natural numbers

nodes.summary: The first base `a` of `a :: rest` is either unpaired, or paired with `rest[k]` for some `k ≥ m` with `pair a rest[k]`, splitting the rest into the enclosed part `rest.take k` and the outer part `rest.drop (k + 1)`. Exponential-time specification; the usual `O(n³)` table memoizes it on the intervals of `s`.
nodes.title: The Nussinov recursion

nodes.summary: Every secondary structure has at most `nussinov pair m s` pairs.
nodes.title: Soundness bound

nodes.summary: Some secondary structure has exactly `nussinov pair m s` pairs, so the recursion computes the maximum number of pairs over all non-crossing structures.
nodes.title: Optimality

nodes.summary: Positions `i` and `j` of `s` both lie in `s` and carry complementary bases.
nodes.title: Complementary base pairing of two positions

nodes.summary: Inside recursion over a commutative semiring `R`: `inside pair m s w i len` is the weighted sum over the secondary structures supported in the interval `[i, i + len)` (proved in `inside_eq_sum`). Base `i` is either unpaired, or paired with `i + 1 + k` for some `k ≥ m` with `CanPair pair s i (i + 1 + k)`, which contributes `w i (i + 1 + k)` times the inside values of the enclosed interval `[i + 1, i + 1 + k)` and of…
nodes.title: Inside recursion

nodes.summary: Outside recursion (McCaskill 1990) over a commutative semiring `R`, for a sequence of length `n = s.length`: `outside pair m s w i j` is the weighted sum of the parts outside the pair `(i, j)` of all structures containing it (proved in `outside_mul_eq_sum`). Either no pair encloses `(i, j)`, leaving independent structures on `[0, i)` and `[j + 1, n)`, or there is a unique innermost enclosing pair `(a, b)` (`a < i`,…
nodes.title: Outside recursion

nodes.summary: The secondary structures on `s` (`IsStructure pair m s`) all of whose pairs lie in the interval `[i, i + len)`.
nodes.title: Secondary structures within an interval

nodes.summary: All secondary structures on `s` with minimum hairpin `m` (see `mem_structures`).
nodes.title: Set of all secondary structures of a sequence

nodes.summary: The weight of a structure: the product of the weights of its base pairs.
nodes.title: Weight of a secondary structure

nodes.summary: `structures` is exactly the set of secondary structures on `s`.
nodes.title: Membership in the set of secondary structures

nodes.summary: The inside recursion sums the weights of all secondary structures supported in the interval `[i, i + len)`, over any commutative semiring.
nodes.title: Inside algorithm

nodes.summary: The inside value of the whole sequence sums the weights of all its secondary structures.
nodes.title: Inside value sums the weights of all secondary structures

nodes.summary: Outside algorithm (McCaskill 1990): for a candidate pair `(i, j)` (`i + m < j` and `CanPair pair s i j`), the outside value times the pair's weight times the inside value of the enclosed interval `[i + 1, j)` sums the weights of all secondary structures containing `(i, j)`.
nodes.title: Outside algorithm

nodes.summary: With every base pair weighted `-1` in the min-plus semiring `MinTropical (WithTop ℤ)` (addition `min`, multiplication `+`), a structure with `k` pairs has weight `-k`, so the inside value of the whole sequence is minus the Nussinov maximum number of base pairs.
nodes.title: Tropical semiring

nodes.summary: Waterman's recursion for the number `S_m(n)` of secondary structures on `n` points with minimum hairpin `m` when every pair is allowed: `S(0) = 1` and `S(n + 1) = S(n) + ∑_{m ≤ k < n} S(k) S(n - 1 - k)` (Waterman 1978; Stein–Waterman 1979). For `m = 0` these are the Motzkin numbers (`watermanNumber_zero_eq_motzkinNumber`); for `m = 1` the Stein–Waterman numbers `1, 1, 1, 2, 4, 8, 17, 37, …` (OEIS A004148).
nodes.title: Waterman's recursion

nodes.summary: The number of secondary structures on `n` points with minimum hairpin `m`, when every pair of positions may pair, is Waterman's number `S_m(n)`.
nodes.title: Counting semiring

nodes.summary: For `m = 0` (no hairpin constraint) Waterman's numbers are the Motzkin numbers `M(n) = ∑_k C(n, 2k) C(k)`: the number of non-crossing partial matchings on `n` points.
nodes.title: Waterman numbers with no hairpin constraint are Motzkin numbers

nodes.summary: An additive base-pair energy model: the free energy of a structure is the sum of the energies `e i j` of its base pairs (in the same units as `RT`).
nodes.title: Additive base-pair energy model

nodes.summary: The partition function `Z = ∑_S exp (-E(S) / RT)` over all secondary structures `S` on `s` with minimum hairpin `m`, for the additive energy `e` at thermal energy `RT` (physically `0 < RT`; the identities below hold for every real `RT`).
nodes.title: McCaskill partition function of RNA secondary structures

nodes.summary: McCaskill's algorithm (inside part): over the sum-product semiring `ℝ` with Boltzmann weights `exp (-e i j / RT)`, the inside value of the whole sequence is the partition function. This is an algebraic identity valid for every real `RT`.
nodes.title: McCaskill's algorithm

nodes.summary: The base-pair probability `P(i, j)`: the total weight of the structures containing the pair `(i, j)`, divided by the total weight `Z` of all structures. For nonnegative weights `Z ≥ 1` (the empty structure has weight `1`), so the denominator is positive; for Boltzmann weights this is the probability of `(i, j)` under the Boltzmann distribution on structures.
nodes.title: Base-pair probability

nodes.summary: For a candidate pair `(i, j)`, `P(i, j) = outside(i, j) · w(i, j) · inside(i + 1, j) / inside(0, n)`.
nodes.title: McCaskill's base-pair probabilities

nodes.summary: For nonnegative weights the total weight of all structures is at least `1`, the weight of the empty structure; so the denominator of `pairProb` is positive.
nodes.title: Total structure weight is at least one

nodes.summary: Base-pair probabilities are nonnegative for nonnegative weights.
nodes.title: Nonnegativity of base-pair probabilities

nodes.summary: For nonnegative weights, the probabilities that base `i` pairs with some later base `j` or some earlier base `j` sum to at most `1` (`∑_j (P(i, j) + P(j, i)) ≤ 1`).
nodes.title: Each base pairs at most once

nodes.summary: The score `∑ᵢ W i (s i)` of a site `s` of width `w` under a position weight matrix `W`.

nodes.summary: The likelihood `∏ᵢ p i (s i)` of a site under the product (column-independent) site model `p`.
nodes.title: Site likelihood under a column-independent model

nodes.summary: The likelihood `∏ₖ q (x k)` of a sequence of length `m` under the background of independent letters with law `q`.

nodes.summary: The log-odds matrix `log (p i b / q b)` of a site model against a background (natural logarithm).
nodes.title: Log-odds matrix of a site model

nodes.summary: For a four-letter alphabet (DNA) and the uniform background, a column carries between `0` and `2` bits.

nodes.summary: Under the site model, `E[score] = log 2 · ∑ᵢ IC(pᵢ ‖ q)`. This is an identity for every `q` (both sides use the same logarithms); it is an expected log-likelihood ratio for a positive background.

nodes.summary: The M-step maximizes the EM objective over PWMs with positive entries and normalized columns: for every `θ'`, `Q(θ' | θ) ≤ Q(mStep θ | θ)` (Gibbs' inequality per column).
nodes.title: The M-step maximizes the EM objective

nodes.summary: The motif likelihood is nondecreasing along the EM iterates.
nodes.title: The motif likelihood is nondecreasing along the EM iterates

nodes.summary: The moment generating function `∑ₐ ∑_b pₐ p_b e^{λ s_{ab}}` of a pair score under independent letters with law `p`.
nodes.title: Moment generating function of a pair score

nodes.summary: Karlin–Altschul `λ` (Karlin and Altschul 1990): if the expected score under a positive background distribution is negative and some score is positive, there is a unique `λ > 0` with `∑ pₐ p_b e^{λ s_{ab}} = 1`.
nodes.title: Karlin–Altschul `λ`

nodes.summary: The implicit target frequencies `q_{ab} = pₐ p_b e^{λ s_{ab}}` of a score matrix.
nodes.title: Implicit target frequencies of a score matrix

nodes.summary: At a root of `pairMGF p s λ = 1` the target frequencies form a distribution on pairs.
nodes.title: Target frequencies form a distribution on pairs

nodes.summary: Every such score matrix is a log-odds matrix (Karlin and Altschul 1990): `s_{ab} = log (q_{ab} / (pₐ p_b)) / λ` for every `λ > 0`; at the Karlin–Altschul root the `q_{ab}` form a distribution (`isDist_targetFreq`), the implicit target frequencies.
nodes.title: Every such score matrix is a log-odds matrix

nodes.summary: The relative entropy of the target frequencies (Altschul 1991): `λ ∑ q_{ab} s_{ab} = ∑ q_{ab} log (q_{ab} / (pₐ p_b))`, which is nonnegative.
nodes.title: The relative entropy of the target frequencies

nodes.summary: At the Karlin–Altschul root `λ > 0`, the expected score `∑ q_{ab} s_{ab}` under the target frequencies is positive.
nodes.title: The target score is positive

nodes.summary: The one-hot encoding of a letter: `oneHot a b = 1` if `b = a` and `0` otherwise.
nodes.title: One-hot encoding of a letter

nodes.summary: The response of a convolution (cross-correlation) filter `W` of width `w` on the one-hot encoded sequence `x` at the window starting at `i`: `∑ k, ∑ b, W k b * oneHot (x (i + k)) b`.

nodes.summary: The window of length `w` of `x` starting at `i`.

nodes.title: The convolution response is the PWM score of the window

nodes.summary: Global max pooling over the `m + 1` windows of a sequence of length `m + w`.
nodes.title: Global max pooling

nodes.summary: Every window's PWM score is at most the max-pooled output.
nodes.title: Every window's PWM score is at most the max-pooled output

nodes.summary: Some window attains the max-pooled output.
nodes.title: Max pooling returns the best PWM hit

nodes.summary: Pooling `max (conv + β) 0` over the windows gives `max (maxPool + β) 0`.
nodes.title: Bias and ReLU commute with max pooling

nodes.summary: Dropping the first letter shifts the responses by one window.
nodes.title: Translation equivariance

nodes.summary: The reverse complement of the length-`L` prefix of `x`: position `j < L` holds the complement of `x (L - 1 - j)`.
nodes.title: Reverse complement of a sequence prefix

nodes.summary: The reverse-complement filter: `rcFilter W k b = W (Fin.rev k) (comp b)`.
nodes.title: Reverse-complement filter

nodes.summary: On a sequence of length `m + w`, its response at window `i ≤ m` is the response of `W` on the reverse complement at window `m - i`.
nodes.title: The reverse-complement filter scans the other strand

nodes.summary: Max pooling the reverse-complement filter equals max pooling `W` on the reverse complement.
nodes.title: Max pooling the reverse-complement filter equals max pooling `W` on the reverse complement

nodes.summary: The responses only read the positions `< m + w` of a sequence of length `m + w`.
nodes.title: Filter responses read only positions within the sequence length

nodes.title: Both-strand convolution score

nodes.title: The both-strand score is invariant under reverse complementing the sequence
Profile scores for amino acid substitutions

nodes.summary: The profile log-odds score `log (p a / q a)` of residue `a`: `p` is the position-specific profile probability (estimated from aligned homologs), `q` the background probability. Meaningful for `p a, q a > 0`; otherwise Lean's `log 0 = 0` and `x / 0 = 0` give junk.
nodes.title: Profile log-odds score of a residue

nodes.summary: For a sequence `s` over independent positions with profiles `p j` and background `q` (all positive), the summed profile score is the log of the likelihood ratio `∏ p_j(s_j) / ∏ q(s_j)` of the profile model against the background.
nodes.title: The score is a log-likelihood ratio

nodes.summary: If `p` and `q` are probability vectors and `q` is positive, the expected score under the profile, `∑ p a log (p a / q a)` (the Kullback–Leibler divergence), is nonnegative.
nodes.title: Gibbs' inequality for the profile score

nodes.summary: If `p` and `q` are probability vectors and `p` is positive, the expected score under the background, `∑ q a log (p a / q a)`, is nonpositive.
nodes.title: Expected profile score under the background is nonpositive

nodes.summary: The PSIC score difference of a substitution from the wild-type residue `wt` to the mutant residue `mt`: `profileScore p q wt - profileScore p q mt`.
nodes.title: PSIC score difference of a substitution

nodes.summary: The PSIC difference is the log of the ratio of the two residues' likelihood ratios.
nodes.title: PSIC difference as a log ratio of likelihood ratios

nodes.summary: The PSIC difference is positive iff the wild type is more enriched in the profile, relative to background, than the mutant.
nodes.title: Positivity criterion for the PSIC difference

nodes.summary: A two-class naive Bayes model: class *damaging* has prior `prior ∈ (0, 1)`, class *benign* the complement; each feature `j` takes values in the finite type `X j` with class-conditional probabilities `damaging j` and `benign j`, assumed positive; features are conditionally independent given the class. The tables are estimated from training data.
nodes.title: Two-class naive Bayes model

nodes.summary: The joint probability of class `c` (`true` = damaging) and feature values `x`: `π ∏ P_D(x_j)` or `(1 - π) ∏ P_B(x_j)`.
nodes.title: Joint probability of class and features in naive Bayes

nodes.summary: The joint law of class and features is a probability law.
nodes.title: Naive Bayes joint law is a probability law

nodes.summary: The posterior probability that the variant is damaging given feature values `x` (Bayes' rule on the joint law).
nodes.title: Naive Bayes posterior probability of damage

nodes.summary: The log-likelihood ratio `log (P_D(v) / P_B(v))` of value `v` of feature `j`.
nodes.title: Log-likelihood ratio of a feature value

nodes.summary: The naive-Bayes score: prior log-odds plus the features' log-likelihood ratios.
nodes.title: Naive Bayes score

nodes.summary: The posterior probability of *damaging* is the logistic function of the score.
nodes.title: Naive-Bayes posterior

nodes.summary: The posterior is strictly monotone in the score.
nodes.title: Naive Bayes posterior is strictly monotone in the score

nodes.summary: Let feature `j` carry a numerical value `g v` (for example a PSIC-difference bin) such that its likelihood ratio `P_D(v) / P_B(v)` is monotone in `g v`. With the other features fixed, the posterior is monotone in `g`.

Zuker's minimum free energy algorithm

nodes.summary: A loop (nearest-neighbor) energy model: energies of hairpin loops closed by `(i, j)`, of stacks, bulges and interior loops closed by `(i, j)` with inner pair `(k, l)`, and the affine multiloop parameters `a` (per multiloop), `b` (per branch) and `c` (per unpaired base). The exterior loop has energy `0`. Units: free energy, e.g. kcal/mol.
nodes.title: Nearest-neighbor loop energy model

nodes.summary: `q` lies strictly inside the pair `p`: `p.1 < q.1` and `q.2 < p.2`.
nodes.title: Strict enclosure of one base pair by another

nodes.summary: The branches of the loop closed by `p` in `P`: the pairs of `P` strictly inside `p` that are not strictly inside another pair of `P` strictly inside `p`.
nodes.title: Branches of a loop closed by a base pair

nodes.summary: The exterior branches of `P`: the pairs not strictly inside any pair of `P`.
nodes.title: Exterior branches of a secondary structure

nodes.summary: In a secondary structure every pair is either an exterior branch or a branch of exactly one pair of the structure (and not both): each pair is shared by the loop it closes and exactly one enclosing loop, possibly the exterior loop.
nodes.title: Unique loop decomposition

nodes.summary: The energy of the loop closed by `p = (i, j)` in `P`: a hairpin with no branch, a stack, bulge or interior loop with one branch `(k, l)`, and the affine multiloop energy `a + b · r + c · u` with `r ≥ 2` branches and `u = (j - i - 1) - ∑ (l - k + 1)` unpaired bases.
nodes.title: Energy of the loop closed by a base pair

nodes.summary: The free energy of a structure in the loop model: the sum of the energies of the loops closed by its pairs (the exterior loop contributes `0`).
nodes.title: Free energy of a structure in the loop model

nodes.summary: A pair with no branch closes a hairpin loop.
nodes.title: A pair with no branch closes a hairpin loop

nodes.summary: A pair with exactly one branch `q` closes a stack, bulge or interior loop with inner pair `q`.
nodes.title: A pair with one branch closes a stack, bulge or interior loop

nodes.summary: A pair with at least two branches closes a multiloop with the affine energy.
nodes.title: A pair with two or more branches closes a multiloop

nodes.summary: Every position has a unique innermost strict container (not loop membership): a position `x` either lies strictly inside no pair, or there is a unique pair `p` with `p.1 < x < p.2` such that no branch of `p` has `x` strictly inside it. This is an innermost-container assignment, not the conventional loop decomposition of positions: endpoints are excluded from the loop they close (a position `x = q.1` or `x = q.2` is…
nodes.title: Every position has a unique innermost strict container

nodes.summary: Zuker's recursion on the interval `[i, i + len)`, with `j = i + len - 1`, returning `(V, WM)`: the least of the hairpin energy `hairpin i j`, the interior-loop energies `interior i j k l + V(k, l)` over `i < k < l < j`, and the multiloop energies `a + WM(i + 1, u) + WM(u + 1, j - 1)` over `i < u < j - 1`; unpaired base) is the least of `V + b`, `WM(i + 1, j) + c` (base `i` unpaired), `WM(i, j - 1) + c` (base `j`…
nodes.title: Zuker's recursion

nodes.summary: The exterior-loop recursion on the prefix `[0, len)`: `W(0) = 0` and `W(len + 1) = min (W(len), min_{i ≤ len} W(i) + V(i, len + 1 - i))` (the last base is unpaired, or closes an exterior branch `(i, len)`).
nodes.title: Zuker exterior-loop recursion

nodes.summary: Zuker's minimum free energy of `s`: the exterior recursion on the whole sequence.
nodes.title: Zuker minimum free energy

nodes.summary: Zuker's algorithm (Zuker and Stiegler 1981; Zuker and Sankoff 1984), here with the affine multiloop energy of Jaeger, Turner and Zuker (1989): the Zuker recursion computes the minimum free energy over all secondary structures on `s` with minimum hairpin `m`, for any real loop energies (of either sign). The minimum ranges over a finite set that contains the empty structure, so it is never `⊤`.
nodes.title: Zuker's algorithm

nodes.summary: The minimum free energy is at most `0`, the energy of the open chain (the empty structure).
nodes.title: Minimum free energy is at most zero

Counting binary phylogenetic trees

nodes.summary: A planar rooted binary tree with leaves labeled by `α`: a leaf `leaf a`, or an internal vertex `node l r` with left subtree `l` and right subtree `r` (the children are ordered).
nodes.title: Planar rooted binary tree with labeled leaves

nodes.summary: The multiset of leaf labels.
nodes.title: Leaf labels of a planar binary tree

nodes.summary: Every planar tree has at least one leaf.
nodes.title: Every planar binary tree has a leaf

nodes.summary: One swap: exchange the two children of one internal vertex (anywhere in the tree).
nodes.title: Swap of the children of an internal vertex

nodes.summary: The planar drawings of rooted binary trees on the taxa `X`: planar trees whose leaves are labeled by `X`, each taxon labeling exactly one leaf.
nodes.title: Planar drawings of rooted binary trees on a taxon set

nodes.summary: The rooted binary phylogenetic trees on the taxa `X`: planar drawings with leaf set `X` modulo exchanging the two children of internal vertices, i.e. rooted binary trees with unordered children and leaves labeled bijectively by `X`, up to label-preserving isomorphism.
nodes.title: Rooted binary phylogenetic tree

nodes.summary: On `n ≥ 1` labeled taxa there are `(2 n - 3)‼ = 1 · 3 · 5 ⋯ (2 n - 3)` rooted binary phylogenetic trees (`1` tree for `n = 1` and `n = 2`, `3` for `n = 3`, `15` for `n = 4`). For `n = 1` the natural-number subtraction gives `2 - 3 = 0` and `0‼ = 1`, the conventional value `(-1)‼ = 1` of the formula; the empty set of taxa (excluded here) has no tree (`isEmpty_rootedBinaryTree_empty`).
nodes.title: Schröder's count of rooted binary phylogenetic trees

nodes.summary: An unrooted binary phylogenetic tree on the taxa `X`: a finite tree `G` on a vertex type `V` whose degree-one vertices are labeled bijectively by `X` (`label`) and whose other vertices all have degree three.
nodes.title: Unrooted binary phylogenetic tree

nodes.summary: Two unrooted binary phylogenetic trees are isomorphic when some graph isomorphism maps the leaf with each label to the leaf with the same label.
nodes.title: Isomorphism of unrooted binary phylogenetic trees

nodes.summary: A binary hierarchy on a finite set `S`: a family of nonempty subsets of `S` containing `S` and every singleton, any two members nested or disjoint, and every member with at least two elements the disjoint union of two members. These are the cluster systems of the rooted binary phylogenetic trees on `S` (Semple & Steel 2003, Section 3.1).
nodes.title: Binary hierarchy on a finite set

nodes.summary: The members of a binary hierarchy below a member form a binary hierarchy.
nodes.title: Binary hierarchy restricted below a member is a binary hierarchy

nodes.summary: On a nonempty finite set `S` there are `(2 |S| - 3)‼` binary hierarchies, as many as rooted binary phylogenetic trees on `S`: a tree corresponds to the leaf sets of its subtrees.
nodes.title: The number of binary hierarchies

nodes.summary: The cluster of a vertex `v` seen from the leaf labeled `a`: the taxa `x ≠ a` whose leaf lies beyond `v`, i.e. `v` is on the path from the leaf `a` to the leaf `x`.
nodes.title: Cluster of a vertex seen from a leaf

nodes.summary: The clusters of all vertices seen from the leaf labeled `a`. (The cluster of the leaf `a` itself is the set of all other taxa, which is also the cluster of its neighbor.)
nodes.title: Cluster set of a tree seen from a leaf

nodes.summary: Isomorphic trees have the same clusters.
nodes.title: Isomorphic trees have the same clusters

nodes.summary: The clusters of a tree seen from a leaf form a binary hierarchy on the other taxa (Semple & Steel 2003, Section 3.1).
nodes.title: Clusters of an unrooted tree form a binary hierarchy

nodes.summary: Two trees with the same clusters seen from the leaf `a` are isomorphic: the clusters determine the tree.
nodes.title: Clusters determine an unrooted binary tree

nodes.summary: Every binary hierarchy on the taxa other than `a` is the cluster set, seen from the leaf `a`, of some unrooted binary phylogenetic tree (vertices: the leaf `a` and the members of the hierarchy; each member is joined to the smallest member strictly containing it).
nodes.title: Every binary hierarchy is a cluster set of a tree

nodes.summary: Unrooted binary phylogenetic trees up to label-preserving isomorphism correspond to the binary hierarchies on the taxa other than `a`, by their clusters seen from the leaf `a`.
nodes.title: Unrooted binary trees correspond to binary hierarchies

nodes.summary: The count `(2 n - 5)‼` of unrooted binary phylogenetic trees holds from `n = 2` taxa on: for `n = 2` the single tree is one edge and `2 · 2 - 5 = 0` in `ℕ`, `0‼ = 1` (the conventional value `(-1)‼ = 1`). For `n ≤ 1` there is no tree while the formula gives `1`.
nodes.title: Number of unrooted binary phylogenetic trees

nodes.summary: On `n ≥ 3` labeled taxa there are `(2 n - 5)‼ = 1 · 3 ⋯ (2 n - 5)` unrooted binary phylogenetic trees up to label-preserving isomorphism.
nodes.title: The number of unrooted binary phylogenetic trees

nodes.summary: Felsenstein's pruning algorithm, tabulated on the states `Fin n`: the vector of partial likelihoods of each subtree is computed once, with `O(n²)` operations per internal node.

nodes.summary: `G` with the taxon placement `ι` is a binary phylogenetic `X`-tree: `G` is a tree, `ι` is injective, the leaves (degree-one vertices) are exactly the taxa, and every other vertex has degree three.

nodes.summary: The taxa on the `a`-side of the edge `{a, b}`: those whose vertex is still joined to `a` once the edge `{a, b}` is deleted.
nodes.title: Taxa on one side of a tree edge

nodes.summary: The contribution of one split `{A, Aᶜ}` to the neighbor-joining score of the pair `x, y`: the number of taxa on the far side of the split when `x, y` lie on the same side, and `1` when the split separates them.
nodes.title: Contribution of a split to the neighbor-joining score

nodes.summary: In a tree, the two sides of an edge partition the taxa.
nodes.title: Two sides of a tree edge partition the taxa

nodes.summary: In a tree, the splits of any two edges are compatible: one side of the first edge lies inside one side of the second.
nodes.title: Splits of two tree edges are compatible

nodes.summary: The leaf side of a pendant edge holds only the leaf's taxon.
nodes.title: Leaf side of a pendant edge

nodes.summary: Every side of every edge of a binary phylogenetic tree holds a taxon.
nodes.title: Every edge side of a binary phylogenetic tree is nonempty

nodes.summary: At an internal vertex `a` with neighbor `b`, the `a`-side of `{a, b}` is the disjoint union of the far sides of the other two edges at `a`.
nodes.title: Edge side at an internal vertex as a disjoint union

nodes.summary: The path length between two taxa is half the sum, over the darts (oriented edges) of the tree, of the lengths of the edges whose split separates them.
nodes.title: Split decomposition of a tree metric

nodes.summary: For a compatible system of splits with positive weights, containing every trivial split and binary (every side with at least two taxa is the disjoint union of two sides), on at least four taxa, a pair maximizing the total `splitGain` is a side of some split.
nodes.title: Cherry lemma for split systems

nodes.summary: The Q-criterion of two singleton clusters at the start of neighbor joining: `Q({x}, {y}) = (|X| - 2) d x y - ∑_z d x z - ∑_z d y z`.
nodes.title: Q-criterion of two singleton clusters

nodes.summary: If `d x y` is half the total weight of the splits `A e` separating `x` and `y`, then `(|X| - 2) d x y - ∑_z d x z - ∑_z d y z = -∑ e, w e * splitGain (A e) x y`.
nodes.title: The Q-criterion of a split-decomposed dissimilarity

nodes.summary: A side holding a single taxon `z` is the leaf side of `z`'s pendant edge.
nodes.title: A singleton side is a pendant leaf side

nodes.summary: If a side of the edge `{a, b}` is the pair `{x, y}`, then `a` is a common neighbor of the leaves `ι x` and `ι y`: they form a cherry.
nodes.title: A two-taxon side forms a cherry

nodes.summary: (Saitou & Nei 1987; Studier & Keppler 1988; Bryant 2005). Let `d` be the path-length metric of a binary phylogenetic `X`-tree `(G, ι)` with positive edge lengths `w` and at least four taxa. If the distinct taxa `x, y` minimize the Q-criterion over all pairs of distinct singleton clusters at the start of neighbor joining, then `ι x` and `ι y` have a common neighbor.
nodes.title: On a tree metric, a pair of taxa minimizing the Q-criterion is a cherry

nodes.summary: On the path-length metric of a binary phylogenetic `X`-tree with positive edge lengths and at least four taxa, any pair of clusters that neighbor joining may join from the initial singletons consists of two taxa with a common neighbor.
nodes.title: The first join of neighbor joining on a tree metric joins a cherry

nodes.summary: Let `S` partition the taxa of a binary phylogenetic `X`-tree `(G, ι)` with positive edge lengths `w` and path-length metric `d` into sides of edges. Then there is a system of splits `A e` (`e : E`) of the set of clusters with positive weights `w' e`, closed under complement, pairwise compatible, binary, and containing every trivial split, such that edge with both endpoints internal; splits separating `s` from `t`,…
nodes.title: The path metric on a partition into sides

nodes.summary: Let `d` be the path-length metric of a binary phylogenetic `X`-tree `(G, ι)` with positive edge lengths `w`. Then every complete run of neighbor joining (stopped with at most three clusters) forms exactly the splits of the internal edges of the tree: a set of taxa `A` or its complement is a formed cluster if and only if `A` is the set of taxa on the `a`-side of an edge `{a, b}` with both endpoints internal.
nodes.title: Neighbor joining is exact on tree metrics

nodes.summary: Let `(G, ι)` be a binary phylogenetic `X`-tree and `D` any dissimilarity. Suppose that whenever a run of neighbor joining on `D` has reached a partition `S` of the taxa into sides of edges of the tree (with at least four clusters) and joins two of its clusters, their union is again a side of an edge. Then every complete run of neighbor joining on `D` (stopped with at most three clusters) forms exactly the splits of…
nodes.title: Neighbor joining forms the splits of a tree when every join forms a side

Let `A e` (`e : E`) be a compatible binary system of splits with positive weights `w`, containing every trivial split and closed under complement, on at least four taxa, and let `d x y` be half the total weight of the indices whose side separates `x` and `y`. Let `μ` be a lower bound on the weight…
