nodes.summary: The selection step of Atteson's theorem (Atteson 1999), with a proof after Mihaescu, Levy & Pachter (2009, Theorem 16). Let `d` be the path-length metric of a binary phylogenetic `X`-tree `(G, ι)` with positive edge lengths `w` and at least four taxa, and let `μ` be a lower bound on the lengths of the internal edges (edges with no taxon at either end). Let `D` be a symmetric dissimilarity with zero diagonal such…
nodes.title: Robust cherry lemma for neighbor joining

nodes.summary: Under the hypotheses of `exists_adj_adj_of_qCriterion_min_of_abs_sub_lt`, any pair of clusters that neighbor joining run on `D` may join from the initial singletons consists of two taxa with a common neighbor.
nodes.title: The first join of neighbor joining on a perturbed tree metric joins a cherry

nodes.summary: Along every run of neighbor joining on a symmetric dissimilarity `d` with zero diagonal there are weights `α s` (nonnegative, supported on `s`, summing to `1`) and row terms `κ s` such that the cluster dissimilarity vanishes on the diagonal and `D s t = ∑ x, ∑ y, α s x * α t y * d x y - κ s - κ t` for distinct current clusters. Joining `a, b` takes `α (a ∪ b) = (α a + α b) / 2` and…
nodes.title: Neighbor joining averages up to row shifts

nodes.summary: The shifting lemma (Mihaescu, Levy & Pachter 2009, Lemma 4): if `D'` agrees with `D` on the diagonal of `S` and `D' s t = D s t + f s + f t` for distinct `s, t ∈ S`, then the Q-criterion of every pair of distinct clusters drops by the same amount `2 ∑_{c ∈ S} f c`, so both have the same minimizing pairs.
nodes.title: The shifting lemma

nodes.summary: Atteson's theorem: neighbor joining has `ℓ∞` radius `1/2` (Atteson 1999). Let `d` be the path-length metric of a binary phylogenetic `X`-tree `(G, ι)` with positive edge lengths `w`, let `μ` be a lower bound on the lengths of its internal edges (edges with no taxon at either end), and let `D` be a symmetric dissimilarity with zero diagonal such that `|D x y - d x y| < μ / 2` for all distinct taxa. Then every…
nodes.title: Atteson's theorem: neighbor joining has `ℓ∞` radius `1/2`
Neighbor joining and balanced minimum evolution

nodes.summary: The generalized Pauplin coefficient of the pair of clusters `u, v` in the tree `T_ab` obtained from the star on `S` by joining `a` and `b`: `1/2` for `{a, b}`; `1/(2(|S| - 2))` when one of `u, v` is `a` or `b` and the other is not; `1/(|S| - 2)` when neither is. Values on the diagonal `u = v` are never used.
nodes.title: Generalized Pauplin coefficient of a cherry tree

nodes.summary: The balanced minimum-evolution length of `T_ab` for the dissimilarity `D`: half the sum over ordered pairs of distinct clusters of `cherryCoeff S a b u v * D u v`, which is `∑_{u<v} cherryCoeff S a b u v * D u v` when `D` is symmetric.
nodes.title: Balanced minimum-evolution length of a cherry tree

nodes.summary: For `D` symmetric and zero on the diagonal of `S`, `|S| ≥ 3` and distinct `a, b ∈ S`: `cherryLength S D a b = (∑_{u ≠ v ∈ S} D u v + Q(a, b)) / (2 (|S| - 2))`.
nodes.title: The BME length of a join in terms of the Q-criterion

nodes.summary: The BME length of `T_ab` on the current clusters for the current cluster dissimilarity `D`. This is the local star identity; it is not the full Gascuel–Steel comparison on all taxa.
nodes.title: Minimizing `Q` is minimizing the local star BME length of the join

nodes.summary: Along a run of neighbor joining on a symmetric `d` with zero diagonal, the cluster dissimilarity stays symmetric and vanishes on every current cluster.
nodes.title: Neighbor joining preserves symmetry and zero diagonal

nodes.summary: At every state of a run on a symmetric dissimilarity with zero diagonal and at least three clusters, a pair of distinct clusters minimizes the Q-criterion (the pairs NJ may join) if and only if joining it gives the smallest `cherryLength`, the BME length of the join tree `T_ab` on the current clusters for the current cluster dissimilarity `D`. This is the local star identity only: it does not compare partially…
nodes.title: Q-minimality is cherry-length minimality at a run state

nodes.summary: Let `T_ab` carry real edge lengths: `ℓ c` on the pendant edge of each cluster `c ∈ S` and `m` on the edge between `u` and the center. If `D` is its path-length dissimilarity (`D a b = ℓ a + ℓ b`, `D x c = ℓ x + m + ℓ c` for `x ∈ {a, b}` and `c` another cluster, `D c c' = ℓ c + ℓ c'` for two other distinct clusters), then `cherryLength S D a b = ∑_{c ∈ S} ℓ c + m`.
nodes.title: The coefficients give the tree length
Pauplin's formula and balanced minimum evolution

nodes.summary: A rooted binary tree with leaf labels in `X`; `node a l b r` has the child `l` at the end of an edge of length `a` and the child `r` at the end of an edge of length `b`.
nodes.title: Rooted binary tree with edge lengths

nodes.summary: An unrooted binary tree, rooted at its edge of length `len` that joins the roots of the rooted binary trees `left` and `right`.
nodes.title: Unrooted binary tree with edge lengths

nodes.summary: The Pauplin coefficient `2 ^ (1 - τ)` of a pair of leaves at topological distance `τ`.
nodes.title: Pauplin coefficient of a pair of leaves

nodes.summary: The total length of the edges.
nodes.title: Total edge length of a rooted binary tree

nodes.summary: The leaves, each with its label, its distance to the root and its number of edges to the root.
nodes.title: Leaves of a rooted binary tree with root distances

nodes.summary: The unordered pairs of leaves, each with the two labels, the length of the path between the two leaves and its number of edges.
nodes.title: Leaf pairs of a rooted binary tree with path lengths

nodes.summary: Kraft's equality for a rooted binary tree: `∑_{leaves} 2^{-depth} = 1`.
nodes.title: Kraft's equality

nodes.summary: The total length of the edges.
nodes.title: Total edge length of an unrooted binary tree

nodes.summary: The leaf labels (with multiplicity).
nodes.title: Leaf labels of an unrooted binary tree

nodes.summary: The unordered pairs of leaves, each with the two labels, the length `d_T(i, j)` of the path between the two leaves and its number of edges `τ_ij`.
nodes.title: Leaf pairs of an unrooted binary tree with path lengths

nodes.summary: The balanced minimum-evolution length of the topology of `T` for a dissimilarity `d` (Desper and Gascuel 2002): `∑_{i<j} 2^{1-τ_ij} (d(i, j) + d(j, i)) / 2`. It depends on `T` only through the topological distances `τ_ij`. Each term is symmetrized, so the value does not depend on the orientation `T.pairs` happens to assign to a pair: swapping the children of a node, or the two sides of the root edge, leaves…
nodes.title: Balanced minimum-evolution length

nodes.summary: Pauplin's formula (Pauplin 2000): the total edge length of a binary tree with real edge lengths is `∑_{i<j} 2^{1-τ_ij} d_T(i, j)`, the sum over pairs of leaves of the path length weighted by `2` to the power one minus the number of edges on the path.
nodes.title: Pauplin's formula

nodes.summary: If `d` is the path-length dissimilarity of `T` on its leaves and `d` is symmetric, `bmeLength T d = length T`. Symmetry is needed because `bmeLength` averages the two orientations of each pair.
nodes.title: The balanced minimum-evolution length of a tree metric is the tree length

nodes.summary: Kraft equality for unrooted binary trees: for every leaf `i` of a tree with distinct leaf labels, `∑_{j ≠ i} 2^{1-τ_ij} = 1`.
nodes.title: Kraft equality
PhyloCSF coding classifier

nodes.summary: The leaf data of an alignment column `col : L → S`: the indicator of the observed codon at each leaf.
nodes.title: Leaf data of an alignment column

nodes.summary: The likelihood of one alignment column under the model `(t, π)`.
nodes.title: Likelihood of one alignment column

nodes.summary: The likelihood of an alignment of `m` independent columns: the product of the site likelihoods.
nodes.title: Likelihood of an alignment of independent columns

nodes.summary: The PhyloCSF score (natural-log scale): the sum over the columns of the log-likelihood ratio of the coding model `(tC, πC)` against the non-coding model `(tN, πN)`. The published PhyloCSF score is reported in decibans; see `score_decibans` for the conversion. Thresholds for this `score` are in natural-log units.
nodes.title: The PhyloCSF score

nodes.summary: `10 * log₁₀(L_C / L_N)`, i.e. `(10 / log 10) * score`, since `log₁₀ x = log x / log 10`.
nodes.title: The published PhyloCSF score in decibans

nodes.summary: Decibans are the natural-log score rescaled by `10 / log 10`.
nodes.title: Deciban score as a rescaled natural-log score

nodes.summary: Each site likelihood is computed by Felsenstein's pruning algorithm.
nodes.title: Site likelihood by Felsenstein's pruning algorithm

nodes.summary: The score is the log-likelihood ratio of the alignment when all site likelihoods are positive.
nodes.title: The score is the log-likelihood ratio of the alignment

nodes.summary: The threshold test on the score: call the alignment coding (`1`) iff the score exceeds the cutoff `c`.
nodes.title: Score threshold test for calling an alignment coding

nodes.summary: With positive site likelihoods under both models, a randomized test `φ` whose weighted size under the non-coding weights is at most that of `scoreTest c` has at most its weighted power under the coding weights. Small parsimony problem

nodes.summary: The cost semiring: `MinTropical (WithTop ℕ)`, with `min` as addition and `+` as multiplication.
nodes.title: Min-plus cost semiring

nodes.summary: The total substitution cost of a labeling `x` of the non-root vertices of `t` with root state `s`: the sum over all edges of the cost `untrop (P a b)` from the parent's state `a` to the child's state `b`.
nodes.title: Total substitution cost of a labeling

nodes.summary: The labeling `x` (with root state `s`) agrees with the observed states `σ` at every leaf.
nodes.title: Labeling agrees with the observed leaf states

nodes.summary: The leaf weights of the observed states `σ`: the tropical one (cost `0`) at the observed state and the tropical zero (cost `⊤`) at every other state.
nodes.title: Tropical leaf weights of observed states

nodes.summary: The weight of a labeling in the tropical semiring is its edge cost if it agrees with the leaf states and `⊤` otherwise.
nodes.title: Tropical weight of a labeling equals its edge cost

nodes.summary: The minimum cost of the subtree `t` given the state `s` at its root, computed by Felsenstein's pruning recursion over the tropical semiring.
nodes.title: Sankoff's algorithm

nodes.summary: `sankoff σ t s` is the minimum total edge cost over all labelings of the non-root vertices that agree with the observed states at the leaves (with root state `s`).
nodes.title: Sankoff's algorithm computes the small-parsimony cost

nodes.summary: Sankoff's cost is a lower bound for the cost of every labeling that agrees with the leaf states.
nodes.title: Sankoff's cost is a lower bound

nodes.summary: Sankoff's cost is attained: if it is finite, some labeling that agrees with the leaf states has exactly this cost. (It is `⊤` exactly when every agreeing labeling uses a forbidden change, or when `t` is a single leaf whose observed state is not `s`.)
nodes.title: Sankoff's cost is attained

nodes.summary: Sankoff's recursion at a leaf: cost `0` at the observed state, `⊤` elsewhere.
nodes.title: Sankoff's recursion at a leaf

nodes.summary: Sankoff's recursion at an internal vertex: the cost of state `s` is the sum, over the two children, of the minimum over the child's state `a` of the edge cost from `s` to `a` plus the child's cost at `a`.
nodes.title: Sankoff's recursion at an internal vertex

nodes.summary: The unit cost: `0` for no change and `1` for a change of state.
nodes.title: Unit substitution cost

nodes.summary: Every edge of the tree carries the unit cost.
nodes.title: Tree with unit costs on every edge

nodes.summary: The set of candidate states at the root of the subtree and the number of changes counted so far. The edge weights of the tree are ignored. Each child is evaluated once per node, so the recursion makes one call per vertex.
nodes.title: Fitch's algorithm

nodes.summary: On a binary tree with unit costs, Fitch's count equals the minimum, over root states, of Sankoff's cost.
nodes.title: Fitch's algorithm computes the small-parsimony score

nodes.summary: On a binary tree with unit costs, a root state is in Fitch's set if and only if Sankoff's cost at that state is the minimum.
nodes.title: Fitch's root set is the set of optimal root states
Pulley principle, LogDet distances and Felsenstein zone

nodes.summary: A family of transition matrices `P t`, indexed by branch length, is a reversible semigroup for the distribution `π`: it satisfies the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation and detailed balance `π a P t a b = π b P t b a`. With rows summing to `1`, detailed balance makes `π` stationary; the pulley principle uses only the two equations below.
nodes.title: Reversible semigroup of transition matrices

nodes.summary: Swapping the two subtrees of a node does not change its partial likelihoods; with `likelihood_node_comm` this lets the rerooting move `likelihood_reroot` reach either child.
nodes.title: Partial likelihoods are invariant under swapping subtrees

nodes.summary: Swapping the two subtrees of the root does not change the likelihood.
nodes.title: Likelihood is invariant under swapping root subtrees

nodes.summary: With the root on the edge between the subtrees `l` and `r`, at distances `s` and `t`, the likelihood is that of the root placed at the root of `l`, with `r` at distance `s + t`.
nodes.title: The root can be pushed to the end of its edge

nodes.summary: Moving the root along its edge does not change the likelihood (Felsenstein 1981).
nodes.title: Pulley principle, sliding

nodes.summary: Let the root sit on the edge between an internal vertex `x` (at distance `s₁`) and the subtree `C` (at distance `s₂`), where `x` has the subtrees `A` and `B` at distances `a` and `b`. Moving the root to the edge between `x` and `A`, at distance `u₁` from `A` and `u₂` from `x` with `u₁ + u₂ = a`, gives the same likelihood: the unrooted tree and its edge lengths are unchanged (Felsenstein 1981).
nodes.title: Pulley principle, rerooting

nodes.summary: A reversible continuous-time model gives a reversible semigroup: if `π` is in detailed balance with the generator `Q`, the transition functions `exp (t • Q)` form a reversible semigroup for `π`.
nodes.title: Reversible continuous-time models give reversible semigroups

nodes.summary: The LogDet (paralinear) distance of a joint distribution matrix `F` (`F i j = ℙ(X = i, Y = j)`): `-log |det F| + (log det Π_X + log det Π_Y) / 2`, where the diagonal marginal matrices have determinants `∏ i, ∑ j, F i j` and `∏ j, ∑ i, F i j`. It is a distance only when `det F ≠ 0` and the marginals are positive; otherwise the value is Lean's totalized logarithm (`log 0 = 0`).
nodes.title: LogDet (paralinear) distance

nodes.summary: The distance of a vertex to itself is `0`: the joint distribution of `X` with itself is the diagonal matrix of its (positive) marginal.
nodes.title: LogDet distance of a vertex to itself is zero

nodes.summary: Under a nonnegative, nonsingular transition matrix, a positive distribution stays positive: every column of `M` has a positive entry. This puts the LogDet logarithms in their domain.
nodes.title: Nonsingular transition matrices preserve positive distributions

nodes.summary: Additivity of the LogDet distance at a separating vertex (Steel 1994; Lockhart et al. 1994; Lake 1994). Let `Y` have distribution `p` (positive) and let `X` and `Z` be conditionally independent given `Y`, with transition matrices `M` (from `Y` to `X`) and `N` (from `Y` to `Z`) whose rows sum to `1` and whose determinants are nonzero. The joint distribution matrices are `F_XY = Mᵀ Π_Y`, `F_YZ = Π_Y N` and…
nodes.title: Additivity of the LogDet distance at a separating vertex

nodes.summary: For a Markov chain `X → Y → Z` with `X` distributed as `p` (positive), transition matrices `A` (nonnegative) and `B` with unit row sums and nonzero determinants, `d(X, Z) = d(X, Y) + d(Y, Z)`, where `F_XZ = Π_X A B`, `F_XY = Π_X A` and `F_YZ = Π_Y B` with `Y` distributed as `p A`.
nodes.title: Additivity of the LogDet distance along a chain, one step

nodes.summary: The product `M 0 * M 1 * ⋯ * M (n - 1)` of the transition matrices along the first `n` edges of a path.
nodes.title: Product of transition matrices along a path

nodes.summary: Additivity of the LogDet distance along a path (Steel 1994; Lockhart et al. 1994): for a Markov chain `v₀ → v₁ → ⋯ → v_n` along a path, with positive initial distribution `p` and nonnegative nonsingular transition matrices `M i` with unit row sums, the LogDet distance between the ends is the sum of the distances of consecutive vertices. The joint distribution of `v₀, v_n` is `Π_{v₀} M 0 ⋯ M (n - 1)`, and that of…
nodes.title: Additivity of the LogDet distance along a path

nodes.summary: The symmetric two-state model on one branch: the state changes with probability `p`. As a model, `0 ≤ p ≤ 1/2`.
nodes.title: Symmetric two-state model on a branch

nodes.summary: The quartet `((A, B), (C, D))` on the taxa `0 = A`, `1 = B`, `2 = C`, `3 = D`, with change probabilities `pA, pB, pC, pD` on the pendant edges and `pI` on the internal edge. The root sits at the `AB` end of the internal edge (the edge to the `AB` cherry vertex has change probability `0`); by the pulley principle its position does not matter.
nodes.title: Four-taxon quartet tree model

nodes.summary: The leaf weights of a site pattern `σ`: the indicator of the observed state.
nodes.title: Leaf weights of a site pattern

nodes.summary: The probability of the site pattern `σ` on the quartet, with the uniform root distribution (the stationary distribution of the symmetric model).
nodes.title: Probability of a site pattern on a quartet

nodes.summary: The pattern probabilities sum to `1`, for all parameters.
nodes.title: Site pattern probabilities sum to one

nodes.summary: The pattern probabilities are nonnegative for change probabilities in `[0, 1]`.
nodes.title: Nonnegativity of site pattern probabilities

nodes.summary: The site pattern `σ` supports the split `{a, b} | {c, d}`: `a, b` agree, `c, d` agree, and the two pairs differ (a parsimony-informative pattern for that split).
nodes.title: Site pattern supporting a split

nodes.summary: The expected frequency of the patterns supporting the split `{a, b} | {c, d}`.
nodes.title: Expected frequency of patterns supporting a split

nodes.summary: With change probability `P` on the long non-sister branches to `A` and `C` and `Q` on the other three branches, the expected frequency of patterns supporting the wrong split `AC | BD` exceeds that of the true split `AB | CD` by `(1 - 2 Q) (P ^ 2 - Q (1 - Q))`, for all real `P, Q`. This is Felsenstein's equations (16)–(17) (his four-species model has equal probabilities of change `0 → 1` and reversion `1 → 0`).
nodes.title: Felsenstein (1978), the exact comparison

nodes.summary: The wrong split `AC | BD` against the third split `AD | BC`: the difference of expected frequencies is `(1 - 2 Q) (P - Q) ^ 2`.
nodes.title: Wrong split against third split frequency difference

nodes.summary: The true split `AB | CD` against the third split `AD | BC`: the difference of expected frequencies is `Q (1 - 2 Q) (1 - 2 P)`.
nodes.title: True split against third split frequency difference

nodes.summary: The rooted quartet `((a, b), (c, d))` with unit costs, for Fitch's algorithm.
nodes.title: Rooted quartet with unit costs

nodes.summary: The Fitch parsimony score of the site pattern `σ` on the quartet `((a, b), (c, d))`; it is the small-parsimony score by `Parsimony.fitch_score_eq`.
nodes.title: Fitch parsimony score on a quartet

nodes.summary: On four taxa, the parsimony scores of two quartets differ only on informative patterns: the score on `AB | CD` minus the score on `AC | BD` is `1` on patterns supporting `AC | BD`, `-1` on patterns supporting `AB | CD`, and `0` otherwise; likewise for `AD | BC`.
nodes.title: Difference of parsimony scores of two quartets

nodes.summary: The expected Fitch parsimony score of one site on the quartet `((a, b), (c, d))`.
nodes.title: Expected Fitch parsimony score on a quartet

nodes.summary: The Felsenstein zone (Felsenstein 1978): if `0 ≤ Q < 1/2` and `P ^ 2 > Q (1 - Q)`, the wrong quartet `AC | BD` has strictly smaller expected parsimony score per site than both the true quartet `AB | CD` and the third quartet `AD | BC`. The statement is algebraic in `P`; the model has `0 ≤ P ≤ 1/2`.
nodes.title: The Felsenstein zone

nodes.summary: Parsimony is inconsistent in the Felsenstein zone (Felsenstein 1978): if the sites `σ i` are pairwise independent and identically distributed with the pattern distribution of the quartet, and `0 ≤ Q < 1/2`, `P ^ 2 > Q (1 - Q)`, then almost surely, for all long enough alignments, the wrong quartet `AC | BD` has a strictly smaller total Fitch score than the true quartet `AB | CD` and the third quartet `AD | BC`.
nodes.title: Parsimony is inconsistent in the Felsenstein zone

nodes.summary: The JC transition matrix along a path whose branch lengths are listed in `ts`: the product of the branch transition matrices `jcProb μ t`.
nodes.title: Jukes–Cantor transition matrix along a path

nodes.summary: The JC transition matrix along a path is the transition matrix of the total length.
nodes.title: Chapman–Kolmogorov along a path

nodes.summary: JC-corrected distances are path lengths (Jukes & Cantor 1969): the JC distance of the probability that the two ends of a path differ is `μ` times the total branch length.
nodes.title: JC-corrected distances are path lengths

nodes.summary: The empirical p-distance of the taxa `x, y` over the first `n` sites of the alignment `seq` (`seq i x` is the base of taxon `x` at site `i`): the proportion of sites where they differ.
nodes.title: Empirical p-distance

nodes.summary: The JC-corrected empirical distance `jcDistance (pHat seq n x y)`.
nodes.title: Jukes–Cantor corrected empirical distance

nodes.summary: Neighbor joining recovers the tree within radius `r` of the dissimilarity `d`: every complete run of neighbor joining on a symmetric dissimilarity `D` with zero diagonal and `|D x y - d x y| < r` for distinct taxa forms exactly the splits of the internal edges of `(G, ι)`. Atteson's theorem gives this for the path-length metric of a binary phylogenetic tree with `r` half the shortest internal edge length…
nodes.title: Neighbor joining recovers a tree within a radius

nodes.summary: For pairwise independent, identically distributed sites, the empirical p-distance of every pair of taxa converges almost surely to the probability that the two taxa differ at a site.
nodes.title: Strong law for the p-distances

nodes.summary: Let `d` be the path-length metric of a binary phylogenetic `X`-tree `(G, ι)` with positive edge lengths `w` whose internal edges (no taxon at either end) have length at least `m`. For `μ > 0`, neighbor joining recovers the tree within radius `μ m / 2` of the scaled metric `μ d`. This is `njRun_splits_of_abs_sub_lt` (Atteson 1999) for the edge lengths `μ w`.

Time-reversible nucleotide substitution models

nodes.summary: The GTR rate matrix (Tavaré 1986) with base frequencies `π` and exchangeabilities `s`: `s i j * π j` off the diagonal and minus the off-diagonal row sum on it. The diagonal of `s` is not used.
nodes.title: General time-reversible (GTR) rate matrix

nodes.summary: The rows of the GTR matrix sum to `0`, for all parameters.
nodes.title: Rows of the GTR rate matrix sum to zero

nodes.summary: With nonnegative base frequencies and nonnegative off-diagonal exchangeabilities, the GTR matrix is a rate matrix (the diagonal `s i i` is not used by `gtrRate`).
nodes.title: GTR matrix is a rate matrix

nodes.summary: With symmetric exchangeabilities, the GTR matrix is in detailed balance with its base frequencies, `π i Q i j = π j Q j i` (Tavaré 1986).
nodes.title: GTR is reversible

nodes.summary: The base frequencies are invariant for the GTR generator: `π Q = 0`.
nodes.title: Base frequencies are invariant for the GTR generator

nodes.summary: The base frequencies are stationary for the GTR transition function at every time.
nodes.title: Base frequencies are stationary for the GTR chain

nodes.summary: Detailed balance of the GTR transition function with the base frequencies, `π i P t i j = π j P t j i` for every `t` (time-reversibility of the GTR chain).
nodes.title: Time-reversibility of the GTR chain

nodes.summary: The HKY85 exchangeabilities: `κ` for a transition (indices of equal parity: `A ↔ G`, `C ↔ T` in the order `A, C, G, T`), `1` for a transversion. The diagonal (also `κ`) is not used by `gtrRate`.
nodes.title: HKY85 exchangeabilities

nodes.summary: The HKY85 rate matrix (Hasegawa–Kishino–Yano 1985) with base frequencies `π` and transition/transversion ratio `κ`: rate `κ π j` for a transition to `j`, `π j` for a transversion.
nodes.title: HKY85 rate matrix

nodes.summary: The F81 rate matrix (Felsenstein 1981): rate `π j` to every other base `j`.
nodes.title: F81 rate matrix

nodes.summary: The K80 rate matrix (Kimura 1980): equal base frequencies `1/4`, rate `κ / 4` for a transition and `1 / 4` for each transversion.
nodes.title: K80 rate matrix

nodes.summary: With nonnegative base frequencies and `κ ≥ 0`, the HKY85 matrix is a rate matrix.
nodes.title: HKY85 matrix is a rate matrix

nodes.summary: With nonnegative base frequencies, the F81 matrix is a rate matrix.
nodes.title: F81 matrix is a rate matrix

nodes.summary: With `κ ≥ 0`, the K80 matrix is a rate matrix.
nodes.title: K80 matrix is a rate matrix

nodes.summary: HKY85 is in detailed balance with its base frequencies.
nodes.title: Detailed balance of the HKY85 model

nodes.summary: F81 is in detailed balance with its base frequencies.
nodes.title: Detailed balance of the F81 model

nodes.summary: HKY85 with `κ = 1` is F81.
nodes.title: HKY85 with κ = 1 is F81

nodes.summary: Equal base frequencies `1/4` and equal exchangeabilities `4 μ / 3` give the Jukes–Cantor rate matrix `jcRateMatrix μ`.
nodes.title: JC69 is the equal-rates GTR model

nodes.summary: The equal-rates GTR transition function is the Jukes–Cantor transition probability `jcProb μ t` (by `JukesCantor.jcProb_eq_exp`).
nodes.title: Equal-rates GTR chain is the Jukes–Cantor model

nodes.summary: For `μ ≥ 0` the Jukes–Cantor matrix is a rate matrix.
nodes.title: Jukes–Cantor matrix is a rate matrix

nodes.summary: K80 with `κ = 1` is JC69 with substitution rate `μ = 3/4`.
nodes.title: K80 with κ = 1 is the Jukes–Cantor model
Codon substitution models and dN/dS

nodes.summary: A codon: three nucleotides, each in `Fin 4` (order `A, C, G, T`).
nodes.title: Codon as a triple of nucleotides

nodes.summary: The positions at which two codons differ.
nodes.title: Positions at which two codons differ

nodes.summary: Two codons differ at exactly one position.
nodes.title: Codons differing at exactly one position

nodes.summary: Every differing position is a transition (same parity: `A ↔ G` or `C ↔ T`).
nodes.title: Codon change consisting of transitions

nodes.summary: Differing at exactly one position is symmetric.
nodes.title: Symmetry of single-position codon changes

nodes.summary: Being a transition change is symmetric.
nodes.title: Symmetry of transition codon changes

nodes.summary: The Goldman–Yang exchangeability between codons `i` and `j`: `0` unless they differ at one position; otherwise `κ` for a transition (`1` for a transversion), times `ω` if the amino acid changes.
nodes.title: Goldman–Yang codon exchangeability

nodes.summary: The Goldman–Yang exchangeabilities are symmetric.
nodes.title: Symmetry of Goldman–Yang exchangeabilities

nodes.summary: The nonsynonymous exchangeabilities are linear in `ω`, the synonymous ones do not involve it.
nodes.title: Dependence of Goldman–Yang exchangeabilities on ω

nodes.summary: The Goldman–Yang rate matrix (Goldman & Yang 1994): the GTR matrix with codon frequencies `π` and exchangeabilities `gyExchange`.
nodes.title: Goldman–Yang codon rate matrix

nodes.summary: The stationary rate of synonymous substitutions per codon, `ρ_S = ∑_{i ≠ j, aa i = aa j} π_i Q_ij`. This is the stationary rate when `∑ i, π i = 1`; for unnormalized weights it is scaled by `(∑ i, π i) ^ 2`.
nodes.title: Stationary rate of synonymous substitutions

nodes.summary: The stationary rate of nonsynonymous substitutions per codon, `ρ_N = ∑_{aa i ≠ aa j} π_i Q_ij`. This is the stationary rate when `∑ i, π i = 1`; for unnormalized weights it is scaled by `(∑ i, π i) ^ 2`.
nodes.title: Stationary rate of nonsynonymous substitutions

nodes.summary: The number of synonymous sites per codon, counted under `ω = 1`: `S = 3 ρ_S(1) / (ρ_S(1) + ρ_N(1))`.
nodes.title: Number of synonymous sites per codon

nodes.summary: The number of nonsynonymous sites per codon, counted under `ω = 1`: `N = 3 ρ_N(1) / (ρ_S(1) + ρ_N(1))`.
nodes.title: Number of nonsynonymous sites per codon

nodes.summary: The synonymous rate per synonymous site, `dS = ρ_S(ω) / S`.
nodes.title: Synonymous substitution rate per synonymous site (dS)

nodes.summary: The nonsynonymous rate per nonsynonymous site, `dN = ρ_N(ω) / N`.
nodes.title: Nonsynonymous substitution rate per nonsynonymous site (dN)

nodes.summary: Off the diagonal the Goldman–Yang rate is `gyExchange i j * π j`.
nodes.title: Off-diagonal entries of the Goldman–Yang rate matrix

nodes.summary: With nonnegative frequencies, `κ ≥ 0` and `ω ≥ 0`, the Goldman–Yang matrix is a rate matrix.
nodes.title: Goldman–Yang matrix is a rate matrix

nodes.summary: It is in detailed balance with its codon frequencies.
nodes.title: The Goldman–Yang chain is reversible

nodes.summary: The synonymous rate does not depend on `ω`: `ρ_S(ω) = ρ_S(1)`.
nodes.title: Synonymous rate does not depend on ω

nodes.summary: The nonsynonymous rate is linear in `ω`: `ρ_N(ω) = ω ρ_N(1)`.
nodes.title: Nonsynonymous rate is linear in ω

nodes.summary: There are three sites per codon: `S + N = 3` when `ρ_S(1) + ρ_N(1) ≠ 0`.
nodes.title: Synonymous and nonsynonymous sites sum to three

nodes.summary: `dN / dS = ω` in the Goldman–Yang model with sites counted under `ω = 1` (derived; see the module docstring for the site definition), provided `ρ_S(1) > 0` and `ρ_N(1) > 0`.
nodes.title: `dN / dS = ω`

nodes.summary: `ρ_S(1) > 0` if the frequencies are nonnegative, `κ > 0`, and some synonymous single change joins two codons of positive frequency.
nodes.title: Positivity of the synonymous rate

nodes.summary: `ρ_N(1) > 0` if the frequencies are nonnegative, `κ > 0`, and some nonsynonymous single change joins two codons of positive frequency.
nodes.title: Positivity of the nonsynonymous rate
Tree metrics and the four-point condition

nodes.summary: `d` is a tree metric: there are a finite tree `G` on a vertex type `V`, positive edge lengths `w`, and a placement `ι` of the taxa on vertices such that `d x y` is the total length of the (unique) path from `ι x` to `ι y`.
nodes.title: Tree metric

nodes.summary: The four-point condition: `d x y + d z t ≤ max (d x z + d y t) (d x t + d y z)`.
nodes.title: Four-point condition

nodes.summary: Tree metrics satisfy the four-point condition (the easy direction of Buneman's theorem).
nodes.title: Tree metrics satisfy the four-point condition

nodes.summary: A symmetric dissimilarity on a finite set that vanishes on the diagonal and satisfies the four-point condition is a tree metric.
nodes.title: Buneman's theorem, converse direction

nodes.summary: A symmetric dissimilarity on a finite set that vanishes on the diagonal is a tree metric if and only if it satisfies the four-point condition.
nodes.title: Buneman's four-point theorem
Splits, compatibility, ultrametrics and UPGMA

nodes.summary: A hierarchy on a finite set `S`: a family of nonempty subsets of `S` containing `S` and every singleton, any two members nested or disjoint. These are the cluster systems of the rooted phylogenetic trees on `S` (Semple & Steel 2003, Section 3.5).
nodes.title: Hierarchy on a finite set

nodes.summary: A binary hierarchy is a hierarchy.
nodes.title: A binary hierarchy is a hierarchy

nodes.summary: Adding `S` and the singletons to a family of pairwise nested-or-disjoint nonempty subsets of a nonempty `S` gives a hierarchy.
nodes.title: Pairwise nested-or-disjoint clusters form a hierarchy

nodes.summary: Every family of pairwise nested-or-disjoint nonempty subsets of a nonempty `S` is contained in a binary hierarchy on `S`, the cluster set of a rooted binary phylogenetic tree on `S` (Semple & Steel 2003, Proposition 3.5.2 and the refinement of a rooted tree to a binary one).
nodes.title: Hierarchies are refined by binary trees

nodes.summary: A binary hierarchy on `S` has `2 |S| - 1` members: the `|S|` singletons and `|S| - 1` internal clusters (stated without subtraction).
nodes.title: Number of members of a binary hierarchy

nodes.summary: The splits `A | Aᶜ` and `B | Bᶜ` are compatible: one of `A ∩ B`, `A ∩ Bᶜ`, `Aᶜ ∩ B`, `Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ` is empty (Semple & Steel 2003, Section 3.1).
nodes.title: Compatible splits

nodes.summary: Compatibility is symmetric.
nodes.title: Symmetry of split compatibility

nodes.summary: Compatibility depends only on the split, not on the side used to store it.
nodes.title: Compatibility is unchanged by complementing the first split

nodes.summary: Compatibility depends only on the split, not on the side used to store it.
nodes.title: Compatibility is unchanged by complementing the second split

nodes.summary: For the sides not containing a fixed taxon `a`, compatibility is being nested or disjoint: splits seen from a root are clusters.
nodes.title: Compatible clusters are nested or disjoint

nodes.summary: The binary characters `χ` and `ψ` show all four gametes `(0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)` on the taxa.
nodes.title: Four-gamete condition for binary characters

nodes.summary: The split of a binary character: the taxa in state `true`.
nodes.title: Split of a binary character

nodes.summary: Two binary characters give compatible splits iff they do not show all four gametes (Buneman 1971; Estabrook, Johnson & McMorris 1976).
nodes.title: The four-gamete test

nodes.summary: The split set of `T` computed from the leaf `a`: both sides of every cluster of `T` seen from `a`. It equals `edgeSplits T` for every `a` (`splitSet_eq_edgeSplits`).
nodes.title: Split set of a tree computed from a leaf

nodes.summary: The clusters seen from `a` do not contain `a`.
nodes.title: Clusters seen from a leaf omit that leaf

nodes.summary: The side of the edge `p – v` containing `v`: the taxa whose leaf is closer to `v` than to `p`.
nodes.title: Side of a tree edge containing a vertex

nodes.summary: The edge splits of `T`: the sides of all its edges (both sides of every edge).
nodes.title: Edge splits of a tree

nodes.summary: The two sides of an edge are complementary.
nodes.title: The two sides of a tree edge are complementary

nodes.summary: The cluster of a vertex `v` seen from `a` is the side of `v` of the edge from `v` to its neighbor `p` toward `a`.
nodes.title: Clusters seen from a leaf are edge sides

nodes.summary: The split set computed from any leaf is the set of edge splits.
nodes.title: Split set from any leaf equals the edge splits

nodes.summary: The split set does not depend on the leaf used to compute it.
nodes.title: The split set does not depend on the leaf used to compute it

nodes.summary: Any two splits of one tree are compatible.
nodes.title: Splits computed from a leaf are pairwise compatible

nodes.summary: Any two splits of one tree are compatible.
nodes.title: Edge splits of a tree are pairwise compatible

nodes.summary: Splits-equivalence theorem, binary form (Buneman 1971; Semple & Steel 2003, Theorem 3.1.4): on at least two taxa, a family `F` of proper splits (both sides nonempty) is contained in the split set of some unrooted binary phylogenetic tree iff its members are pairwise compatible. The tree is a binary refinement of the tree whose splits are exactly `F` and the trivial ones.
nodes.title: Splits-equivalence theorem

nodes.summary: `T` is a perfect phylogeny for the binary character matrix `M` (taxa by characters): the split of every non-constant column is a split of `T`, i.e. every character changes state on exactly one edge.
nodes.title: Perfect phylogeny for a binary character matrix

nodes.summary: Perfect phylogeny and the four-gamete condition (Estabrook, Johnson & McMorris 1976; Gusfield 1991): a binary character matrix on at least two taxa has a perfect phylogeny iff no two of its columns show all four gametes.
nodes.title: Perfect phylogeny and the four-gamete condition

nodes.summary: The Robinson–Foulds distance: the number of splits in exactly one of the two trees. Each split is counted once, by its side away from the leaf `a` (its cluster seen from `a`); trivial splits are common to all trees and cancel. The value does not depend on `a` (`rfDist_eq_rfDist`).
nodes.title: Robinson–Foulds distance

nodes.summary: Each split is counted twice in the symmetric difference of the split sets (once per side), so the Robinson–Foulds distance is half of it.
nodes.title: Robinson–Foulds distance as half the split symmetric difference

nodes.summary: The Robinson–Foulds distance does not depend on the leaf used to compute it.
nodes.title: Robinson–Foulds distance is independent of the base leaf

nodes.summary: The Robinson–Foulds distance from a tree to itself is zero.
nodes.title: Robinson–Foulds distance from a tree to itself is zero

nodes.summary: The Robinson–Foulds distance is symmetric.
nodes.title: Symmetry of the Robinson–Foulds distance

nodes.summary: The Robinson–Foulds distance satisfies the triangle inequality.
nodes.title: Triangle inequality for the Robinson–Foulds distance

nodes.summary: The Robinson–Foulds distance vanishes exactly on isomorphic trees (Robinson & Foulds 1981).
nodes.title: Robinson–Foulds distance vanishes exactly on isomorphic trees

nodes.summary: The Robinson–Foulds distance is invariant under isomorphism, so it is a metric on the trees up to isomorphism.
nodes.title: Isomorphism invariance of the Robinson–Foulds distance

nodes.summary: On `n ≥ 3` taxa it is at most `2 (n - 3)`, the number of nontrivial splits of two binary trees (Robinson & Foulds 1981).
nodes.title: Maximum of the Robinson–Foulds distance

nodes.summary: The majority splits of a finite family of trees `T i`: the clusters, seen from `a`, of more than half of the trees (repetitions in the family count).
nodes.title: Majority splits of a family of trees

nodes.summary: Majority splits are compatible (Margush & McMorris 1981): two clusters each in more than half of the trees are both clusters of a common tree (pigeonhole), hence nested or disjoint.
nodes.title: Majority splits are compatible

nodes.summary: The majority splits are clusters of one unrooted binary phylogenetic tree (a binary refinement of the majority-rule consensus tree).
nodes.title: The majority-rule consensus tree

nodes.summary: Bootstrap support (Felsenstein 1985) of the split with side `A` away from `a`, for a tree estimator `est` and an alignment `M` of `m` sites: the fraction of the `m ^ m` site resamplings with replacement `w : Fin m → Fin m` (uniform draws, whose site counts are multinomial) for which the tree estimated from the resampled alignment `M ∘ w` has the cluster `A`. This is the exact bootstrap proportion; Felsenstein's…
nodes.title: Bootstrap support

nodes.summary: Bootstrap support is a frequency: it lies in `[0, 1]`.
nodes.title: Bootstrap support lies in the unit interval

nodes.summary: A split has bootstrap support above one half iff it is a majority split of the bootstrap replicate trees; so the splits with support above one half are pairwise compatible and form one tree (`exists_tree_majoritySplits_subset`).
nodes.title: Bootstrap support above one half means a majority split

nodes.summary: `d` is an ultrametric on the taxa: symmetric, zero exactly on the diagonal, and satisfying the three-point condition `d x z ≤ max (d x y) (d y z)` (equivalently, of the three distances among any three taxa the two largest are equal).
nodes.title: Ultrametric on taxa

nodes.summary: `d` is the metric of a dated rooted tree, encoded by its clusters: a hierarchy `H` on the taxa with dates `h` (`0` at the leaves, strictly increasing from a cluster to any cluster strictly containing it) such that `d x y` is the date of the smallest cluster containing `x` and `y` (their most recent common ancestor). With edge lengths `(h D - h C) / 2` from each cluster `C` to its parent `D`, `d x y` is the path…
nodes.title: Metric of a dated rooted tree

nodes.summary: Ultrametrics satisfy the four-point condition (Semple & Steel 2003, Section 7.2), so every ultrametric on a finite set is a tree metric (`IsUltrametric.isTreeMetric`).
nodes.title: Ultrametrics satisfy the four-point condition

nodes.summary: Every ultrametric on a finite set is a tree metric (via Buneman's four-point theorem).
nodes.title: Every ultrametric is a tree metric

nodes.summary: Ultrametrics are dated tree metrics (Semple & Steel 2003, Theorem 7.2.5): on a nonempty finite set of taxa, a dissimilarity satisfies the three-point condition (and is a metric) iff it is the metric of a dated rooted tree.
nodes.title: Ultrametrics are dated tree metrics

nodes.summary: The average linkage between two clusters: the mean of `d x y` over `x ∈ C`, `y ∈ D`.
nodes.title: Average linkage between clusters

nodes.summary: The states reachable by UPGMA (Sokal & Michener 1958) on `d`: a partition `P` of the taxa into blocks and the heights `c x y` recorded so far. It starts from the singletons; each step merges two distinct blocks `C`, `D` of least average linkage (ties broken arbitrarily) and records `avgDist d C D` as the height at which every `x ∈ C` and `y ∈ D` are joined (the distance between them in the output tree; their common…
nodes.title: States reachable by UPGMA

nodes.summary: In every UPGMA run on an ultrametric, the recorded height of two taxa in the same block is their distance. In particular a completed run (one block) reconstructs `d`, i.e. the dated tree, exactly (Semple & Steel 2003, Section 7.2).
nodes.title: UPGMA is exact on ultrametrics

nodes.summary: UPGMA always completes: from the singletons it reaches the single block `univ`.
nodes.title: UPGMA always completes

nodes.summary: A rooted triplet `xy|z`: `x` and `y` are closer to each other than to `z`.
nodes.title: Rooted triplet

nodes.summary: The cluster system `H` displays the triplet `xy|z`: some cluster contains `x` and `y` but not `z`.
nodes.title: Cluster system displaying a triplet

nodes.summary: The Aho graph of the triplets `R` on `S'` (vertices `S'`, an edge `x y` for each `xy|z ∈ R` with `x, y, z ∈ S'`) has a cut: a partition of `S'` into two nonempty parts with no edge across, i.e. the graph is disconnected.
nodes.title: Cut in the Aho graph

nodes.summary: A rooted binary tree is determined by its triplets (Semple & Steel 2003, Theorem 6.4.1): two binary hierarchies on `S` displaying the same triplets are equal.
nodes.title: A rooted binary tree is determined by its triplets

nodes.summary: Correctness of BUILD (Aho, Sagiv, Szymanski & Ullman 1981; Semple & Steel 2003, Section 6.4): a set `R` of triplets on a nonempty `S`, none of the degenerate form `xx|x` (which no tree displays and no cut detects), is displayed by a rooted binary phylogenetic tree on `S` iff for every subset `S'` of at least two taxa the Aho graph of `R` on `S'` is disconnected. BUILD splits along the components and recurses; the…
nodes.title: Correctness of BUILD

nodes.summary: `T` displays the quartet `xy|zw`: some edge split of `T` has `x, y` on one side and `z, w` on the other.
nodes.title: Tree displaying a quartet

nodes.summary: An unrooted binary tree is determined by its quartets (Semple & Steel 2003, Corollary 6.3.8): two trees displaying the same quartets are isomorphic. Already the quartets containing the taxon `a` suffice; they are the rooted triplets seen from `a`.
nodes.title: An unrooted binary tree is determined by its quartets
Evolutionary conservation scores

nodes.summary: The upper tail `P(X ≥ k) = ∑_{i = k}^{n} C(n, i) p^i (1 - p)^(n - i)` of the binomial law `Bin(n, p)`.
nodes.title: Upper tail of the binomial distribution

nodes.summary: `P(X ≥ 0) = 1`, for every real `p` (the binomial theorem).
nodes.title: Binomial upper tail at zero equals one

reading_title.source: Binomial upper tail vanishes beyond $n$

nodes.summary: `P(X ≥ k) = 0` for `k > n`.
nodes.title: Binomial upper tail vanishes beyond $n$

nodes.summary: The tail is nonincreasing in `k` for `p ∈ [0, 1]`.
nodes.title: The tail is nonincreasing in `k`

nodes.summary: Derivative of the binomial upper tail in the success probability: for `1 ≤ k ≤ n`, `d/dp P(Bin(n, p) ≥ k) = n C(n - 1, k - 1) p^(k-1) (1-p)^(n-k)` at every real `p` (the sum telescopes).
nodes.title: Derivative of the binomial upper tail

nodes.summary: The binomial upper tail is nondecreasing in `p` on `[0, 1]`, for every `n` and `k`.
nodes.title: The binomial upper tail is nondecreasing in `p` on `(0, 1)`

nodes.summary: The binomial upper tail is strictly increasing in `p` on `[0, 1]` when `1 ≤ k ≤ n`.
nodes.title: The binomial upper tail is strictly increasing in `p` on `(0, 1)`

nodes.summary: The conserved count `k` of a motif with `N` occurrences, standardized under `Bin(N, p)`: `(k - N p) / √(N p (1 - p))`. This is an approximation to Xie et al.'s MCS, not their exact score.
nodes.title: Binomial z-score approximation to the motif conservation score

nodes.summary: The MCS approximation is strictly increasing in the conserved count, for `N ≥ 1` and `p ∈ (0, 1)`.
nodes.title: Motif conservation score approximation is strictly increasing

nodes.summary: The MCS approximation of the number of conserved occurrences among the first `n` is the de Moivre–Laplace standardized sum.
nodes.title: Motif conservation score approximation as a de Moivre–Laplace sum

nodes.summary: If the conservation indicators of the occurrences are i.i.d. Bernoulli(`p`) with `0 < p < 1`, then for every `z`, `P(z ≤ MCS approximation of the first n occurrences)` tends to the standard normal mass of `[z, ∞)`.
nodes.title: De Moivre–Laplace for the MCS approximation

nodes.summary: The SiPhy rate matrix `Q a b = ω R a b π b` for `a ≠ b` (Garber et al. 2009, Eq. 10), with rows summing to zero: `ω` times the GTR matrix with exchangeabilities `R` and base frequencies `π`.
nodes.title: The SiPhy rate matrix

nodes.summary: With `ω ≥ 0`, nonnegative `R` and nonnegative `π`, the SiPhy matrix is a rate matrix.
nodes.title: SiPhy matrix is a rate matrix

nodes.summary: For symmetric `R` it is in detailed balance with `π`, for every `ω`.
nodes.title: `π` is the equilibrium of the SiPhy matrix

nodes.summary: The expected complete-data log-likelihood of a rate matrix `Q` and root distribution `π` (Garber et al. 2009, Eq. 6): `∑_{a ≠ b} n a b log Q a b + ∑ a, τ a Q a a + ∑ b, r b log π b`, for expected substitution counts `n`, expected state durations `τ` and the root posterior `r`.
nodes.title: The expected complete-data log-likelihood

nodes.summary: The expected total number of substitutions `N = ∑_{a ≠ b} n a b`.
nodes.title: Expected total number of substitutions

nodes.summary: The weight `c b = ∑_{a ≠ b} n a b + r b` of state `b`: substitutions into `b` plus the root posterior of `b`.
nodes.title: Weight of a state: substitutions into it plus root posterior

nodes.summary: The time-weighted exchange rate into `b`, `e b = ∑_{a ≠ b} τ a R a b`.
nodes.title: Time-weighted exchange rate into a state

nodes.summary: The part of Eq. 6 that depends on `π` (for fixed `ω`): `∑ b, (c b * log (π b) - d b * π b)`.
nodes.title: Part of the SiPhy objective depending on the constraint vector

reading_title.source: Constant $n \log R$ term of the SiPhy objective

nodes.summary: The `n log R` constant of Eq. 6.
nodes.title: Constant $n \log R$ term of the SiPhy objective

nodes.summary: For `ω > 0`, positive off-diagonal `R` and positive `π`, `expectedLogLik = N log ω + ∑_{a ≠ b} n a b log R a b + piObjective c (ω e) π`.
nodes.title: Eq. 6 for the SiPhy matrix

nodes.summary: The SiPhy rate update (Eq. 7, for fixed `π`): `ω = N / ∑ b, e b π b`.
nodes.title: The SiPhy rate update

nodes.summary: The rate update maximizes Eq. 6 over `ω > 0` for a fixed positive `π`, when the expected number of substitutions `N` and the time-weighted rate `∑ b, e b π b` are positive.
nodes.title: The rate update maximizes Eq. 6 over `ω > 0`

nodes.summary: Any other `ω > 0` gives a strictly smaller value of Eq. 6.
nodes.title: The rate update is the unique maximizer

nodes.summary: For positive `c` and nonnegative `d` on a nonempty finite alphabet there is exactly one `γ` with `d b + γ > 0` for all `b` and `∑ b, c b / (d b + γ) = 1`.
