nodes.summary: The mean squared imputation error: `𝔼 (z_t - ẑ)² = Σ_tt - 2 wᵀ Σ_ot + wᵀ Σ_oo w`.
nodes.title: Mean squared imputation error

nodes.summary: For the ImpG weights (`Σ_oo w = Σ_ot`, i.e. `w = Σ_oo⁻¹ Σ_ot` when `Σ_oo` is invertible) the imputed statistic has second moment `wᵀ Σ_ot = Σ_to Σ_oo⁻¹ Σ_ot`; for `Σ_tt = 1` this is `1 -` the linear-prediction residual variance, ImpG's `r²_pred`.
nodes.title: Second moment of the statistic imputed with ImpG weights

nodes.summary: For the ImpG weights (`Σ_oo w = Σ_ot`) the mean squared imputation error is `Σ_tt - wᵀ Σ_ot = Σ_tt - Σ_to Σ_oo⁻¹ Σ_ot`, the linear-prediction residual variance (the conditional variance only under the Gaussian ImpG model).
nodes.title: Mean squared error of imputation with ImpG weights

nodes.summary: The moment matrix `Σ_oo` is symmetric.
nodes.title: Symmetry of the typed-marker moment matrix

nodes.summary: If `Σ_oo w = Σ_ot`, then for any weights `w'`, `𝔼 (z_t - w'ᵀ z_o)² = 𝔼 (z_t - wᵀ z_o)² + (w' - w)ᵀ Σ_oo (w' - w)`.
nodes.title: Excess error of a linear imputation

nodes.summary: The weights solving `Σ_oo w = Σ_ot` minimize the mean squared error `𝔼 (z_t - w'ᵀ z_o)²` over all weights `w'`.
nodes.title: ImpG is the best linear imputation

nodes.summary: For any weights `w` with `wᵀ Σ_oo w > 0` (for example the ridge weights solving `(Σ_oo + λ I) w = Σ_ot`), the statistic `ẑ / √(wᵀ Σ_oo w)` has second moment `1`, so it has unit variance under the centred null.
nodes.title: Normalized imputed statistic
Latent causal variable model

nodes.summary: The latent causal variable model of O'Connor and Price (2018, Equation 3) on a probability space: `α_k = q_k π + γ_k` with `π` independent of `(γ₁, γ₂)`, the law of `(γ₁, γ₂)` invariant under each sign flip, `π` of mean zero and unit variance, and both `α_k` of unit second moment. Fourth moments are assumed finite.
nodes.title: Latent causal variable model

nodes.summary: The marginal effect `α₁ = q₁ π + γ₁` on trait 1.
nodes.title: Marginal effect on the first trait in the latent causal variable model

nodes.summary: The marginal effect `α₂ = q₂ π + γ₂` on trait 2.
nodes.title: Marginal effect on the second trait in the latent causal variable model

nodes.summary: The excess kurtosis `κ_π = E(π⁴) - 3` of the effect on the latent variable.
nodes.title: Excess kurtosis of the latent effect

nodes.summary: The genetic correlation is `E(α₁ α₂) = q₁ q₂` (O'Connor and Price 2018, after Equation 1).
nodes.title: Genetic correlation in the latent causal variable model

nodes.summary: Mixed fourth moment (O'Connor and Price 2018, Equation 2): `E(α₁³ α₂) = κ_π q₁³ q₂ + 3 q₁ q₂`.
nodes.title: Mixed fourth moment

reading_title.source: Mixed fourth moment $E(\alpha_1 \alpha_2^3)$

nodes.summary: The mirror image of Equation 2: `E(α₁ α₂³) = κ_π q₁ q₂³ + 3 q₁ q₂`.
nodes.title: Mixed fourth moment $E(\alpha_1 \alpha_2^3)$

nodes.summary: Unit variance of `α₁` forces `q₁² ≤ 1` (the non-mediated part has variance `1 - q₁²`).
nodes.title: Mediated coefficient of the first trait is at most one in size

nodes.summary: Unit variance of `α₂` forces `q₂² ≤ 1`.
nodes.title: Mediated coefficient of the second trait is at most one in size

nodes.summary: `E(π⁴) ≥ (E π²)² = 1`, so the excess kurtosis is at least `-2`.
nodes.title: Fourth moment of the latent effect is at least one

reading_title.source: Centred mixed fourth moment $E(\alpha_1^3 \alpha_2)$

nodes.summary: The centred mixed fourth moment: `E(α₁³ α₂) - 3 ρ_g = κ_π q₁³ q₂`.
nodes.title: Centred mixed fourth moment $E(\alpha_1^3 \alpha_2)$

reading_title.source: Centred mixed fourth moment $E(\alpha_1 \alpha_2^3)$

nodes.summary: The centred mixed fourth moment: `E(α₁ α₂³) - 3 ρ_g = κ_π q₁ q₂³`.
nodes.title: Centred mixed fourth moment $E(\alpha_1 \alpha_2^3)$

nodes.summary: If `κ_π ≠ 0` and `ρ_g = q₁ q₂ ≠ 0`, then `|E(α₁ α₂³) - 3 ρ_g| ≤ |E(α₁³ α₂) - 3 ρ_g|` iff `q₂² ≤ q₁²`.
nodes.title: The centred moments order `q₁²` and `q₂²`
Excess kurtosis of the latent effect is at least −2

nodes.summary: If `κ_π > 0` and `ρ_g ≠ 0`, then `|E(α₁ α₂³)| ≤ |E(α₁³ α₂)|` iff `q₂² ≤ q₁²` (O'Connor and Price 2018, after Equation 2, which states the forward implication).
nodes.title: The paper's uncentred comparison, under its sign condition

nodes.summary: If `κ_π < 0` and `ρ_g ≠ 0`, then `|E(α₁ α₂³)| ≤ |E(α₁³ α₂)|` iff `q₁² ≤ q₂²`. So the paper's uncentred criterion needs `κ_π > 0`; the centred criterion `abs_centredMoment_le_iff` does not.
nodes.title: The uncentred comparison is reversed when `κ_π < 0`

nodes.summary: The genetic causality proportion `gcp = (log|q₂| - log|q₁|) / (log|q₂| + log|q₁|)` (O'Connor and Price 2018, Equation 4). Meaningful for `0 < |q₁|, |q₂| ≤ 1` and `ρ_g² < 1`; for `|q₁| = |q₂| = 1` the denominator vanishes and the value is `0` by the convention `x / 0 = 0`.
nodes.title: Genetic causality proportion

nodes.summary: `gcp ≥ 0` iff `q₂² ≤ q₁²`, for nonzero `q₁, q₂` with `ρ_g² = (q₁ q₂)² < 1`.
nodes.title: Sign of the genetic causality proportion

nodes.summary: The genetic causality proportion solves the paper's Equation 1: `q₂² / q₁² = (ρ_g²) ^ gcp` with `ρ_g = q₁ q₂`, for nonzero `q₁, q₂` with `ρ_g² < 1`.
nodes.title: Genetic causality proportion solves the defining equation

nodes.summary: `gcp ≤ 1` when `q₁² ≤ 1` (for nonzero `q₁, q₂` with `ρ_g² < 1`).
nodes.title: Genetic causality proportion is at most 1

nodes.summary: `-1 ≤ gcp` when `q₂² ≤ 1` (for nonzero `q₁, q₂` with `ρ_g² < 1`).
nodes.title: Genetic causality proportion is at least −1

nodes.summary: The paper's criterion for `gcp ≥ 0` (O'Connor and Price 2018, after Equation 2), under the sign condition `κ_π > 0` that it needs: if `ρ_g ≠ 0`, `ρ_g² < 1` and `|E(α₁ α₂³)| ≤ |E(α₁³ α₂)|`, then `gcp ≥ 0`.
nodes.title: The paper's criterion for `gcp ≥ 0`
LD-score regression

nodes.summary: The normalized cross product `r j k = X_jᵀ X_k / N` of markers `j` and `k`. For a standardized genotype matrix (`IsStandardized`) it is the sample correlation of the two markers; for other matrices it is only a scale-dependent dot product.
nodes.title: Normalized cross product of genotype markers

nodes.summary: The LD score `ℓ j = ∑ k, r j k ^ 2` of marker `j` (an LD score in the sense of the cited paper for a standardized genotype matrix).
nodes.title: LD score of a marker

nodes.summary: The genotype matrix is standardized: every marker column has mean `0` and sum of squares `N` (unit sample variance).
nodes.title: Standardized genotype matrix

nodes.summary: For a standardized matrix each marker has correlation `1` with itself.
nodes.title: A standardized marker has correlation one with itself

nodes.summary: For a standardized matrix the correlations lie in `[-1, 1]` (Cauchy–Schwarz).
nodes.title: Correlations of standardized markers lie in (-1, 1)

nodes.summary: The random-effects model of LD-score regression (Bulik-Sullivan et al. 2015), stated at the level of raw second moments, for `N` individuals and `M` markers with heritability `h2`.
nodes.title: Random-effects model of LD-score regression

nodes.summary: The heritability is nonnegative when there is at least one marker.
nodes.title: Nonnegativity of heritability in the LD-score model

nodes.summary: The heritability is at most `1` when there is at least one individual.
nodes.title: Heritability is at most one in the LD-score model

nodes.summary: The phenotype `y = X β + ε`.
nodes.title: Phenotype in the LD-score model

nodes.summary: The `N`-normalized score `β̂ j = X_jᵀ y / N` of marker `j`. For a standardized column (`∑ i, X i j ^ 2 = N`) it is the marginal least-squares estimate of the effect of marker `j`; in general that estimate has denominator `∑ i, X i j ^ 2` instead of `N`.
nodes.title: Normalized marginal score in the LD-score model

nodes.summary: The association statistic `χ² j = N * β̂ j ^ 2` of marker `j`.
nodes.title: Association statistic in the LD-score model

nodes.summary: The exact expectation of the association statistic built from the `N`-normalized score, for an arbitrary genotype matrix: `𝔼[χ² j] = N h² / M * ℓ j + (1 - h²) * (∑ i, X i j ^ 2) / N`. (For `N = 0` both sides are `0` by the convention `x / 0 = 0`.)
nodes.title: Expected association statistic for an arbitrary genotype matrix

nodes.summary: LD-score regression (Bulik-Sullivan et al. 2015): for a standardized genotype matrix (`IsStandardized`, so that `ldCorr` is the sample correlation and `ldScore` the LD score) and `N ≠ 0`, `𝔼[χ² j] = N h² / M * ℓ j + (1 - h²)`. The expected association statistic is affine in the LD score, with slope `N h² / M` and intercept `1 - h²`. The proof uses only that column `j` has sum of squares `N`; the rest of the…
nodes.title: LD-score regression

nodes.summary: The mean LD score `ℓ̄ = (1 / M) ∑ j, ℓ j`.
nodes.title: Mean LD score

nodes.summary: Polygenic inflation: for a standardized genotype matrix with `N, M ≠ 0`, the mean expected association statistic is `1 - h² + N h² ℓ̄ / M`.
nodes.title: Polygenic inflation of the mean association statistic

nodes.summary: The phenotype with a stratification shift: `y i = (X β) i + ε i + s * c i`.
nodes.title: Phenotype with population stratification

nodes.summary: The `N`-normalized score of marker `j` under stratification, `X_jᵀ y / N`.
nodes.title: Normalized score under stratification

nodes.summary: The association statistic `N * β̂ j ^ 2` under stratification.
nodes.title: Association statistic under stratification

nodes.summary: Stratification inflation: for a probability measure and mean-zero effects and noise, `𝔼[χ² j] = N h² / M * ℓ j + (1 - h²) (∑ i, X i j ^ 2) / N + N s² (X_jᵀ c / N)²`.
nodes.title: Expected association statistic under stratification

nodes.summary: Stratification inflation for a standardized genotype matrix and `N ≠ 0`: `𝔼[χ² j] = N h² / M * ℓ j + (1 - h²) + N s² (X_jᵀ c / N)²`.
nodes.title: Expected statistic under stratification for standardized genotypes

nodes.summary: With a constant stratification term (`s² (X_jᵀ c / N)² = a` for every marker), the expected statistic is exactly affine in the LD score, with slope `N h² / M` and intercept `1 - h² + N a`.
nodes.title: LD-score regression with constant stratification

nodes.summary: With a constant stratification term `N a`, the mean expected statistic is `N h² ℓ̄ / M + (1 - h² + N a)`.
nodes.title: Mean association statistic with constant stratification

nodes.summary: The attenuation ratio `(intercept - 1) / (mean χ² - 1)` of Loh et al. (2018).
nodes.title: Attenuation ratio

nodes.summary: With a constant stratification term `N a`, the attenuation ratio of the exact intercept `1 - h² + N a` and the mean expected statistic is `(N a - h²) / (N h² ℓ̄ / M + N a - h²)`.
nodes.title: Attenuation ratio under constant stratification

nodes.summary: With a constant stratification term `N a`, the share of the mean inflation above the exact null level `1 - h²` that is due to stratification is `N a / (N a + N h² ℓ̄ / M)`.
nodes.title: Confounding share of inflation under constant stratification

nodes.summary: The confounding share `N a / (N a + N h² ℓ̄ / M)` lies in `[0, 1]` when `a`, `h²` and `ℓ̄` are nonnegative (as they are in the model: `a` is a square, `h² ≥ 0` by `Model.h2_nonneg`, LD scores are sums of squares).
nodes.title: Confounding share lies between 0 and 1
Genomic prediction from summary statistics

nodes.summary: In a target population whose marker genotypes `x j` have raw second moments `∫ x j * x k = [j = k]` (standardized, uncorrelated markers), the scores `xᵀ a` and `xᵀ b` of two effect vectors have raw cross moment `aᵀ b`. With mean-zero genotypes and a probability measure this is the covariance of the genetic value `xᵀ β` and the polygenic score `xᵀ β̂`.
nodes.title: Cross moment of two polygenic scores

nodes.summary: The effect-estimate model behind polygenic-score accuracy (Daetwyler et al. 2008; Dudbridge 2013), at the level of raw second moments, for `M` independent markers: true effects `beta k` with `∫ β k β l = (h² / M) [k = l]`, estimation errors `err k` with `∫ e k e l = s² [k = l]`, orthogonal to the effects. The estimates are `β̂ = β + e` (`betaHat`). For a probability measure and mean-zero effects and errors these…
nodes.title: Effect-estimate model for polygenic score accuracy

nodes.summary: The model forces `h² ≥ 0` when there is at least one marker.
nodes.title: Nonnegativity of heritability in the effect-estimate model

nodes.summary: The model forces `s² ≥ 0` when there is at least one marker.
nodes.title: Nonnegativity of the sampling error variance of effect estimates

nodes.summary: The estimated effects `β̂ = β + e`.
nodes.title: Estimated marker effects

nodes.summary: The squared correlation of the genetic value and the polygenic score as a ratio of expectations, `𝔼[βᵀβ̂]² / (𝔼[βᵀβ] 𝔼[β̂ᵀβ̂])`: by `integral_score_mul_score`, `βᵀβ̂`, `βᵀβ` and `β̂ᵀβ̂` are the covariance and variances of `xᵀβ` and `xᵀβ̂` over a target population of standardized uncorrelated markers. It is not the expectation of a squared correlation.
nodes.title: Squared accuracy of a polygenic score

nodes.summary: `𝔼[βᵀβ̂] = h²` (for at least one marker).
nodes.title: Expected cross product of true and estimated effects

nodes.summary: `𝔼[βᵀβ] = h²` (for at least one marker).
nodes.title: Expected squared norm of the true effects

nodes.summary: `𝔼[β̂ᵀβ̂] = h² + M s²` (for at least one marker).
nodes.title: Expected squared norm of the estimated effects

nodes.summary: Polygenic-score accuracy as a ratio of expectations: `r²_g = h² / (h² + M s²)`. (If `h² = 0` both sides are `0`.)
nodes.title: Polygenic-score accuracy

nodes.summary: With sampling variance `s² = 1 / N`, `r²_g = N h² / (N h² + M)`.
nodes.title: Daetwyler–Dudbridge formula

nodes.summary: The training genotype matrix has orthogonal columns with sum of squares `N`, `∑ i, X i k * X i l = N [k = l]`; for centered columns this says that the markers are uncorrelated, with unit sample variance, in the training sample.
nodes.title: Training genotype matrix with orthogonal standardized columns

nodes.summary: The effect-estimate model obtained from the LD-score model when the effects are estimated by the normalized scores `β̂ = Xᵀ y / N` on a training matrix with orthogonal standardized columns: the error is `e k = ∑ i, X i k ε i / N` and its sampling variance is `(1 - h²) / N`.
nodes.title: Effect-estimate model derived from the LD-score model

nodes.summary: The estimates of `ofLDScore` are the normalized scores `Xᵀ y / N` of the LD-score model.
nodes.title: Estimates of the derived model are normalized scores

nodes.summary: With orthogonal standardized training columns, `β̂ = Xᵀ y / N` and residual variance `1 - h²`, `r²_g = N h² / (N h² + M (1 - h²))`. The cited `N h² / (N h² + M)` takes the residual variance to be `1`.
nodes.title: Polygenic-score accuracy in the LD-score model

nodes.summary: The marginal least-squares estimate `x_jᵀ y / x_jᵀ x_j` of marker `j` (single-marker regression without intercept, on centered genotypes and phenotype as in Yang et al. 2012).
nodes.title: Marginal least-squares estimate of a marker effect

nodes.summary: The diagonal `D = diag(XᵀX)` of the Gram matrix.
nodes.title: Diagonal of the genotype Gram matrix

nodes.summary: `Xᵀ y = D β̂` for the marginal estimates `β̂` (Yang et al. 2012). This holds for every genotype matrix: a column with `x_jᵀ x_j = 0` is zero, so both sides vanish there.
nodes.title: Genotype-phenotype cross products from marginal estimates

nodes.summary: COJO joint estimate (Yang et al. 2012, eq. (5)): the joint least-squares estimate `(XᵀX)⁻¹ Xᵀ y` equals `(XᵀX)⁻¹ D β̂` in terms of the marginal estimates `β̂`, so it can be computed from summary statistics and `XᵀX`. (Stated for every `X`; it is the least-squares estimate when `XᵀX` is invertible.)
nodes.title: COJO joint estimate

nodes.summary: For markers uncorrelated in the sample (`XᵀX` diagonal) without zero columns, the joint estimate is the vector of marginal estimates.
nodes.title: Joint estimate equals marginal estimates for uncorrelated markers

nodes.summary: The unconditional algebraic formula from Yang et al. 2012, eq. (15): `(X₂ᵀX₂)⁻¹ X₂ᵀ y - (X₂ᵀX₂)⁻¹ X₂ᵀX₁ (X₁ᵀX₁)⁻¹ X₁ᵀ y`. When both Gram determinants are units, this has the usual interpretation as the block-2 fit conditional on the block-1 fit. For a singular Gram matrix, Mathlib's nonsingular inverse is zero and the value can be a junk value.
nodes.title: Conditional estimate of second-block effects (COJO)

nodes.summary: COJO conditional algebraic formula from summary statistics (Yang et al. 2012, eq. (17)): `b̂₂|b̂₁ = (X₂ᵀX₂)⁻¹ D₂ β̂₂ - (X₂ᵀX₂)⁻¹ X₂ᵀX₁ (X₁ᵀX₁)⁻¹ D₁ β̂₁`.
nodes.title: COJO conditional algebraic formula from summary statistics

nodes.summary: Unconditionally, the conditional formula equals the nonsingular-inverse formula applied to the algebraic residual `y - X₁ ((X₁ᵀX₁)⁻¹ X₁ᵀ y)`. If both Gram determinants are units, these are the successive least-squares fits on blocks 1 and 2. With a singular Gram matrix they need not minimize residual error. This is in general not the block-2 part of the joint formula on both blocks (the formulas agree when…
nodes.title: Conditional estimate as a fit to the first-block residual

nodes.summary: The stratified normalized-cross-product score `ℓ(j, C) = ∑_{k ∈ C} (X_jᵀ X_k / N)²`. For a standardized genotype matrix this is the stratified LD score of marker `j` with respect to annotation category `C` (Finucane et al. 2015).
nodes.title: Stratified LD score

nodes.summary: The stratified LD-score model (Finucane et al. 2015), at the level of raw second moments: annotation categories `cat c ⊆ {markers}` (possibly overlapping), per-category contributions `tau c`, effects with `∫ β k β l = [k = l] ∑_c τ_c [k ∈ cat c]`, noise with `∫ ε i ε i' = σ²_e [i = i']`, effects orthogonal to noise. The cited model normalizes the phenotypic variance so that `σ²_e ≈ 1`; the confounding term `N a` is…
nodes.title: Stratified LD-score model

nodes.summary: The phenotype `y = X β + ε`.
nodes.title: Phenotype in the stratified LD-score model

nodes.summary: The `N`-normalized score `β̂ j = X_jᵀ y / N`.
nodes.title: Normalized score in the stratified LD-score model

nodes.summary: The association statistic `χ² j = N β̂ j ²`.
nodes.title: Association statistic in the stratified LD-score model

nodes.summary: The exact expectation of the association statistic in the stratified model, for any genotype matrix: `𝔼[χ² j] = N ∑_c τ_c ℓ(j, cat c) + σ²_e (∑ i, X i j ²) / N`.
nodes.title: Expected association statistic in the stratified LD-score model

nodes.summary: Stratified LD-score regression (Finucane et al. 2015): for a standardized genotype matrix and `N ≠ 0`, `𝔼[χ² j] = N ∑_c τ_c ℓ(j, cat c) + σ²_e`. Full-matrix standardization makes every normalized cross product in `stratLDScore` a sample correlation.
nodes.title: Stratified LD-score regression

nodes.summary: One causal variant (the LD-proxy noncentrality; Pritchard & Przeworski 2001): if the genotype matrix is standardized and the only category is the single causal marker `c` with variance `τ`, then for a marker `m` and `N ≠ 0`, `𝔼[χ² m] = N τ r m c ² + σ²_e`.
nodes.title: One causal variant

nodes.summary: The in-sample normalized cross product `∑_{i ∈ S} X i j X i k / |S|` of markers `j`, `k` in the sample `S` of a pool of individuals (the sample LD correlation for a matrix standardized within `S`).
nodes.title: In-sample LD correlation

nodes.summary: The bivariate LD-score model (Bulik-Sullivan et al. 2015b), at the level of the cross second moments that enter `𝔼[z₁ z₂]`: a pool of `n` genotyped individuals with genotype matrix `X`, two GWAS samples `S₁`, `S₂` of the pool (possibly overlapping), effects `β₁`, `β₂` with `∫ β₁ k β₂ l = (ρ_g / M) [k = l]` (genetic covariance `ρ_g`), noises `ε₁`, `ε₂` with `∫ ε₁ i ε₂ i' = ρ_e [i = i']` (residual cross-moment `ρ_e`…
nodes.title: Bivariate LD-score model

nodes.summary: The scaled marginal score `z₁ j = √N₁ X_jᵀ y₁ / N₁` of marker `j` for trait 1, computed on `S₁` with `y₁ = X β₁ + ε₁`. The model does not assert the normalization needed for a z-score.
nodes.title: Scaled marginal score for the first trait

nodes.summary: The analogous scaled marginal score `z₂ j` of marker `j` for trait 2, computed on `S₂`.
nodes.title: Scaled marginal score for the second trait

nodes.summary: With `N₁ = |S₁|`, `N₂ = |S₂|`, `𝔼[z₁ j z₂ j] = √(N₁ N₂) (ρ_g / M) ∑_k r¹ j k r² j k + ρ_e (∑_{i ∈ S₁ ∩ S₂} X i j ²) / √(N₁ N₂)`, with the in-sample normalized cross products `r¹`, `r²` (`sampleCorr`).
nodes.title: Cross-trait scaled-score identity, exact form

nodes.summary: If the two samples have the same normalized cross products with marker `j` and the overlap marker is standardized at `j` (`∑_{i ∈ S₁ ∩ S₂} X i j ² = N_s`), then `𝔼[z₁ j z₂ j] = √(N₁ N₂) ρ_g ℓ_j / M + ρ_e N_s / √(N₁ N₂)`. Here `ρ_e` is only the residual cross-moment specified by `CrossTraitModel`; this theorem does not state the Bulik-Sullivan phenotypic-correlation overlap formula or establish z-score normalization.
nodes.title: Equal normalized-cross-product specialization of the residual cross-moment identity

nodes.summary: The number of individuals `N = ∑ (r i + s i)`.
nodes.title: Number of individuals in a case-control genotype table

nodes.summary: The trend numerator `U = ∑ i, i (r i S - s i R)` with `R = ∑ r`, `S = ∑ s`.
nodes.title: Numerator of the Cochran–Armitage trend statistic

nodes.summary: The pooled genotype-score variance `∑ i² n_i / N - (∑ i n_i / N)²`, `n_i = r i + s i`.
nodes.title: Pooled genotype-score variance

nodes.summary: The Cochran–Armitage trend statistic with scores `0, 1, 2` (Armitage 1955): `N U² / (R S (N ∑ i² n_i - (∑ i n_i)²))`.
nodes.title: Cochran–Armitage trend statistic

nodes.summary: The squared sample correlation of case status (`1` for cases, `0` for controls) and the genotype score over the `N` individuals of the table.
nodes.title: Squared correlation of case status and genotype score

nodes.summary: The pooled frequency `p = ∑ i n_i / (2 N)` of the counted allele.
nodes.title: Pooled allele frequency

nodes.summary: Pearson's statistic `n (a d - b c)² / ((a + b)(c + d)(a + c)(b + d))` of a `2 × 2` table `[[a, b], [c, d]]` with `n = a + b + c + d`.
nodes.title: Pearson's chi-squared statistic of a 2 × 2 table

nodes.summary: The allelic test: Pearson's statistic of the `2 × 2` table of case and control allele counts (`2N` alleles).
nodes.title: Allelic test statistic

nodes.summary: The trend test is `N r²` (Armitage 1955): the Cochran–Armitage statistic is `N` times the squared sample correlation of case status and genotype score. (In degenerate tables, where a denominator vanishes, both sides are `0` by the convention `x / 0 = 0`.)
nodes.title: The trend test is `N r²`

nodes.summary: The observed score variance minus the Hardy–Weinberg score variance `2 p q`: `Var - 2 p (1 - p) = (4 n₀ n₂ - n₁²) / (2 N²)`.
nodes.title: Departure of the genotype-score variance from Hardy–Weinberg

nodes.summary: Allelic versus trend test (Sasieni 1997): with cases and controls present, a pooled allele frequency strictly between `0` and `1` and a positive score variance, `allelic · 2 p q = trend · Var`.
nodes.title: Allelic versus trend test

nodes.summary: The allelic test equals the trend test iff the pooled sample is in Hardy–Weinberg proportions (`n₁² = 4 n₀ n₂`; Sasieni 1997), whenever the trend numerator is nonzero.
nodes.title: The allelic test equals the trend test iff the pooled sample is in Hardy–Weinberg proportions
Mendelian randomization

nodes.summary: An observational linear moment model: variables `Z`, `X`, `Y` and `U` on a probability space, all square integrable, with the algebraic decomposition `Y = α + β X + U`. The residual `U` is an arbitrary observed-variable function. Consequently `outcome_eq` does not exclude direct effects of `Z` under interventions, and `β` is only the coefficient in this decomposition. Orthogonality (`Cov(Z, U) = 0`) and nonzero…
nodes.title: Linear moment model for instrumental variables

nodes.summary: The covariance of any square-integrable variable with the outcome splits along the observational decomposition: `Cov(V, Y) = β Cov(V, X) + Cov(V, U)`.
nodes.title: Covariance with the outcome in a linear moment model

nodes.summary: The Wald covariance identity: if `Cov(Z, U) = 0` and `Cov(Z, X) ≠ 0`, then `Cov(Z, Y) / Cov(Z, X) = β`. For a two-valued `Z` the ratio is the grouping estimator of Wald (1940), the difference of the group means of `Y` over that of `X`. This is a moment-condition identity, not a formal causal-identification result.
nodes.title: Wald ratio identity

nodes.summary: The Wald covariance identity when the instrument is independent of the residual.
nodes.title: Wald ratio identity for an instrument independent of the residual

nodes.summary: The Wald ratio as a ratio of regression slopes: the slope of `Y` on `Z` divided by the slope of `X` on `Z` (the form used with SNP–outcome and SNP–exposure associations) is `β`. This is again an observational moment identity.
nodes.title: Wald ratio as a ratio of regression slopes

nodes.summary: The ordinary least-squares coefficient identity for `Y` on `X` is `β + Cov(X, U) / Var(X)`, which differs from `β` exactly when `Cov(X, U) ≠ 0`.
nodes.title: Bias of the ordinary least-squares coefficient under confounding

nodes.summary: The ratio estimate `β̂_{Yj} / β̂_{Xj}` of SNP `j` (Lean's `x / 0 = 0` gives `0` when `β̂_{Xj} = 0`; such SNPs carry weight `0` in `ivwWeight`).
nodes.title: Ratio estimate of a single SNP

nodes.summary: The first-order inverse-variance weight `w_j = β̂_{Xj}² / σ_j²` of the ratio estimate of SNP `j`, where `σ_j` is the standard error of `β̂_{Yj}` (Burgess, Butterworth & Thompson 2013).
nodes.title: Inverse-variance weight of a ratio estimate

nodes.summary: The inverse-variance-weighted (IVW) estimator `∑ β̂_{Xj} β̂_{Yj} σ_j⁻² / ∑ β̂_{Xj}² σ_j⁻²` (Burgess, Butterworth & Thompson 2013). The standard errors are positive in the model; it is the junk value `0` if every `β̂_{Xj} = 0`.
nodes.title: Inverse-variance-weighted estimator

nodes.summary: The weighted residual sum of squares `∑ (β̂_{Yj} - b β̂_{Xj})² / σ_j²` of the regression through the origin with slope `b`.
nodes.title: Weighted residual sum of squares through the origin

nodes.summary: The IVW estimator is the weighted mean of the ratio estimates with weights `w_j = β̂_{Xj}² / σ_j²`. This holds for all data: a SNP with `β̂_{Xj} = 0` has weight `0` and contributes nothing to either side.
nodes.title: IVW estimator as a weighted mean of ratio estimates

nodes.summary: The IVW estimator is the weighted least-squares slope through the origin: it minimizes the weighted residual sum of squares. This holds for all data: if every `β̂_{Xj} = 0` the sum does not depend on the slope (and `ivw` is the junk value `0`), and a SNP with `σ_j = 0` has weight `0` on both sides by Lean's `x / 0 = 0`.
nodes.title: IVW estimator minimizes the weighted residual sum of squares

nodes.summary: The total weight is positive as soon as some SNP has `β̂_{Xj} ≠ 0`.
nodes.title: Positivity of the total IVW weight

nodes.summary: Without error, IVW recovers the proportionality coefficient: if `β̂_{Yj} = β β̂_{Xj}` for all `j` and some `β̂_{Xj} ≠ 0`, then the IVW estimate is `β`. This algebraic statement does not itself give `β` a causal interpretation.
nodes.title: IVW recovers an exact proportionality coefficient

nodes.summary: Unbiasedness of IVW (Burgess, Butterworth & Thompson 2013), with the SNP–exposure associations `β̂_{Xj}` treated as fixed: if `β̂_{Yj} = β β̂_{Xj} + ε_j` with integrable mean-zero errors, the IVW estimator has mean `β`.
nodes.title: Unbiasedness of the IVW estimator

nodes.summary: The first-order variance of IVW (Burgess, Butterworth & Thompson 2013): with the `β̂_{Xj}` fixed and `β̂_{Yj} = β β̂_{Xj} + ε_j`, where the errors are square integrable, pairwise uncorrelated (for instance independent) and `Var(ε_j) = σ_j²`, the IVW estimator has variance `(∑ w_j)⁻¹ = (∑ β̂_{Xj}² / σ_j²)⁻¹`.
nodes.title: Variance of the IVW estimator

nodes.summary: The weighted mean `∑ v_j a_j / ∑ v_j`.
nodes.title: Weighted mean

nodes.summary: The weighted covariance `∑ v_j (a_j - ā_v)(b_j - b̄_v) / ∑ v_j`, where `ā_v` and `b̄_v` are weighted means.
nodes.title: Weighted covariance

nodes.summary: The MR-Egger slope (Bowden, Davey Smith & Burgess 2015): the slope of the weighted linear regression of `β̂_{Yj}` on `β̂_{Xj}` with an intercept, `Cov_v(β̂_X, β̂_Y) / Var_v(β̂_X)`. The paper's weights are `v_j = σ_j⁻²`.
nodes.title: MR-Egger slope

nodes.summary: The MR-Egger intercept `β̂̄_Y - slope · β̂̄_X` (weighted means).
nodes.title: MR-Egger intercept

nodes.summary: The weighted residual sum of squares `∑ v_j (β̂_{Yj} - a - b β̂_{Xj})²` of the line with intercept `a` and slope `b`.
nodes.title: Weighted residual sum of squares of a line

nodes.summary: The MR-Egger line is the weighted least-squares line: for nonnegative weights and `β̂_X` of nonzero weighted variance (so the total weight is positive and `β̂_X` is not constant on the support of the weights), it minimizes the weighted residual sum of squares.
nodes.title: MR-Egger line is the weighted least-squares line

nodes.summary: The MR-Egger slope under pleiotropy (Bowden, Davey Smith & Burgess 2015): if the SNP–outcome associations are `Γ_j = α_j + β γ_j`, with pleiotropic terms `α_j` and SNP–exposure associations `γ_j`, the Egger slope of `Γ` on `γ` is `β + Cov_v(γ, α) / Var_v(γ)`.
nodes.title: MR-Egger slope under pleiotropy

nodes.summary: The MR-Egger intercept under pleiotropy: it is the weighted mean pleiotropic effect `ᾱ_v` minus `Cov_v(γ, α) / Var_v(γ) · γ̄_v`.
nodes.title: MR-Egger intercept under pleiotropy

nodes.summary: The finite-sample InSIDE identity (Bowden, Davey Smith & Burgess 2015): if the pleiotropic terms are uncorrelated with the instrument strengths in the weighted sense, `Cov_v(α, γ) = 0`, the MR-Egger slope is the coefficient `β` and the intercept is the weighted mean pleiotropic term `ᾱ_v`. This identity alone does not encode a causal interpretation.
nodes.title: InSIDE identity for MR-Egger

nodes.summary: Directional pleiotropy biases IVW: if `Γ_j = α_j + β γ_j`, the IVW estimate is `β + ∑ γ_j α_j σ_j⁻² / ∑ γ_j² σ_j⁻²`. For example a common pleiotropic term `α_j = α ≠ 0` biases IVW whenever `∑ γ_j σ_j⁻² ≠ 0`, whereas a constant `α` satisfies InSIDE, so `eggerSlope_eq_of_inside` gives MR-Egger slope `β` and intercept `α`.
nodes.title: Directional pleiotropy biases the IVW estimator

nodes.summary: A ratio with a Gaussian denominator has no first moment (a classical fact, recalled in the weak-instrument analysis of Burgess & Thompson 2011): if `D ~ N(m, v)` with `v > 0` and `N` is independent of `D` and not almost surely `0`, then `𝔼|N / D| = ∞`. Applied to the ratio estimator `β̂_Y / β̂_X` with a normally distributed SNP–exposure estimate `β̂_X`.
nodes.title: Ratio with a Gaussian denominator has infinite first moment

nodes.summary: The ratio of two independent normal variables, the denominator with positive variance and the numerator not almost surely zero (`(mN, vN) ≠ (0, 0)`), is not integrable.
nodes.title: Ratio of independent normal variables is not integrable

nodes.summary: The four compliance types of Angrist, Imbens & Rubin (1996), determined by the pair of potential treatments `(D(0), D(1))`.
nodes.title: Compliance types of Angrist, Imbens and Rubin

nodes.summary: The compliance type of the potential treatments `(D(0), D(1)) = (d₀, d₁)`.
nodes.title: Compliance type of a pair of potential treatments

nodes.summary: A potential-outcomes model with a binary instrument and a binary treatment (Imbens & Angrist 1994; Angrist, Imbens & Rubin 1996): the assigned instrument `Z`, the potential treatments `D(z)` and the potential outcomes `Y(z, d)`, all measurable. The observed treatment is `D(Z)` and the observed outcome `Y(Z, D(Z))`. The identifying assumptions (independence, exclusion, monotonicity, relevance) are separate predicates.
nodes.title: Potential-outcomes model with binary instrument and treatment

nodes.summary: The observed treatment `D = D(Z)`.
nodes.title: Observed treatment in a potential-outcomes model

nodes.summary: The observed outcome `Y = Y(Z, D(Z))`.
nodes.title: Observed outcome in a potential-outcomes model

nodes.summary: The compliance type of a unit.
nodes.title: Compliance type of a unit

nodes.summary: The compliers, `D(0) = 0` and `D(1) = 1`.
nodes.title: Compliers in a potential-outcomes model

nodes.summary: Independence (random assignment): the instrument is independent of the vector of all potential treatments and potential outcomes.
nodes.title: Independence assumption for an instrument

nodes.summary: Exclusion: the instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment, `Y(0, d) = Y(1, d)`.
nodes.title: Exclusion restriction for an instrument

nodes.summary: Monotonicity: assignment never decreases the treatment, `D(0) ≤ D(1)`; there are no defiers.
nodes.title: Monotonicity assumption (no defiers)

nodes.summary: The mean of `f` in the arm `Z = z`, `𝔼[f | Z = z]`, the expectation under the conditional measure. It is the junk value `0` when `P(Z = z) = 0`.
nodes.title: Mean of a variable within an instrument arm

nodes.summary: The observed treatment as a `0`/`1` real variable.
nodes.title: Observed treatment as a 0-1 real variable

nodes.summary: The Wald (instrumental-variable) estimand `(𝔼[Y | Z = 1] - 𝔼[Y | Z = 0]) / (𝔼[D | Z = 1] - 𝔼[D | Z = 0])`.
nodes.title: Wald instrumental-variable estimand

nodes.summary: The first stage (Imbens & Angrist 1994): under independence and monotonicity, with both arms of positive probability, the difference in treatment rates between the arms is the proportion of compliers.
nodes.title: First stage: treatment-rate difference equals complier share

nodes.summary: The reduced form (Imbens & Angrist 1994): under independence, exclusion and monotonicity, with integrable potential outcomes and both arms of positive probability, the difference in mean outcomes between the arms is `𝔼[(Y(z, 1) - Y(z, 0)) 1_complier]`, for either `z`.
nodes.title: Reduced form: outcome difference is the complier-weighted effect

nodes.summary: The unrestricted algebraic identity behind LATE. If the complier set has measure zero, both sides totalize to `0`; therefore this theorem is not an identification or complier-average claim at that boundary. Use `waldEstimand_eq_late` for the source-faithful result with relevance.
nodes.title: Unrestricted algebraic identity behind the LATE theorem

nodes.summary: The local average treatment effect theorem (Imbens & Angrist 1994, Theorem 1; Angrist, Imbens & Rubin 1996): under independence, exclusion, monotonicity and relevance, with integrable potential outcomes and both arms of positive probability, the Wald estimand is the average treatment effect among compliers, `𝔼[Y(1) - Y(0) | complier]` (read at either instrument value `z`, which exclusion makes irrelevant).…
nodes.title: Local average treatment effect theorem
Posterior of the heterozygous selection coefficient

nodes.summary: Mean PTV allele count `n U / s` at deterministic mutation–selection balance, for `n` sampled chromosomes, PTV mutation rate `U` and heterozygous selection coefficient `s > 0`.
nodes.title: Mean PTV count at mutation-selection balance

nodes.summary: The balance mean is antitone in `s > 0` for `n U ≥ 0`.
nodes.title: Balance mean is decreasing in the selection coefficient

nodes.summary: Posterior of `s_het` is stochastically nonincreasing in the PTV count, any antitone mean: for a prior `μ` on `s_het` concentrated on `(0, ∞)`, a Poisson count with mean `λ` nonnegative and antitone on `(0, ∞)`, integrable likelihoods and positive marginal likelihoods, `P(s_het > t ∣ k') ≤ P(s_het > t ∣ k)` whenever `k ≤ k'`.
nodes.title: Posterior of `s_het` is stochastically nonincreasing in the PTV count, any antitone mean

nodes.summary: With the balance mean `n U / s_het` (`n, U > 0`) and any probability prior on `s_het ∈ (0, ∞)`, the posterior probability `P(s_het > t ∣ k)` is nonincreasing in the observed PTV count `k`.
nodes.title: Cassa et al. (2017) model
Principal-component correction for stratification

nodes.summary: The adjusted (residualized) `y`: the residual of the least-squares regression of `y` on the subspace `V` (`y` minus its orthogonal projection onto `V`).
nodes.title: Residualized vector after adjustment for a subspace

nodes.summary: Residuals are orthogonal to the adjustment subspace.
nodes.title: Residuals lie in the orthogonal complement

nodes.summary: Residuals are orthogonal to every vector of the subspace, in particular to every axis.
nodes.title: Residuals are orthogonal to every axis

nodes.summary: The residual is the orthogonal projection onto `Vᗮ`.
nodes.title: Residual as projection onto the orthogonal complement

nodes.summary: Residualization is additive.
nodes.title: Additivity of residualization

nodes.summary: Residualization is homogeneous.
nodes.title: Homogeneity of residualization

nodes.summary: The residual vanishes exactly on the subspace.
nodes.title: Residual vanishes exactly on the subspace

nodes.summary: Adding a vector of the subspace (stratification lying in the axis span) does not change the residual.
nodes.title: Stratification within the axis span does not change the residual

nodes.summary: Vectors orthogonal to the subspace are their own residuals: stratification outside the axis span is not removed.
nodes.title: Vectors orthogonal to the subspace are their own residuals

nodes.summary: Regressing on an orthonormal family of axes one axis at a time gives the joint residual: `y - ∑ₖ ⟪aₖ, y⟫ aₖ`.
nodes.title: Residual with respect to an orthonormal family of axes

nodes.summary: Frisch–Waugh–Lovell, uniqueness: in any least-squares decomposition `y = c + β g + e` with `c ∈ V` and `e ⊥ V ⊔ span {g}`, the coefficient `β` is the coefficient of the regression of the residualized `y` on the residualized `g`, and the residual `e` is the residual of that regression.
nodes.title: Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem, uniqueness

nodes.summary: Frisch–Waugh–Lovell, existence: the coefficient of the residual-on-residual regression gives a least-squares decomposition of `y` on `V ⊔ span {g}`.
nodes.title: Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem, existence

nodes.summary: The EIGENSTRAT association statistic `(N - K - 1) ⟪r_g, r_y⟫² / (‖r_g‖² ‖r_y‖²)` of the adjusted genotype `r_g` and adjusted phenotype `r_y`: `(N - K - 1)` times their squared cosine, which is their squared sample correlation when both are centered (Price et al. 2006). When either adjusted vector is zero the ratio is the junk value `0`.
nodes.title: EIGENSTRAT association statistic

nodes.summary: Adding vectors of `V` to the phenotype and the genotype does not change the EIGENSTRAT statistic.
nodes.title: Stratification in the axis span is removed

nodes.summary: The EIGENSTRAT statistic is nonnegative when `K + 1 ≤ N`.
nodes.title: Nonnegativity of the EIGENSTRAT statistic

nodes.summary: A genotype lying in the axis span carries no signal after adjustment (its residual is zero, and the statistic is the junk value `0` of the zero denominator).
nodes.title: Genotypes in the axis span carry no signal after adjustment

nodes.summary: The allele-frequency estimate `p̂ⱼ = μⱼ / 2` of marker `j`, where `μⱼ` is the mean variant-allele count of column `j` (autosomal diploid data, counts in `{0, 1, 2}`).
nodes.title: Allele-frequency estimate of a marker

nodes.summary: Patterson's normalized genotype matrix `(C i j - μⱼ) / √(p̂ⱼ (1 - p̂ⱼ))`. For a monomorphic marker (`p̂ⱼ ∈ {0, 1}`) the denominator is `0` and the column is the junk value `0`; Patterson et al. use polymorphic markers only.
nodes.title: Patterson's normalized genotype matrix

nodes.summary: Patterson's `N × N` matrix `Ψ = M Mᵀ / (number of markers)` of the normalized genotypes, whose top eigenvectors are the axes of variation.
nodes.title: Patterson's relatedness matrix

nodes.summary: Patterson's matrix `Ψ` is positive semidefinite.
nodes.title: Patterson's relatedness matrix is positive semidefinite

nodes.summary: The all-ones vector is in the kernel of `Ψ` (columns of the normalized matrix are centered), so at most `N - 1` eigenvalues are nonzero.
nodes.title: All-ones vector lies in the kernel of the relatedness matrix

nodes.summary: The axes of variation: an orthonormal eigenbasis of `Ψ`, in decreasing eigenvalue order.
nodes.title: Axes of variation

nodes.summary: The eigenvalues of `Ψ` in decreasing order, matching `axes`.
nodes.title: Eigenvalues of the axes of variation

nodes.summary: The span of the top `K` axes of variation, the subspace EIGENSTRAT adjusts for.
nodes.title: Span of the top axes of variation

nodes.summary: Each of the top `K` axes lies in their span.
nodes.title: Each top axis lies in the span of the top axes

nodes.summary: The top `K` axes span a `K`-dimensional subspace.
nodes.title: Dimension of the span of the top axes

nodes.summary: Patterson's sequential count of significant axes: among the first `K` statistics, the length of the leading run of statistics exceeding the threshold `t` (testing stops at the first non-significant one).
nodes.title: Sequential count of significant axes

nodes.summary: At most `K` axes are declared significant.
nodes.title: At most K axes are declared significant

nodes.summary: The first `numSignificant stat t K` indices are exactly those `k < K` whose statistics and all earlier ones exceed the threshold.
nodes.title: Characterization of the axes counted as significant

nodes.summary: Every axis counted as significant has a statistic above the threshold.
nodes.title: Significant axes have statistics above the threshold

nodes.summary: At least one axis is significant iff the leading statistic exceeds the threshold.
nodes.title: Criterion for at least one significant axis

nodes.summary: A higher threshold declares no more axes significant.
nodes.title: Count of significant axes decreases with the threshold

nodes.summary: For decreasing statistics (such as ordered eigenvalues compared with a fixed threshold) the sequential count is the number of statistics above the threshold.
nodes.title: Significant-axis count for decreasing statistics

nodes.summary: If, under the null hypothesis, the `k`-th statistic exceeds `t` with probability at most `1 - F t` (the Tracy–Widom approximation with `F` the TW₁ distribution function, taken here as a hypothesis), then the rule declares more than `k` significant axes with probability at most `1 - F t`.
nodes.title: Conditional error bound
Proximal contamination in mixed-model association

nodes.summary: The mixed-model (generalized-least-squares score) statistic `χ²(V) = (xᵀ V⁻¹ y)² / (xᵀ V⁻¹ x)` of the marker `x` for the phenotype `y` under the phenotypic covariance `V`. For positive definite `V` and `x ≠ 0` the denominator is positive.
nodes.title: Mixed-model association chi-squared statistic

nodes.summary: For positive definite `V₀` and `c ≥ 0`, `(V₀ + c x xᵀ)⁻¹ x = (1 + c xᵀ V₀⁻¹ x)⁻¹ • V₀⁻¹ x`.
nodes.title: Sherman–Morrison applied to the candidate marker

nodes.summary: Including the candidate marker `x` in the covariance, `V = V₀ + c x xᵀ` with `V₀` positive definite and `c ≥ 0`, divides the mixed-model statistic by `1 + c xᵀ V₀⁻¹ x`, for every phenotype vector `y`: `χ²(V₀ + c x xᵀ) = χ²(V₀) / (1 + c xᵀ V₀⁻¹ x)`.
nodes.title: Proximal contamination

nodes.summary: Including the candidate marker in the covariance never increases the mixed-model statistic: `χ²(V₀ + c x xᵀ) ≤ χ²(V₀)` for positive definite `V₀` and `c ≥ 0`.
nodes.title: Including the marker in the covariance never increases the statistic
Signed LD profile regression

nodes.summary: The in-sample LD matrix `R̂ = Xᵀ X / N`, with entries `ldCorr X j k`.
nodes.title: In-sample LD matrix

nodes.summary: The linear phenotype model of SLDP regression at the level of first moments: integrable random effects `β` with means `meanBeta` and integrable noise `ε` of mean zero. (SLDP's model takes `meanBeta = μ v` for a signed annotation `v`; second moments are not needed for the first-moment identity.)
nodes.title: First-moment phenotype model of SLDP regression

nodes.summary: The phenotype `y = X β + ε`.
nodes.title: Phenotype in the SLDP regression model

nodes.summary: The vector `α̂ = Xᵀ y / N` of marginal correlations between the (standardized) markers and the phenotype.
nodes.title: Marginal marker-phenotype correlations in SLDP regression

nodes.summary: Conditional on the genotype matrix, `𝔼 α̂ = R̂ 𝔼 β` with `R̂ = Xᵀ X / N`.
nodes.title: First-moment identity, exact in-sample form

nodes.summary: SLDP first-moment identity (Reshef et al. 2018, Methods, Equation 5): if the true effects have mean `μ v`, then `𝔼 α̂ = μ R̂ v`, a multiple of the signed LD profile `R̂ v` of `v`.
nodes.title: SLDP first-moment identity

nodes.summary: For any weight matrix `W` and signed LD profile `s = R̂ v` with `⟪s, s⟫_W = sᵀ W s ≠ 0`, if `𝔼 β = μ v` then `𝔼 [⟪s, α̂⟫_W / ⟪s, s⟫_W] = μ`, where `⟪a, b⟫_W = aᵀ W b`. SLDP uses the inverse of `Ω = σ² R² + R / N` as `W`.
nodes.title: Unbiasedness of the weighted least-squares estimator

nodes.summary: Unbiasedness with covariates (the signed background model): suppose the true effects have mean `μ v + U γ` for background annotations `U` (columns `u_b`) with arbitrary coefficients `γ`, let `A = R̂ U` be their signed LD profiles, and let `z⊥ = R̂ v - A w` be the weighted residual of the signed LD profile of `v` on `A` (`Aᵀ W z⊥ = 0`) for a symmetric weight matrix `W`. If `⟪z⊥, z⊥⟫_W ≠ 0`, then…

nodes.summary: The random-effects model of stratified LD-score regression at the level of raw second moments: marker `k` has effect variance `sigma2 k`, the noise has variance `sigmaE2`, and effects and noise are orthogonal in `L²`. As in `LDScore.Model`, the measure is arbitrary, no means are assumed, and all statements are conditional on the genotype matrix.
nodes.title: Random-effects model of stratified LD-score regression

nodes.summary: The phenotype `y = X β + ε`.
nodes.title: Phenotype in the stratified LD-score model

nodes.summary: The `N`-normalized score `β̂ j = X_jᵀ y / N` of marker `j` (as in `LDScore.Model.betaHat`).
nodes.title: Normalized marker score in stratified LD-score regression

nodes.summary: The association statistic `χ² j = N * β̂ j ^ 2` of marker `j`.
nodes.title: Association chi-squared statistic in stratified LD-score regression

nodes.summary: The LD-score regression model of `LDScore` is the stratified model with equal per-marker variances `h² / M` and noise variance `1 - h²`.
nodes.title: LD-score regression model as a stratified model

nodes.summary: The stratified statistic of `ofLDScore D` is the statistic of `LDScore`.
nodes.title: Stratified statistic agrees with the LD-score statistic

nodes.summary: Expected statistic with per-marker variances, for an arbitrary genotype matrix: `𝔼[χ² j] = N ∑_k r_jk² σ²_k + σ²_e (∑_i X_ij²) / N`. (For `N = 0` both sides are `0`.)
nodes.title: Expected statistic with per-marker variances

nodes.summary: For a column with sum of squares `N` (a standardized marker) and `N ≠ 0`: `𝔼[χ² j] = N ∑_k r_jk² σ²_k + σ²_e`.
nodes.title: Expected chi-squared statistic of a standardized marker

nodes.summary: The LD score of marker `j` with respect to annotation `C`: `ℓ(j, C) = ∑_k a_{kC} r_jk²` (Finucane et al. 2015 for binary annotations; Gazal et al. 2017 for continuous ones).
nodes.title: Annotation LD score of a marker

nodes.summary: Stratified LD-score regression (Finucane et al. 2015; continuous annotations, Gazal et al. 2017): if the per-marker variances are linear in the annotations, `σ²_k = ∑_C τ_C a_{kC}`, then for a standardized genotype matrix and `N ≠ 0`, `𝔼[χ² j] = N ∑_C τ_C ℓ(j, C) + σ²_e`.
nodes.title: Stratified LD-score regression

nodes.summary: Frequency-dependent architecture (the α model of Schoech et al. 2019): if the per-allele effect variance of marker `k` with allele frequency `p_k` is proportional to `[p_k (1 - p_k)]^α`, the variance of the effect of the standardized genotype is `σ²_k = c [p_k (1 - p_k)]^(1 + α)`, and then, for a standardized genotype matrix and `N ≠ 0`, `𝔼[χ² j] = N c ∑_k [p_k (1 - p_k)]^(1 + α) r_jk² + σ²_e`. (The real power is…
nodes.title: Frequency-dependent architecture

nodes.summary: The heritability `h²(C) = ∑_{k ∈ C} σ²_k` of category `C`, for a labeling `cat` of the markers by categories.
nodes.title: Heritability of a marker category

nodes.summary: The number `M_C` of markers in category `C`.
nodes.title: Number of markers in a category

nodes.summary: The enrichment of category `C`: its proportion of heritability divided by its proportion of markers, `(h²(C) / h²) / (M_C / M)` with `h² = ∑_k σ²_k` (Finucane et al. 2015).
nodes.title: Heritability enrichment of a category

nodes.summary: For a partition of the markers into categories (a labeling `cat`) and nonzero total heritability, the marker-proportion-weighted enrichments sum to one: `∑_C (M_C / M) * Enrichment(C) = 1`. Empty categories contribute `0` on both sides of each term.
nodes.title: Marker-proportion-weighted enrichments sum to one

nodes.summary: The design matrix `[1 | N ℓ(·, C)]` of stratified LD-score regression with a free intercept; column `none` is the intercept and column `some C` the scaled annotation LD score.
nodes.title: Design matrix of stratified LD-score regression

nodes.summary: A real matrix has injective `mulVec` iff it has full column rank.
nodes.title: Injective matrix action iff full column rank

nodes.summary: Under the annotation model, the vector of expected statistics is the design matrix applied to the parameter vector `(σ²_e, τ)` (intercept first). Hence the parameters are determined by the expected statistics of all markers, whatever their values, iff `(design X a).rank = Fintype.card (Option ι)` (`injective_mulVec_iff_rank_eq_card`).

nodes.summary: Admixture followed by drift: if `C` is an `α : 1 - α` mixture of `A` and `B` that then drifts along a private edge `c` (not traversed by `A` or `B`), then `f3 C A B = len c - α (1 - α) f2 A B`; post-admixture drift can mask the admixture signal.
nodes.title: f3 of an admixture followed by drift

nodes.summary: Three-population test, converse direction: a nondegenerate pure admixture (`0 < α < 1`, `f2 A B > 0`) yields a negative `f3 C A B`.
nodes.title: Nondegenerate pure admixture gives negative f3

nodes.summary: If `X` is an `α : 1 - α` mixture of `Y` and `C`, then `f4 A O X C = α * f4 A O Y C` (bilinearity of `f4`, together with `f4 A O C C = 0`).
nodes.title: f4 of an admixed population scales with the mixture proportion

nodes.summary: f4-ratio estimation of the admixture proportion. f4-ratio estimation (Patterson et al. 2012). Let `X` be an `α : 1 - α` mixture of a source lineage `Y` and of `C`, where `Y` is unsampled but sister to the sampled population `B` relative to the `A–O` path, so that `f4 A O Y C = f4 A O B C`. If this value is nonzero, the ratio `f4 A O X C / f4 A O B C` of two estimable statistics recovers the admixture proportion `α`.
nodes.title: f4-ratio estimation of the admixture proportion

nodes.summary: Hudson's `F_ST` denominator at one site: `p_A (1 - p_B) + p_B (1 - p_A)`, the probability that two copies, one from each population, differ. The numerator is `(p_A - p_B) ^ 2`.
nodes.title: Hudson's F_ST denominator at one site

nodes.summary: Hudson's `F_ST` over sites `s` in the ratio-of-averages form of Bhatia et al. (2013): `∑ s, (p_A s - p_B s) ^ 2 / ∑ s, hudsonDen (p_A s) (p_B s)`. It is defined when the denominator is positive (it vanishes only if every site is fixed for the same allele in both populations); otherwise Lean's value `0` is a junk value.

nodes.summary: At each site Hudson's numerator is at most the denominator for frequencies in `[0, 1]`: the difference is `p_A (1 - p_A) + p_B (1 - p_B) ≥ 0`.
nodes.title: Hudson's numerator is at most the denominator

nodes.summary: Hudson's `F_ST` lies in `[0, 1]` for frequencies in `[0, 1]`. (When the denominator vanishes the junk value `0` also lies in `[0, 1]`, so no positivity hypothesis is needed.)

nodes.summary: The sample frequency is unbiased: for `X ~ Bin(m, p)` with `m ≥ 1`, `E[X / m] = p`. (For `m = 0`, `X / 0 = 0` is a junk value, hence `m ≥ 1`.)

nodes.summary: For `X ~ Bin(m, p)` with `m ≥ 2`, `E[X (m - X) / (m (m - 1))] = p (1 - p)`.
nodes.title: Unbiased heterozygosity

nodes.summary: Unbiased `f2` (Patterson et al. 2012, Appendix): with independent binomial samples `X_A ~ Bin(m_A, p_A)`, `X_B ~ Bin(m_B, p_B)`, `m_A, m_B ≥ 2`, `E[f2Hat] = (p_A - p_B) ^ 2`, the population `f2` at the site.
nodes.title: Unbiased `f2`

nodes.summary: Unbiased `f3` (Patterson et al. 2012, Appendix): with pairwise independent binomial samples, `m_C ≥ 2` and `m_A, m_B ≥ 1`, `E[f3Hat] = (p_C - p_A) (p_C - p_B)`.
nodes.title: Unbiased `f3`

nodes.summary: For four populations sampled independently across the two pairs (`m ≥ 1` each), `E[f4Hat] = (p_A - p_B) (p_C - p_D)`; no correction is needed.
nodes.title: Unbiased `f4`

nodes.summary: Hudson's denominator is unbiased (Bhatia et al. 2013): with independent binomial samples (`m ≥ 1` each), `E[hudsonDenHat] = hudsonDen p_A p_B`.
nodes.title: Hudson's denominator is unbiased

nodes.summary: Summed over sites, Hudson's numerator estimator `∑ s, f2Hat` is unbiased for `∑ s, (p_A s - p_B s) ^ 2` (independence is needed only within each site).

nodes.summary: Summed over sites, Hudson's denominator estimator is unbiased for `∑ s, hudsonDen (p_A s) (p_B s)`.
nodes.title: Unbiasedness of the summed Hudson denominator estimator

nodes.summary: Hudson's `F_ST`, ratio of averages (Bhatia et al. 2013): the ratio of the expected summed numerator and denominator estimators is the population `hudsonFst`. nodes.summary: The recursion at an admixture node `X` with parents `A ≠ B`: with `α = prop X A`, `w X = α w A + (1 - α) w B + w₀`, where `w₀` puts weight `α` on the edge `(X, A)`, `1 - α` on `(X, B)` and `0` elsewhere.

nodes.summary: The drift model of an admixture graph: the populations are the nodes, the root frequency is `root`, the edge increments are `incr` (square integrable and pairwise uncorrelated), the drift length of an edge is the second moment of its increment, and the weights are the lineage weights of the graph.
nodes.title: Drift model of an admixture graph

nodes.summary: A tree-shaped admixture graph induces a drift model with binary loadings (all weights `0` or `1`).
nodes.title: A tree-shaped admixture graph has binary loadings

nodes.summary: The three-population test on a tree-shaped admixture graph: `f3 C A B ≥ 0`.
nodes.title: Three-population test is nonnegative on a tree

nodes.summary: The three-population statistic at an admixture node `X` with parents `A ≠ B`, proportions `α = prop X A` and `β = prop X B` (`α + β = 1`), in a drift model with the graph's weights: `f3 X A B = α² ℓ_{XA} + β² ℓ_{XB} - α β f2 A B`, where `ℓ_{XA}`, `ℓ_{XB}` are the drift lengths of the two admixture edges.

nodes.summary: With no drift on the admixture edges, an admixture node `X` with parents `A ≠ B` and proportion `α = prop X A` has `f3 X A B = -α (1 - α) f2 A B` (the hypothesis of the seed's `DriftModel.f3_admixture`, here derived from the graph).

nodes.summary: The covariance of the allele counts at the two loci of one gamete drawn from the gamete frequencies `x`: `∑ g, x g a(g.1) a(g.2) - (∑ g, x g a(g.1)) (∑ g, x g a(g.2))`.

nodes.summary: The diploid genotype covariance is twice the haplotype one, `z = 2 D`: the two same-gamete terms each contribute `D` and the two cross-gamete terms vanish by independence (Loh et al. 2013, Eqs. 2–3).

nodes.summary: Gamete frequencies right after the pulse: with probability `α` the gamete comes from `A`, where the loci are in linkage equilibrium with `'1'` frequencies `pA` and `qA`, and otherwise from `B` (frequencies `pB`, `qB`). The biological domain is `α, pA, qA, pB, qB ∈ [0, 1]`; the identities below hold for all reals.

nodes.summary: Admixture LD right after the pulse: `D₀ = α (1 - α) δ(x) δ(y)`, with `δ(x) = pA - pB`, `δ(y) = qA - qB` (Chakraborty and Weiss 1988).

nodes.summary: Admixture LD after `n` generations of random mating with recombination fraction `r`: `D_n = (1 - r)^n α (1 - α) δ(x) δ(y)`.

nodes.summary: Recombination keeps gamete frequencies summing to `1` over any number of generations.

nodes.summary: The diploid genotype covariance in the admixed population `n` generations after the pulse: `z(x, y) = 2 α (1 - α) (1 - r)^n δ(x) δ(y)` (Loh et al. 2013, Eq. 3, with the exact discrete-generation factor `(1 - r)^n` in place of `e^{-n d}`).

nodes.summary: Joint law of the local-ancestry labels at the two loci right after the pulse (`true` = descends from `A`): every gamete is entirely from `A` (probability `α`) or entirely from `B`. This is `sourceMix` with perfectly differentiated markers (`pA = qA = 1`, `pB = qB = 0`).

nodes.summary: Pulse admixture: after `n` generations of random mating the local-ancestry indicators at two loci with recombination fraction `r` have covariance `Cov(I_x, I_y) = α (1 - α) (1 - r)^n` (for every real `α`, `r`; the biological domain is `0 ≤ α ≤ 1`, `0 ≤ r ≤ 1/2`). The ancestry labels obey the two-locus random-mating recursion of `Linkage.recombine` (Chakraborty and Weiss 1988).

nodes.summary: The mean frequency `p̄ ω = (1 / n) ∑ X, p X ω` across the `n` populations.
nodes.title: Mean frequency across populations

nodes.summary: The centred leaf covariance `K X Y = 𝔼[(p X - p̄) * (p Y - p̄)]`: the second moments of the frequencies centred across populations (not over `Ω`).
nodes.title: Centred leaf covariance

nodes.summary: `f2` from the centred leaf covariance: `f2 X Y = K X X + K Y Y - 2 K X Y`.
nodes.title: f2 from the centred leaf covariance

nodes.summary: The centred leaf covariance from `f2`: `K` is half the double centring of the `f2` matrix, `K X Y = (f̄2 X· + f̄2 ·Y - f2 X Y - f̄2 ··) / 2`.
nodes.title: Centred leaf covariance as the double centring of f2

nodes.summary: f-statistics determine exactly the centred leaf covariance. f-statistics see a model only through its centred leaf covariance: two square-integrable frequency models have the same `f2` at every pair (hence the same `f3` and `f4`, by `f3_eq_f2` and `f4_eq_f2`) if and only if they have the same centred leaf covariance.
nodes.title: f-statistics determine exactly the centred leaf covariance

nodes.summary: Lineage weights of the star tree on three populations `0 = A`, `1 = B`, `2 = C`: edge `e` is the leaf edge of population `e`.
nodes.title: Lineage weights of the three-population star tree

nodes.summary: Lineage weights of the admixture model: `A` and `B` sit on edges `0` and `1`, and `C` is an `α : 1 - α` mixture of `A` and `B` followed by drift on its private edge `2`.
nodes.title: Lineage weights of the three-population admixture model

nodes.summary: Edge lengths of the star tree matching the admixture model with edge lengths `a`, `b`, `c`: `(1 - α)(a + b)`, `α (a + b)` and `c - α (1 - α)(a + b)`.
nodes.title: Edge lengths of the star tree matching an admixture model

nodes.summary: In the admixture model, `C` is the `α : 1 - α` mixture of `A` and `B` plus its private edge.
nodes.title: Admixed population's weights in the admixture model

nodes.summary: The star-tree model has binary loadings.
nodes.title: Star-tree model has binary loadings

nodes.summary: For `α ∉ {0, 1}` the admixture model does not have binary loadings.
nodes.title: Admixture model lacks binary loadings

nodes.summary: The star tree and the admixture model have the same `f2` at every pair of populations.
nodes.title: Star tree and admixture model have equal f2

nodes.summary: The star tree and the admixture model have the same `f4` (hence the same `f3`) at every quadruple of populations.
nodes.title: Star tree and admixture model have equal f4

nodes.summary: The matching star tree has nonnegative edge lengths when `0 ≤ α ≤ 1`, `a, b ≥ 0`, and the private drift of `C` is at least `α (1 - α)(a + b)`, i.e. when `f3 C A B ≥ 0` in the admixture model.
nodes.title: Nonnegativity of the matching star-tree edge lengths
Fitting admixture graphs by least squares

nodes.summary: The qpGraph score `S1(g) = -½ (g - f)ᵀ Q⁻¹ (g - f)` (Patterson et al. 2012, eq. 6) of predicted statistics `g` against estimated statistics `f` with error covariance `Q`.
nodes.title: Generalized least-squares qpGraph score S1

nodes.summary: The least-squares qpGraph score `S2(g) = -∑ᵢ (gᵢ - fᵢ)² / (Qᵢᵢ + λ)` (Patterson et al. 2012, eq. 7). A term with `Qᵢᵢ + λ = 0` is `0` by the convention `x / 0 = 0`.
nodes.title: Least-squares qpGraph score S2

nodes.summary: `S1` is basis independent: under an invertible change of basis `A` of the statistics, with the covariance transformed to `A Q Aᵀ`, the score is unchanged. (The identity holds for every `Q`; for singular `Q` both sides are `0` by Mathlib's convention `Q⁻¹ = 0`.)
nodes.title: Basis independence of the qpGraph score S1

nodes.summary: `S2` is not basis independent (Patterson et al. 2012, after eq. 7): there are a positive definite covariance `Q`, an invertible change of basis `A` and statistics `f`, `g` such that, for every `λ`, the score changes.
nodes.title: The qpGraph score S2 depends on the basis

nodes.summary: `S2` is twice `S1` with the covariance replaced by the diagonal matrix of the `Qᵢᵢ + λ`, when these are nonzero.
nodes.title: Score S2 as score S1 with a diagonal covariance

nodes.summary: The qpGraph design matrix of basis statistics `f4 (A i) (B i) (C i) (D i)` for lineage weights `w`: entry `(i, e)` is `(w Aᵢ e - w Bᵢ e) * (w Cᵢ e - w Dᵢ e)`.
nodes.title: qpGraph design matrix of basis f4 statistics

nodes.summary: In the drift model, with the admixture weights fixed, the predicted statistics are linear in the edge lengths: `g = B ℓ` for the design matrix `B`.
nodes.title: Predicted f4 statistics are linear in the edge lengths

nodes.summary: GLS maximizes `S1`: for positive definite `Q`, a solution `ℓ̂` of the normal equations `Bᵀ Q⁻¹ B ℓ̂ = Bᵀ Q⁻¹ f` maximizes `ℓ ↦ S1(B ℓ)` over all `ℓ`.
nodes.title: Solutions of the normal equations maximize the score S1

nodes.summary: Uniqueness of the GLS maximizer: for positive definite `Q` and a design matrix of full column rank (`B.mulVec` injective), a vector `ℓ` with the same score as a solution `ℓ̂` of the normal equations equals `ℓ̂`.
nodes.title: Uniqueness of the generalized least-squares maximizer

nodes.summary: For positive definite `Q` and a design matrix of full column rank, the GLS Gram matrix `Bᵀ Q⁻¹ B` is invertible.
nodes.title: Invertibility of the generalized least-squares Gram matrix

nodes.summary: The closed-form GLS estimate `ℓ̂ = (Bᵀ Q⁻¹ B)⁻¹ Bᵀ Q⁻¹ f` solves the normal equations when the Gram matrix is invertible.
nodes.title: Closed-form generalized least-squares estimate of edge lengths
Outgroup f3 and admixed branches

nodes.summary: With binary loadings, `f3 O A B` is the total drift length of the edges shared by the paths `O–A` and `O–B` (on a tree, the path from `O` to the `A–B` path).
nodes.title: f3 statistic as shared drift on a tree

nodes.summary: Outgroup `f3` (Raghavan et al. 2014): with binary loadings, if the lineage of `O` shares no edge with the lineages of `A` and `B`, then `f3 O A B` is the drift from the outgroup to the root plus the drift shared by `A` and `B`.
nodes.title: Outgroup f3 statistic

nodes.summary: For a fixed outgroup `O` and population `A`, the outgroup `f3` ranks candidates `B` by the drift they share with `A`.
nodes.title: Outgroup f3 ranks populations by shared drift

nodes.summary: MixMapper's mixed drift `α² ℓ_a + (1 - α)² ℓ_b + ℓ_c`: the only combination of the terminal drift lengths that enters the `f2` statistics of an admixed population.
nodes.title: MixMapper mixed drift

nodes.summary: The admixed-branch identity (Lipson et al. 2013): if `Mx` is an `α : 1 - α` mixture of the endpoints of the edges `a` (below `A`) and `b` (below `B`), followed by drift on `c`, and `A`, `B`, `X` do not use `a`, `b`, `c`, then `f2 Mx X = α f2 A X + (1 - α) f2 B X - α (1 - α) f2 A B + mixedDrift α ℓ_a ℓ_b ℓ_c`.
nodes.title: Admixed-branch identity for f2 statistics

nodes.summary: Identifiability of the mixture proportion (our formulation): with the split points `A`, `B` given, two references `X₁`, `X₂` satisfying the hypotheses of `f2_admixedBranch` and with different contrasts `f2 A Xᵢ - f2 B Xᵢ` determine `α` from `f2` statistics.
nodes.title: Identifiability of the admixture proportion from f2 statistics

nodes.summary: Given `α`, the mixed drift is determined by the `f2` statistics of one reference `X`.
nodes.title: Mixed drift determined by f2 statistics

nodes.summary: The genetics of continuously varying traits: decomposition of genetic variance, resemblance between relatives, kinship, mixed models and the response to selection.
nodes.title: Quantitative genetics
Breeder's equation

nodes.summary: The linear parent–offspring model on a population described by a probability measure `μ`: the parental (mid-parent) value `parent` and the offspring value `offspring` are integrable, `mean` is the population mean of the parental value, and the offspring value regresses linearly on the parental value, `𝔼[O | P] = mean + h2 * (P - mean)` (equivalently `O = mean + h2 (P - mean) + e` with `𝔼[e | P] = 0`). Here `h2` is…
nodes.title: Linear parent–offspring regression model

nodes.summary: The selection differential `S = 𝔼[P | selected] - μ` of the selected group `s`.
nodes.title: Selection differential

nodes.summary: The response to selection `R = 𝔼[O | selected] - μ`: the mean offspring value of the selected parents, relative to the population mean.
nodes.title: Response to selection

nodes.summary: The breeder's equation (Lush 1937): if the selected group `s` is determined by the parental value (an event of `σ(P)`) and has positive mass, the response to selection is the heritability times the selection differential, `R = h² S`.
nodes.title: Breeder's equation

nodes.summary: Selecting the whole population gives no selection differential, `S = 0`.
nodes.title: Selecting the whole population gives zero selection differential

nodes.summary: Selecting the whole population gives no response, `R = 0`.
nodes.title: Selecting the whole population gives zero response
Dominance linkage disequilibrium

nodes.summary: A diploid two-locus genotype under random union of gametes: the haplotypes `(X₁, Y₁)` and `(X₂, Y₂)` are independent and identically distributed, with square-integrable allele codings.
nodes.title: Two-locus diploid genotype under random union of gametes

nodes.summary: The allele frequency (mean coding) `p = E X₁` at locus `A`.
nodes.title: Allele frequency at the first locus

nodes.summary: The allele frequency (mean coding) `q = E Y₁` at locus `B`.
nodes.title: Allele frequency at the second locus

nodes.summary: The haplotype variance `V_A = E (X₁ - p)²` at locus `A`.
nodes.title: Haplotype variance at the first locus

nodes.summary: The haplotype variance `V_B = E (Y₁ - q)²` at locus `B`.
nodes.title: Haplotype variance at the second locus

nodes.summary: The gametic linkage disequilibrium `D = E (X₁ - p) (Y₁ - q)`.
nodes.title: Gametic linkage disequilibrium

nodes.summary: The additive coding `a_A = (X₁ - p) + (X₂ - p)` (centred allele count) at locus `A`.
nodes.title: Additive coding at the first locus

nodes.summary: The additive coding `a_B = (Y₁ - q) + (Y₂ - q)` at locus `B`.
nodes.title: Additive coding at the second locus

nodes.summary: The dominance coding `d_A = (X₁ - p) (X₂ - p)` at locus `A`.
nodes.title: Dominance coding at the first locus

nodes.summary: The dominance coding `d_B = (Y₁ - q) (Y₂ - q)` at locus `B`.
nodes.title: Dominance coding at the second locus

nodes.summary: Additive LD: `E(a_A a_B) = 2 D`.
nodes.title: Additive linkage disequilibrium is twice the gametic one

nodes.summary: The additive coding has second moment `E(a_A²) = 2 V_A`.
nodes.title: Second moment of the additive coding at the first locus

nodes.summary: The additive coding has second moment `E(a_B²) = 2 V_B`.
nodes.title: Second moment of the additive coding at the second locus

nodes.summary: Dominance LD: `E(d_A d_B) = D²`.
nodes.title: Dominance linkage disequilibrium is the square of the gametic one

nodes.summary: The dominance coding has second moment `E(d_A²) = V_A²`.
nodes.title: Second moment of the dominance coding at the first locus

nodes.summary: The dominance coding has second moment `E(d_B²) = V_B²`.
nodes.title: Second moment of the dominance coding at the second locus

nodes.summary: The additive coding at `A` and the dominance coding at `B` are uncorrelated: `E(a_A d_B) = 0`.
nodes.title: Additive and dominance codings at different loci are uncorrelated

nodes.summary: The correlation of the additive codings is the gametic correlation `r = D / √(V_A V_B)`.
nodes.title: Correlation of additive codings equals the gametic correlation

nodes.summary: Dominance LD is the square of additive LD (Palmer et al. 2023, graphical abstract): the correlation of the dominance codings at two loci is the square of the correlation of their additive codings.
nodes.title: Dominance LD is the square of additive LD

nodes.summary: The dominance encoding of a biallelic genotype `g ∈ {0, 1, 2}` (count of the allele with frequency `p`): `p²`, `-p (1 - p)`, `(1 - p)²`. Dividing by `-p (1 - p)` gives the encoding `-p / (1 - p)`, `1`, `-(1 - p) / p` of Palmer et al. (2023).
nodes.title: Dominance encoding of a biallelic genotype

nodes.summary: For `0`/`1` allele indicators the dominance coding `(X₁ - p) (X₂ - p)` depends only on the genotype `X₁ + X₂` and equals its dominance encoding.
nodes.title: Dominance coding of allele indicators equals the dominance encoding
Fisher's decomposition of genetic variance

nodes.summary: The mean genotypic value `μ = ∑ i ∑ j p i p j G i j` under Hardy–Weinberg proportions.
nodes.title: Mean genotypic value under Hardy–Weinberg proportions

nodes.summary: The average effect of allele `i`, `α i = ∑ j p j G i j - μ`: the mean value of the genotypes carrying `i` (the other gene drawn from the population) minus the population mean. This is the average excess; under Hardy–Weinberg proportions it is Fisher's average effect, the coefficient of the least-squares additive fit (`domVar_le_sum_sq`).
nodes.title: Average effect of an allele

nodes.summary: The dominance deviation `δ i j = G i j - μ - α i - α j`.
nodes.title: Dominance deviation of a genotype

nodes.summary: The genetic variance `V_G = ∑ i ∑ j p i p j (G i j - μ) ²`.
nodes.title: Genetic variance under Hardy–Weinberg proportions

nodes.summary: The additive genetic variance `V_A = 2 ∑ i p i α i ²`, the variance of the breeding value `α i + α j`.
nodes.title: Additive genetic variance

nodes.summary: The dominance variance `V_D = ∑ i ∑ j p i p j δ i j ²`.
nodes.title: Dominance variance

nodes.summary: The decomposition `G i j = μ + α i + α j + δ i j` (an identity by definition of `δ`).
nodes.title: Decomposition of the genotypic value

nodes.summary: The average effects have mean zero: `∑ i p i α i = 0`.
nodes.title: Average effects have mean zero

nodes.summary: Orthogonality of the dominance deviations: `∑ j p j δ i j = 0` for every `i`.
nodes.title: Orthogonality of dominance deviations in the second allele

nodes.summary: Orthogonality of the dominance deviations for a symmetric genotypic value: `∑ i p i δ i j = 0` for every `j`.
nodes.title: Orthogonality of dominance deviations in the first allele

nodes.summary: Among all fits `c + a i + a j` of the genotypic value by a function additive over the two genes, the additive fitted genotypic value `μ + α i + α j` minimizes the weighted squared error `∑ p i p j (G i j - c - a i - a j) ²`; its error is `V_D`.
nodes.title: Least squares (Fisher 1918)

nodes.summary: `V_G = V_A + V_D`.
nodes.title: Fisher's variance decomposition

nodes.summary: The covariance of the genotypic values of a parent and its offspring: the parent has genotype `(i, j)` (frequency `p i p j`) and transmits `cond b i j` (each with probability `1/2`), and the offspring's other gene `k` comes from an unrelated mate (frequency `p k`).
nodes.title: Parent–offspring covariance of genotypic values

nodes.summary: The covariance of the genotypic values of half sibs: the common parent has genotype `(i, j)` and transmits `cond b i j` to one offspring and, independently, `cond b' i j` to the other; the second genes `k`, `l` come from two unrelated mates.
nodes.title: Half-sib covariance of genotypic values

nodes.summary: The covariance of the genotypic values of full sibs: the sire `(i, j)` and the dam `(k, l)` are unrelated; the first offspring receives `cond b i j` and `cond e k l`, the second, independently, `cond b' i j` and `cond e' k l`.
nodes.title: Full-sib covariance of genotypic values

nodes.summary: `Cov(P, O) = V_A / 2`.
nodes.title: Parent and offspring (Fisher 1918)

nodes.summary: `Cov(HS) = V_A / 4`.
nodes.title: Half sibs (Fisher 1918)

nodes.summary: `Cov(FS) = V_A / 2 + V_D / 4`.
nodes.title: Full sibs (Fisher 1918)

nodes.summary: Allele frequencies at a biallelic locus: `A₁` (`true`) has frequency `q₁` and `A₂` (`false`) has frequency `1 - q₁`.
nodes.title: Allele frequencies at a biallelic locus

nodes.summary: Genotypic values at a biallelic locus on Falconer's scale: `A₁A₁ ↦ a`, `A₁A₂ ↦ d`, `A₂A₂ ↦ -a` (the origin is the midpoint of the homozygotes).
nodes.title: Genotypic values at a biallelic locus on Falconer's scale

nodes.summary: With `p = q₁` and `q = 1 - q₁`, `V_A = 2pq (a + d (q - p)) ²`. An algebraic identity, valid for every real `q₁`; it is a variance for `0 ≤ q₁ ≤ 1`.
nodes.title: Additive variance at a biallelic locus (Falconer & Mackay 1996, ch. 8)

nodes.summary: `V_D = (2pqd) ²`, for every real `q₁`.
nodes.title: Dominance variance at a biallelic locus (Falconer & Mackay 1996, ch. 8)

nodes.summary: A single locus under random union of gametes: allele frequencies `p` on a finite allele set and symmetric genotypic values `g a b` (the mean phenotype of genotype `{a, b}`).

nodes.summary: The population mean genotypic value `μ = ∑ p_a p_b g(a, b)`.
nodes.title: Population mean genotypic value at a single locus

nodes.summary: Fisher's average effect of allele `a`: `α a = ∑_b p_b g(a, b) - μ`.
nodes.title: Fisher's average effect of an allele at a single locus

nodes.summary: The dominance deviation `δ a b = g(a, b) - μ - α a - α b`.
nodes.title: Dominance deviation at a single locus

nodes.summary: The genetic variance `V_G = ∑ p_a p_b (g(a, b) - μ)²`.
nodes.title: Genetic variance at a single locus

nodes.summary: The additive variance `V_A = 2 ∑ p_a α_a²`.
nodes.title: Additive variance at a single locus

nodes.summary: The dominance variance `V_D = ∑ p_a p_b δ_{ab}²`.
nodes.title: Dominance variance at a single locus

nodes.summary: Average effects are centred: `∑ p_a α_a = 0`.
nodes.title: Average effects are centred

nodes.summary: Dominance deviations are orthogonal to every allele: `∑_b p_b δ_{ab} = 0`.
nodes.title: Dominance deviations are orthogonal to every allele

nodes.summary: Fisher decomposition of the genetic variance: `V_G = V_A + V_D`.
nodes.title: Fisher decomposition

nodes.summary: The additive variance is nonnegative.
nodes.title: Nonnegativity of the single-locus additive variance

nodes.summary: The dominance variance is nonnegative.
nodes.title: Nonnegativity of the single-locus dominance variance

nodes.summary: The additive fit is least squares (Fisher definition of average effects): every additive fit `c + h a + h b` has mean squared error at least `V_D`, the error of `μ + α a + α b`.
nodes.title: The additive fit is least squares

nodes.summary: The mean product of genotypic values of two non-inbred relatives that share `0`, `1`, `2` alleles identical by descent with probabilities `k₀, k₁, k₂`: given the IBD state, the non-shared alleles are independent draws from `p`.
nodes.title: Mean product of genotypic values of two relatives

nodes.summary: Covariance between relatives at one locus (Fisher 1918; in the IBD form of Falconer and Mackay ch. 9): for IBD probabilities summing to one, `E[G_X G_Y] - μ² = (k₁ / 2 + k₂) V_A + k₂ V_D`, i.e. `2φ V_A + Δ V_D` with kinship `φ = k₁ / 4 + k₂ / 2` and `Δ = k₂`.
nodes.title: Covariance between relatives

nodes.summary: Cockerham–Kempthorne variance components up to order `n`: `V i j = V_{A^i D^j}` is the component of `i` additive and `j` dominance factors (`V 1 0 = V_A`, `V 0 1 = V_D`, `V 2 0 = V_AA`, …). They are nonnegative, there is no `(0, 0)` component, and the genetic covariance of relatives with `2φ` and `Δ` is `∑_{i, j ≤ n} (2φ)^i Δ^j V i j`. This structure is the stated representation; it is proved for one locus by…
nodes.title: Cockerham–Kempthorne variance components

nodes.summary: The genetic covariance of relatives with coefficients `2φ = twoPhi` and `Δ = Δ`.
nodes.title: Genetic covariance of relatives in Cockerham form

nodes.summary: The additive variance `V_A = V 1 0` (zero if `n = 0`).
nodes.title: Additive variance of the Cockerham components

nodes.summary: Falconer's estimator under the ACE model, in covariance form: monozygotic twins have `2φ = Δ = 1`, dizygotic twins (full sibs) `2φ = 1/2`, `Δ = 1/4`, and both share the same common-environment covariance `C`; the estimator is `2 (Cov_MZ - Cov_DZ)`.
nodes.title: Falconer's estimator

nodes.summary: Falconer's estimator is `V_A` plus the non-additive components weighted by `2 (1 - 2^{-i} 4^{-j})` (derived from Cockerham's coefficients).
nodes.title: Falconer's estimator in terms of Cockerham components

nodes.summary: The phantom-heritability inequality in covariance form: `V_A ≤ 2 (Cov_MZ - Cov_DZ)`.
nodes.title: Phantom heritability inequality

nodes.summary: Equality holds iff every non-additive component of order `≤ n` vanishes.
nodes.title: Equality case of the phantom heritability inequality

nodes.summary: Phantom heritability on the correlation scale (Zuk et al. 2012): with phenotypic variance `V_P > 0`, the narrow-sense heritability `V_A / V_P` is at most the ACE estimate `2 (r_MZ - r_DZ)`, where `r = Cov / V_P`.
nodes.title: Phantom heritability

nodes.summary: The one-locus model as Cockerham components of order `1`: `V 1 0 = V_A`, `V 0 1 = V_D`, `V 1 1 = 0`.
nodes.title: Single-locus model as Cockerham components

nodes.summary: The one-locus covariance between relatives is the Cockerham form of `toComponents`.
nodes.title: Single-locus covariance between relatives in Cockerham form

nodes.summary: With monozygotic twins (`k₂ = 1`), dizygotic twins (`k = (1/4, 1/2, 1/4)`) and a common environment `C`, `2 (Cov_MZ - Cov_DZ) = V_A + (3/2) V_D`.
nodes.title: One-locus phantom heritability, unconditional

The reference allele has frequency `p ∈ (0, 1)` (a polymorphic locus), and `ibd c d` is the probability that the copies `c` and `d` are identical by…
