nodes.title: The GCTA diagonal estimator is unbiased for `1 + F_i`
Lande's selection gradient

nodes.summary: Stein's lemma for the normal law `N(μ, v)`, `v > 0`: if `g` is differentiable with derivative `g'` and `g`, `(z - μ) g z` and `g'` are integrable, then `𝔼[(z - μ) g z] = v 𝔼[g' z]` (Stein 1981, Lemma 1).
nodes.title: Stein's lemma

nodes.summary: The mean fitness `w̄(μ) = 𝔼[W z]` of a population whose trait is distributed as `N(μ, v)`.
nodes.title: Mean fitness of a normally distributed trait

nodes.summary: The directional selection differential `S = 𝔼[(z - μ) W z] / w̄`: the mean trait of the selected parents, weighting each individual by its fitness, minus the mean trait `μ` before selection. If `w̄ = 0` the division returns the junk value `0`.
nodes.title: Directional selection differential

nodes.summary: The derivative of mean fitness with respect to the trait mean is `d/dμ w̄(μ) = 𝔼[(z - μ) W z] / v`, for bounded measurable fitness and `v > 0`.
nodes.title: Derivative of mean fitness with respect to the trait mean

nodes.summary: Lande's equation for one normally distributed trait (Lande 1979): the selection differential is the phenotypic variance times the derivative of log mean fitness with respect to the trait mean, `S = v · d/dμ log w̄(μ)`.
nodes.title: Lande's equation

nodes.summary: The Lande–Arnold selection gradient for one normally distributed trait: for a differentiable bounded fitness function with integrable derivative, `β = S / v = 𝔼[W' z] / w̄`, the average slope of relative fitness `W / w̄` (Lande–Arnold 1983).
nodes.title: The Lande–Arnold selection gradient

nodes.summary: The mean fitness `w̄(μ) = 𝔼[W z]` of a population whose trait vector is distributed as `N(μ, P)`.
nodes.title: Mean fitness of a multivariate normal trait

nodes.summary: The directional selection differential `S = 𝔼[W z · (z - μ)] / w̄` of a trait vector distributed as `N(μ, P)`: the fitness-weighted mean trait vector of the selected parents minus the mean `μ` before selection. If `w̄ = 0` it is the junk value `0`.
nodes.title: Multivariate directional selection differential

nodes.summary: The gradient of mean fitness with respect to the vector of trait means is `∇_μ w̄(μ) = P⁻¹ 𝔼[W z · (z - μ)]`, for positive definite `P` and bounded measurable `W`.
nodes.title: Lande's gradient of mean fitness for multivariate traits

nodes.summary: Lande's equation (Lande 1979): for a multivariate normal trait vector, the selection differential is the phenotypic covariance matrix applied to the gradient of log mean fitness with respect to the trait means, `S = P ∇_μ log w̄(μ)`.
nodes.title: Lande's equation
Linear mixed models and BLUP

nodes.summary: The phenotypic covariance `V = Z G Zᵀ + R` of the linear mixed model `y = X b + Z u + e` with `Cov u = G`, `Cov e = R`.
nodes.title: Phenotypic covariance of a linear mixed model

nodes.summary: Henderson's mixed-model equations for `y = X b + Z u + e`, `Cov u = G`, `Cov e = R`: `[Xᵀ R⁻¹ X, Xᵀ R⁻¹ Z; Zᵀ R⁻¹ X, Zᵀ R⁻¹ Z + G⁻¹] [b; u] = [Xᵀ R⁻¹ y; Zᵀ R⁻¹ y]`.
nodes.title: Solution of Henderson's mixed-model equations

nodes.summary: `V = Z G Zᵀ + R` is positive definite.
nodes.title: Positive definiteness of the phenotypic covariance

nodes.summary: Henderson's mixed-model equations (Henderson 1975; Robinson 1991): for positive definite `G` and `R` and `V = Z G Zᵀ + R`, `(b, u)` solves the mixed-model equations if and only if `b` solves the generalized least-squares normal equations `Xᵀ V⁻¹ X b = Xᵀ V⁻¹ y` and `u = G Zᵀ V⁻¹ (y - X b)`.
nodes.title: Henderson's mixed-model equations

nodes.summary: The MME solution is the GLS estimate and the BLUP (Henderson 1975): if moreover `Xᵀ V⁻¹ X` is invertible, the mixed-model equations have the unique solution `b̂ = (Xᵀ V⁻¹ X)⁻¹ Xᵀ V⁻¹ y` (the GLS estimate) and `û = G Zᵀ V⁻¹ (y - X b̂)`.
nodes.title: The MME solution is the GLS estimate and the BLUP

nodes.summary: BLUP as a conditional law (Henderson 1975; Robinson 1991): in the Gaussian mixed model `y = X b + Z u + e` with fixed effects `b`, random effects `u ~ N(0, G)` and residuals `e ~ N(0, R)` independent, `G` and `R` positive definite, the conditional law of `u` given `y` is `N(G Zᵀ V⁻¹ (y - X b), G - G Zᵀ V⁻¹ Z G)` with `V = Z G Zᵀ + R` (for almost every `y`).
nodes.title: BLUP as a conditional law

nodes.summary: BLUP is the conditional expectation in the Gaussian mixed model: `𝔼[u | y] = G Zᵀ V⁻¹ (y - X b)` almost surely.
nodes.title: BLUP is the conditional expectation

nodes.summary: The LDpred-inf posterior (Vilhjálmsson et al. 2015; the likelihood `β̂ | β ~ N(R β, R / N)` of Zhu and Stephens 2017): with `M` markers, `N` individuals, heritability `h² > 0`, effects `β ~ N(0, h² / M · I)`, an LD matrix `R` that is positive definite, and marginal estimates `β̂ = R β + ε` with `ε ~ N(0, R / N)` independent of `β`, the posterior law of `β` given `β̂` is…
nodes.title: The LDpred-inf posterior

nodes.summary: The `N`-normalized marginal association estimate `β̂_j = X_jᵀ y / N` of marker `j` for the phenotype `y = X β + ε` (fixed effects `β`, noise `ε`).
nodes.title: Marginal association estimate of a marker

nodes.summary: The mean of the marginal estimates (Zhu and Stephens 2017): for fixed effects `β` and noise with mean zero, `𝔼[X_jᵀ y / N] = (R β)_j` with `R = Xᵀ X / N` (`ldCorr`).
nodes.title: The mean of the marginal estimates

nodes.summary: The raw residual-product second moment of the marginal estimates (Zhu and Stephens 2017): if `𝔼[ε_i ε_i'] = σ² [i = i']`, then `𝔼[(β̂_j - (R β)_j)(β̂_k - (R β)_k)] = σ² / N · R_jk`.
nodes.title: The raw residual-product second moment of the marginal estimates
Pedigree kinship and inbreeding

nodes.summary: A pedigree on the individuals `Fin n`, numbered so that parents precede their children (every finite pedigree, a finite DAG, has such a numbering). `parents i = some g` means that `g 0` is the father and `g 1` the mother of `i`; `parents i = none` means that `i` is a founder. Founders are unrelated and not inbred (their `2 n_F` gene copies are distinct).
nodes.title: Pedigree

nodes.summary: `a` is a parent of `b`.
nodes.title: Parent relation in a pedigree

nodes.summary: `a` is an ancestor of `b` (a parent, a parent of a parent, …).
nodes.title: Ancestor relation in a pedigree

nodes.summary: No individual is the offspring of a selfing (father ≠ mother), as in Wright's setting of a bisexual population.
nodes.title: Pedigree without selfing

nodes.summary: A gene-dropping outcome: `ω i k` is the Mendelian coin of the copy `(i, k)` (`k = 0` the paternal copy, `k = 1` the maternal copy), saying which copy (`0` or `1`) of the parent `g k` of `i` it inherits. Under gene dropping all `4 ^ n` outcomes are equally likely.
nodes.title: Gene-dropping outcome

nodes.summary: The founder copy from which the gene copy `c = (i, k)` descends under the gene-dropping outcome `ω`: a founder copy is its own origin; a copy of a non-founder descends from the copy `ω i k` of its parent `g k`.
nodes.title: Founder origin of a gene copy

nodes.summary: The probability, under gene dropping (independent fair Mendelian coins), that the gene copies `c` and `d` are identical by descent, i.e. descend from the same founder copy.
nodes.title: Probability of identity by descent under gene dropping

nodes.summary: The kinship (coancestry) coefficient under gene dropping: the probability that a copy drawn at random from `i` and a copy drawn at random from `j` are identical by descent.
nodes.title: Kinship coefficient under gene dropping

nodes.summary: The inbreeding coefficient under gene dropping: the probability that the two copies of `i` are identical by descent.
nodes.title: Inbreeding coefficient under gene dropping

nodes.summary: The kinship coefficient by Malécot's recursion, computed in the order of the numbering (the tabular method): for `i < j`, `φ i j = (φ i f + φ i m) / 2` with `f, m` the parents of `j` and `φ i j = 0` if `j` is a founder; `φ i i = (1 + φ f m) / 2` with `f, m` the parents of `i` and `φ i i = 1 / 2` for a founder; symmetric for `j < i`.
nodes.title: Kinship coefficient by Malécot's recursion

nodes.summary: The inbreeding coefficient by Malécot's recursion: `F i = φ f m` for the parents `f, m` of `i`, and `F i = 0` for a founder.
nodes.title: Inbreeding coefficient by Malécot's recursion

nodes.summary: The tabular recursion for `i < j` with `j` a non-founder.
nodes.title: Tabular kinship when the second individual is a later non-founder

nodes.summary: The tabular recursion for `i < j` with `j` a founder.
nodes.title: Tabular kinship when the second individual is a later founder

nodes.summary: The tabular recursion on the diagonal for a non-founder: `φ i i = (1 + φ f m) / 2`.
nodes.title: Tabular self-kinship of a non-founder

nodes.summary: The tabular recursion on the diagonal for a founder: `φ i i = 1 / 2`.
nodes.title: Tabular self-kinship of a founder

nodes.summary: The tabular recursion for `j < i` with `i` a non-founder.
nodes.title: Tabular kinship when the first individual is a later non-founder

nodes.summary: The tabular recursion for `j < i` with `i` a founder.
nodes.title: Tabular kinship when the first individual is a later founder

nodes.summary: The tabular kinship is symmetric.
nodes.title: Symmetry of tabular kinship

nodes.summary: The ancestral paths from `i`: the lists `[i = v₀, v₁, …, v_k]` with each `v_{t+1}` a parent of `v_t` (`k ≥ 0`; the path `[i]` has no edge).
nodes.title: Ancestral paths from an individual

nodes.summary: The ancestral paths from `i` that end at `A`.
nodes.title: Ancestral paths ending at a given ancestor

nodes.summary: Every path in `ancPaths i` starts at `i` and is nonempty.
nodes.title: Ancestral paths are nonempty with the starting individual as head

nodes.summary: A founder copy is its own origin.
nodes.title: A founder gene copy is its own origin

nodes.summary: A copy of a non-founder descends from the chosen copy of the corresponding parent.
nodes.title: Origin of a gene copy of a non-founder

nodes.summary: Ancestors precede their descendants.
nodes.title: Ancestors precede their descendants

nodes.summary: A parent is an ancestor.
nodes.title: Parents are ancestors

nodes.summary: Two copies are identical by descent of themselves with probability `1`.
nodes.title: A gene copy is identical by descent with itself

nodes.summary: Identity by descent is symmetric.
nodes.title: Symmetry of identity by descent

nodes.summary: One step of Malécot's recursion for identity by descent.
nodes.title: Malécot's recursion step for identity by descent

nodes.summary: `φ i i = (1 + F i) / 2` under gene dropping.
nodes.title: Self-kinship under gene dropping

nodes.summary: The inbreeding coefficient of a founder is `0`.
nodes.title: Founders are not inbred

nodes.summary: The inbreeding coefficient of `i` is the kinship of its parents, `F i = φ f m`, under gene dropping.
nodes.title: Malécot

nodes.summary: Malécot's recursion under gene dropping: if `j ≠ i` is not an ancestor of `i` and has parents `f, m`, then `φ i j = (φ i f + φ i m) / 2`.
nodes.title: Malécot's recursion

nodes.summary: A founder `j ≠ i` that is not an ancestor of `i` has kinship `0` with `i`.
nodes.title: Zero kinship with an unrelated founder

nodes.summary: Gene-dropping kinship is symmetric.
nodes.title: Symmetry of gene-dropping kinship

nodes.summary: The kinship coefficient computed by Malécot's recursion is the probability of identity by descent under gene dropping.
nodes.title: Malécot's recursion computes gene-dropping kinship

nodes.summary: The inbreeding coefficient computed by Malécot's recursion is the probability of identity by descent of the two copies of `i` under gene dropping.
nodes.title: Malécot's recursion computes the inbreeding coefficient

nodes.summary: The only ancestral path from a founder is `[i]`.
nodes.title: Ancestral paths from a founder

nodes.summary: The ancestral paths from a non-founder: `[i]` and `i :: q` for a path `q` from a parent.
nodes.title: Ancestral paths from a non-founder

nodes.summary: Every individual on an ancestral path from `i` is `i` or precedes it.
nodes.title: Individuals on an ancestral path are its start or precede it

nodes.summary: Every ancestral path from `i` starts with `i`.
nodes.title: Ancestral path as its start followed by a tail

nodes.summary: A path from `i` ending at `i` is `[i]`.
nodes.title: An ancestral path returning to its start is trivial

nodes.summary: `[i]` is an ancestral path from `i`.
nodes.title: Trivial ancestral path

nodes.summary: Wright's path formula in kinship form: `φ i j` is the sum, over common ancestors `A` (including `i` or `j` themselves) and pairs of ancestral paths `p` from `i` to `A` and `p'` from `j` to `A` that share no individual other than `A`, of `(1/2) ^ (n₁ + n₂ + 1) * (1 + F A)`, where `n₁ + n₂ + 1 = p.length + p'.length - 1` is the number of individuals on the loop.
nodes.title: Wright's path formula

nodes.summary: Wright's path formula for the inbreeding coefficient (Wright 1922): if `i` has parents `f = g 0` and `m = g 1`, then `F_i = Σ (1/2) ^ (n₁ + n₂ + 1) (1 + F_A)` over common ancestors `A` of `f` and `m` (including `f` or `m` themselves) and pairs of ancestral paths from `f` and `m` to `A` (with `n₁` and `n₂` edges) that share only `A`. Here `F` is the gene-dropping inbreeding coefficient.
nodes.title: Wright's path formula

nodes.summary: Dynamics of biochemical reaction networks and gene regulatory circuits: mass-action kinetics, enzyme kinetics, ultrasensitivity, feedback, metabolic flux analysis and gene expression noise.
nodes.title: Systems biology
Coherent feed-forward loop

nodes.summary: The variation-of-constants solution of `z' = P(t) - α z`, `z(0) = z₀`: `z(t) = z₀ e^{-α t} + ∫₀ᵗ e^{-α (t - s)} P(s) ds`. Used for `t ≥ 0`.
nodes.title: Variation-of-constants solution of a linear relaxation equation

nodes.summary: The relaxation solves `z' = P - α z` at every time where the (locally integrable) production rate `P` is continuous.
nodes.title: Relaxation solution satisfies its differential equation

nodes.summary: AND-gate production in the logic approximation: rate `β` when `K_x < x` and `K_y < y`, else `0`.
nodes.title: AND-gate production rate in the logic approximation

nodes.summary: Single-input production in the logic approximation: rate `β` when `K_x < x`, else `0`.
nodes.title: Single-input production rate in the logic approximation

nodes.summary: `Y` after an ON step of `Sx` from `Y(0) = 0`: `Y(t) = (β_y/α_y)(1 - e^{-α_y t})`.
nodes.title: Intermediate factor after an ON step

nodes.summary: The ON-step delay `T_on = (1/α_y) log(1 / (1 - K_yz / Y_st))`, `Y_st = β_y/α_y`: the time at which `Y` crosses the activation threshold `K_yz` of `Z`. Meaningful for `0 < K_yz < Y_st`.
nodes.title: ON-step delay of the feed-forward loop

nodes.summary: `yOn` solves `Y' = β_y - α_y Y` with `Y(0) = 0` (for `α_y ≠ 0`; at `α_y = 0` Lean's `β_y / 0 = 0` makes `yOn` identically `0`, which is not a solution).
nodes.title: Intermediate factor solves its production–decay equation

nodes.summary: The ON delay is positive.
nodes.title: Positivity of the ON delay

nodes.summary: `Y` exceeds `K_yz` exactly after the ON delay: `K_yz < Y(t) ↔ T_on < t`.
nodes.title: Intermediate factor exceeds the threshold exactly after the ON delay

nodes.summary: The FFL target after an ON step of `Sx` at `t = 0` from `Y(0) = Z(0) = 0`, with `X* = 1` and `K_xz < 1`.
nodes.title: Feed-forward loop target after an ON step

nodes.summary: The simple-regulation target after an ON step of `Sx` at `t = 0` from `Z(0) = 0`.
nodes.title: Simple-regulation target after an ON step

nodes.summary: The FFL target stays at `0` until `T_on`.
nodes.title: ON delay

nodes.summary: After `T_on` the FFL target relaxes from `0` towards `β_z/α_z`: `Z(t) = (β_z/α_z)(1 - e^{-α_z (t - T_on)})` (for `α_z > 0`, `K_xz < 1`).
nodes.title: Delayed rise

nodes.summary: Simple regulation responds without delay: `Z(t) = (β_z/α_z)(1 - e^{-α_z t}) > 0` for all `t > 0`.
nodes.title: Simple regulation responds without delay

nodes.summary: The FFL target after `Sx` is removed at `t = 0` (`X* = 0`), starting from `Z(0) = z₀`, for an arbitrary trajectory `Y` of the intermediate factor.
nodes.title: Feed-forward loop target after an OFF step

nodes.summary: The simple-regulation target after `Sx` is removed at `t = 0`, from `Z(0) = z₀`.
nodes.title: Simple-regulation target after an OFF step

nodes.summary: For a nonnegative threshold `K_xz`, whatever `Y` does, the FFL and simple regulation decay identically after an OFF step: `Z(t) = z₀ e^{-α_z t}`.
nodes.title: No OFF delay
Complex balancing and the deficiency-zero theorem

nodes.summary: A chemical reaction network on the species `S` with reactions indexed by `ρ`: reaction `r` turns the source complex `src r` into the product complex `prod r` (stoichiometric coefficients).
nodes.title: Chemical reaction network

nodes.summary: The stoichiometric subspace: the span of the reaction vectors `prod r - src r`.
nodes.title: Stoichiometric subspace

nodes.summary: The mass-action vector field with rate constants `k`: `x ↦ ∑_r k r (∏_s x_s ^ (src r s)) (prod r - src r)`.
nodes.title: Mass-action vector field

nodes.summary: The mass-action rate `k r * ∏_s c_s ^ (src r s)` of reaction `r` at concentrations `c`.
nodes.title: Mass-action reaction rate

nodes.summary: Concentrations `c` are complex balanced for the rate constants `k`: at every complex `z`, the total rate of the reactions with source `z` equals the total rate of the reactions with product `z`. (Complexes that occur in no reaction give `0 = 0`.)
nodes.title: Complex-balanced concentrations

nodes.summary: The pseudo-Helmholtz function `G(c) = ∑_s c_s (log c_s - log c*_s - 1)` relative to the reference concentrations `cstar` (Horn & Jackson 1972). It is meaningful for positive `c` and `cstar`; elsewhere `Real.log` takes junk values.
nodes.title: Pseudo-Helmholtz function

nodes.summary: The rate of change of the pseudo-Helmholtz function along the mass-action vector field, `∑_s (log c_s - log c*_s) f_s(c)`: the derivative of `pseudoHelmholtz cstar` at `c > 0` applied to `massActionField k c` (`hasDerivAt_pseudoHelmholtz`).
nodes.title: Rate of change of the pseudo-Helmholtz function

nodes.summary: Complex balance at `c` rewrites the rate-weighted sum of any function of the products as the same sum over the sources (for all real `c` and `k`).
nodes.title: Complex balance exchanges source and product sums

nodes.summary: A complex-balanced state is an equilibrium of the mass-action system (for all real `c` and `k`). Source: Horn & Jackson (1972).
nodes.title: Complex-balanced states are equilibria

nodes.summary: If `c*` is a positive complex-balanced equilibrium for positive rate constants, the pseudo-Helmholtz function does not increase along the mass-action vector field at any positive `c`. Source: Horn & Jackson (1972); Feinberg (2019), ch. 15.
nodes.title: Horn–Jackson inequality

nodes.summary: Under the hypotheses of `helmholtzRate_nonpos`, the rate of change of the pseudo-Helmholtz function vanishes at a positive `c` exactly when `c` is an equilibrium. Source: Horn & Jackson (1972).
nodes.title: Equality in the Horn–Jackson inequality

nodes.summary: If a mass-action system with positive rate constants has a positive complex-balanced equilibrium, then every positive equilibrium is complex balanced.
nodes.title: Horn–Jackson

nodes.summary: If `c*` is a positive complex-balanced equilibrium for positive rate constants, the positive equilibria are exactly the positive `c` whose `log c - log c*` is orthogonal (for the dot product) to the stoichiometric subspace. Source: Horn & Jackson (1972); Feinberg (2019), ch. 15.
nodes.title: Horn–Jackson: the positive equilibria

nodes.summary: For any subspace `W` of `S → ℝ` and positive `a`, `b` there is a positive `c` with `c - b ∈ W` and `log c - log a` orthogonal to `W` (for the dot product). Source: Birch (1963); Horn & Jackson (1972).
nodes.title: Birch's theorem, existence

nodes.summary: Two positive vectors whose difference lies in a subspace `W` and whose logarithms differ by a vector orthogonal to `W` are equal.
nodes.title: Birch's theorem, uniqueness

nodes.summary: If a mass-action system with positive rate constants has a positive complex-balanced equilibrium, then each positive stoichiometric compatibility class `(x₀ + 𝒮) ∩ ℝ_{>0}^S`, `x₀ > 0`, contains exactly one positive equilibrium. Source: Horn & Jackson (1972); Feinberg (2019), ch. 15.
nodes.title: Horn–Jackson: one equilibrium per compatibility class

nodes.summary: The pseudo-Helmholtz function has time derivative `helmholtzRate` along a solution of the mass-action system, at any time where the solution is positive.
nodes.title: Pseudo-Helmholtz function along positive mass-action solutions

nodes.summary: Along a solution of a mass-action system with positive rate constants and a positive complex-balanced equilibrium `c*`, positive and differentiable (two-sided) at every `t ≥ 0`, `G(x t)` is nonincreasing on `[0, ∞)`.
nodes.title: The pseudo-Helmholtz function does not increase along solutions

nodes.summary: The complexes of the network: the sources and products of its reactions.
nodes.title: Complexes of a chemical reaction network

nodes.summary: The directed reaction relation on complexes: `y ⟶ y'` if some reaction has source `y` and product `y'`.
nodes.title: Directed reaction relation on complexes

nodes.summary: The undirected reaction graph on the complexes: distinct complexes are adjacent when one reacts to the other.
nodes.title: Linkage graph of a reaction network

nodes.summary: The number of linkage classes: connected components of the undirected reaction graph.
nodes.title: Number of linkage classes of a reaction network

nodes.summary: The deficiency `δ = n - ℓ - s` (number of complexes, linkage classes, dimension of the stoichiometric subspace).
nodes.title: Deficiency of a chemical reaction network

nodes.summary: The network is weakly reversible: for every reaction `y → y'` there is a directed path of reactions from `y'` back to `y`.
nodes.title: Weakly reversible reaction network

nodes.summary: A weakly reversible mass-action network of deficiency zero has, for any positive rate constants, a positive complex-balanced equilibrium. Together with `existsUnique_equilibrium_of_isComplexBalanced` this gives `existsUnique_equilibrium`.
nodes.title: Horn–Feinberg: complex balancing for every choice of rate constants

nodes.summary: A weakly reversible mass-action network of deficiency zero has, for any positive rate constants, exactly one equilibrium in each positive stoichiometric compatibility class.
nodes.title: Deficiency-zero theorem, weakly reversible case

nodes.summary: A mass-action network of deficiency zero that is not weakly reversible has no positive equilibrium for any positive rate constants.
nodes.title: Deficiency-zero theorem, non-weakly-reversible case
Goldbeter–Koshland ultrasensitivity

nodes.summary: The value of `V₁ / V₂` for which the mole fraction `W` of modified protein is at steady state (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 8): `W (1 - W + K₁) / ((1 - W) (W + K₂))`. Meaningful for `0 < W < 1` and `K₁, K₂ > 0`; at `W = 1` Lean's `a / 0 = 0` gives the junk value `0`.
nodes.title: Rate ratio at a given steady-state modified fraction

nodes.summary: The Goldbeter–Koshland function: the steady-state mole fraction of modified protein when `V₁ / V₂ = v` (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 7, rationalized so that it also covers `v = 1`, Eq. 9). Meaningful for `v, K₁, K₂ > 0`.
nodes.title: Goldbeter–Koshland function

nodes.summary: The response coefficient `R_v`: the ratio of the values of `V₁ / V₂` giving 90% and 10% modified protein at steady state (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981).
nodes.title: Response coefficient of a covalent modification cycle

nodes.summary: The fraction of a Hill response `Sⁿ / (Kⁿ + Sⁿ)` with half-saturation constant `K` and Hill coefficient `n` (meaningful for `S, K > 0`, `n > 0`).
nodes.title: Hill response function

nodes.summary: Steady state of the modification cycle (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 8). For `V₂ > 0`, `K₁, K₂ > 0` and `0 < W < 1`, modification and demodification balance, `V₁ (1 - W) / (K₁ + 1 - W) = V₂ W / (K₂ + W)`, iff `V₁ / V₂ = rateRatio K₁ K₂ W`.
nodes.title: Steady state of the modification cycle

nodes.summary: `rateRatio K₁ K₂` is strictly increasing on `(0, 1)` for `K₁, K₂ > 0`: it is the product of the positive increasing functions `W / (W + K₂)` and `1 + K₁ / (1 - W)`.
nodes.title: Rate ratio is strictly increasing in the modified fraction

nodes.summary: For `v, K₁, K₂ > 0` the Goldbeter–Koshland function lies in `(0, 1)`.
nodes.title: Goldbeter–Koshland function lies strictly between 0 and 1

nodes.summary: The Goldbeter–Koshland function is a steady state (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 7): for `v, K₁, K₂ > 0`, `rateRatio K₁ K₂ (goldbeterKoshland v K₁ K₂) = v`.
nodes.title: The Goldbeter–Koshland function is a steady state

nodes.summary: Uniqueness of the steady state (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 7). For `K₁, K₂ > 0`, if `0 < W < 1` and `rateRatio K₁ K₂ W = v` with `v > 0`, then `W` is the Goldbeter–Koshland function.
nodes.title: Uniqueness of the steady state

nodes.summary: Equal maximal rates (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 9): for `V₁ = V₂` and `K₁, K₂ > 0` the steady-state modified fraction is `K₂ / (K₁ + K₂)`.
nodes.title: Equal maximal rates

nodes.summary: The response coefficient (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 10): for `K₁, K₂ > -0.1`, `R_v = 81 (K₁ + 0.1)(K₂ + 0.1) / ((K₁ + 0.9)(K₂ + 0.9))`.
nodes.title: The response coefficient

nodes.summary: For `K₁, K₂ > 0` the response coefficient exceeds `1`: the switch is never infinitely sharp.
nodes.title: Response coefficient exceeds 1

nodes.summary: For `K₁, K₂ > 0` the response coefficient is below the Michaelis–Menten value `81`.
nodes.title: Response coefficient is below the Michaelis–Menten value 81

nodes.summary: As both `K₁, K₂ → ∞` the response coefficient tends to `81`, the value of a Michaelis–Menten response.
nodes.title: First-order limit

nodes.summary: As both `K₁, K₂ → 0` the response coefficient tends to `1`.
nodes.title: Zero-order ultrasensitivity

nodes.summary: Hill response coefficient (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 11). For a Hill response with `n > 0` and `K > 0`, if `S₉, S₁ > 0` give 90% and 10% response, then `S₉ / S₁ = 81 ^ (1 / n)`.
nodes.title: Hill response coefficient

nodes.summary: Michaelis–Menten response (`n = 1`): going from 10% to 90% of the response takes an 81-fold increase of the stimulus.
nodes.title: Michaelis–Menten response
Integral feedback and perfect adaptation

nodes.summary: A single-input single-output linear time-invariant system `ẋ = A x + u b`, `y = c ⬝ x + d u` with state space `n → ℝ`.
nodes.title: Single-input single-output linear time-invariant system

nodes.summary: The vector field `A x + u b` at state `x` and input `u`.
nodes.title: Vector field of a linear time-invariant system

nodes.summary: The output `c ⬝ x + d u`, measured from its adapted value.
nodes.title: Output of a linear time-invariant system

nodes.summary: For every constant input `u`, the output vanishes at every equilibrium.
nodes.title: Perfect adaptation

nodes.summary: A linear functional `z = k ⬝ x` of the state integrates the output, `ż = k ⬝ (A x + u b) = y`, for every state and input.
nodes.title: Integral feedback

nodes.summary: The steady-state (DC) gain `d - c ⬝ A⁻¹ b`; for nonsingular `A` the output at the equilibrium for input `u` is `dcGain * u`.
nodes.title: Steady-state (DC) gain of a linear system

nodes.summary: Integral feedback implies perfect adaptation.
nodes.title: Integral feedback implies perfect adaptation

nodes.summary: For nonsingular `A`, the unique equilibrium for input `u` is `x = -u • A⁻¹ b`.
nodes.title: Unique equilibrium of a nonsingular linear system

nodes.summary: For nonsingular `A`, the output at the equilibrium for input `u` is `dcGain * u`.
nodes.title: Output at equilibrium equals DC gain times input

nodes.summary: For nonsingular `A`, perfect adaptation holds iff the steady-state gain vanishes.
nodes.title: Perfect adaptation iff the DC gain vanishes

nodes.summary: Integral feedback is necessary (linear systems with nonsingular `A`): perfect adaptation holds iff some linear functional of the state integrates the output; one such functional is `k = c A⁻¹`.
nodes.title: Integral feedback is necessary

nodes.summary: Along a trajectory `ẋ(t) = A x(t) + u(t) b`, the functional `k ⬝ x(t)` of an integral-feedback system has derivative `y(t) = c ⬝ x(t) + d u(t)`: it is the time integral of the output.
nodes.title: Integral-feedback functional is the time integral of the output

nodes.summary: Integral feedback gives robust perfect adaptation (nonlinear form). Let `F p` be the vector field and `y p` the output of a system with parameters `p`, and let `z` be a differentiable state function with derivative `z' x` satisfying `z' x (F p x) = y p x` for all `p`, `x` (so `ż = y` along every trajectory, for every parameter). Then the output vanishes at every equilibrium of every `F p`.
nodes.title: Integral feedback gives robust perfect adaptation
Intrinsic and extrinsic gene expression noise

nodes.summary: Two-reporter intrinsic noise strength `η_int² = ⟨(X - Y)²⟩ / (2 ⟨X⟩⟨Y⟩)`.
nodes.title: Intrinsic noise strength

nodes.summary: Two-reporter extrinsic noise strength `η_ext² = (⟨X Y⟩ - ⟨X⟩⟨Y⟩) / (⟨X⟩⟨Y⟩)`.
nodes.title: Extrinsic noise strength

nodes.summary: Two-reporter total noise strength `η_tot² = (⟨X² + Y²⟩ / 2 - ⟨X⟩⟨Y⟩) / (⟨X⟩⟨Y⟩)`.
nodes.title: Total noise strength

nodes.summary: Two-reporter decomposition (Swain et al. 2002; Elowitz et al. 2002): for any square-integrable reporters, `η_tot² = η_int² + η_ext²`.
nodes.title: Two-reporter decomposition

nodes.summary: Two reporters of the same gene given the extrinsic σ-algebra `m`: equal conditional means, equal conditional second moments, and conditionally uncorrelated. Conditional independence with identical conditional laws given `m` implies these three conditions.
nodes.title: Identical reporter pair

nodes.summary: Identical reporters have the same mean.
nodes.title: Identical reporters have equal means

nodes.summary: For identical reporters the covariance is the extrinsic variance: `Cov(X, Y) = Var(E[X | m])`.
nodes.title: Covariance of identical reporters equals extrinsic variance

nodes.summary: For identical reporters half the mean squared difference is the intrinsic variance: `⟨(X - Y)²⟩ / 2 = ⟨Var(X | m)⟩`.
nodes.title: Half mean squared reporter difference equals intrinsic variance

nodes.summary: The two-reporter extrinsic noise is `Var(E[X | m]) / ⟨X⟩²` (Swain et al. Eq. 8).
nodes.title: Two-reporter formula for extrinsic noise

nodes.summary: The two-reporter intrinsic noise is `⟨Var(X | m)⟩ / ⟨X⟩²` (Swain et al. Eq. 8).
nodes.title: Two-reporter formula for intrinsic noise

nodes.summary: The two-reporter total noise is `Var(X) / ⟨X⟩²`, and it splits into the intrinsic and extrinsic parts by the law of total variance.
nodes.title: Total noise splits into intrinsic and extrinsic parts
Michaelis–Menten kinetics and the quasi-steady state

nodes.summary: The Michaelis constant `K_M = (kb + k₂)/k₁` (Briggs–Haldane). Meaningful for `k₁ > 0`.
nodes.title: Michaelis constant

nodes.summary: The mass-action rate of the substrate, `s' = -k₁ e s + kb c`.
nodes.title: Mass-action rate of the substrate

nodes.summary: The mass-action rate of the complex, `c' = k₁ e s - (kb + k₂) c`.
nodes.title: Mass-action rate of the enzyme–substrate complex

nodes.summary: A solution of the Michaelis–Menten mass-action system on `[0, ∞)`: `s' = -k₁ e s + kb c`, `c' = k₁ e s - (kb + k₂) c`, `e' = -c'`, `p' = k₂ c`.
nodes.title: Solution of the Michaelis–Menten mass-action system
Enzyme conservation
Mass conservation

nodes.summary: The quasi-steady-state value of the complex, `c = e₀ s / (K_M + s)`.
nodes.title: Quasi-steady-state value of the complex

nodes.summary: The Michaelis–Menten rate law `v(s) = V_max s / (K_M + s)`.
nodes.title: Michaelis–Menten rate law

nodes.summary: With total enzyme `e₀` (so `e = e₀ - c`), `k₁ > 0` and `K_M + s ≠ 0`, the complex is stationary iff `c = e₀ s / (K_M + s)`.
nodes.title: Quasi-steady-state manifold

nodes.summary: On the quasi-steady-state manifold the product forms at rate `k₂ c = V_max s / (K_M + s)`, `V_max = k₂ e₀`.
nodes.title: Briggs–Haldane rate law

nodes.summary: On the quasi-steady-state manifold the substrate is consumed at the Michaelis–Menten rate: `s' = -V_max s / (K_M + s)`.
nodes.title: Substrate consumption at the Michaelis–Menten rate under QSSA

nodes.summary: The rate law is strictly increasing on `s ≥ 0` for `V_max, K_M > 0`.
nodes.title: Michaelis–Menten rate is strictly increasing

nodes.summary: The Michaelis constant is the half-saturation substrate level: `v(K_M) = V_max / 2`.
nodes.title: Michaelis constant is the half-saturation substrate level

nodes.summary: The rate law is below its maximum: `v(s) < V_max` for `s ≥ 0`, `V_max, K_M > 0`.
nodes.title: Michaelis–Menten rate stays below its maximum

nodes.summary: Saturation: `v(s) → V_max` as `s → ∞`.
nodes.title: Saturation of the Michaelis–Menten rate

nodes.summary: The fast transient of the complex with the substrate frozen at `s̄`: `c(t) = c* + (c₀ - c*) e^{-k₁ (s̄ + K_M) t}`, where `c* = e₀ s̄ / (K_M + s̄)`.
nodes.title: Fast transient of the complex with frozen substrate

nodes.summary: The fast transient solves the boundary-layer equation `c' = k₁ (e₀ - c) s̄ - (kb + k₂) c` for `k₁ > 0` and `K_M + s̄ ≠ 0`.
nodes.title: Fast transient solves the boundary-layer equation

nodes.summary: The fast transient converges to the quasi-steady-state value for `k₁ > 0` and `s̄ + K_M > 0`.
nodes.title: Fast transient converges to the quasi-steady state

nodes.summary: Rigorous QSSA (Tikhonov 1952; Heineken–Tsuchiya–Aris 1967). On the slow time scale `τ = e₀ t`, the substrate of the full Michaelis–Menten system with `s(0) = s₀`, `c(0) = 0`, `e(0) = e₀` stays within `C e₀` of the solution `S̄` of the reduced equation `dS̄/dτ = -k₂ S̄ / (K_M + S̄)`, `S̄(0) = s₀`, uniformly on `[0, T]`.
nodes.title: Rigorous QSSA
Stochastic mass action, metabolic control and flux balance

nodes.summary: The stochastic mass-action propensity of reaction `r` in state `x` (molecule counts): `k r * ∏_s x_s (x_s - 1) ⋯ (x_s - src_s + 1)`, the falling factorial `Nat.descFactorial x_s src_s` (it vanishes when `x_s < src_s`). Anderson, Craciun & Kurtz (2010), §2.
nodes.title: Stochastic mass-action propensity

nodes.summary: The state reached from `x` by one firing of reaction `r`, `x - src r + prod r` (meaningful when `src r ≤ x`, the only case in which the propensity is nonzero).
nodes.title: State after one reaction firing

nodes.summary: The state from which one firing of reaction `r` leads to `x`, `x - prod r + src r` (meaningful when `prod r ≤ x`).
nodes.title: State before one reaction firing

nodes.summary: The product-form Poisson weight `∏_s c_s ^ x_s e^{-c_s} / Nat.factorial x_s` of a state `x`.
nodes.title: Product-form Poisson weight of a state

nodes.summary: The generator of the stochastic mass-action chain restricted to a finite set `Ω` of states: `Q x y = ∑_r λ_r(x) ([fire r x = y] - [x = y])`. It is a rate matrix when `Ω` is closed under firing (`isRateMatrix_classGenerator`).
nodes.title: Generator of the mass-action chain on a finite state class

nodes.summary: Global balance of the product-form Poisson weights (Anderson, Craciun & Kurtz 2010, Thm 4.1): if `c` is complex balanced for the deterministic mass-action system with rate constants `k`, then at every state `x` the total outflow `π(x) ∑_r λ_r(x)` equals the total inflow `∑_{r : prod r ≤ x} π(x - prod r + src r) λ_r(x - prod r + src r)` for `π = poissonWeight c`. This is an algebraic identity valid for all real `k`…
nodes.title: Global balance of the product-form Poisson weights

nodes.summary: The restricted generator is a rate matrix when the rate constants are nonnegative and `Ω` is closed under the reactions.
nodes.title: Restricted mass-action generator is a rate matrix

nodes.summary: Anderson–Craciun–Kurtz on a finite class (Anderson, Craciun & Kurtz 2010, Thm 4.1–4.2): if `c` is complex balanced and every state of `Ω` from which a reaction leads into `Ω` lies in `Ω` (`hbwd`), the Poisson weights restricted to `Ω` are invariant for the restricted generator: `π Q = 0`, for all real `k` and `c`. For a closed communicating class of a weakly reversible network with positive rate constants `hbwd`…
nodes.title: Anderson–Craciun–Kurtz on a finite class

nodes.summary: The Poisson weights normalized on a finite set `Ω` of states.
nodes.title: Normalized Poisson stationary law on a finite state class

nodes.summary: Stationary law of the stochastic mass-action chain on a finite class (Anderson, Craciun & Kurtz 2010, Thm 4.1–4.2). Let the rate constants be nonnegative, `c > 0` complex balanced, and `Ω` a nonempty finite set of states closed under the reactions in both directions. Then the restricted generator is a rate matrix, and the normalized product-form Poisson law `π(x) ∝ ∏_s c_s^{x_s} e^{-c_s} / Nat.factorial x_s` on `Ω`…
nodes.title: Stationary law of the stochastic mass-action chain on a finite class

nodes.summary: Reaction rates `v_i(e, s) = e_i f_i(s)` proportional to enzyme levels `e`.
nodes.title: Reaction fluxes proportional to enzyme levels

nodes.summary: The steady-state fluxes `J(e) = v(e, σ(e))` along a steady-state map `σ`.
nodes.title: Steady-state fluxes along a steady-state map

nodes.summary: The flux control coefficient `C^{J_j}_{e_i} = (e_i / J_j) ∂J_j/∂e_i`. It is meaningful when `J_j ≠ 0` and the steady-state flux is differentiable at `e`; otherwise Lean's `x / 0 = 0` and `fderiv` of a non-differentiable map, `0`, give junk values.
nodes.title: Flux control coefficient

nodes.summary: The concentration control coefficient `C^{s_m}_{e_i} = (e_i / s_m) ∂s_m/∂e_i`, meaningful for a positive concentration `s_m` and a steady state differentiable at `e`.
nodes.title: Concentration control coefficient

nodes.summary: The elasticity `ε^{v_i}_{s_m} = (s_m / v_i) ∂v_i/∂s_m`, meaningful for a nonzero rate `v_i` and a rate law differentiable at `s`.
nodes.title: Elasticity of a reaction rate

nodes.summary: A regular steady state at enzyme levels `e₀`: `σ` is differentiable at `e₀`, the rate laws are differentiable at `σ e₀`, `N v(e, σ e) = 0` for `e` near `e₀`, and the Jacobian `δ ↦ N ∂_s v(e₀, σ e₀) δ` is injective (it is square, so this is its invertibility).
nodes.title: Regular steady state of a metabolic network

nodes.summary: If `s₀` is a steady state at enzyme levels `e₀`, the rate laws are continuously differentiable at `s₀`, and the Jacobian `δ ↦ N (e₀ ⊙ f'(s₀) δ)` is injective, then the steady state continues to a map `σ` with `σ e₀ = s₀` satisfying `IsRegularSteadyState`.
nodes.title: Regular steady states exist by the implicit function theorem

nodes.summary: Concentration summation theorem (Heinrich & Rapoport 1974): for a positive steady-state concentration `s_m`, `∑_i C^{s_m}_{e_i} = 0`. The positivity hypothesis is the domain on which the scaled concentration control coefficients have their biological meaning.
nodes.title: Concentration summation theorem

nodes.summary: Flux summation theorem (Kacser & Burns 1973; Heinrich & Rapoport 1974): for a nonzero steady-state flux `J_j`, `∑_i C^{J_j}_{e_i} = 1`.
nodes.title: Flux summation theorem

nodes.summary: Flux connectivity theorem (Kacser & Burns 1973): when all steady-state fluxes are nonzero, `∑_i C^{J_j}_{e_i} ε^{v_i}_{s_m} = 0` for every flux `J_j` and metabolite `s_m`.
nodes.title: Flux connectivity theorem

nodes.summary: The feasible fluxes of flux balance analysis: `S v = b`, `l ≤ v ≤ u`.
nodes.title: Feasible fluxes of flux balance analysis

nodes.summary: The optimal value `max {c ⬝ᵥ v | S v = b, l ≤ v ≤ u}` of flux balance analysis (the supremum; it is `0` by convention when the problem is infeasible).
nodes.title: Optimal value of flux balance analysis

nodes.summary: Dual feasibility for flux balance analysis: `y` prices the metabolites, `α, β ≥ 0` the upper and lower flux bounds, and `Sᵀ y + α - β = c`.
nodes.title: Dual feasibility for flux balance analysis

nodes.summary: The dual objective `b ⬝ᵥ y + u ⬝ᵥ α - l ⬝ᵥ β`.
nodes.title: Dual objective of flux balance analysis

nodes.summary: A feasible flux balance problem attains its optimum.
nodes.title: Feasible flux balance problem attains its optimum

nodes.summary: Weak duality for flux balance analysis.
nodes.title: Weak duality for flux balance analysis

nodes.summary: Strong duality for flux balance analysis: a feasible problem has a dual feasible point whose value is the optimal value.
nodes.title: Strong duality for flux balance analysis

nodes.summary: The optimal value is concave in the right-hand side `b` on the set of feasible `b`.
nodes.title: Concavity of the flux balance optimum in the right-hand side

nodes.summary: Shadow prices (Orth, Thiele & Palsson 2010): at a feasible `b`, the metabolite prices `y` of the optimal dual solutions are exactly the supergradients of the optimal value: `fbaValue b' ≤ fbaValue b + y ⬝ᵥ (b' - b)` for every feasible `b'`.
nodes.title: Shadow prices

nodes.summary: Two diagonal scalings of a positive matrix to doubly stochastic form differ by a positive scalar.
nodes.title: Uniqueness of Sinkhorn scaling

nodes.summary: Symmetric matrix balancing (Sinkhorn 1964; the "equal visibility" normalization of Imakaev et al. 2012): a symmetric matrix with positive entries has a unique positive vector `d` with `diag(d) A diag(d)` doubly stochastic.
nodes.title: Symmetric matrix balancing

nodes.summary: A square matrix has total support if it is nonzero and every positive entry lies on a positive diagonal: for `A i j > 0` there is a permutation `σ` with `σ i = j` and `A k (σ k) > 0` for all `k` (Sinkhorn & Knopp 1967; Csima & Datta 1972).
nodes.title: Total support of a square matrix

nodes.summary: Necessity of total support (Sinkhorn & Knopp 1967; Csima & Datta 1972): if a positive diagonal scaling `diag(d) A diag(d)` is doubly stochastic, then `A` has total support. The proof uses Birkhoff's theorem. The converse for symmetric nonnegative `A` is `exists_symmetric_balancing_of_hasTotalSupport`.
nodes.title: Necessity of total support

nodes.summary: In the interaction graph of `f : {0,1}ⁿ → {0,1}ⁿ` there is an edge `j → i` when the `i`-th coordinate of `f` depends on the `j`-th variable.
nodes.title: Interaction graph of a Boolean network

nodes.summary: The interaction graph of `f` has no directed cycle (loops included).
nodes.title: Acyclic interaction graph

nodes.summary: Robert's theorem (Robert 1980): if the interaction graph of `f : {0,1}ⁿ → {0,1}ⁿ` is acyclic, `f` has a unique fixed point `p`, and every synchronous trajectory reaches it within `n` steps.
nodes.title: Robert's theorem

nodes.summary: `t : ι → ι` is a spanning in-tree rooted at `r` (each `i ≠ r` points to its parent `t i`): `t r = r` and iterating `t` from any state reaches `r`.
nodes.title: Spanning in-tree rooted at a state

nodes.summary: The total weight `∑_t ∏_{i ≠ r} Q i (t i)` of the spanning in-trees rooted at `r`.
nodes.title: Total weight of spanning in-trees

nodes.summary: A rate matrix is irreducible if every state reaches every other state through positive jump rates.
nodes.title: Irreducible rate matrix

nodes.summary: Markov chain tree theorem (King & Altman 1956; Hill 1966): the in-tree weights are invariant for every matrix with zero row sums, `w Q = 0`. The proof matches both sides with the maps `g : ι → ι` whose functional graph has its cycle through `j` (Anantharam & Tsoucas 1989).
nodes.title: Markov chain tree theorem

nodes.summary: For an irreducible rate matrix every in-tree weight is positive.
nodes.title: In-tree weights of an irreducible rate matrix are positive

nodes.summary: For an irreducible rate matrix every invariant vector is a multiple of the in-tree weights: the stationary law is proportional, at each state, to the weight of the spanning in-trees rooted there.
nodes.title: Uniqueness in the Markov chain tree theorem

nodes.summary: There is a finite set `T` of pairs `(y, u ⬝ᵥ α - l ⬝ᵥ β)` with `(y, α, β)` dual feasible, such that for every feasible `b` some pair in `T` is optimal: `y ⬝ᵥ b + κ = fbaValue S l u c b`.
nodes.title: Finitely many dual solutions suffice

nodes.summary: There are finitely many affine functions `b ↦ y ⬝ᵥ b + κ` whose minimum is the optimal value at every feasible right-hand side `b`.
nodes.title: The FBA value is piecewise linear

nodes.summary: If `b` is an interior point of the set of feasible right-hand sides and `y` is the only metabolite price vector of an optimal dual solution, then the optimal value is differentiable at `b` with derivative `b' ↦ y ⬝ᵥ b'`.
nodes.title: Shadow prices are derivatives when unique

nodes.summary: Statistical tests of neutrality and genome scans for selection based on polymorphism, divergence and haplotype structure, and models of the distribution of fitness effects.
nodes.title: Detecting natural selection
Composite selection scores

nodes.summary: A composite-score model (Grossman et al. 2010): a prior probability `prior` that the site is under selection, and for each of the `k` component statistics a positive score function `sel` under selection and `neut` under neutrality (unnormalized densities: only positivity is assumed). Conditionally on the hypothesis the components are independent, which is what makes the joint scores the products below. The…
nodes.title: Composite selection score model

nodes.summary: The Bayes factor of component `i` at the observed value: the ratio of its score function under selection to its score function under neutrality.
nodes.title: Bayes factor of a component statistic

nodes.summary: The CMS score: the product of the component Bayes factors.
nodes.title: Composite of multiple signals (CMS) score

nodes.summary: The normalized composite score: the normalized ratio of the products of the component score functions. This is the posterior probability of selection given the observed component values when the score functions are normalized densities (see `sum_joint_eq_one` for the normalization hypothesis).
nodes.title: Normalized composite score

nodes.summary: Every component Bayes factor is positive.
nodes.title: Positivity of component Bayes factors

nodes.summary: The CMS score is the ratio of the two joint densities.
nodes.title: CMS score as a ratio of joint densities

nodes.summary: Bayes-rule identity for conditionally independent components: the posterior odds of selection are the prior odds times the CMS score. This is an algebraic identity for the normalized score; it is a genuine Bayes rule only under the normalization hypothesis of `sum_joint_eq_one`.
nodes.title: Posterior odds equal prior odds times the CMS score

nodes.summary: On the log scale the evidence is additive: the log posterior odds are the log prior odds plus the sum of the log Bayes factors of the component statistics.
nodes.title: Additivity of evidence on the log-odds scale

nodes.summary: The posterior probability is a strictly increasing function of the CMS score, so the two rankings of sites agree.
nodes.title: Posterior probability is strictly increasing in the CMS score

nodes.summary: The model is a probability model: with normalised component score functions (each a density with respect to a common base measure), the joint distribution of the observations sums to one. This is the validity hypothesis that makes `posterior` a genuine Bayes posterior.
nodes.title: Normalization of the composite score model

nodes.summary: The probability that a lineage at position `y` escapes a sweep located at `x`, with compound strength parameter `α > 0`: `1 - exp (-α |y - x|)` (Kim and Stephan 2002; Nielsen et al. 2005). The parameter `α` is proportional to the recombination rate per unit distance divided by the selection coefficient.
nodes.title: Probability of escaping a selective sweep

nodes.summary: No lineage escapes at the swept site itself, and nowhere else.
nodes.title: Escape probability vanishes only at the swept site

nodes.summary: The escape-probability profile determines the sweep location and its strength. Positivity of one of the two strength parameters is enough: the location is the unique zero of that profile, and the strengths then agree by injectivity of `exp`.
nodes.title: Escape profile determines sweep location and strength

nodes.summary: A mixture of two distinct laws determines its mixing weight.
nodes.title: Uniqueness of the mixing weight of a two-component mixture

nodes.summary: Identifiability of the sweep parameters from the per-site frequency spectra. If the neutral spectrum `f` and the post-sweep spectrum `g` differ, and two sweep parameter pairs give the same mixture at every position, then the parameters coincide. This is what the composite likelihood of SweepFinder maximises over.
nodes.title: Identifiability of sweep parameters from frequency spectra
Distribution of fitness effects

nodes.summary: The expected number of sites with `i` derived copies in a sample of `n`, `1 ≤ i < n`, is bounded uniformly in the selection coefficient: `|E ξ_i(σ)| ≤ |θ| C(n, i)`.
nodes.title: Uniform bound on the expected site-frequency spectrum

nodes.summary: The expected unfolded site-frequency spectrum under the distribution of fitness effects `μ` (a law on the scaled selection coefficient `σ = 2Ns`): `∫ E ξ_i(σ) dμ(σ)`, where each new mutation draws its own `σ` from `μ`.
nodes.title: Site-frequency spectrum under a distribution of fitness effects

nodes.summary: The Poisson-random-field frequency density averaged over the distribution of fitness effects `μ`: `∫ φ_σ(x) dμ(σ)`.
nodes.title: Frequency density averaged over a distribution of fitness effects

nodes.summary: For `1 ≤ i < n`, the expected spectrum `E ξ_i(σ)` is integrable in `σ` against every finite measure.
nodes.title: Integrability of the expected spectrum in the selection coefficient

nodes.summary: For a finite measure `μ` of selection coefficients and a segregating class `1 ≤ i < n`, the DFE-averaged spectrum is the binomial sampling integral of the DFE-averaged frequency density: `∫ E ξ_i(σ) dμ(σ) = ∫₀¹ C(n, i) x ^ i (1 - x) ^ (n - i) (∫ φ_σ(x) dμ(σ)) dx`.
nodes.title: Mixture identity

nodes.summary: A DFE concentrated on one selection coefficient gives the single-`σ` spectrum.
nodes.title: Spectrum under a point-mass DFE is the single-selection spectrum

nodes.summary: The spectrum is additive in the (finite) DFE.
nodes.title: DFE spectrum is additive in the measure

nodes.summary: The spectrum is homogeneous in the DFE.
nodes.title: DFE spectrum is homogeneous in the measure

nodes.summary: The gamma distribution of fitness effects (Boyko et al. 2008): the scaled selection coefficient is `σ = -T` with `T ~ Gamma(a, r)`, shape `a > 0` and rate `r > 0` (scale `1 / r`), so new mutations are deleterious with mean strength `a / r`.
nodes.title: Gamma distribution of fitness effects

nodes.summary: The gamma DFE is a probability law.
nodes.title: Gamma DFE is a probability measure

nodes.summary: Under the gamma DFE no mutation is beneficial.
nodes.title: No mutation is beneficial under the gamma DFE

nodes.summary: The mean scaled selection coefficient under the gamma DFE is `-a / r`.
nodes.title: Mean selection coefficient under the gamma DFE

nodes.summary: The variance of the scaled selection coefficient under the gamma DFE is `a / r ^ 2`.
nodes.title: Variance of the selection coefficient under the gamma DFE

nodes.summary: Rescaling a gamma DFE by `c > 0` (for example from `s` to `σ = 2Ns`, `c = 2N`) keeps the shape and divides the rate by `c`.
nodes.title: Rescaling a gamma DFE divides its rate

nodes.summary: Under the gamma DFE the fraction of new mutations with `σ < -c`, `c ≥ 0`, is the gamma tail `Γ(a, r c) / Γ(a)`.
nodes.title: Fraction of strongly deleterious mutations

nodes.summary: The fraction of new mutations whose strength `-σ` lies in `(c₁, c₂]`, `0 ≤ c₁ ≤ c₂`, is `(Γ(a, r c₁) - Γ(a, r c₂)) / Γ(a)`.
nodes.title: Fraction of mutations in a strength interval under the gamma DFE

nodes.summary: The spectrum under the gamma DFE as an integral against the gamma law of the strength.
nodes.title: Site-frequency spectrum under the gamma DFE

nodes.summary: The Poisson log-likelihood `∑ (k_i log E_i - E_i - log k_i!)` of counts `k_i` with means `E_i`. Meaningful for `E_i > 0`; at `E_i = 0` Lean's `log 0 = 0` gives a junk value.
nodes.title: Poisson log-likelihood of counts

nodes.summary: The joint law of independent Poisson counts with means `E_i` gives the count vector `k` the probability `∏ e^{-E_i} E_i ^ {k_i} / (k_i!)`.
nodes.title: Probability of a count vector under independent Poisson laws

nodes.summary: For independent Poisson counts with positive means `E_i`, the log-probability of the observed counts `k` is `poissonLogLik E k`.
nodes.title: The Poisson-random-field log-likelihood

nodes.summary: The derivative of the log-likelihood in the parameter `ψ`, when the means `E_i(ψ)` are positive and differentiable at `ψ`: `∑ (k_i / E_i(ψ) - 1) · DE_i(ψ)`.
nodes.title: Derivative of the Poisson log-likelihood

nodes.summary: If `ψ` maximizes the Poisson log-likelihood over a parameter set `S` that is a neighborhood of `ψ`, and the means are positive and differentiable at `ψ`, then `∑ (k_i / E_i(ψ) - 1) · DE_i(ψ) = 0`.
nodes.title: Score equations

nodes.summary: With means `E_i = θ f_i` linear in the mutation parameter, positive `f_i` and at least one count, every `θ > 0` has likelihood at most that of `θ̂ = ∑ k_i / ∑ f_i`.
nodes.title: Profile maximum in `θ`
Ewens–Watterson test

nodes.summary: The number of permutations of `n` letters with cycle type `π`, `w(π) = n! / ∏ j, j ^ (a j) * (a j)!` with `a j = π.parts.count j` (Cauchy's formula).
nodes.title: Number of permutations with a given cycle type

nodes.summary: The probability `P_θ(K = k)` that a sample of `n` genes carries exactly `k` distinct alleles under the Ewens sampling formula.
nodes.title: Probability of a given number of alleles under the Ewens formula

nodes.summary: The conditional probability of the allelic partition `π` given that the number of alleles is `K = K(π) = π.parts.card`, under the Ewens sampling formula with parameter `θ`.
nodes.title: Ewens conditional probability given the number of alleles

nodes.summary: The conditional upper-tail p-value of a statistic `T` of the allelic partition: the conditional probability, given the observed number of alleles `K(π)`, that `T` is at least its observed value `T π`. It is written with the cycle-type weights and so does not involve `θ` (by `ewensCondProb_eq` it is the conditional tail probability for every `θ > 0`).
nodes.title: Conditional upper-tail p-value of the Ewens–Watterson test

nodes.summary: The sample homozygosity `F(π) = ∑_i (n_i / n)²`, the sum over the alleles of the squared sample frequencies (Watterson 1978); `n_i` ranges over the parts of `π`.
nodes.title: Sample homozygosity of an allelic partition

nodes.summary: The cycle-type weight is positive.
nodes.title: Positivity of the cycle-type weight

nodes.summary: Factorization of the Ewens sampling formula (Ewens 1972): `P_θ(π) = θ ^ K(π) / θ^{(n)} * w(π)`, with `K(π) = π.parts.card` the number of alleles.
nodes.title: Factorization of the Ewens sampling formula

nodes.summary: `K` is sufficient for `θ` (Ewens 1972): for `θ > 0`, the conditional law of the allelic partition given the number of alleles is `w(π) / ∑_{K(π') = K(π)} w(π')`, which does not depend on `θ`.
nodes.title: `K` is sufficient for `θ`

nodes.summary: The cycle-type weights of the partitions of `n` into `k` parts sum to the unsigned Stirling number of the first kind `|s(n, k)|`.
nodes.title: Cauchy's count by number of cycles

nodes.summary: Law of the number of alleles (Ewens 1972): `P_θ(K = k) = |s(n, k)| θ ^ k / θ^{(n)}`. As an identity between the defining sums it holds for every real `θ`; it is a probability for `θ > 0`.
nodes.title: Law of the number of alleles

nodes.summary: The Ewens–Watterson conditional law (Ewens 1972; Watterson 1978): for `θ > 0`, `P(π | K = K(π)) = w(π) / |s(n, K(π))| = n! / (|s(n, k)| ∏ j, j ^ (a j) (a j)!)`.
nodes.title: The Ewens–Watterson conditional law

nodes.summary: For nonnegative masses `q` on a finite set `s` and a statistic `T`, the upper-tail p-value `p x = ∑_{y ∈ s, T x ≤ T y} q y` satisfies `∑_{x ∈ s, p x ≤ t} q x ≤ t` for every `t ≥ 0`.
nodes.title: Validity of a discrete upper-tail p-value

nodes.summary: For `θ > 0`, every number of alleles `k` and every level `t ≥ 0`, the conditional probability given `K = k` that the conditional upper-tail p-value of `T` is at most `t` is at most `t`.
nodes.title: Conditional validity of the Ewens–Watterson test

nodes.summary: Validity of the Ewens–Watterson test (Watterson 1978): for every `θ > 0` and every level `t ≥ 0`, the Ewens probability that the conditional upper-tail p-value of `T` is at most `t` is at most `t`. With `T = homozygosity` this is the test against excess homozygosity, with `T = -homozygosity` the test against a deficit of homozygosity.
nodes.title: Validity of the Ewens–Watterson test
Extended haplotype homozygosity

nodes.summary: The window of radius `d` of haplotype `i`: its alleles at the `d` sites closest to the core, in the direction indexed by `ℕ`.
nodes.title: Haplotype window around the core

nodes.summary: Two haplotypes have the same window of radius `d` exactly when they agree at every site `k < d`.
nodes.title: Equality of haplotype windows

nodes.summary: The number of ordered pairs of distinct haplotypes of `C` whose windows of radius `d` agree.
nodes.title: Concordant haplotype pairs at a given radius

nodes.summary: Extended haplotype homozygosity at radius `d` of the haplotype set `C`: the probability that two distinct haplotypes drawn from `C` without replacement agree at all `d` sites nearest the core (Sabeti et al. 2002). For `#C ≤ 1` the denominator vanishes and the junk value `0` is returned; every statement below that needs the probabilistic reading assumes `2 ≤ #C`.
nodes.title: Extended haplotype homozygosity (EHH)

nodes.summary: Outside the domain `2 ≤ #C` the definition returns the junk value `0`.
nodes.title: EHH is zero for a set of at most one haplotype

nodes.summary: At radius `0` every pair of haplotypes agrees, so `EHH(0) = 1`.
nodes.title: EHH at radius zero equals one

nodes.summary: EHH is nonincreasing in the radius: widening the window can only break ties.
nodes.title: EHH is nonincreasing in the radius

nodes.summary: EHH as the sampling-without-replacement homozygosity of the partition of `C` into window types: `EHH(d) = ∑_t c_t (c_t - 1) / (#C (#C - 1))`, where `c_t` is the number of haplotypes of `C` with window `t`. This is the form in which EHH is usually defined.
nodes.title: EHH as homozygosity of window-type counts

nodes.summary: The number of ordered pairs of distinct haplotypes of `C` whose core alleles (under `core`) agree and whose windows of radius `d` agree. The extended haplotype includes the core, so pairs carrying different core alleles are never concordant, even when their outward windows match.
nodes.title: Concordant haplotype pairs sharing a core allele

nodes.summary: Extended haplotype homozygosity with core-allele labels: the probability that two distinct haplotypes drawn from `C` without replacement share both their core allele and their window of radius `d`. For a set `C` of carriers of a single core allele this is the same count as `ehh`; for a pooled set `D` carrying several core alleles it excludes the cross-core pairs that plain `ehh` would wrongly count as concordant.
nodes.title: Extended haplotype homozygosity with core-allele labels

nodes.summary: Relative extended haplotype homozygosity: the core-labelled EHH of the core-allele carriers `C` divided by the core-labelled EHH of the pooled set `D` of haplotypes carrying the other core alleles. The denominator counts only pairs sharing a core allele, so cross-core pairs never inflate it. This is the statistic of the long-range haplotype test (Sabeti et al. 2002). It is a junk value `0` when the denominator…
nodes.title: Relative extended haplotype homozygosity (REHH)

nodes.summary: With a positive reference EHH, the relative EHH exceeds `1` exactly when the core allele's haplotypes are the more homozygous ones.
nodes.title: Criterion for relative EHH to exceed one

nodes.summary: The probability that no recombination falls on the genealogy of a pair of lineages within genetic distance `d` of the core, given that the pair coalesces at time `t` (time in units of `2N` generations, `ρ = 4Nr` the scaled recombination rate per site): the two lineages carry recombination events at total rate `ρ * d` until they coalesce.
nodes.title: Probability of no recombination on a pair's genealogy

nodes.summary: The no-recombination probability decays in the distance from the core.
nodes.title: No-recombination probability decays with distance

nodes.summary: Averaging over the pair coalescence time `T₂`, which is exponential of rate `1` in units of `2N` generations under the neutral coalescent, the probability that no recombination falls on the pair's genealogy within distance `d` is `1 / (1 + ρ d)`. In a mutation-free model, since a recombined lineage can still carry an identical haplotype, this is a lower bound for `E[EHH(d)]`; without that assumption the bound is…
nodes.title: Mean no-recombination probability under the neutral coalescent
Hudson–Kreitman–Aguadé test

nodes.summary: HKA's expected number of segregating sites `θ C(n)` in a sample of `n` genes with scaled mutation rate `θ` (use `f θ` for species `B`).
nodes.title: HKA expected number of segregating sites

nodes.summary: HKA's variance of the number of segregating sites, `θ C(n) + θ² C₂(n)`.
nodes.title: HKA variance of the number of segregating sites

nodes.summary: HKA's expected divergence `θ (T + (1 + f) / 2)`.
nodes.title: HKA expected divergence

nodes.summary: HKA's variance of the divergence, `θ (T + (1 + f) / 2) + (θ (1 + f) / 2)²`.
nodes.title: HKA variance of the divergence

nodes.summary: Expected divergence (Hudson, Kreitman & Aguadé 1987): if the ancestral coalescence time `τ` is exponential with rate `2 / (1 + f)` and, given the genealogy σ-algebra `m`, the divergence `D` has conditional mean `θ (T + τ)`, then `E D = θ (T + (1 + f) / 2)` (for `f > -1`). No integrability hypothesis on `D` is needed: if `D` were not integrable its conditional expectation would be `0` (Mathlib's convention), and the…
nodes.title: Expected divergence

nodes.summary: Variance of the divergence (Hudson, Kreitman & Aguadé 1987): under the hypotheses of `integral_hkaDivergence`, if moreover `D` is square integrable with conditional variance `θ (T + τ)` given `m` (as for a Poisson count), then `Var D = θ (T + (1 + f) / 2) + (θ (1 + f) / 2)²`.
nodes.title: Variance of the divergence

nodes.summary: The HKA statistic for `L` loci with polymorphism counts `SA i`, `SB i`, divergences `D i`, parameters `θ i`, `T`, `f` and sample sizes `nA`, `nB`: the sum over loci of the squared standardized deviations of the three counts from their HKA expectations.
nodes.title: Hudson–Kreitman–Aguadé statistic

nodes.summary: HKA's variances are positive in the biological domain: `θ > 0`, `n ≥ 2`.
nodes.title: Positivity of the HKA polymorphism variance

nodes.summary: HKA's divergence variance is positive for `θ > 0`, `T ≥ 0`, `f > -1`.
nodes.title: Positivity of the HKA divergence variance

nodes.summary: If every count is square integrable with the HKA mean and variance (as derived above under the neutral model), with `θ i > 0`, `T ≥ 0`, `f > 0` and `nA, nB ≥ 2`, then `E X² = 3 L`.
nodes.title: The HKA statistic has mean `3 L` at the true parameters

nodes.summary: HKA's estimating equations (Hudson, Kreitman & Aguadé 1987) for parameters `θ i`, `T`, `f` given the counts: the totals over loci of polymorphism in `A`, in `B` and of divergence match their expectations, and at each locus the total of the three counts matches its expectation. (Only `L - 1` of the per-locus equations are independent of the totals.)
nodes.title: HKA's estimating equations

nodes.summary: The true parameters solve HKA's estimating equations at the expected counts.
nodes.title: True parameters solve the HKA estimating equations
McDonald–Kreitman test

nodes.summary: The Smith–Eyre-Walker estimator of the proportion of adaptive nonsynonymous substitutions, `α̂ = 1 - (D_s P_n) / (D_n P_s)`.
nodes.title: Smith–Eyre-Walker estimator of adaptive substitutions

nodes.summary: The neutrality index `NI = (P_n / P_s) / (D_n / D_s)`.
nodes.title: Neutrality index

nodes.summary: `α̂ = 1 - NI`, for all real counts (the junk values of division agree).
nodes.title: Adaptive proportion estimator equals one minus the neutrality index

nodes.summary: Expected counts of the MK table without a slightly deleterious class (see the module docstring): synonymous and nonsynonymous mutational targets `Ls`, `Ln`, neutral fraction `f₀` of nonsynonymous mutations, polymorphisms and neutral fixed differences per unit of neutral target `polyRate`, `divRate` (`θ_P`, `λ_D` in the module docstring), and `A` expected adaptive substitutions.
nodes.title: Expected-count model of the McDonald–Kreitman table

nodes.summary: Expected synonymous polymorphisms `E P_s = θ_P L_s`.
nodes.title: Expected synonymous polymorphisms

nodes.summary: Expected nonsynonymous polymorphisms `E P_n = θ_P f₀ L_n`.
nodes.title: Expected nonsynonymous polymorphisms

nodes.summary: Expected synonymous fixed differences `E D_s = λ_D L_s`.
nodes.title: Expected synonymous fixed differences

nodes.summary: Expected nonsynonymous fixed differences `E D_n = λ_D f₀ L_n + A`.
nodes.title: Expected nonsynonymous fixed differences

nodes.summary: The proportion of nonsynonymous substitutions that are adaptive, `α = A / E D_n`.
nodes.title: Proportion of adaptive nonsynonymous substitutions

nodes.summary: (Smith & Eyre-Walker 2002): `1 - (E D_s E P_n) / (E D_n E P_s) = A / E D_n`.
nodes.title: `α̂` at the expected counts is the proportion of adaptive substitutions

nodes.summary: The proportions of nonsynonymous changes among expected fixed differences and expected polymorphisms agree iff there are no adaptive substitutions.
nodes.title: The MK null is neutrality

nodes.summary: Let `Dn i, Ds i, Pn i, Ps i` be the counts at locus `i`; suppose each of the four sequences consists of pairwise independent, identically distributed, integrable variables whose means are the expected counts of `M` (the loci are exchangeable copies of the model). Then almost surely `α̂` computed from the counts summed over the first `m` loci converges to `α = A / E D_n` as `m → ∞`.
nodes.title: Consistency of `α̂` over loci
Selective sweeps

nodes.summary: The logistic trajectory of a favourable allele with genic selection coefficient `s`, starting from frequency `x₀`: the solution of `x' = s x (1 - x)` with `x 0 = x₀` (Maynard Smith and Haigh 1974).
nodes.title: Logistic trajectory of a selective sweep

nodes.summary: The trajectory stays strictly between `0` and `1`.
nodes.title: Sweep trajectory stays strictly between 0 and 1

nodes.summary: The logistic equation: `x'(t) = s x(t) (1 - x(t))`.
nodes.title: Sweep trajectory solves the logistic equation

nodes.summary: The time the logistic trajectory with selection coefficient `s` takes to go from frequency `a` to frequency `b`: `(1/s) log (b (1 - a) / (a (1 - b)))`, the difference of the logits divided by `s`.
nodes.title: Duration of a logistic sweep between two frequencies

nodes.summary: `sweepDuration s a b` is the exact time at which the trajectory started at `a` reaches `b`.
nodes.title: Sweep trajectory reaches its target at the sweep duration

nodes.summary: The time to reach a higher frequency is positive.
nodes.title: Positivity of the sweep duration

nodes.summary: A complete sweep in a population of `N` diploids, from a single copy `1 / (2N)` to `1 - 1 / (2N)`, takes exactly `(2 / s) log (2N - 1)` generations in the deterministic logistic model. (The familiar `(2 / s) log (2Ns)` is the conditional expected duration of the corresponding stochastic sweep, a different quantity.)
nodes.title: Duration of a complete deterministic sweep

nodes.summary: The probability that two carriers of a swept allele are identical over a window of genetic length `d`, in the star-genealogy model of Voight et al. (2006): all carriers coalesce at the start of the sweep, a time `T` ago, and the pair is identical exactly when neither of its two lineages recombined, each at rate `r * d` per unit time.
nodes.title: EHH in the star-genealogy sweep model

nodes.summary: The star-genealogy EHH is the square of the probability that a Poisson number of recombination events with mean `r d T` on one lineage is zero.
nodes.title: Star-genealogy EHH as a squared Poisson zero probability

nodes.summary: Haplotype homozygosity decays with the window length.
nodes.title: Star-genealogy EHH decays with window length

nodes.summary: The one-sided integrated haplotype homozygosity: the area under the EHH decay curve in one direction from the focal site. Voight et al.'s iHH integrates in both directions; see `ihh_twoSided`.
nodes.title: One-sided integrated haplotype homozygosity

nodes.summary: The two-sided integrated haplotype homozygosity of Voight et al.: the sum of the one-sided integrals in the two chromosome directions.
nodes.title: Two-sided integrated haplotype homozygosity

nodes.summary: In the star-genealogy model the one-sided integrated haplotype homozygosity is `1 / (2 r T)`.
nodes.title: One-sided iHH in the star-genealogy model

nodes.summary: In the star-genealogy model the two-sided integrated haplotype homozygosity is `1 / (r T)`.
nodes.title: Two-sided iHH in the star-genealogy model

nodes.summary: The integrated haplotype score of Voight et al. (2006): the log ratio of the integrated haplotype homozygosities of the ancestral and the derived allele, whose star genealogies have ages `T_A` and `T_D`. The factor of two between the one-sided and two-sided integrals cancels in this ratio.
nodes.title: Integrated haplotype score (iHS)

nodes.summary: In the star-genealogy model the integrated haplotype score is the log ratio of the two ages, so the recombination rate cancels.
nodes.title: iHS as the log ratio of genealogy ages

nodes.summary: The integrated haplotype score is negative exactly when the derived allele's star genealogy is the younger one, i.e. when the derived allele swept faster.
nodes.title: iHS is negative exactly when the derived allele is younger

nodes.summary: Combining the exact sweep duration with the star-genealogy decay: after a complete sweep of a favourable allele with selection coefficient `s` in a population of `N` diploids, the extended haplotype homozygosity at genetic distance `d` is the power law `(2N - 1) ^ (-(4 r d / s))`.
nodes.title: Power-law EHH after a complete sweep
Cross-population haplotype homozygosity

nodes.summary: The pair of statistics `(X, Y)` is exchangeable under `μ`: the joint law is unchanged by swapping the two coordinates. This is an additional calibration assumption for a two-group haplotype test, stronger than the ordinary neutral null. Defined as `IdentDistrib` of the two orderings, so the measurability of the joint laws is part of the hypothesis rather than restored separately in each theorem.
nodes.title: Exchangeable pair of statistics

nodes.summary: Applying the same measurable function to both statistics preserves exchangeability.
nodes.title: Exchangeability is preserved by a common measurable map

nodes.summary: The difference of an exchangeable pair has a symmetric law.
nodes.title: Difference of an exchangeable pair has a symmetric law

nodes.summary: Equal tails: the upper tail of `X - Y` at `t` has the same probability as the lower tail at `-t`.
nodes.title: Equal tails of the difference of an exchangeable pair

nodes.summary: A two-sided rejection region splits into two tails of equal probability.
nodes.title: Two-sided rejection region splits into equal tails

nodes.summary: For positive statistics, the log ratio — the XP-EHH form — has equal tails.
nodes.title: Equal tails of the log ratio of an exchangeable pair

nodes.summary: The same statement for the ratio itself, the form used for relative EHH: the probability that the ratio exceeds `c` equals the probability that it falls below `1 / c`.
nodes.title: Equal tails of the ratio of an exchangeable pair

nodes.summary: The cross-population extended haplotype homozygosity score (Sabeti et al. 2007): the log ratio of the integrated haplotype homozygosities of the same core region in two populations. Both arguments must be positive for the score to be meaningful. Outside that domain `Real.log` is totalized by Mathlib, not by the stated junk value: `Real.log 0 = 0` and `Real.log (-x) = Real.log x`, so for example…
nodes.title: Cross-population extended haplotype homozygosity (XP-EHH)

nodes.summary: XP-EHH computed from two star-genealogy sweep models with the same recombination rate is the log ratio of the two ages, with the opposite sign to `ihs`.
nodes.title: XP-EHH in star-genealogy sweep models

nodes.summary: Under exchangeability, the XP-EHH score has a symmetric law: the two tails of the two-sided test carry the same probability.
nodes.title: Symmetry of the XP-EHH law under exchangeability
Tajima's D

nodes.summary: Tajima's `D` (Tajima 1989) for a sample of `n` genes with mean number of pairwise differences `π` and `S` segregating sites: `D = (π - S / a₁) / √(e₁ S + e₂ S (S - 1))`. It is meaningful for `n ≥ 4` and `S ≥ 1` (`tajimaVarEstimator_pos`); otherwise Lean's junk values for `x / 0` and `√` of a nonpositive number apply.
nodes.title: Tajima's `D`

nodes.title: Tajima's $c_1$ vanishes for two genes

nodes.summary: For two genes `c₂ = 0`.
nodes.title: Tajima's $c_2$ vanishes for two genes

nodes.title: Tajima's $c_1$ vanishes for three genes

nodes.summary: `c₂ = b₂ - (n + 2) / (a₁ n) + a₂ / a₁² > 0` for `n ≥ 4`.
nodes.title: Positivity of Tajima's $c_2$ for at least four genes

nodes.summary: The denominator of Tajima's `D` is well defined: `e₁ S + e₂ S (S - 1) > 0` for `n ≥ 4` and `S ≥ 1`.
nodes.title: Positivity of the denominator of Tajima's D

nodes.summary: The rejection region of the Chebyshev test of neutrality at level `α` and hypothesized `θ₀`: `|π - S / a₁| ≥ √((c₁ θ₀ + c₂ θ₀²) / α)`.
nodes.title: Chebyshev test of neutrality

nodes.summary: If Tajima's numerator `π - S / a₁` is square integrable with mean `0` and variance `c₁ θ₀ + c₂ θ₀² > 0` (as under the standard neutral model, by `KingmanTimes.integral_tajimaNumerator` and `KingmanTimes.variance_tajimaNumerator`), then for every `α > 0` the test rejects with probability at most `α`.
nodes.title: Level of the Chebyshev test

GISTIC permutation null for copy-number scores

nodes.summary: The permuted score at marker `m`: `∑ j, x j (σ j m)`.
nodes.title: Permuted GISTIC score at a marker

nodes.summary: The GISTIC permutation null at marker `m`: the probability that `∑ j, x j (σ j m) = g` when the permutations `σ j` of the markers are independent and uniform.
nodes.title: GISTIC permutation null distribution

nodes.summary: The number of marker choices `u : Fin S → Fin M` (one marker per sample) with `∑ j, x j (u j) = g`.
nodes.title: Count of marker choices with a given score

nodes.summary: (Mermel et al. 2011): the probability of the score `g` is the fraction of the `M ^ S` marker choices with that score, whatever the marker `m`.
nodes.title: The GISTIC permutation null is the law of a sum of independent per-sample draws

nodes.summary: With no samples the null is the point mass at `0`.
nodes.title: GISTIC null with no samples is a point mass at zero

nodes.summary: Adding sample `S` convolves the null of the first `S` samples with the empirical law of the new sample, `P_{S+1}(g) = ∑_v (1 / M) P_S(g - x_S(v))`.
nodes.title: Convolution step

nodes.summary: The minimum of `y` over the window of `n + 1` consecutive markers starting at `i` (GeneGISTIC's per-sample gene-level value for a gene covering those markers).
nodes.title: Window minimum over consecutive markers

nodes.summary: GeneGISTIC null (Mermel et al. 2011): permuting the per-sample minima of all running windows of `n + 1` markers gives, at every window `i`, the law of a sum of independent draws of one window minimum per sample.
nodes.title: GeneGISTIC null
Molecular timing of copy-number gains

nodes.summary: A single copy-number event on a region: `copies` original copies, of which copy `i` has `desc i` copies after the event (`0` if lost, `2` if duplicated).
nodes.title: Copy-number gain history

nodes.summary: The copy number `c₁ = ∑ i, desc i` after the event.
nodes.title: Copy number after a copy-number event

nodes.summary: The number of original copies amplified by the event (`desc i ≥ 2`).
nodes.title: Number of amplified copies

nodes.summary: Expected number of mutations of multiplicity `m`: `μ t #{i | desc i = m} + [m = 1] μ c₁ (1 - t)` (per-copy rate `μ`, event at time `t` of the normalized history `[0, 1]`).
nodes.title: Expected number of mutations of a given multiplicity

nodes.summary: `∑_m m E_m = μ c₁`, summing over all multiplicities up to a bound `B ≥ max(1, max_i desc i)`.
nodes.title: The multiplicity-weighted total is time-invariant

nodes.summary: The mutations of multiplicity at least two number `μ t #{i | desc i ≥ 2}` in expectation: they all arose before the event, on an amplified copy.

nodes.summary: An event that amplifies some copy leaves a positive copy number.
nodes.title: Positive copy number after an amplifying event

nodes.summary: If some copy is amplified, two parameter pairs `(μ, t)`, `(μ', t')` with `μ, μ' ≠ 0` and the same expected multiplicity spectrum are equal.

nodes.summary: A single-copy gain `1 + 1 → 2 + 1`: one copy duplicated, the other kept.
nodes.title: Single-copy gain

nodes.summary: Copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity `1 + 1 → 2 + 0`: one copy duplicated, the other lost.
